I liked this book a lot - not an overly hard read but not mind candy either... will definitely read the pre and sequels.

Tana French's thrillers are anything but relaxing, they are gripping, hold-you-by-the throat-and-not-let-you-go reading. 
 Set after In the Woods, the first book in the Dublin Murder Squad series, this book focuses on detective Cassie Maddox, the best friend of Rob Ryan, the narrator of the first book. In this installment, Cassie narrates, as she is pulled into an old undercover role 
 A woman is found murdered and she'd been using Cassie's fake (and discarded) undercover identity of Lexie Madison. To complicate matters, Cassie is a dead-ringer for this this murder victim. Her commander from undercover comes up with a plan -- leak to the media that Lexie wasn't actually dead, but in a coma, and for Cassie to go back into undercover once again as the murdered Lexie to lure the killer to finish the job. 
 I know - say what? Utterly implausible! But when Ms. French is telling a story, you suspend disbelief as she takes you on a thoroughly gripping ride. 
 Cassie/Lexie assumes the persona and has to return to the house she shared with Daniel (who inherited the house), Rafe, Abby and Justin -- an insular group of university students who enjoy a close and intense friendship. 
 As the murder squad investigates the (now revisionist) attempted murder, they confiscate the other housemates phones giving Cassie videos that she relentlessly studies in order to act, talk and "become" the murdered Lexie. Eventually Lexie returns to Whitethorn House having come out of her coma but suffering (convenient) memory loss 
 "It took my breath away, that evening. If you've ever dreamed that you walked into your best-loved book or film or TV program, then maybe you've got some idea how it felt: things coming alive around you, strange and new and utterly familiar at the same time; the catch in your heartbeat as you move through the rooms that had such a vivid untouchable life in your mind, as your feet actually touch the carpet, as you breathe the air; the odd, secret glow of warmth as these people you've been watching for so long, from so far away, open their circle and sweep you into it." 
 The Likeness excels at its psychological insights especially for Cassie, who in her real life is lonely and shattered from her previous case. She finds friendship -- nay, family, among her new Lexie friends. These blurred identities are made believable with the beautifully written scenes and well developed characters who live, love and murder within the walls of Whitethorn House. The setting and moods glitter with life. But Cassie gets lost inside her assumed identity and finds herself in a maze of murder quickly spinning out of her control. This is breath-holding stuff, 
 As others have said, there are many similarities to Donna Tart's A Secret History - both have dreamy academic types living together in a beautiful, run-down house. 
 But The Likeness makes you feel for Cassie -- what she lost and can never regain. The heartbreak of assuming a new identity, being part of a loving family, and finding a home in the world ~~ but in the end, it's only a likeness. 
 See all my reviews at http://www.bookbarmy.com

I'm a bit disappointed. The storyline in this book was just alright. Although there's a minor surprise at the end, it's never really followed up on, so once again we're left with a couple questions. The mystery in these books end up being so lackluster to me because 70% of it is spent on introspection from the main character, that is just too much to be enjoyable, and instead feels like overkill. I don't think I will end up reading the rest of the books in this ongoing series.
I could not get into this book. It is 466 pages long and could have been told with 300 pages. Tedious is the only word I can use to describe my experience with this Tana French book.

Publishers, please oh please save us from sophomore books! French's first book was a fairly good read. This one was anything but. The premise was ridiculous and about as unrealistic as you can get. The plot dragged on and on and on. There were pages and pages (or rather since I listened to the audio version, minutes and minutes) of exposition--exposition of the most boring and irrelevant kind. 
 You know how silly and unrealistic it is when the villain explains his/her master plan to the hero? Take that and multiply it by a gazillion and you can get a glimmer of what awaits you in the last quarter of this book.

This is the followup to "In the Woods," which I loved, so we'll see... 
 It's back on the "to-read" shelf because I got to about page 20 and had to take it back to the library b/c someone else had requested it. Libraries are great, except... 
 3/15/09: Just got ahold of another copy for a little while and got to page 153 before I had to give it up again. Very compelling. Not as good as "In the Woods," but still a fun and easy page-turner. I'm looking forward to getting it back to find out what happens... 
 6/10/09: Done! 
 Several people recommended this book to me and I started it several times before I actually got ahold of a copy for long enough to finish it. Like its predecessor, In the Woods, once I got into it, I could hardly put it down. It's not as good as that first book, but almost. The best moment for me was just about at the climax when everything turns: 
 Daniel took off his glasses and polished them on his handkerchief. Without them his eye looked blank, blind. "There's a Spanish proverb," he said, "that's always fascinated me. 'Take what you want and pay for it, says God.'" 
 The words fell into the silence under the ivy like cool pebble into water, sank without a ripple. "I don't believe in God," Daniel said, "but that principle seems, to me, to have a divinity of its own; a kind of blazing purity. What could possibly be simpler, or more crucial? You can have anything you want, as long as you accept that there is a price and that you will have to pay it." (335) 
 The book isn't really about lessons or morals; it's just a mystery with some light adventure in there. You could call it a psychological thriller of sorts, but it's mostly just a great story with vivid and fascinating characters. Still, this is what I will take away. You can have anything you want, as long as you accept that there is a price and that you will have to pay it. 
 Knowing what you want is the true challenge...

The premise for this story is nuts, it would never be feasible in any way shape or form. And yet, I bought in to the set up, I wanted to see what would happen and I happily read till the end. This is the second in the Dublin Murder Squad series. A police detective is approached by her old supervisor from her undercover days with a proposal. A young woman has just been found dead, and said deceased woman is not only the splitting image of our detective, she was using the detective's undercover identity. Why not pretend the deceased did not die, substitute in the undercover detective and solve the case????!!!! This was enjoyable from start to finish despite the you got to be kidding me set up. French is a talented writer and the added level of character development and detail to her writing brings this up a notch from your typical genre thriller. 4 stars.

This definitely wasn't as good as the first one. For one thing, it seemed like Cassie, the main character, was a little too detached. Like, she was telling the story, but it's not like it mattered or anything. She didn't seem all that realistic to me, whereas in the first book she was. But the writing was beautiful, as always. The only other thing was that this didn't feel anything like a suspense mystery or psychological thriller type. It was more about the growing relationships between people, living and dead, and a slice of life story (the kind where you enter into a house or a town for a week or so). Of course, there was a mystery, but it wasn't a typical one, and there weren't clues and trails for the reader to follow. 
 It was a little long, especially for a book that had a lot of analyzing people and relationships going on. The conversations between characters are completely spelled out, no skipping anything. Whereas In The Woods was easier to deal with since there was stuff going on, this was like listening in on a phone conversation when you need to call someone. 
 Also, and this is probably a pet peeve of mine, what in the world was going on with Sam? Here's Cassie, going along, being ornery to everyone and not seeming to care about him one way or another, super ambivalent, and then suddenly, he's her soul mate. Don't get it, don't like it.

Pretty entertaining; kind of a mind-bender. I really liked the concept of this book but felt that the author took about 100 pages too long to execute it... it started feeling a little tedious to me around the middle. I understand that she was setting a very elaborate stage for the ending, but still.

I adored 'In the Woods' and consequently had pretty big expectations from this book. But it fell flat on so many levels, it's almost painful to recount. The beginning was slow-slow-slow and repetitive, the dialogue was shallow and cheap for the most part, and I won't even get started on how stupid and far-fetched the plot was. 
 The characters were the only good thing about this novel - and no, I am not counting the main one here...Cassie aka Lexie was so far off what she was supposed to be as a detective, I owe her character a huge amount of my frustration. The last few dozen pages were also pretty good, or at least much better than the rest of the book. 
 Sorry Tana!
I know people hate the set up but I think French did a good job of earning it, and I'm sorry but I just wanted to spend as much time in that house with those people as possible.

If you can get past a plot that is absurdly far fetched to say the least(that a cop looks/sounds/acts enough like a dead girl to fool her close friends/roommates, then it is a good literary mystery. Sequel to the far superior In the Woods. Freench is a terrific writer.
Beautiful and suspenseful, 100 pages too long.

Now this was a book I absolutely hated! First, it was painfully slow-paced and in my opinion, way too long. Second, the novel completely fails in so many ways! I don't want to spoil it for anyone but the storyline is so (!!!!) far-fetched that I thought the main mystery here was whether the book had an editor or not. 
 Plus, my favorite character from the first book was completely missing and I don't gave a single f*** about the fate of all the other shallow characters who bored me to death on 466 pages.

book_b.title: A Head Full of Ghosts
book_b.user_review:
paul tremblay interviews me, or "me" here: 
 https://thelittlesleep.wordpress.com/... 
 this book is about a fourteen-year-old girl named marjorie, her eight-year-old sister merry, and the events leading up to marjorie's exorcism. your attention, i have it, yes? this is both a horror novel and a psychological suspense novel, but then it goes the extra step into self-referential metafiction in a way that is natural and not gimmicky-annoying, probably because that part involves a delightful character named karen brissette. on the one hand, this rests firmly in the canon of possession lit, and all the expectations are met: the voices, the vomit, the levitation, the inappropriate sexual acts, but there's a cheekiness to it at all times - a little wink as it slightly adjusts these elements so that they are present, but slightly "off." this isn't played for horror, more for unease and a sort of evaluation of the possession genre itself. 
 the book is mostly told through the eyes of merry - now twenty-three years old - meeting with a woman who is writing a book about marjorie and the family's experiences. it cuts between merry-now and merry's immersive recollections of the events that destroyed her family. when marjorie began acting erratically, her parents sent her to a psychiatrist and she was put on medication. when her condition worsened, and events more sinister and inexplicable occurred, her unemployed father turned to the church in desperation. under the direction of the inscrutable father wanderly, an exorcism was prescribed and somehow the whole thing became a media event and was filmed for television as a reality show. since we are relying on the memory of an eight-year-old who was kept out of the planning stages, the how of this is unclear but it doesn't come across as implausible or silly, the way it does in what i just wrote. the family was struggling financially, and this helped them out of a tight spot. desperate people do desperate things, things they might later regret. so their house is overrun by camera crews, marjorie continues to creep through the hallways, and merry tries not to get lost in all of it, whatever "it" is. 
 essentially, it boils down to what all exorcism scenarios are beneath their shrieking theatrics: what is "really" happening - is it madness? is it actually demonic possession? is it the cry for help of an abused child? this is a novel concerned more with perception/perspective than with truth. there are no easy answers here, and you can draw your own conclusions: the supernatural explanation is just as plausible as the psychological, but no matter which way you lean at the end, there are prickly stickers that will make you doubt your choice. 
 but tremblay adds another layer on top of this familiar storyline with the reality show element, and in life's delicious synchronicity my reading of the book coincided with my starting to watch black mirror, so all the themes of suffering-as-entertainment and the complicity of the viewer in demanding and therefore perpetuating another person's humiliation is fresh in my mind. two things right off the bat - he doesn't fall into the ready trap of either satire or preachiness. this is not wry chuckling at reality teevee and the ethical ramifications are put forth in very natural ways by characters who would indeed question these things, so it doesn't feel like reader-directed "shame on you" (which makes it better than black mirror, but i've only seen two episodes) 
 and now let's get to the best part of the book: MEEEEEE!!! 
 the karen brissette character writes a horror blog which is running a 15-year-anniversary feature on the show. it's not ME-me, but it's clearly written by someone who has read a review or two of mine. while i would never use the word "funky" or ever say anything in r'lyehian, there is a very familiar enthusiasm and a chatty, distracted voice that both delighted me and made me squirm a little when i was reading it in my head, in my voice. i'm a little alarmed that i am so easy to parody/spoof. it actually reads like a mash-up of me and pms, where the thinky parts sound like her and the puppy-energy parts sound like me. and i so cringed when "karen" dropped that das unheimliche thing because YES, that is something i have done WHEN APPROPRIATE but i did feel a miniature shame for it to be pointed out. 
 and except for the ugly capital letters sprinkled throughout her blog posts, there's something uncanny (DO YOU SEE WHAT I DID THERE? <---- also something the book reminds me that i do. stalk much, tremblay?) about the voice: 
 And we the viewers watch from this eerily liminal vantage point. I mean, we're there with them but not really there. We watch from the spaces between their spaces, and that's always where the monster dwells. Dwells, I say!!! 
 SCARRRRYYYY! I mean, damn, so here we are in the opening minutes of the final episode and we discover that we actually know jack and shit about the house's layout and ARRGGGH, OUR HEADSSSS ARE EXPLODINGGGGG! 
 so, yeah. it's pretty sweet. 
 "karen's" role is to place the reality show's situation in a historical and pop cultural context and draw our attention to what the show (and by extension, the book itself) owes to its predecessors. she brings up salem, The Exorcist, House of Leaves, The Haunting of Hill House; all of those literary and filmic touchpoints and she analyzes what it is we find so compelling about these kinds of narratives. 
 because our fascination with this shit isn't new. the salem witch trials were a precursor of reality teevee - young girls playing for cameras that hadn't yet been invented, spectators shivering with shock and can't-look-away revulsion as fornication with demons was described in little-girl lisps. and there's plenty to say (and karen does) about the misogyny inherent in exorcism-narratives as white men hover over virginal girls writhing on a bed spluttering obscenities and there is such glee in her deconstruction of the show - it's a really fun sort of lit crit that i anxiously hope is something has some basis in the efforts of her namesake. 
 it's not often that you get critical commentary of a book in a book as it is happening. but it's a neat little trick. there are so many opportunities to call out the references - the sunroom with its yellow wallpaper inspires a discussion of gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper; not in a "look how clever i am being" way, but in an almost exhausted way, in the same manner marjorie recites the steps of the exorcism or the details of her possession. we've seen this. we know how this goes. we are steeped in references, influenced by pop culture, there's a precedent in everything we do, but the calling attention to it ironically renders it novel and strange. 
 the idea of audience is very important here. not just the audience of the show, or the fact that watching the show turns merry into an audience of her own life's experiences, but the fact that marjorie's symptoms intensify when merry is in the room, the way people being filmed amplify their behaviors for the benefit of the imagined viewers, the way the presence of cameras can stifle natural behavior and can modify a dynamic as a subtle power play. 
 there's also some commentary on how media manipulates our memories, but also how we manipulate them all on our own. in one of my favorite quiet scenes, grown-merry is sitting with rachel, the writer, going over some of the key moments in merry's past: 
 Sitting here in the coffee shop with her outlining her research findings, I'm getting the sense that she's hiding something from me. I don't know how that would be possible. 
 She wasn't there when it happened. And I was. 
 but memories are not always the truest truths. merry was young, shielded from parts of her family's life, fuzzy on the details, confused over what she saw, and it's just a nice moment that highlights that distance we all have from our own past, and how we interpret our memories in frequently incorrect ways. 
 there are lots of fantastic little details here - how merry never got over her childish need for attention/affection and the way she behaved around the crew as an eight-year-old; pleasing the reporters, playing for the camera is mirrored in her relationship with rachel as a grown woman. she's fragile, arrested, vulnerable, and with good cause. 
 it's a surprisingly meaty book - much more than a typical horror novel but one that will nonetheless satisfy the discerning horror fan. plus - a version of meeeeeee!! which is something stephen king has yet to do, to his detriment. 
 ********************************************************** 
 MOVIE NEWS!! 
 http://deadline.com/2015/05/a-head-fu... 
 i would like to play myself in this movie, please!!! 
 ********************************************************** 
 paul tremblay is a clever man. 
 this book features a character named karen brissette who says writes things like: 
 I promise I'll get to the fun gory horror stuff eventually, but you have to indulge me first... BECAUSE KAREN SAYS SO!!! 
 i mean, that karen's slavishness to the capital "i" aside, there's no way i can give this fewer than five stars, is there? 
 clever, clever man...

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoyed reading this book, it was fantastically written and a entertaining story. But I really didn't like the end, I guess I was just hoping for something more exciting.
Not as good as I was made to believe it was through the reviews! Boooo! Not sure how this made it as a contender as a best horror book!

I absolutely LOVED this book. There's very little I can say without giving it away, but if you are a fan of possession-type stories that center around the family dynamic, you'll surely enjoy this book.

This is a book about an old trope -- possession/exorcism -- that, like the Scream franchise, is put in a self-aware, contemporary setting. 
 When a broke family's daughter starts showing signs of possession, they agree to make the girl the subject of a reality television program. The family hopes this will bring in both money and help. 
 Is the girl actually possessed, or is it all an elaborate ruse? She can, after all, use the Internet to look this sort of thing up -- but is she intelligent enough to spout all of the things she does? 
 Is she faking everything to save her family? 
 You spend the whole book not knowing. And the ending is super-fucked-up. This book's pretty epic.
standby by for scathing review.
meh

merry berrett is an 8 year old girl who is living in the worst hell imaginable. her family has no money, her sister pinches her nose shut at night, and she gets her head filled with someone else's ghosts. the worst part? her sister has a demon inside- or does she? is she really possessed? does she have schizophrenia? or is she faking? i continuously went round and round with these thoughts throughout the story. 
 although this book is more psychological than it is gory, i didn't feel all that frightened. some stories, like We Have Always Lived in the Castle and The Shining instill a deep, unsettling feeling that i can't quite name. those are the books that i cling to and read vehemently without seeming to breath. i actually put this book down to clean, ya'll- seriously. the fear merry had found it's way into me, but it was unreliable. i would love to ring up king and ask if this book truly scared the living hell out of him, so if anyone would care to share his direct line, i'd be more than grateful. 
 to trembaly's credit, the ending did surprise me and i liked the blog posts in between the story. i discovered fangoria through this, and i am sooooooooo excited! 
 After your performed the exorcism, how did you know that demon wasn't still in there, hiding? How do you know it didn't go in a hibernation state, quieting down to come out later, years and years later when no one would be around to help? Hey, how do you know if the wrong spirit left? What if you expelled the person's real spirit and only the demon's spirit was there to take its place? If I believed in any of that stuff, I'd be afraid that was going to happen to me.

Loved the whole book except the ending. After the last word, I turned the pages hoping it somehow had more. Just felt it could have ended so much better! Great, interesting and scary twist on the possession story.

A Head Full of Ghosts is on several Best of 2015 lists. People really like it. Stephen King likes it. I think I belong to an outlying class of reader you can dismiss from survey results, like a child who hates macaroni and cheese. I found this book plodding, awkwardly structured and unconvincing. It was very difficult to finish. Constantly referencing the very best of the genre certainly didn't help. I thought the scariest part of the book was the synopsis of Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper". Like I said, outlier. Carry on.

3 Things I Liked: 
 -the blurring of the lines between mental illness and possible demonic possession 
 -parts describing Marjorie's episodes were very scary 
 -twist ending 
 Things I Didn't Like: 
 -didn't enjoy the writing style 
 -parts describing the filming, blog, and present day were extremely boring to me 
 -disliked the characters except for Marjorie 
 Overall, the scary parts were what kept me from putting the book down. The author was good at scares, I wish there had been more. I found myself skimming through paragraphs thinking "why does this part matter?"

,,Glowa pelna duchow" jest lektura niesamowita, ktora w pelni moga docenic starzy wyjadacze horroru, wlasnie te ,,stare psiska", ktorym nieobce sa dziela popkultury grozy, stanowiace ten jeden, najwazniejszy kanon. Oczywiscie mozna powiesc Paula Tremblaya czytac bez znajomosci czegokolwiek, ale otrzymamy wtedy smutna, splycona wersje czegos, co w literaturze mielone jest od lat, w uproszczonej, niczym niewyrozniajacej sie wersji. A taka lektura bylaby jedynie na szkode ,,Glowy pelnej duchow", ktora staje sie czyms o wiele wiecej, jesli odczytamy ja jako meta-ksiazke, jako opowiesc, ktora skrywa w sobie niejedna tajemnice, ktora daje do myslenia i zostaje w glowie na bardzo dlugi czas, stajac sie kolejnych glosem niemozliwym do uciszenia.

I'm quite disappointed... I came to know about this book from a book podcast I really like and someone called it the Bird Box of 2015. And I love the Bird Box. This is far less gripping than the Bird Box. I'm not very sure what the author wanted to focus on. To portray the tragedy of a family with a possessed teenage girl? Or to present that there are different possibilities of what actually happened? I feel that the author wanted to do the latter in the 2nd half of the story but it's not very consistent... The book is not bad because I finished it. But I didn't catch quite a chunk of it (I was listening to the audiobook)and I didn't feel it make any difference... Does it mean some parts of it aren't even "necessary" in the book? I don't know because I didn't care enough to go back and find out what I missed. 
 It's no Bird Box... It's just a lesser horror. But if you don't have that expectation and you have a lot of free time, then it doesn't hurt to read this one. And I have to say the narrator did a fairly good job.

Something about possession in literature and film absolutely fascinates me, for that reason this book was a must read, and certainly did not disappoint. 
 This wonderfully structured novel evokes all the feelings of fear, tension, terror, excitement and dread that are fundamental within the classics of the genre. 
 The story brings the subject right up to date, the historic concept of possession is brilliantly portrayed in a modern setting and the introduction of a film crew documenting the events gives the tale a very current, and very topical feel. 
 Terrific and terrifying in equal measure, and up there with my favourite books in the genre.

I found this an entertaining read. I liked all the nods to classic horror tropes (not just The Exorcist!), I found both the adult and child Meredith an interesting character, and the reality TV was an interesting angle on truth vs fiction. I was surprised that Stephen King found this book scary because it didn't feel that way to me really. In fact, having finished the book, I have come away feeling thoughtful and a bit sad, which isn't a bad thing, just not what I expected!

Unfortunately, a killer ending can't completely save this one. Other than a couple flashes of brilliance in the third act, I thought this was tedious and felt a lot longer than 286 pages. Part of the problem is the three prong narration. The three POVs here aren't entirely effective (especially the blog posts) and dilute the impact. Thankfully, the perspectives are mainly whittled down to one in the second half. I had read rave reviews of this, but was pretty disappointed.

I don't remember where the recommendation for this book originated from but I think it will always remain in my memory as one of the worst books I've ever read. The shocking ending, the books one redeeming quality, made slugging my way through the rest of it ALMOST worth it.
The idea of the story and the twists are very intriguing, but the writing is rather jumpy and unfocused that I had to skip some parts.

One review I read said, "This book scared the hell out of me." This person must still sleep with his blankie. With the lights on. 
 Not only don't I think this qualified as a horror novel, but I don't think it even qualified as a good one. It is a play on tropes, a play on genres. The book, mostly told from the viewpoint of an 8 year old girl who witnesses her older sister's descent into madness, tried hard to be "unique," and in doing so, came off as fan fiction. 
 Not that the author didn't pay homage to the original books and movies he "borrowed from" - he did. He confessed that the entire first third of the book was fashioned, almost scene by scene, after The Exorcist. This doesn't excuse what is, in my opinion, a weak attempt at legalized plagiarism. The story is told by the 8 year old Meredith, then in a satirical blog by the grown-up Meredith, some years later. The story utilizes the concept of reality TV - another pathetic attempt at making the book "timely and relevant." 
 The Shining was scary. The Exorcist was scary. The Omen was scary. A Head Full of Ghosts was not scary. It was annoying, shallow, and trendy. Are those three terms synonyms? They might as well be. 
 I listened to this on Audible, and although I think the narrator did an okay job on all the female voices, her male voices were pathetic. 
 To those whose reviews say, "This scared the hell out of me," I have this advice: Don't read a REAL horror novel. You might just have a heart attack.

I started reading this as a sample on my Kindle based on author reviews alone. It's a classic straightforward possession story, or is it? I have to say, I've never seen a male author render female characters so well before, especially children. Most of the book is seen through the eyes of an 8 year old witnessing the changes her elder sister is going through. The end is a shocker, but I'm not sure spending the bulk of the book wading through the life of an 8 year old is worth it for the big pay off. It is an interesting take on a classic theme, interjecting blog posts, interviews, reality TV, and corrupt church officials in the mix. It's worth a read if its on sale or on Kindle Unlimited.

This one crossed a few genres, was genuinely creepy and left you guessing what really happened to this poor family. Was it a mentally disturbed teenager? was it a mentally disturbed Father? was it a mentally disturbed 8 year old? Or was it really a demon? Perhaps we need to define "demons" better in order to figure this one out. Yes, it borrowed from "The Exorcist" a bit, but twisted (sorry) it for a jaded, reality show audience. Fun stuff.

Really wanted to like this book. It had some very interesting ideas. It played on common horror and "exorcism/possessed girl" tropes, while being very self-aware, which I found enjoyable. However, this plot feels like it shits the bed right at the end and it left a poor taste in my mouth, too bad really. It's a short read, so definitely not a total waste of time.

I like to take my time getting to books that are receiving a lot of hubbub, and baby this book had hubbub to spare! It earned it, though. I admit that the first 20 pages or so were rocky in that I had a hard time adjusting to the writer's voice and cadence, but then the story snagged me and I was immersed. 
 If you want a recap, read another review. I will say that the tension and the "is she really...?" aspect was at just the right temperature to keep me hooked but not maniacally so. I'll definitely read more by Paul Tremblay and I double recommend this book.

A fantastic read. Tremblay creates something substantial from relatively little, weaving in Big Themes without once slowing down a fast-paced narrative. The characters are sympathetic and interesting. Oh, and it's very scary. Tremblay ratchets-up the tension whilst never once abandoning the ambiguity that makes this such a refreshing novel. Head Full of Ghosts comfortably and confidently takes its place alongside The Last Days of Jack Sparks by Jason Arnopp and Weathercock by Glen Duncan to form an unholy trinity of intelligent, challenging and genuinely unnerving exorcism novels.

This book probably could have been better, but was weighed down by inauthentic dialogue and characters and by the author's incessant need to tell us that something bad was going to happen before it happened. The key to horror is the suspense of not knowing what or when things will go wrong, and the "little did we know" nonsense ruins this.

It's hard to believe this is the first horror novel I've read in a long, long time. Mostly I liked it, but it also reminded me why it's been so long since I've read a horror novel, and why I quit the Horror Writers Association. 
 Imagine The Exorcist as a reality TV show with running commentary about the evils of a patriarchal society. That's pretty much A Head Full of Ghosts. The story is told by a grown woman who was an eight-year-old girl when her sister may or may not have become mentally ill or possessed by a demon. The father -- who can't provide for his family after the factory he worked at closed -- can't handle the loss of his power and may also be going crazy, but before he goes he finds the Catholic God and arranges for the Church and his family to do a reality television show called The Possession showing how they deal with the demon-infested 14-year-old girl. 
 There was too much look-how-much-I-know-about-the-horror-genre commentary thinly disguised as the girl's research for her Fangoria blog. Plus the social commentary was annoying and just reminded me way too much of the HWA message board flame wars. 
 And it was pretty easy to see where the story was going to end up. 
 Since I listened to this in audio I can't say if it was written in such an annoying way or if it was the woman doing the narration, but I wanted to throttle her. Her male voices were deliberately dumb and her teen girl voices were over-the-top with slang and annoying inflection. 
 If you like the recent spate of predictable PG-13 demon movies you'll like this book. If you don't laugh at Friedkin's The Exorcist, you'll likely be entertained enough while reading, but won't remember much about this one a few hours after finishing it.
Did I accidentally buy a YA book? I don't get it. Horrible.

I read this for Spookathon 2016. 
 This was a mind bend. The twists are unexpected and great. I am still thinking about the book and the ending. I went into this totally blind and that seemed the way to do it. I don't want to say to much because of spoilers but.... wow.

This book was buzzing on all of my favorite horror author's blogs, so I had to read it. What an awesome surprise. The book is about Merry and Marjorie, two sisters who are very close. Marjorie begins acting very strangely, and terrorizing Merry and the rest of the family in increasingly bizarre ways. The book riffs on reality TV and blog culture, as soon enough a TV crew is brought into their house. So many twists and turns are in this book. Merry is quite the loveable character and narrator. I will not spoil too much here. Read this. 
 P.S.I nerded out slightly when a character named Dr. Navidson appears, which I can only assume is a subtle nod to House of Leaves.
I am a fan of horror books, but A Head Full of Ghosts is not that scary (based on the title lol) even though some parts made goose bumps and I don't know, a little bit confusing for me, sort of.

I need to start off by stating very clearly that I officially hate Paul Tremblay. 
 No writer should be this good. 
 This book absolutely blew me away on so many levels. Merry is a wonderfully drawn character, as adult, as blogger, and especially as an 8-year-old. Marjorie is finely nuanced and terrifying. You never know where she's going to come from next. 
 And the story. The story. Everyone I know that wonders why I love horror (especially when I read so much of it and bitch about how shitty it is), now I have a contemporary book (read that as, something other than Stephen King), to point to and say, "This. This right here is EXACTLY why I love horror." 
 This novel has everything a finely crafted horror story needs. Extremely little gore (only twice, and handled very well). Instead, the story burrows into your head, makes you question whether it's real or not. It makes you uneasy. It fills you with dread. 
 And it delivers the payoff beautifully. 
 Honest to God, I could write about all the things I loved about this novel for the rest of the day. Instead, I'll just stop here and say that this is tied with Sarah Lotz's The Three, and Lauren Buekes' The Shining Girls and Broken Monsters, as not only the best horror novels I've read this year, but likely the best horror novels I've read in the past decade. 
 Blew. Me. Away.

Boring. Every character, with the exception of eight-year old Merry, are utterly flat, two-dimensional cardboard cutouts with dialogue balloons taped above their heads. I don't know how Tremblay managed to at least lift the young Merry off the page and feel like an actual little girl when he failed so miserably with everyone else. 
 Tremblay takes the easy way out with the plot by structuring the whole thing as an interview given by an adult Merry to a journalist, together with blog posts written about the reality show done around the events she discusses. He only bothers to come back to either conceit a few times in the book. Once Merry gets going he just keeps on writing. You forget that she's being interviewed. Apparently so does he (no wonder, really, given that the journalist is basically just a name). 
 As for the blog posts, they're needed for two reasons. First, Tremblay wants you to know exactly where the ideas for this book came from, so they're filled with explanations of all the pop culture sources and references he's used. Second, and most importantly, he needs some way to tell the reader that, a few weeks after the exorcism, Merry's father poisons and kills himself, her mother, and Marjorie. . And he needs to do that because he has to turn that around a few pages later and have Merry in her "interview" reveal that it was she who poisoned the family, tricked by her sister into spiking some spaghetti sauce. 
 That's the twist, the supposed big "gotcha" moment where the reader gasps and his/her jaw drops in shock and surprise. And once Tremblay tells you that, the book's over. The interviewer exits stage right with nary a reaction or response, the spotlight fades to black on Merry, and the reader is left to ponder the many other enjoyable ways he/she could have spent the afternoon. 
 To say this was lazy writing is an understatement. Tremblay's story is assembled from scenes that anyone who's seen any of the classic horror/supernatural sources he cites in those blog posts will recognize straight away. Actually, if you've seen The Exorcist or anything of its ilk, you'll have basically read this book. The only difference will be that "twist" but don't worry about that as Tremblay will just check off that box himself at the end. 
 This is one of the very few times when I genuinely don't understand where all the rave reviews are coming from.
HOLY SMOKES. This book is a roller coaster ride that you never want to get off of. I cannot recommend this book enough!

Did Not Finish. YUCK! About 25-30% though there is a scene which I hate to even summarize. It involved underage masturbation, blood, deification, and urination, as viewed by a pre-pubescent child. Ugh! I wish I could un-read it, wipe the memory, and have my time back!
According to the reviews I read, this was supposed to be scary. I kept thinking, when am I going to be scared? I liked the ending.

I did enjoy this but was disappointed I did not find it as scary or disturbing as others had - perhaps because I had been intending to read it for so long my expectations were too high, or perhaps real life is currently scarier than the book!

I love my book club because it gets me to read things that I wouldn't normally consider like A Head Full of Ghosts. And, we'll have plenty of things to talk about tomorrow night: the relationships in the family, the connection between schizophrenia/magical thinking/psychosis, religion vs science, evil within vs evil from without, media in modern society, bullying... yeah, there's a lot. 
 Personally, I didn't enjoy A Head Full of Ghosts because it brought up some old baggage for me and I had a really hard time enjoying a story about a young girl who's world was imploding because it was far too easy to see my own kid in the narrator. But, for people who like to read horror, don't have a 9 year old, and aren't bothered by someone who may or may not be having a psychotic break, this is the book for you.

This was good, but it wasn't great. I liked the relationship between the two sisters, but there were other things I didn't like. Without giving anything away...I didn't like Merry's blog posts. I didn't love that Marjorie's diagnosis wasn't absolute, but I think that's probably a reality with mental health. Im not an expert on dark fiction, but I'd say this is worth 3 stars...

Paul Tremblay's A Head Full of Ghosts is half an epistolary novel via horror blog entries by Karen Brissette and from the protagonist's, Meredith "Merry" Barrett, POV. 15 years prior, Merry, then 8 years old, was involved in a reality TV show called The Possession. 
 The Possession focused on her older sister Marjorie and her abnormal and increasingly erratic behavior. Now, she could be suffering from schizophrenia or it could be demonic possession. Unfortunately, an unscrupulous suggests the latter and is the sole reason why The Possession into existence. The show becomes an instant hit and when it ends in tragedy, the show ascends into a cult classic legend. 
 I'm not going to lie. I picked up this book because it's has the same title of a Bad Religion song. Therefore, that and Stephen King liked it, was all I really had to go on. Tremblay was effective in writing the tense atmosphere in some parts. It definitely gave me pause during my early morning readings. 
 I wasn't entirely a fan of Merry. At times, I thought she was a bit whiny. However, I did like how she was pathological and a bit of an unreliable narrator. Merry went through something extremely traumatic and never really recovered. The rest of her family I didn't like though there were times Marjorie was hella creepy. 
 A Head Full of Ghosts was good and I'm glad I read it but I could have lived my life if I didn't.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ambiguous and annoying. This book could have been good and interesting, but it only ended up boring me. I wanted to like it, but the characters were all so unlikable. The premise of Marjorie being possessed/not being possessed by a demon entity had potential, but I just could not like any her or sympathize with her issues. I also could not invest in the idea that they were filming a documentary series at the house and it would be on television a week later. Really? No editing time necessary? Unrealistic. A lot of anti-religion sentiments were peppered throughout the work as well. I found them to be distracting and unnecessary. Many times "The Exorcist" is referenced, but I think it was all to keep readers thinking that this story could get really twisted and good, but ultimately, it only disappointed. If the author wanted this to be a modern take on the Exorcist horror, he missed the entire mark. By the end, I was hoping that everyone would have eaten the spiked spaghetti sauce and then maybe there wouldn't have been a horrible retelling of an uneventful event in the lives of this dysfunctional family.
omg that ending though. I keep thinking about the guy in Troll 2 who is like "OHHHHH MYYYYY GODDDDDDDDDD"

2.5 stars. I just did not enjoy this rather unpleasant story about mental health and the breakdown of a family. A sad and creepy little tale...it reminds me a little of Shirley Jackson, where the atmosphere and tensions provide the 'horror'. It did scare me, and I think that's why it needs a low rating from me. That doesn't seem fair but there it is!
Slogged through to the end, so 2 stars.

"Set in suburban Massachusetts 15 years after a family's alleged possession ordeal was captured by a reality show, Tremblay's intricate, dizzying thriller weaves commentary about social media, blogging, and pop-culture obsession in the internet age into a jaw-dropping reinvention of familiar tropes. And beneath the complexity and exquisite construction is a nerve-shredding odyssey into darkness whose ending will chill the heart." --THE ONION A/V CLUB........ Amazing book. I will add that it's a disquieting look at the effect mental illness has on families, especially when meddled with by zealotry and greed. I found the book to be scary at times, profound at others, and ultimately heartbreaking. A great way to start off the new year and I highly recommend it. It avoids cliches (and in fact criticizes those cliches) and leaves you with questions that have answers if you can find them.

Honestly, I had to sit on this book for a while because I couldn't decide if I liked it or not. This was a random audio pick from my library. In A Head Full of Ghosts, teenager Marjorie starts exhibiting signs of schizophrenia be cause she claims that voices are telling her to do things. Her father and his priest are convinced that she is possessed. In order to pay off bills, the family makes a deal with the devil. OK, not the devil, but a TV network to have their ordeal turned into a reality TV show. I'm not sure there is much difference. The story waffles between the present where Merry is being interviewed for a book about her experience and the past as Merry relates her version of events with her sister and family. 
 I think I'm just going to have to say this book was just OK. I think it had the potential to be a good horror story. In fact, the beginning was really creepy. But as the book progressed, it got more and more disappointing. What I thought was going to be a good horror story turned into a somewhat negative commentary about reality TV, religion, and moral obligation. The blog posts that are sprinkled throughout the book were disruptive and threw off the pacing of the narrative for me. The last 1/4 was equally disappointing. Yes, there were a couple of twists, but they weren't as shocking as I think they were meant to be. The final scene has kind of an ambiguous ending and that was frustrating. 
 I have seen a lot of rave reviews on this book. but I just can't agree. I think if you go into the book not expecting horror or even a spooky story, you might like it more than I did.

I came into this book on the recommendation of a fellow horror fan over at Reddit's HorrorLit sub-reddit. Repeatedly, I heard comparison's to Danielewski's House of Leaves, which I haven't yet read but continue to hear good things about, and decided to give it a go. I'm glad I did. 
 That said, this book is not horror. It is more of a psychological thriller, if anything, but even that doesn't feel like an apt description. 
 The story, in a nutshell, is told by Merry as she relives her tragic, troubled childhood for her biographer. Her childhood home is beset by fear, tension, and wholesale discord, when her sister becomes possessed by a demon. Or does she? Network television and the Catholic church seem to think so, or at least see the chance for profit, and the family becomes the stars of their own reality TV show, The Possession. 
 Is Margaret possessed? That is the central question behind Paul Tremblay's Head Full of Ghosts. The story gives you enough to lead you one way, but then keeps you guessing about the other right up until the terrible, unexpected end. The final pages of this book pack a punch that I didn't see coming. It's a testament to the author's creativity and storytelling that the sense of unease which so permeates this book never relents, even when its biggest questions seem to be answered. 
 Head Full of Ghosts was not what I expected from the lofty praise of horror fans. This is not a book steeped in terror or easy gross-outs. It is disquieting and uncomfortable, yet also incredibly genuine and at times very touching. This, Tremblay's most popular work, in an intersection of genres -- horror, drama, mystery, thriller. It is also worthwhile no matter which genre you call home. Read it.

Meh. Basically, this book is meh. 
 As a horror, it fails. There are a few scary scenes but it's completely bogged down by the set up and structure. It just didn't work for this. Instead of having a quick succession of horrors strung together, the way this is set up makes it impossible to keep the tension. 
 It's just an awkward set up. It truly is. 
 Basically, you have the past events, then you have the interviewing portion (Merry is being interviewed by Rachel), and beyond that, you have this blog that is basically a retelling of what happens on the show. At one point, the author decides it's much better to have this blogger analyze what happened in the video so you basically get two retellings of events and the POV of young Merry. 
 My other issue was the language. No one in this books speaks like their age, and beyond that, there was a clunky word choice. That's the only way I can describe it. Most were words that you'd not necessarily think of being plucked from a thesaurus, so virtue of that poor book is probably okay, but they were odd enough that you wouldn't hear them in any daily conversation. 
 Finally, the ending. That ending. It was so completely underwhelming that I literally just sat back and thought "really?" It was infuriating or anything. It was just so stupid and unsurprising that I was just sort of floored that anyone would think it was clever. Honestly, given the book, it would've been the first thing I'd've considered. I actually did consider it but chucked it away thinking that even going with the obvious set up would've been better then that. I might've given this 3 stars if not for that. 
 Overall, I suppose I say that the feeling I got from this book was one of an author who didn't want to write horror, even found it trite and boring, but felt he couldn't publish in any other genre. 
 The allusions to this book being like the numerous classic horror was also incredibly annoying. Why do some authors try to make that allusion? Your work will always suffer. Whatever props I gave this book for having the quote from 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (one of my favorite horror stories) was completely taken away when the author tried to say that Marg was like the woman in that short story.
Uhhhh mixed feelings about this. Mostly it gets two stars because I did not like one character in the book and the plot was very predictable. Zzzzzz.......

They sell it to you as a thriller, but it is not, it is just a drama about a family having a hard time as the elder daughter goes schizophrenic. And it is quite boring at that. 
 By the way, the blog posts were super annoying and totally unnecessary.

I'm kind of at a loss as to how to start this review/rant. 
 For the first half of this book, i was completely blown away by how much i was enjoying it. It takes a lot...A LOT...to freak me out/make me uncomfortable while reading a book, and this book...in the beginning at least, did both those things big time. 
 Around the 50% mark though, i started to get a weird feeling. A feeling that told me that this book was possibly going to start to go down a path I was not happy with. One that would have left me feeling both annoyed and have me rolling my eyes at the sheer predictability of it all. Well, what i ended up feeling by the end of this book was out and out anger. Angry at the fact that the book showed so, so much promise, only to have it turn into this massive, silly train wreck that made me feel like pounding my kindle into a wall when i turned the last page. 
 *deep breath* 
 Okay, i might sound a bit melodramatic here, but honestly....there is nothing i love more than a good, scary read. And because i am a huge horror movie fan, and have basically grown up watching any horror movie i come across, i tend to be more cynical when it comes to horror/suspense fiction. I can count on one hand the times i have considered myself to be unsettled by a book...and have yet ever really find myself being scared by one. But, the beginning chapters of House Full Of Ghosts knocked me on my butt with how well the author set a genuinely creepy tone. There are scenes early on (especially between the 2 sisters) that were so well done, that i nearly had to stop reading because i felt like it was a bit too unnerving to take in all at once. 
 As i mentioned above, around the half way mark i started to get the idea that the story was going to take a turn i would have been very disappointed in. But, I was still enjoying the overall story so much that i tried to put it out of my head, and just kept going. It's worth mentioning that all of my issues with the book actually started around the time that the family started to film their reality tv show. I thought that might be an interesting aspect to the story, but it just came off as gimmicky....which might or might not have been intentional. 
 With the exception of one scene, the entire last 25% of the book turned into a completely ridiculous hot mess. It is almost mind boggling to me how much of a complete turn around this book took in my opinion. It's hard to get into the specifics of what happened that drove me crazy without giving away huge plot elements, so....cue the spoiler-filled cut .......> 
 First off all....I got the impression that it was going to turn out that Marjorie faked being possessed. Which was the first thing that i wasn't happy about, because the book was so much more effective when it seemed like all the supernatural elements were true. Once the idea of her pretending started to creep into the story, it lost a lot of it's punch. 
 Also, it was VERY obvious that Merry had a lot of emotional and psychological problems. And it wasn't surprising in the least that she ended up being this mysterious blogger who posted her cynical observations on the authenticity of the reality show & the supposed exorcism. Unfortunately, that entire sub-plot of why Merry acts the way she does...why she seems almost childlike in her manner of speaking and the way that she interacts with the woman hired to help write her book....just ends up being one of the many loose ends that the book throws at us. 
 The actual ending of the book...the last 20-30 pages...is where i have my biggest problems. I'm okay with an author deciding to leave a book open ended, or up to interpretation, but this was just a case of a sloppy, poorly constructed conclusion. In fact it didn't even feel like any kind of conclusion...open ended or not. It felt like the author got to the end of a sentence and said, "You know what? I think that's a good enough place as any to end this." Are we to assume that Merry made a lot of her story...the parts that didn't air on the reality show at least...up? That she in fact was the one who poisoned her family and it was just more convenient to let her poor, mentally unstable sister (or father) take the blame for it? Based on the reaction of the writer after she listened to Merry tell her "true" account of the story, i am also wondering if the writer herself wasn't a figment of Merry's imagination as well. 
 I am truly sick of the "unreliable narrator" trope being used these days. Very rarely, if ever have i come across a story that actually works well when this device is used and i for one hope to never find myself reading something along those lines again. 
 I hardly ever write reviews that are this negative, and i realize i have an unpopular opinion based on all the glowing reviews this book has received. I wish things had turned out differently. I wish this book had stayed on the course i thought it would...or would have at least found a way to resolve SOMETHING by the end of the book. I feel both cheated and angry that a book that showed such promise ended up being so cliched and so melodramatic .

3.5 really. This book kept me turning the pages, and wanting to know how it was all gonna fall into place. For the most part, it did just that. In a good way. I'm not giving 4 stars only because the very end kinda left me thinking, ' really, just going to end like that? '

reference_books.title: Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil
reference_books.review_text: This was a story that took me a little while to figure out. It is a mix of true crime & narrative concerning a murder which takes place in the hot, steamy city of Savannah Georgia. I loved the author's colorful tales of the residents that lived there, as well as the main crime that takes place between a local millionaire & his secret lover (an explosive drug addict). However, I was really disappointed by the ending and if I ever do get around to watching the movie--I hope it is different!

reference_books.title: Dead Wake: The Last Crossing of the Lusitania
reference_books.review_text: I gotta be honest, this was definitely my least favorite Erik Larson book that I have read to date. I still really like his style of non-fiction writing (he talks about the events in real time pulling from a variety of different perspectives) however, I think it was the event itself that did not keep my attention. The sinking of the Lusitania, which was VERY interesting to read about because I had no real prior knowledge of the event, was rather anti-climatic to read about. As a reader, I KNEW the ship was going to be torpedoed and to some extent, I just wanted the event to happen and then read about the aftermath of the tragedy. That's not really what happened. Most of the book was devoted to the build up (which makes sense) but I found myself stopping for awhile and then diving back in and finishing the story. I found a lot of the little details fascinating and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this one to a history or World War buff. For myself, in the Garden of Beasts & Devil in a White City are the ones that I will keep at the top of my list.

reference_books.title: In a Dark, Dark Wood
reference_books.review_text: Honestly this book was a complete disappointment. I wanted it to be a tense thriller...instead it was more like a wet blanket. The plot focused on a writer named Nora who was invited to a bachelorette party for her former best friend. Only a few people could come and of course it was at some creepy cottage which right away made the plot seemed way too cliche for me. Also, I found it completely unbelievable that Nora is unable to get over her HS boyfriend (from 10 years ago!!) which is supposed to add a sense of betrayal to the story since her former best friend is marrying said former boyfriend. Anyway, crazy things start happening at the cottage and an awful tragedy occurs...which of course Nora can't really remember. Blah....definitely save yourself for suspense writers like Harlan Coben, Karin Slaughter or the Kellermans.

reference_books.title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
reference_books.review_text:
I picked up Wild in the airport when I was headed to Boston for an intimidating education conference sponsored by the U.S. Department of Education. Unfortunately, I didn't read it on that trip but I engrossed myself in it this week as I was on spring break. 
 The book is a memoir of Cheryl Strayed's journey down the Pacific Crest Train after her mother passed away, she divorced her husband and proceeded to experiment with heroin and meaningless relationships. Although the book was very detailed about the trail itself (which I sometimes found confusing since I have never been to the Pacific Northwest), I thought Strayed's introspective journey to be honest, unflinching and really poignant. Although sometimes I skimmed through her rantings, I found the text overall to be really sincere and empowering for anyone going through a depressing period of life and needing a reboot. 
 I want to give a few copies of this book to girlfriends of mine who are going through issues in their love life and overall I would look back at this book if I had my own negative life moments.

reference_books.title: The Last Summer
reference_books.review_text: A predictable beach read about two sisters and their friend Paul who have spent their summers on the Atlantic coast their whole lives. The narrative is a predictable triangle between Alice's and Paul's love and Riley's (the other sister) illness. The only thing that was really interesting was Alice's insight on her sister's illness--I read the book in a day and had guessed the ending within minutes.

reference_books.title: The Handmaid's Tale
reference_books.review_text: A futuristic view of a world in which women are only valued for what their ovaries can produce. Also, the world has gone back to a much simpler time. I read this book in college for a feminist literature class at MSU and I have to say at the time the concept seemed so far out. However, the more I read, the more believable the premise seemed. You root for the narrator the entire time and I really enjoyed the whole thing in the end.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Honestly I read this book because it always grabs my attention when a book becomes a topic of conversation especially in an era where we seem to discuss movies & media to the 10th degree but books are far behind. Anyway, I have read Anais Nin & have read many books with episodes of erotica so it wasn't like I was unprepared to begin the book. So, pros? The sex scenes were terrific and the plot although over-the-top simplistic is just what the doctor ordered when you want to read a no-brainer sex novel. Cons? the first book REALLY pissed me off when it came to the backwards gender roles between Mr. Grey & "Ana". My God, "Ana"....have some FREAKIN' backbone when it comes to sex. And REALLY EL James you had to make your main character a college graduate VIRGIN who happens to meet a guy who has a SEX DUNGEON?? I mean as I'm typing this I can't even believe someone had the balls to write this stuff down!! To be fair, if you are reading this expecting to absorb some high-brow literature, then be prepared to be disappointed. But, if you are reading this because it's summer and you want to see what all the fuss is about, then have at it!

reference_books.title: The Hate U Give
reference_books.review_text:
So let me just start off by saying--I LOVED this book. I was worried because so many people liked it that it would not live up to the hype but it did, wow. Easily the best YA book I have read in a LONG time. Please make sure that if you have time to read this summer, to read this one. I will be placing it in my classroom bookshelf for sure as well as recommending this text to anyone who wants to dive deep as an ally and as recognition of their own experiences. 
 The story centers around a black teenager named Starr who is growing up in Garden Heights, New Jersey. Early in the book (like Chapter 2) she witnesses the shooting of her childhood friend Khalil at the hands of a police officer, and Khalil is unarmed. What happens next causes Starr to question her and her community's place in society and her responsibility in the entire situation. 
 Thomas's writing style is accessible, creative and refreshing to read. She approaches her readers like friends and even though my skin color is white, I identified with Starr's feeling of powerlessness and being from two different communities. Also, there were so many quotable lines about current society, race and humanity today. Starr's parents and family were so well-written I wanted there to be a series...each one of them had their own unique story. 
 So...I could go on and on about this one but I'll leave this review with three words: READ. THIS. BOOK.

reference_books.title: Bossypants
reference_books.review_text: I have to be honest I was really underwhelmed with this memoir.Maybe it was because I was expecting a lot--I had read the letter she wrote in the book to her daughter on a pinterest site and thought it was amazing, and I really admire every interview I've seen of her. On one hand, the book had that awesome letter to her daughter and traced back her thoughts on growing up (hilarious), her impression of Sarah Palin and other anecdotes about Saturday Night Live which I found interesting. However, I felt like the book really shied away from being even CLOSE to personal and honest. She glossed over a lot of the obstacles and issues she probably has faced throughout her life and I just wanted more details than she seemed willing to give her readers. Also, at times there were large swaths of her life that were just not really that interesting. I was bummed...I had really hoped for a lot from this one. Sigh, at least I have that speech to give my daughter!

reference_books.title: Gone Girl
reference_books.review_text:
so I really really REALLY wanted to like Gone Girl more than I did. I was captivated by the his & her chapter structure, the sheer dysfunctional"ness" of the marriage between Nick & Amy, and I loved the supporting cast of characters that kept ducking in and out of the narrative. BUT. 
 the end? really?? I was so disappointed by the anti-climatic STOP that the author decided to go with that I looked up interviews with Gillian Flynn as soon as I was done. One thing I was annoyed about is that her response to criticism about the novel was "well, what did you want to happen?" Want? Want? I want an ending! It's not so much that I need justice, but I would like some sort of resolution with the characters not just this edgy tension. If I wanted that, I would have checked out some of the Oscar nominees for this year. Overall, I just wish I would have read reviews first so I wouldn't have started reading with high expectations of a thriller with a satisfying conclusion. If you are going to read it, be warned!

book_a.title: This Lullaby
book_a.user_review:
On my quest to read a lot of YA lit (which I started in 2013), this book became my next victim. A lot of my students talk about reading Sarah Dessen books so I thought I would give her another try. Sigh....this book just really didn't make the cut. It took me awhile to get through (always a bad sign) and I really tried to root for Remy, but she just kinda irritated me. 
 The whole plot centers around a girl whose habitually marrying mother marries again and meanwhile she struggles with being with any boy for over a certain period of time. While I can relate (I'm a reformed commitment-phobe), I felt like her reasoning was a little shallow and she really didn't delve into Remy's background enough to make me feel sympathetic to what she was going through. Also, some of the dialogue was pretty cheesy and the whole sidebar with her not being able to listen to "this lullaby" was pretty weak. I would have liked more backstory on her mother & father's quickie relationship. 
 On the other hand, it is harmless chicklit and made for a light read. This would be a great one to have at the beach...too bad there's 2 feet of snow outside!

sample_reviews.review_text:
"This Lullaby" is one of those books that is hilariously funny at times, and at others, makes you bawl your head off. 
 I found myself entranced with the ideas, relating to my life, and completely depressed when I was through. I know I won't get the words right, but here's why I liked this book: 
 Because.. 
 "this lullaby is just a few words 
 a simple set of cords..."
It's a 4.5 really. Love Sarah Dessen. :)
I thought this was one of her best books yet!!
Very sweet. You wanted to keep reading. Loved it.
I hate sarah dessen. Haters do hate when they want to hate.

I rate this book 4.5 stars. 
 My book blog: nazishreads.net 
 My twitter account: @NazishTVDSwift 
 My Instagram accounts: @nazishreads, @nrcharmed01, and @nrh20justaddwater 
 And I also have a facebook fan page for my blog. 
 To view the full post and other reviews, click here This Lullaby 
 I know that there are newer covers now, but it's edition that I read, so I decided to post that specific cover. 
 Gore: No 
 Magic: No 
 Romance: Yes 
 Pacing: 4 stars 
 Plot: 4 stars 
 Eighteen-year-old Remy Starr doesn't believe in true love or at least she thinks she doesn't. That is until she starts spending more and more time with Dexter. 
 Remy became this way because of her mom's love life, she had four marriages (technically 3), but they all failed, and now she's working on husband #5. So even though Remy does date, she only does for a certain amount of time, when things start getting to serious, she dumps the guy even though he didn't do anything wrong, which is cruel, she should at least warn whoever she's dating, it's not fair to the good guys that she's just playing around, it actually kind of makes her sound like a slut even though she's not really. She does this because this way she thinks that no one will get hurt, while she acts tough, she's actually afraid. 
 Remy is looking forward to her last summer before she goes off to college, in fact, she's more excited about college starting, than the summer. Her summer doesn't go as she planned, thanks to Dexter. 
 Remy has rules about who she will and will not date, like no musicians. 
 Dexter is in a band with his friends and he is nothing like the boys Remy's dated before, he's also the complete opposite of her, meaning that he's a slob while she's very organized and neat. Despite this, she ends up dating him. Another thing that is different about her and Dexter's relationship than we she dated other boys is that she hasn't slept with him (I don't understand why people think that isn't serious and how people do that so easily with random people, it just sounds so gross), and she keeps feeling things that she hasn't felt with other boys before. Her friends start to question what is wrong with her and quickly realizing that shes in love, which Remy herself doesn't believe. This summer (like with most of Sarah's books) changes her life. 
 Unlike the other Sarah Dessen books I've read before (That Summer, Along for the Ride, Someone Like You, and Keeping the Moon), this book doesn't start out slow, it starts out interesting right away, especially when she talks about her mom and the typewriter, lol. 
 I couldn't put it down, I loved it. It also has some interesting realistic characters. I've read Sarah's first four books as well and I love that Sarah keeps on getting better with each book. I didn't like her first two (That Summer and Someone Like You), I enjoyed the third one (Keeping the Moon), and then there's the fourth one (Dreamland), which I can't really compare to this one because it's totally different than this book. 
 Remy is also very organized (as I've said before), almost to the point of OCPD (but I don't think she has that, she's just really organizational), it really bothers her if something is out of place or dirty or any clothes are wrinkled. Funny thing is, she's a lot like me in that way. It was nice to see her start to doubt what she believed about love when she started hanging out with Dexter. 
 I liked Dexter, but I felt like for him, it was love at first sight, which is one of things that I didn't like about this book. He didn't even know her name, he just thought she was hot and fell in love with her, isn't that lust, not love? Later on he does get to know her and loves her for real, though. Dexter is funny, I loved the crazy things he would do and come up with from time to time. 
 I also liked some of the other characters as well. Remy's mom is childish, but she has her moments of being a good mother, like when near the end or in the middle she gives Remy good love advice. I also liked that despite so many marriage failures, she still had so much faith in love. It seems that she doesn't get discouraged easily. 
 I also liked Dexter's friends and bandmates, they were an interesting bunch. There's so much I want to say about them, but I can't because then this review would be way too long. 
 Scarlett from Someone Like You is also mentioned and even has a few scenes in this book. In this story it's been 3 years since the end of Someone Like You. I hear that this is the first book where Sarah started bringing some characters back from her previous novels for cameos. I love it when authors do that, if it's a character I like, I just smile and get excited, even though it is only a few pages. 
 In case you're wondering, the This Lullaby was a song that Remy's dad wrote for her when she was born. This song stayed with Remy even after her opinion of love changed. 
 Like with Sarah's other novels, there's always a lesson the main character learns, which I love, and it's something I don't see very often in many YA novels these days. 
 Overall it's a light, happy, and fun summer read. 
 This Lullaby is entertaining, has great, interesting and fun characters, has many sweet, funny moments, and is a fun summer read, even though I read it about a week ago. 
 They seem like people I could be good friends with. That's one of the things I love most about Sarah Dessen and John Green's stories, their unique, hilarious, interesting, and relatable characters. 
 I can't wait to read Sarah's other books. So far I've read (in the following order): That Summer (I think this was 2 or 3 years ago, then I stopped reading Sarah Dessen's novels until the end of August of this year), Along for the Ride, Keeping the Moon, Someone Like You, This Lullaby, and I'm currently reading The Truth About Forever and I'm enjoying it so far.

I first read this book when I was in 8th Grade. I remember passing it around to all of my friends because I enjoyed it so much. The protagonist, Remy Starr, is a cynical, narrow-minded high school senior who is completely over love. Enter, Dexter, a free spirit who completely shakes up everything Remy knows, or think she knows about life and love. This is defiantly my favorite Sarah Dessen book, and quite possibly my favorite straight teen romance. I have read, and reread this book many times. The characters are all very charming and carefully crafted (like Remy's family and her friends) and I love watching the story unfold. I think I enjoy this book so much because you really get to watch Remy change as the book progresses.
Silly summer read. Wanted more to the ending.

This is my third (or fourth. I lost count) Sarah Dessen book, and this is by far the most depressing one I've read. I was hoping it would be like 'The Truth About Forever' (which by the way, a book that I come to love, and will definitely read it again) and 'Along For The Ride' but unfortunately, it came out as a total shock. I should, however, be relating well to Remy given the fact that I had a dysfunctional family, and had been to many relationships (thirteen, to be precise) before I found my 'Dexter'. 
 Anyway, for the benefit of my valuable readers who, despite of my negative feedback, are still willing to endure a good four-hours (depending on your reading skills) to read this book. Here goes: 
 "Remy always knows the perfect time to give a boyfriend 'the speech' telling him it's over: right after the first romantic rush, but before any real emotional involvement happens. And Remy should have perfect timing, since she's had plenty of experience dumping guys. Not to mention what she's learned from watching her own mother, who's been married four times and is heading for wedding number five. 
 So then what is it about Dexter that makes it so hard for Remy to follow her own rules? He's everything she hates: messy, disorganized, impulsive, and worst of all, a musician like her father. The father Remy never knew, the one who wrote a famous song for her but disappeared from her life. Remy has never had trouble getting out while the getting is good. But there's just something about Dexter. Could it be that Remy is finally finding out what all those love songs are about?" 
 Let me tell you something about Remy's character, two words: anal retentive. She's a neat-freak and is an achiever (I guess all of Sarah Dessen's lead character are like that)! But what make Remy's character stand out is because she's the ultimate player, has vices, and does NOT believe in love. The latter part actually threw me off since I'm a hopeless romantic, which by the way mean (per Google search): one who looks for a person that makes their world come together. They're not to be confused as stalkers or creepy (There! I'm not a creep, okay?! Enough said). 
 I think Dexter is the hopeless romantic one but he's actually not the type of guy I would WANT to date with. He's a slob, clumsy, don't know how to do his laundry properly (I mean, my husband can do better job than him?! Sheesh), and not a husband material. Two things I like about him though: he's funny AND a musician! I always have a soft spot for musicians. I don't know why but I'm glad that I didn't end up with one. I don't want any groupies around my man, that's for sure! 
 You can see that Remy and Dexter are absolutely opposite! In every. Freaking. Way! But I guess love can overlook anything. It can move mountains. It can even launch a thousand ships and lead a country to war (I know, I know its Helen's beauty not love but it's a very good example, right?). Moot point is nothing is impossible when it comes to love. I'm not a love psychologist or anything, I don't even have a plaque of recognition for that. Just an avid-reader who wants to vent out. 
 And I've come to conclusion that this book did not do anything good for me. I was disappointed, ergo, the one-star. 
 Even so, I'm still recommending it to all Sarah Dessen fans, young-adults who lost hope in love, and just any avid young-adult fiction reader. This one got rave reviews from Goodreads, so I think its just me and my subconscious who think its bad. 
 Enjoy!
