Meh. That's literally how I felt about this book. I admit I was excited to read but I had not a big BIG expectation about it... I was like cool, this looks nice it must be great and that's it. My hopes weren't too high for me to feel kinda sad for it not being what I expected or "obligated" to like it. 
 I don't know, I think the problem was that I really didn't like the characters at all. I mean, Remy was good and she had some sad definition of love and it's understandable why she does, why she think that things are always meant to end given her mom has had 4 marriages and she is planning her 5th one . 
 Plus she finished high school and she is going to college in another city and she doesn't want anything serious and she had a pretty large history with a lot of guys so she already knows how it's going to be. That's the only thing that hasn't changed (because she stopped smoking and drinking a lot and partying 'hard' in general) until she "meets" Dexter... or more like, until she decides to give him a chance. I only liked him in a few parts... like in 30% of the book. I honeslty didn't like his stalking manners. The way he first bumped into Remy was abrupting and it was obvious that she wasn't interested. Still he insisted a bit and well, I thought it was okay but since then I didn't like them as a couple. 
 I know maybe the word "stalker" is not too appropriate because there where gaps when he was keeping his distance, but he still was kinda obsessed with her and without even really knowing her... until she finally gives in, even though she is sure it's just a summer thing and then she is scared because with him it's all different and she thinks about him more than she thought after they "break-up" and blah blah blah Remy still has this misconception about love, that it never lasts and that it's kind of a waste, but then she has a talk with her mom whom she thinks was miserable when all her marriages don't work, but actually she was content and not giving up on love after so many failures . I also didn't like the Dexter's band storyline, it was in general dull and (what a surprise) I didn't find the band members interesting. The only character I mildly enjoyed was Chloe.

The book would have been so so so so so much better if it was about her working through her disposable-boy reputation and her mother's zillion marriages and her daddy abandonment issues WITHOUT the catalyst and major influence being a boy. I did really like Along for the Ride, so maybe it's just crankiness right now, or that specific book.

They're fun to read when I just need a serious break from life, but not for a steady diet. It was REALLY fascinating in This Lullaby how Remy's mother was modeled on Nora Roberts, and ended her romance novel with the main character going off into the sunset alone and independent, and yet REMY didn't get that great ending.  I didn't like the characters....Remy was so selfish she just wanted to be only for herself.... and never thought about the others when it come to feelings she just cared for her own feelings.... I read Dessen's book Keeping the Moon this past summer and liked it a lot, so I was looking forward to checking out another one of her books. This one, however, didn't really do it for me. I still love Dessen's writing style and her un-preachy attitude towards teens drinking and having sex. I was even OK with Remy's crabbiness toward guys, since it's grounded in her mother's string of failed marriages and general flightiness. But I just didn't believe anything about Dexter, and worse, I didn't like him. He shows his feelings for Remy by being creepy, stalker-y, and immature. Literally the only thing that makes his actions OK is that he somehow "just knows" he and Remy are going to end up together. She tells him "no" over and over and he just ignores her. I hate to be the one taking the "what are we teaching our children??" tack, but I just cannot get behind a book whose message is "you'll know when you find THE ONE because he won't take no for an answer." 
 I also found the whole musician dad subplot troubling. I get that allowing Dexter to sing her dad's song represents Remy finally yielding the most private part of herself to Dexter, but the emotional impact that that change was supposed to have never really resonated with me. 
 I do like stories like this, where a crabby jaded girl learns to take risks and let herself love again. But I really wish Dessen had found a way for Dexter to break down Remy's defenses that was a little more respectful of her boundaries.

 Remy is a great character and I think she's the reason why this This Lullaby will stay near the top of my favourite books list. She had to take on some more responsibilities than she should have when she was younger. Nothing too drastic, but her mom always seemed to need an extra push or helping hand - like with planning yet another wedding. Remy is incredibly organized. In fact, calling her anal would not be out of line. She's an 18 year old girl who is desperate to move on to the next stage in her life - college - and trying her hardest to keep love out of her life. She's strong, smart, and terrified of love. Dexter (literally) crashes into her just when she needs it and he does his best to convince her that he (and love) is worth a shot. 
 This is one of Dessen's novels that has a lot to do with the romance but it's not really the love story that is the point. Remy needs to work on herself and her belief that love is a sham and anyone who falls for it gets their heart broken. What I like about her novels is that the romance is there and lovely but not in an "in your face" kind of way.

I am a little surprised that this book is rated as high as it is. It isn't a bad book by any means, but I don't think it was 4+ worthy. I felt like the main character, Remy, tried to be a bad girl, but all of her bad girl cred was from the past that the reader only gets mention of. For some reason I noticed that the characters kept saying things "flatly." I guess the bottom line is that I really didn't care too much about the characters. Remy's mom seems clueless, Remy's friends are forgettable, and there seem to be so many of them that I can't keep track. Dexter and his bandmates just seemed annoying to me. I think this book may have just been a little too young adult for my tastes. Not a bad book, just didn't interest me as much as it could have.

This review contains some NON-SPECIFIC spoilers... 
 I read this book as part of our Pie Plate Publishing online bookclub, and I'm posting this review on our collective behalf. We only had a few readers for this selection. There were more in the beginning, but participation dropped dramatically a few chapters in. Perhaps we're all tired of mysteries, or maybe this isn't a good chatty book for a bookclub selection? Perhaps as the writing itself lost its steam, our enthusiasm followed... 
 First, let's preface our review with some positives - we did find the writing itself to be good, we were interested in the characters (at least at first), and the book included all of the basic elements necessary for a compelling mystery/suspense: a grizzly crime, a large cast of characters to suspect, lots of loose ends, a backstory to confuse things, and a few twists. That said, by the end of this book, we felt like we'd been led on a merry chase. Themes that were introduced were not resolved, and [spoiler alert] the killer gets away with the crime. 
 According to one of the bookclubbers: "I felt that the ending was completely anti-climactic. I was disappointed. I really wish there would have been some resolution to at least one of the main themes." (Roxanne H.) 
 The most disappointing thing for me was that the main character (our narrator) started off to be a character I liked. I thought he would be our hero, breaking the rules on the job to get to the real story, solving not only today's crime but a decades old crime as well. I thought there was something special about Detective Robb, only to find out that he was just a messed up guy with unresolvable issues in the end. His insight into the case becomes muddied by his inability to control himself. He ruins his relationship with his partner. Midway through the book, he becomes someone I dislike, and when I lose faith in the narrator, I lose faith in the story. I don't really care anymore about his perceptions and feelings. I just want him to go away. His downward spiral isn't compelling or really related to the case at hand, and the writing begins to feel indulgent and distracting. 
 We've heard there is a follow up sequel to this book. Based on our experiences with this one, we're hesitant to read the next. It's does not read as though this was meant as a continuation, intended to be the first in a serial. There's definitely a final conclusion to it - and it stinks. If there is a sequel, it seems as though it was written as an afterthought, to capitalize on the success of the first. We're not sure we're ready to go down the road again with this author...she hasn't earned our trust. 
 Roxanne H. says it best: "It makes me think, well, this book ended with no resolution and no teasers, why would I want to invest any more time in these characters?"

A very engrossing, very melancholy read. The main character falls very short of being a likable protagonist. As the story is told through first person POV and the narrator directly addresses the reader several times, he is aware that he isn't painting himself in the best light. So we get nothing held back as we see him through his struggles of solving he Katy Devlin murder along with trying to figure out his own diluted, splotchy past whose tendrils reach into this case. 
 I've never said "Trigger warning" in a serious context before, but if you're prone to depression I would avoid this book.

So conflicted. French has a strong grasp of what I think of as poetic prose and an amazingly sharp eye for detail. This was both her strength and her undoing, after awhile it becomes tedious. My first issue with the story was that I kept forgetting the narrator was supposed to be a man because the voice and observations were decidedly feminine (in my head anyway) until about 250 pages into it. Another 100 pages or so and French slipped back out of it and Detective Ryan started sounding more like a girl again. The plot was brilliantly woven but it was not paced to be a true novel of suspense. It was more about a detective's experience going through a case, than about the case itself. And it was sadly predictable. For anyone who reads or watches a lot of police procedurals or spent any time studying crime....it was too obvious almost from the first introduction of the guilty character. All that being said, I did enjoy reading it. Even though I knew who it was going to be I wanted to see how it would be played out. Toward the end though, French started to lose me. I didn't buy Detective Ryan's weakness for a certain person. And then on 409, she lost me altogether when she claimed, "(the guilty person) fooled me, but (guilty person) fooled you too." Um no. And to say it is almost arrogance. I've heard this line in plays and movies, it was a cheap device. BUT! But I liked her grasp of language and detail. For writing skill I would give her 5 stars. For plot, 3. So I leave it at a happy medium of 4. It's not a fast read, unless you want it to be. You really have to be committed to it, I felt. And yes, I'll read The Likeness. But not right now. I want something with a little better pacing (assuming The Likeness will be like In The Woods) for right now. As a murder mystery this book should have been AT LEAST 100 pages shorter. It's like Hamish MacBeth on steroids.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I have to admit I'm disappointed with the ending. Two cases, and one isn't resolved in the least. I understand that authors use that to prove a point about a character, etc. etc. but I wanted closure! However, I did enjoy the novel until the last 20 pages when I realized I wasn't going to get all the answers I wanted! I'm tempted to pick up another French novel, if only for her wonderful use of description. I'd recommend this book if you're looking for a good story, just don't expect a conclusion.

One of the best books I've read this year, but an unexpected great book for me. Not usually the type of book I like so much. This book by author Tana French does a great job of playing with your emotions. By the tagline and what's described on the back of the book, you know it's going to be dark. But the relationship between the two main characters, Cassie and Adam Ryan, give you a lot of other emotions from over-the-top happy to over-the-top sad. I think a good book has to have at least one moment where you put down the book, look up to the ceiling and go, "Wow, that just happened." Well, this book does that about three or four times. I didn't want this book to end. That's another great sign. I can't describe this book too much as I don't want to give anything away, but the basis of it is that three kids in 1984 go into the woods near Dublin. Only one kid comes out, although he has a tough time remembering what actually happened. That one kid later becomes a cop and 20 years later he is investigating a murder in the same area. Are the two crimes related in any way? Will the detective be able to handle going back? This book also features a very, very good first chapter that sets the tone for the rest of the book. A very good mystery and I look forward to reading more by Tana French.

**Spoiler Alert** 
 So I was in a mood to read a Dark book and the book fulfills that promise.Some parts of the book were really scary. Also the mystery element is truly nice. 
 What I was disappointed about was that some of the questions remain unanswered in the end. For e.g. What happened to the kids in the woods? Why did only the main character come back? 
 These unanswered questions were really frustrating. 
 Otherwise the book is a really good read :)

*Spoiler Alert* 
 I was all set up to enjoy this book immensely, but my faith in the story began crumbling about two-thirds the way through and was never redeemed. 
 To begin with we, the readers, are given a tantalizing mystery: a little boy and his friends go into the woods. The boy, with blood filled shoes, is found later. There is no trace of his friends, and he can't remember a thing about what happened. The story itself begins 20 years later when the boy has become a detective and sets to work on a case that promises to uncover all the secrets of the past. 
 In the first part of the book, the characters are intriguing and well written. French has a good handle on dialogue, and though the relationships she sets up between her characters are a little stereotypical, I enjoyed reading about them. As they hunt down leads in the present case, small bits of the past case begin floating up, teasing the reader and promising more. 
 Starting somewhere around chapter 17, the protagonist, Rob, suddenly goes insane. I don't mean this in a plot-driven, logical-reaction-to-developments sort of way. I mean he suddenly turns into an ass and an idiot for reasons that aren't adequately explained or supported. Until this point, I'd been willing to believe in his inner demons and minor character quirks. Sure, he managed to blank out part of his memory in reaction to trauma and he's got a soft spot for floozies. But after he spends his night in Knocknaree and finally succumbs to the expected night of passion with Cassy, his personality shift defies the bounds of reasonably suspended disbelief. Nothing the author did ahead of time prepared me for it, and in the scene where they realize Rosalind is involved, I was downright offended by his opaque idiocy. 
 I would have been willing to forgive all that if final revelations about his childhood trauma had given us more insight into his demons, explaining away his irrational behavior. It was not to be. Perhaps in some misguided bid for realism or attempt to defy literary conventions, the original mystery is left unsolved. In the right circumstances, I don't mind when authors leave a bit of ambiguity or let the reader draw their own conclusions based on a story that provides enough information to be able to draw a conclusion... But this was not the case here. The mystery is left perfectly open ended. Yes, we can draw our own conclusions, but we can draw ANY conclusion. Aliens abducted them. Alligators ate them. Adam killed them himself. 
 I've decided the ending is so disappointing because the very premise of the book promises an answer. The book pulls you in because you want to know what happened to that little boy with bloody shoes and his missing friends. You expect a shocking and satisfying conclusion. Better luck next time.

I decided to read this book from a list of great books you can't put down, and a few others, "spoiler alert" the story began with Adam Ryan's mystery which never gets solved or even comes close to it, the person who murdered Katy was mentioned very briefly and when I found out he did it I didn't even care. The narrator was an asshole, which lead to many disappointments. I did guess from the beginning that the older sister had something to do with it but she gets away with it, you think when the diary is found that yes finally she is going to have to pay, after all she is an evil psychopath, but no, not enough just another let down. It ended and I was left with no satisfactions on any part of it. and who writes a murder mystery and doesn't solve the murder???? why even bring that into it if there is nothing connected to it or it being solved. The end could of brought it all together, but instead it left you just plain disappointed.
I liked it, even tho it was kind of disturbing. A more literary mystery than some.

This is the first of French's amazing Dublin Murder Squad series, but I'm reading them all out of order and it doesn't matter. They all feature flawed, troubled protagonists, a beautifully rendered, gritty Irish setting, and suspenseful story lines. This, her first novel in the series, is about Adam Robert Ryan, a detective investigating the murder of a 12-year-old dance student near the very spot where he and his two friends were abducted in the 1980s. He hides this possible conflict of interest from his bosses, but shares it with partner Cassie Maddox, who is appropriately skeptical of his insistence that his past has no impact on his investigation. The relationship between Ryan and Maddox was for me a huge part of the book's appeal, and I suppose a benefit of reading the series out of order is knowing that Maddox is going to show up in other books. 
 The other appeal of the series is how French incorporates contemporary Irish issues into her plot lines. In this book the conflict between developers and scholars over the bulldozing of an important archaeological site plays a major role in the mystery, and it was just plain interesting in its own right.

This book was amazing! The characters are so deeply written, you feel like you know them. I think Tana French did an outstanding job for her first novel. I can't wait to read more from her. This book easily became one of my favorites!!!!
Beautifully written thriller with an excellent plot--except for the ending, which (spoiler alert!) left me a bit flat.

The most frustrating mystery I've ever finished, which is a shame since the writing is so good. I read the prologue and was dazzled. Unfortunately, the story then began. The mystery is more the lazy observations of a hipster who works in a coffee shop, not a supposed cop. There is zero tension, very little conflict, no brilliant investigatory insight. Worst of all, the narrator/hero is a deeply unlikable guy. Immature, lazy, whiny, and very, very stupid. At the end, he even tells the reader: "I know I'm stupid, but hey, the killer fooled you too, right?" WTF?!! A terrible book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It had a lot of promise, but started to meander toward the end and sort of lost me. It was a little bit risky of her to leave Rob Ryan's personal mystery unsolved, and I can respect that -- but the focus on his relationship with his partner was a bit overwrought and made the thing drag on, particularly at the end. The fact of Cass ending up with Sam in the end was a bit too romance-film ironic for me and I wish she'd gone ahead and left that thread a bit loose.

I've been hearing buzz about this series all around the internet, but I just don't understand why. It started off well; I was pulled in by the two separate mysteries and the creepy family. But it was really obvious who the murderer was very early on in the story, and since the entire middle section of the book is devoted completely to red herrings, I found a large part of the narrative pointless and boring. I also hated how the narrator kept saying things like, "Oh if I had only known X, maybe that would have changed what would come next," or "Even after everything that has happened, I still feel X." It made me feel like something big was coming, but then when the events finally transpired, they were actually quite anticlimactic. I kept reading thinking that surely something exciting would happen, but it never did. I found Det. Ryan's behavior pretty unbelievable. Not telling his boss about his history as a missing child was certain to come out and get him in trouble. Why would he keep that a secret? Why would his partner agree to it? Don't the police have background checks? They really should have known that already. I also didn't believe that his behavior toward his partner would change so drastically. I understand some awkwardness between them after the stuff that was going on, but his complete 180 degree turn wasn't fitting with his character. There are some mysteries still left on the table at the end of the story, and that completely irked me. I would have understood if the series continued with this narrator, but the next installment follows a different character. That means that these loose ends will never be tied up, and that feels like a cop out to me. I would not recommend this book to others, but I might read the next book in the series because it follows a character I like.
80% complete, and just quit...which I rarely do. I no longer cared.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I will agree that this book is gorgeously written, and the characters are well crafted and sympathetic. That's what kept me reading through the various absurd plot points. An example: the narrator, as a child, is found in the woods, his shoes full of blood, with his two best friends mysteriously missing. He comes back years later as a detective to investigate another murder in the same small estate, and no one recognizes him including the mother of one of those best friends. Oh, PLEASE. And then, after all that, while you do find out who committed the recent murder, the question of what happened to the protagonist and his friends years ago is never resolved. I mean, WTF? the murder of Katy Devlin is a McGuffin--a plot device that motivates the characters or advances the story, but the details of which are of little or no importance otherwise. The real mystery is left hanging in the air. 
 I put the book down at the end and said out loud, "are you [bad word:] KIDDING ME?" 
 So, the kindest thing I can say about this book is "enjoy the journey, but realize you're going to roll your eyes in disbelief a lot on the way, and then you're not going to end up anywhere."

Well written, the book really grips the reader through three quarters of the story. The undying questions--who killed Katy, and what happened to Pete and Jaime--stay...and build urgency. The lead investigator, Robert (Adam) Ryan, gets stupid...like men are wont to do with women they love, and all detectives on the case make common mistakes. 
 Between graft, corruption and politics that underlays most human societies, this tale, set in Ireland, doesn't hedge on reality. Neither does it present a story that conveniently ties up all loose ends. It's a good read, but I wouldn't call it great. It's real, and it's definitely a character-driven novel that will hold you, at least until Rob takes an emotional dive. Disgusted, you will, then read to the end to find out what happens, but your momentum might not be quite as driven and your satisfaction will be tainted by the outcome.
This was the best detective novel I've ever read. Looking forward to reading the rest of the series.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Reading challenge category: book popular author's first book. Some major annoyances - many echoed by others. Rob being an idiot when it came to his predictable interactions with women, Cassie's reason (after too much build up) to finally break down and cry, and the childhood mystery. Unexplained references to monster birds flapping in the woods? Very Lost tv show. That story was the hook. I was most invested in solving it. Especially the bloody shoes. I am still curious. 
 HOWEVER, I really did enjoy the book up until it started to change pace. Seems like the ending was just rushed. 
 Also, there is no way that shed would have gone without being searched in a real crime scene. Come on.
Ok. I have tried several times this year, but murder/mystery thrillers are not for me. I am sad about that, but I surrender.
This book is straight booty. Characters are bland, boring and the story goes nowhere. Waste of time and money.

At first, this book reminded me of a hipper, cooler, Irish version of Law and Order: there's a feisty female detective who's as sharp as a pin, and a hip but somewhat elusive male detective who are partnered up and working on the case of their careers - the seemingly senseless murder of a young girl. 
 And then there's the twist (this isn't a spoiler - it's right there on the book jacket): the male detective, Rob Ryan, was also involved in a missing children's case... as a victim. As a child, he was the only known survivor in the disappearance of three young friends, and he has no memory of what happened to himself or the others. 
 But comparing such a great suspense thriller to Law and Order is admittedly a terribly shallow way to describe it. This story is much more complex, riveting, and dark. I'm not sure if it's due to the author's multinational upbringing (she grew up in Ireland, Italy, the US and Malawi) or because it's set in Ireland, but there was just something about the writing style and the atmosphere that was set that was so unique and beautiful and lush and compelling to me. It had a way of letting the tension and suspense of the story sneak up on you until all of a sudden you'd realize that you were gripping the book really, really tightly. 
 The first half of the novel worked to enthrall me. The second half - I gripped. 
 The relationship between the two main characters was brilliant. I loved every minute of them together, on the case and off, happy and sad. I almost wish that it had been written to have a sequel, but this book was so good on its own that I'm happy to leave it be. (Hold on a sec - it DOES have a sequel: The Likeness. It's officially been added to the "to-read" list.)
Couldn't get into this book at all. Had to quit with it. Just wasn't interesting to me.
I'll think of what to write later.

I loved this book and would recommend it to others. 
 The lead characters were fantastic and throughout their detective work they went down many blind alleys trying to find out who murdered a 12 year old girl. This made the book believable as you followed every twist and turn with them. The relationship between Adam and his partner was so true to life and if I'm honest I wanted things to turn out differently for them both. 
 The fact that there were unresolved mysteries didn't spoil the book. I'd read previous reviews and had this on my wish list for some time as I'd been put off by the negative comments but so glad I went ahead and bought it. 
 I'm now going to read Tana French's other two books!
Not overly impressed. If you like hard boiled crime stick to Raymond Chandler.
The story was intense throughout, and the descriptions of the characters made them come alive - sometimes with good results and sometimes bad. Great book.

This book reminded me of Gillian Flynn - and it's a good thing. I love Flynn. 
 I also enjoyed the characters; I understood why they acted like they did. The plot and development didn't feel forced, dialogues were good and yes, sometimes I was annoyed by how they acted, but it's only because I thought that characters were three-dimensional, realistic, and consecuential. 
 The only reason I didn't give it five stars is ***kind of spoiler*** because of the bleeping mystery that isn't solved. I can only hope that Tana will at some point tell us what happened. 
 If you like good mystery books with believable characters, suspense, and a loose end, go for it.

I'm a little back and forth on this one. At times it was slow and others I couldn't put it down. Overall I thought the story was well written, but I'd figured it out long before it was over. I think the author must get better from here as her books turned into best sellers later. Will try the next one.
I'll let it go once I find a spoiler; too chatty, don't need the male character passing judgement on women who eat salads as a general rule

It's well-written, sort of. One of those books that's very lyrical, with some passages verging on poetry. The only problem is that there are two central mysteries, one of which is never resolved. I'm sure the tentativeness with which it was left was some sort of artistic decision, but as a lifelong mystery reader I prefer my mysteries a little less arty and a little more solved. If you can't do both, that is.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What a huge disappointment. This book had a great story and kept me wanting to read it till the last few chapters when you realize the author is never going to reveal the whole main story line behind the book. I was digusted when I put it down last night. Major bummer way to end a good story.
I really liked this book but it was a bit slower paced than I expected. It gets really good at the end if you stick with it!

Not a fan. Too long and too pointless. Sounded like a great mystery. Totally lame. Didn't solve the underlying story. A whole lot of time wasted on this book. Frustrated I read it waiting for SOMETHING awesome to happen. Bleh.

Week 22 of the 2016 Reading Challenge: The first book in a new to you series. My feelings for this book were all over the place. The murder part of it was good although it dragged a bit in the middle and I was annoyed with what happened at the end. The primary detective though really ticked me off by the end. I started out liking him a lot but by the end, I thought he was a total ass.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I loved this book- this was a book that I read until 2 am nonstop until I finished. The relationships, the dialogue, the mystery all were very well written. The end was not quite the ending I had hoped for- especially the late night phone call to Cassie, and what we did and didn't learn about the 1984 disappearances.
I liked the premise and all the secondary characters. I could not stand the narrator and am so happy he isn't the narrator of book 2 - which I will definitely read.

UGH. What was with the ending?! I absolutely loved almost everything about this book (even the horrible decisions that the mc made) except for the ending! There are so many questions I want answered. Somebody quick please tell me that the subsequent books answer these questions to tie it all in a neat little bow! The writing was so good I just can't believe she would put that much detail into weaving the story only to leave so much unfinished.
It would have gotten three stars but the last 20 pages were terrible. A good story with characters you can't connect to but the last pages ruin it all.

I really like this book at the beginning. And then I got to the end and wanted to rip it to pieces. Nothing is resolved - it's like the author got tired and decided to just slap something down so she could be done with it.

A fun way to spend a rainy day. I'd give this 3.5 stars, really. 
 SPOILER SPOILER SPOILER ALERT!!!!! 
 This was perfectly delicious entertainment but I think I was expecting more...I don't know... depth, I guess. I was underwhelmed by the 'whodunit' of this thriller- it was a little too "Law and Order"-ish for me and pretty obvious. I could also hear the insistent clicking of Manolo Blahnik heels and Gucci loafers as Hollywood execs lined up to secure film rights.... 
 Ryan's train wreck as a police detective was exasperating- I just didn't buy that someone so intuitive and insightful could be so incredibly thick - that he would have become involved in the investigation in the first place is just implausible- as if it wouldn't come out that his history tied him profoundly and disturbingly to the case at hand. But then there wouldn't be a story ;) 
 French's writing was far more akin to Patricia Cornwell or John Grisham than Benjamin Black or Colm Toibin- a testament to her international upbringing and the globalization of popular fiction. She is thoroughly modern and homogenized- none of the lyrical, dark and mystical tendencies that define "Irish" writing for me. 
 But I did enjoy French's snappy writing; the pacing of the plot was terrific, the characters had depth and she drew a complete story. I wasn't bothered by the threads left hanging at the end- she created a great anticipation for the next and the next thriller. I was very drawn to Cassie and cheered her on. I've got The Likeness waiting on the coffee table and I'm pleased read in the book jacket that it focuses on she who is likely to become Dublin's female counterpart to the DI across the puddle- Edinburgh's Rebus. 
 I have to close with a recommendation for an intense, disturbing Irish thriller that also happens to be an extraordinary work of literature IMO (and one that came to mind when I first read about French's novel- it seemed an odd coincidence...): Edna O'Brien's In The Forest, based on true and terrible events in Ireland in the late 1960's. This one will really haunt your dreams- O'Brien's writing wraps around your soul and gut like a wraith of mists rising from a bottomless bog... 
 _______________________________ 
 I'm probably the last kid in our neighborhood to read this book! Brendan and I picked up a copy on the cheap from the bargain bin at Third Place Books, Ravenna. He's hooked! I'm reading it while he's away because the sequel, The Likeness, just appeared on my hold shelf at the library; one look at the queue behind me and I know it will be 6 months before I can get it again.

** spoiler alert ** 
 F this book. You don't take up half the back of the book description talking about the plot point that won't be solved. That was what interested me in this book, and not solving it was a failure.
Most. Disappointing. Ending. Ever. The story started off so well but the ending was just the worst. Wish I hadn't wasted all the time it took me to finish it.

One of the most unsatisfying endings I've ever read. I also realized who did it early on and spent most of the book frustrated with the MC for not seeing it too. All that aside, I enjoyed French's writing. She is great with characters and atmosphere and I'll definitely be continuing with the series.

** spoiler alert ** 
 well written. was expecting more suspense. The ending was not very fulfilling. Was hoping to find out what happened to adam's childhood friends.

I had such high hopes for this book. I guessed who the killer was very early on became increasingly infuriated at the main characters for not noticing or not saying something. Awfully disappointed and while I do plan on reading the next book (actually it was a review from the town library on the next book that made me borrow this one first), my expectations will be considerably lower.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Typical thriller, leading the reader down one road and then surprise plot twist, but really if she'd been killed at the site the first place they should have looked was the sheds and did crime scene analysis there. This book was too long with unnecessary delvings into Ryan's mind and psyche that had nothing to do with the killer and his friends' killer is never found. Were the woods haunted? Too many open ended questions that for the amount of time spent on them should have been answered. And what's with the weird roommate of his. 
 Compared with Gone Girl this book just doesn't cut it.

Three children set out to play in the woods. Two are never found, and the third, Rob Ryan, is found gripping a tree trunk, wearing blood filled shoes and unable to remember anything. 
 Twenty years later Rob Ryan is a detective in Dublin and keeps his past a secret. A twelve year old girl is found murdered in the same woods and Decective Ryan and his partner find themselves investigating a case similar to the one in Ryan's past. 
 This book gripped me from the beginning and kept me reading. That being said, I felt that the author was wordy and drug things out, making this a longer book than necessary. 
 The ending was so unfulfulling for me. One murder was solved, and I didn't figure out who did it, but the second older murder was never solved. I felt cheated.

reference_books.title: Stories I Only Tell My Friends
reference_books.review_text:
At the beginning of the book, Lowe explains his fascination with stars which he had as a young person. He explains that in our media-centric culture, the characters we get to know and follow become friends, extended family. Events in their lives become mile markers in our lives. They have a status in our society that gives them the opportunity to do real good. Lowe goes on to tell stories of himself as a child meeting stars until be becomes a star. It's always nice to know how normal the lives of movies stars can be - divorced parents, being bullied, bullying and moving to new neighborhoods with good and bad luck. 
 I've always enjoyed Lowe in his films and TV shows and have the impression he is a terrific guy. He doesn't top the list of memoirs I'd like to read, but his book received wonderful reviews and I figured it would be fun. I was right. One of the fascinating things about any memoir is the back story and the other folks we know coming in and out of the story. Lowe has known, worked with and befriended hundreds of folks you'd expect and never suspect. From JFK Junior to Princess Stephanie of Monaco. Lowe's style is conversational as be tells small stories from his life. The stories come in chronological order which makes it a biography, but each story stands by itself. It's as though you just ran into an old friend and he says "hey, you know what just happened to me..." The book is charming. 
 This book won't change your life and there is better literature, but as celebrity memoirs go, it's fantastic - funny, well written, easy to read and full of fun details. Well worth reading.

reference_books.title: Moby-Dick or, The Whale
reference_books.review_text:
When I was in 5th grade I had a teacher who read us Moby Dick. I had always believed I knew the work and had listened to it. So many of the passages and descriptions where so vivid that I remember them 40 year later - but she did not read us the full work. I found an abridgement for children which she must have read and I made note that I should read it for real. This book is so much a part of popular culture that along with Huck Finn and others, this book is critical to anyone claiming to be an educated individual - or so I believe. When a friend mentioned he was planning to read it this summer, I picked it up and have found it delightful. 
 Ishmael is the narrator and main character. The part he plays on the crew is a young sailor restless for the see and willing to be a minor crew member on a whale ship. In actuality Melville uses Ishael's voice to not only tell the tale, but to act as an omniscient narrator who not only tells the tale at hand, but gives a history of whaling, humanity and the sea, and reflect in poetic terms on the whaling as a metaphor for life, spiritual reality and eternity... he really goes off. 
 I have to say, I really liked this book. Melville's prose are exquisite. His rants on the beauty of the sea and mysteries of the deep are engaging and hypnotic. At almost 700 pages of 19th century romanticism, this book is not for the faint of heart. But for those with the time and energy, once again, this is a classic for good reason. The tale captures the romantic passion of the American Spirit to engage the world adventure and live to tell the tale. Good Read!

reference_books.title: A Christmas Carol
reference_books.review_text: This is my annual re-read. "God bless us, every one!"

reference_books.title: Dracula
reference_books.review_text:
Last year I began the Vampire Chronicles after reading Christopher Moore's vampire series. In the Christopher Moore books, which are comedy, at one point the boyfriend of a novice vampire struggles to help her by collecting all the vampire fiction he could find. His comical references to the differences are funny and made me curious. Having completed 4 Anne Rice novels, I thought I'd go back to where it all began and read the classic. 
 The style is, of course, a bit funny since it is stiff, proper and full of words that are less used today. Never the less, the style of narrative via letters, diary entries and notes is clever and gives the reader the feeling of having stumbled across a secret archive. While there isn't the blood and gore of some modern horror tales, Stoker creates real ambiance in his lavish descriptions and subtle details. This was a clever writing style and quite enjoyable. Now I know why this caught on and has become so iconic. Like so many classics, characters and phrases have entered the lexicon to the extent that I recognized much of this book. 
 Final Note: I had thought Carfax was a service that faxed reports of cars. In our modern age it seemed quaint that this business would make itself seem older by referencing 80s technology. However, Carfax is the name of Dracula's estate in England! Could it be that the nice car history report people are actually blood sucker?

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This is a work aimed at a teen audience written with limited vocabulary and short sentences. At first the rhythm reminded me of Hemingway, but it is not particularly sophisticated. The story is a Handmaid's Tale style world wherein villages of the empire send tribute/sacrifices as reparation for an uprising that happened almost 80 years ago. The "Tributes" have to fight to the death on television. The game takes place in the woods while viewers send support and bet on the contestants. Very quick read. There are 2 sequels. They may be easy enough to read that it would be worth covering the series, but really, this is enough to know what it's about and I'd like to go back to full sentences with grown up vocabulary.

reference_books.title: Goliath (Leviathan, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Really, really fun. This is the 3rd in a stream punk, alternative history of World War I fought between the Darwinist powers who use genetically modified beasts against the machines of the "clanker" powers. I've already discussed the series in two other reviews. There is little new here, just an extension of the adventure with a rather satisfying conclusion. 
 As I've noted, this is a teen oriented fantasy, well written and nicely detailed. I highly recommend this series if you are a fan of the genre. I am happy to place this on my bookshelf next to His Dark Materials, Stoneheart and The Chronicles of Narnia.

reference_books.title: Club Dead (Sookie Stackhouse, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
In the third installment of the Sookie Stackhouse mysteries, our heroin finds herself in Jackson Mississippi trying to find Vampire Bill. In this one we learn that the feudal system of the old world has been re-created in the new world in a network of "districts" ruled, ultimately, by kings and queens. While on a job for the Queen of Louisiana, Vampire Bill finds himself in the clutches of an old love on the estate of the King of Mississippi. Eric and Pam are on the scene, as always, and we meet a whole new community of werewolves and shape-shifters as the world of Sookie Stackhouse continues to unfold. And, just in case one starts to take anything to seriously, Vampire Elvis is always on hand to add comic relief. 
 As I've explained in other reviews, this is VERY light reading. It's lots of fun in a fantasy world with some supernatural beings and a pretty, young heroin who narrates in the first person. While the whole series seems targeted directly at a young adult audience with what look like children's drawings on the cover and the promise of lots of adventure for Sookie and her supernatural friends, there is graphic violence and explicate sex at every turn. This is new for me since I tend to like my teen fantasy fiction somewhat more chased. Having watched a bit of The Game of Thrones and then read all the books, it seemed to me HBO made more of the sex in The Game of Thrones than was necessary to relate the books accurately. In the books, sex is part of the earthy, brutal medieval background. In the show, there are whole episodes of technique being taught to prostitutes - not necessary. The relationship between Sookie Stackhouse and True Blood is the opposite. The books go into more graphic detail than can be shown without drawing an XXX rating. So, fun, light vampire adventures with lots of sex and violence - and despite the packaging, not for young teens.

reference_books.title: Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas
reference_books.review_text:
If Hemingway's Paris is a movable feast, Thompson's Los Vegas is a movable drug fest. This is less a story than a snapshot of a few weeks with Thompson tripping, drinking, smoking, vomiting, wrecking cars and trashing hotel rooms. I didn't see much point. Imagine running into an old friend who has developed an alcohol or drug problem. He or she isn't quite right but has to tell you a great story. The story ends up being about how someone got soooooo high and saw a dog and thought it was a dragon and then someone said "hey man, that's a cop" and everyone freaked out... it was awesome. This book does that for 200 pages. 
 As a look into the drug culture of the 60s, this book has some value, though the focus is alarmingly on two characters. Thompson and his "attorney" are on there way to Vegas, high in Vegas, trying to get out of Vegas, sick, high again, renting cars, sick, trying tying to leave, on their way back... not much here. 
 Since the book is somewhat iconic, I am glad I read it, but like the old friend who had to tell you how cool being high was, I put leave this book thinking that if this was really how Thompson's life was, it was a shame.

reference_books.title: Lord of the Flies
reference_books.review_text: Hated this book. Read it years ago because I try to keep up with what kids in the school where I work are being assigned. I know it's a study in sociology which raises lots of cool questions for discussion, but I hated it.

reference_books.title: The Time Machine
reference_books.review_text:
The format is similar to A Turn of the screw. A gathering of men, in Victorian Age club, gather to hear the tale of a "time traveler", an inventor whose machine had taken him to the future. The story he tells is of a distopian world in which humanoid creatures who live below ground feed on the humanoids above ground. The telling of the tale is pompous and full of observations that reek of Victorian sensibility. Ultimately, the setup and story are quaint, though it is obvious that Wells intended it to be shocking and thought provoking. 
 I can understand the significance of the work. In the period when Wells wrote, social and political issues indicated a future which must lie within a range of known possibilities. Given the advance of technology and the availability of information, that range has expanded. The simple logic of Wells, while progressive in 1895, is provincial and just plain silly. Never the less, it's a classic for good reason. The Time Machine was a large step for the genre and remains influential for it's style and structure. I am happy I read it since I believe it is valuable to be familiar with cultural icons. However, I will not suggest that it was compelling, surprising or exciting in the way that a reader at the turn of the 19 to 20th century might have found it.

book_a.title: Dead Ever After (Sookie Stackhouse, #13)
book_a.user_review:
Equal to all the books in the series in every way. However, since it's the last in the series, I was hoping for some closure - there is very little. Sookie so seldom "closes the deal" on anything, that ending up with Sam but saying "let's take it slow" is no different from any other book. Some of the fun of the series is the tension between Sookie and her various suitors. It appears Eric is gone, but he leaves still proclaiming his love. Bill just fades away. Charges aren't dropped, Amelia and Bob? Pam and Karen? All the fairies, the demons and witches? All we know is that Sookie survives the latest attempts on her life with a half dozen casualties and Sookie and Sam hook up - not the satisfying ending I was still hoping for as I entered the last chapter. If she had spent half the book winding down, it might have been anticlimactic. However, heading home with the vague suggestion that Sookie might end up with Sam leaves too many loose ends. 
 I've apologized after every review. I read everything from fairly heavy non-fiction to teen fantasy fiction. This series is in a category that seems intended for 20 somethings give the sex and drugs and so forth, though the writing style is clearly very young. I thought Harris might have created some atmosphere, which she did here and there, but ultimately this is a bunch of folks whose lives orbit a couple of nightclubs experimenting with life-styles and solving murder mysteries with lots of super-natural soap opera style drama. Light, fun and finished.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Alisha: The fan who is neither crazy, nor entitled rants 
 Update: 
 So I've been on Amazon, watching the reactions. Lots of sock puppets and rabid Charlaine fans giving this turd 5 stars. Even Anne Rice is weighing in! I'm uber suspicious of all reviews that say, "She tied this up nicely, way to go Ms. Harris! and I look forward to reading the Coda in October!" Gotta hand it to Penguin, they are on top of this. 
 "Hey everyone! Look over here! Disregard the bad reviews. Those people are CRAZY!" 
 There's been a lot said about this final installment of Sookie. There have been angry fans, sad fans, furious bloggers, and Charlaine sheeple. Fans of Charlaine and maybe free speech? are calling the upset masses entitled and crazy. If you didn't like the book, you are a crazy Eric/Sookie shipper. Just check out the Wall Street Journal's crap article, How to Kill a Vampire Series if you don't believe me. 
 It's a mess. In the end, this will sell plenty of books, but a good portion of readers will remember that their emotional trust was broken. Say what you will, that is a legitimate feeling. There is a relationship between reader and writer and that is built on trust. When a writer chooses not to just add a twist, but to twist a knife into the reader, it's sometimes permanent. 
 The world of Sookie has changed. I've thought a lot about why Harris would write an arc that heavily favored Eric, then dismantle the entire work in three books. My guess is that Harris, being tired of Sookie isn't in the same frame of mind she once was when writing the frisky waitress/telepath. Of course she isn't in the same place she once was. We change. What once was exciting and fresh, can become dull and stale. Likewise, with Sookie, Harris' ability to do what she wanted in light of True Blood, crazed fans, and simple boredom all took their toll on the work. 
 I've read books 1-9 at least five times each. 10-12? Why bother? 
 I'm not a whiny girl who didn't get her way. 
 I did not read this final installment and I don't plan to, but not for the reasons that you might think. I'm not an entitled douche bag. I don't want to make Harris my bitch. I've been known to read a book or two, and despite what Harris' PR camp is spinning, I won't be attempting suicide or threatening the author any time soon. Most likely, I'll just read something else. 
 Here's my complaints, since I know the ending and I've read all the reviews on Amazon. 
 Bad Plot Devices 
 Alisha takes offense. Harris thinks that rape is a appropriate plot device, selling Eric into sex slavery for the next 200 years. Lets salt that and add that Pam is forbidden to go with him. What's troubling is that I doubt she would have made the same choice for a female character, because RAPE! Holy crap! . Try saying that out loud to someone who hasn't read the books and see if they don't laugh at the absurdity of that particular choice. "She did WHAT to Eric?!?" 
 1. I waffle between thinking that Harris hates her fame or or fans or the book. I can't tell which one. Then I think, no, she's just tired of it. But after her choices for DEA, I am back to thinking that she's a bit vindictive. Why? I haven't a clue. It could be the fans, or True Blood/Alan Ball hate. I can't say. I do feel her choices for Eric were vindictive. Let me restate that. I feel this. YOU are free to feel other stuff. 
 But Alisha! Wait! Harris can do whatever she sees fit. See my last comment, but also... 
 Sure, she can and she did. I ask you though, how did Moning conclude the Fever series? How has Gabaldon treated Fraser and Claire? How did Mead conclude Vampire Academy? You can literally insert any couple into this example and get a similar outcome. That outcome being that not everyone is satisfied with conclusions, but the readership did not freak the fuck out. 
 2. Harris wrote the love between Eric and Sookie. Eric always had Sookie's back even when she didn't realize it. He graveled her drive, and replaced her coat. He called her brave and self-less. He tried to protect her from a bond with Andre. Harris also wrote Sookie saving Eric. In those books, many of us became invested readers. 
 3. Harris wrote the friend/boss/big brother relationship between Sam and Sookie. There was a kiss here and there, but we READ that it could never work because Sookie could hear his thoughts unless he was actively blocking her. But now, it's all good. Thoughts, shmoughts, is what I always say! 
 4. Harris wrote that Sookie was worried (annoyingly concerned) that the bond between her and Eric was influencing her feelings of love, so much so that she broke the blood bond. And yet, Sookie is willing to overlook the use of the Culivial Dor on Sam because...we don't know. Sookie decided that reading Sam's thoughts didn't matter, so maybe it a new life choices/attitude thing. Maybe her clock is ticking? Settling worked well for Tara, right? After all, Tara has twins! 
 5. Harris wrote Sookie as brave in the beginning and accepting of other supes because people had always treated her like crap. She was open to others, but now, to live a happy life she must shun other supes and try to live as humanly as possible? 
 6. I'm not okay with the way it ended for Eric. Rape happens and so does sex slavery. I know it's just a book, but it leaves a horrible taste in my mouth. CH wouldn't make this choice for a female character, but it's okay for a man? *face palm* Just kill him off! This choice is cruel and the sex slavery is icky. We know what happened between Eric and his maker and we know he was abused sexually. That was sad. Now it's full circle? Jesus. I just can't... 
 My hard-hearted husband laughed up when I told him what Harris did to Eric. He said I ought to charge Harris with committing a McMurtry in the first degree. If you don't know what I'm referring to, see Lonesome Dove and the sequel, The Streets of Laredo. 
 But wait! There's more weird plots! Why would Sookie's gay cousin, Claude want to kidnap and rape Sookie? He was foiled by homophobes? Right wingers save the day! Again, I didn't read this, but there are some heated rants of tumblr that are discussing this peculiar plot device. 
 If you don't want to end up a spinster, it's time to settle! 
 Back to my point. I'm not reading the book because Sookie isn't fun anymore. That character I loved has devolved into a bigoted old woman, hell bent on nitpicking every aspect of her life. Sookie settled! She settle for line dancing, kids, and casseroles. That is NOT BRAVE. Remember ladies, when a woman nears thirty, it's time to quit being picky. The music is about to stop, so pick a chair! Charlaine wrote that too. 
 SVM books once involved a mystery, some witty banter, a bit of fantasy with a smidgen of lust. When it worked, it was magic. 
 Sadly, the magic is gone. Luckily, there are other books in the sea, err...library.

This final books starts out rather different than the rest of the series which gave me some reservations but Charlaine Harris is a master story teller and I should never for a moment have doubted her skills. 
 While I am not sure this is how I would have wanted the series to end, I can not truthfully say I'm unhappy. 
 Kudos for Ms. Harris staying true to her world and her books and not bowing to fans which (whether they know it or not) would have not done Sookie a service. On the contrary, I think any other ending would have felt false and completely ruined the entire series.

I have read a lot of book over the years. I know you don't always get the "Happy Ever After" you think the character(s) should have. Heck, sometimes your favorite character gets killed off... or everyone does. But I have NEVER read a book where the author so blatantly gave all of her readers the proverbial finger. I said I'd go into this book with an open mind and a heavy heart, but I know I will never again read anything she writes. Dead Ever After was as horrible as we were all told and I now wish I had just slept instead of reading it. 
 FULL review coming soon.

SO glad to be done with this series. if anyone knows how to screw up a good, yet poorly written series, charlaine harris does. fortunately, this was a fast read and packed with yet more attempts on sookie's life. very glad to get to move on and not think about sookie in any other context than the hbo true blood series.

Better than I thought it would be. I had a bit of a time getting into it. I think because this book has more viewpoints to it. I am use to Sookie. What worked really well for me was that the author seemed to go back to her earlier story. The characters were more like the people I knew and loved or hated. I disliked the feeling I got towards the end that Ms Harris was trying too hard to wrap up the story while leaving enough open for another book. After all this was suppose to be the final book but we were fooled. I am not so certain Sookie ended up with anyone. I do think the ending was a typical Sookie man action with a lesson learned aspect. I missed Pam. She is my favorite, (and I totally would be psyched with a Pam spin off), and was just not in this book enough. I wasn't as satisfied with the ending as I would have been if this were the final book, but I am giving it 4 stars. It is more in line with the first books.

I have been a fan of this series since a friend of mine recommended them to me, so I am sad to see it end! There are things that I did not particularly agree on in this last book, but I was not comepletely disappointed nonetheless. All loose ends were tied up, and although I would have preferred Sookie to end up with someone else, I was still happy with the way things played out. I recommend this series to anyone who is interested in this genre. I agree that the first ones in the series were much better, but I still had a difficult time putting even this one down.

Ok i haven't had the courage to open DEA. I pre-ordered it a while ago and it's been there compelling me to read it. 
 On Tuesday 7th I was reading on my iPad (Game of Thrones, excellent book so far, I highly recommend it) and all of the sudden the reminder of the book release appears in the center of my iPad screen, anxiety and excitement cursed through me as I pressed the "library" button on the top right corner of the screen, and after so many months and 13$ less (I thought the book was really expensive BTW), there it is, the arrow that tells me that I can start downloading my new book, and I just....couldn't do it. It was like something was telling me to wait, and weirdly enough not for the right reasons; so I decided to finish GoT before I start DEA. it's so disappointing to see so many bad reviews after all this years of loyal reading and readers. It literally pains me knowing that I will not like the book and that I, as my fellow readers and companions in my sadness; will end up being extremely disappointed with it. I've read literally hundreds of different reviews in hopes that maybe, just maybe the book its not as bad as everybody says, but no and I'm still shocked to see how bad they are. Some of them are really enraged towards Harris, which I admire (haven't read the book yet, so give me time) and I mean, as a writer she has the right to do whatever she wants to do with her characters, I think you become a writer to tell a story and create whatever a world you want, the perfect world as u see it, in a way you become God. You have the power to do whatever you like in this world who actually owes YOU, it's existence. I'm a big fan of the TV Show True Blood, and I just think, if Harris wouldn't had dared to create this world we wouldn't had have Alexander Skarsgard as Eric Northman (such a beautiful sight can't be denied to the world) or Joe Manganiello as Alcide (another gorgeous man) or Bill Moyer...but I'm babbling, what I'm trying to say is that I hope we are not being to hard on Harris, after all we have to respect everybody's work, but I as I stated before I haven't start the book, (give me two min after I'm done with this review) and I just hope that the disappointment and unfairness that I hear and read in other people reviews isn't as bad for me as it is for them. 
 Wish me luck!

Wow. What happened? Harris' books used to be fun, and at least competently written. This one was no fun at all (Could it have been any more boring? ENDLESS paragraphs about Sookie cleaning, Sookie dressing, Sookie moisturizing her legs) and the writing was atrocious. It was like the worst fan fiction ever written. I'm so relieved this is the last book, because now I won't be faced with the difficult decision on whether or not to give another of her books a try. I definitely will not be. 
 The only bright spot was that she ends up with Sam . Of course she did; that ending was broadcast loud and clear from the very beginning. And he is absolutely right for her. I'm just sorry that their relationship had to resolve itself in this particular book. Worst sex scene ever in the history of bad sex scenes. Well, okay. Maybe not the worst, but I do feel the need to scrub out my brain.

Oh. My. Goodness. 
 I have spent years loving the Sookie Stakhouse novels and waiting patiently for them to be released one after another. Though I didn't find them until after 2005 (the first was published in 1999) I became a big fan of Sookie and have enjoyed the Sookie Stackhouse saga. 
 I was not disappointed with this last book necessarily. Well, not at all... as you can see I gave it a 5/5. It was a great ending to a phenomenal series. I'm just not 100% positive I gel with the person she ended up with. Not that I don't like the character the ends up being "The One" for Sookie. He's great! I just don't feel like Ms. Harris got you warmed up enough to the idea before throwing you in to it. 
 Needless to say, I consider Sookie Stackhouse to be one of my best literary friends and I wish her fictional-future to be nothing but happy! 
 Dead Ever After was a great final book. Not only does Ms. Harris tie up a BUNCH of loose ends that were just blowin' in the wind there for a while... she does so with enough finality to make the readers comfortable with leaving Sookie alone. There's hope for her having a happy life after all. 
 I was surprised by (though shouldn't have been) by the sheriff swap. I wasn't sure what was going to happen in that department but it came together nicely. 
 Also... WHAT THE HECK, NIALL!? 
 Alright. Anyway. Ms. Harris uses her last book as an opportunity to reintroduce characters that the reader hadn't heard from in a while... she also takes great care in making sure that each of Sookie's love-interests are either "off-limits" enough or "out-of-mind" enough for there never to be any future requited love issues going on there. Which is good... because Sookie sure did know how to fall for some pretty dangerous guys! Yoiks! 
 In the series Sookie dated 2 vampires, a werewolf, a were tiger, and a shape-shifter. She was also pursued by multiple other-creatures including fairies. I mean, yikes. This girl had an interesting love-life and, honestly, I'm going to miss hearing about it! 
 Sookie Stackhouse was a brave, unique, sassy, and out-of-the-norm heroine. Not only is she a SOUTHERN girl... she's also been described as being a size 10 with a healthy appetite. I could go on and on about how I appreciate a book with a main character that isn't "slim waisted", "waiflike" or "athletic". 
 Ms. Harris managed to create a female character that could stand up for herself without coming off too cold or bitchy. She made Sookie juuuussst vulnerable enough to make us feel like we weren't reading about a stone-cold, emotionless female. However, I never felt like Sookie was the "Rescue me" damsel in distress, either. She knew how to take care of herself and when to let others help take care of her. 
 The entire LGBT underline was well done and perfectly displayed. Though these books were romance/action/mystery/supernatural all woven together in a harmonious saga of awesome... they were also a commentary on today's human rights movements. 
 Anyway... I'm sad that the series has ended but I'm happy that I got a chance to enjoy it for 13 full books. Also, I'm happy to hear that Ms. Harris will be releasing a book with information about the fates of many of her characters after the end of the series. 
 This book is called "AFTER DEAD" and will be released October 29, 2013. 
 If you're a fan of supernatural books and you HAVEN'T read any of the Sookie Stackhouse books then you need to GET ON IT! NOW! But, if you're like me and thousands of other Sookie fans you'll be anxiously awaiting the next Charlaine Harris book... whatever its topic may be. I'll help pass the time by reading her Aurora Teagarden mysteries for now!
I thought it was a good book. Sorry that it had to end. I think her choice for Sookie to be with Sam was a good way to end the book. I'm glad also that Pam got to be the new sheriff for the vampires.

Loved how the author tied everyone back into the last book somehow! I wasn't sad about who Sookie ended up with, just sad that this awesome series came to an end! Was glad to be given this awesome ride!
Terribly disappointing! ITA with another reviewer who said that this series ends with an apathetic shrug.

My God this book sucked. 
 The Sookie Stackhouse/True Blood series has been going downhill pretty steadily for some time now. The last couple of books were barely readable. 
 This one made me want to kill myself multiple times. 
 Had I not been listening to it as an audio book, I highly doubt I would have gotten through it. 
 I don't know if Charlaine Harris had a stroke or what - maybe she's just playing a game where she figures out how badly she can write a book and still get it published? Whatever the reason is, she really sucked it up on this one. She was LAZY. The parade of past characters is one of the laziest things an author can do, and her's was never ending in this book. 
 At the end, when Sookie was explaining to Sam what happened he said to her "That's pretty convoluted" and I'm thinking "Convoluted? Seriously? Understatement of the YEAR." 
 When we first met Sookie she was cute and spunky. 
 Now she's just tired all the time. And apparently not as cute as she once was, since none of the bar patrons are harassing her. 
 Sookie used to be smarter and tougher than she thought she was. 
 Now she thinks she's a whole lot smarter and tougher than she really is. 
 Sookie used to practically vibrate with emotion. She had so much LOVE for her friends and family. 
 Now she's just dead inside. That should have been the name of this last book, Dead Inside. LOL. Seriously, tho, nothing upsets her or excites her or even makes her mad. She breaks up with Eric, gets shot and kidnapped and hooks up with Sam and I never felt any emotion about any of it. 
 Sookie used to be sexy. So were all the guys she was with. The sex scenes used to be hot. 
 Not anymore. The sex scene between her and Sam was just awkward. Harris's use certain words just seemed icky! 
 I could go on, but I won't. 
 I will say that I own all of the books in this series except the last one, and after reading it, I'm considering getting rid of them all. These last few books - especially this one - really dragged the whole series down :( 
 Thank God it's over.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Bull..sh*t. That's what this last book was. I read all the other books in the series so I am one of those people that MUST finish a series out once I have started it. I made it through the first 12 books pretty much unscathed. This one I felt like Harris just pushed me overboard and went "LOL". To add insult to injury, Sookie did not end up with who I was rooting for...not even my second in line, OR THIRD. Are you kidding me, woman?! I should have known. I felt it coming, but kept denying it, saying no way would she go through all this writing just to let her end up with him. SAM?! SERIOUSLY? Ugh. His character makes me want to gouge my eyes out. I think I honestly would have preferred a random stranger blowing into town and kidnapping Sookie to make her his sex slave because that is just as realistic as her being with Sam. I am sorry, I just do not see them having much in common besides the obvious. Anyway, moving on before I continue stabbing Sam with my thoughts.. 
 Well, where is there to go from there. The plot was..wait, what plot? NOPE. I honestly hardly remember anything because it was that boring. Oh no, Snookie was accused of a murder? NO WAY. AGAIN?! Come on. Stop. I can't do it anymore. I really have nothing more to add. Garbage. Plain and simple. I am glad it is finally over because I really do not think I could another book.
ugh... done... and dusted...

Final book and both sad at the end and not sure I feel completely satisfied, but then again, it is so difficult to end such a series with a true sense of completion. It's been a good run of enjoyable books.
I'm so glad that I borrowed this book from the library and I didn't fork over the money to buy it, because if I did, I'd be pissed.
so disappointing... I love this series but this last book broke my heart and left me empty.
Disappointing doesn't come close.
OMG this book was a let down.! There aren't words to describe the utter disappointment. Hey fanfic authors please rewrite and fix this hot mess. Seriously!

WOW! I was hoping all the BAD reviews were not accurate. What a disappointment. Does Charlaine Harris have no friends or editors or readers who warned her that this was a terrible idea? The characters aren't even the same as they were at the beginning of the series. This was the only series from her that I enjoyed, so i guess I won't be reading anything else from her.

Kept me entertained. I've read every book in the series and I accept them for what they are: a guilty pleasure read, one that doesn't require me to think or analyze, something to waste time with. I really enjoyed the series, sad that it is over.

First thing this has spoilers. 
 Second I am so glad this series is finally over. It had become so unbelievably ridiculous and the plots took so many unnecessary directions and characters instead of evolving just got more unlikable and less like people. 
 This book I pretty much figured sookie would end up with Sam you knew the author wasn't going to turn her and as much as I hoped she would died that apparently wasn't in the cards either. 
 The final plot didn't seem to actually come to the climax I thought. I found the ending not worthy of gar first 5 or 6 books and wish the author has done a better job in telling not just the Aries, but the ending of it as we, 
 Ll.

Sookie is still reeling from her use of the cluviel dor, her resurrection of Sam, and the fact that her and Eric seem to be in the middle of a fight. But she's Sookie Stackhouse, and something else is bound to pop up. Pop up it does--in the form of the death of Arlene Fowler. Sookie ends up as the main suspect in the murder. A bunch of the gang show up to help acquit her and solve the murder. Although, Eric, Bill, and Sam are all tend to be a little more hands off than expected. 
 While these series are penned as mysteries, romance is a big part of them. So, naturally, a large part of the anticipation of this book stemmed from figuring out who Sookie will end up with, if anyone at all. For many readers, I'm sure the romantic results are one of the biggest matters of contention, and that's fair. While I certainly had my preferences about who Sookie would end up with, even if I seemed to care less as the series' progressed as a sad side effect of caring less about Sookie. I was not unpleased with the finale romantic wrap-up. The writing has been on the wall for a long time with this one. In fact, the romantic results may have been the only thing Harris thought long term about. Although, she didn't seem to really thing about how to get it there, because all the sudden there it was. Still, the signs have been there. 
 However as mysteries are at least publicized as a large part of the series, that part of the novel shouldn't be ignored. If you've been reading along with the whole series, the thirteenth installment will not shock you. You've gotten used to plot turns that really make no sense and constantly lowering stakes. Here's the deal: I've seen Sookie in mortal peril before. What is different about this time? How does she react differently? What does she get out of it? What does it teach her? After all, one of my biggest problems with the series is generally that Sookie can tend to "reset" after an adventure. She'll just go right back to telling us about her tanning and her romance novels and her word of the day calendar and over describing her outfits. With the exception of the word of the day calendar, Dead Ever After does not disappoint on this front. 
 But if you can't give me that growth, at least give me a better mystery. First of all, why Arlene? If there was supposed to be some sort of closure inherent in this, some coming full circle, I missed it. There was a good deal of dramatic irony employed in this book, in that the reader knew more of the possible suspects than Sookie. However, the "twist" at the end didn't make me go "wow, what a shocker." Instead I opted for, "wow, that does not seem to fit with the world we've established. In addition, the climax of the novel itself felt very anticlimactic. 
 I think that's my biggest critique of the series itself. It felt anticlimactic. This does not feel like a series that had a planned and plotted ending. Instead, it felt like it ended because the quality of the books were going downhill. And this one certainly fits that trend.
Dead Ever After wrapped up the Sookie Stackhouse series very well. I'm going to miss these characters, it was a lot of fun.

If I could give 0 stars to this book, I would have given 0 stars. 
 What I did not like in the book: 
 -There is no story worth mentioning. At least the previous 12 books had a story with a beginning and an end. 
 -Eric is not Eric. Who is this person and what did he do to MY Eric? 
 -Harris is throwing the dreams of the majority of her fans to the bin. What kind of HEA is this??? 
 What I liked in the book 
 -hmm maybe nothing.... and I used to be a devoted fan... It's really such a pity :-(

I am thoroughly disappointed in this novel. This series is one of my favourite. I loved reading each one of the books in the series. Somewhere in between I fell in love with vampire Eric. His character was like a tornado......totally unexpected and destruction follows. 
 Sookie was too much egoistic. She said she loved Eric but she was not ready to give up light or sun to stay with him for eternity. Love means sacrifice. One can't have both ways. I knew something was coming coz earlier novel of this series was also very disappointing. There was a distance in Sookie- Eric's relationship and in this novel finally they broke up. I feel Eric has been cheated. He was counting on Sookie to be his rescuer but she ditched him. 
 All in all,I am not happy with the ending and not really satisfied. 
 We say, All's well that ends well. But I do not believe it ended well. 
 This ending was no ending for me. 
 I will think that Sookie is still with Eric. For me, There cannot be any other ending for this series.

I have a penchant for being unable to abandon a series that I once enjoyed, no matter how much I wish that the author had ended it sooner and how painful it is to get through the book. The Sookie Stackhouse series, (around book 9-10) is the penultimate example of this painful experience. Every ounce of love, care, and connection I had for/to the characters disappeared due to an onslaught of convoluted, unnecessary plotlines and unjustified/strange character choices. 
 The last book in the series only served to magnify these faults. It's almost as if the author purposefully turned all of Sookie's previous love interests into petulant and selfish little boys in order to justify her final 'choice.' Don't get me wrong, I would have accepted who ever Sookie ended up with and respected Charlaine Harris' decision...if and only if it was explained in a believable way. It wasn't. Almost everyone acted out of character and the author's attempt to tie up all loose ends while still adding an element of mystery to the book's central narrative missed the mark entirely. Not only did the the book leave me unsatisfied on it's own merit, it was also highly unsatisfactory as the final book of a series.
I'm giving the book 3 stars since its a good book. The emotional part of me, gives it no stars. So just to be fair...1 star!!!

The ending was pretty flat and boring... It felt very "safe"... Somehow I expected something more... Interesting. I didn't like how Sookie just goes back to a normal life after all that happened to her.
Wrapped up everything nicely

Dear Sookie Stackhouse: Good riddance. I hope never to read about you again. You started as a light, fun read to look forward to every year and you ended as the most pointless, useless series I've ever had the misfortune to read. I'm sorry I wasted so much of my finite time on this Earth on you. 
 As for you, Charlaine Harris, you might think these characters are yours. This story is yours. But you know what? That's bullcrap. When you put out a story for consumption by readers, it BECOMES a story. Otherwise, it's some crap you made up in your head.
