And when you DO put out a story for consumption and charge people (frankly astronomical prices) to read it, you do enter into a contract with these people. You're obligated to give them a good story for their money. You are not supposed to build up relationships and characters and point the entire direction of the series one way, only to get pissed at your fans (you know, the ones who MADE you all that money I was talking about?) and with one fell swoop, destroy the world we paid for. You are not supposed to start the story with a timid telepathic barmaid, give her these amazing men to love, send her on countless adventures only to bring her full circle back to a barmaid who's content settling for the man who can give her babies. What sort of message is that in this day and age? "Look girls! Don't be with the man you've loved all along! Don't have any sort of personal growth, even! Just hook on to a decent dude (one you've never even seriously considered as a romantic choice!) who can knock you up, settle down and raise them babies! Yee-haw!" 
 I'm not just one of the angry Eric fans (though, he is one of the best characters you created). I would have been FINE with Sookie not ending up with Eric if you'd given Eric SOME sort of worthy ending. Forcing him into a marriage that equates to legalized sex slavery is a mean and nasty way to punish a character who's responsible for quite a bit of that money you're enjoying spending -- and separating him forever from Pam is the final kick in the nuts. What the Hell made you HATE Eric so much all of a sudden? Because the author that wrote the earlier books clearly liked him. 
 As much as it pains me, I won't be taking these books to the used book store. I won't foist this crap on anyone else's unsuspecting head. Nope. I think I'll save 'em all up until winter and use them as kindling. At least then I might actually get some use out of all that money I spent. 
 I have many (MANY) of your other books. I never got around to reading them. I bought them because I trusted you -- trusted you to give me a fair amount of entertainment for the money I spent. Don't know if I'll even bother reading them, now. They're looking mighty like kindling themselves. 
 Speaking as someone who's known a lot of fledgling authors -- amazing people with loads of talent -- I have to say that when I see someone with your good fortune it makes me very angry. How many good people went without book contracts while you laughed in the faces of the people responsible for yours?
http://kathleensbookreview.blogspot.c...
Not a great ending but better than the last four books. 2.5.

What a sad way to end a wonderful series. I can't even say I like any of the characters after this final installment. If you want to read this series, just read books 1-10, the last three are painfully awkward.
Oh! *sob* goodbye Sookie! *sniffle* I've loved you!

UGH! This was the final book in this series that I used to love. Harris really needed to end the series about 4 books ago before it all went down hill. It's obvious she simply wrote more books to make more money. Sookie seems to be getting dumber and was really driving me nuts. The last 3 books could seriously have been written as 1 book with 100 pages or less. I really could do without the detailed lists of the contents of Sookie's drawers, her grocery list, or the exact steps she takes to wash her hair or cook dinner. Besides the fact that Eric was pretty much missing from this book. UGH.

This book just left me so incredibly sad..... why build up this great love just to trash it in the final books and replace it with a sparkless relationship with someone that seems more fatherly than lover. I think Eric and the fans deserved better especially considering that I'm more broken-hearted that Sookie is.....

Oh god, Charlaine why did you give up in the last third of the book, cashed your cheque already? NOBODY wanted that dismal, boring happy ending. Where is the blood, where is the gore, where is the sex, WHERE IS ERIC. glad it's the last one, think the last chapter actually rotted something in my brain.
Very satisfying ending!

Can I give zero stars? 
 Sookie was so far OOC I didn't recognize her. She looked upon all her friends and even Jason with such contempt it made me uncomfortable to read. The first half of the book didn't match the style or tone of the rest of the series. This improved with the second half, but by then I was just bored with it all. The changes in POV were a bit odd. Particularly jarring was the scene at Sookie's house when she wasn't there. That POV change wasn't even necessary. 
 A lot of scenes and details weren't needed for the narration and pulled me out of the story. I'm still not sure I understand why the antagonists were after Sookie in the first place, other than they didn't like her. Did they have a motive? 
 Sadly, this series finale had so much potential, but ended up being a lackluster read that was torture to finish. In fact, the only reason I finished it rather than stopping halfway through was out of a sense of loyalty to Sookie and the series I had invested so much of my time and money in. And that makes ME sad.

After reading the last few books in this series, hating them, and having similar expectations for this installment, I was not disappointed. This book was not the worst in the series, but deserves one star mostly because it was the worst ending to a series I've ever read. Completely anticlimactic and, well...boring. There was nothing overly entertaining about it. I can only say that the author partially redeemed herself by putting a little more effort into the quality of writing, which was slightly better than the previous two/three books. So sad that a series which started out so great ended on such a flat tire.

I am a Sookie Stackhouse novel and True Blood fan. I was so excited to get my hands on a copy of the last book in the series. Once I started reading the book, the story immediately began to drag and the vague description of two of the villainous characters made it feel completely out of place and relevance questionable. Each time I would pick up the book to read a bit more, it was no time until it honestly put me to sleep. When I read the first four books in the series, I couldn't put them down. I was intrigued from start to finish. This one had me saying, "forget this". I wasn't pleased with this novel or the author's inability to capture the reader's attention or suspense.
meh
This book sucked sweaty hairy balls. So bad. So so bad.

Disappointing end to an enjoyable series. What the hell would possess Harris to think that ending was an acceptable one?!?! This is the last time I will be reading her work, that is my way of punishment to her no matter how insignificant it may seem. She should be ashamed at the disloyalty that ending gave to her readers who grew to know & love these characters. Plain & simple fact is she sold out by putting it on TV & in the end didn't care about the written product.
Utterly forgettable
Sookie ended up with the man I thought she should have been with all along.

Only read it because after 12 books I had to finish the thing and admittedly I skimmed the last 100 paged because I was totally picking up where it was going and then some of it I just could barely stand to even skim. *sigh* Just. Disappointing.

WHAT A TERRIBLE, AWFUL, PIECE OF CRAP!!!! Charlaine Harris got lazy with this book, and that is SO disappointing since I am so attached to this series. book_b.title: The Haunting of Hill House
book_b.user_review:
The Haunting of Hill House is a classic and an archetype for good reason. The story is reasonable and rational. Then, it is full of beautiful prose. Then it get confusing and spooky. Then it gets evil! Jackson does a great job of creating sympathetic characters who end up being worked upon by malevolent forces which she leaves undefined. 
 The secret to great horror is the unanswered question: what is the evil here? The reader will find beauty and innocent juxtaposed by evil and debauchery. This has all the elements of great horror and given it's age, defines the genre. A great read if you are looking for great horror. 
 My only note is that, given it's age and the number of stories that have gone beyond it, it is fairly tame as haunted tales go. Never the less, like Frankenstein and Dracula, it is the archetype for haunted house stories and well worth reading.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is one of my favorite books. I have read it twice and both times it gave me the chills. It is a very well written haunted house tale that leaves the reader looking over a shoulder. In my book, it is a classic.

I did not like this book at all! I found it really tedious... 
 I didn't like the style of writing or the story line. 
 It did not live up to my expectations.

I actually started reading this audiobook way back in September for the Readers Imbibing Peril challenge. It's only 7.5 hours long, so I thought it'd be a quick read. I think the fact that it wasn't demonstrates quite well how not drawn into the story I was. This is a classic haunted house tale that perhaps might not work for the modern reader, depending on how much horror they generally imbibe. 
 This is going to be a quick review because I honestly don't have too much to say about the book. Four people arrive at a house. Things appear normal, except one of them, Eleanor, clearly is a bit more emotionally unstable than the rest. She is, for instance, shocked that anyone is interested in her or asks her questions. She also has trouble with her own identity, such as knowing for sure what she likes to eat. Odd things start to happen in the house, and because Eleanor is odd, the others aren't sure if it's the house doing them or Eleanor herself. Eleanor becomes overly attached to Theodora. Drama ensues. 
 None of the house horror scenes really got to me, because frankly I've seen worse in plenty of other horror I read. I do love the genre. The parts that actually disturbed me were when the others in the household were inexplicably cruel to Eleanor. That dynamic of an odd woman randomly tossed in with strangers who proceed to be mean to her in a highschoolish way held my interest more than the house did. People and their cruelty are so much more frightening than a haunted house. I understand that the book is sort of leaving it up to the reader to wonder if the house or the people really drive Eleanor crazy, but frankly I think the ending removes all question on this point. 
 Similarly, there are definitely some undertones in the Theodora/Eleanor relationship that indicates they might possibly have had a fling early on and then Theodora abruptly distances herself from Eleanor when she gets too clingy. None of this is said outright, however it is heavily implied that Theodora's roommate back home is her lover who she had a quarrel with, and she and Eleanor establish a close bond early on in the book. The problem is this all stays subtext and is never brought out in the open of the book. I get it that this book was published in 1959 so it probably had to stay subtext and was most likely shocking to a reader in the 50s. But to me, a modern reader, it felt like the book kept almost getting interesting and then backing off from it. The combination of the former issue and this one meant that I was left feeling unengaged and uninterested. Basically, I feel that the book didn't go quite far enough to be shocking, horrifying, or titillating. 
 The audiobook narration by Bernadette Dunne was excellent as always, and the main reason I kept listening rather than just picking up a copy of the book and speed reading it. I love listening to her voice. 
 Overall, this classic was boundary pushing when it was first published but it might not come across that way to a modern reader. Readers who read a lot of modern horror might find this book a bit too tame for their tastes. Those interested in the early works of the genre will still enjoy the read, as will modern readers looking for horror lite. Readers looking for the rumored GLBTQ content in this book will most likely be disappointed by the subtlety of it, although those interested in early representation in literature will still find it interesting. 
 Check out my full review.

Although it's not nearly as scary today as it undoubtedly would have been at the time it was published, what this book is is a lot of fun. The characters are witty and the dialogue is engaging and brilliantly written. The pacing works very well. The characters, especially central character Eleanor, is relatable and easy to care about as are the other haunted house explorers. Some of the plot and narrative seems cliched to a modern reader, but the likeliest explanation is that this story is a prototype for much of what followed. Don't dismiss this as genre fiction or judge it by the awful film version. This is a psychological horror story of great literary merit that is well written and developed. Jackson is an underrated writer who deserves more attention.

I'm beginning to think Shirley Jackson just recycles 3 or 4 different characters in every one of her stories - the unstable younger woman, the slightly older/slightly more stable woman, the arrogant playboy misogynist and the cruel/angry townspeople. No more, Shirley, no more. I loved The Lottery as a teenager, but I'm quitting you now.

1 stars 
 Scariest book? I've read scarier Goosebumps books than this.

 Dr.Montague, a scientist, sets out to pursue an investigation of paranormal activities at a possible haunted house, Hill House. He invites 3 quests/assistants, Eleanor, Theodora, and Luke to stay in Hill House for some of the summer to prove the existence of paranormal events. When they get there they find a creepy house but is it haunted and filled with paranormal activities? 
 _____________________________________ 
 I chose this book after Googling scariest books and this was on top 10 in most lists, boy was I disappointed. This book was just slow for me. Even though it was a short book I had to force myself to keep going and often found myself making excuses to why I was "too busy" to finish it, when in reality it was just boring. I'm not saying that all Shirley Jackson's books are like this but this one certainly did nothing for me. 
 The character dialogue was just odd and jumpy, which at first I thought maybe it was because the time period in which it was written but from reading other reviews it's not rather than Jackson's writing choice. 
 Dr.Montague didn't do much investigating, he mainly drunk and played chess with Luke. Luke wasn't interesting. 
 Theodora and Eleanor was drama queens. Eleanor was so insecure at times it made me roll me eyes. 
 I found Mrs.Dudley's constant repeating herself funny. That's about it for the characters. 
 I kept waiting and waiting for something to happen and nothing ever did. I take that back, there was a few "creepy-ish" things that happened like the time where Eleanor thought she was holding Theodora's hand in the dark room and turns out it wasn't her hand, that was kind of creepy but not enough to keep me interested in reading. 
 I think that it had potential but just felt flat for me. I think that this book is either a hit or miss for people, and for me it was a miss. Maybe I'll give Shirley Jackson's other works a try someday.. Maybe. 
 1 Stars.

I've wanted to try Shirley Jackson's work for a long time, and now I have! THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE is billed as a horror classic, though in my opinion, it was eerie but not scary. After finishing the book, I'm left with several questions without definite answers, like who (or what) exactly was doing the haunting -- the house itself, the doctor and his test subjects, or something else? Was anything supernatural actually going on, or were the unexplained events a figment of an unreliable narrator's imagination? I have my own theory, but I won't share because of spoilers. 
 THOHH is a well-crafted psychological thriller that makes readers decide for themselves what went down at Hill House. I enjoyed Ms. Jackson's straight-forward writing style, and how she was able to make something as innocuous as a cold spot on the floor downright spooky. The characters were okay. They all irritated me to some degree, and I also thought that the dialogue between characters could get pretty unrealistic and silly, like "Oh, Nell, my Nellie!" or some such. The character I liked the most was the housekeeper, Mrs. Dudley. I loved her totally weird ways. 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading THOHH, and I can see why the book has been a big influence on the horror genre since its publication in 1959.

After the haunting opening, I wanted to be haunted more. However, this is more of a haunting psychological story rather than a supernatural one. 
 There were definitely vivid characterizations with Mrs. Dudley's robotic monotones of ominousness and Mrs. Montague's extremely annoying personality. 
 This is probably one of those, "if I was in the right mood" books that I would appreciate better with different expectations and circumstances.

Because I've seen both film adaptations of this book, a lot of the surprise and suspense was removed for me. As typical with the printed word, the characters' psyches were far more explained and I found myself wondering, along with Eleanor and the rest, if the hauntings were real or a product of Eleanor's imagination and manipulation. It is definitely a read-worthy book. The story has stayed with me and my mind continues to debate its actual events.
DNF at 15%. Couldn't get into it, didn't wanna waste precious time.

Story: 4 stars 
 Character Development: 4 stars 
 Prose/Language: 3 star 
 Technically, this should be a 4 star book review. But I didn't feel like I could emotionally sink into the story. There was always something distracting me, pulling my attention elsewhere. It's a solid story with great writing and impressive character dev for such a short book. Hill House is creepy in a way that makes me never want to visit. The Haunting of Hill House is a classic. It read like a classic, but it wasn't really in my wheelhouse. I enjoyed the book, but I found it a little boring. The book got more monotonous when the doctor's wife arrived. The last quarter of the book is littered with the woman's constant bitching. I really hated the woman by the time the book was over. Ms. Jackson was skilled with the written word, and I'll be reading We Have Always Lived in the Castle soon.

The often light tone of Eleanor belies a whole can of worms. 
 I expected and received a rather fine ghost story in a haunted house, of course, but I was actually more interested in how Eleanor was always so unhappy in the beginning and how everything changed for the better when she moved into the house. How all her priorities and her descent into crazyville was directly linked to the tragic house, about how she wanted to be afraid, changed this rather simple tale into one that actually applies nicely to all us horror fans just begging to be scared. 
 What? The crazy girl is just like all of us? No way! :) 
 But what about the ghost? The ghost investigation? All the automatic writing and spooky stories? 
 It's great. :) 
 It's not over the top like what we usually get with our modern sensibilities, but he psychological side of this makes up for the simple story by actually managing to be profound. Nice work. :) 1959 and hardly dated at all! Color me impressed. And spooked! :) 
 Happy Halloween!

This was a weird, spotty little book. Parts of it I adored (Eleanor, the group's dynamic, the descriptions of Hill House), parts of it terrified me (holding hands in a dark room, the closing doors), and parts of it felt off-kilter and baffling (though I'm sure this was purposeful on Jackson's part). I can see why The Haunting of Hill House has become a seminal ghost story for so many contemporary horror writers, but, overall, I found its conclusion to be less satisfying than I had hoped it would be.

Don't get me wrong. Shirley Jackson is a fantastic writer. The world she creates--of the gothic, imposing Hill House, nestled at the base of hugging hills--is stark, dark, troubling, and surreal. She has an intriguing knack for getting inside the head of her protagonist (although that tends to be uncomfortable, as the protagonist is a couple of cards short of a full deck); and her dialogue is clever and often engaging. That said, Jackson's classic "masterpiece", THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE, misses the horror mark by a phantom mile. Why? Because it's little more than a 182-page pity party/catfight. 
 While I'm ambivalent about Dr. Montague, the other characters in this novel are completely and irretrievably unlikable. Luke is an immature playboy, while Theodora and Eleanor are 24/7 drama queens competing for not only the attention of the men they are sharing Hill House with--but for the attention of Hill House itself. And then Jackson, late in the novel, introduces two even more unpleasant characters in Mrs. Montague and Arthur; I so disliked all of them I kept hoping some manifestation would cart them all off. (Alas, it didn't happen.) 
 Spoiler alert. There are no monsters are ghouls who appear in this novel, and there's nothing wrong with that; a horror novel doesn't have to have a physical entity growling about to be effective. What we do have are bumps in the night, freezing cold air, invisible laughter and voices, and scribbling on walls--yet we don't know if they are real, or products of a psychotic imagination. Furthermore, we get to embark on a most uncomfortable trip as shy, insecure, unstable Eleanor steadily goes bats--a trip having Eleanor pay the ultimate price. In the end, Hill House wins, but as a reader trudging through THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE I was much too ambivalent to care.

This is Shirley Jackson's pivotal ghost story about a girl named Eleanor Vance who is summoned to the haunted establishment called Hill House by a Doctor Montague, an earnest and intelligent psychologist. Beautiful and so stylistically unique, this story has quickly become one of my favorites. Utilizing terror rather than horror, the chilling paranormal aspects of Hill House ingrain itself upon the residents, mostly Eleanor and her friend Theodora, creating a stunning balance between beauty, peace, and disconnect. The audience is left wondering what exactly the haunting is and what the connection is between Eleanor and Hill House, but this just amplifies the amount of fear in the reader. Definitely a must read!
The story as a whole was just ok, but it has one of the best first paragraphs I've ever read.

This book was NOT scary or eerie or creepy but just plain boring! Wasted time getting to know characters who would never matter in the plot. So much detail of the house and the landscape and character thoughts when it's advised as a thriller... I just didn't get it. I'll probably never pick up a S. Jackson again... Major let down.

Four strangers are gathered at Hill House, a decrepit old residence, to see if they can find some actual evidence that is is haunted. Well, it wouldn't be much of a story of no evidence appeared, would it?

** spoiler alert ** 
 Supernatural thrillers have certainly come a long way since Shirley Jackson penned this novel in 1959. I liked "We Have Always Lived in the Castle" much better. But Hill House is considered a classic of the genre, so who am I to dispute that. I've seen several movie versions of this story, and since they are far more dramatic than the book, I think the movies have influenced my expectations of the story. In the end, Eleanor simply crashes her car into a tree. Her spirit wasn't taken up to become a permanent resident of Hill House; she just crashes her car into a tree and that's the last we hear of her. A recent movie version of the story did a much better job. The book is very good at illustrating how a writer uses the omnipotent voice and merges it with the second person voice. At any rate, it took me a long time to read this book because I read it mostly at bedtime and not every single night. I think if it weren't for the 1960s version of the story, I wouldn't be able to imagine the creepiness of The Haunting of Hill House and its events.

I have chewed on this book for a long while. As I've been reading the recently published Shirley Jackson biography, by Ruth Jackson, it has come back to me; it's truly the definitive Jackson book. 
 Franklin writes this: "In Hill House, which appeared in 1959, Jackson gathered powerfully all the objects of her longtime obsession: an unhappy, unmarried woman with a secret trauma; the simultaneous longing for a mother's love and fear of its control; the uncertain legacies handed down by previous generations; and finally the supernatural as a representation of the deepest psychic fears and desires. The result, a masterpiece of literary horror on a par with Henry james's The Turn of the Screw, is arguably her best novel, and certainly her most influential." 
 Eleanor is the young protagonist of the novel. She is neither woman nor child; she is homeless, although she dreams often of the perfect home that will belong only to her. For many years Eleanor has been sequestered in an unhappy home; caretaker to a sour mother who she cannot ever please. When her mother dies, Eleanor seizes the chance to participate in a paranormal experience. Her own background hints at 'sensitivity' to paranormal phenomena, as she and her sister were subjected to three days of a shower of stones (not quite a literal stoning, but close) after their father's death. So Eleanor steals her sister's car, and drives herself to Hill House - whose ghosts include a mother, tragically killed, and two squabbling sisters. 
 There are many brilliant descriptions in this book, and one of the most memorable is that of the physical building of the house which defies symmetry at every turn - every angle and line of it just wrong. Its oddness, and deliberately unnavigable quality, make it the perfect counterpart and foil to Eleanor. The four participants in the experiment - and inhabitants of the house - include Eleanor, the insouciant Theodora, Dr. Montague and Luke (a young man who is the future heir of Hill House). From the beginning, Eleanor seems the most affected by the house - the most sensitive to its ghostly messages. But neither the reader, nor Eleanor herself, ever quite knows what is external and what is internal; in other words, is the entire story just Eleanor splintering, and losing her tenuous hold on reality? Interestingly, the other characters - particularly Theodora - accuse Eleanor of seeking attention. Like a child who blames an imaginary friend, Eleanor seems to be the perpetrator (or is it the victim?) of a series of small yet malevolent mischiefs. There is also a death-wish in this book, a decidedly murky one. We never know quite for sure if Eleanor is merely making 'a call for help' which she desperately hopes will be heeded, or if she has an inexorable impulse to self-destruction.

I got this book off of a "10 most scariest books to read" list & there was nothing scary about it at all. Apparently there was a movie made after it was written & I can already imagine how boring & flat the acting would be. Don't waste your time, unless the thought of an ugly looking house scares you.

Meh. I don't get all the hoopla. I expected an exquisitely creepy story from everything I've read about this book. It should have occupied my mind even after I set the book down at the end of reading sessions. I was very disappointed. 
 The story took forever to get to the actual starting point and was still slow after that. The description wasn't all that amazing, so many opportunities for creepiness were missed, and the ending was a let down. There were interesting crumbs sprinkled throughout the book, but none of them were followed up on. Maybe I'm just jaded on horror or skimmed over the important bits.

A book club choice because it was written by Shirley Jackson, whose short story The Lottery used to be required reading by many high school English students. We were all disappointed, and it wasn't just because this novel, published in 1959, seemed dated. Set in an old house, this is a not-very-compelling ghost story without real ghosts. Not only wasn't it scary, but the characters were unlikeable.

As a voracious reader - and specifically the horror genre - I follow a lot of blogs and websites about books. Just about every list of "Top horror books you must read" includes The Haunting of Hill House. I finally decided to give it a try. 
 I can only say I truly must have read a completely different book than the authors of those lists read. The plot was nonexistent, the characters were cold and forced, the dialogue pedestrian at best, and if some knocking on walls is considered horror then let me bang out a bunch of best sellers. 
 In a nutshell, there is a supposed haunted house that a doctor and three students stay in to document the goings on. Eleanor - the stories "central" character starts to have a breakdown. That's it... End of story... Oh, there's an unexplained cold area in the nursery, some banging and wall shaking, and words written on the walls in blood. If anything, this was more a psychological thriller - not horror. And I really didn't care what happened to Eleanor at the end. All I did hope for was that someone would slap the hell out of the Doctor's condescending wife, who came to visit in the last quarter of the book. 
 While this wasn't the worst piece of drivel I've ever read, it certainly ranks up there with one that I wouldn't even give a second glance to. Had someone actually slapped the Doctor's wife, I would have given it two stars. 
 I have never done this before, but I need to ask - if you've read this book and enjoyed it (or think that it belongs on those Best Lists), please, for the love of all that is written, write me a note telling me what I missed. 
 If you are even the least bit curious and are thinking about reading this, do yourself a favor - paint a wall and watch it dry... It's more entertaining.

I had a hard time making myself finish this one. 
 I love Poe's psychological horror and mentally unstable protagonists, yet Jackson's psychological horror with a mentally unstable protagonist did not interest me much. The plot was too slow for my liking, and Eleanor (the protagonist) seemed weak and silly instead of threatening. Mostly, I just wanted to tell her to grow up and get ahold of herself. I found her annoying, and that made me dislike the book.

No one ever did it better. And Stephen King says it best: "Shirley Jackson, who never needed to raise her voice." 
 I've read this book multiple times and it never, ever fails to disturb me.

While Shirley Jackson's ghost story The Haunting of Hill House is very well written, I found it to be a bore. I was expecting a really easy, pulp-horror, type of novel...based off the two films, base off the novel, that were mediocre at best. I was wrong, Shirley Jackson knows how to write. Descriptions were interesting, passages were eloquent. I just was bored throughout ninety percent of the novel, which is not what I want from a ghost story.

It's the home I've dreamed of," Theodora said. "A little hideaway where I can be alone with my thoughts. Particularly if my thoughts happened to be about murder or suicide--" 
 Houses catch a bad rap. Some curse them as conduits, others as tombs. The shelter provided leaves a record of sins and scars. One could imagine the sum of voices gathering as well. Huddled and harboring. Echoes vie with whispers as dust motes measure the empty turn of the seasons. The curse of Hill House renders certain voices eternal. They don't just speak, they inquire and condemn. 
 Ghosts are absolved, at least in my book. Life's cruelty is the villain of The Haunting of Hill House. Elenor was a brilliant character of human failure. Her missteps and insecurity were impeccably realized. I also liked the presence of Mrs. Montague; she and Mrs Dudley maintained a gothic smirk, an antidote of the psychological parlour games occupying the chief characters and their "research." 
 Fear has a smell. Shirley Jackson achieves the impossible by conveying such to the page. 
 4.5/5
This was so boring and not scary at all. It's not that it was badly written, it's just that the story was impossibly bland. Nothing happened. That's the bottom line. Absolutely nothing happened.
Eugh.....very badly written so quite honestly, can't be arsed.

Absolute classic Gothic horror. There are bumps in the night, strange writing on the walls and mysterious 'cold spots'. But this is not a cliched read. Recluse Eleanor, is the main focus. Having looked after her invalid mother for years, she now has the freedom she longs for when she accepts an invite to stay at Hill House along with psychic researcher Dr Montague, flamboyant artist Theodora and lovely Luke, amused by the whole set up. Over susceptible, Eleanor is almost absorbed by the house; begging the question, is the house haunted, or is she?

I read this book after seeing the black and white film when I was younger (my dad brought it home for me) and for a 7 year old I was pretty terrified.I read the book and was surprised how much was NOT in the movie. I guess at the time the original movie was made the censorship issue was what kept a lot out even if not much in the book was offensive (really nothing if I remember correctly). Eleanor kind of annoys me as a protagonist, I like Theo better. It's spectacularly chilling and I do recommend that you check it out!

Sigh!This book supposed to be a scary book but I didn't find it spooky at all.I am speechless at how this can even get a 5 star rating from anyone.After reading the synopsis(very interesting),I was expecting a lot from this book but I was disappointed and felt irritated with the characters(especially Eleanor).Meh.
This story is so atmospheric. I found it to be a creepy, slow burning horror novel. The characterisation is excellent.

If you have already seen one of the many movie versions, borrow this from the library. I paid $13 to B&N not realizing that it is only 173 pages (including the 20 page introduction). The ending kinda leaves you hanging as to whether Hill House was truly haunted, or was it all in Nell's head. It has nowhere near the violence or gore the movies had. So I would say it is safe enough for the middle schooler looking for a quick scare.
A very scary classic.
It was horribly disappointing. Not at all as creepy/scary as you're led to think when you see it in any kind of "top scariest novels" list.

Ok, this book defined a whole genre. Ok, Shirley Jackson writing is fine. Ok, this is a horror classic that every fan of the genre must read. BUT, I just found it boring and dull. The main character is just annoying! I was waiting all the time that somebody just force her to shut up.I was annoyed by her from the beginning of the book, and I felt the same way until the end. 
 I didn't like this book and I trully think it's quite overrated. But hey, everybody loves it... so maybe I just skipped the good part of it by mistake.

Picked this up on Halloween after seeing it listed as one of the scariest books ever. I waited for the scary to start but it never really happened for me. I struggled to get through it. Thinking the "scary" is more psychological or theoretical on some levels and perhaps I missed some of the deeper points? Oh well. Not so scary in my opinion.

This book had me interested right up until about the halfway mark, although I'm not really sure I would characterize it as horror. I finished it. Barely, and then I was ashamed of myself for reading it. It was almost as if the author had given up on the story.

"Journey ends with lovers meeting" Eleanor kept on saying then and now, which is to become true in a tragic way, a one line story to mull over. "No live organism can continue for too long to exist sanely under the conditions of absolute reality" and there it starts, a conspiracy to dull the expectations down in order to unleash the horror on oneself. 
 The characters were dull and confusing and so many things were unexplained or left to guess, which is great but not on this magnitude. There were not more than instances where it felt a little scary. The book is moderately written and the description of hill house was beautiful in a horrifying way. 
 Mrs Montague, a woman of high elegance annoyed me with her every sentence, Dr Montague, (Mr Sassy) is not good enough, Luke was whiny and Dudleys were creepy for no apparent reasons. Theodora was funny and okay until the first hundred pages. Eleanor,on the other hand kept feeling sorry for herself and ended up meeting her lover in the end finally, death. 
 Hill house, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within; it had stood so for eighty years and might stand for eighty more. Withing walls continued upright, bricks met neatly, floors were firm, and doors were sensible shut; silence lay steadily against the wood and stone of hill house, and whatever walked there, walked alone. 
 I WOULD NOT READ YOU AGAIN
Suitably spooky with some good creepy moments. I couldn't work out what was going to happen next so the ending was a genuine surprise.

reference_books.title: The Goose Girl (The Books of Bayern, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
In Hale's re-telling of: "The Goose Girl," both the princess and her lady-in-waiting 
 are given names: Ani, and Selia. 
 They also become more rounded with better motives for their actions and behavior. 
 The modifications contemporize the story without loosing the fantasy aspect.

reference_books.title: City of Heavenly Fire (The Mortal Instruments, #6)
reference_books.review_text:
The plot is a blend of Philip Pullman's: "Subtle Knife," and Rowling's: 
 "Deathly Hallows." 
 Sebastian Morgenstern is set on destroying all of the Shadowhunters. 
 Clary and her friends are all the Shadowhunters have to save them from the final end. 
 At the end of the story, Clare sets up the story for a future spin-off series.

reference_books.title: The Dream Thieves (The Raven Cycle, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Stiefvater's plot is a complex blend of the modern world that is filled with ancient Celtic magic. 
 Ronan Lynch is on a quest to find Glendower, in order to save his friend Gansey. 
 A repeated reference to street racing, disrupts some of the story, but eventually does make sense.

reference_books.title: The House of Silk
reference_books.review_text:
What makes this story unique is that it is authorized by Doyle's estate, unlike the countless 
 others which were written and published without such permission. 
 The story is set in 1891 London and narrated by Doctor Watson. 
 The story is two mysteries which eventually illustrate why Doyle retired his famous detective.

reference_books.title: The Dark Days Club (Lady Helen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The story is set in 1812, London with eighteen year old Lady Helen Wrexhall as the main character. 
 Helen vacillates between wanting to rid herself of her new powers and at the end does a sudden 180 degree reversal that reads too much like "God in the Machine."

reference_books.title: Strands of Bronze and Gold
reference_books.review_text:
The story is narrated by Sophia Petheram, and is set in 1855 Missippi. 
 Nickerson mentions: "The Robber Bridegroom," inside the text of her story, this is an earlier version of "Bluebeard." 
 Nickerson describes plantation life through Sophia's eyes. 
 The issue of slavery works well with the dark fairytale that deals with secrets and murder.

reference_books.title: The Golem and the Jinni (The Golem and the Jinni, #1)
reference_books.review_text: An intresting way to show immigrent life in 1899 New York. The plot dwells on the theme of consealing the true self and how both the Golem and Jinni of myth are slaves to their masters.

reference_books.title: The Raven King (The Raven Cycle, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
The entire series is over written and in need of serious editing. 
 Stiefvater plot's ineffective use of several powerful archetypes made the story 
 weak and convoluted. 
 Better authors: 
 Neil Gaiman: American Gods, which is being turned into a television series 
 Nancy Springer: The Hex Witch of Seldom 
 Pierce Anthony and his: Incarnates of Immortality series

"Not every tale has a happy ending. In fact, many of them are grim."-this is probably one of my favorite quotes from the book! Mina Grime, descendant of the Brothers Grimm and present target of the Story curse, must "finish" the tales that the Brothers Grimm started in order to break the curse that's responsible for taking out several of her ancestors. Couple of problems, of course. First, the Story doesn't play nice. Second, if Mina fails, that means Mina is dead. Third, we're talking about a couple hundred of stories. Uh oh... 
 Luckily, Mina's a smart and brave heroine, and she has friends, a cheat sheet, and a mysterious helper to give her a hand in finishing the tales. Mina is such a fun characters as she's so disaster prone and awkward, yet trying to cope with it. She's so likable as she tries to deal with a growing relationship with her previously unattainable crush, fight off bad guys, train to fight with her recalcitrant helper, and tries to figure out how to complete the stories. The secondary characters and the interactions between them are great. Her best friend Nan, a social media queen who at first I questioned if she really was her friend, turns out to be greatly loyal side-kick, and a fun comic relief character. She was my favorite out of the secondary characters, but there were many other fun ones. 
 I liked the spin on faery tales that Ms. Hahn decided to go with. The premise is pretty simple so there isn't too much mythology to go through. The setting is in modern day and in our world so there are references to iPhones, tweeting, etc. However, there are fae creatures and magical battles that I enjoyed reading. With her writing style, I could picture Mina's adventures, which made the story so much more entertaining to read. The magic scenes were easy to visualize. This is told in third person through Mina's viewpoint so reading about things that Mina didn't know added some suspense as the story (not to be confused with the Story!) unfolded. I have mixed feelings about the ending; I did not see the that coming at all although it does make sense and there were allusions to it. Unenchanted does not end in a cliffhanger since there is closure and you don't have to worry about the fate of major characters. However, it's clearly a first book to a series, and the ending makes you want to pick up the next book to see what happens next. 
 I did want to disagree with some of the early reviews that the book got about the book having pacing, POV, and spelling/grammar issues. Ms. Hahn must have put out a revision, because I didn't see many of the issues that the early reviews pointed out and took off stars. There *are* typos though, but not enough to warrant the response that made me expect it to be really badly edited. Instead, maybe one more pass with an editor would fix the remaining errors. 
 Overall, this is a promising start to a series that I look forward to following. I'm definitely recommending it to all ages and those that love faery tales. This is a 5 out of 5 for me!

Unenchanted by Chanda Hahn 
 How I heard about the book: It was a free kindle book and looked interesting so I gave it a shot. 
 Summary: (from Goodreads) 
 "Mina Grime is unlucky, unpopular and uncoordinated; that is until she saves her crush's life on a field trip, changing her High School status from loser to hero overnight. 
 But with her new found fame brings misfortune in the form of an old family curse come to light. For Mina is a descendant from the Brothers Grimm and has inherited all of their unfinished fairy tale business which includes trying to outwit a powerful Story from making her its' next fairy-tale victim. 
 To break the fairy tale curse on her family and make these deadly occurrences stop, Mina must finish the tales until the very Grimm end." 
 My thoughts: A very pleasant surprise! Such an interesting story and awesome characters. 
 Good/Liked- 
 Story- A very interesting take on the Grimm Brothers. I myself am a fan of the show Grimm but even this is very different from that. I love the originality of the story. 
 Bad/Disliked- 
 Romance- Kind of got annoyed with the classic to good to be true relationship that happens in the story. 
 Editing- More than a few errors here but hey it was a free book, I can't complain much. 
 Would have enjoyed to see more action on the protagonists part and would have liked to see promise of her growing in character. 
 Overall: It's a good series to read if you are one for fantasy and a good story. 
 Recommendations: I would recommend this book to anyone who loves fantasy. 
 Rating: I give this book a 3.5 out of 5.

No. Just no.

One of my goals for this year is to read if not all, then atleast half of the total books in my TBR before purchasing new ones. Kind of hard actually, haha, but I'm keeping a hardcopy of the list of books that I am purchasing soon. It's still February but I've almost written a whole first page of my notebook lol). 
 I'm not quite sure how long this story has been in my TBR, but I'm guessing it's been more than a year lol. So yep, while browsing for some books to read, I've stumble to this one. It easily caught my attention because of the simple yet interesting cover. Besides, I'm a YA freak so I'm sure I'm going to like it. 
 The first few chapters was fine, nothing special really, just a typical girl who is so clumsy that I think that's her natural talent. Basing on the cover, I know this is going to be fantasy, but I've finished chapter 2 still no flying wizards or supernatural things happened. Then, all of a sudden, the weird action of Mina's (main female character) mother stinks like a rotten fish. 
 So yeah, after that, my first reaction about this story changed and I am really so adamant to know what's behind her mother's odd reaction. But before finding that out, I was introduced with this kinda sweet teeny-weeny romance (which, not to mention I'm a total sucker hah!) between Mina and her ultimate crush in the whole wide world, Brody, which really made my reading experience romantic, ayeei! Well, at first, I was suspecting about his true intention for Mina. He was this rich unattainable heartthrob to Mina, then in an instant, a sick puppy inlove with her. Quite a turnout of events actually. I don't know what happened, but I just find myself grinning like crazy lol. Well, it can't be help especially if I'm this hopeless romantic lol. 
 Aside from the teeny-weeny romance, my most anticipated revelation finally came. I'm not really sure how to react about it because it was kind of hilarious actually. I don't want to offend anyone, but I kinda laugh. I don't want this review to be a bummer so I'm not gonna tell, but maybe I'll drop some clue once in a while *wink. As I get further with the story, I kinda understand how it goes now. How the whole idea of this story fits so well that I am starting to doubt my knowledge about the Grimm fairy tales. 
 So yep. I'm totally convinced now how great the idea of this story is. But. Yep, there's a but. This story would have been great, but I've noticed some mistakes in the word usage, punctuation and structure. Even if I find the story interesting, there were still some times that I am on the verge of flipping off. I love the added romance (who wouldn't eh?) but I can't deny that the story's development was kinda off sometimes. Like there are some scenes that doesn't makes sense which I think just added there to make this story longer. There are over 200 tales for Mina to complete but she only gets through two stories. It would have been convincing if she were atleast get through 10 tales with those 235 chapters. Also, the conveying of information about Mina's family curse wasn't delivered flawlessly that's why there were times that I was confused that I need to read some parts all over again. 
 Most of the time, the ending of the story makes me decide to change my overall rating. It could make or break it. I would have given this story a 4-stars rating but the ending is just meh. It's just too convenient which I think was given only a minimum amount of effort. 
 That said, my rating would have been just 3-stars. But this story surprisingly kept me awake late just to finish it. Plus, I'm still interested to read the next book from this series. And that my friend speaks something, so yep, that's how my 3.5 stars was created. 
 If you love YA fantasy, you might want to check this one out. 
 Rating: 3.5 out of 5 stars

This one doesn't quite live up to YA standards (at least those standards that do not include books like Twilight). In my mind, a YA readers should be given much more credit than this book gives them. I'd say this is a beginning chapter book. 
 First off, kudos to Mrs. Hahn for finding time, imagination and courage to write. That in itself is inspiring. However, marketing this to YA's doesn't say much for the discerning reader. 
 Not even one full chapter in, I questioned the believability: 
 Brody Carmichael: jock, aristocrat, family with old money, a clothing company and racehorses! 
 Guess what, girls. He goes to public school! 
 Because of such rampant passive voice, descriptions seem forced, stilted, and lacking dimension. It is much easier to pick on tense and time-frame than to wobble between a few. (But for this, we must accuse the editor of this cringe-fest rather than the author who has such a wonderful idea.) 
 As I must be a grammar Nazi, please ignore my rant if you can overlook those kinds of mistakes. If you can ignore the lack of depth in character and such basics as setting, if you can suspend your disbelief to a far greater level than I who cut my teeth on Stephen King and Melanie Rawn and read Madeleine L'Engle in grade school.... 
 I truly hope you find enjoyment from the story. I can see from the reviews that some of you can and have. 
 Normally, I cannot wait to recommend books to my kids. I can only recommend this one as an example of what not to do, despite the entertaining concept. 
 What any author wants is to get the story out there for people to enjoy. They write for the pleasure of writing. They write for the few to which it may appeal. Mrs. Hahn has achieved that. Maybe, I'll pick up one of her later books some time in the future and appreciate the growth of her authorial voice. 
 Until then, my grammar Nazi self cannot get past the third chapter. And I truly feel that I'm missing a great story.

Review courtesy of Dark Faerie Tales 
 Quick & Dirty: Will Snow use her powers to save the world she's left behind? 
 Opening Sentence: First kisses sometimes wake slumbering princesses, undo spells, and spark happily ever afters. 
 Excerpt: No 
 The Review: 
 It was soooo difficult to choose an overall rating for Stealing Snow because I alternated between three and 3.5 stars throughout the book! It's a retelling of the Snow Queen but I've not read that so I don't know how much of a retelling it really was....The story was interesting but it took me longer to finish than I would have liked, which for me is always a bad sign. 
 "Does everyone here lie?" I asked. 
 "Everyone lies everywhere. I saw your world, too, Princess. Not much of it. But enough." 
 I hadn't seen much of my world, either. And definitely, not enough. 
 Snow is a fearsome protagonist with a dangerous temper. Living in the asylum most of her life is bound to unhinge anyone but Snow found that her friend, Bale, kept her going. Then she kisses him, discovers her magic and all hell breaks loose. Bale is kidnapped and taken to another world and Snow is determined to bring her true love back. 
 Stealing Snow reminded me too much of Alice in Wonderland with the crazy characters, escaping the asylum, walking through mirrors and so on. Although there were a fair number of original concepts like the robbers that steal faces and 'steal' magic, my first impression stuck! 
 "They're scales," the girl explained, touching the leaflike things attached to me. "They draw off all the bad." 
 Great. I had been saved only to be tortured by crazy wannabe witch people. 
 Aside from Bale, there are two other boys Snow becomes tangled up in: Kai and Jagger. For someone who has just escaped an asylum, I found her love life very promising albeit unrealistic. If I'm completely honest, I think Snow thought she was more in love with Bale than she really was, probably because of the time they spent locked up together (and the fact that they were both high on who knows what!). I didn't really like Bale, maybe because he's portrayed as a drugged-up arsonist? I don't know why Snow is adamant that Bale is the perfect guy for her... I thought it was her guilt that was making her trek through another world to find him, only to learn that there's countless other lives depending on her. 
 Ironically, he was looking at me closely, as if he was memorizing my eyes for later, in case I ever took him up on the new face thing. At Whittaker, I was the queen of staring contests, but I looked away. 
 "You should watch out for Fathom. You should watch out for everyone, really..." 
 "Except you?" 
 "Especially me." 
 Snow's aim to save Bale and go home is understandable but I thought she would have changed her mind once realised what the stakes were. Besides, what home was she returning to? The asylum? Snow would rather run away with her friend than try to save a world she has a duty to! Snow has been through a lot but that's pretty heartless, even for her. 
 To conclude, it was certainly a fun read packed full of action but I felt that there were too many elements 'borrowed' from Alice in Wonderland at the start, making it harder to appreciate the originality later on. 
 Notable Scene: 
 Most people usually ran in the other direction when I exploded. But not Bale. He stood right next to me. He didn't touch me. He just stood patiently until I was done. When I stopped seeing red, and the intense, all-consuming wave of anger subsided, and everything in the room finally quieted down, he held my hand. That's when I fell in love with him, too. I wanted my hand in his from that day to forever. Even if he did break it in two places eventually. Because no one really understood what it was like to live with this kind of rage and pain, like fire and ice, inside you. No one but us.

I received an ebook of Stealing Snow via Netgalley for a fair and honest review. Thank you to the author, Danielle Paige, and the publisher, Bloomsbury Childrens for the opportunity to preview this book. 
 Snow is a seventeen-year old girl who's spent most of her life living within the confines of the Whittaker Institute - a high security mental facility located in New York. She knows that she's not crazy, but that she is different to everyone else, a fact confirmed for her when she meets a new orderly within Whittaker's and begins dreaming of a strange tree. Snow plots to escape and and find the tree, and when she does, the lines between the reality she knows and the newer, stranger one she finds herself in begin to blur and she needs to unravel the truth from the lies in her own life. 
 The premise of Stealing Snow was very appealing to me, and while I enjoyed the book I don't think it quite lived up to my expectations. 
 It was a fairly easy to read and there are a lot of really interesting characters - which I think for me became a bit of a drawback because we met so many characters that seemed to be integral to parts of the story but I don't feel like we got to find out as much as we needed to about them. We get these snippets of them (in this book - perhaps they'll be expanded on in subsequent books) but sometimes it felt more like adding more puzzle pieces without a clearer sense of how everyone is connected. 
 Snow, as a main character fell a little flat. As a character who's spent most of her life living in an institute, she's used to accepting orders and instructions from people and while I'll accept that she's not had that much experience making decisions for herself, there are some decisions that she makes in this story that I felt were quite strange and didn't make a whole lot of sense. 
 There's also three love interests, and while I can handle one or two in a story, three felt a bit much. 
 I found the world that Danielle Paige built to be fascinating. There are definite fairytale elements, as well, and I think this was what I was most excited about, however I feel some of this got lost amongst the infinite characters. 
 Would I recommend this book? I do know a few people who would enjoy a story like this and would probably enjoy it more than I did. I would be interested in reading a follow-up book, to see what character development happens and how the plot evolves. 
 Overall, I gave it 3 stars.

 This book really drew me in with the concept. I'm a total and utter sucker for fairy tale re-tellings and a Snow Queen type retelling sounded just up my street. Unfortunately, it turns out that this book was several time zones away from my street. 
 Firstly, what I liked; I really liked the idea. It sounded a little different from the usual, run of the mill re-tellings I'm used to picking up. I also liked the world itself - mirrors are a cool portal to another world in a lot of stories, but I like the trope and so was happy to run with it. Likewise, I have seen the whole "mental institution patient turns out to by world saving princess" thing done a thousand times - but I love it when it's done well. A world frozen over by an evil overlord sounds very Narnia, but again, I like Narnia, so why not give a re-telling of its central concept a chance? 
 However the things I didn't like could probably fill a significantly longer book than Stealing Snow. It felt rushed beyond belief - way too many plot threads, half fulfilled characters, insipid bad guys...we skipped from happening to happening with barely a pause for breath. There were moments of good writing hidden in amongst the full on sprint to the finish line, but they were almost buried under the intense and yet also strangely unfulfilling plotting and pacing. 
 I also full on detested the love quadrangle. Yes you heard that right. As in square. The main character had not just two love interests, but three. This is excessive in the confines of any story. In one which seemed to struggle with pacing so much as Stealing Snow, it was a major negative. For me, the least featured love interest was my favourite; Kai. I think he has a lot of secrets which have yet to be revealed; and his sister being a part of the story too gave him some grounding for me. Jagger and Bale were equally uninteresting but if I had to cut one then try hard Robber Jagger would have to go. 
 Then, finally, the greatest weakness; Snow herself. Princess Snow is as dull as they get. There wasn't anything I can recall from reading Stealing Snow which made her stand out for me. She grasped the use of her powers with startling ease. She was locked up in an institution for a number of years but seems completely sane - which no one, not staff or visitors or other patients seemed to notice. She has men falling all over themselves to kiss her. Her every action seems orchestrated to make convenient plot points add up. 
 Overall, I'm not hooked enough to seek out the sequels, which is a massive shame. This seems like such a fantastic concept, I know that Danielle Paige can write well. However Stealing Snow did nothing for me and I can't really recommend.

Snow has spent most of her like behind the walls of the Whittaker Institute. The high security asylum is meant to help rehabilitate troubled patients, like Snow, let go of their delusions. 
 But Snow doesn't think she's crazy. Not really. 
 Being near Bale makes like at the Institute bearable. At least until Bale claims he can see what Snow really is when they kiss. And breaks her hand in two places. 
 When mysterious hands grab Bale and pull him through a mirror, Snow knows that she has to follow. A voice in her dreams tells Snow exactly what to do in order to escape. Following the voices directions, Snow makes it outside and finds herself in the wintry world of Algid. 
 Snow soon learns that Algid is her true home and her father is determined to do everything he can to hold onto the throne--and keep Snow far away from it. As magic, mayhem, and trickery collide, Snow will have to decide who she can trust if she wants to rescue Bale and make it out of Algid alive in Stealing Snow (2016) by Danielle Paige. 
 Stealing Snow is the start of Paige's new series which is a dark retelling of The Snow Queen. 
 Paige goes for a darker tone right from the start with Snow residing in an asylum that seems to come straight from the pages of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. While this setting offers a gripping backdrop for the opening of the story, it also often defies logic as readers realize Snow has been at the Institute since she was a child (and is, in fact, still only seventeen suggesting there should have been at least some type of schoolwork or high school equivalency studies). 
 The story picks up considerably when Snow actually arrives in Algid and more of the novel's characters are introduced. Snow finds a veritable band of misfits as she makes her way through Algid trying to find her father, the Snow King, and rescue her love Bale. 
 Along the way Snow encounters numerous love interests, her own snow magic, and vast conspiracies that stretch between Algid and our world. While this series opener raises many questions about Snow, her family, and Algid, readers will have to wait for future installments for most of the answers. 
 Stealing Snow is a fast-paced adventure with a sharp-tongued narrator who isn't afraid to be ruthless. Paige takes some of the familiar elements of The Snow Queen and shakes them up with an inventive reimagining of the this fairy tale and the frighteningly evocative world of Algid. Recommended for readers looking for a new fairytale retelling that is extra dark. 
 Possible Pairings: Splintered by A. G. Howard, Princess of Thorns by Stacey Jay, Reign of Shadows by Sophie Jordan, Winterspell by Claire Legrand, Cinder by Marissa Meyer, Snow Like Ashes by Sara Raasch, Ruined by Amy Tintera

 Then fished something out of her pants pocket and tossed a glowing blue vial at me.

-POTENTIAL SPOILERS- 
 Well, this was disappointing. Don't get me wrong, it had a lot of good ideas in it, but the overall product was way too rushed for me to really understand anything that was going on. 
 The Snow Queen is one of my most favorite fairy tales, second only to The Princess and the Pea, and even though I think the story is perfect and can't be retold in any other way, I'm still open to retellings of the fairy tale. It'd be interesting to see how the Snow Queen came to be in this world and how she turned crazy, but the book doesn't really show that. I know there's supposed to be a sequel, but by the end of this Snow isn't even on the path to becoming crazy or cold or distant like the original Snow Queen. 
 I did like the element of the robber society, and the Robber Queen, instead of there being just one robber girl like in the original fairy tale. I liked their magic and how they made dresses that could fly, but I also didn't think it was explored well enough. 
 Kai and Gerda are names from the original fairy tale, the boy who gets kidnapped by the Snow Queen and the girl who goes out and finds him, but they don't really have much to do with this story. Snow meets them, but that's pretty much it. 
 The basic plot was interesting, it was similar to the Snow Queen where the girl's friend gets stolen away to a magical world of snow and ice, and there were lots of broken mirrors, but again, it wasn't explained very well. I did like how the main character was using her sheltered knowledge of what she's seen on TV to try and survive in this world; that's something I can relate to a lot. Everything I know too comes from TV! 
 This was my first Danielle Paige book and I'm not a fan of her writing style, here it felt way too rushed and held-back. Apparently her Dorothy Must Die series is better, so maybe I'll give that one a try instead. 
 And why is the magical world inspired after Norway instead of Greenland like in the original story?! Kai and Gerda were Inuit in the original story; I'm so sick of people retelling this story in Norway. Is your thought process like: "Well the original fairy tale is already ethnic, so we don't need to do it anymore!" I also wasn't a huge fan of all the guys in this story. In the original, Gerda either helps herself or gets help from other girls and women, like the robber girl, the Finnish woman, and the princess. It's a good story of girl power. 
 Overall, I liked the general idea of this, but it was way too-rushed and poorly thought-out to be any good. Maybe her sequel and other books are better, maybe not. I do admire the attempt to retell an already-perfect fairy tale, but in this case, this was an example of why you shouldn't do that.

This book was very much just...meh. It's suppose to be based off of Snow White, but if the main character's name hadn't happened to be Snow, I probably would have never guessed this fact. The story jumps around all over the place and the pacing just seemed off and jarring. One minute she's stuck in an insane asylum and then the next there's this huge destiny around her where her father is a King from another world and is intent on killing Snow because she has magical snow powers...yeah. There are also three love interests who are pretty much interchangeable. More than two is one too many in my opinion (Even two is pushing it). 
 There was also a lack of cohesiveness to the story that made it a very hard book to finish. 
 And like the love interests almost all the supporting characters were hard to tell apart because they all sounded exactly the same...I wanted to like this book but it just wasn't my fav.

For a highly anticipated read, I found myself... disappointed. While the writing style was wonderful, I couldn't connect to the story. It seemed very disjointed, jumping from a coming-of-age-plot to rebellion-plot to heist-plot to romance-plot. The romance... that was even more all over the place. DNF. UGH.

This book was interesting, and not in a good way. There were moments where I loved it, and there were moments where I HATED it. I LOVED the second half of the middle section; the rest I HATED. I didn't like the main character AT ALL. She never saw what was right in front of her, and when she did, she denied it and had a bad attitude. Also, she never accepted who she truly was, which bugged me SOOO MUCH. Another part that bothered me was the romance portion of the novel. The main character had THREE LOVE INTERESTS, I repeat: THREE LOVE INTERESTS. In my opinion. that's excessive and unnecessary. I didn't even see a reason for one of them to even be a love interest. Kai. I didn't like him at all and he honestly didn't even need to be in the book at all The only character I liked was Jagger, but that's it. I got SOOO FRUSTRATED whenever she didn't trust him, or didn't give him hope of their love. He was trying SOO HARD and she just had her eyes for Bale, who I also didn't like. I also really enjoyed when she was with the Robbers. That was such a cool setting, and I loved all the characters in there. Another thing I didn't like was that Snow took control of her powers too quickly. She only had around 3 practices and then she had complete control. A main thing that I don't like about her is that she refused to see what was right in front of her. She was really stubborn, and that REALLY bothered me. The ending went really downhill for me also. The world was really interesting, and there was so much potential to explore that world, but we never did. Another thing I didn't like was that this book seemed really choppy. Nothing really connected with each other. Snow met so many new people, some of them I saw no reason to even be in the novel. Overall, this book was disappointing for me, and I won't read the rest of the books in the series. I don't recommend this one.

I was able to finish STEALING SNOW, but only because I skipped a lot of it by skimming paragraphs to get to the end. 
 I can't think of anything in STEALING SNOW that would make me recommend it to someone. I was so completely bored and for some reason, instead of putting it down and marking it DNF (did not finish) I forced myself to keep reading in hopes that it would get better. Unfortunately it never did. 
 Where was the world building? I was thrown into a world that I didn't know anything about and at the end, I still felt like I knew nothing. I had a hard time picturing where the characters were and when I could picture where they were I felt like something else was introduced before I could get comfortable in knowing the last place. There was a LOT of jumping around going on and I was always left feeling like things were unfinished. Snow jumps from group to group and never really finishes anything with any of them. 
 The love triangle--or should I say square?-- was just another part of STEALING SNOW that I couldn't stand. Snow is in love with Bale, a fellow insane asylum patient, but then he's kidnapped and on her mission to find and save him there is Kai. But wait, it gets better! Here enters the thief. There is a lot of kissing other boys while her 'love' is sitting in a dungeon somewhere or maybe dead. I wasn't feeling any of her feelings at any time in STEALING SNOW. 
 I am really surprised I didn't put STEALING SNOW down and was able to make it to the end. I absolutely hate that I was insanely bored with everything about it because I hate writing bad reviews. There was just way too much going on with zero development to fall back on in every part of this book.

 I really went back and forth on even writing this review, because it hurts my heart to say negative things about Danielle Paige's writing. She is one of the sweetest authors I have interacted with, so please remember that I feel that way through this review. 
 Now, I was super excited to pick this up at BEA, not only to meet Danielle, but to get to read it because I loved the Dorothy Must Die series. I read some negative reviews before starting, but chose to ignore them and give it my all as I usually do. I was pretty interested for the first several chapters, but then I kept finding my mind wandering. Still, I stuck with it and read, but just could not make myself be interested in what was going on or invested in the characters. I think I would have liked a little more background on Snow and a little more struggle with her trying to learn how to use her newly found magic abilities. I can't help but think of the scenes from the Twilight series where Bella is learning to use her powers after becoming a vampire as an example of more of what I would have wanted. I'm not sure why it just didn't sit well with me. I also didn't care for any of the love interests (and yes there was more than one, even more than two actually) and didn't find myself rooting for any of them to be the one for Snow. Overall, I just couldn't stay focused and I feel like I missed a lot of details because I wasn't paying attention. I don't think I'll investigate this series further, but that won't stop me from purchasing it for my library and letting some students try it out. Maybe it just wasn't my cup of tea, maybe I just liked Dorothy Must Die so much because I've always been a bit obsessed with Wizard of Oz...I'm just not sure. I wouldn't discourage others from reading this one, I just wouldn't pick it up again myself. Again, I love Danielle Paige, and I'm sorry that I didn't love this particular book.

DNF at page 130 
 Why I DNF'd: The story. Where the heck was the story?? 
 I wanted to like this so bad!! You see, I don't read a lot of fantasy, but I want to try to broaden my horizons and read more of it. I've had luck with retellings, so this was all over my radar!! Alas, I was just not feeling it. 
 It starts with Snow in a mental hospital, and that was the only part I liked. I felt like that world was explained and the characters felt real. Once she left there it was like an outline took over instead of an actual book. There was no world, it was just oh you fell down a tree and here you are in Algid... and BTW it's cold here & you are a princess with powers. And Snow's just like-- are all these guys here single??(cause she crushes on EVERY guy she comes across). After that random things started happening just to happen. It didn't feel believable, it felt... lazy? I don't know where this book goes from there, but I don't really care. I don't feel like the author took enough time to care about the world, so I'm not going to take time to care to read it.

 there were twists and turns, love interest galore and fights... but it felt rushed. the relationships were too much in too short a period. ending was abrupt. I know you're probably setting up for a second book but I've never felt so short changed in my book loving life.

Well, this was definitely a case of everyone else was right. When people started reviewing ARCs or whatever they had of this I was surprised. Many of the people on my Goodreads wall disliked it, but it looked AWESOME. It's been there, mocking me on my to-read list for ages. So what if I didn't really like Dorothy must Die? This book should have been written just for me! 
 But alas, it wasn't. Instead of the cool Snow Queen retelling I was envisioning, I got a random mish mash of subplots, prophecies, random kissing, random training and I'm not even going to sugar coat, some of the most simplistic and terrible writing I've ever encountered. I used to proof read English assignments for some of my friends, many of whom had never read a novel. Reading their disaster work would be a blessing after some of the work I just read. I just...no. 
 So I really don't have a problem with the main character going around and kissing hot boys. If I did, I wouldn't still be reading Anita Blake after all these years. My problem is when all three boys are the exact same characterization. There is nothing to define any of them, except they are all brooding bad boy types with hearts of gold. They also have a magical ability to be around other pretty girls and only see Snow -gag-. 
 Add all of this together with too many prophecies, awesome unique magic skills, unknown twin sister, absent parent who truly loves them both! poor action/fight scenes and this made for an excruciating read for me. Ahem. This is definitely a time where I should have listened to the reviews ;_; But still, it takes all sorts and I was determined to try this for myself. Maybe someone else will enjoy it more, because it's going in my donation pile for the Op Shop! :/

*Warning: Rant below* 
 This was SO DISAPPOINTING! I was so excited about Stealing Snow that I actually preordered it despite how much I disliked Dorothy Must Die. This book was written very similarly to Dorothy Must Die it's like the author used the same formula for both books. This was such a mash up of different plot lines that nothing made sense. Our main character starts out in an insane asylum, gets transported to a magical land and just accepts everything without question. There is NO world building it's hard to have a clear picture of anything in the novel. There is a magical training plot line that ends abruptly and then turns into a heist story. There is a LOVE SQUARE, guys. A LOVE SQUARE. Why? When is that ever necessary? I can handle a love triangle, and there are a few love triangles that I actually enjoy, but you throw one more love interest in there for shits and giggles and I'm gonna hate it. There is absolutely no reason for our main character to have 3 love interests at all. The whole point to the story is for Snow to rescue the guy she loves who was kidnapped and brought to this magical land, but she somehow falls for two random guys she meets along the way. Why? It made me hate Snow as a character. This was so badly written that half the time I wasn't sure what the characters were talking about, but maybe that was the lack of world building. There are a few 'plot twists' that you can see coming from a mile away, like every single plot twist (there's 3 that I can think of) I guessed early on in the book. I really cannot think of one redeeming thing in this book, not a single thing comes to mind that I actually enjoyed. I finished this book last night and I've already forgotten half of the characters names and things that happened to them. This book took me two weeks to read (I started and finished more than 10 books in that time, and all of them were much better than this) and everything about it is easily forgotten. I love the original Hans Christian Andersen story of The Snow Queen (and Disney's version as well, don't judge me!), it's one of my favorite fairy tales, but this was so terribly done that it didn't feel anything like the story at all. 
 I'm so upset by this book that I don't know if any of my rant is coherent, but seriously, save yourself the aggravation and skip this one.
Hey guys, I read a book!

Started in a psych ward and then moved to a magical land. 
 A magical land of death, pain and manipulation. I mean, really?! Both parents of Snow are trying to kill her. The boy she loves is trying to kill her and she's required to kill lots of people to become queen of this land. 
 Might as well have stayed in the psych ward.
