 Ok, not gonna lie, my disappointment with Yellow Brick War may have colored my reading of Paige's next novel A LOT. 
 I'm not familiar with the story of The Snow Queen, so I can't compare this retelling with the original. 
 I went back and forth between things happening too slow and things moving too fast. Once Snow joined up with the Robbers, things really sped up and not necessarily for the best. 
 Will I read the next in the series...hard to say.....

I'm usually fairly careful when choosing which books to read, but this time, apparently, I've chosen grossly wrong. At first glance , it had all the elements that usually appeal to me - snow magic, a fairytale retelling, asylums &etc. But frankly, at the end of the day, it was like listening to a computer voice reading a book out loud with a plot that was supposed to be exciting but turned out to be very dull indeed. It was just so... emotionless, I feel like reading something truly angsty after this just to cleanse myself.

Well this is weird. 
 The asylum angle is BAD. The twists on the fairy tale are interesting, especially the focus on the mirror. Ending - too soapy. Still uncertain what Snow is actually like. EH. 
 Also, compared to DMD, the plot arc is... shallow, familiar. Confused, angry girl travels to pretty land full of hidden evil, gives up on one branch of magic, embarks on "training" in some other branch of magic that all has a lot to do with eye candy, teens in a clubbing army, Dragonball Z-style five-episode-long Final Confrontation that isn't even final. Also, boy drama. Not impressed.

Curse my inability to stay away from retellings. 
 Just like Dorothy Must Die, I found myself not rushing to read the first few chapters and doing exactly the opposite when I got near the end. The story and the pacing were okay, well, the story needed time (or should I say lots of pages) to build its way around your imagination and make it easy for you to imagine Algid. I didn't like how the MC kept jumping from one place to another and having each guy from that place fall for her, it just felt a little funny for me that her main motive in the story is to save the boy she claims that she truly loves but fall for each guy she meets along the way. I mean there were just two guys, but still. This is just book one. Will there be more love interests in book two???? Because I'm here to see how her powers would improve and if what Margot said about her having more access to the elements is true. Not as to who Snow ends up with in the end. SMH 
 I think the characters need more pages to grow on me. They just felt weak for me at the moment. Their roles, I mean. There were lots of characters which I don't mind, but there was too much drama, and maybe it's just the author trying to give the readers a taste of what's more to come, and that in the end everything will be tied up in a big ol' ribbon, but ALL the revelations felt too sudden. 
 But like I said, the story appealed to me even though the writing style felt flat...and I'm still anticipating the next installment of this series because, just like Dorothy Must Die, Stealing Snow left me hanging. But not in a good way.

I listened to the audiobook of this one. I really enjoyed it for a nice light read. The actor sometimes seemed like she was forcing her lines and the main character got a bit annoying with being so flighty in her romantic interests. But over all I enjoyed it. I plan to get the sequel when it comes out-if there is one.

This book was so terrible. I don't know why I kept reading it. It was seriously more painful than Twilight (or whatever other book you dislike.) 
 It started off well enough, but the writing was pretty juvenile. "Oh well," I thought. "if that's the worst it gets, it's going to be great!" 
 NOPE. 
 SO WRONG. 
 The plot didn't completely suck, but the writing was so bad. And the characters. Does everyone have to fall all over themselves at Snow's pretty princess feet? She's not nearly that interesting. But it seems like every teenage male she meets just HAS to kiss her. And considering she only met 3 teenage males in the course of the novel... yep. So much stupid kissing. 
 Skip this one. Not worth it in the least.

So basically I was supposed to fulfill some kind of major destiny in a month. And I had no idea this place even existed until now. 
 (+deg#deg)+( +-+ REALLY? REALLY?! 
 I love retellings. I even loved Dorothy Must Die, despite the scandal surrounding the publishing of that book. It had spirit. It was fun. The setting of the book was recognizable, but there was creativity in the way the book built the mythology around the original. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same for this book. This was simply a dull, plodding book. 
 To be fair, I entered the book with a misconception. I expected Snow White. This book was more of a retelling of 
 The Snow Queen 
 with elements of Snow White - she calls her medications the "dwarves." One of the only bright things about the book was that throughout the book, I was imagining one of my favorite k-pop idols - also named Kai - as the love interest. 
 Can you blame me? HNNNNNNNNNGGGGGGGGGG 
 The book had many faults. Unfortunately, life is short, and I shall limit myself to listing three. Never mind. Four. 
 1. The casual and one-dimensional interpretation of mental illness. Snow is crazy. She bites people. That's it, she bites people. The people in the asylum are generic crazy people acting out. There is no depth to them, there is no true portrayal of any type of mental illness besides acting generally insane and taking lots and lots of pills and dealing with orderlies. 
 2. THE LOVE TRIANGLE. Holy fuck, why?! Snow is IN WURVE with this one boy, Bale, in the mental institution. She gets pulled into this other world and all of a sudden she's kissing this HAWT, MYSTERIOUS STRANGER NAMED KAI. To be fair, I would have kissed the aforementioned Kai if he looked like that gif above. Again, HNNNNNNNNNNNNG. 
 3. ZEE CHOSEN ONE. AGAIN, WHY?! OF ALL THINGS. Haven't we had enough of these stupid chicks with prophesied powers that all of a sudden emerge for no fucking reason other than they were the product of a special sperm and a special egg? 
 There was a prophecy spoken on your birth to the three most powerful witches in the land. Remember, you are the daughter of magic on both sides of your lineage. You have magic within you. Powerful magic, probably the strongest that Algid has ever seen. 
 4. What world building? I honestly am not sure where I was in the book, what the point is, and why I should care? There was no world building, there was random slapdash elements of a generic, and I do not use that word lightly, fantasy world. Magical stuff and magical people without an iota of explanation or personality for me to give a fuck. 
 This book was such a 180 from the author's previous one that it's nearly incomprehensible.

reference_books.review_text: Simple, short and sweet story. I felt that the style of writing was a bit fan fictiony but it was a nice easy read. reference_books.title: Falling Kingdoms (Falling Kingdoms, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Ok so let's start out with the good points about this book. Book cover is pretty cool and the idea of this story is promising. Here's the bad news. I was pretty disappointed with this book. The characters drove me nuts and the book seemed to be on the verge of a older young adult book but the characters are what killed that idea. The characters drove me nuts and I honestly felt like there was an invisible Cupid shooting people with his arrows throughout the book. This book was very predictable and I highly doubt I'll continue this series. I wanted to like this book and I desperately tried to like it but this book just didn't work for me. The book covers still draw me to the books but the content doesn't. This book wasn't a match for me. Overall, I would say this book is a 1 out of 5.

reference_books.title: Shatter Me (Shatter Me, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Ok so first of all I had somewhat high expectations because I've seen this book everywhere and I've heard a lot of good/bad reviews. The description of the book seemed kind of unique and intriguing so I had high hopes but I'm sad to say that this book was disappointing. I can't deny that the book made me feel sad for the character and that the oddly creative descriptions were intriguing at first but the style of writing really got tiring around 40% into the book. I understand the state of mind that the main character is in and it explains why she describes things the way she does but after a while it got to be a bit too much. I can't deny that some of the descriptions were so ridiculous that there were eye rolling/eyebrow raising/laughing moments. I just feel that the author tried way too hard to be poetic/creative when writing this book. It got tiring really quick and I honestly really wanted to like this book but I felt like I was reading fan fiction. The writing seemed choppy and the story was centered around main points and didn't really have any calm/in between moments (if that makes sense?). The story was too centered around romance which highly disappointed me. I thought the overall idea of the storyline was good but didn't live up to itself. The storyline reminded me of Divergent and Delirium quite a bit. I honestly don't know if I'll read the next book because of how annoying the book was but maybe I'll just read the next book to find out the ending. *shrugs* I wouldn't really recommend this book to someone but either people love this book or hate it so I guess if you really want to read it I can't say I didn't warn you.

reference_books.title: Matched (Matched, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book was not worth my time. I was led to believe that this book was sort of like the Hunger Games with the whole society ordeal. But sadly it wasn't. This book just isn't worth your time. I also didn't really like the way this book was written. The author made the main character, Cassia, seem a lot younger then she actually was. I was looking forward to reading this book but not anymore.

reference_books.title: Winter (The Lunar Chronicles, #4)
reference_books.review_text: Wow. It's so hard to believe that this book series is over. The book in its entirety was enjoyable and overall satisfying. It's always sad to finish a book series that you've become well aquatinted with and have loved. The author did an excellent job overall with this book and book series in its entirety. The only character that got on my nerves was Winter because they kept on going on and on about her beauty but I guess that's just part of the story. I would totally and completely recommend this book. It's well worth the time. I can fully say that this is by far one of my favorite books series. :)

reference_books.title: Crooked Kingdom (Six of Crows, #2)
reference_books.review_text: Why is this series over with?!?! :( This book was awesome. I enjoyed this book the entire time and I'm so sad this is the last book. Why can't this series be longer?! I can defiantly say, hands down, that this book is going on my favorites list. The whole atmosphere of the book gives off a Black Sails/ Pirates of the Caribbean/ Sherlock Holmes(Robert Downy Jr. version) vibe which is totally a positive thing. I absolutely love the unexpected twists and turns that you think you know about but you actually don't. An incident towards the end of the book was totally unexpected and I'm just wanting more from this book series. I just can't express how much I enjoyed this series. I'll defiantly look into other books from this author. Overall, amazing 5 star book!

book_a.title: When Dimple Met Rishi
book_a.user_review: To be honest, I wasn't overall impressed with this book. I loved the idea of learning about a culture but I found the story line not really exciting. I honestly thought that certain "events" were going to happen towards the end of the book and not half way. Overall, kind of disappointing.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book had so much potential, but it was a couple of different cute tropes smashed into one so that none of them were as satisfying as they could have been. For example, Dimple and Rishi get off on a really bad start, but ended up kind of stuck together as partners in the same place for six weeks. That sounds like a delightful hate-to-love story, but somehow ended up feeling like insta-love. There was no sense of pacing. 
 In addition to that, I found Dimple so frustrating. She started off so well, resentful of her mother's expectations and with huge ambition. But she was just so cruel. And although she did come to some realizations, it felt like Rishi changed a LOT more. 
 Some stuff with the supporting characters was also badly done. Again, mostly a pacing issue.

This was so adorable and cute, and cuLTURALLY DIVERSE!! I loved loved LOVED how we saw how Dimple and Rishi differed in their views of their family traditions and how Dimple in particular struggled with them. I love the messages this book sends out, like pursue your dreams, and I love how we saw Rishi and Dimple's relationship develop; it was so adorable and precious! I just kinda disliked the secondary characrers though, and would've liked it if they had played a bigger/more significant role in the plot or something. This book is definitely a 4,5 stars rating for me!

What a disappointment. At first I thought this book was cute but the more I read the more annoyed and bored I got. 
 The biggest problem with the book is that there's no romantic or sexual chemistry between Dimple and Rishi. They're supposed to go from (one-sided) dislike to friends to lovers but it just wasn't convincing to me. If the book was about their friendship, it would be much more believable. It didn't help that the POVs kept switching way too fast. And that subplot with Ashish and Celia was unnecessary and just as unconvincing. 
 Both Dimple and Rishi are competing in Insomnia Con (really bad name). It's supposed to be a web development program, and we never get to find out much about it, but if I understood correctly they're making a mobile app. Web development and app development are very different things, so this doesn't make sense. The book takes place during the six weeks of Insomnia Con but it doesn't seem like they're there at all, that's how little they talk about it. They spend much more time talking and preparing for some ridiculous talent contest. This talent show has nothing to do with tech industry but apparently everyone has to participate. And there's a statistic that says 78% of talent show winners also won Insomnia Con - but those are completely different competitions that have nothing to do with each other! Why would your ability to dance or sing have anything to do with how good your app is? 
 I really wanted to like this book, it had so much potential. But it was too predictable. And I think the author avoided writing about the details of app development because she doesn't know anything about it - but that's why writers need to do research. I feel like I would have enjoyed this much more if I read it ten years ago.

I think I am just gonna DNF this one. It is too damn cliched for my liking. Found the story quite.. not mature too. Romantic or sentimental readers might love this but too bad I'm neither romantic nor sentimental. 
 Plus I am quite unhappy with the Hindi terms in the book. If the author wanted to make the story original and unique, at least insert some side notes or footnotes of the meaning of the terms and not expect all the readers to understand Hindi. I mean, what the heck man. I like to know every details in the story. Stuff like this is just not cool.

 and then meet Dimple who actually is saying to her parents ( F** you guys I will do what I want and ain't no body gonna stop me ) 
 their parents wants them to marry 
 what happens when they meet ? .. Dimple wins .. EVERY . SINGLE . TIME .. and Rishi being used to being the underdog straight up falls in love with her with no real reason !!, WTH ? whatever Dimple says it will happen like magic with no regards to how Rishi feels .. man this was so frustrating to me 
 there were some cute moments when they reference some of my favorite Indian movies, and the ending was nice .. but man that was a tough ride for me .. another disappointment over a hyped book

This might be my favorite book of the summer. Dimple and Rishi are engaging characters who shuck many YA conventions while the story plays out in a relatable way. 2.5/5 stars. This was a very sweet YA story, but some of the dialogue seemed very contrived and unrealistic. Some of the side characters seemed really stereotypical. Lots of juvenile behavior and shenanigans. My favorite thing was a male protagonist who was really earnest and expressive.

This was really cute! I'm always wary at first of potentially stereotypical representations of Indian parents, and I wasn't sure about Dimple's mom in the beginning, but actually most of the family dynamics in this book played out in a believable way. Also, to me at least, Dimple is really relatable as an Indian-American teenager, especially in terms of self esteem (varies from knowing she's smart to feeling unfavorably desi, i.e. not cute/cool). Also she's relatably grumpy, because high school and rich white kids and Indian patriarchal pressures suck. Anyway, she gains confidence throughout the course of the story, which is nice to see. 
 As far as the romance aspect, even though you do have to accept a certain level of rom-com cheesiness (mostly only at the beginning of the story), Dimple and Rishi have an easy rapport, friendship, and ~chemistry~. Their challenges/differences reflect a realistic gendered dynamic I've seen in real life where RIshi wants to respect his parents' traditions and wishes re: education and marriage, and Dimple is more interested in freeing herself from obligation, finding independence, and developing her interests/career. They have to work to understand and respect each other's needs if they want to establish any kind of friendship or relationship. 
 The setting, a six-week web development camp at San Francisco State University, is fun and it moves the plot along at a nice pace. Because the people and places around the camp are new and exciting for the characters, they're also new and exciting for readers, creating an atmosphere of unpredictability and possibility that can be especially engaging for a teen audience. 
 I'd recommend this as a fun read and also as an example of healthy relationship dynamics (especially for straight and "westernized" brown kids -- American-Born-Confused-Desis -- but for others too!)

Two and a half stars. 
 When Dimple Met Rishi is simply a love story of two Indian teens. It started with marriage arrangement that ended with consent commitment. It's one of Bollywood movie that's 'written in the stars' with a twist of American contemporary young adult. The story is rich with Indian culture and diversity, which is what YA world wants and needs right now. 
 It's just the execution is not quite like it sounds in the blurb. I get it that the MC was 'independent, strong woman' but did she have to prove it by punching the love interest in ribs becaude she was 'not like other girls'? Maybe she was trying too hard or maybe she was just abusive. The MC pretty drives me confused and mad. 
 Actually, I have a bad feeling about her from the very first chapter, when her mother was carrying tea cups with trembling hands and she didn't even flinch, let alone help. If I were her mother I'd have had her on my lecture. And then, she continued her annoying attitude to Rishi who tried to be nice to her all the time. Was she trying too hard to show that she's important? Other characters were confusing as well, some of them even stereotypical, although not as bothersome as the female protagonist. 
 And it's not just about the characters. The writing style, too. At first it was okay, and then it goes like generic YA with sentences like 'I want you. I want you so bad' and other cheesy examples. I... wow. A reviewer said it sounds like middle grade writing, and I agree with her. It sounds childish and over the top. It's a miracle I can stand it until the end, LOL. 
 Last, the universe Dimple and Rishi in. I just didn't buy the Cons they attend (okay, maybe I enjoy Little Comic Con more than Insomnia Con). Or maybe I need to research about that kind of coding convention/coding camp. It's kinda unfortunate because I'm insterested in coding world Dimple is involved in, but there were very little coding story in the con itself. 
 Here's the good thing though: besides interesting Indian culture, when Dimple is not abusive, she and Rishi can have fascinating deep conversation about principle and what they see in life, affected by their experience and how they are raised. I think marriage arrangement has its own perks, one of them is when two parties share their vision and mission in relationship, until they realize they need to compromise instead of changing each other. 
 So... this book actually has potential especially because it offers diversity. However, the MC, writing style, and 'world building' just doesn't meet my liking. Maybe it'd appeal to some of romance contemporary readers, so you may as well give it a go if you feel interested in this book.

 I know people say do not judge a book by its cover, but damn, this book is absolutely GORGEOUS. When I got it in the mail, it was so bright and orange. After reading the premise and reviews for this book, my hopes were soaring. A contemporary, young-adult, romantic novel with two non-white characters? Please take my money! Being half South-Asian, I was ecstatic to see this book getting rave reviews on social media. The only South-Asian characters I can remember from a book are the Patil twins from the Harry Potter series. 
 Dimple is heading off to Stanford in a few months! She is passionate about coding and establishing a career in computer science. However, she struggles to find a balance between her American and South-Asian roots. Dimple does not want to get married or have children at an early age. Since Dimple has no desire to pursue a traditional life, she feels like she is a disappointment to her mother. On the other hand, Rishi is a hopeless romantic who wants to follow tradition and please his parents. Despite agreeing to study engineering at MIT, Rishi secretly draws comic books to get away from the stressors of life. Their parents have set them up to have an arranged married (and not the selling your daughter to Rumpelstiltskin kind of way) because they seem suitable for each other. When they Dimple and Rishi meet at Insomnia Con, the pre-university coding camp, things are going to head for a surprising turn. 
 In my opinion, the way Sandhya Menon portrayed Indian culture in When Dimple Met Rishi was HIGHLY accurate. The fact that I felt like I was reading my life on these pages is a good sign. It was the small details that caught my attention. From the Hindi phrases, family gatherings over chai and biscuits, Bollywood music and Indian snacks. It all made me reminisce and I am thrilled that other non-Indian readers are getting a glimpse at my upbringing. But there were also a lot of serious topics the author touched on too. As a South-Asian woman, I definitely felt the internal struggles Dimple went through. From my experience, there is a lot of pressure put on women to wear makeup and nice clothes for the purpose of landing a suitable spouse. There was much less emphasis on establishing a career or obtaining a solid education. It can often be difficult to navigate between two cultures. 
 Although I loved reading about the cultural bits in this book, I felt like the story itself was lacking and it kills every inch of my soul to say that. I really wanted to like this book, but I can only give it an okay rating. To be honest, the beginning of this book was a bit hard to get through. I was shocked at how immature some of the characters in the book seemed. In university, people tend to be a bit more mature than they were in high school. I would even say the characters in this book acted like they were in middle school. 
 I felt like the lackluster secondary characters took away from the story. I know a lot of people who gave this book negative reviews disliked Dimple and I can understand why. She sometimes look down on girls who wear makeup, provocative clothing and join sororities. But this part never threw me off. I think a lot of books sadly praise girls for not acting in a stereotypical manner. The example that comes to my mind is Hermione Granger and Ginny Weasley (both of whom I adore) from Harry Potter. While girls that cry, giggle, wear makeup or dress up are looked down upon. 
 The chemistry between Dimple and Rishi was cute and well-paced. In my opinion, it never felt forced but natural. It felt like they were growing to love each other. Despite this, I found the beginning of their relationship to be boring. Without getting into spoilers, I loved the dynamic of their relationship near the end, but it was hard for me to read through the beginning. It was like eating an upside down cupcake. Although I found this book slightly disappointing, I am glad books like this exist and are paving the way for diverse characters to exist in our stories. I still enjoyed parts of it and I would recommend reading it if you like cute and contemporary stories. I think Menon is an awesome writer and I look forward to reading more of her up-coming releases in the future.

I originally had no intention of reading Sandhya Menon's When Dimple Met Rishi because I generally avoid straight-up romances; but with people seeming to love it on Twitter and the fact that the protagonist is Desi, I figured I'd give it a try. Having read When Dimple Met Rishi now, I have mixed feelings about it. 
 On the one hand, I loved how I could relate to Dimple so much. Guys, the pressure to find a good husband is real, and the conversations Dimple has with her mom regarding marriage are definitely similar to ones that I've had with older female family members. I also loved how Menon blended Indian culture into the experience of a teen growing up in America. For example, Hindi is integrated seamlessly in conversations between Dimple or Rishi and their parents. 
 On the other hand, I wasn't crazy about the romance, and was kind of disappointed that the coding aspect of the plot was overshadowed by it. I also found Dimple to be very self-righteous at times and didn't like how quickly she judged others. For example, Dimple describes Isabelle as "the blond girl who wore a perpetual sneer as if she were too good for all of this" (p. 54) even before getting to know her. 
 Despite its flaws however, I'd recommend giving When Dimple Met Rishi a chance if only because of how authentic Dimple and Rishi's voices felt as South Asian-American teens.

So I started reading When Dimple Met Rishi with high expectations. I have heard a lot of people say they absolutely loved it and that it was so diverse, cute, and one of the best books this year. I was slightly disappointed to find out it didn't live up to my expectations. Shame on me for expecting anything to be what I expected, right? I shouldn't put that much pressure on a book. 
 It was diverse because it was about two teenage Indian Americans trying to break through their standard expected lives to try and be themselves when their parents want them to take the route they were born into, like arranged marriages. 
 Dimple was a feminist, which at first I was all for, but then I noticed she was kind of annoying, and a throw-it-down-your-throat feminist who was already on her own route to life but still wanted to complain and moan about her parents, claiming they weren't accepting or didn't want her to happy in life, when actually it seemed they did, they just wanted to be parents and see if her and Rishi were a match. No biggie. After all, I don't recall her thanking them for introducing them, *wink wink* 
 I also didn't really like when they were speaking in Indian and I had no idea what they were saying, maybe only twice when they actually translated it. 
 In the beginning I was loving the story and really liked Dimple and Rishi, but once I was 3/4 i started to not enjoy it as much. I thought it was too cheesy and not as exciting as before, I started to not enjoy Dimple, or any of the characters actually. I almost put the book down but wanted to see how it ended. I like how it ended, though, it ended like a cheesy contemporary would, giving the reader satisfaction and relief.

I'm so angry at this book! 
 I preordered it months ago based on the description: A YA POC romance involving a tech savvy nerdy girl. What could be better? This sounded like my jam. 
 Oh, I was wrong. Prepare for a rant. 
 The story takes place at a web dev summer program/competition inappropriately called "Insomnia Con" which is neither a 24 hour codeathon nor a convention. Obviously, the author is out of her tech league here. There's a total of ~3 pages talking about working on the app Dimple and Rishi drafted over six weeks. The rest of the time is spent moving from fancy restaurant to fancy restaurant, going on "non-dates", and, for some bizarre reason, practicing for a talent show. Yup. You read that right, a performance talent show where Dimple and Rishi dance on stage for an audience. This has NOTHING to do with coding or web development but the story forced it in so heavy-handedly to even include a passage about those who win the talent show usually go on to win the competition. An app design competition. If I attended this "Insomnia Con" I'd ask for my money back and site this as a gross incompetence. But the part that threw me completely over the edge was that Dimple and Rishi only completed a wireframe of their app for final submittal. They had six dedicated weeks to build something and they only finished a wireframe?! WTF Menon?! Once again, I'd ask for my money back if all the students finished in six weeks was a wireframe. Oh, but the rage gets better: the "judges" for this "competition" are two rich people in their sixties, because everyone knows old people are the best judges for up-and-coming apps, and nepotism plays heavily in the outcome. The author is soooooo ignorant of the tech community it's embarrassing. If this really went down in the Bay Area it would lose all credibility. 
 Just because stories about women in STEM are popular doesn't mean everyone should write about them. Know your subject matter.

That this wasn't the case was the first thing that threw me off a bit. 
 The second thing were the characters. 
 I liked the main characters well enough, even though both Dimple and Rishi annoyed me at time, but the supporting characters just felt a bit two-dimensional to me, personally. They just didn't seem like real persons, they were just characters in a book and I think that's part of the reason why I couldn't quite dive into the story completely. 
 The third and last thing that kind of destroyed the buzz I felt about reading this story was the way it was exerted. The writing was solid but sometimes did not really work in favour of me falling deeper into the story. For example 'it was funny and fun'. Maybe that is some kind of stylistic device I don't get or I just can't appreciate but it really kicked me out of the story at that point. This is the most extreme example but there were other phrases/ situations/ parts of dialogue that destroyed the story's flow for me as a reader. 
 What I can say about this book is that I expected something completely different and that may have tarnished the experience for me.

 I'm not sure how Kiera Cass has so much power over words to be able to produce such swoon worthy books. Her books are so light, romancey, and just easy to read. I really appreciate that. Having been a faithful reader of The Selection series from the start, I was rather excited to pick up this book and see if Eadlyn picked the same boy I did. (PSST - She did!) 
 This story starts out with Eadlyn trying to figure out how to continue with everything in her life after the sudden heart attack her Mother suffered. How can she continue with the selection process while trying to run a country at the same time? Eadlyn reminds herself that she was born a princess and as such, she will continue to rule with grace and beauty. Eadlyn does have her struggles along the way. She truly never thought she would find love in any of the thirty-five boys chosen and was only doing this selection to make her parents happy. However, she is slowly discovering that she doesn't have to keep her walls up all of the time and it is okay to let someone know the personal part of yourself. How else will she be able to find that magic and chemistry that her parents have? 
 It has been no secret that Eadlyn's character annoyed the snot out of me from the beginning. She starts out as one of the most self-centered, self-absorbed, entitled little brats I have ever seen in written form. Granted, I'm sure Ms. Cass meant to do that but it made the story that much more difficult to get through. I'm happy to say that Eadlyn found a way to grow and mature as the story progresses. While Eadlyn did grow up and realized that the world did not revolve around her, her emotional state was seriously all over the charts. It was almost too much at times. One moment she is rock solid sure of herself, then something small happens and she starts to question everything she has ever done in her entire life. She questions who she is as a person and who she would be as queen due to the simplest comment from someone that doesn't even matter. It almost gave me whiplash how back and forth she was. That is probably the one complaint I have about her. 
 The pacing of the story was pretty good, keeping a steady flow which made the story go relatively fast. Sure, there were parts that were fluffed up for the sake of the story, but since it is a short book, it was good. Here is the one issue I have with the ENTIRE book: it felt like everything was wrapped up in the last two pages of the book. ARE YOU SERIOUS? Is that necessary? NO. It isn't. Eadlyn makes her choice of who she wants to marry (no spoilers, I promise) and then *BAM* - attempts to make a crap-ton of things happen all at once. That crap should have been spread out over a chapter or two. There was no need to snowball into a word-vomit tirade that ended the entire book. When it was over, I sat staring blankly ahead wondering what just happened. It wasn't a good "what just happened?!" either. It was a "did that just happen?!" reaction. I really, really dislike when authors rush the ending. TAKE. YOUR. TIME. The reader is obviously invested in your story, keeping them for another chapter or so won't hurt anyone. 
 Overall, yes, I enjoyed the book. Would I recommend? Ehhhhhhhhhhhhhh.... it was a good tag on to the first part of the series but it isn't something I would urge people to rush and buy unless they are die hard Kiera Cass fans (like me).

Eadlyn is bratty and irritating to read in The Heir, and her development in The Crown just feels too forced and sudden. reference_books.title: The Song of Achilles
reference_books.review_text:
So...I didn't hate it. I mean, I kind of did, but this book's saving grace is Miller's expertise with the Classics, and that she laid out Ancient Greece and its culture in a way that was both interesting and accessible. My only complaint there is that the world would be even better if it was shown, instead of told. 
 I hate romance novels, though. And this...this is a standard romance novel. That it's about the love between two men doesn't make me like it any better than I like straight-couple bodice rippers. 
 Possibly that's because Patroclus is written in such a way that he is identical to a damsel in distress--one pulled straight from a dime store smut novel. 
 Sigh. At least I didn't pay money for this. I'm going to need a good long break before I try another GLBT novel because so far, they're all like this.
