reference_books.review_text: I was pretty hooked on this at first. It has some really good, spooky scenes in the first act. Buuuut the pacing sort of lost me about 100 pages in. I'll probably come back and finish this one when I don't have such a huge stack of other books that I'm wanting to read, but for now, back to the library with you, book.

reference_books.title: The Night Circus
reference_books.review_text:
Beauty without substance. Two-dimensional characters. The end. 
 I mean the circus was cool, but it would have worked better as a painting or comic book than a novel.

reference_books.title: Outlander (Outlander, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I knew I'd never pick this series back up when people were horrified at a man being raped in the show but continue to swoon over it happening to women. 
 This goes in the same pile as Game of Thrones: the pile of books I let my cat shred.

reference_books.title: Beat the Reaper (Peter Brown #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The narrative style was almost simultaneously engaging and forced. How is that possible, you ask? Read it and see. 
 It kept throwing me out of the story, so I'll admit, I ended up not finishing it. (I would've had to renew it from the library to do so, and I decided there were things I wanted to read more.) 
 That being said the footnotes were informative and funny, and it's action packed. I'll most likely pick up something else by this author and hope I like the characters more.

reference_books.title: The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo
reference_books.review_text:
Meh. I didn't hate it but reading this was like being told different jokes with identical punchlines over and over. And over. 
 Maybe I just need to be in the mood to read about a straight girl talking about sex! (Which, side note, I applaud women being unashamed of their sexual freedom. I actually think it's great that we have female celebrities who are willing to be as boldly outspoken about their choices as men are 'allowed' to be. It's why I gave this book four tries. But, Amy, come on. Shake up the act a little, huh?) So yeah, I have no idea when I would ever be in the mood to read something like this when there's a TV to depict it in slightly less repetitive detail.

reference_books.title: Twilight (Twilight, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is the story of Bella, the girl who forgets to breathe, doesn't know where her lips are, and hates anyone who isn't supernaturally beautiful. Especially those horrible ordinary people at her new high school who inexplicably try and try again to befriend her. 
 The key to the plot is this: she's such a miserable little nonperson, she will literally try to kill herself unless she has a controlling, borderline-abusive, much older boyfriend telling her how to blow her nose. 
 ...The End.

reference_books.title: The Blind Assassin
reference_books.review_text:
I don't know why, but this book was impossible for me to get through. I normally love Margaret Atwood. I got 2/3 of the way in and couldn't even be bothered to remember the characters' names. That's when I realized it was time to just give up. 
 The prose was, as always, beautiful, though.

reference_books.title: Fight Club
reference_books.review_text: I wish I had read this before I saw the movie, but because I didn't, the twist was spoiled for me. Without the surprise, almost everything about the book fell flat for me.

book_a.title: Damned (Damned, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Oh, Chuck. His books are even more hit and miss than Windows OS releases. 
 I didn't actually finish the book. I'm all for shock but I got to the bit with the severed head and the giant and at that point it felt like the book had jumped the shark. Which is a shame because that was only 70 pages in, and apparently there's a sequel. 
 I didn't hate the book, but I don't like getting secondhand embarrassment for a book. Damned really is like watching a junior high boy try really hard to impress someone, and that's...that's about all I can say about it.

sample_reviews.review_text: Distinctly Palahniuk. Funny and gross and wildly imaginative. Not as fantastic as his earlier works but if you've already read Choke, Diary, Lullaby, Rant, etc...then add another to the list.

I'll admit I'm not a big Palahniuk fan (even though I've read a lot of his books). The premise was interesting, but I got tired of the repetitive structure and the humor just isn't my style (and I was flat out disgusted with many parts). It's a creative setting and I can see how some people would really enjoy it, I'm just not one of them. I finished it because it was a quick read, but I was definitely ready for it to end.

Hello Satan, are you there? Don't be hurt, but I didn't like this book. I never gave up hope but then I guess that is what Hell is, it is hoping that there will be some enjoyment after trudging past shit river listening to this whiney ass self victimized thirteen year old Breakfast Club wannabe as she slowly takes over Hell. Did I miss something? I mean I get it, she becomes a self empowered bully which did not bring me as much enjoyment as maybe it does others. In the end I learned people in Hell are not honest and the same can be said for people on earth so when this book was recommended I thought okay, and I read it. But then of course I am passing it on to someone else and telling them, yeah read it; it's good. So read this at your own risk.

I keep reading Chuck Palahniuk books hoping I'll re-discover the feeling I had going through Haunted for the first time. Never quite gets there for me. And reading the reviews below, it sounds like I'm not alone --- a lot of readers think back to the one, earlier Palahniuk novel that they absolutely loved. For some it's Fight Club, others it's Survivor, and for me it's Haunted. So is it unfair for me to give 2 stars to an author who clearly knows how to write well, just because I dislike the content and characters of the book I just read? Maybe in my earlier years (my much, much earlier years) I would have found Palahniuk's description of Hell really inventive, radical, and delightfully gross. As is, this book just doesn't fit my personal tastes and I'll pass on whatever few Palahniuk books come out next. Side note -- I laughed out loud reading Jacob's review below; it's brilliant. Well done, sir!

Just a bad book by almost any measure. Boring, forced, ill plotted...a mess. The potential redeeming factors were in the weirdness and absurdity of the topic, but instead these just reinforced the lack of internal coherence in the novel. It was clear little thought was given to the effects of the internal rules of his subcreation, instead only looking to what would create a fun scene. Even the vulgar absurdities that Palahniuk built his career upon seem calculatingly 'vulgar', 'offensive', and 'shocking'. These bits felt like Paris Hilton stepping out of her limo without panties, or Janet Jackson at the Super Bowl. 
 It was a dull book that seemed convinced it was clever.
Not shocking, boring. Or maybe shockingly boring. Like listening to a 3 hour recitation of someone you keenly dislike's acid trip. I loved Fight Club but I've officially given up on Palahniuk now.

A refreshing first person narration which takes a peek at life through the eyes of a dead rich tween girl. This is a fun quick read that has the ability to reveal some humorous, philosophical truths without ever feeling like a motivational or self help story. I can't comment on the Judy Blume style since, "never ever have I read any of those books", however it has been said t hat this story was written with those books in mind. This book could possibly be the most pleasant and even perky possibility of hell I have ever entered in word form. With that, if your looking for a quick fun ride to hell or maybe not all that obvious story filled with a few laughs and a few ironic characters, open this world up.

It's mostly dirge-like with the occasionally witty one-liner thrown in. Overly repetitive, frivolous, and boring on all accounts, but I did like the whole "people are the devil more than the devil" motif; I just had higher expectations for the humor.
I've read better books by Chuck.

I tried to listen this, which was some of the downfall. I do think that Palahniuk nails the repetitive nature of teenage girls, and their spirally thought patterns, but I just couldn't continue after trying for a few days.

I like Palahniuk and as many others have said in the past, Fight Club is genius. So I thought, what the heck let's try one of his newer books. However, this book was a disappointment with its tired trope of how hell is SO much better and more interesting than heaven. He throws in the standard amount of snide intelligentsia comments about right wing politics, celebrity culture, and environmental/health issues. And he does it all with style, actually, he does it all with many different styles and none of them are well thought-out or cohesive. The story changes direction at odd times and in odd ways, but not in a "good" kind of odd. It is just jarring in a "what the hell" kind of way. This isn't so much a novel as it is a writing exercise gone horribly awry. There is parody here, but it is unfortunately Palahniuk becoming a parody of himself. I've read some of his other stuff and he is so much better than this. Take my advice, don't let this book be your initial introduction to him.

2.5* This book was like a fever dream you'd have while high on acid. I did enjoy the unapologetic approach to describing Maddie Spencer's life on earth as well as the depiction of hell (aka the pool of unborn babies - seriously who comes up with this stuff). My issue with this was the stale, one-note characters that I was having a seriously hard time rooting for. But man, did I love the absurdity of this!

"Read" would be an over-statement but read 30 pages is more like it. There are many repetitive lines, like in a poem, in novel form. The book is well written, I must give the author credit for doing that, it was as if a 13 year old actually wrote it; the heroine being a 13. I found it annoying (the repetitiveness) and overall a bit boring. Did not finish.

The author's view of hell is gross and wonderful. The protagonist is delightful and her journey is worth taking. The story gets meandering at times. There is an arc, but the story feels incomplete, but a continuation is threatened. If it comes, I'll read it.
Ouch...it hurts me to not love this book, but I did not. Definitely not up to par with his usual.

2 1/2. Started reading this and didn't think too much of it, Palahnuik doing Bizarro-Lit. Then from reading some Goodread reviews I noticed they were mentioning Judy Blume alot, decided to look her up (having never been a pre-pubescent girl I've not had the prior need seemingly...) and then this book made alot more sense. However it did drag on a bit and just became Palahnuik doing Bizarro-Lit and imitating Judy Blume's writing style. Which is alright, but not amazing. 
 Then it ended with a To Be Continued... 
 *sigh*

Okay, so what happened to the sexiness that was Tell-All? 
 This book was just blah. The beginning was great, but I got bored by its monotony that I actually skipped a lot of chapters past the half of it. 
 Chuck may be a genius, but I think Damned turned out to be a fact book with a bit of plot instead of a novel with bits of fact. There's just too much fillers. 
 Thumbs up for the effort, though.

I only got 3 chapters in before I gave up. Each chapter repeated text from the previous where Palahuniuk's main character kept asserting she was a 13-year-old dead girl in hell. Between the repetition, and the fact that Palahniuk can't write a believable 13-year-old girl, especially in the first person, I lost interest. I am a fan of clever snark, and he has mastered that verbal trick in some of his other work. Just not this one.
Chuck always amazes me with new creative ways to right a book.
I'm unimpressed. I didn't like the characters or the story so it was hard to get into and even more difficult to get through.

I have a pretty high tolerance for Palahniuk weirdness (and grossness) but this one did me in before I got past the 6th chapter. It's just really freakin' gross. But more than that, there is also a running thing (I hate to call it a gag, cuz it's not funny the first time and it's just like nails on a blackboard the more it's done) where the heroine will use a big word in a sentence and then say, something like, 'Yes, I know the world inclement. I'm a dead teenager, not an idiot." The idea of however many more of those gags being used was more than I could stand. But mostly I just could not see this going anywhere I wanted to go, so I bailed. Happily.

Ever wondered what it'd be like in hell? Even in my worst nightmares, I never came up with the visions in Palahniuk's head, which includes lakes of vomit, deserts of dandruff, and mountains of toenail clippings. The swamp of partial birth abortions or the demons that devour you and spit out your bones... there is something in this hell to turn anyone's stomach. And for a 13 year old girl who never got the chance to grow breasts or have her first period, it's not so bad. At least, not with her friends, the rebel, the nerd, the jock, the prom queen... why you're right, it is kind of like The Breakfast Club in hell. 
 Not as much of an ick factor as some of Palaniuk's works, but brutal and in-your-face as you'd expect. Interesting concept.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book started slow and annoyingly. By the end of the book I was much more into reading it. If there is a sequel (as is somewhat hinted at) I would read it. Definitely not Palahniuk's best work though.

I've seen nothing but bent out of shape reviews of this book. People all pissed off that it's not Fight Club or that Palahniuk isn't Vonnegut. News flash! If you want to read about a mayhem mastermind with MPD, don't read this book, reread Fight Club. If you want Vonnegut, read The Slaughterhouse Five. 
 This book is by Chuck Palahniuk. It is a fictitious autobiographical account of a thirteen year old dead girl's experiences in the afterlife. She's a lot nicer than I was at thirteen, in general. She's also very defensive. It was kind of fun, kind of irreverent, fairly ridiculous, and very fast. I enjoyed it more than I did Diary and less than Rant or Survivor.
This book was horrible...I'm starting to wonder what I ever like in Chuck to begin with...wondering if it wasn't some author I picked up because someone said it was "cool".....it isn't.

I will forever love Chuck P. for writing Rant, but this one was full of gimmicks with out delivering much in the end. It was hard to determine exactly what the main character was trying to acheive for much of the book which made the whole thing confusing and uninteresting. I really wanted to like it,but I just couldn't.
This is the first Chuck Palahniuk book I've ever read. It will also be the last. Way too creepy and weird for me.
Only read part of it, but thought it was god awful. Am I missing something? Young teen-aged girl is dead and reporting about how it is in hell - pretty disgusting is how it is!

I have to return this book to the library soon, because despite putting it on hold, it has another hold on it already. Already. This Chuck Palahniuk guy sure is popular. Yet I feel as if I should do my civic duty and put a sticky note inside this book that reads, "Don't bother." That's pretty much my review of Damned, in two words. 
 Madison Spencer is a thirteen-year-old girl, the daughter of rich-but-eccentric parents who love her but are not close to her. She overdoses on marijuana on her thirteenth birthday, dies, and goes to Hell, which it turns out runs on candy and forces people to work, usually as telemarketers. (It is Hell, I guess, so that's fair.) 
 Madison Spencer is really concerned with letting you know that she is well aware of who Judy Blume is and that she has a good vocabulary. That's why she starts every chapter with a faux-naive address to the Prince of Lies himself: "Are you there, Satan? It's me, Madison," and why every time she uses a word that you might doubt a thirteen-year-old would know, she lampshades it by challenging you and reminding us of her bookish habits, because she feels alienated and angsty (unlike any other teen in the history of ever). When she isn't sharing her thoughts on her own sexuality, she's rubbing decaptitated heads into giant clitorises, telling living people that dying and going to Hell is a bucket o' fun, and punching Hitler and ripping off his moustache as a trophy (because why not?). 
 Going to be honest: I kind of stopped paying attention after the punching Hitler part. But by that time I was too far in to quit, and I rather hoped that Palahniuk would somehow pull a redemptive ending out of his ass that would, if not make my time sunk into this worth it, at least give me something marginally positive to say in this review. 
 Alas. 
 Damned occurs entirely in the first-person voice of Maddy. And that's where it falls flat for me: Chuck Palahniuk does not convince me that this is a thirteen-year-old girl, or at least, not any thirteen-year-old girl I want to sympathize with: 
 A crew of sinister Snarky Miss Snarky-pants girls at my old boarding school, the infamous three who taught me the French-kissing Game, they once professed toe ducate me about human reproduction. As they told it to me, the reason boys desire so desperately to kiss girls is because, with each kiss, the activity makes the boy's wanger grow larger. The more girls a boy can kiss, the larger a wanger he'll eventually possess, and the boys boasting the largest are awarded the best-paying, highest-status jobs. Really, it's all very simple. All boys devote their lives to amassing the most elongated genitals, growing the nasty things so that when they eventually wedge them inside some unfortunate girl, the distant end of the enlarged wanger actually breaks off--yes, the wanger flesh becomes so hardened that it shatters--and the broken portion remains lodged within the girl's hoo-hoo. This natural event is much like those lizards that live in arid deserts and can voluntarily detach their squirming tails. Any amount, from the pointed tip to almost the entire wiener, can literally snap off inside a girl, and she's fully unable to remove it. 
 WTF, Chuck? The above language sounds like something I'd more likely find in 
 Worst. Person. Ever. 
 --and you wish you were as darkly hilarious as Coupland. Not only is that just crude, but it's not even the type of crude that would actually slip out of a thirteen-year-old girl's lips. Trust me, I asked a couple of people who were once thirteen-year-old girls. Did you? 
 It's not even the "thirteen-year-old" or the "girl" parts that Palahniuk fails so badly at: Maddy just doesn't seem like an actual person. She is a badly written character. And given the equally-bad twist at the end, maybe that's intentional Palahniuk is just trying to be uber-meta and clever--but I'm just not charitable enough to cut him such a large length of slack. My slack is incredibly short supply these days, and I cannot dole it out to just anyone. You have to earn some of my slack, Chuck, and you don't do that here. 
 Even if I cut you slack on Maddy--and I'm not--the rest of Damned is still a disaster. Let's talk about Hell: 
 I explain the seemingly arbitrary rules of which people run afoul, how each living person is allowed to use the F-word a maximum of seven hundred times. Most living persons haven't the slightest idea how easy it is to be damned, but should anyone say fuck for the 701st time, he or she is automatically doomed. Similar rules apply to personal hygiene; for example, the 855th time you fail to wash your hands after voiding your bowels or bladder, you're doomed.... 
 Such yawn. Much boredom. 
 And yes--I will say this explicitly, lest someone reads these criticisms and challenges me on the grounds that I did not "get it"--I get it: Palahniuk is trying to make Hell sound boring and drab and overly bureaucratic. The problem with that? It's boring (and drab). Matthew Hughes does a far superior job depicting an overly-bureaucratic Hell. And he manages to do so while exploring some interesting moral and philosophical issues. Palahniuk just seems to be working out some prurient plotlines that don't actually go anywhere. 
 One reason I got so far into the book before realizing I should bail is that I was waiting for something to happen (beyond the going to Hell part). Maddy spends the first hundred pages stuck in a cell or wandering aimlessly around Hell with her friends before we even get a glimmer of the wider structure of the place. Even then there seems to be little hope of an over-arching storyline. Maddy veers from one remembrance of her parents' terrible parenting to another, and all the while she has conversations with living people over the phone. Oh, and then she goes off on some kind of sabbatical and ends up punching Hitler. 
 Because ... why not? 
 Then there's the twist at the end. Without spoiling it, all I can say is it puts Maddy in a Satan-killing mood, and that's where the book ends. On a cliffhanger. After less than three hundred pages. Maybe if you had led with the twist, Chuck, and built an engrossing story around it, then I would have liked Damned. As it is, now I just feel like you spent an entire novel working up to the real story, in Doomed. The irony here is that the only reason I read Damned is because my Dad gave me a copy of Doomed many Christmases ago, and I thought it sounded very interesting but that I should read the first book in the series before I read it. 
 Past!me, you were so wrong, it is not even funny. 
 Damned is crazy, and not in a good crazy way. I'm guessing Palahniuk wants to be clever in a shocking-look-at-me-for-how-outrageous-this-is! kind of way. It all falls very flat, and the result is nearly three hundred pages of boredom topped only by my disbelief--in everything. It has been a long time since I've read a book, and finished it, and not had anything good to say about it. I'm less than 10 books into 2015, and already I think I have a solid candidate for worst book I've read this year. 
 My two words still stand: Don't Bother. Read anything else. Read another Palahniuk book. Read a Twilight book. Read Twilight fanfic. But leave this one on the library shelf where it belongs. Don't even think about putting it on hold.

You know that sensation when you're unable to shower for a day or two? For example, you're camping, or on a marathon car trip or long international flight... your skin develops an ultra-thin film; an ever-present additional layer of grime that hugs you and leaves you feeling uncomfortable until the next time you can clean yourself up. 
 That's exactly what the experience of reading a Chuck P book is like. Each one explores a different rabbit hole in the burrow of human depravity. They're certainly not for everyone. 
 Just as reading a Brett Easton Ellis novel will leave you feeling that there's no point to life and people are just nihilistic, narcissistic douchebags, Chuck P (gave up trying to freehand-write his last name years ago) novels leave you feeling that, deep down, we're all disgusting creatures, unworthy of the regal notions we ascribe to ourselves. 
 Like I said, not for everybody. 
 In Damned, Chuckers take us on a trip through hell via the experiences of 13-year old Maddy Spencer, and her journey to find meaning in the afterlife. 
 The good: the setting. I mean, c'mon, how many books are set in hell? (right, right, Dante. Shut up.) From the start, I was excited to see how the twisted mind of Chucky P would build the world of the damned. And he's smart about it... the details are given out achingly slow at the beginning. He does, over the course of the first half, build a demented and funny world for Maddy to explore. One little example (no spoilers after this, I promise): everyone in hell has to work. You have a choice of two jobs: you can either perform depraved and vile sex acts on webcam for earthlings, or you can work in telemarketing. 
 The bad: like most Chuck P books, there's a plot twist near the end. While it's well-done and surprised me, it doesn't really go anywhere. Maybe that's because there's a sequel coming out next year and Chuckkity P planned it that way, but I thought this story deserved more of its own resolution. Fulfill me, Chuck, I've earned it.
Is it just me or has Chuck Palahniuk been writing the same book, just with a different setting. I liked his style the first few times, but this is getting ridiculous!

After reading Survivor, Choke, Rant and Fight Club, most of which I liked, Damned is very disappointing. I used to be able to say that I like Palahniuk's books but now I'm not even sure anymore. With this book it becomes painfully apparent that he's got stuck repeating himself endlessly and it can't end well. Damned put me off so much I'm not sure when I'm willing to start another Palahniuk book. 
 2/5 because I didn't hate it but can't say I liked it either. It's probably closer to 1.5/5 but half stars are not available. 
 If you're thinking about reading one of Palahniuk's books for the first time, don't choose this one. Also, if you already like his previous work, don't read this at all. It'll spoil everything.

Oh look it's a book by Chuck Palahniuk the guy who wrote Fight Club (you didn't read the book but you liked the movie) maybe you should read something he wrote! 
 And look this one's cover is cool and the description says something about The Shawshank Redemption meets The Breakfast Club set in Hell, READ IT! 
 This was what went through my head when i came across this book. 
 And this is what i learned after reading it: 
 Don't judge a book by it's title, author, cover or description, lesson well learned.

Oh Chuck, why must you continue to disappoint me so much? How can he write such amazing books like Fight Club, Invisible Monsters, Choke, Survivor, and Rant... and then publish this uninspired garbage such as Pygmy, Tell-All, Snuff, and Damned. Damned is the worst one yet in my opinion. Sorry to be harsh on the amazing Chuck Palahnuik, but I have pretty much given up on his stuff these days. Don't bother with this one.
why

I really didn't enjoy this book. I understand what Palahniuk was going for, but it's just so goofy. I also feel like this book just copies from multiple other works of literature in a similar way to what Weird Al Yankovic does with his music. The landscape of Hell the author creates is interesting, but at times difficult to actually picture/imagine with it being so crazy and unbelievable. That was probably my biggest problem with the book, though how the story jumps around also made it heard to read. It was so weird, the main character had just formed a group to go adventuring, but right after their first victory, they all go to work as Telemarketers. Eventually the adventure continues, but it's again so unbelievable. The author tries to bring it to a close with a goofy "you're my ultimate creation" with a semi 4th wall breaking deus ex machina. Then instead creates a cliffhanger where the main character is going to battle with Satan. All I hope is that Palahniuk doesn't decide to come back to this story, though it would probably be something quick and easy to write.
My first Chuck Palahniuk novel. Thirteen year old Madison is dead and in hell. It's a funny book but irreverent and raunchy.
Didn't finish. Chuck is now nothing more than a cliche of himself.

I've just experience my first heartbreak as an aspiring writer. 
 Last weekend, I was browsing in Barnes and Noble, when I came across Chuck Palahniuk's Damned. I'm a fan of Palahniuk and Damned, now in paperback, had slipped my attention. I picked it and read the description. Devastation. The story seemed to be remarkably similar to the novel that I'm currently writing and one that I have been workshopping. 
 I calmed myself. Maybe it just seemed to be similar. I bought the book to check it out for myself. Although it is very different than what I'm writing ( and hell, just Palahniuk's tone is so unique to him), there are enough similarities to make me rethink key components of my story. 
 Heartbreak. 
 PLOT - Thirteen year old Madison Spencer is the newest arrival in hell. The daughter of an eccentric celebrity couple, her life on earth was mainly lived as another accessory for her parents. Fat and awkward, popularity has not come easily to Madison. She is unsure of how she died, but she suspects that it may have been a marijuana overdose, occurring while getting stoned with her adopted Russian brother. 
 Hell is a confusing place. Demons run rampant and are quick to devour and torture the deceased, only to have the dead reappear for more torment. It's easy for most people to land in hell. Honk your horn too many times or litter and you might not get a pass to heaven. The landscape is littered with rotten candy, mountains of toe nail clippings and rivers of hot saliva. Telemarketers work from hell, communing with the living through phone surveys. 
 It's hard enough being an awkward thirteen year old girl, but Madison must figure out why she is in hell and how to live in her new existence. 
 LIKE - I liked Palahniuk's vivid imagination in describing hell. It's disgusting and hilarious. Palahniuk's unique style of wit is on every page of the story. I grew to like Madison as our unlikely heroine and I liked her Judy Blume style of writing letters to satan to start each chapter. I'm glad that at the very end of the book ( I'm not going to spoil it), he explained why hell has so much candy. It was a cleaver little twist. I liked the transformation of Madison's character. She's a kick-ass towards the end! 
 DISLIKE - In all of the imaginative details, the stakes got lost. Other than the demons at the start of the story, the characters didn't have a sense of urgency or danger. The consequences were low, which made my interest wane. Along with the stakes, the general plot played second fiddle to the creative details and humor. This isn't to say that Damned wasn't a fun read, but it could have been a more compelling read. The story ended with a "to be continued" and I'm not sure if I would continue with the story. 
 RECOMMEND - If you're a Palahniuk fan, you're going to have to read Damned. This book would have definitely crossed my path at some point. However, if you've not read a novel by Palahniuk, don't start with this one. I enjoyed Choke or Invisible Monsters. 
 Like my review? Check out my blog!
Really irreverent but at times really funny. I like Palahniuk's work and I am glad I am writing this because I can not pronounce his last name.

The novel starts out as a hilariously refreshing and tastefully vulgar (it is a thing) story. But as I continued to read, Palahiuk got so engrossed in setting details or minute descriptions of character personalities that it began to feel like it lacked plot progression and major character development. It felt like a series of short, repetitive moments in the narrator's past. 
 Had I stopped at Chapter 5, I would have definitely recommended this. But you could easily just read the first 2 chapters and the last 2 and get the main gist.
What the actual fuck?

I consider myself a new fan of Chuck Palahniuk; I loved Choke and Fight Club and quite enjoyed Diary so when I heard about the impending release of Damned I was pretty excited. 
 Well :( 
 I found the whole novel to be completely 'wrong', it may have been tongue in cheek but on the whole it didn't work and to certain reader's it would be very offensive. I know that is his intention, and I guess sensitive readers would be avoiding his work anyway, but there only some depths you can sink to. 
 I think I may read his earlier and more worthy novels, this one was most definitely not worth the wait.

Really interesting concept but I wasn't that impressed even though I LOVE Palahnuik. Madison, the protag, really annoyed me after a few chapters. Also, the representation of Hell is a bit far fetched for me and kind of defeats the purpose of it being Hell. 
 I wouldn't recommend you this book. But you should read Fight Club.

The only positive compared to other books I have hated was that it was relatiely quick. It was not painless, however. It was very repetitive and lacked much of any revelation or twist, or any real reason for being.

If you've read one Chuck Palahniuk, you've read them all, except containing just maybe a little less inspiration, depending on how many novels he's put out before. The narrative styles really don't change, and we've gotten used to the formula. And now the sequel to Damned is out. You think I'm going to read it? Of course I am, because the real damnation is going along on this journey, reading book after book, hoping that Chuck can somehow make us feel the way we did when we first read his words.
This was a strange book. The writing was excellent, but I detested the MC. Palahniuk got incredibly graphic in places, and there was no real conclusion. I've been disappointed.
Don't bother ... so redundant and boring

Not sure I'll read any more of his work. Seemed like he was trying to mimic Judy Blume's style and failed miserably. The story arc lost me when Archer convinced her to attack Hitler. Here she had been trying to get out of Hell and now she wants to take over? Just didn't see the motive for the transition.

There are parts of this novel that are interesting but, overall, the plot just doesn't sustain. Hell is presented as more of a psychological horror than a spiritual/physical suffering so, given that, the place is too surreal to be scary or believable. Hell becomes too predictable - almost what you would expect. No real mystery here. Madison, yes, you develop sympathy for but she is very egotistical and pathetic - which I guess makes sense given she's been damned.

book_b.title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
book_b.user_review:
I go back and forth on giving this one star. I hated this book, but I can also see why so many people (and so many of my friends) love the series. I scoff a little when I hear people talk about this like Martin is the second coming of fantasy lit, but you know what, the books aren't the worst in the genre. 
 But maybe they are the most hyped. My first experience with a fan was eerily similar to the experiences I've had with enthusiastic evangelicals, but that didn't bother me that much. I was a huge Tolkien fan at the time! I was reading Robert Jordan, I had torn through Terry Goodkind's series. I could totally handle high fantasy, even if it came with prose so dry it just about chapped your lips. 
 So I started to read this way back before HBO had even announced they were considering doing a tv series. (And by the way, Sean Bean as Stark, Lena Headey as Cersei? Cruel fate. It's like HBO was trying to engineer mental crack just for me.) But sadly, Martin's prose is long-winded as well as painfully flat. It's the sort of thing I imagine I would listen to when I needed a good nap. 
 Except I wouldn't ask Uncle Georgie to tell me a story, because then I'd just dream about children being raped and random people getting their heads whacked off. 
 Every fan I had spoken to then and have spoken to since tries to tell me how different it is. It has more political intrigue, yes. But in the end what I hated most about this series is what a lot of other people have already said, so I'm just going to quote the person who best says what I also feel: 
 "Alternatively, some fans may find it tempting to argue "Well this media is a realistic portrayal of societies like X, Y, Z". But when you say that sexism and racism and heterosexism and cissexism have to be in the narrative or the story won't be realistic, what you are saying is that we humans literally cannot recognise ourselves without systemic prejudice, nor can we connect to characters who are not unrepentant bigots. Um, yikes. YIKES, you guys." 
 - Rachael

sample_reviews.review_text: After reading through a few chapters, I skipped anything that didn't have "Daenerys" written on the top. She was the only remotely interesting character in the series because I actually cared what happened to her. I pretty much fell asleep when anyone else was narrating (particularly if it was one of the interminable chapters at the Wall...). How could a book that starts with the walking dead on page 1 be so bloody boring?
...Wow

UGH ok I had to stop myself from commenting in the thread because it would serve no purpose, but I have to vent here a little. 
 Just got done reading a series of posts on here where readers expressed their shock that people who didn't fall all over themselves for Game of Thrones existed (great quote here "god forbid they should hate the series" - and then they speculated as to why that is. 
 To date the thread has two main speculations: 
 - they can't stomach the rape (it's realistic in a medieval setting!) 
 bullshit - GRRM *MADE UP* the world that GoT takes place in. He intentionally chose to include rape. As for realism? So dragons and magic and whatnot is believable but omfg a medieval-ish fantasy without rape.. NO WAI! 
 My "favorite" of these was 
 "GRRM is still the best out there, so it's a huge shame that some people can't get past whatever pre-conceived notions [referring to the sex and paedophilia] they have to enjoy these books. " 
 Not liking rape is a perfectly valid reason for not reading a book, the part that bugged me is that this was frowned upon. Which implies that I should "get over" being offended by something (one commenter actually says this) in order to enjoy the books. No - I am sorry.. I don't think I'm going to _get over_ rape being portrayed as ok. Also childbrides and their subsequent rape - no thanks not in my fantasy! 
 - they can't read long books 
 That _must_ be it. I am just not intelligent enough of a reader to make it through a long book. Also the tie-in that because I don't read long books I also won't read books twice. (for the record I've read LoTR about 23 times AND I've made it through the Simarillion SO BITE ME) 
 I wish these people could take a step back from their fanboy/girl ism and take a minute to actually read what it is that they're typing and consider what it is that they are saying. 
 I didn't comment in the thread because doing so would make me have to join the group - something I didn't want to do. But thanks for reading the rant!

I don't know what else can I say that has not already been said about this book. But for those who are still thinking about reading it, I highly reccomend. It's damn good fantasy, well written, never boring.

Lo que no me gusto: 
 - El estilo de escritura. El autor hizo un info-dump masivo en este libro. Pienso que existen mejores maneras de dar informacion sobre el mundo, los personajes, etc. 
 - Lo aburrido que fue el libro. Me costo mucho mantenerme interesada, creo que me tomo mas de un mes terminarlo. La idea es buena, pero a mi parecer estuvo mal ejecutada. 
 - Que no me importo ninguno de los personajes. Sinceramente, pudieron haber muerto todos y me hubiese dado igual. 
 - Tener que lidiar con Sansa y Danaerys. No se que tanto le ven a esas ninas... 
 - Haber gastado dinero en el boxset. 
 Lo que me gusto: 
 - Que logre revender el boxset lololol.

Finished the ebook with less than an hour before it expired... whew! 
 What a great story! I expected the kings and knights of old; I didn't expect the undead, mages and dragons! Can't wait to get my hands on book 2: A Clash of Kings.
I did think the ending was a pretty good surprise. It just took a long time to get there. A long, long time...

I was pretty daunted by the prospect of starting this book, mainly because I had trouble making it through Lord of the Rings, and I had heard there were lots of names and families to keep track of in this book, too. However my fears were pretty much unfounded. I did look in the appendix once to check who somebody was, but most of the names aren't too weird or anything. Even though the book is pretty long, I had trouble putting it down because there was just so much intrigue. This isn't the kind of book I normally pick up, but I had heard so much about it that I just had to find out. It turned out I really liked it! I'm sure I'll be continuing with the series, but might have to read a few shorter books first.

Excellent book. Great character development and intricate plots lines. Throughly entertaining. 
 I'll do a full review when I finish the series.
Even if you have watched the show it is still well worth reading this book. There is much that is not covered in the tv show as is always the way.

As far as heart-piercing impression goes, I give A Game of Thrones an average 3. 
 For quality writing I have mixed feelings; It covers everything from crude figure of speech and gross descriptions to gigantic plot twists and vigorous dialogues. 
 What it lacks in World-building specially (imho) landscape characterization which is immensly important to me as a fantasy reader I think it manages to make up for with a heavy cast of interesting characters almost each crazily driven by ulterior motives. It's true that this is one of the book's advantageous qualities. I hear they salute the series because the world and its inhabitants humans ring true to our modern society, I wouldnt have an idea, is every random stranger either a filthy smelly rapist or a bloodthirsty power hungry lordling? The political and overtly cynical aspects of the story that are supposed to make it dark, mature and allegedly humane are not enough. They either sound contrived or downright annoying. If I was not familiar with the series, I think I would have able to appreciate the realism of the first book which now only seems harsh and forced. to what end? I am reading a thousand thousand pages to see well developed and promising characters randomly tossed to an early grave! It's not your typical fantasy, granted, but nor does it make it automatically a good one. I think I prefer my fantasies to engage me 'deeper' with the crazyness, the history, the life and uniquness of its world. I would want to read more about 'The Others', The Children of the Forest and Winter, The Lands across the Narrow Sea, The Sorcerers and Magic. All we get in this books are legends. That and women; Sure, Dany is becoming a badass queen but how do we see her up until the end? Right to the end she stricks me as self-conscious of her sex. Is Martin assuming all women walk around painfully conscious of how silk feels between their thighs or is he fantasizing about being a women? Lysa Arryn's breast feeding a grown child is also another example. Talk about fetish!! 
 This book cannot stand alone of course, as these thousand pages are only marking the beginning of the story. The actual appearance of the Dragons is promising... well, that is if you haven't watched the series. 
 GoT is a 3 for me, It could be a near 4 had it not been for the bad treating it gives women but all the same it could've hit better spots yet.

An excellent Fantasy series. Heavy on politics, relationships and struggle, light on your standard fantasy elements. It's a bit of a soap opera but well-written, engaging and worth reading. Word of warning, don't get attached to any one character, Mr. Martin likes to kill them off at a rapid pace.

I like the tv series better. The book went into detail about the wars that were being fought that I don't care for, I guess. Too much logistics for my taste. Not sure if I want to continue the series.
I don't get the hype. People hacked by swords, heads on spikes, people burned alive, eating raw horse heart....It was a gross-fest without a point.

I'm sorry; I just couldn't stand this book. I tried to read it once before the show ever came out, but I couldn't get past the part where the brother and sister...well. 
 I gave it a second try after I watched a few episodes of the first season, but that failed badly after I realized the writing was long-winded and utterly unfocused. 
 I tried again, but I just couldn't get over the brother and sister thing and the sheer depression in the novel. I know people like to say, oh wow, so damn realistic, but last time I checked, my life had absolutely nothing do with whoring, rape, incest, incest, incest and oh, incest. 
 This is not gritty realism. It's gritty. The realism got lost in all the ugliness. I think Martin might have forgotten what the hell he was doing somewhere between the first and second page. What baffles me most of all is G R R Martin's obsession with perverting the relationships between family members. 
 I know the diehard fans think this books shits gold, but I'd rather get my balls shot off than read the next one. 
 And there's more. In the first half of the book, there are almost twenty references to rape, and I counted them, so I'm not making this up. Someone should get a psychologist to look at this. I'm sure a person fetishes show themselves in what they write. Game of Thrones is one big excuse to talk about 'manhoods', as Martin puts it, and other things I don't want to be in the same room with. 
 ,,|,, 
 ,,|,, (just in case you didn't see it) 
 And no, don't quote statistics on rape and incest. Just because it's happening doesn't mean we should have to read fantasy novels about it.

I have to admit this took me some time to get through since kept putting it down to read other books since kept getting confused on who is who, relation to each other and where they all lived. 
 However, kept with it & so glad I did. Going to get the 2nd one in the series today.
I can't wait to read The clash of kings!!! Awesome book.

It's a grand book. Excellent, engrossing writing, exceptional characterization. Makes me wonder at the sort of planning that must have gone into writing this book. Excellent. No wonder it is so famous.
I tried reading this a few years ago and it never hooked me. I do like the show though.

Wow. Just...wow. 
 It's been far too long since I've read a book this captivating. This was a breath of fresh air compared to what I'm used to seeing from traditional 'fantasy' books. I'll try to be brief in this review, but it's difficult not to get excited when a series like this comes along. 
 The first thing I enjoy about this is how the reader is left to decide who they're rooting for. There is no clear 'villain' nor is there a clear 'hero'. Every character has their vices and virtues, and we are left to decide (or not to decide), who we want to win. 
 George RR Martin does a fantastic job of presenting things neutrally. There is no 'right time' to be horrified or to get angry at a character, etc. We get to decide what parts to romanticize. I really enjoyed that we get to see every win and loss from both sides; the subtle ways the characters interact are nothing short of intriguing. I can't wait to see their stories merge more as the books go on. 
 And by God, the foreshadowing. I wanted to scream at my book because George RR Martin, like myself, is a bit of a sadistic writer at times. 
 While many dislike his frequent killing off of characters, I think it makes the novel all the more exciting, because for once, I can't remain apathetic when my favorite character gets into a dangerous situation. There is no 'oh, well they wouldn't kill them off,' because anyone is fair game! 
 And while we're talking about characters, let's talk about how delightfully human the people in this book are. We have disabled characters, virgins, whores, feminine women and masculine women, abuse survivors--and all of them have different personalities! Maybe that seems like I've set the bar low, but so many authors fail to write a diverse cast with diverse personalities, and Martin nailed it. Characters face racism, classism, ableism, sexism, the list goes on. Nothing is glossed over. 
 However, that brings me to my next point, which is the reason this lovely book will be receiving four stars and not five from me. This may be a matter of personal taste, but sometimes Martin's descriptions were too graphic. I distinctly remember a scene in which a woman getting gang raped was described in detail. I can handle sex and nudity to a degree, but this was a bit much for me, and while I praise Martin's 'neutral' way of writing, in which he simply describes something without bias...some things need to be treated with sensitivity. 
 Overall, this was a brilliant novel, and I will without a doubt be reading the rest of them. If you like well written female characters, brilliantly developed fantasy worlds with a rich history, and ancient magic, then I wholeheartedly recommend this book to you. 
 Oh, and 
 dragons

This author is one of my favorites, he writes so well. I picked up A Game of Thrones on a recommend from on of my friends and couldn't put it down for the next several days, I was fascinated by the command of language that George R.R. Martin is able to muster in order to weave the tapestry that is this enchanting and involving story. He is also able to show restraint and not introduce a myriad of characters with a cast list so long it could be compiled into a book itself. More time is given to the main characters and the story, a fascinating read, to be sure.

Battle tactics and strategy in "A Song of Ice and Fire" are at an imbecilic level. Such a disappointment. Especially the "I'll pile up my whole army in one place and you'll do the same" principle (which basically reduces the war to a single battle, but of course, you can fix the situation by increasing the amount of enemies), siege (does that guy even imagine what siege is???!!!). The Tullies release the floodgates in the first volume and Riverrun turns into an island, with waters touching the walls of the castle. That would wash or at least dampen the foundations of the castle after a couple of tries and would do the job of a fine siege technique - when a part of castle wall's foundation is taken away and the wall, being solid and long, breaks. Of course, if Tullys haven't build castle upon a gigantic solid chunk of rock that "accidentally happened to be there". Et cetera, et cetera. 
 Also, the whole series can be described with a passage from it: 
 "Sansa stared at him, seeing him for the first time. He was wearing a padded crimson doublet patterned with lions and a cloth-of-gold cape with a high collar that framed his face. She wondered how she could ever have thought him handsome. His lips were as soft and red as the worms you found after a rain, and his eyes were vain and cruel." 
 That's what the book is - vain and cruel. With no clear plot, concept, hero, morale, idea. Just a bunch of power-hungry assholes and stupid, cruel women. 
 The author has no ethics towards heroes and the reader. Especially when he makes everything interesting in Jon Snow's chapters and feeds us another lump of primitive and boring politics. If he wrote a book about the coming of winter, White Walkers on the background of a war, I'd forgive him it. But up to the 5th tome the White Walkers and Winter are on the background. And the rest is like Leo Tolstoy's "War and Peace". 
 And the winter concept is borrowed from Ursula K. LeGuin. 
 Also, every time Martin carelessly mentions yet another mention of a rape (throwing in a couple of meaty details), I promise myself to throw the book into the nearest garbage can. 
 Female characters are mostly stupid and disgusting. And those who aren't, become such in time, as in Arya's case. 
 Et cetera, et cetera. Now my list of "least favorite fantasy writers which are worth mentioning" contains three names: Clive Staples Lewis, Andrzej Sapkovski and George R. R. Martin. 
 Guess I'll go back to Charles de Lint and Philip Pullman for a while, to wash the aftertaste.
These books could be less stressful. The things I do for my love of Sean Bean, I swear. (Also fuck you Sansa for getting your wolf killed.)

I'll admit this straight up: fantasy is not my cup of tea. But I decided to give this a shot because of my experience with Harry Potter and The Lord of the Rings (and because I wanted to stay in the loop with what's crazy hot on TV). Martin definitely had a good story up his sleeve, but he lost it somewhere in the mundane details.

I'm torn on this book. I wanted to like it, and I did some. But in the end it lacked an ultimate good. 
 I liked: the story telling, the scope of the story and that it all interconnected, and the feeling that it occurred in a much earlier time, hundreds of years ago. 
 I didn't like: The frequent crudeness (though I consul myself with the idea that this may have been what it was like in a less civilized time. I can forgive a lot in epic tales of good and evil, but sadly, there was no ultimate good here to find. There was cunning, deceit, and violence. The characters you grow to love, become invested in, and think are good, don't win, and so the book becomes disappointing. I'm told the next books get better? Perhaps I will revisit one someday.

This book had me laughing and swearing and wretched with suspense for pretty much every single page. George R.R. Martin has always been one of the staples for fantasy novels, and now I understand why. 
 At first I was turned off by the multiple viewpoints and the rapidly increasing amount of names to remember (in fact, I still probably don't know most of them. This is a huge cast of characters, after all), but the plot moved along so fluidly and the characters who were important were so striking that the book came alive in my hands. 
 Needless to say, I'm already digging around for the next book, because holy crap, am I relieved it doesn't end there. Suspense! Intrigue! Not a whiff of romance, but man even if that is usually the thing I look for first in a book, A Game of Thrones totally doesn't need it.
The story line was interesting, but the story was too graphic for my tastes.

This book was excellent and I totally loved the characters, though I'll warn you that there are a pretty lot of them. I don't know what to say honestly, but I deeply regret Eddard Stark's death. . Good book, am looking forward to the second one.

In the Seven Kingdoms, winter is no momentary hardship. Summer has already lasted more than ten years, and winter is expected to be at least as long. In winter, dead-alive beings from the cold country will have time to take over the Seven Kingdoms, if they are allowed. During the long summers, children grow up who have never seen one of the Others, and there are many people who have forgotten they exist. 
 In the Seven Kingdoms, the preoccupation is ruling-class politics. King Robert, under whose leadership the mad king Aerys II and his family were deposed, is busy roistering. He is leaving the governing to his representative, the King's Hand, and his council. Robert hates his ambitious queen Cersei, but he does nothing to control her as she positions her family, the Lannisters, to take over the Kingdoms. People have begun dying by poison, and the whisperers know who is responsible. 
 Obviously the Lannisters will have to be opposed. The one clear leader among the nobles is Eddard Stark, Warden of the North. Eddard was at Robert's side as King Aerys was conquered, and unlike Robert, he has retained his honor and integrity. Robert promotes Eddard to King's Hand, to rule the Kingdoms and create a balance of power with the Lannisters. That makes two rivals for power in the Kingdoms. Across the sea are two children of King Aerys. The daughter Daenerys has married a powerful lord of the Horse People, in a deal meant to win their family's throne back. That makes three. And have you forgotten the Others? Just about everybody in the Kingdoms has, except the Black Watch. The Black Watch is strung inadequately out across the northern Wall, against the time when the Others will again attempt to overrun the Kingdoms. 
 This is an overview of a complex situation. Author George R.R. Martin doesn't describe it the way I have. He tells the story by having eight people live it for us. Simplified down to one personal viewpoint at a time, each sees a different portion of events. 
 Eddard Stark, dragged reluctantly from the North to control a situation Robert has already allowed to go too far. 
 Catelyn Stark, Eddard's wife, forced to deal with an attack that drives her into a premature offense. 
 Sansa Stark, Eddard's daughter, betrothed to the crown prince Joffrey, blissful because he looks just like her dreams of the perfect knight. 
 Tyrion Lannister, the queen's younger brother, a bitter dwarf whose cleverness is bent on winning respect by any means necessary. 
 Daenerys Targaryen, daughter of King Aerys, sold into a marriage alliance by her brother Viserys, finds more potential in herself than anyone ever expected. 
 Bran Stark, Eddard's younger son, crippled in the Lannister attack that ultimately leads to war. 
 Arya Stark, Eddard's rebellious younger daughter, on the run from a Lannister vendetta, which she ignited when she forced Joffrey to expose his true nature. 
 Jon Snow, Eddard's illegitimate son, hasn't forgotten the Others. They are his problem. He is in the Black Watch. 
 A GAME OF THRONES is a masterly interweaving of all these elements and more, so vividly written you can't look away. At 800 pages, there is plenty of room for characters to evolve, country to be explored, and mysteries to emerge. The last page is definitely not a stopping place, so have the sequel A CLASH OF KINGS ready. The throne of the Kingdoms is up for grabs.

It's difficult to say anything about this book that hasn't been said. I really appreciate all the detail that George RR Martin has put in every little thing of this awesome story. I loved it. It has everything. You can tell how the best fantasy books had a deep influence in him. And he wanted to make a masterpiece that included everything. And besides the plot is formidable and develops at a perfectly-timed pace, what makes this story so fascinating for me, is its characters. Each of them is a treat, same for heroes as for foes. This book is a must for anybody that enjoys epic fantasy stories.
This book does not need to be in the youth section of the library. If books had ratings it would be R. Adults go for it, but children and young teens stay away!

I truly loved the unique quality of this book. The characters where strong and the plot line was evident. George R. R. Martin is a modern authour who has taken a fantasy genre and weilded the pen like no other. A modern counter part to J. R. Tolkin's classic series. 
 Would reccommend it to anyone who enjoys political drama, classic warfare and a good old dose of writing magic.

Martin. My man. I fell in love with the HBO series and knew that the books were on my to do list. I've borrowed the entire collection from a friend of mine, and am slowly working my way through them. I found George's writing fantastic, and I fell into the world of Westeros and the Dothraki Sea once more. I found that because I already knew what happened to some of the characters, I had to trudge through the reading, unwilling to relive the tragedy. It'll probably be that way for the 2nd and 3rd books but I look forward to them nonetheless.

I went into reading this book expecting to like it, but I was sorely disappointed. Despite its vast size I felt the story and her characters fell very flat. At one point, probably close to halfway through the book, I realized that I was imagining the characters by what I'd seen in the TV show and not by what was written in the story because there really wasn't much character development in the story itself. I'm a huge fan of fantasy. I love a big fat book with a massive character list. But this one just did not come close in my mind. 
 I think I'll forgo the remaining books and stick to the TV show.

I'm a big fan of the fantasy genre. However, this book was just too political, and not enough fantasy. 
 The bit where it got to her breast feeding the baby dragon, was where I stopped.

I got thoroughly addicted to the show before reading the books. I know that's a cardinal sin, but I'm glad I did. The show has more humor to balance out all the darkness. I loved pointing out all the differences in the books, like more women warriors and ages.

I plowed through the first four books of this series more because I was enjoying the HBO series than because the books themselves had an appeal. I assumed that as is usually the case, the books would be better than the show. I was wrong. 
 There is a lot of (depressing and ugly)action in the books, but little internal motivation for the characters. The first book is full of characters that we correctly expect to see later in the series. Learning their names and thinly drawn personalities hardly prepares us for the author's treatment of them. He seems to resolve problems of plot and character by making each character do something completely unexpected and out of character given what we know about them while killing them or some other key character off. By the fourth book we are down to a manageable number of names, but no closer to a cohesive plot. The characters pointlessly cross and recross a smaller area of Westeros but nothing is gained from their near misses of each other. I have heard the series compared to LOTR, but without a clear vision of where the story is going the characters just flounder around, dying in unusual and gruesome ways, sometimes several deaths for each character. The device of seeing the story from the POV of several characters should be interesting, but because the characters seem to have little internal life and are in general so unlikable it is rather ineffective. New character added later often make no sense or do not live long enough to make it clear why they were added to the story. 
 I will probably watch the next season of the HBO show, because the excellent production values and cast make it worth my time, but I doubt I will continue reading the series. I purchased my kindle edition as a bundle of the first four books, thinking that they comprised the whole of the series. Now I think it has become an endless slog of giant books that won't hold my interest. 
 I have enjoyed genre fiction all my life, but this series has lost me. It's just not good enough. I am clearly not the target demographic for this product, and whether that is because my age and sex are not optimal for the product or because I have read and can compare it to too many better examples to hold it in high esteem is another question. I really have no explanation for why I trudged through four of the books, when by the end of the second I was pretty sure the series was dreck. If I had not had the expressive interpretations of the HBO cast in mind as I read I think I would have stopped reading long before I did.
Lo lei tras ver su adaptacion televisiva, tal vez, por eso no me impacto tanto. Lo cierto es que aunque conocia la historia y sus giros, el libro me gusto.

I stopped reading this book. It was just far too graphic for my tastes and too many of the really good people were being brutally murdered or mistreated. Some people like books like that, like the harsh plot twists and all that. I don't.

What to say, what to say: 
 Incredibly rich with imagery and amazing description. GRRM is great at dramatic irony, although it can be said that the reader thinks that they know what is going on but perhaps is just as clueless as the characters, quite the paradox. 
 GRRM loves to throw curve-balls, much to the excitement and utter dismay of the readers. Do not get attached to anything in these books because as a friend constantly says to me when I proclaim disbelief at a passage I have reader, "No one is safe". 
 It started off a bit slow for me but after awhile the action just kept coming and never stopped. Your jaw will definitely be open at the end of every chapter. 
 Except for Bran. Or Catelyn. They're kind of boring/annoying.
I loved this book! Although it took me awhile to finish, I became so wrapped up in the characters and the world. I can't wait to continue reading the series.
One of the best book i have ever read.The characters were amazing-kalisi , tirion ,Jon Snow , Arja , Ned... Also soooo many twists and action.*ane so many death .

There is little I can add to this review: 
 http://www.goodreads.com/review/show/... 
 except that I gave up on this after the first couple hundred pages. Time is expensive, especially mine. Much too valuable to spend on such pretentiousness. 
 I was interested to see two things there: 
 The review which best matches my own take is by someone who like me loves Leiber and Moorcock and finds Tolkien also fairly boring. This can't be coincidence! 
 Like Lois McMaster Bujold's Vorkosigan books this one gets styled a soap opera (one in fantasy, the other in scifi) and I hate that format and its conventions already when it's applied to the real thing, to TV-series. I do not think that is a coincidence either.
Loved this book, and the series, little long winded and the writing is slow, but still got drawn in to the characters.
Al principio me parecio aburrido, pero sigues leyendo y leyendo y no puedes parar.
I could not finish this book because I could not get into this book. It's not my cuppa.

I am like the last person on the planet of readers who read this, so not going to spend too much time crafting a eloquent and intelligent review. It has all already been said. Really. There are about 4.2 million reviews of this book, some are classic This Sucked/Ruled and Here's Why, and others that qualify for master's level thesis. 
 Some of the things I liked were also things that I didn't like. For the most part, I liked the characters. They are weird, unique and varied. Some of the "bad" characters are the most interesting. However, some of the "good" ones are super boring and those chapters dragged on too much. Ned, I'm looking at you. Are there too many characters? Yep, sure. But that doesn't really matter too much. 
 I liked the intrigue, the game of thrones, and the deals being made. I hated the battle scenes. I also found it disturbing that the main characters are all children. They don't have to be. Why is Dany 13 and Robb 15? Just make them in their early 20s and it would be the same story.
George R.R. Martin does an amazing job of really taking the reader into the world of kings, knights, and betrayal. I absolutely love this book and look forward to continuing the series.
Engaging but confusing at times, new characters introduced too often, although following POV characters is exciting a lot of the time

I didn't finish it and won't. It's exactly like every other adult fantasy series out there ( Goodkind, Jordan). Violent, creepy sex scenes, twenty thousand characters that I can't keep track of, and endless violence. My thoughts during the first few chapters were " I already read this stuff in my teen years.... I don't need to do this again." So I didn't. The end.

reference_books.title: Gone Girl
reference_books.review_text:
Ummmm. That's it? That was: 
 For me, anyway. I feel like I just wasted my time with this one. 
 I was kind of surprised at some point but that's all the emotion (besides disgust) that I felt while reading this. Also, this book was 400pages but it felt even longer. I was just, "can this end already?"

reference_books.title: The Queen (The Selection, #0.4)
reference_books.review_text:
He tucked a strand of hair behind my ear. "You will be the only thing in this world that is truly mine. And I will put you on a pedestal so high, it will be inpossible for anyone to adore you." 
 I think this novella is quite okay despite it being fairly short. 
 The other girls in the competition came out bland. Of course we know, Amberly will be Queen since we've read the series but yeah. I wished there was more depth for the other girls. 
 I see why Clarkson chose Amberly and his reasons made sense. Though I don't know. It looked like he wants a Queen that will follow all his orders and he didn't even tell Amberly that he loves her. But then again, this was just a part of their story so I wouldn't know if he actually did. Clarkson was like a different person here it's so weird after reading about him in The Selection. 
 Anyway, an interesting addition for the series. 
 ----- 
 Uhm, so I just saw an article about this author 'behaving badly'. 
 I don't know. I just think authors are different from their works. Works shouldn't be defined by who wrote them. I mean, it all came down to 'Did I like it after I read it?' Well, that's my take on it. After all, we have different tastes in books. It's different though when an author didn't take a bad review in a good way and they say something really nasty to a reviewer. That's... so awful. 
 I might be sort of weird but I find this series entertaining nonetheless even though yeah, it was kind of predictable and some characters are stupid and annoying. But my opinion might change as I grow older. XD I mean, this is what I like now but really, change is constant.

reference_books.title: Tangled (Tangled, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
A charming and confident guy noticed a girl one day. He was used to getting what he wants and right now, he wants her. He started flirting with her. The girl was not affected by his charms (on the outside, at least). Well, surprise surprise! They exchange verbal insults and retorts back and forth but they're actually foreplay. The boy seems to be different now. He doesn't want to be with other girls anymore, just her. Finally found his match, huh? Well, that was original. 
 Not. 
 Summary sounds familiar? To me, yes. Duuuuh? That's like the plot of many other romance stories out there. Just edited here and there, put some twists on some parts and then.. BAM! New book. Puuuuh-lease. 
 The narrator, Drew, was actually kind of amusing at first. It was refreshing to read something from a guy's POV. It was honest and different. He spoke what is really on his mind, no holds barred. 
 But unfortunately, he is an annoying bastard! He likes to hurt someone just to keep her from noticing he's hurt, too. I mean he's the kind of guy who doesn't mind wounding other people's feelings when he saw it fit and convenient for him. After he told us why he got the "flu", I just stopped sympathizing with Drew. I mean dude, what the hell is wrong with you?! I think he deserved what he got! I didn't like what he did and I don't care how sorry he was after that. That is just unacceptable in my book. Yeah people do stupid things when they're hurt. But gaah, this man is just plain mean. 
 The woman, Kate, has a fiance on the story. They were together for almost 11 years already. Well, of course, the author made the readers see that this guy is an absolute jerk. In other words, he's nothing compared to Drew. Yeah, yeah. I swear this character, Kate, is not that interesting. And I don't like a girl who can cheat with her fiance. There is nothing special about her really but Drew seems to think differently. Well, of course, he'll think that since this woman seems to be immuned to his charms. 
 I also didn't like how proud Drew was about his sexual encounters and how he boasts about it. It makes the women felt... small and unworthy. Like they're an object, not a person. So there's this saying that if someone doesn't seem to respect herself, you're not entitled to give it to her. That is just wrong. I think some people just needs someone to respect them in order to be different, in order to change their way of living. Well, that is what I think anyway. 
 The only thing that I managed to like in this book is MacKenzie, Drew's 4-year-old niece which is such an adorable girl, and some funny moments. But other than that... Meh. 
 Overall, not impressed. I've seen this kind of story many times already and the main character is such an ass. 
 Final Rating: 1.5/5 stars

reference_books.title: City of Lost Souls (The Mortal Instruments, #5)
reference_books.review_text:

 So here's my thoughts about this one: 
 Clary. Woah. This made me remember her stubbornness. She's reckless and impatient. She asks for permission about some things but when she's not allowed to do it, she do it anyway. I don't like the way that she always gets what she wants. But still, I liked her loyalty to her friends and loved ones. 
 Simon. Oh goodness I forgot how funny Simon could be. 
 "You don't just get to say no."

 "Simon-" 
 Simon patted the seat beside him as if someone was sitting there. "Let me introduce you to my good friend no."

 Sebastian. One word. Ew. I can't believe I shipped him with Clary before. Mind you, that was only for a minute but still.. Ew. Ugh. I wish he would die. And he would, of course. But after having some casualties.

reference_books.title: Ugly Love
reference_books.review_text:
Ummm. Wow. And I use that "wow" in a bad way. 
 Why I didn't like this one: 
 1. Jerk hero. Miles. I don't care if your past is shitty. You don't treat others like that. Ehhh. I don't care if you're hot and handsome and adorable and hurt and depressed. Being hurt doesn't give you the permission to hurt somebody else. I am annoyed at his continuous "I can't give you more than this." line. Gaah. "Tell me to stop, Tate." Seriously? How about you stop? Argh! 
 2. A too stupid to live heroine. Tate. I don't know if I should pity her or scream at her. Ugh. I don't really think that girls could give herself to a guy without giving a part of her. Or maybe that's just me? I don't know. 
 3. I was already on half of the book and I don't even care. Ugly Love is one of my most anticipated reads last month but it didn't reel me in like I expected it to. It was rather disappointing. 
 Colleen hoover writes so beautifully though. It was something I loved from her other books since the beginning. I mean, if I ever recommend NA books it will be those written by her! This was an exception, though. This is terrible, in my opinion. 
 Anyway, maybe my expectations were just too darn high. If you're a fan of Ms. Hoover, don't expect to much from this book.

book_a.title: Succubus Blues (Georgina Kincaid, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Actual Rating: 3.5/5 stars 
 "We all have moments of weakness. It's how we recover from them that really counts." 
 Georgina did something terrible in her life that she made a deal with the devil to be a succubus in order for the people she wronged to forget about her. And they did. Their memories was totally wiped out. 
 I don't know what is a succubus though. So I went on Google to search what a succubus was and they are like immortal, evil creatures who seduces men in their sleep to absorve energies or something. Succubus sucked the life out of their victims. if they take too much. 
 I've been on a Richelle Mead roll and I noticed that the really strong suit she have on her books was her heroines. They do bad things all the time. The made mistakes and then regret it. They weren't perfect and maybe that's why I really enjoy reading about them. Also, Georgina likes books. She have this certain book and she's reading 5 pages a day to make it last and it's so charming. 
 "Because...Because it's so good, and there's only one chance to read a book for the first time, and I want it to last. That experience. I'd finish it in a day otherwise, and that'd be like...like eating a carton of ice cream in one sitting. Too much richness over too quickly. This way, I can draw it out. Make the book last longer. Savor it. I have to since they don't come out that often." 
 But Georgina wasn't happy about being a succubus. She has to deal with it though because really, what choice does she have? 
 I was kind of confused about the love interest though. Well, I was of course rooting for the writer. He was mortal though. Georgina's favorite author, Seth, was awkward at first but man was he so sweet. He was caring and I actually pity him for seeing a lot of weird happenings. 
 The epilogue nearly brought me to tears. Awww. 
 This was an adult, urban fantasy book though so there was a lot of steamy scenes and I do mean A LOT. Of course, these acts were in a succubus nature so yeah I guess I'm saying is that don't be too shocked about those things. 
 I am looking forward to where this story would lead. It was different and it's quite refreshing to read about.

sample_reviews.review_text: Definitely better the second time reading it. Didn't feel like I was rushing to just finish it. Enjoyed the story more this time and making me want to continue the story to see what happens next for Georgina and Seth :)

Had a harder time getting into...I love Ms. Mead's writing style and especially her YA books, but this was a little too graphic for my tastes...but I'd totally recommend any of her YA books - especially the Vampire Academy Series & Bloodlines - her new series spin off from VA. :)

 Review: OMG this was such a fun beginning to a new series for me. I really liked Georgina--she was smart, sassy, and works in a book store. The fact that she is a Succubus well that is just her life. She does really have 2 bosses: her succubus boss (who knew that came with quotas) and her bookstore boss.
