I've tried reading it but it was so BOOOOOOORING... Vampire Academy series,which I love, is a total masterpiece in comparison to this garbage.

I read this book because it's the same author with Vampire Academy. Georgina Kincaid is an adult series about a Succubus who seduces mortal men to gain energy and survive. Georgina have a complicated past life thus stopping her to have a normal romantic love life. 
 This book is interesting but I didn't enjoyed it much.

I tried to read this book; four times I tried reading it. I even skipped ahead 20 pages and tried again. I wanted to read it! I just couldn't read it. 
 The main character was just too pathetic for me to take an interest in her well being. There were attempts to give her depth (the scene where she takes off her shoes, the scene where she remembers the necklace given to her by her husband-to-be), but these were disarmed by random raunchy attitude toward her by the men around her, particularly her boss at the bookstore. Also the second main character, the writer, seems to have a split personality with the difference between his writing abilities and his everyday speaking abilities. It's hard to feel much for either. The plot development also left me with the feeling of confusion, not mystery. So I guess I'll pass this one, and the remaining books in the series, to others.

Oh what a perfect book to follow up the took-too-long-to-read literary Pulitzer slog I just finished. I read the entire thing in about 4hours and loved it. Just easy, fun and sassy. The banter is some of the best I have read in this type of book - smart and sexy and not feeling forced or fake. A book that can make you laugh out loud is the perfect thing for a cold winters night in front of the fire. 
 The writing is solid but not brilliant. The characters though are very well portrayed and I absolutely enjoyed meeting Georgina and her friends (and foes). I was expecting (since the title does have succubus in it) a sex-fest but pleasingly it was mostly plot and only a little bit of sexing which is my preferred ratio. I will hunt out book 2 next! I read some of the reviews for later books and get the feeling this might suffer from series-itis (you know, where the author doesnt know when to stop) but will continue on until I get tired of it.
So I really enjoyed this book and well Carter and Cody both have been added to the book boyfriend club !

This was laugh out loud fun. I would place it in the category of "Twilight" for adults. Anyone who watches Supernatural will enjoy this. It is all about angels and demons in the human world. It is definitely R rated but I flew through it because it was fun and well written.

I read this on a friend's recommendation. I like UF and I'm good with kick ass females (though they can be so stereotypical and generic that I get bored). SB has a lot to recommend it with decent amount of action, a love triangle, lots of hellish demons that you can't help but root for and a relatively smooth writing style. I found the book very easy to listen to though I never quite connected to the characters. I definitely am not invested in the book or series but I like it enough to continue. 
 SB introduces Georgina Kincaid, ancient succubus by night and bookseller by day. She sold her soul to the devil to pay for cheating on her then husband. Now she has to seduced men, corrupt their souls, and steal their life energy to survive. It's a hell of a job. She has a few close friends, namely a couple of vamps, a demon, and an imp, and several humans that revolve in her world - all men. In this book, Georgina must contend with a few suitors while trying to figure out who's attacking her immortal friends and killing off her enemies. 
 The plot itself holds the book but is largely predictable. I guessed what was going to happen pretty easily - and much faster than the sharp leaps Georgina took to figure it out - but that didn't bother me so much. It'd be nice if the story had been more subtle or nuanced but for a quick, light, fluff UF romance read it's fine. The writing helps with a slick style that moves easily and quickly from scene to scene , introducing new men at a rapid pace but never overwhelming the reader. 
 What really kept me from engaging and loving this story is the sole female - Georgina. She's flawed, very much so, and I found it hard to root for her. She clearly loves and craves the attention she gets from men and needs that attention even separate from her succubus duties/needs. She tries to "be good" and stay away from good men but she purposefully plays a thin line that teases the men. She shapeshifts and dresses in such a way to attract their attention but then laments for chapters about how she doesn't want to hurt them. She's inherently selfish and that, above all, is what I found hard to really like about her. The ending regarding Seth and her deal with Jerome is entirely selfish on her part, while understandable, I found her dislikable because of it. 
 She's not without charm though as her initial meet-cute with Seth is adorable and likable. Her inability to find a good balance with him at the beginning helped me overcome some of her flaws, as did her behavior regarding Roman. I thought the men in her life gave her too much credit/forgiveness given her actions but then again I guess that's her charm/succubus wiles at work. 
 Overall I liked this well enough but I don't particularly care for the lead female. She's too selfish and attention seeking. I think Carter (who's definitely my favorite character next to Seth) said it best when he questioned why she chose such a provocative shape if she wanted the good guys to leave her alone. There was never a good answer to that. I'll read the next book and see if I like her anymore.
Loved it!

** spoiler alert ** 
 So after reading Richelles VA series I thought about giving this series a shot this first book started of s bit slow for me a the start but Georgina is such a interesting character so I enjoyed the slow start learning about her life and the events that occurred in the book took me by surprise especially such characters as Roman turning out to be the nephelim and finding out about Georginas past like always Richelle never disappoints she's an amazing written and im of to read the next book in the series and see what Georgina is up to next
3.5 stars. I enjoyed this book. There were some slow parts, but I think the others in the series will be faster paced.
Very mehh. I expected much more since VA is one of my favorite series.

Let me start by saying that I almost never read fantasy. However, I could not resist getting sucked into the tumultuous, sassy world of Succubus Blues (and the resulting sequels). This was Mead's first novel, and is less well known than her Vampire Academy series. Georgina Kincaid is a succubus and just so darn human . Mead's prose is snappy, witty, intelligent, and irresistible. Plots twists and revealed secrets kept me reading this gem into the wee hours of the night. Girly urban fantasy at its finest. 
 Five bubbly stars. 
 Lily M.
Overall I found Succubus Blues to be a good story. I enjoyed the inclusion of angels and demons as a bit of a fresh spin on the urban fantasy genre which is really very saturated right now.

I had only a vague idea of what a Succubus was before I started reading this story. I learned about Succubi, Imps, Nephilim, Guardian Angels, Angels, Fallen Angels, Demons, quirky Vampires, book stores, Seattle bands and a introverted writer by reading this story. It was a fun romp through the landscape of Seattle and a bunch of counter intuitive personalities of this wide range of mortal and immortal actors. I enjoyed the contrast between the emotional impulses of the Succubus, Georgina Kincade and the constant battle she has with her natural inclination to suck the life forces from honest true blue odie coloney guys who are the best to feed upon but her natural inclination is to feed on the evil dirtbags who don't offer much to one with her attributes and skills. Georgina is a walking bundle of sarcasm and sexual innuendo resulting in an amusing character dialogue interplay. If you like playful verbal banter, this is will be an enjoyable read for you. Who ever heard of an evil creature with a good heart. That's Georgina! I enjoyed the story and learned a lot. The dancing classes alone were worth my investment. It is hard not to like a beautiful, sexy alluring woman who has an immortals lifetime of learning to share. Never a dull moment. Hard to read fast enough to satisfy your curiosity.

I very rarely find a book I can't finish, but this was it. I didn't like the heroine from the beginning, and she just diminished for me from there. Very slow, and didn't hold my attention. I don't see the hype for this series.
That cliffhanger of an ending ensured I'll be reading the next installment though!

My summary: 
 Start of a series, by same author as Vampire Academy. About a succubus who seduces and pleasures mortal men (while sapping their life energy), but also longing for what she can't have, a true love. This was ok, not as bad as Bitten, but not great either. Good writing but a weak plot. I may read another one in the series to see if it gets better. 
 See my full review here: 
 http://readingaftertwilight.wordpress...

The only thing keeping me from giving Succubus Blues one star is my current obsession with Mead's Vampire Academy series. After all, if Mead has the ability to write such an awesome story line for a YA series ~ her adult novels (about a succubus, no less!) should be amazing, right? Sadly, it was not. 
 The main issue with this novel is Georgina Kincaid herself. As a succubus, Georgina possesses an unnatural amount of charisma and is able to bend both men and women to her will... supposedly. We see this trait in the beginning of the novel, then it is pretty much non-existent. The reader is subjected to Georgina's whining and complaining, and only rarely do we see her use supernatural succubus charm to get her way. This would perhaps be understandable if she was new to the whole succubus scene and was still figuring out/strengthening her powers. But no, Georgina has lived as a succubus for a millennia. 
 Despite her longevity, Georgina is fairly clueless about many aspects of the immortal world. In fact, when attempting to solve the "mystery" Georgina turns to an older, mortal human guy who works at a new age bookstore for information about immortal myths and history. Again ~ believable if she were a new immortal. But the reader is expected to believe that an outgoing woman who loves to freaking read has not found time in the last one thousand years to learn about her own immortal society and culture???? Sorry, Mead, but I'm not buying it. 
 And while Georgina is strangely uninformed about her fellow immortals, she is able to remember very precise details about her pre-succubus, human life. Not only does she remember these details, but they still affect her quite strongly. Ok, I realize that this is an author's prerogative for the point of making a well-rounded character and providing a bit of background. But again, I just don't buy it. Granted, none of us know what it is like to experience so many years of life. But even in our own short lifespan, memories fade and hurts heal. It seems to be a common thread in novels that any creatures which have been turned from mortal to immortal not only forget much of their pre-immortal existence, but they also become more... vampire, werewolf, or whatever... and less human as time goes on. Georgina is very much a modern woman. 
 It's been difficult for me to write this review because there is so much I just didn't like about Succubus Blues. But I guess it mostly comes down to Georgina being unbelievable and inconsistent. The other characters really aren't better. There are no noteworthy female characters. Georgina's friends and co-workers are a demon, an angel, an imp and two vampires. But rather than have unique personalities or stories they simply exist to bolster Georgina's ego. In addition to my irritation with Georgina and the underdevelopment of the supporting characters, the mystery was ridiculously simple to figure out. Perhaps I expected too much because the Vampire Academy series is just so good? Succubus Blues has been on my TBR list forever, and all I can say is that I am glad to have found Vampire Academy first. Had this been the first Mead book I discovered, I am sure it would have been my last.

Got to the end of chapter four... and that's it. I'm done. 
 I wanted to ditch this book after the 1st chapter because I dislike the 1st person narrative that characterises the PNR genre, but decided to persevere anyway. I really wanted to hold out for the good stuff, but I just cannot read a book with the sort of too-stupid-to-live heroine who lets a total stranger (who blathers on about how his own name sounds like something out of a romance novel. WTF?) know where she lives 5 minutes after meeting him.

I really enjoyed this book. I had no idea what a succubus was before I read this book, but now I have found a whole new paranormal theme that I will be looking into. This book had the perfect amount of romance, mystery, and humor--the main character could be so sarcastic! I loved this book and can't wait to read the next one in the series.

It seems that I am very much in the minority here but I really disliked this book. It actually made me so uncomfortable that I couldn't finish. It was this paragraph that finally did me in: 
 He stayed quiet a few moments before finally saying, "You're a pretty girl, Georgina." 
 I started. So much for serious talk. "Did you drink more than that beer?" 
 "I forget, though," he continued, ignoring my question, "that you're also a smart one." 
 OMFG! 
 By the way this was a conversation she was having with one of her self proclaimed best friends. Guy by the way. He had to REMIND himself that she was intelligent!! He goes on to excuse this disgusting line by claiming he is so used to being around women who are only concerned about their looks. 
 She then goes on to FUCKING DISAGREE ABOUT BEING SMART! 
 There is so much wrong ....I...just....cant....even... 
 But it didn't start out much better. I only made it through 15% of the book, but in that time the main character is physically assaulted, verbally abused by her coworkers, scary sexually harassed, forced to walk home with a man she said no too MANY times, and through it all is a constant stream of self doubt and self hatred. 
 Maybe my big problem is that I don't think a thousand year old Succubus would have the self respect of a cockroach or the inability to defend herself. But I think what really bothers me is the underlying disrespect to women that this book has. Ugh. 
 And I don't care if it "gets better" or she finds her inner bitch. I don't want to read a book that essentially insults the intelligence of my entire gender. There is plenty of that in RL already.

Georgina Kincaid is a succubus. However, for someone who steals life energy from men by having sex with them, she has a terrible social life. She just can't carry on a meaningful relationship with anyone. So what happens when she has not one but two suiters? Who will she pick? 
 I enjoyed the world that Richelle Mead has built. I like the main character. I thought the story was good. I like the banter and dialog. If only the writing were a bit stronger. Now, in most urban fantasy novels (that i have at least read) succubus are usually relegated to the peripheral bad guys category. They are not usually physically or psychologically threatening enough to hold your interest. So as a succubus Geogina cannot be the bad ass character that kick ass and take names in stilleto and leather that i so love in urban fantasy novels. It would have been better if she's more predatory in her seduction, but alas she seem to just send out phermones or whatever to make her attractive to the opposite sex without her doing much of anything just stand there and look pretty. Even her relationship with her boss being the teacher's pet making her get away with a lot of things, making you think of the pretty cheerleader you love to hate in high school. Also for somebody who supposedly lived for centuries she lack the wisdom and confidence most immortal creatures have. All in all the basic problem is that the lead character lacks challenge, everything is handed down to her on a silver platter that you find it hard to believe that she will spend the time and energy to figure out who is doing the killing in the story. And another thing just a though she has no work ethics i mean she signed up on this deal and she's coping out on damning souls to hell. I'll admit I was hesitant to read a series with a succubus as the heroine. My chief concern was lots of promiscuous sex without any plot. But, Mead pulls it off by placing her heroine in a strictly grey moral area. I'll try and explain. 
 After years of succubus indentured servitude, Georgina just craves normalcy, which is something a succubus can't have. Georgina has a cat, a job in a bookstore, and a tight knit group of paranormal buddies. Fine, she has to have sex to survive and fill a quota, but that doesn't mean she has to like it. As a subversive act, Georgina won't sleep with good guys. Instead, she feeds off of men whose souls are already tainted. The problem is that Georgina can't have a normal relationship with a guy without taking years off his life if they even kiss. 
 Ok, so there's not a lot of depth to the book or the characters, but it's a book about a succubus. How much depth was I expecting? Georgina's group of friends ranging from humans, imps, angels, demons, and vampires are what really glue the story together. They're funny and endearing. But, on the downside, there is an annoying love triangle. However, with Georgina being a succubus, a certain amount of appeal to many males is to be expected. The mystery was well done with enough red herrings to keep me guessing through a good bit of the book.

This is how I feel about this book... 
 When I first started reading this I thought "Thank the good lord" because reviewers whom I follow and adore all rated it highly. Also, I've been reading far too many YA-Contemporary/YA-PRs lately and this seemed like it would provide me with a much needed break. I thought it would clear my intellectual pallet of the sugar it's been fed these past two weeks. Don't get me wrong, sugar can be a good thing. Sometimes it's just the pick me up I need. But too much of it can rot your teeth. And brain. 
 Unfortunately this book was less like a break for me and more like a trial. I can't even tell you how proud I am that I didn't rage-quit it because on several occasions I had to restrain myself from committing the ultimate act of literary blasphemy and burning it. I had so many problems with it that it took me twice as long to read as it should have because I kept pausing to scribble down angry notes before looking heavenward for patience and forcing myself to continue on. 
 The issues I have will probably sound like hate spam and I apologize for that because I really don't want to offend anyone but I feel like someone has to point these things out, so here goes... 
 The first question I asked myself was this: Does everyone hit on Georgina? 
 By the end of the book I had my answer: Jesus Rollerblading Christ, YES THEY DO. 
 The rest of this review is probably one big giant SPOILER and I'm too lazy to keep covering them up, so... 
 There is almost zero world building here. Within the first chapters you learn that vampire hunters are in the media but do common citizens really know about them or the vampires they stalk? I have no frigging idea, Mead never elaborates. Which is a popular theme. 
 Georgina, the MC, is over a millennia old yet she seems completely clueless about the preternatural part of the world she's inhabited for the past thousand or so years. Did someone just tell her she was immortal one sunny day and she took it at face value, assuming nothing could kill her? I don't know, it's never explained (surprise!). I'm sorry, but who in her shoes wouldn't make damn sure they knew everything about their altered existence? If you didn't, you'd be TSTL, which she is IMHO. But lo and behold she's still alive, so what the hell do I know? 
 No really, how can you be 'close friends' with vampires and not know that they can't kill each other? Or that they can't kill you? Oh, but don't worry if you come across a really nasty vamp because you can just call up one of the "certain mortals" that are able to kill them. And not just with a stake to the heart but it seems any blunt object will do. But make sure you definitely send a "certain mortal" to do the job because unfortunately the same weapons wielded by anyone else are ineffective. Would you like to know why that is? 
 SO WOULD I, GODDAMN IT! 
 Another question I have is how can someone live so long and still be so neurotic? You hate getting hit on all the time yet get pissed when people don't throw themselves at you, you constantly second guess yourself and everyone around you, you can't make up your mind and you let a thousand year old DEAD relationship dictate almost every move you make. Don't you think in all that time you'd come to terms with yourself? Isn't a thousand years about 950 years longer than it should take to get over heartbreak and your own stupidity? More to come on this later. 
 The first time I almost quit this book was when I got to the random swing lesson Georgina holds in the bookstore she works at after hours. And no, this is not the wife/husband swapping kind you might expect from a 'morally corrupt' succubus but the DANCING kind. The entire staff and even one of her vampire friends attend it. Really? Not one person was like "No thanks, I'm cool"? Of course not! Who could say no to Georgina? She's irresistible! 
 This was the note in my reading journal regarding this: 
 "WHATTHEFUCKISGOINGON?! I feel like this book keeps getting hijacked by random bullshit filler scenes. Goodbye plot, goodbye world building, HELLO ZOOT SUITS!!!" 
 Here's an example of the dialogue between ole Georgie and Roman, one of the love interestS (Anita? Is that you?), that took place during said dance lesson and will also serve to double as an example of why my eyes almost rolled out of my skull while reading this: 
 "Group date, huh?" 
 "For my safety. I've always found it best to keep a few dozen chaperones on hand." 
 "You'll need a few dozen more in that dress," he warned in a low voice, those eyes molesting me from head to toe. 
 I flushed, taking a few steps away from him. "You'll have to wait your turn, like everyone else." 
 ...did she just call herself a slut? She must have because if this was supposed to be a dancing reference I missed it. Also, molesting? That's the word you go with here? One with serious negative connotations? After you eye-humped him first, you bloody hypocrite? 
 To distract herself from this little tete-a-tete Georgie makes a sexual innuendo to the group gathered for the dance lesson about Doug not being able to last longer than five minutes during sex. You see, its okay for her to insinuate but damn it, nobody else can! This is because there aren't enough double standards in this book already. 
 Oh, and just in case you find yourself wondering who the hell Doug is, don't worry, you don't really need to know him, just that he--like many of the male characters in this book--was created for the sole purpose of constantly hitting on/ogling Georgina to constantly remind you of how irresistible she is. And really, you need that reminder, because otherwise you'll realize that there is NOTHING sexy or redeeming about her character, spike your book on the ground with a muttered "Fuck this" and walk away to find solace in ice cream or vodka (or if you're me, the two blended together with ice and a few other ingredients - yum!). 
 The single redeeming character in this book for me was Seth, another love interest. I liked him. He seemed to be the only male in the universe with some immunity to Georgina's "charms", at least in the beginning. I liked his social awkwardity (yes that's a real word...or at least it should be. Say it out loud a few times and tell me you don't agree). Unlike other reviewers I didn't mind that he was a beta male and I liked that he only seemed able to express his feelings through writing. But on second thought maybe that was just the case with Georgina because her interactions with him sent so many mixed signals that he didn't know how to talk to her in person. First you want to flirt with him, then you slam on the brakes and play ice-queen, then want to start talking again and get irritated when he doesn't immediately fall all over you but then when he finally asks you out you shut him down again and are then disappointed when your refusal doesn't seem to ruin his life. Oh, and then you cave and go out with him. This would be another example of the neurosis I spoke of earlier. 
 At this point I began to demand that she make up her fucking mind. She refused to do so and instead enthusiastically donned a tiara and a sash reading 'Queen of Mixed Signals'. 
 Let's continue along this theme. Warren, yet another love--sex--interest (Anita? It really IS you!) wants to sleep with her. Because she's so irresistible remember?! She tells him no. He ignores her. They get steamy. 
 Now back to Roman. She grudgingly goes out with him. At the end of the date(s) they have this conversation: 
 Roman: "Go out with me again." 
 Georgie-Porgie: "No." 
 Roman: "We had a great time tonight and we get along really well." 
 Georgie-Porgie: "No." 
 Roman: "But I'm so charming and you're really lonely." 
 Georgie-Porgie: "Okay fine but only if you promise that we can have this same inane conversation next time too." 
 Roman: "Oh Georgina, you know I could never say no to you. You're just so irresistible" 
 Not only can she not make up her mind, she doesn't know when to shut the hell up. She threatens people when she has zero fighting experience and allegedly abhors violence. I don't mind some barking if you have the bite to back it up. She doesn't. Like a Chihuahua she's weak, prone to cowering when really threatened, has a propensity for yapping, at best is capable of non-life threatening nail scratches and small puncture wounds, tires herself out quickly and could easily be vanquished with a well placed punt. 
 I'm not really sure what to say about the preternaturally themed plot line other than it was weak, was dragged out in small snippets throughout the book and ended quickly. I kept forgetting there was even a murder-mystery because I was constantly distracted by all the other bullshit that took up the MAJORITY of this book. I think if you cut out Georgie-Porgie's social life this would be thirty pages. Tops. This isn't the only book I've read that fills space with personal drama but for some reason this time around it irritated the shit out of me. 
 Speaking of her social life, for a book about a succubus this really lacked the sexiness I was expecting. Yes there was some sex but I thought it was pretty uneventful. There was no build up, no slow ratcheting up of sexual tension. Maybe that's why I'm so disappointed with it. I have literary blue balls. 
 Nope. I'm disappointed for more reasons than that. And offended. I almost quit for the second time after this brilliant revelation: 
 "In that moment, I suddenly understood the power women had over men. It was surprising and exhilarating. Never mind issues of property and politics; it was in the bedroom women ruled. With flesh and sheets and sweat." 
 Welp, I guess I should just quit my job now, since the only real power I'll ever have will come from between my legs. Vagina for the win! What a great message. 
 After that I started skimming, which is probably a good thing because otherwise this review would likely be a few thousand more lines of ranting. 
 In short I won't be reading the next book, nor would I recommend this to anyone. Ever. 
 This review can also be found at The Book Eaters.

I picked up this book out of curiosity for its trashy title and flashy cover and found myself very pleasently surprised! 
 Succubus Blues is the first book in a series about Georgina Kincaide - a succubus living in Seattle. In the "world" that Mead creates the forces of Heaven and Hell are all around us, and the saving and corruption of souls is just all part of the day job. Having joined the ranks of the immortals, on whichever side and for their own reasons, these supernatural creatures have their quotas to fill and around this they live their own lives. It's an intriguing premise and I enjoyed the way Mead blurs the distinction between the good guys and bad guys. 
 This book is part mystery, part romance, and all fun. Georgina and her friends are put at risk when a vigilante starts killing off other supernaturals. Mead writes skillfully and weaves a plot that leaves you suspecting everyone and kept me guessing for much of the book. Her characters are warm, witty, and likeable - whichever side they work for and this fast paced book kept me throughly entertained throughout. 
 Fans of Charlaine Harris and Jim Butcher would say that her mystery plot isn't quite on a par with their writings. Fans of Sherrilyn Kenyon and Laurell K Hamilton would probably find the romance element of this book to be better than either of those. All in all I'd rate this book as fairly middle-of-the-pack when it comes to naming my favourite authors. That being said I immediately ordered the whole series from Amazon and if the others are as good as this first installment I can see this being one series that I'll read again. 
 Very entertaining and I'd certainly recommend it.

Despite the lone star, my experience of Redeeming Love was sometimes good. I liked the inner change the heroine went through throughout the book. It was a reminder that being good to those who don't deserve it can produce better results than giving them their due. 
 The storytelling was full of cliches and cheesiness (naming the leading man Hosea?). Many parts of it were positively cringe-worthy, such as the part where the errant heroine is suddenly too stupid to know that her employer is giving her nonsensical chores to give her husband time to arrive and whisk her back home. And I'm not sure I'd be too pleased if my partner called me a fertile valley while in bed, as the hero does making love to his wife. 'You're like the earth ... the Sierras, the fertile valley and the sea.' The writing was less than good. I am yet to make my peace with writers who think on behalf of their readers -- who tell and tell and tell when they have the option to show. 
 Back to sex, I found it strange that the author of this book was so shy about it that I sometimes had to go back and reread to find out that this MARRIED COUPLE had done it. This is a book based on the biblical Hosea, husband to a prostitute. Funny enough, the author was willing to paint a graphic picture of an eight-year-old being raped by a grown man. But sex between husband and wife? God forbid! 
 But after reading the author's views on God and godliness, as aired in this "inspirational" book, perhaps I shouldn't complain about the author's bleak writing. 
 On God: 
 The author seems to believe that he, the author of marriage, will tear a wife away from her husband because the husband has become too attached to her. 
 'Why did you drive her from me?' 
 Thou shall have no gods before me. 
 'When have I worshipped anyone but you?' 
 You became hers. 
 On wives: 
 'I promise to love and cherish you, to honour and sustain you ...until I die ...' 
 'And what do I have to promise you?' 
 'To obey?' 
 (In case it wasn't clear, this man asking for obedience from an adult woman is the good guy, the one I, the reader, am supposed to fall in love with) 
 John Altman was clearly in charge and would tolerate no disrespect or rebellion, but it was clear that he was not held in fear by his wife ... 
 On the purpose of women: 
 'It's a woman's reason for being, isn't it? Our divine privilege: to bring new life into the world and nurture it.' 
 'It's what being a woman is all about, isn't it? Miriam called having children a divine privilege.' 
 And on women: 
 'Bathsheba was an adulteress.' 
 Also, the author consistently made the heroine the bad guy, and never made her husband's bro-in-law pay for demanding sex from his "brother's" wife. In fact, the woman's husband acted like nothing had happened. 
 I think it's sad that many Christians believe in a god who would take away what they love because he had no other way of teaching them better, who thought women's place in their families was the same as those of the children they've brought into the world, who has created women with brains, motivation and competence but who ultimately considers them good only for childbearing and child-rearing, who blames women for being abused and taken advantage of but lets a man who took advantage of a woman off the hook. I don't hold such views, therefore Redeeming Love was not very redeeming to me.

My girlfriends convinced me to read this book because they said it "changed their lives." 
 I appreciate what Francine Rivers did to the classic Hosea story--making it modern and applicable. But. If you treat this book like a love story between a man and woman, you'll be disappointed. Michael Hosea acts about 48 years old when he's said to be 26, and is about the closest character to Jesus Christ that you can make. He's loving, strong, and practically holy.

I didn't get very far into this before realising that it was R rated. Luckily I got it free so haven't wasted any money and can happily throw it away. One of the most troubling things about this book is that there are a number of reviews from non-Christians commenting on the graphic nature of this book and stating that they wouldn't have thought the writer was a Christian. That alone explains why Christian authors need to be careful with their content, they are representing Jesus. 
 I am aware that this is meant to be based on the book of Hosea in the Bible. However, Rivers presents her main character as a prostitute prior to her marriage... 
 What are the moral implications of God's command for Hosea to marry a prostitute? It appears best to see Gomer as chaste at the time of marriage to Hosea, only later having become an immoral woman. The words "take yourself a wife of harlotry" are to be understood proleptically, i.e., looking to the future. An immoral woman could not serve as a picture of Israel coming out of Egypt (2:15; 9:10), who then later wandered away from God (11:1). Chapter 3 describes Hosea taking back his wife, who had been rejected because of adultery, a rejection that was unjustifiable if Hosea had married a prostitute with full knowledge of her character. 
 (https://www.gty.org/library/bible-int...) 
 The first few chapters dealt with child rape, child trafficking, brothels, drunkenness, adultery, death.....that was enough. If Rivers was trying to relay events in Hosea, I don't understand why she felt the need to include child rape and trafficking in her narrative. It just makes a tragic story even more depraved. The point of Hosea is God's love towards unfaithful Israel despite their waywardness. It is not focused on the graphic exploits of Gomer. 
 I don't recommend this book which is full of graphic detail for shock value. For those who will no doubt comment that the book of Hosea also contains graphic scenes of a similar nature. It doesn't. The whole focus is on Israel's unfaithfulness and God's pending judgement. It is not on the details of Gomer's sin. 
 The popularity of this book and some of the comments are representative of the "God as love" or some kind of "divine romancer" beliefs that are prevalent, as if God needs us and is desperate for us, rather than the other way around. The author writes that God says, "Though you deny me, I love you with an everlasting love." That is not in line with Scripture, where God does not love with an everlasting love those who deny Him. God hates sin (and sinners) and demands obedience. Yes, God loves us and forgives us when we sin if we approach Him through trust in Jesus, but that doesn't give us a licence to sin or to presume upon His grace. Redemption (the supposed theme of this book) should lead to a complete transformation of heart and life.

This book was recommended to me by a friend who read it a very long time ago and loved it. Since she is reading one of my recommendations right now I thought it would be fun to be part of a book swap. Here are my thoughts: 
 Good stuff about the book: 
 Content notwithstanding, the story was written in a page turner fashion. Very fast paced and easy to read....and you did want to just keep reading. A lot of stories taking place in a historical setting tend to spend a lot of time with scene description. This author did not spend time doing this and seemed to assume the reader could do this on their own. Fine with me! Allowed me to read it pretty quickly. 
 Stuff I didn't like about the book: 
 Here we go. Generally, I didn't like the content of the story itself. Meaning....like an artist that appreciates the canvas but didn't like the final painting. So...the story is about a young girl sold into sexual slavery/prostitution at the age of 8. She was the daughter of an illicit union between her mother and a married man. Her father wanted nothing to do with his illegitimate daughter. When the mother dies, she is sold into prostitution. She survives as a prostitute for 10 years until a man named Michael notices her on the street one day and professes he will marry her no matter what. He spends all his money to meet with her at her brothel but only to talk with her and try to convince her to marry him. She says no and wants nothing to do with him. 
 So what does he do? He waits until someone beats her half to death and marries her while she is semi unconscious and doesn't even really know what's going on. That was the only way to justify him taking her away from the brothel and to his own home. She eventually heals and basically does chores for him...doing laundry, cooking his food....cleaning his home....working in the fields. She tries to escape a couple of times and he finds her and brings her back both times. Basically she has left one form of slavery into another. She does not love him. He sleeps with her without her loving him. 
 Oh...and the reason he did all of it is because God told him to. 
 At the end of the story she runs away from him a final time. She is in San Fransisco for a few years facing her demons and finding Jesus. Then Michael's friend comes to bring her back because he is tired of seeing Michael so sad about being without his wife. And she obliges because God told her to. 
 At the end of the story the two of them are quite happy. I didn't like the way it happened. Should it be ok to marry someone without their fully fledged consent? Was that ok in the 1850's? I mean...I know women had less rights back then, but this was ridiculous. I should mention that this book mirrors entirely the story of Hosea and Gomer in the Bible. Hosea, who marries a prostitute that keeps running away from him,loves Gomer even though she has children with other men. It's also a good read and would be good to have that story handy to reference as background while reading this novel. 
 My opinions on how this story portrays women aside, I can see why people in general liked the book. On the surface...it's the story of a damsel in distress (although she didn't know it) who is rescued by a prince charming and he loves her no matter what she does. It's the story of someone living a not so good life who is rescued by someone who seemingly leads her to lead a very good life. On the surface. 
 If you read it with an open mind you will see all facets of the story.... 
 Not one I would read again, and probably will never read this author again. But still glad I read it. I love reading things from my friends. 
 On to my next book. Happy reading.

Redeeming Love has over a million copies in print and has been through several editions since it was originally published in 1991. I just finished reading the 2005 edition, which includes a study guide by Peggy Lynch with some really thought provoking discussion questions. As I write this review in December 2013, Redeeming Love remains on the ECPA and CBA Best Seller Lists. I think the case can be made that this book has become a classic of Christian fiction. I am happy to have read it and I would recommend it highly to Christians and non-Christians alike. It can be read as an allegory with significant Christian themes, exploring God's unconditional love, even for those who don't feel worthy of that love. And it can be read as a beautiful and emotional love story between two very complex and memorable characters. 
 Redeeming Love is set in California during the time of the Gold Rush. It tells the love story of a godly man named Michael Hosea who is called to marry a prostitute known as Angel. She is a beautiful woman who was sold into prostitution as a child, and feels herself incapable of loving Michael back or living any other kind of life than the one to which she is accustomed, despite the unhappiness it brings her. Michael loves her continually and forgives her repeatedly, despite the pain she brings him, and God uses this to begin the process of redemption in Angel's life. But it isn't until she comes to know God's unconditional love for herself that her redemption can be complete. 
 I found this to be an engaging and deeply moving story that dealt with tough issues revolving around sin, shame, and forgiveness in a very tender hearted way. The allegory is there, just as it is in the Book of Hosea from the Bible on which this story is loosely based, but it's subtly woven into the fabric of the romance and doesn't feel at all forced or contrived. 
 The prologue sets up the story by describing Sarah's childhood and how she came to be the woman Michael would know as Angel and later as Amanda. It goes a long way toward making her feel real, believable, and sympathetic, even when her actions might tend to make her seem cold-hearted and unsympathetic, much as she is seen by Paul and other characters who do not know her well. 
 "Head-hopping" is a storytelling technique that has fallen out of vogue in recent years, in which the viewpoint from which the story is told jumps from one character's thoughts to another character's thoughts and back within a single scene. The argument against head-hopping, is that these jumps can confuse the reader and prevent him or her from developing a close rapport with a single character. In some cases, I think that can be an issue. In this case, I thought the technique was handled deftly with clear clues provided each time the viewpoint was changed preventing confusion. And I thought it added depth to the story to be able to see it from multiple viewpoints more or less at once. Given the dichotomy between Angel's thoughts and actions and the way her actions were interpreted by other characters, I think the technique played a useful role. 
 This story moved me to tears at a couple of points near the end of the book. I felt my heart breaking right along with Michael at some of the decisions Angel made over the course of the story, but I just had to keep reading to see how it would end. Redeeming Love was a beautiful exploration of love in all its manifestations from the platonic love of friends to the love between a husband and wife, to self-sacrificial love, to the love of God for mankind. All in all, an enjoyable and thought provoking read. Highly recommended. 
 Note: This review was first published on my blog at www.karencollier.com. Please consider visiting for additional articles, reviews, and discussion questions.

I could go on forever about the extent of abuse in this novel, but suffice it to say, don't read this traumatizing novel, and if you read it anyway, and you think this relationship reminds you of your own, GET OUT of that relationship and GET HELP. In no way do I intend for this review to be a slam on Rivers as I admire her greatly. Redeeming Love is a powerful story of redemption, but Rivers has clearly grown as a writer since penning it.

It's been a week or so, but I think this book has slightly traumatized me. 
 Written by a reformed romance writer turned Christian, the author clearly had some moral points she wanted to make about love and redemption and self-worth and our value as God's children, using a 1800's prostitute as the main character. 
 Great. Sounds good. I just read a similar story a couple months ago and I really liked it. I could go for another uplifting story of love and acceptance. Yay. 
 Nay. 
 This book, though incredibly like the other I read, was vastly different. It wasn't darker, necessarily, though definitely uglier. This author's descriptions of scenes and events were not only more detailed, but also more depraved. Physically, sexually, and psychologically more violent. 
 Not just the girl, not just the men and women involved, but pretty much everyone in the entire story is abusing other people in one way or another, and they are all MESSED UP. 
 Ok, not everyone, but most. The thing is, even the guy who saves her isn't necessarily all that great. He gets really mad. A lot. And he talks about killing people. Often. 
 Good intentions, maybe, but poor execution when it really comes down to it (for the author as well), because he kind of just wants her for the sex, too. And man, is there a lot of sex. But even when it's supposedly loving and good and safe, it's still kind of ugly, too. After writing smarmy bodice-busters, I don't feel like the author has a very good grip on what that should look like. 
 As in the other book I mentioned, this also deals with young girls being sold into prostitution. It's not pretty, but it's real, even now. I get that. 
 But I did NOT sign up for details. I wasn't looking for Margaret Atwood. I can get the idea, and if I care to, I can imagine. But I don't want to vomit from having it spelled out to me. 
 And finally, this view of Christianity was not typical and certainly not like my own. These characters get a ton of direct talk-time with God. Like, way more than most biblical prophets. Also, some doctrine is interpreted quite differently than what I've seen. It's all just a wee bit much. 
 What it really comes down to, is that calling this "inspirational" isn't accurate. Historical romance is more appropriate.

Okay, so I've been complaining, kicking and screaming about reading this book so I figured I would go ahead and chronicle my reaction to the book. If it wasn't for the fact that this is my book club book - I would never have made it through the prologue. I do not find reading about child rape or prostitution entertaining. I know that Redeeming Love is the retelling of the Prophet Hosea's struggles with his former prostitute and adulterous wife, Gomer. However, Redeeming Love is difficult for me to get through. It's hard for me to even want the main character, Angel/Sara/Mara/Amanda/Tizpora/whatever else the author wants to call her, to actually want to fall in love with Michael Hosea. I mean I don't know about you, but I would be freaked out and rebellious about the idea of a man hauling me off into the mountains when I was sick and then semi-forcing me to be his wife. Is it any surprise that she runs away? I would have! There is something very cultish about his behavior that would scare me. If you've ever met people who are that fanatical about something, it can either be inspiring or terrifying. I think Michael Hosea would be terrifying; I'd never drink any kool-aid he'd offer me! 
 And does Michael ever do anything but play with her hair and lean his hip against things? I'm being cynical, I know, but I find it challenging to believe his character. He's an ideal, many, sensitive, religious, person I could list tons of other things about and never encompass all that he is supposed to be - and yet he lacks some character that makes me really not believe him. He is anything and everything that the author needs him to be. He is always patient - except when it suited for the plot to have some conflict. The man had no faults; he was too perfect. I'm sure even the prophet Hosea had flaws. 
 At least Angel/Sara/Amanda/Mandy/Mara/whatever - at least her character is for the most cut defined though I wouldn't be surprised if she were diagnosed with bipolar something or other. She held onto these ideals these things that were the bedrock of her person and you saw - at least for the most part - her change. Okay, in three places she's all nope, no, noway - OKAY! 
 And I think it's rather funny, but Thanksgiving wasn't even really considered a holiday until 1863 and it wasn't a national holiday until later. The book takes place in the span of 1850-1856ish I believe. 
 For me, the first few hundred pages were a war to read. I read them because I had to. There's nothing anyone could have done to have kept me in Angel/Sara/Amanda/Mandy/Mara's place with a man like that. It's the last 100 pages that make the story. I'll never read it again, I'm not actually even a fan of this book. I think there are some things wrong with the characters and the narration of the story is wacky. Rivers does have a way with painting the setting so beautifully that does pull you along and that's the spell that kept me reading. 
 It also made me think of Seven Brides for Seven Brothers. I kind of want to watch that now.

Cleanliness: Although this is a Christian book and based on the story of Hosea and Gomer, I think this book goes beyond "painting the general idea" and gets too intimate in the couple's tulmultuous love story. While the sex scenes stop before sex, the paragraphs leading up to it are emotionally and sensually rousing and somewhat graphically detailed. 
 Of course prostitution is mentioned (as that is what Gomer was) but there is also an entire scene with a pedophile who plays with and rapes a little girl.

reference_books.title: Poughkeepsie (Poughkeepsie Brotherhood, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've read several novels recently that began as Twilight fan fiction and have been pleasantly surprised at how good they were. This novel had that same potential - the premise was promising and it sounded interesting - it even had a good trailer. However, the author completely failed in the execution of this story. From the storyline, to the writing, down to the dialogue, this novel was a failure. 
 As a reader, I want to care about the characters I'm reading about. I want to see and feel what they do. This didn't happen. I cared nothing for these characters, felt nothing. I feel like I didn't even get to know them. They were flat and one-dimensional: each character had one distinct personality trait and seemed to have blinders on when it came to exhibiting any other kind of emotion. 
 *****SPOILER ALERT***** 
 The rest of my review will contain spoilers so don't read any further if you don't want to know what happens. 
 The main storyline of the novel just didn't make a whole lot of sense. Because of something that happened in Blake's (the "hero's") past, he thinks he is made out of glass. This has caused some psychological problems and he has difficulty forming relationships. He is also "homeless." I use the homeless word rather loosely because that doesn't make much sense either. He has two foster brothers who do have homes and whom he sees rather frequently - so he isn't too homeless since he is always clean and has clean clothes. Most of the homeless people who live around here don't have such accommodations. Regardless, the "heroine" Livia falls in love with him almost instantly and decides to leave her boyfriend of several years for this crazy, homeless guy. 
 After the first 50 or so pages however, the novel's focus shifts and the main couple becomes secondary to all the other characters in the book. While the other storylines aren't much more believable, they are certainly more interesting than primary one. This shouldn't be the case. The novel should have focused on our heroes instead of pushing them to the back burner in favor of everything else. Much of what happens between the two of them happens "offstage" and the reader only hears about it through other characters. What's the first rule of writing? SHOW don't TELL. Apparantly the author doesn't follow this school of thought. 
 I've never read a book with worse dialogue than this book has. Livia's sister, Kyle, and Blake's brother, Beckett, have some of the worst dialogue that I have ever had the displeasure to read. Here's a sample: "Holy fucking dogs! You scared the uterus out of me." Who talks like this? I'll tell you: no one. There is also too much vulgarity in the language. I'm no prude - crude language can be necessary to the story in terms of characterization or plot. However, just adding more curse words to a sentence purely for the sake of adding more curse words to a sentence is not good writing. 
 I also had a problem with Livia and Klye's father. The author tries to portray him as a stand-up guy; he's a police officer who supposedly will do anything to protect his girls. Yet he allows them to hang out with known criminals (Beckett) with little more than - and I'm paraphrasing here - "Well girls, you know best, just be careful." Sorry, any father worth his weight would not allow this. Livia and Kyle don't seem to mind either that they are friendly with a man who commits murder as easily as breathing. sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm not one for writing reviews but this book kind of demands it. 
 I'm not a big fan of Stephen King's novels. He has the tendency to drag on the beginning way too long and make it boring. 
 This book literally threw you into the plot immediately and was a great story until the last scene. I think I read it in about four days, and it usually takes me about a month to finish his books. 
 I definitely suggest it to anyone who likes horror and apocalyptic themed books.

 This isn't it. What it IS is midly unnerving nonsensical B-roll Stephen King. Ok for a beach read if that's what you're into. Otherwise, go reread The Stand.

Thank you, Mr. King, for yet again wasting my time and making millions of dollars you don't deserve. Take some pride and time with your novels, sir. This book has the patina of just being thrown together. It's just amateurish, with terrible plot turns and corny action scenes. I hated this book.

Something no Stephen King book should ever be: Boring. Sad but true. I didn't care about the protagonist, the situation wasn't interesting (and it should have been!), the ending fell flat. Sad. 
 Worse than Doctor Sleep because it's not a sequel. Those are the only two Stephen King books I don't own.

I really don't know what to say about this book. At first, I really liked it. I felt I was in the middle of everything that happened. But soon my opinion drastically changed and often I found myself thinking if I should read it on or not. I read it on, but I wish I didn't, because I feel that I wasted a lot of time.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The general rule of thumb is science fiction isn't Stephen King's forte, and that holds true here. A couple of suggestions are thrown out as to what the Pulse is and who created it, but nothing definite is said about it. I don't like this ambiguity. The idea of brains being "reset" is intriguing but it's only half-realized before the book ends. 
 I also don't like the structure of the book, a linear sole-strand narrative of the main characters. You just ended the world - what's going on besides what's happening to these people? What is left of the U.S. government? How are they handling things? This book badly needed the cutaway to a second storyline, because so much of what we get is the heroes walking, walking, and then walking some more. (I understand there are cars littering the road but, until they commandeer a schoolbus towards the end, I found it hard to believe they couldn't get an offroading SUV from somewhere). The characters are somewhat well-drawn, but they don't have much to do and it drags the pace of the book down. 
 And then King goes and kills off the girl, who was one of the best things the book had going for it. 
 Outside of the beginning, there isn't much action. You have zombies, but they're lying prone on the ground for large chunks of the time. OK, the heroes blow them up spectacularly, but then at the end, they do the same exact thing. And then, uh, the book kinda ends. The way it ends seems so much like King gave up. It also seems like a copout, just like not fully explaining the Pulse. 
 The grating single-focus of the narrative reminds me of Delores Claiborne. At least this book is in chapters, but I think Claiborne was the better read.

My Review: I say this with love in my heart- Cell is not Stephen King's best work. Rarely do I find myself halfway through a King tale feeling distracted and disconnected from the characters. Even as I read the final chapters, the plot still hadn't truly pulled me in. It was more gory than story, as they say, and I've never been a fan of the shock factor without an intriguing plot to back it up- I've always seen it as lazy writing. 
 I do love the cliffhanger ending, though, so I must give credit where credit is due. No fairytale happy endings for Mr. King, even in his less-than-effortful novels. Props! 
 Want to check it out for yourself? Buy it here!

King fanboys/girls--avert your eyes. Quickly. Yer not gonna like this. 
 I honestly feel dishonest giving this book one star, even. 
 Mr. King, you honestly lost me as a fan at Insomnia. I came back for the rest of the Dark Tower series, because I loved the first four so... but you've changed. Sir, with respect you did good work in your earlier years, and I think it's time to hang up the pen. Be remembered for the good books in the beginning. Quit turning out this half-assed, slapdash shit. To paraphrase your own words in On Writing: do it right, or don't fucking bother. Well, my man, quit bothering. 
 This book is the very epitome of the "New King"... uninspired. Lazy. Compared to his earlier works, this is the new mass-produced cookie-cutter pottery, vs a Ming vase, for example (the Ming piece being his older work, in case there was any confusion). 
 Mass-produced. Cookie-cutter. That's how this book feels. King leaves the barest descriptions of character, even going so far as to violate one of his cardinal rules he presented in On Writing: SHOW me, don't TELL me. 
 Prime example... the character Alice. We know she's 15. We know she's a blonde. We know she plays soccer. And we know, because King TELLS us, that "she's still pretty, even at 3AM." This phrase is useless to me. For one, it's so vague as to be absolutely meaningless, it brings NO imagery to the mind. WHAT about her is pretty? Does she have ice-blue eyes that glitter a bit in the light? Is her hair straight as an arrow and golden like ripe flax? Hell, does she have a lanky soccer-player's bod with a pair of soccer balls up front? I mean come on! "pretty even at 3AM"??? Wow. Lazy. 
 As others have pointed out, there isn't much memorable about this book. The characters are uninteresting, and for the situation, don't seem to react too realistically. With the exception of Alice, who vacillates from the more realistic "freaking-out teen" to a wannabe Ellen Ripley or her Resident Evil namesake: the stereotypical "balls bigger than the guys" heroine. 
 However, her cohorts for much of the book, Comic-Book Guy and the Not-Quite-Stereotypical Gay Dude (I can't even tell you WTF Tom did, that's how forgettable these characters are), seem pretty composed and together, for a couple guys basically witnessing Armageddon coming down round their heads in the opening chapters of the book. 
 While there are a few "visceral" scenes that make ones eyes pop with a bit of gore or violence, those die away pretty quickly, and one is left with little more than a bunch of hum-drummery involving playing "keep-away" from the phoners, which becomes laughably easy as they discover the phoners go into "turpor" at night. 
 There's very little tension-release, except at the very beginning, and somewhat towards the end of the book. This book, for me, had no "wow" moments, nothing that really moved me ... even the one character's death scene was pretty much a "cut-copy-paste" from Dark Tower... I dont remember if it was VI or VII. King snipped and edited a bit, but otherwise, yep, it should spring immediately to mind. Like I said. Lazy. Uninspired. 
 And that laziness, lack of attention to detail, is what remarks this whole steaming pile of feces that King hands us and expects us to lap up because "it's King". Fuck that, and fuck you, Mr. King. You've sold yourself out for a few extra bucks, and now you demean yourself to the level of hypocrite as well. 
 I'm an avid reader and love books... and I love Mr. King's older work. But this new stuff? I refuse. It's rare that I honestly regret buying or reading a book, but this one? Absolutely. 
 I plan on purchasing his new short story collection, because short stories seem to be something he shines in, even in these later years (Everything's Eventual was good stuff), but for novels? No more. I was dearly disappointed by the final three of the Dark Tower series... and this was the straw that broke the proverbial camel's back.
Man, I was really looking forward to this one here. *uncontrollable sobbing*

El vive (quien conoce a King ya se lo imagina) en Maine y es artista, estaba en Boston por un asunto de trabajo cuando el fenomeno se expande por todo el mundo. "El pulso" ataca unicamente a las personas que utilizaban su celular el primero de octubre a las 3:03 pm y los transforma en una clase de zombies. Quienes no tenian celular o no lo estaban usando en la hora del pulso son los sobrevivientes de esta historia. 
 Clay, nuestro protagonista esta aterrorizado, sobretodo porque esta lejos de su reciente ex esposa (a la cual todavia quiere) y de su hijo de 12 anos. Su preocupacion por su hijo te llega, estuve con un nudo en la garganta cada vez que contaba cosas del pequeno. 
 De a poco se va transformando en una historia que conocemos todos: La mayoria de la gente se convierte en "zombies" Las personas no afectadas se juntan para esconderse, y si es necesario, pelear contra los locos. The one reliable thing about Stephen King books, even the c----- ones (Insomnia), is that the people are always interesting and you kind of want to know what happens to them, even if it's stupid. ** spoiler alert ** 
 In which King Technophobe turns everyone with cell phones into zombies--or rather, into the Borg. I was more into this in the early chapters when it was survivors vs. zombies; the Borgian bits bored me a little. I was also a little skeeved that King chose to make a black man in a Harvard sweatshirt the leader of the Borg army--there's so much nasty stuff one could read into an educated black dude being used as the representative of the mind-enslaving Big Bad. But I am afraid to touch Stephen "magical Negro" King's racial issues with a ten-foot pole, so I'm just gonna leave it at that. 
 I'm focusing on the negative rather early here, aren't I? That's actually not all that fair--there was in fact a lot about this novel that I enjoyed. King is great at envisioning post-apocalyptic landscapes; what you've got here in Cell is basically a more succinct version of the good parts of The Stand. So while it never achieves the heights of the best parts of The Stand, it never hits that book's low points, either. Also, remarkably for King, one of the main characters is a gay man--a gay man who's awesome! And who actually survives! The friendship between this fellow, Tom, and Clay, our everyman hero, is by far the best part of this novel. It's also slashy as hell. At one point, oh-so-hetero Clay actually thinks about how much he is going to miss Tom's smile. Hee! How has the internet seemingly failed to produce fic for this? I want to read all about Clay and Tom's wacky post-apocalyptic adventures! Because if surviving the end of the world isn't the perfect excuse to experiment with your sexuality, I don't know what is.

Excerpt from my full review at seattlebooks.tumblr.com: 
 I wanted to like this book. 
 It had so many things going for it: Rainbow Rowell's glistening reputation among BookTubers and Goodreads reviewers, a quirky premise, the promise of dated 90s references, a cute story. All factors that I took into account when selecting a novel for my Memorial Day weekend getaway. 
 Rowell chronicles the saga of a young man named Lincoln O'Neill, a recent hire at a newspaper office who has been assigned to flag emails with questionable content. He lives with his mother, is often berated by his sister, and has not quite recovered from a broken relationship with an ex-girlfriend that resolved nine years ago. He inadvertently finds himself sucked into the daily correspondence of two fellow employees - Jennifer and Beth - and their amusing over-sharing makes him feel as if he knows them. 
 As you may have guessed, Lincoln develops feelings for one of the women and begins to feel guilty for his invasion of privacy, especially once it becomes apparent that he lacks the willpower to turn them in for conversing on company time. He admits this to his friends, who agree that his behavior has overstepped the bounds of privacy and decency. Nevertheless, Lincoln's attraction to his coworker continues to overpower his ability to do the right thing. 
 My friends and I have a saying that perfectly applies in this kind of situation: It's romantic if you're into him, creepy if you're not. Even under the guise of love, this is creepy behavior. Lincoln begins to fall in love with a woman based on a few emails he's read -- which, while revealing about her character and personality, only provide him the smallest glimpse of her life. Inhibited by natural shyness and feelings of guilt, he cannot bring himself to interact with his coworker face-to-face. It is too easy for him to continue invading her privacy and treating her as a beautiful illusion, rather than a person deserving of respect and space. 
 This in and of itself would be alarming enough, but Lincoln continues to perpetuate other traits of the stereotypical "nice guy," the one who just can't catch a break when it comes to dating. When he goes out to a bar with his more outgoing wingman, Justin, he has the following conversation with a young woman named Lisa: 
 "When you think about that guy--who, by the way, we both know isn't me--when you think about meeting him, do you think about meeting him in a place like this? In a place this ugly? This loud? Do you want him to smell like Jagermeister and cigarettes? Do you want your first dance to be to a song about strippers?" 
 She looked around the bar and shrugged again. "Maybe." 
 "Maybe? No, of course you don't." 
 Lisa tells him off, but we still get the picture: Lincoln has set ideas about what women find romantic and appealing, even when he solicits the advice of a woman who tells him that he is wrong. Before he interacts with Lisa, he has already made up his mind that the atmosphere and circumstances are too surreal for him to treat her as anything more than an idea of a person: 
 "This place and this girl were so far outside his everyday life, they didn't seem quite real. Definitely less real than the women he felt avoiding him on sidewalks and in hallways." 
 When it comes to the girl that Lincoln really wants, the one he imagines and pines for, he treats her with no more consideration. Although he loves her, he can't quite bring himself to believe that she is real. 
 "He knew why he wanted to kiss her. Because she was beautiful. And before that, because she was kind. And before that, because she was smart and funny. Because she was exactly the right kind of smart and funny. Because he could imagine taking a long road trip with her without ever getting bored. Because whenever he saw something new and interesting, or new and ridiculous, he always wondered what she'd have to say about it--how many stars she'd give it and why." 
 Rowell pens a character who appears to love his coworker for all of her inner qualities, but it's important to remember that he doesn't know her. He glosses over her insecurities instead of fully realizing them. To him, she is a beautiful, quirky fantasy. 
 And, while he doesn't seem to judge her for her outward appearance, it quickly becomes apparent that she doesn't do the same. She gushes about his rugged good looks and broad shoulders, even going so far as to stalk him from time to time. As in most romantic comedies, this behavior is excused because it looks less creepy when a woman obsesses over a man - especially a man as gentle and down on his luck as Lincoln, especially when the woman has an inattentive and distant boyfriend. 
 As I said earlier, I wanted to like this book. I believe that Rowell could've pulled off a beautiful love story without resorting to the tropes that pervade today's romantic comedies - men who don't listen to women, women who are consumed by the minutiae of their love lives, and the saccharine ending that is rarely found outside of Hollywood.

 Light read...pure fluff...a few laugh out loud moments, but a very unrealistic (and sometimes flawed) story.

Sooooooo cute. This book is so cute! We start off with Jennifer and Beth, BFFs and co-workers at an Iowa newspaper. (Or maybe it was Nebraska. Whatever, same difference.) Told via their email exchanges, their chapters are smart and funny with great dialogue and chemistry. Think Tina Fey and Amy Poehler, or you and your best friend. Then the chapters alternate to Lincoln, the guy in charge of IT security at the paper. The story is told from Lincoln's perspective, and whereas we only get to see Jennifer and Beth through their emails, we learn about Lincoln and his background. And that's where we, and the story, run into a slight problem -- because Lincoln for all intents and purposes is kind of a loser. Let's look at the evidence: 
 1. He lives at home with his mother. 
 2. He hasn't had a relationship since he broke up with the love of his life. 
 2A. It was his high school girlfriend. 
 2B. They broke up 9 years ago. 
 2C. NINE YEARS AGO!! 
 2D. After he followed her out to college in California. 
 2E. He's been adrift ever since. 
 3. He spends his Saturday nights playing Dungeons and Dragons. 
 In the first few chapters, Jennifer and Beth's snap crackle pop were what kept me reading because Lincoln was just so sad and dull and pathetic. And then came Lincoln's physical description. 
 He's basically Joe Manganiello. YES. That plus the fact that he became less woe-is-me made the story pick up and then zoom into AWESOME territory. 
 Plot: Jennifer and Beth write typical BFF emails to one another detailing the minutiae of their lives. They use their work emails despite knowing that Big Brother or IT Guy can read them. IT Guy Lincoln does read them because they keep popping up on his security filters. As he reads them, he finds himself falling for Beth. He doesn't know what she looks like, but he loves her personality. (That's the dream, isn't it?) Beth, however, has a long-term, live-in boyfriend who is a musician and therefore absentee. Remember that Lincoln isn't Prince Charming either (see evidence above). Yet. 
 Overall, I was pleasantly surprised and charmed by this book. I loved the female dynamic. I've had some, if not most, of the exchanges that Jennifer and Beth have with each other. And as I read, I began to appreciate Lincoln more and more. First and foremost, I love that he's not a Darcy. He's shy and awkward and nice -- a totally normal guy (except for the whole Joe Manganiello thing). As a reader, you're not swooning over him in the beginning because there's nothing to swoon over! You grow to like him as he grows. I would've probably stayed up all night to finish this except my Benadryl kicked it. A fun, enjoyable read, I highly recommend it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 (Some spoilers) I have heard amazing things about Rainbow Rowell's work, so I decided to start with a book set in the '90s and told partly through emails. The premise was rather interesting to me and throughout the book I liked the alternating points of views between the characters. 
 I thought the book was funny in all the right places and a fun, fast read overall. However, it was not all I thought it would be before I read it. 
 Since in the past I've been a complainer of love and relationships portrayed in YA, I thought I would give one targeted to adults a chance. After all, these characters are almost 10 years older than me, so I believed that this would allow me to finally find something realistic and not corny. I'm sad to say that that's where the book was at fault. All of the work Rowell put in to get us to their first real meeting supplies us only with kisses that end with people biting shirt collars. I was very confused. The dialogue during their first meeting and the rushed ending also made me feel like it was eyeroll-worthy. I don't understand characters that discuss how they are GLAD they don't have to spend one moment apart, like the perfect relationship is one where you are stuck at the hip 24/7. Is this what people 10 years older than me believe? 
 I also thought that Beth and Jennifer were hard to tell apart until about 3/4ths of the way in. I kept asking myself, "Is this the one with Chris? Is this the one that never wants to be pregnant? Is this the one with the sister getting married?" I had to stop and differentiate between the two characters. Overall, I didn't even really understand Beth/Lincoln. We never got to see them really interact. We got to see why Lincoln liked her, but all we got from Beth is that Lincoln was "The Cute Guy." I kind of need a little bit more than that to believe that these people are practically meant to be together forever and will be stuck to the hip for the rest of their lives.

This book is so good, so so so soooo good. Growing up in the 90s, I remember AOL, celebrating the new millennium, driving old cars, CDs and record players, the good old days when connections weren't depended on technology. Granted, I grew up in the 90s, I didn't get to fully experience it like the characters in Attachments, so I felt like I was going back in time and it was amazing. 
 I really like Lincoln. He's just a standard nice guy-he loves his mom, likes helping out people, is a complete gentlemen, and always tries to the right thing. I sometimes feel like he is a bit too nice and naive, that people tend to take advantage of him. I found it interesting that we do not get his physical description until we are about half way through the book, so I imagined him as being tall, scrawny, ect but he's actually this big, buff guy? Total doesn't match his quiet and introverted personality, and I loved that. 
 Jennifer and Beth's friendship was absolutely adorable. I like their deep conversations about life, and where they are at but I also enjoy their trivial conversations about gossip. That's how a real friendship is-"it doesn't matter what the conversation. just as long as you called" (Yes, I did just quote a 98 degrees song). 
 This wasn't so much a cute love story (like I had originally thought), but it's more about finding yourself and what you want out of life. For Lincoln it was realizing that in order for him to be happy, he couldn't keep the same routine day after day. He was still in love with his past-his fantasies about his ex-girlfriend, his love for college-and for him to be happy, he had to let that go and take control and steer his life in a different, unknown direction. 
 This book is such a relatable read, and I enjoyed the story a lot. The only bone I had to pick with it, is the fact that it dragged on, a lot. I felt like the story either had to be much shorter, or things had to have happened much quicker.
