** spoiler alert ** 
 I just finished Naomi Novik's Uprooted, which is supposedly a reworking of "Beauty and the Beast." I don't see it myself. I liked her first dragon book (quit the second a few chapters in) so I thought I'd give this new book a try. Just as in her earlier books, her female characters are tolerable but the male characters are very...one-dimensional, shall we say. If you're going to create a (heterosexual) romance, you need a hero who can do more than sneer at the heroine. He should have some positive personal traits in evidence, maybe he could even be somewhat attractive. Otherwise, why is the heroine going to fall for him? More to the point, why should we want her to? Dragon, the Wizard, protects a small rural community from the Forces of Evil with his powerful magic. In exchange, he takes one of their daughters every ten years to live with him in his fortress. Nice guy, right? I can't for the life of me see why anyone, male or female, would be interested in him as a mate. All of the wizards in Uprooted are nasty pieces of work, actually. It was a mildly entertaining, fast read, but if I'd paid for it instead of checking it out of the library, I'd feel like I'd wasted my money as well as my time.

Do you know that old saying, "If you don't have anything nice to say, then you shouldn't say it at all." Well this doesn't apply here. 
 How on earth has this book got a 4.14 star rating? This book was really difficult to read. I had to put it down at times because I was so confused and disgusted by what I had read. 
 I have a lot of grievances with this book but my main one is this. WHY ARE PEOPLE SO OBSESSED WITH A FLAWED HEROINE, FALLING IN LOVE WITH SOMEONE WHO TREATS THEM LIKE ABSOLUTE CRAP?! WHY? WHY?! 
 At one stage The Dragon (who isn't a dragon at all but a powerful sorcerer or magician...whatever) drags Agneshkia (The heroine) down a flight of stairs (Oh! That is so dreamy). He demeans her, belittles her, yells at her. Look, he is just basically awful, both physically and emotionally abusive to her the entire time she's with him. Oh, and the fact that he took against her will and kidnapped her, there's that too. 
 I'm really sick of these flawed protagonists, girls who are clumsy, who aren't the "prettiest" or "smartest" to make them more relatable? That's really messed up. They'll fall head over heels in love with an impossibly handsome male, who they think is on a whole different level to them and that they'll never be together. He'll be "mean" to them in the beginning but really, deep down inside they mean well and are just big softies at heart. Fuck that shit. I'm so sick of this goddamn formula. 
 The best thing about this book was the cover. It really is one of the most beautifully designed covers, which really drew me to it.That's the only thing I'll say that's positive about the book. 
 I really can't believe Ursula Le Guin and Patrick Rothfuss recommended this. I'm kind of at a loss for words. Did they really read the same book?

4.5 stars. 
 Uprooted is very evocative of traditional fairy-tales, while not being a retread of any. It alludes to familiar folkloric concepts while remaining a modern fantasy novel that deals with things like political schemes, and building relationships. The way the book shows the maintenance of friendship as the parties grow up and away from each other is refreshing, as so few fantasies seem to include friendships at all. The gradual build of respect and friendship between Agnieshka and the Dragon works well, though the transition to romance may be more abrupt. My biggest criticism of this book is probably the development of Agnieshka's magical talents. Toward the end of the book her magic seems to become super-powered, and the rules established in the book for magical systems seem cast aside. I found the protagonist enjoyable though, and the antagonistic force of the dark Wood was one of the more malevolent villains I've read. The villainy of the Wood really gives the story a lot of it's delightful flavor and shape.

This book was a massive disappointment. I had heard so many great things about it and read a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately, mine isn't. I did not feel invested in this book at all - it annoyed me to no end. The main character wasn't just young and innocent, she was intolerably naive and completely clueless. That did grow a little better throughout the story, but not until the end. She's chosen to live with the so-called 'Dragon', a sorcerer who picks a village girl to come live with him every ten years. This sorcerer is utterly unbearable, but suddenly, for no visible reason, the main character likes him. Also, when the prince comes to visit and tries to assault her, she merely deems it unpleasant but not the biggest deal, which is quite incomprehensible. When it comes to the plot, this book was all over the place. There were quite a few interesting parts, but so much happened that it was just too much to even want to keep track of. All in all, it was fairly well written and well thought out, but for me, it lacked a lot of character depth and control over the story.

I had heard such great things on this book. Those beautiful words were exactly what drove me to even pick up the book in the first place. At first, I did realize why the book was given such high praise. I was happy with having had picked up the book, but then came all the problems... 
 The first problem for me was how annoyingly detailed it was. Like, excessively so. There were details about things that hardly even needed a description as well as details UPON details. I love a good descriptive book, but this book was about 45% description alone. 
 My second problem was the grammar. Maybe it was me trying to focus on anything else but the descriptions, but they were everywhere, and it was grating my nerves. 
 My third problem was my biggest. It bothered me to NO end how she would call her teacher "The Dragon" in one breath of a sentence, and the next it was his real name. She did that for "The Falcon", too, and if I didnt know any better, I would have thought both the author and the main protagonist were confused. 
 The final problem for me was the... uh, "chemistry" between the two main characters. I went in the book and I was thinking, "Hmm, I wonder who will love her." I thought maybe even this were just a fantasy book without a need for romance. 
 I was wrong. 
 Then, I thought maybe she would fall for her Kasia. I thought this was finally a good enough book to include a well told lesbian story. 
 I was still wrong. 
 Then I thought The Dragon would change drastically and they would fall in love. 
 I was almost wrong there, because as I thought this and as I was waiting for their chemistry to show up...he kissed her. Either I had missed details, or the author was just throwing stuff in there to peak interest. 
 So I tried to go along with it, even when the book got excessive and boring, and then even when I forgot what the book USED to be about. But then came the extremely random sex scene? And I had to finally put the book down and wonder what the hell was happening. 
 Sex?? Love?? Her and this pompous and unwavering dick?? 
 Needless to say, I did not finish the book.

After seeing Naomi Novik's newest, UPROOTED, recommended a couple of different places, by people whose judgment I trust, I promptly ordered it. And I'm so glad I did! It was a wonderful novel: rich, warm, deeply-rooted in the best kind of folklore. It felt familiar and new all at once, set in a world vaguely recognizable as Poland (here: Polnya) with magic. 
 Agnieszka has grown up in the shadow of the Dragon, the reclusive wizard that protects her valley from the Wood. Every ten years, he selects a village girl from the valley to come back to his tower. No one knows exactly what he wants them for (though of course there's gossip), but after ten years when he releases the girls, they never come home again. Oh, they might visit, but they're unalterably changed. Agnieszka belongs to the cohort of girls from whom the Dragon will chose his next girl, but everyone knows he's going to choose her best friend, the best and brightest and prettiest of the girls. Imagine her surprise, then, when the Dragon chooses her. 
 Her surprise deepens when she discovers, in the Dragon's tower, a latent talent for magic. A talent that might just be called upon to save not only her beloved valley but the kingdom itself from the encroaching evil of the Wood. 
 I think one of the things I loved about the story is that the hook here isn't huge: it's not some end of the world, wizards pitted to the death kind of scenario. But it's no less compelling and fast-paced for all that. The wood is a very real menace: the kind of thing nightmares are made of. (And the ultimate secret of the wood is startling and wonderful). 
 I loved Agnieszka. I loved the Dragon. (And I'm nerd enough to feel chuffed that I figured out the source for the Dragon's name: he goes by Sarkan, a variation of sarkany, a Hungarian shape-shifting dragon--a minor bit of trivia I would not have known except I've recently been immersed in Hungarian folklore for bookish purposes). Their unfolding relationship is sweet and spiky and charming. 
 This book isn't for everyone--there are a couple of adultish scenes that make it inappropriate for young teens. But I loved it.

It's nor here nor there. I'm going to steal a bit from Chester and say this is the epitome of Blur Rating. 
 Are you one of those readers who really gets fed up with series? 
 It's like every corner you turn, every book you read, you find out it's a trilogy. Or some kind of saga. I remember I used to whine and cry about this all the time because I don't know about you but if I read a book today you can sure bet your butt that I will not remember details about it in two months time unless it was utterly epic, and even then. And unlike most readers, I refuse to reread so I trudge on to the next book most of the time not knowing what the heck is happening until my memories resurface or a friend (usually Brit) so kindly refreshes my mind. 
 You may be asking yourself, why the heck is Melissa blabbering on about series and trilogies? 
 Well, because this book made me appreciate them. It dawned on me, that some plots just need to be turned into a saga because smashing them into a 400 page book is like forcing a size 9 foot into a 6 inch 7 1/2 size heel. 
 It's murder. 
 Cold blooded murder. 
 This novel is too dense. It's too layered and runs from one plot to another without giving us time to digest the previous one, making this one tough cookie to swallow. When it's not the overly descriptive surroundings, it's the tedious never ending rendition of magic, one that, by the way, still left a lot to be desired. 
 See, that is one thing I'm able to appreciate from the Throne of Glass series. I'm not its biggest fan (having actually only really enjoyed the second book) but I was able to enjoy how the plot thickens and gets layers added as the series progresses but if you try to do that in such a short novel, it just becomes hard to swallow and digest. 
 But at the same time, if it wasn't going to be written into a series, than this needed to be slimmed the heck down cause I just read 3 stories in one. I mean, I know this is only 440 pages or so and I've read longer books in one sitting but daaaamn at times this book read like a textbook. 
 And ain't nobody got time for that. 
 As for the writing 
 You know how some authors have a way of writing in a lyrical and slow paced manner but when you enter an action scene they have a way of making your heart pound and adrenaline sky rocket. That art of being able to make your breathe hold still and your anxiety hit the roof? 
 ...This one doesn't. 
 A friend had previously warned me about the writing style but I did not heed caution cause in my mind you don't have to be a poet to woo me. But crap, you at least have to have some finesse. 
 As for the magic 
 Look, honestly I'm not one to fidget about this. I usually don't care and they don't necessarily have to have some kind of system or consequence theme going on but, honestly? This magic was weird as heck. There was times she used spells but most of her magic was some sort of weird ass humming. If she wanted a twig to turn into a tree she would go... 
 hmmmm...you are a tree, you have leaves. You grow branches...You are a tree...grow...grow...You are a tree and have leaves and branches...You are a tree...hmmm 
 Ok, so that may not be an exact rendition but that sure is as close to it as it comes. 
 As for the romance 
 Just no. I can honestly say this is one of the worst romances I've read in a book. You know when reviewers rant about the lack of chemistry between characters? Well my friends, here it wasn't even a lack of it, it was a total absence! 
 When I got to the scene where he kissed her I was just... 
 Where the heck did that come from?!?! The romance sucks and not just because of the absolute lack of chemistry but because he never backpedals on being a total unrelenting inconsiderate jackass. 
 Like I said...Just no. 
 As for the characters 
 In all honesty? I just liked the Wood and I'm not really sure if that's a character. 
 But as for Sarkan (who was always snapping, glaring, and growling, reminded me of my rabid chihuahua) and A-jkidhl (because you can't honestly expect me to recall her name right?) 
 Sooo this just got awkward cause all I remember are the cons. But there are pros, I just can't really remember them. I mean, it couldn't have been that terrible, I did finish it, so there's that. Also, the story is good but I just didn't like how it was told. And the Wood is creepy (not buts here). Yeah...I'm shutting up now. 
 P.S. Also, this actually the first book I finished this month. So YAY me! I will conquer you, you neverending slump!

**Upon reflection, I think the 4.25 overall rating is completely merited. READ THIS BOOK!!** 
 At first, I was extremely drawn in and hooked on this book. I'd heard plenty of good raves and was really enjoying the feel of the world. I kept wondering if this was another take on the Beauty and the Beast story, because the beginning was certainly feeling that way, but I was pleased that it veered in its own direction. 
 Loved the main character Agnieszka, though at times I found her annoyingly naive/almost unable to make her own decisions. Also quite liked the Dragon and how he never quite turned into this wonderfully handsome prince-like perfect guy. I think it was good for there to still be the romance aspect without that being the focus of the book. I'd been under the impression that this was a young adult novel, and was a little surprised at the full-on sex scene, as well as the multiple gory battle scenes. I mean, it was in no way a very graphic sex scene, but something a 14 year old me would have found semi-scandalous. I thought that the descriptions of the battles/deaths were much more disturbing and very real, in a not-sugar-coating way that was great to read. 
 Kasia was a great character too. At the beginning it was hard to see why the two girls were friends because Kasia is described as being so perfect, but I think that their friendship was an important part of the overall story and was beautiful because it wasn't all about other people. I grew to care for Kasia in the same way that Agnieszka did, which is an obvious demonstration of a great friendship, and I like that Kasia did not overshadow Agnieszka after being in the Woods. 
 One other great thing that I loved was the language and vocabulary in the book, and I'll admit that I grabbed the dictionary twice. I perhaps have been not reading particularly challenging material recently, but this book's usage of thesaurus words was fun and I think tied to the way magic was so language-based. Speaking of which... 
 The magic in this world was very interesting, in that there are magic words and that how you put them together and pronounce them makes a difference. I rolled my eyes a bit at the same old trope of the main character suddenly finding out that she is special/has magic and that that is where the story starts, but I was pleased that her harnessing her magic (while she seems to be super good and super strong unbelievably quickly) took effort on her part and learning, and that she also had the "price" of being worn out and that the magic was almost like a muscle she had to work to use. It would have been easy for her to find out she had magic and just be spectacular without trying or even wanting it, or for magic to have no physical toll at all, and I think having these elements was great. 
 The Wood was a cool source of "bad" and I think the managing of this element was great at the beginning. I liked that there were incidences of varying "degrees" of contamination and that also there were situations when there were indirect consequences too (not just walking into the wood, but the pollen that blew from the wood to contaminate the crops). 
 For me, the major downfall of this book was really in the solution. Once the Queen of the Woods character was introduced, I thought that was an unexpected sharp left. I wasn't following who that character was, why she was a) still alive or b) evil, and I felt that the perspective of Agnieszka suffered at this point in the story. We as the reader were no longer following along with her reasoning and we were more watching the events unfold. I felt that I was missing out key information and the scenes about her being in the tree and sort of seeing memories and history were not resonating with me. Maybe I just read it too late at night, because I was not understanding about how the Queen's story led to the evil of the Wood, nor did it make me care for her or the other tree people. 
 I was really invested in the characters and enjoyed the book until that point. I was a little disappointed that Agnieszka was the one to figure out how to solve the problem and that she did it alone and became this odd witch woman that the people didn't really know how to interact with. 
 After reading a few other reviews, I think a re-read of the last hundred pages would be merited, as I may have just been too eager to devour the story that I missed key details. 
 2nd read through: 
 I definitely understood the Wood Queen and her role better this second time through. I still felt like this plot line was unexpected. There had been really no mention of any other peoples or species or races except the creatures in the Wood, so for Agnieszka to discover this long-lost entire type of people was odd. I understood better how the Queen had been hurt and traumatized and despaired, but not how this could have affected so much land/area, nor have lasted so long. 
 I understand that the story has to be about our main character and that she should be the one doing the discovering and solving, but was a little tired to see her be so special and strong so quickly. 
 Still like the Dragon! Still like the magic! Was annoyed that Agnieszka seemed to (later in the book) not really be casting spells so much as "pushing" and "throwing" her magic at things to make stuff happen. The beginning of the book implied that spells are longer sequences of words. Even she has to sing words in a repeat to melodies or just sort of repetition, but sometimes it felt like she was just using a force. 
 The Summoning was a bit of a deus ex machina by the end. 
 Still didn't really love the impression of Agnieszka just being a wandering witch lady that the people feared. I know she was doing important and good works, but it didn't seem to leave a lot of room for her own happiness, which I wanted after getting to know her so well.
The magic was strong and good in the beginning but petered out into one long drawn out struggle of good vs. evil.
It was a decent book. It didn't blow me away, but it was just enough fluffy fantasy for me to enjoy once in awhile.

 Have you ever felt like a book was written just for you? 
 Not even in a vague "this is my JAM!" kind of way, but more like the author performed a lobotomy on you while you were asleep, scanned and catalogued every part of your brain for all the things that click and make you happy, and then wrote a book, specifically for you, about those things? 
 Er... maybe not the unaware lobotomy part. That's kind of gruesome, and not behavior that I would normally condone. 
 ANYWAY! 
 Uprooted was written just for me, I'm sure of it. Dark, twisted, enchanted forests? Grumpy wizards? No-nonsense heroines? Magical books? Spells that take the form of stories? 
 I went in to Uprooted knowing next to nothing, and honestly, I'd recommend the same for others (though knowing more wouldn't hurt!) All I knew was that once every ten years, The Dragon demands that a maiden be sent to his tower, where she spends the next decade and when she returns, she is wholly changed. By her experiences? New knowledge? Nobody knows... but what Agnieszka does know for certain is that there's no way she will be chosen. The Dragon always takes the most special girl in the valley, and that girl is not her, but her best friend. 
 But of course, Agnieszka gets taken, and hijinks ensue. 
 The best way I can think of to describe the mood and feeling of Uprooted would be to say that it's like Howl's Moving Castle... for grownups. 
 If Howl's Moving Castle is like a warm, comforting cup of hot cocoa with mini marshmallows, then Uprooted is rich, dark chocolate mint cocoa- with a hefty splash of Bailey's. 
 COME TO ME.

Every ten years, the Dragon comes down from his tower and chooses a girl to come live with him for the next ten years. (No, not like that. Although, the towns do think that way.) When she returns, she leaves her home town for the security of a place far from the dangerous, corrupted Wood. Agnieszka grew up knowing the Dragon would choose her best friend, Kasia, as his companion when the time came, but for whatever reason, he chose clumsy, disaster-prone Agnieszka. As the Wood struggles to gain the upper hand in its constant battle to take take take, Agnieszka struggles to reconcile why she was chosen with what she thought she knew of the dragon, of her home, and of herself. 
 At first, I was worried Uprooted would end up being a fantasy novel that fell into all the tropey traps that fantasy novels tend to, but I was pleasantly surprised. It did fall into a few of the genre pitfalls, but not in a jarring way that would ruin the story. Overall, the story flowed very well from one event to the next and the characters felt as real as any characters could. When Agnieszka felt tired, so did I. The characters played well with each other, even when they didn't exactly play nicely together. Novik clearly knew these characters inside and out and knew exactly what they would do in the situations, not a single choice made by them felt out of place or wrong. Now, my question is: 
 When do I get a sequel??

So. This book was ... weird. It was good-weird. Definitely good-weird. 
 So when Agnieszka is taken by the Dragon instead of Kasia, she expects to live the next ten years as a servant (and possibly sex slave). But that is so far from what happens, you'd almost laugh if you knew where the story really ends up going. It's so imaginative and interesting and moving. Really, really good read. 
 Uprooted is good old-fashioned high fantasy. It has all the ingredients - evil kings, magical humanoids, mad wizards, witches, villagers, and evil being and a farm boy/girl with an Epic Destiny. It reminded me a lot of Kristen Britain's excellent Green Rider series. In fact the more I think about it, the more it reminds me. Not that they havethe same storyline or anything, but the tone of the book was very similar (and I enjoyed Green Rider a lot as well). 
 I know practically nothing about Eastern European folklore or fairytales, so I couldn't say howmuch the author has borrowed, but it felt fresh and new and interesting. Agniezska has been one of my favourite characters so far this year - I loved how confident she was without being arrogant and how passionate and wild. 
 And a standalone fantasy. Hallelujah. Give me more books that I don't have to wait a year for the second part for, please. 
 And that ending. Brilliant. 
 I liked the understated romance vein that threaded its way through the story. I loved the way Agniezska made her own decisions and how she and her lover were totally different but complimented each other so well. 
 I've only just finished it and I wanted to write my review straight away before I forgot anything. I'm really glad I picked this book up. I've enjoyed it immensely.

"They come and go like seasons, the winter that gives no thought to the spring." 
 I went into this one thinking it would be about a girl who was led to a man donned 'The Dragon', about her growth and journeys and adventures. Then I started thinking it would be about their relationship. I was wrong. 
 I found out it was a story of magic, about an ancient twist in the path that had gone horribly twisted, that it was up to a handful of characters to brave it out and try to set the paths straight again. The story isn't about the protagonist as much as it is about the larger picture looming in a horizon. 
 The story starts simply enough before it branches into unique complexity; she is chosen instead of Kasia, the beautiful one who everyone had always assumed would be taken instead. At first the reader will pause in confusion along with the protagonist and the villagers, but it eventually becomes clear why she must be the chosen, and then the story erupts from there. 
 Uprooted is one of those stories where the back blurb and the first quarter make it seem easier and simpler than it looks, but it's a deceptive surface covering something much deeper and more sinister. She doesn't stay in the castle, and the magic grows and grows to involve others, political struggles, kingdoms and heartbreaks, magic and battles, discovery and illusion. 
 The protagonist is fun at first because she's awkward, clumsy, a true tomboy who cares little for appearance. As her friend Kasia remarks, it's almost as if the magic inside her demands she dirties everything she wears, swearing one time that she even saw a branch reach out to soil her clothing when she was leaving the woods. The Dragon is definitely not a charming man - he is a reclusive, irritable wizard who has lost his hold on his own humanity while he battles to keep the humanity in the village from losing itself to the Wood. 
 The Wood is the biggest player for the story, a creatively woven and structured backbone that raises the story out of mediocre territory into richer, fertile imagination. There's violence and surprising twists, sadness and despair, but as with most dark fairy tales - light can exist at the end of these tunnels. 
 I applaud the author for her imagination - the story keeps getting more complex as it grows and it's not possible to guess all of the conclusions and wrap-ups. She writes differently - simply and easy to comprehend but not with elementary, stilted words. The pacing is sluggish sometimes, hence the four star rating, but it did plant itself firmly enough inside my reader zone that I couldn't help but continue following the trail. 
 A fantasy definitely worth reading.

reference_books.title: The Murder Complex (The Murder Complex, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This is exactly the kind of book I'm always looking for - interesting characters, unique plotting & page-turning action. Meadow has been trained by her survivalist father to overcome obstacles in a messed-up dystopian world. Zephyr thinks his only job is to clean up the murdered corpses in the morning after nights of violence. He has a not-so-secret from himself nighttime life killing those he cleans up in the am. He's tortured, she's uniquely capable. The plot twists & turns run in tandem to their growing relationship, which is just the best kind of YA angsty fun. Excellent! Very much looking forward to the next installment . . . .

reference_books.title: Panic (Panic, #1)
reference_books.review_text: This never really worked for me. As much I as love Oliver's writing, I never warmed up to the characters or their stories. Kept putting it down, hoping it would draw me in the next time, and sadly I had to force myself to finish.

reference_books.title: The Hunt (The Hunt, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Gene hides his human/heper status in a world full of vampires. In order to entertain the masses, a reality tv show (a la Hunger Games) will give select vampires an opportunity to hunt down the final known humans/hepers. In overlong chapters, Gene plots to control his body odor, hair and human reactions and figure out how to survive as a human in hiding. A final last sentence cliff-hanger was annoying, and lowers this to a 2 star rating. The book/writing/characters should be compelling enough that I want to read more - a cliff hanger is just a cheap trick cynically intended to sell more books. ugh.

reference_books.title: The Testing (The Testing, #1)
reference_books.review_text: An adult mystery writer tries to cash in on the YA market by writing a not terribly interesting, completely unoriginal, and sin of all sins, boring dystopian ripoff of Hunger Games.

reference_books.title: I'll Give You the Sun
reference_books.review_text: Loved "The Sky is Everywhere", but got irritated with the characters in this one. Jude is too self-absorbed, and Noah's gayness should not really be the problem that it's made out to be.

reference_books.title: Hidden (Firelight, #3)
reference_books.review_text: slightly disappointing conclusion to series - having said that, finished it in one sitting

reference_books.title: Legend (Legend, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A bit of Hunger Games Lite - June & Day are on opposite sides in a dystopian future. There's something about a plague that requires the government to control its' citizens, but that's just the set-up. Day is a rebel, June is a star of the government's forces. She believes he killed her beloved brother. Unknowingly, he takes her in when she's undercover. They bond. They kiss, but she still turns him in - only to realize that what she's believed all along is wrong. The torture scenes when Day is in the custody of the evil gov't are fairly graphic, and unfortunately although somewhat gratuitous are the most believable parts of the second half of the book. Characterization is slight, the action is acceptable, and the overall world building is too shoddy to make this a highly recommended read.

reference_books.title: 172 Hours on the Moon
reference_books.review_text: After all the hype, this just didn't live up to the advance billing. Too many plot holes - no way NASA would have chosen only 3 kids to stake their campaign on. At the least, it seems likely that several would have been nominated, then tested to see who was best suited. That kind of short shrift is emblematic of much of the rest of the book. In a hurry to get to a specific scene or vision, the author neglected to fully flush out the details - an almost unforgivable mistake in scifi.

book_a.title: Requiem (Delirium, #3)
book_a.user_review: Final book in the Delirium series - landed with a bit of a thud on first quick read-thru, but I enjoyed it much more the second time around. While Hana's story was much less engaging than Lena's, and the love triangle with Julian & Alex felt forced at times, it still worked, and the final chapter of Alex's experiences away from Lena, along with the ending brought it up to a 4.

Wait I'm confused, is there another book after this? I personally didn't even known this was a series after finishing the first book. I was content with it ending there, and a bit disappointed when I did find out it was a series. (Don't get me wrong, I was so torn up about Alex's death but kind of happy it didn't end so cliche) Now I've read all three, and I'm glad it ended up as a series now because the last two books, i feel, are so much better than the first. faster, more action. Although, I'm content with it ending the way the third book did and not finding out what happens to the characters. (Don't hate me) 
 I feel like Lauren Oliver stuffed a LOT of concepts into these three books (despite some of my annoyances with the plot of the book itself-the dystopian 'love outlawed' theme has some bugs that I will dutifully ignore at the moment) and I got a lot out of it, so that I ended up really enjoying the series. Great writing, which is getting harder and harder to find nowadays, and descriptive! But not so much that I'm falling asleep. And I can actually feel all the characters's personalities without me feeling like the author is somehow making the main character magically able to read the minds of everyone around them (isn't that annoying when that happens). 
 I'm annoyed with cliff hangers but Oliver ends it in such a way that I AM OKAY WITH IT. If it ends here I won't go ripping off doors and blog slamming her all over the Internet because I kind of get that books will never really end, that there will always be something after even though, yes it's made up. Again, it's not the characters that matter here (no matter how much we get attached to them) but their concepts, which I think we're manifested beautifully in this last book. I'm all for her getting together with Alex, but I always feel disappointed when the author FINALLY picks who ends up with the main character because they do it in such a way that, in the beginning it's like "oh my god, how will she ever choose!?" Into "wow that was stupidly obvious" and I'm left here like "cool, happily ever after, whatever". Is it wrong to hope for a twist to an ending? (See Allegiant) 
 Plus, if they do succeed in taking over Portland, then they have the entire rest of the US to conquer, plus reclaiming relations with other countries and reverting back into what is present day America, but you see, we already knew that. Again, it's not what happens to the society, because deep down we know what's going to happen, but Lena's journey (which was, I'm sorry, a bit of a let down because the entire time she was basically whining abut her love life when it was so obviously completely inappropriate with the events at the time. I miss her back in the first two books -hence the missing star- but liked the book despite her flaws -hence the other stars) and really we've already learned from it, and its kind of nice to let her choose who she'lI end up with without our prying eyes. 
 Honestly, the only thing I could think of that's missing is something about what the hell is going to happen to poor confused Hana. But that could have possibly been wrapped up into an epilogue. I just pray this series isn't overly extended (see The Mortal Instruments) or that the plot doesn't attempt to become too political and fail due to the brevity of a comeback into a sane state (See also Allegiant -it has it's good and bads-) that would be utterly disappointing.

Rowling did in the Deathly Hallows. So you just get a sense of closure after all the action.

No!!! Please, no! That it so not the end of this series! 
 Golly, come to think of it, I've more or less started all my reviews from Lauren Oliver's Delirium series with a "no" (see Delirium and Pandemonium reviews). I'm starting to think whether this is because I have an arguable explanation for saying so or it's just my refusal to accept what's at hand every time the books reach their endings... yeah, both. 
 [Be warned, this will contain spoilers from the first two books...and a bit from book three too. Okay maybe a lot. Sorry. I have to vent out some things.] 
 Let's do a little recap... (I'll make it quick, don't worry) 
 We follow Lena's story first through Delirium, where she is set on getting the cure for deliria, but then she meets a boy named Alex who shows her what love feels like. Falling in love with Alex made Lena decide not to take the cure anymore and instead run away with Alex into the Wilds, which first she thought was dangerous. In their attempt to flee Portland, Alex ends up being shot and left behind while Lena escapes into the Wilds. 
 This then follows on to Pandemonium where Lena is now living in the Wilds along with other un-cureds/Invalids. She thinks that Alex is dead. On the effort of trying to move on with her life, she takes on a mission for the movement against the DFA. Through her mission, she meets Julian, the role model of young individuals of the society, typically telling all the people that being cured is the right - and only - choice. So Lena, although grieving over Alex's supposed death, manages to fall in love with Julian, which then leads to them running off to the Wilds together, that is after Lena rescues Julian and all that. I know... vague details. You'll all get it once you read both books (if you haven't yet that is). So anyway, although Lena is now happy having Julian with her, surprise, surprise - Alex is alive and has found his way back to her... and so here is where Requiem takes the lead... 
 Those who oppose the "Deliria-Free America" law of the domineering government continue on with their goal - to give people the freedom to act without the need of the cure. Lena, Julian and Alex are all part of this group, which isn't exactly comfortable for any of them. Lena is determined to stand by her decision but Alex's presence makes things complicated. 
 Compared to the first two books, Requiem has a faster pace. Although most of it involved Lena travelling with her companions to seek other rebels and finally fight against the DFA, and watching Hana prepare for her upcoming wedding to Fred, whom I'd like calling the "ultimate villain" of this story. 
 In Pandemonium, we got alternating views of the "Then" and "Now" of Lena's life in the Wilds, here in Requiem, we get alternating points-of-view of Lena and - wait for it... Hana! Yeah. If you've read the ebook entitled Hana, her side of story showed that she betrayed Lena which led to the misfortune that happened in Delirium. So imagine reading from her now that she's cured... but guilt seems to be eating her up inside. I was so excited to see how she and Lena would eventually come face to face here. 
 Majority of the book revolved around the love story between Lena, Julian and Alex. To be honest, this love triangle was rather stressful. You see, I find Lena a bit annoying here for the whole "torn between two lovers" bit. But I admire her for trying to stand firm on what she has chosen. 
 I was heartbroken to see my dear, dear Alex come back as someone I don't know anymore. *sob* The Crypts sure have done a hell of a job on him. I'm still no fan of Julian even though he's done nothing but his best to fit into Lena's world. I do love the brawling scene between these two. Probably one the most entertaining parts of this book. LOL. Sorry. *sheepish grin* 
 Still, I really feel that this is just too exhausting. It feels like one of those Tucker-Christian (from Cynthia Hand's Unearthly series) slash Adam-Warner (from Tahereh Mafi's Shatter Me series) moments. Seriously, are these authors talking and plotting against their readers? *glares* 
 Now let's get to the part where my "no", at the beginning of this review, fits in. I hate the ending. Let me explain... Have you watched the movie, Inception? You know the part at the ending where Leonardo DiCaprio spinned his totem on a table to see if that part was a dream or not (if it's not a dream the totem stops, if it is then the totem keeps spinning), so when he walks away it just keeps spinning until it agonizingly slows down (and just barely even) then - boom! Screen goes blank then the credits roll. And you sit there stunned thinking: "did it stop spinning or not?" and no one gives you the answers... that's how Requiem's ending was. Damn it! 
 I refuse to believe that "bringing down the walls" scene was the only goal of this Resistance. There has got to be more than that. And the whole Lena-Julian-Alex mess? No way did that get settled as simple as that! And frankly I don't think Lena should get off the hook that easily. 
 So I have to ask... there is going to be a spin off or something right? Because that CANNOT be the ending. It's not fair! 
 For more of my reviews, please visit my blog: 
 The Blair Book Project @ www.theblairbookproject.blogspot.com

 I read Delirium and absolutely loved it. I read Pandemonium and thoroughly enjoyed it. As for Requiem I certainly LIKED it, but I did have a few issues, which I will submit you to now. ;) 
 I suspected it from the moment I picked up book 2 and by the end I knew it was inevitable. Brace yourselves... the love triangle is coming. I'm afraid I rather dislike love triangles. I think it was sparked by Twilight, and then bolstered by countless other books with the same tired formula. I'd rather just focus on the one couple, and bypass all the drama that comes with a second suitor. I'm certain love triangles can be done right but... I'm just a bit tired of seeing them done wrong. 
 In Delirium I completely fell for Lena and Alex. I relished every scene they had together; they seemed such a sweet, perfect couple. As a result I went into Pandemonium ready to hate Julian and... didn't. In fact I really love Julian, and that only intensified with this instalment. He's been through so much and his world was turned upside down, yet he never wastes a moment feeling sorry for himself. Instead he focuses on adapting to life in the wilds, and soon proves his worth to the rebels. This is all in spite of Lena's complete lack of support, as she is absolutely awful to him from the moment Alex reappears. I was really, really disappointed with how petty and mean she becomes. The only time she is nice to Julian is when she's using him to distract herself from Alex, or trying to make him jealous. 
 Speaking of Alex, I didn't find him very sympathetic in this instalment. At the end of Pandemonium I was actually (unpopular opinion alert!) not that happy about him turning up again. Because I knew the love triangle was imminent, and because I really. like. Julian! After the big Alex shaped space in book 2, I needed Requiem to remind me why I adored him so much in the first place and sadly, it didn't deliver on this front. He has a much less significant role than I expected, and spends most of it either cosied up with Coral or trying to rival Lena in the pettiness factor. I was really annoyed with his whole "I never really loved you" thing, and I can't believe Lena bought it. Pleeeease! You are both better than this. 
 Luckily there is much more to Requiem than the relationship drama. After the events of Pandemonium the government have stepped up their campaign against the 'invalids', and the time has come to make a stand. The tension had me glued to the page throughout and there was a certain fatality that absolutely ripped my heart in two... As well as following Lena's story we also rejoin her former best friend Hana, who has been cured and is preparing for marriage to Portland's mayor to be. At first this may all seem a bit irrelevant, but we soon learn Hana's new life is not as simple as it seems, and eventually the two story lines converge in the finale. 
 I really did enjoy this final instalment to the Delirium series, despite my issues with the love triangle setup. I liked the hopeful, open ending and the last few paragraphs gave me goosebumps! (the good kind) By the way, was I the only one who wanted to belt out "Do you hear the people sing?" from Les Mis as I turned the last page? Probably... but doesn't it fit well?!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ok spoiler alert spoiler alert. 
 So you read the first book of the series and you think its a dystopian book with heavy romance...the first book doesn't tell us much about the government. The second book goes from past and present pushes us more into what the resistance is doing, has us fall in love with Julian, and has us finding Alex at the end. This book is more into the resistance and also focused on Julian and Alex as possible love interests for Lena, but the entire book is just meh. Alex shows up and Lena pulls away from Julian, Alex starts to hang with Coral more and it hurts Lena so she uses Julian to feel better. Then Alex leaves and still loves her but he is gone.....and on and on. There is ZERO resolution to the book, what was the point? The really cute message to keep fighting? I didn't read this story for morals and values and to be uplifted. I read it to find out who Lena would choose and what happens to their government. Almost all of the dystopian books I have read have a conclusion as to what has happened with the government- this one does not. It is a waste of time. I'm sure I would have been more up in arms if I was not aware of this being the case from other reviewers to friends who have read the book. I absolutely hate books with no resolution. I need answers, I want to know what happens now, you can't just end the series like that, what a cop out. Clearly if that's where they ended there was more to be told. What happened to Fred did he die? Hanna? What happens to her? Let's pile on the questions shall we. Waste of my time. It could have been good it could have even been great, but it is not. And because of that I have rated it two stars.

Here's the problem, you can't finish a series about the freedom to love with a book that has no love in it. What this book should have been about was Alex and Lena finding each other and learning to love the new people they have become after their experiences in Pandemonium while Julian (who, as far as I'm concerned was never a serious romantic rival for Alex) becomes the figure head of the resistance movement. Instead, what I got was Lena pointlessly walking around in the Wilds interspersed with a post-procedure Hana (Hana?!?) ambivalently wondering around Portland kind of feeling guilty about turning in Alex and Lena and kind of not. Another problem, I couldn't care less what is going on with Hana. Instead of wasting time checking in with Hana in Portland we should have been getting Alex's POV on what was happening with Lena and how he was feeling about the whole situation. For some reason, instead of running into each other's arms and never letting each other go again, which is what ANYONE IN THE WORLD would do when a love that you thought was dead is miraculously alive again, Alex is mad at Lena for I'm not sure what and Lena believes him when he says he never loved her so she just continues things with Julian like nothing even happened. And that's pretty much how they go on throughout the book until the end when Lena finally sits down to have a conversation (novel idea there) with the girl she thinks Alex loves who tells her Alex still loves her and never stopped loving her blah, blah, blah. Suddenly she's over Julian and back on the Alex train where she should have been the whole time. Despite all this there is no satisfying conclusion to their love story and, along with a lot of other stuff, we're left to draw our own conclusions on how it all plays out. The end is another big problem for me. After wondering around in the Wilds for the whole book and seeing bombings and massacres by the government I'm supposed to believe that a poorly planned and disorganized group of rebels can pull off a successful coup, tear down the wall and suddenly everything's going to be ok and everyone lives happily ever after? Sorry, don't buy that. Pretty much everything is wrong with this book. It's not the story that should have been told and is a completely frustrating and unsatisfying conclusion to the series. Everything that happens is pointless and irrelevant and ultimately a massive disappointment. I feel about this book how cureds feel about life, disinterested and uncaring. What a waste of time. Verdict: Silver Linings Playbook this mess.

Meh. 
 There is nothing interesting in this book. The heroine is the typical bland character that allows readers to insert themselves into the story. The love triangle is uninspired, and while usually I find myself pulling for one pairing over the other, I didn't like any of the three characters (Alex is the quiet brooder type - no thank you; Julian is the doormat type - again, no thank you; and the interest in Lena is baffling - both guys would be better off without her). 
 Requiem is quite preachy, going on and on about choices and consequences. I don't disagree with the sentiments, but they aren't anything novel. I suppose the idea was to sound high-minded, but instead it came off as pretentious. 
 Lastly, what is up with the language? Did the other two previous volumes have so much language in them? At times like this, the saying comes back to me: profanity is the effort of a weak mind to express itself forcefully. Yeah, that applies to writers as well. 
 I have one more boring dystopian YA trilogy finale to read, and I'm thinking I might scrap the attempt. These stories are all the same, and I've wasted enough time reading them. If you have a recommendation of an original dystopian novel or series, please share. I'm done with whiny insipid heroines and plot-lines.

If you aren't familiar with the Delirium trilogy, Requiem is the third and final book. In the Delirium series, love is a disease and the folks in the books have a procedure done to be cured from amor deliria nervosa (love). 
 As I stated in my review of the first book, Delirium, love isn't just about the romantic love between two people. It's the love of friends, the love of hobbies, the love of the small details as well as the large. 
 Like most dystopian books, there is a lot of suspense, darkness, and conflict in this series. Good times (for the reader). The second book was kind of lackluster for me, but the ending... oh, the ending. I'm not normally a fan of the cliffhanger, but I did love the ending to Pandemonium. I needed Requiem after that ending! 
 Thus, I've been waiting and waiting to read Requiem which you know if you follow my blog. I hoped Requiem would pick up just seconds after Pandemonium, but I was very pleased with how Requiem began. In fact I was pleased with most of Requiem. I'd seen the low ratings. I'd read some of the spoiler free reviews. I was happy I was loving it so much because my expectations were no longer high. 
 Once I reached the end of Requiem, however, I understood all too well why this book was not well received. My poor hubby had to hear so much bitching from me last night. My main beef with this book (and the entire series I have devoted so much time toward) was there was no ending. No ending, no resolutions. I'm all for literature that makes me think. I have no problem when things are left up to my imagination, but when you leave the actual story up to my imagination, I feel robbed. 
 I feel robbed.

I Bought Requiem by Lauren Oliver off of Amazon to read and share my honest review. Requiem is the continuation of the Delirium trilogy by Lauren Oliver, it is the third and final book in the trilogy. Taking that into consideration I obviously cannot share every detail because it is the last book but I will share what I can. 
 I enjoyed the plot in this story because there is not just one place. Since there are two point of view's in the book, the plot bounces back and forth between Lena's hometown of Portland, and then the wilds. The more interesting chapters in my opinion were the ones in the wilds, and the reason I say this is because whenever you were with the invalids there was never a dull moment something was always happening. The chapters in Portland kind of annoyed me because I got bored with them so quickly but some of them did make the story. 
 I did not enjoy Lena's character in the first book Delirium but since then in the second book Pandemonium and now in the last book Requiem her character has really developed into someone that I enjoyed reading about. She no longer seems weak and unable to speak her mind, which is good because watching her sit there and take orders and mope around in the first book got old quickly. We saw more of Hana (Lena's best friend from Delirium) in this book as well, now I cannot really tell you much about her because it will ruin what you find out about her but lets just say she has changed as well since the first book, but right now I am not quite sure if she changed for the better or for the worst. 
 A character that we met in Pandemonium also showed up as well as we all knew he would and that is Julian whom you will know if you read the second book. I enjoyed his character very much he starts to branch out and be adventurous which I think surprised Lena as much as it did me. Lets talk about Alex for just a second (this is not a spoiler if you read Pandemonium so do not worry!) I have to say that even though I fell in love with Alex in the first book I absolutely hated his character throughout this whole book. Everybody has definitely changed in their own ways but Alex changed in awful ways! 
 Overall the story was great seeing people fight for what they believed in throughout this whole trilogy is very inspiring. It shows that no matter what people know the difference between right and wrong and they knew that what the society was doing to these people was very wrong. The book gets a 4 out of 5 stars and I cannot wait to pick up more of Lauren Oliver's books!

What did i think? 
 I think Requiem was a goddamn hot mess.

The momentum is lost when waiting for the next book. You can't quite remember all of the earlier details and why you loved the last one so much. For Requiem, my love never fully came back so it was just an okay ending to what started out so well.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It pains me to rate this book so low. I had been looking really forward to reading it. I've had a hectic schedule with no time to read and the first chance I got I dug in. I expected to tear through the pages and I expected to be so heartbroken in the last pages being this is the end of the series. Instead, I found myself trudging through the pages, wondering when the action would pick up, and finding myself irritated with Lena and her back and forth feelings for Alex and Julian. I've typically no issues with love triangles but this one was getting on my nerves. I felt bad for Julian because she was playing him like a fiddle and the poor guy was so smitten (he gave up his entire life for her after all) that he just let her walk all over him. There was no emotion between Lena and her mother when they finally get to spend time together. We don't hear anything from her mother about her time away from Lena. There were so many areas in the novel where more could've been done, especially in a series finale, that it's a shame so much was left out. And then the end, well, I don't even know where to begin. This is one of the worst endings I've ever read. There was no closure at all in any situation in the book. It did not feel like an ending. It felt like a cliffhanger for another novel. The raid on Portland, and all the other areas across the country, had just begun. Lena made absolutely no decision on whether she was going to choose Julian or Alex. We have no idea what happened to Hana. She just walked away from her husband, knowing the building he was in was about to explode, wondering if someone was going to kill her for her betrayal. There was not one single loose end tied up at the end of this novel that I'm completely baffled that this is it. I walk away from this series entirely disappointed. I loved the first two so much and the last just sucked all the life out of it. However, with all of that said, I still love the beautiful way that Lauren Oliver has with writing prose. I just wish she'd focused more on the plot and the story.
One of the worst endings!!!!!! Reminds me of the end to the soprano series. WTF!!!!!!!!!!

I'd like to warn you that this review contains spoilers, but I'm not sure how you can spoil a story that had absolutely no resolution whatsoever. After loving Delirium and Pandemonium, I anxiously awaited the ending to the story. I was let down from page one. There was so much forward momentum going at the end of Pandemonium, and it came to a screeching halt within the first pages of Requiem and never got started again. This felt like a half-assed effort from Oliver; almost as if she needed to meet her deadline and figured she'd take the easy way out and let us make up our own minds about what happened to Lena, Hana, Grace, Bee, Julian, Alex, and the rest. (Either that, or she figured she was home free with the cash in the bank selling the rights for the TV show and felt she didn't have to fully flesh out the rest of the story.) I don't think I've ever been more disappointed in a finale to a series than this one, and it's not because she left us hanging, it's because the entire book, all four-hundred and some pages, was nothing more than fluff filler. There was nothing in it that made me care about any of the characters, and their story arcs were flat, disjointed and pointless. I really feel that Oliver let her readers down on this one, in a BIG way.

I couldn't do it. I made it 32 pages into the book and had to stop. Maybe it gets better as the book goes on and the 18 year old writer protagonist matures. But I didn't find it worth going through the beginning to get there. It reads like a teenager wrote it, and maybe Scott Westerfeld intended it that way. In fact, I hope he did, because there's no other way to justify plument in the quality of his writing style. I'm a fan of his, particularly of his Leviathan trilogy, and this in no way measures up. The descriptions are bland, the interactions over the top cheesy and the dialogue painfully to the point or cliche. 
 My impression is that it's meant to encourage young writers to participate in NaNoWriMo, and give them hope that their novel will one day be published. (Which I support, as long as the author does a lot of self-editing before submitting it anywhere) But if this is the writing style that he's claiming will be picked up by big New York publishers, then I worry about the future of YA publishing. If fact, I cringe that this book is being published and will do well just because it has Scott Westerfeld's name on the cover.

Darcy es una adolescente india, que escribio un bosquejo de novela en un mes y decide abandonar a su familia y mudarse a New York (para ser una gran escritora). La novela que escribe es sobre una chica atacada por terroristas en un aeropuerto que, al tratar de sobrevivir, se hace la muerta. En el momento que pierde la conciencia cruza al Otro Mundo, donde conoce a otros seres (fantasmas y no tanto). 
 El problema es que ambos relatos estan entrelazados y la parte de Darcy es taaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaan aburrida. El padre le dice: "pero, podes escribir en tu tiempo libre y aun ir a college" "No, escribi la novela en un mes y casi me mata" (WTF!!!???) Es tan poco comun que una familia de origen indio promueva la educacion de mujeres en vez de insistir en que se case, que es molesto ver como desprecia todo ese apoyo familiar. Como se puede ir de la casa si "no sabe ni lavar su propia ropa". Ademas, cual es el sentido de la cultura india, si se comportan como sino lo fueran... ya se, es prejuicioso, pero el audiolibro es muy explicito en el acento. 
 No creo que complete la serie

I purchased this book at the TTBF last year and was not disappointed. Scott Westerfeld wrote a very good book which was actually two books in one. I loved the layout of one chapter being the viewpoint of the writer and the next chapter being that of the actual book "Afterworlds." Unique concept. I could have done without the writer part of it but it was still good. The actual story of "Afterworlds" was very creepy but the book held my attention so I read it in record time and just finished reading it at 1:25AM. A very good read. I can see whay he is a New York Times bestselling author! If you like creepy and a little romancy...this book is for you!

A disappointing book written by a usually reliable author, Afterworlds is actually two full-length novels inter-cut with each other. The first is a tiresome wish-fulfillment fantasy for wannabe writers, depicting an 18 year-old author, Darcy Patel, who moves to New York City after selling her first manuscript. The second is the novel Darcy has written - a bland supernatural romance about a girl who discovers the ability to see ghosts. 
 Let's start with Darcy. Darcy's story is totally devoid of conflict and therefore the most boring story I have ever read. She gets everything she wants without any effort whatsoever. She gets $300,000 dollars for a crappy first draft she wrote in a month, she moves to NYC and finds the perfect apartment, everyone loves her books - from her instant girlfriend to distinguished authors she barely knows, she goes on an amazingly successfully pre-publicity tour, blah, blah, blah, blah. Honestly, the only obstacle that Darcy ever faces is the occasional slight insecurity which she quickly overcomes. She's the most boring character of all time! She never faces any hurdles; she never has to try particularly hard. This fact is made ever more deeply ironic because at one point in the story Darcy tries to convince a crowd that conflict is the most important element in any story! Maybe the author should have listened to his own advice and actually included some conflict in Darcy's story. 
 I appreciate that Westerfeld has tried to show what "real" YA writing is like - the pressure from editors to make books marketable, the long delay before publication, the pressure to write sequels, the total necessity of publicity and networking. All that is great. But without any conflict, Darcy's story is just a series of unengaging events. By the end, I was actively irritated by her for getting everything she ever dreamed of without any cost or consequence. 
 In addition, while I appreciate the gesture of a 50 year-old straight white man deciding to write a teen lesbian romance about a woman of colour, I was utterly underwhelmed by Darcy and Imogen's romance. Most everything about their relationship was unconvincing, inauthentic and unmoving. I don't want to criticise Westerfeld for attempting to write a YA lesbian romance - the world most definitely needs more of them - but I honestly wished he cared enough to make the romance real, not some ridiculously diluted-down version of lesbian romance written by a straight man for a presumably straight audience. 
 And as for the story Darcy writes... Well, that's a whole different level of atrocious. Darcy's novel about Lizzie Scofield, a teenage girl who survives a terrorist attack and acquires the ability to see ghosts, has got to be the most horrendously generic supernatural romance I have ever read in my entire life. Lizzie's love interest has no personality whatsoever - he's a hot guy who shows up and Lizzie falls instantly in love with him. There's no substance whatsoever to their relationship, just PG-rated kisses. Lizzie's relationship with him isn't even that relevant to the plot and plays such a minor role it could easily be dropped entirely. 
 Lizzie's friendship with the ghost of a murdered girl takes up much more time and it's also more emotionally engaging and actually drives events. Except that Lizzie's story is so shapeless! She gains the ability to see ghosts and then hangs out in her house for a while. Every time she gets into a problematic situation she just summons her hot boyfriend to save her instead of solving things herself. Lizzie appears to have a few plot goals involving a serial killer and a ghost collector, but even those plot lines turn out to be too brief and insubstantial to amount to much. And THIS is the story that all the characters in Darcy's story are crazy about!? It's absurd! 
 The worst part is that Westerfeld is very obviously aware of the shortcomings of his book, but he just doesn't care. The book features a lot of meta-commentary about YA writing in general and, in particular, about cultural appropriation. Darcy wonders if it's okay to include a Hindu god in her story "for the purposes of YA hotness." But the book never properly resolves this issue, nor acknowledges that it's actually 
 Scott Westerfeld 
 who has appropriated a Hindu god into his story for the purposes of YA hotness. Lampshading a trope doesn't suddenly make it okay. Lampshading is not a get-out-of-jail-free card. 
 And what's more, there's very little point to inter-cutting the two stories. They never really influence each other; they never intertwine; they are always merely the sum of their substandard parts. I was longing for the moment that the two stories would mesh together and become some mind-bendingly post-modern self-parody of YA literature. That was honestly the only thing that could have saved this book. Alas, Scott Westerfeld is not so self-aware. 
 This book has totally changed my opinion on Scott Westerfeld. Previously I saw him as a solid, varied writer who occasionally misses the mark. Now I see him as a mediocre, generic writer who occasionally finds a decent idea. This is definitely one of Westerfeld's worst.
Stopped reading on page 392. Just not worth finishing at this time.

I did like the concepts that were brought out, and the fear of the supernatural that you don't quite understand. The darkness reminded me a little of A Great and Terrible Beauty by Libba Bray.

I am kind of at a loss with Scott Westerfeld. He's never once irritated me enough to make me want to stop reading his books. But on the other hand, I've now read quite a few of his works, and there wasn't a single one that made excited to be reading it. He skates by on "fine," and it hasn't really changed with this book. Although there were a few moments early on that made me think that maybe this would be his breakout book in my affections, in the end, it was...fine. Not bad. Just not great.

 The idea of writing an entire novel feels so foreign. The only thing I really know about the publishing process is from "Romancing the stone" and tweets that authors make (especially Ally Carter). So an entire novel that takes me through the writing process? Yes please! 
 It starts off with Darcy Patel getting her novel published, she's freaking out, ditching college to move to New York. No one in her family has read her book, and she can barely believe its real, It only took her thirty days to write the entire novel. 
 Then starts chapter two, now all of a sudden she's in an airport and there's a terrorist attack. Wait. Not her... some girl named Lizzie? Who is she? And why has her story started? Then we go to chapter three and now we're back with Darcy? 
 Apparently every other chapter would be a scene from Afterworlds, it's a story inside of a story. I personally don't like ghost stories. I'm a huge scaredy-cat and they just freak me out so I half-skimmed all the Afterworld chapters. Which means I didn't get the whole "experience" but it was a cool idea. 
 As for Darcy's story she frustrated me so much! She moves to New York on a budget and instead of following the budget she goes all crazy and buys an expensive loft and eats exotic ramen. I think I was more stressed about her budget than anything else. She was also so wishy-washy. She doubted herself nearly every other page. In the beginning it was okay but near the end even I didn't believe in her anymore Another huge part was her friend Imogen. Not gonna lie there were a few unexpected parts there, but I think it made the whole story more unique. 
 Imogen Is also a writer who has been in the publishing world longer than Darcy has. She starts to show her the rope and helps her meet the right people. She's also the first person to read Afterworlds and giver her feedback, other than her agent. Other characters that I really liked where Carla and Sagan. It was cute how they were these book nerds whose best friend is now this hot up and coming debut author. 
 Last positive thing about this story was the fact that we go to see Darcy's dreams come true! She not only met her favorite authors but was able to get blurbed by them, which must be the dream 
 . 
 Overall it was a fun story about a debut author, a great story for any paranormal lovers
