Not a fan of this one. I've read some Westerfeld, but I wouldn't say I'm a huge fan. This one though, not for me. Just not enough uumph. I found the narrators, both of them, rather annoying and there wasn't enough plot development here to keep me interested. I had this one as a galley copy on my e-reader, so you just never know how many pages the book actually is. It just went on and on and...you get the picture.

This is unfortunately a DNF for me :/ I really tried to give it a chance but I just wasn't interested enough. This book has 2 stories. One is about a girl named Darcy who writes a book during NaNoWriMo and gets it published. She goes to New York and lives the life of a writer. The second story is the book that Darcy got published. It's about Lizzie, a girl who survives a terrorist attack and goes to the afterworld and it changes her. Honestly, I liked the story about Lizzie. I wish I could finish her story, but I can't handle reading a book and skipping chapters. Darcy's story is so uninteresting to me. I don't know why Scott Westerfeld published two ENTIRELY different stories in one book. I really wish he had published the book about Darcy and then, like Rainbow Rowell is doing with Simon Snow, published the Lizzie story separately. 
 Unfortunately this wasn't for me. 
 I won't say if I recommend it or not, simply because it's not the writing or anything that was bad, just poor choices on the authors part.

3.5/4 stars 
 This is my first Scott Westerfeld book and it was so different for me! Im always about the romance and a book making me experience something different, and this book was TOTALLY different! 
 For starters there is two stories in one! :D BONUS! 
 and the cool thing about the book is that it goes back and fourth between Darcy story and Lizzie story and it is easy to keep up with as well. Darcy story has regular white pages and Lizzie story has black columns on the top and bottom of each pages, and that really helped with keeping track of which story your reading and also made the book look amazing and different, but regardless of the pages it is pretty easy to keep track of each story and follow them. 
 Review of Darcy story: 
 Darcy was a very different character for me to read. Her love interest and life is different then what I'm use to reading but it was still fun to read. I felt that you would really need to know about the writer/author lifestyle in order to know how writing and publishing process takes place and what needs to be done during the process and Scott Westerfeld really did a great job in showing us what needs to be done and he gave us a hint of what writers go through. I did feel myself wanting to just get back into Afterworlds because certain times I got a little bored with Darcy story and her complaining about her writing and her ending of her book for like half of the whole book. I couldn't really connect with her because of her personality I felt that her personality was sort of stand off-ish and then when she got talking about her religion and stuff It was interesting but didn't really hold my attention for long, and it was interesting to see how Darcy family do certain things and how Darcy and Nisha don't call there mother "mom" it was weird for me. I found it shocking and exciting to see Darcy talk about her book but would be shocked or upset when she mentions things from the book that hasn't came up yet. It honestly felt like I was getting spoiled! but I see that it was approriate because it got us seeing how the story we are reading developed and had it's ideas and make you want to finish Darcy story to see what happens. I felt that Darcy part of the story ended ok I felt that it could of ended a little better. 
 Review of Lizzie story: 
 Lizzie and the Afterworlds was what kept me hooked on this book, I couldn't wait to see what happened next, The beginning part of Lizzie story was so amazing and interesting reading about the terrorist attack, and experiencing the Afterworlds with her, and reading about the bad man and his murders. There was so much actions and events in the beginning and a little in the middle parts of the story. But after certain events happens I felt that the story went down a hill a little, it wasn't as exciting and even though it wasn't that predictable the ending section wasn't another special which sorta sucks. But overall Lizzie story was still cool and fun to read. 
 Overall, Afterworlds as a book was a new experience for me, It was fun to read one story and then have another one in the next chapters. I thought this idea was very creative and smart. 
 Thank you for reading!

DNF at page 177 
 2/5 stars 
 I haven't picked this up since it was announced that this didn't make the shortlist. Maybe I'm just trying to justify my laziness here, but I don't really like this book. 
 The reason why I won't finish this is because I don't have the motivation to continue reading it, and I've convinced myself I no longer like it. Specifically, the fact that Lizzie's storyline is uninteresting, the links between the two stories are so tenuous that they might as well not be there, and the (mild spoiler) INSTALOVE IN DARCY'S STORYLINE WHICH TOTALLY CAME OUT OF NOWHERE AND IS COMPLETELY UNEXPLAINED AND WILL NOT END WELL FOR ANYONE. Also there's the fact that Darcy took the dead childhood friend from her mother's life, which will not end at all well for their relationship (I can't believe that she was so stupid as to think that doing that would be a good idea) . And I haven't even gotten to Darcy's sister, who is 14 (I think) and a complete maths genius and how does Westerfeld show us that? By having her create Darcy's "budget" (which she seems to be ignoring anyway) for her and telling the reader that she check's their parents tax forms. 
 NO. JUST NO. 
 One of the things I hate most (and it happens so frequently in YA novels with 16/18 year-old protagonists) is when the main character has a younger brother/sister who is so smart/clever/sporty/fantastic at this, yet ACTS LIKE A 8 OR 10 YEAR-OLD . In Afterworlds, the little sister is smart enough to check tax forms for her parents, yet she immediately goes to touch everything and act like a spoilt 6 year old at Darcy's temporary apartment. 
 NO. That's not how people work. 
 Maybe I'll finish this one day, maybe I'll just read Darcy's story and skip Lizzie's - except I won't do that because of the INSTALOVE WHICH CAME OUT OF NOWHERE - so, perhaps I'm justified in DNFing this. 
 Either way, 2/5 stars.
Overall an intriguing read.
Parts of this book are good, but, the plot holes needed a rope ladder to get across.

In my opinion, the story Darcy wrote was better than the actual story about Darcy. I love writing, so seeing what it was like to be a nearly published young adult author was really cool to read. The story she wrote, Afterworlds, was even better because the story was different, though both were still really good!

Afterworlds made me want to be a teen YA writer living in New York for the first time, and I won't be the only one. It will also inspire NaNo novelists the world over to bludgeon agents with their half-baked masterpieces on December 1, which is a very bad idea, but we can't really blame Westerfeld for that. 
 This is two books folded into one. First, there's the story of Darcy Patel, a teenaged debut novelist who defers college and uses her entire (hefty) advance to move to New York, live in an insanely expensive apartment, and work on her two-book deal. Told in alternating chapters is the book that's landed Darcy her NYC dream life, a slight but compelling YA paranormal romance that starts with a firecracker first chapter featuring a terrorist attack in an airport (as her agent and publisher keep reminding her, it's that first chapter that made them want the book). 
 Darcy works on rewrites, meets her first love, has writerly highs and lows, and generally has a blast. Readers will, too. Two books for the price of one, PLUS an insider's pass into the life of a YA writer in New York! I'm pretty sure Westerfeld filled it with writerly in jokes, but I didn't get them all. There's a John Green stand-in, and a lot of shade thrown at the youthful ebullience of debut novelists, and it's all a lot of fun. Read it!

I loved Scott Westerfeld's Uglies series, so I was particularly excited to read this book, however, this book was just a mess. It was extremely difficult for me to summarize the events of this book because there were so many events, most insignificant, that happened in the story. I didn't like how it switched from Darcy to Lizzie and honestly didn't even know why we were told Lizzie's story. The book felt all over the place to me. It was long and reading it was like sludging through the River Vaitarna. What I had a problem with was the fact that Darcy was suddenly gay. She had no idea that she was even gay. How can you be 18-years-old and not know which gender(s) you are attracted to? Because LGBQT issues are so popular and "hot" right now, I feel like having a lesbian character was just an addition, something that wasn't thought out--like having a random asexual character in a story just "to be cool." I also didn't understand the tagline of the story "Darcy writes the words. Lizzie lives them." It makes it seem like this is a story about a person named Darcy who controls a person named Lizzie. In a way, this is true, but it makes it sound like a whole different story, like a Stranger Than Fiction type of story where a real person is being controlled by an unknown force and they have no idea why. I found Darcy's Afterworlds extremely dull. I honestly couldn't understand why Darcy's publishing company gave her so much money for it, nor did I know why it was expected to be so popular. Lizzie's story was actually my least favorite part. There was nothing enthralling about it. It felt like I was being tugged every which way in this story and I had no idea where the story was going and why I was supposed to care. It was especially weird because the ending of this story was described as "brutal" by one of Darcy's fellow authors, but there was nothing altogether brutal about it, besides the death of the FBI agent that was hired to protect Lizzie after the terrorist attack. There was so much left unsaid and unanswered at the end of the story, which I guess is why there is supposed to be a sequel for it. In both stories, all of the characters felt lifeless. I didn't care about any of the characters nor their relationships. I felt nothing for Lizzie and Yamaraj or Darcy and Imogen. There was little imagery and it was hard for me to immerse myself in this world. The setting was as dull and gray as the afterworld. If Westerfeld hadn't of written Uglies, and wasn't a popular author, I don't see any young adult truly enjoying this. The cover is appealing, it is what the cover of Darcy's novel Afterworlds looks like; it features spreading black ink which represents the River Vaitarna and a teardrop, which represents Lizzie's teardrop shaped scar which she got after being exposed to tear gas in the airport during the terrorist attack. The cover is very YA appealing. It's unusual and it does make one stop and say "Hmm---wonder what this is about?" In fact, one of my fellow librarians picked it up because she found the cover so appealing. If only the story had been as appealing. If I had to recommend this to any age group, I would say someone who is 18+. This is more for those who are college-aged/new age as Darcy is college-aged and it isn't dealing with any YA issues, really, other than the brief paragraph on Imogen discussing the hardships of being gay. LGBQT issues are so rarely brought up that I'm a little bit baffled by this being a featured LGBQT book on YALSA. Reading this book has discouraged me from wanting to read any of Westerfeld's other books.

I enjoyed Westerfeld's Uglies series, so when I saw Afterworlds at the library, I decided to check it out. The premise sounded interesting, and as I got into the first few chapters, I loved the Vedic influence. I wasn't as interested in the publishing world, the dual story being told, and it came off a little self-conscious as Westerfeld is in effect praising his own writing within the story itself and that's just...weird. 
 Interesting premise aside, I see where this story is going, and I'm done with it. If I want to read a story with Hindu influence, I'll stick with Roger Zelazny's Lord of Light (https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/1...). Contrary to what characters in the book said, it has been done before (Vedas/Hindu influence in fantasy). 
 Unfortunately, it feels like the new trend in YA lit is to throw in as many minorities and same-sex relationships as they can (Stiefvater did the same with her Raven Cycle books), and it comes across as a forced effort to somehow show how progressive the YA genre is or something. We do need more minorities represented in American literature - my children are of mixed heritage and we enjoy learning about different cultures and peoples - and I am not afraid of the diversity of people and lifestyle. But, first and foremost, I read a book for the story it tells me and if that story gets lost due to some agenda, I'm done. 
 *I will say I enjoyed the little dig at Twilight. That was pretty funny.

I don't know how I feel about this book? It was really hard to get into because the book was two stories alternating, Darcy's story, and Afterworlds, the book she presumably wrote. Once there was some kind of intense part going on with Lizzie, the chapter'll end there and start off at Darcy's dilemma with writing or the apartment. I'm not 100% sure what's the whole point behind having the two stories. I suppose to kinda give insight of what the writing process is? But then you get some of Darcy's personal life and it's just really distracting. I ended up chopping up the book and reading Darcy's stuff first and then Afterworlds, which probably isn't what Westerfeld intended to happen. Nevertheless, Afterworlds is an interesting new twist and I did enjoy kinda nosing in on Darcy's life.

I give it 4.5 stars. Brilliant read. I've had this book sitting on my shelf for nearly a year, waiting for a full weekend to get to enjoy it properly. 
 I loved the interwoven tale of Darcy exploring her writing career, and Lizzy who lives the tales. I think I enjoyed Darcy's perspective more. She was a very relateable character living in a plausible society. As she went through the writing process, I had the urge to get on my computer and start trying to write a book myself. She faced struggles both with her books and with her personal life, allowing for a multidimensional and realistic character. 
 Lizzy's tale was also very fascinating. Scott Westerfeld did a great job of creating a unique mythical universe with some romance, without having the entire book be driven by that romance. While Yama and Lizzy where clearly in love, they each had their separate purposes, and they each understood that. 
 This book was very unique. I have read many YA books, but I have never read one woven together quite like this. It was nice to see a new concept beyond traditional supernatural or realistic fiction. This provided for a bit of mixed genre, as you switched back and forth between different perspectives/ storylines. I'm curious to see what Westerfeld will do with a sequel. 
 I highly recommend this book to YA lovers!
Thoroughly enjoyable.

There were parts of this book that were fascinating to read...like the idea of a novel-in-a-novel, and "inside" details of what debut authors' lives are (or could be) like. In the writing/publishing aspect, I felt like those parts of the book were almost a love letter to fans and book lovers that also want to be authors. 
 But...the swearing. I mean, hardcore swearing, like the F-word on almost every page. And I did not enjoy reading about the romance, either. I tried to skim over Darcy's parts after a while. In these aspects, I almost feel this book should have been an adult novel. 
 Some smaller things that also bothered me were several glaring typos, and the characters in Darcy's novel didn't feel very real. It was hard to care about them, and I wondered, if I had just read the black-bordered pages, would it have been a pretty short/thin book, and would I feel satisfied after reading it? Because it was a novel-within-a-novel, sometimes it wasn't as noticeable that not much was really happening in "Afterworlds"--and especially pretty much ZERO happening in Lizzie's real life. Time apparently passed, but we know virtually nothing that went on in her "real" life. Also, I really did not agree with a certain action that Lizzie did. (Spoiler alert: Lizzie is a MURDERER?! Couldn't her "Breakup" with Yama have been achieved some other way? Seriously, a 17-year-old murderer?! And she suffers no consequences of any kind for such a terrible crime, no matter how justified she may have felt in doing it?!

**2.5** 
 I rarely rate books below three stars, but there were just so many things in both plots that could have been amazing that were too flat! To imitate the multitude of awkward metaphors scattered all throughout it: this book drips with potential, but my imagination was left parched. The concepts are all super intriguing, but none of them are ever fully explored. Imogen is the only interesting character. Darcy is only Indian to give Westerfeld an excuse to use Yamaraj, Lizzie is far from a sympathetic protagonist, and Yamaraj is SO "mysterious" that he is boring. Hardly any of the conflicts in either plot actually cause much obstacle, leaving no doubt that Darcy and Lizzie will achieve their goals. 
 Darcy's unrealistic luck didn't bother me like it did many other reviewers, because there is a certain amount of stretching the truth that an author must do to set things up. We need that feeling of unrealistic luck for Darcy's future to feel unstable. It wasn't very effective, despite her utter disregard for financial prudence, but I see what Westerfeld was trying to do. The dialogue was awkward in both plots, and much information was inconsistent or poorly explained. To be honest, I am really tempted to interpret this whole book as satire against publishers' focus on sales over quality and the romanticized teenage dream of writing. 
 Despite my negative review, I really appreciated the experience of reading Afterworlds. I loved exploring a new and unique (as far as I know, anyway) concept of the afterlife. My main disappointment is that I wanted to be able to explore it more. There are many layers of it alluded to, but we only get to see the very basic workings of it.

Review initially posted at Wyz Reads. 
 Wow. It has been a while since I reviewed a book. I've read a lot of good ones along the way. However, for whatever reason, none of them compelled me to write a review. There were a few I wanted to, but the words just didn't come. Then Afterworlds came along. Something about this book is so. . .unique, it just had to be written about. 
 To begin with, it's important that we realize that Afterworlds is actually two books in one. It is part Afterworlds, a novel written by fictional 18-year old Darcy Patel, and part the story of Darcy becoming a published author. These two stories are told in alternating chapters. 
 I won't bore you with the details of either story, because, quite frankly, they're good, but not the most interesting part of this book. The most interesting part is reading and watching Scott Westerfeld wield his pen and do magical things with this book. 
 First off, there's the fact that the story-within-the-story is written by an 18-year old girl named Darcy, not a 51-year old man named Scott (who actually wrote the story). It's also not only Darcy's first published novel, but she wrote it in a month, and has spent a year revising it. I don't know how he does it (probably because the man is a genius), but Westerfeld manages to create a novel (Darcy's Afterworlds) that a publisher would take a chance on, but also reads like a debut novel from a teenage girl. By itself, it may not get a second glance from me, but the story is interesting. 
 Okay, I mentioned the story; perhaps I should talk about it a bit. The story of Darcy's novel is of a girl named Lizzie (and yes, the fact that a girl named Darcy wrote about a girl named Elizabeth is addressed in the book). Lizzie is in an airport when 4 gunmen come in shooting up the place. A 911 operator suggests she play dead, so she does. Lizzie then discovers that she can sort of pass through between worlds -- the overworld where we all live, and the afterworld where we go when we die. The story goes from there, there's some paranormal romance type stuff going on, and she's faced with difficult decisions along the way. You know, kind of like a debut novel from a teenage girl would read. 
 Then there's the other half of Scott Westerfeld's novel. The story of Darcy herself. As someone who has often been intrigued by the publishing world, I find this story fascinating. Darcy decides to postpone her freshman year of college to move to NYC and work on both Afterworlds and the sequel. She deals with her editor, her agent, and fellow writers. She finds love, and deals with being a young adult in the big city. 
 In this story, I can see Scott Westerfeld's experience coming through. His experience as an author in the publishing world is evident, as he has been through the ins and outs of this process many times. Reading this book felt at many times like a veteran pulling up the curtain and poking a flashlight around for everyone to see what really goes on backstage. His experience as a writer comes through in ways I didn't fully anticipate. 
 I have never written a book. I have a few I've started, but none I've seen all the way through. I imagine, though, that if I write a book and have it published, I would love to tell my readers certain things to look for -- little pieces that I'm particularly proud of or that took a lot of effort on my part. Darcy, through Scott Westerfeld, gets this opportunity. 
 By telling us Darcy's story of getting the book published, Scott Westerfeld can guide our thoughts on the book. We can see the connection between a ghost in Darcy's book and a "ghost" from Darcy's mom's past. We can see how much work has gone in to the ending, so we will read it more eagerly, knowing what could have happened, or what was an earlier draft. We can even keep an eye out for a few words to make their appearance, as Darcy mentions they'd be good to use. How often does an author get to do this? Never. Never times. It's a unique look into the mind of an author as she is creating the book -- even if it is all entirely fictional. 
 That is the mastery of this book, and that is the genius of Scott Westerfeld.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I didn't like the ending but the rest was good. I also think there should be a squeal. I found the story about Lizzie more interesting than Darcy's story.

Oh my goodness! I am awestruck by this glorious cover! Sadly, that's really the only good thing about this book. I had 1000 problems with this book and I will share some of them with you. 
 The premise of this book is interesting. It was delivered not as good as it could have been written though. 
 1. The Characters 
 Darcy was one of the most bland plain characters in YA. She was so immature and very irresponsible. She was so quick to assume that Imogene wrote something rude about her in her diary without even knowing if it was her. 
 Imogene very frusterating. I can understand being a funny character but I guess I just couldn't connect with her. 
 Lizzie was very cookie cutter. I couldn't see if she was just supposed be that way, or if Westerfeld didn't write with as much zing. 
 The writing was different. I adore Scott Westerfeld and it saddens me to see his writing change.

I was expecting a lot more than I got. I would like to read more but I can't. It takes too much effort to get through a single page. 
 I don't know if it's intentional because it's supposed to be a teenage girl writing but Lizzie's story is unbearably bad. I just can't go on any more.

First off, let me forewarn you. This book would seem to most like a massive undertaking, what with the considerable amount of pages. However, I'm here to tell you that this book is anything but a task. The book, I will not lie, was a part of the Red Dot Award reading list for Mature Readers, which I was - am determined to work my way through. Once I picked up the book, it took... Read the rest of this review on my blog - http://www.foreverchicbooks.blogspot....

Like many of the other reviews I wonder if this is a parody or joke or something. I cannot believe this is a serious attempt at a novel. The story about Darcy and her literally overnight success as a newbie author is the reason that writers get zero respect. Seriously. I cringed so much while reading the Darcy storyline that I nearly developed a tic. IT IS THAT BAD. The other story line is interesting but the pacing is bad and some of the plot is tired. Honestly, reading this book yesterday put me in a bad mood.

Forgive me, Scott Westerfeld, this one-star rating. You are an amazing author. This book was well-written. I just could not care less about the plot. I did, however, love that your main character was a POC AND a lesbian (bi? Pan? Whatever. She's dating a girl, and that's good enough for me). Possibly this book was too meta for me--books about characters who know they are characters in books or books about writers make me nauseous. I'm glad to see that others are enjoying your excellent work though, even if I cannot.

Have you ever read a book you loved? Have you ever read a book you hated? This was the combination of both, in alternating chapters. While Lizzie's story kept me turning pages, Darcy made me seek out distractions. The story of Aafterworlds was beautifully crafted, and expertly told, while the story of Untitled Patel (aka Darcy) felt like an afterthought with big words to make up for the inaccuracies. Though many of Scott Westerfelds novels would have me re-reading them within a week, this book is bound to stay on my shelf for a long time. 
 Some other grievences I had about afterworlds came not from the story or plot, it came from the binding. There are tears, and now a missing letter on the spine of my copy. If you're planning on picking up this novel anytime soon, take good care of it. It doesn't feel as sturdy as it should.

I thought the book was okay. It seems a little too unrealistic and too easy for Darcy to automatically just be published like that. There were moments where I just wanted to slap Darcy for being so......Darcy. Something about her just bugs the crap out of me. I don't know what it is but I didn't like her. I enjoyed Lizzie's story much more than Darcy's. 
 I feel as though that this story could have been more developed character wise but it was an interesting premise. 
 I'm not saying this is a bad book, I guess it just wasn't for me.

Both plots in this story fell completely flat for me. I wasn't interested in either story to get past the first 50 or so pages. Also, I was uncomfortable that impressionable, young Darcy winds up in a girl/girl romantic relationship. I'm open to authors writing those stories, but I'm not interested in reading them.

So here's the thing. I have a reading list a mile long and very limited time in which to read. So even if I find a book interesting, and respect it on many levels, if I don't love it I'm not going to finish it. This is one of those. 
 Major quibbles: 
 You can see that Westerfeld is trying to be new and different and relevant today by having a protag who is: 
 1. Female 
 2. POC (person of color) 
 3. Gay 
 It's like he's trying to win at minorities Bingo. However, although he's always been good at #1, he fails at #2 and #3. Although Darcy is Indian, this doesn't matter in any way--besides her last name, she's 100% white American. Her parents allow her to follow her dreams, live on her own, and be in a homosexual relationship--but all of these things run counter to traditional Indian culture and values. This is highly problematic, yet completely ignored, because as a white man Westerfeld cannot make judgments on Indian culture by including traditional values that Americans would consider sexist and homophobic. Therefore the author completely whitewashes them so his white readers can think, "Oh Indians are cool, they're just like us, how progressive of Westerfeld to include them." And in regards to the love story, Darcy has no feelings besides friendship for Imogen when she's transformed by a kiss of insta-love. This is always highly unsatisfying and a common complaint of many reviewers in straight romances, so it's too bad the author didn't deal with it better. 
 Minor quibbles: 
 I feel like this book could have used a heavier editing hand, as I say about practically every book I've read in the last couple of years. Mechanically there were a few hiccups. Also, the word "psychopomp" is really unwieldy and awkward, although Westerfeld admits that fact and makes fun of his own terminology. Finally, this book really reminded me of Neal Shusterman's Everlost, which bothered me but maybe it's totally accidental.
I gave this a good 250 pages and decided to give up. Two stories in one book - great! However, both stories are so damn boring.
It was OK. That's all I can say. Some parts were interesting, but I couldn't connect with any of the characters in the book. It just wasn't for me.

3.5 stars is my real rating. This is really two books: the story of a teen whose book gets published and the book she wrote. The chapters alternate the two tales. On the one hand, I couldn't put it down. On the other hand, both stories on their own were a bit weaker than how they interplayed. So many issues were tackled in the "real life" story that I lost any sense of reality, especially in terms of an 18-year-old on her own in New York, renting her own apartment, etc. Still, a good YA read.
Bailed halfway. Just wasn't for me.

This is one of the worst books I've ever read. 
 Afterworlds is boring and has flat characters. I skimmed the second half. 
 Darcy's story was the only reason I kept reading (and because I wasted $30 on this book). As a writer, I want to read about writers and get some kind of an insight into the writing world. This did not give me that. Darcy's struggle was entirely self-induced and unbelievable. Oh, you're struggling for money even though you got a massive advance? Get fucking part time job, or stop spending so much money. Jesus Christ, woman. 
 This girl spent 18 months making out with her girlfriend, going to bars underage, and complaining that she didn't have her next book written. I have a revolutionary idea for her: 
 write the damn book. 
 I know, it's crazy, right? But hear me out, you can't get a book written if you don't try. Butt + chair + computer = writing. Try that next time, Darcy. 
 Also, I've decided I hate instafame even more than I hate instalove. This book had both *stabs eye with a fork* at least now I don't have to read it anymore. 
 I learned a new word though. 
 Neophyte: noun. Person who is new to the subject, skills, or belief. 
 So, yeah. There's that.
Hated it.

Got an ARC of this from Edelweiss after missing out on a copy at BEA. And maybe it's because I'm a writer and I love reading about the writing process, or maybe it's the surreality of reading a book where the characters attend BEA, but I really enjoyed this. It's a massive departure from Westerfeld's usual style and genre, but once I realized how the structure works, and how the Lizzie parts do and don't relate with the Darcy parts, I found it quite fun. Recommended, with caveats.

To clarify, I didn't finish this book. I loved Uglies and the sequels. But this book, not interesting at all to me. Also, the use of the F word multiple times in a YA novel to me is surprising and not ok. The characters were self-absorbed and trite. For those reasons I only made it about a hundred pages in, which is rare for me, I hardly ever put a book down once I pick it up.

I had to give up on the novel within a novel about halfway through because (a) it's not the kind of thing I want to read and (b) I found Darcy's actual story much more interesting. 
 This was a love letter to writing, and I really enjoyed that, though I did have some qualms with the romance, but these are my own issues and no one else's, probably. 
 At any rate, an interesting book, even if I did find Darcy a little flat. Oh, and I really thought Imogen was some kind of Cassandra Clare stand in, but her backstory was so tame and, as a result, kind of boring. Oh well.
Two books in one sounded like an interesting idea but I was completely let down by the author's sudden overuse of profanity and sexuality. I normally love Westerfield's work but this was horrible.

reference_books.title: Takedown Twenty (Stephanie Plum, #20)
reference_books.review_text:
Another madcap Stephanie Plum novel. So light and funny that reading it is effortless. 
 I sometimes have trouble remembering which number/title goes with which plot, so I hereby dub this The One With the Giraffe.

reference_books.title: The Burning Sky (The Elemental Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Loved it! Good world-building--the Domain and its connections to 19th century Britain, otherwise spells, the Crucible, elemental magic, mind magic, blood oaths--were all richly detailed and hung together. I especially enjoyed the relationship between Iolanthe and Titus. I must hunt down book two.

reference_books.title: Etiquette & Espionage (Finishing School, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
YA steampunk. Delightful characters, including some younger versions of minor characters from the Parasol Protectorate series, fun action scenes, good world-building and Carriger's amusing turn of phrase. A lot of fun. 
 Quibble: Sophronia never really had much at stake, so I had trouble caring about the mystery prototype.

reference_books.title: Ender's Game (Ender's Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Reread this to my son. Still a darn good book, even if I find the lack of girls in Battle School more annoying these days.

reference_books.title: Beyond the Shadows (Night Angel, #3)
reference_books.review_text: Excellent conclusion to a great trilogy. Lots of action, cool magic, complex characters... everything you could want in an epic fantasy series. I enjoy epic fantasy, but they often take a long time to read. This one zipped along.

reference_books.title: Chime
reference_books.review_text: After sitting on my to-read shelf for over two weeks, I finally picked this one up because it was due at the library. It didn't really get rolling for me until I'd crossed page 100, but then I stayed up til midnight to finish it. Briony is a complicated character, full of self-hate (in chapter one she confesses to witchcraft and asks to be hanged). I really liked her relationship with Eldric. One of the two revelations at the end was dead obvious, but the other one was a nice twist.

reference_books.title: Fuzzy Nation
reference_books.review_text: A "reboot" of H. Beam Piper's fuzzy novels. Fast-paced and quite enoyable with an excellent courtroom trial climax.

reference_books.title: Raised by Wolves (Raised by Wolves, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Good world-building with a definite sense of werewolf culture, a strong female character, and a quick read.

reference_books.title: The Horse and His Boy (Chronicles of Narnia, #5)
reference_books.review_text: Another childhood favorite I read to my daughter. Shasta and Aravis's story held up fairly well: the talking horses, Shasta being mistaken for Prince Corin, the flight across the desert, etc. Some of the Aslan bits seem heavy-handed to my adult eyes--but flew right over my daughter's head.

reference_books.title: The Elite (The Selection, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I'm a little ambivalent about this one. On the one hand, it was a smooth read and America is a well-drawn and believable character. On the other hand, here in book two the constant back-and-forth of the love triangle started to wear on me (to be fair, I am not the book's intended audience age range wise) and the action scenes lacked tension and felt repetitive. (Rebels attack, they hide in a safe room until it`s over.) I did like the developments with Marlee and the revelation about Maxon near the end, so I`ll probably finish the series some day.

book_a.title: Burn for Me (Hidden Legacy, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Devoured this one. Bought it yesterday, read it all evening, finished early this morning--and just spent my noon hour rereading my favourite bits. An exciting new world with magic following inheritance lines and head of House Primes with near-infinite scary power. High-stakes plot. An awesome heroine with human lie detector skills and a quirky family to support. Great scenes with witty banter and lots of heat between Nevada and 'Mad' Rogan. 
 Quibble: Not entirely sure why this is being classified as paranormal romance instead of urban fanasy. Yes, there is a stronger romance element than in other Ilona Andrews books, but it's still a subplot and IMO the book fits better as UF. (First person POV, characters don't meet until p. 90, series with continuing characters and no HEA in book one. THIS IS NOT IN ANY WAY MEANT AS A COMPLAINT--I'm greatly looking forward to seeing Nevada and Rogan earn their HEA as the series continues.)

Sono disperata. 
 Aprile. 
 DUEMILADICIASSETTE? 
 Ma dico, stiamo scherzando? E' tra un anno e mezzo!! T___T 
 La mia disperazione e' infinita... 
 Andiamo con ordine. 
 Come sempre gli Andrews hanno un'immaginazione che non ha pari nel mondo dell'urban fantasy, questo e' il loro quarto "universo" e ancora una volta mi hanno conquistato. 
 Nevada e' una giovane donna che fa l'investigatrice privata per la sua agenzia di famiglia, fondata dai suoi genitori e ampliata da lei stessa. Tutta la famiglia lavora per l'agenzia ma e' lei la titolare e colei che risolve i casi. In realta' l'agenzia non e' propriamente sua ma fa parte di una multinazionale che l'ha acquistata quando la famiglia aveva bisogno di soldi... Ma questo non e' mai stato rilevante, almeno finche' l'MII non decide di usare i vincoli che li legano all'agenzia di Nevada per affidargli un caso. Uno di quelli "persi in partenza" dove se Nevada non accetta l'MII si prende l'agenzia di famiglia ma, se accetta, ci sono ottime possibilita' che ci lasci le penne. 
 C'e' anche da considerare una piccola cosa, tipo la magia... 
 Nel 1800equalcosa e' stato creato un siero capace di far espandere la magia nell'uomo, rivoluzionando cosi' tutte le sorti della storia! 
 Ci sono vari livelli di magia e vari tipi di magia... C'e' chi sa muovere una penna e chi sa far collassare palazzi, chi accende cerini e chi produce delle vere palle di fuoco, degne del miglior mago di D&D! 
 Insomma, ci sono quelli con poteri distruttivi come Adam o come Connor. 
 Ovviamente, entrambi incroceranno la stessa strada di Nevada... 
 Consigliatissimo ma, si' c'e' un MA, il secondo volume verra' pubblicato ad Aprile del 2017 :( per cui potrete leggerne un'estratto a fine libro ma se poi finirete come me, cercando invano di comprare il seguito su amazon per poi scontrarvi sulla data....beh, io vi avevo avvisato.

Mad Rogan (H) and Nevada 
 fantasy story with explanations of Magic are done well. 
 I love a strong heroine who displays some vulnerability and then gets up to do the task she needs to do. I also am fond of slight bits of reality in stories, like when Nevada realizes she can't use up all the hot water on her sisters and cousin and finishes up her shower. she's the responsible oldest sibling and head of the investigation company and is done believably and consistently throughout the novel. 
 there's also funny bits for example when Nevada explains why she bought Adam a t-shirt and of course many of the scenes with Grandma. 
 The 2ndary and 3iary characters are well rounded too with other pillars of strength found in the mother and grandmother.

SOOOO GOOD!!

3.5 Stars 
 I've learned from past experience that books with man titty on the cover are generally not for me, but for Ilona Andrews I'll take a leap of faith. As it turns out, Burn for Me is one of those books that rides the line between urban fantasy and paranormal romance. Thankfully, there's no insta-love (plenty of insta-lust, though), no gratuitous sex, and no destined/eternal soul mates. The only elements that make Burn for Me lean towards paranormal romance is the narrator's constant inner monologue about how scorching hot the hero is, plus a few steamy kisses. 
 As an urban fantasy, on the other hand, Burn for Me is exactly what I've come to expect from Ilona Andrews. The worldbuilding is unique, rich, and evocative; the supporting characters are intriguing and well fleshed-out; and moments of humor help lighten an otherwise dark and gritty story. I loved reading about a heroine with a happy, healthy family life for a change. Even though the writing isn't quite as polished as Andrew's other books (and maybe it's just me, but Nevada and Rogan's voices sound eerily similar to Kate and Curran's), Burn for Me definitely makes the grade as an urban fantasy. 
 Besides the needlessly long descriptions of the hero's sexiness, the only thing I disliked about the book is the hero himself. He's arrogant and manipulative, and he acts like a complete asshole 99% of the time. But what bothered me the most was how he kept pushing and pushing Nevada to get with him, even after she explicitly told him she wasn't interested. I can get down with the whole alpha-male personality, but it's not romantic when a guy repeatedly disrespects a woman's boundaries (verbally, emotionally, or physically). Not even Nevada's family called him out on this, acting like she was the silly one for resisting his aggressive advances. Again, I can see shades of Kate and Curran in this relationship dynamic, but Burn for Me takes it to another level. Quite frankly, I found it a little disturbing. 
 Despite my problems with Nevada's love interest, I'll probably continue reading the series for the awesome worldbuilding and the overarching mystery that was hinted at in this installment. I also have enough faith in Ilona Andrews' writing that I'll hold out hope for the hero's behavior to change. Maybe after Nevada warms his cold, dead heart he'll actually become somewhat likable.

I have a love/meh relationship with Ilona Andrews books. And this book was a "meh" for me. It felt a little careless in places, like it could have been revised further to give more substance but they decided it was good enough. 
 As usual, the world building and magic system are interesting, and the MC was likeable. However, it lacked the extra something special that makes me adore the Innkeeper books - it is standard urban fantasy/romance fare. The romantic interest, Rogan, is a rich alpha meathead, Nevada is a scrappy detective with money troubles and mysterious abilities. They are thrown together because Rogan agrees to find his cousin, who is mostly forgotten about for the rest of the book. The ending has a bit of a cliffhanger, but it wasn't interesting enough to sell the next book to me.
LOVE IT! Seriously, this was only the first book in the series and I'm completely hooked. I want to read the next book now, now, now!
This cover and title make this sound like a pretty cheesy romance novel. Ok there was some romance and cheese, but it was deeper than that. Good quick read. I love this authors Kate Daniels series.

Another great book by Ilona Andrews. These 2 can't go wrong. I loved everything about this book: the quirky family, the bad-ass mom, the fun grandma, the warring sisters, the geeky cousin... The kick-ass heroine who knows her limits and studies her options is a huge plus. No TSTL moments and no obnoxiousness. The psychopathic hero is a nice touch. I loved the guy. A bonus is also the great humor and sarcasm. All in all a mostly flawless book. Too bad I'm gonna have to wait till 2017 for the next one.

4.5 stars 
 if Stephanie Plum were competent and responsible (Kinsey Millhone without the orphan-y angst) and lived in a world where magic was a thing, she would be Nevada Baylor: not a romance per se (no HEA), and not really much smut, but a fun thriller, urban fantasy; really like the strong female characters throughout; besides Nevada, her mom and grandma are portrayed as strong, sex-positive, unique individuals, but still human. looking forward to more scenes with the heroic DA too 
 spoiler alert, note to self: betting that future books will reveal that Nevada's magic level is much higher than she knows, maybe even Prime; also that her sense of right and wrong is an extension of her Truthseeker gift

2.5 stars 
 Billionaire romance set in an urban sprawl with some interesting superhero elements. It feels familiar, but at the same time, uniquely Ilona Andrews. I see the attraction. I'm just not feeling it this time. 
 This one is not sitting well with me for many reasons, the main one being the romance in question. There's a huge power imbalance in the relationship, and the love interest comes off as a major asshole. I just don't see it working out. This is why I don't read billionaire romance, or basically anything with a billionaire in it, but that's a personal preference.

Nao sei bem... talvez 3.5 estrelas para esta releitura. Foi uma semana em que nao estive muito concentrada, mas reconheco que este mundo de fantasia e muito giro e teve cenas que me deixaram bem disposta. O Mad Rogan e tao poderoso, para ele e tao facil fazer um predio cair em cima de alguem ou esborrachar alguem debaixo de um autocarro que, quando acontece, fico estupefacta a olhar para a pagina a pensar se li bem antes de me rir. 
 Gostei da relacao de Mad Rogan e Nevada, sao muito fofos e as picardias entre eles sao mais fofas ainda. 
 Tive dificuldade em algumas cenas muito descritivas e ha aspetos no mundo de fantasia que incluem magia que nao me agradam muito e fico ali a enrolar as palavras...

It's kind of embarrassing admitting how many times I've reread this thing. Especially with that sophisticated cover! 
 It's just a happy-fun read that hits the spot every time. Funny, witty dialogue. Simple yet believable world building. Awesome secondary characters, especially Nevada's family. The sexual tension crackling between Mad Rogan and Nevada? Swoon. Butterflies. 
 Remember when they were trapped under rubble for a bit? Rogan asks Nevada to please stop squirming because "thinking about baseball only goes so far." They're all cranky attraction, no mushy lovey dovey stuff going on. Neva can deny it all she wants, but I know she's hot for his tots. 
 One order of Mad Rogan tots please! Actually, make that three. I want ALL the books!

The writing duo of Ilona Andrews is very readable. The cover is ridiculous and frankly Ilona Andrews would do well to limit the sex; they are better at action plots and moderate romance. Still, the book is readable and interesting enough that I will read the next one in the series.

Nevada Baylor is faced with the most challenging case of her detective career--a suicide mission to bring in a suspect in a volatile case. Nevada isn't sure she has the chops. Her quarry is a Prime, the highest rank of magic user, who can set anyone and anything on fire. Then she's kidnapped by Connor "Mad" Rogan--a darkly tempting billionaire with equally devastating powers. Nevada must join forces with Rogan to stay alive. Rogan's after the same target, so he needs Nevada. But she's getting under his skin, making him care about someone other than himself for a change. I think I'm getting to the point where I've read too much by the Gordon team. Yes, there is such a point. I'm starting to catch their plot tricks and story fillers, and they're starting to bother me a bit. That does not mean I won't be continuing -- this was a fun book, and a great way to give myself a break after some heavier reading, and I'm all for fun.

The world we know has been changed by the introduction of magic. The most powerful in the world are magic users and the Primes have that claim tied down. There are somethings that you just don't want to take part in. Then there are somethings you have no choice but to get involved in no matter the outcome. 
 Nevada has been contracted to bring in a deadly Prime. She has not the skills to do this. She has only her family and their bonds to do what it takes to care for the other. Then comes in the picture a Prime just as deadly if not more so than the one she has been contracted to capture alive, Mad Rogan. 
 I loved getting involved in this world. I loved finding that connection to Nevada and her family. I loved seeing things that only Nevada got to experience with Mad Rogan. I look forward to seeing where they go from here. This was on par with Kate Daniels and her introduction to the world.

Yet another magical universe for the Ilona Andrews husband/wife author team, with different magical rules and consequences. Their great female heroines are a constant in each of their series, and I appreciate that. I also like the eccentric families that surround the characters in both this series and the Edge books (family in the Kate Daniels books is...a little more complicated). Another thing that stays the same, though, is the One True Alpha Male Romantic Lead across all of the series. Him, I'm less fond of. They're always a little over the top, for my tastes. They're all so very manly that people on the streets literally either run away from them or stare with their mouths open, overcome by such a supremely manly presence, and they're all pretty much jerks to women (except our heroines, eventually, because they are DIFFERENT), and they really don't do much for me.

I really loved this book. I've read some of the Kate Daniels books and liked them but I really love this new series. 
 I was confused at first because I couldn't remember who Adam was our who Rogan was. I completely contribute this to the fact that I had a lot going on and would only read a page or two at a time. once I was able to sit down and pay attention, I couldn't put the book down. I've stayed up till nearly 4am reading the past two nights because of this. 
 I love the interaction between Nevada and Mad Rogan. I love the slow build in their relationship. 
 I love this new world. I love the magic and the Houses and I'm really looking forward to the next book. As of right now, it's only supposed to be a trilogy but I think it's going to do well and more books will be ordered. I hope.

Having now read this I can say with certainty that the cover is...wrong, on so many levels. What on earth were the publishers thinking? This isn't romance, it's barely PNR. Let's break it down: 
 PNR: 
 The romance is central to the plot. Everything else is a subplot. 
 A new couple for each book in the series. 
 A HEA for each book (or a HFN at a stretch). 
 Man-chest book cover 
 UF: 
 Action / adventure / mystery is central to the plot. Romance may be present, or not. It's not essential. 
 Long series arc with character progression throughout. 
 Unlikely to have HEA until the end of the series, if at all. 
 Kick-ass MC on the cover. 
 *The Fever Series (the first five books - let's not mention the others ;) ) is UF BUT the publishers here too seemed to struggle with the book covers. Manchest? What? YA flowing dresses? Seriously? C'mon, we all know it's UF at it's core. See below: 
 UFRomance: is a sub-genre of UF. It plays fast and loose with the HEA and generally keeps the romance close, but not driving the main plot. 
 Many tough chick UFs have elements of urban fantasy romance and are mostly aimed at female readers. Tough guy UF, such as Dresden and Iron Druid have very thin romantic sub-plot and are mostly aimed at male readers. 
 Thus ends the lesson in urban fantasy. *There is police procedural and many sub-sets of UF, but we're focusing on the above for now. 
 Back to Burn For Me. This is squarely in the UF genre, with a bit of a superhero feel. We have a mystery main plot and a romantic sub-plot that will likely be woven through the entire series. I have to admit, it didn't immediately wow me, but neither did the Kate Daniels first in series. (UF first in series all have flaws because of the expected long series arc). 
 With Ilona Andrews you always know you're in for a treat, no matter what. I hope their publishers eventually take note of the reviews and deliver some covers the series deserves.

So... I just finished this book. Ilona Andrews is a power writing couple and have recently on my auto-buy in paper/hardback copies. 
 Don't let the cover or title fool you. 
 Yes, it looks like a tame romance novel, but this story is more Urban Fantasy rather than romance. Of course, the love interest isn't the main focus but it doesn't sit too far on the back burner either. In a nutshell, it's one badass book with equally badass characters. 
 One of the reasons why I enjoy books like Burn For Me so much is because of the non-insta love crap. We meet Nevada Baylor who can be tough as nails but would rather lead the normal life. In many ways, she echoes the qualities of Kate Daniels (awesome series by the same authors btw). She's power in her own right, but she rather hide it than deal with the power play. She may not be as much of a smart ass as Kate was, but the humor was great. 
 I did particularly enjoy Rogan. I even got a bigger kick out of always referring to him as Mad Rogan and the Scourge of Mexico. I can't wait to get more of POV especially now that he seems like he's putting his full attention in winning Nevada over. Oh yeah, and dealing with his massive fallout within his family. 
 Anyways, the entire premise of the book is fantastic. An entirely different and new world has been created where we have magic users. Magic was introduced over 150 years ago with the Osiris serum; a serum that manifested magic in human beans. Of course, everything went wrong and there was a huge fall out from in. Years and year later to the present, we see that magic has taken over the city. In a big place like Houston, there is a pecking order according to how much magic you have. At the top of the food chain are the Primes, powerful sons of bitches who get whatever they want, when they want and roll in piles of filthy money. Lots of money. They are assholes and they are scary. They're a product of breeding and careful pedigree which is a rather sad existence. 
 But don't mind me... just, sitting here and salivating in the corner. Totally normal.

So...that cover. It's the worst part of the book and the only part that I don't like. Honestly, I'm almost embarrassed to have it on my shelf, and I can't imagine actually reading it in public. I seriously debated whether I even wanted it on my favorites list because ok, maybe I'm that shallow, but I have a hard time forcing myself to even LOOK at that cover. 
 Ilona Andrews is one of my all time favorite authors and the fact that it's a pseudonym for a husband and wife team just makes it that much better. I knew this book would be great, but I still didn't think it would be as awesome as it ended up being. I do have to say that the male and female heroines in this book bear strong resemblance to the Kate Daniels characters (one of my all time favorite UF series), but hey, when it's that good, what's bad about bringing on more of the same? 
 Meanwhile, I'm going to pray that this series ends up becoming super popular as it deserves to be, makes it into hardcover, and new covers will be made eventually. Please, dear God.

If it were possible to go back in time and unread this book, I would - just so I could read it for the first time all over again and be again struck by the pure awesomeness that this book is. 
 I wasn't so sure when I first read the blurb about the book, since the Kate Daniels series already pushes the about of 'magic' I like in a book, I read the Kate Daniels series for the shapeshifters. I was drawn to that series for that sole reason there were shapeshifters, but I do love the series. Kate and Curran are also my all time favorite couple, but I fear that Nevada and Mad may take that spot. Ilona and Gordon Andrews know how to write a couple, they make it real. The couple is not perfect and everything is not roses (or carnations in this case) and things don't come together in one book, but the relationships develop over the series. I love it but I hate it. I hate that I have to wait until the next book comes out to find out where things go. I love that I can't stop thinking about what could happen next and how they're going to work everything out. 
 I don't want to give anything else away about the book, but trust me even if you don't like to read about magic, you will still love this book. 
 This was the best read for me this year!

This was so fun to read! Great balance between mystery, action, and hotness. The characters were engaging and you felt as if you were on the adventure with them. I loved how the setting of this fantasy did not veer too far from contemporary times so that I never felt lost in a strange world. I cannot wait for Hidden Legacy #2!

First I need to ask this: Who chooses these covers people?! Really. Someone actually gave this poor guy a shirt and made him use it as a PROP. 
 Cover apart, this book was amazing. It took some time for it to start going, but when it did it made the wait worth it. It's full of action and plot twists, and the heroine is so beautifully intelligent it made the whole experience that much special. I was actually proud of her. You know those moments when you are reading a heroine/ alpha male interaction and you just want to scream "Noooo, who does he think he is?! Don't let him get away with that!"? Well, Nevada doesn't. She demands respect and I loved that about her. Even though the world of this series is full of magical elements, the relationships between the characters as a whole felt very real.

Honestly? 3.75ish 
 There's confident and then there's smarmy asshole confident. And he is a way too blase and unrepentant serial killer.

I had forgotten that I'd read this one. Shame on me. Another wonderful novel in a wonderful new series. The Ilona Andrews duo are among my favorite writers. Always strong male/female leads with lots of weaponry, mage work and violence. Highly entertaining. Now I have to run see if there are others in this series out.

I'm giving this book, which I devoured the second half of in record time, four stars because the beginning was a little hard to get into. Admittedly, I was still emotionally attached to Kate Daniels when I started this book, but Nevada took a little time to grow on me. There's something about her character that didn't quite jive with me, but that didn't stop me from getting really into this book once the action got started. The characters, as always with Ilona and Gordon, are believable and exciting. The action was exciting and unique but gave you enough time to breathe in between action scenes. I'm really into the romance between Nevada and Mad Rogan, but in typical fashion we'll have to wait 3-4 books before they get together. The way they set it up in this book? I'm not even upset that we'll have to wait! 
 All in all, this was a great read (or, listen, as I checked out the audiobook) and is setting up a very intriguing story for Nevada Baylor. I will anxiously await the next book in this installment. Hopefully they will find a better cover artist between now and then.

Now I see what all the fuss is about with these authors. I loved this book! Can't wait for more, and I need to get on reading their other series stat. Tho I will say, I do not care for this cover at all, and I'm certain Nevada wouldn't appreciate it either.
This took me a minute to get into because there was so much world building (which is necessary btw) but it was worth it. Another great start for an Ilona Andrews series!
Can't wait for more in the series!

I love Ilona Andrews. That said, at first I wasn't too sure about this book as I thought it was slow to get going. And it finished with a sequel set up which is not one of my favourite devices, as even in series I prefer each book to be completely stand alone. But with those two provisos I ripped through this book and was sorry it was over. I nearly went back and read all their previous books just so I didn't have to say goodbye. 
 It's a great story of young woman who is the stalwart of her family. They are just getting it together after tragedy and she made one wrong decision by taking out a mortgage to get them through. That decision comes back to haunt her when the mortgagor takes advantage to send her and her family Private Investigation company on a suicide mission to bring in a renegade Prime magic user. 
 In the process she comes up against, and then partners with, (sometimes hard to tell the difference in practice), another Prime magic user. Keeping the upper hand when she is insanely attracted to him and he knows it, keeps her on her toes and him plotting. 
 Clever, funny, imaginative and suspenseful. Enjoy.

Buddy read with my girl Lana. 
 MAN! What words to use to describe how much I'm in love with this book?? I completely devoured it. I was hooked from page 1. I should probably give you a little description. 
 You have Nevada Baylor and her family who run Baylor Investigative Agency. Their work consists of light cases such as following cheating spouses and ratting them out to their significant others. Sometimes the case gets a bit dangerous because it's not always regular humans they're dealing with. You see there was this serum that gave humans magical powers back in like the 1800's and ended up passing to future offspring. The city is divided into specific Houses that are dedicated to the highest level of magic users called Primes. Some of the powers include telekinetic, pyrokinetic and aquakinetic. 
 Now of these Primes, you have the biggest badass of them all; Mad Rogan. Nobody truly knows how much power he really has but he is greatly feared. Nevada gets a case where she's tasked with going after Adam Pierce of House Pierce, who's a serious pyrokinetic, and bring him home alive. Adam has been going on arson sprees and needs to be stopped before cops put a bullet in his brain. Nevada doesn't have much choice in whether she gets to pass on the case or not because the man who owns her business threatens to make her family homeless. She ends up on Mad Rogan's radar and they work together to stop Adam before he burns down the city. 
 I absolutely, positively LOVED Nevada's commentary. Whether she was talking with family members, enemies or Mad Rogan, she was FANTASTIC! She's tough as nails and brutally honest. It may be a trait because of her special power but I think even without she'd still ridiculously honest with herself and everyone around her.  I read this book for the Unapologetic Romance Readers' New Years 2017 Reading Challenge. For more info about what this is, click here. 
 I'm not very good at fangirling, but some books make me want to try. BURN FOR ME makes me want to try. It was so good. The heroine, the villainous antihero, the magic system, the world-building...it was all so, so good. Reading this transported me to childhood again, when I could completely immerse myself in fantasy stories and they all felt real - 
 Except no childhood fantasy story ever had Mad Rogan in it. 
 (Phwooooar!) 
 BURN FOR ME is the first in the Hidden Legacy series, which takes place in an alternate universe where a magic serum has given various human beings X-Men-like abilities. Some control the elements, some control minds. Nevada Baylor, a private investigator, has the ability to discern truth. And right now, she's hunting down a powerful pyrokinetic named Adam Pierce who seems to want to set the whole city of Houston up in flames. 
 Mad Rogan is a powerful tactile who can level large buildings with the same ease that he can peel splinters of a chopstick, layer by layer. (And that's not the only thing he'd like to peel layer by layer *cough*) He's after Adam, too, although when he meets Nevada, he decides that he might just be after her, as well. You know, while he's at it. 
 The result is a tug-of-war between the various powerful mages, called Primes, with poor Nevada bouncing around between them like a ping-pong ball, as she dodges gunfire, actual fire, mutant turf wars, and the sexual advances of a very attractive, possibly sociopathic telekinetic, all the while trying to prevent the destruction of the entire world. 
 One of my friends recommended this book when she found out that I love villainous heroes, and Mad Rogan definitely fit the bill in that regard. Goddamn, that man is the type of bad that inspires X-rated fanfiction. He had some amazing lines, and some super steamy scenes with Nevada. Did I maybe skim ahead a bit, looking for said scenes? No, no of course not. That would be sacrilege. (Maybe.) It's so hard to find urban fantasy novels with romance that don't put the world-building in the backseat. In BURN FOR ME, it's front and center, and instead of detracting from the romantic elements, it makes them that much more stronger and compelling. 
 I want to say more about this book, but to be honest, I wouldn't know where to begin. I could tell you that the secondary characters are just as colorful as the ones in a Stephanie Plum novel, and I could tell you that reading this book gave me those same "this is good fantasy" vibes as I got from His Dark Materials and Harry Potter. I could tell you that Mad Rogan has a place in my exclusive heroes hall of fame, and I could tell you that I am insanely jealous of my friends who seem to have acquired ARCs for not just book 2 (which isn't out yet) but also book 3 (which also isn't out yet). I could tell you all these things, but you should probably just read the book for yourself. 
 Also, for all you people saying Mad Rogan is yours? Back off, he's mine. I WILL FIGHT YOU. 
 4.5 stars

This was amazing and I loved every word of it. I bought book 1 and 2 together and I ordered 3 because I have a feeling I'll be needing it very soon. 
 Urban fantasy isn't always the most easy genre for me. Most of the time I dislike the heroine because she tries to hard at being a badass, but this has been a really great read. I genuinly like Nevada and how she can take care of herself and most importantly, her family. She puts them before anything and everything and the connection between all of them feels real. 
 A guy like Rogan would never be my type in real life, but he's right up there with Jericho Barrons from the Fever series, who will be forever branded into my memory as a hot, massive chunk of manliness and lust. Glad he finally has somebody to chat with in there, and I dunno, exchange a few -coughs- pointers? 
 If you have any doubts, don't let the horrible cover stand between you and this really great book. I'm not the only one complaining about it, but at least you don't spend most of the time looking at the cover while reading it. So buy a copy and go read it, now!

This is an original review from http://bookedandloaded.com ~ All opinions are my own and are not influenced in any way. 
 Burn for Me is Ilona Andrew's first installment in the Hidden Legacy Series. Honestly, if you don't know who this husband/wife team is, you need to come forward and present yourself to the COUNSEL OF WHERE HAVE YOU BEEN? Their previous Urban Fantasy series will forever remain one of my all time favorites and are definitely in the reread category. 
 And now onto to this new Series! 
 Burn for Me is a fantastic story. I loved the dynamic Nevada had with her family and reading about all of the different personalities under one roof made me long for that kind of life. The world building was easy to understand and all magical. So be warned, no vamps or weres were contained on the pages of this book! It was a great fresh feel with new rules about magic and the society around it. Andrews throws out such unexpected similes, keeping the whole feel stunning and awe-inspiring. 
 I also want to address something. I accidentally read a snippet of a review for this book and I normally don't do that, but it happened. It was only a piece and I honestly don't know what the end of the review stated about it. Good or bad - I have no idea. This review stated that the name of one of the main characters, "Mad" Rogan was shaming him for a disability. There was a fancy word that was used and I seriously had to look it up to know what it meant, but I am not sure I agree. Mad was certainly not "normal" but I don't believe he had a disability. Unless that disability was narcissism. Not sure we should be calling everyone with a little quirk "disabled". He was the most powerful man in the book. So much raw power, both physically and mentally. Mmmmm. Wait. What was I saying? Oh, yeah. I didn't feel calling him Mad Rogan was insulting. That being said, he was kind nuts. In a way that is great for fictional characters, probably not so great in real life. I would not classify him as an Alphahole - more of a socially awkward bad ass that doesn't understand normal people logic. 
 The chemistry was sizzling, but that was about as far as it went. This title read much more like a Urban Fantasy than a Paranormal Romance. This aspect contributed to feeling a bit discontented at the end. Where was the love? Where was the Happily Ever After? When I read romance I want to be swept off my feet by the chemistry and dance of the couple. I want to journey into their internal struggles and then overcoming them to be happy at the end. I want to be clear on this warning - there was no HEA and I would never call this title a Romance. However, this was a great read and I truly enjoyed it. I would highly recommend to any Urban Fantasy lover or magical fiends!

PJV Quickie: I am always wary of a favorite author starting a new series. Being that this is Ilona Andrews, though, I had high expectations going in to Burn for Me, and to say I was not disappointed is a huge understatement. Burn for Me grabbed my attention and kept me turning the pages until the end. I cannot wait until the next installment in this fabulous new series. 
 Review: 
 Burn for Me is set in a version of our world that is full of magic. The magic is carefully cultivated and passed down through family lines and magical dynasties have been created. 
 Nevada Baylor is a private investigator in her small family firm. In the magical caste system, her family is not important at all. Due to a series of unfortunate circumstances, they had to sell their independent firm to a larger corporation in order to stay in business. When the corporation calls her up to handle a particularly difficult (and dangerous) case involving a powerful firestarter, she knows she won't be able to bring in the culprit but does not have the option of turning the case down. 
 Mad Rogan is a legend. His magical abilities are epic and his family is one of the most powerful in the world. He is searching for his nephew, an accomplice to the firestarter and wants to know what Nevada has uncovered. She refuses to talk and he's intrigued by her ability to resist his magic and wants to know what secrets she's hiding, unrelated to the case. 
 Nevada soon realizes that if she wants to stay alive, she's going to have to work with Mad Rogan. As they track down the firestarter, an attraction grows, but Nevada knows that as a 'nobody', she doesn't have any hope of a relationship with a powerful magic user like Mad, and she doesn't want to fall for him and end up hurt when he's done with her. 
 ~~~~~~~ 
 The summary above doesn't express what an awesome book Burn for Me is! Parajunkee reviewed it a few months ago here, and she was spot on - I loved this book! The worldbuilding was cool, I like the idea of magic being "discovered" and the repercussions of that through successive generations. In addition to the interesting plot, which kept me guessing, the characters were genuinely interesting. Nevada was a great heroine: ethical and family-oriented and fiercely loyal to her clients. Rogan is my idea of a perfect bad-boy hero: strong, powerful and protective, but dangerous and deadly too. The secondary characters kept me entertained; there were times when Nevada's family members stole the show. I'm not sure if I should admit that I kind of liked the flirty, spoiled bad-boy firestarter right up until the end. (Hmmm...I may have a soft spot for bad-boys) 
 Don't let the cover turn you away - Burn for Me is an Urban Fantasy read with *just enough* romance to keep my romantic little heart happy. The smoldering tension is soooo good, but really as far as sex there's only a kiss or two. 
 Recommendations: 
 Fans of UF and PNR should both like Burn for Me; it's got action and humor, but enough romance (and promise for more in the future) to satisfy someone who normally reads romance. It's a given that fans of Ilona Andrews will love Burn for Me, but if you haven't read any of their other books, Burn for Me is a good place to start.

Ilona Andrews has once again outdone themselves with this spectacular series. MUST READ! The world-building is so lovable. It is urban fantasy, so it's the "normal" world, but infused with magical talents and magical family houses. The magical talents are very unique and endearing. There is a family aspect to this series that makes it very heartwarming. The two main characters are the real draw, though. Nevada is easy to relate to and her love for her family and sense of duty make her an inspiration. Mad Rogan is incredibly sexy and enticing. Nevada + Rogan = hot, hot, hot! Love this series, and the books get even better as they continue.
Good Book, Can't wait for the next one!

In 1863, in a world much like our own, European scientists discovered the Osiris serum, a concoction which brought out one's magic talents. 
 So begins this absolutely fascinating book. Magic users have been separated into families or Houses and designated as Minor, Average, Notable, Significant and Prime. Nevada Baylor runs a small family owned business that investigates fraud and cheating spouses. The business was bought out by the Montgomery House after the death of her father. Nevada is tasked to apprehend Adam Pierce, a Prime pyrokinetic who is responsible for the death of a security guard following a fire at a bank. Nevada realizes the case is a suicide mission but has no choice but to take it. Enter Connor "Mad" Rogan. Mad is a Prime so off the charts that he has become a folk legend. Mad's cousin is the second suspect in the fire and he has promised to find him for the family. Mad kidnaps Nevada to force information from her. 
 I'm trying very hard to not reveal spoilers of the story. Mad is a seriously scary man yet Nevada stands her ground repeatedly. The magic that occurs between the two of them is amazing. I love the character building, the unreal situations and the tension of the inevitable relationship. Adam is such a strong demented character. His spoiled rich boy persona starts to wear thin but he is the ultimate sociopath. 
 I believe my reaction at the end of the book was just "Wow!" I am so ready for the next one in the series. Excellent, excellent read!

This book was great! Imaginative, exciting, and funny. The sole reason I gave it four stars instead of five was the totally misleading, corny, and flat dumb cover art. This is not a romance novel. There is a bit of a love story, but it is not central to the narrative. I have a hard time believing this cover helps to sell books.

Only a few chapters into the fourth book and I just can't handle the character (and by extension, the author as clearly Harry Dresden IS REALLY Jim Butcher!) any longer. This series is making me irrationally angry and I just plain HATE the "good guy". I can't do it any more. 
 Fuck this garbage.
Culmination of the previous three. First one I've felt like you need the backstory to really get, it doesn't function as a standalone. Grittier. He's definitely out of his league this time.
Better than earlier Dresden books, though still bound heavily to old urban fantasy tropes.

I never considered reading about faeries, but it was a mandatory thing for me to do so because I really like the Dresden Files. Harry Dresden is no doubt one of my favorite fictional characters. Witty and crazy will always be a perfect match. 
 This novel was about faeries, and thrones. I really enjoyed how Butcher portrayed both. I've never read anything faerie related so I had no background knowledge of them. Based on the first three novels, Butcher is known for putting his own twists in the supernatural creatures. He makes them his own, and it works most of the time. I like his portrayal of the faeries, and it makes me want to read more of them. Main reason would be to know if he made his own shit up again, but also because he made them sound so damn interesting in the first place. 
 This fourth installment in the series was face paced and consistent. I can't remember any slow points in the middle of the novel. The characters were great as usual, with an addition of a few new great ones. There were good and bad faeries, and both were great characters. I was not expecting to like faeries more than ghosts, but Butcher made them seem so cool. While the third novel was better overall, the creatures in this novel were a bit better. 
 4.25/5 stars. While it was such a fast read because it was so enjoyable, I was still a bit disappointed with the ending. I didn't find it phenomenal, but honestly I haven't read a good ending written by Butcher based on the four novels I've read of his. But aside from the ending, there's nothing more I can complain about. This series keeps improving. If you haven't started reading this series yet, then you're missing out a lot.

This is a great modern or urban fantasy. I've read the first nine books in the series and don't intend to review all of them, so this is a review of the series. There is a formula to the series, and it becomes a bit too apparent about mid-way through the books I've read, but the writing is good enough to overlook it. 
 The characters are interesting and the action is well paced. Highly recommended to anyone interested in magic set in the modern world.

I tried to finish this last night, but was so tired that I fell asleep still in my clothes, with the book on my belly. 
 Another Dresden misadventure, this time with faeries, sprawling battles between the vampires/White Court and winter/summer fae folk. Dresden, as usual, has his work cut out for him: He needs to somehow figure out who killed the summer knight (champion to the Summer Queen), why they did it, and stop the two faery groups from destroying each other, and unbalancing the entire world in the process. 
 Add in the fact that his former flame (who helped his master try to bind and turn him to evil, many years past, and who he thought he'd killed) shows up unexpectedly, his current love is MIA (and craving blood), and throw in a few werewolves, pixies, changelings, and sidhe, and you end up with a typical Dresden book. 
 Fun, as ever.
As always, Jim Butcher has come up with a great story that is action-filled and lots of plain old fun to read in Summer Knight. It is a terrific addition to the Harry Dresden series.
