3.5 stars, better than the previous 2 books. While I get a little tired of Harry being so put upon & taking so much on himself, this plot twisted in some very unexpected ways. Great action & tons of suspense.

I was introduced to this series by a good friend, and I am glad she recommended it. I am four books into the series and I am looking forward to the 5th. Personally I love that Dresden is not a hero. He is a man who has his own code, rough, unrefined, and jumps first. He reminds me a little of myself.

"How long were her legs, Harry?!" 
 This is what I've taken to shouting as my husband reads these aloud to me, every time a female character steps onto the scene with her long, coltish, shapely, miles of lithe limb. I almost promise that I'm almost positive that this'll be the last time I bring up that we tend to know a new girl's measurements before we know what color her hair/eyes are. I probably won't belabor it too much longer possibly maybe... 
 Anyway. This was the weakest Dresden book so far for me. So much effort spent trying to make this whole fairy smackdown look like an intricate and ingenious game of chess, every move of which Harry will miraculously puzzle out after receiving a single subtle clue. Until then, of course, he'll kick down every door he finds and bellow "Did you kill [insert vic's name here]?" apparently expecting someone to reply, "Yep. Please zap me with fire now." 
 This ham-fisted investigative technique will do nicely as filler until it's time for Harry to deduce the entire rest of the plot to the Nth degree, receive a couple of plot devices from his beneficent all-powerful allies, and save the day in spite of overwhelming and hyperbole hyperbole odds. Plus we still have room to cram in the "and everything worked out wonderful and we'll tie all the loose ends up in a bow and we all laugh and fade to black" final chapter that I can't stand. 
 Summer Knight has helped me realize that what works for me about the Dresden books is the combination of Harry's goofy, practically slapstick character that I just adore mocking and...I don't know...the bloody simplicity of being chased by a werewolf, or getting fed to a pack of vampires. Ye gods, try to put that boy in a White Council meeting (make it STOPPPPPPP) or a struggle for political power on a global scale (thanks, plot devices!), and it all falls flat. It's a snooze fest with a lot of bad jokes--as opposed to Grave Peril where you roll your eyes through the bad jokes because at least the action's intriguing. 
 Recognition is owed for the much-improved "Hell's bells" count* (now with 70% fewer bells!) and for SOMEBODY calling Harry ANYTHING other than "Mister Dresden". I continue to get the impression that Butcher took great effort to overcome the criticisms of his previous books, but I'm a little disappointed that Grave Peril got me thinking "Here we go! Now we're getting there!" and then Summer Knight dropped, tripped over, and deflated the ball. I needs me some monsters to get me back to the pro-Harry side, please no more of the big bad just being mystically manipulative, mystically sexy women. 
 With mystically long legs, of course. 
 = = = 
 *After reading this review, my husband admitted that I'd taken to complaining about "Hell's bells" so much that he just stopped saying it when it was printed, replacing it with "Hell" instead. So...yeah...the 70% fewer bells were just my husband trying to avoid making me grumpy. Next he'll be telling me he clipped the descriptions of womens' legs short.

I have to say this series gets better with every book! Harry seemed much more in control this time around and although he is still the wizard that everyone loves to hate he is much less the victim. The pace of this story is very fast with good action sequences throughout. I can't understand why it took me so long to read thid series but am I ever glad that I picked it up. Highly recommended.
Series definitely getting better with this one, though I felt the stakes didn't feel as high even though I knew they were. Interested to see what happens in the next book.

An excellent fourth installment of The Dresden Files series by Jim Butcher! 
 This book has it all and more in my opinion! *Watch out for spoilers below!* 
 The opening scene leads to action and also pertinent info, the White Council is coming to Chicago that day. For, among other reasons, to talk about the war with the Red vampires that Harry started in the last novel over Susan Rodriguez. 
 In the last while Harry has been obsessively working to find a cure Susan now that she has been turned by the Red vampires. So fr he has had little luck at all and has been neglecting other duties, such as work. When he does get his first client, he could have never expected to find himself talking to a Fae... 
 In this book I believe Harry comes to a lot of realizations, we get loads of action, mystery, suspense, surprises and much more. It is pretty fast paced plots though I admit that it was a little different from other books, we don't have much human interaction in this book. We mostly get supernatural/paranormal. Which I didn't mind, I think it lets us see Harry in a new light; see him compared to creature of almost perfection and in the end I think I like and admire Harry even more now than I did in the last books. 
 I would recommend this book to anyone looking for a great paranormal/urban fantasy read.

Well, I actually finished reading this a while back and I've been a bit slow on the blog posts. My apologies. Without further ado, my review of Summer Knight, by Jim Butcher. 
 Up to now, I have not been aboard the Dresden Files train. I read Storm Front a few years back and was unimpressed. It was a quick, fun read, but nothing to write home about. Then last year, he was doing an author event here in Kansas City (he's from my home town, Independence, MO) and I attended. I thought it would be good to hear from a local author, to pick his brain a bit. It was a good time and I got a signed first edition hardcover for my money. 
 I also ran into friends there who ARE on the Dresden Files train. The peer pressure began. I was also driven to keep reading after he said (paraphrasing), "the problem with a 14-book series is that people have to start at the beginning, when I didn't know what the hell I was doing." After writing my own first novel and deeply understanding the sentiment, I kept reading. 
 Book 2: a non-stop action sequence. 
 Book 3: a little better. 
 Now Summer Knight is book 4 and it looks like Jim has finally found it voice. I felt this way about J.K. Rowling as well. She found her voice and her pace in the fourth Harry Potter novel. Butcher has finally found the balance between his masterful action sequences and the character introspection every novel needs. He also digs much deeper into the world he's created, making the reader really want more and more of it. The beginning characters are breaking out of their stereotypes. The novel ideas are becoming fleshed-out and meaningful. 
 Okay, Jim. I'm on board. Call me a Dresden Files fan. Well done.

 I'm listening to the series on audiobook with my husband - who is now an avid Dresden fan. : ) I had struggled a bit with the detail during the first read through of Summer Knight, but the story was so much better the second time around. Now that I'm more familiar with the characters, it was easier to understand the organizational structure of the White Council and Fairy Realms, allowing me to simply enjoy the story.  Ah...another great adventure in the world of Harry Dresden! It's been 9 months since Susan left and he's been working night and day to find a magical cure-all for her blood cravings. When he isn't working in his basement, he's dodging Bianca's hired assassins who are looking for any opportunity to exact revenge. Harry's depressed and withdrawn over Susan and has clearly let himself go in the hygiene department. Luckily he has Billy trying to set him back on the right path. Gotta love Billy and The Alphas! They might be young, but I think Harry needs them more then they need him at the moment. 
 His troubles get worse when he's forced into service by the Winter Queen, who has purchased the "bargain" from Harry's fairy godmother. After a rather unpleasant demonstration of her power, it's obvious she will not take "no" for an answer. Add being called in front of the White Council to account for his actions against the Vampires and it turns out to be a really bad day. On a side note... The scenes with Harry in front of the white Council had some of the funniest dialogue I've read in a very long time! It's classic Harry. No holding back, even when he sticks his foot in his mouth or makes himself look silly. He doesn't hold back, even if it will get him killed. 
 There was quite a bit of world building surrounding the Winter and Summer Fairy realms, but I love where this series is going! We meet many new characters and are get yet another glimpse into Harry's past. I found that I liked Elaine more than I planned and was pleased with her advice to Harry at the end of the book. The Alphas are back, as is Toot-Toot and Bob. Murphy is still recovering form her ordeal in the last book, but it's good to see their friendship is back on track. 
 The action scenes were fantastic and had that spark of humor that kept my spirits up even when things looked bleak. Harry is making new enemies and new allies with each new adventure. I'm curious to see what catalyst will throw them all together for a common goal in the future.

Harry's in big trouble this time. The Red Court of vampires is sending assassins after him, the White Council wants to strip him of his wizard status and he's in real deep to fae queen Mab. The only way for Harry to face all his problems is by embroiling himself in sidhe politics and discovering who murdered Summer's Knight. 
 By the fourth book in the series, Jim Butcher has really worked out exactly who Harry Dresden is as a character. He still has a massive hero complex and is annoyingly chauvinistic, but he's not the borderline misogynist he was in books one and two and he has startes to rely on friends' advice... and even their help. Harry has become an iconic character, someone that stands apart from the cookie-cutter heroes that fill the pages of the urban fantasy genre. 
 I hate to admit it, because she's such a bitch, but I really like Mab. She's smart, ambitious and dangerous. Evil and untrustworthy without ever reducing herself to anything as banal as a villain. Jim Butcher does baddies well, almost better than his good guys.

I'm not sure why I keep reading this besides the fact that they're on my kindle. It's a little sexist and the protagonist just suddenly puts everything together with seemingly no evidence and little explanation. I prefer heroines.
Exciting and funny, as always!

Summer Knight is another quick, action-packed read. Harry's ass is on the line (when is it not?) as he contends with an impending Fae war and the nervous, vindictive White Council. 
 He has to solve a murder, find a thief, and prevent all of heaven and earth being torn asunder. At the same time, he must prove his worth to the crotchety Senior Council members who'd love to see him fail. Oh, and help a few damsels along the way. Will the poor guy ever catch a break? 
 Although there are some interesting twists and turns, it felt as though Harry made zero progress until more than half the book had flown by. Lots of closed doors and enigmatic statements held him back, and the Big Reveal was delivered in too neat a moment of "here's what happened." 
 Despite those faults, there's more than enough to entertain. Harry starts off in a desperate state, and it's nice to see the Alphas reappear to rally around him and pull him out of the doldrums. Also, as many enemies as Harry makes along the way, he still manages to pick up some important, loyal allies as well; these folks offer a bright spot against the pity party Harry's been holding since the events of Grave Peril. 
 Mostly, Summer Knight is engaging for its expansion of the Dresden universe, and for Harry's acceptance that sometimes a man can't do it all on his own. Butcher is well-able to suck me in. I'm looking forward to following Harry into the next harrowing mess.

Good stuff. It just keeps getting better and better. Solid work, with each book. "4.5 stars" Summer Knight was a much better read for me than the last book of the Dresden Files series. Even though I was really tired again while reading this one and occasionally dozing off (just like last time:-)), I had no trouble at all following the story. There's lots of action, mystery, intrigue, and plenty of supernatural occurrences. The climactic battle in the Nevernever in the land of Faerie kept me on the edge of my seat. I loved that Jim Butcher finally gave his readers some more insights into Harry's background. I'd been getting really antsy waiting for Harry's character to develop more fully, so this new information was very much appreciated. The author also utilized several secondary characters who were already on the canvas from previous stories, and it was nice to see them again. Most exciting of all was a surprise character from Harry's past who showed up and became an unexpected ally. Everything combined to make Summer Knight a very enjoyable read. 
 In this installment, Harry is still reeling about nine months after the events of Grave Peril. He's been in a major funk ever since his girlfriend, Susan, left town after being bitten by a vampire. He also feels guilty about what happened to her, thinking it was at least partially his fault. He's been obsessively searching for a cure for her condition, without success, and it's strongly affecting his life. His apartment has turned into a pigsty, and he's about to be evicted from both it and his office. He needs money fast, but the only "job offer" he receives is working as an emissary for one of the faerie queens to clear her of a murder. After being screwed over by his fairy godmother, working for one of the Fae is not an appealing prospect, but when he discovers that his fairy godmother sold his debt to the Queen, he doesn't have much choice. Not to mention, the White Council is breathing down his neck for starting a war with the Red Vampire Court, and if he doesn't succeed in his mission, there could be hell to pay in more ways than one. Harry was definitely in fine form in this story. I've always loved the fact that he isn't an all-powerful wizard. His magical powers do have their limits, but I think this makes both him and the stories more interesting, because it gives him vulnerabilities, which adds conflict to the stories. Sometimes, he simply has to use good old-fashioned ingenuity and/or brute force to get out of sticky situations. However, his powers can also be pretty impressive, and I get the feeling that they may be gradually growing, that there could be a lot of untapped potential in him, which is a good thing for future stories of the series. 
 Susan may be temporarily (presumably) out of the picture, but there were plenty of other secondary characters to fill in the gap. Harry reconciles his friendship with Karrin Murphy, and we get to learn a little more about her background. She's still struggling emotionally with the supernatural things that happened to her in the previous books, but it seems she's finally forgiven Harry. She ends up being one of the few people Harry feels he can trust completely, and her warrior woman instincts help him out of a life-or-death situation. Billy and his Alphas werewolf pack from Fool Moon return to help Harry with his investigation and the coming battle. Toot-toot, the pixie who was first seen in Storm Front, is back to help Harry, along with his adorable little faerie army. The way Harry can always trick them with food is just too cute. We're introduced to a number of new characters including Ebenezar, Harry second mentor, and several members of the White Council, who I have a feeling will factor prominently in future books. Then there's Mab, the faerie queen who hires Harry. I'm sure we haven't seen the last of her, because Harry still owes her two requests before his debt will be paid in full. There are also a group of half-mortal, half-fae young people who are instrumental players and some of whom will likely have roles in coming books as well. Of course, there's the mysterious character from Harry's past that I mentioned earlier, but I can't say much more about that without giving away a major spoiler. Suffice it to say, I liked this part of the story and hope we'll see more of this person as the series progresses, because I didn't feel like their history had been fully reconciled yet. This is only a fraction of the broad and varied supporting cast, but some of the ones I felt were more memorable. 
 Overall, I liked Summer Knight, and in the end, I waffled a bit on how to rate it. The ending was just so good, I almost gave it the full five stars, but as I considered a few minor quibbles I'd had throughout, I decided to knock off a half star. The writing needed a few more contractions, because the dialog and/or prose was occasionally a bit stilted without them. There are so many supporting characters, I sometimes found myself forgetting who they were, especially when they appear in an early chapter and then aren't seen for several more. Last but not least, while I did enjoy the book, I can't really say I felt a burning need to get back to it when I had to put it down, at least not until those climactic final chapters. I can't put my finger on exactly why this is, but normally, I only give five stars to those books where I could barely put them down. Other than the couple of minor things I mentioned though, I can't say that there was anything wrong with the story. In fact, I thought it was very well done. It held my interest quite well, and even though I probably never would have guessed the villain (that's not one of my strong suits anyway), once everything came out, it made perfect sense. So, ultimately, Summer Knight was a near-perfect read that has put the series back on track for me, and I'm looking forward to reading more Dresden books in the coming year.

reference_books.title: The Snow Child
reference_books.review_text:
As much as I wish it, "The Snow Child" is simply to incoherent and vague in its message to ever truly become interesting. The concept of losing a child in its early ages is of course an important emotion to be explored but Eowyn Ivey's take on the old russian fairytale of Snegurochka is far from being a version anyone will remember for very long. The endless descriptions of snow may have an effect during wintertime but a strong book must also be able to deliver on its promises even outside its main element. Here the snow simply seems an unnecessary excuse for preaching the beauty and purity of newborn life. 
 Further on, Ivey's lack of a coherent focus on the mystery of the Snowchild leaves the reader with a feeling of a barren emptiness. At the end you still sit with countless of questions that are never resolved: Who is the snowchild really? Where did she really come from? Why did she leave during summer? Where did she go during summer? None of this is ever truly explored and it seems to me that Ivey simply couldn't come up with clear answers to the plot she had borrowed from the old fairytale. 
 Whatever Eowyn Ivey's real intention with the book was one can only get disappointed by the end result of her writing. Of course, one could always excuse it with her lack of experience in writing novels. This is, after all, her first published work but as usual this is a far too simple excuse that doesn't make her book better. 
 Bottom line: The Snow Child is a disappointing and overrated failure. 
 2/Stars

** spoiler alert ** 
 Over the weekend I finally read "The Hobbit" after intending to ever since the movie came out. I am usually a stickler for reading the book before the movie, so I still haven't seen either of the movies yet! Since the third and final film is coming out this December, I knew I was running out of time to read the book, and thus the stage was set for me to tackle my first Tolkien. 
 Full disclaimer that, fantasy is not usually one of my favourite genres (with exceptions for Narnia and Tamora Pierce), and I have tried in vain multiple times to watch the LOTR movies. With this in mind, it is no surprise that this is not one of my favourite book, but there were definitely still sections I enjoyed. 
 One of the things that annoyed me the most was the bizarre quasi-musical vibe of the book. The characters kept breaking into song at the most inopportune times. I also found the story dragged on a little long and soon the obstacles started to blur together. At the very end, Bilbo is reminiscing about his adventure, and I didn't even remember they had battled trolls at the beginning. It sounds silly to say I found this novel somewhat boring, but I definitely felt disengaged from the plot much of the time. 
 That being said, it is clear that Tolkien is a gifted writer and there were many passages of prose that made me pause and roll them over in my brain again to really enjoy their weight. Maybe it is because I went on my first big trip sans parents this summer, but I also really connected with the passages dealing with adventure, travel, and the importance of seeing the world for yourself. 
 The character development of Bilbo was another aspect of the novel that I appreciated. At the beginning he is reluctant to join the company of dwarfs and questions his utility and ability to contribute to the quest. Watching his self confidence and aptitude grow, demonstrated in part by his increasing sword skills, was one of my favourite parts of the book. For me this was especially evidenced by his orchestration of the dwarves' river escape from the elves. In my opinion, the importance of believing in your own abilities and having faith in yourself was one of the key take-aways from the novel. 
 Ultimately, even though it wasn't my favourite book, I am still glad I gave it a chance, because I think it was a worthwhile read and there were a number of allegorical lessons/truths (those outlined above and those dealing with materialism and environmentalism) that I enjoyed. If you enjoy fantasy, adventure, or travel, I would certainly recommend you consider reading "The Hobbit".

 I like the way Tolkien is able to make helplessness cute and funny. Doing it any other way, (ie the Girl that Loved Tom Gordon, or The Solitude of Prime Numbers' opening chapter, with the girl breaking her back and soiling herself while waitin to die) would not have been welcome here. Instead, you get ''Even Bilbo was given a high seat at the table, and no explanation of where he came in - no songs had alluded to him even in the obscurest way -was asked for in the general bustle.'' 
 Maybe what's important for me now is the whole Underdog aspect of it, and the fact that the post-graduate years a person is liable to commiserate a great deal, since you're out on your own and supposed to be able to feed yourself. But the actual specifics of what the challenges are regarding Bilbo are unimportant and leave me cold. The spirit of the thing matters more, though it is a good story, no problem there. 
 Why does this not seem more exciting? Well, I never get the sense that they're in real danger. Either Gandalf or Tolkien himself will save them. And the fact that we get bombarded by the same stuff in every video game we've ever played and half of the cartoons that ever were. 
 In the same way that Morocco has ruined Bowles for me, while still being able to appreciate this intellectually and how well it's done, (and looking at the language side is thrilling) part of it still seems forced and lifeless and I cant get super excited about it. In this case, I think it's my age being a factor, and how I should have read this when I was on my Dean Koontz / Stephen King kick in 6th grade.

I'm sorry... 
 too boring for me...

I have read and reread this book more times than I can remember over the past 15 years, and before that my mother was constantly reading it (and The Lord of the Rings) to me. I will never not get that feeling of excitement when I read that very well known first line: "In a hole in a ground there lived a hobbit." 
 We are introduced to Mr. Bilbo Baggins in the very first chapter. Bilbo is a well-to-do Hobbit living in a hole in the ground in The Hill (not a nasty, dirty, wet hole, mind you!). Bilbo is quite content living peacefully in his "little" hole, never going on adventures or straying far from his day-to-day routines. That is, he is fine until a surprise guest (or fourteen) show up on his doorstep and somehow convince him to embrace his more adventure prone inner Took. 
 From that point on, his once fairly boring life is never to be the same. He journeys with dwarves, faces horrifying trolls, stays with beautiful, mysterious elves, and encounters a creature - and more importantly an object - that would forever alter the fate of Middle Earth. 
 JRR Tolkien's writings, though I haven't read most of his lesser known works (yet!), never cease to amaze me. The scope of his imaginings and the world that he created makes my mind spin. And the Hobbit is just the tip of the iceberg!

The most unadventurous adventure book I have ever read. The Hobbit fails to elaborate on any character development beyond Bilbo's whiny complaints of wanting to go home. The majority of the characters serve no meaning to the thinly laid out plot and the characters that are remembered by name are dull, annoying, and useless. Gandalf abandons the party when his magic would have aided the party in the monster-infested forest, Thorin's sole purpose in the book was to mope about his gold (both stolen and retrieved), and Bombur is a lazy dwarf that does nothing other than being a nuisance to the party. Bilbo unrealistically manages to escape every single threat because of his (dumb) luck, which makes every action scene tensionless and flat. Character deaths are unmoving because there is no emotional connection between them and the reader. The narration is boring, the journey is mostly described through walking, and the action is told through a few measly paragraphs. Despite it being 330 pages, The Hobbit dragged into unnecessarily long descriptions of settings and songs that drove the plot to nowhere.

book_b.title: Dark Matter
book_b.user_review:
I am going to be brutally blunt about this book and give it 1 star. It would be easy to just simply state that this book has a paper thin plot, is overmelancholic and sappy in writing. A lot of the time the author repeats the same sappy emotional state of our main character by making him cry about how much he loves his wife and kid and how much he misses them. 
 The book is also promoted as a book that deals with the question of what if or are you happy with your life, and the elements of choice through quantum mechanic theories based on, yet it is full of nonsensical descriptions of "Everett's many-worlds theory" which tend to contradict the whole premise of his book when the characters travels through infinite universes. Crouch elegantly manages to get around the issue by simply showing us that choices are like doors in our lives. You walk through them and gets to a new place where you had made a different choice. How does that apply? What door can you choose? By simply thinking about certain elements the doors will give you a world similar to your thinking. Rather conveinient. 
 The issue lies primarily in the premise of the book. We are told it is a story about choice. Good, then give us a story about consequences of our choice. You would have thought that such a story where a character travels from one dimension to another seeing would be about seeing himself through various choices in his life, right? Yet, Crouch's book this far from the case. Instead our main character visits dimensions which basically presents artificial and non-relevant presentations of alternate realities that doesn't have much to do with our main character. A few of them are post-apocalyptic which Crouch takes his time to describe while he perfectly skips many other worlds where the characters choices actually have an influence on their lives. But then what is the meaning of discussing choice and consequences if the worlds they visit are not based on the characters choices but on external events and happenings like a virus-epidemic or a world layed bare to a presumably nuclear war or a world where winter is harsh? 
 That Crouch seems to have had a greater focus on repeating the sappy thoughts of the main character than on actually focusing on giving us insight to the paradoxes of choice in a meaningful way is also illustrated by the rather short visit to the first world he appears in; the alternate reality Jason whose life is carreer-wise a huge succes. He is barely in that world for very long, missing a significant chance to at least dig a bit deeper into whether Jason actually would have liked a world where he choose career over family. Instead the author conveniently kills of important characters in order to push back to the path of pseudo-exploring different realities that essentially are simple filler for the overarching plot: Complaining about how much family means to the main character. 
 There is nothing wrong in expressing traditional conservative values about family; that family is the way to strive for happiness and that career is all good and fine, but in the end it is having family that makes us happy. Just be upfront and honest about it instead of trying to sneak it in through the backdoor by making the unhappy villain, the career-orientated Jason, into a woman/family snatching creeper-nerd. Based on that story the line between career and family is heavily tilted towards the latter, thus easily destroying any deeper meaning for the book as a discussion point since, well, the book already gives you the "right" answer. 
 But what about the action? What about the tension that this book creates, making you seat at the edge of your worn chair? In fact, the amount of action in the book is fairly limited and the tension rises only on a few occassions when the main character is faced with a simple external threat such as people wanting to capture or kill him. No offence, but I do believe most people are capable of implementing such a simple "action-component" to any story they might write making this book only exciting if you are into sporadically meaningless action-sequences with a sappy character running around crying about his lost life. 
 Maybe there is some alternate version of me in some obscure dimension that likes, perhaps even loves, this book. But for that to happen he probably has to be a sappy regretful whiner with nothing else to do than critize books that are more meaningful than this "version" of Dark Matter.

 Pros:

 Favorite lines:

 Her breath is wine-sweet, and she has one of those smiles that seem architecturally impossible. It still slays me.

I always try to finish books but I just couldn't get into this book, it's an interesting concept but it really didn't grab my attention
another crazy multiverse story showing the abuse of science and technology

This is one twisty, suspenseful, mind-f*ck of a book... and I mean that in the best way possible! 
 Like... wow. I could not put this book down. I mean, edge of seat, biting the nails, all in. 
 But enough gushing. Let's talk about why this is such a great read. 
 In Dark Matter, the author (a) creates a scenario that feels actually possible, even though it's pure science fiction; (b) trusts that his readers are intelligent enough to follow the plot down the physics rabbit holes; and (c) creates characters who we can truly care about. 
 Poor Jason. Of all the ways a life can go wrong, I'm sure he never expected this one! One day he's teaching college physics, married to a lovely woman, father of a pretty awesome teen boy. Next thing he knows, he's kidnapped, drugged, and waking up in a strange lab to applause and cheers, surrounded by people who seem to be his super-impressed colleagues. 
 It all comes down to quantum physics. Of course. Years earlier, Jason and Daniela each compromised on their dreams -- Jason to make the kind of physics breakthrough that changes the world, Daniela to achieve renown as an artist -- in order to focus on family and marriage. But what if there's a world where Jason made different choices? In the multiverse concept (as explained by me, a non-physicist, so be kind and forgive anything I get wrong), each decision a person makes spins off an entirely new universe from that decision point (okay, yeah, that's totally simplistic, but best I can do in a quick digest)... and Jason, being a world-class physicist, can appreciate the dilemma of worlds colliding and splitting more than most. 
 I really don't want to say too much about the plot of Dark Matter. It's complicated and fast-moving, will occasionally make your head spin, and moves along its path in all sorts of WTF-ish ways. 
 I loved the complexity of Jason's situation and the seeming hopelessness of his quest. The climax of the book includes scenes that are absolutely out there, but also kind of perfect. There are shades of grey and some practically impossible decisions that must be made. And oddly, beyond being a very cool and fascinating science fiction novel, I think it's fair to say that Dark Matter is also a love story. It's Jason's love for Daniela and his son Charlie that propel him through his despair and force him to keep trying when all hope seems lost.
This was SO good and I can't wait for the inevitable movie adaptation that I can only assume will star Matt Damon.

First half of this one was gangbusters, but it kind of went off the rails a bit toward the end with an over-complicated and slightly ridiculous finale. Still fun, but had Crouch been able to execute the ending, it would have really been a great entry into the alternate timeline genre. The pace is breakneck though, just hang on for the ride once you begin.

For the most part, I did like reading this book. However, some parts were too disheartening to enjoy. I was annoyed at times by the plot going round and round, while the writing sometimes made too much use of short phrases and paragraphs. I don't believe I would recommend this book unless you were really interested in an Intersteller-esque ride through dimensions and heartache. It did make an easy beach read this July 4th weekend, which is what I was looking for.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Why don't more people write about alternate timelines, you said. It'll be fun, you said! 
 P.S. Yo Crouch where my Amanda-centric sequel at? You know the one where she picks a great alt universe and has the perfect life but keeps her spare ampoules secreted away just in case and never tells the people she loves even though it threatens to tear them apart and one day-- I'll stop. But no, really.

***2.5 stars*** 
 This is a book about the idea of multiple universes. About the idea that each decision we make could have gone the other way and at that point in time another reality splits off. Another world is formed in which you made the other decision and life moves forward from there. That there are an infinite number of worlds out there in which we made every decision possible at every point possible. It's enough to make your head spin! 
 This was a fun, quick read- but I think the hype killed it a little for me. This is the thing I hate about hype- it can distort my experience of a book in a way that is usually negative. 
 It seemed like everyone was talking about this book- about the pacing, the action, the can't-put-it-down factor... And for the first 255 pages I was waiting for that to hit me. For the first 255 pages I was thinking: this seems like an average book about an interesting subject; these characters feel flat to me; every plot point feels predictable; when is the amazing-ness going to start? 
 There is a lot of material to be mined from a subject like this and on page 256 there was a turning point for me- it finally took an unpredictable and fascinating twist. I felt like it was the first time in the story I was surprised by what happened. But it kind of felt like too little too late. 
 Overall it's a fun, quick read about a really cool, interesting subject. But proceed with caution- unfortunately I don't think this one lives up to the hype.

The book started well and had a good core concept. But then it started going convoluted and there were plot-points which were difficult to swallow. From middle part onward, the story started to drag and at the end became slightly ridiculous. I wish the writer has kept it simpler and leaner, because there was much promise. 
 Not a recommended read.

Pretty fun take on a somewhat tired trope (CAN INTERDIMENSIONAL TRAVELERS HAVE IT ALL) but unable to achieve what it could because of Crouch's unfortunate decision to opt for the first person. In my more naive moments I have read some advice for novelists and they almost always contain a prohibition on the first person. Now I understand why! 
 Crouch's protagonist is supposed to be among the most brilliant theoretical physicists on earth but he reads like the most banal action movie Everyman you could imagine. As I read the book I uncharitably assumed that this was a product of an author unable to outsmart his audience. But maybe the alternative doesn't work, either: once all of your eggs are in the first person basket, your choice between a relatable or unlikeable narrator becomes very black and white. No one likes a smarty pants. 
 I suppose a book that thanks its film development team in the acknowledgements is obviously only somewhat concerned about literary merit. And the book mostly works, in what you'd have to call a cinematic way. 
 But the finale makes no sense. Without spoiling anything (I think): you can't posit an infinitely branching timeline in one plotline and then have it converge on a singular timeline in another plotline. It's such an obvious plot hole. Ugh. 
 Like a surprising number of other books, this made me think of The End of Mr Y. That book will hit many of the same notes and stay with you much longer. I'd start there. But this was definitely fun.
Nope.

Entertaining and fun read. Clearly written with a movie adaptation in mind. Explored themes of love and identity. While it may label itself science fiction, the science itself is very dubious and just provides a very convenient plot device.

I received an advanced copy from Netgalley for an honest review. 
 I see that the reviews for this are mostly very positive. People like Lee Child and Tess Gerritson are giving it amazing blurbs. Unfortunately these authors are not science fiction writers nor probably science fiction readers. I have been struggling to find a really mind blowing new author or book to praise and make a staff pick at work. This is not that book. 
 This is by the author of "Wayward Pines," which was turned into a TV series. I watched the first episode and then tuned out. The setup on shows like this are always intriguing but the attempt to make it interesting beyond the initial concept does not always work. See "Under The Dome" for a cute concept that fell flat quite quickly as the initial thrill stalled when trying to maintain stories that did not bore the audience. 
 This is the story of Jason Dessen and is told from the first person. Jason is really the only character that is given any sense of character development. Jason is a physics professor at a local college in Chicago. He attends a celebration at his local pub for a friend who has won a major science award, an award that he was en route to winning fifteen years ago, before he decided to marry his pregnant girlfriend. He still has regrets about his decision even though he truly does love his wife, Daniela, and his son, Charlie. Coming out of the celebration, Jason is kidnapped at gunpoint and forced to drive to a secluded part of Chicago where he is forced to strip and is injected with some substance. When he awakens, people he does not know are welcoming him back and his wife is not his wife and his son was never born. From this point on it degenerates into a standard multiverse thriller. 
 We see Jason and then Jason and Amanda, a psychiatrist from an alternate world who helps him escape, going from world to world trying to locate his prime world. It does touch on concepts such as regret and missed opportunities, but does not really tackle these in a thought provoking or even philosophical way. I have read better tales, such as E. C. Myers' "Fair Coin" and the short story and Israeli short film version "Impossible Dreams" and even the old TV series "Sliders," which have dealt with the multiverse in much more interesting and thrilling fashion than this. The reason I don't give this a lower rating is due to the competent writing style and a twist near the end, but it is too little, too late to salvage the story. The story just did not resonate with me. So I am still trying to find a really good, knock out book to promote.

I honestly was expecting to be mindblown... it didn't happen. Don't get me wrong, the story is fine but this was heralded to be one of the best science-fiction reads of its year and it just wasn't. The "science" is barely explained, and not believable. I'm not saying it has to be possible, I'm just saying it has to sound believable. I found this too simplistic, the writing somewhat mediocre and -to me- everything was so predictable and that it ruined the reading experience. It's not bad, it's just not what I was expecting from one of the alleged "best reads of 2016." Definitely "over-hyped."

Wow. I don't even know where to begin. I guess I'll start by saying that I don't normally read main stream, super popular books but I am so glad I took the plunge with this one! 
 Have you ever wondered if there were multiple versions of you living different lives than the one you're currently sitting in? I know I have, and this book explores that possibility in frightening clarity. 
 This is one of the best books I have ever read, because it is so different. Jason is an incredible, intelligent, brave man and I can't imagine how he felt going through all he does in this twisted tale of multiple dimensions. 
 I am praying for a book to follow this one, it ends in a cliffhanger of sorts. I was pleased with what we left with but dying to see where the lives of these characters go. I am so attached to Jason it's kinda sickening. And Amanda! Ugh I can't even begin to explain my feelings for her. She's wonderful. The kind of person everyone wants on their side. 
 Blake did an outstanding job of bringing Dark Matter to life, and giving you the thrill you didn't know you were searching for. 
 A million stars, a highly recommended novel. If you haven't read it- do it.

As with many books I've read this year, this one started off with an interesting premise, and then got tedious. I think a lot of these problems would be solved with hacking off 75-100 pages of all of these.

Incredible. Short, precise and well flushed out. I don't remember a single time I put this book down and didn't feel regret for not being able to continue. The science is reminiscent of other things, particularly Sliders and other great many-world advertures, but Crouch still manages to keep me guessing and moving at lightning pace.
I think this is my favourite book I've read this year. Incredibly gripping and heart wrenching. I'm going to recommend this book to everyone I know.

I wanted it to get SO MUCH BETTER AND IT NEVER DID UGH THIS WAS A GODDAMN PIECE OF WHITE MALE GARBAGE. 4.75

I only took a little bit off because sometimes when the text got super 'science-y' i found myself drifting off but everything else about this book was truly amazing.

Wow. What an amazing ride. 
 The author has a very unique writing style. Clean cut and fast paced. I couldn't put it down. The ending will have you wondering for days of what happens next.

Crouch's "Dark Matter" reads like the literary offspring of a union between "The Secret" author Rhonda Byrne and Michael Crichton, exploring concepts rooted in quantum physics -- that the addition of living consciousness affects ultimate outcomes in both science and life. 
 The main character gets a chance to see what life could have been like had he gone down the paths he didn't choose in life and work. And who hasn't had these thoughts? While the book illustrates philosophical concepts, it's also just great fun -- for me, it felt good to read a novel like this again. I hadn't read one in a long time that seemed to turn the pages for me, with a strong plot and high-concept ideas that drive the action, yet populated with characters that feel relatable. 
 Crouch also wrote, or is writing, the screenplay; I think the film version of this is going to be really good. Now planning to check out the "Wayward Pines" trilogy too.

Three stars +. I read this novel in a weekend. Interesting, compelling, not totally surprising, the romance a bit over done. Time travel but the time doesn't change. "'It's terrifying when you consider that every thought we have, ever choice we could possibly make, branches into a new world'"(112).
Whoa. Mind bending.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I can't bring myself to like this book. I like the idea, but the idea seems to get too big for the author to handle. So instead of exploring it deeply, it only brushes surface and leave more questions on the logic (how does Jason 1 ends up in the Jason 2's right world in the first place). Not to mention the ending - it's like the author wrote himself into the corner and don't really know to best end it. I felt also that the author kept on "telling" on how we should feel or think instead of making us arrive to that conclusion ourselves.
Interesting, but not believable enough for my taste.

DARK MATTER Well i really don't know what to say ! I'm completely shocked and stunned by this book although i gave it a 4 out of 5 stars because it left me with millions of questions that I'm dying to get answers for, i mean the book was great the plot was awesome but the ending was mmmm okay, let me make myself clear now, , i can't help but thinking of the amount of Jasons left in Chicago!! I mean what's going to happen to them ?? And what if they follow the real Jason and his family through the box again?? I would really appreciate it if the author would write a little Novela or maybe a second book to complete the story and also to tell us what happened exactly to Amanda because she disappears and we never heard of her again through the book , but overall this book hooked me in from its first page and it was an incredible read
Wow! What a ride!!!!

Ever feel like you are just missing the piece that makes everyone love a book? That's how I feel about Dark Matter. People love it. I thought it was okay, but not outstanding and the ending annoyed me a bit. And, since I had high expectations, just "okay" was really a let down. 
 At heart, Dark Matter is a love story with a bit of philosophy thrown in. It does make you think about how choices affect who you are, the life you lead, how far you would go to hold onto the life you have, how big the universe(s) can be. 
 It's also a thriller, complete with guns and violence and blood. It was fast-paced and a quick read, but I've read a lot of thrillers. I'll grant the twist was interesting, but couldn't carry the book for me. It was the only part that felt really unique, though. 
 But I was expecting sci-fi. I don't read a lot of sci-fi, only four in the last year, according to my Goodreads list. The Fold had alternate universes with different versions of the same people, so even that felt recycled. Interestingly enough, it also had a genius who instead of doing BIG THINGS, teaches, like our Jason. Is that a common sci-fi thing? I'm going to assume the science was at least somewhat believable, even if it seemed wonky to me. And there was at least one plot point that seemed impossible, even if we buy into the rest of it. 
 Then there's the end. Except I was convinced if I kept tapping my Kindle it would eventually turn to the next page. It didn't. That was the end. I'm not a fan of that type of ending, the kind where I don't realize it's the end. It worked for the story, just not for me. At least it was a happy ending. (Hope that wasn't a spoiler.) 
 Several times while I was reading it, I told Amber bits and pieces. When I finished (and complained out loud when I realized no, there was no next page), Amber said something to the effect of "Wow, you didn't like it at all, did you?" I'm clearly in the minority though.
WOW THIS BOOK. Jason is such a beautiful character

A fun mind-bendy thriller with an interesting idea or two to think about (providing you don't think too hard). It was much easier for me to get on board with the hilarious insanity of the premise than it was to get on board with the writing, which occasionally managed to achieve the subtlety of an air-horn. That said, for the most part, I was willing to keep turning the pages at all costs. A brain-neutral pleasure!
This book is mind blowing. Absolutely amazing. A brilliant work of science fiction, and by far the best book I've read in a long time.
Closer to 3.5 stars. I liked the middle third of the book a lot and was kind of unenthusiastic about the first and last sections. Maybe thrillers just aren't my thing.

Unpopular opinion, this this just didn't do it for me. I loved that it was set in Chicago. I initially loved that it was a quick, punchy read, until I realized it was also lacking a lot of its substance. The science in here is great. But the whole time I was kind of like, "why do I care?" It was action driven, though often it felt like action for action's sake. I appreciated Jason's driving want, but the characters felt so thinly drawn it isolated me from this a bit. Like, imagine drawing in the importance of choice from a position of knowing a more firm version of Jason. It just all felt so easy for how hard it really was. 
 Ultimately, it felt like this wanted to be a movie. And it would probably make a decent one. But I wanted more from the book. Though it wasn't my favorite, I am excited to donate my copy to the high school. I think teens will respond to the fast-paced nature of the book. And it will introduce some cool science.

By the end, I was racing through the pages because I needed to know what happened. Fans of sci-fi will appreciate this a great deal, but general fiction fans should give it a try. It really made me think!

Jason Dessen, a fairly ordinary college physics professor, is kidnapped and wakes up in a world where he is a genius scientist but never married his wife and his son was never born. 4.5 Stars

I've never read anything quite like Dark Matter before. And I don't think I will again. 
 Jason is physics professor with a wife he adores and cherishes after all these years and a son that's his pride and joy. He was an up and coming star in the field, but he chose the family life instead. It's a regular night, dinner with the fam until he decides to catch a drink with an old school buddy and he doesn't make it home. 
 I don't know how to review this book. Without spoilers I can't discuss the best part: the thrilling sci-fi ride along and all the implications. I'm still thinking about the consequences, the results, and how police will handle the disturbing trail left in its wake. 
 Dark Matter's blurb is good, but the Netgalley description needs to be included because I can't agree more: 
 From the author of the bestselling Wayward Pines trilogy, Dark Matter is a brilliantly plotted tale that is at once sweeping and intimate, mind-bendingly strange and profoundly human--a relentlessly surprising science-fiction thriller about choices, paths not taken, and how far we'll go to claim the lives we dream of." 
 I haven't read Blake Couch's previous work, but I plan to now and I'll be watching his new releases. 
 The Good: 
 + Solid blend of science and sci-fi that's easily understandable 
 + Phenomenal pacing and plotting 
 + Unpredictable 
 + Loved Jason and his journey, his progression, his family, his mind and character 
 + Staying power, lingering questions and paths to wander after finishing 
 + Ending is open, emotional, and impeccable 
 The Bad & The Other: 
 -	Uh??? 
 You know all those over-used cheesy descriptions like mind-blowing, and mind-boggling? Dark Matter is the kind of book those should be saved for because it brings them back to life with a purpose. 
 Dark Matter explores well, dark matter. I'm a layman interested in science but honestly, the science of physics is beyond me. So I was uneasy going in, wondering if I would be able to keep up. 
 Thankfully, Jason is an excellent guide through Schrodinger's Cat, the multiverse, and game theory. I feel like I understand the concepts better than I ever have. I wasn't lost or confused ever during the winding travels and tribulations. 
 I learned much reading Dark Matter, beyond the science. It made me think about the choices I've made and ponder how small variations could drastically alter...everything. Before I've had occasional thought about "the path not chosen" but never to this extent, to the minute, to this satisfaction. I'm more content with where I am and what led me here after reading Dark Matter. My choices won't result in such a...calamity but it makes me appreciate it all the more anyways. 
 In the end, we're left pondering what happens next. While I usually loathe open endings, it's perfect for Dark Matter. It feels right with trepidation, hope, and the next generation leading the way. 
 If you want a thriller with legitimate thrills, science fiction based on real science, or an unstoppable page-turner, you should read Dark Matter.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Part Sci-fi, part thriller with a good dose of romance- this book was a strong mix of genres with an undeniable emotional core. The story-line (man on a mission to get his life back) never faltered in its detailed and coherent constructed world nor in its forward moving momentum, and culminated in a very satisfying end. 
 I enjoyed the Sci-fi aspect of this book in which an alternate Jason has created a device or "box" that allows one to move between multiverses, to visit or even inhabit worlds that have split off from one's own world through the infinite small or large decisions one makes everyday. 
 I also liked that love was such a central part of the story. Jason battles everything from confusion, violence, poverty and hopelessness but never gives up because he needs to get back to the love of his life Danielle. 
 There wasn't too much whimsy in the narrative, but the little there was was good. I especially appreciated the part where the various Jasons had a group chat going. 
 I could have done with a little less violence, but that's a small critique when this book was full of adventure, smarts, passion and humor. 
 Lastly, this book reminded me of one of my favorite reads of 2016: The Hike by Drew Magary, as both were primarily about men suffering through horrible and absurd obstacles to get back to their beloved families.

I was really impressed with Dark Matter by Blake Crouch. I gave it five stars - and it was truly five full stars for me. Crouch's descriptions of alternate worlds were so vivid, at some times bleak, and at some times deceptively lovely - I found myself lost in his words.

 My major issue here was the theory behind the science of the plot. This story treats the Box like a TARDIS that can't travel through time, only universes (if only - #tenrose for life). But that's not the theory here. The Box would need to already have existed in these universes to allow this sort of travel. But in the main universe Jason disappears from, there is no Box. It was never invented. That's LITERALLY THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS STORY. Jason 2 should not be able to somehow manifest the Box in a universe where it was never invented. The only universes he could theoretically travel to through the Box would be other universes where the Box exists. This bothered me throughout the entire story and kept me from really feeling invested.

A new paranormal romance series by Gena Showalter. WAs originally going to be a trilogy, but has now plans for 6 at least in the series. It is darker than most of her books on theme and the use of pain and pleasure. Interesting idea with the Titans and Greek gods. I love the new take on Pandora's box. Each Lord of the Underworld is a warrior that was punished for defying the gods by being cursed to "house" the demons they released. For this specific tale, we have Maddox who is possessed by the demon/spirit of Violence. He is also cursed to die each night with the assistance of Pain and Death (other demon lords of course). 
 Ashlynn is an innocent female who enters into their world seeking a way to control the voices that she can never silence. She knows no peace and is hoping that the "angels" or "demons" that these strange warrior men are referred to by the citizens of Buda can help her. Much to her surprise, they are not what she expected and things get weird fast. 
 Overall, the story seemed very chaotic. A lot of world building and set up forced the "romance" to almost take second stage. There were so many introductions it was hard to keep up at first with who housed what. Plus, it was hard to see the "beast" side being tamed so easily considering these are supposed to be "Evil" spirits to begin with. I guess the "evils" from Pandora's box weren't that evil afterall. I was a tad disappointed with that, but willing to let it go. The book itself was a fun romance that by the ending had me wanting to read the next to find out what happens with each guy. We kept having so many elements being introduced it was hard to relax into the story. The men are definitely alpha men with the whole "mine" possessive attitude that Christine Feehan does in her Carpathian series. The meet their potential mate (hard to say loved ones considering) and become obsessed despite themselves. I had mixed feelings about that. It seems such a cop out to have a couple meet and instantly "fall in love" without knowing each other or speaking. Falling lust I can understand. But terming it love? Nah. 
 It was an interesting, unique story. Nice to pass the time with. The second book read easier and flowed better than this one. Like I said, it was more set up for the whole series I think. Still good for fans of Showalter or paranormal romances that like J.R. Ward and Feehan's books. They are definitely set up to get more complicated with each book so I will be sticking with it though I don't think I will keep the books.

So, I started this one a long time ago, got about halfway through, then put it down because: somehow, I doubt someone being burned alive over and over in Hell would be having such mundane thoughts while smiling. I mean, come on. I get that Maddox is used to being burned, but smiling? Doubtful. Hey, my skin is melting off and I'm turning into ash, let me smile now! I'm in love, so it doesn't hurt for me to be burned alive anymore. In fact, I'll laugh and do the tango while my bones get charred to cinder! 
 Characters. 
 Maddox. 
 Now, I don't feel any special connect with Maddox, but I do like him. He seems like a good "guy," and he was very preotective of Ashlyn and very loving. I could tell he cares for the other lords very much, and feels guilty whenever he hurts any of them. Oddly, I found him sort of sweet. He's the typical alpha, possessive type, but not in a way that really bothered me. Besides, with a curse like his, I'm impressed that he hasn't gone utterly insane! 
 Ashlyn. 
 Okay, okay, so she is a little on the stupid side, but I got over that pretty quickly and learned to like her. She's sweet, caring, tender, selfless, and is willing to do anything for the man she loves, who happens to be Maddox. I loved the way she tried to defend him when the lords were killing him--and she even went so far as to use a sheet to climb out a window and swing over to the balcony a room over (even when she was pissed at him) just to get to Maddox. Now THAT is love. THAT is a heroine. I was beginning to forget what real heroines are like! Ashlyn totally reminded me. 
 Right now, the characters that stand out to me the most are Gideon and Torin. Gideon because his curse is hilarious! Everything he says has to be a lie, and it's cute when he gets all worked up about it. Plus, he's got blue hair and blue eyes, which is just sexy. And Torin, well, he sounds majorly yummy as well, but, on top of that, he helped Ashlyn hide when the other lords were going to use her as bait. AND, I feel so sorry for him, not being able to touch anyone. Aww. Most of the other lords aren't doing it for me at the moment. 
 Relationship: 
 Yes, things moved ridiculously fast, but I've come to expect that in PNR, so it didn't bother me. Plus, it was refreshing to have a hero and heroine who actually LIKE each other. Plus, they meshed well, had good chemistry, and as for their love--I was definitely feeling it. The sex scenes were a little on the riduculous side, but...again, it didn't bother me overly much. And what Ashlyn did for Maddox at the end--epic. She's such an amazing heroine, and here she truly proved her lover for her man. Usually, in romance, it's only the man who has to prove himself, but here, they both proved their love, and I adored it. 
 All in all, this is a pretty enjoyable book, and I'm sure the rest of the series will improve.

I found myself wondering how Showalter was going to write a book about each of these guys. Their 'curses' are way more ickier than Ward dreamed up for her BDB. 
 I wanted to like this one - I found the premise interesting, with the whole Pandora's box idea, and there are tons of 5 star reviews on GR. The Hero being stabbed to death every night and spending the night burning in Hell (or whatever it was going on) was very dramatic. A novel approach to be sure, except it woke up my snarky inner troll. Troll snickers, 'it's like a gory version of Groundhog Day'. 
 The we meet the heroine on a quest to Budapest to find these secret dudes, and discovering that the voices in her head that plague her are silent when she is near Maddox and snarky Troll pipes up, 'shades of Sookeh!' 
 Then as I'm reading further and I couldn't think of how one silly girl would be able to change thousands of years of a curse with anything other than the power of lurve (there's that damn Troll again) and I realized I just couldn't make myself care about the rest of it. 
 So ends my foray into Paranormal Romance. 
 I think.

 Brother! Okay, there was a shower scene. But when the demon-man realizes his "damsel in distress" and this woman who he decides he MUST protect at all costs, even if it means fighting and/or killing his brothers in arms of hundreds of years, is a virgin -ack!- oh, my....the stops go up and there is no way he is deflowering this fine specimen in the shower. I actually got confused between the voices in her head that she hears from times gone by, current thoughts, and out loud thoughts. Geez. And why all the secrets? The only secrets one should be keeping are Christmas gift secrets. Unless, you know, said Christmas gift is a set of fine combs for her long hair. AmIRight? 
 I know character evolution and storylines need some conflict, some man vs man, that kind of stuff, but holy crap. Be honest with what is going on and save yourself, the people around you, and the readers reading some time and agony over silly misunderstandings.

 The Darkest Night and The Darkest Kiss (books one and two, respectively) kick off Gena Showalter's Lords of the Underworld paranormal romance series. This series has been on my radar for a while and has been recommended to me several times since I do enjoy a good paranormal romance. It seems as though a lot of people compare this series to the Black Dagger Brotherhood series by J.R. Ward. While it has it's similarities, the BDB series is, in my opinion, immensely better. 
 I'll be honest - the series does have an interesting premise. There are several Lords of the Underworld - it seems as though most, if not all, of the Lords were involved in the opening of Pandora's Box back in the day. As a punishment for unleashing Pandora's evils out on the world, each Lord of the Underworld is cursed to carry one of the evils/demons that had previously been living within Pandora's Box. As is the thing with these kinds of series, the men have had to endure the curses for centuries, but all seem to find love and/or redemption around the same time. 
 The Darkest Night introduces us to Maddox, cursed to carry the demon of Violence, and to Ashlyn, a human woman with a penchant for hearing voices. Ashlyn seeks out the Lords in an attempt to try and stop the voices in her head. She stumbles upon Maddox who initially thinks she is Bait (humans who are used for...well...bait by the Lords' enemies - the Hunters) while he is out seeking Hunters that are trespassing on the grounds. The two team up to fight the powers that be and...hopefully this shouldn't come as a spoilery surprise...they fall in lust (er, love?) and the plot moves on. 
 The Darkest Kiss then moves on to Lucien who is cursed to carry the demon of Death. This second installment starts out rather abruptly (and, in my honest opinion, quite awfully) with Anya (the goddess of Anarchy...a "minor" goddess in the Pantheon, but don't tell her that apparently) stalking Lucien in a club while the other Lords (or maybe it was just Paris, the Lord saddled with the demon of Promiscuity? I can't remember) have sex on the dance floor with women. Anya has her own issues as the daughter of a promiscuous daughter and the product of an affair. Anya is cursed by Themis to an unfulfilled, unhappy love life because of the sins of her mother. Anya has angered the Titan god Cronus...so much so that Cronus has ordered Lucien to kill Anya. So begins the cat and mouse game that's peppered with lust (er, love? Maybe?). 
 I just didn't like these. I didn't really enjoy the first book and I only gave the second one a whirl because it came up as the book of the month in a bookclub I enjoy. In both books, the characters are flat, the writing boring and somewhat awkward, and the love just isn't there. Oh, there's lust aplenty. But, a "lust story" holds no appeal for me. I wonder if the series doesn't get better as the author matures in her writing style and as the characters grow (and I don't know enough of Showalter to know whether or not these were written early on in her career or not). 
 I just don't know if I will continue on in the series to find out if they get better.

 I don't think it's a surprise that I don't like new adult. Most of the NA books I've read have been a big disappointment and I decided I wouldn't read another one for a very long time. But when I found out that Jennifer L. Armentrout (aka J. Lynn) wrote an NA book, I put my opinions aside and I read Wait for You. And I'm happy to report that I didn't absolutely hate Wait for You. It wasn't the best book I've read but it was great entertainment. 
 The plot line for Wait for You seems to be like every NA book out there: innocent, inexperienced girl, college, sexy bad boy, sexytimes, sex and a main character with a tortured past. BUT I liked how J. Lynn took these themes and changed them around. Not only did Avery have a past but Cam did as well. Better yet, the plot for Wait for You featured Avery's and Cam's slow friendship turned to romance. While they are both attracted to each other, there is not kissing or sex until about one hundred pages into the book. THAT my dear friend, in my opinion, is how it should be done. No insta love or "no, they got to know each other for two weeks, that is not insta love." For me, I knew what was going to happen (I guessed Avery's background well ahead of its reveal) but for Wait for You, it worked. 
 But I have to say this: this book features sex and masturbation in detail. For some, it will be too much but for others it will be okay. Personally, I wasn't expecting it to be as explicit as it was (I recently read an adult romance and that had a more PG love scene, lol) so I just skimmed some of those scenes but they didn't feel out of place. 
 As I said, the plot isn't all that original but J. Lynn's writing is what made the difference. J. Lynn obviously knows how teens talk today and she was able to put that experience into Wait for You. The dialogue in Wait for You, like in many of J. Lynn's books, was my favorite part. It was fast, snappy, snarky and I could imagine my friends talking like the characters in the book. 
 I want to put something out there before I talk about the characters: I've never experienced the things Avery has. No assault in any form or rumors or slut shaming have been a part of my life so far (and I plan to keep it that way) so it was hard for me to connect to Avery. Sure I could imagine how I'd feel if I had Avery's past but that was it. I liked Avery's character: she wasn't completely naive but her innocence was believable. As far as I know, Avery's reaction to her past seemed real enough so I appreciated how J. Lynn wrote a believable character. 
 I personally loved Cam. I really thought that he would be that same old cocky, confident, bad boy with a heart but Cam turned out to be a complete sweetheart. His anger wasn't something to worry about and I loved his relationship with Avery. I also liked the secondary characters but I didn't think they were as developed as Cam and Avery. I especially didn't like Avery's parents but I wanted to know them more. 
 Overall, I liked Wait for You. One day I was bored and I needed something fun and light and Wait for You delivered. I'm not sure which couple is going to be featured in the next book in this series (why is it a series again?) but I know I'll read it for sure! If you like new adult, I'd recommend this book but for those who need an entertaining book but not too much depth, I'd also recommend this book!

Avery is running from her past. College is an excellent excuse to put thousands of miles between her past and the new life she hopes to start. Her goal is to focus on class and maybe make a few friends. Cameron doesn't want to be Avery's friend. Tall, athletic, and charismatic, Cameron threatens the safe little world Avery is building for herself. Being with Cameron means facing her past or hiding part of herself. But when her past catches up to her in emails, text messages and phone calls, Avery knows she can't hide forever. 
 Jennifer Amrentrout definitely knows how to draw a swoon-worthy male lead. Cameron is every twenty-something's ideal. He's incredibly tall, good-looking, sweet and relentless. He pursues Avery with a single-mindedness that is endearing. Armentrout perfectly balanced the sweet and the swagger with this character, which is fortunate as Wait for You, to me, is character driven. The interaction between Avery and Cameron are the strongest points of Wait for You. Their dialogue is fun and playful and always stays just shy of too emotional. 
 Wait for You falls into a fairly new genre: New Adult. I'm still not entirely sure what sets New Adult and Young Adult apart aside from more sexual content. I am finding a commonality among New Adult: dark pasts that usually include some of abuse, sexual or otherwise. Our female protagonist is damaged by her past, but eventually rises above her circumstances to become a stronger, if not wholly self-actualized, person. I'd have like to have seen what Armentrout could have done with a fresher plot line.

I finished reading this book two days ago, and I still can't get over it. I simply can't stop playing it in my mind, and I want to start reading it all over again. 
 Wow. I'd guessed I would like this, but get obsessed over it? Definitely not. 
 I loved the story from the beginning. From the moment Avery bumped into Cam, from that first 'sweetheart' I was hooked. 
 This book is romantic, is sweet, is funny, is sexy, it's simply amazing. 
 I loved that they didn't just fall head over heels with each other after the first chapter, because this gave me the chance to get to know them better and feel for them. I loved how their relationship evolved from friendship to love, and how Cam just waited for her. I loved their banters, the way they kept teasing each other, I highlighted lots of them, they made me laugh out loud. The dialogues were brilliant and truly entertaining. 
 Avery is a great heroine, who went through a lot when she was still very young, but managed to get back on her feet years later and get away from her family, running away from her past and starting a new life where nobody knew what had happened to her. I loved her personality, her strength and her weaknesses. 
 Brit and Jacob were great secondary characters and I loved how they interacted with Avery, and with Cam. Jacob was simply hilarious! :-) 
 As for Cam... well, what do I say about him? He's the absolute perfect hero, and I'm still thinking of him days after finishing the book. He's the typical heartbreaker, but he turns into the perfect boyfriend after falling for Avery - I was swooning every time he starred in a scene. It wasn't just because he was absolutely HOT (black curls and blue eyes - my very favorite combination!), but it was everything about him that made me fall so hard for him, making me wish throughout the book that he was real. He was sweet, romantic, funny, baked cookies!!! - now, how cool is that in a man??!!, and owned a tortoise named Raphael, which is totally sweet! No matter how hard I try, I can't get that scene in the first chapters when Cam rescues Raphael from Ollie out of my mind :-) 
 I loved how he didn't let Avery's attempts at turning him down discourage him; I loved how he didn't let their past get in the way, and how protective he was of her, after she opened up with him and told him the truth. Well, I simply loved Cameron Hamilton, and he's probably climbing up my personal chart of book boyfriends really fast. I'm pretty confident he's already reached number 2 close to reaching number 1. 
 I really really enjoyed reading this book, in spite of typos here and there. I would love to read more about Cam & Avery, and personally I would have liked to see things through Cam POV, maybe in a sequel?

There are a lot of book boyfriends out there who set the bar so high you can only hope to wish someone like that in person but Cameron Hamilton sets it even higher for the book boyfriends we have learned to love. 
 I have read a lot of books in my 24 years, and I have fallen in love with a lot of characters and even got obsessed with some. ;) But Cameron Hamilton trumps them all. First of all, he has blue eyes, is an athlete, can cook and bake, an overprotective brother and my most favorite trait of all, he was NOT an asshole. LOL And I mean, come on, who can resist those cookies? 
 "I'm beginning to think cookies is a code word for something else." 
 "Maybe it is." He tugged on my bag again as he took a confident step back, forcing me down another step. "And just think about it. If cookie was a code word, whatever it symbolizes, it's been in your mouth, sweetheart." 
 Wait For You is one of the books I have read over 10 times, and is my favorite re-read whenever I just want to get that warm fuzzy feeling. :) I guess that's the reason why I bought the book three times over; one to lend to my friends as one of my most recommended reads, one for myself to read over and over, and one to not touch ever and display on my shelf. :) 
 The characters in this book are to die for. I remember the first time I read this book, I couldn't really put it down cause it was funny, and realistic and teaches you that you need to accept your past and live in the present in order to move forward. 
 "As long as the sun's shining, shit can't be that bad." 
 The book is told on Avery's perspective, and it's really nice cause you get the full effect of the swoon-worthy Cam and realize Avery is not crazy for turning him down over and over cause she is going through a lot in that brain of hers. I wouldn't have minded alternate perspectives, but I totally forgot about it when Trust In Me got released for Cam's point of view. :) 
 It is funny, definitely a page-turner, a light and easy read. You will find that you won't stop smiling going through the pages, and it will get you hooked from the moment Avery plowed into Cam. You must definitely pick up Wait For You and can you believe it? This is the first in a series of standalone/s.

 Full review: 
 Some of you know that my favorite author is Jennifer L. Amrentrout (A.K.A J. Lynn). I love all of her books, all of her characters, everything. So, I was really excited to read this book and it did not disappoint, not one bit. Jennifer L. Armentrout did it again, she weaved a tale of love, despair, and healing. All of it was great, the characters, the plot, the story in general, are just outstanding. 
 The plot in this book had so much depth to it, like all of her books do, but this book felt like it had more depth and reality in it. I think that's what really made me love this book, because it didn't just feel like a made up story, it felt real. I like books that have a plot that feels like that and Mrs. Armentrout did this very well, because it was deep, but not to deep that it felt like you were suffocating.  One of the best things about this whole book was the relationship between Avery and Cam. I felt real and not fake. It didn't feel one bit forced or unrealistic. And because you feel such a connection with the characters you want them to fight for their relationship, you want them to try.
