book_b.user_review:
Distopian? SF? YA? Yes and no to all. This fabulous novel transcends all genres. An original and compelling first novel, that's for sure. Must now read the second one. 
 I love the premise -- Amy leaving typical teen life behind to be frozen and launched on a ship for 301 years of travel to an earth-like planet in a different galaxy. A second narrator -- Elder -- a young man destined to be the leader on this aircraft transporting Amy, her parents, and the other scientists and settlers for the destination planet. 
 But much as this sounds like it would be all about transponder rings and metal hats, it isn't. Against a backdrop of a believable future, we get nuanced characters, a murder mystery, lots of suspense, and a hint of romance. 
 Well done.

It was fine. Good. I liked it. 
 Even though I know there are more books after this one I'm not entirely satisfied in the end. I'll read them because I am curious, but I am not so invested in the world or the characters. The story is really interesting, but I think it's missing something that I can't really place. I think maybe it needs more development...? Hopefully the rest of the books will give me what I need. Though, I do really appreciate Amy's character, I like her spunk and she is not one to just give in. 
 That being said, her life sucks Bertie Botts Every Flavor Beans. Seriously.
Ok I give up on this one too. I've read the first five chapters and I can't take it any more. I love Sci-Fi so I thought I'd like the whole space thing but I can't take it any more. Sorry.

I picked this as the second book to read during #Xmasbooktubeathon 2014. I will talk more about it in my video but I started it at 10:30pm and finished it at 2:15am, so there's that....

** spoiler alert ** 
 Amy is a strong, vibrant character. Immediately, I sympathized with her and wanted her to be able to run under an open sky. Because of this, it got REALLY hard to read through the middle and end of the book--especially when I realized that the situation was going to get worse without relief. It was gut wrenching to watch it all go down in the end. A bit of a depressing ending. 
 It didn't have to be a happy ending--but I think some smaller victories for the character I loved so much would have helped. I'll have to read the next book to find out.
This book was really inappropriate an should be rated R.

Review 7 out of 5 
 Seventeen-year-old Amy and her family leave Earth to colonise a planet which is 300 years away. But she is brutally woken fifty years before she was supposed to be. Amy feels so alone, but there is someone who wants to protect her. Elder is sixteen, but he is to be the new leader of "Godspeed" when it's his time. 
 Can Amy and Elder unravel the secrets and lies and get to the truth? Can they find the killer before more lives are lost? 
 I absolutely LOVED this book! Those who know me know I very rarely, if ever, swear. BUT - O.M.G. - This book is fantastic! 
 I had heard on the review grapevine that it was good, but to me it's an understatement! This is one of the most exciting science fiction novels I have read in a long time! The characters are so life-like, that I couldn't believe that they only existed in the author's imagination. This book is told from both Amy's and Elder's point of view. 
 Amy is a typical teen, but she has to make a hard decision whether or not to join her parents on a 300 year journey to a new planet. She is very brave, because if I was in her position, I don't think I would go through with it. After being woken, she has to cope with her new reality. 
 Elder is a not so typical teen. He has been raised on ship to be the next leader. When Amy is woken up, he takes her under his wing, trying to protect her from an unknown murderer. 
 There are some other great characters in this book too. I especially liked Harley, Elder's friend. There are some disturbing issues brought up in this book, but I think that they (the issues) need to be examined and are quite relevant today, as I'm sure they were in the past and will be in the future. After I finished reading, I sat for a bit thinking "WOW, that's some story!". 
 Beth Revis has found a new fan in me, and I'm now looking forward to reading the sequel, A Million Suns. I highly recommend this book if you love YA/science fiction/adventure/action/mystery.

Actual rating 1.5 stars. 
 This was poorly written but the worst part was that she was a seven year old, not a teenager. It creeped me out, how can someone miss so bad in targeting the age?

Liked the premise, didn't care for the structure. Was engaged in the initial story, but lost interest after the jump ahead. 
 First in a trilogy I won't be reading.

This was an okay book. For my first YA Sci-Fi Novel, I was really expecting more... 
 Not to spoil it for anyone else, but I saw EVERYTHING that happened at the end of the book within the first half of the book. All of it. The revelations, the secrets, the reasons everything. It was kinda disappointing. 
 CHARACTERS: 
 Amy and Elder are the main characters and the novel jumps back and forth from their perspectives. Honestly, I didn't see much difference between their viewpoints. Both of them had the same narrative style, they just had better insight into some area of the story (which is fine, it just made it a little confusing resuming the read half-way through a chapter). 
 I was more than a little disappointed that neither character showed much development or change by the end of the story. Amy was still upset, and Elder was still confused and torn. The romance felt a little one-sided to me, and forced. 
 STORY: 
 A really novel (ha-ha) idea. I was really expecting more of a star-trek feel to the book, but was surprised when it kept reminding me of the Giver (dystopian, a ban on emotions and free thought, a single individual chosen to carry on duties as ruler, love interest with flaming red hair, etc.). The Giver freaked me out, but still, I pressed on. 
 There's a few moments that made me antsy in reguards to the sci-fi/YA world. The whole 'season' thing, I could have done without and I don't think the story would have suffered for it. And for those of you who have read it, i don' think Amy needed to go through what she did in the cornfield for the novel. I really didn't see the point. You traumatized her, and them moved on. Not realistic. 
 Finally, I should mention that there's and awful lot of characters talking about death and suicide. I mean, a lot. There's at least two characters who were referenced as having killed themselves, and it plays a big part in the story in two places. 
 OVERALL: 
 Worth it, but know what you're getting into. It's a good read. I'd say it's the giver in space. It's definitely not for the younger YA readers. I'd say 17+ for some of the subjects in it... I might read the next book. I haven't decided yet.

Buddy read with Elizaveta.. Mission complete! 
 Across the Universe is so much more than a Sci-Fi Dystopian book. It has tragedy, romance, action, and even a faction of depression that's usually found in Contemporary novels. The story itself blows your mind and as you discover more secrets about the ship, it draws you in more and more. 
 Story begins with Amy and her parents saying goodbye to each other. Giving an opportunity of a lifetime, they have to be frozen, only to arrive 300 years later at a planet that was recently discovered. But Amy's dad gives her a choice: either to leave her whole life behind and get frozen or stay on Earth. What I loved the most is that she chose family. 
 When she gets unfrozen, she realizes that someone tried to kill her just like they have been doing with several other members. The mystery remains while noone is trying to do anything about it. Amy realizes that the ship itself is a huge mystery and Earth's history may be forgotten a long time ago. 
 With all the mystery and secrets, it usually pretty obvious what happens at the end. But definitely not in Across The Universe. I did not see that coming. At all. And I'm pretty good with freaking things like that. So BRAVO to the author who made me be in the dark until everything was revealed. Definitely recommended for anyone who likes Sci-Fi and doesn't mind the world-building in the ship.

 I have mixed emotions about this book. It's one of those books where I'm not quite sure how I feel. I both did and didn't like it. The thing is.....there isn't anything actually wrong with it. For the most part, it's a perfectly good book. The writing is excellent and the plotline is incredibly detailed; you can tell the author put a lot of thought and effort into creating her world. I'm usually a fan of paranormal books and I think the fact that this is a Sci-Fi book is what makes me feel the way I do. It's outside my comfort zone and it was a bit too scientific for my taste. 
 Going into this book was really looking forward to it. I think I had a picture in my mind of what it would be like and when I started reading I discovered that was I got wasn't what I thought I would. The story fell short in my opinion. 
 Also, taking into account of the detail that went into the writing and story, I feel like the main two characters were lacking at some times. While both Elder and Amy were great for their purpose in the story I feel like they lacked real depth and emotion. 
 Elder was an alright male lead. To begin with, everyone within the Godspeed had no emotions, so I suppose that just the fact he began to question things should really say something. And yet it doesn't.....if that even makes sense. I think I wanted a much stronger lead than what I got. 
 And Amy? She annoyed me at times. I can completely understand how horrible her situation was. I can't even begin to imagine what it would be like waking up long before you were supposed to and to the world she did....where everyone acted mindless and emotionless, but come on! I just felt like she should have acted different. I don't even know how....just different. However I was glad that she forced Elder to look into everything that was going on and to seek out the answers Eldest were keeping from him. 
 People mention the romance in this book, but to be honest I didn't feel it. While it was obvious Elder was attracted to Amy and they liked one another there wasn't a lot of romance and romantic moments between the two of them. I also didn't see the chemistry that I was expecting to see. 
 The whole twist that Elder was actually the one who unplugged Amy to begin with completely threw me. I thought perhaps it may have been Harley or Orion, but never Elder. Usually when something similar happens within a story the author will throw little hints in....you know, making the character feel bad about something that happened, and even though you as the reader don't know what, it still is a clue. In this, there was none. There simply came a moment where Elder thought back to that situation where he unplugged her and he knows he has to fess up to Amy. 
 It was just strange. 
 And yet she accepted it very easily. Yes, she freaked out and hit him, but it seemed like she wanted to move on at the end. She was upset and angry, and even though she's not ready to forgive him just yet she began to let it go. Me personally, I would have ranted and shrieked a bit more and told him I never wanted to see him again. But then again....he is one of the better people on the ship. 
 All in all, not a bad book. It's not really my thing, but fans of The Uglies series and similar books should eat this up.

 My mind is reeling after finishing this book! There are so many complex themes I could talk about, that I hardly know where to start. 
 ...so I'll start from the beginning. 
 Beth Revis began her tale with Amy, who watches her mother as she is frozen in preparation for being sent off to space; a scene so well-described, I almost didn't want to read any more. I found myself cringing and shuddering at the description...but at the same time, I had to know what happened next. And what happens next, is one heck of a tale. 
 The setting on the ship, Godspeed, is so mind-blowing, that it is almost unbelievable. But Beth manages to describe it in a way that makes it feel tangible. The descriptions are wonderful, and allow you to imagine the entire ship in your mind. Everything about the book--from people, to the emotions they feel--seems real, allowing the story to come alive and take hold of your mind. 
 The characters are complex, and show the reader many believable personalities, each character true to their circumstances. The contrast between hearing the story from Amy, and then from Elder, allowed the story to be told through the eyes of two very different beholders, each with different thoughts and beliefs. I am so grateful for their relationship, which was more of a friendship that slowly grows. It was a relief to not have two characters who were thrown together, and instantly matched. The way it was written is believable, and--I found--preferable, given their situation. 
 Some of what I did not like, however, was that although the characters were so real, I did not see a lot of character development until the very end of the book. I would have liked to see a more gradual change, but it seemed to happen all at once. The ending happened very fast as well, and it seemed like everything that was building up to that final moment, was gone too quickly. 
 Across the Universe covers huge themes, like the different ways people take on leadership, and the way humans respond to change. I think do Beth did a fantastic job in creating a society--complete with its own language variations--that had evolved and progressed, over the hundreds of years it had been around. All-in-all I think the book was a unique, fresh, take on science fiction, and I had a great time reading it! 
 Read this if 
 ...you want to experience the confines of life across the universe, and you don't mind solving a little mystery along the way.

Is a one star rating warranted if there are aspects of the book that I enjoyed? In this case, I'd say yes.

 I mean, for fuck's sake, the ONLY reason she's even there is because that idiot Elder takes a fancy to her and wants her awake during The Season aka the time where most people on the ship mate like crazed rabbits. And if you haven't guessed yet, I don't like that. At all. 
 Otherwise, she has little to no importance to the plot. 
 Which brings me to Elder and the alternating POVs. Although I enjoyed being in Amy's head, I dreaded reading his point of view. Normal on the outside, rotten on the inside, that's Elder. And just when I think he's finally waking up and smelling the coffee, realizing the absolute craziness around him, he goes and thinks another effed up thing and I think: that's it! 
 Also, the book features an almost rape scene . The aftermath is a bit mishandled and everything is kind of glossed over. 
 Nope. Just no.

The premise of this book was very interesting. But, the romantic relationship (which is what I read all books for) was lacking. Amy and Elder didn't have much chemistry and their relationship lacked development.

 Se gia la copertina (che rimane invariata anche nella versione italiana) non mi avesse stregata, lo avrebbe fatto di certo la trama. Across The Universe entra di fatto nella mia top ten dei romanzi piu interessanti letti da un po' di tempo a questa parte. Non solo per la trama fantascientifica (che io apprezzo notevolmente), ma soprattutto per lo stile narrativo scelto dall'autrice. Questo continuo cambiare di prospettiva, di voce narrante, forse e la vera novita del romanzo. Infatti la storia viene raccontata dalle voci dirette dei due protagonisti, Amy e Elder, alternandoli continuamente per permettere al lettore di vedere e capire ogni singola reazione e pensiero dei giovani ragazzi. Diciamo che ho un gran debole nei confronti delle narrazioni multiple e dei cosiddetti romanzi corali, quindi non ho trovato molto difficile seguire il filo logico della narrazione e le vicende alternando di continuo luoghi, situazioni e personaggi. Passato questo "scoglio" voglio addentrarmi un po' nella trama del romanzo. 
 --- SPOILER ALERT --- 
 La vicenda inizia con l'ibernazione della madre di Amy, offertasi volontaria per mostrare alla giovane il processo doloroso e traumatico che la aspetta. Entrambi i genitori sanno perfettamente che la giovane non vorrebbe partire con loro per questo progetto della BRF (la Borsa Risorse Finanziarie, "un'alleanza multinazionale con un solo scopo, il profitto"), perche lei ama la Terra e in particolare ama il suo ragazzo Jason, che non potra partire con lei. Sara suo padre, pero, che le fornira subito un'occasione per uscire fuori dal progetto e vivere la sua vita nella Terra con gli zii, infatti l'uomo le dice chiaramente che non si aspettava che lei sarebbe partita con loro e le da il benestare per rimanere nella Terra, lasciando a lei l'ultima decisione, in quando ultima nel processo di ibernazione. La giovane sembra tentennare alla sua offerta, ma subito decide di rifiutarla per seguire gli amati genitori nella loro missione. Subito dopo, saltiamo al "presente" nella nave spaziale Godspeed, dove il giovane Elder, futuro leader della nave, studia per prendere il posto dell'anziano Eldest, attuale capo della nave. Eldest appare sin da subito come una figura schiva che nasconde parecchi segreti. Forse sembra troppo prevedibile un suo futuro coinvolgimento nelle vicende che seguiranno. Tornando alla nave, la Godspeed e una nave organizzata in tre grossi livelli: quello dei Custodi, dove vivono e hanno accesso solo Elder e Eldest, quello dei Naviganti, dove si trova il centro di ricerca e lavorano gli scienziati, e infine quello degli Alimentatori, dove si trova e vive di fatto tutto il resto della popolazione. Una societa di fatto profondamente classista, con un centro di comando forte e indiscutibile come solo il leader Eldest sa essere. Una piccola distopia dentro un romanzo sci-fi, dove tutto viene controllato nei minimi dettagli da Eldest, persino le nascite e la morte dei singoli individui che abitano la Godspeed. L'unico periodo in cui, infatti, e permesso (e di fatto viene incitata la procreazione) e la Stagione, che si svolge poco prima del cambio di potere tra un Eldest e un Elder, cosi infatti si chiamano le cariche di leader e vice-leader della nave. Sara proprio sulla Godspeed che la giovane Amy si risvegliera, inavvertitamente o quasi, molto prima del loro arrivo nella nuova Terra-Centauri. 
 Che dire? Tra colpi di scena piu o meno prevedibili (che Orion, il misterioso archivista che sembravano poter incontrare solo Elder e Amy, fosse l'Elder creduto erroneamente morto non ne avevo dubbi sin dall'inizio), misteriosi omicidi (prevedibili, ma interessanti dal punto di vista della trama), rivelazioni sorprendenti (la vera storia dell'Epidemia, in primis, ma anche il finale) e personaggi secondari a cui si ci affeziona subito (Harley <3) "Across the universe" rimane di fatto un libro ben scritto e con personaggi ben caratterizzati (sebbene ho letto che molti si siano lamentati del fatto che i personaggi principali fossero poco delineati - si tratta pur sempre di adolescenti che stanno crescendo, non di adulti, suvvia!), con punti di vista sempre diversi e interessanti e una confessione finale che mi ha lasciato davvero a bocca aperta. Non vedo di leggere gli altri libri della serie, sperando che possano arrivare anche qui in Italia molto presto. 
 Consigliato: a chi ama il genere sci-fi, ma anche a chi ama i romanzi distopici.

Couple of notes: 
 This one flowed really well. YA sci fi with some romance, but not a whole lot. 
 Following two characters who alternate chapters. 
 Amy is frozen and put on the Godspeed with her parents and other colonists for the long 300 year journey to another planet. There is also a crew that keeps the ship going, families who live their entire lives on the ship and their kids take over the next generation of ship's crew. Then she gets woken up 50 years early. 
 Elder is the future leader of the Godspeed, living in a highly regimented society founded after the Plague decimated most of the ship's crew. He is set to take over from Eldest soon, but although he has always respected him as a leader, Elder is having doubts about what he's been told. 
 Amy is thrust into a society so bizarre, she can't believe everyone is human, and although she wants her parents with her, she is also scared because someone keeps unfreezing people, and people are dying. 
 Lots of questions on what it is to be human; is it better to have total peace or individual truth, how much do we need lies in order to live. 
 Can't say that any of the themes were new for me - have read them before, but I do think that this book is a good way to get new, younger readers into sci fi. 
 Some violence, sex, and an attempted rape make it a bit more adult than other YA.

I had big expectations for this book and I was a bit disappointed. The world building and the characters were good, I loved the claustrophobic feeling this book managed to give me. But other than that, it was nothing special. 
 What bothered me most was how stupid the characters were most of the time. Some of the plot "twists" and the answers to pretty much all of the questions were obvious long before the characters figured out the truth. I like books that challenge me to keep up, rather than ones that leave me waiting for 100 or so pages for the characters to figure out something that is painfully obvious.

Amy has been cryogenically frozen for centuries with her family as they make the long voyage to colonize a new planet. Elder is the young leader-in-training on the generation ship that has housed Amy, her family and the rest of the colonists for 250 years. The ship is more than a vessel - it's a whole society of people, kept peaceful and productive under the absolute rule of Eldest. But then someone wakes Amy up 50 years too early. Her presence alone is enough to destabilize the carefully balanced society Eldest cultivates, but there's more -- the same person who woke her is killing more of the cryogenically frozen colonists. Who is this unknown murderer and why would they jeopardize the ship's 300-year mission? Well, maybe you'll be able to find out, dear reader, because I could not finish this boring hunk of drivel. 
 It's sad to have to put this book on the old "stopped reading" shelf, but I tried, I really did. I read halfway through -- 180 pages -- before giving up because nothing was f*cking happening. The premise is so interesting; sci-fi, murder mystery, fish out of water story; but the execution fell short. Waaaaaay short. Let me enumerate: 
 1. The story is told in alternating chapters from Elder and Amy's POV. A standard device. But wait! This includes chapters where Amy is frozen the whole time. Does that sound boring to you? Well it is. There are about 7 chapters of Amy, the human popsicle, having nightmares and flashbacks. One would have more than sufficed. 
 2. Amy has an acute case of Mary Sue-itis. OMG - she's so different! Her hair! Her skin! She'll tear society apart just by standing around and pouting! This cannot be! Gag me with a spoon, people, I so over this kind of character. 
 3. The only thing the romantic leads have in common is that they are equally whiny and unlikeable. Yes, the situation they're both in is stressful. Elder is under a lot of pressure from Eldest. Amy's entire world has gone up in smoke. But let's have some real anguish, not just a couple of kids whining about how they can't do what they want. 
 The characters never come off the page, and the setting -- this huge, awesome, ship-planet where people have lived for centuries -- never becomes more than a cardboard backdrop for teen angst. What a f*cking disappointment. 
 Read these instead: 
 Living Hell 
 The Knife of Never Letting Go

 This book is all over booktube, which is the reason that I picked it up. 
 Across the Universe is a sci-fi romance novel and I enjoyed reading it. It details the journey of a ship, the Godspeed and the development of the people living on it. It was a relatively enjoyable read and it's errors, while present, were not so bad that they majorly influenced the likableness of the story. 
 Plus it's a nice change of pace from the usual post-apocalyptic dystopians. 
 Sci-fi is not usually my choice of genre. I hate the subject of astronomy. In sixth grade, we did moon journals and I hated it with a fiery passion. 
 Even so, I wish that Across the Universe had had more information about the science behind the Godspeed. We're treated to loads of information about the citizens and history behind the ship, but what I want to know is the technology. How does the ship run? How do they manipulate and reuse resources? The book skimmed over a lot of the science behind the methods used on board. Revis does a fantastic job building up the setting details and while she did have some of this information, I still want more. 
 (But not as an info-dump, which thankfully, wasn't a problem in this book) 
 The characters were alright. Amy can be unbearable at times, but some of it can be attributed to her high amount of panic when she realizes, "Oh shoot I've been woken up early". I do think that she was too inconsiderate. She doesn't understand that the Godspeed IS NOT LIKE Earth and that the ship has essentially been reduced to a homogeneous society. She doesn't realize that her different appearance might cause the people on board the ship to rebel. She's selfish and doesn't know what she's doing half the time. 
 On the other hand, I'm not really sure if I like Elder that much. :/ He's naive and kind of dull. Half the time he was talking about how beautiful Amy was and it's really obvious that he wants to get in her pants. I also felt like he was a doormat. Too meek. However, his creative friend, Harley, was really great. 
 The plot was pretty predictable what with the reader knowing who the enemy is within the first fourth of the book. There were a few plot twists that I didn't expect, but looking back, I honestly probably could have predicted them had I been focusing more. 
 There were both good and bad things about the romance. Very insta-love-y on Elder's part. Kind of annoying reading all about his obsession with Amy 24/7. But hey, at least there wasn't any love triangle and the love isn't forced on Amy. 
 I liked this one a lot.

I read Olive Kittridge and liked enough that I decided to try another by Elizabeth Strout and picked up My Name is Lucy Barton from the library. 
 I am really glad the book was as short as it was. A rambling meandering mess of a book. Lucy is an older adult looking back at a time when she was sick in the hospital for an extended period. Then, she was married with kids but her husband was a wuss afraid of hospitals and she had been estranged from the rest of her family for years. Her husband arranged for her mom to fly in and come see her in the big city in the hospital and they had this ...totally non-bonding .. time. They talked about everything, except the important stuff, about random people you never meet or hear about again in the book. The visit is so surreal, at one point I wondered if it really happened. I thought perhaps she had a high fever in the hospital and hallucinated her mother being there. 
 This episode is spliced between Lucy's current life as a writer and her childhood, which she remembers as abusive and poverty stricken. The poverty is the truth. The abuse seems pretty ordinary coming from a generation in which kids were pretty regularly told to go pick a switch from tree for a whipping. Not that I am agreeing with it, I am just saying that it is not something extraordinary that the book was exploring. It was just boring. There was no big reveal. She never really reached any understanding of her mother or herself. She didn't resolve the conflict with her father. There was no resolution or even understanding reached. On top of that, Lucy wasn't even that likeable. A disappointing read from an author that I hear great things about.

 My Name is Lucy Barton is literary fiction. Which means that not much happens. So fair warning, this is going to be one of those reviews where I end up talking a lot about how the book made me feel, rather than what the book was about. 
 Because I'm not quite sure what this book was about, at least in the sense of what the plot might have been. Or even if there is one. 
 Instead, this is a novel about relationships. And it is also very much a story about secrets, especially the ones where the need for secrecy becomes so ingrained, that we no longer even tell them to ourselves. 
 The ostensible story is about Lucy's unexpected extended hospital stay, but it is clearly told from a point much later in her life. And as her thoughts roam over the whole of her life, she hints at memories from her childhood and adolescence. 
 It's clear that there was a lot wrong in the Barton household while Lucy was growing up. The family was poverty-stricken, but that wasn't either the real or the whole of the problem. Sparked by an extremely unexpected visit from the mother she hasn't seen for years, in the quiet of her own mind Lucy hints at the things that went wrong. But she never speaks of them, not even to herself, at least not in detail. 
 There's a monster lurking somewhere in that dim past, but the habit of never revealing that truth, whatever it was, is so ingrained that Lucy doesn't even let herself think it. Consequently, the reader never does know precisely what happened. 
 What we do know is that those long ago troubles shaped Lucy's life, and that her mother's inability to even touch on those difficulties is part of their estrangement. At the same time, Lucy longs for real connection with her mother. And even though she is terribly grateful that her mother is there for those long, uncertain days in the hospital, Lucy still doesn't get what she needs. 
 Escape Rating B-: I finished this, I found it interesting enough to keep turning back to over and over throughout the day, but in the end, it didn't move me. There was no catharsis, no true ending. 
 Throughout the story, Lucy hints at terrible secrets, but she never reveals them, even to herself. As a reader, I felt let down at the end. I expected a resolution, or at least a reveal, that never came. 
 At the same time, part of what kept me coming back was the tenuous relationship between Lucy and her mother, which had some uncomfortable parallels to my own relationship with my mother. And maybe that was the point of the whole story. Not that Lucy tells us what happened to her, but that it makes the reader reach for the resonances in their own story. It's not what the story gives us, but what we bring to it. 
 And that's an uncomfortable thought.

In My Name Is Lucy Barton Elizabeth Strout, Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Olive Kitteridge accomplishes a great feat - she tells the story of a woman's entire life in just 193 pages, and manages to be both thorough and economical. Because of its brevity we know to pay attention to each moment, for they are all significant if we want to understand Lucy's life. 
 Growing up in extreme poverty in rural Illinois, with a father who had PTSD before PTSD existed, a mother who was emotionally distant, and two siblings from whom she could not have been more different, Lucy Barton's childhood was lonely, and hungry, and frequently cold. An excellent student, she attended college on a scholarship, married her first husband at age 20, and settled in New York City. She made two friends, had two daughters, and then complications after an appendectomy landed her in the hospital for an extended recovery. Her estranged mother visits her in the hospital, and the conversations Lucy has with her during this time frame the novel. 
 This novel reminds me of Kent Haruf's Our Souls at Night and Thomas Christopher Greene's The Headmaster's Wife, deeply human stories that pack a real emotional punch in relatively few pages. Highly recommend.

I really doubt my review can do this book justice, but I'll do my best. 
 It's quite difficult to categorize this book. There isn't much of a plot; most of the book takes place in a NYC hospital where Lucy Barton is fighting off an infection she contracted after surgery. She wakes up one day and her estranged mother is sitting by her bed, and for the next five days, though she spends longer in the hospital, her mother rarely leaves her side, and she and Lucy discuss the stories of people they knew back home in Illinois, where Lucy grew up. Interspersed among these discussions are flashbacks to Lucy's childhood, which we slowly realize was quite unhappy and quite impoverished, and she lets slip stories about her parents and her siblings that are quite sad and at times disturbing. We also realize that Lucy's time in the hospital is a flashback of its own, as we see Lucy as she is now, much older with children now grown. 
 This is a story about relationships, about people, about not feeling safe or comfortable in a family when that's the place you're supposed to feel safest and most comfortable. We do learn a measure of compassion, however, since Lucy's father was very damaged by his time fighting in World War II, and we get a sense that he would have been a much better husband and father and person without the trauma he experienced during the war. It's also hinted that Lucy's mother had had a difficult childhood of her own, and I feel like Lucy tries so hard to forgive her parents for her own hard childhood because she knows they were both so damaged. 
 I'm surprised to find out that I've read another book by Elizabeth Strout, Amy and Isabelle, when I could have sworn that this was my first by her. But Strout's beautiful writing is evident in both books, and there are times that my eyes fairly flew across the page and just absorbed the words into my soul. This isn't a book I'll forget quickly. 
 An interview with Elizabeth Strout that aired on NPR can be read online here. I found it quite fascinating, and now I feel like I must read Olive Kitteridge.

This was the first really disappointing read of the year for me. 
 The writing was okay, nothing remarkable, but the characters were so grating. Stargirl was absolutely the Manic Pixie Dream Girl. While I have mixed feelings about this trope, I have to concede that she fit it perfectly. She would dance in the rain, dress outrageously, bring her pet rat to school, among plenty of other odd things. An oddity here and there isn't terrible, but Spinelli had absolutely EVERYTHING about her be so different from everyone else, that she just wasn't the least believable. Not only did she play the ukelele to sing to people on their birthdays (whether they liked it or not), she was also very naive and sensitive and kind. Again, those aren't bad things, but wrapped up altogether, she just did not seem real at all. It might have been better if it had been from her perspective or third person, but it was not. 
 One review I read put it best when they said it seemed like the message of the book was not to necessarily be yourself, but to be as different as possible. Instead of being a testament to individuality, it was more like a guide for being purposely weird. Some of the things Stargirl did was nice, but others were really not as nice as the author tried to make it seem. Following people around the mall is creepy and technically stalking, it isn't cute and quirky. Someone tells her to not sing to them on their birthday, and she does it anyway, but not looking at them. The author makes very arrogant assumptions that people should just go along and be spontaneous, rather than thinking of the varying levels of comfort and consent people have and can give. 
 In addition to that, all of these characters are completely one-dimensional. Of course the most popular girl in school is a mean blonde who doesn't like Stargirl. Leo, the narrator and eventual admirer of Stargirl, is very bland and hates to stand out but can't help being interested in her. I didn't hate Stargirl, despite how forced her character felt, but I strongly disliked Leo. He was not a good person, trying to make Stargirl change herself so he could be seen with her. The only relationship I was really interested in was Stargirl and Doris', the only friend who would eat with her in public and was consistently supportive of her. 
 Outside of the characters, the plot really dragged on. For a small book, I had a hard time staying engaged in the story. It honestly could have been cut down even more. Again, the take-home message is supposed to be to believe in and just be yourself, but it really did feel more like 'be as different from others as possible'. I can see this being a kids introduction to teen novels as the content was very tame, but I personally prefer something a little more realistic. 
 (I will also say that for the longest time, I was under the impression that this was a story about the Holocaust. I thought that's where the title came from...)

This is the sort of book that, if you're a writer, makes it extremely difficult to concentrate on Your characters and Your plot and Your syntax, because all the above are flitting through your head all day, like stained-glass butterflies, begging to be paid attention to. 
 Growing up, I wonder if Jerry Spinelli was a fan of The Wonder Years . . . I was. While I did not imagine Fred Savage as Leo Borlock or Josh Saviano as Kevin or "Winnie" as Stargirl, there is something within the tone of the narrative that made me think of the voice-over narration for which the show was iconic. Something humorous and teenage, and at the same time poignant and serious. I am left with an impression like a safe cut. Does that make sense? Stargirl is going to make you bleed a bit, but it's because you have to climb something important, something with thorns. 
 Stargirl herself has inspired me. Kind and gentle and weird and passionate. It's been a long time since I have cared this much for a character. There is one scene in particular where I wanted to reach my arms through the pages and wrap them around her. I wanted to look into her eyes and say all the things Leo wasn't saying to her but should have been. I wanted her to know that rare, beautiful things are often the recipients of ugly words and hateful people. But of course she already knows all of this. She didn't need me to tell her. And Leo . . . Leo was young, and I have confidence in the man he is yet to become. 
 I want to express how special I believe this book to be. It's moments like this I wish I had a megaphone, through which I could speak to the world, whisper in their ears, "Read this book. Read it fast. Then read it again, slowly. Then sit and let the nuggets rise up like gold in a miner's pan." 
 I should have been writing down all my favorite quotes. That's how I know I was engrossed. I forgot, up until almost the end. I managed to get this one down. 
 "Thin as a minute, he appeared to lack the heft to carry his own name." 
 Thank you, Jerry Spinelli. I am ever so grateful to you!
Beautiful descriptions.

It was kind of a funny book, just to see what Stargirl would do the next day. It also had an ok story line. The only thing I didn't like was the ending. I think she should have at least done something back to the mean girl, or at least stayed in town with the guy.
In a world of "normal" we all need a Stargirl!
I think I could re-read this book, this old favourite, dozens of times and never get bored of the story and its messages.

Spinelli captured what it's like to be different in a world of normal through this novel. It showed how cruel high school can be. This book also shows signs of true love. Spinelli's idea was simple (a different girl in a conformed school) but his imagery and narration were true to what high school students talk and think like. 
 I feel in love with this book. It reminded me just how important it is to be nice to everyone. Stargirl is the ultimate friend and charity worker. This story wanted me to change how I was acting and being. That's when you know you have a great book on your hands. Spinelli was dead on in his characters. Needless to say, this book is a keeper!
This is a good book. It inspires some of my own social experiments. People are so funny.

This is a tremendously odd book. Stargirl follows the course of events at Mica Area High School after the arrival of a new (and almost indescribable) student. The book did make me think, which I'm sure was the intended result, but it involved a bit too much navel-gazing for me, and I thought the writing was a bit pretentious at times (and its level of writing seemed really mature for a book aimed at intermediate level children). Probably the worst example: 
 "Like so many of Archie's words, they seemed not to enter through my ears but to settle on my skin, there to burrow like tiny eggs awaiting the rain of my maturity, when they would hatch and I at last would understand." (p. 103) 
 Auuugh. The book reminds the reader just how cruel and unforgiving teenagers can be; even the main character, who is not overall a bad guy, has bought into the hype about being like everyone else so thoroughly that he can't see past it to what is really important. 
 I didn't really enjoy this book very much, but I am still somewhat curious about the sequel.
Stargirl is clever and an inspiration to be... you.
The most boring piece of literature I have ever read. Besides from twilight.

This is just such a different story I have ever read and a great one too. It has a good writing style and the plot is fantastic. It's hard to explain a book with such difference but not at all at the same time.

Quick read. Not too big of a fan. Leo was boring. Stargirl was not...but she was a bit TOO odd. Not that that is a bad thing, because I like the message the author is trying to send but I feel as if Leo and his classmates learned nothing, she was shunned up until the very last day when she left...This book left me unfulfilled, and usually even with books aimed for a younger audience, I can appreciate them, but this one? Not so much.

I wanted to like this book. 
 The more I think about it, the more I hate to rate stories negatively. Because they're stories. They are written for a variety of purposes and they impact people in different ways. I thought about this a lot while listening to this book. Stories are important. 
 But, I guess, I'm not rating the value of this story. I'm rating the value of this story to me. 
 So I'll say that it comes across as pretentious. And a bit too preachy. It reads almost like a parable - like an obviously fake story that is written just to make a point. Also, like a parable, it kind of hits you over the head with its message. 
 And the people on the stories just don't seem real. In fact, Stargirl is the ultimate Manic Pixie Dream Girl. (With my apologies to Nathan Rabin who coined the term and is calling for its death.) Maybe this breaks down in the sequel where we have a story from her perspective, but I didn't like this well enough to read further. 
 Archie plays the wise mentor, but too often he seems like he's spouting the stoned philosophizing I hated in On the Road. 
 It feels like the author wants to say "be yourself"; but it comes across as "try to be different". Which really aren't the same. 
 Ultimately, I have to say the story didn't hold much value for me.

A modern young adult classic. Makes a point about the value of individuality and the conformity of not just high school and the suburbs, but human nature. My only complaint is that Stargirl is a little too good to be true.
One of my 7th grade students asked me to read this book, I'm glad I did. I laughed and I cried. This was a great kids book and has many life lessons for kids.

1) It is not possible to generate a living story out of a topic. 2) A character trait is not a premise. 
 This a fundamental misunderstanding of storytelling. And this is why Stargirl is the sum of all cliches you can find on a esoteric fair and the personal narrator sounds like a forty years old accounting clerk. 
 There is not story at all. It is more like a book treatment, told from the distance.

Wow. This book was fantastic. It's written in the voice of a high school student, but anyone can relate to the characters in this story. I think we all can think of kids that didn't seem to fit in with the rest of the school. In this case, there is one girl in particular, and she leaves an indelible mark on the lives of everyone she encounters. You'll have to read to find out why she's called Stargirl.

Sat down to read this and finished it in a day. Such a good book with lessons that even adults can learn from. Stargirl's story will stick with you and make you re-examine how you treat and look at the people around you.
A fun, easy read. It was short and sweet and had some really cute moments during the book. Stargirl was a super lovable character and it was pretty realistic (the emotions and people at least)

I loved this book. Stargirl reminded me a lot of myself when I was in high school, except she was a much better person than I was. I think this is a great YA book, but I think once you are out of high school you can appreciate it even more.
Was not as good as I remembered it.
This had a great moral to the story, great for pre-teens.

The trouble with miracles is, they don't last long. 
 Honestly, I don't understand what it is about this book that many people seem to love so much. 
 I read this at the start of the year and am only catching up with the reviewing now, so my memory of it might not be as fresh as it should, but my general opinion stands. 
 Stargirl is a very, very annoying character. Yes, she's supposed to be special and unique and outlandish, but at the core she is simply irritating. She's also supposed to be friendly, yet she doesn't respect people's wishes, like not singing to somebody on their birthday, which can be understandably uncomfortable and embarrassing. Things like making a book about a young child that isn't your own and wanting to give it to the parents. I can't imagine any parent appreciating that; they would be more worried about somebody watching their child like that. As for running onto a football pitch and taking the ball? Rules and social norms are there for a reason. She isn't being revolutionary for doing things like that, she's being disruptive. It isn't fun, and nobody would ever stand for it for a second. 
 In terms of personality, she is very borderline Mary-Sue. She's supposed to be unique - and the book is desperate to remind you of that every single second - but her behaviour could quite easily be attributed to attention-seeking. Furthermore, her character plays into the 'homeschooled oddity' stereotype, and portraying those who are home educated as being without social skills etc. is just ridiculous. 
 Protagonist Leo is a very, very boring character. Not just ordinary, dull and boring. There was no reason for Stargirl to fall in love with him, and their 'love' seemed childish and out-of-nowhere, which is, in my opinion, the worst way to write romance. While Stargirl has a high school setting, the characters and situations read as very immature, more like middle school at the most. I struggled every second to imagine the young people as being high school teenagers. 
 The writing, while it has a few shining moments, is mostly simply and doesn't flow. There are many short, basic sentences, which is a style that works with certain writers and certain genres, but doesn't work here. Leo has many moments where he is captivated by Stargirl, and his comments are obnoxiously pretentious. Nobody thinks like that, and the phrases used don't even always make sense even in quite an abstract way. 
 The 'system' of popularity the author uses is unrealistic and, again, very childish. Well, unless things are very different where the book is set, which is possible, but unlikely to such a degree as this. 
 With so little to redeem the book, I have to honestly say that I struggled to reach the end, which, I feel I should add, was also nothing impressive or enjoyable.
I was very touched by this book. It has a great message about being yourself and accepting others.
Weird, but cool weird.

reference_books.title: The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight
reference_books.review_text: Sadly, I read reviews of this book, and they were not good (on this site), so I was trying to go into this book with an open mind. However, I was very disappointed and found this book to be very fluffy. The main character, Hadley has just missed a plane to England that will bring her to her father's wedding. Hadley hardly approves of the marriage. She meets a guy at the airport, and they have a long chat on the plane ride there. And then she decides in the middle of the ceremony that she needs to find this guy in England. The story was far fetched and the characters were cliche and unenjoyable.

reference_books.title: The Silver Star
reference_books.review_text: I really loved Walls other two books, and was excited to read this one. I was willing to buy it but am very glad i got it from the library. The novel is about two sisters who have an erratic, crazy mother, much like in the Glass Castle. When she leaves the kids alone for a long time, they go to visit an uncle who they barely know and live in the town their mother grew up in. The characters were somewhat interesting, but I felt that I was reading a VC Andrews novel, that was slightly elevated. I did not like the ending in the least, I felt it was way too neat and also thought the last page ended rather abruptly.

reference_books.title: I've Got Your Number
reference_books.review_text: In Sophie Kinsella's latest comedic romance, a woman discovers a cell phone in the trash that is thrown out by a PA of an exec named Sam. In a ridicolous but enjoyable twist, she begins answering his emails and responding to his texts. Meanwhile, she is set to be married to the handsome Magnus, who has a very smart family that leaves the narrator, Poppy, feeling a bit dumb. This book, like many other Kinsella novels is very very light and fluffy, yet very fun. I enjoyed this book, and despite it being a 400 page book, it was a fairly quick read. If you've read Kinsella's other jaunts, you will enjoy this one as well.

reference_books.title: Love Anthony
reference_books.review_text:
This is my third attempt at a Lisa Genova 
 novel and most likely the last. The premise is that a woman has lost her son to autism discovers a secret about a woman who is having marriage issues. This book was slow moving, bordering on dull and also had flat 
 characters who I did not connect with nor did I find remotely interesting.

reference_books.title: The Shade of the Moon (Last Survivors, #4)
reference_books.review_text: This book was completely awful, in several ways. The first book I really enjoyed. The second book in the series was equally good, the third one, not so much, and this book was awful. The book had a bunch of mistakes, I'm going to crack this up to being an Advanced Reaidng Copy but I'm not sure. The plot was hard to follow, and there were pointless deaths that did nothing but to move the plot around. Characters that were beloved in the first two books have become boring shells of themselves. The main character, Jon, was a character who was barely in the other two books, and he was someone who I did not particularly care about. The author should have stopped writing these books after the first third, and possibly after the first two. BLAH!!

reference_books.title: The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry
reference_books.review_text: This was my favorite book so far of 2014. IT was well written, had great characters, and was just a good overall read. It didn't drag in the least and was the perfect length. The premise is that a man lives on a small fictional island in the US and owns a bookstore. He is bitter and hard to get along with because he suffered a great tragedy in the loss of his wife. He is visited by reps from different publishing companies, and he has a remote interest in Amelia, one of the reps. But suddenly, an event occurs that changes his entire life, and as a result his entire personality as well changes. I really loved the main character, as well as the characters of Maya, Amelia and Lambiase. I'd recommend this book to nearly everyone, and it especially appeals to a literary lover.

reference_books.title: The Truth About Alice
reference_books.review_text: This book surprised me in a good way. The book starts out with the focus being on a girl named Alice who supposedly did bad things with two boys at a party. Her reputation at the school is tarnished and she has no to turn to. The book is divided into chapters with different characters telling their stories. Some of them are more likable than others naturally, but the book unfolds like a flower blooming and eventually you find out what really happened to tarnish Alice's name. My favorite character was Kurt, who served as a good nerdy anti hero. Overall, a great read.

reference_books.title: The Night Strangers
reference_books.review_text: I've been a fan of Chris Bohjalian for a while. I didn't love his last book, but I was excited to get this book..until I read the reviews on Goodreads. Several of my friends gave it a poor rating. However, I did NOT want to believe them! A ghost story! A good author who is literary! I should have known better. A family moves to New Hampshire where they buy a house that has a bolted door. The husband has flashbacks of a flight he piloted that crashed. The family has two twin daughters who are lonely. And they become friends with the "plant women," who are women named after plants, which just seemed stupid. The description promises characters that you cared about, I didn't care about any of these characters. I barely got through this book, and it moved very slowly and didn't catch my interest at all.

reference_books.title: Conversion
reference_books.review_text: This book started out being very exciting. A girl attends an all girls school and one of the students suddenly has a seizure. Soon after, other students begin having seizures. Is this a repeat of the Salem witch trials? This book takes place in Danvers, which contrary to popular knowledge, is where the actual Salem witch trials took place. This book kind of dragged on, and my biggest issue were the flashbacks to the time of the witch trials, which I found extremely boring. I would have enjoyed the book much more of it actually took place entirely in the present.

reference_books.title: After Dark
reference_books.review_text: This was my least favorite Murakami. The plot is about a girl and a few other characters who do activities after dark. She goes to Dennys, meets a guy, and then is asked to translate something that a female Chinese prostitute is saying. The book was kind of dull, and didn't feel like his other books, which was a huge disappointment.

book_a.title: Lone Wolf
book_a.user_review:
A new Jodi Picoult novel. Let's go through the Jodi Picoult checklist, shall we? 
 Family Drama? Check! 
 Courtroom scenes? Check! 
 Twist Ending? Check! 
 Lots of angst? Check! 
 Oddly named characters? Check! 
 Told from different perspectives? Check! 
 Social issue? Check! 
 This book really wasn't great. I didn't care about the wolves, nor the family, and the last 100 pages made me just skip to the end, which wasn't impressive.

sample_reviews.review_text:
This was my first Jodi Picoult book and I'm still kind of digesting it but wanted to do the review while it was fresh in my mind. 
 I have to say I identified the most with Edward in the story though it was hard not to be empathetic towards Cara as well. While the story is mostly about family and the things we have to get through that will either tear us apart or make us a stronger unit - it also brings up trust and sincerity issues between siblings. Having just gone through something similar with my sister, the decision to pull the plug or not, I found the story a bit heartbreaking as I relived the aftermath. 
 My favorite parts involved the wolves and how we humans could learn a lot by watching them interact as a pact. This is true of other animals in the animal kingdom as well. Animals don't have the emotional range that humans do so there will always be conflict, hurt feelings, and selfishness. It is sad to say but true. 
 I did think Luke was a bit crazy for living with a pack, eating raw meat, etc. Quite frankly, it grossed me out. No matter how we might try to change our spots, we are, in fact, human with human attributes. We aren't wolves, lions, or any other pack animal. We are humans with human needs and human families. I know that isn't coming out the way I want but basically I'm saying that a wolf is a wolf - a human is a human. We can learn a lot from them, but we can never become them nor them us. 
 I thought the book drug in a few places and had some things that could have been cut without it changing the dynamic of the story but that is me. I don't like oodles of details that could just as easily been left out. 
 I give the book an A. I can't swear I will read more of Jodi Picoult - I can't swear that I won't either. I thought she'd make it to my best author's list but she didn't - I am rather neutral on her as a writer. Good story, a bit of a tear jerker, but interesting none-the-less.

This is definitely my least favorite Jodi Picoult book (an honor that was previously reserved for Harvesting the Heart). Half of the book was completely predictable. The other half was completely unpredictable, but only because everything that happened was so bizarre. Most of the characters, especially Luke, were poorly developed and none of their actions or thoughts really seemed to fit together as a cohesive character. There was also way too much anthropomorphism going on with the wolves. Wolves are interesting and social animals, but they were elevated to be these magical creatures and I don't buy all of the wolf "facts" that were thrown in there. The last three pages were ridiculous. I saw that coming and sort of thought she wouldn't actually go there. Totally did.

This is now one of my favorites by Jodi Picoult. It is almost as good as Nineteen Minutes and House Rules, almost. It kept me guessing but there was one detail left unexplained to my satisfaction. I won't say what it is due to spoiling the book for others. I highly recommend this and could not put it down.
I am finding that Picoult's books seems to drag on forever. I couldn't even get threough all of this one. It was horrible!

Jodi Picoult delivers again ... an intimate look at making a choice for life or death. Mostly it shows that any decision about anothers life is really based on the life of the person deciding it(and dealing with it)and not on the person it is decided for. A great subject and a nice view of the complexity that is ... a family.
eh. Not very good. All the characters sounded the same and I didn't care for any of them. I thought I would like the wolf-y bits but they all rang very false to me so I didn't.

I usually love Jodi Picoult's books and can't wait til the next one comes out but I just couldn't get into this book. I tried really hard to like it and I rarely stop reading books once I've started them but this one I just couldn't get through. The wolf stuff was just too weird. Hope her next book is better :(

The lowest stars I have ever given to one of Jodi's books. I usually love her books but this one is just to bland, boring. it felt like Jodi herself didn't really feel this story. The characters are not to the usual Picoult depth. The whole tone of the book felt like she had a looming deadline and just wrote whatever came to mind with little thought. It's like she forgot she had a book to write so pulled an all-nighter to get it done because she was so distracted by other things.

I enjoyed the research that Jodi Picoult did to present this book, and I had heard of a similar person who "lived with wolves". That's why I chose this book. Reading the first part of the book, I honestly thought it might be "different" than his other books, however it wasn't. I guess I'm just a bit tired of her books being so predictable. She does write about real life challenges and moral/ethical issues, and that is what I liked about her writing when I first read her books, but to me, it becomes so predictable. Her writing however flows nicely, and her books are "quick" reads. They just don't leave me satisfied at the end. The correlation between wolves and humans is most interesting though!
Whew! Glad to be done with that one. It was physically hard to read this book. Don't think it was a good intro to Jodi's work. I will try another and hope for better.
It was an interesting story of family. Not my favorite of hers and I really did have to force myself at times to keep going, but it was still a decent read.

So disappointing. What was she thinking? It is really hard not to give a good rating to a Picoult book. She is one of my faves, but I just can't imagine where this one came from, what inspired it or why. 
 The characters weren't very likeable, especially Cara, the daughter of Luke (the "wolf man" himself). She came across as selfish and whiney, although devoted to her father, who didn't really deserve it, not like her mother did. One thing I did like was the separation of chapters by the different characters point of view, one of my favorite formats. 
 Yes, apparently it's been done before in real life, but Luke himself was hard to believe. I couldn't imagine why an intelligent male with everything to live for would leave his young family, wife and children and go off to live with wolves for experimental purposes, and enjoy it. He felt "at home" with them, like his own family. There had to be something wrong with this guy. He ate bloody, raw, fresh-killed animals with them, that had often been urinated on (which was disgusting to read about), first to earn their trust, then to survive. He slept with them, and missed them when he wasn't around them. I half-expected that he would have sex with one of them, that is how much he was into the wolves. It wouldn't have surprised me. Sorry, I didn't like this guy. 
 His wife divorces him and marries a Phillippino lawyer, Joe Ng (now how does one even pronounce a name like "Ng" couldn't she have picked something else? At least he was likeable, as was his wife, but not so much that would make the read worthwhile. The most interesting part of this was the legal part of the story, when Luke is in a coma, brain dead, and the family must decide whether to terminate life support, but that is not exactly an original plot line. I skimmed the parts about Luke, I just wasn't interested in his life with wolves, especially upon learning that it wasn't even based on true facts about wolves (read some of the other reviews). 
 I am so glad I read the library copy, I wouldn't spend money on this one. I hope her next one brings us back to the Jodi we've come to love and eagerly anticipate releases from.

Jodi Picoult has done it again in her latest book "Lone Wolf". Jodi Picoult takes a life issue and lets you see from all different sides of the issue but she doesn't stop there. Instead of just challenging what you think you know and feel about the subject she also makes you take a long hard look at the facts. Did I change my mind about what I think I know and feel regarding this issue? No, I just found a lot more gray area that I didn't realize was there and it makes me go deeper into myself and realize that a yes or no answer would take more time to process. Along with the life issue that this author brings to our attention she also takes us into the personal lives of each character as they react and respond to a life and death situation that provokes such complex humanity. Their family history slowly evolves and takes unexpected turns with the complications that makes all of us human. 
 Jodi Picoult keeps to form with her trademark in the literary world. She surprises us and she pulls the insides out of us that makes each of us who we are while throwing in the ironies of life. 
 I really liked this book as I have with her many other books for all of the same reasons. 
 If you want to be entertained then don't read this book. But if you want to feel the wow at the conclusion of this story by making you feel educated, challenged and insightful then please read this book. It is a journey you will not regret taking.

I really did not like this book. I could never bring myself to care about the characters, except to dislike pretty much all of them. Let's see: we have the spoiled, bratty and selfish daughter; the son whose actions dont make much sense; the selfish and obsessive father who ends up only actually acting like a father once in the book... And on and on. I kept reading it only to learn a bit more about wolves but feel I would have been better off reading the real wolfman's book instead. I can tell by the writing that Picoult's other books are probably better, but as others have said it feels like she hammered this one out just to make a publisher deadline... Bummer.

Jodi Picoult has written some of my favorite books and this one lived up to my expectations in most aspects. The descriptions of Luke and his wolf pack were fascinating - definitely more interesting than I'd expected - and it's clear that Jodi did lots of research for his point of view. Cara's description of the accident in the end had me in tears, which was a good thing, but the reason this book got 4 stars instead of 5 was that I found some of the characters a little flat and I wasn't as attached to them as I was with characters in her other books. Also, I expected more of a "wow" ending like in other Jodi Picoult books and this one didn't have that wow factor. All in all though, this book had some beautiful passages in it and it was an enjoyable read.

2.5/5 stars 
 In the past I have enjoyed Picoult's books and I look forward to her future books. Unfortunately, this book was not one I enjoyed.

This is the eighth book I read by this author. I always learn something from her books. I think she researches them very well. Lone Wolf is about a man who studies wolves. He studies their behavior and wolf packs. He goes to live with them for two years. He builds a sanctuary for them. He loves the wolves so much, he abandons his human family. One day, he and his daughter are in a terrible car accident. They are rushed to the hospital. His daughter recovers but her father doesn't. He is in a coma. Hard decisions need to be made. The story is told by the different perspectives of the main characters. I found the information about the wolves to be interesting. I recommend any of her books.

If you read this book you will discover many fascinating facts about the behavior of wolves. I listened to the audio book which was performed by various narrators which added interest. The moral dilemma that Picoult poses in the novel is timely and being a work of Picoult family dynamics is front and center. It was just a little too drawn out and long and I wished it would have moved a bit quicker.

http://www.crandomblog.com/?p=251 
 This book... I am not really sure where to start. I guess I should stay I messed up, because I borrowed it from a friend and I gave it back to her prior to writing this review. I gave it back so soon because I know how it is to lend out books and having to wait and worry about whether or not you will ever actually get them back. I baby my books, they are all spoiled and well taken care of, so when not in my care I worry about their well-being and if they are being treated properly or if I will get them back with cup rings on them or worse. Anyways, before I digress further, I should give you more information about the book. 
 I forget where exactly it takes place, but I want to say New Hampshire, or somewhere like that. It's a northern state in the USA and it is one that gets a lot of snow. Please forgive me for not taking note. Cara Warren is a 17 year old girl, daughter of Luke Warren and Georgie. Her parents are divorced. Her father practically lives at a park that is pretty much an amusement park. During the winter, the park is deserted of everyone but the caretakers. Her father stays there to take care of his multiple wolf packs. Cara lives there with him, she idolizes her father. Edward, Luke and Georgie's son, lives in Thailand where he moved after a huge argument with his father. 
 There is an auto mobile accident, that isn't exactly explained in the beginning. They unravel the story behind the accident as the story progresses and just when you think you have the reason for the accident down, something else happens. As a result of the accident both Luke and Cara end up in the hospital. Luke is in ICU, clinging to his life with a serious head injury that messes up his brain. Cara has to have surgery to fix her shoulder. Georgie is seriously worried about her daughter and she knows that her son needs to know, even though they haven't talked in about six years she calls him and lets him know. Family is family, no matter how mad you are at someone, and he flies home to the states in order to see his family. 
 When he arrives at the hospital, Cara is still upset with him for leaving all those years ago. His mother is delighted to see him and his estranged father is unable to even react to him being there. From his arrival, him and his sister are completely opposite on what they want. Cara wants to keep her father alive no matter the cost and Edward wants to discontinue life support and let him pass away. The novel is an emotional roller coaster, you get to see the point of views of both of the children of Luke and even his view on his life and his wolf. It's an awesome novel, very touching. It had me going back and forth as to what I wanted to happen. 
 In the end, I ended up crying my eyes out. My fiancee walked into the room, looked at me like I was nuts. Maybe I am, but he understands how attached I get to my characters. He makes me feel like the luckiest girl ever. <3 5/5 stars. Next on my to read list by Jodi Picoult is The Storyteller, however is in the lower numbers of my next five to read. Currently 50% done with Blueberry Hill by Bette Lee Crosby. Also just finished up Charlotte's Web by E.B. White.

Edward and Cara Warren must decide if they should take their father off life-support, but they do not agree. Luke, their father, was in a car accident with Cara. Luke Warren is a wolf expert and left his family when they were young to live in the wild with wolves for two years, which left a lot of bitter feelings. Like the other Jodi Picoult books I have read, this one is a family story wrapped in a courtroom drama, featuring a social interest. Previous books have dealt with rape, adoption, gay marriage, autism and organ donation. 
 The plot centers around an environmentalist who goes to live with wolves in the wild and Picoult beats us over the head with metaphors to remind us of the importance of family. 
 I find myself enjoying her writing less and less with each book. This one contains characters that add nothing to the story and, like her other books, is told by multiple characters in alternating chapters. 
 One of the techniques she uses in this book is to have us experience chapters from the environmentalist's book, which one of the characters is reading. Sound confusing? It is. I'm sure there had to be a better way to get us to understand the characters without this bit of "creativity." 
 If you are really fascinated by wolves, you might be interested in this book. For everyone else, this one has to go on my not-recommended list.

book_b.user_review: In this very quick read, we are introduced to Maddie, a very sad 17 year old who has spent her entire life indoors due to a rare illness that causes her to be allergic to nearly everything. She spends most of her time with her mother, her nurse Carla and a small handful of teachers. The process to visit her involves a long period of time standing in a decontaminating airlock. But one day, a moving van pulls up next door and Maddie is captivated by the young boy in all black, Ollie. They communicate through their bedroom windows and eventually move to email. Will Maddie ever get the chance to meet Ollie? And if she does, what will happen to her very tightly lidded world. The book was well written and contained a few twists and turns that I did not expect. Overall, it was a great read and one I would recommend for fans of books like The Fault in Our Stars.

 I'm finding it difficult to sum up my feelings for this book. At first I was bored, then mid-way it was okay, but then it just got silly and I sat there contemplating what my rating would actually be. I settled on a good 2 stars. 
 I got this book with RavenPost with the theme 'Isolation', and it's a book I've definitely seen around but never really considered picking it up. Still, it was an interesting read. I've not read a story of someone who has to stay inside and never leave their house due to terrible allergies, so it was quite new to me. I just the story lacking in some areas. 
 Firstly, it was a bit slow. Maddy was inside and basically just reading and spending time with her mum or nurse, all the while pining for the normality of a regular teenage girl. Of course that's to be expected, she's isolated. But then her neighbours move in. And one of them a handsome young man called Olly who takes her fancy. From there, this book is mostly just Maddy wanting to be with Olly and cursing her illness for trapping her in her home. Which leads to my other issue with the book overall - romance. 
 Maddy and Olly speak a few times online, meet face to face twice and then THEY'RE IN LOVE. It's instalove, and it's too unrealistic for my liking. Not only that, but Maddy makes some terrible decisions and does pretty questionable things just to be with him, right up to risking her life. It's pretty careless of her. Literally risking everything just for a boy she's just met. Instalove isn't a seller, I don't know many people who like it, so I wish authors would stop writing that in. I, for sure, am not a fan of it 
 Also, there is a plot twist in this book. Sadly, I kind of suspected that there would be one. The book was a little too slow for there to not be. When it happened, I wasn't that surprised. I did have a reaction along the lines of 'WHAT' because I wasn't sure that would even be an option. If you know what it is, you'd think 'surely this can't be after everything that's happened.' Yet it did. It's not easy trying to explain without spoiling, so go read the book and let us know what you thought about the twist! 
 There was also a part of the story which I really didn't like (can't say due to it being a spoiler), but I felt that Maddy was really stupid and acted on impulse without thinking. It ended up being extremely bad for her and others around her. I was reading it thinking 'Why do this, and what made you think this was a good idea?' 
 She learnt the hard way. 
 With the characters, I wasn't a fan of Maddy. Her bad decisions, dramatic nature (mostly near the end of the book, crying over such a small issue), and her slight lack of consideration for others. As soon as she saw Olly outside from her window, she was obsessed. I got bored of that very quickly. 
 Near the end though, she was just so emotional and crying so much (for about an hour - maybe longer!) over something and I was like 'what is she even crying about?'. I know she's a teenager, but I was genuinely not sure what was wrong. If it's about Olly, it's honestly her own fault for making silly decisions, getting people in trouble and nearly dying for her reckless attitude. 
 Speaking of Olly... he was alright actually. He was quite patient with her, and he wasn't pressuring in any way. His penchant for climbing on everything and stuff was a little strange, but it's not really a bad trait. He was quite a nice guy. I do think he should have knocked some sense into Maddy, though. Sometimes it felt like he should say 'Alright, stop now. You need to be careful', if he really cares about her. He was just as reckless as Maddy in the end, and should have been a bit more decisive in some cases. 
 The other characters were interesting, but didn't really stick out much. I quite liked Carla - she was a warm and caring character, a bit more lenient and sometimes funny. There aren't many characters in this book, but considering the type of story it is, you don't need too many. The number itself was enough. I just wished that some were fleshed out a bit more. There was time, for sure. 
 Olly's family was quite interesting to read about. His overall story and what was going on in his life was sad and I wish we learnt more about that. Of course, the male lead as well as the female lead needs a sob story. We had quite a bit of pagetime with Olly, so again, more fleshing out of his life would have been good. Ultimately, it was all about Maddy. 
 I did like that the main character was half-Japanese and half-African American. It certainly makes a change. I'm all for diversity, especially in YA. I just wish I enjoyed the story more, considering it was a kind I'd never read before. I haven't read many books revolving around isolation and it's one of those rare ones that I read that's about sickness. As a hypochondriac, I tend to avoid them. 
 I'm not entirely sure how I feel about this book. I forced myself to read it, I did get into it but then I was left feeling like it was lacking something. Hence my 2 star rating.

 Everything, Everything was humorous, engaging, conflicting, hopeful, frustrating and so many more complicated emotions. 
 This story encompasses so many complex situations and emotions, and the difficulties of rectifying one with the other. We see Maddy transform, and begin to make choices for herself for the first time in her life. She pushes herself outside her comfort zone so far and so fast because she wants to thrive in a life she isn't guaranteed. We see Maddy trying to come terms with her health, her relationships, and her life now, as her world begins to change- and the conclusions that she face are not necessarily happy, or even completely formed. 
 Everything, Everything is a story about the complexities of life in all it's components and quirks and disappointments, and how we try to do more than survive the life we're given.
