 I liked this book. It was pretty well written and the characters were well-developed. But I guessed on PAGE EIGHT that the mother had some kind of Munchausen by proxy syndrome (not exactly, because her motivations were different, but she imagined the whole illness thing). I think you can enjoy the book without having the surprise of a plot twist. However, it's a little like hearing a joke you think is funny the second time. Once you know the punchline, it's just not the same. 
 Here are some questions that occurred to me: 
 Olly lives in an abusive family; his dad beats him and his mother. Does Madeline live in an abusive family too? 
 Do you think Madeline's mother is aware of what she is doing? What incidents in the plot would read very differently if she were? 
 Is it credible at all that Carla wouldn't realize that Madeline is not really sick? Does her strained relationship with her own daughter explain why she might not question Madeline's mom? 
 The Little Prince plays an important part in the book. Is Madeline the Little Prince and Olly the rose? Or is the mother the Little Prince and Madeline the rose?

I was about a quarter of my way through the book when I was completely smitten by Maddy & Olly (Oddy? Molly?). They are just such cute characters. 
 Maddy Whittier, as per the back cover description, has Severe Combined Immunodeficiency disease; basically she is allergic to the world. Maddy lives in an environment controlled house. Everything is white. Everything is sterilised. Decontaminated. 
 Maddy's whole world takes place inside the four walls of her house, and have done since she was 6 months old. She's never been to school, never had a friend, never played in the park, never been kissed. Maddy experiences life through her beloved books, and is home schooled via Skype. 
 Maddy's mum is very protective of her, partly because of her disease, but mostly because Maddy's older brother and Father were killed in a car crash when she was only a few months old. Mrs Whittier is a doctor, and makes sure that Maddy is well cared for by a full-time nurse Carla, and protected from the rest of the world in the controlled climate of their home. 
 Maddy is disappointed that she doesn't get to go out into the world, but she is generally happy. She has her books, her mum, and Carla. That is until they get new neighbours... 
 The Bright family are loud, noisy, and chaotic. Maddy loves watching them through the window. Olly is the teenage son, good looking and parkour enthusiast. His sister Kara seems like a typical sullen teen, and there is obviously tension between the parents. 
 Mrs Bright sends Olly and Kara around with a Bundt cake to Maddy's mum, who won't accept the cake, and refuses to allow them to meet her daughter. 
 Olly becomes intrigued with Maddy, and finds a way to contact her over the internet. Thus begins a wonderful but dangerous relationship between Maddy and Olly. They can never get too close to each other, or Maddy could die, but is friendship enough? 
 Olly is such a physical character; he can't seem to sit still, whereas Maddy has a very calming, thoughtful personality. I love the way that they interact with each other. Most of their communication is through IMs, emails, and they are just adorable. 
 I love how the author mixes up traditional narrative with diagrams, illustrations and charts. Also, Maddy's book reviews are hilarious. 
 Yoon is also quite sneaky! I thought I'd guessed the ending of the book, but then there was a turn of events, and I thought I was wrong, but then something else happened- sneaky sneaky! 
 I really enjoyed the story, and it's a very quick read; only 306 pages with lots of pictures and pages with only a brief paragraph.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not a fan of love at first sight, which is what happens in some respects in this book. Maybe, to be honest, I should say that it's like at first sight, and the relationship between Maddy and Olly builds through looks and messages from their windows, via emails and IMs, and finally culminates in a visit. Why is that visit so important? Eighteen-year-old Maddie hasn't been out in the world since she was very young because she has Severe Combined Immunodeficiency. Her mother, a doctor, has installed safety precautions on their house to protect Maddie from possible infections or diseases. She also has a devoted nurse, Carla, who monitors her vital signs constantly. Although Maddie has been content with her safe world, protected in the bubble fashioned by her mother, once she and Olly connect, she wants more. When her mother finds out about the relationship, she grounds Maddy. At first Maddy goes along with the program, but eventually she concocts a plan to fly to Hawaii with Olly. Although I suspected the truth about Maddy's illness at some point, I still loved how the author told this story. Her prose made me care about Maddy and hope that this hopeless love of hers might somehow be possible. The use of diary entries, charts, lists, brief book review spoilers, medical reports, and plane tickets as well as lovely artwork sprinkled throughout the book adds to reader interest and will engage even the most reluctant of readers. The writing is exquisite and appealing, Maddy and Olly are both extraordinary, and the drama that plays out next door among Olly's family members is so typical of suburbia that it is almost impossible to resist reading and cheering this unlikely couple on. While it is easy to understand Maddy's wish to remain safe and sheltered, readers will surely also understand the pointlessness of never taking risks and keeping one's heart shrink-wrapped, safe, protected, and yet untouched. Even the book's first line in which Maddy proclaims to have read more than anyone and her fondness for The Little Prince, which she is constantly reading are wonderful aspects of the book that reveal her character quite well. It's hard to resist Everything, Everything, and yes, I liked just about everything, everything about it. I'll be thinking about this one and what love prompts us to do for a long time.

 UPDATE: Not sure why I gave this 4 stars to start with. The more I think about it, the angry it makes me. 
 Sigh. 
 Okay, short summary this is a good book and you should read it. 
 But to delve into this a little more... this book is very problematic. I love the integration of drawing and email it rounded out the book. At the same time the romance was way too insta-lovey and contrived. The plot was incredibly weak. Original, but weak. I guessed the "twist" after about 75 pages in. The relationships between the characters were contrived and their emotions felt fake. 
 All that being said, the writing is really beautiful and all of these rough and wonky parts came together well-ish. 
 The book just needed more meat, and in all honesty the "twist" felt like a total cop out. Making Maddy's disease "real" was something I think Yoon mistakenly shied away from. However, if she really committed to having Maddy persevere and keeping her hope through the reality of the disease I feel that so much more depth could have been brought to the table.

tl;dr It wasn't bad, per se, but it wasn't long enough for me to figure out what it was enough to like it. Also, teenagers being stupid and I just kinda wasn't in the mood. 
 Look, sometimes teenagers do stupid things. I don't think this makes them stupid, I think it makes them teenagers. 
 I am not really sure how I felt about this book. I should probably let my opinion settle and then write the review but too bad! I am writing the review now. 
 So, in no particular order and in most cases with neutral judgement, here are some things about this book: 
 -This book is a very simple story. The whole plot, rising, climax, falling, resolution, could be summed up in one sentence, easily. Very simple story. 
 -Very quickly readable. Light, fast. The narrative is simple, the book itself is short. I don't even know if it's actually compellingly written or not, I just know that it was so easy to read that I went right through it without even thinking about stopping bc it simply took no effort. 
 -Extremely short. I hope I am not demeaning the entirety of YA book readers when I say that I can see why this book is a super best seller and also why it got a movie adaptation so quickly. Easy: it's short. There are illustrations and diagrams and little non-textual snippets, which I may talk about later, but their main effect is that this book, which was physically maybe 300 pages long, has an actual narrative maybe 2/3rds of this. And since everyone knows that it's actually short stories and not novels that make the best fodder for movie adaptations, this is a great candidate. The movie won't have to cut anything bc there's not too much in the first place. I'll try not to talk about the movie again (I haven't seen it, and if I get all speculative about adaptation theory I'll never finish the actual review), but I must say that they had better do a good job. Not because this book means a lot to me emotionally, but just because this is a relatively easy story to adapt, it would take effort to screw this up in a major way. 
 -Maddy is a character who is made of words. I don't feel like she is letting us in, totally, so she doesn't feel like a real character who is a person. She feels like a bunch of words. She feels like she's careful of words even when she's describing physicality, like every detail we get from her has a word carefully chosen for it before she tells it to us. This is good, I guess, in that I felt Maddy behind this and not the author, but it still felt off and strange to me. I'm not sure if it's bad or good, but it is definitely not what I'm used to. There just didn't seem like it accessed anyone's real emotions. Even when I could visually see what I was reading about, I could never realllllly feel it. 
 -So, this is not really a literary critique in the slightest but my favorite part of this book by far, probably the only thing I'll remember about it in a year, is how charmingly Maddy argued that the meaning of life was found in books and Olly argued that it was definitely found in math. 'You needed a whole branch of mathematics to tell you that' 'Chaos theory, yeah. You knew that?' 'Books! Olly, I learned if from books!' 
 Actually, now that I think about it, that was my favorite part of The Sun Is Also A Star too, when they argued science vs poetry. I think in my opinion Nicola Yoon should only write two kids arguing on that strain, just like I think that John Green should only write teenage best friends ribbing on each other with quality your-mom jokes and the like. 
 -Now, I come into this book, right from the first I heard from it, from the angle entirely of a person who has, on purpose, read both Alex Flinn's Towering and Cindy C Bennet's Rapunzel Untangled, which I have to list both of them bc they have more or less conflated into one book over the years. One of them had kidnapped people and one of them had a continuously constructed house with doorways to nowhere and one of them had a boy with a terribly stupid name she made friends with on Facebook, I just can't keep straight which was which. It doesn't take a genius to link the premise of Maddy's situation to the premise of a Rapunzel novel, so... [and here's the spoiler part so seriously, don't read the spoiler if you want to read this book bc it takes probably 40% of the fun out of it] I always suspected the Mom. The whole big reveal? It was just a matter of time for me reading this book. And yeah, I don't know how suspicious a person who hasn't read nine different Rapunzel novelizations would be, so maybe every person's brain goes down this track and I'm not special. Extremely likely. But I must say, that Maybe that reveal would have upped this a star, made this book something interesting and unexpected, if I hadn't seen it coming from reading the blurb the first time. Also, AT ALL COSTS, keep first time readers, especially young or reluctant ones, from knowing about this reveal. This is mostly me saying this @me concerning my little sister. 
 -I mean, as far as I can go with recommendations is that this is a book where teenagers do a lot of stupid things. So maybe you are a teenager, and when you read this you'll be like 'amazing, that is a thing I wish I could do' because the only thing more universal than teenagers doing stupid things is teenagers wishing they could do stupid things. Which is fine, genuinely. Or maybe you are a teenager and your thought will be 'why are these characters so stupid,' which is also fine, bc you can't see that these characters are just being stupid bc they are teenagers. Or maybe you aren't a teenager and you're basic only reaction will be 'well there they go again, doing stupid teenager things just because they are stupid teenagers, I can't even blame them because they are stupid teenagers and will one day see how stupid they were' (and then maybe, just maybe, you will suddenly feel the vague presence of your 35-year-old self watching you have this reaction and laughing at you for being so self-righteous and condescending about teenagers at the ripe old age of twenty-one) (vividness of hypothetical situation obvious tell-tale that this is exactly what happened to me) I mean, I need to have one moment, maybe two. Join me in the spoilers, if you will. okay, two things. The whole buying of plane tickets and just going for it made me think of Josh & Isla going to Barcelona in Isla & the Happily Ever After. So clearly a bad idea, so clearly with no regard for consequences on themselves or anyone else (can't get over the fact that Olly mentions most of the way through the trip that he doesn't like leaving his sister and mother with his abusive father. That was the only time in this book I felt any deep emotion for Maddy, though unfortunately it was anger with her that she would not think of that, that she would be so selfish. Urgh. Can't forgive her for that, for some reason.) Second thing: let's discuss a thing I had to read with my own two eyes, and that is Maddy, the dear sweet Maddy, musing about the Big Bang and the dictionary definition of the word 'infinite' after (during? It's always fuzzy once the metaphors kick in) having sex for the first time. GIVE ME A BREAK. I literally turned into Sebastian the crab at this point. "TEENAGERS. THEY THINK THEY KNOW EVERYTHING." (although good on her for buying the condoms: 'fourteen ninety-five, they have everything at that souvenir shop' that's a bamf move if I've ever heard one) 
 Trying to think of anything especially eyeroll-inducing that I need to bring attention to while I'm in hidden spoilers but honestly I still can't recover from turning the page and reading 'infinite' and screaming because I just lost my admittedly limited ability to take anyone in this book seriously after that. 
 -Why doesn't she have any friends? I mean I know the answer, logically, both from an in-universe reason and just the fact that this book is so short but still I am upset that she doesn't have any friends. In fact, I have just written a whole different book in my head where instead of a teenager with a cute boy next door [side note: why do their windows face each other haven't these authors ever seen a real neighborhood in their life, people don't build houses like that bc it's creepy af], it's a twelve year old who makes friends with twin girls who move in next door and then it switches to the perspective of one of the twins and turns into a mystery novel about uncovering the [spoiler] and there is no romance and no teenage stupidity and everything is middle grade friendship land. Yes, I have a chronic condition and that is that I take ten year olds more seriously than seventeen year olds. 
 I really need to stop writing marathon long reviews for books I don't care that much about. I mean, this review has taken me probably almost a quarter of the time reading the book in the first place did, how does that make sense. 
 -I feel like I need to have an opinion on Olly but I don't have an opinion on Olly. I also can't muster up an opinion one way or another on the doodles/inserts/ etc. I can't tell if they made Maddy's character more clear to us or if they just made the book more interesting to flip through. There was something original about this book, at least. I just don't think I get Yoon's approach with this stuff, it was the same way for TSiaaS. Is she trying to promote thought? Is she trying to fill pages? I can't figure it out, and I have no opinion on it. 
 Okay, one last thing, and that is a disclaimer that I may not have just been in the mood for this book. I mostly read it because it was there and Caroline was going to read it and I was putting off reading Middlemarch. I loved The Sun Is Also A Star when I read it a couple of months ago, but there's a chance if I'd read The Sun Is Also a Star yesterday I also would have been rolling my eyes. Some days you just want to watch pretty, naive teenagers fall in love bc it's pure and silly and young and somedays you just want to slap them upside the head. I don't think this one could have swept me away the way other books have and TSIAaS did, but, again, it's just because it's short. This book is so short, guys. I know I keep mentioning it, but it is just so short. I'm so not used to reading novels this short.

 Everything, Everything is a gorgeously written, pure YA novel about freedom and first love. 
 Maddy suffers from SCID, a disease where she isn't allowed in the outside world, and it isn't allowed in hers. 
 She's confined to her home, homeschooled and monitored day in day out, with no one but her mother and nurse to interact with. 
 Until all-black-wearing, parkour-loving, Olly moves in next door. 
 Loved, LOVED this book. Loved the innocence of first love, the drawings and snippets throughout (though a little small to read on my Paperwhite Kindle), loved the plot and imagination of the characters. I knocked it down half a star, probably my own fault for guessing the plot twist.

reference_books.title: The Girls
reference_books.review_text: 3.5 stars: As others have mentioned, the writing is overblown, but that didn't bother me. I actually enjoyed some of Cline's unusual metaphors, and I thought the writing (on a sentence by sentence level) was the best part of the book...kind of reminded me of a young Michael Chabon. The thing that annoyed me more was the way the plot didn't seem to drive the story. For a book about a violent cult, I was expecting something with more momentum and more tension. It was an odd incongruity to have a violent plot in a book that felt mostly calm and quiet...strange. I think Cline is a writer to watch.

reference_books.title: All the Birds in the Sky
reference_books.review_text: Not my thing. This book read to me like a young adult novel (I don't think that was intended given the amount of sex and other adult topics). Something about the writing style seemed flippant and simplistic perhaps? Also, I generally do not read it fantasy or science-fiction novels, so this was outside my comfort zone. I'm sure I'm not the best (most reliable) critic of this novel.

reference_books.title: Eligible (The Austen Project, #4)
reference_books.review_text: I love Jane Austen, and I've also enjoyed several of Curtis Sittenfeld's prior novels, so I was excited to see that Sittenfeld was chosen by Penguin Random House to tackle the modern retelling of Pride and Prejudice, my favorite of Austen's novels. I am very familiar with P&P, so I was worried that I would find Sittenfeld's 500+ page retelling somewhat boring, but I needn't have worried. Sittenfeld so cleverly updates the story that I was just as enthralled by her retelling as when I reread P&P (something I do every few years). All of the major plot points are here but moved to modern-day Cincinnati, complete with cell phones, the internet, and the home shopping network. Instead of wealthy country gentry, Bingley and Darcy are successful doctors. Mr. Collins is still as awkward and unappealing as ever, but he's now a rich software entrepreneur. Kitty and Lydia are cell phone-crazed and crude and in their early 20s, while Jane and Lizzy are, gasp, approaching 40 without husbands. The best part of this novel is the witty dialog (similar to Austen's classic). It's much more edgy than Austen's but also very funny and filled with sly social commentary, just as Austen would've wanted it. This is a fun read and would be a great vacation book.

reference_books.title: A Brief History of Seven Killings
reference_books.review_text: I very much respect what this book is attempting to do, and I found parts of it to be compelling. All in all, though, I had a difficult time getting into this story and these characters. The book's extreme violence, patois, and disjointed (on purpose) structure combined to make reading this book feel like an academic exercise. It was challenging, and I was pushed to work hard to follow the story, both good things, but I didn't particularly enjoy the experience.

reference_books.title: Vanity Fair
reference_books.review_text: Couldn't finish this one...finally gave up. Just too baggy and disorganized and boring. Probably just the wrong time for me to read this, and I hope to pick it up again later.

reference_books.title: An Untamed State
reference_books.review_text: This novel is the most harrowing reading experience I have ever had. At a point about two-thirds of the way through the novel, I had to set it aside and switch to lighter reading for a few days. Like the female protagonist, I have an infant son who is still breastfeeding, and I believe that coincidence is one reason why this novel affected me so much. If you are in a similar position (or have a close friend or relative who is), then this book is likely to be even more affecting for you. Never have I been more happy and grateful to be woken up multiple times during the night by a crying baby as I was while reading this book. This book will make you grateful for your family and your comfortable life, and it will make you think and worry about those who do not have similar gifts.

reference_books.title: A Little Life
reference_books.review_text: For me, two words capture this book: relentless and cumulative. I'm sure I've never read another book that so relentlessly takes the reader through a character's troubled life--day after day after day--for decades. Though there are four primary characters in A Little Life and dozens of well-drawn supporting characters, all of the focus, really, is on Jude. After finishing this book, I now feel like I know Jude personally. I've been there in his office with him as he pulls all-nighters on so many occasions that I know what the sunrise looks like as it comes in his office windows. I've sat through all those meals he struggled to eat despite lacking an appetite. I know where he goes for Thanksgiving and for his summer vacations, and I know what his body looks and feels like. The cumulative effect of 700+ pages of close observation is truly astounding. It's also truly exhausting, in an emotional sense, to make the journey that A Little Life demands of its readers. If you decide to make that journey, be prepared. 5 stars for being unlike anything I've read before and also something I'll never forget.

When I first saw the title I thought 'Great a geeky book like 'Ready Player One' or 'Reamde''. Reading the cover explained it would be about a travelling circus. I admit, this was a bit of a bummer, but I was still excited to read it, because the life of a family of weird creatures would entice nearly everyone to start reading; including me. 
 And admittedly the first 50 pages or so fly by, new stuff happens every page and it is all rather entertaining. But after that, in my opinion, all juice has been squeezed out of the lemon and the reader is left sucking the dry peel. 
 I don't know what exactly is wrong with this book, but I feel it just tries way too hard to be everything. It wants to be wacky, which it is, but at the same time wants to be philosophical and have a screwed up chronology, have all characters deepened out in both the dark and the light (which somehow ends up making them a bit of a caricature of the real persons they start out as) and be poetical and literature worthy. In all it is just a jack-of-all-trades, but a master of nothing. 
 I don't often put a book away after I have read more than 20%, let alone 50%, but this I just can't finish.
