Well. I can't exactly explain why I didn't like this book, I can only offer that it didn't really gel with me. Geek Love reserves the spot of The Weirdest Book I Have Ever Read, and despite its disturbing quirkiness, I found myself slightly bored more than anything. I liked Katherine Dunn's writing style, but thought some of the character's motivations to be unconvincing and a handful of scenes quite tasteless. I think I might be having issues as a reader in 2017 about what to think about how this novel approaches themes of disability and deformity - I'm not saying the author's approach is bad, I just don't know how I should feel.

i hated this book and i try not to be offended that so many people i know liked it. basically it was too insanely triggering to me to get any enjoyment out of it whatsoever. i generally don't really enjoy people using metaphors taken from other people's experiences, and this happens a lot around amputation. since amputation is something i have actually experienced, and has impacted my life in ways i can still only begin to understand or describe, there is nowhere for me to go with a book like this. this is a tale of parents' profiting from the manipulation of their children's bodies, the horizontal abuse between siblings, the feelings of entrapment as "freaks"/disabled people who can't leave their family, and cult status of one of the children who convinces followers to amputate their limbs. what should i take from this, other than the fact that people are entertained by the freak show still. there can be no dialogue between my experiences and those of the characters - they are trapped in the reality of the author's imaginings. i can't look to them for survival skills, just a reflection of the confines i already feel in the world.

I picked this up for a book club, got about one-third of the way through, and couldn't bear to finish it. It was as if it was deliberately constructed to turn the reader off in some sort of 'last (wo)man standing' race to the finish. The moral and physical repugnance of each and every one of the characters was just painful to watch unfold.

My sister recommended this book to me, and I'm about seventy pages into it, but I'm having a really difficult time engaging with it. Dunn's writing style is very floral and descriptive, and I'm enjoying it, but for some reason, i am having a difficult time getting into the story. It's about a family of circus freaks, which you would think would be interesting. I'm told it gets stranger and worth the read. Here's hoping! 
 It did get stranger, but it really didn't get any better. The ending made me angry, as I found it completely out of line with the character that had been developed up to that point. The ending went against all of the family values that had been examined and feverishly held throughout the novel. Dunn does do an excellent job challenging the reader to examine their own family, social and cultural values, illustrating that normalcy is relative, but the novel still left me wanting.
It's about circus geeks in love.

***THIS REVIEW CONTAINS MILD SPOILERS*** 
 This book boasts many strange characters, vividly and believably drawn. The Binewski children, intentionally bred to have deformities by their parents, in order to draw crowds for their traveling carnival; the Bag Man, who lives without a face; Dr. Phyllis and Miss Lick, women who, for different reasons, have made it their lives' work to enact radical surgical amputations. In the world of these characters, abnormality is valued; the more deviant from the "norms" the better. In fact, the narrator, Oly--a hunchbacked albino dwarf--is a bit of a disappointment to her family because her deformities aren't unusual enough. She certainly doesn't fit in with the norms, but her abnormalities aren't spectacular enough for display. Instead, she works as a barker for the show, and is a slavish devotee of the show's star: her brother, Arty. 
 It is hard for me to picture what Arty looks like, not because he isn't well-described, but because he has flippers instead of hands and feet. Unlike other deformities described in the book, Arty's isn't based on a real condition. (There is the case of Chick, but I will get to him later.) But if you can get past that, his personality is clear and real enough: he is a megalomaniac, controlling and insecure. He is the villain of the book, though mostly people love him, to the point of obsession and their own ruin. Oly, hopelessly in love with him, is treated by him as a contemptible toadie to fulfill his demands, poses no threat. However, the Siamese twins--Elly and Iphy--rival him for stardom. 
 What I loved most about this novel is how it inverts the whole normal/abnormal dichotomy. I found out about this book through David T. Mitchell and Sharon L. Snyder's Narrative Prosthesis, a critical book about depictions of disability in literature. They cite Geek Love as one of the more positive and nuanced portrayals of disabled characters. While I wouldn't quite say that Geek Love shows disability in a positive light, it does play with our assumptions about normality. 
 Characters willingly embrace deformity, as in the case of the Binewski family. Or they are seduced into it--as with Arty's cult, attendees at his shows who come to believe that they can achieve enlightenment through amputation, or Miss Lick's prodigies, attractive women whom she convinces to surgically alter themselves so as to lead more fulfilling lives. Yet, bodily alterity comes with the same traits of vanity, jealousy, ignorance, and cruelty that accompany mainstream norms of healthy, attractive bodies. Dunn often describes the strange world of the Binewskis with beautiful prose, but she does not flinch from stark depictions of dysfunction and loathsomeness. 
 We definitely need more books like this, narratives that challenge assumptions about attractiveness and bodily norms. Yet the novel also connects the embrace of freakery with commercialism, manipulative tendencies, and unstable behavior. I would like to see a book that takes on some of the ideas of Geek Love, with prose and plot that are similarly powerful and compelling, while portraying characters with disabilities or deformities in a more truly positive sense. Unfortunately, this seems very hard to do. The comic book character of Daredevil, a blind superhero whose other senses are super-advanced, is a rare example of such an attempt, but his other senses so offset his lack of sight as to render his disability almost nonexistent. Most examples of disability in literature take on a single disabled character, and like with the Daredevil figure, erase the disability to an extent. Few books take on abnormality as a thematic concept in the way that Geek Love does. 
 Some aspects of this world aren't totally convincing or compelling. The most difficult part of the narrative for me was not being able to like our narrator, Oly. She is aware of her own flaws, but is so full of self-loathing, self-pity, and spinelessness that it made me more annoyed than sympathetic with her. She is shrewd, even manipulative, but cannot seem to transcend her obsessive devotion to others--whether it is to her psychotic brother or daughter, Miranda. She shifts back and forth between her life in the family carnival, and her present watch over Miranda and her now mostly blind and deaf mother. I believed that, given that she served others all her life, she would be protective of her child, but her ultimate actions to do so didn't make a whole lot of sense to me. 
 Speaking of endings, the climatic conflagration at the end of the carnival story disappointed me. Dunn rushed through it in a page or so, and the chain of events felt disjointed and forced. I felt that Dunn needed to wrap it up, and wanted us to see the disaster as inevitable, which I didn't quite buy. 
 I also have to wonder about the choice of Siamese twins as Arty's rival. The girls draw crowds by playing the piano. Really? That's spectacular enough to threaten Arty? Siamese twins seem almost too "normal" to be that interesting, even if marginally musically talented, especially given that other than being conjoined, their appearance is conventionally beautiful. They seemed like the blandest characters to me, without much personality or interesting qualities other than the fact that, unlike Oly, they stand up to Arty. 
 One other part of the novel that I grappled with is Chick, the Binewski child who appears "normal" but who has telekinetic powers. OK. He becomes sort of like Oly, devoted to the family but not really fitting in. I liked this idea of freaks who are not freakish enough, outcast from both the norms and the freaks. And they seemed to be the most compassionate people in the book (but then maybe they had to be, to feel some level of acceptance). Still, the whole telekinetic thing felt out of place. I'm a fan of stories of the paranormal and supernatural, but why include that here? I mean, I understand that his ability is seen as having a biological basis, a deformity of sorts just like those of the other children, but why not stick to more realistic conditions? And the fact that, like Oly, he helps rather than has his own show--because his parents supposedly worry about the government finding out about him and taking him away--just doesn't convince me. His role seemed more like a plot device. 
 Despite its flaws, the novel was one of the most intriguing books that I have read. I loved the strangeness of the characters, though it was hard to like most of them. I loved the complexity of the plot, though it stretched credulity at times. And the writing is rich enough to feel that I could get something out of revisiting it again at some point.

This book is messed up but I couldn't put it down. A family of carnival freaks, freaks created on purpose by giving a cocktail of drugs to the pregnant mother. Throw in a cult that amputates body parts and it makes the book even more messed up. The only thing that I think let it down was the ending, it just seemed so neat and cleanly wrapped up it didn't go with the rest of the story,

The large cast of characters and some early jumps in chronology make GEEK LOVE initially jarring, enough to potentially keep some readers from continuing. But the persistent reader will be rewarded, as the family dynamics explored among a cast of side-show freaks is at times morbidly interesting, at times disgusting, yet always endearing.

Thank god that's over. I had the book in my car multiple times to take back to the library but I really wanted to be able to say I've read it. It was very well written but that didn't redeem it much for me.

Loved this book! 4 stars because objectively it's kind of messy: structurally weird with a rushed ending, but subjectively, it just made me happy. Er you know...happy, in that way that depressing and disturbing stories do.
I guess it was interesting, but it wasn't for me. Something about circuses and circus "freaks"...creeps me out.

i had such high hopes for this novel, but i was sorely disappointed. the writing was great, and i love a story about underdogs, or people "different" from the norm, whatever that means, but the characters in this book are just gross. Her argument about outsiders, and embracing ones uniqueness, would have gone a lot further with me if i felt any shred of sympathy for her creations.

This book was horrible. It was boring yet disturbing, sick, and twisted all at the same time. The characters were the most unlikable characters I've ever read about in my life. The family dynamics were sickening and this book was total smut. The author is sick in the head to have dreamed all this up. Two parents breeding children to be circus freaks? A murderous, evil child running a cult where people cut off their limbs to show their devotion? Two siblings sharing a child? It's gross and it's not like there was even a point or a "lesson" at the end.

I absolutely LOVE this book. But I don't think I would've been able to read it if it hadn't been assigned to me. It's very horrifying in lots of ways, but not in obvious ways. There aren't any typical monsters or cold-blooded murders. Nothing pops out at you. Just the characters and events are so bizarre that they make you uncomfortable. It's beautiful, in a way, but mostly very telling about us and our society, especially how we see our bodies, how we see those who are "others," and how we treat people who are different. I read it in a class that talked about racism and ablism, so it was interesting to read it in that light. It is not for the the faint of heart or those who prefer to read always pleasant things, but for those who want to venture, it WILL be worth it.

Katherine Dunn is a crazy person. How and why did she think of these characters. And why did I read this book? I wanted to quit it, but was afraid it would haunt me wondering what happened to everyone. SPOILER ALERT: they all die, except one character who has lost her mind anyway. Horrible. Horrible. Addicting.

hmmmmm; what to say about this book........ 
 Geek Love is a book you can read. I'm not going to say it is a good book, but it is a book you can read. Personally, I wouldn't recommend that anyone read it, but it is a book you can read. 
 I read it. I read the whole book and I still don't quite understand why; I have given up on books that were better than this. If you could just remove most of the plot and throw all the good bits together, you might have a pretty good short story. 
 I didn't find this book to be very shocking, but I was annoyed by how shocking it was trying to be. 
 The characters were not engaging. To be honest, I once read a book in which a can of beans, a dirty sock and a jelly spoon were more intriguing, compelling and more fully realized characters. 
 Nothing to like here, people, move on.
A strange, painful and wonderful read.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book literally took me forever to read as I just couldn't get into it.... Finally when it came to how Arty started to get his 'followers' I started to get interested then for it to be all torn down with the weak and super quick and under descriptive end to the Binewinski family (well most of them) then for it to skip to Oly living on years later to also show her quick demise... So very annoyed with this book giving it 2.5 stars as it could have had so much more potential!!

This novel is an engrossing and disturbing read...I couldn't put it down! The character development of the Bolenski family members is well done, and the story line takes you on quite a ride. READ THIS BOOK!
I couldn't get into this book at all. I don't know why. It just was not appealing to me.

This book did not go the way I thought it would. At all! And the ending felt very abrupt - I was not prepared for all of that to happen. Still, it was an intriguing read, somewhat witty in places, and quite creepy. Very enjoyable!
deeply disturbing, yet fascinating

Let me start by saying I had no idea what I was getting into when I picked this book up. I was under the impression that geek was synonymous with nerd. I thought it would be some light, entertaining reading after some books I didn't particularly like. Boy, was I wrong. I was quite surprised when the first page started talking about biting chickens heads off. 
 The book is more or less about a circus family who look down upon "norms." The weirder you are, the higher your stature. The mother takes various drugs to try and make the most screwed up children she can. Now I know some people could be disturbed by this. I was okay with the concept, but a boy with flippers, conjoined twins and a hunchback just weren't that entertaining to me. I could not get into the book AT ALL. I know people who love it draw parallels to the world and how normalcy is overrated but I just thought it was annoying drivel. I skimmed through a lot of it just to finish the book.

This is a weird book written by a Portland author that I kept planning to read, but finally found at Goodwill. It is narrated by a albino hunchback dwarf named Olympia. Her parents were carnival folk and developed a master plan to breed their own children as sideshow attractions using drugs and other methods. They end up with Olympia (considered a disappointment as she is weird, but not AN ATTRACTION), an "aqua boy" with flippers, siamese twins and a son that can move things with his mind. It's interesing that this book was a runner up for the National book award, because it is ..so dark and strange. It really goes places that I had not imagined..cults, dismemberment, incest..I cound not stop reading it, but was unhappy with the end which seemed rushed. Not one for everybody, but I guess I liked it. I mean, I can't get it out of my head, so I guess it accomplishes it's mission.
Not a fan...I could not even finish. Decided to stop and get ahead for upcoming months book club reads.

This book made my keeper shelf many years ago, and I re-read it last year for book club. The folks in our club either loved it or hated it, so in a way, it's a hard book for me to recommend. However, no one regretted reading it. 
 Dunn is a fascinating writer. The subject matter can be hard going for some folks--Dunn doesn't pull any punches, and she takes the situation and the characters to extremes that can be unsettling. As the title implies, the exploration of love, in all its many forms--tender, obsessive, twisted, maternal, pure, and not so pure--is front and center in this book. This book will move you, perhaps in ways you don't like, but you won't walk away from it unaffected.

The real question is, how and why did I even finish this book? Something in it might have compelled me to finish, maybe I finished because the back of this book promised: ...Geek Love throws its sulfurous light on our nations of the freakish and the normal, the beautiful and the ugly, the holy and the obscene." And I just kept hoping it would deliver. Sadly, I never felt it did. 
 This novel is an overflow of all things carnival. This is Dunn having a party with all the darkest and freakiest things and humans she can possibly think of, and I must say she is inventive and in that way the novel is impressive and compelling. But I need more from a novel than inventiveness, and I do not think this one is more than that. It sometimes had interesting and semi-original thoughts, but mostly it is "just" entertaining. 
 The prose was maybe the novels weakest feature, it is over the top and sometimes incomprehensible in its desire to be freakish.
I'm hating this. life is too short to force myself to listen to books that irritate me. I hate the Artie character and there's not enough to hold my interest.

I recognize this is a book that many people love. I did not and I'm not sure why. It had all the elements, but I just never connected with any of the characters or the pace of the plot. Anyways, I wanted to like it and it just didn't take.

This book is a pretentious piece of crap. 
 Okay, if you want to know more: the writing is unbearable. It reads like the author was trying to pretend to be Tom Robbins, except that Tom Robbins is amazing and this author's talent is about the size of a grain of salt. It drags and moves painfully slow. The plotline is also horrific: circus performer parents, or geeks, want to raise children who are circus worthy simply by their appearance, or freaks. By taking drugs and other things not recommended in pregnancy, they get a kid with fins, Siamese twins, and a few others. Their most disappointing child is Olympia, a bald-albino-hunchback dwarf. The book starts off with adult Olympia narrating, and it's clear that Something Very Bad happened to the family as the novel backflashes. This plotline could have worked had the book been a dark comedy. Instead, it's quite serious. The flipper kid is a sociopath who creates his own cult of people who willingly remove their limbs to achieve higher enlightenment, or something like that, thus usurping his parents for control of the circus. Throw in a doctor who mutilates animals to make them into freaks, a wealthy woman who pays beautiful women to become permanently disfigured, and a man without a face for no reason whatsoever. The Something Very Bad denouement happens in roughly 1 small paragraph, whereas we're treated to nearly a full chapter about the faceless man's history, which accounts for nearly all of his presence in the book. In short, I'm mad that I wasted so much time reading this book.
if your freakshow is losing money, why not just breed a whole new one? disfunctional family dynamics at their most bizarre.
everyone who reads this book loves it. it was enjoyable enough, but i don't absolutely love it. why do you all love it?

Couldn't finish.. 
 great premise but not working for me.

Oh I dearly hated this book. Had I not been stuck on a plane with nothing left to read, I'd have stopped. It was recommended to me as being "a bit like Night Circus" which I loved. It is a bit like Night Circus (they both involve carnival/circus folk) in the same way King Lear is a bit like Jerry Springer (they both feature dysfunctional families). This book was WELL past creepy and into the gag reflex zone. Imagine a cheap, bad 80s horror flick, and you've got the picture. The writing was sloppy and I hated every single character in the book. I was hoping for the grumpy tiger to escape and eat them all. The ending (which I won't reveal) was so pointless and just plain silly I was stunned that this thing was recommended for anything but the recycle bin. So, so sorry to have wasted my time on this. Must learn to always board a plane with my kindle or 2 books, in case one is this bad.

This is such a hard book to review. It's totally weird in every sense of the word. (SPOILERS AHEAD) It's about a family who runs a traveling carnival/freakshow and the parents purposefully try to create freak children: the mother takes all kinds of drugs during pregnancy. Sometimes it works and they have a child who just has flippers for arms and legs (he's billed as Aqua Boy), Siamese twins (who later get pregnant), an albino hunch-backed dwarf and a child with strange powers. There are the misses though, and the children who died either at/before birth or early in life are kept in jars filled with formaldehyde and put on display. There are many subplots and it's hard to even say what the main storyline is. It's a very dense book with small single-spaced typing so it took me longer to get through. It's also kind of difficult to read since there is some horrible callousness on the part of almost every single character. The end was strange and unexpected but I guess it goes with the rest of the book. It's definitely not an easily forgettable read.
Hated it!

When I think about dysfunctional families, I always have a few to chose from, but this is by far the most work I had to put into while reading a book to try to empathize and connect to the characters. 
 That being said, I found the book to be abject not only from the story's point of view, but how it was written as well. 
 I had a lot of anger while reading it, it felt stretched and with a lot of details that really weren't helping the story (I will never get the image of moss growing on Arturo's testicles) but I refused to abandon it because I wanted to be able to give it one star with the full understanding of why I hated it so much. 
 So by the end of the book I found out something about myself: that I am a masochist that will carry on reading a book she dislikes just to be able to never give that book any "power" over me.

I think I would have enjoyed this book if I had read it 15 or 20 years ago, or not. It had the elements of a fantastic read in the beginning, but then it began to lack congruency and fiber and I found it difficult to stay focused. This is the meat of my problem with the book. I should be fascinated with content that includes genetically bred (sort-of) freaks, cults and carnies but, sadly I wasn't sucked into that world.
I found this book disturbing, but I couldn't "look away."

To be fair to the author, I only got through two chapters. But I can tell I don't want to finish this book. 
 NC

I can't believe I read the whole thing! Really awful story with lots of incomplete details throughout. Reads like a diary. I couldn't care about the under-developed characters, who probably could have been interesting as symbols of various pathologies within the grossly dysfunctional family, but weren't. I kept waiting for something to happen that never did. Very flat ending.

Geek Love is the guts of a dysfunctional family. The Binewskis family not only looks dysfunctional on the outside, but within its ranks the siblings have a very common rivalry. A spiteful competition of sales between Arturo and the twins is constantly aired, and Arturo makes no attempt to conceal his disdain for Chick's normal appearance and apparent favoritism from their father. 
 The story flashes back and forth between present day and the childhood of Oly. When her estranged daughter moves into her apartment building, she struggles with whether she should tell her about her true origins. 
 Most of the story is told from Oly's point of view. She is an albino hunchback, and describes her outwardly appearance as not abnormal enough. The whole family describes how norms (the term they use for normal people) must have it rough since they will never be unique. This is the type of thinking is the basis of the story when Arturo offers norms a unique way for them to see the world. 
 The heart of the story is centered on love and all its many branches. It dives deep into the things people will do for love, and it displays the fallouts caused by jealously and greed. My only complaint would be the narrative voice came to me as emotionless, which seems to defeat the purpose, but overall the storytelling was unique and grips the reader's attention.

Why, why, why did I ever read this book? It must be art because it made me feel something, but the feeling was horrible and completely unsuited to the Mexican beach on which I read it. I just wish the vile imagery would go away. See..art.

book_b.title: Brown Girl Dreaming
book_b.user_review:
I listened to this memoir as an audiobook. The book is narrated by Jacquelyn Woodson herself, so it feels like a personal experience to listen to the narration. The beauty of Woodson's language really comes through in the audiobook, though I missed seeing the form of the poetry. I'm sure that some of the power of this books is tied up in the form of the words on the page, and I wasn't able to experience that. On the other hand, those who are intimidated by reading a book-length prose poem might try the audiobook, which doesn't even sound much like a poem when it's read out loud. 
 Overall, this memoir is a touching and honest evocation of growing up as a "brown girl" in a white world. I particularly enjoyed learned about how Woodson developed her love of writing, and it was heartbreaking to hear how, as a child, almost all of the books she encountered were populated with people who looked nothing like her. I know this book is usually described as "young adult," but I think it's one of those that would be equally enjoyable for adults.

sample_reviews.review_text: An inspiring story beautifully told.

I liked this memoir of Jacqueline Woodson's early life fine, but I wasn't wowed by it. I'm not an especially big fan of free verse novels, so maybe the format was preventing me from getting the full emotional impact that other people seem to be raving about. However, this is definitely recommended for fans of Rita Williams Garcia's book One Crazy Summer, or Inside Out and Back Again by Lai.
Gorgeous

I don't read many verse novels but I really enjoy them. I really like that it was a memoir written in verse. I did read a few of Jacqueline Woodson;s book in elementary school. I would say I was intrigued by how she wrote. She wrote differently than most authors which I liked. This is one of my favorite books of hers, though I do wish she continued her stories in the book. Recommended for everyone.
DNF, Audiobook monotone.

Brown Girl Dreaming is a must read for young people, a journey through Woodson's discovery of herself and her many identities as a child. It is about memory, family (born into and made), identity, race, culture, American history, and the drive to Be in all its forms. It's hard to put into words, but this is a wonderful and accessible way for children to start asking important questions about themselves and the world around them, and to begin considering how the world is and how they are in it. It's kind of impossible to describe, but it's a wonderful collection of poems.

Written in free verse, this book is an autobiography of Jacqueline Woodson growing up in the 1960s. She brings perspectives from the North and South. Although marketed for kids, I think the perfect audience is adults. Kids most likely will struggle for context; but for adults, the context is well-known. The language is beautiful and succinct and is a wonderful expression of her life.

This book is autobiographical, a memoir, telling the story of the author in free verse. There is a cadence and rhythm to the story that is very appealing for read-alouds. It could be used in any 5th grade or higher classroom. It would be especially useful for reading groups with a historical/social studies perspective.

If I had to summarize this book into one word, it would be boring. I usually love books in verse, and this book's language was really pretty, but for some reason it didn't work for me. I'm not sure if it's because of the verse format that it was difficult to read, or just that the plot itself wasn't very interesting in the first place, but I definitely had to push myself to want to read this. But like I said, I did enjoy the writing in some parts. Was it life changing and inspiring and so great and amazing and worth a bajillion awards? No. Would I recommend it? No.
Beautiful! I've never read a novel in free verse and it was absolutely wonderful!

Rating: 4.5/5 
 Just beautiful.
Beautiful. I think "poignant" is the right word, even if it's overused. Poignant, but not depressing. Just...though provoking. Loved it.
Sublime. What else can I say? She is a genius. I had no idea this book was written in free verse until I opened it and it thrilled me.

Jacqueline Woodson's is a voice of generosity, grace and wisdom in literature today. This, her memoir of childhood, is as good as anything she's written. I loved her choice to write it in poems -- each memory distinct on the white page and all building a narrative arc of her growing awareness as a writer. Congratulations for winning the National Book Award for this are well-deserved.

"How amazing these words are that slowly come to me. 
 How wonderfully on and on they go."
I listened to the audio version which may have been the reason I didn't enjoy it as much. Narrators can make or break an audio book.
I didn't love this, but I can see why other people do. I'll be passing it along to my niece and maybe she'll be the right audience.
http://savvyverseandwit.com/2015/06/b...

This book is so important and beautifully written. I particularly enjoyed the audio version because Woodson read every word as she meant it to be read. The story flowed well and the poetic text exuded Woodson's experience and sentiments. It is a story I will be reading to my children. A critical story in the canon of children's literature.
love love love
I enjoy reading free verse poetry novels. The history was also very interesting.
I can't do this book justice by writing a review about it. It is THAT good. Wonderful writing style. Poignant. A voice that needs to be heard. Please read it!

This was a beautiful book, and so enjoyable to read. It's a great introduction to the civil rights movement, there are plenty of opportunities for discussion, without the true horrors for sensitive readers. Not just a YA book, I enjoyed it as much (if not more than) my children (13, 11 and 10.)

This is a great book. A memoir written in verse, Jacqueline gives us insight into her family history that came before her and that frames her story of coming of age in the 1970s, of course a moment of great change. I think this book is one of the more accessible books in verse I've tried to read, and it would appeal to young poets, aspiring writers, and people interested in cultural history alike. The writing drew me in rather than alienated me. Moreover short poems feels so appropriate for a memoir. After all, memory doesn't have a beginning, middle and end like a fully fleshed story. Memory happens in fits and starts and is about small details and revelations. So I loved how the author wove her story this way. 
 I haven't heard feedback from teens on this one yet, but my hope is that this isn't a book that wins awards just because the adults love it. I can imagine many teens connecting with the author both in story and her writing/storytelling style.

A wonderful autobiographical book written in prose. Jacqueline has the unique ability to transport the reader to childhood and capture the voice of a child so perfectly, yet still write with the beautiful maturity that moves you. clearly I am not the writer that Jacqueline is! The chronological vignettes, some more touching and others more telling, pieced together in a way that made you feel the love for her family and gave you an understanding of the complexities of growing up and finding your way in the world. A beautiful book.

This is one of those books I feel a lot of pressure to like, and I find myself strangely resistant to that pressure. It has not one, not two, but THREE shiny award stickers on the cover. And I'm not saying it's bad, by any means. It just didn't jump and and down and yell, "Best book EVER!" at me. 
 I do envy her her grandpa ("Daddy") though.

I do love poetry but I don't give it the time I should because I'd rather have a story. This is a story in poetry, a powerful, sometimes difficult to face, sweet, thought filled, poetic stream by a girl whose young life was a study in opposites, and who believes in opposites coming together some day. I do, too. Thank you Jaqueline with a J and a Q for inspiring me to keep on believing and for taking me through your journey with such grace.

I usually don't like books written in verse, but the verses here were actually poetry. I loved this book! I'm not sure what kind of audience it will have in my library, but I thought it was beautiful. I had to read some of it aloud just to feel the words in my mouth. Woodson has a gift. I'm glad she chose to share it with us.

Written in poetry form, the story of Jacqueline Woodson as she grew up in the 60s and 70s in the south, then in New York City -- truly tells what it was like to be a child at that time and split between two very different cultures. I loved that her ability to write was slow, but her love of stories started very young and helped create an amazing writer.

A Newbery Honor winner this year, I deeply loved this book. I honestly didn't think I would as it is also written entirely in verse. It is a memoir of Ms. Woodson's memories growing up and it is absolutely beautiful. While I probably would have enjoyed it written in novel form, I think the use of verse is stunning as it almost feels like little tributes to the people, events, and feelings that she focused on in each section. 
 Her life and the story moves from her birth in Ohio, to living with grandparents in South Carolina, and then finally moving to New York City as a little girl. She continued to spend summers in South Carolina with her grandparents for a few years and I loved her comparisons of struggling to feel home in one place or the other. They both felt like home and her thoughts honored the fact that we often leave pieces of our heart in the many places we live and love.

I liked and admired this but it was episodic and lacked a narrative pull. It *felt* like a classic, like a book that would be read alongside A Tree Grows in Brooklyn or Little House in the Big Woods or something. I didn't connect to the parts that were about becoming a writer, however, and I wanted more about her siblings - wanted to hear more about them and their adventures. The audiobook helped because I enjoyed the author's narration.

1)Twin Text: Inside Out and Back Again by Thanhha Lai (2011) 
 2)I chose to pair these two books for a few reasons. They are both about a young girl who struggles with a move from what she has always known to be home, to a new, different place. Inside Out and Back Again is historical fiction in which the main character moves from Saigon to Alabama due to the war taking over her homeland. It depicts the struggles she has not only moving from what is familiar to a new country, but a part of the country (deep South) where race is a volatile issue. Brown Girl Dreaming also has a connection to the deep South and the struggles Jackie faces moving north and feeling like she doesn't fit in. And, last, but certainly not least, both texts are written in verse. This brings in another element of compare and contrast. 
 3)Brown Girl Dreaming is written very descriptively, but also chronologically. 
 4)I would use a compare/contrast strategy with these two books. We would compare/contrast main characters, plot, setting, conflict (internal and external) and the way the verse is used/written. I have helped develop some graphic organizers for our Differentiated Literature groups that I believe would work well for these two texts.

The good thing about starting this as an audiobook is that I could hear Jacqueline Woodson's voice reading to me even after I switched to print. 
 The poem about discovering the children's book full of black children was my favorite.

This memoir about the author's childhood is written in verse and it's beautiful. She grew up in South Carolina and New York during the Civil Rights Movement. It's one of those rare books that can be enjoyed by readers of all ages. Look forward to reading more of her work.
Such a lovely read. Jacqueline Woodson really has a way with words. Each poem was so vivid and beautiful to read.
Loved the verse--quick read. Also loved how Woodson unspooled her coming of age as a tale of someone who discovers what she loves.

"Even the silence 
 has a story to tell you. 
 Just listen. Listen." 
 What a beautiful, rich memoir. I listened to the audio version and was utterly captivated by the rhythmic prose.
This book was beautiful and moving. I was hesitant to read it because it was written in verse but I am glad that I read it. The poetry made it even more amazing.

Books in verse can be hard to pull off well, and to me this memoir was lacking. Woodson didn't flush out most characters, and the pacing lacked momentum. On the plus side, its discussion of the Civil Rights Movement is powerful and inspiring.

4.5/5 
 This is a beautiful story. I love to read books written in verse, but sometimes feel as though they are missing something essential - whether it be plot, character development, or tone. Yet, Woodson managed to get it all right. 
 I listened to the audiobook version of this novel, read by Woodson herself. Listening to her read was wonderfully atmospheric - I truly felt myself transported into her story, into the different ways of life and her experiences in both the North and the South. 
 This is a powerful true story of growing up, dealing with change and prejudice, and coming into oneself. I would highly recommend you give it a read!

This deceptively simple book is quite powerful. I really enjoyed the stories told here, and feel a real kinship with Ms. Woodson and her family. We have a lot in common! The poems really touched me. The writing is excellent, and this is a book both kids and parents can enjoy. Highly Recommended!

3.5/5 stars 
 I enjoyed the story behind Brown Girl Dreaming, especially Jacqueline's relationship with her grandfather. However, I feel like the writing in this book does not live up to its hype. While I found some of the passages beautiful and inspiring, I overall wasn't impressed with the writing.
Where is the 6th star?
very good book.

Wow...this could have been such a quick read, but I found myself purposely slowing down to take it all in. 
 Some parts light & humorous, others just plain heartbreaking; all verse, all powerful. 
 I loved the poems labelled "How to Listen" and how Jackie talks about being a writer. 
 Beautiful.

Read this for a book discussion group. I am not familiar with Woodson's other work, as I am not a YA fan (and never was, even at the target age), but, although targeted at the same age group, this is autobiography, and so goes down easier with me than YA fiction. I particularly enjoyed the insight into what it was like to be black and living in the south during the Civil Rights Movement, and would have liked more of that. That was not, however, Woodson's main focus--she wove that into a bigger picture of what it was like to be a child moved from one home to another--Ohio to Greensboro, NC to New York City. This is a very fast read, and it does create a vivid portrait of family and social life in the early 60s. I also enjoyed it a bit more than I might have a week ago, I think, because I went to Montecello last weekend and so the Woodson story is fresh in my memory.
Wonderful book. Loved learning about the author's life in her own beautiful words.
I did not finish this poetic book. It did not grip me.

This is a tender introduction into the civil rights movement told through the eyes of a young person living in the North and South during that time period and trying to make sense of the events surrounding her. It's also a moving portrait of the emergence of a young writer. There is some beautiful writing here, though I did find it to be a slower read.
This is a beautiful little book. The poems are so evocative, they form a vivid picture of the people and places of Jacqueline's growing-up years. There's a nice little surprise at the end, too.

reference_books.title: The Catcher in the Rye
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I enjoyed J.D. Salinger's style of writing. For me it was very intimate the way Holden Caulfield told his story. I pictured him at a bar with his scotch and soda and a cigarette (keep in mind he is about 15 or 16 years old) telling a fello patron his story. And then at one point, it seemed almost like a confession until I realized there was nothing to confess just a rambling story. 
 Which brings me to my next point...what was the point of the story?! OK, so Holden is flunking out of a private school and pretty much hates everyone and/or is annoyed by everything everyone does. So?! It's suppose to be a coming of age story, right? 
 Holden gets kicked out of 3 private schools (over a period of time) and then decides to run away until his little sister decides she is running away with him. He tells her it's important for her to stay in school which he then takes his own advise to heart and decides to try school again in the fall. 
 Is that really "coming of age"? Because he realized that he needs to take responsibility and apply himself in school if he wants to get anywhere in life? Of course I'm adding words here because that isn't exactly what Holden said. Basically he said he changed his mind (about running away) and he's going straight home after dropping his sister off at school. 
 I'm trying to understand why this would have been required reading in high school and why it's such a classic. Was there some great message about staying in school that kids would have gotten out of this book? My thoughts are probably not. However, circa 1970 yes, perhaps. 2010 not so much.

reference_books.title: Lolita
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 One of the most annoying books I've read in a long time. I read this book because it is one of Amy Tan's favorite authors and she spoke of this book often. I wanted to know what the hoop-la was all about. It's a love-hate book for me. 
 H.H. is shockenly stricken by a very young Lolita. He describes her beauty in great detail and his thoughts are very well laid out. However, the only way to get to this young girl is the marry the mother. However, now the mother is in the way between H.H. and Lolita. One afternoon while cleaning H.H's study Lolita's mother reads a journal with very private and explict details about her daughter's sexual being and how much H.H. is in love with her. She confronts him and threatens to leave taking Loltia with her. So of course, he decides to murder the mother while Lolita is a camp. 
 However H.H. doesn't tell Lolita that her mother is dead he instead tells her that they are going on a trip. They have their first sexual encounter and Lolita is very relaxed about it. So relaxed that it's very unnerving. H.H.'s raw emotional feelings and very over-powering and soon Lolita learns to control H.H. by either giving him what he wants or holding out. And so the story continues... 
 Vladimir Nabokov does a fabulous job and showcasing all sides of the story. The torrid love affair and the raw all- to consuming sexual emotions that we had with our first real loves. He reminds us what it was like to feel everything for the first time; the mix emotions, the can't breathe, eat, sleep, and how sexual emotions can take over our lives. But then he shows us the side of the unwanted attention. The ugly side of brutality, the side that shows us what some people will do in order to get that. A side that is almost common place in some parts of the country. And just when you think you might have it figured out...Vladimir Nobokov shows us the side of Lolita who uses that raw sexuality to make men do things. And ultimately destroying a man.

reference_books.title: On the Road
reference_books.review_text:
I finally read this book and while I was thinking this would be a fantastic story, it wasn't. I often felt like I was reading a Henry James novel filled with adolescent bullshit and the senseless wanderings that it didn't equate to an epic adventure. One word - bored. 
 I understand that On The Road is really an autobiography of Jack Kerouac's travels across America with his friends. Why he choose to pen it, still puzzles me. 
 The main character, Sal travels across the US not once but 5 times each time looking for adventure, freedom, girls and his friends. Along the way he picks up strangers, loses friends, finds a new love, friends get married/divorced, car breaks down, wins money, loses money...on and on. Could this have been the original brat pack in the making, maybe. But the story didn't capture the reader like it should have.

reference_books.title: The Horse and His Boy (Chronicles of Narnia, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
This particular book wasn't as exciting as the last 4 books in The Chronicles of Narnia. Was it because I had a greater adventure on my mind - Harry Potter? Perhaps, however, I am reminded at how simple this series is. 
 Book #5 is about a young boy, Shasta, who wishes to run away before being sold to a Prince. While he is planning his escape, he finds an unlikely partner, a talking horse named Bree, who convinces the boy to run away to Narnia and North. Obviously from there adventures ensues. 
 In this book, King Edmund and Queen Susan return as rulers of Narnia, except they are more mature and Aslan doesn't come to save the day but rather he helps events unfold.

reference_books.title: The Notebook (The Notebook, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I still have mixed feelings about this book. When I think about it, i like it and then at times I don't. I don't know how to judge this book. 
 Basically it's a "remember when..." story. Two elderly people whom you assume are friends tell you their story about how they met when they were younger. They did date and were in fact lovers at a very young age - well, in their early 20's if not 18-19 years old. She of course was from a wealthy family and he was just a dreamer working for the local mill. 
 Very hot and heated these two made. But it annoyed me to know end how bossy and snobish the girl was. She pretty much led this poor lad on a wild chase, then would denounce him, then send him on a wild chase again. Is it my age? Did we really do this? 
 Towards the end, she is marring a wealthy business man in another town. But for some reason she feels compelled to go back to her hometown and find this young boy. Once she does, she falls back in love and again the cat and mouse dance begins. Even more annoying! 
 Well, they end up getting married against all better judgement of her parents. So the elderly couple is him and her and she has alzheimer. So the "remember when" is the husband telling his wife about her life as he remembers it. So, when you look at that way, it's rather romantic and I enjoyed it. But when they were young...UGH!!

reference_books.title: Tropic of Cancer
reference_books.review_text:
...because it was onced banned. 
 Unfortunately banning this book only fueled interest and in a sense landed Tropic of Cancer as a masterpiece. Upon reading this exhausting story it is anything but a masterpiece. 
 Tropic of Cancer is basically the meandering thoughts of a tortured soul, oversexed, often poor and homeless man (Henry Miller) who fancies himself as a writer. He often shares company with not only various prostitutes, but other men who are in the field of the arts and who dole out money to support him in his time of need - or habit, which is quite often. Henry Miller as the author uses vulger and obscene language which at first I was startled by but after a while I realized that it was his way of writing without editing and using words that you don't normally see. Basically shock value. However, shock value has no value in my opinion. 
 "I have made a silent compact with myself not to change a line of what I write. I am not interested in perfecting my thoughts, nor my actions." 
 "...Now we shall have a vessel in which to pour the vital fluid, a bomb which, when we throw it, will set off the world. We shall put into it enough to give the writers of tomorrow their plots, their dramas, their poems, their myths, their sciences. The world will be able to feed on it for a thousand years to come. It is colossal in its pretentiousness." 
 Give me a break! Henry Miller comes across as such an ass that the one word that he uses quite liberally is really what I think of him. He has such a blantant disregard for women that not only can he not live without them and sex for hire, but upon looking at the female anatomy he ponders life and the "cancer" that is eating at our society. WOW - that's deep?! (no pun intended) However, Henry Miller has a chance to change his life and "start over" but just can't give up women and his cunning ways.

reference_books.title: Girl, Interrupted
reference_books.review_text:
Girl, Interrupted is about the author, Susanna Kaysen, and her 2 year stint in a mental hospital plus some events leading up to her stay, her life afterwards, and her own diagnosis. 
 Unfortunately or rather sadly enough, Susanna Kaysen probably didn't have a personality disorder but was rather unmotivated in life. At the time she was 18 with no direction. She thought of suicide, had self-image issues, had multiple boyfriends, didn't want to go to college, didn't enjoy school, felt trapped by her over-achieving parents, didn't have long-term goals or career choices and basically (in the grand scheme of things) wrist banged. Not self-mutilation, mind you. WOW - what a nut case, right? Hmm - sounds like every teenager I grew up with in the midwest. In fact, it still sounds like a lot of teenagers I hear about. 
 However this was in the 60's and a true story. 
 Susanna Kaysen poignantly quotes her past psychiatrist on borderline personality disorder as what they call people whose lifestyle bothers them.

reference_books.title: The Blood of Olympus (The Heroes of Olympus, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
This the 5th and I should think final installment of The Heroes of Olympus. 
 The Doors of Death have been closed and all demigods, giants, monsters and everyone from Roman and Greek camps are converging at Camp Half Blood in the final battle to eliminate all demigods and Gods alike, to wipe out the Earth and let only those who helped Gaea return to rule shall inherit the Earth...or so she says.

reference_books.title: The Sound and the Fury
reference_books.review_text:
What?! 
 OK - I wasn't ready for this book after my epic read of The Mists of Avalon. 
 The Sound and the Fury is the MOST complicated book I've ever read. I found myself reading and then going back to re-read what I've already read because what I thought was a boy was later a girl. Or who I thought was telling a story ended up being someone else. 
 William Faulkner wrote of all sorts of characters and then wove their thoughts among other characters so I constantly questioned myself on who I was reading about. Again going back a couple of paragraphs to find the original narration. 
 The book is in the narration of Benjy who at first is named Maury then is changed to Benjamin then shortened to Benjy. It's of his family and basically the curse of the family. Not only is Benjy mentally retarded or should I say, mentally challenged, but he is also 33 and not a baby as everyone seems to call him. Still confused? Just wait...Benjy has a sister, Candace (Caddy for short), and two brothers, Quentin and Jason. Once Candace finds herself pregnant, she marries a bank owner but after the baby is born too soon, she finds herself divorces with a little girl named none other than, Quentin. Quentin, her brother, who loves his sister like a women comits suicide while her other brother, Jason has emence hatred for Candace. All the while, the mother is bed ridden and claims that she will not live long manages to continue to live for another 18 or so years. 
 I have a headache from reading this book. UGH! Maybe I'll rent the movie - it has all the makings of a really good psycho thriller.

reference_books.title: Beloved
reference_books.review_text:
UGH! This was a difficult read for me. Not only did the story track back and forth from past to present, but the story was extremely depressing. 
 Beloved is about an African American woman, Sethe, who is bought, sold, and traded to various farms. It's about her fight for freedom, the lost of her children, the reuniting of her children, and the unforgetable act Sethe does to protect her children from slavery. 
 I gave Beloved 4 stars because it was difficult to follow. I know this was made into a movie, however, I won't be renting it. 
 This book was a 1988 Pulitzer Prize winner for fiction. I believe it's probably due to the acute story telling of slavery and the misuse/mistreatment and degrading of African Americans in our time.

book_a.title: The Girl in the Spider's Web (Millennium, #4)
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 UGH! This book was a complete disappointment. Not only did the (new) author languish over rudimentary details but he got lost in the art of storytelling. I spent well over 250 pages reading descriptive BS that didn't capture me as a reader but instead Mr. Lagercrantz tried to play "catch up" in a story I was well versed in. Not only did the characters not ring true but the dialogue was off and fundamental like I was reading a badly written tweener book. Worse of all the author was predictable. 
 The Girl in the Spider's Web is about a murder and stolen intelligence leaving a young boy as the only witness. Unfortunately this young boy is handicapped leaving inept people solving the case. In comes Salanger to save the day. Bore!

sample_reviews.review_text:
This book was given to me, like as a birthday present not by the author, and I was dubious. The author is well dead, and his girlfriend didn't want the trilogy touched, but the father and someone else inherited the legacy and they said yes. I get why people want to live off the dead. Apart from money. There's always that cheeky money monkey suggesting we take, steal and borrow. But as I had it in my house I figured i should read it. 
 And it's okay. He does no harm to Lisbeth, and it's a nice touch introducing the twin sister. The beautiful but naughty twin sister. This story is all about hacking, but the relationship between the autistic child and Lisbeth is sweet. 
 I don't recommend the book because I feel like someone has robbed Larsson's grave, but I do love the Lisbeth character and if you want more, then Mr Lagercrantz gives us more.

While it felt great to be reading about Blomkvist and Salander again, this book felt rushed. It's like it only reached the surface of what Larsson would have written. I don't love how things just seemed to fall into our laps instead of us having to work for the information by getting little glimpses and clues throughout the novel. Normally it would take quite an adventure to find out vital information that in this book seemed to just be handed to us in huge chunks by supporting characters. I still give it a 3/5 because I was happy to be back in their little world for awhile.

This is a functional narrative that ticks a lot of boxes but ultimately left me feeling flat. There was little in the way of twists and turns - even the identity of the antagonist didn't come as a surprise - and the level of expositional backstory was off the charts (although I seem to recall this being an issue I had with the other instalments in this series, so that's hardly Lagercrantz's fault). But then, a formulaic story is fine as long as it's told well, and unfortunately this is where my real problem with the book lies: the writing just lacks life. I can't tell if this is Lagercrantz's problem or whether the spark was just lost in the translation, but none of the characters have distinctive voices (especially the peripheral characters who provide Blomkvist with background) and I felt that the factual material (on autism, mathematics etc) could have been much better integrated. Add to that the pacing (the narrative didn't really pick up speed until at least the halfway mark) and this was a pretty rocky read for me.

I am surprised at how disappointed I was with this book. Unfortunately the third book should probably have been left to wrap up the story. This book didn't fit with the others. The characters didn't come together and the story really wasn't about Lisbeth at all. I really hope that another book is not in the works.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Overall it captured the style of the Millennium series very well, but I wasn't crazy about the ending. The author was obviously intending for this book to kick off additional books in the series, and the ending was way too open-ended for my liking. It felt like the only reason the main antagonist wasn't caught was to further the series, and not the story itself. 
 I did appreciate Lagercrantz's changes to the Blomkvist character. One of his criticisms of the existing books was that the Blomkvist character had way too easy a time getting women to go to bed with him. They would walk up to him and proposition him after no more than a few paragraphs of dialogue. Thankfully here Blomkvist sticks to just Erika as his lover and his lothario-like ways are no longer a focus of the narrative.

My first "ditched" book of 2016. I am SO glad I didn't pay for this book. It is so obviously a cash grab, the writing is horrible, and I honestly just can't be bothered. I read about 100 pages, and in that time I found myself thinking "Lisbeth wouldn't do/say that". The characters we have come to know and love are not resurfacing with this book. Instead they are new, unlikable characters who have nothing in common except their names and physical description.

Once I let it be different, I liked it well enough. There was an overall feeling of shallowness, I don't know how much I'd like it if the (original) author hadn't already established the characters for me.
There were moments that brought be right back into world of Lisbeth Salander and I was so happy to back! Decent plot line however it just didn't live up to the originals for me.

Was afraid that the continuation of the series would be a disappointment, but that turned out not to be so. 
 Of course there are differences in the writing style and the level of suspense was not as high as in the other 3 books but it was a good read nevertheless.

An enjoyable spring break read- like meeting up with old friends. That said, not sure how I'm feeling about the series possibly going on and on- as it surely could, given the ending. Is this what Stieg Larsson had in mind? I doubt it. Also, despite some badass moves, Salander seems to have lost her edge a bit in this book. All in all, this novel's not as sharp as the trilogy.

An absolute train wreck. A professional attempt to slaughter and other writers career with ham-handed politics, goofy pros and a desire to please all the right people without ever telling any kind of story. Noteto the publisher: please stop you're ruining this series. The family the author should sue you for everything that you're worth.

Sadly David Lagercrantz is no Stieg Larsson. 
 Despite, no doubt, honourable intentions, I fear the damage done by Lagercrantz is irreversible and contaminates the rest of the Millennium series. It is boring, stilted and generally tries too hard. 
 The last straw, for me, so to speak was when listening to the audiobook, the character "Balder" asked someone to be "pacific" about a threat. Just, no!

Incredibly slow, tedious and 100 pages too long. I felt the author was more interested in lecturing his readers about industrial espionage as it related to the state of artificial intelligence than writing a good story. Lisbeth Salander was a fascinatingly complex and dynamic character until her unfortunate literary turn here. Too bad because she might have resuscitated what I found to be a wholly unreadable novel. I believe Steig Larsen would have been disappointed.

This was disappointing for several reasons: 1- the translation was awkward in some places which I found distracting; 2- despite the listing of some characters in the front of the book, there are too many others to keep track of; 3- I liked the Lisbeth parts and wish there were more. Stieg Larrson, I miss you. R.I.P.

What a chore it was getting through this book. I had the upmost giddiness in picking up from the continue of Steig Larsson's Millennium series. The love of the characters I had before, had no spark of trepidation, it was a flickering wet match. I smelt a wet dog plot. (And yes, Mikael Blomkvist is such a skilled journalist which was on and on (did I mentioned he is a respected journalist everyone is in awe of) throughout the book, and has become a rather old man fart.) Lisbeth Salander felt like a hollowed out character of herself. Her ghostly presence was just merely there. It felt as the author was talking down to you. The book read more as a textbook then a fiction, quick paced book. Disappointing for a fan of Steig Larsson's Millennium series.

While I really enjoyed the first three books, this one had no verve, no flair, no reason to continue. I abandoned it after about 20 pages in hardcover. 
 Maybe it was the writing that was wooden and clumsy or perhaps the translation, but it was very off-putting for me. 
 I have now read some of the other reviews and found how this happened to be written. An excellent example of why one should always write a will.

Took me awhile to finish this one. It was good, but not quite as compelling as the previous novels by Larsson. I enjoyed the story and the characters were done well enough to be intriguing and interesting, but I had a hard time getting used to a different author providing the voice of the characters. 
 One major drawback for me was the lack of pages that were actually about Lisbeth. For a novel of nearly 500 pages I would guess less than 100 were about her, perhaps less than 75. Lisbeth is the character that makes the story interesting so having to read 400 pages or so about Mikael and other secondary characters is a tad disappointing. 
 I will read the next book in the series when it is published. Lagercrantz did well with this one.

Disappointed! I'd put this aside and had been looking forward to reading it over the Christmas season but it turned out to be something of a wet squib. To be fair, the plot was interesting enough and covered issues that are particularly relevant today (NSA misuse of their powers) but the characterisation fell very flat. Blomkvist is fine but Lisbeth is despairingly bland and I'm not entirely sure why. It is a bit of a worry though when your side plot (machinations over the control and survival of Blomkvist's Millenium magazine) is actually more interesting than the main plot.

I was prepared to be disappointed. Not just prepared. I expected to be disappointed. But, as you can tell from my rating, I was not. The only disappointment I felt was when the last word was read and the story came to an end. 
 IMHO, Lagercrantz did justice to the character of Lisbeth Salander, the series, and the late Mr. Larsson. I am aware that the writing and publishing of The Girl in the Spider's Web came with much controversy and drama, but, putting that aside, this book was damn good and I savored every word of it. 
 *Ratings Note: Normally when I vacillate between four & five stars I more often than not go with four, but, after reading a 1-star review that was given out of spite without the reviewer having even read the book, I went with five. Piss on that.*

DNF. I was quite open to liking this - though I'm generally not keen on series being carried on by new authors, I'm not so invested in the Millennium trilogy that the idea offends me - but, dear god, this reads like a cash in. The translation is unbelievably clunky (even if the fault lies with the original, I can't believe an English speaking editor let this through - nobody speaks like an actual person), the plot feels a terrible combination of incoherent and unbelievable, and the editing feels like it comes from the fifties. In a book supposedly all about future technology, it feels perverse to use editing where all acronyms are punctuated (even such common ones as O.K.): it jars the eye, slows the pace and makes this even more of a slog.

I wish I had never picked up this novel. It's as dull as dishwater and is a pale imitation of everything I loved and was gripped by in the original trilogy. 
 Worse still, for a series that's about fighting men who hate women...it's written almost completely from the male characters' point of view and the heroine of the trilogy is barely in it. I really missed Lisbeth. 
 The writing is all over the place. Every few paragraphs the POV shifts to someone else like a child who can't sit still. I am so done with this book!

If you are thinking of giving this a try, don't. Save yourself the pain. Lisbeth and Mikael are finished. They are no more. Let them go. 
 Simon Vance (All hail the Great Simons--Vance and Prebble) tried, but this book is so bad that not even his narration could save it. 
 Where to start...how about with the action? But wait! I can't start there because there was so little action, it doesn't matter. One or two gun fights, a quick rescue, and lots of driving around talking and standing around talking and sitting down talking--talking on the phone, talking in person, talking via memos. Talk. Talk. Talk. Talk. Talk. Talk. TALKING DOES NOT COUNT AS ACTION!!! 
 What about the plot? There was a plot...at least I think there was. Problem with it was that it was so convoluted and inane and, at times, so down right trivial that I just gave up caring. I kept thinking it would get better, but nope. It didn't. 
 What about the characters? Tissue thin doesn't even begin to describe them. If I hadn't already cared about Mikael and Lisbeth, I wouldn't have cared. By the end of the book, I didn't care. Didn't care at all. I just wanted it to end. 
 The writing? This book could be used in an Intro to Creative Writing course to show how to piss off your reader. Let's see... 
 1) Interrupt a conversation right when it FINALLY gets interesting by switching to another scene. Do this not once or twice but just about every freaking time something important is about to be said or happen. (Extra points for putting so little action in the book that this interruption irritates the reader even more.) 
 2) Make sure the reader knows that someone is going to be killed, then draw it out over several chapters (using process described above). Do this so blatantly and slowly that even though this character is a darling, the reader begins to shout at her audio device "Kill him! Kill him!" 
 3) Take a stereotypical character and rather than give him some interesting characteristics make him/her even MORE stereotypical. The innocent person is not just innocent--he/she is excruciatingly innocent. Obnoxious--excruciatingly obnoxious. Rude and outspoken--excruciatingly so. 
 4) Rather than try to convey your characters' inner thoughts/conflicts by actually writing well, just do it the lazy way--give 'em a dream! It is so much easier to have them dream about their conflicts than by having to figure out how to SHOW those conflicts via the characters' actions. 
 There is more, but honestly, this book isn't worth the keystrokes. And it definitely was not worth the audible-dot-com credit or the time I wasted listening to it in the hopes it would get better.

 How do you honor one of the best crime series of the decade? I had my doubts about Lagercrantz, especially once I heard that much of the story would involve the US and the NSA, but he's proved me wrong. I think this works because Lagercrantz doesn't try to be Larsson -- he pays respect to him while still making this book his own. It's not a easy task to breathe new life into such beloved characters like Salander and Blomkvist, but I think readers will happy with the results. 
 Like the previous novels in the series, a series of seemingly unrelated characters and events are tied together intricately. The plot is complex, well-thought out and has the impressive touch of an expert, even if gets a bit over the top at times. All of the business with the NSA intertwines with all of the Swedish conspiracies and politics quite nicely, it also adds another layer of relevancy considering how often the security organization makes headlines. 
 Yes, readers read these books for the twisty mysteries and enticing Blomkvist, but we're all really just here for Salander. Lisbeth is just as fucking amazing as one would expect, there's a reason why she's the "girl" who's featured in the titles. Salander has always been somewhat of a mystery and Lagercrantz gives readers a peek into her childhood with Zala, illuminating little details that paint a better picture of our favorite heroine. Though it does destroy partially some of that air of mystery she carries around her, it also makes readers want to cheer her on even more. 
 Mikael Blomkvist is just as stubborn, obsessive and horny as readers remember and reading about him for the first time in ages felt like getting reacquainted with an old friend. It was interesting to see how Blomkvist and Millennium try to adjust to the more digital age and attempt to stay relevant. It's clear that our journalist hasn't lost his touch and still is just as engaging as readers remember. 
 I was worried that this book would be just glorified fan-fiction, but it's clear that Lagercrantz really cares about Salander, Millennium and Larsson's novels. I'm eagerly awaiting the inevitable sequel and all I really want is just more Lisbeth kicking ass. I don't think that's too much to ask for.

 Unfortunately, I was supremely disappointed, so much so that I can't face going back to the book after making it halfway through the audio. First of all, these are not the same characters of Lisbeth and Mikael that I know from the trilogy. Lisbeth seems to have reverted to one of two modes - sloppy hacker or hungover boxer - no depth, no motivation, nothing interesting. It could be that we reached the end of her story in the trilogy. Mikael is unmotivated too, can't stand to be at work and arriving late to the scene of an important crime that finally happens midway through the book. 
 The author spends TOO much time describing things that don't matter - an hour (I listened to the audio) on the current status of Millennium, the news publication that Mikael has worked on; the storms, frequent descriptions; and Mikael's white fur coat. He hasn't bothered to explore the characters themselves. It isn't written about intelligently enough to feel like high stakes. This is set in the present day. If I wanted a thrilling read about AI and the singularity I would look for it in science fiction, where it is handled with interesting variations and frightening possibilities, NOT in a Swedish crime novel. It makes no sense.) 
 I would be happy if someone came along who convinced me that this book turned a huge corner and I should have kept reading... but I doubt that will happen.

 When I first saw that there was going to be another book in the Millennium Series, I jumped for joy. Having read The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, The Girl Who Played with Fire, and The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest, I was very excited to see what was going to happen next for Lisbeth and Blomkvist. However, I was also very surprised. I didn't expect there to be another book in the series because the author of the original three books Stieg Larsson died in 2004. So when I found out about The Girl in the Spider's Web, I was very excited to see how David Lagercrantz would continue Larsson's story. 
 And what a story it was. Lagercrantz did an excellent job in writing this book with the same style and feel as the rest of the series. 
 What I love about the series the most is Lisbeth and Blomkvist's relationship throughout the series and The Girl in the Spider's Web doesn't disappoint in continuing to grow that relationship. What I love about their relationship is how both characters come from different walks of life. But yet, they are able to form a connection with each other out of the oddest of circumstances and still able to live their own separate lives. 
 I also love Lisbeth as a character. I love her character because she just doesn't give a shit. She has her own personal views and she sticks by them until the end. Lisbeth has a way of handling things and disregards what others tell her to do and I love that about her character. 
 Another aspect of The Girl in the Spider's Web I enjoyed was all of the action that took place in the story. Like the rest of the series, this book has a lot of action that keeps the reader on their toes and makes them want to continue reading to find out what happens next. It is a thrilling read that any crime loving book nerd would be interested in checking out. 
 I also love how The Girl in the Spider's Web switches perspective. Not only do we get Lisbeth and Blomkvist's perspective but we also get to see the story from the villain's point of view as well. I love reading books like this where you have those changing perspectives because it gives the reader access to what the main antagonist is thinking. Having these different perspectives allows the reader to get a better understanding of the antagonist's actions and see them as more human capable of making bad decisions. 
 The one thing with The Girl in the Spider's Web that I didn't enjoy was the ending. I didn't like the ending because I want to know what's going to happen next. Yes, they caught most of the bad guys, but I still have questions about what's going to happen. I also didn't like it because it sounded final as if this book is going to be the last book in the series. While there is the possibility of there being another book after this one, Lagercrantz leaves us hanging with no details or hint of there being another book after The Girl in the Spider's Web. 
 However, I overall enjoyed reading this book just as much as the rest of the books in the series. Seeing Blomkvist and Lisbeth's characters once again was really nice and I really enjoyed reading a book in this series again. David Lagercrantz did a wonderful job with this book and I can't wait to see what else he's written. I highly recommend reading The Girl in the Spider's Web to anyone interested in reading a book with a set of diverse characters and an action packed story that will keep you wanting more.

First and foremost: I am glad to be back. Several things in my personal life came up at once, preventing me from having any spare time for reading or blogging.  Arguably the most popular character created by author Charles Dickens, Oliver Twist is the orphan who dared to ask for more gruel. The tragic story of workshops, thievery, and murder set against the bleak backdrop of London's Victorian Era, this novel is quintessential Dickens. It hosts a large cast of characters (though not as large as his readers would see in his later works), all with fascinating back stories and motives. 
 You probably think you know the story if you've never actually read it -- Oliver Twist living in pitiful conditions in a workhouse, starving . . . and while that is part of the story, it's the first part only. Soon after, Twist runs away and ends up living with two different families, becomes caught up in a gang of robbers, and the story unfolds from there. It's pretty interesting stuff! 
 What's funny about this book is I loved every character . . . except Oliver. I have two reasons for that: 1.) He is wildly complacent, and goes along to get along. He never, ever stands up for himself, and he's a huge whiner to boot. I totally understand that he has had an awful life, but damnit he can be a chore to read about sometimes. Luckily, despite being the title character, he's actually not in a whole lot of the story once it really gets going. And 2.) He never 'feels' or reads like a kid to me. His dialogue and actions are not that of a child. I understand this was only the second novel written by Charles Dickens, and I've heard his child characters in later novels feel much more realistic, so I guess I'll see eventually! I wanted so badly to like Oliver, and the terrible things he goes through do create a certain amount of sympathy for the boy, but after a few hundred pages I was sick of the brat. Just my opinion. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed this book. It was a highly enthralling read, and I wish I could have read more of it at a time than just a chapter or two. It's Dickens, so there's a bit of overwriting, but the writing itself is simply divine. Almost two hundred years after initially getting published, Dickens' mastery of the English language trumps almost any other novelist or poet. Oliver himself was a bit of an annoyance to read about, but the rest of the characters (especially Nancy -- oh, how I loved Nancy!) are a pure joy. If you're one of the few people who have yet to experience this story, what are you waiting for?
