 This is Dickens' second novel, first published in serial form over 2 years. Later Dickens, from the bits I've read, may come across as more polished and sophisticated, but all the typical ingredients are here: the genius for characterisation, the biting social satire, and - unfortunately - the sometimes mawkish sentimentality that he seems to have shared with his fellow Victorians (I'm reminded of Oscar Wilde's typically ruthless observation that "One must have a heart of stone to read the death of little Nell without laughing"). 
 Some of the social observation and banter now seem either dated or impenetrable to a modern reader (q.v. the Dodger, Fagin and Master Bates (!)), but I'm sure they were spot on for a contemporary one. Taken as social commentary, the heartlessness of the parish workhouse system is laid bare mercilessly: the pompous hypocrisy of Mr Bumble the Beadle and the parish board members; the mercenary Mrs Corney, starving her charges into an early grave. I doubt there was much exaggeration needed on Dickens' part, and any sentimentality is far outweighed by such keen eyed dissection of human faults and prejudices embedded in the system. It's great stuff. 
 The other downside concerns the charge of anti-semitism. Dickens, it seems, was no anti-semite - or at least he vehemently denied it, merely arguing that it was a common fact of the street that most criminal's of Fagin's class were Jews. However, Fagin is not the only Jewish character in the novel, and it seems fair to say that Dickens does little to dispel harmful racist stereotypes, and much (if inadvertently) to promote them. But then maybe the fact that Fagin remains one of his most popular and well-known characters - a lovable and charming rogue - is something that should argue in his favour (though possibly this is more due to Ron Moody's portrayal than his depiction in the novel). Let readers make up their own mind.

 One of several classic Dickens books which I had not previously read, and which eventually worked to the top of my list. I am sure that it was spell-binding social commentary in 1838, but the character of Oliver seemed to me much too good to be true. Any child coming from that sort of brutal institutionalised background would have pretty serious psychological issues; in fact all Oliver need is a comfortable bed and a cuddle and he turns into an angel. The implication is that Oliver, as a Good Boy, is therefore part of the deserving poor, and the Artful Dodger and so on, as Bad Boys, are part of the undeserving poor, a distinction I find rather invidious - copper-fastened at the end by the fact that Oliver does inherit wealth, but on condition of his goodness rather than his absolute rights as his parents' son. There seems little room for redemption, and Nancy, the fallen woman who tries to redeem herself, gets killed off. The portrayal of Fagin must surely have appeared gratuitously anti-Semitic even by 1838 standards. I'm glad that I have read and enjoyed later Dickens, because I think if I had started here I would have written him off.

First, let me disclose that I listened to an unabridged (13 CD's) audio version of this tale, published by Tantor and read by Simon Vance. Vance's voicings of the characters (and there are a lot of voices to master here) are truly amazing. They really brought this novel to life in a way that I never would have experienced had a I simply read the novel and "heard" the dialogue with my mind's ear. Here's his website. http://simonvance.com/ The guy is a true pro. Now, on to Mr. Dickens... 
 Amazing novel, this. Somewhat contrived in plot (no spoilers, here, folks) in terms of seemingly coincidental relationships, but filled with memorable characters - mostly criminals. Jack Dawkins, (a/k/a "The Artful Dodger"), the evil and scheming Fagin, the profane and brutal Bill Sikes, the tragic Nancy, have achieved something akin to literary immortality. Dickens of course delivers with razor skill harsh social criticism and mocking satire of England's workhouses for paupers, the hypocrisy and corruption of the "parochial"/church administered "homes" for orphans and indigent children. Dickens describes in rich prose and often lurid detail the cruelty of an early industrialized urban society -- the filth and degradation of certain parts of London (Islington and Bethnal Green mentioned in the novel were still rough areas of the city when I spent time there in the early 1970's), the harshness of its treatment of the poor, and the rough justice meted out to criminals, petty and otherwise, with little of what we would consider due process. 
 Oliver Twist himself is somewhat overwrought as a character. His dialogue with other characters sounds too mature and refined, almost "precious", given the circumstances of his birth and early upbringing -- almost as though he were speaking in blank verse in an Elizabethan play. Dickens intended, I suppose, for this to serve as a contrast to the rough an slangy speech of the Dodger and his confederate, Charlie Bates. The character of Rose Maylie, a refined 17-year-old pure and beautiful heroine (the "mirror" of the coarse and decidedly unrefined Nancy), speaks in such emotionally ornate and contrived sentences, as to to make you want to slap her, God bless her. Many readers and critics have also criticized Dickens' repeated references throughout the novel to Fagin as "the Jew." Yeah, it got old, but Dickens does not caricature Fagin's supposed ethnicity; if anything, Fagin is probably the deepest and most complex character in the story, treated with no small amount of sympathy, I think, as much a victim as victimizer in the final analysis. I never saw the movie "Oliver", so I didn't have images of Ron Moody (Fagin) and Oliver Reed (Bill Sikes) swimming in front of me to spoil my imagination. 
 Despite some flaws, this is a compelling story: "fiercely imagined" as we now often describe a novelist's efforts, and worth the effort to experience, whether you listen to it or read it. For Dickens' sophomore effort in the realm of novels, you have to marvel at his genius. 
 Now on to David Copperfield!

Every once in a while a book comes along that you know will be one of your favorite books of all time. This is one of them. I borrowed the hardcover from the library -- checked it out the day it was released -- and will have to go buy it at full price, just so I can re-read it several times whenever I feel inclined. Which come to think about it, is exactly what has happened to The World According to Garp over the years. If John Irving isn't our greatest living author, it's only because his subjects aren't likely to be everyone's cup of tea. Do you get the sense that I adore this book yet? 
 It was so hard to finish this book, because it's written in a way where there can't be a sequel, and I just never want to leave Billy Dean's world. I'm jealous of Elaine in the same way that Tom was jealous of Madame Bovary. Even though I was around other people, I couldn't stop from bursting into laughter at some of the delightful situations and phrases found throughout the book. I've read quite a bit of John Irving over the years, but this also reminds me that I have to go back and read everything I haven't read yet, and re-read the ones I already love, like Garp. Maybe I'll even watch some of the movies too, like Rob Lowe in Hotel New Hampshire. 
 I can't imagine anyone I'm friends with not loving this book. My only quibble is that he does skip around a fair amount, but given that the way Billy tells his life story is exactly how someone telling their life story would tell it -- not perfectly linear -- maybe it's not even fair to call it a quibble. I'd give it a 10 if I could.

John Irving has done it once again with his 13th novel. He has created three dimensional characters that pass through the decades with emotions and incredible depth. This is probably Irving's first gay, bi-sexual, transgender, straight primary novel that deals with all the taboos of the subject with informative, heart felt narrative. 
 'In One Person' is extremely well written and moves at a rather good pace considering the seventy year span of the novel. Opening just after WWII and carrying through to the present day, he weaves back and forth between time frames without contentions nor at the risk of losing narrative focus. 
 The sex within the book is very plentiful and he does cover some quite taboo sex that includes straight, gay, transgender and bi-sexual with an astute awareness. He never gets down and dirty with it but he captures the act with affirmation. He also doesn't make any excuses and neither is it highlighted to cheapen the story. It is used as a natural narrative that needs no explanation, the characters are what they are. A bit like people, they are what they are, not everything has to have a reason. 
 If you are new to Irving, this book will feel incredibly fresh and new. If you are a long standing fan, like myself - the novel has some drawbacks. 
 There are many fragments from his other works. 'The World According to Garp', 'The Hotel New Hampshire', 'A Prayer for Owen Meaney', 'Son of the Circus', 'Widow for a Year', etc plot points all make an appearance. Vienna plays a part, Amsterdam, parental situations, wrestling, New England, etc all play an important so it is very deep rooted in Irving's sense of writing. At times, this comes across as endearing but at times, you do kind of wish he try something slightly different. I do understand that a writer writes from what he knows about but I am sure that in the past forty years, he has experienced something a bit more to tie his characters together. As I said, if you are a fan of Irving, this will mean something to you. 
 All in all, the book ending comes at a natural point and is filled resolution without being cheated or weakened. I would highly recommend this book as it is very thought provoking, eccentric characters, real emotions, great worldly settings and probably the best gay fiction novel to be written by a heterosexual ever. This is a must read.

I was looking very forward to reading this book before I got it. The last John Irving I had read was The Cider House Rules and My Movie Business about making the movie for Cider. Both were good books, not excellent, but very good. Irving has a unique style of writing, some writers occasionally go off on tangents, for Irving the whole book is a tangent. The plot is moved ahead by rememberances of this that have passed in a usually non-linear remberence. 
 What I ultimaely liked about Cider House was that you could write a novel about abortion and make a 500 page book contain 495 pages that were not about abortion, with so many side roads and side stories you get lost on the way. But the thing that I think held the book together was the abortion thread, that despite the many pages about things like the main character's first fumblings with a girl in a drive in movie theatre ( I remember that from reading the book 10 years ago), the book was going somewhere. 
 With In One Person, who knows where the book is going, and frankly, who cares. I got this along with two other people I know and all of us have put it down and stopped reading. I had been determined to plow through until I hit page 180, and the person the narrator had sex with was just to ridiculous, so unbeliveable, I gave up. I am done. 
 The main character is not relatable or nice, or anything other than bland. The only character I cared about was Kitenridge and even him I couldn't remember his first name - and he says in the beginning nothing ever happened with Kitenridge so I knew it wasn't going anywhere. 
 The book is a hodge-podge of genders and crushes and Shakespere and summers in Austria, but it really doesn't go anywhere, it's not going to be anything you care about, and while I would have brief moments where I cared about what happened, something else would turn me off and I would always be looking for any excuse to read something else. 
 Untimately as I said, despite all this I was still determined to get through it, then the sex on page 180 happened and I was done. The spell, however lightly cast, was broken.

The novel has a breadth and depth spanning four generations and the subtle and not so subtle shifts in attitudes towards sexuality and gender. Typical Irving themes are present: wrestling, cross-dressing, New England boarding schools, complex mother/son relationships and a cast of eccentrics. 
 The main critique I have is Irving seems to be trying way too hard to get his tolerance point across. The narrative lagged if it drifted towards the preachy. The eccentric characters more than made up for this indiscretion. 
 I listened to the vast majority of this on audio, while reading just a few chapters. The audio experience can differ from the written experience. My wife is reading the book and is driven nuts by the repetition and sloppy writing. I realized that this book had been a remarkably easy listen because of the very same repetition that made the reading a slog. The book could easily have been half the size and covered the same story and plot. 
 Also, apparently in my heterosexual bent, I missed Irving's lapses into male hetero stereotypes of bisexual and homosexual men. They didn't jump out at me like they did to my wife -- lisps, crying, predatory older homosexuals, etc. Even in a paean to tolerance, stereotyping falls flat.

In One Person is reminiscent of The World According to Garp in many ways: the absent biological parent, the New England boys boarding school, wrestling as the prominent sport, Billy's studies abroad in Vienna, Austria, and characters that Irving terms "sexual suspects." In Garp, the sexual suspects-people who have been unfairly relegated to the margins of mainstream society because of their sexual preferences and/or gender identity-play semi-marginal roles; In One Person places them center stage (in more ways than one). At the heart of In One Person is a request for tolerance (at the very least) of all people, no matter their sexual preferences or gender identity, and a call for us not to succumb to the very human trait of labeling and categorizing each other-an act which strips us of our individuality and our complexity. As Miss Frost puts it so well, "My dear boy, don't put a label on me-don't make me a category before you get to know me!" 
 [...] 
 In One Person incorporates everything I have come to love about John Irving's writing-great storytelling; wonderful characters; humor, heartbreak, compassion, and everything in between. I highly recommend it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I picked this book up because of the LGTBQA+ characters, and shortly after I did, #DiverseAThon was announced. Perfect timing! I could use it for my first book of the week. Sounded like a great plan at the time... 
 ...Unfortunately, doing so turned out to be the biggest cautionary tale of reading #OwnVoices books of all time. John Irving is not gay. He is not transgender. And it shows in the writing of this book. Be careful when you are picking "diverse" books. Try to pick books by actual POC authors, LGBTQA+ authors, mentally ill authors. Don't only pick authors who are writing about those characters. 
 The following is unpleasant, so I'm going to put a trigger warning on it. But I want to illustrate WHY you should be careful about reading books by authors who actually come from the cultures you are reading about. I'm going to gray out the triggering stuff. Skip that, if you need to. 
 This is not a book that is kind to transgender people. The narrator is so conflicted about his own sexuality and desires that while he is not completely homophobic-he IS sort of transphobic. He is sexually attracted to those he calls "she-males" and "transexuals." At one point he dismissively tells us that he won't use the term transgender because they didn't ever call them that and so why should he change now? 
 ...Are you cringing yet?... 
 He speaks about the transgender women in his life cruelly, as if they are something Other. He does not understand them, why they would want to change the bodies he finds perfect and is offended by that need. They are his playthings and not people he totally respects. 
 Now, the narrator was extremely unreliable. Probably one of the most unreliable narrators I have ever read, even against Harry Potter. We are completely in this guy's head. But I still don't find that as an excuse for such awful narration. 
 The other stomach churning thing about this book is the multiple adult-youth sexual relationships. The only reason I call them that and not the abuse they actually are is that the narrator sees them as consensual relationships. He sees them as seduction. He has his own, after hearing about two of his friends having them...but again, unreliable narrator...he does not realize how uncomfortable his friends are, and how not seduced they were. 
 I stopped reading this book about 3/4 of the way through. As the narrator grew older, the story only grew worse, and less interesting. I left him in Europe bullying a vomiting, anxious friend. 
 I get the general idea of where Irving was headed with his novel, and why he wrote this the way he did. But it was too disgusting to finish.

Do you ever finish a book and want to hug the author? That's what I wanted to do after finishing In One Person. I didn't think John Irving would ever write another novel as full of life as Garp, The Cider House Rules or A Prayer For Owen Meaney. How happy I am that I was wrong about that. Billy is unapologetic about who he loves and is attracted to. Fortunately, he has the right people in his life to allow him to develop this way. But as usual with Irving, there is an undertoad of menace. The Kitteredge mystery had me burning through the pages. At times, I wondered if there was a little too much Shakespeare and Ibsen in the sections on Bill's theatrical upbringing, but literary allusiveness is one of Irving's charms. Sure, the parts of the book that describe Bill's childhood are more fully developed than his sketchily filled in later years, but this is a minor quibble. He follows even the smallest characters in the book to their final fates, leading to a lot of moving epilogues. But no one in the book compares to Miss "Al" Frost, the heroine John Irving was born to create and who he has been preparing us for in his other twelve novels. John Irving has written a novel which is perfect for our times. In One Person is a book that entertains and that will also save lives with its prescription for self-acceptance.

Like his last few books, this one feels off-key in places. Here we have another Irving novel with the New England prep school upbringing, the quirky relatives, the missing biological father, the wrestling, the writing about writing, the cross dressers and other sexual edge cases. The first-person narrator is bisexual -- a twist! The book takes us through the early days of AIDS for its dramatic turning point, but others have told that story better. Irving always seems to be pulling his emotional punches right when things seem about to get interesting. I keep waiting for a return to the books with the sweep and impact of "Owen Meaney," "Cider House Rules," or "Garp," but maybe Irving has just run out of steam.

I cannot believe that I have given an Irving novel less than 3 stars. If it wasn't for the fact that the "modern day Dickens" wrote this book, I don't believe I would have finished it. Upon completing the book, I placed it beside the author's other great works and I immediately looked at all the other titles. 
 Has Irving written a book that I have disliked more? 
 Now, I admit that I did put "A Son of a Circus" aside after about 20 pages and picked up another book. And, I have never gotten back to it. The subject matter (India, dwarves,) didn't really interest me at the time. "Water Method Man", "Setting Free the Bears" and "150 lb Marriage" I have never picked up. But, now I am on a quest. I will pick up these novels, and try to read "A Son of a Circus" because dammit they have to be better than "In One Person". 
 The plot is very basic. And, what's worse is that it is predictable. To the point that you say outloud: "are you kidding me? Now, I know that this is coming across as a very harsh review, but, that is because of the author. I expected a lot more from this book. An alternate title should have been: "A Touch of Frost". Miss Frost is the character that I was most interested in. But, she was thrown aside after her involvement with the narrator was used up, and had aided in that character following his predictable path. 
 Maybe the book is suppose to reflect a parody on it's subject matter. By this I mean that the majority of the family, and friends that Bill Abbott has are either gay, lesbian, bi, transexual, or a cross dresser. The fact that the book begins in the 50's, when homophobia and just plain hatred were the norm, I am a firm believer that if the American government had found out that a quaint little Vermont town had this high a percentage of LGBT individuals they would have nuked it. Okay, maybe not that far...but, atleast they would have tested the water supply! 
 I really enjoyed "Middlesex", which dealt with the issue of hemaphrodites. But, I found that the controversial theme in that book blended very well with the plot. 
 Sorry John. I just didn't appreciate this effort. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm gonna pick up my copy of "A Son of a Circus".

When I talk about a book by John Irving, I have a habit of talking about all of his books. Maybe I picked the habit up from my dad, the Irving super fan who first loaned me his books. So I'll say I liked In One Person about as much as I like The 158-Pound Marriage, which is to say less than I liked The Fourth Hand and Until I Find You, but more than I liked Last Night in Twisted River, which comes in last in my ranking mostly for not being memorable, at all. 
 The book is narrated by the protagonist Bill, a man navigating bisexuality over the course of several decades. Sexuality and gender identity are the major topics of the book, but some of the characters didn't seem to have any other characteristics beside their "sexual differences." Bill's lifelong attraction to trans women seemed more like fetishizing than representing, and his reluctance to update his terminology with the times is jarring, if not entirely out-of-character. Then there's the whole *don't label me* business, which is fine, but even if you don't want a label, you should respect the ones that others have chosen for themselves. 
 Some characters were more rounded, even despite their brief appearances- I finished the book wanting to know more about Gee and the cast of Romeo and Juliet, this next generation of LGBTQ activists who Bill hopes he has helped in some way. I even warmed up to Bill by the end, which can happen when you're reading a coming of age novel about an annoying kid who grows into a decent adult. 
 The style is still Irving, which is what I came for- the voice that is unique to the character but also to the author, always the perfect choice of words, the nonlinear chronology and the amazing bald-faced foreshadowing that never takes away the emotional impact (Oh, of course Character A is dying- he told us 300 pages ago that that was going to happen, but buried it well enough that it still a shock when it does happen). I would recommend this one to other die-hard Irving fans. And who knows, maybe a lonely, questioning teenager will find in this novel what Bill found in the books he was borrowing from Miss Frost.
A bisexual Forrest Gump; talky and clumsily plotted, it's not Irving's best. If you like Irving, though, it's still worth your time.

I love John Irving's novels; they depict detailed characterization that is often both humorous and emotional. The story lines are creative, but also speak to some greater societal truths. It was with this in mind that I began reading "In One Person". I wanted to love it; I really did, but as I was reading, I felt that there was something fundamentally missing when compared to Irving's other novels. This one has the story line along with some intriguing themes, but the detailed characterization is missing. It's like the framework of the story is in place, but the meat hasn't been added yet. I want to know more details about the relationships between William and the characters he encounters: his grandfather, Miss Frost, Richard, even his mother. There aren't any holes story-wise; I just want to know more about them.
Penso proprio di non finirlo.

** spoiler alert ** 
 OK. I understand that I'm coming to this book from a place within the LGBT community and the issues in this book are likely a little closer to my heart than the average reader. I also don't think that the things I disliked in this book were unreasonable for me to dislike. 
 While some of the story was implausible - like the fact that just about everyone the main character came into contact with ended up either gay or transgendered, that wasn't my biggest problem. It seemed to me that all of the gay and trans characters had something MAJOR happen to them - as if some sort of trauma caused their deviation from regular straight appropriately-gendered society. There is incest, and bullying and a couple of instances of adult-teen seduction. I was deeply uncomfortable with the cause and effect it all implied. 
 That being said, I did actually enjoy the book. John Irving can spin a really good yarn, even if it is a flawed one. I believe Irving did an excellent job representing the widespread seemingly endless tragedy the AIDS crisis brought to the gay community in the 80s and the horror of having everyone you know die around you. I loved the relationship between Billy and Eileen. Grandpa Harry was, by far, my favorite character. In my head, any movie version would have to cast Allan Arkin! 
 Worth a read, but not as good as his other work.
Not my favorite John Irving at all.
Just made it to page 120. While Irving is one of my favorite authors, sadly this book just didn't do it for me.
I am officially over John Irving. The German, the wrestling...I was surprised there was no bear. Too many times to the well.

Was waiting for the author to quit obsessing over the various sexual abnormalities, peccadilloes and perversions of all the characters and begin the actual story. Well, that IS the actual story! To spare you from all 425 or so pages of this dreck, here is a summary: Some men like to wear bras! Some men want to be women! Some men pass themselves off as women! Wrestling is an incredibly homoerotic sport! AIDS is bad! Reagan was bad! And so on.

This is a novel that meanders. There's no other word for it. In the hands of an aging narrator, the reader is drawn both forward and backwards in the life of Billy Abbott, a bisexual man coming of age (of course) in the 1950s and '60s. Billy's family is darkly quirky and full of more secrets than love. There's a lot of potential there, but it's mostly unexplored. Billy's character begins and ends with one thing: he is attracted to both men and women. His family and friends are painted in relation to how they respond to his sexuality. Billy's bisexuality defines him to the exclusion of anything else, and leaves this well-written book without a plot. Billy is a symbol of his sexual choices, a cultural touchpoint for how the American understanding of sex and gender has changed over time. His experiences are thought provoking and sympathetic, and the writing is sharp and lovely. But there's no story. Billy's character is passive, letting the waves of attraction and loathing wash over him, letting others lead him and make his decisions for him. 
 At the end, I felt like this was more of a message than a novel, an educational piece about how complex a person's sexual relationships can be.

I got about 1/3 of the way through this book and realized I just didn't care about it. I was listening to the audio version and the narrator didn't seem to care about the story either. There are too many good books in the world to spend time finishing ones you don't like.

Definitely read more like a memoir than a novel. At the end I so desperately wanted to find Bill Abbott and thank him personally for sharing his experience. I suppose I will have to settle for writing this review in which I commend writer John Irving for creating a character with a formidable voice and point of view that helped me better accept and understand my own sexuality. One of my social work professors recommended this book to me in order to better prepare me for working with trans* people. I'm not sure if I learned anything new from the book in that regard because I've done a lot on my own to integrate LGBTQ positive and informed care into my practice. However, I would definitely recommend this book to anyone with any curiosity about what it would've been like to grow up gay and/or trans in the 60s and 70s. I would especially recommend this book to anyone wanting more information about bisexuality or (like myself) craving some validation and realistic depiction of what it is to be bisexual.
How did John Irving do this?! Owen Meany energy and power, grown up. Elegiac, thrilling, gorgeous.

John Irving is such an immensely talented writer, one wishes he would show more enthusiasm for his work. A trend that has become more and more tedious in his writing since Son of the Circus is that Irving can't seem to let his characters relate to one another in any way other than sexual attraction. I don't object to this for reasons of prudery (I actually love the idea of more queer characters in mainstream fiction), but it does result in very one-dimensional, dull characters. Take the narrator in this book, for instance. Apart from the fact that he is bisexual, I can't think of a single thing I learned about his personality in the 425 pages of this book. How one misses the colourful and complex characters from Garp and Owen Meany.

Didn't liked it. Dicks, vaginas, can't believe it, haha, it permanently damaged my wish for sex. Ok ok, I'm probably exaggerating, but seems it reflects how some people (with neurosis) see sex. Not delicious with lots of flat, boring problems (about flat boring dicks or vaginas, of course and flat and boring sex), and I like no boring sex. Character doesn't seem to be neurotic, but book is - neurosis expressed in sketchiness. 
 Just read some say it's the stand for same sex marriage or kid adoption. Don't see how that could work, and I know nothing about life in LGBT community, but there is simple answer for any opponent: "not your fucking job to be so overly interested in what's happening in other people beds". Usually who are interested, they are just crazy neurotics having no own life and thus trying to control others. 
 Probably could be done differently. Author lost full fucking crazy magic of testosterone.

Well, I didn't read this long enough to encounter Irving't trademark bear (if there is indeed one in this novel), but I did read long enough to get very weary of the constant sexual longings of the male adolescent narrator -- gay and straight. 
 When I flipped through the upcoming pages, it appeared to be just more of the same. 
 Yawn!
Normally, a big fan of Irving. I did not care for this book, however.

Like many John Irving books, this one took me forever to finish. His character development is amazing. It really made me think about what it would have been like being gay in NYC at the height of the HIV crisis.

I have transgendered relatives so I was not upset about the topic but was concerned that an author whose other books I have enjoyed would foist this book on the public and find a publisher for it was too much. This book was so badly written that I thought Irving had a colleague write it and pen his name to it. The plot was implausible but the characterizations were worse.
I'm sorry. He's just so hopelessly neurotic.
Classic and courageous Irving!

I was quite engrossed by the first half of the book, and I feel like it should have ended with the wrestling scene. The rest of the book seemed more like a halfhearted sequel to everything else. The memoir-feel of the book can sometimes make for lackluster reading at times (especially all the time jumps), but for the most part, I didn't mind it. I think what bothered me about the second half of the book was the inclusion of the modern-day high school characters. It was uplifting, but it had a somewhat generic, Glee aftertaste. It was a huge let-down after the novel's strong beginning.

For the record, I USED to LOOOOVE John Irving. But his last three books haven't been worth the price of admission. 
 Here are his go-to elements: 
 Set in New England? Check! 
 Has an all boys prep school? Check! 
 Has a young man protagonist in love with older man or woman? Check! 
 Has a wrestling team? Check! 
 Does the main character spend time in Austria and/or Germany? Check! 
 C'mon, Irving! You're better than this. Or you used to be. Dig a little deeper. 
 And not to self, I won't be purchasing any more of your books. They'll be from the library from now on.

It took me a really long time to actually be interested in the plot of the story. It took some revelations about halfway through for me to finally care about finishing it. I did find parts of it funny, other parts rather depressing and heartbreaking. 
 I really like some of John Irving's other books, which is why I picked this one up, but in the end it didn't meet my expectations.

I wanted to like this more. I assumed I would. I like big, sprawling novels that introduce us to eccentric characters. Such as Dickens' and Wolfe and Irving. There is much charm in this book and much that I enjoyed. I enjoy the recurring motifs that tell you you've wandered into Irving country: wrestling, New England, characters coming of age, all of which are accounted for here. I appreciate Irving's embrace of diverse sexualities, how he honors them, treats these characters with respect, and generally goes where most straight male writers would fear to go. So what's my problem? 
 There were so many times I felt pulled out of the story by questions or reservations. A small New England town in the 1950s would allow the local librarian to be transsexual, a boy they had known as the star wrestler at the local high school? Really? I decided to accept these things as the world of John Irving. Maybe not true to the way the world was at this time but true to the world Irving has created. But so many of these piled up. When the librarian is caught having sex with an underage boy she loses her job. Not arrested? No matter how the reader feels about this, or who in town supports her, it seems society would demand harsh punishment. There seem to be a huge number of straight men who seem most comfortable wearing female clothing and it's pretty much accepted. I wasn't sure I really knew Billy by the end of the book. I knew his habits, his opinions, but did not have a deep understanding of him as a man. 
 As a gay man, I do appreciate Irving treating diverse sexualities with respect, but this felt more like a fable than a novel of real people. Perhaps that's my problem for wanting a book that Irving didn't write.

John Irving is one of my favorite authors, but I came into this book warily because of the mixed reviews. All in all, I enjoyed it. To me, it was an odd mix of "The World According to Garp" and RENT. It was an engaging story, especially if you go into it expecting to read a story, not to read a political novel. As a political novel, it falls short for me. It doesn't really bring anything new to the table, although I was overjoyed to see bisexual and transgender people represented in a mainstream novel, because it's so rare that that happens. I was so excited by that, and I continue to be. In that respect, I think the book succeeded, in bringing some super marginalized queer identities back to the forefront, at least in literary circles. 
 As a story, like I said, it's similar to Garp and Owen Meany. It goes through the main character's entire life, birth to old age. I was invested, I didn't get bored. It was entertaining enough for me to rate it a four, as a lot of my criticisms are petty and nitpicky. I did love Elaine and Bill's friendship, and it's complications. I always love how Irving writes his main characters relationships with people. They are always complicated and unique and realistic, in my opinion. I think he did an excellent job of showing homophobia/queerphobia/transphobia across the scale of it. I think a lot of people think these phobias have one face, when really they have many, and I think Irving showed that well. His characters are well-written, as they always are. It's an extremely well-written book, and I enjoyed it. 
 Also, as hard as these scenes were to get through, the portion of the book devoted the AIDS epidemic, in my opinion, was wonderful. I read my mother a few passages (my mother knew quite a few people who died of AIDS, as she was heavily involved in the gay community once upon a time), and she expressed how realistic they were. Realistic enough it was almost impossible for her to listen to them without getting emotional. Yes, this book makes it seem like everyone was dying AIDS when many did survive. However, I think this generation is forgetting how awful AIDS is and was (it's making a resurgence among gay populations who, in some cases, are attracting it ON PURPOSE), so maybe we need a reminder. Irving did a great job of showing how it must have felt to see so many around you dying. I think it was very effective that he focused on the people who did die rather than those that survived. 
 That being said, another writer character, Irving? Really? And another thing, while I understand Bill was heavily involved in the gay community (and that during much of the years this book takes place, queer people really didn't have non-queer friends most of the time), the sheer number of gay and transgender people who happened to be in Bill's class at First Sister Academy seemed unrealistic. There were too many of them, it felt odd to me. I think the tipping point was Kittredge, at the end. The discovery that he had gender reassignment surgery just ended up being one too many for me. 
 My final criticisms are that I don't think the ending was as strong as it could, and should, have been. It seemed to sort of end really suddenly, without any real closure. Normally, I accept that as an author's choice, but in a book that tells the story of a lifetime of one person, closure is important to me. And finally, the scene where Bill meets his father and his father's lover seemed out of nowhere, and I don't know if it really added anything.

I sm s John Irving fan. I really enjoyed Last night in Twisted River and many of his other books. I was very excited to pick this one up from the library and start reading....but it was not good. I don't know how anyone can make it through this book. It was almost like the whole point of the book was to see how many times you can say the names of sexual body parts. It was just inbearable to read and not good.

i loved it! i am officially a Jojo Moyers fan. i loved the sense of humor loved the romance in it and how it was not the main focus but still it was there. loved the story and where she took it and how she developed it. it started out slow and had some slow parts in between but it was bearable. overall a great book and story.

One of my favorite books that I read in 2014. It's sort of silly and outlandish in plot, but you don't care, because you're just riveted, wanting to read it as quickly as possible. Jess is a down-on-her-luck mom of two (her daughter, Tanzie, plus stepson Nicky), whose husband has abandoned her so she has to work two jobs to make ends meet. She meets Ed, a millionaire who is also a bit down-on-his-luck (oh just some investment fraud charges and such) while cleaning his vacation home. Eventually Ed comes to their rescue (literally, as the family is sitting on the side of the road) and helps drive them to a math competition for young Tanzie, who is a maths expert. Along the way, a lot happens. You'd think the novel would be pat and predictable, but it's really just... lovely. And one of the few books I've really loved that I actually think would make a good movie, provided I can approve all casting choices, of course.

This is exactly the sort of book to read on a day you feel pessimistic, or question whether you might be overly optimistic. Also a great read if you are currently in love, madly or otherwise, or wish you could be in love.
Touchy
Nothing terribly wrong with this book, but it's a reminder that I'm just not a big fan of predictable romance novels, especially the "man saves the woman" type

Eh, this book was okay. Closer to a 2.75. It was WAY too similar in theme and style to Moyes' other books. Annoying main characters, completely predictable. I'd give it only 2 stars, but I'll admit that it was readable and slightly entertaining, so it gets 2.75.

This story was slow going at first for me. I had trouble seeing how the story lines would intersect at first and then it all started to make sense. I had a perpetual ache in my throat for the difficult things that were taking place for the main characters. This was another fast read for me. Once I started it, I had to read through to the end so that I could find out what would happen. It was very well written, it didn't have the same emotional impact on me that "The Girl You Left Behind" or "Me Before You" did, but it was still a great story about overcoming obstacles and overwhelming odds in more than just one way. I really can't give specifics of the story will be given away...you will have to read it and get that satisfied feeling all on your own.
Not the most honorable characters, but laugh out loud funny. I devoured it!

She just keeps getting better and better. I loved all of the characters, but especially Jess, an eternal optimist who I could only hope to be like in trying times. I devoured this book and there is nothing like a book that makes you laugh AND cry, sometimes in the same paragraph! Can't wait to meet her next week, hopefully so that I can tell her face to face what a great reading experience she gives her fans.
Entertaining. This book is definitely chick-lit. It was predictable and cliche. A good beach day book.

After falling in love with Me Before You, I was eager to read another book by Jojo Moyes. One Plus One was my follow-up attempt and it was a very enjoyable romance, but somewhat predictable. It simply lacked the magic of Me Before You, but I found it enjoyable nonetheless.

JM is becoming one of my favorite authors. I've read "Me Before You" and "The Girl You Left Behind" and really enjoyed both books. This one topped them. Her books are sweet, heartbreaking, not all "warm and fuzzy, unicorns and rainbows!" which I appreciate and think add a relateable quality to her stories. I cannot wait to read more by her.

I don't know, I just loved it a lot. It wasn't perfect but I loved it. The characters were real and lovable and sweet and they deserved so much better than they got but they were perfect. I didn't like the beginning because Ed seemed like a total asshole but god, the character development was great and he fit perfectly into the family. I really, really loved Nicky and Jess and Tanzie and even Ed (and Norman the dog) and there was one chapter that was the best example of sexual tension I've ever read. I definitely cried a couple times in the book (either tearing up or a few short gasps at one part) but the whole thing was just very good. The ending felt a little rushed, especially since there seemed to be multiple climaxes throughout the long story but everything was perfect, really. The plot was smooth and the dialogue was great and mostly everything was completely relatable. The three day car ride was wonderful and pitch perfect -- it just had this really great, comfortable feeling, and the plot just kept building and building and building -- so much so that the ending wasn't that satisfying, but the process of getting there was amazing. Every part of the writing had so much life and just reading back on random pages there is just so much comedy and reliability and honesty and vulnerability and hiding and comfort and happiness and sadness. Every single sentence has some sort of mood and they are all perfect. 
 The most memorable moments: 
 -Nicky sees an asshole teasing his sister and gets fucking even 
 "One of the teachers stepped in front of him then, one hand raised, his face questioning. 'Excuse me? Did I just see you--' 
 "'Wishing him luck? Yes. Great kid. Great kid.' Nicky shook his head, as if in admiration, then headed for the Gents to fetch Tanzie." (pg 216-217) 
 -Ed finally visits his sick father after months of telling off from his sister 
 "The woman looked at him, disbelieving. Her jaw dropped, and for a moment Jess thought she was going to say something. 
 "'It's good to s--" he began. From nowhere, the woman's hand shot out, smacking Ed across the face. The sound actually echoed down the corner. 
 "Ed staggered backward, clutching his cheek. 'What the--' 
 "'You fucking wanker,' she said. 'You fucking, fucking wanker.'" (pg 260) 
 -After all that shit: 
 "'See, Mum?' He said, chewing on a piece of bread. 'You were right. Things can change.' 
 "Jess say very still. She looked at the newspaper, then back at him, until he realized what he had called her, and she could see him coloring, hoping she wouldn't make a big deal out of it. So she swallowed and then she wiped both her eyes with the heels of her palms and stared at her plate for a minute before she began eating again. 'Right,' she said, her voice strangled. 'Well, that's good news. Very good news.'" (321) 
 I more than teared up here 
 And I cried a few sobs when Nicky seemed like he might actually forgive his shitty dad because his dad did not deserve forgiveness of and ownership over those two beautiful kids
Typical feel-good book, with the depth of a well-made soap opera. Wasn't bored, I finished it, but it will leave me next to nothing.
An entertaining read. Good to read on vacation.

Jojo Moyes is such a clever author. How did she weave those characters and then entwine their lives together. This book actually made me laugh out loud on more than one occasion. Something I rarely do when reading. I cry usually but that's a different story. 
 I really loved reading this book.

DNF at p.102 I just didn't click with this one. 100 pages in and they finally begin the road trip. It took 100 pages for the author to lay out the back story of the two main characters and I still don't connect with either of them. It was just boring to me.

Nothing life changing here, but a solid little plot and a memorable couple characters. 
 A struggling family of a mom, a very smart daughter, and a socially different step son live in a not nice neighborhood. The mom is a maid. She cleans house for this successful man who is getting sued for insider trading and his father is seriously ill. The daughter gets the chance of a lifetime to go to an amazing school and they need to raise funds, so they enter her in a competition in Scotland. Their car breaks down on the way, in swoops the successful guy and he drives them. The plot is fun and perfect for the beach. I really enjoyed the characters. The stubborn mom who doesn't want to ask for help, the quirky smart girl, the nerdy / heart of gold guy, the distant but observant and loving son.

Ditched by her husband, living on the breadline in a housing association estate, 27 year old Jessica Thomas finds providing for her family to be a constant battle. She tries her best, she sees herself as a glass half full person, but she never stops working - or worrying. In her job as a cleaner alongside her friend Nathalie, and her second job as a barmaid, she gets glimpses into other peoples' lives and they never match up to her own. Daughter Tanzie, 10 and a maths prodigy, has the opportunity to go to public school via a scholarship. Goth stepson Nicky, a sulky 16, is bullied at school by the local hooligans and finds it hard to cope, seeking solace in cannabis. The scholarship will remove Tanzie from the bullies' orbit, but how will Jess ever find the money? 
 Moyes has a knack of putting together "damaged" individuals who would ordinarily never have a relationship with each other. One of them is always "out of the other's league" and this person has to go through a humbling, life-changing experience to effectively "bring them down" before a relationship can blossom. Enter Ed Nicholls. He's a wealthy computer nerd with a massive problem; he's facing jail for insider trading. Their worlds collide when Jess cleans his South Coast holiday retreat, setting off a chain of events that are quite unbelievable. Ed's good deed is indeed very odd. However, he has been a victim of his own weakness with a former university crush, driven, I think, by his determination to finally win "the one that got away". 
 Faced with finding the contribution to the scholarship, Jess finds out that all Tanzie has to do is to win a maths competition. Small problem - it's in Aberdeen and how will they get there? Somehow Jess persuades Ed to drive them there - the whole family, including Norman the dog. This seemed unbelievable to me, although without it there would be no story. All kinds of madness then ensue as a bonkers road trip gets under way. 
 I think we fall into the trap of thinking authors are always sympathetic to their main protagonist. Were we meant to like Jess? I'm not sure that I did. Having persuaded Ed to drive them heaven knows how many miles, she hides from him the fact she has pocketed PS800 that dropped out of his wallet when drunk, proceeds to sit with her feet up on the dashboard of his car (that image is horrid) and gets them all into so many scrapes we think she's bonkers. A lot happens in these four days; Jess comes face to face with her ex-husband Marty, a completely ridiculous and unsympathetic individual who was only included to complete the story arc, allowing Jess to move on. The best storyline belonged to Nicky. It was great to see him come out of his shell under Ed's influence and out of his usual environment. But, my most favourite character of all was Norman the dog. 
 This was an amusing read, and on the whole kept my interest, but it worked better for me as a funny road trip than a romance. I thought the love element happened far too quickly, and felt it quite irresponsible and selfish of Jess as a parent to sleep with a complete stranger in front of her children. (Not literally, but they knew what was going on). I thought it took the theme of the kindness of strangers just a little TOO far and I really didn't like it. This author seems to have a theme of pitching together characters who wouldn't touch each other with a bargepole without some cataclysmic event happening to make them "in each other's league". In his "Me Before You" life, Ed wouldn't have looked twice at Jess. It was also completely morally wrong of Jess to have stolen from Ed. His reaction was reasonably justified, but I think the old Ed wouldn't have forgiven her; she wouldn't even have been on his radar. 
 It was our book club read and I felt it well worth reading, though somewhat unrealistic in the romance stakes.
Another astounding masterpiece by Jojo Moyes. I couldn't get over Tanzie; very jealous of her love and excellence in math. She was one of my favorite characters along with Ed.

This was very different from the other books I've read from Jojo Moyes. This book offered a more lighthearted story with real life hurdles rather than the hard truth and despair she tends to serve up with many of her others. I really loved the characters, each one was brought to life in such a great way. This story was heartwarming and fun, but nothing spectacular, a great summer read!
A lovely romatic story about a family with a dog and their memorable trip to Scotland with Ed.

I don't want to rate this. It's just not my genre. It was entertaining up to the point where I was constantly thinking "enough already" for the "coincidendes". I liked the girl being the math geek and the boy being the goth and the main character being a tough woman though.
Not the most poetic or the most complex plot, but the characters will live with me for a long, long time.

This book was really similar to Jojo Moyes' first book, Me Before You, in that the characters were likable and the love story parts cute, but definitely not overwhelming. The writing was good, but not great, and the plot was interesting in the way that you actually look forward to reading the book instead of kinda bemoaning it until you are immersed in the story again. I liked Tanzie a lot-- she's definitely my favorite. I like how in the UK they say "maths," instead of math. I like how this book was definitely made for an older audience not because it is explicit at all, but because it deals with a divorced man in a business scam and a single mother of 2. I like reading books like this because the characters seem more real. They are responsible for food and money and more money (enough to pay for St. Anne's, at least). Norman was a nice touch, and I liked hearing about his antics a lot. I liked that he was a big part of the family and Moyes took the time to write about him instead of just inserting prettily into the pages that they had a dog. While the ending tied up really nicely for the characters, it was probably highly unrealistic, but I do like a good, happy ending. Jess was also really relatable and I appreciated character because we actually saw the kinds of bills and problems she faces. Most of the time, books ignore things like that because who wants to hear about poor people's problems? Some complaints: the voices of all the characters were the same, and Moyes could have done a better job trying to make them sound differently. The whole plot line of Jess' ex with a new gf was cliche, and the overall writing of the book could have been better (ie, more adjectives are needed). Still, fans of her first book would definitely like this one, and I'm glad people are reading One Plus One. I feel like the story of a poor, desperate single mother and her children is not told as much as it should be, and I feel like older audiences would definitely be able to relate. Kudos to writing this, Moyes.
The story line was okay. It was too much language for my preference.

Actually, I'd say this one is a little less than a 4. It was slow getting started but once underway it was good. I had a hard time remembering all the characters and keeping track of everything and everyone. Once they all got together and the story really got going it was hard to put down. The ending was a bit predictable but how they got there wasn't. The book renews one's faith in human nature and the need to pitch in and help one another. There's nothing like taking a look at life from someone else's perspective. My favorite Moyes book is still Me Before You.
A little too "Harlequin romance" for me.
Heartwarming! I loved to read this so much!

I liked One Plus One by Jojo Moyes but it wasn't one of my favourites. I went into the novel super exited, honestly jumping up and down when I got accepted from Netgalley to read a copy. Maybe it was because I had super high expectations or maybe it was because I thought One Plus One was a different kind of story (based on the back of the book review) but either way I came out of the novel happy and pretty satisfied...unfortunately I didn't feel like telling everyone it's a must-read. 
 One Plus One is about the messy lives of our two main characters, Jess Thomas and Ed Nicholls. Jess is a single mom with two kids (Tanzie and Nicky), a massive dog named Norman, two jobs, and an ex-husband who does not help support the family. Ed seems to have it all, a vacation home, money, his own company, and a satisfied work life, yet he recently got himself into a ton of trouble that has the chances of shattering everything he knows. These two characters eventually cross paths and end up on a road trip to Scotland to take Jess' daughter Tanzie to a math competion. The book progresses as each character (Jess, Ed, Tanzie, and Nicky) hit a new obstacle and attempt to overcome it. The ending was okay...I wish there was a bit more details but it gave a pretty little picture of how life is moving for everyone. 
 I work in a bookstore and cannot tell you how often I hear what a fantastic writer JoJo Moyes is...yet I haven't read anything by her. I thought One Plus One sounded like a perfect introduction to her. I believed the novel was a light fiction story just right for the summer, and although that description does fit I don't think I'd find myself re-reading the novel. Personally, I was looking for a cute story, and instead found a book about tough life choices and situations that wrapped up in a happy way. 
 I would still like to recommend this book to everyone. The writing is superb and the story has nice life lessons. I just found that the book didn't fit the picture I had of it in my head, and therefore didn't live up to what I thought would happen. Maybe one day when I feel like reading a lighter, lesson-based novel I'll give One Plus One another shot. 
 A copy of this novel was provided by the publisher through NetGalley in return for an honest review.

This is the second Moyes book I've read and I really like her style. These are fun, quick, quirky reads. I shed a few tears and laughed pretty hard several times while reading this one. Both heartbreaking and heartwarming.

Somehow, this is the second book I've read by Jojo Moyes. (Look, I was bored at work. Don't judge.) (Ok, maybe judge.) 
 Having read, and actively disliked, two separate novels by her, I'm starting to get a hang of what exactly is going wrong in her books. 
 Number one, all of the side characters are awful. Like, unrealistically so. Everyone is an utter monster to an unbelievable degree. From the demonic neighbors to the evilest bad dad to the worst ex ever to repulsive random strangers encountered on the road, every single side character is despicable to a degree not normally witnessed together. 
 Number two, the main characters are also pretty awful. Despite Moyes' attempts to make her two leads likable yet flawed, I rather disliked both of them. Jess and Ed are kind of irritating to read about. They just aren't that interesting. Even reasonably likable characters, like ten-year-old math whizz Tanzie, became irritating by proximity. 
 Not to mention when Jess and Ed finally consummate their nonexistent sexual tension, it's when Jess is high and has just crashed a car. Calling that dubious consent is being generous. Wow, Ed. Just wow. 
 I need to stop doing this to myself. Even if I am bored at work.

reference_books.review_text:

 Bu kitapta tahmin edersiniz ki pek de iyi islenmemis. Jake kitabin basinda kalbinin sahibiyken, Kacey'nin Travis'e karsi bos olmadigini anlamasi biraz damdan duser gibi oldu. Fazla hizliydi. Sevmedim. O hisler cok guclu de verilmemisti ustelik. 
 Yani yillardir bir adama asik oldugunuzu dusunuyorsunuz. Sonra bir hafta sonu onun yillardir gormediginiz abisini goruyorsunuz. Adam kasli, yakisikli... Ah bir de gamzeleri var. Ve bam! Bir anda ona asik oldugunuzu anliyorsunuz. 
 Yani okurken... Kamoooooonnnn... moduna girmeniz olasi. Adam kasli ve cok yakisikli oldugu icin mi birinden digerine dondun diye dusunuyor insan. 
 Keske biraz daha uzun olsaydi ve o ikilem, duygu gecisleri gercekten guclu islenebilseydi. Cok kotuydu diyemem. Ama beklentimi karsilamadi. :)

reference_books.title: Bad Romeo (Starcrossed, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Vay canina! 
 Once bir durup, derin nefes almam gerek. 
 Gercekten! 
 Cok guzeldi. 
 Cok. Cok. Cok guzeldi! 
 Kitapla ilgili beklentim cok yuksekti. Cok sevmek istiyordum. Ama bir taraftan da hayal kirikligi yaratabilecegi durumu vardi ki, kabul etmek istemiyordum. Son birkac kitapta oyle olmustu ne yazik ki. 
 Neyse efendim... Yoruma geceyim. :D 
 Kitabi Cassie'nin bakis acisindan okuyoruz. Cassie Taylor ve Ethan Holt universitede tiyatro bolumundeler. Ethan'in gecmisiyle ilgili sakladigi bazi sirlar, daha da onemlisi onune gecemedigi korkular var. Ancak buna ragmen Cassie'ye karsi koyamiyor. Ne zaman uzaklasmayi denese, hemen sonra daha hizli bir sekilde ona cekiliyor ve bu yuzden de kendinden nefret ediyor. 
 Cassie gorup gorebileceginiz en acik sozlu kadin karakter. Sacma sapan triplerle karsisindaki erkegi yormuyor. Hatta aksine, adamimiz ondan uzak kalmak icin deli gibi cabalarken, Cassie onun uzerine gidiyor. Onu sinirlendiriyor, tutkuyla yanip tutusmasini sagliyor ve onu nasil istedigini asla ama asla inkar etmiyor. Ve onun o edepsiz ic sesi... :D Gercekten harikaydi. Acikcasi yazari boyle sevilesi bir karakter yarattigi icin kiskandigimi soylemeliyim. Kadin karakterlerin sevilmesini saglamak bence ciddi bir yetenek.. :P 
 Romeo ve Juliet'i sahneledikleri surec, ozellikle provalari harikaydi. Ethan'in surundugunu, savastigini ama her defasinda yenik dustugunu gormek cok eglenceliydi. Kiskancliklari sapsik sapsik siritmama neden oldu. :D 
 Amaaaaaa... Gel gelelim hala sirlarimizin tamami aciga cikmadi. Ethan'in yaptigi okuzlugu neden ve nasil yaptigini hic bilmiyoruz. 2. kitapta ogrenecegimizi umuyorum. Ama bu sekilde olmasinin hosuma gittigini de soylemeden edemeyecegim. Beklemek guzel olacak, hissediyorum. :D 
 Spoiler vermeden yorumumu bitireyim bence. :D Sadece sunu soyleyebilirim. Bu kitabi kesinlikle okumaniz gerek. Yani okumadan ne demek istedigimi anlayamazsiniz. :D 
 Bad Romeo uzun zamandir gercekten her satirini ayila bayila okudugum nadir kitaplardandi. Kikirdadim, kahkaha attim, sinirlendim, gozlerim dolu dolu oldu ve her defasinda gozlerimden kalpcikler fiskirdi. :D Ethan Holt ve Cassie Taylor ile tanismak beni inanilmaz sarsti. 
 Ethan'in icinde yatan o gizem, indirmeyi basaramadigi koruma kalkani ve bunun ardindaki zayiflik, beni gercekten cok etkiledi. 
 Ayrica kitabin bir gecmisi bir gunumuzu anlatmasi da ayrica hosuma gitti. Sanirim flashbackli anlatimlari nasil sevdigimi bilmeyen yoktur. :P

 "Benim kadar inatci olup da guvensizliklerin kazanmasina izin verme. Birak da biz kazanalim. Cunku beni sevmenin berbat bir risk oldugunu ve ihtimalin dusuk oldugunu biliyorum ama sana sunu belirtmeliyim ki ben, hic suphesiz varim. Denesem de seni sevmeyi birakamazdim. 
 Beni inciteceginden hala cok korkuyor muyum? Tabii ki de. Muhtemelen senin de benim seni incitecegimden korktugun kadar.

Mitoloji sever misiniz? 
 Ben bu konuyla ilgili cok fazla kitap okumasam da, her zaman ilgimi cekmistir. 
 Pegasus Yayinlari 'ndan cikan KARANLIGIN EFENDILERI SERISI de iste tamamen bu konudan yola cikiyor. Mitolojiden. 
 Pandora'nin Kutusunu acarak iblisleri dunyaya salan, guclu, seksi ve karsi konulmaz savascilarin hikayeleri anlatiliyor bu seride. Ve Tanrilar bu iblisleri onlarin bedenlerine yerlestirerek hepsini lanetliyor. 
 Siddet, Olum, Aci, Suphe, Gazap, Yalan, vs vs... Tum bunlar iblislerin ozellikleri ve savascilarimiz da iste bu ozelliklerle lanetleniyorlar. 
 Macera ve tutkunun enfes bir sekilde harmanlandigi Fantastik bir seri... Savascilarin iclerindeki iblisle tamamen butunlestigini soyleyebilirim. Tabii bu durum onlari epey zorluyor. :D 
 Ilk kitap En Karanlik Gece "Siddet" iblisinin muhafizi olan savascimiz Maddox'u anlatiyor. 
 Savascilarimiz Budapeste'de bir kalede insanlardan uzak yasiyorlar. Onlara zarar vermemek adina... 
 Ancak Ashlyn isimli kizimiz kalenin sinirlarina girdiginde Maddox'un hayati tepetaklak oluyor. 
 Diger savascilarin iblislerle ic ice olmaktan baska cezalari yokken, Maddox Tanrilar tarafindan baska bir seyle daha cezalandirilmis. Pandora'nin kutusunu actiktan sonra Pandora'nin kendisini de olduruyor Maddox gecmiste. Bu sebeple de Tanrilar hem siddet iblisiyle birlikte yasamanin, hem de her gece yarisinda tipki Pandora'yi oldurdugu gibi 6 kez bicaklanarak olmesi, sabah tekrar dirilmesini ona ceza olarak uygun goruyorlar. 
 Ilk kitap seriye giris niteliginde. Tanrilari, iblis savascilari taniyor, ozelliklerini ogreniyoruz. Tabii Maddox ve Ashlyn arasindaki tutkulu ask da hikayeyi ateslendiriyor. 
 Cok severek okudugum, inanilmaz guzel ve ozgun bir seri. 
 Kesinlikle tavsiyemdir. 
 Bu seriyi okumakta tereddut eden varsa, kesinlikle etmesin. Okuyun. Okutun. <3 :D

FREAKING LOVED IT! <3 <3

Originally reviewed on my blog Reading the Best of the Best. 
 The cover and synopsis of Cinder had me entranced. A futuristic sic-fi re-telling of Cinderella? Yes, please! Sadly, I wasn't happy with this book at all. While I enjoyed certain aspects, like the characters, it wasn't enough for me to love this book. I do have Scarlet, the second book in the quartet on hand and I'm hoping it's better. 
 Let's start with the plot. I want to point out that there was so much potential for the plot to be amazing but sadly, it was really predictable. Besides knowing who's going to end up with who (after all, this is a re-telling), I figured out a key aspect of the plot almost 15% into this book. There was no sense of surprise in this novel for me and that was not okay. I found myself getting bored and I even admit to skimming some pages because I just didn't care. I thought about not worrying about it since this was Marissa Meyer's debut novel but that seemed wrong. The second half of the book had much more action which was fantastic because the first half was a chore to get through. 
 I was also surprised at the lack of world building. As I said, this is considered a sci-fi book but I found some aspects to be border line fantasy. All of the special powers that some of the characters possess seem to just be there. I really wanted more background as to how it all came to be. The only explanation was that it was because they lived on the moon. Being the science nerd I am, I began to wonder if it had to do with DNA changes or particles in the air or something else that caused the powers. But nothing was explained and that was rather sad. 
 I did like many of the characters. Cinder was a fantastic protagonist. She was brave and smart and loving. She was also willing to do whatever she needed to to help her step sister (the one who likes her anyways) and for the people she cared for. Even though she was strong willed, I liked the aspects in which she was confused or sad since it made her seem more relatable. Iko was hilarious and a much needed distraction from all of the drama but she was also the best friend Cinder needed. Kai wasn't as fleshed out as I had wanted him to be but I was willing to put that aside. Honestly, I wasn't in love with their relationship. I felt like there was no spark and all of the times there should have been tension between the two, I felt nothing. 
 Overall, I didn't like Cinder. I liked out protagonist but combined with the predictable plot and lack of world building, it wasn't a book I enjoyed. I want to give this book more than 2 stars but really, the 2 stars come from liking Cinder and Iko. I will be reading Scarlet and I'm hoping to love it!

I received this as a Christmas present and started reading it immediately. Then I got busy and put it down and didn't pick it up again until 2 days ago. I started from the beginning and burned through it in 2 days. Very entertaining retelling of Cinderella with lots of twists, although I did figure out who Cinder was early in the book. I'm looking forward to reading the remaining books in the series.

This was a nice hybrid mix between cinderella and sailor moon with a dash of cyberpunk. The lack of vampires or magic (the lunar effect could be explained through science so I do not count it as magic)was refreshing but the book could have had so much more potential! The background for the storyline was bleak and underdeveloped. I would have loved to see the author explain in a more understandable way the migration to the moon. I understand this is meant to be a young adult romance novel, which it is and I would much rather my adolescent daughter (if I had one) read this rather than twilight or any other vampire-ridden book (special apologies to Anne Rice and Bram Stoker who's books I am not reffering to here) but if the author took the time to work on the history of earth, description of the city and scenery as well as the mechanics then this would be one heck of a cyberpunk romance novel. Ommitting the many cultural and historical inadequacies, I found some things to be a nice twist in the retelling of Cinderella such as: 
 -> one of the stepsisters being actually amiable 
 -> a companion to make witty remarks (although those fell quite short. I do appreciate the effort) 
 aaaand that's it. There were too many things going on here that deserved better descriptions and explanations but instead built up an unnecessary parade for the love plot which even though was inventive in having such a surrounding background fell short for my taste. Now that i think about it, the whole story could have used a bit more drama. Either that or the internet has made me an emotionless zombie or I am simply not 16 anymore. 
 Overall it's a nice one-time read with a refreshing new scenery. The love plot wasn't overdone in a sick way as I've seen it in many YA dystopian novels from the past 2 years but could have been worked on a bit more story-wise. The writing style wasn't all that bad either and was quite comprehensible. It sadly also had no surprising twists as figuring out the plot was a no-brainer early on. 
 But i'm babbling again. 
 Give it a read. Get inspired to read more cyberpunk literature and go find better books ;) or just go read sailor moon. Because all this book gave me is an immense need to take apart my wrist watch and crossbreed it with my toaster :) 
 PS. Be kind rewind. This is my first review here on goodreads. Please don't pulverize me.
A really fun, fast paced book. Before this I had never read a fairytale retelling and I was not sure what to expect. But I absolutely loved it!
Review to come soon.
I found this to be very compelling. I enjoy how the story doesn't follow the original tale so closely that you can predict what will happen next. Can't wait for Scarlett to arrive on my desk!

I am not the kind of reader who can force myself to finish a book once I lose interest. I'm aware of my bad habit, so I gave this book 3-stars, which I thought was fair, considering I couldn't finish it. 
 The positive: imaginative world and interesting concept. Cyborg cinderella? Pure gold. Love it. I enjoyed Cinder's world and loved reading about her cyborg-ness. That was the best part of the book for me. I actually wish we could have seen more of her day-to-day life as a mechanic working in a small stall. Gave me Star Wars flashbacks. I found the narration strong and funny at times. 
 The Negative: Most of the characters fell flat. The Lunar Queen was a vicious villain, but not very intriguing. Her motives were pretty transparent from the get-go, though all the other world leaders seemed confused and indecisive. Prince Kai was also very wooden. He didn't seem to have much of a personality and I really couldn't get into his character at all. 
 The book lost me about 75% of the way through when a bunch of political blah blah started taking place. First, the political conflict in the book was cute but not real enough for me. I couldn't figure out if Beijing was a world power or more of a third-world country where the Lunar queen was trying to get her foot in the door. I get that she wanted to marry a prince...but with her voodoo mind control powers that can waylay an entire mob, why not just brainwash some 50-year-old sugardaddy politician and take it from there? Yeah. 
 Also, Ms. Meyer needs to work on subtlety. The foreshadowing was so in-your-face I figured out Cinder's real identity, the lunar queen's motives and Prince Kai's hang ups at about 50% through the book. Once I figured all that out, the rest felt like a waiting game for the characters to catch up. Eventually I lost the need to keep reading. 
 I think I'm getting too old for the YA genre, which saddens me. I really wanted to like Cinder. I hope some day, someone rewrites this idea for an older audience. It would be spectacular.

I was pleasantly surprised by this book. Going in I thought it was going to be just another YA spin on the classic Cinderella story that would be nice to kill an afternoon, but would really have no substance. 
 But this book took the Cinderella story and turned it on its head (the girl loses not only her shoe, but her foot running from the castle, her foot!!). Meyer shoves a lot of different goings-on in this book (cyborgs, moon-people, a killer plague), but it works. It works well. My usual complaint about these type of YA novels is that there is not enough information to make me understand the why and how of every issue the book brings up. I didn't have that problem in this book, however. 
 And all the great Cinderella tropes are there: the handsome prince (with substance and character!); the evil step-mother and step-sisters (well, one is anyway, the other is pretty darn sweet); the fairy-godmother (a cute little sassy android house servant); and the pumpkin (an old beat-up car). 
 It's a well-written fairy tale/sci-fi mash-up.

Actual rating: 3.5

 I'll give Meyer credit in terms of creativity and writing, but the truth was, I just plain didn't like the story. Cinderella being a cyborg was the biggest problem, as well as this ridiculously huge, unexplained aversion normal people had towards them. It also appears Meyer did absolutely NO research when it came to modern Chinese culture. She may as well have gone to Chinatown in some American city and read a bunch of comics for her research and not asked any questions from the locals about how things worked. Her earth of the future makes little sense, nor does the lax treatment of the Leutmosis plague that's been a problem for earth for 12 years prior to the story. You'd think the scientists would have figured out the cause far earlier than that. It sounds especially like a cheesy Asian anime with all the little "android" robots running about in everyday society. (She apparently can't tell the difference between androids and robots at all). 
 I'm also not buying these Lunars. There's no way, not even through centuries of genetic manipulation, that human lunar colonists would have developed such mental abilities that allowed them to project illusions, or manipulate other people's thoughts and behavior. It doesn't fly with me. In fact, I'm surprised they didn't have issues with earth's higher gravity when visiting. Human beings living in such low gravity would have become taller, thinner, and way less strong compared to humans living on earth. Maybe if Meyer had written them as beautiful, pale, humanoid aliens that had colonized the moon a short time ago, maybe the story would have been more believable. Otherwise, it sounds stupid. 
 The book was also far crueler and darker than it should have been, with the nice stepsister dying of the plague, Cinder's beloved android friend getting trashed by her ogress of a stepmother, and arriving at the ball by crashing an ancient orange car and looking like a drowned rat from the rain that was falling during the event. The prince also seemed very immature for a guy who was supposed to have been groomed to take up the torch in the future after his father, and the fact that he was still acting like a rebellious teenager shows that either the author knows nothing about royalty, or she chose the cheap route of the overdone coming-of-age cliche too many teen authors use these days.

I've been wanting to read Cinder for a while now. Pretty much ever since I met Marissa Meyer at ATBF this year. I'd been glancing at the book before that, but then meeting her and hearing her talk about her book--which was about a CYBORG CINDERELLA--I couldn't resist. So now here I am. I read it. And...it was pretty good. 
 The concept of this book was amazing. It was a great, fresh retelling of one of the most well-known fairytales. Cinder wandered from the beaten path a bit, but still stayed true to the main storyline well enough to be recognizable and lovable like the story we all know and love. I was so interested to see and learn about Cinder's world in New Bejiing, and in turn see how her life fit into what was the original story of Cinderella. 
 Character Rundown: 
 Cinder: Cinder's one of those strong, stubborn characters. She can take care of herself and you're going to let her do it whether you like it or not. Normally, I'm all for a female protaganist like this. Strength, when used positively, is always a good thing, right? But, honestly, Cinder's attempts to protect herself with lies bothered me. Call me naive, but I think she should have been straightforward about the fact that she was a cyborg from the beginning. I understand why she lied, but I don't agree with it. If he couldn't like her for who she truly was, he didn't deserve her, anyway. Being the strong character that she is, I kind of hoped Cinder would realize that sooner. Then again, every character DOES have their flaws. 
 Kai: GUYS. He's a prince. A totally swoon-worthy prince. He's caring and kind and cares so much about the people he rules over. For the most part, I flipping love this boy. But as I said, every character does have their flaws, and Kai...well, Kai made me want to slap him. Doesn't mean I don't love him, though. Can't wait to see more of him in Scarlet! 
 Plot. This was a wonderful story. Well written and unique. BUT. Yes, but. But I saw the plot twist coming from a mile away. I was not very surprised at all in the reading of this book. That does not by any means indicate that I did not enjoy reading this book. I did, very much. But I was somewhat let down by the predictability of the plotline. 
 Boy + Girl. Kai & Cinder! I just want these two to be TOGETHER already. Like, for real. They obviously care for each other, and the reasons they've been holding back are silly. When two people are so obviously dancing around each other throughout the whole book, only to have an ending like these two had, I want to slap things. At this moment, it'd probably be Kai's face. I love him and all, but he should get a nice slap. And...I can go around in circles forever on this. The main point I'm trying to make here is that I want them to be together. They are adorable. 
 The ending. [insert sigh here] Can Scarlet just, you know, COME OUT ALREADY? I'd be very much obliged if it did. Thanks. 
 Overall, Cinder was a very enjoyable story that was different from other books I've been reading lately. Though this book was not perfect, it was certainly worth my while and I cannot wait to dive into the next book in this series. When I happen to get my hands on it, that is. It's based off of Little Red Riding Hood! Is that cool or what? I love the idea that all the books in this series are going to be based off of different fairytales each time! Personally, I'm excited for the Rapunzel one. But first, I repeat: I NEED TO GET MY HANDS ON SCARLET. 
 Oh, and yes. You should totally give Cinder a shot. That's what I've been trying to tell you this whole time. :) 
 You can find more from me on my blog: Just a Booklover
