reference_books.review_text:
Slogging through this book by my favorite author... Don't like the constant references to plays and other literature. Makes me think he's bragging and showing off how much he's read. Parading as we used to call it. 
 OK, I got through the book, and it was dreadful. I dropped it to one star (I was going to go for 2 just because I liked some of the characters) when the ending was so dreary, predicable and disappointing. But that was the entire book for me. 
 I can't stand that Irving keeps insisting that he's "imagining" these situations and characters. He writes so knowledgeably about that--particularly the AIDS deaths--that I can't believe he hasn't experienced them somehow. 
 Usually, I crave every page of an Irving novel. Trying to take my time. Trying to prolong the experience. Not this time. I skimmed the last 100 pages and still felt like I was reading something that had no value. Sad. I hope this isn't the beginning of the end for him with me.

reference_books.title: The Taking
reference_books.review_text: I thought there would be a different ending to this book particularly since the characters reference War of the Worlds several times. But then the end comes and it's the same kind of ending, just a different alien. Strange book, creeped me out. But I guess that's the point, right?

book_a.title: The Good Neighbor
book_a.user_review: OMG I can't believe I read this entire book. Totally a chick book, but the plot was so convoluted and not credible, I wanted to put it down a dozen times. But still I plowed through, hoping that it would get better. It never did and now I'm upset I wasted so much time on it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
First: Two stars isn't totally fair. This book was ok - it kept my attention, and it was a quick read. But it felt underdeveloped and rushed. I kept running names of characters who I didn't recognize, and by the time the "twist" was revealed it was exactly what I expected. The main character (Sarah?) was an idiot. She seemed nice enough, but was locked in a bubble of distrust due to her fathers shitty choices when she was a kid. None of the characters where very deep, and I'm bothered by the author's assumption that there is a man anywhere that every woman is going to want. There were some storylines left unfinished: what's happening to Jessie? Is Mia actually ok? What about her grandma's health issues? Who was the "other woman" stalking Johnny? 
 I'm sure this book will have scores of people who adore it. It just was not quite up to snuff for me. 
 I got this book through the Kindle First Reads program.

I do like the plot twists within this book and want to like the characters but they are written in a stereotypical way. The story itself was like every other lifetime movie; women bonding together in solidarity, the neighbors in each other's business but not really knowing each other, the once promising teenager now filled with angst and dating an abusive jerk, the question of is the husband cheating or not, even the injury the wife suffers causing her to question her judgement. Sorry, but if I wanted an atypical story line I would have just watched a random lifetime movie.
This was a quick and easy read. Kind of entertaining but not really a "psychological thriller." It was free on Amazon...you get what you pay for....
This might be the worst book I've read in a long time.

"A riveting psychological thriller with twists and turns I didn't see coming."; dubbed as the next "Gone Girl". Nope. I think not. This is not a fair description of the book. First off, just about all "twists and turns" were predictable. Secondly, I wouldn't classify this as a psychological thriller or even a mystery. It read more like a Lifetime movie wannabe. I truly enjoyed the first half of the book. I zipped through. It was engaging and exciting and then it seems as if the author gave up, grew tired, and threw every situation she could think of to write the ending. It could have been a spectacular read if more attention were given to the wrap up. My rating went from a three to a two because of this.
I would rate it less if I could. Could not get through this mess of a book. Publisher should be ashamed of allowing this book to be published

** spoiler alert ** 
 Just eh. This was a quick, easy read. I am disappointed in the ending/killer. We spent so much time getting to know the neighborhood and then it ended up not being one of the original neighbors. I also have so much contempt built up towards the husband that now I feel guiltier than the wife that he was innocent. All in all, not amazing but if you're looking for a quick read then go for it.

Garbage 
 I was looking for a thriller. I'm not sure how this was recommended, or how anyone thought this deserved to join the other books deemed fit for human consumption, bc this is literally garbage.

I found this book dull and the characters were bland. I couldn't identify at all with the main character, and some of the characters I couldn't tell apart, they were just faceless names. I did read this book in one sitting because I kept waiting for the psychological thriller that Amazon had promised me. I was not thrilled and it was three quarters through the book before even a mystery was hinted at. 
 The book did open with a cut scene of excitement but by the time I'd read enough of the book to reach the slice that was shown in the beginning I'd forgotten about it. I knew this wasn't the book for me when I start talking about it with the phrase: This book would've been so much better if... 
 And the author really used the 5 senses description, I've never read a book that told me what everyone and everyplace smelled like. The downside is the lack of description, so and so smelled like sage, but didn't go into anything about how sage smells. 
 The upside is the book is a short, light read, if you need to a couple hours to waste.
Soooooo bad. Don't waste your time.
DNF at 25%. Writing is utterly soulless.

It wasn't the worst book I have ever read, but definitely not great. I am not sure if their is a followup book, but the way it ended made me want to throw my book across the room. Not a thriller at ALL. Not suspenseful at ALL. Save yourself the trouble, don't read it.
I didn't hate it. It was just okay.

A fast paced mystery - can be read from cover to cover at ease. The writing is crisp, chapters are kept short, and the narration sticks to the story line with no unnecessary details. 
 The story is narrated by a woman who is perturbed about the sudden strange happenings in her neighborhood which start with a fire accident. Things only get more intriguing with people not considering it an accident and her husband acting secretive which makes her suspect him of cheating. The ending was a reasonable explanation and end to the mystery however, it didn't thrill me as much as I would have enjoyed it, especially after such a strong build-up.

Usually when people think of horror they think of ghouls, goblins, stalkers, psychopaths, werewolves,clowns... but a happily-married couple? That's more like something you'd see in a romance novel... 
 Unless you take into account the husband's secrets, the wife's suspicion, and the possibility that the people she trusts the most might be more dangerous to her than even the furthest strangers. Really creepy book and one that any thriller fan would enjoy. :)

I had high hopes for this book and it simply did not deliver. The plot was poorly constructed and the characters were insufficiently developed. The climax is puzzling and disappointing, coming out of nowhere with no tie in to the rest of the book. The reader is not given a view into the motivation behind the characters actions. This book is equivalent to craving a donut and finding it stale upon eating.

I love that it was a quick and easy read. I was hooked right away and had to know how it ended. I was a little disappointed by the simplicity of the ending. Also, what was the point of the cliffhanger? IMO, this isn't the sort of story that needs a sequel. I do want to emphasize that I enjoyed reading it. Not a perfect story but I was read it as quickly as I could.

This was in interesting story. It starts right out of the gate with the main character in the river fighting for her life. Then it immediately switches to the back story that leads up to that incident. Although, I would call this a mystery I wouldn't classify it as a thriller. The story moves along at a reasonable pace but I almost wishes for more suspense. That being said I did not anticipate who the bad guy was or the ending.

This book was fast paced and it was well written in a way that kept building up to the climax. Simple story, but plenty of suspense to get you hooked in. It reminded me of a good old fashioned suspense movie. Sarah Phoenix is a newly married author of children's books. She lives in a quiet cul-de-sac with her dermatologist husband Johnny. A raging fire starts at her neighbors house in the middle of the night while Johnny is away at a conference. Sarah is a hero and saves the neighbor's daughter Mia, while her parents perish in the fire. Sarah & Johnny's house catches on fire too and so they move to a cottage offered by neighborhood realtor Eris. Turns out Eris is a patient of Johnny's, which Sarah didn't know. Sarah finds out from another neighbor, that Johnny may have had an affair with Mia's mother, who perished in the fire. Suspicion and self doubt start to cloud Sarah's thoughts about her husband. Sarah starts to question everything Johnny does and says. She sees him enter the house of a neighbor at the cottage they are staying at. Is he having an affair? Who keeps calling his phone and hanging up? More twists and turns, even to the very end.

Amazon did a bit of a push on "The Good Neighbor" kindle daily deal, showed up as a special offer on my Kindle, so when I noticed it was in the lending library I thought I'd give it a try seeing as it was in "Thriller" and "Suspense" category. After reading it I googled the definition of suspense to see if it had changed since I was last in school. "Suspense, noun, a state or feeling of excited or anxious uncertainty about what may happen." Yup still the same so it's official this book didn't deliver. 
 The book is well written with great descriptions which made me feel as if I was out there in the rainy PNW with them, but that's about all I have that's good to say about it. The characters are static, straightforward and predictable. The plot line is just there with no real suspense. There is a traumatic event at the beginning, which throws in to question a lot of what the main character, Sarah, believes is true. Is her husband cheating on her? Not very original nor suspenseful. Is someone trying to kill her? It would be suspenseful if it were more of a major part of the story line, but it isn't. In the end a majority of the plot is how Sarah recovers from this traumatic experience that she had which, quite frankly, I didn't find that interesting. 
 In the end there is a suspenseful ending but it really felt as if it came out of nowhere? There seemed to be little buildup to see it was coming (except that I was close to the end of the book) and no real way to guess who it was going to be since there were no hints along the way. I just felt disappointed when I reached the end of the story.

One of the worst books I've ever read. I saw that the author, in response to someone's question said their question might be answered in the next book and it turned my stomach. Nothing in this book was working, move onto something else! The story lacked imagination, talent, intrigue, and even common sense.
Dumb. Literally, dumb.
Sappy--

Bit Silly 
 Predictable story with a silly protagonist that gets bogged down in unnecessary melodrama instead of focusing on what could have been a more more compelling A-story. Telegraphed the twists too obviously. Some nice writing, though.

This book is very average. It's not stellar and it's not terrible. It's meant to be a light read and that it is. There are certain parts that could have been spruced up and the entire thing would be immensely better with around 10,000 more words but it's still not a dreadful read. 
 The story starts out with a girl named Sarah waking up to find her neighbor's house on fire. During the course of the fire she gets injured while also saving the life of a child. What happens afterwards is a downward spiral as secrets unravel. 
 My biggest grievance with this is the dull dialogue. It didn't feel realistic or free-flowing in the least. There weren't any creative quips or human elements to the writing. It was as if the interactions had the sole purpose of portraying a message to the reader and when that message was portrayed the story jumped right to the next scene. It didn't allow for much in the way of character depth so there was very little in the way of emotional ties. It was interesting seeing how things would play out but I really would not have felt strongly if the protagonist lived or died. 
 There was also the odd detail of everyone in the community being beautiful. Each woman was described as voluptuous, gorgeous, and extravagantly dressed. It's not realistic and makes the only character with apparent flaws the antagonist. Well the protagonist had some but that was just her neediness and insecurity. 
 On a good note, the book was a fun and easy read. The price(free) was right and I'm not sitting here dreading the amount of time I invested into reading it. It could be better, it could be worse, but all-in-all it couldn't be more average.

This was OK but nothing to be excited about. I also listened to the narration. Lots of time, when I find a book a little slow or boring I'll buy the accompanying audio book (usually through Amazon for $1.99) and that gives the story some life but this, unfortunately, was just a boring book. I felt like the characters were really shallow and fake. The narration really made them sound cheesy. There was a twist at the end and for that I gave it two stars but not a lot of follow through and really just skimmed the surface for me.

Entertaining and well paced, this is a quick read for any psychological thriller fan. 
 Full spoiler free review on the blog: 
 https://miareads.wordpress.com/2016/0...
The characters didn't come to life for me and the dialogue felt forced.
Really quick read (only 190 pages) so it is hard to get too dark, crazy, and twisty. However, it did provide some good suspense and really, overall an enjoyable read.

the opening of this book held so much promise but it did not deliver. bad dialogue, superficial characterization. i skimmed to get to the end and was glad when it was over- now i can read something good. the ending hints at a sequel, but this was so bad, i would not even consider it. i'm shocked there are so many good reviews on amazon. it was like a really bad lifetime movie.

A gripping psychological thriller about a woman and a man. Sarah is a writer; Johnny is a dermatologist, and they are madly in love. That is, until the night when a fire in their next door neighbor's house destroys lives. 
 Questions arise over the situation, and Sarah wonders how well she knows her husband. With twists and turns galore, this one is a non-stop roller coaster of a suspense thriller until it ends the bumpy ride. 
 Who to trust? Who not to trust? Where is the truth? And who is the good neighbor? This is one that the reader will think about long after the final paragraph.
Reads like a LMN movie.

I struggled to finish this book. Why it has received so many five star ratings I will never know. While it's not the worst book I have ever read, it was still not up to the standard of well written books I have read recently, and all through 2015. The story just didn't have that easy flow to keep you interested. 
 The plot was predicable and I felt that the main character Sarah was whiny and annoying. Really glad I only paid 99c for this one.

Uggghh. The suspense is so nonexistent that it's not even frustrating, just offensive, when the twist is so unsatisfactorily random after zero foreshadowing. The main character reeks of the author inserting herself into the story for validation and wish-fulfillmemt - her books are super successful, she dresses frumpy but still wins the guy, she's a friend to everyone, and she rescues children from mortal danger and teenagers from themselves. And she's apparently supposed to be having this deep awakening about how little we can know the people we spend our lives with, but she comes off as just emotionally and intellectually stunted - she's never asked her obviously secretive husband about his past but gets upset when there's stuff in it she didn't know about, and even after her awakening, she sees men as either bastards or heroes, nothing in between, and women either unimportant extras with only a handful of speaking lines, or crazy bitches who exist only to drive plot because in fact, the climax and suspense (or lack of it) both hinge on not one but two women being straight up obsessed with a guy who, honestly, is not interesting enough to warrant it, and none of the minor characters have enough agency to substantially affect the plot. These are the big chunks of awfulness, and they float in a bland and forgettable soup of bad writing. I say again, uggghh.

Whodunit/what-did-he-do 
 Decent story line. Liked characters, but not enough development on some of them. Writing not terribly developed - weak imagery.
I feel like the study was building momentum and then just ended too quickly with questions not answered

1.5 stars. The actions and paranoia of the main character about the actions of her husband before they were married - and before she even knew him - just seemed irrational to me. It annoyed me the entire book. The conclusion seemed far fetched to me.

I had high hopes for this book, as it came recommended, but I found it wanting. The characters were a bit flat and I found the heroine quite irksome. I think she was supposed to come across as "stronger than she knew" but she struck me as far too needy and tiresome. The story itself was ok, although became a bit predictable by the end and when I put the book down each day, I struggled to find the motivation to pick it up again the next time. It was simply written, not particularly challenging to read and a bit on the boring side. Not the worst book I've read, but not one I'd recommend further, either.
I liked it! The mystery was a little predictable, but the red herrings were pretty good. The writing was a little simplistic, but the story was engrossing.
What the fuck did I just read? This was horrendously bad. I have no idea how this was labeled as a psychological thriller. And that ending was atrocious. Save yourself some time and skip this.

I have really mixed feelings about this book..the first few pages I thought wow , this is going to be good, and then it started being just meh..it didn't always flow well, st times I felt like I had missed a section, or maybe even a page. It did pick up again but it was at the very end of the book.
DNF at 30%. The plot is boring, the characters are unbelievable and plain, the writing awfully repetitive. It needs more editing
Meh... a bit predictable and formulaic, but ok entertainment for an airplane.

I didn't DNF this, but I also didn't listen to the whole thing. I may have skipped to the last two chapters to find out who done it and how right I was about my guesses, and see how predictable it was. I'm sure I missed a lot of in between things, but I listened to about 50% of it, and I was getting annoyed with every bit of it. Everything has to be dramatically descriptive that's either completely beautiful or dark. The dialogue between characters were either one after the other without any description of what is going on while they are talking, or too descriptive about what someone smells like or is wearing.

This might be the worst book I've read all year. I can totally see this being a whack made-for-tv movie. 
 Update: I wanted to come back a write a fair review for this book but I can't even remember the main character's name. What does that tell you? #iTried
It sucked. I hated everyone in the book.

I did not enjoy this book at all. 
 The number one reason I didn't like this book was the main character, Sarah. She lacked any common sense. She was very big on being in denial. Sarah is not smart and it was infuriating reading about her idiocy at times. She lacked any type of confidence. She was not a woman I could relate to. It was extremely frustrating and annoying to read about her and getting to know her throughout the story. For example, who goes out into the night looking for their husband and doesn't turn on the lights outside the house? 
 The plot was bad. Every event that led up to the ending was unexpected in a bad way. There was also a side plot with a young girl in an emotional and physically abusive relationship that had nothing to really do with the story besides to maybe make the reader think the girl and her boyfriend are the perpetrators. This story was all over the place and the ending could have been so much better. The ending was a bid disappointment. 
 I would not recommend this book. There are better mystery/thrillers out there.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The protagonist is an unbelievable super woman who climbs a ladder into a burning house to rescue a neighbor's child. She then goes on to rescue the same child from drowning in between having doubts on, who is the bad guy. If you enjoy a light thriller romance this book is for you. As for me, I need to stay away from Kindle First books for awhile.

Good thing this was free - I would be upset I spent money on it. 
 I really can't even tell you the plot because there isn't one. It just kind of follows the main character around for a while trying to create suspenseful situations, but nothing of the sort happens. I feel like if it was more than 200 pages it would have been a DNF for me.
This was a quick read and held my interest, but wasn't phenomenal. I would consider reading another book from this author though.

book_b.title: The Bone Clocks
book_b.user_review: Never read anything by him. But I did see Cloud Atlas movie. Started this book and enjoyed it, but the fantasy/horror got to be too unbelievable. Ended it less than halfway through. Sad. Thought it had potential.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 ::SPOILERS::SPOILERS::SPOILERS:: 
 Really wish I could give this even 2 stars, but I didn't like it even that much. Which is especially disappointing, considering how much I loved Cloud Atlas. 
 I felt like this was a bit of a rehash of "Cloud Atlas", in terms of the structure (superficially), but where that book drew the reader forward then back through time, this one just kind of . . . rambles. The author uses different sections of the book to explore different characters, jumping forward in time within their lifetimes -- more or less. The problem is that this jumping forward left me feeling very removed from the characters Mitchell made me care about in the first place. We meet Holly Sykes at 15, JUMP now she's in her 20s, JUMP now she's 30-something, JUMP now she's 40-ish, etc etc etc. And there's too little explanation of what's happened in the interim to make me really care about this "new" Holly -- kind of like meeting an old friend you haven't seen for 20 years, then realizing you don't really have that much in common anymore. 
 Mitchell piles on detail in many areas, but they're the mundane details of everyday life that aren't especially interesting -- all while leaving the BIG things (such as Ed's death) to be gleaned through snippets here and there. 
 I had a hard time understanding what some of the characters were even doing in this story -- from reading other reviews, I guess they're there because they're characters from other books? How disappointing. 
 I'm not even going to start on the whole Horologist / Anchorite thing -- that is just too big of a mess to even bother with. 
 Truthfully, I'd recommend reading "Cloud Atlas" again, and giving this one a miss altogether.

Ugh. I give myself 5 stars for reading this entire book. I must be a simpleton. I give Mitchell credit, he can write from many a perspective. He uses words I don't quite understand and his plot wasn't awful. I read to be entertained. I fancy myself as someone that enjoys a challenge intellectually as well. However, I struggle with books that require me to go back and reread paragraphs so as to confirm I'm as confused as I was the first go around. After fighting through 550 pages...to read the final chapter was depressing. SPOILER *** 
 ***Our society is destroying the world for our children. Too bad. Hope we are all gone before it happens. It felt like I waited all day in line to buy something I really enjoy...only to see the only inventory left was a sh*t sandwich.

If there is one phrase to describe this book, it would be... 
 "This is the book that won't end." 
 I didn't like this book, because unfortunately I am not a big fan of huge disappointments. This book was not my pick for our book club, and I was really excited because the person who suggested it said it had a huge following. It even has it's own semi-textbook to help you understand it? After the first couple of chapters, believe me, I was hooked. Although it steadily was a downhill slope from there, until eventually I fell off of the cliff of boring material, to land in the pit of horrible plot development. 
 I have heard about other books that this author has done, but if this book is any indication of his work, I'm thoroughly uninterested.

2nd audiobook in a row that I've quit! Argh! 
 Despite the positive reviews for this book, I just couldn't get into it. Or rather....just as I started to get into it, the plot/narration shifted so dramatically that it was like I had to restart my efforts to get into it. 
 Apparently this book is told in six different POVs (at least, there were six narrators listed for the audio). Each follows a different person in a different time period. They all start out feeling like just regular realistic fiction (a teenage girl running away from home, a college boy getting into financial trouble, a photojournalist losing his marriage), but then after we get good and invested in their story, BAM! Suddenly some mystical, confusing, rambling side characters come in and introduce the current protagonist to a fantasy subplot with a lot of meaningless names that (I assume) will tie all of the different POVs together eventually. Then the protagonist gets some other kind of Big Plot Changing Event...but instead of following through with that, the author drops their story, jumps forward several years, and dumps us with a new protagonist. So, all of that time we spent investing in the last plot feels a bit like wasted time. Sure, after a while, we eventually make connections with the previous plot and the current one (college boy meets that former teen runaway where years late she now works at a bar, etc), but it still feels disjointed. Whichever POV you're currently on is so detailed and richly written that you feel like THIS is the story you're supposed to pay attention to.....but no, it turns out that it's all going to be irrelevant in a bit because we're going to move onto someone else. Don't pay attention to all of these details and relationships, because they're not actually important to the BIG plot, which is about the mystical spooky people who can apparently live forever. 
 Magical realism is tough to get right. You can't tell a regular realistic story about every day drama, and then tack on some fantasy at the very end. The magical bits need to blend in better with the rest of the story, otherwise it just feels like an after thought. A teenage girl running away from home and having to make it on her own while pregnant is a deep enough story on its own. A college aged boy squirreling away tons of money by creating a false identity and swindling an elderly man out of his valuable stamp collection...that is story enough on its own. A middle aged photojournalist and on the brink of divorce as he travels through war torn Iraq......that is story enough on its own. But, no, NO. Forget all of that interesting plot that you've just gotten invested in because now we're going to toss in some immortal people and telepathy and body possession. Got that? Good, now let's move on to the next interesting plot with new characters. 
 Frustrating. Quite possibly, the next three POVs also have interesting plots, and quite possibly the fantasy subplot wraps it all together brilliantly in the end.......but there's a lot of fluff to read before you get there. Either the magical stuff needed to be spread out more, or the regular realistic subplots needed to be shortened so that there was less time between the fantasy bits.

Goodreads FirstRead 
 This book was hard for me to get into. My hubby and I tried to watch the movie Cloud Atlas and I marked it as one of the worst movies we watched that year. I then received this book in my mailbox from GoodReads FirstRead and thought I would give it a shot, books do tend to be better then movies. 
 Overall, the book was not enjoyable and I marked that it was okay. Took me months to get through it (even with the cheating/skimming through chunks). The only saving point was Holly. 
 The first section of the book was hard to get into, felt like the story was all over the place and I completed several other books before I even got to the second section. Second section had me skimming the pages. Reading a paragraph here and there (I am not proud of this :( I really love to read and pride myself on giving every book a chance). As the character Holly Sykes developed in later parts of the book though I became interested in her character. Cut out all the rest of the book and I would have marked this book much higher. 
 The story line bounced from one crazed idea to another and most made no sense to me. Maybe reading other books by David Mitchell would provide greater insight into his writing style but with a bad movie and book under my belt I think I will pass on his work for now.

So it's one of those David Mitchell novels that is a series of interconnected novellas in which various characters keep turning up in reincarnations or whatever. Wait, haven't I read this novel before? It was called, like, Cloud Atlas? And it was far better then, too. It may well be that David Mitchell is a genius and I am a dullard but to me this is some kind of unholy and not especially interesting mash-up of realistic and fantastical genres. I enjoyed some of the earlier sections quite a bit, but by about page 450 the book's gone into karma mumbo-jumbo land and I just lost interest. I actually abandoned this at about that point, which is something I never do - abandon a book 75% of the way through. But that's the way I felt about it. 
 I still like David Mitchell a lot; I really loved The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet, Cloud Atlas and Black Swan Green. This is the first of his that I'm unhappy with.

Because this book was told from so many perspectives I liked it only sometimes. I enjoyed Holly's story, but the Crispin Hershey section felt needless in the grand scheme of the story. The showdown section was way too far fetched for me. Didn't love it though felt I needed to due to its attempt at being an epic.

This was an amazing novel, but I'm resisting giving it five stars. While it was amazing in scope and execution, I found the switching-between narrators jarring at times. Each chapter was like starting a new book, with new characters, which only eventually flow together. When it worked, it really really worked, but when it didn't I had to struggle a bit to keep going. 
 Overall: pretty great

The Bone Clocks makes you rethink the concept of "genre" and "novel." The author does not let others' views of the novel depict how he expresses his creativity and art. 
 Holli Sykes, the protagonist, narrates two of the six sections of the novel, while important characters around her narrate the other four. Crossing genres and ages, some how Mitchel convincingly gets into the head of them all, each using a first-person narrative. The first section begins in 1985, and each section progresses forward from that point in history to 2043 in the future. 
 This book is so fresh and enjoyable, I def want to buy this book so I can reread as much as I want. ;)

There's almost nothing i can say that will do this book justice. It's great. He's a wonderful storyteller and a master wordsmith. This book fits very nicely into his oeuvre. It's not as ambitious as Cloud Atlas, but more cohesive, and chock full of wonderful easter eggs recalling characters and events from his other books.

If Neil Gaiman and Margaret Atwood had a baby it might write something like this, however Mitchell tries too hard and is at times downright preachy and repetitious. 
 And his attempts to create a whole new mythology fails, leaving the reader confused and confused and confused (Bone Clocks is no American Gods!) 
 It does redeem itself in the last pages, however Mitchell relies on the pulling of the reader's heartstrings to get there. 
 All in all - hardwork with little reward.
Hey, I've never read anything else by David Mitchell but I couldn't put this one down. So funny and odd and insightful. Is this part of a series? Should I be reading other ones?
Need to read again!

Challenge #50 A book you started and never finished (popsugar reading challenge 2015) 
 Initial thoughts: Though that ending really has me wanting to give this book 5 stars I know that there were parts of this book that I really didn't like. 
 Review: This book is told in 50-100 page sections that introduce a new character and setting each time, and the book spans from the 70s to the 2040s. They all are somehow connected to the main character, Holly Sykes, who is the narrator of the first and last sections. I went through a lot for this book, it took me about 9 months to finish it. I started reading it in January this year, and I absolutely loved the beginning. But once I hit the section on Chrispin Hersey I lost all interest. I realize you aren't supposed to like him, but I just couldn't deal with his character. After multiple tries to get through his section, I finally finished it. Then, read the rest of the book ~300 pages in a couple days. 
 I truly enjoyed the book in the end, despite my hate for one of the characters. I thought that the prose was elegant without becoming too convoluted and flowery. The story was really interesting; in fact, Mitchell doesn't really let on what is going on until the second to last section of the book. But by that section the reader has a loose grasp on what is going on. 
 The book moves from stories that are completely grounded in reality to stories that are incredibly fantastical effortlessly. This makes the book perfect for someone like me, who prefers the magic to not be the main point of the book but to still be present. Because what is the point of reading without a little fun. 
 I really grew attached to Holly Sykes, but she seemed to be the only character I really cared for. The others (except Hersey) were interesting, but they were just a means for me to see what was going on with Holly. I think this was because I knew if I grew attached to them, I would have to say goodbye in the next 50 pages. My two favorite sections were the ones with Holly as a narrator. 
 The last section of the book might have been my favorite. Not only did it have a nice conclusion, but it was a realistic and interesting look into the future. The reality of Mitchell's made up future scared me a bit, but I liked that he didn't make it completely hopeless. 
 I really had to take my time with this book. Since it is almost like reading many short stories that intertwine, I think it was ok spending as much time on it as I did. Overall it was a really interesting read. 
 4/5 
 If you liked TBC try Slade House by David Mitchell! It is a companion book where we see some familiar faces!

I feel like David Mitchell tried to cover way too much in this book. I'd often be left thinking, "who is that again?" "Where are we again?" What's a horologist again? Maybe it's because it took me Soo long to read it. I found the best part to be the section about the young men partying it up on a ski holiday in the alps... Yet somehow it ended on a farm in Ireland/a boat in Iceland with almost completely different characters to where it began or visited. Next book please!

'We sort of live on, as long as there are people to live on in.' 
 This had all the David Mitchell trademarks that I love so much. It tells of a hidden war taking place through time by two different ' immortal with terms and conditions' groups. I don't want to say any more really about the plot as part of the joy of a David Mitchell novel is actually working out what is going on and how it all relates. 
 The story is told through the viewpoint of several characters, each one at a jump of a few years. They intertwine and weave together as we go along but Holly is the main character and has a part in all of the stories. 
 This book came out a few years ago now and I had been planning to read it on its release. However, the novel didn't seem to be too well received. As a fan of David Mitchell, I didn't want to be disappointed, but finally I picked it up. It ticked all the boxes for me. It covers so much ground I don't even know how to shelve it- a little dystopia, fantasy, psychosoteric..plus a dash of history- all my favourites! 
 Recommended.

I tried to read this for a book club meeting but found it v disjointed and bizarre. The initial 50 pages about Holly was disrupted by some weird surreal phenomena, and just I thought the character was filling out, the second part was completely off course. I could not read any more.....
I loved the first few chapters and then the magical fantasy parts began. skimmed the rest to discover more of the same. opps. I picked the wrong kind of book.

Alternated between confusing, tedious and interesting. But at about 75%, the tedious and confusing just became too much. With such a long book, 25% remaining is a lot to slog through. 
 I liked Holly and I found the interwoven stories appealing whenever I figured out what was going on. The supernatural component was intriguing. Until it was explained in excruciating detail. 
 Cool concept. Way too long.

I've seen a lot of structural comparisons to Cloud Atlas, but I don't see the similarity. This is more like the interconnected stories of Olive Kitteridge or the Carpet Makers or A Visit From the Goon Squad (the Goon Squad and Bone Clocks are similar markers of mortality as well). Time marches forward. Holly Sykes, our narrator in the first section, makes small appearances in the other sections, and when we return to her head at the end it is a reward. In between are sections that work to greater or lesser degree. Two have absolutely unlikeable narrators but compelling prose. The weakest (and arguably most unnecessary) was the one that followed a self-centered author through the twilight of his career; it seemed designed for overclever meta-commentary more than plot advancement. The section I had the most trouble getting into was actually the climactic fifth, but by the time the sixth ended I was weeping. Mitchell is a writer who engages my head but sneakily grabs my heart when I'm not paying attention.

I enjoyed this novel. There were times when it got a little long winded, but i felt it paid off in the end. Compared to Cloud Atlas i liked that there was a central character through the whole novel. I liked that we got to see Holly through different periods of her life, including the very confusing next to last chapter. After all of the hints at the supernatural i am probably one of the few people who was glad that all of the information was given to us in the Marinus chapter. I think I would've felt cheated if he hadn't, but then i was glad for the Atwoodesque final chapter where we get to see the civilized world falling apart. I really felt for Holly and all of the villagers and i was glad that Mitchell brought the story back to his main character. I think this was a great read and i can't wait to get a chance to go back and read all of Mitchell's backlist.
More like 3.5 stars - a little difficult at times, but an intriguing story spanning over 50 years with tales told from the perspective of different characters.

This is a bit of a tough book for me to review since I think it does some amazing things but falters hard in many areas. 
 First, the magic system is pretty unique and interesting. I was consistently picking this up because I wanted to know more. Unfortunately, the horology (magic) is barely talked about. I would have loved more from the Atemperals. Point of fact I loved Marinus' story. Also just more of the rules of it, Mitchell hints at it but then flips to other stuff. 
 With that I would like to bring up my biggest issue with this book. There is so much filler in here that doesn't serve a purpose. Telling Holly's story through other characters is an interesting device but we get so much of it that it really drags the book down. After a couple of the same cycle I just wanted to get to the bits where they would interact with Holly and then horology stuff would happen. I will say the quality of writing does make getting through the fluff not nearly as bad it could be. 
 Finally, their is a section after the story feels like it concludes that feels like an extremely long epilogue. Just felt completely pointless, it could have been a paragraph and conveyed the information in it just as well.
I liked the first bit about Holly Sykes and then he lost me completely, so I am not going to waste my time on this, I'm done!
I liked Thousand Autumns and Cloud Atlas better than this book. In some ways, the prose seems written for direct translation to a screenplay. Still an interesting read.

There are books that are so good they stay with you. You can't stop thinking about them. You expect scenes from the book to stay with you throughout your life. 
 With the Bone Clocks, I realized the same can be true of a particularly terrible book. This is an intense and focused disgust that will last me years. 
 The problem is that there are about 5 books in this book, and I liked 1/5 - the story of immortals secretly working to save the world. However, this book has already been written: please read Steven Brust's The Incrementalists - it does the same thing, but better, for a whole book. 
 The other books are a classic young adult tale of a run-away, a character examination of a misogynist sociopath, a tortured author who is kind of a jerk-off, and a really depressing post-apocalyptic tale that is somehow trying to say something about global warming, the common thread being "this one woman who hasn't done shit to anyone is tortured from age 15 to age ??? for no reason." 
 I can get behind a good post-apocalyptic tale (though, I prefer a more subtle implication of global warming than constantly bashing the reader over the head explicitly with "WE RUINED OUR LIVES") - but I had no desire to read those other "genres." 
 I am now an interesting combination of mad, depressed, and driven to re-read Steven Brust.

An excellent and interesting novel that jumps in time, from narrator to narrator, form the 1980s forward to the future. There is an story interlaced between the different segments that builds and unfolds along with the lives of our narrators. Always interesting and engaging, often heartbreaking as well.

Audio version - good narration, although the same problem I always have with multiple narrators - the voices for dialogue aren't consistent between different narrators, so the same character will sound really different in different sections of the book. 
 The book itself? Didn't really work for me. Some really nice scenes, even some nice vignettes, but as a novel? It felt self-indulgent, as if the author wanted to include bits because he wanted to include them, not because they served the story. The entire section from Ed's POV was only there, as far as I could tell, to give support for one instance of Holly's supernatural abilities. So an entire novella is included in order to show one scene that could have been easily shown in a paragraph or two from Holly's POV. And the novella from the novelist's POV is similarly unimportant to the overall plot. It felt shoehorned in, to me. 
 Actually, I felt like both of those parts were included as a way for the author to give a political rant about the Middle East and a series of in-jokes/digs at a fellow novelist, respectively. I don't follow novelists as celebrities so the in-jokes mostly went over my head, and the political diatribe (including the environmental message from the last section)? 
 My politics are very closely aligned with the ideas presented in the novel, and I STILL resented the lecturing and hectoring tone. If the political ideas had fit seamlessly into the plot of the story, fine, but they sure didn't. 
 So-some really nice bits of writing, but not a successful novel for me.

I like David Mitchell's writing, but this barely eked out three stars for me. The opening section was led by a brash, interesting character and a good supporting cast, all toned with a touch of surrealist mystery. Each section thereafter -- in typical Mitchell fashion, told by a different narrator in a different time and place -- dropped down a notch in quality until I was reading a book that, while still reasonably well-written, had long lost the initial excitement and no longer had any sort of discernible binding story. Mitchell still tells a story well, but by the novel's end there wasn't a clear enough central theme to feel satisfied with the whole. 
 (Warning: Slight spoilers ahead...) 
 Crispin Hershey: I am baffled by this character -- neither likable nor interesting, his purpose and value to the story was unclear, yet the characters seemed to behave as if he was somehow important. I didn't enjoy reading about him, but somehow he was strongly connected to the other central characters? Huh? What part did I miss when that happened? (Was number9dream required reading to understand Crispin?) The later section showing the Horologists in action read like an unpleasant mash-up of a Harry Potter knock-off and a weird manual to an imaginary cult daydreamed up by a higher school student obsessed with a coming up with a (seemingly) unique take on immortality (by not using the word "vampires" except once). And the final section when it all comes back to together? I had already long lost whatever thread bound the sections of the novel together and the final section did nothing for me in terms of connecting and elevating the earlier story. 
 Perhaps my biggest gripe, the jaw-dropping one for me where I nearly the dropped the book as well as my jaw, was the altogether pointless "tie-in" reference to Jacob de Zoet. Did I miss something? That reference seemed to have *nothing* to do with the book and was weirdly, weirdly superfluous and out of place. I started to get a little worried that Mitchell was starting to buy into his own theory that "everything is connected" a little too literally. I read Ghostwritten and Cloud Atlas a little too long ago to realize there were question-of-purpose-evoking character overlaps with those books as well. 
 While not a waste of time reading this book, but I had high hopes which were let down by a lack of a strongly binding theme and story across Mitchell's jumps between time, place, and narrators.

Really enjoyed the first third and the last fifth of this novel. The three-fifths in the middle I found slow and hard-going, with a ton of backstory it would have been better to edit out. Holly is a brilliantly drawn character, and the parts from her viewpoint are superb. Alas, this feels like three separate books, with the middle one as dull as a history text.
Did Not Finish--This book is crazy bizarre . . . .

My review is below, but first let me tell you why I love David Mitchell... 
 I became a fan of DM after reading his first two books and being in awe of his almost Shakespearean ability to portray characters. At a reading in September 2014 in Seattle, in response to an audience question, Mitchell said that we all have the ability to create characters because we all have a unique way of understanding the people in our lives. He said, think of the way you understand your parents, your friends, your co-workers, your classmates, or anyone else that you meet. A character is constructed in the same way you understand any person. I found his remarks to be instructive and helpful, because from a very early age our heads are filled with theories of characterization. We learn about protagonists, the hero's journey, the stock characters of genre fiction, etc. We are strongly encouraged to create characters that match these templates, and this limits our ability to create characters from life and the unique way we understand people. I am grateful to David Mitchell for speaking out to empower writers to trust themselves and their own unique abilities. 
 Now for my review of The Bone Clocks... It's a poor novel, and David Mitchell doesn't create vivid and differentiated characters. Instead, they all share a similar voice across their 1st person narrations, a hipster voice in which every sentence abounds with ironic playfulness. Many characters are cliched, for example, Holly Sykes is just another symptom of 80's nostalgia, a goth teen a la Nancy Spungen, or Molly Ringwald. Since I was a teenager in the 80's I feel well qualified to say that every high school had at least twenty girls who dressed like Molly Ringwald, and they didn't have daddy issues, and they didn't want to sleep with middle aged men. So what kind of effed up wish fulfillment is taking place thirty years later, when middle aged writers fondly remember their adolescent lusts? Mr. Mitchell, this characterization is predictable and disappointing. 
 Other characters are bungled conceptually, like Aoife, a five year old girl, who speaks like an adult hipster. The effect is horrifying, like when a medieval painter tries to paint Baby Christ, but instead paints a miniaturized adult. Mitchell seems incapable of depicting the way a character is changed by time and experience. For example, we keep meeting Holly Sykes again after fifteen year interludes and each time she seems like a completely different character. It's as if Mitchell has never bothered to develop his writing ability to evolve a character, because it is easier to rely on his talent to spawn new characters and simply name them Holly Sykes. 
 If we move on from characters, his plot is also very weak. With its touch of the supernatural, and its continuous hinting at a deep conspiracy, it reads like a Dan Brown novel. With its plot about good immortals versus bad immortals, and an attractive mortal girl caught in between, it reads like Stephanie Meyer's Twilight. The entire book abounds with very bad authorial decisions, resulting in entire sections that seem irrelevant. For example, the section called "The Wedding Bash" is set in the green zone in Baghdad, but listening to Mitchell opine about the Iraq war was a jarring experience because he has simply applied his prose style to a new subject area, the journalist's perspective on the Iraq war. To any reader who read a newspaper sometime between 2003 to 2012, Mitchell's ideas come across as the most superficial level of political talking points. They could have been copied and pasted after an hour of online research. The Bone Clocks reveal Mitchell as...not exactly a hack, but someone with a pleasing prose style who tends to choose the easiest authorial path. I had hoped that he would turn out to be what I want a novelist to be, a wise soul.

Interesting, but not that fun to read. Totally confused with all the terms that just too much for me. 
 To be honest, the first part is pretty enjoyable. I can understand that this is a story from different person that somehow tied each other in fate. The problem is, the tie is not twisty and tangling enough that I, a reader, strangled in its ropes and struggle to breath for more pages. 
 The only thing that I really appreciate is the reality this book portray. After all that magical and full of psychothingy, reality hits Holly like a train. The ending is not that happy. He didn't live happily ever after, but at least he can live with assurance that people he love the most can get a better future. 
 The last line from this book really get me, draining my thought nearly the whole day.

Much of this book is disjointed. The reader frequently doesn't know who is narrating the story from one paragraph to the next. To make matters worse, characters sometimes refer to themselves in the third person - and then switch to first person in the same paragraph. Many times, a story line is suddenly stopped, and the next chapter occurs years later, with a different set of characters. Nevertheless, there were some memorable scenes and even one line that I had to copy into my list of memorable quotations. I won't include the quote here, because it might offend somebody. However, it speaks of the futility of reasoning with certain types of people.
I slaved through 500+ pages and couldn't finish it. I wanted to like it I really did, but it was...just boring.

We start off by meeting Holly Sykes, whom is seemingly disgruntled with many facets of her life. I'd like to think of it as the teenage angst period! You may think this would be a story of how she comes to terms with her life, and it is, yet it is oh so much more! 
 Many complicated ideas are presented, which involve you believing the possibility of: psychic abilities, the existence of souls with the belief that some souls for what ever reason drift through time from one being to another and are reborn in them. Usually they re-inhabit a child that would of otherwise have died, These souls are looking in a way for answers that essentially would help mankind from those ill - intentioned. They are gender neutral, changing the host body from male to female and vice versa with each lifetime they inhabit, They are referred to as Horologist, but there are another type whom aren't this way naturally. They are called anchorandites, they desire the ability to live on forever, the drink the souls of the young "gifted" children to lengthen their own existence and remain at the same age when they first become an anchorandite. These two fractions are at war with each other. 
 These beings are interwoven in Holly's existence or perhaps, it is better to say her existences is interwoven in theirs. 
 At times I wished, I had a key to remember whom was whom previously of the horologist, as they speak of their past lives, and with gender switching it became more complicated. 
 We are introduced to the loves that come into Holly's life, and I often wondered why am I going off reading about this character - perhaps thou to realize that no character is simple, that there is depth, and more to us then at the surface. 
 In many chapters, your reading in the first person, through their thoughts/voice, but it isn't clear whom you are. This was irksome and maybe simply putting the name before the chapter or switch in character would of been nice. I didn't like to read a few pages in before I knew whom I am. 
 Overall, this complicated story held my interest, presented many idea. Some of which also beg me to reread the whole story to grasp the full depth of what is occurring. 
 The story left me with the feeling of "hmmmmm" It drew me in yet, left me more questioning, not being totally involved.

Fifteen-year-old Holly Sykes runs away from home, and though she soon regrets it, is determined to prove she can make it on her own. As a child, she heard "radio people," and was surrounded by strange events--the voices left her after a visit to a specialist, but now the strangeness is returning--with deadly consequences. Holly has gotten tangled up in the war between two groups who have each achieved power and immortality, but disagree about the means. And then her family suffers a loss that forces her home--a mystery that affects her through her life, wrapping itself around the people she cares about. 
 This mystery reaches a variety of people caught up in the same war as Holly was, from across the world, a variety of occupations, ages, and philosophies. These life stories intersect and break away from each other, often returning, forming a larger picture of conspiracy and secrets. 
 This is one of those stories that the pay off takes a little while. In the beginning, the separate stories don't seem connected, but when they start to pull together, you can see the shape of the story as a whole. There's a lot of unexpected moments, and it stretches farther than you might expect. Not content to leave loose ends, it follows several stories through to their conclusions, which are, unsurprisingly, rather peculiar.

Mitchell has spun out a series of novellas of varying genres, among them a YA, a satire, a rollicking sci fi clash of the titans, and an unsettling dystopian future. For each of the 6 substories, the reader must recalibrate to a new voice and style, but there is an underpinning of a larger story, a story part of a larger uberstory that Mitchell has been rolling out over many of his books. 
 There are so many things I've been loving about Mitchell whatever I say here will be truncated. 
 * The metastory metauniverse thing he's doing wherein characters from other equally-fantastic books feature in this one? Love. 
 * The humor parsed out side by side with the fantastical and the mundane? Love. 
 Side comments to Mitchell: 
 * You are nearly my favorite public speaker of all the writers who give readings. You are affable and have great comic-timing. Please drop by for coffee or tea any time. 
 * Thank you for your inclusion of Three Lives Booksellers in NYC in this story. In my head, I've built a backstory of your attachment to the place and the warm people who work there. I've wiled away some time talking books with them and echo your appreciation. 
 * Extra points to Mitchell for successfully negotiating his stammer to become such a fluid public speaker and also kudos from a fellow special-needs parent for his reflections upon parenting his son who is on the autism spectrum. 
 Mitchell has been exploring with structure in his novels. I prefer the symmetry of Cloud Atlas, but still enjoy what he's done with Bone Clocks. Although he ranges far afield in setting, style, and plot, his novels are tightly-edited. Things do not appear without reason. 
 If it seems as if I've conflated Mitchell the person with his writings, I have a bit. His personality has, however, only been a pleasing bonus to his exceptional books.

Like in Cloud Atlas and Ghost Written, The Bone Clocks has sections which link to each other, though the links aren't always immediately apparent. However, unlike Cloud Atlas and Ghost Written, it is told chronologically and focuses more or less on the life of one protagonist, Holly Sykes. The Bone Clocks also links in a big way interestingly enough, to the The Thousand Autumns of Jacob de Zoet, which will have readers re-thinking a certain character from that novel as well as some of the story itself. Apparently David Mitchell has said in interviews that all of his books are really part of one enormous story arc, which makes me look forward to reading number9dream and Black Swan Green to complete the uberstory. My only real disappointment with The Bone Clocks was the reveal of the Horologist and Anchorite factions. For me, this took something that was satisfyingly nebulous and metaphysical and made it prosaic and tangible. I liked it better not knowing.

This is a huge book, with literally hundreds of characters, many who appear for a short period and then never come back. The author however takes the time to flesh each character out, no matter how irrelevant they are to the story. This book could have come in at a couple of hundred pages with a bit of normal editing. 
 This is the life story of Holly Sykes, who we first meet as a young girl being regularly visited by her invisible friends, who it turns out are souls engaged in a war of good souls v. bad souls, holly's invisible friends are on the bad side, but she's cured of them by a psychiatrist who is really a good soul in human form. Yeah, they can do that. The psychiatrist, Dr. Maroness reappears regularly throughout the story, becoming somewhat of a guardian angel for Holly. The story regularly flashes back and forth throughout the entirety of Maroness' existence, from early human existence to a very dark and bleak not so distant future. Suffice it to say that it is all wrapped up rather tidily and quickly, and left me thinking that the author, much like myself, wanted to hurry and get this over with. 2 stars, mostly for the concept of the story. I could have easily put it down, but I kept thinking it would get better. It didn't.

Author was capitalizing on his superficial knowledge of psychic phenomena. As one of his characters who is an author says in the book, an author often wants to "tell the world the state of affairs". Unfortunately, this wasn't enough. He doesn't really know. But it ends with a scenario that everyone ought to be familiar with. He writes well but lacks Something. A Da Vinci code story that is interminable for the first 4/5 of the book and then a can't put down read for the last 1/5.

Stayed awake late last night to finish this one. I always find David Mitchell's books tremendously fascinating. The scope of his imagination leaves me breathless. I would list Cloud Atlas and The Thousand Autumns of Jacob De Zoet among my top ten ever reads, so I had ultra high expectations of this one. 
 The Bone Clocks did not disappoint! Such incredible characters, and what a complex and challenging story. I love the way this writer paces everything, feeding us morsels of plot without ever rushing for fear we would lose the thread. I confess there was a section where I struggled a litte about two thirds of the way through. A bit too high fantasy for me (says she who writes about witches and fairytale detectives!), but the beauty of the writing and the assuredness with which Mitchell handles his material got me through. Sticking with one of his books is always worth it, and it does us good to be tested and challenged. 
 The ending had me in tears. An all round wonderful book.

I wish I could bump this review up to 3 1/2 stars, as I'm torn on this book. I've read everything Mitchell has written, and I've enjoyed them all. Part of the problem, of course, is that he wrote Cloud Atlas, and his other works just haven't gotten to that same level (which is completely understandable). 
 In this book,he's definitely trying to get to that level again, but it just doesn't work for me. I enjoyed the first 2/3, before everything gets rather fantastical, much more than I did the final third. I thought the story actually lost energy there, especially after the big climax. In fact, I could largely see the ending coming from close to 100 pages away, which is never good. 
 All of that said, even average Mitchell is still pretty darn good. It's a solid read, and I'm glad I took the time to read it. I enjoyed getting to know the characters and their world. I wish I would have learned more about both of them, but he took the book in a different direction.

Very disappointed in this book--70% thru and I'm done. Novelettes woven together with a thread. The story is not evolving...maybe it all comes together in the end but at this point, I've stopped caring.
I couldn't follow this plot. Gave up halfway through.

Wow, that took a long time. It was going to be 4 stars for much of it. Six novellas featuring one linking character - the psychic Holly Sykes - taking place from 1984 to 2043. The first four I liked a lot. Very down to earth stories which became fantastical in places. When the fantasy took over I got lost, or did I just lose interest? 
 I'd give the same author's 'Black Swan Green' 4 stars.

3.5 - There were moments I was blown away and moments that I had to push through. This book is unlike anything I've read before. 
 Did anyone else notice all the references to birds in the novel? Often nearby, singing, during or just after a major scene. Also, several references to a bird sitting on a spade, either in a painting (Vinny's house) or actually present at the scene. I Googled to see if I could find out more about what they might have symbolized, but no one else is talking about it.
I got halfway through the book and decided I didn't want to spend anymore time on it. I couldn't seem to keep the characters straight with what was happening in the book.

I was really into this book for awhile because I was expecting all the different subplots to go somewhere. They didn't. I stopped reading in the second to last section (after a scene that was supposed to be climactic). I decided to read a review of what happens at the end, and according to this one (http://www.morbidoptimism.com/culture...) I didn't miss much.
As much as I loved the first third of this book, the final third I loathed. The middle I was bored by. Star rating conflicted by how utterly charming David Mitchell was at the reading.

book_a.user_review: Could I have cared less? Maybe. Who cares.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I am on the side that views Christopher McCandless as the kid who was did not respect nature enough, rather than the Walden seeker in the woods. Who goes into nature without a map or skills? Who wants to die of starvation a few miles from aid? I thought Krakauer was biased in his research, straining to make McCandless into what he wanted him to be. I wanted to read this book after first watching the movie, and I was disappointed to discover how unprepared, naive, and selfish Alex Supertramp turned out.
My teacher made me read this. I didn't like it at all. This book was very lack-luster. It was very alike to a reference book.

I thoroughly enjoyed the epigraphs that precluded each chapter in this book. The immortal words of Jack London and Thoreau echoed the sentiments of Alex Supertramp's story, helping readers understand the way Chris pursued solitude and sincerity in nature. 
 However, while I applauded Krakauer for completing such a comprehensive and thorough examination of McCandless' journey, I found his personal interjections to be distracting -- and almost annoying -- at times. He tended to also repeat premeditated thoughts and opinions regarding McCandless' decisions, which interrupted the way I tried imagining Chris. It was only through watching Sean Penn's film, "Into the Wild", that I regained a true vision of Alex Supertramp. Seeing the charismatic, tortured soul on screen, set against the brutal landscapes of the wild, made this all the more real. In fact, I appreciated the way the movie exposed each layer of Chris' life, seamlessly tying together the pieces of his life. There were no other comparisons, and nowhere to go except alongside Chris. 
 In this way, I fully understood the tragic idealism of Chris McCandless' young but starry life.

Read for the second time due to some bizarre circumstances. I am not at all fascinated or interested by Chris McCandless, and Krakauer's other books seems so much more interesting. So many more nonfiction books could and should be in the canon.

 3. I sense in Chris a youthful exuberance/stupidity that I believe was aptly described as hubris and hubris, by definition, leads to a fall. 
 4. Chris seemed adverse to work. Many other travelers (Woody Guthrie comes to mind) would work while on the road to earn his food and shelter and respected and revered the idea that work is how you earn a living, literally, and the people who did hard work. Chris seemed to only want to work when he absolutely needed money for food or something. He did great work for Wayne but that seemed mostly due to the fact that he liked Wayne.  5. Chris was rebelling but if he cared so much about conditions in the world (like his wonderful donation to oxfam suggested he did) he should try and do something to change it. The back of this book categorizes it as a "travel essay", but I'd consider it more of a biography or character study. The book follows the last several years of the life of Chris McCandless, who set off after college to explore the country. Alone, living off the land or as a "hobo" (even riding the rails at times). His story became notable after he was found dead of apparent starvation in the bush of Alaska. 
 Krakauer began chronicling McCandless' story with a magazine article and then expanded his story into the novel. Within it, he pieced together an account if what led McCandless into Alaska and to his death, even figuring out the most likely direct cause. 
 The book itself is well crafted and complexly structured. The author makes heavy use of quoting other books, including the journal of his subject. In this case, it works because reading was such a big part of McCandless' world and identity. The story is strengthened by the author's adventurous experience, lending credibility to his speculations about McCandless. 
 It wasn't a difficult read or too challenging but the author is a big fan of $10 words when 50 cent words would do. I found myself looking words up more often than I normally do. 
 I think the big thing almost every reader of this book will do is form an opinion of McCandless and what they think if his death. Is he an adventurer? Selfish? Troubled? Independent? Crazy? In my opinion, young and an adventurer, possibly if not probably, a bit troubled, but not beyond that. He was so young and had such good luck for the most part, I think he really think he believed he was ready and would make it out alive. So "selfish" is a stretch. 
 A good read and an intriguing story. I recommend it.

I fail to see the heroism in Chris McClandess's actions. I wouldn't even say that his is a case of noble intentions but poor execution. 
 Biographies are difficult. With the sheer act of writing about a person's life, you'll inevitably deconstruct them into something they're not. Obviously, Jon Krakeuer took some artistic liberties when telling the story of Chris McClandess's death. Yet Into the Wild is just as much rooted in fact as it is speculation. And so this is where the dilemma of rating nonfiction comes in. 
 Do I rate this based on personal opinions, enjoyment level, or literary merit? Do those things even matter when the events of this book already happened? How do I fit real-life people and real-life events on a scrawny 5-star scale? And should some homage to McClandess be factored into that that? 
 SO MUCH CONFUSION. 
 Maybe McClandess was a martyr, maybe he was an imbecile. Maybe he was overly arrogant, maybe he was just incredibly naive. All that I can say with reasonable certainty is that he was human. 
 That's not meant to sound deep and profound or anything. It's the simple fact, and a fact that I feel like we often forget in the wake of those polarizing figures with tragic tales to accompany them, figures like Christopher Johnson McClandess.

But after reading Unravel Me and falling head over heels in love with Warner, I had to read this. 
 Click to read the full review on The Library Canary!

I'm reading this long, long after I've read Unravel Me, which I think is both a positive and a negative. A positive because I'm not hankering to know what happens next, but a negative because the experience of reading Unravel Me would have been richer for knowing what this novella contains. 
 Destroy Me isn't enough to make me switch to Team Warner: in fact, when it comes to this series my feet are firmly planted in Team No-one. Although I loved Adam in the first book, his character failed to impress me in the sequel. And I don't think I'll ever want Juliette to be with someone who regularly murders and tortures, no matter how sympathetic this novella tries to make him. 
 The novella answers a lot of the questions I'd had about Warner, and I do feel I turned the last page with a greater understanding of what makes him tick. I admire that Mafi has decided to write such a reprehensible character. His motivations are clearer, as is his background, and I concede that with the family life he's had, he was bound to turn out the way he did. But that doesn't make me like him on a human level. 
 I think Mafi has done an amazing job in placing us inside Warner's head. I'm so used to Mafi's writing being synonymous with Juliette's unique way of thinking - rambling and overly metaphoric, but Warner's voice is completely different: militaristic and stark. I'm looking forward to reading Fracture Me, which will be from Adam's point of view, which I think will showcase how versatile this author is. 
 Destroy Me is a great novella, and I am saddened that reading would have made my experience of Unravel Me quite different, because I don't particularly like the trend of writing novellas between each full size novel in a series, and don't think they should be mandatory reading. This is basically what I hate about Throne of Glass: all the world-building and character development I'd looked for in the novel were present in the four prequel novellas that were released prior to it. But Destroy Me is still an enjoyable read, and has reminded me how much I love this series, and how desperate I am for Ignite Me.

Disclaimer: This review contains spoilers about the first book of this series, "Shatter Me". Please, do not read this review if you haven't read the first book yet. 
 "Destroy Me" is a novella that takes place between the first and second book of the Shatter Me Trilogy. In fact, it starts right after Juliette shoots Warner at the end of Shatter Me. It is written in the point of view of Warner and how he lives the few weeks after the incident as he searches for Juliette. 
 I have to say it, this book was great. It really made me understand Warner better and where he comes from. I finally got the reasons why he acts like he does and I have to say that they are pretty good ones. When I first read Shatter Me, I absolutely hated him and did not understand why any readers would like him. Or prefer him to Adam, love triangle speaking. Even though my heart still goes to Adam, I really enjoyed discovering other aspects of Warner's personality and hidden qualities and I now don't see him as the cold hearted boy the way I used to. 
 In conclusion, I am still totally amazed by Tahereh Mafi's writing style and I thank everyone who pushed me into reading this novella because it just amazing!

 "Destroy me" e una novella che ha come protagonista principale Warner e racconta, dal suo punto di vista, tutti quegli eventi che si svolgono dopo che Juliette lo ferisce con un colpo d'arma da fuoco. Eventi, pensieri e sensazioni di cui altrimenti non saremmo mai potuti venire a conoscenza. 
 Mi e piaciuto moltissimo entrare nella mente di Warner, anche se solo per poche pagine, e credo che questa sia una tappa fondamentale per poter comprendere meglio un personaggio cosi complesso. Questa novella e molto utile per capire anche il passato di Juliette, alcuni sprazzi della sua vita passata, di quegli anni vissuti in isolamento all'interno di quelle stesse quattro mura in cui poi un giorno incontrera Adam. Mi e piaciuto il fatto che qui si ha modo di scoprire come Juliette venga vista da un osservatore esterno, da Warner in questo caso, e come questo incida sullo stile della Mafi. L'autrice e infatti stata bravissima a rendere la differenza del punto di osservazione anche dallo stesso stile narrativo. Non sono piu presenti quelle frasi brevi, sintetiche, a volte anche contraddittorie cancellate con un frego, che tutti abbiamo imparato ad amare in "Shatter me". Questa loro assenza mi ha fatto capire che tale impostazione era un qualcosa esclusivamente legato al modo di ragionare e di esprimersi di Juliette, e non un "marchio di fabbrica" della Mafi. Si, lo stile e diverso ma non per questo meno bello, anzi! Adesso ci troviamo di fronte a qualcosa di piu profondo che esprime perfettamente lo spessore di questo personaggio senza perdere la sfumatura poetica gia incontrata nel libro precedente. 
 Warner e uno di quei personaggi impossibili da inquadrare con un solo sguardo, ma che basta un attimo per rendersi canto che sotto quel loro atteggiamento, quella loro scorza dura e impenetrabile, si nasconde molto altro. Per lui l'apparenza e tutto, "tutto" nel senso che rappresenta l'unico modo per sopravvivere, e qualcosa di essenziale come l'aria che si respira. E una persona estremamente meticolosa e legata a doppio filo alla quotidianita, vive seguendo schemi ben precisi e la parola "imprevisto" non fa parte del suo vocabolario. Tutto cio che fa ha un senso, un obiettivo e uno scopo bene preciso, niente nella sua vita e lasciato al caso. Gli inconvenienti per lui sono qualcosa di inaccettabile poiche infrangono l'equilibrio che faticosamente e riuscito a creare intorno a se. Il suo bisogno di essere amato e accettato da un altro essere umano e smisurato. Sente di avere tantissime cose in comune con Juliette, eventi del passato, stati d'animo e sentimenti. Crede che lei sia l'unica persona in grado di comprenderlo e capirlo e questo lo porta a provare amore verso di lei. Secondo me la ama perche sono due spiriti affini, si rispecchia in lei e questo lo fa sentire meno solo. Non so se questo possa definirsi amore, non so se basta sentirsi simile ad una persona per poter affermare di amarla, ma il solo fatto che lui provi un qualche tipo di sentimento che non sia indifferenza, o che gli importi di qualcuno piu che di se stesso per me conta molto. Questo e la grande complessita della sua psiche mi hanno permesso di comprendere meglio questo personaggio, rivalutarlo e apprezzarlo di piu. Nonostante tutto cio pero continuo a credere che la persona giusta per Juliette sia Adam, o meglio non credo che Juliette sia la persona giusta per Warner. Lui ha bisogno di una ragazza che lo completi, che sia la sua esatta meta e non di qualcuno che sia solo lo specchio di se stesso, come potrebbe esserlo Juliette. 
 Fantastica anche la parte finale in cui sono state inserite le cartelle cliniche di Juliette, gli appunti di studio di Warner sul comportamento della ragazza e i fascicoli personali redatti della Restaurazione su alcuni dei personaggi della serie. Una vera sorpresa e una piccola gratificazione alla mia curiosita.
