reference_books.title: The Fault in Our Stars
reference_books.review_text: I don't get the hype. Yes, John Green is a good writer. Yes, I can appreciate his nuances and his format. Yes, his characterization is great. But honestly, this was ultimately just a sad teen melodrama. If he'd had Hazel fall in love, but ultimately find another way to cope with and be at peace with her cancer, I'd be better with it. She was a relatable, strong woman, even if she was fragile at times. I hated to see her reduced to simply a moping teenager. She started out as so much more. To be honest, this really isn't my type of book, and now I remember why.

reference_books.title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A good book from a great author. While this was very different from the Harry Potter series for which she is known, J K Rowling still shows her talent for words. So many clues, and so many suspicions keep you guessing until the confirmation at the end. I look forward to reading more of Cormoran Strike's adventures.

reference_books.title: Death Comes to Pemberley
reference_books.review_text: A nice sequel to Pride and Prejudice that is not quite the norm. While most sequels tend to focus more on the romance and drama side of the story, this novel takes it in a whole other direction by creating a murder mystery. While James clearly outlines that she feels Jane Austen would not approve, I think James does a fantastic job of staying as true to the source material as she can, even going so far as to structure her sentences and vocabulary in the style of Austen. This was a fun read with characters that I love.

reference_books.title: Night Film
reference_books.review_text:
This was quite a good book. Very suspenseful. I would have finished it much sooner than I did if I hadn't been sick. The narrative was well-paced, and I thought it was going to go in a completely different direction than it did. However, I'm glad everything turned out as it did. It made for an ending that keeps with the tone of the book nicely. 
 I think my favorite feature of this was the interactivity of the book. I liked that, as McGrath read articles or webpages, we too got to read them. It made me immerse myself deeper in the story, as I wanted to find out if my conclusions were true. Again, a good, solid, well-written novel.

reference_books.title: Full Dark, No Stars
reference_books.review_text: Stephen King has once again proven why he is the king of short stories. King's novels often tend to ramble, and while he does a great job of setting up the story and characters, the basic plot often goes into incoherence. King is best when his narratives go in short doses. As evidenced by this book. These novellas are long enough to flesh out the characters well, but short enough to keep King from going on and on and rambling about insignificant details that distract from the story itself. I've been a fan of King's short stories for a long time, and this collection proves why. This is King at his best, and sometimes creepiest.

reference_books.title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows (Harry Potter, #7)
reference_books.review_text: A perfect end to a perfect series. I recently reread this book after having only read it the week it came out. I have actually read it less than the others. I read the others twice and this one once, so I am going to have to reread it, but I still picked up on so much that I missed the first time when I was reading for plot. Rowling did a wonderful job in tying up loose ends in a satisfactory manner. Yes, there were some hard deaths, but we all knew going in that there would be. This is a wonderful culmination of an extraordinary series of children's literature. The joy I feel in reading these books can only be expressed in a single act: when I finished this one, I hugged it to my chest tightly. It really is near and dear to my heart.

reference_books.title: Grave Mercy (His Fair Assassin, #1)
reference_books.review_text: What a good book! I know nothing about this time period, and went into it essentially blind. I thought the way Lefevers blended history and fantasy was excellent, and not overdone at all. This was a gripping, page turning book. Can't wait to read the rest!

reference_books.title: Untamed (House of Night, #4)
reference_books.review_text: One of the better HON books. I liked that there wasn't as much sex in this one. It didn't seem forced. It was a nice balance of thriller, mystery, and teen romance. Good stuff!

reference_books.title: Wishful Drinking
reference_books.review_text: What a fantastic memoir! Carrie Fisher has a painfully heartbreaking life, but she writes about it in such a way as to make it bearable. The woman is insanely strong. And the book is insanely good. I read it in about 2 hours total. A quick read, but a very satisfying one. Great job, Carrie!

reference_books.title: Rook
reference_books.review_text: This book was a struggle to get through. I actually almost put it down several times. However, I made myself power through. And I'm glad I did. The last 150 pages or so were well-paced and worth it, but the beginning was slow and convoluted. Know that you're in it for the long haul, and you'll be better prepared.

book_a.title: Fahrenheit 451
book_a.user_review: A fabulous book. I can't believe I've never read this until now. I think what is most amazing about it is the fact that in 1950, Bradbury predicted many things that would happen in our society. He is fabulously intuitive when it comes to human nature. This was a wonderful, and very scary book. I don't want to think about living in a world like this.

Everyone spends there time watching their "parlor walls" which is basically television projected onto the walls of the home. Everyone is kept occupied with no real time to think. There is always a war going on and knowledge doesn't seem desirable. Montag did his job for years , secretly keeping some books but usually supressing the need to really read through them or tell anyone about it. After meeting a young girl who is constantly asking questions and pointing out to Montag the many things he doesn't notice and is missing, his eyes are opened and he starts to question his life and realize there might be more to it than burning books.

As I write this, Ray Bradbury died almost a week ago. Five days ago I was looking for something new to read, and his death inspired me to pick up Fahrenheit 451, which had been sitting on my bookshelf for some time, waiting to be read. 
 I can't say that I enjoyed the time I spent with F451. A book of this size--barely novel size, novella, really--should have taken me no more than two days to read, took me 4 days. I even started to fall asleep a few times, a phenomena that rarely happens while I'm reading a book. I even wondered if the thing was worth finishing. I vowed to finish it, and finish it I did, but not without skimming and skipping pages. And it still took me 4 days to finish it. 
 I guess that sums up how I feel about the book and maybe I should stop there. But I won't. I will say what I've been itching to say since I picked the damn thing up. I may be slaughtered for such honesty, but to hell with it. 
 It's an overrated bore! Lifeless prose, unlikeable characters. A short story stretched out to novella size--Bradbury admits as much in the Afterword, which I have to say, was more interesting than the book itself. It should have remained a short story, in which it undoubtedly could have been a more enjoyable read. 
 The idea was good, but how could such a good idea become such a boring novel? In this age of e-Books, and Kindles and Nooks and etc. this book does not transcend time, and I wouldn't be opposed to every paper and hardback copy of this book being burned. I'm thinking about burning mine just for the fun of it in vengeance of the time of my life I will never get back and the lack of fun I had reading it. Does anyone want to buy it? 
 Bradbury may have been a talented storyteller, but he did not impress with F451. May he rest in peace, for if all of his works are as boring as this one, it will save people their valuable time of reading it and from having such heinous thoughts of wanting to burn it.

I'm listening to the audiobook that I borrowed from Dallas Public Library, but I have read it many times before. 
 This is actually my favorite book of all time, by my favorite author. This audiobook is read by the author. His reading voice is not entirely clear, but it is worth it to hear his book in his own voice. I own a hard copy of the book, but I borrowed the audiobook from the Dallas Public Library. 
 This year I am participating in World Book Night and The Big Read and both of them feature this book. I will be giving away 20 copies as part of World Book Night and I will be working with my library's Big Read programs to give away more copies. 
 Everyone should read this book. One of the most interesting aspects of it is in the story when characters claim that the situation was not caused by official government censorship in the beginning, but by the public's loss of interest in books. I love some of the futuristic gadgets that became true in some way, like the seashells that are a lot like our earbuds and the "robot tellers" at the bank (ATMs)! 
 Bradbury's worry that too much interest in mindless entertainment from the "boob tube" would be the death of books isn't necessarily true, but there are fewer book stores these days. All is not lost, though. We might be, unfortunately, losing some of the small bookstores and chains, but there are still the big box book stores you can find in most decent sized malls, like Barnes and Noble. A lot of people are getting books through Amazon, Kindle and other ereaders, Half-Price Books, and of course libraries. Libraries might be using funding, but they are still around and lots of people use them. 
 Well, I got on a book soap box. Back to Fahrenheit 451- It is a flawless, perfect book about the importance of reading and the value of keeping our cultural history alive

A dystopian novel that describes a world where the banning of books has created a culture that only asks "how" rather than "why." Its real value to me was in the message, not the plot. It was (intentionally) inconclusive in much of the narrative, but the descriptions of an unthinking world hypnotized by entertainment were haunting.
Great Science Fiction read.

"The good writers touch life often. The mediocre ones run a quick hand over her. The bad ones rape her and leave her for the flies."That is a very unpleasant metaphor, and Fahrenheit 451 is an unpleasant book. It feels like it was written by a teenager, and if I were his teacher I'd give it a B- and not let my daughter date the weird little kid who wrote it. 
 Its protagonist, Montag, lacks any character; he changes as Bradbury's shitty story requires him to, from the dumbest kid on the world (his cousin once offered to pay him a dime to fill a sieve with sand and he sat there for ages crying and dumping sand into it - I understand that's a metaphor, but it's a metaphor for a moron) to a mastermind (telling Faber how to throw the Hound off his scent). You ever see film of someone skipping a pebble in reverse? Me neither, but I bet it's like this: plop plop skip skip wtf? 
 Each other character exists solely to advance the plot. There's the hot underage Manic Pixie Dream Girl - "her face fragile milk crystal" - who teaches him how to smell dandelions (and whose beauty is harped on endlessly) and then disappears off-stage; Faber, who's all of a sudden like best friends and then disappears off-stage; the bonfire circle of retired professors who happen to be right there when he stumbles out of a river looking for them. 
 There's his wife - "thin as a praying mantis from dieting, and her flesh like white bacon." He seems to loathe her, and all real women. 
 "Millie? Does the White Clown love you?" 
 No answer. 
 "Millie, does - " He licked his lips. "Does your 'family' [TV entertainment] love you, love you very much, love you with all their heart and soul, Millie?" 
 He felt her blinking slowly at the back of his neck. "Why'd you ask a silly question like that?"There's a real conservative streak to this book. It looks backwards, as conservatives do. Bradbury blames his world's disgust with books on "minorities," what we nowadays call "special interest groups": 
 "Colored people don't like Little Black Sambo. Burn it. White people don't feel good about Uncle Tom's Cabin. Burn it."These are the only specific examples given during Captain Beatty's central speech about why literature has been banned. 
 There are some nice moments here. A disturbed and immature but intelligent kid flailing around will hit a few marks. The central idea? No, no props for that; book-burning was invented centuries ago. But the moment when the TV instructs all citizens to open their doors and look for Montag, that's nice. And the suicidal Captain Beatty is the book's only living character, although his speech is littered with what I swear are just random quotes. I even like the idea of a circle of book-readers, each responsible for remembering a certain book - but it's dealt with so lamely here. "We've invented ways for you to remember everything you've ever read, so it's no problem." Well, in that case I got like half the Canon, y'all can go home. Losers. Wouldn't it be cooler if these people had to work for it? 
 Point is, those little flashes of competence are so overwhelmed by terrible philosophy and so ill-sketched themselves that I have no idea how this book has escaped the bonfire of apathy, the worst and most blameless fire of all. It's just a lame, lame book. 
 I wouldn't burn this or any book. But I'll do worse: I'll forget all about it.

I love Something Wicked This Way Comes, and look forward to reading more Bradbury eventually, but I did not particularly like *this* novel of his. 
 Why not? Because of all the sociopolitical satires or didactic fictional works I've ever read, this one is the most unsubtle. It is the literary equivalent of grabbing someone, violently shaking him or her, bellowing "CENSORSHIP IS BAD! IS THAT UNDERSTOOD?" in his or her face, and then clubbing them with a blunt object for good measure. As a work of literature, it's nothing great, and it frustrates me that almost everyone loves it.
I don't really know what to say about this book. It has a excellent conception and a good lesson behind the story but I don't think it was a couldn't-stop-reading-book. It was ok.
You're books!
Still pondering how this is a classic.

I need to reread this. 
 This is the first time I rate a book 1 star and I have read only good reviews about it, that makes wonder if I'm missing something here. 
 Fahrenheit 451 you'll get another chance, but for the time being one star is all you'll get from me.
Interesting... reminded me of Brave New World. I did like it and it was a pretty easy read. He's not too far off the mark for futuristic writing. I'm glad I finally took it off the shelf!

Wonderful. I especially loved part one of the book. It was desolate and barren and just great imagery. The kind of prose that makes you stop and read it again because it was just so good. A real classic.
It was so much more fun and true when it WAS science fiction

Reminds me a little of Catch 22 in the fact that some of the plot makes sense and then it goes into a section where nothing makes sense. I understand that this to stimulate the idea that the world is changing and that nothing will ever be the same but realistically could get really confusing. 
 I really enjoyed reading the book despite all this. I liked the main character and could identify with the idea that some people need to change the world to feel better about themselves.
It was a really wierd book. Very confusing. Switched to 1st person to 3rd person on and off in the book.
the afterword was the best part

I had high hopes. Perhaps it was just because I read this right after 1984, which I loved, and I had heard from a friend that this was better... it didn't live up to my expectations. 
 I liked the premise and characters, but there was something about the writing that just felt...flat. It couldn't hold my attention. Sorry Ray Bradbury, I don't think I liked your book. I did try though.
keren, gak nyangka kalo ceritanya akhirnya bakal seperti ituh. tapi sayang pas bagian.......tttttttttttttuuuuuuuutttttttttt....... (kena sensor)
I guess its kind of a 'classic' but I didn't really like it that much.
I got his autograph twice; he wrote all of 451 fahrenheit at the Los Angeles public library. He spent ten dollars in dimes using their type writer.

Esta es otra cacotopia en la linea de "1984" de Orwell y "Un mundo feliz" de Huxley, sin ser tan fatal y negativo como los otros, teniendo tintes mas naives. Cuenta la historia de Montag, un bombero que se dedicaba a quemar libros. Y como en su ciudad donde todos eran felices y estaban rodeados por pantallas con las que interactuaban incesantemente, Montag empezo a tener ideas y darse cuenta que quizas, no era tan feliz como deberia ser.... 
 El libro me parecio interesante y agil, no muy engorroso. Con un estilismo que me parecio bastante mas interesante que el contenido en si, entre romantico y realista: 
 "Vio que la luna se hundia en el firmamento. La luna alli, y su resplandor, ?producido por que? Por el sol, claro. ?Y que iluminaba al sol? Su propio fuego. Y el sol sigue, dia tras dia, quemando y quemando. El sol y el tiempo. El sol el tiempo y las llamas. Llamas. El rio le balanceaba suavemente. Llamas. El sol y todos los relojes del mundo. Todo se reunia y se convertia en una misma cosa en su mente. [...] 
 El sol ardia a diario. Quemaba el Tiempo. El mundo corria en circulos, girando sobre su eje, y el tiempo se ocupaba en quemar los anos y a la gente, sin ninguna ayuda por su parte."
I didn't like this book

Sono perplessa... davvero questo libro sarebbe un classico? 
 Personalmente l'ho trovato illeggibile. Si, ok, mondo distopico, libri proibiti, i buoni leggono, i cattivi guardano la tv... ma nessuna trama, per quanto bella sia (e non e questo il caso), puo convincermi ad affrontare un libro scritto in un modo che mi ha fatto sfiorare l'attacco isterico. Possibile che ogni parola necessiti di due aggettivi, un paragone e una metafora? Non puoi venirmi a dire che e una "scrittura poetica"... questo non ha niente di poetico, e solo frustrante da morire. Roba che quasi quasi ci do fuoco.
I read this in high school, but actually loved it this time. Makes you think about the world around us a lot more.

Fahrenheit 451 
 An exquisit short novel that I really enjoyed. The account of an awakening, in the midst of a society where instant gratification has become the norm, and life has become void of deeper more lasting values. The story seems relevant even today, and some of the details seem eerily accurate to todays technical environment, even though it is was written almost 60 years ago. The prose seems to me fragmented, verbally astounding in parts, and almost a bit rushed and mundane in others. 
 Highly recommended.

Audio book read by author. Not a huge fan of author readings but when it is Mr. Bradbury, well, I'm willing to make exceptions. I knew this story but had never read this story. Wow. If you were 18 the last time you read this book, I highly recommend picking it up again. It is one amazing read-and still relevant (and I would argue even more relevant) in 2012. Surprise on the audio: the last disk is an interview of Mr. Bradbury where he discusses the book, his life and everything in between. He had me laughing out loud one moment and crying the next. He loves the written word so deeply which shows in his work as well as in his life.
This book moved very slow and took me a while to get through it...

book_b.title: Practical Magic
book_b.user_review: This book was okay. To be honest, it really didn't start getting good until the last third. Slow start, but a good ending. I rarely say this, but in this case, the movie was better than the book. I like the tone of the movie a lot better. The tone of the novel is gritty and despairing until the last third, and then the women get stronger. It was just not what I expected, knowing and loving the characters from the movie, I really had trouble with the book.

sample_reviews.review_text:
As we're nearing the release of 
 The Rules of Magic 
 , let's look back to where it all began. Back in the 90's when I was but a wee lass, there was 
 Practical Magic. 
 Which wasn't just a book - it became a beautiful movie too! In fact, that's how I come to know this wonderful story of Alice's - through seeing the movie when I was a child, or maybe a teen. 
 (if the images don't load, you can read this post on my blog.) 
 And then we waited for years, without even knowing we were waiting. 
 I was really excited to read 
 Practical Magic 
 , because I really loved the movie, but I suppose that's what made my experience worse than it would have been, had I approached the book as a blank slate. 
 The movie has quite a few differences to the book, so if you expect the same story - forget about it. 
 That's not necessarily bad, of course - it's just that after having loved the movie as a young teen, it's impossible to, well... Unsee it. 
 Had I read this book on its own though, I would probably have loved it much more - as I love nearly anything that Alice writes. You can feel the same style, the same passion - even though it's an older work of hers. 
 However, I had a few problems with this story - for example, the portrayal of love. 
 The book makes it sound like physical love is pretty much all there is to it! I refuse to accept that - certainly, that's not my experience. Where is companionable love, where's soul love? Where is the rest of it? Aside from that, 
 it makes it sound like only incredibly beautiful women are loved. 
 That's... harmful. I know the author probably did not mean it that way, but having always felt one of the plainer ladies myself, it was... a little hurtful to read it. We are constantly barraged with messages that we're not beautiful enough - every woman is today. 
 We don't need to be told that only pretty ones are loved, moreover - we absolutely don't need to be told that one pretty woman's looks can act like a spell and take true love away. Certainly that's not true, or at least - not always true? There's definitely more to love than that! 
 If you can put that aside though, the book grows on you. Alice has such a beautiful writing style, she can tell a story like it's a fairytale, and maybe a dark, adult one - that's what I love about her books the most. Reading her works, you feel as if the world you're reading about (and quite possibly, the world you're even living in) is not as simple as it seems - 
 it's magical, secretive and probably quite dark. 
 Other than that, I think it was a job well done writing about an abusive relationship and shedding light on all of the feelings and causes of one. Alice always does a splendid job with these things. But even though the feelings are very well written, this novel doesn't come too close to the characters - it's more like a camera that keeps watching from the corner of the room - not making assumptions, not judging the characters - it's just there. 
 Differences from the movie? Let me use a spoiler tag for those who still want to read 
 Practical Magic. 
 The story doesn't take place in the aunt's house, that's one thing. Another thing - the whole tone of the story. The fact that the sisters are never absolved in front of the community. The fact that Gillian never did kill her husband. Or the fact that Sally's girls are not little, they're almost grown. The fact that Gillian takes a lover too, it's not just Sally who's got a happy ending. And also? Gillian is blonde! 
 Read Post On My Blog | My Bookstagram | Bookish Twitter

I checked this out from the library because Alice Hoffman is coming to Frederick as part of the libraries "Frederick Reads" program. I don't think I'll go to hear her speak. The book is entertaining, but feels gossipy/dishy. It dwells on satisfying personal desires. Sally is depicted as backyard for being so responsible and trying to fit into society. 
 Did not finish. Listened to 3 disks out of 8.
Loved this more than the first time I read it!
One of the most stupid books i have ever read.
I must say this was a pretty good book. Obviously the movie and book are different but they did a good job translating it onto film.
Amber, this is another quirky author you would enjoy and one I want to read more of. Meg, she does kids books also.

I think I liked the parts where she didn't talk about magic best. 
 "The only advice the aunts offered was that a baby was easier to prevent than to raise, and even Gillian, as foolhardy as she was, could see the truth in that". 
 "It's easy to forget what you do in the dark, if you need to". 
 "...it's just that she doesn't want them to see who she really is, when she herself doesn't know".

This is the second book I attempted by this author.....I figured, hey, the movie wasn't that bad, so the book's got to be better, right? Wrong. Not a fan of Hoffman's writing at all....it lacks substance to me and after reading two of her books, I won't be subjecting myself to a third.

This is one of those rare examples of the movie being better than the book. Yeah. I somehow managed to get through it, but this book was like one never-ending series of mood-setting lists. An example: 
 "Sally thought long and hard each time she hung up the phone. She thought about the girl in the drugstore and the sound of Antonia's footsteps on the stairs when she went to bed without a good-night hug. She thought about Michael's life and his death, and about every second they had spent together. She considered each of his kisses and all the words he had ever said to her. Everything was still gray-- the paintings Antonia brought home from school and slipped beneath her door, the flannel pajamas Kylie wore on chilly mornings, the velvet curtains that kept the world at bay. But now Sally began to order things in her mind-- grief and joy, dollars and cents, a baby's cry and the look on her face when you blew her a kiss on a windy afternoon. Such things might be worth something, a glance, a peek, a deeper look." 
 I count 4 lists in just one paragraph. Within the next page, the total of similar lists goes up to 8. In two pages. This kind of writing feels sloppy when it is used beyond the beginning stages of scene setting, and when it is almost the only way the author seems to able to convey meaning it becomes teeth-gnashingly annoying. Add to this a complete lack of momentum and a generally meandering story line and you get a sad face (or maybe bitch face if I'm being honest) and a thumbs down from me.

One star because the Goodreads rating system aptly sums up my feelings on it: did not like it. I only finished it because I have a uni class that requires I do so, else I would have DNF'd it last week. I didn't care for the writing, the characters, the plot, the setting, the use of 'magic' and 'witchcraft' (which seem questionable at best in this novel) and an overabundant reliance on using metaphor as magic in place of writing actual moments of fantasy. Thanks for reminding me why I don't read Alice Hoffman novels anymore, though!
It was alright. Not my favourite, I really did like the movie better (maybe because of my weakness for Sandra Bullock), but it holds up well on its own.

I enjoyed it ... not at all like the movie. Comparing them is apples to oranges. 
 I remember sweeping poetry, discussions of fall and love. Definitely not my usual - but I enjoyed it very much.

A good story! I kind of wish I had read it before I saw the movie. Although both stories were quite different, I couldn't help comparing the two in my head. This was a quick, easy read, not too deep in my opinion. This is my first read by this author and while it was good, I wasn't overly impressed. Honestly, I think I liked the movie better.... Which is a rarity for me!
What a strange story. Nothing like the movie except for the characters names. I was not expecting the kids to grow up and have such an intricate role.

I know this is sacrilege, but it happened: I finally found a movie that was better than the book. 
 I was really torn about whether to give this book 2 or 3 stars. I've never read a book I disliked so quickly - I just wanted it to be over so I could move on to something I liked, but at the same time, the writing was strong enough that it didn't turn me off completely. That shifted it from a 2 star (the plot) to a 3 star (lovely writing). But then I wrote this review and realize I was more angry than I thought I was about the romance, so I dropped it back down to 2. 
 The problem with this book is twofold: the main characters, and the portrayal of love. 
 Every main character is a nightmare human who is so self-obsessed I'm surprised they even know the names of their close loved ones. They never give a thought to anyone else until close to the very end, they're constantly messing up their lives and blaming it on everyone else, and they're just generally not very nice. This resolves a bit near the latter part of the book; it was divided into thirds, and the final third made up for the first two in that at least the characters learned and grew, though the circumstances that led to it were pretty flimsy. How were their deep character flaws solved? Simple. They fell in love. 
 Because, ladies, the moral of this story is that love is instantaneous, based on nothing but appearance and fate, and everlasting. Acting like a stalker is okay because it's romantic! Giving up everything about who and what you are is good because love! Don't ever get to know anyone or put work into relationships, that's a waste of time, true love is blind and instant and based on nothing and will hunt you down whether you want it to or not! Also it's inevitable, so there's that. Ugh. Gag. No thank you. That is not romance. It's a half-hearted fantasy that only teenage girls would actually want for themselves, because the rest of us have figured out love is more than that, and better for it. But this book is NOT written for teenage girls. Every time the author threw out a 'fuck' or a 'dick' amidst the otherwise flowery poetic language my whole body viscerally reacted. I don't have a problem with sex scenes or swearing, but it felt wildly out of place in a book that otherwise was painting a highly stylized portrait of life. 
 Would not read again. Might read a different book by the same author, but only after careful research of reviews to make sure the plot was as different as could be.

I didn't have high hopes for this after reading some of its reviews. I have to agree with everyone who has said that in this case the film is far superior. 
 This version of the story is nowhere near as touching which is so disappointing. 
 I wouldn't recommend this book to fans of the film, and to anyone who is unsure I would say don't bother with this.

Practical Magic seemed so cool on the outside, but most of it is just filler. I was really disappointed with its unoriginality, generic style and the sections that just dragged on unnecessarily. Books like these are sad because they have the potential to be something greater but they never really reach it. :(
Rarely will I EVER say this about a book, but WATCH THE MOVIE!!!!!

I don't remember when I read this book exactly, but I really loved it. It is beautiful and magical. Reading the words on the page was like reading a long poem it flowed so constantly smoothly. There is not one jagged corner to snag your mind on, only pretty words threaded together. Somehow the book entertained me, grabbed me and soothed me all at once. Beautiful writing, excellent story, and full of wisdom we should absorb and keep. It was seriously magical on every level and is a book I will return to again and again, forever.
Finally read this and watched the movie. Hands down the book is better than the movie, in fact I didn't even finish the movie, I thought it was so terrible.

For the first time in my life, and as a book nerd this truly pains me to say, but the movie was better! I grew up watching Practical Magic, and it has shaped who I am as a person. I was over the moon to finally find the book. However highly disappointed, when it fell short of my love for the Owens sisters! It's not bad, Infact is is a good story and had I not been a P.M. Fan I most likely would have given this book four and half stars.

I picked this book up because I loved the Sandra Bullock movie so much--naturally, there were a lot of things different (aren't there always?), but still I am glad I read it. It probably would have been a five-star had a read the book first--but then I wouldn't have liked the movie as much, most likely. Ah, well. A double-edged sword. Still, a highly enjoyable read.

Practical Magic is one of my absolute favorite movies so I figured it was high time for me to read the book it was based on. It's not often that I watch a movie based on a book before I read the book and it's even more rare for me to say that I like the movie more than the book but I'm going to say it, Frankly the movie was better. 
 Usually when you compare a book to it's movie counterpart something is lost in translation. In this case the movie focuses more on the magical and mysterious lineage of the Owens women making it, in my opinion anyway, a far more interesting story. In the movie the aunts are main characters to the story whereas in the book the aunts play a less pivotal role. This makes for two very different stories. 
 Comparisons aside, Hoffman does write fairly well. I wouldn't mind reading more by her.
I can't believe I'm writing this but, the movie was so much more entertaining than the book. The book was dark and depressing and I can't say that I liked any of the characters.

This book was ok. I'm glad I had already seen and loved the movie much because it was very different. I thought the book added a whole new dimension that I liked, however I'm not a fan of the f-bomb and there were too many.
One of those rare cases where I preferred the movie.

I kept reading this book thinking that it has got to get better... but page after page, the suck just kept going! This book is the Energizer bunny of the terrible book world. 
 I'll usually give a book 100 pages to convince me to keep reading, this one was so bad that I had a morbid fascination to see if it got any better... it didn't. In fact, hard as it seems, if anything... it got worse. 
 I'm sorry, I have to go wash my brain...

This book made me want to fall in love every day and start making soaps and jams out of ingredients from my organic garden. 
 I loved it. Between a 4 and 4.5.
I was expecting more from this book. The plot never "grabbed" me and it took me a while to finish.

This was a great book. I really enjoyed the movie and decided to read the book finally. The book of coarse was very different from the movie. The Aunts weren't as big of characters like in the movie. Don't get me wrong I would have loved the book even more if I had read the book first. I did like the book and I'm glad I read the book but I liked the movie better. But it could be because I saw the movie first.
Great movie, great book!
I was disappointed. I'm not sorry I read it - but it left me wanting more.
*MUCH* more literary than the movie. I have to admit, I liked the movie better.

Beautiful, poetic, and it flows so easily from start to finish. I've watched the movie that's based on this book over and over for the last decade and I absolutely love it, but this was my first time reading any of Alice Hoffman's work. Oh, the things I've been missing! I love what the writers of the movie did to make the changes so the movie would be visually entertaining, but it also borrowed from the book and made it even better (or at least equal to). I'm now going to read other Hoffman novels, and the next on my list is The Ice Queen. I've read a portion of it on amazon.com and it starts off beautifully enough and left me wanting more. I'm absolutely looking forward to reading much more from this author.

I really, really wanted to like this book because I absolutely love the movie, but the movie was just 100% better. The writing was sloppy and had no real continuity. The plot was dark and, ultimately, not very moving. I'll be sticking to the movie from now on.

loved the movie. shoot me you book junkies. I'm one of those book junkies. It's a case of having seen the movie about ten times and loving it. don't get me wrong Hoffman's writing is great. I usually dig her. so read the book then see the movie, or pick one.

I think this is the first time I can say that I liked the movie better than the book. The bitterness and jealousy of the sister's in this story is overly irritating to me. The story line is similar whereas the movie takes bits and pieces of the story and condenses it in a way that the characters are much more enjoyable.
not as good as the first time I read it
The movie was soooooooo much better. This barely had any magic and the aunts were gone for most of the book.

I've loved the movie for so long that I figured I should read the book. While the two are not faithfully similar I was not disappointed. Hoffman doesn't just write women characters, she writes women's soul. The relationships between the three sets of sisters are complicated, emotional, and painfully accurate; which also goes for their romances. Hoffman switches from the lyrical to the profane in a single sentence with the same dexterity and grace of a cat. It's simply magic!
This is one of those rare cases where the movie is better than the book. I didn't enjoy this one.

This was just bad. I've read a few Hoffman books before and enjoyed most of them. This was hard to read and not at all what I expected. Very little magic, not the great relationships between women that I was expecting, crappy setting for most of the book. More than one rape threat in this book as well, one in the thoughts of a man that we are supposed to see as a good guy, and one towards a kid! Disgusting and horrible. 
 I have watched the movie, though it was probably over 10 years ago. While I remember very little of the movie, it was definitely better than this book.

Well... this book was weird. 
 Let me preface this by saying that I have pneumonia. I can't do anything at all without huffing and puffing like I've just run a marathon. That trip to the bathroom? Yeah, it took me ten minutes to catch my breath when I came back. 
 So, I'm not doing anything but reading and watching tv for the moment. And I'm also drugged, so maybe that's a contributing factor to this review as well. So take from it what you will. 
 This is a cute book that's written oddly, and there are other issues. 
 I've never seen a book with so many characters and so little dialog. It's all internalized thoughts, remembrance, and description. That's a little weird. 
 The way the tenses jump in this book makes me want to strangle cuddly animals. It was also weird. No, it was way worse than weird, it was third person present future past. 
 Now onto the other issues: 
 Men: Most importantly how no female can live happily without them, including the 13 year old girl. This made me roll my eyes. Each woman/girl has this fucked up life and it is all just magically better because penis. Eh. I wish it worked that way in real life, I really do, because penis is a dime a dozen. 
 Beauty: I don't even know. Women in this book are so beautiful that men just jump up and start doing crazy shit for them, like dancing the hoochiecoo in a puddle of water while angry competitive suitors throw plugged in toasters at them. (That didn't happen, but I bet it could have.) It's really important in this book to be drop dead I came in my pants beautiful. Even the old lady is described as the most beautiful Owens woman ever and at that point you wonder, "If everyone is this fucking singularly beautiful than no one can be." 
 Magic: Fuck that logic. We're not witches and we do no magic unless we are in which case we do but we're just normal. Got it? K. 
 The Aunts: They aren't named until the end and you don't know much about them and you're kept waffling between thinking they're really great people who took in two orphans to wondering if they're evil because for some reason a sweet lovesick girl deserves to have her life ruined because she's not old enough to understand yet that you can't have everything you want. I don't know. I've thought about this way too hard but I'm pretty sure I'm on team, "Fuck these bitches!" when it comes to the aunts.
It's a rare thing, but I liked the movie better!

This was difficult to read. The author kept switching between past and present tense. She would also start talking about another character and switch to their point of view without a transition. I had to go back a few times and see if I had missed something. The worst part was the use of the author's favorite word, F_ _ _. She loved that word and used it constantly. This is a case when the movie is much better than the book.
Nothing like the movie but still really interesting. A little slow at times but still a really good story.
Movie was better
The writing as writing is nice. The characterization is interesting. The story is slow, and not a lot happens, but I'm pretty sure the author wanted it that way.
Rare instance of the movie was better.

I was intrigued with the story, but Alice Hoffman does what I thought writers were never supposed to do - write huge information dumps and then proceed to use 10 words when just one or two would suffice. I got so tired of hearing about those damn lilacs and how every single person in this book from main character to unnamed minor character is awash in grief and secret pain. She really lost me after she used the phrase "... drenched in a thousand tears." No joke, she really uses that phrase. 
 I don't think I'll be picking up any more of her books in the near future. So glad I got this from the library so I don't feel bad about wasting any money.

reference_books.title: Wildwood (Wildwood Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Well I wanted to love this one. Being a fan of the Decemberists, loving the artwork, a favorite genre all mixed together was a for sure win in my hasty opinion for reading this one. I have finally abandoned it with 5 chapters left to go. I kept trying to keep Going, to finish, but this book is soooooo damn looooong! Five chapters would just take me another few days to get through. Just couldn't do it. 
 As a children's book I believe this one would lose the interest of most 10 year olds attention. The writing is actually very good and would definitely expand any child's vocabulary. The story is highly imaginative in its world building and takes great care creating and developing its characters. However keep in mind this is a children's book. All those elements would work if the book were cut on half. 
 Here are some other problems I had with the story. Pru who is 12 is left in charge of her baby brother whose a year old, and when she takes him out a bunch of crows steal him into the woods which starts her adventure to look for him. This is the basic premise of the story. At one point while she is in the land of Wildwood she meets an older man in a van and gets a ride from him. Personally, I felt creeped out that she would get into a van with a strange old man she didn't even know. It wasn't so much that it was in the book, it's more that pru didn't seem to question or ask herself if this was ok, just blindly went to him. Another bit I didn't like had to do with the kids parents, won't say what it was it would be a spoiler. Just know that it made me seriously question what kind of people these parents are. 
 I admit I'm not a fan of talking animals in books so that was off-putting for me personally. Lastly, because of its length, it tended to get boring for me. I have read 1000 page books that fly by, leaving me wanting more, but this was killing me. I'd definitely pass on this one.

reference_books.title: The Orchardist
reference_books.review_text:
When I began this book, I was literally swept away by the lovely, slow-paced writing, the easy, gentle way the story unfolded, much like its main protagonist, Talmadge. His story of growing up on the orchard farm, the devastating loss of his sister along with his quiet solitude for some reason made me care very much for this man. One day two teenage, pregnant sisters show up in his orchard, alone and afraid. His slow, kind way of trying to connect and help them was beautiful. He was almost trying to tame them as if they were wild cats. His kindness and patience so unusual in a man. This is where he shows his strengths. However, his shortcomings for where actions needed to happen I did find ultimately frustrating. 
 Carolyn Middy, his good friend, was another character I became fond on. Mostly for her sand and grit. She was a tough but kind woman who was very capable. A woman you could go to if one needed help or a kindness. The story of how these lives touched and completely changed each other made me want to turn the pages to find out more. There are disturbing things that happen in this story that are not pretty, but written in such a way as to not be graphic and gratuitous for entertainment sake. A nice change for me. 
 I do have gripes about this book which is why the 3 stars. It was way, way too long. The author went on a lot about nothing for long stretches through the book that I found completely unnecessary and added no value nor did it move the story forward in any way. I also became frustrated with Tamaldge at times for his inaction. A man that made many regrets by sitting b and watching and thinking his way through his,life rather than doing and living it. A kind and thoughtful man, but he needed a good swift kick in his ass. 
 Also, the ending. This ending was most unsatisfying. For me, it just ran out of steam and faded away. The first half was very good and was waiting for the set up for things to come to a climax, only to be vastly disappointed that that did not happen. 
 Overall a pretty good read.

reference_books.title: The Shack
reference_books.review_text: I couldn't get past page 40. This book is way too preachy. I think the message it wants to give about redemption is a positive, but it doesn't reach out to all faiths and all people only a select. I also found it to be poorly written. I don't believe this book converted anyone like it seems to want to do, only attracted the same like-minded people and was written for just that audience.

reference_books.title: Invisibility
reference_books.review_text: First of all I love David leviathan and I have never read Andrea cremer. These two writing a book together did not flow at all!! This started out strong with a boy living alone (dad left mom died) and he is invisible. He's never even seen himself. His thoughts and feelings gave a wonderful sense of his life of isolation. I loved the description of his days and how he managed himself up to his 16 year old self. Then comes along a new neighbor, Elizabeth and her gay brother Lorrie, who I did love. Elizabeth could see Steven!!! The first person ever. This premise had such promise. I think I could tell where leviathan ended and cremer began. So I had love/hate going on a lot. The whole story was ruined by two things, the rushed "I love you". This happened way to soon. I still cannot tell you what they loved about each other since they didnt really know each other. The other part completely fell onto utter nonsense with evil curses and spellcasters and overall awfulness. I'm so sad and disappointed in this book that had such a great idea only to see it thrown away. I gave it two stars for leviathan writing and Elizabeth's mention of the Tardis.

reference_books.title: The Monsters of Templeton
reference_books.review_text: I gave it my best shot, but I really had to stop and put this one down. Just couldn't get into it although I tried hard.

reference_books.title: Ender's Game (Ender's Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I thought long and had about reading this book. My son, who is not a reader was assigned the book in school as are many kids, it's also hailed as one of the classics of sci fi. Now the movie is coming out so I thought, ok, I'll give it a go. 
 I got through it, I finished it. That's about it. I was not wowed by this book at all. The one thing that did impress me was the use of blogging and role playing video games which were not yet around back in 1977. I always love when sci fi does that. Other than that, I found the writing so repetitive! One chapter bled into the next about the battle scenes and they all just blurred together for me. The psychological aspect of training kids by use of manipulation and isolation was interesting yet full on child abuse. Leaving Ender to live with what he did was plain awful. Overall, it's an interesting story. Movie may play out better. 
 I won't read anything else by this author, as I hear most the rest of the series has a "religious" agenda that I'm not interested in. Also, I think this guys a one hit wonder and overall not a good person. Like Mel Gibson, ill just pass on this guy all the way around.

reference_books.title: Ordinary Grace
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed this little book. Being told through the eyes of a 13 year old boy set in 1961 brought back memories of my own childhood and for that alone, I liked it. Frank drumm tells the story of how deaths surrounding his small town in Minnesota change his life and forces him to grow up sooner. His father is the town preacher, he has a Brother that stutters and a mom who has become merely tolerant of her life as a preachers wife. 
 Frank tells the story some forty years later. You get a wonderful sense of the sixties in small town america. I loved the flashbacks of watching the wonderful world of Disney of Sunday nights, the excitement of watching TV on TV trays in the living room. The way the kids ran all over town until nightfall when they knew to come home. A lovely feeling of nostalgia. 
 As for the murder and the mystery that surrounds it, I was pretty engaged in up I til a certain point. Then I realized and figured out "who did it". The red herring became all too clear and i felt the overall who done it was a cliche and not at all that surprising. Although the mystery left me disappointed, the story itself did not. I found my characters believable and enjoyed the easy style of writing very pleasurable. For that alone, I would recommend.

reference_books.title: The Jungle
reference_books.review_text: WOW!!! This was one of the most amazing books I've read. Powerful in every way. This shows the true underbelly of how America boasted it's freedom and liberty for all out of one side of it's mouth and how once the immigrants bought off on that story, came here only to find that they were the slaves of corruption and greed, which we call American freedom. How our meatpacking companies were allowed to feed the American people food not fit to serve a dog was sent out to our tables everyday and how the best of the meat was sent to Europe because of their tough inspection laws and how the worst of our meat was sent to our soldiers, the ones who die for the sake of our "freedom". I invite anyone with a strong stomach and a strong heart to read this amazing book.

reference_books.title: This One Summer
reference_books.review_text:
I am not sure what age group this is intended for, but it's way too mature themes to be for anyone under 15. The cover and being a Caldecott winner is deceiving, it screams YOUNG. 
 This is an fairly depressing story involving two friends who see each other over summer vacations with their families to the beach. The overall tone is quite the downer making this not very enjoyable when thinking about it for a kid to read. It's all too realistic drama weighs heavy on you while you going through this story. There is lots of contents, f bombs, sex, bloke jobs, porn, pregnancy, suicide. All the negative elements not much positive. The pictures are wonderful, but is the only reason for the 2 star. 
 This should be 15 on up.

reference_books.title: Just Kids
reference_books.review_text: We should all be able to experience as profound a friendship as Patti and Roberts. What a beautiful tribute to Robert who was in very many ways her artistic soulmate. Patti smith seamlessly weaves her story of the beginnings of her and Roberts artistic adventure letting us meet the likes of Janis Joplin, Jimmy Hendrix, Andy Warhol, Sam shepherd and many more. You get a wonderful sense of the times and the life of true artists. Highly recommend

This book is all about opposites-light and dark, tragedy and joy, happiness and misery. In one corner we find Anna, married to an important government official, but bereft of love. When she finds it in Count Vronsky, she gives up everything to grasp it. Unfortunately her ties to her old life and the intense resentment she receives causes her to retreat into isolation with only Vronsky to keep her company. And because of all of these pressures and a growing sense of distrust to Vronsky, she begins a decline into sadness and despair. 
 In the other corner we have Levin, a 'hands-on" type of guy who loves to work the fields of his country estate alongside his servants. There are many a long passage describing his passion for new methods in farm laboring. He is content with this life, except he lacks one thing: a wife. He sets his sites on Kitty, the younger sister of Anna's brother's husband (have I lost you yet?). Through no level of drama on their account they attempt to forge a union that will last a lifetime. While their story isn't glowingly happy, it is much lighter than Anna's. 
 I liked this book-the writing style is so rich. I felt like I was in those fields during threshing, or at the theater with Anna. Its exquisite detail really immerses you into the society of Russia in the mid-1800s. It seems like every other person is a princess or a countess or whatever, and they flaunt their wealth extravagantly. But witnessing the downward spiral that is Anne and the tangled web that Kitty and Levin weave was completely engrossing. Yes, there are times when the author takes a trip into left field to air his political stance or talk about farming or religion (it loses a point for those), but on the whole it is a masterpiece, and I'm glad I read it.

I'm really not certain how to even begin this review, as this was unlike any reading experience I've ever had. To start with, it is the most in-depth book I've ever had, and one of the longest, at a whopping 940 pages. It also is not a book you can take down in huge chunks, at least that's not the way I approached it. Often times I'd read no more than 20 pages per day, which of course meant I spent several weeks working my way through this. 
 The main characters are among the most well-constructed figures I've ever read, which is something you would certainly hope for given the book's length. The title figure, Anna Karenina, is an enchanting high-born Russian lady who, at the beginning of the novel, is married to Alexander Karenin, an important Russian figure in government. Anna has a sort of magnetism to her that is evident from the reactions of both men and women to her throughout the novel, and she knows how to use this magnetism when she wants to. It is this magnetism that attracts the bachelor military man Vronsky to her and really kicks off the various plotlines of the book. 
 To go too deep into the plotlines of this book and analyze them would turn this review into a term paper because of how numerous the plotlines are. But the essence is that Anna falls for Vronsky, runs away from her husband and sun with him, and once they are truly together, she begins to wonder just how well they truly go together as a pair. Running concordantly with that thread is the story of the agrarian Levin, whom I was unsurprised to discover was based heavily on Tolstoy himself, and the life he establishes with his wife, Kitty after she originally shuns him in hoping for a proposal from Vronsky, which she of course does not get. 
 The prominent theme that Tolstoy puts out in this book is the changing nature of people, and our own desire to change ourselves and those around us. Unfortunately, the way he did it got a bit repetitive and irritating by the 3/4 mark and didn't stop causing me to grind my teeth until I got to the end, where one of the characters at last seems to understand that, yes, people change and what we resolve to be cannot always last forever. But until that point, it was a revolving door of characters stumbling upon a new idea or attitude, or being affected by another person's attitude, resolving that they will never be the same because of this, and then ten pages later either realizing that they were wrong or that their new attitude is untenable. We get it, Tolstoy. 
 The other criticism I have of this book is from a modern viewpoint. I'm guessing it was a style common in this era of Russian literature (though I have never read any other Russian lit from this era), but the lengthy diatribes on industry, political views, and farming were often very difficult to plow through because of how little they relate now. Obviously I can't fault Tolstoy for including this, but it was tiresome after a while. 
 All in all, I'm proud to have finished this book, and I am a better reader and student of literature for it, but it wasn't the most enjoyable time I've had reading.

Time magazine calls "Anna Karenina" one of the ten greatest books of all time (many other, reknown readers and writers call it "the best"), and while I probably haven't read enough books to say whether or not this is true, I have read enough to say I can't imagine anything ever written any better. 
 AK, published in serial installments from 1873 to 1877 in "The Russian Messenger", tells the overlapping and contrasting stories of Anna Arkadyevna Karenina and Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin. Anna is a married woman and mother who falls in love with a man who is not her husband. The novel unfolds her plight as an adulterer...how she is scorned by society and abandoned by her friends and family, and how her loneliness and isolation plunges her into a deep despair. 
 Levin is a confused, misguided young man who falls for a naive young girl. His path in life leads in another direction, as his relationship and growing family lead him toward stability and spiritual growth. The stories of these two characters which are interesting enough on their own, also serve to give the reader a glimpse of the social, political, and philosphical issues of the day. 
 Anna Karenina is named as an example of literary realism, and that is what I liked best about the novel. Tolstoy wrote life as it really was...not only as it was lived in day-to-day activites, but as the characters thought out their actions, their lives, their decisions. Once you've read such a realistic depiction of society, it makes it hard to read highly imaginative fiction--it all feel so insincere, so impractical, and unnecessary. Why would you want to read someone's highly idealized re-telling of life, when you can experience the magic of someone who can actually put into words what people think and why they do what they do? If you truly want to read life, read Anna Karenina.

Like many people who begin reading Anna Karenina, I was intimidated by the size of the novel. As I'm a slow reader, I took it at my own pace. It's 900+ pages took me just under 2 months to read. 
 Now that the story is over, I miss my window into Tolstoy's world. I loved the array of characters in this novel and while I found that I identified with certain characters more than others, I think there's something for everyone in one story line or another. I did find that there were parts of the novel that bored me, such as Levin's confusion at the election process and the hunting trip that took place in the later part of the book. However, I was captivated by Levin's struggle to find meaning in life and his consideration of what it means to have morals without religion. 
 I enjoyed getting into Anna's head, but also appreciated understanding the feelings of her husband as well as her lover. Tolstoy's ability to write from different perspectives and opposing points of view, male and female, was my favorite aspect of the book. 
 Oblonsky was, without question, my favorite character. You meet him right away, and though he's not always a key player in the novel, Anna and Levin's lives always intertwined with Oblonsky just enough to leave me wanting more. His character is larger than life, and one I will keep with me as a literary favorite.

Actually, I'd give this 4.5 stars. It's a wonderful book. Does a fantastic job of putting us into the world of 19th century Russia and the lives (and problems) of nobility. Also contains probably one of the best horse racing scenes I've ever read in a novel. 
 The only thing that's dropping this book by 1/2 a star is the ending, which seemed to wander into a less interesting reflection/crisis on religion by one of the main characters. It's interesting because the point where everyone remembers (and talks about) the book ending is actually a solid nineteen chapters before the book actually ends. That said, I liked the characters enough I was okay to hang out for a while longer with them, even if it did feel a bit like wandering. I'm definitely going to read War and Peace now, thanks to this book, though that won't happen until after I get out of Grad School for sure.

So I finally finished Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina. It took me most of the year. Did I like it? That's kind of a loaded question. It was a fascinating book. More interesting for me, perhaps, than it would be for most others, because I actually know someone who is JUST LIKE Anna. 
 Anna is flawed in the worst sorts of ways which makes her a fascinating character, but rather annoying at the same time. For those who don't know, this book is about a married woman who has an affair with a younger man. That's not a spoiler. The affair begins near the start of the novel. She makes her decision to have the affair, which will ostracize her in the eyes of nineteenth century Russian society. 
 If that was what she wanted and she was willing to deal with the consequences, I could be okay with that. But that's not what Anna does. She flaunts her decision for all of this puritanical society to see, and then gets mad when a scandal hatches. She's the kind of woman that creates drama, then sits around crying because there's so much drama in her life. 
 By the end of the book, I wanted to throttle this woman! Yet, there is a lot of truth in Tolstoy's story because, as I said, I know someone who has made many of the same choices Anna did and is exactly like her. I think Tolstoy must have known just such a person. He describes this type of personality perfectly. 
 If you like tragic period pieces with class-system drama, this is the book for you! It's a bit slow moving and kind of hard to stay in, but persistence pays off. I read 1-2% a day until I was done. And I must say, I'm glad I did. I view it as an accomplishment and now I can boast that I've read Tolstoy. Yea! 
 About the writing: it's kind of hard to read. This is the type of book that would never get published today. There's a lot of meandering, repetition, and passive voice. Of course, this could be because the novel was originally written in Russian and translated. But, if you're going to tackle this one, be forewarned. 
 Overall, I thought the story was interesting and rang of truth. I'm glad I read it but I'm also glad to be done. :D

sample_reviews.review_text:
Here were my thoughts still reading it: Oh my God this book is awful. I'm going to try and keep reading for Dante's sake but it's just really boring and poorly written. Great premise, it's a shame. 
 Here's what happened shortly after: I gave up. It was just too boring and not worth my time when I have so many other books to read. It's difficult to keep the main characters straight (mostly the ones with like 10 words in their name), I got really tired of reading "My dear Dr. Holmes," "honestly my dear," etc., and the overall flow was horrible. 
 Update: A friend of mine read it and apparently the ending wasn't horrible. It made sense. So read at your own discretion. My friend told me what happened and I'm done with it.
"I can't even get through one page. Terrible writing. Even the grammar trips me up. The pronouns float without clear antecedents. What's up with this?"

It's 1865, the Civil War has just ended, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and the other members of the Dante Club are translating Dante's "Divine Comedy" for the 600th anniversary of Dante's birth. When a pair of murders occur that seem to take their inspiration from the tortures in "Inferno", the Dante Club decides to investigate. What is revealed is that 19th century poets make poor detectives and boring characters. Longfellow is treated liked some kind of poet-god, Holmes is a whiny little bore, and Lowell and Fields are interchangeably nondescript. In fact, none of the key characters other than Oliver Wendell Holmes are developed very much and Holmes is not an especially likable person. 
 Although using historical figures in a mystery can be interesting, the problem is that since we know that none of the members of the Dante Club were murdered by a serial killer in 1865, it's hard to create much sense of danger. Normally, an author will add additional fictional characters, make us care about them, and then put them in danger so that only the heroes of the story can save them. But Pearl doesn't go this route, instead putting his main characters at risk but this doesn't create any real tension. In fact, Pearl seems to realize this so the danger he places his characters in is quickly dispelled. The book starts off fairly well for the first chapter but then drags as Pearl introduces the Dante Club. A big problem is the dialog. Here is a random sample: 
 *Lowell mumbled, "Did not Dante himself once write that no poetry can be translated? Yet we come together weekly and gleefully murder his words." "Lowell, peace," gasped Fields...* 
 Perhaps Boston poets did speak this way in the 1860's but it makes for tedious reading. In the acknowledgments, Pearl reveals that much of the dialog is taken from essays written by the various members of the Dante Club. Since people don't speak the same way that they write, perhaps this is the source of Pearl's problem. After struggling through the first hundred pages, the book finally starts to move as the mystery deepens and our heroes start their investigation. But the story quickly begins to drag again as the "detectives" reveal their incompetence. 
 Which leads us to the denouement of the story in which all is not revealed. The holes in the solution to the mystery are vast and the "detectives" make no effort to fill them. So the story seems mostly an excuse to discuss some issues with the translation of Dante. The murders are brutal but poorly described. Boston of 1865 could have been an interesting character (as New York City is in Ragtime and The Alienist) but instead Boston is barely described. In fact this is the key to the book's failures... Pearl isn't a very good descriptive writer which is critical in fiction but especially in a mystery. 
 I should add that the book has a foreword which gives away a key plot point (one of the few of interest in the first part of the book). Skip the foreword and return to it later... you'll thank me.

 Enough of stone throwing, I don't want to keep on writing words on words about a book which I did not like. Keeping the plot aside, there were some parts I did like, the ambiance being but one of them.

Pusing, itu yang saya rasakan waktu membaca novel ini, teman saya sampai kagum ketika saya mengembalikan novel ini kepadanya dan saya bilang saya sudah selesai membacanya.

 Terus terang saya tidak tau, apa yang benar-benar membuat saya pusing, tapi kemungkinan dikarenakan terjemahan ke Bahasa Indonesia nya yang tidak tepat, seperti yang dikeluhkan oleh beberapa orang.

I started this book at the beginning of January, and just wasn't motivated to finish it... 
 I'm getting to the age where - if a book doesn't hook me (I gave it till page 78), I give up. 
 I feel the author is a smart person - he goes to great lengths in the book to let you know you're reading a smart author... So, the theme is great, and the setting is cool. Maybe Pearl should've trusted his research and spent more time making engaging characters instead of two-dimensional cliches. Also, the plot is there, but it is lethargic as Hell! (See what I did there? Dante? Hell?) 
 He went form concept to book without developing engaging, intriguing, empathy-inducing characters. Subsequently, on the 4th of April in the year 2017, I gave up on this book and put it in the donation pile...

The voices of the poets were very believable, and I was touched by the account of post-traumatic stress disorder in Civil War soldiers. It was a pretty good murder mystery, but the pace was too sluggish for me. I understand that Pearl was trying to recreate the style of the 19th century poets and writers, but it wast really my cup of tea. So I say this is a solid novel, but not spectacular.

Despite the attention grabbing start the book failed to really get going for some time, with the narrative unecessarily wordy and over-worked. I was thinking about giving up after a quarter of the book but the pace improved and the plot developed well. The Dante connections were well delivered if a little far fetched. 
 All in all a decent read, but it's going in the charity shop bag!

This book is a great guilty pleasure for the Dante's Divine Comedy nerd inside of me. The plot isn't very good though. Actually the plot just flat out stinks. There I said it, it Dan Brown stinks. The descriptions in the book and the interactions of the characters more than make up for it though. I would recommend this to any literary nerd looking for a fun read.

I liked the plot of this historical fiction based on well-known literary men, who in translating Dante's Divine Comedy from Italian to English discover a killer is using their Dante translation to perform gruesome acts of murder. I enjoyed their quest to find the identity of the murderer, and I liked the personalities of each character; however, i got weighed down in the many muddled and mundane details the author used. I was certainly ready to be finished.

The summary of this book boasts, "A series of grisly murders...are no ordinary killings. Each is inspired by the hellish visions of Dante's Inferno." I have currently read 84 pages of this book and have only read of one 'murder' which did not contain many gory details or any suspense what-so-ever. So far this book seems to only contain dialog between stuffy professors/poets who only want to talk about why Harvard should allow them to translate Dante. The text is incredibly slow and I find myself losing interest only a couple sentences in. This book has not kept my attention.

By the time I got to the middle, I really wanted to know "who dunnit," and that's the main reason I finished the book. The ending was totally unexpected, but unless you really love Dante or poets of the 1860s, I'm not sure I'd recommend it.

Maybe it is unfair to try and read a book in the middle of NaNo (National Novel Writing Month) but I did start this book before. I just could not get into it and finally when the second notice came from the library to please return this book I took it back without finishing it. I may give it another try in a few months or maybe not.

I generally love historical fiction and mysteries, but this one missed the mark. If it had not been an audiobook that passed the time for my commute to work....I'm sure I would not have ever finished it and it would have been added to my "throw-away" pile.

The beginning was glorious. Unfortunately after the big start the story ground and ground until I wondered if we were supposed to collect a sack of corn meal at the end. 
 Vastly disappointing.

This book started out as a "hey, this isn't too bad" type of book to a "wow, this is cool and I can't put it down" book. I really like the plot, and I learned more about Dante than I knew before. Someday I will read the Divine Comedy, but hearing about Inferno is enough for me for now. Maybe when I have a break between semesters I'll try to read The Divine Comedy for real.
