book_a.title: Kitchen
book_a.user_review:
I started this book because it was a recommendation in Anna and the French kiss, I think. I've been wanting to read for some time now, and I finally got to it. The author is really praised for her novels that bring to light the struggles of the human heart. I was expecting a marvelous story about loss, finding yourself and leaving the darkness behind, but this book was a little disappointing. 
 It starts with Mikage losing her grandma, her last relative, and it follows her through the day to day struggles of loneliness, to end up with a substitute family. At the beginning she's lost and utterly depressed, with time she turns to cooking as a hobbie to deal with time. 
 Anyway, the story is a little monotonous and without a real plot. It feels like a lot of sad scenes put together in order to develop a story. I wasn't able to finish this book because I was too bored. Seriously, I just couldn't get through it, between this lack of plot and slow pace narrative. It's just not for me, even though I liked the Kitchen metaphor.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Can cooking help you cope with the despondency you feel from loss? I'm not talking about wolfing down garlic mashed potatoes from a pan; I'm talking about a multi-course gourmet meal that you are willing to toss out if it's not perfect and start all over again. That's the theme of Kitchen. Our main character is a twentyish-woman who lost her father at an early age and then her mother. She went to live with grandparents but her grandfather died, and then her grandmother, and now she has no living relatives. 
 She turns to her kitchen. But she is also invited to live with the family of a young man she has known since childhood. Now here's a modern family: just two people, the young man and his mother. But did I tell you his father is his mother? Or, to phrase that more correctly, his mother is his father? It's a transgender situation. The two young people are drawn to each other but then he is hit by loss. They grapple with trying to help each other, maybe love each other, or maybe just pity each other, and try to stop each other from jumping over the edge. 
 This very short novel has a short story appended at the end: Moonlight Shadow. This story, also about loss, and it could be the same woman, takes us into magical realism. Maybe they do come back, at least to tell you they're ok. 
 I found the two stories very moving and fascinating to read. Translated from the Japanese. 
 Photo: Model of a Japanese kitchen, ca. 1880, from peabody.harvard.edu

A story about a young woman, a young man, their care-givers that function as loving anchors connecting them to the world, and the loneliness and isolation that persists as the human condition. Beautifully written, it was a pleasure to read.

How can such sort stories be filled with so much emotions? This was the first thought that came to mind when I finished reading Kitchen and indeed this book was an emotional rollercoaster. Both of the stories were deeply touching and heartfelt, although they were short and concise. 
 Kitchen, the first and longest story included in the publication, is about a young woman named Mikage, who has lost her grandmother. She struggles to get over the grief, but it's too difficult for her, because she's left alone in the world, without another blood relation. But she finds hope when she moves in with a young friend of his grandmother, Yuichi, and his mother Eriko. After that she slowly gets closer to both of them, she finds a job and a new apartment. When tragedy comes to Yuichi she has to make an important decision, if she will stand beside him or let him deal with it alone. 
 In its core Kitchen is a love story, although death and loss and how to go on living after such a difficult situation are present all the time. But there is not a great dramatic gesture or a confession, or even sweet loving words. The feelings develop under the surface and the understanding comes from little gestures, like sometimes happens in real life. Sometimes to bring a takeout is enough, in order to convey the feeling of wanting to be together even if everything is so uncertain. 
 Full review at: http://thereadingarmchair.blogspot.gr...
2015 Popsugar Reading Challenge Item 44: A book that was originally written in another language.

3.5/5 
 This book is split up into two short stories, the first one being a little over 100 pages, and the second one being a little under 50 pages. Both of them deal with grief and loss of a loved one whose passings were unexpected. Banana Yoshimoto's writing style is beautiful and eloquent, however I found that there was something quite elusive about her prose. I found myself not really immersed in the story at times, particularly in the first story. I also enjoyed Yoshimoto's inclusion of a transgendered character, who was never used as the butt of jokes, but stood as the nurturing, wonderful human that she was. 
 With the first story, while I registered the sorrow of the main characters and the themes that came up, I just couldn't connect with the characters. I have never dealt with the loss of a relative who I have been very close to and I think because of that, I wasn't able to understand their sense of anguish. I do see the importance of being present for those who are dealing with depression, no matter how little you can contribute to helping them in finding joy again. This is something I can connect with as I have been through this in the last couple of months actually. You should be there for other people, but not at the expense of your own well being, particularly if you find their emotional state triggering for yourself. I ended up giving this story a 3/5 rating simply because I feel that it is a good story that is also very well written, but I think this is just a case of me reading the right story at the wrong time in my life. 
 The second story I enjoyed much more. I was really able to empathize with the character and I definitely felt more drawn to her narrative than with that of the previous story. There were subtle elements of magical realism as well, which I really liked. While the first story took me several days to read, I finished this story is one sitting and I liked the allusions it made in mental illness (depression) being similar to having a fever. The toughest parts are hell to pull through but once you make it out of that alive, slowly and surely you will find the joys of life again. This story did a really good job and showing the normality of depression and our coping methods, no matter how strange they may seem to those who have never gone through similar situations. It normalizes the actions of those who suffer in a very real and relatable and I really commend Yoshimoto for doing that. I ended up giving this story 4/5 rating. 
 I highly recommend this book for those who may be going through a rough patch in life, whether it be the loss of a loved one or simply feeling like you are falling into a black hole. I am glad this book came into my life and I will be sure to return to this later on in my life.

From what I understand, this is stylistically very "Japanese". While I appreciate the simplicity in a lack of prose, I found this story to be monotonous in tone. It was good... but I suppose I had hoped for better with the reviews that I read on it and the author's ambitions so unabashedly grand.

The book works in a little patches only. It's neither boring nor entertaining. 
 The other ratings I found on this were over hyped. The problem with the book was it should have been a little more longer, either writing out the characters more or progress story in any one of the 'genres'.
Hilarious. Humor is an excellent remedy for tragedy and loss, if we're brave enough to stomach the first dose.
152 pages about death, thinking of death, depression, thinking of depression and a bit of cooking. Life is too short for books like this.

depth beyond the sweetness with tiny clear painted images that stay forever.

This book came highly recommended to me when I was looking for female authors versus the white male variety. I thought: what an adorable name...Banana Yoshimoto, what on earth could her one-word titled books be about which are a worldwide sensation? Lizard, Asleep, Amrita, Kitchen. 
 The same week I reserved Kitchen at the library, I also found it in a nearby Goodwill sifting through an elaborate fiction section on Sunset Boulevard. Two, in fact. I thought: fate is bringing this great book to me, and look how small and quick to read it will be. I thought: this cover is super cheesy...is that the author? 
 Then flipping through the book I saw that it had been translated from Japanese by a Megan Backus. That sounding like a name of English origin, I had my doubts for a fair interpretation. My doubts were justified with rudimentary prose, if one can even call it that, and a story about an unconsummated relationship between a girl and a boy, inspired by the death of close family members affecting both. 
 I suppose it's meant to be bittersweet the way these kids are there for each other when they are lonely, sad and grieving. Groundbreaking or controversial the way the boy character's mother is actually his father with a sex change, who dies in a bar fight at the hands of an obsessed admirer feeling ashamed of his attraction. 
 You'd think with a premise that inspiring, the story would pretty much write itself with little to no need for style, or even closure to give the story some depth or a stick-to-the-guts consistency. There was a second story, too, also about untimely demise and cross-dressing...I skimmed that one. 
 I'd hate to think that my heart could've formed a wall of ice around it overnight, but Kitchen to me was flat, uninspiring, but just as cute as the cover. For Yoshimoto to be the sensation she is, I must assume it has a lot to do with the kitsch of her name, or with the fact I missed something in the translation of it, which must read as fantastic in Japanese. Otherwise, I never thought my life would be better off, with one less Banana in it.

"In the uncertain ebb and flow of time and emotions, much of one's life history is etched in the senses." 
 There is such simplicity and gentleness to this writing. Banana Yoshimoto writes so honestly about the experience of death. I kept thinking: Yes, this is how we feel. Yes, this is how we experience the beauty of life, the sadness of death. 
 She managed to talk of death without being sentimental, or even particularly sad. "In places where a loved one has died, time stops for eternity." 
 I was a little disappointed after Kitchen. For me, it should have been longer, or shorter. Moonlight Shadow though was perfectly satisfying.

I have read that Japanese author Banana Yoshimoto's debut novel Kitchen remains a phenomenal success in Japanese publishing history. If there is one thing that I can say with some confidence about the book, she certainly plays to her audience. Unfortunately for me, that audience comprises of an awful lot of love struck girls. 
 Ostensibly the tale of family, grief and love, Kitchen is replete with food-based imagery and metaphor. For me, this is the strongest aspect of the novel. Perhaps this is due to the fact that there is a certain licence to describe what's on the table. Unfortunately, this is also a tale of grief and love, and the constant telling rather than showing the central characters' (intense) feelings very much wears you down. 
 I'm not sure how suited I am for the unbridled sentimentality that forms the heart of this book. An uneven translation probably doesn't help, as the frequent 'Americanisms' do jar when spoken by Japanese characters. That said, it's an interesting peek at the lives of young Japanese. It explores a world that balances tofu and pickled vegetables against KFC and doughnuts, and gives me a peek at a life quite different from mine. 
 A long way from the work of Yukio Mishima or Shusaku Endo, I don't think that Kitchen was a waste of my time but I am sure that Banana is my cup of tea. That said, if you're young and in the throes of your first love, I'd recommend it.

This is a sweet little book about Mikage, who was orphaned as a young child and then raised by her grandmother. When her grandmother dies, she finds solace in her friend Yoichi and his mother Eriko. The three of them become a new kind of family, and the book details their relationship as well as how the losses the three of them suffer, independently and as a unit, affect each of them in a myriad of ways. 
 There were some things I absolutely loved about this book. The writing is really pretty, flowery without being over the top, descriptive but not to the point of being annoying. The way Yoshimoto describes grief and its hold on a person's soul is absolutely gorgeous. I also loved how the relationships between the three main characters went places I wasn't expecting while at the same time remaining very true to their personalities. Another thing I loved was Yoshimoto's handling of a trans character in Eriko. Eriko used to be Yoichi's father and is now his mother, and the way that Yoshimoto has the characters handle this fact is SO nonchalant, like it's no big deal whatsoever (as it shouldn't be) is really amazing. The way that Yoichi explained it to Mikage, and how Mikage just accepted it and loved Eriko exactly the same as she did before she knew this information about her, was really incredible to see in fiction. 
 While I loved certain aspects of Kitchen, overall it was not my favorite novel. I appreciate that it was slim, but I wanted more from it. I wanted more emotion, I wanted to get to know the characters even better, and I wanted to feel a deeper connection to them. This could possibly have been accomplished by making the novel longer, but I'm not sure that Yoshimoto's style could have made that happen for me. Either way, I can see what people love about this author and there were definitely things about the book that really worked for me.

This is actually two stories in one. The main story, Kitchen, was just over 100 pages long and the companion story, Moonlight Shadows, was only about 50 pages. 
 Kitchen had so much potential, and seemed like it could have been a really good story. But it felt to me like the outline got published instead of the actual story. The whole structure of the book was choppy and broken from the character and story development, to the paragraphs and even the actual sentences. There were many little nuggets throughout the story that I really liked, a paragraph or a sentence that felt really profound and touching. These little treasures were scattered throughout the whole story and just when I would be frustrated and ready to give up, one would appear to redeem the story for me. Since nothing really ever got developed thoroughly though, I never got attached to the characters or anything that was happening in their lives. I'm not sure if this was meant to be a love story, or a remembrance of a loved one who had died, or an inspiration to others to be who they want to be (even if that mean becoming a transsexual). There was a small amount of hope threaded through what felt to me like a lot of darkness and pessimism. All of the loved ones in the main characters life have died and you can feel how this has broken her in her story telling. I thought this was a relatively pointless and depressing story that was not well developed at all. 
 The reason this book gets two stars for me is because of the rare wonderful insights that I found in Kitchen which really touched me, and the fact that Kitchen was only 100 pages long and therefore a short read. However, that alone was not enough, the main reason I gave two stars was because of the companion story Moonlight Shadows. This was also quite a depressing story of loved ones lost, but it flowed so much better and seemed to convey more of a message of hope and a lot less pessimism than Kitchen. This short little story touched me a lot more than the main one, and redeemed the book for me. 
 I wouldn't really recommend this book to anyone, but I would possibly recommend Moonlight Shadows to someone who has recently experienced the loss of a loved one and needs to hear a story of hope from someone who obviously understands.

 So yesterday, having finished my first Murakami shortly on the heels of The Vegetarian, I was stubborn about wanting to leave this corner of the world. I was looking at lists of books and this book featured in several including one (not sure) saying books by lesbians of colour.

 What struck me, and I made sure of, was that kitchen is definitely not magic realism. Realism, but it is so sparkly and rainbowy and pretty it borders on magic. BTW, it's a novella, and there's a second shorter story in most editions.

And I mean this in a good way. Also, not sure, but I think her books are meant for a younger audience. Gosh this review needs so many edits. Typing from the phone is a pain.

I first read this book in high school as an assignment, but I really enjoyed it, although I was too young to really understand any of it. Then in college I was assigned it again. This time I read it more closely, & I was pretty shocked at how deep I found it the second time around. 
 The story is basically about love & death, but dealt in this unique, non-cliche way that makes you appreciate it a little more. It's quirky & very clearly a Japanese story, so if you're not into that don't bother. The story starts off with Mikage, the main character, sleeping in a kitchen while dealing with the death of her grandmother. She suddenly meets Yuichi who knew her late grandmother & the two slowly fall in love. Mikage moves in with him & his parent, where she develops a love for cooking. 
 I really enjoyed the symbolism of food in the story, & how these little, unexpected events which could easily become clunky & schmaltzy were actually very touching. I would suggest this to anyone looking for a quick read without a sacrifice in quality.

Wow so I found this book by reading the jacket on the book in the story. This blurb given there was so cryptic it intrigued me. Now that I've read it I know why the blurb was so cryptic as this book is hard to make a summary for. It has so much in it. Creatures never seen before, angels, magic, giant puppets, fallen, and war. It had love and hardship, it had friendship and morals, and the meaning of values and how they shape people. Taylor did an incredible job making the characters have internal conflicts. She twisted an amazing tale of love that lasts through the ages even after death. It mixes magic with the ethereal and absolutely entrances you from the very first page. 
 This book is about a girl named Karou who was raised by chimera. She knows she's not ordinary and in the beginning that's all she wants. Her 'family' use peoples teeth to grant wishes and she helps them collect those teeth. When she's not doing that she goes to an art school in Prague where she shows still life's of Brimstone, Issa, and other chimera but people think are just her imagination. All of that changes when scorched hand prints start showing up a doors all around the world signaling that the war fought between seraphim and chimera for century's has found its way into their world. Karou is faced with her past and who she really is. She meets a seraphim named Akiva that she feels she knows but just doesn't know how she knows him. He hold the key to her past but if she remembers will she still love him or will that love turn to hatred? She must decide if her love for the enemy or her love for her 'family' is more important. 
 The imagery in this book was spectacular. You felt like you were standing there in Prague or India or where ever. The characters were phenomenally written. The plot was original and intriguing. The world was beautiful and creepy at the same time and Taylor did a great job portraying that. This book and its characters were so unique I honestly had no idea what was going to happen. It was unpredictable and it kept you riveted from the very first sentence. I could not put this book down. 
 The characters were so deep and vivid it was hard not to completely love all of them. Karou is strong-willed, bold, but also has an innocence to her that makes her totally intriguing. She was naive and a little childish but she learned and grew and I loved watching her do it. Her heart was pure, but strong like the heart of a lion and she was not afraid to be herself in all things...most of the time. Akiva was wow. He was so heartbroken and tormented that when he finally finds her again would can't help but rejoice for him. He is standoffish and has a no nonsense attitude but that's what I love about him. 
 I recommend this book for everyone. There were some places that were slow but the imagery and the world made even thoughs parts completely intriguing.

I've been hearing so many good things about this book for so long that I thought it was time to see what the fuss was all about. I wound up with an audiobook version, and I really liked the person who read it. The book itself was terrific- I loved the premised, liked the characters, and was intrigued by the locations. I found myself sometimes getting a bit lost as to what time/location the story was currently taking place in, but I think that is more a function of the audio rather than any issue with the writing. 
 Karou is an art student at a university in Prague. She is known for her drawings of fantastical creatures, though little do her friends know the characters in her sketchbook actually exist in her life. After a devastating loss of those she has always called family, Karou embarks on a journey to discover what happened and where her "family" has gone. Discovering that the man who should be her mortal enemy seems to be, in fact, her soul mate tips her world on its side as she seeks to find out who she really is.

I've been contemplating about reading this novel for sometime now because it takes place in Prague, I've been told it's well written and it's about monsters. I love stories about monsters. But I had a bit of a drawback because some people told me, "You'll love it because it's flawless." Nothing is flawless. The story felt extremely flawed. Yet. I felt addicted throughout. Laini Taylor does an excellent job at combining words into such beautiful sentences. As somebody who loves to write, I learned a lot from her. In fact, I would suggest this novel to anybody who is interested in writing because there is a lot to learn from Taylor. 
 Laini Taylor writes in third person about a mysterious girl named Karou. She lives in Prague, she's an art student and oh. . .she works for monsters. But she does not understand her past. The plot does delve into her past later. Half it it tells of Karou's errands that she runs for monsters collecting teeth. Why teeth? Read the book to find out. It honestly is creative and shows Taylor's talent at brilliant world building--for aspiring writers. While Karou is on an errand she meets an angel and learns that these angels are "back" and so everything starts to become interesting. So enters Akiva. He is an angel who is attracted to Karou because of her mysterious nature. Who is Karou or as some others say it, what is Karou? Akiva introduces interesting character elements, development and humor. 
 Anyhow. I did enjoy this novel a whole lot more than I originally thought and I am excited about reading the next novel. It was the fun read that I've been needing in my life. I would suggest this to anybody who is interested in writing or loves novels that are prose heavy. Also. A great read for monsters. And if you think you know anything about Young Adult books and judge them. Then I also dare you to read this novel because you know nothing. 
 So. Thank you everybody who has gradually been telling me to read this. I'm glad I did.

Disclaimer: After continuing on with the series I was utterly and competely infatuated, and gave the other two books much higher ratings. OMG I ended up loving it so much. 
 Well, hmm, I didn't love this book as much as it seems that everyone else did. Considering this book has been reviewed out the wazoo I'll do a quick rundown of the things that I liked or disliked. 
 I'll start with dislikes, because I prefer to finish on a positive note. I did not like the "astral" "ethereal love." I did not like it because it was not tangible, it was not something that we see grow and thereby expand the characters themselves. It just happened and was all "oooh butterflies." I've been with my husband for 7 years now, real love may start as butterflies, but butterflies it ain't after the first year (pardon the colloquialism). Granted it turns out that they've met in a previous life, and so the true love becomes something much more meaningful, however, this happens in the last three chapters of the book, so has little to no bearing on the first several hundred pages . Second, the constant descriptions of that same astral love seemed to become more and more repetitive. (Granted, if I had read this at 16, I would have been head over heels, and it is YA, so these are all more complaints geared to the older crowd). Third, I have no problem with the much-much older being stalking the nubile young thing, it's a trope and it doesn't bother me, creepily stalking someone and watching them sleep does bother me though. Oh well, I can get over that. I'll even forgive Karou for sometimes being annoying, the girl is 17, I was probably a terrible person at 17, it's just that I never really felt I gelled with any of the characters. They didn't do much for me. My only other issue is that sometimes the narrative seemed erratic. I think this was more of an editing issue than an authorship issue, they probably should have asked her to soften the edges between flashbacks, flashforwards, and all the gobbeldy goo inbetween. 
 Things I liked are just as numerous, however, as the things I disliked. I like the tone of the narrative; I enjoyed the flow of the author's words. I appreciate that the author managed to be highly descriptive, but it seemed that the narrative itself was plain, and not too flowery, so you were better able to lose yourself in the world. And the world! Boy! I really did enjoy the world. I love the angels, I loved loved loved the chimera, I loved the price of magic; I thought it was really superb world creation. I particularly enjoyed the ending of this book, I just wished that it had come about 100 pages earlier. If anyone is reading this review, and feels that they are flagging in the middle of the book, I highly encourage them to finish- it picks up, I promise. I particularly enjoyed the convergence of stories. I also found that the book's treatment of sex as part of growing up was an incredibly healthy attitude, and this is something that I feel a lot of older YA either lacks or doesn't confront. Also, FANTASTIC cover art. I'm a big fan of cover art, and I really feel that this cover grabs the tone and the beauty of the story inside. These things should not be underappreciated. 
 All in all I felt that the read was worth it. It's not my favorite series or anything, but it's fun brain candy nonetheless. I will read the sequel, but I'm not breathlessly awaiting its arrival either. 
 Edit: The author gets extra points for having awesome pink hair.

DNF at 170 pages. 
 I'm starting to think that fantasy isn't my thing anymore. I'm still enjoying authors I found a while ago, like Amelia Atwater-Rhodes, but with the sole exception of Neil Gaiman, it's been months since I found a fantasy author I liked. For the most part, this was no exception. It wasn't all bad, but I found it dull and not interesting enough to complete. 
 Everybody's going to complain in the comments if I don't say this, so I'll get it out of the way first: yes, the writing was phenomenal. Absolutely phenomenal. Among the best I've ever seen. Taylor's control of language and imagery skills are astounding, and the pictures she paints with her words are vivid and real. I might not have liked the book that much, but man, it's worth picking up just to see some of this prose. You'd think the dialogue would be overly-formal and awkward, but it wasn't - Taylor did a great job of making it authentic and realistic. There: I hereby acknowledge that the writing is just as good as everybody says. 
 That said, I just couldn't get invested in the story. The pacing was pretty slow - even 170 pages in, where I stopped, I wasn't quite sure what the overarching plot was supposed to be. There was some mystery to it, but it felt manufactured; I could tell Taylor wasn't really interested in writing a real mystery, and she just wanted to throw it in to make The Truth more surprising. It didn't seem to be going anywhere, and it didn't interest me enough to find out The Truth. 
 The worldbuilding, though, is where I had real problems. I'm really shocked by how few people have been complaining about the tedious infodumps here. At the beginning, it seemed like every few paragraphs, Taylor launched into some tedious and (usually) unnecessary explanation of how we got to where we were. The world wasn't even that complex, really, but damned if Taylor didn't find a way to make it complex. The explanations got so tedious that I often found myself skimming without even realizing it. I just didn't care, and not even the great writing was enough to get me invested. 
 The characterization could've worked fine, except that it mostly relied on telling rather than showing. Taylor had a pretty complex personality worked out for each character - she told us as much - but Karou was the only character where it really came through in how she acted. She was a pretty engaging character, but she was the only one. Everyone else just felt bland - it could've worked better with less telling, but the way it was, I didn't enjoy it. 
 With all the hype surrounding this book, I really did expect a lot more. It turned out to be very dull and forgettable. Taylor's writing really is excellent, and I hope that at some point, she finds a more engaging story to tell with it. But until then, I'm not the audience for her writing.

This book.*sigh* 
 It is one of those books where 5 out of 5 just doesn't feel like a high enough rating. It is unlike any other YA book I've read before; it had an originality about it that's hard to find these days. It was beyond amazing. Brilliant comes to mind. 
 When I say it is a MUST READ I am not using the word lightly. 
 The quote on the back from Patrick Rothfuss reads, 'Wow. I wish I had written this book.' And he is not alone. I am seething with jealousy wishing I had written it too. 
 You know when you discover a book and you just know that you'll love it? Well, after I read the following, I just knew I was going to love it. 
 Errand requiring immediate attention. come. 
 The note was on vellum, pierced by the talons of the almost-crow that delivered it. Karou read the message. "He never says please," she sighed, but she gathered up her things. When Brimstone called, she always came. 
 In general, Karou has managed to keep her two lives in balance. On the one hand, she's a seventeen year old art student in Prague; on the other, errand-girl to a monstrous creature who is the closest thing she has to family. Raised half in our world, half in 'Elsewhere', she has never understood Brimstone's dark work - buying teeth from hunters and murderers - nor how she came into his keeping. She is a secret even to herself, plagued by the sensation that she isn't whole. 
 Now the doors to Elsewhere are closing, and Karou must choose between the safety of her human life and the dangers of a war ravaged world that may hold the answers she has always sought. 
 Sound good? 
 This is an urban fantasy, with the fantasy side fantasy. 
 Karou is a blue haired girl whose sketch book is full of monsters that no body knows are actually real. Mysterious handprints start showing up all over the world on the doors to 'Elsewhere', and then they are burnt down. Karou's life is suddenly turned upside down. And then she meets an angel, Akiva. He is not our idea of an angel, but an angel from another world, and he has an amazing, unbelievable tale he shares with Karou. 
 This is a story within a story and it has you on the edge of your seat the whole time it is unravelling. It is achingly romantic and mysterious and imaginative. Laini's prose painted such a vivid, beautiful picture in my mind. 
 Just look at this example: 
 'Everything was between them, everything he'd felt suffuse the air while they faced each other over the rooftops. Being near her was like balancing on a tipping world, trying to keep your footing as the ground wanted to roll you forward, hurl you into a spiral from which there was no recovery, only impact, and it was a longed-for impact, a sweet and beckoning collision.' 
 You will devour this book quickly as you will be un able to put it down. For every lover of fantasy and romance this is THE book to read.
I think I loved the language and the creativity more than the actual plot, if that makes sense. The world-building was good, it just wasn't a world I wanted to be lost in.

 MAY 12th: 
 I understand why this book and trilogy are so loved. I get it. 
 Wow. That was fantastic. 
 The characters were rich, complex, mysterious, and lovely. Everyone from Zuzana to Brimstone to Karou to Akiva were fantastic. 
 The writing style is legendary. So gorgeous, so perfect, so completely brilliant. I ate it up. 
 Also, I really appreciated the world. It was confusing (until I got answers) but unlike anything I've ever read. Which was so nice. Sometimes I feel like these fantasy books kind of run together and just change little things but this one was so unique. 
 The main thing I'm taking .5 off for this book is because of the insta love. I know, Madrigal and Akiva loved each other and Karou is Madrigal reborn. But still, I felt like they're love moved too fast. But let's be honest, at this point I'm kind of looking for things to be wrong with this book. 
 In the end, I would recommend this to everyone who loves fantasy. As with every fantasy, you have to be patient and learn the world (so expect to be confused until you get answers).

 I would recommend this to people who want to read a writing style unlike anything I've read. One that will have you reading for hours and you can't stop because it's that great.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I really wanted to like this book. Really. The plot line is stunning, and not to mention Taylor's writing and her way of telling the story is so fluid, so river-like, satin-like smooth, that drew me from one page to another. 
 I did finish the book, hence I could rate it (I would never rate a book I don't/can't finish). But eventually, I resign to the fact that perhaps, it's not for me. 
 Usually I don't mind descriptive language - I love it, even, being a lover of fantasy/adventure books, because I'm a sucker of vivid, lush world-building and rich characters, and obviously I relish in details. Daughter of Smoke and Bone is poetic, and this makes it even more alive. It's like a moving picture for me. 
 It is narrated from the third point of view, I know, but I guess I still really can't understand why the lead characters are made so capable, so eloquent to simultaneously feel and capture and process all sensations and feelings in too much detailed a thought. One example is: 
 But this was different. It couldn't be contained. She sometimes imagined it streaming out of her like light. Happiness. It was the place where passion, with all its dazzle and drumbeat, met something softer: homecoming and safety and pure sunbeam comfort. It was all those things, intertwined with the heat and the thrill, and it was as bright within her as a swallowed star. 
 It's pretty. But to be honest when I feel happy, I simply feel happy. The feeling bursts out, alright, but I guess I would never imagine, consciously imagine at the same time, that something bright lights up, comes out from within me and I would also consciously compare it with a swallowed star. 
 Of course, again, it's 3rd point of view, which makes it all possible. 
 But what bothers me the most is because I'm not convinced with what Karou and Akiva has. While I could understand their immediate magnetic attraction to each other in the modern time because of their history, a precedent past that connects and binds them together despite of time and dimension and race - despite of everything, I still fail to comprehend how easily Madrigal fell in love with Akiva and Akiva with Madrigal. First time they met when Akiva had been on the verge of death and Madrigal had saved him - such a brief moment, yet momentous. Two years after that, they met again for the second time during the ball in Loramendi, each was disguised by masks and Madrigal already wanted to lean in to his chest as she relished in the smell of salt and spice coming off from the masked stranger in front of her. A stranger who she only recently discovered as an angel she'd happened to save 2 years ago. Akiva. An enemy. 
 So, you see, Madrigal had been so troubled when she'd first decided to save a Akiva that the thought of it still lingered in her mind in the couple of years to come (yet she still wished him to be alive). 
 But then there was no slight hesitation, even the slightest wariness in her when, after running away from the ball and Thiago together with Akiva, they unmasked each other and eventually... kissed. And slept together. 
 She fell in love with Akiva so easily, disregarding the facts that the eternal war fought between their races, chimaera and angels, has been ongoing for centuries; dismissing their cultures, beliefs, and what they have been thought. Suddenly and instantly they became star-crossed lovers that defied everyone; everything. Not to forget the fact that the universe has conspired in getting them together simply because were meant for each other (like Romeo and Juliet). 
 Well... I know I'm not the writer. But I'm only saying that it would have been believable and convincing if both Madrigal and Akiva had shared their dream of a world filled with love and no war together, and then fallen in love. 
 Just my 2 cents. 
 Anyway, I'm really sorry I don't like this book. 
 But I'd still definitely read Taylor's other books.

I LOVED "Daughter of Smoke and Bone". Laini Taylor is a beautiful storyteller; she was able to combine the beauty of Prague with paranormal romance to create an epic fantasy novel. 
 The characters are one of a kind. Brimstone is a monster that sells wishes for teeth. Yes, you read it correctly, TEETH! At the same time, he is part of the only family that Karou has ever known. Karou herself is wonderfully mysterious. She has tattoos and "naturally" blue hair, is extremely artistic, runs dangerous errands, was raised by monsters, and has no idea who she is. Karou is a strong female character searching for her identity, but nothing can prepare her for the truth. 
 The way Laini Taylor described Prague transported me back to this beautiful, historic city. Prague is a fantastic city and is the perfect setting for this book. It is so romantic with great old-world charm that I could totally picture there being secret doors that lead beyond our world. 
 On top of characters, plot, and beautiful storytelling, there is this huge war that has taken over two civilizations for hundreds of years and Karou is getting sucked in. I know this probably doesn't make a lot of sense, but you will just have to read the book to find out how all these pieces fit together. 
 "Daughter of Smoke and Bone" is filled with so many mysteries that it hooks you from the first page until the last. And let me just say that the last page will blow your mind hole! How can Karou be family with monsters? Why does Brimstone collect Teeth? Who is Karou? Honestly, just go buy "The Daughter of Smoke and Bone. It is awesome and one of the best books that was released in 2011.

I saw the movie first, and I'm not entirely sure that that wasn't a mistake. You know when books get made into movies that they're going to be, in some fundamental way, different from the words on the page. Not necessarily in a bad way, but there are things that are easier to capture in words than in movies, And in the same way, you can do different things with visuals than you can with words. But, on a fundamental level, movies often aren't as deep because it's hard to get the complexity of inner thoughts and feelings in their entirety up on the screen.

I shared this book with with my 10/11 year old students just before the Christmas holidays and they were wildly enthusiastic about it. (Several of them came back in January and told me that they had done their holiday book report on this novel.) 
 Unsurprisingly, most of them loved the fact that there were LOTS OF ILLUSTRATIONS. I, too, enjoyed the illustrations . . . but I really liked the fact that the children were brave and resourceful, and that they managed to resurrect all sort of treasures - including the legacy of one of the first French film-makers. One of the really fascinating things about this book, to me, is the way that Selznick weaves the true history (and some of the images) of film-maker Georges Melies into his fictional story. Selznick is known for his work illustrating biographies, but with this book he pursued one of his particular passions -- and it really shows.
Seriously. What was the big deal about this book???

The Invention of Hugo Cabret by Brian Selznick is a story about a lonely, clock keeper boy named Hugo living in a Paris train station who has a secret. He steals to eat and to fix an automaton that was once his father's obsession. When an elderly toy store owner takes his father's book with drawings of the mechanical man, Hugo befriends the man's goddaughter who wants to help him get it back. Soon Hugo is swept up in the secrets connecting the automaton and the toy store owner and when he discovers the answers to those secrets, his life will never be the same. 
 Selznick uses his black and white pictures to tell half of this magical story and his crisp, smart words to tell the rest. Hugo is a young, secretive character that has a lot on his shoulders but that only makes him want to fight for his dreams more. You will also be on the edge of your seat waiting to unlock all the secrets of this book.

 The Invention of Hugo Cabret by Brian Selznick won the Caldecott Medal in 2008. As I'm sure most of you are aware, the Caldecott Medal is awarded annually to the artist of the most distinguished American Picture Book for Children. It's akin to receiving the Newbery Award for children's books, or the Printz Award for young adult. 
 Hugo Cabret was an especially interesting win for the Caldecott, because although it does contain a lot of beautiful illustrations (284 in a 533 pg. book) it's a 533 page novel. The front jacket describes this as a book "combining elements of picture book, graphic novel, and film" which "breaks open the novel form to create an entirely new reading experience." 
 The dust jacket does not lie. Reading this book was unlike anything else I've ever read and it was wonderful. I was hooked from the first page, "A Brief Introduction by Professor H. Alcofrisbas" to the last page as we visually watch the moon as it disappears from the sky. The illustrations are... beyond brilliant. Designed to look like sketches, they are surprisingly complex and deceptively simple. As I mentioned in my review of American Born Chinese I am increasingly shocked by what you can portray and how much story you can tell with just one picture. 
 The story itself was wonderful. Hugo Cabret is a wonderful character just trying to find his place in life. He is a young boy living alone in the middle of Paris in the 1930s, trying desperately to survive. He has no money, but he feels bad every time he is forced to steal something to survive. He is such a good character. He is so confused and desperately searching for something tangible to bring him hope. I loved the secondary characters as well. Questioning and spunky Isabelle, hurting and bitter old Georges, and loving and protective Jeanne. Each of the characters are incredibly well developed. Even the minor characters are given more depth than we normally see. 
 This book was marvelous. It's definitely one that I am going to want on my own shelf sometime soon. It's beautifully illustrated and wonderfully written. This is a book that can be enjoyed by people of any age, at any stage of their life. I'm enjoyed reading this one so much, that I am definitely looking forward to seeing what else Mr. Selznick has to offer the literary world.

 Initially gave this book 3/5 stars, but after giving it some more thought, lowered it to 2/5 stars. I greatly enjoyed the previous books, and this one was a letdown. 
 The book starts with Belly as a college freshman, Jere a sophomore at the same college, and Conrad going to some distant university in California. Jere and Belly had been together since the end of the second book. Jere made a mistake a boy must not make when in a relationship. As he asked for forgiveness from Belly, he pitched in that one question every girl wants to hear from the man of her dreams. She then came up with decisions that made her question if what she and Jere had was true love, or whether she still hasn't gotten over Conrad. 
 The author had 3 books to build up the love story between Conrad, Jere and Belly. Despite the numerous backstories, I wasn't convinced that Jere really loved Belly and vice versa. It's like they got together out of convenience and familiarity, rather than love. 
 Which is why I was irked by Jere asking Belly to marry him. To me he appeared as a happy-go-lucky, immature, marriage-belittling, selfish guy who wanted to secure Belly for himself before Belly could decide to breakup with him. It wasn't justified why he wanted to marry Belly so bad in the first place, what that would entail that was so much different from their present boyfriend-girlfriend situation. They were only teenagers, aged 19 and 21, with barely any money to pay for the wedding. What's with the rush? It was annoying how it was easy for Jere to ask for Belly's hand in marriage, and then later on with Conrad back in the picture, had the nerve to doubt Belly's decision to marry him the day before the wedding itself. Even though, deep down he knew, Conrad still had a place in Belly's heart. It was unfair, to be mad at Belly, when all she did was for Jere's benefit and happiness. 
 The wedding was like an event thrown lamely into the story to give rise to a conflict that will result to only one outcome: Belly finally choosing between Jere and Conrad. 
 The book concludes with a glimpse into Belly's happy ever after a few years later. I wish that the author wrote more about how Belly, and the one he ended up with, got together.

She's a pretty flat and boring character from what I can see. Even in the end, she's like this teenage girl throwing tantrums and running away from challenges. I don't think she treats anyone in her life right. She takes Taylor for granted, she doesn't listen to her mom, and she never even thinks about Steven that much even though he clearly cares about her. 
 And the last book... Really? REALLY??? Wedding planning with one boy and then blow off the wedding and that boy is never mentioned again as she ends up with the other one. What the hell? People might hate me for saying this, but I never liked Conrad, I don't get him, either. But I did like Jeremiah, just a little. To me, Conrad really acts like a jerk most of the time in this series. I know he has his reasons, but I don't like the kind of character who bottles up their feelings and make everyone around them worry. And ALL the characters are so inconsistent with their decisions and behavior. Maybe except Belly, who hasn't changed from when she was five years old. 
 I'm not sure if I'm done with my rant, my point is, this book was really not my cup of tea.

So, Belly is dating Jeremiah at the start of this and all seems pretty great until Belly finds out that during a Ross and Rachel kind of break, Jeremiah had sex with some girl during spring break in Cabo. Jeremiah's way of atoning for this fuck up? He proposes. 
 And Belly accepts! 
 Not only are they too young for this and ill-prepared but why was this the answer to their problems?! Was it just a way to bring Conrad back into the picture so he could fuck with Belly's heart again? Jeremiah became a bit of a douche. Like a frat boy douche that you knew meant well and was a really good guy, but had to get partying and all that junk out of his system first. Conrad, pre-med, was kind of above all that. So was Belly. 
 I kind of felt like Jeremiah's character took some unnecessary hits. I wasn't really Team Conrad or Team Jeremiah to begin with. I felt like Belly needed something other than them in her life. 
 I was pleased with the ending even if I still thought that Conrad was an ass. Even in his confession to her about how he still loved her he was a jackass. And then to attempt to take it all away and say he was drunk just for the sake of pride...? No. It just made him look like an ass to do that. Even in taking blame he still managed to blame Belly for his mistakes.
Best. One. Yet.

No. No no no no no no no no no. No. 
 I did not enjoy this book. At all. I'm suspecting it has a lot to do with the fact that the main character's name is Belly. 
 Other than that, the infamous Belly also pissed me off quite a bit by her horrible decision making skills. I am very serious. It went Jeremiah, no Conrad, wait Jeremiah, oh Conrad for the entire. fucking. book. 
 I will have you know - I read this in the summer, in my car, in the muggy heat, while my mum went to get groceries. Weird? Probably. But, while I was in there, I literally felt as though I was in a torture chamber; it was that fucking awful, people. Belly here also sends out a gr-eat message to young girls everywhere - please, marry a guy when you're barely legal drinking age just so you can get back at your fucking ex and sooth those feelings you still have for him. This is the sort of education that girls need these days. 
 That up there is what I wanna do to you, bitch. Seriously! Why is your nickname Belly?! 
 Enough of this garbage. I gotta read and review books I actually happen to like, unlike this piece of YA junk. Bah, humbug!

Goodness, no. Do I think that it was worth it? Yes. I took me 3 days to read this trilogy. A book a day. I'm proud.

reference_books.title: The Hundred-Foot Journey
reference_books.review_text: Inevitably comparing book to movie. Movie was more compact and differently-emphasized. So ultimately, book and movie were two different stories, each good in its own right.

reference_books.title: Paper Towns
reference_books.review_text: Now that I have read this John Green book, I don't see a need to read more of them. Reason 1, I can check the Manic Pixie Dream Girl novel off my list. Reason 2, the story was not half bad, but the lecherous conversation was a real downer. High school exposed me to many adolescent males who talked that way, and I was happy to leave that kind of talk behind when I left high school.

reference_books.title: Dietland
reference_books.review_text: Refreshingly bold rejections of dieting, the fashion industry, and the unquestioned pursuit of being defined as attractive. I loved Plum's transformation into someone who valued and accepted her body instead of resorting to surgery to alter it. So why only two stars? Because for me, the discussions of pornography were too graphic and the profanity too heavy-handed. The messages in this book are important, but I didn't relish trudging so deeply into the muck.

reference_books.title: The Great Gatsby
reference_books.review_text: My embarrassments: 1) Didn't remember anything from the first reading. 2) Didn't have natural empathy for the tragic figure of Gatsby. 3) Didn't pick up on the theme of Old Money versus New Money. I seem to be an indifferent clod.

reference_books.title: Things Fall Apart (The African Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed this insight into the culture and perspective of Africans prior to and during colonization. Although I did not agree with all of Okonkwo's actions, he certainly lived in accordance with his values. It disappointed and angered me that the white men of the government presumed to impose law and order on the village, yet did not act in accordance with law and order, because they did not deal honestly with the Africans.

reference_books.title: Inkheart (Inkworld, #1)
reference_books.review_text: An imaginative premise, but bogged down by a repetitive and tiresome cat-and-mouse game in which the "mice" keep returning to the cat's clutches.

reference_books.title: The Good Lord Bird
reference_books.review_text: Sorry, but after 190 pages, which I feel is a very thorough attempt, this book simply failed to make me care enough to finish. I won't hold it against James McBride--I will still try other books of his.

reference_books.title: Something Borrowed (Darcy & Rachel, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Dear continuity editors: Montana is not in the Midwest region of the United States, and a person who had grown up in Indiana would know that.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text: Such an original idea--life as a palimpsest! I was hooked to see if, or how, Ursula would overcome her various fates.

reference_books.title: The Wednesday Wars
reference_books.review_text: Like real life, a chronological progression of small defeats and victories, with no climactic "final battle between good and evil", yet enjoyable in its verisimilitude. I absolutely loved that it was Holling who rescued his sister.

book_a.title: The Alchemist
book_a.user_review: Mixture of encouraging truths and misleading platitudes. The former: "Whenever we do something that fills us with enthusiasm, we are following our legend." Yes. The latter: "When you want something, all the universe conspires to help you achieve it." Nope!

I'm not sure about how to review this novel. I always feel terrible when I have to give a novel or book less than three stars. I'm too empathetic in that sense; I just think about all the effort the author must've put in their novel, like coordinating and constructing the proper structure for their plot, how to arrange the dialogues and finding the proper words to express what they want their characters to say, finding ways to develop their emotions and conveying a believable synergy to the reader among other things. When I think about all these things I feel both bad and amazed, the prime because I didn't like the novel and the author put effort into it and I feel bad for disliking it, the latter because, well, the effort must've been big. However, I cannot force myself to like a novel, and I just didn't like this one. 
 The spiritual and metaphysical basis of "The Alchemist" seems to be a combination of Christianity, Pantheism, Mysticism and every speech any public motivator would want to deliver an audience. The novel sums up in the following words: " 
 Follow your dreams and do not give up, no matter what the circumstances are. 
 " 
 I almost feel as if Darth Vader was trying to say in the most polite and protracted way possible: " 
 Use the force, Luke! 
 " 
 Unfortunately, I consider this novel to be filled with the trite, over-used and hypersensitive phrases we have all heard before: "Don't give up!" "Follow your dreams!" "You can do anything you want!", and that's simply not my cup of tea. I like cold, hard truths and different point of views, not recycled phrases I can read on-line. Now, with all that being said, I'm not certain if Coelho's objective was to help his readers grow and feel more confident about themselves, or if he simply wanted to use demagogy at its finest to win his readers and have a larger audience for his next novels. Quite frankly, this novel is both demagogic and boringly trite, so in short words: I didn't like this novel. One star.

If anything, it's preachy and leads people into thinking that if they want something hard enough, the universe will fucking conspire for them to get it. And all that without lifting a finger.

 I don't understand. I just cannot. I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone. With all the hype around it, I'm seriously disappointed.

If George S Clason's 1926 book, The Richest Man in Babylon, could be blended with James Redfield's, The Celestine Prophecy, the result would be Coelho's, The Alchemist. While there are a few thought provoking and quote worthy lines, the majority of the novel is an amalgamation of religious mysticism and magical fantasy set in a quest to find treasure and truth. After a series of mishaps that always ends in a Celestine Prophecy type of outcome in which greater wealth and wisdom miraculously result, the true treasure is where one started. Additionally, regardless what the protagonist did, he perpetually increased his wealth, like Clason had his characters do; the difference is that Clason's sitting is Babylon, while Coelho's ranges from France to Egypt. Overall, I am not impressed with the Prayer of Jabez style novel.

Oprah, have you met -- ? Oh, of course. Of course you have. Yes, I should've known you go way back. I can totally see how you guys would get along. I mean, you and Paulo are both about following dreams and making them come true and stuff. How do I know Paulo? Well, a long time ago, a beautiful girl gave me a copy of The Alchemist and made me promise that I'd read it, but it seemed like a bad imitation of Kahil Gibran, who's bad enough already, and all the dialogue sounded like Obi-Wan Kanobi or Morpheus in The Matrix, so I was like, "Nope! I ain't gonna read it!" Then it sat on my shelf for a long time, and last week I got really sick and I was looking for the simplest stuff possible to read, and there was The Alchemist and I thought, "Maybe this will do." Of course all of the "philosophy" in the book is crazy-person stuff. I mean, crazy people think just like the boy protagonist, or the Morpheus figures who keep appearing to tell the boy that the world, or the universe or whatever, is conspiring to help him, and reading a book like this one is only going to make crazy people crazier. Also, of course, it's really a book for children, which means that, in today's world, it's read primarily by "adults." But I guess The Alchemist for me is like a wildly popular TV show that I know is corny and hackneyed and so on, but if I were really honest, I'd have to admit I was entertained by it, in spite of all of my huffing and puffing and eye-rolling. So I'm going to admit all that and give The Alchemist three stars, and I'll leave you, Oprah, alone with Paolo to discuss your crazy-person philosophy, which has really worked out well for both of you. Yes, you both look magnificent on your gold thrones. But Oprah? I think you've got a piece of spinach stuck between your teeth. Oh, that's an emerald? My mistake. Sorry.

The Alchemist tells the story of a young everyman character, Santiago, and his quest to fulfill his destiny. Guided by a recurring dream and a mysterious king, he leaves behind his life as a shepherd and embarks on a journey through Egypt in search of buried treasure. Depending on how you feel about it, it's either an allegory about self-realization, or a self-help book masquerading as a fairytale. I tend to think of it as the latter. 
 There are a lot of aspects of this book's philosophy that I can agree with: thoughts have power; an unspoken language unites all things; obstacles can be opportunities for great growth and learning; by finding what it is you love to do, and doing it, you're better able to improve yourself and your surroundings than if you bustle around just for status and money; but it can require a great deal of courage to part with familiarity for the sake of pursuing what you love. 
 What I found bothersome, in terms of message, is its one-sided view of life: a life can be lived well by just "following your heart". Near the beginning of the tale, Santiago finds himself in a bad situation because he carelessly trusted a stranger. One might think that the lesson he learned was to exercise more discernment next time, but instead he finds that things turn out well anyway--because he's following his heart. I'm not sure how well this works in practice. It's good to trust in the Universe watching out for you and bringing you the things you need, but keep your wits about you; your own sense of judgment is also part of the Universe. Heart and head are both essential, and striking a balance between them seems to be a better way of living than blindly throwing yourself to one extreme or the other. 
 In terms of how the story is written... it left much to be desired. It was too long and involved to be feel like a parable, but not long and involved enough to feel like a decent novel. It's been praised for the simplicity of its prose, and it certainly was simple, but not in a good way. In addition, the term "Personal Legend"--with capital letters--made me feel as though I was reading an informercial for a product that Coelho was trying to sell. I almost wish he'd have skipped the attempts at storytelling and written a self-help book outright; the plot and characters are generally flimsy, and he spells out every concept instead of allowing the reader to discover and absorb the ideas on their own. 
 I should mention that the main reason I picked up this book was that I'd heard it compared to The Little Prince. Um, no. Both are simply written and involve young men in deserts, but The Little Prince is charming, moving, and deftly written, while The Alchemist is none of those things. The Little Prince speaks its messages softly, while The Alchemist crams them down the reader's throat. 
 **slight spoilers ahead** 
 Lastly, I was bothered by the lack of "Personal Legends" for the female characters. When Santiago meets other men, he often learns what their Personal Legends are, and whether they're being fulfilled. This is not the case when he meets women. The most important female character--she and Santiago fall in love before either of them say a word--is only important insofar as she's part of Santiago's destiny. Blowing kisses is all very well, but it would have been nice if she'd been shown to have her own legend to follow, apart from anxiously awaiting her lover's return. Santiago learns the important lesson that people who truly love him don't hold him back from achieving his dreams, but he never seems to question whether he might be preventing someone from achieving theirs.
This book helped me get through a very difficult time in my life. I give it as a present to everyone who feels a bit lost.

One of the worst things that I have ever read in my entire life. Clumsy, repetitive and horrifically twee throughout. I had to stop myself from throwing the book across the room and, if I didn't have a weird thing about finishing books, there's no way I would have finished this. 
 Take a simple premise - follow your dreams and don't give up. Personify everything from your heart to the weather to sand. Add a liberal amount of door-knocker spirituality. Come up with a straightforward plot. Bing! You'll have a book just as bad as this one. 
 If you don't believe me how bad it is, read this: 
 "That night the boy slept deeply, and, when he awoke, his heart began to tell him things that came from the Soul of the World. It said that all people who are happy have God within them. And that happiness could be found in a grain of sand from the desert, as the alchemist had said. Because a grain of sand is a moment of creation, and the universe has taken millions of years to create it. 'Everyone on earth has a treasure that awaits him,' his heart said. 'We, people's hearts, seldom say much about those treasures, because people no longer want to go in search of them.'" 
 Absolute piffle. If you like this, and want to hear it over and over again, then definitely read this novel. You'll enjoy it. 
 On the other hand, if you like this, and want to hear it over and over again, I congratulate you for actually being able to read because you're obviously not that smart.

My expectation about Paulo Coelho was wrong but he did overwhelmed me with this story. I already considered him as my favorite writer even though I haven't read anything in one of his works. But when I saw his books, I got so attracted, especially the one who's plot got me interested with. I just manages to read every summary at the back of his pocket book in the national bookstore and give me an expression that he is a great and interesting writer. 
 Then I thought of liking him in Facebook and I did. I saw lots of good quotes/phrases in his page. That made me thought that he is really an awesome and ideal writer. So I declared him as my favorite author without even reading one of his works :D 
 But as I read this pocket book which I just borrowed to my best friend, FaithMemory, the way he detailed the story was not not that professional. Maybe, my expression about him was affected because the last book I read seem professional and in detailed. The way that Dean Koontz tell his story was really in detailed and has a good flow. 
 I expect that Paulo Coelho would be the same. But he was a good spiritual writer. I like the philosophical way of his story and the feelings it give me as I read it. I really like the prologue, the old man's story about the wise man, the alchemist story and especially the ending! It has a good impact to me. It give me a WOW feeling. He's definitely a good writer! I want to read more of his works :) Oh! and the way Santiago fall in love is funny and cute xD Especially when he met Fatima :D

What an overhyped and overated piece of crap. This book is full of pretencious bullshit.
