 It just added to all my skeptimism... 
 Ive read PLENTY of books better. An okay kinda book. Waste of time i guess...

I did get sucked in to this at first. Having been a middle school girl, it's easy to step back I to that mindset and think Edward is the perfect man. Only after thinking about how creepy Ed is and how shallow and awful Bella is did I regret this series. The only good part is that it references classic literature that could get kids to read actual literature instead of this garbage.

I learned that vampires are attracted to clumsy idiots, and that clumsy idiots are attracted to extremely creepy jerks! 
 Blech. Boring story; only the thinnest sliver of plot; puerile writing; a heroine who is a weak and stupid damsel-in-distress cookie-cutter character; completely unmotivated characters. All in all, a perfect example of how NOT to live your life/ handle your relationships/ write a book for teenager girls. 
 That this book has become so popular makes me despair for our next/current generation of women. Seriously, ladies-- go read Jane Eyre or something.

I very much enjoyed this book! I didnt really like the movie however it was quite different from the book. once I started reading I just couldnt put it down. if you have seen the movie and have not read the book, I suggest that you get off your lazy but and read it i give it a ten star!!:)
Vampires do not sparkle. Hate it

Awful writing, awful book. Basic plot. OMG he's a vampire. Yeah. Okay, I'm done. 
 This book killed me inside.

I recently came to the conclusion of why I didn't like the Twilight series. 
 For the first three books, the obstacles that Bella would have to face if she were to become a vampire were constantly brought up (to name a few): Insatiable human blood thirst, risking breaking the treaty, losing her family, and losing her friends. 
 Apparently, if you spend enough time fearing that you will become a monster, then you just magically won't become one according to Stephanie Meyers. I thought that we would get to see Bella's struggle to keep her humanity, but instead the writer waved her magic pen and decided that nope, it wasn't going to be a big deal after all. Check. If one of the pack imprints on a person, no one from the pack was allowed to harm that person, so Jake imprinting on Renesme nicely got rid of the problem of that pesky little treaty violation. Check. I guess Charley was okay with the changes, but didn't want to know what they were. After spending three books terribly concerned about her, he suddenly seemed not to care. What kind of self-respecting, over-protective father wouldn't ask what was going on? Check. Her so-called friends weren't even mentioned after the wedding. Not that she really cared about them anyway, seeing as how she completely forgot about them in New Moon for a few months. Check. If you're building something up for three previous books, you should at least have some sort of struggle in the last book. But no, these were wrapped up all nice and neat with a little bow. 
 Throughout New Moon and Eclipse, she literally could not decide between Edward and Jacob. She said that she loved both. Ultimately, she went with Edward. So there was this huge build up of Bella being attracted to both for two entire books, and then suddenly when she changed into a vampire, *poof* it was neatly taken care of. As a vampire, she found Jacob's scent repulsive and he was no longer pleasantly warm but too hot. Also, after the birth of Renesme, she no longer loved him or was attracted to him in any way, because apparently the part of her that was like that was now Renesme. Then, Jacob found Bella repulsive because she smelled like a disgusting vampire. He was no longer attracted to her, because he imprinted on Renesme. Well, that love triangle was tied up nicely, don't you think? Completely realistic, no? I didn't think so either. I guess the lesson here that girls were supposed to learn is that if you're having a tough time deciding between a guy you'd have to change to be with and the one you wouldn't, go with the one that you have to change yourself for because those feelings for the one you didn't have to change to be with will just evaporate the second you change. It's like magic, don't you know? I seem to be saying that quite a bit... 
 Then there were the two main love interests themselves, and their relationships with Bella. First is Edward. He found her fascinating because he couldn't read her mind and he wanted to know what was going on inside there. Understandable, but then he creeped on her by watching her sleep. Personally, if someone admitted to doing that to me, I'd call the police. Then he's controlling. He not only told her she can't do something, he went out of his way to make sure she complied. He took some sort of plug out of her truck so she couldn't drive to the reservation to see Jacob. Then there was the time that he broke up with her because he felt he was putting her in danger. She said she didn't care, and really it should have been her choice. He left her suffering from depression for months while he was away. He forced her to marry him, even though she didn't want to. Edward was an unrealistic ideal that no boy could possibly live up to when dating a girl Twihard. He was beautiful, he won't age, he won't gain weight, was incredibly wealthy, and refused to have sex until after marriage. Second is Jacob, who had much more personality. He let her make the choice of whether or not to use the bikes (until it becomes clear that she's not quite right in the head). He also urged her to not abandon Charley, or her friends. He was there to pick up the pieces Edward left behind when they had broken up. He was more realistic, because he wasn't doting on her every second of every day. He had a bond with his pack, and his friends whom he hung out with when Bella was not around. Jacob also worked on his Rabbit and various vehicles, at the same time as going to school to learn things he didn't all ready know for decades. He was impulsive, passionate, and loyal. He tried to push Bella away for her own safety when he first phased, but soon realised that the decision of whether or not they should hang out was not his to make so he let her choose, and was fine with the decision. He didn't constantly whinge about it. Some Team Edward supporters would say "But Jacob was controlling too, he told Charley about the bikes so that he'd punish Bella." Put yourself in Jake's shoes. He despised Edward. When Edward broke up with Bella, she fell apart and went into a depression for several months. He spent that time trying to put Humpty Dumpty together again. Then, when Charley and the people on the Reservation (who were kind and friendly to Bella during her depression) needed her the most, she left witthout a second thought to save Edward from his own selfishness (aka suicide... did he not think of his family at all?) Wouldn't you be even a tiny bit angry or hurt? Jacob was 15 at this point. He was a teenager, he's allowed to act a little immature like tattling on her to get her in trouble, unlike Edward who after 100 years should know better. 
 I know it seems as though I'm on Team Jacob, but I'm truthfully not any more. It would have been much better for the books (and Bella would have therefore been a good role model) if she said, "You know what? My entire sense of self-worth is based upon whether or not these two boys like me. It's unhealthy. I need to base it on something else, so I'm not emotionally crippled if one of them leaves/falls for someone else. Being alone is a scary thought right now, but it's what I need to do for me." That's why I like Tamora Pierce's heroines, not all of them who have romantic interests in the books end up with someone by the end of the novels. If they do end up with someone, they don't just settle for the first one that comes along, either. 
 Bella was the worst role model ever. She spent all her time worrying about whether first Edward, then Jacob liked her. She ditched her own friends the minute she and Edward started to date. When they broke up, she was reduced to a suicidal schizophrenic (jumping off cliffs just to see/hear Edward). Teenagers don't take that long to get over a relationship, especially one that was for only a few months. I could see depression and whatnot taking over for that long if it was a married couple because they had more invested in the relationship... Bella also worried too much about what other people thought about her, which was her reason for not wanting to marry the vampire she supposedly loved. She also fell to pieces again when she went for a while without Jacob speaking to her. Then, magically once she turned into a vampire (read: changed everything about herself to be with Edward), all her problems just disappeared. Tell me if I'm wrong about this, but that's a horrible message to send to young girls (change yourself to be with your man, and you'll live happily ever after). 
 There was also the problem of the Volturi. From the end of New Moon on, there was this build up to a big battle with them, which was over in just a few minutes, with only one casualty which we had no emotional investment in. It was nothing like the heart-wrenching battle for Hogwarts at the end of Deathly Hallows, where we lost Colin Creevey, Tonks, Remus, Fred,and even Harry for a time... I was expecting both Edward and Bella to die, and Jacob to raise Renesme (which is wrong on a few levels) based on the lead up (and repeated allusions to Romeo and Juliet) but no, it was a perfectly happy ending and everyone except the Volturi were perfectly happy at the end of the perfect little story. Bella didn't become the queen instead of a pawn, like Meyers wanted the cover of Breaking Dawn to suggest. She just became even more of a Mary-Sue than she all ready was (I took the Original Fiction Litmus Test for Bella, she's an Uber-Sue). 
 Just because you have an idea of the end of a story (in this case, Bella, Edward, and Renesme) when you first go to write, doesn't mean you have to keep it that way even after the first draft is done. I thought that was Writing/Revision 101. The only reason I kept reading the books was because I hoped Bella would smarten up and decide not to be with Edward.When that didn't happen, I kept reading in the hope that at least it would end like Romeo and Juliet because of all the allusions... but no such luck there. I did like learning about the other vampires and their pasts, as well as all the Quileute legends. Too bad the secondary characters were so under-used, as they were the most interesting. 
 This book is filled with plot lines with tons of build up which were wrapped up much too quickly and easily, a Mary-Sue for a main character, a love interest that is too high of an expectation to live up to for any guy, under-used secondary characters, and just shoddy writing overall. I doubt I'll be picking up "The Host" or any other book written by her any time soon.

God, this book. It was /horrible/ to read. I literally spent three fucking months reading this. And it wasn't even worth it. 
 I read this book in year 6 and became absolutely obsessed with the story, but now re-reading it 6 years later, I'm left disappointed. The story was boring, the characters were boring and taxing, the scenes written like they're coming from a twelve-year-old's fan fiction. I spent this whole book cringing, really. 
 Hated it. 
 Two stars, because of sentimental value.

I wanted to like this book, I really did. All the other women in my immediate family had nothing to say but great things about it, and I'll admit it: I wanted in on the party. But from the opening chapter, I just couldn't get into the story at all. The writing style seemed naive and underdeveloped, and I couldn't form a connection whatsoever to the protagonist or find myself caring at all about her so-called problems. I also found the romance to be intensely creepy: not in a scary-but-seductive creepy way, but the full out contact-the-authorities-and-arm-yourself kind of creepy. 
 I managed to finish the book, only to ask myself why.

EUGH. 
 there is no end to how much bad I can say about this book, but what I hated the most was just how badly written it was. 
 I understand that it's YA, but there's no excuse for how simplistic this book is. 
 The characters are obtuse and Bella's only personality traits are "clumsy" and "in love with Edward." She is a perfect example of a Mary Sue protagonist. 
 I just... 
 I can't even think about this book long enough to review it properly.

I'd walked past the book stand in my local supermarket a few times and each time the movie cover of twilight caught my eye (I know, you should never judge a book by its cover but hey, its too late now) and after a couple of weeks my curiosity got the better of me and I ended up buying it and boy, am I glad I did. 
 I was sucked into the story completely and ended up reading it in one sitting. My inner fangirl was definitely jumping for joy! I've always been a sucker for love stories and have always enjoyed delving into fantasy and horror, so this book sort of merged the two. I felt that Bella was easy to relate to in certain aspects and Edward certainly filled the role of the mysterious love interest. 
 I hadn't felt this excited for a book since Harry Potter, and was glad to give my bookworm a jump start back into the reading world.
I was skeptical at first considering that these books were not meant for a twenty something male, but I love it. Its fun.
a really good mental potato chip . . .

Teen-angsty love affair between a sexy, brooding vampire and a smart, loner every-girl? Yes please! Sure it's cheesy and cliche, but it's also entertaining and gratifying. Total guilty pleasure, esp. when I didn't dwell too much on representations of race and gender, didn't read too closely or ask too much from the characters, and did read with an overactive imagination to fill in the gaps. I'll admit it--I can't wait to see the movie.

oh where to even begin? i've read this book 1 and a half times. the half time comes from me trying to read it again, trying to see if maybe i just hated it on principle, nope. i couldn't make it past the first 1/4 of the book. (i didn't even get to vampire baseball! dang!!) so here goes... 
 the characters are horrible. 
 bella is whiny. edward is broody, emo and a stalker. (did i mention he freaking sparkles? what the freak!!) 
 the writing is horrible. 
 did stephenie meyer even have an editor? what is with some of her word choice? 
 this book is just horrible. 
 it teaches teenage girls that your life basically needs to revolve around the 'love of your life'. at the ripe old age of 17 you should be willing to leave your parents and cling to your one true mate? uh, what? (did i mention that she is 17??) 
 there are so, so many things wrong with these books. unfortunately i can't go into details without being spoilery. suffice it to say these are some of the worst books i've ever read and the hype is outrageous. 
 if you want a good YA series read Harry Potter. want a good YA/Supernatural series? read The Mortal Instruments. there are so, so many other books out there that are so much better than Twilight! read them :)

Although I like my vampires more evil and murderous as opposed to, um, sparkly, I guess I can see why these books are popular, especially with teen girls. Since I am no longer a teen girl I thought the whole Edward/Bella thing was more creepy than romantic. If my husband acted that way (obsessive and rude) I'd punch him. Which is what I'm sure Rosalie would do as well. (I did like Rosalie and Emmett. I need a lot more of them.) Thankfully it was a quick read because the book was way too long. The beginning was so drawn out I was afraid that nothing was ever going to happen (besides 'I love yous' and rain). And when we finally do get some action it's crammed into the end like an afterthought. Even the bad vampires don't eat people. I just don't get it. 
 All that aside, of course I'm going to read the next one, because I like to torture myself and I'm under the impression (thanks to the eleventy-hundred times I've been forced to watch the movie trailer on tv) that there are werewolves in book two (who probably don't eat people either but I can always hope.) It's like "Jennifer's Body" all over again, only without Megan Fox. Very disappointing.

It was better than I thought it would be. I am always suspicious of books that are really popular. But I will say that I am disappointed that the world Stephenie Meyer created isn't more thorough. I think I'm spoiled by my Sci-Fi reading, but I always want good reasons and backgrounds, and don't feel like I get that here.

Lo dejo en tres porque lo que este libro significo para mi en su momento. Cuando lo lei hace cuatro anos, pasaron muchas cosas. En primer lugar ame la saga, me indujo a escribir, me volvio adicta a la lectura (un gusto que siempre estuvo ahi pero nunca recibio el empuje necesario hasta ese momento) conoci mucha gente maravillosa en el fandom... Sin embargo, anos despues y millones de libros leidos, mis gustos han cambiado y mi percepcion es otra. Los vampiros nunca me gustaron en primer lugar, pero me gustaba esta saga y por eso los vi con otros ojos. Sigo pensando que Eclipse es el mejor libro de la saga, pero hoy dia soy capaz de encontrarle millones de errores, cabos suelos... personajes que me gustaban los veo con otros ojos. Cuatro libros fueron innecesarios, se pudo haber contado todo en dos, maximo y hubiese sido mejor. Me importa un soberano pepino lo que digan por ahi, me gusto mucho y eso nunca lo negare, sin embargo, si hoy dia me ofrecieran un libro de la misma tematica, dudo que me caiga de la misma manera.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Alternately boring and annoying for the first 3/4 of the book. The dramatic tension that finally makes an appearance toward the end has an unsatisfying resolution, as the point of view character is unconscious while the conflict is resolved, and only hears about what happened after the fact. 
 Many of the supporting characters are really intriguing. Sadly, neither the protagonist nor her love interest is.

Well, one of the worst books I've read lately. Such of waste of time. I was just about to say that I just don't get how in the world it became a world success, but then I remembered that human kind is so unpredictable. The book is so boring; the silly story could have been told in 100 pages, but the author decided to torture us with more than 500, full of shallow and repetitive conversations between Bella and Edward. I assume it was aimed to female teenagers who dream about falling in love with a gorgeous and perfect guy, but I wonder if all of those girls think of themselves as Bella does: a silly, insignificant, ugly, unattractive girl. I would expect that an author would show a little bit more affection towards his/her characters, but Mrs Meyer seems to hate Bella. Or is Bella a self projection? My question all along the reading was "Why in the world Edward, as perfect as he is, can fall in love with such a waste?" And why in the world a common girl would fall in love with a vampire, risking her life (which she doesn't seem to really appreciate) in just two ore three days and just because "he is so perfectly handsome"? Isn't that as shallow and stupid as it can be? My God, this is the only case I know in which the movie is much, far better than the book... and I hated the movie! And yes, I know Mrs Meyer is making a lot of money with these books. So are doing drug dealers around the world and they're not making any good either.
Not my usual reading material but found the young adult viewpoint intriguing

I really didn't like it. 
 That is all.
ugh.
Loved the characters, loved the fantasy. Team Jacob;)

Read the whole book one day while I stayed home sick from school. 
 I should have just slept.
I gave it a chance I can't say I liked it. it just wasn't my cup of tea.

In lettura... 25.09.2012 due frasi emblematiche: 
 1) Sentii un'ondata di vero terrore. Sapevano quel che sapevo io? E a me era permesso di sapere che sapevano che sapevo? 
 2)Sospiro:"Se chiedo scusa mi perdoni?". "Forse...se sei sincero. E in piu se prometti che non lo rifarai". 
 .... 
 Ma poi qual e il senso di dover scrivere continuamente BMW? La Meyer non aveva abbastanza soldi per pubblicare da sola il libro? Inoltre, non ho mai visto niente di piu fastidioso di dover leggere ogni dieci pagine la parola "pick-up". 
 24.10.12 Finito. O meglio, non proprio. Mi mancano 80 pagine circa ma ho perso ormai da tempo la voglia di continuare a leggerlo. Proprio no.
I couldn't make it past the second chapter. This book is absolutely horrendous.

Had to return it to the library before I got the chance to start it. Will try again at a later date. 
 Tried. Hated it. Total wallbanger. 
 The writing was stilted and charmless. The characters were wooden parodies of every other trope and stereotype ever created. The heroine, Bella, was the epitome of TSTL. Edward was just plain CREEPY. The power dynamic between Bella and Edward is monstrously effed up. He'll sneak into her house, watch over her while she sleeps, and shift moods with alarming speed, while she mopes around in the background being the weak, spineless creature that she is. She's a mishmash of every teen stereotype, like Frankenstein's monster ... and like Frankenstein's monster, that sh*t is messed up in the head. 
 Now, I lurrrve me some angsty heroes, and I lurrrve me some intense romance, but Edward's intensity comes off as creepy not swoon-worthy. 
 Total fail.

Read this so that I would be able to speak knowledgeably with students about it. I can see why young girls are drawn to this story, but I personally have concerns with the obsessive nature of the Edward/Bella relationship. The book provides parents with a good discussion with their daughters about what IS love... and what they see in this book? It isn't love

I couldn't put it down when I began reading this book. The subject is interesting: vampire and campus romance. Especially the latter, the author has wonderful writing skills in describing the mental working of a 17-year-old girl. 
 I sort of didn't want the early stages of the romance to end. I knew there would be some violence. Vampires were living there anyway, there had to be some bad guys to fight. 
 I was not surprised to find out later that the violence part was less thrilling than the romance part.

My god!! What a horribly written book. The level of english was pathetic, the story line was very interesting though. I prefer watching the movie of course but what a waste of my precious time. This book is ideal for 12 - 14 year olds only. 
 Did not even complete this book! LOL!
Why boher? This is a teen romance book... lots of longing glances and heavy sighs...

The Twilight books were the type of amusement, I needed at a very busy and stressfull time, but I doubt I will read the books again. It is no great litterature nor future classic, nor a story that would be interestning the second time you read it. 
 When all that is said, I have to confess, that I enjoyed the four books about the grat love story between Bella and Edward. It's an exciting story, it's interesting, the passion and love are all-consuming and the danger is always present. 
 When reading the books, you have to remind yourself, that they are young adult books and you have to leave all your usual litterary criteria behind - beacuse Twilight is a young adult series, and you can't expect nothing but just that! And with that knowledge in mind, I think the books are great! 
 All in all - great for young adults and good entertainment for the rest of us.

Mesmerizing! I forgot how fun it was to pick up a book that you really didn't want to put down...and I was so pulled in that I finished the entire series over the next couple days. 
 Before I started reading I was put off by the subject matter, I love fantasy, but falling in love with a vampire...please. And yet, Twilight started out so human and high school. New girl, normal insecurities, regular high school concerns. Then we meet Edward and I was just as fascinated by him as Bella was. I loved the tension, the danger and the dialogue of their relationship. I really enjoyed this book!
I loved it.

Is it me or this book too dull for words? Or maybe I am just to cyncial and bitter to enjoy it ... Officially stopped caring and will be donating this and volumes 2 and 3 to the Library. I may need to add a note: dear reader, not all men want to suck the life out of you ... don't use this book as a guide for your future boyfriends.

I absolutely hated this book!!! The writing sucked big time. So many times I just wanted to burn it. The funny thing is I saw the movies ran out and bought all the books. It was like pulling teeth getting through the Bella and Edward saga. Yuck, after twilight I never cracked open the others and never will.
Much better than I remembered. Appreciate more now I'm older.

I stayed up very late to finish this book. There are only a handful of books that I read in under a week or in the span of a few days- and this one was one of them. 
 And then after I finished the other two books currently out I re-read this one in the same month. Safe to say I really like this. Mad Props Stephenie Meyers

I didn't really have much interest in this series, but I decided to see what all the fuss was about, and what fun it was! There's nothing like your first love, but adding the human/immortal twist makes it interesting. This was also an interesting take on vampires, not exactly going against all myths, but explaining why they exist.

Given this book as a gift. 
 Shoot me if I ever pick it up and read it again. 
 Got maybe about 3/4 of the way through it. Characters were vapid, and childish.

Thanks Miriam for the recommendation - it's always somewhat insightful to read what many girls in my World Lit class are reading. I can't say I really loved it though. It was a fun read - I stayed up to 4am this morning to finish the thing. (I wish WW2 history books had the same effect on me and I wouldn't be so behind in my grad reading.) But I didn't feel like there was anything too complex about the book. I think I remember a time in my life when the "way-too-obsessed-about-a-boy" theme really struck a chord, but at this point it became a bit annoying. And the whole adolescent awkwardness, fitting in at high school stuff got a little tired for me. The end of the book was probably the best part - lots of action, some good vampire bits. Overall I enjoyed the book - it provided a nice break from heavy, dense text, but I'm not going to read the next one in the series until Winter Break because I can ill-afford to burn through two nights that should have been devoted to history. It sure was nice though!

** spoiler alert ** 
 The fact that so many millions of people have read this story leaves me to wonder a bit about the human race. What bugs me even more are the people that want to read about "strong heroines" and still adore this novel. 
 Bella Swan is truly the weakest wimpyest heroine I've had the misfortune to read about. From the start of the novel she makes no sense. Her family life with both parents is utterly ridiculous, and the fact that Stephanie Meyer chooses not to explain why she's gone to live with her father, Charlie in Forks until the story is about a quarter of the way in, just proves what a lousy storyteller she is. 
 Then there's the fact that Bella doesn't quite grasp vampires. Now I know this is fiction, but its present day fiction, where people have heard of vampires, mummies and the holy ghost. How does she not understand in the least about Edward's hunger and why she might be in danger from it? 
 I find very little about Bella to endear her to me. Mostly I just want to punch her in the face. I was actually cheering for the tracker vampire at the end to finish her off, but I knew it would never happen what with 3 more books in the series ahead. 
 And then there's Edward. Perhaps if I could see the real attractivenes in the actor, which so many find sexy I could understand Edward's appeal on paper. But that said I can't. He's a stalker! And he talks down to Bella the whole time, though that's understandable, because Bella begs for it. 
 She's the classic dutiful woman..cooking for her father, obeying Edward most of the time and generally being disgustingly docile. 
 Oh and then there's the whole Cullen clan, denying their existence as vampires for the most part. Why does every vampire not want to feed on the human race! Dammit that's what they are supposed to do. And the sparkly vampire shit is damn damn annoying. Turn into dust please!! 
 If this sage (melodrama) weren't the most popular piece of tripe out now, I would seriously say that only the tweens would find it enjoyable. I'm not sure how to explain off the adults that bought into this, except that years of reality tv have turned so many brains to mush.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I gave it a shot...and it wasn't that bad for the first third. I thought perhaps the author would have some interesting ideas. Then the meadow scene happened, and it was pretty much downhill from there. The rescue scene was massively anticlimactic (how do you NOT write a big vampire fight?), and the main character is simply beyond saving. But I guess it's what teenage girls want, right? Gotta play to the audience..even if they're not that bright.

This book just sucked me in. I liked the characters and the plot moved quickly. I thought that Bella's clumsiness was played up a bit too much and Edward was a bit too perfect, but I liked them both anyway. Meyer's did a great job of making it seem perfectly possible that a family of vampires could be living in a small town. I can't wait to start the second one. Sometimes, you can't beat a good romance novel!

Anyone who compares this to the Harry Potter series is unequivocally not my friend. 
 I get the allegory between teenage hormones and vampires' desire for blood. It is a somewhat interesting premise but NOT at all a clever microcosm of fantasy in the way Harry Potter is. It is like a Sweet Valley High novel except the popular high school hunk happens to be an amiable nocturnal beast. Precisely HALF of the book is about how dreamy Edward Cullen is. I sort of want to finish the series out of sheer morbid curiosity but dammit life is too short to read bad books. 
 I can understand why it is a teenage phenomenon but NOT at all why it is an adult phenomenon. I feel like I just drank an entire gallon of Capri Sun.

Yes, I liked it. Other people's reviews are fun to read though, because it's such a mix bag. I read the book for pleasure and it was entertaining. Besides, my teenage daughter thinks its cool I read it and we can have interesting discussions.
A perfect summer read. A humorous and fun look at vampires in a Northwest community.

Goodreads needs a sixth star - "HATED IT". Or, if they need to be nice to the authors, "hated it". "Didn't like it" is so much nicer than this book deserves. 
 Horrible writing, boring and dim characters, and vampires that sparkle. 
 I tried writing a review where I didn't rant about how abusive the relationship is between Edward and Bella, and I couldn't. Ignoring the actual vampire bits (because Edward is just...NO. Across the board NO.), the romance is non-existent and bland. The only chemistry between these two people lies in looks and smell. Oh, and the fact that Edward wants Bella's blood. 
 Props to Meyer for getting people to read and putting a new, albeit horrendous and somewhat hilarious, spin on vampires. But that's all I can thank her for. 
 I'll read the the other books in the series one day, mainly because I need to know how much worse this train wreck gets before it's over. I definitely won't be paying for them, however. These types of books are why libraries exist.

reference_books.title: Peter and the Starcatchers (Peter and the Starcatchers, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A fun, well written addition to the world of Peter Pan. Sort of a "before the legend" type story. And one that I very much enjoyed. I definitely need to reread this soon. (Damn, I need to reread a lot of books, don't I?) & look at that cover! So pretty. Lanie need! This is an excellent middle grade/young adult novel. Perfect for any who loves Peter Pan.

reference_books.title: Awakened (House of Night, #8)
reference_books.review_text: Aren't books supposed to get better and better with each book? These just keep getting worse and worse. This unorganized dreck isn't even fun to laugh at anymore.

reference_books.title: Virals (Virals, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
"Virals" combines science fiction with mystery and manages to do it fairly well. :) the story is fun and full of adventure and excitement. The writing is serviceable and easy enough to read. & the characters, while somewhat flat, are likable. The mystery unfolds at a good pace and actually balances well with the outrageous science of mutant wolf kids. 
 If you enjoy teen mysteries, or are a fan of James Patterson's young adult series "maximum ride", I'd definitely recommend this one two you.

reference_books.title: Eleanor & Park
reference_books.review_text:
I hate that I didn't like this. :( I wanted to so badly! I absolutely fucking adored "fan girl" & I very much enjoyed "carry on" but I just couldn't get into "Eleanor and Park." 
 :/ the writing is good. The characters are decent enough. I loved the beginning part of the novel. 
 But after The scene where they talk on the phone... I don't know. It just feels so... Dull. It getting boring to me. :( I don't know. I do know it's only about 330 pages and it's taken me FOREVER to read. So that must say something about it, right? 
 Its boring. But also, I think I really didn't like it because it went from this beautiful budding friendship/romance to insta love. 
 It just got a little painful and hard to swallow. It was just so... Desperate. You know what I mean? I mean, I get that they are teens. I get that Eleanor is obviously attention & loved starved. But just because they are teens doesn't mean they have to have this insta love crap. after Her declaring how much she hated this type of Romeo and Juliet thing, the obsession feels a bit insulting. 
 :/ this book was not for me. Other readers might really enjoy it, but i didn't. It had a good opening but it just went down hill after that. 1.5 stars, but I'm rounding down instead of up because I found the book to be such a bore. If you want a really good book by this writer, pick up "fan girl". Skip this one.

reference_books.title: A Monster Calls
reference_books.review_text:
I don't get it. :/ 
 The hype or the stories the monster told. 
 Picked this up cause the name and cover made it look like a creepy horror book. Very appropriate for Halloween yes? 
 It's honestly a very misleading cover and title. 
 But that's ok, so long as the story is good... Right? 
 And it was. I guess. It was ok. It wasn't a bad book, really. It just wasn't for me. 
 Maybe it's just because I've never lost anyone close to me. So I really can't relate to this. But I just don't get the hype. It seems oddly... I don't know....Bland to me. I mean, For a book about a mom dying of cancer and a angry little boy trying to deal, I found it very unmoving. :/ I thought it was kinda sad. That scene with Connor and his mom in the hospital room was pretty sad. 
 but really, I had trouble feeling very bad for him when I was so focused on how selfish Connor was being about the whole thing. 
 Sorry, not sorry. 13 is plenty old enough for him to realize that he's not the only person going through crap. That he's not the only person loosing someone here. Look, I know your mom is dying and all but that does not give you the right to be a dick to your friends and grandma. 
 But really, I think my big issue was the writing. It's just so bland. Boring. Nothing special about it. No flourish to it, not strong voice. And that's very sad, because I know what this author is capable of. "The knife of never letting go" was the first book to ever make me truly cry. 
 But "a monster calls"?.... It just left me with a "meh" feeling. Not bad. but not great. Certainly the not as great as everyone else seems to think. Guess I'm the black sheep, huh? & It kept my attention for the few hours it took me to read it. the illustrations were great. 
 I just wasn't very impressed. Definitely not a book for me. Plenty of other readers are sure to enjoy 
 Just not me. If you want a book by Patrick Ness, try his "chaos walking" trilogy. It's much better.

reference_books.title: Destined (House of Night, #9)
reference_books.review_text: My god. This was painful. An unorganized, badly edited, mess of teen pettiness & drama disguised as a super cool, hip vampire series. The characters are all dick. I've seen better writing in fanfics. :( ugh. The 1st few books are fun in a trashy book, ha-ha this is so terrible it's funny kinda way. This though... "Destined" is just beyond sad.

reference_books.title: A Child Called "It" (Dave Pelzer #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The Poorly written string of the tortures suffered by an abused child. It's sad & depressing over course. No one should suffer like this. 
 But honestly, a lot of it seems like it was embellished for dramatic effect. :/ 
 & after hearing and reading several things about the author buying his own books in bulk to increase sales records, & how his family said a lot of it was made up in interview, it make me wonder if "non-fiction" is really the right category for it. :/ 
 I don't care if it true or not, because, frankly, I don't really care. & Even if it was all true, I'd still have to give it one star for its piss poor writing. 
 Not recommended.

reference_books.title: Variant (Variant, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Was not impressed.

reference_books.title: Breaking Dawn (Twilight, #4)
reference_books.review_text: So sad. All that build up for a very disappointing ending.

reference_books.title: Delirium (Delirium, #1)
reference_books.review_text: i never really could figure out what it was that i disliked about this book. maybe it was the fact that i don't beleive that it's possible to get rid of love. or that getting rid of love could essentially destroy parental instincts. i know, i know, its fiction. but i at least what my fictional worlds to at least be believal! it doesn't make sense that a governement could convince an entire nation to believe that love is wrong. or maybe it was the complete lack of personality to our 'heroine'. i wanted to like her, i just couldn't do it. not good. if you wany a futuristic story that's actually good, try "Unwind" or "The Knife of Never Letting Go".

book_a.title: Trapped
book_a.user_review:
Maybe I didn't enjoy it very much because I'm just not that into realistic fiction. There's only a handful that I really like. I'm more of a fantasy & science fiction kinda gal. Manga & horror are great to. The darker & bloodier & emotionally draining the better. >:D 
 "Trapped" was ok. There wasn't anything particularly wrong with it. The writing wasn't good or bad. Just serviceable. None of the characters were overly annoying, really they were just... There. The story was ok to, progressing at a decent rate. 
 Kids trapped inside a school with no heat and no help coming while a blizzard rages on for day? 
 On the surface it sounds very exciting. 
 I just found it very underwhelming. Just not for me. :/ 
 others might enjoy it more. Recommended to readers who enjoy contemporary adventures stories.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Trapped has a premise that would catch any reader's attention -- a group of students get trapped alone at school when a disastrous snowstorm hits the area. Anyone would be intrigued, and start thinking of what these teens would do in order to survive. Unfortunately, readers won't be given much of anything. 
 There was really no attempt to connect the readers with the characters, to get them involved in the plight. The idea of the story can only carry someone so far, and when there is practically nothing happening, no step to move forward, the reader will quickly grow bored. 
 Similarly, the ending isn't any better. Although the main character is rescued, the only sense of relief anyone would feel is that the book is finished. There is no word on the other students who were trapped, no sense of what's been happening in the outside world, nothing. As a result, the ending, like the rest of the story, falls completely flat. 
 A real let-down.

I was kind of excited about this book when I read the summary of it but was kind of left disappointed in the end. I had never heard of another book taking on this topic and I thought it would be really good. The beginning was good especially when the snow kept falling and falling and wasn't going to stop anytime soon. But towards the middle and right before the climax (snow coming through the roof of the school) and then at the end I kept wanting to read more to figure out if the kids would be saved. 
 Didn't really like Scott (main character), thought he was kind of annoying and acted like a girl rather than a strong male character. Also the other students weren't very well developed and I felt like I still really didn't know them at the end of the story. Also I felt like the kids weren't really smart with trying to stay warm too. 
 Also, what happened to the teacher that left? I'm assuming he died but I dunno. 
 I thought this book had a lot of potential but kind of fell.

If I could give 0 stars I would. 
 The plot interested me - a group of teens stuck in their high school during a storm and conditions get worse and worse. However, Absolutely nothing happens in this story. Nothing. It was cold, the kids ate food, then they slept. Over and over for 220+ pages. 
 What's worse was the writing. The author clearly hasn't been a teenager in a very long time. His attempts to be "cool" were awkward and so annoying I got too angry to keep reading. I toughed it out to see what happens at the end, where it abruptly ends with the character saying something irrelevant. What a waste of time.

Bored now. Information in this book is relayed in first-person format and is rather like a cross between a novel and a shopping list. There are scattered foreshadowings which are probably supposed to be teasers but instead are annoying reminders of what hasn't happened yet. I kept hoping the pace would pick up and someone would go "rogue cannibal". Alas, life is too short to read dull books.

The writing is very simple and there is a lack of sensory details. The narrator (Scotty) speaks like a teenager. Yes, I get the point, the kids are teenagers. However, readers cannot go a couple sentences without reading the words "seriously", and "kind of" and things like that. The book was narrated toward the audience, but there were too many hypothetical questions. They were pretty lifeless characters. There was no character development and the characters are pretty standard- the regular guys, the troublemaker, the strange kid, and the girls. There was nothing really special about them. They also missed all types of foreshadowing. I could easily guess what was going to happen way before the characters did. The plot was not bad, it was just slow. The events were all necessary and important. Some events I was impressed with, but others just were very obvious. I liked the idea of the story, but the little things tore it down. The ending was not what I wanted it to be. It ended too suddenly, like someone just yanked the book out of the author's hand while he was still writing it. Read more of my review at http://pagesforthoughts.blogspot.com/...

Thinking about natural disasters and such...it scares me. I live in an area where the only crazy weather we would receive would be a snowstorm, so I can relate being stuck somewhere, businesses closing, losing electricity, no water, and other things because the snow is horrible. 
 Trapped pretty much is just a story about seven freshmen and sophomores being stuck at school when a nor'easter snowstorm hits their area and their survival during the days they are stuck at school. I almost didn't see a point to the book, why was the book written in the first place? The only thing that got my brain thinking during the book is if we teach enough "real world" information in school such what to do in an emergency, what a credit score is, and how to write a resume and put less emphasis on algebra. I think many of us leave school without common knowledge on things that we need to know to function in everyday society. 
 Another thing that bothered me a little in the book: cell phone battery life. Me personally, my phone goes dead at least once a day even if I don't use it, but I have a phone known for sucking the life out of a battery and I have access to a plug with electricity and an extra battery. What I want to know is how long can a cell phone battery last when it's being used only occasionally like for seeing if you have a message or using it as a "flashlight." I'm thinking 1 to 2 days tops depending on the phone. The whole time I just kept thinking "Your batteries on your phones should already be dead!" I had a talk with my sister and did some research and maybe that could happen where a cell phone's battery can last longer then what I'm thinking in certain circumstances and there were some circumstances in this book, but it still bothered me for some reason. 
 I will probably remember this book a little bit just because I think it's the only book I've ever read involving a natural disaster and plus snow worries me at times. And I do have to add that the cover was probably what sold me on buying this book.

Totally totally riveting. I read this during breaks at work, and had to tear myself away everytime my breaks were over. I'd come out and rave to my coworkers. This is a slim volume of just 232 pages, and the chapters are really really short. There's a dramatic sense of suspense, as Northrop foreshadows how horrible the trauma will be from the very beginning. 
 Seven teens are "trapped" in a high school during the mother of all snowstorms. As the snow piles up, the power and water goes out, and after a while, the snow covers the whole first floor, where the cafeteria and other niceties are. The kids are stuck in a classroom in the second story. Interpersonal struggles don't make things any easier. 
 I definitely agree with those who say the ending is abrupt, but the rest of this is good enough that it's ok.

Scotty is a Sophomore at Tattawa Regional High School in New England. When an unexpected blizzard comes to town, seven kids are stranded at school, including Scotty and two of his friends Pete and Tommy. Les, Elijah, Krista and Julie are the other four students. 
 Scotty is one of the survivors, so we hear his story of being trapped at school for seven days. 
 Before I started reading, I wondered how Northrop would manage to have seven students still at school during a snow storm. I couldn't help thinking, everyone would be on their way home, making this scenario impossible. But the author quickly made it seem very possible. After that is was easy to lose myself in Trapped. It's a serious page turner. 
 Everything that happens, from the school losing power to physical violence was inevitable. What makes this story that much more powerful and scary is the fact that it doesn't seem that far out there. 
 " I remember the snow, drifting sideways into half crescents in the windowpanes, and I remember that I didn't eat my corn. I don't know if I took a bite and thought it was a little too soggy or if I just remembered that it had been soggy the last time, but I left it there on my tray. 
 As dumb as this sounds, that bothered me for days. I mean soggy or not, it was decent corn prepared by people who were at least borderline professionals. It was definitely a whole lot better than what I'd end up eating soon enough, and I'd just thrown it away, I still remember the little flash of yellow as I pushed the tray onto the conveyor belt that took it into the back of the kitchen, where the giant, hissing dishwashing machines were. Whoever thought you could be haunted by corn niblets? 
 Trapped is great winter time read. It's that much easier to picture the never ending snow. While walking in the cold, I found myself sympathizing with the characters, and wondering what I would do if I was in their situation. Imagining being stuck with six people anywhere thanks to a week long blizzard is scarier then any fantasy novel because of the possibility factor.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Firstly I was super stoked to have won this novel free from Goodreads First Reads!! I like and disliked the story, I found it funny at times and loved how the main character, Scotty would interpreted the way things were said as code for something else. I was a little erked by a couple of sentences in the first chapters when Scotty says that not everyone makes it, at that point you don't think of the teacher as the one who doesn't make it. It was fun to see the competition between the three best friends and Jason's determination to make something of that Go-Kart. I am sad that everyone seems to interpret Jason's behavior to Pete when he wants to take it out and try to get help as if he doesn't want anyone on "his work" when that wasn't the case.
So much wasted potential! This story could and should have been a fun read, but the kids lack imagination, and ultimately it's mostly about acne and frozen pudding. Very disappointing.

I love the idea of this book. The tactic of capturing a group of people in a place where they cannot get away from each other and then watching them interact (in books - not reality television) has always been a favorite of mine. This book does not disappoint. The tension in the group of students grows, changes, re-shapes, lessens, and grows again throughout the story in a very claustrophobic way that I really enjoyed. I was impressed with Mr. Northrop's ability to flesh out these teen characters just enough to keep them a bit mysterious. He also did not feel the need to borrow from the likes of Saw movies to keep the pace moving which seem to be the only comparison reviewers can draw from with claustrophobic group tales. 
 As a fan of books with a male first-person narrative, I found this book to be a teensy bit disappointing. In the midst of a very large crisis, Scotty managed to be one of the most hormonal guys I've ever read. He focused a bit too much on girls with little to no pay off for that up close scrutiny he treats us to in the story. And the in depth look at his burgeoning pimple and its aftermath was just irrelevant to the plot and made me wrinkle my nose in a bit of disgust. However, I do have to say that his voice otherwise was really realistic and interesting. He was not always predictable and he was able to give everyone around him a pretty fair assessment personality-wise, even changing his mind about some of them as the story progresses. 
 The story moves a little sleepily along and could never be considered to have much fast-paced action. But the interactions between the characters is almost deliciously voyeuristic without the ridiculous, hyped up drama created by reality television shows. Watching each of them react to the crisis at hand through Scotty's eyes makes the read very worthwhile as does the slowly building sensation of the ominous as things begin to go wrong and the teens must react to survive. 
 I read one review that said the ending felt contrived but I disagree. The story promised the ending from the very beginning. Reading this book was not about intense, racing survival and dread. It was about watching how the characters interact with each other and their environment, speculating how you may have responded in the same situation, and rooting for the snow to please, come to an end! Sort of like those of us who have had a ton of snow dropped on us over the past few weeks. I have to say that actually added to my enjoyment of the book because I sort of lost the line between reality and the book (in a fun way) and kept waiting to see the snow piled up past my own first floor window!

Living in a place that gets snow for a good six months, I often wondered what would happen if I ever got snowed in at school (back when I was in elementary and high school) with no way for anyone to come get me (almost happened at work, once. I had to walk halfway home!). TRAPPED takes my question and answers it in the most extreme way possible. 
 Seven students are stuck at their high school when a snowstorm hits. At first, they don't think that anything is wrong - they believe they will be picked up and safe at home before the day is over. As the storm continues to rage on, and the power goes out, they come to the conclusion that their rides cannot make it through the snow, and will be spending the night in the school. The snow keeps rising, and the days start to add up. As they run out of emergency light, scavenge the cafeteria for food, and get progressively colder, Scotty, Pete and the others trapped in the school hear an ominous creaking from the roof, and realize that not only is no one coming, but it may be possible no one even knows they're there. 
 Through Scotty, our narrator, you get to know the seven teens as much as possible. Divisions and friendships change up as the situation becomes worse, and tempers are quick to flare. For all that you do get character insight, I saw the book more as a survival story than a character interaction/development story. The draw for me was the challenges that the seven faced and how they dealt with their situation. I didn't need a whole bunch of back story - the few bits presented throughout the story as they're needed were perfect. Michael Northrop has great mood writing; I was drawn right into the setting and storm, and the descriptions of the cold, the dark and Scotty's worries really stood out and added depth to the story. It was easy to imagine the anger and lack of hope they feel when they begin realizing that things are a lot worse than they originally thought. Their worries for family members that may or may not have made it home from other places just adds to the stress you know they are all feeling. 
 I was happy to see the attention paid to details, like lights, cold, needing food, finding a radio, etc. I would have liked a bit more to the ending, I thought it was rather abrupt, but it does work with the book. It's more personal preference that I wanted to see more of the "after" of the storm. TRAPPED is a bit of a slower book, like I mentioned above, it is definitely a survival story. Not too much action but a lot of development and enough tension to keep the book going at a good pace. The decisions the teens eventually have to make in order to survive were heartbreaking, and I have to say - the book gave me chills. 
 Review originally posted at Escape Through the Pages

Great if slow set-up to an exciting survival book. Seven teens trapped in a rural high school with no end to the accumulation of snow and no escape or rescue apparent. The abrupt ending ruined it for me though. What no denouement or epilogue? Come on Mr. Northrop! We read the entire book and you don't let us know what it was like after the rescue? I feel cheated.

I felt like the book had a horrible plot. The main character could have obviously thought of making snowshoes before the end when kids are dying in a school. It was just bland. I rarely dislike books to this extent because I usually try to find some sort of merit, but I just couldn't handle this book.

Pros: 
 Fast Read 
 Good for guys 
 Disaster Fiction (one of my fav's) 
 Good for reluctant and/or not as advanced YA readers 
 Cons: 
 I thought it ended too abruptly. I wished there had been a bit more description or an epilogue or something. 
 Just so you know: 
 There is no sexually explicit material in this book, but there are many references to the things that happen with boys when they are over hormonal about girls. I don't care, but some people might.

Maybe if I'd read this during a snow day I would've appreciated it more. I normally love stories about being stuck somewhere (LOVE when Nova Lee has her baby in the Walmart in Where the Heart Is), but these characters were so under developed and immature that I couldn't connect or relate.

Anyone who knows me knows that I absolutely love survival stories. It is probably my favorite genre ever. Before this, I have read five YA survival books - three of them made it onto my list of favorite books ever. Alas, this was the first that I really didn't like. In fact, I liked it so little that I couldn't finish it. It wasn't worth it. This was one of the worst books I've read in a while, and I'll certainly never be reading anything by Northrop again. 
 The worst part was the writing. I'll give you a couple examples of it in the form of character descriptions, because they exemplify the consistent problems in Northrop's writing, and they'll come up again when I talk about the characters. First, Scotty: 
 My name is Scotty Weems. I prefer Scotty, but most people, even my friends, call me Weems. I guess it's easy to say, and maybe some people think it's funny. It doesn't bother me that much. I'm just glad that Snotty Streams never really caught on as a nickname. 
 Anyway, I'm an athlete, so I made peace with my last name a long while ago. Since I was a little kid in T-ball, I heard it shouted every time I did something right and every time I screwed up, too. These days it's on the back of my basketball jersey. I like to think that someday people will be chanting from the bleachers: "Weems! Weems! Weems!" Chanting fans make any name sound good. 
 Anyway, that's me. I'll be sort of like your guide through all this. Some of the others might've seen things differently, and some of them might've told it better, but you don't get to pick. You don't because, for one thing, not all of us made it. 
 This is his friend, Pete: 
 Pete was just, like, a normal kid. It was sort of his role. It might sound strange, being known for what you aren't, but Pete wasn't a jock or a Future Farmer of America or a student council member, and he wasn't super hip or incredibly smart. He was just a normal sophomore. [...] You needed some kids like that, otherwise all you had were competing factions of freaks, all dressed in outfits that amounted to uniforms and trying to play their music louder than yours. 
 And finally, here's Krista: 
 Krista was wearing a blue wool hat, even though she was indoors: a blue hat and a sweater. [...] She had thick brown hair and her eyes were sort of blue-gray. Her skin had just a few reddish brown freckles here and there. But it wasn't the colors as much as the way it was all arranged. [...] 
 And did I mention her body? Because I will, repeatedly. She wasn't tall, but she had that awesome combination of just enough curves on a tight athletic body. [...] Really, they shouldn't let girls like her mingle with the general population, not in high school anyway. Half the time the guys here were so stuffed with hormones and frustration that we walked down the hallways stiff-legged and ready to burst. 
 (Don't worry, I'll get to that body thing later, believe me.) 
 These passages show off some telltale signs of his Northrop's bad writing. It's awfully simplistic for YA, with no real descriptive details, even when it would be appropriate. And the teenspeak... dear lord. Hardly a sentence goes by where Northrop doesn't add some variation of 'seriously', 'I mean', 'like', 'you know', ect. I don't care if that's how real teenagers talk - it sounded plain out awkward and annoying in the writing. It also led to a few awkward misuses of the word where it felt obligatory such as: 
 Cell phones weren't allowed at Tattawa, and they were kind of not kidding about that. This kind of thing really felt like it belonged in middle-grade, not YA. 
 The writing was equally amateurish when it came to the use of literary devices. The Chekhov's Gun of the high school being out in the middle of nowhere was spelled out for us at its first appearance. There wasn't foreshadowing so much as Scotty telling us outright what was going to happen, like in the first quote where he said that some of them didn't make it. It's almost an implied diss: teenagers are stupid. They won't notice and appreciate things like foreshadowing if it's not as blatant as possible. Well, guess what? We're not that stupid. And it makes you seem stupid to misuse foreshadowing like that. The purpose of it is not to tell the reader what the twist will be, but have them be prepared for the twist so that it doesn't come out of nowhere. 
 And now for the characters. They were flat. Lifeless. Boring. Hardly recognizably human. Remember the description of Scotty I gave above? He never grows beyond that, he never shows any signs of being anything beyond that. The only thing we know about him is that he likes basketball. Same goes with his friend. And the cast made up a stereotypical Disney show: you have the three normal guys (Scotty, Pete, and Jason), the bully (Les), the weird kid (Elijah), and the hot girls who are OMGBFFs! (Krista and Julie). All we're missing is the unrealistically smart nerd, and we have a fully Disney cast. These characters didn't feel like real people. Not once. 
 Oh, and remember when I said I'd get back to Krista's description later? Well, get ready for a rant. She had no personality apart from being hot. There was not a single interaction with her in which her hotness wasn't mentioned. I almost felt sorry for her, because that's all that Scotty could see her as, not as a real person. THIS IS NOT HOW TEENAGERS THINK! It is an insult to teenage boys such as myself to imply this way that we only notice the physical looks of a girl. BECAUSE I DON'T! 
 Not to mention the misogyny of it. (Which, I didn't mention originally, but I'm fixing it now.) It is not okay to sexually objectify women like that. We don't exactly see a whole lot of women - only two, in fact. But both of them are characterized like that. As I said earlier, not a single scene went by when Scotty didn't mention Krista's hotness. THAT IS NOT OKAY! Not only to assume a teenage boy would think that way, but also to characterize women that way, like their sex appeal is their only characteristic. I'm not saying Northrop thinks that way - he may not have meant for that attitude to come across in his writing - but it certainly comes across that way, and Scotty is definitely misogynistic, no matter how you spin it. 
 There's also something that I didn't read (it came after I gave up in the narrative). I don't really feel qualified to talk about it, so I'll just quote a friend's review: 
 Also, what truly pissed me off was that ONE scene that did not necessarily need to be written[. It] was when one of the other 6 students, Julie [...] was leading boys on with her "Oh, I'm helpless" vibes, [and] triggers the boy that has a crush on her, Pete, to assume that the bad boy of the group, Les, has molested her. And of course, there's a two paragraph length of just Pete and Les semi-brawling it out when it was just a MISUNDERSTANDING. 
 Gah, what the fuck? WHY was that written? As if Scotty's attitudes towards Kristia weren't fucked up enough, now we have a female character being used as a tool to characterize someone through her sexual abuse. It is not okay to use your female characters like this. And it turned out not to be true, making it even more useless and rage-worthy. This is probably the most misogynistic shit I've ever read. 
 The plot wasn't nearly as bad as the characters or the prose, but it wasn't anything special either. The pacing was sorta slow - 70 pages in, and they still hadn't gotten serious about survival yet. It was boring. I don't normally mind a slow pace in survival stories, but you have to put it to good use, which character development or emotion. (See The Way We Fall). This was not good use of it. Without even survival elements, the plot was nothing. Absolutely nothing. 
 Everything about this book felt like it was made specifically so that it could be enjoyed by reluctant readers. I mean it, all of it: the slang, the familiar characters, the lack of complexity in the plot, the blatant use of foreshadowing to increase the suspense in the most bland way possible, all of it would appeal to reluctant readers a lot more than regular ones. Two problems with this: 
 1.) You cannot write something specifically for reluctant readers. Because guess who's more likely to read it? That's right, readers who know how to form opinions, teenagers who aren't morons. (Yes, Northrop, those people exist. You clearly don't know that from the way you wrote this book, but they do.) These readers will immediately see through this shit that you've written; I did. 
 2.) It's been proven, time and time again, that the books reluctant readers enjoy are the books that are made so that everyone can enjoy them, not just the people who don't read very often. Just look at Harry Potter! Just look at Animorphs! Both of these books are written in simple language, with action and characters that teenagers will be able to identify with without much work. But they also have intelligent writing, character development, emotion, and interesting plots. I feel as if Northrop doesn't understand this: you cannot write for anyone without these elements. If you don't include them, everything you write will receive reception just as harsh as this one. 
 I'm sorry. But I feel as if Northrop has no grasp at all of what makes a book good. It's like something I wrote when I was in 5th grade: all action and badly thought out plot, no emotion or character development, and with painful slang to boot. 
 So, yes. This was truly, truly awful. It was an insult to my intelligence and to the fact that I am a teenage boy. If I were to speak frankly, it pissed me off in a way that books rarely can. It's the only book I've ever read where I can honestly say that I didn't like a single thing about it. Nothing. Whatsoever. I would recommend it for no one.

 This is another book I probably wouldn't have read if not for the Contemps spurring me onward. The basic premise is that Scotty Weems and seven classmates are stuck at school after the storm of the century strikes, trapping them there for a week with limited electricity and food, and the knowledge that no one knows they are there. 
 This was quite a frightening book in that the monster snow storm that appears last about a week, covering even two-story buildings and pulling down the phone and power lines. Now they are in a school, so there are bathrooms, food in the cafeteria, and rooms aplenty. Unfortunately as the week progresses that becomes less important as the water, the lights, and the heat fail. 
 The beginning of the book suggested the death of some of the seven stuck at the school. Not Scotty who narrates the entire book, but perhaps one of his friends Jason or Pete, one of the girls Krista or Julie, or one of the other guys Les or Elijah. I was disappointed with the conclusion of this plot line as I thought it would get a lot darker than it actually did. Additionally as high school students they navigate the roles of cliques and interactions with each other in order to survive. Their efforts to survive were sometimes ingenious but frequently repetitive without providing additional depth to my understanding of their character, which is my main complaint against the book. Perhaps it would work better for readers who are 14/15, the ages of the characters in the book. 
 I'm been debating if this would be more fun to read when it's really cold and snowy outside or when you know you are safe because of the very nice weather. I think I'm the kind of person who prefers the latter so I'm glad I live in a warmer area that doesn't get snow.

I love books and films in which a group of disparate survivors are thrown together in seemingly dire circumstances. It's worked well for books like Stephen King's The Stand, or movies like Dawn of the Dead, 28 Days Later, or The Mist (also by King), and I'd hoped it would do so for Michael Northrop's slender YA book, Trapped. 
 Unfortunately, while there was a lot of potential story to be mined in this tale of seven high-schoolers trapped in their school during a nor'easter that lasts an entire week, almost none of that potential was reached. 
 For most of the book, things move along at a decent pace. Several threads are introduced that add suspense and urgency to the story - the apparently violent Les, the weirdly reticent Elijah, the narrator's fear for the fate of his mother, the development of illness among the students, even the structural integrity of the building in which they're trapped. But few of those subjects are addressed by the jarringly abrupt end. And when I say abrupt, I mean shockingly, disappointingly so.

sample_reviews.review_text: A quirky and hilarious little book. I couldn't resist picking up the sequel.

I'll admit it: I was a holdout. I don't know if it was the fact that it was SUCH a big deal, or if it was the cartoony element (back before cartoons in books were a common as they are now - in other words, it was something new), or if it was the fact that when I opened it up to a random page, I got the page where he plays a prank on his best friend and my thought was, "This Wimpy Kid is a sucky friend, which is the opposite of awesome." Let it suffice to say that I was not eager for Kidlet Number One to discover these books. 
 Until he did. 
 It was one of those days. We were in a bookstore. We were waiting to see the amazing Libba Bray (more on that later!). The line was long. He was wilting. I told him to go pick a book - any book - from the pre-teen section and if he liked it, he could buy it with his allowance. And he came back with... Dun-dun-DUUUNNNNN: THE BOOK WHICH WAS NOT NAMED. 
 To my discredit, I argued with him. I told him that I hated that book with a passion that burned with the power of a thousand suns. (Yes, I actually said that. About a book. In a bookstore. I am a cretin.) But standing there surrounded by book-lovers, reason (and shame) prevailed. We can read this together, I thought. And then we can talk about it. 
 And then I laughed pretty much nonstop for over 45 minutes. This book is hilarious. 
 From the moment Greg says that he specifically told his mother not to get him something that said "diary" on it (and then follows it up with a cartoon illustrating his fear: a bigger kid beating on him because of it), I knew that this was a book that would speak to the hearts of every middle-grader out there. Through Greg, Jeff Kinney gives us a picture of Middle School that echoes the universal Middle School experience: trying to find your niche in a universe that seems to have no niches left. From the Halloween mishap to the Christmas play shenanigans, Greg speaks for all middle-schoolers out there as he navigates the perils of hallway bullies, fights with his best friend, unreasonable parental expectations, and clueless teachers. 
 There are still definitely things about Greg's behavior that I didn't like: he treats his supposed best friend pretty badly from the very beginning, and he sneaks around a couple of times breaking his parents' rules. But these are things that echo the true middle-school experience, and while I don't like them and I don't want my kids feeling like it's okay to do these things, I do think that this book is a better way to bring up these issues and to illustrate why it's important to treat our friends well and listen to our parents, even when we don't know why they make the rules that they make. In other words, this book has some great talking points in it, and I encourage parents to read this book with their kids so that you can ask them questions and discuss those moments and find out what they think about Greg and his escapades. 
 As for me and my kid, we're already looking forward to laughing our way through the second book in this deservedly popular series.

An excellent book for parents who want their children to grow up lazy, spoiled, entitled, disgusting and rude all the time. I understand that it's a children's book (or YA? I was in grade seven when the film adaptation came out but I only recently noticed the franchise). But Greg is self-absorbed and a nasty teenager. He expects everyone to throw him a pity party and vents his concerns, yet he has nothing to be unhappy about. Sure, most kids don't like school, but they usually appreciate having an education, which they realize as they get more mature. Greg on the other hand wallows in his own self-worth and heavily criticizes his family, classmates and neighbors. He has nothing to be sad about! He has a caring family, a pretty comfortable lifestyle (I was living in a musty old rented-out house on an army base all through middle school, and kids at my school were taught by their parents to be bullies on purpose so it certainly wasn't a cakewalk for a lot of kids I knew at the time or myself, my sister and brother). Greg has a hoard of toys, books, video games and money and never has to worry about grief or loss of any kind. He's an ungrateful little jerk who could use a few trips to boarding school if you ask me. 
 Diary of a Wimpy Kid is one of those books that appeals to the "lowest common denominator": it's got loads of toilet humor, fart jokes, nose picking jokes, crass jokes and name-calling. One of the reasons why kids today can get away with using "f*ck" as a comma in their conversations and why they're growing up to be failures is because at an early age these days they're taught that crude humor is funny, that apathy and laziness is cute and that bullying is "just fun and games". Crude humor isn't funny. Bullying is hurtful and nasty and acting like the world revolves around you is just pathetic. This generation needs a wake-up call, and so do the parents who should be teaching their kids to be decent, good people, not cell-phone-toting couch potatoes who find a kid being beat up to be a laugh-riot. There isn't any swearing in any of the Wimpy Kid books but the crude humor and Greg's horrible attitude only get worse as time goes on. 
 This series had potential to be really good, and it did have a few genuinely funny moments. Why Kinney didn't work with that and leave the stupid filler out of it is a mystery to me. :(

giggles

Jeff Kinney's books might be recommended for 9+,but I can always rely on DOAWK to get me out of a reading slump or make me laugh. DOAWK follows the story of an out-of-place and dorky pre-teen who has to navigate his way through middle-school and family drama.All the books are hilarious,fun and totally mood lightening.Greg might not be the ideal role model,but he sure is entertaining.Diary of a Wimpy Kid books are easy-reads and take me on average an hour or so to finish(that's if I EVER get an hour of my life ALONE in peace to read!).I don't think I'll ever outgrow Greg(hopefully).

I've been meaning to re-read this series again, especially considering I watched the third movie installment last night for the first time. 
 So, things I've learned since re-reading the book. 
 Greg is a relatable character. 
 He's also an asshole. 
 The way he treats and manipulates situations and how selfish he can be is really astonishing once you actually pick up and devour the book in under an hour and really consider the situation at hand - the comic book scenario, the fact that he hoped he would get a better present from Rowley's family because they have a lot more money, the fact that he didn't appreciate Rowley's Christmas present, he didn't appreciate his dad's, etc. I can kind of understand why he didn't appreciate his Uncle's. I mean - who really wants a photo of their Uncle for Christmas. I guess we know self-centredness runs within the family. 
 And despite the fact that I didn't really laugh out loud, or even breathe an excessive loud amount of breath from my nose, I can still see how the book would be humorous to youngsters, or hell, even people my age. I still found it humorous and addicting despite not actually laughing. 
 I'm still giving this a five star rating, or maybe a 4.8 - either way, I still see myself enjoying these books despite the main characters general selfishness and lack of understanding towards other people's feelings. It's realistic in that sense.
