reference_books.title: Supernaturally (Paranormalcy, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Fans of "Buffy The Vampire Slayer" will probably enjoy Kiersten White's wonderfully cute, special and kick-ass "Paranormalcy"/"Supernaturally" series. 
 I must say that I really did enjoy these fast-paced, entertaining and oh, so fun books. Both this one and the previous novel in the series; "Paranormalcy". As a first-time author with these two books; Ms. White writes like an old pro and was able to capture the essence of what it means to be a very special young woman in a world more messed up than most people could or would ever know. The sweet romance intermingled within the heart-stopping scenes of action and plot twists had me red-eyed in the mornings and chugging caffeine like it was going out of style due to staying up those nights glued to the book and Evie's story. Evie's point of view was a refreshing drink of ice cold water after all of the lukewarm human-meets-other love stories I've been running across. It was nice to see a main heroine who knew her own mind, had sass enough to spare and could kick some butt if need be. Plus, her "specialty" made her all the more interesting and endearing.

reference_books.title: Thirteen Reasons Why
reference_books.review_text:
I don't know. Maybe it's because I haven't been a teenager myself for many years, (hey, now! Not that many!), and I don't feel quite as deeply or as rawly as a lot of hormonal teens do, but as I am reading this book it doesn't strike me that she would have reason enough to end her own life. I understand that bullying and being ostracized is traumatic, hell, I went through both in various degrees growing up having been shoveled from grade school to grade school due to having nomadic parents and several times I had a breakdown in the middle of class and my home life was nothing to write home about but I never once considered offing myself. I don't know. Maybe I just need to feel for the character more, but what she went through didn't seem like it was so bad when compared to what another character goes through! For the first half of the book I was thinking to myself that here's a little girl who needs some attention and, watch, at the end we'll find her still alive and the tapes were her cry for help. I'm almost done with the book now so I know that's not going to 
 happen, but I still can't understand what would make someone believe that there is no more hope for them and decide to kill themselves? My younger brother committed suicide a few years ago and when I read this book and think about him I don't think think that I will ever understands what can drive someone to do such a thing. I guess no one can. Not until they have been there themselves. So I take back what I just wrote above; No one can really know or understand what makes something too much for a person to go through. It's a sad, poignant book that will probably stick with me long after I turn the final page. 
 Edit: I finished it. Still have the same opinion and thoughts I had at 80% of the way through, which you just read if you didn't skip my entire review just to read the end. On to the next book!

reference_books.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
reference_books.review_text:
Edit: Having just finished this book my first impression is still the same; but it did keep my attention a little better the second half through. In my opinion the story was good but the writing left much to be desired and got in the way of this book truly being the emotional roller coaster of a story the author was undoubtedly attempting, and failing to tell through it's milquetoast and naive, (read: dull and stupid), protagonist and narrator. At least it was short and hopefully the movie is better. 
 Overall impressions: In a word? "Meh". 
 To me, it reads like Charlie is much younger than 15, and it feels like something from the 1950s or some other more innocent time. There are some parts that are cute and/or funny and some sincerely touching moments, but so far I have to seriously say that I really don't understand what all the hype around this book was all about. Going into it I had heard a lot of positive spin about it due to the movie being made and thought I was heading into a little bit of "Running With Scissors" type of book, but "Running" was ten times what "Wallflower" only dreams it could be. Maybe it's one of those books where the movie is better; with "Running With Scissors" the book was awesome, but the film just flopped. Maybe it will be other way around with "Wallflower" because the book, so far, (40% through as of this writing), to me, is nothing to write home about. I'll finish it, though, because it's so short I'd feel like I was just being lazy to not finish such a brief book.

reference_books.review_text:
100% A lot of crazy stuff, sex, passive aggressive control freak and Happy ever after. Roller coaster ride is right! I feel seriously emotionally drained after finishing this book. Two stars; for the slight enjoyment that kept me barely involved, and the negative stars are due to how very unrealistic it was throughout. 
 50% 
 OK, now I am getting more of a Full picture of the borderline domestic abuse in this book. Red flags galore from Travis's temper tantrums everytime he even suspects Abby of wanting to leave and just stay the night away, much less break up! There's a few scenes where I'm sure if she'd been around him he would have hit her. If the author wants to go that route then to stay True to form the next book should have him isolating her, (if they are still together), refusing to let her make decisions, taking over her finances, etc and then the final outcome: Lying to friends and family and sunglasses to hide the bruises. Travis and Abby's violence relationship doesn't make this book addictive, it makes it sick and twisted unless the author was going for a cautionary tale rather than a romantic fantasy. 
 40% 
 So far I don't see what makes this book any more addicting than any other? To be perfectly honest I'm having trouble forcing myself to stick with it. Maybe I'm missing something or it gets really good in the last 50%. 
 About 20% through: 
 There are too many books where the main love interest falls madly into love with the main character right out of the starting gate so it's nice to read a book where they are friends first, which is how all realistic and long lasting relationship should start out as; friends first, lovers second. 
 Just Started: 
 Well, several people on GRs have said how addicting this book was for them and having a so-called "addictive personality" I thought I'd give it a whirl.

book_a.title: The Glass Castle
book_a.user_review:
I realize the review below for the first half of this book is pretty judgmental, but I tend to have that kind of knee jerk reaction when presented with depictions of abuse and neglect. I have finished the second half and thus the rest of the book and I'm no longer looking at the author's adult family members as villains but as flawed individuals who were trying to keep afloat during hardships and who were all products of their time and situations. I applaud the author for being able to break the cycle of addiction and abuse that her father and mother suffered from. This book, from beginning to end pulls emotions from the reader as myriad as a rainbow and twice as vivid; starting with disbelief, shock, disapproval and loathing and ending with bittersweet triumph as well as peppered here and there with sparkling raindrops of dry humor. All in all a satisfying read from page one to the final chapter of the author's adventure through her formative years on this planet. 
 Below is the review I wrote after reading the first half of the book: 
 The first paragraph below is the only spoiler I'm including here and it won't ruin the book but if you don't want to read it just scroll down past it... 
 ~*SPOILER*~ 
 In the beginning of this book the author at three years old is injured laying in a hospital bed. Her mother had entered a contest using something of the little girl's and won a free helicopter ride. When the family visited the author in the hospital they tell her about her winning a ride in a helicopter. Excitedly the little girl asks her parents when she's going to get to go up on a helicopter ride and nonchalantly the mother says; "We already went. It was fun." 
 ~*END OF SPOILER*~ 
 I know it was a mixture of mental health issues and addiction that caused the author's parents to appear half the time as quirky, free-spirited sporadically caring parents and the other half as complete and utter douches not worthy of taking care of a middle school flour sack "baby" much less real live children! 
 This is the second autobiographical book by Jeanette Walls that I've read, the first being 
 , and, so far, I have to say that this book is far more interesting. I say "interesting" in the way people who can't help rubbernecking horrible car wrecks use that word, for this book is akin to a most horrific vehicular accident worthy of a prime time medical soap opera two-porter that you really and honestly want to drive past and not look but you just can't stop your neck muscles from twisting around or your eyeballs from bulging from their sockets at the carnage and mayhem. This book reads like an original V.C. Andrews' book, if someone had just begun telling me about it but failed to mention the author or that it's a memoir I'd probably assume it was a lost V.C Andrews' or her estate's ghostwriters' manuscript and not a real life account of one girl's childhood to adulthood. It's probably one of the most distressing look at familial dysfunction and poverty in the United States that I've ever seen in an autobiography. It's amazing what the author and her siblings went through, even more so when you think about how many countless others had grown up during that same era where a lot of what we would consider child abuse and neglect today was considered normal for the time. I won't give too much away other than to say there were several sections of the book that had me exclaiming aloud in outrage at the indignities, pain and humiliation piled on the main children of the story.

I enjoyed this book well enough, and I think Jeannette Walls is a good writer (unlike so many memoir writers). However, there were two issues that leaped out at me: 
 1) Though she didn't mind providing a detailed story of her childhood, she really skimped on her adult life. She didn't need to give us every sordid detail of her life to date, but giving at least a reasonably full picture of life as an adult would have made the book more well rounded to me. 
 2) The book ended very abruptly. I felt there were still a few things that needed to be said in order to end it with a satisfying conclusion. Perhaps providing an epilogue with a brief update to tie up some of the loose ends (i.e. Maureen visiting or not, the current situation regarding her mother's apartment building, etc.) would have helped. 
 Overall it was a fairly good book & decently written. It didn't affect me as negatively as other memoirs of this nature have (Angela's Ashes, for example), so I suppose that's a good thing. It has its flaws, but I've come to believe that the majority of memoir writing will by its nature have flaws. I'm not sure perfection is attainable within this genre, because it's so wide open in terms of structure & style. To be able to write a good but flawed personal account of one's life that people want to read is a goal worthy of achieving, and Walls has done that.
Loved the beginning, but then. It seemed to just keep sounding the same note.

After seeing so many accolades for Walls' "The Glass Castle", I decided to pick it up to see for myself how great this memoir was. Walls' tale of growing up in abject poverty with an absentee yet well-meaning alcoholic father and flighty, artistic mother was quite an eye-opening experience. The material ranges from hilarious, to sad, to heartbreaking, sometimes in the blink of an eye. It is clear that Walls memoir is a testament to her great love for her terribly dysfunctional family, even after all the shame she endured at the hands of peers and all the years that (as a child) she had to assume the role of parent to her siblings (and mother/father) due to her mother's refusal to parent and her father's horrific struggles with alcohol addiction. It would be easy for one to throw in the towel after the childhood that Walls experienced, but her story proves triumphant as she mustered up the courage and scrappiness to rise above her ineffective parents and turbulent childhood. It is sad that her parents could not (or would not) escape the throes of addiction, malaise and chaotic lifestyle resulting in them remaining homeless after their children's careers took off. Highly recommended.
While I appreciated the struggle and thought the writing was great, it made me so angry/sad I couldn't wait for it to be over.

I am a reader of the "troubling memoir" genre (that I just made up!), so I found Walls' book compelling. Walls' story of her childhood includes extreme poverty, an alcoholic father, and a horribly unstable, artistic mother. Her family lived in conditions that do not seem possible in the contemporary history of the United States. The actions of her parents, particularly her mother, are almost incomprehensible and never fully explained. While her mother is not violent or physically abusive, she is obviously very mentally ill. This is an issue that I have with the book; it never addresses or even deeply questions the reasons behind the mother's behavior. I also thought the pacing of the book was a bit off. 
 Minor events often seem to take up a great deal of time, such as describing a specific event or dialogue in incredible detail; while major events, such as how she, her two sisters, and her brother ultimately escaped poverty and hopelessness, are rushed through. 
 This book is a definite page turner, but ultimately it left me wanting for answers, particularly about Walls' mother. If you liked A Child Called It, Running with Scissors, or Dry, you will probably find this book interesting. I would primarily recommend it to "troubling memoir" enthusiasts, such as myself.

Yes, memoirs of dysfunctional families and abused children are quite popular among adults now as they are among teens. "The Glass Castle" could be grouped into this genre, but it is set apart by the fact that Walls' parents are not overtly abusive--they seem to love their children--but they are so neglectful that it defies imagination. How the Walls children managed to grow up and escape a life of poverty is a great read. 
 Walls' father was an alcoholic and her mother was an (unsuccessful) artist. Both are completely impractical and have no parenting skills. They allow the kids to do as they please and to raise themselves. Jeannette severely burns herself when she is three because she catches fire trying to make herself a hotdog. The dangerous mix of children and fire still doesn't sink in for the parents, and there are several close encounters throughout the book. 
 Mrs. Walls has a teaching certificate, but is rarely employed because she doesn't like the routine or getting up in the morning. She has an excuse for everything about her life and nothing seems to bother her too much. If the family doesn't have the money to feed its pets, then all the better--the pets are learning survival skills. Rex Walls is very intelligent, but he always has pie-in-the-sky schemes and resorts to alcohol and arguing on the job, which routinely get him fired. He seems to make more money playing poker than he does working. Thus the kids have to learn survival skills just as the pets do. They sleep on cardboard boxes and cover themselves with a plastic raft to keep the rain off when the roof leaks. They scrounge for food and eat out of the schoolyard trashcans. If the family accumulates too much debt--or just gets the itch to move--they 'skedaddle.' They don't pay to have the garbage collected, and it ends up in a large hole the kids had dug in the yard--a hole that was supposed to be for the fountain of the 'glass castle,' a dream house that Rex is always modifying plans for and never building. 
 While the kids are young, they are able to believe in the glass castle of their future. Their father has sometimes delightful ways of disguising his negligence--such as the Christmas when the kids will get no presents, but he takes each of them outside to name a one of the stars in the night sky as their own. However, ultimately, the children must place themselves in reality.

Ten years on and off the NYT Bestseller list, 3 million copies sold, and only 2 stars. What gives? 
 I think The Glass Castle, and its success, say too many bad things about our publishing industry and our culture at large. 
 Memoir authors routinely sell their families down the river for fame and fortune. Because, as The Glass Castle illustrates, we have learned--through psychobabble and liberal self-involvement--to demean, devalue, and (in the case of Walls's Mom) starve and freeze our family. 
 Much more at my book blog https://2manbookclub.wordpress.com/20...

enjoyed as an audiobook; touching but not a self pitying look a growing up in an incredibly dysfunctional family.

God! Some people should just get sterilized BEFORE they have kids ...

A dispassionate look at the trials of a neglected childhood. With such an upbringing I don't understand the author's choice to convey such serious and heartbreaking matters so evenly. To convey numbness? Is this writing style commenting about how her upbringing left her feeling about it? Maybe. But I can't shake the feeling that she was convinced to write about her past, yet was reluctant to do so, so she gives the barest of stories with little reflection or hints about how she coped/felt about/reconciled/grew from her early family life. While there was a bit of plot trajectory via the main character perpetually sculpting plans for a 'way out', I felt for the most part like I was reading a laundry list of general awfulness. And then it was done. I don't understand why she wrote this book.

I can't exactly say I liked this book, but it kept me glued to its pages. Parts felt a little "and then this happened,and then that happened, and then and then and then," but this is a minor complaint. 
 Anyone who thinks they had a tough childhood might do some rethinking after reading this...
This is another book that I really liked it made me laugh out loud probably when I should not have, it was heart breaking, but well worth reading.

Wow. Reading this book brought on a wide range of emotions, but most noticeably, it felt EXACTLY like watching an episode of Hoarders: horrifying, shocking, and with a sense of "how can this go on and no one does anything about it??" I got so frustrated with Rex and Rose Mary Walls I wanted to scream. Having a five-month-old son did not make me any more sympathetic, because it just intensified my horror at the things they allowed (or sometimes encouraged) their children to do. Also, their constant lies and whacked perspective on things drove me up a wall. As a parent, the idea that someone would keep a diamond ring to "boost their self-esteem" rather than buy food or clothes for their children is abhorrent. I just could not muster sympathy for these people. 
 What amazed me most of all was that their daughter wrote this book with a great deal of sympathy, and with great respect for the positive qualities her parents did have. She learned a great deal from her parents, who were both avid readers and intelligent people with great understanding of science, the arts, and nature... unfortunately there was no sense tempering their behavior. 
 I'd definitely recommend this book because it's enthralling. But it's also very, very frustrating. (I'd also recommend reading the companion semi-novel about Walls' grandmother, Half-Broke Horses.)
Fantastic! What the author overcame in her childhood and never complained about is amazing. I don't think i could've done the same! I heard they are making this into a movie
American memoir....recent/current US....unconventional family life with parents unmotivated to provide financially. No pity, just how it was.

I finished this memoir, and felt that books were ruined for me for awhile - I couldn't bear to pick up something new to read for a few days. I'd heard how wonderful THE GLASS CASTLE was ever since it came out in hardcover, but it took me awhile to pick it up. When I finally did pick it up, I was hooked from the first page: Walls is a fantastic storyteller. She is able to tell the story of her childhood, of her neglectful and abusive parents, without bitterness and anger. In fact, her recollections are often told with humor, and wonder, and even with love. Her family's "skedaddles" across the country can seem like adventures, and not just flights from the government or people to whom they owe money. Walls' story is both heartbreaking and compelling, and a testimony to the strength of the human spirit. A beautifully written memoir.

Like 
 I understood J's commitment to her father never doing wrong. However, I couldn't help but hate him after he whipped her with his belt just because her mom didn't like the way her daughter was talking to her. He made it known that J was his favorite child & I think he loved her more than he did his wife, but I couldn't forgive him for the whipping. Why start acting like a father at that point? I wonder if maybe the parents were genius IQs? Could that explain their eccentric & depressing tendencies? Or maybe they had some sort of mental health issue? Nevertheless, this story was riveting & I couldn't put it down. Hard to believe people grow up like J & still manage to live a good life.

I enjoyed this book. It was an interesting and often heartbreaking memoir. Many love this book. I didn't love it as it seemed that the writer kept the reader at an arm's length from her experience. Maybe she had to. Some of the book is funny, quirky, and the author chronicles pieces of her life with tales of her childhood and the absolutely crazy things she experienced without one bit of self pity. There is also little vulnerability which was a draw back for me. It was well written and the characters so well recreated on the page.
What a family! What a life! Gripping.

I hated this book so much. I'm not sure if I've read (or rather listened to) about such grotesque villains as Walls's parents and at the same time as horrified as I was by their behavior I am nearly equally horrified by Walls's defense of it. I realize that these types of memoirs are meant to inspire or demonstrate how the author overcame such obstacles to become a success, but the reality is that the cases like Jeannette are the exception and not the rule - they are few and far between. If not physical, the psychological damage that such "parents" inflict on their children is tremendous to overcome in order to grow into functioning adults. The parents constant refusal to be employed and take care of their own children while at the same time denying access to public assistance and labeling it as "bohemian" or "alternative" is vilely inaccurate. I literally screamed in anger when the relentlessly selfish mother decided to keep a 2 carat diamond ring over putting food on the table for her four children who were eating out of the trash and the one selfless thing that the father does by giving Jeanette money so she can continue college is practically erased by all of his drunkenness, violence, and nearly prostituting his own daughter. And while Jeannette and most of her sibs triumphed over their nightmarish upbringing, the reader can't help but notice that the youngest child, Maureen winds up stabbing her mother and going to a mental hospital before dropping out of contact with her family. 
 I also did not care for the way Jeannette Walls read her own memoir (her voice or inflection would get on my nerves), nor her writing style, too many sentences started off with "one day," making timelines a little difficult to understand.
I think it should have been short story rather than a book. It was quite repetitive in the squalor descriptions and the dads drinking. Then the last hundreds pages or so, were brilliant.

I did not enjoy this book, though so many others seem to love it. I can't for the life of me see the point of it--why did the author choose to write it? She told her autobiographical story with little to no emotion. The style was very journalistic and detached. She did not necessarily blame her parents for her childhood--she seemed to accept it. So the only conclusion I can come to is that she wrote this simply to make money or capitalize on it. Good for her, I guess. I did listen to the audio book in its entirety. There were some interesting parts to it and it moved pretty quickly. I never felt like I didn't want to finish it. But when I was finally done I thought, "ok, so what was the point of that?" 
 I think a better story would've been from her sister's point of view or more details around how her sister was impacted by her parents. How had her sister been negatively effected by her childhood? That would have been more interesting to me, and I think also more helpful for readers if the ultimate goal was to educate people on this. But again, the only goal I can see--other than to publicly embarrass her parents, if that's possible--is to make a buck. I'd give it 2.5 stars if I could, it was only average. 
 There are so many good memoirs out there. If you want to read a true story of abuse and triumph, I would suggest Dave Pelzer's books, or Sickened.
I loved this book. It is really scary that it was based on actual experience. I highly recommend.

Wow. 
 That story was out of control. At fist I was just so floored by the never-ending tragedies that seemed to befall her family. And then I got mad. I tried to give her parents a LOT of leeway in the beginning. I didn't want to label them "bad parents" but instead tried to really think of them as eccentric and free-spirited. But after a certain point, I really just couldn't do it anymore. They were absolutely horrid parents. My parents are fairly eccentric. Her parents were downright neglectful and abusive. And maybe my upbringing had something to do with the way I felt about her parents. My parents have always been a little on the weird side, and our family did a lot of things differently than other people. But my parents were still parents. My mom was also an artist, like Jeannette's, but unlike Jeannette's she realized that being a starving artist wasn't good for her family, and whether it was her life's dream to be an art teacher she did it because her family needed to eat (and have clothes, books, etc.). She committed to being a parent. Jeannette's mom just wanted to cry and moan about life's injustices and in the process, made her children suffer. It was just appalling. Her father was also appalling, but I think for a number of reasons I am less "shocked" by this. First of all, he's an alcoholic. Not that being an alcoholic is an excuse to be a crappy dad, but at least I can recognize that he has a disease. Secondly, he's a dad. Again, that's not an excuse to be a terrible parent, but it's less surprising when dads fall down on the job. When a mom falls down on the job it's pretty big. When my parents divorced and we lived with our dad it was pretty abnormal, and our mom was still involved with us, we just didn't live with her. So to have a mom who so clearly sucked at all things mom was pretty alarming. I was thinking about this after I finished the book and I was wondering if Jeannette's mom has an undiagnosed mental health condition. This is the only reason I can even begin to understand as to why she would behave the way she did. But maybe that's just me trying to come up with an excuse for her (like her father's disease). When Maureen loses it at the end it made me wonder if there was a history of mental illness in the family and maybe her mother was mentally ill as well. 
 Overall I liked the story, but I'm not sure if I want to read another book by Jeannette Walls. At least if it has to do with her family, and especially any more stories from her childhood. This book seriously disturbed me. I woke up with bad dreams three different times last night. I hate the thought of children being abused and neglected. It makes me so sad. If you can get past the horrible neglect and abuse I would very much recommend this book.
From this book I learned that even if you're the poorest and most free-spirited parents around your kids can still grow up to be materialistic Manhattan socialites.

i didn't see this as an inspiring book like others did.. As a child i witnessed horrific child abuse and neglect of a friend of mine and this book was almost her story. The parents in this book are not inspirational, eccentric or unique. They were abusive, selfish and neglectful. Their daughter did not 'overcome' hardship even though she became a celebrated journalist.. The truth is this type of abuse is not overcome and people live with those scars the rest of their lives.. I don't care how different parenting people have but letting your kids feed on butter out of desperation and allowing sexual abuse of your own child is child abuse no matter how open your interpretation of parenting is.

I cannot comprehend how this book can get so many raving reviews or why some people I know told me how much they love it. Maybe, they all read a different book? I kept on coming back to read reviews while trying to make it through the book .. wondering if maybe it does change or makes it all worthwhile in the end. It does not. 
 I'm at a loss how to even review the book. 
 On the good side, the writing wasn't terrible. It also wasn't great, but I've seen worse. 
 It's basically a memoir focusing on the crazy (and completely abusive) childhood of the author. Every chapter contains description of either neglect or physical, emotional and sexual abuse and here and there, some moments of cruelty toward animals. And, it's written in a way that excuses all that because in the end, it's all good for something? I found it awful to read and not in the sense of heartbreaking. I think it's the writing style of the author who comes across quite narcissistic the way she presents herself .. especially in her older years. In the end, I'm having a hard time relating to her or even believing anything she writes (and I'm not saying it isn't true, it's just written so arrogantly). Ugh. I have to honestly say that I hated this book and feel like reading it was a complete waste of time.

I started this book last winter on the recommendation of my daughter. I put it down. So depressing. Then towrd the end of school, two of my colleagues were discussing the book. I picked it up again and could not put it down. Depressing? Yes. Walls perserverence through such dysfunction is the glimmer of hope.

Memoir of a girl growing up with transient parents who are neglectful and abusive. Pretty good read. It grabs you right in the beginning, the girl telling the story, Janette, starts where she is three years old, her mother is in the other room painting pictures while Janette is boiling hot dogs when she sets her dress on fire receiving third degree burns and has a long hospital stay.

Sunt zile in care ei nu au ce sa manance sau unde sa stea, cand tremura de frig si de foame, insa speranta rasare cand isi dau seama cat de puternica este legatura dintre ei. It's been months since I read this book, and I still find myself thinking of it. Absolutely read it. Beautiful, disturbing, and gorgeously written.
ok, tried this. couldn't go on much past chapter 5. Depressing and abrasive. don't waste your time.
Wow. I am a good parent:)

I know this is an incredibly popular book, and it came out at the height of the memoir frenzy...but more than anything, it just made me anxious. Between the terrible conditions and near catastrophes (or sometimes just catastrophes), and Ms. Wall's flat writing, I mostly wanted to avoid this book. 
 I think all memoirs are (at least) tinged with fiction and of course a compelling story has to be told, but some of Ms. Wall's recollections seemed like tall tales...and of course everything just works out in the end. 
 Ultimately this was a low stakes read that I could pick up and put down. I originally picked it up because I thought I'd want to see the movie, but I think I'll pass.
good book. Screwed up family. Strong children. Who did you have less sympathy for, the mom or the dad?

This was a fascinating story, but the author's writing style was too detached for it to be really enjoyable for me. She has quite a story to tell but I thought it could be much more gripping and interesting to read.

I'm glad that I read this book (almost finished) but I wonder what's the point? It's basically a big list of really awful experiences all strung together.... the redeeming concept is just that Walls overcame all those experiences-- proved by the first chapter and maybe again at the end but I haven't gotten there yet... 
 (update) I finished to book and think it's amazing how successful Jeanette became... however it's still a list of awful childhood experiences... almost like reading about poverty in another country b/c I didn't know people in the US ever could live this way..

I had to read this for the worst class I've ever taken, which might affect my rating. I feel like this is of the Augusten Burroughs school of fucked up childhood memoirs. It's a madcap romp of sexual and emotional abuse and mental illness and OH! How chipper I am! 
 I don't know why I react so negatively to these, but man, do not like.

I spent the entire book going "Why isn't someone removing these children from the home?" That sentiment ruined the book for me. I have zero tolerance for people not caring for their children. 
 I also didn't like that after all she went through, she grew up to become a gossip columnist, the scourge of the journalistic world, in my opinion.

book_b.title: The Catcher in the Rye
book_b.user_review:
A few spoilers and reader's opinions ahead.... 
 Now, I don't agree with the banning of this book, or any book at all, but with the references to underage drinking, prostitution and rape I can understand why parents of middle school age kids wouldn't be too happy about their children reading this before they've had a chance to speak with them about it. I don't believe banning a book solves anything. In fact, the fastest way to get someone to do something is to tell them they can't. Kids are notorious for participating in the old reverse psychology thing. 
 Instead of banning books I think we should let kids read what they want but with the clear stipulation that whatever they want to read the parents will read as well and then, afterwards, a discussion could be had where everyone's questions are answered and fears put to rest. I was lucky enough to grow up with a bookworm grandmother who was more than happy to let me read what I wanted and wanted to read whatever I was reading and she always told me I could talk with her about whatever I read in a book. 
 But, I realize not everyone has adults like that growing up. But, just because I don't believe in banning books doesn't stop some books from just being bad. Of course, 'good' or 'bad' is a personal decision when it comes to reading, but for me "The Catcher In The Rye" is a pretty crappy book. It wasn't bad due to the content or themes, it was bad due to the writing itself. The plot pretty much went nowhere, the story was mediocre and the characters were all mostly one-decisional in my opinion. Including special snowflake Holden, who seemed to regard himself as misunderstood and too good for anything throughout much of the book. There were a few vague references to sexual assault as well and in both instances Holden seemed to regard the act of rape as an inconvenience or an annoyance more than anything else. In one part he tells the reader about a double date he went on in which he could hear the girl from the other couple fending off the unwanted advances of her date from the back seat of their car and Holden remarked that the experience was 'embarrassing'. 
 Then there was another scene where he reminisces about past close-encounters with sex and how it was never the right time or place and that his dates would often ask him to stop but that later on he'd wish he hadn't. So, in other words, Holden regrets not becoming a teenage rapist. Jesus H. Christ. 
 For all the hype of this classic I was expecting a lot more. Basically what I got out of it was "upper middle class teenager feels that he is special snowflake and misunderstood and decides to give up when things aren't going his way and run away from his problems and consequences." Why didn't he just go home and face the music? It would have been hard but a lot better than running away and causing the problem to snowball out of control due to avoidance and procrastination. But, I guess that's part of being a teen; when seemingly insignificant issues to adults can be world-enders to teens. 
 Anyway, I guess we should just be happy these days, full of computers and video games, when kids actually want to read a book, no matter what our own opinions on said book might be.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Let me start off by saying that I love books about troubled people, especially if they feel like they are written by the main character and have a distinct voice. I love them. 
 BUT: 
 I decided to read The Catcher in the Rye because it seems to be one of those "essential" reads, and about 13% through I realized why it is essential. People either love this book or despise it, which I think is the reason it's so important. Holden is either relatable or he isn't, and I cannot relate to him whatsoever. 
 The thing is, I probably would have loved this book if I would have read it when I was thirteen, still painting my eyelids red and putting the letter "x" on either side of every username, but right now, at the tail end of age twenty, I absolutely could not stand it. Even the rebellious thirteen-year-old in me wanted to smack the hell out of Holden. In my opinion, he wasn't even a well-rounded character, because he had absolutely zero likable characteristics and that makes for a very flat characterization. 
 I asked my boyfriend a little ways into the novel if Holden ever shoots somebody or something interesting like that happens because I found myself completely bored with the monotony of his vapid existence. I'm fine with annoying characters like him if they have some sort of eye-opening experience or at least one likable quality, but he lacks any of that. There weren't even secondary characters that were at least mildly interesting. 
 Needless to say, I'm going to spend my time reading about worthwhile protagonists (who do not have catchphrases that make me want to knock them out) rather than repetitive, annoying, pointless, unchanging ones like Holden Caulfield. 
 He's got a great name, though.

My teacher actually managed to convince me it deserved more than 1 measly star - so 2, but with a lot of reservations. 
 BONUS TIME! 
 Counting of catch phrases! 
 And all - 338 times. 
 Goddam - 237 times. 
 Killed me/her/him - 50 times. 
 Phony - 45 times. 
 Hate/drive him crazy/pisses him off - 51 times. 
 Boy - 74 times. 
 Repetitive? It is repetitive, it really is, if you want to know the truth.
I think I'm the only person I know who hated this book, found it incredibly overrated....

I do not and probably wont ever understand what makes this such an American classic. I don't even know why they teach it in schools because you can't even learn a lesson other than "Gosh nobody likes an over-dramatic spoiled brat who thinks they have the worst life ever." Thank goodness its a short book because if it were any longer I probably wouldn't have been able to finish it.
Augh - What are people thinking? This was a horrible book. I felt like I was reading some very very bad high school writing project. No story, no point, bad grammar. A total waste of time.

What's all the hubub, Bub? Maybe it's a coming-of-age thing from '60s nostalgia of a time past, but I don't get it. Holden was annoying, but it was not just that. I expected so much more, and sometimes hyped expectations are disappointing. Maybe I should have read it earlier in my life to appreciate the angst. 
 I need to re-approach this book some other time in hopes my disappointment was about timing.
Hated this book! Is there even a storyline? I kept waiting for it to come to life, but it never did.

I don't like this book for two reasons. 1. Holden is a whiny, obnoxious, self-centered baby and I find reading about him unpleasant. 2. I don't like the style of Salinger's writing. 
 In high school this was one book I refused to read. I had to teach it a few years ago, and my students had the same reaction to it that I did.

I don't know if it holds up when you're an adult, but it's rather life-changing to read as a teen or college student. Salinger's profane Holden Caufield was the first kid of his kind I'd ever experienced on the page, then I looked around and saw dozens of him in the hallways at school.

I had read this book back in High School. And then Promptly for got it. All that crap on the cover about you may like it. you may hate it, but you will never forget this book. Not true!I fogot it bigtime. Over the holidays I was digging in my son-in-laws library and thought I have heard of this book pick it and it suck worse the second time. Catcher in the rye is for gotten forever this time.
Great to read as a teenager but loses a lot when read from the point of view of an adult. It comes off as pretentious and unfocused.

I've been reading this book for like 6 months now. Why? because I couldn't seem to bring myself to endure the annoyance that is Holden Caulfield. Everything he says makes you wanna either kill yourself or find a way to get through the pages and stab Holden repeatedly till he shuts up. Never had I been so incredibly bored and irritated whilst reading a book as I was during this one. I wanted it to end so badly. 
 I skipped some pages and the damn thing wouldn't end. 
 All the time I kept saying 'what's so special about Holden? Why is he deemed a god amongst teens and even adults? Why is it a literary masterpiece? Nothing happens. Absolutely nothing! Holden narrates his disturbed and boring life using the same stupid curse words and lame catchphrases all through his provocative jaunt. The only redeemable thing about Holden is his relationship with his little sister. And guess what? We don't get a whiff of that until the last few pages of this travesty. Too late J.D. You failed miserably in demonstrating something of value or even entertainment. I don't recommend this book to anyone, at all. 
 One more thing, Holden claims that everyone is phony, when he himself is the biggest phony in the world.
I really hated the protagonist, the story dragged on and on. I don't even remember the point of the story. I don't see what the big deal is with this book, it made zero impression on me.
I just finished reading this book in class, I wish I could say I enjoyed this book but to be honest it was a bit of a bore. I would not read this book again, but if I had to I would think about it.
Interesting story!

One of my favorite books of all time. My boyfriend and I both reread this book often - the pages are all worn from use. I love this book for the things J.D. Salinger chooses to leave to the imagination as much as for what he chooses to include. Really lovely book.

Didn't get what all the hype is about..
I hate Holden Caulfield. The book isn't that bad, if the main character weren't so damn unsympathetic.
Holden - the only sane one but not so perceived in the beginning
I read this when I as 15. Now at 63 I see it a very dated book.

(1.5-2) Huh. Not what I expected; I'm glad I read it, because it's a classic and now I can say I've read it. haha. But I didn't really care for Holden or any of the characters. Phoebe was alright. This book was nothing like I thought it was going to be. I didn't like it, I found it depressing.

One of the few books I have read twice
This was the most overrated book I ever have had the misfortune of reading.
if i wanted to hear a white boy constantly complain about nothing, i'd just go talk to one
Much ado about nothing!

Rating: 2.5 
 I did like it towards the middle but I couldn't really handle reading Holden's dialog the whole time. Most of the time I just wanted to grab him by the collar and yell in his face because how dumb he was acting. The ending made sense but as it was only 1 1/2 pages long, the resolve I wanted wasn't there. It wasn't a bad book but it isn't a book I would necessarily recommend to other people.

I can't believe this book is on the High School English reading list! I never got to read it in my high school years so I picked it up because it had recently been banned from the HS reading lists and I wanted to see what all the hub-bub was about. I'm sorry, but there was NO POINT to this book at all. It was just one big ramble about some kid that gets kicked out of school and doesn't want to tell his parents because it was like his 3rd strike or something and if he ever got kicked out again he was going to have to pay a heavy price, something down those lines. So he thinks he'll go stay with his brother in California. From there we follow him around - inside his head - so to speak - trying to get to his brother but he sort of finds other things more interesting. For instance, he meets this girl and he wants to kiss her and I can't remember if he gets the kiss or not but the build was pretty lame. There was no moral to this story at all. If there was? Well. I missed it.

It's bad but I seem to find this a recurring problem when it comes to certain 'classics' at the moment. I just don't get it. What was the point of that whole story? If it can even be called a story. There was no beginning. No middle. No end. All it was about was a stupid 16 year old boy who didnt appreciate what he'd got running around New York after getting kicked out of school. The writing style reminded me too much of a clockwork orange. Heavily disappointed with this!

I'm a phony. Holden Caulfield is a whiny little wanker. 
 Most painful book a teacher ever made me read.

I actually didn't finish this one which is a rarity for me. Clearly I'm in the minority on this one. I forced myself to try the first 50 pages then just said enough is enough. Not for me. I couldn't stand the main character (how does one like a book if you don't like the mc at least a little bit?), found it extremely repetitive and poorly written. I'm stumped why this is a "classic" and adored by so many. Perhaps I'm missing something.

There were definitely thought-provoking insights through the novel; some I got. I really did. But I kept waiting for something interesting to happen. Nothing ever did. It was a quick read that after reading I though "well um...huh." and put it away. Not a 'life changing' novel for me. Call me crazy.
I'd really like to punch Holden. But overall it was a pretty enjoyable book and I laughed a few times.

"I don't understand boring guys. I really don't." -says guy in story about nothing 
 Oh lord... I liked this book way better before actually reading it. I used to work at Chapters and could recommend so many titles when people mentioned this one. Needless to say, I had to see what the fuss was about. 
 ...And now I wish I hadn't. 
 K, I understand that sexism was common when this book was published, but that does not mean I have to tolerate it. Then it was bordering onto homophobia and xenophobia... 
 Plus Holden was whiny and manipulative. There was nothing charming in his compulsive lies. If relating with him is what it takes to enjoy this book, then I'm perfectly happy to be the odd one out. 
 That's not even the worst of it. The repetition drove me 
 INSANE! 
 You could cut this book nearly in half if we edited it out. It got so ridiculous that felt like reading a picture book. Can I put this on my Middle Grade shelf? 
 Seriously, just read this: 
 "She'd hand in her basket and then go someplace swanky for lunch. That's what I liked about those nuns. You could tell, for one thing, that they never went anywhere swanky for lunch. It made me so damn sad when I thought about it, their never going anywhere swanky for lunch or anything. I knew it wasn't too important, but it made me sad anyway." 
 The only reason I still appreciate this book is because it's inspired some good books. But it's also inspired some super dry and plot-less stories too. 
 "He had one of these very raspy voices, and he never stopped talking, practically. He never stopped talking, and what was awful was, he never said anything you wanted to hear in the first place." -hypocritical main character who can turn one sentence into five 
 ...I rest my case.
Must read for every teenager

READ FOR A VERY LATE #BookBuddyAThon 
 Ok, this book was weird. 
 The main character Holden Caulfield gave me Percy Jackson from the PJO series and Charlie from The Perks of Being a Wallflower, vibes. 
 This book was the perfect size, and fast-paced. 
 J.D. Salinger's writing-style was a little bit familiar and he filled the pages with beautiful metaphors about life. My favorite one was the one who gave this book its title (the one from the poem).

ugh. was that language necessary? the conversations in this book consist in someone saying "god damn!" and being answered with "god damn!". also, whats that "youre depressing me" thing? according to this book, being annoyed equals "getting depressed", being mad equals "getting depressed". i hated it.
Meh.
Just NO. Annoying kid. Maybe I just read it too late

I had a strange high school experience where I somehow didn't read all the required reading that most of my friends had. 
 I had never read any of Salingers novels and this one being so controversial and all, I thought I'd give it a shot. 
 At first, I didn't like it. Holden, the main character, is your typical teenager...self righteous and self involved...to be fair, I don't really like teenagers at this point in my life. the more I read however, the more I enjoyed it. By the end, I felt a strong connection towards him and was able to put aside my own biase surrounding my preconceived notions and enjoy the story. At points, I found myself saying, one more chapter...just one more chapter before bed. 
 His deep connection towards his siblings, his love for them and his own self worth drew me in and I was able to understand him in his own lost ways with school, friends...life. 
 it's a quick little read and I would strongly recommend it to anyone who has not read it simply for the fact that it created such a stir when published (I mean, look what we put on tv these days and how widely that is recieved). 
 I liked it. 
 the end.

It was kind of hard to read about this kid's downward spiral, but at the same time I can relate to totally losing control of your life for a couple of days at a time, and in that sense it was comforting. I'm sure there's a lot more to this than I took out of it, and I would like to read it again someday, and look at some criticism and some interpretations of the text. But sometimes it's nice to not think like an English major and just read something and get what I get out of it, no matter how little.

reference_books.review_text:
Reading this book is like walking through ankle-deep water, expecting to hit the deep side of the pool at any moment. There is no depth here. 
 The characters are all one-note (and rather inauthentic, if I may say so). Madame Mallory is probably the most interesting character in the book and she is shoved out of the story halfway through the book only to die of old age offstage after being mentioned a handful more times . What a waste. 
 I imagine the character of Hassan goes through life without any serious problems (even a terrible accident that burns much of his skin is never mentioned again after a brief rest to recover ) and appears to lead a charmed life to prove some sort of point about destiny or some such. In the second half of the book, we spend barely a chapter with Hassan in his thirties and then suddenly we've skipped a decade and he's in his forties, only to skip again shortly after. 
 Hassan's father is probably the most exaggerated (and I'll be honest, a bit offensive) caricature of an Indian man in a country where he does not speak the language. The beginning of the book is set in what is essentially a slum in India (as is fashionable, apparently), complete with descriptions of children shitting on the side of the road and religious violence. 
 The whole thing is riddled with no depth, no real hardships for any of the characters, conveniently large amounts of cash when required by the characters, etc. I found the whole thing really silly and unsatisfying.

reference_books.title: Lumberjanes, Vol. 1: Beware the Kitten Holy
reference_books.review_text:
I was expecting something along the lines of Rat Queens here: a bunch of (adult) women who are ok with swearing and kicking ass stumbling into interesting adventures. Can you blame me for reading the title Lumberjanes and expecting the story of expectorating women in the woods with axes? Turns out the Lumberjanes are basically the equivalent of the girl scouts, but the squeaky clean rebels of that world. This results in them being daring enough to sneak out of their cabins at night to follow a mysterious bear-woman because curiosity, but not daring enough to actually swear when in danger, or cast off their babysitter-esque cabin leader lady. 
 A bit disappointing, I must say, but probably well suited for younger readers.

reference_books.title: Into the Wild
reference_books.review_text:
I'm sure some would find this book a fascinating account of a young man with wanderlust. I found it dull, and possibly better suited to an article. 
 Chris McCandless wants to live off the land in Alaska. He finishes college, engineers a situation where he disappears shortly after graduating without informing any of his family. He bizarrely chooses to use the name Alexander Supertramp on his travels and proceeds to hitchhike to Alaska in complete ignorance of basic preparations and lacking any material possessions (including and up to clothes to keep warm in Alaska, although he does carry a 25 pound bag of rice with him). 
 The author bombards you with stories of Alex/Chris as told by people he encountered (and manage to unanimously charm). I felt there would be more dramatic tension in the book is Alex's fate is not revealed very early in the book. 
 The reason I feel this book should have been an article is that the writer clearly runs out accounts of Alex/Chris' travels shortly and switches focus midway through the book to some other well-known young men who disappeared into the wilderness for a temporary or permanent time. Ironically, the author's own account of his interest in mountain climbing and one particular mountain in his youth is more interesting that the tale of Alex/Chris's arrogance and ignorance (and pretentious ideas). 
 I have no idea why anyone would enjoy this book. It is competently written in the factual manner of a seasoned journalist, but goes on too long and has an uninteresting subject. It is also clear that the writer semi-idolizes Alex/Chris, which is annoying to anyone with a modicum of good sense.

reference_books.title: The Wise Man's Fear (The Kingkiller Chronicle, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I love this series, and especially this installment, since we move beyond just introducing Kvote and make our way to the edges of the empire and meet some very interesting new people along the way (the Adem are my favorite). Very enthusiastic thumbs up for this series and cannot wait for the third and final installment. 
 Update: The Felurian part is a bit dull but still five stars. I really enjoyed that we move far from the established setting of the University and hear about the far reaches of this fantastic world. I can't wait for the final installment, but these books, like all good fantasy, are so rich that everytime I re-read them, I spot yet another interesting bit that fits in with my theory about what finally happens. Highly recommended!

reference_books.title: World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War
reference_books.review_text: Started off a bit oddly, with a disjointed narrative made up of many stories, but the longer you read, the more the various threads form a rich (and enjoyable) tapestry telling the tale of humans defeating the zombies.

reference_books.title: Ghost World
reference_books.review_text:
I don't "get" this. I mean, I understand what it is: two girls fresh out of high school while away their days taking (figurative) dumps on everything. Things are either generically lame or incredibly lame, at which point they become cool again until they become lame again. Everyone knows people like this, sure. What I don't get is why anyone would want to spend an entire graphic novel reading the inane thoughts of people like these. I suppose it may be more palatable to me in parts, as the comics were originally released rather than in one condensed setting. 
 Yeah, I don't really get why this is so popular. I give it two stars for an accurate representation of that obnoxious type of person (or depending on who you are, that phase of your life). I plowed on in the hope of a satisfying conclusion of some sort, but this never materialized either.

reference_books.title: Black Hole
reference_books.review_text:
I didn't enjoy this at all. 
 This was too thin on plot for me. It seemed that there was some thin narrative thread between hallucinations, dreams, memories, and random sex scenes with tails and mouths growing out of necks. I just don't get it, I'm afraid. 
 The art was also a wash for me. I don't know what it is but the character style is so androgynous that I have trouble recognizing who it is the narrative is following when it suddenly shifts. 
 I couldn't wait to get this done and over with to be able to say that I gave it a chance because there was nothing here for me at all.

reference_books.title: I Am Not A Serial Killer (John Cleaver, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
John Wayne Cleaver very much reminds me of a 15 year old Dexter Morgan. The only difference between the two is that John Wayne Cleaver is desperately trying to avoid his darker impulses while Dexter takes care to regulate and channel them according to a code. 
 I would have given this book four stars save for the excellent characterization of a character who should, by all accounts, be quite unlikeable. I actually find his struggle to suppress his darker impulses quite endearing. I would also have preferred it if this book had not taken the supernatural route for the killer, but this is another way it differs from Dexter, which is very much grounded in a non supernatural reality. 
 I would recommend this book for anyone interested in a good (fairly short) read and also anyone who enjoys the subject matter of the TV show Dexter.

reference_books.title: A Quest of Heroes (The Sorcerer's Ring, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Good things about this book: 
 1. The plot is interesting and moves forward at a fast pace. 
 Bad things about this book: 
 1. The plot can be a little contrived at times and a bit predictable if you have read any fantasy books before. 
 2. Holy shit, does this book need the services of a decent editor. Some instances of modern words pulled me right out of the story, such as "crap" (noun) and some instances of missing words refused to parse ("in that way she was like her (missing word brother) Roderick"). The author seems to be enamoured of certain one word summaries of characters to create a more vivid picture in the reader's mind. In one instance, slovenly is used so many times in a single paragraph to refer to a shady merchant that I found myself facepalming. 
 3. Characters. The characters are archetypes of fantasy. The good and benevolent (and handsome) King has multiple children who may inherit: an illegitimate eldest son (another very good looking young man) who is described tediously frequently as the finest man I have ever known, the schrewd, manipulative and scheming second son (predictably his features resemble those of a weasel) who expects to inherit but is not shrewd and clever enough to hide his shrewd and manipulative nature from anyone (he is also gay, of course), the beautiful and wilful younger daughter of the King (we all know where this is going) and the youngest son who immediately befriends a common boy. I've deliberately left out an elder daughter who is only used as a plot point because her marriage kicks off the exciting events, and a drunkard lout son who we never understand anything about except that he is unpleasant. 
 4. The animals. In the real world if you find a random animal or one is gifted to you as a pet, you do not "form a deep and immediate spiritual bond" with the creature. In this universe, apparently, you can only stumble across animals that want to kill you or ones that want to form a spiritual bond with you. Oh, and all animals are apparently rare, except chooks and boars. 
 5. Last but not least: our hero, Thor. I'll assume I don't need to explain why naming your main character Thor is mildly silly. Thor is what I have come to recognize in fantasy novels as the "Fine Young Man" archetype. Everyone he meets will think he is a fine young man and embodies all the good qualities necessary for the situation. He will prove himself bold and loyal in combat situations, having a keen eye to foil an assassination attempt when no other (more capable) person in the group notices said assassin, he is appropriately enigmatic and handsome so as to capture the eye of the predictably interested princess, he has a mysterious gift that allows him to save the life of a knight and so the King adopts him (WTF? Will get to this later), he is sufficiently honorable to protest keenly when steered towards excessive drink and prostitutes, etc. It seems the hero can do no wrong, aside from constantly wondering why the rest of his comrades in the training program hate him. Here's a hint: you did not get selected and then essentially shoved your way in and got admission by unfair means. 
 5. Convenient but nonsensical plot points. Some really inorganic developments in the plot (which make sense only because in typical fantasy fashion, you know what should be coming up next) happen. Thor takes immediate liking to no less than ten people in this book. This is possible because handsome people in this world are always good and anyone described as an unfavorable animal (weasely, as in the case of the manipulative prince) or evil-looking (I shit you not, people are described as "evil-looking") are immediately identified as villains. There is a sword in the stone (very original) and only people from the King's line of descendants can try to lift it. This... makes no sense but it explains why it may be necessary for the King to randomly decide to adopt Thor. Thor also has prophetic (and strangely literal) dreams, which serve as convenient reasons for him to should about danger, have nobody believe him and then be vindicated later on. 
 Summary: The story, despite some silliness, kept me engaged. Perhaps a more seasoned fantasy reader would have flung the book away by now, but I kept going so I will read the next one in the series. However, I wonder why a writer who has published fourteen books in this series so far never thought to go back and edit the earlier ones or at least fix the very obvious problems.

book_a.title: The Lovely Bones
book_a.user_review:
I was directed to this after reading The Time Traveler's Wife, the back cover of which contained an enthusiastic quotation from someone calling it "the new The Lovely Bones...". Like a trusting fool, I immediately purchased the book and attempted to read it. 
 Based on my distaste and the general public's enthusiastic embracing of this book, I had assumed my taste was simply off. Reading other, far more eloquent rants about why this book was simply not good has made me feel better, hence I happily banish this to the depths of my "Will never recommend to anyone" pile.

sample_reviews.review_text: I think the reason I gave this three stars is my own visceral reaction to the book. I think I had such difficulty with it because I have a thirteen year old daughter. Then, the POV was sort of distracting to me. It was an effort in sustained suspension of disbelieve through out the entire novel for me.

I read this standing up at Wal-Mart. Not a scintillating read. Did not really hold my attention. Characters seemed based on other characters. Having an admittedly not especially bright little girl as the first-person narrator did not seem to work out well. Too much "What Dreams May Come"-ish (I mean the movie, did not read that book) blurry nonsensical wish-fulfillment crap. And how often is a rapist and murderer a boring character? :/
