I hated this book.

It took me a little while to get into this book, but once I did it was fascinating. Narrated from such a unique viewpoint. I can see why it was made into a movie, it reads very much like a movie. Absolutely amazing!

I would actually give this 3 1/2 stars and maybe 4, because I honestly couldn't put this book down. I think I gave it 3 because I like happy endings and this book started out with an unhappy ending so it was hard for me to read. The author did a really good job with the characters and their emotions, although there was a scene in the book that I thought "Really? She chose that to be her wish?" and when you read it, you'll probably understand what I mean!
This book was so memorable that I can't even remember reading it although I know I have. That says it all. Sentimental twaddle..... I won't be seeing the movie.

When I picked up this book a few years ago, I'd heard only good things about it and, as such, didn't even fathom that I would dislike it. Oh, how ill-prepared I was. 
 Now, it has been years since I read this and I am nowhere near willing to pick it up again, so I apologize for not going into specifics. The writing did nothing for me. I could tell the author was going for something pretty and poetic with her descriptions, but often, it just came across nonsensical. Even though I was privy to Susie's most intimate thoughts, I found myself uncaring towards her. She didn't hook me, she didn't interest me, and that is the kiss of death for a book. I didn't care about Susie, I didn't care about what she was doing. The supporting characters fell flat to me as well, and, without any interest in any of the characters, I just could not appreciate the plot. I remember forcing myself to finish this, thinking that it must get better, there must be a reason for such high praise. Sadly, it seems that this book just wasn't for me.

Could not finish. The story idea was a good one but it was not well executed. The characters were hard to like and the plot was dragging and never got interesting. The writing, well, I have seen much better. I tired and I tried to finish but there was nothing holding me in the book: the language, the characters, nor the plot.
I just really liked the writing style - and the suspense in place where, even though you know what happened to her, you're kept turning pages to see if and when other people might learn that.
It was fine and kind of creepy. But I just can't get over the feeling that a ghost possessing someone's body and having sex with that body feels kind of rape-y. And that's it.
Very different - but interesting

I was really enjoying this book during the first several chapters. It wasn't until about 3/4 of the way through that I realized that I, in fact, hate the book. The whole story reminded me of those cheesy "Where are they now" bits of text that get thrown on the ends of movies. You know, the ones that say something like, "Ray and Mary got married that spring and had 3 children. Ray settled down to manage a furniture store in Rock Springs and Mary became ... a painter." 
 These ending are generally silly. I guess I understand them in "based on true story" movies, but I don't like them. I'd rather they leave a bit of mystery to the viewer than them try to wrap everything up in a neat but bland package. Anyways, this entire book was like one of those endings. Nothing really happens. I enjoyed seeing how Suzy's death affected everyone around her, and how everyone became stronger because of it, but that was all after five chapters in. Then it just went on and on and on.
I really liked this but very intense. Have had the opportunity to read it again for several book clubs and couldn't bring myself to do so.

This is easily one of my favorite books, because the plot is so original. I've always had an unusual morbid fascination of what it would be like to watch my family and loved ones from heaven, would they miss me? how would my death affect them? 
 I loved the way Sebold developed all the characters, especially Ruth, the girl who is probably affected the most by Susie's death but a girl who wasn't that close to her during her life. I'll admit, at times I was frustrated when people couldn't tell it was blindingly obvious who Susie's killer was, but I stuck with it. 
 Although it has a sad beginning, at the end I found this story to be somewhat heartwarming. Definitely worth reading, and then telling everyone you know about it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I read this book for a college literature class my freshman year. Basically, the prof decided on this both because we were studying how what happens to one characters (Susie being killed) can change or does it really change other characters (her parents' marriage breaking up). Also, the prof picked the book because it was a more recent book "so I know you might read it" and it was based in Pennsylvania (where I live and go to school in). 
 I liked this book because it was kind of different then other books I read how the afterlife looked.
This was lost on me. Very sad but I thought the end was left a bit up in the air!

Wow, was this book overrated or what! I have three main peeves with this book. One, I couldn't identify with any of the characters, mainly Susie. Second and third would be, *spoilers ahead*------->the sex scene between Ray and Susie (via Ruth's body) and the death of Mr. Harvey. Come on! Death by icicle! Was she serious? Ugh. Maybe I'm cold, but I didn't care much for Susie Salmon or her family. Probably one of the only books where the movie will be better.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I really enjoyed this book. It had been sitting on my bookshelf for more than a year just waiting for me to open it. I never got very excited about it - and then I read the first paragraph. 
 I found the point of view to be interesting (much like the virgin suicides). I enjoyed the fact that rather than most novels involving murder (where you have to wait till the end to find out who did it)we started out knowing who did it in the first few pages. That made it easier to focus on other aspects than the hunt for the guilty. 
 The only part I didn't care for was that there was no real resolution of the murderer getting caught. yeah, he sort of did - but no one who was on the chase (or could have been vindicated by it!) knew about him reaching the end of the line. I realize that that was part of the pull - and that the family didn't need the resolution at that point - but I did! :)
I found the plot simply ridiculous. Well written tripe. Think about it. Rape and another "rape". Two wrongs make a right? I think not. Don't waste your time.

While unique in concept, there are so many things that bothered me about this book, I hardly know where to start. 
 First and foremost, while Sebold achieved great commercial success with this freshman novel, it still reads as a freshman novel. The schtick is clearly the only part of the book thought through and exists to cover the lack of other literary elements. 
 The first person, omnipresent narrative is clunky and not well explained (if the narrator knows what people are thinking show her figuring out that she knows!) and leads to a very much told, rather than shown, storyline. 
 The historical setting is both unnecessary and goes unmentioned for several hundred pages, so when reminded 200 pages in that the date is 1977, it is very confusing. 
 There are a plethora of characters, all of whom seem minor, since not enough time is spent on any for them to be more of a cliche. 
 The pacing is deplorable -- several years will pass over the course of two pages and then 50 pages will be spent on a single day or two, with the years that pass without mention covering such important events as everyone coming to believe the main character's father on the identity of the killer, while the time that we focus on covers the sexual explorations of the main character's little sister. The payload of the book, as it were, comes in the last 20 pages, with no harbinger and no evidence that this was the intended ending. 
 The intended audience is also unclear. The writing style is clearly too juvenile for a larger adult/older teen audience, and the literary foibles are difficult to overlook, even for the audience of adults/older teens who read young adult fiction. At the same time, the focus on the book being rape and murder and several explicit sexual passages make this book at best uncomfortable reading for young teens.

A lovely story, a lovely book - is The Lovely Bones. Alice Sebold is a very sensitive writer. It must take a great amount of sensitivity to write on behalf of a dead young girl's soul/spirit. The characters are so beautifully sketched and developed. Even someone who is just on the fringes of the story like Hal or Ruana. It is Susie's story all through and through her we come to know of so many others. Sebold rises above usual gender biases to give Susie's parents characteristics usually associated with the opposite sex. That Susie's mom Abigail has read Sartre when she was young is beside the point. This is definitely a book one cannot leave halfway and whether one believes in family ties and filial love or not, this is bound to moisten your eyes a bit at some point in the book.
I didn't LOVE the way this story went... It was a good read, but not something I'll be picking up time and time again.
There are a few decent passages, and it starts out OK, but this really doesn't live up to the hype.

This shows how a family transforms from grieving their murdered child and the acceptance that takes place as the child journeys in the afterlife, in which she lets us see the sorrows and tragedies from a man who has been overdriven by lust, madness and loneliness, to her own parents who've almost lost hope but were kept strong by the memories in their heart, guided by their children who portrayed themselves in a very mature way as the years went by. 
 I absolutely admired how this book was written, because it vividly described the feelings and emotions that will trigger something in our hearts. In spite of this, I didn't like how the story shifts so fast because I get a little confused by that. Nonetheless, it captured the voice of an innocent girl, and accordingly, you'll get easily carried by the story.

I read this book a few years ago and really did not like it. I thought it was quite depressing, and I was uncomfortable with how graphic some of the descriptions were. It definitely wasn't a book that left me feeling uplifted at all and I wouldn't read it again.

Las historias de fantasmas normalmente estan incertadas en un genero de horror. Sin embargo, Sebold, se las ingenia narrandonos 'desde el mas alla' el relato brutal de los intersticios del alma del hombre y sus brutales alcances, dejandos desauciados y sin un lugar firme del cual asirnos para no caernos en ese abismo cruento del relato de Susie Salmon. 
 Recomendable leerse a la par del B-side que es Lucky.

While I recognize that this was a well-written and thought-provoking while still being a suspenseful page turner, I can't recommend it simply because it is so freaking sad. To watch multiple lives fall apart after one innocent life is taken is just too depressing.

This book started off really great but it got way too creepy for me, I kept thinking about a unique situation I would be facing that very next day and thinking how the exact same thing or something just as creepy could happy to me. If you can handle a very realistic story-line, I'd recommend you check out this book but it definitely wasn't for me.

Honestly, I never finished this book. I read the first few chapters and then flipped to the last few chapters and skimmed to see what happens to the murderer. 
 I got it as a re-gift (it wasn't new, the cover was battered and nasty looking) for my birthday sophomore year of high school. I believe I gave it away. Beautiful cover, and that's about all it is; a pretty face.

I picked up this book expecting to hate it, given the melancholy nature of the story and the fact that it was not a thriller, my usual genre. 
 However, this book is such a finely crafted portrait of a mourning family told from the perspective of their murdered daughter watching them in heaven that I couldn't help but be completely immersed in the story. Alice Sebold knows how to craft a story out of moments and character turning points that keep you invested in the outcome. 
 With that said, there are things this book is not. Structure and active protagonist there is not: the lead is truly simply a narrator, and the book is tied together through snapshots instead of plot points. The ending left a few things to be wanted, and felt slightly incomplete. 
 However, I found myself not caring about these things and found the emotion of the book to be strong enough to carry the reader, along with the question of whether or not the people on earth would find the murderer. 
 If you like your books to have beautiful character details and heartwrenching portraits of human emotion, The Lovely Bones is for you. If you like your books to have strong structure and a protagonist who propels the story, I'd suggest something else.

I had heard about The Lovely Bones awhile ago. People were telling me what a good book it was and all that jazz, and then it was made into a film which further told me I should probably read it. I kept putting it off and putting it off until I found a copy at my local used bookstore for $2 and took it home. The book centers around Susie Salmon, who was murdered at the age of fourteen, and the lives of her friends and family she watches from Heaven. The reader is taken on the journey of her killer going unnoticed and her family falling apart as they try to deal with her unsolved murder. Her younger sister, Lindsey, becomes a tough, no-nonsense, intelligent girl. Her baby brother becomes the man of the house. Her parents' marriage gets reshaped a couple of times. It all culminates with Susie getting to experience something she never thought she would. I shed a few tears toward the end of the book, but overall I couldn't help but think of how unfair it all was. The book had an okay ending, though not the one I was hoping for.
I know this book was supposed to be The book of the year, and I did stick with it, but I didn't much enjoy it. At the end, I was unsatisfied.
I wouldn't have read this if it hadn't been required for school.

This is one of the few books in my years of reading that I have been unable to finish. Perhaps I should not rate it, for this reason. I do not know why the writing style bothered me, but it did. As well as the plot. I think it was a bit too disturbing for me.

That first chapter made me sob in public and it was all downhill from there (in the best possible way). I read this book a few years ago and I still think about how it made me feel. It also may be the book behind my new rule of not reading in public...

In the words of a wise man, "not my cup of tea. Then again, I don't like shit in my tea" (Ossmo 2007). Started off ok, but got pretty boring and the end was quasi-ridiculous. Then again, how can a book from the point of view of somebody in heaven really not be ridiculous? That's my question.
If I remember correctly, this book was really depressing
I tried ... I really tried to get past the first chapter. It was horrid... why this book is so popular is beyond me.

Had to put it down because I couldn't bear to face what was going to happen to the 14 year old girl but then listened to it as an audio book. Found it annoying and irritating although others whose opinion I respect liked and even loved it. I learned that perhaps I should have stuck to my first reaction to this book and put it aside.

I wanted to read that book as I watched the movie trailer, but I got my hands on it over half a year later when my roommate read it. She barely reads at all and so I got curious about it. 
 As I started I was already suffering at the first page, not because I didn't like the style whatsoever (that came later), but because the topic seems unbearable to me. Anyway I pulled myself together and kept reading on. 
 I decided the book is not my type of liking after 15 minutes. 
 The potential of the book was so big, but I couldn't take it seriously at all! The writing style turned it more into a soap opera than into a realistic situation. See Sarah Aswell's review for that, she states it perfectly and I don't want to wreck my mind about quotes and stuff from this poorly written book. 
 Thank God we have books turned into movies so I don't have to die unknowing. I was quite happy I didn't forced me to finish it, there's no plot at all!
Absolutely hated this book! From the description of the main character's death until the strange, surreal and disturbing final scenes. Of course I don't like CSI or horror movies either.

Its really heartfelt. I almost cried a couple of times-Not really-but yeah, it is kinda sad but happy. Susie Salmons family is completley mortified with Susies unexpected murder and they have to heal overtime.
Terrible book, didn't see the movie. One of the few times that as more details were revealed, the less I wanted to be reading the book.
HATED it, it felt weird reading this. the ending was disappointing. the main character is stupid

On her way home from school on a snowy December day in 1973, 14-year-old Susie Salmon ("like the fish") is lured into a makeshift underground den in a cornfield and brutally raped and murdered, the latest victim of a serial killer - the man she knew as her neighbor, Mr. Harvey. The Lovely Bones is about Susie watching her friends and family from heaven. 
 I felt that the story had great potential for creativity - it seemed a unique idea, and I really wanted to like it, but I was disappointed. There are some enjoyable moments of poetic language and imagery, but most are overdone and unnatural. It was impossible to feel anything for the characters - even Susie herself - as they were as completely underdeveloped. Sebold could have explored the emotions of the Salmon family as they attempted to deal with the senseless tragedy, but instead treated all of her characters with a cold detachment that makes them all seem like shadows rather than real people. 
 The characters were incredibly flat, the scenes disjointed, the storyline contrived, the ending trite - I was left feeling cheated out of the time I spent reading this book. The real proof is here in my review - I can't even think of much to say about The Lovely Bones, and I just finished reading it not 30 minutes ago!

I dug it.Not all of it worked perfectly but it was a intresting idea. 
 I honestly dont remeber Susie Salmon inhabiting a lesbians body 
 to have sex with her highschool crush.Sounds like demonic posession. 
 Im going to reread this book.Maybe I blocked that part out because 
 I really dont remeber that from the book.

Definitely kept me hooked, but slowed down at certain points. It seemed a bit choppy, throwing in suspense with reflective emotional scenes. I don't think I would necessarily say this belongs among my favorite books.

Despite all the negative reviews this book has, I absolutely loved it. Alice Sebold's writing style compliments this novel tremendously. I can see people getting offended by Sebold's concept of "heaven" throughout the book (although it's unwarranted in my opinion) & there are a few parts that are mentally difficult to read due to the nature of the story. Overall I just thought this was a great read. Going to check out her other books for sure.
I couldn't finish it. Not sure what all the hype was about.

book_b.title: The Fault in Our Stars
book_b.user_review:
Some of this book was "trying too hard" for my tastes. I would love to meet intelligent, articulate teens like this, but I doubt they exist. 
 Augustus Waters saved this book for me. By the end of the book, his voice and musings were like a good friend whose tirades and musings you would ignore with an affectionate eye roll. I didn't care much about Hazel, the POV character for this story, but she was tolerable. The other major character in the story, Isaac, is also quite endearing and entertaining. 
 I saw the plot twist coming a mile away, and I'm fairly confident most other readers would as well. Despite that, this book had a lot of heart and not in the cliche'd way you'd expect when dealing with a story about kids with various cancers trying to live life.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There isn't anything unique about this book. 
 However, there are pretty words and amazing meanings. 
 It's a book that you read quickly, with much emotion, and you'll probably remember forever. 
 And even though it wasn't unique, or magical, it was special and worth the read.
I enjoyed this young adult book with very smart characters who are doomed and suffering from cancer. Still not my favorite in the upcoming Tournament of Books.

Finished re-reading The Fault in Our Stars again today. It was just as tear jerking as I remember it being the first time I read it. It brought back memories of my own trials, triumphs and losses in life. And as I came to the end I had the same reaction as I did the previous time I read it- It's over?! I want more!

Rip my heart, why don't you?! 
 You'll need a tissue box. But read it.

This is a reread and was originally finished August 9th 2012 
 My review got deleted for this but basically the 4 stars stay because it's beautiful, but not giving it 5 stars 
 because the writing is very very flawed.

I admit I read this because my daughter loved it. I mean- really loved it-and very passionately begged me to read it. I enjoy reading books she loves because it gives us so much to discuss. That being said, it was very easy to understand WHY my almost 14 year old daughter loved this story. The character of Hazel is so well written, she is SUCH a teenager, that kids can't help but get her. And add to that the gallant, smart, slightly disrespectful but still nice Augustus Waters. Who wouldn't love this guy?? Even Hazel's parents like him. I know that almost everyone out there has already read and reviewed this, so I won't go into the story, except to say it was wonderful, romantic, funny, and extremely sad. If you haven't already, please read this book as soon as you can. And let me know how you liked it! 
 (and if you have a 14 year old daughter, get her this book)
Full of truths, the way only John Green can write. But writing about cancer is tricky, and by the end I found it a little too sentimental. Still a good book.

Once again, I've tried to read it. First time, I made it to about page seven. I didn't even get to the bit on America's Next Top Model. This time, I made it to page nineteen. See, I made progress? To me, from what I read of the book so far and what friends have gushed about to me, Green writes perfect prose -- and he does, the quotes I've read from this book are amazing -- and his characters are teenagers. Teenagers that don't exist. I know that these guys speak and think differently than I do because they had cancer, but I still grew up with teens. Not even the ones who read Green speak like his characters do.

After all the hype, I expected more. I was not impressed by this book. A bit too "teen" for me. I've read books like this before that are better. Yes, it was sad in the end, but it's like everything was okay in it's separate parts and didn't quite come together.

This is the first book by John green I've ever read. I was hesitant to read it because I try to stay away from hyped books and best sellers, and also because I knew it was YA and its not really my genre. However I enjoyed this book. It is fast paced, easy to read, funny and sad, and very complete. I liked the characters, they were very real and relatable. But the thing I enjoyed most in this book was the approach of cancer and death and life. It does not turn the characters into victims, it does not make you feel sorry or pity any of the characters. It celebrates life and the message of living the life you are dealt comes across very strongly. 
 It's pretty deep for a YA book. And although I did find the whole romance thing a bit cheesy, It made me be very grateful for being healthy and alive, and also I think that people who have struggled or are currently fighting cancer would appreciate it, I people treated them like regular people, and see far beyond their illness, because cancer does not define you. 
 I recommend it widely and I'm also curious to read more of this author.
I was surprised that I even read this, especially since I'm not a huge fan of books that aren't fantasy. However, I thought it was pretty good and an easy read.

Another book I set my expectations too high for. Albeit, it had some downright beautiful sentences but I felt there was a lack of something I couldn't quite put my finger on. For me, this book had a slow start and took a while to hook and reel me in. I understood that John Green didn't want to write another "cancer story," but no matter what he says this is just that. Sure, he took a different approach but it's still a story about cancer. Sometimes there were just too many jokes and not enough support among the characters. 
 But the end, that's where it got me. I enjoyed that Hazel dealt with her grief without being incredibly selfish. The end wasn't just about cancer to me, it was about the theme of death and accepting that it's in our lives. I was sure I wouldn't cry, since I usually don't in most books/movies, but I did. It hit too close to the bone watching my best friends death and not being able to grieve selfishly. I had to mourn a certain way for every one else's sake. But even that will catch up with you. 
 The end is the only part of the novel that tore down the walls of a typical "cancer story." Because I've already seen movies and read books where the characters are bitter, sarcastic, and don't want to be a hero within their illness. At least the end of the book exceeded that. This is what gained my admiration instead of distaste. John Green is an accredited and talented writer, but I am starting to see some patterns in his writing. I hope my reviews don't keep declining.
Wow what a book, should come with a warning 'tissues required' such a sad book about how unfair life can be.
"You don't get to choose if you get hurt in this world...but you do have some say in who hurts you."
Finished but wasn't my cup of tea.

This was quite a good read. I had heard mixed reviews before I started so I didnt think I would enjoy it as much but I eventually decided to give it a go. I have to say it is a well written piece of work, realistically depicting the lives of teenagers who are battling with cancer. The book was very sad in parts but there was also humour and romance along the way. I found the relationship between Hazel and Gus both cute and moving. 
 Overall then, this was a worthwhile and quite an easy read, therefore 4 stars from me!

This was one of the first John Green books I read. And let me tell you, I loved this book. The story line was amazing, you fall in love with the characthers. What they are going through is very difficult, but they enjoy their lives to the fullest. Loved this book.

I really liked this book. It's a five star because, well, it was great. It was funny but serious and it really helped put things into perspective, and not just about cancer or sickness in general, although it does for that as well. It's a well-written, thought provoking book for young adults that really shouldn't be limited to just the YA crowd. Not only does this book inspire the reader, but teaches as well. Definitely a good read. So go read it.

John Green's The Fault In Our Stars offers a a dramatic twist on the classic teenage love story. Hazel and Augustus are two teens with cancer that meet at a support group, they share an instant connection right away. Throughout the story, reader's are introduced to the struggles of cancer patients, but also are able to understand that these kids are human just like the rest of us. At first you may make the assumption of a cancer book being so depressing, but the writing style is so witty and entertaining it actually will make you laugh out loud. However, this book also gets very emotional at times. I was hysterically crying by the end of the book because John Green is such a powerful writer. He makes you feel as though you really know the characters personally. I was able to finish the book in just two days because I could not put it down, I was so emotionally attached to it. After reading the book I almost felt lost, as if I just ended my friendships with Augustus and Hazel because the story was over; I just wanted to read it again right away so it wouldn't be over. Everything in this book: the characters, the story, the words, they all have the power to be an inspiration. If you haven't read it, I strongly suggest to take the chance.

There is the subject matter which is excellent. The idea was important and riveting. And then, there was the execution. I can't get over how flat this book came across. it read sort of like a history book instead of literature. 
 The over-use of rather large words did not make the kids sound smart. It made them, however, sound like pedants. Add in the fat, alcoholic, author who they went to see, and I sort of asked myself, 'what is the point of this?' 
 The only part that redeemed this book for me, and managed to not end up with one star was when they sat at the cafe the night before they met senor douchenozzle and his insipid assistant who took them to the Anne Frank House? Welcome sickly children, let us go tour a place where another child died incredibly young, but she was taken out by a cancer of the conscience instead of cancer of the body. 
 From what I understand, Mr. Green is a very intelligent man. And instead of showing us the intelligence of the characters, he showed us extensive vocabulary. Maybe the movie can save it.

The perfect combination of funny and sad. It's heartbreaking and heartwarming at the same time. John Green is a genius and the way the book it's written you can just tell he is a nerdfighter. It's like reading his videos I'm not even kidding
Emotionally gripping, but cliche and written with a market in mind.
This book didn't live up to it's hype. I was extremely disappointed and disgusted by the ending, which was predictable right from the start. This book could have been so much more than it was.

As a newbie to award-winning John Green, I was amazed, humbled, and awed by his insightful, raw, and often funny prose. Technically classified as YA, THE FAULT IN OUR STARS is a fantanstically poignant read about teenagers afflicted with terminal cancer. It's about courage, sadness, love, death, and finding one's place in the world. 
 When Hazel(referred to as Hazel Grace in much of the book) and Augustus (Gus)meet at a Cancer Kids Support Group, the world suddenly shifts from pathetic to brilliant as these teens fall in love tethered by a shared diagnosis and love for the same book written by a fictional author in Amsterdam. The voices of Hazel and Gus penetrate one's very fiber, chatty and full of insight, understanding, and brilliance not always found in teens. 
 John Green crafts a novel that all can appreciate, laugh aloud to, and then cry. Trust me, this book will stay with you long after you finish reading the last line.

I made the mistake of reading this book while waiting for a doctor's appointment. The book is so infuriating that my initial blood pressure reading came back high. I had to explain that my blood pressure is normally textbook perfect but had just gotten incredibly angry at a book. They gave me a moment to calm down and I had a normal reading, but that experience perfectly summarizes my views on the book in a nutshell.

1.5 stars. 
 EDIT: Changed the rating because it's gotten to the point where my sister and I have inside jokes on how stupid and shallow this book is. I can't think about this book without getting angry. 
 I have a history with pretentious people. 
 My biggest mess involved two boys in particular who were so incredibly full of themselves that for the first time in my life, I openly expressed my dislike to them. They know that I couldn't care less about their "hotness" or just how amazing they were. So goddamn full of themselves, spoiled rotten, just overall horrible people. 
 In short, my personality clashes with theirs entirely and there really is no chance of a friendship. I'd dive into it, but then this wouldn't be a book review. 
 And so I move on. 
 The Fault in Our Stars is my first John Green book. 
 Yeah, I know, but I didn't really get into reading up until maybe four years ago. And I'm not too into contemporary, but the opportunity presented itself and I took my first dive. My sister is a fan of John Green. She really loves Looking for Alaska and Will Grayson, Will Grayson and finds Paper Towns to be LfA's quirky New Girl twin that doesn't own up. 
 I almost feel bad for disliking this book, but that's strictly on the idea of cancer. Cancer is horrible, unpredictable, and the worst part is that it's your own cells mutating against you. That's why it's so hard to defeat. That's what I wish this book was about: dealing with the cancer that wants to kill you. Instead, I get a book about a fictional miracle drug that keeps Hazel alive so she can have a boy love her then die (not even on sight either) . 
 I came into this book with an open mind, I assure you. But I ended up really wanting to put the book down several times. From the first few pages, I felt something was actually wrong. Like I didn't know what I was getting myself into. Having finished this book, which, to me, was such a chore to do, I think I've stumbled upon decent reasons as to why I really can't give this any more than two stars. 
 If you didn't know by now, The Fault in Our Stars tells the story of Hazel, a girl whose thyroid cancer has ceased to grow thanks to a magical miracle drug. But because her cancer life is just so boring, a boy has to make it better. 
 Because that is the only way anything gets better in life. 
 Boyz. 
 Cancer People, Dear Readers 
 WRITING 
 This was by far the largest problem I had. Larger than Hazel saying, "I wanna tap that" about Augustus on page 8. This prose was not the voice of a real teenager. It tried, but this did not sound like a teenager suffering from cancer. This was the voice of a teenager who liked to say, "You know what sucks? Cancer. You know what else sucks? Dying." Why? So the reader could laugh. 
 And wouldn't you know it every line is like that. There is no rest for any real emotion or interest. It's all laced with some one-liner or trying to be hilariously philosophical when it's just trying way too hard to keep a reader interested. And this alone, made me find great distaste in the character of Hazel. 
 She is not believable because I never learned anything about her. She just hates Support Group and adores Augustus for reasons that were never clarified throughout the book. Oh you like Gus's smile, his laugh? The idea that he thinks of basketball really as a nod to a baby toy? The idea that he spends money just so he can conduct a metaphor that doesn't do anything but make him look like a pretentious asshole? 
 Oh who am I kidding. This entire book was shallow and pretentious. Everyone thought they were so hilarious because did you know that eggs are restricted to a breakfast food? Those poor scrambled eggs! No, I don't give a flying fuck about scrambled eggs and their apparent oppression. But think about it! We only have eggs for breakfast! Because you choose to point it out as such. 
 Or get this, how about the hurdles event in track? You know what Augustus says about hurdles? He says this after that beautiful basketball connection to a child shoving cylinders into circle holes: 
 "And I wondered if the hurdlers ever thought, you know, 'This would go faster if they just got rid of the hurdles.'" 
 THIS IS ONE OF THE STUPIDEST THINGS I HAVE EVER READ IN A BOOK. 
 Augustus Waters, actual athlete, says something like this about a sport. Sports are a very healthy way to escape stress. If anything, Augustus and his philosophical ass should be wondering what the hurdles represent to the hurdlers. HURDLES ARE A SPECIAL EVENT. The hurdlers are probably doing a running event too! They CHOSE to run the hurdles for the challenge. 
 But this falls on the level of those scrambled eggs. Hey! If we talk about this and make it sound funny, it'll be deep! It'll really scratch the heads of the readers! This just shows how silly and thoughtful Augustus is! Don't you guys just want to get with him and his awesome cigarette metaphor that HE SPENDS MONEY ON FOR NO FUCKING REASON? 
 Guh, you fucking stupid ignorant son of a bitch. This was the line, by the way, that got me in that level of dislike for Augustus that I got on with the asshole dudes that exist in my life. And Hazel just sort of accepts this. Like, what the hell is everyone thinking in this book? What universe are they in? Because this is not a real universe. 
 I think now I'm tracking into character territory so here: 
 CHARACTERS 
 Hazel was the girl who referred to testicular cancer as "cancer to the balls" and then she sees Augustus Waters on page 8 of this book and goes, 
 "Look, let me just say it: He was hot. A nonhot boy stares at you relentlessly and it is, at best, awkward and, at worst, a form of assault. But a hot boy...well" 
 Remember, if you're not drop dead gorgeous, men, your nice glances are only awkward. That's it. You can never go farther, and your delicious insight on life will never win the heart of a girl. Because you are just not sexy enough or Augustinian for it. Hazel likes to do this. She likes to put down other guys for her Gus, even though they still BARELY knew each other. 
 I met Kaitlyn and her (cute but frankly not Augustinian) boyfriend for coffee one afternoon. 
 LOOK AT THAT. What. What is that? This was a nice guy and Hazel's like, "Well he's not a fucking Greek God so no thank you." But what about Augustus, Hazel? You went to his house to watch a movie that you decided was just a silly boy movie that you knew you wouldn't like because you were a girl. MOVIES DON'T WORK LIKE THAT. What are you even doing! 
 You know what I just realized? Hazel is a lot like Mary in The Forest of Hands and Teeth. She hates one thing and loves only one material thing. Hazel hates the cancer support group, and loves An Imperial Affliction. Mary hates the Unconsecrated, but loves the ocean. That's all they have to their name. Which is AMAZING to me that Augustus finds something to love about Hazel. All it is is her John Green wit. 
 If you asked Gus what else was there to Hazel besides this one book thing and her wit, I bet you a hundred dollars that he would respond as Derek in Swan Princess did with "What else is there?" 
 Because that's all their love is. They're not bonding over the fact they have cancer. They bonded over An Imperial Affliction then experienced an intensified Hey Arnold! Episode about visiting the author who, to no one's surprise I hope, was a complete jackass then makes a 180 because...because. Who needs reasons. 
 HOWEVER, the half star is devoted to Mr. Peter Van Houten, who was the only actual character in this book. Everyone else was flat and pretentious assholes. When Van Houten did it, there was history behind it and a REASON. He actually had an arc! He did things! Despite my lack of care for Augustus and Hazel, the way Peter treated them was abhorring and the only way for me to fix that was to stab the man in the eye. But he changed, and revealed WHY he acted the way he did and there was sense made and he was a good character. 
 STRUCTURE 
 Structure was fine. 
 Still flowed okay despite my need to be done with this. 
 OVERALL 
 I honestly thought everything was funny. I laugh at a loooooot of stuff. This, whatever this is, is not really that funny. It's shallow, and not really geared to people who want to know the world of cancer and stepping over the obstacle. It's a cancer-filled girl loving and losing a cancer-filled boy. Oh and they meet their favorite author who's actually an asshole. Cancer is the backseat, and I almost find it insulting. 
 I don't understand why people love this. Tell me all you want that Augustus is a beautiful boy and Hazel just wanted something different in her life, but don't you DARE tell me that this is deep. This is not a deep book, there's nothing that touches my heart except shallow wit and a poor man suffering from the cancerous death of his 8 year-old ray of sunshine. 
 I could go on, but I think this is enough. If it isn't, well that's your opinion. This is mine. You are just gonna have to deal. 
 Final Remarks: 
 This book should have been about what happened to Peter Van Houten. 
 It'd be perfectly parallel to that Hey Arnold! episode I mentioned, but it'd be better than what I read. 
 OR, this book should have been about Hazel WITH THE TERMINAL CANCER. Because her inner conflict with cancer would better clash with her ability to be with Augustus and it would've fleshed her out a hell of a lot more than giving her a magical miracle drug.
There are no words of the brilliance of this book. Though I finally understand the fangirl term kicked in the feels.

I'm sad to say that this is my first John Green book but within the first 100 pages, I vowed to buy the rest on my e-reader. The main reason I bought it the day it came out was because my friend had pre-ordered a signed copy when it was first announced and had been anxiously awaiting the release date ever since. Mine was a first print so it was also signed.(I got a green JScribble and my friend got an orange one.) 
 This book is about Hazel, a 16-year-old girl with a tumor who wants nothing more then to watch a entire season of Americas Next Top Model in one day and reread her favorite book, An Imperial Affliction, for the hundredth time. Her parents however insist she go to her weekly Support Group for kids with cancer. Reluctantly she agrees and meets Augusts Waters who changes her life. 
 This is an amazing book about how much one person can change someone's life, no matter how short or long of a time the two people have known each other. I think anyone will like this book and will be able to "feel all the emotions" as John Green said we would. I'll leave you with the quote that inspired the title: 
 'The fault, dear Brutus is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings.'-Shakespeare, Julius Caesar (Act 1, scene 2).

Let me begin by saying that I am no longer the target audience for this book. That was very apparent to me by the end of the first chapter. By the time I was at 34%, my Kindle said I had two hours left, so I stuck with it. I felt I owed it to Romeo and Juliet Gus and Hazel to finish this tragic love story. I should also say that I knew the ending before I started reading. The book has been a bestseller for two years. If you don't know the ending, you might be living under a rock. 
 Anyway, I finished the book and I'm glad I did. The ending almost redeemed the book. That is why I gave it 2 stars instead of 1. I say almost because I can look past the teenage angst. I feel forced to look past the cancer because I have never had cancer and it would be heartless of me to trivialize the suffering of two fictional teenagers because I don't understand their plight. I do feel like Green uses cancer as a contrived plot device to guarantee the emotional entanglement of his readers. 
 The only cancer related complaint I have is when Hazel says that the only thing worse than having cancer is being the parent of a child with cancer. (I'm paraphrasing but I can see that I need to start underlining quotes that I want to comment on.) Anyway, after reading all about Hazel's teenage existential existence, she gives us this very mature (for a 16yo) statement. It felt like the author was pandering to those readers who might be parents of cancer patients. How would Hazel know what is worse? As evidenced by the entire rest of the novel, teenagers are the center of their own universe. Even more so when they have cancer (if this book is to be seen as realistic.) 
 On to my more pressing complaints. 
 When Hazel first meets Gus, he pulls out a cigarette and puts it in his mouth. She freaks out because she struggles to breathe. She is angry that he would give money for and use a product that creates cancer. Gus quickly explains to her that it is a metaphor. He puts the cancer causing cigarette in his mouth but doesn't light it so that it doesn't have the power to kill him. Magically, Hazel is OK with this. As long as he doesn't light it and only supports the cigarette industry buy purchasing them and giving them free advertising, everything is just peachy. Seriously? Really? This blazing hypocrisy is our first introduction to Gus and Hazel. 
 Another complaint is something that may be completely plausible but it doesn't seem so to me. If Gus was in remission for 18 months, how is it that he didn't know his cancer had returned until it was too late. Did he skip his scans and blood work for those 18 months? One day he just decided to have a PET scan and all of a sudden he lit up like a Christmas tree? With no warning? Seriously? I know Osteosarcoma is a form of cancer created for the book and that there is now way to know how quickly is spreads. But if the original warning signs and subsequent diagnosis were due to a small, highly treatable tumor, doesn't it seem more likely that Gus would have had plenty of warning that the cancer had returned? Does that mean he knew the whole time he was friends with Hazel and just lied to her the whole time? Hazal wasn't kidding about his hamartia! 
 And can we talk about the sex please. How does a kid with full blown Osteosarcoma walk around Amsterdam, climb all the stairs in the Anne Frank museum, help his sick girlfriend through the aforementioned museum and then return to the hotel and have the energy to have sex? Maybe sex is different when your are dying from cancer. It's one of those things I can't comment on without sounding heartless. But he could barely walk the next day. Gus had already started chemo so where did this burst of energy come from? And while this sex scene was relatively chaste why did it have to be included? Why do these dying teens have to have sex to prove their relationship? They don't. They're relationship could have been just as sweet and poignant without the sex. (If you can't tell, I'm not a fan of sex in YA fiction.) 
 But while we are talking about Gus and Hazel's sex scene....wouldn't she have noticed the fresh scar from his recently removed PICC or Central line when they were lying there naked??? Gus told Hazel that he had started his chemo before he left for Amsterdam and stopped to go on the trip. The first time Hazel sees Gus after returning from Amsterdam she notes that Gus has already has his PICC line put in. These events make it most likely that he had his IV removed before Amsterdam. So there would have been a fresh scar. And they were naked. Maybe it was a magical IV that left no trace.... 
 With all those complaints out of the way, I will say that Gus' sickness and death redeemed the book for me. The book seemed more realistic once they returned from Amsterdam. The emotions felt more authentic. Hazel obviously developed and grew as a person. She cared about what would happen to her parents after she died and she finally became aware of why Van Houten was the was he was. 
 It makes me wonder if any of the complaints I have are shared by any teenage readers. The second part of the book (after Amsterdam) was by far better than the first. Unfortunately, the first part was so annoying to me that the second part didn't entirely make up for it. Hazel and Gus somehow manage to turn cancer into a farce. It definitely didn't help me to understand the tragedy of living with cancer or even having a loved one with cancer. The ending is not cancer specific. Most people in the world know the pain of losing a loved one . 
 I do just need to end with saying that I don't hate people with cancer. I swear I don't. I don't even hate tragic love stories. What I do hate is when authors use fake versions of real diseases as a method to garner sympathy for their ridiculous characters and their magical love-at-first-sight tragedies.

Read my review of 
 The Fault in Our Stars 
 .

If you like YA or teen romance, you could do far worse than The Fault in Our Stars, although for the sake of honesty I must admit that I think you could do better too. 
 {Read my full review here}

"And then there are books like An Imperial Affliction, which you can't tell people about, books so special and rare and yours that advertising your affection feels like a betrayal." For me, The Fault in our Stars is such a book. I've waited a week to review it because I get emotional just thinking about it. 
 I'm not going to go into great detail about the plot. It is a heavily read book. So, just briefly it is a coming of age tale where two teenagers, who happen to be fighting cancer, fall in love. 
 I've never read a book where I so completely connected to the characters. Next month (April) will be the 25th anniversary of learning I had cancer. I was seventeen years old at the time and fell in love with the man who would become my husband. I was initially worried this would be an over the top tale about how heroic teenagers with cancer deal with the disease. But, I was incredibly impressed with how well Green tapped into the feelings of a teenager actually going through the ordeal. He captured the frustration of the effects of medicine, the "cancer perks", how relationships with your peers change, the desire to live a life worth living, the affects on the parents, and the uncertainty of being a survivor. One passage that resonated with me, "My final chapter was written upon diagnosis. Gus, like most cancer survivors, lived with uncertainty." I've had two cancer scares in the past 25 years, and I think I will live with that uncertainty for the rest of my life. Even the trip to Amsterdam had a strong connection to my life. The book simply transported me back in time 25 years ago. I was surprised by how raw those emotions still are with me. I loved how I was connected to a character in a book that was connected to a character in a book she was reading. I also loved the significance of the title. 
 I've read criticisms related to the characters being too precocious. I disagree. I remember distinctly growing up overnight. You're entire perspective changes in an instant.
It was ok

Some books change you. If I were to write of my reading life in a Pat Conroy-esque fashion, this book would take on a significant portion of that book. While these are some exceptionally eloquent teenagers, it makes me love them more, because they put such care into what they say when other teenagers and tweens, as I'm accustomed to, spout nonsense just to hear their own voices. Their dialogue was almost a relief. Nevertheless, Hazel and Augustus will continue in my consciousness long after their own has ceased, and I'm happy to say that The Fault in Our Stars has become my own personal An Imperial Affliction.

I have never been so devastated by a book than I was with The Fault in Our Stars. It is one of the most beautiful books I've read recently. The love story between Hazel and Gus grabbed me from the beginning and held me until the end. I devoured the book in one sitting, weeping all the way through. TFiOS is one of the most heart-wrenching depictions of an all-consuming, yet doomed, love between teenagers. There is no falling out of love with Gus just as there is no forgetting Hazel. This book will stay with me forever and I will read it repeatedly, recommending it to everyone I meet throughout the rest of my life.

This book unexpectedly knocked my socks off. It was extremely well-written. I especially appreciated the author's wide use of unique vocabulary. So many lessons to be learned and gleaned from this story, but, most of all, live better and deliberately everyday. Be proud of your choices. Leave a smaller scar on the world.
This book was very flowery and wordy to me. I don't know how to explain it, but I liked it.

There are books that when you finish, you just sigh, put the book down and spend time lost in thought. And so it was with this book. 
 The characters, the story, the narrative - it all felt right and real. That's the highest possible praise that I can give.

Finished in less than 24 hours. Beautifully told story that is both tragic and humorous. This novel is staying on my bookshelf indefinitely. I highly recommend everyone read this book; with a box of tissues handy. You won't regret it.
A-mazing! :) I seriously cried! :)

I feel bad because almost everyone LOVES this book and I just don't. It didn't stick with me, nothing popped out and wowed me, as I'm sure it did for other readers. It wasn't a horrible book and I don't hate it, but it was just sort of neutral for me. There was nothing wrong with the writing, as it was beautifully written, and the characters were decent, I quite enjoyed reading from Hazel's perspective.

After seeing the hype of the book every single where, and how some people claimed how sad the book is and even had cried over it; I decided to give a chance because never in my life, I have ever read a Young Adult book before. I didn't like this book. I only read the first few chapters and then skimming the rest. I couldn't make myself care for the characters at all. I find them all to be unbelievably irritating and annoying, especially Hazel. It was well-written, sad, hopeful... but that's about it. Unfortunately, I'm not as impressed by it as a lot of people are.

I've heard lots of amazing things about the writing of John Green. This book was pretty good, but I don't know if I'd call it the best thing I'd ever read. I do like Green's style, however, and I will certainly read more of his works as I come across them.

Of all the heart-wrenching, soul-crushing, gut-twisting books I could've picked up, I picked up this one. And wow, what a book it is. 
 I managed to hang on till a few minutes after turning the last page, then I wept like mad. If you've ever lost anyone to cancer, you will feel the pain in this book. John Green is ridiculously accurate in his description of the senselessness of the disease. 
 A slight criticism of mine is that it suffers at times from "Juno" syndrome: too many adolescents speaking too eloquently and precociously in off-the-cuff situations. But the more I think about my own teenage years, the more it makes sense. There's that sense of feeling like you know everything and yet ... you know nothing. 
 I feel like I need to cleanse myself from this book before I move on to something else. It leaves a residue of despair, courage, hope, triumph, failure, melancholy, humor and grief that doesn't wash away easily. Nor should it.

reference_books.review_text: I love Jeannette Walls writing. Her stories really come alive for me. However, I would say that this is my least favourite, but more because the other two I have read were so amazing.

reference_books.review_text: Although this didn't pack the punch to the gut that Girl on the Train did, this was still an excellent read. Her writing is top notch, the characters as well. A bit predictable, not one of my favorites, but worth the read for sure.

reference_books.title: The Dark Days Club (Lady Helen, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I must start by stating that I received this book through a Goodreads giveaway. SO...which of my friends now wants to borrow it because I own it, it is a physically beautiful book, and it was GREAT! 
 I really enjoyed the story. I love the mixing of genres: YA, historical fiction, thriller, and supernatural fiction! It was all done seamlessly, accurately and interestingly. 
 The protagonist, Helen, was the type of character I love: flawed but strong. I like that she is not conventionally beautiful, and that some people seem to think she is down right crazy. I like that she is caught in a web of what the era dictates, her rank, her passions, her personality, family, etc, because that is very true to the intricacies of real life as we all try navigate the various roles we play. 
 Anyway, I look forward to reading the next book in this series.

reference_books.review_text: I have done some tidying since reading this, but was not inspired enough to take on the HUGE job she suggests. I feel like her home must feel like a jail cell instead of a comfortable place to sink in and relax. I also feel like she is the type of woman to sleep with her bra on.

Overall, I didn't enjoy it as a novel, stand-alone or in the relationship to To Kill a Mockingbird. It has been years since I read TKAM, but I do not remember the dialogue being so jarring and awkward. I didn't mind the last couple chapters, and I did enjoy the flashback stories of Jean Louise's Scout years.

reference_books.review_text: I had much higher hopes for this. Taming of the Shrew is one of my favourite plays, and I did appreciate how Tyler made it modern without still clearly being assaultive, but it wasn't a very rich retelling and I found the characters boring--although I did enjoy Kate's portrayal at work.

reference_books.title: Morning Star (Red Rising, #3)
reference_books.review_text: The first book in this series is by far the best, but the last one was pretty great too. A range of emotions for sure!

The conflict is less about Dorothy and the Wicked Witch--this is a small plot point rather than the driving struggle--and more about how Dorothy is going to get home to the family that is only kind of meh about her, and her about them. 
 There are aspects of this book that I love, especially the china people and the golden beret. I may read the next 12 (or is it 13?) installments, especially if the kids want to, or I may not.

There are fantasy books that sell more or more enduringly beloved, but "The Wonderful Wizard Of Oz" is perhaps the most influential American fantasy story ever written. 
 And though most people are familiar with the 1939 movie starring Judy Garland, L. Frank Baum's first novel about his magical fantasy land is a whimsical -- somehow darker -- version of the tale. It's a fairly simple tale about a little girl wandering through a magical land filled with strange creatures, but the endearingly familiar companions she picks up along the way and the oddball ideas that Baum peppers the story with keep it entertaining. 
 A little girl named Dorothy lives in the grey expanses of Kansas, on a grey farm with her grey aunt and uncle, and her little black dog Toto. When a cyclone strikes, her house is torn up and sent whirling away... and when it eventually lands, she's in the land of the Munchkins, and has accidentally crushed the cruel Witch of the East. Hoping to find a way back to her relatives, Dorothy takes the witch's silver shoes (yes, movie fans, they're silver) and heads to the City of Emeralds to find the Wizard of Oz. 
 She quickly gains some traveling companions -- a sentient scarecrow in a cornfield, a metal woodsman who suffered a series of involuntary amputations, and a fearsome lion with some anxiety issues -- who also want to ask the Great Oz to grant their assorted wishes. But before they can get what they want, they must deal with the many strange things in Oz: the terrible Kalidahs, poppies that cause narcolepsy, the strange green-tinted City, killer crows, and so on. And when they finally do encounter Oz, he gives them one terrible condition: to get their wishes granted, they must kill the wicked Witch of the West. Easier said than done. 
 "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" is in many ways a straightforward fantasy story for young children -- a young girl is swept off into a magical land, and must find the enchanted means of finding her way back home again. Simple enough, but Baum had a rather lively imagination that spices the land of Oz with various odd little creatures (Munchkins, the Kalidahs, lots of talking animals) as well as some bizarre, whimsical concepts of his own (the City of Emeralds only looks green because... well, Oz got everyone in it to wear green-tinted eyeglasses). 
 And those who have only seen the movie may be surprised by some of the things that happen here, as there were quite a few changes. For one thing, it's substantially darker -- there are more monsters (the fighting trees, a sort of G-rated "Evil Dead" plant threat), the Tin Woodsman's gruesome origin story is outlined in detail, and Dorothy and her friends are effectively hired as assassins. And Oz has creatures that never made it in, such as the bizarre Quadlings and the china people. 
 But Baum presents this with a writing style that is oddly whimsical and cheery, as if refusing to let even the worst events sully Dorothy's adventures for long. It's a pretty simple style, fairly common in the 19th century, but it has a certain charm to it ("Its legs were quite as long as the tiger had said, and it's body covered with coarse black hair"). And his imagination for Oz seems to be almost boundless, as Dorothy simply floats through, encountering one weird thing after another. 
 The characters are fairly endearing ones -- none are particularly developed, but Dorothy's chipper, no-nonsense attitude makes her a pretty likable little girl. And her companions are each pretty charming, each seeking a cure for some perceived deficiency (brains, heart, courage), but not quite bright enough to realize that they have these things already, as shown by their actions in the story. And there are a fair number of intriguing side-characters, such as the Witches (both good and bad, including Glinda and her army of beautiful young women). 
 "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" is basically a fanciful road trip, but Baum's nimble imagination and vivid ideas keep its simplicity from ever becoming dull or cloying. And surprisingly, Dorothy's adventures in Oz are not over yet.

It is very difficult to review children's books, and especially classics that are as well known and famously adapted as The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. This is a silly book. Silly in some good ways, and silly in some tedious ways. The conflict resolutions involve so much deus ex machina that the plot feels like a surrealist generator. It is cute that each of Dorothy's companions already possesses the quality they most desire, and their realization of their traits would be a joyful, satisfying end to their journey, but they instead learn nothing of themselves and rely on false totems. Also unsettling is that each becomes the ruler of kingdoms of which they have almost no knowledge, and of populations that know nothing of them. None have any experience in governance either. I fear reading the sequel and hearing of lawlessness, starvation and civil war as a result of their ineptness. The only culture that seems to have their shit together is the flying monkeys, but rather than destroying the crown it is given to the king of the monkeys which should make Niccolo Machiavelli nervous. If you are still curious I would encourage you to instead read Scottie Young's beautifully illustrated Oz: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, which is a faithful adaption gorgeously rendered.

I have seen the movie many times over the years, but this is the first time I read the book. It is more akin to a fairy tale than a fantasy novel and is written in a simple style. The characters are all very polite to each other (even their enemies) which is sometimes amusing and sometimes irritating. However, this story has great depth despite its folkoric exterior. Dorothy, Scarecrow, Tin Man, and the Cowardly Lion are all searching for something to make them complete. They believe that only the great Wizard of Oz can grant their requests, and so they face many dangers and hardships to win his favor. But the Wizard is a charlatan - a conman with no magic powers. Yet he does, in a sense, grant their wishes, by showing them they already possessed the things they desired. This theme of self-discovery is perhaps what has given this book such staying power. I look forward to reading the other books in the series.

First reaction: well, it was certainly different than I expected. That is to say, different than the movie. In many ways, the movie is much more complexed and well-rounded, even with its cut-and-dry good and evil prototypes. I think the best way to review would be to highlight some ways in which it's similar different than the well-known movie. First of all, very little time is spent in Kansas -- almost none. We're whisked quickly away to the munchkin village. Now, the side-character inhabitants of Oz, and they layout of Oz, is actually an area in which the book was more whole than the movie. 
 the first glaring discrepancy between the book and popular Dorothy knowledge is the fact that her magic slippers are silver, and that the witch she encounters in Munchkin Land is not Glinda, but the old Good Witch of the North. She proceeds to meet her companions in a similar way. The only obstacle they encounter on the way to Oz is the poppies -- there is no sign of the Wicked Witch or her flying monkeys until they're tasked by Oz to kill her. In the end, the detour to Oz is rather pointless -- the book holds the same twist about Oz's true identity, but he's even more useless, and the crew have to journey to find Glinda to get their desires granted (this, in fact, is the first time we see Glinda). 
 I'm trying to imagine if I had never seen the movie and had no fond memories of it -- would I have liked this book? I'm not sure. Possibly, though certainly not as much as I did this time around. For those compelled to enjoy it for sentimental reasons, and who are simultaneously open-minded about realizing what the movie changed (some of the most iconic things -- ie/ ruby slippers -- were not in the book) I think this is a good, quick read.

This beautiful little gem should be on every child's bookshelf! A classic fairy tale that America can claim as its own. 
 There's quite a bit more to the story that we know from the 1939 film. If you'll come along for the ride, there's A LOT MORE ADVENTURE to be had in the Land of Oz! I was happy to see that I recognized many of the scenes from the movie, and it brought a touch of great familiarity to the story as I continued to read. The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are as friendly and delightful as could possibly be imagined. But there are many other fun characters to meet, and new, exciting places to see -- strange and wild of every type! I certainly enjoyed meeting the field mice, the Winkies, and others... plus, visiting the dainty China country, was a rather interesting experience too. 
 NOTE: There's a wee bit of violence that may not be suitable for all youngsters. (It includes chopping off the heads of wolves, which could be a bit disturbing!) 
 Anyways, if you can get a vintage copy with the original illustrations, the pictures happen to add much more charm to the overall story. Toto looks as adorable as ever! -- as do all of our other favorite friends in Oz. 
 I believe there are 14 books in the whole Oz series, and I intend to continue down the yellow brick road and read all of those sequels too. 
 The bottom line? A delightful fantasy tale.

This book leaves you with some serious questions: 
 Is there any reason that the Hammer Heads are the way they are? Why do they live on that hill of sharp rocks? Why do the dolls live in their little porcelain country and become stiff and senseless when carried out of it? Is that the natural state of dolls, or is there some enchantment placed on the space that allows any dolls brought there to come to life? The milkmaid is milking a china cow, but there is no mention of milk being involved, even when the cow knocks over all and breaks off its own leg like some bovine Rumpelstiltskin. Do any of them actually eat or are they just imitating life? 
 Why does the witch die because Dorothy splashes water on her? Does that mark on Dorothy's forehead really protect her from harm on its own, like an invisible barrier that stops them in their tracks, or could someone actually harm her and its up to the good witch to smite the wrongdoer, & everyone's just too afraid to risk it? Everyone talks about the powerful charm on the shoes, but if all they do is act like supercharged Seven League Boots (which, worse than the boots, fly off in the walking) why doesn't the Wicked Witch just snatch them - what else do those shoes do? 
 Annyyyywayyyy...... 
 I remember hating this book as a kid, slogging through the beginning again and again, only ever making it through to Oz's departure on his balloon. I'm pretty sure I've never actually read this book all the way through. 
 That said, I do have really strong memories of vividly imagining Dorothy's first stop to spend the night at one of the Munchkins' houses. Reading it now, I'm not sure how I came to imagine so well, since this book lacks pretty much all detail but the ones you don't need. 
 There are some really serious things that happen in this book - like a couple of scenes of slaughter, where each of Dorothy's companions take turns killing wolves, birds, and bees, and later where the Lion beheads a sleeping Shelob - no, wait - Aragog - oops, dang it - spider that were really kind of shocking. That and Dorothy's slavery to the Wicked Witch of the West - like so many kids books, the author puts in the adult material but writes about it with all the care and emotional impact one would give a slice of toast. I would enjoy seeing a more faithful adaptation of this that explores the frankly dark and gritty side to this story rather than brushing it off as some child's dream. 
 I am actually rather puzzled that the Judy Garland movie with the ruby slippers and all decided to make it all some sort of dreamland at the end. This book and the sequels (I think) insist on this world being an actual place, and the end of the novel shows that Uncle Henry rebuilt the house because the first one flew away, guys.

Thanks to Ray Bradbury's forward, I now see that Oz and Alice in Wonderland are polar opposites. Alice is cold and snide and full of morality lessons, but Oz is warm and genuine and purposefully free of morals. Both are great books, but I only felt good after reading Oz. 
 After growing up on the Hollywood version of the story, I was in for a treat to read the real thing--not the condensed and re-written version. Baum's version is a bit more violent and includes many more scenes involving all 4 quadrants of Oz and many more characters, such as the Queen of the field mice and the China village. There is a lot less mention of the Munchkins and a lot more for Dorothy's traveling companions. Baum also uses the many characters of the book to help solve problems and challenges that come up. Hollywood only used them as clowns. 
 I still have a soft spot in my heart for the Munchkins and the Ruby Red slippers, but now I think I prefer the original.

I knew two things going into this, One, Baum's book would be profoundly peculiar. It's phenomenal success upon publication leaves many modern readers bewildered. Two, I would have to expunge from my mind all images of the film, one of the greatest works of the Hollywood studio system ever made. 
 The peculiarity starts with Baum's introduction to the 1900 first edition. He mentions that the time for the "winged fairies of Grimm and Anderson" has passed. I have not read much Anderson, but I have read the Grimm brothers and I do not remember a lot of winged fairies in their often gritty tales. He goes on to describe the "blood-curdling incidents devised by their authors to point a fearsome moral to each tale," and says that his story is written "solely to please the children of today...with the wonderment and joy retained and the heartaches and nightmares left out." It makes me wonder if he ever read his own book. 
 Page one describes the drought-stricken Kansas prairie where Dorothy lives with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry. 
 The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass...even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else. 
 Ah, the wonderment and joy of it all. 
 But of course Dorothy and her house are quickly whisked away by a cyclone and land in Oz, crushing to death, upon landing, the Wicked Witch of the East. Everyone knows the story. She has to find the Wizard, she meets up with the Screcrow, the Tin Man, and the Cowardly Lion, etc etc. Many adventures, the Wizard is a humbug, but things work out in the end. 
 Baum's pedestrian prose adds little to the book that must have been such a phenomenal success because of the inventiveness he brings to the fantastic residents of Oz. The story is also, in contradiction to Baum's introduction, very bloodthirsty. Dorothy and her friends are sent to kill the Witch of the West. The lion beheads the forty wolves sent to destroy them, leaving their bodies in a pile. The flying monkeys pull out all the Screcrow's straw and toss his clothing into a tree, 
 There are several political interpretations of the novel, but I thought of it in religious terms. (Bear with me.) Oz the Great and Powerful is a total sham, a low rent traveling magician. When he gives the scarecrow brains, the Tin Man a heart, and the lion courage, he is putting on a hollow show. But it works because they believe. He then disappears into the sky. Igmar Bergman could have done a lot with this material. 
 And although I said I wasn't going to mention the movie I have to say this: It naturally streamlines the story by leaving out some extraneous weirdness, but the most remarkable transformation is in the nature of the flying monkeys. Generations of American children remember the flying monkeys as the first truly terrifying things they ever saw on film. In the book, while they are under the control of the Wicked Witch of the West, they are terrifying, but for the last third of the book, once Dorothy gains control of the the golden hat that controls the monkeys, they get her and her friends out of every serious scrape they find themselves in. Ah, wonderment and joy, just like Mr. Baum promised.
this is so different from the movie. a lot of things were left out.

It was fun to revisit my favorite story.. And I truly think this book deserves a second (or first, or fifth) read. Tin Woodman, Scarecrow, Lion idea was really adorable. Book: This Savage Song 
 Author: Victoria Schwab

 I loved this setting...A world where monsters roamed few and two cities at odds with each other. The song that described each of the monsters was simply stunning and I was just in love with the world. Sadly, the unique world of this book was not enough to save it. I was simply bored by the characters and only found myself interested when we got to see the world being built. It was just simply dull. 
 Kate is one of our main characters. She is your typical young adult lead. She is supposed to be a strong and will do anything to get what she wants, even if it means burning down her old school's chapel. She wants more than anything to return home. However, she is not a nice girl and seems to prefer to bully her way to the top. There is a fine line between being a strong, role model like character and an insurgent jerk. Kate does cross that line and I just didn't care for her attitude. She is just a bad character with no sense of inner strength. Inner strength is what I'm looking for in my characters. 
 August is supposed to be our male lead and he's a monster. Well, he is supposed to be the one who readers are supposed to fall in love with. I thought he was kind of boring. He's the tortured soul type, but we just don't get any emotional vibes off him. Hearing him whine about how messed up his life is did get old after four hundred pages. 
 I think the major downfall with the characters and the story was there was no emotion. This book has a lot of character, but it just doesn't come across well on the page. Victoria is a very good writer, but she is just lacking that emotion that makes for a good story. Everything was just too dry and cookie cutter and that is just not what I'm looking for. 
 I really did like the beginning of this one, but it just did not hold my attention for the entire story. It's kind of like Snow Like Ashes for me. Some of the book was good and other parts were just a struggle. 
 Oh, well, off to the next one.

In the future, America has fractured into territories, named after character traits, and values, such irony. Monsters exist in the real world, in cities and towns, brought forth by violent crime. V-City is the setting of our story, and is divided in two, each side run by a different family. The Harker side keeps its own monsters branded, and people pay for protection. The Flynn side fights monsters and patrols the streets to keep crime in check. 
 Kate Harker has finally come home after getting kicked out of her fifth boarding school; the daughter of the Boss, she just wants to prove herself to her father and be a family again. August Flynn goes undercover at the same school as Kate, to keep an eye on her and get information. August is not a true son, because he is a Sounai, a monster who feeds on souls of the wicked, but he just wants to be human. 
 So this sounds like a Romeo and Juliet set up doesn't it? But there is no romance, and Kate and August are enemies., at least at first. It's a series starter that I like very much. I'm curious to see how this plot plays out. The ending is satisfactory but the epilogue sets up the next book nicely.
