A truly monstrous novel that reminds us that sometimes the real monsters are not really monsters at all. One of the best YA fantasy/sci-fi novels I have read this year, 4.5 stars. 
 There are lots of books that ask questions about what it is to be human. Exploring what makes us uniquely 'us' has been a favourite question of authors for hundreds of years and will be for hundreds more. What This Savage Song brings to the table is a desperate urgency to answer that question that will keep you turning the pages long after dark. 
 "It was a cruel trick of the universe, thought August, that he felt human only after doing something monstrous." 
 Our protagonists, Kate Harker and August Flynn are the children of leaders on opposite sides of a divided city besieged by monsters both within and without. The starting point for understanding the monsters in this tale is to ask yourself what would happen if the phrase "Violence breeds violence" was taken literally? Acts of violence manifesting as monsters. It's a brilliant premise, and one which is executed with finesse. There is an air of repressed violence about every single scene, as the threat of it, and an even greater than usual understanding of the consequences of it, hangs over everyone's head. 
 "But Kate didn't need salvation; she simply needed out." 
 I loved both Kate and August, and was cheering for both of them, hoping that Schwab might leave just a little light in the darkness of this novel for each of them to hold onto. Kate in particular was a great character, and one which I will be recommending to teens who are looking for strong female leads. She is the epitome of fierce, flawed and afraid, and she does a lot of learning and growing throughout the novel, which I can't rate highly enough. 
 August meanwhile is one of the most beautiful characters I have read recently, he is so filled with hope despite all the that world has taught him. There isn't a teen out there who can't identify with his thought that "He was just someone who wanted to be something else, something he wasn't." We all want to be what we are not at one time or another, and learning to embrace who we are is a constant struggle no matter our age. 
 "...most people want to escape. Get out of their heads. Out of their lives. Stories are the easiest way to do that." 
 Given the title, it's obvious that music forms a central element to the plot of This Savage Song. What I didn't expect was for the descriptions of music to have quite so much power. They are woven throughout the narrative and give the world both its light and shade, and there is something compelling about using music as a weapon. 
 "...beat of gunfire and the melody of pain and the world was made of savage music" 
 I loved this book, and I can't wait to read the sequel. Victoria Schwab's writing is a joy to read, and as she says in this novel; "Nobody gets to stay the same", least of all readers of This Savage Song. 
 Suitable for ages 13 and up, warnings violence.

2.5 stars. I'm not sure I've ever been in a situation like this before with any book... I did not enjoy this story, but at the same time can't deny that this really is a good book. It just wasn't for me. The quality of this book should get at least 4.5 stars, but I'm going to start with that disclaimer and then give it the rating of my personal opinion instead. 
 "We each have a song. A piece of music that belongs only to us, something we're born with, like a fingerprint." 
 Victoria Schwab is an incredible writer. There really is no denying that. She creates amazingly real worlds with complex characters that are fascinating to read about no matter what they're doing. It took me over two months to get through the first 20% and I almost called it a DNF at several other points, but the writing was so good that I had to see this book all the way through. 
 This was not a fun story. It's a gritty dystopian world with characters who reminded me of much darker versions of Lila and Kell. There is no romance or fun adventure here, though. There's honestly not much that happens plot-wise in terms of events, either. It's more just getting to know August and Kate as characters and seeing where they stand. 
 Verity City is split into two sides and Kate & August's fathers each run one side. There are actual monsters and August is one of them. He's one of the three known Sunai, so Kate wants to turn him over to her cold, ruthless father in order to gain his acceptance. 
 "The Corsai fed on flesh and bone, Malchai on blood, and whose it was meant nothing to them. But the Sunai could feed only on sinners." 
 I guess I didn't realize the book's genre going into it. I just saw the author and was sold. I'm really not big on post-apocalyptic/dystopian worlds (especially ones that are lacking in romance & lighthearted adventure). I want to read about something fun instead of stressful betrayal in a bleak, hopeless world. But even though I didn't necessarily like the story or setting, I was still invested in Kate and August as characters. That alone should show how strong the writing is. 
 This is by no means a bad book; it just really wasn't something I found remotely fun. But I can easily see most of my Goodreads friends giving this 5 stars because of the amazing worldbuilding and complex characters!!! So many people are going to absolutely adore this book... but it just wasn't for me. 
 Thank you to the publisher for sending me an ARC!

I remember Schwab stating that this was the strangest book she'd ever written. This book features: a world where monsters are real, but the worst ones look human and feed on your soul; a human girl who wants to be as ruthless as the very monsters that terrify her world in order to win her father's approval; and a monster boy who wants nothing more than to be human and for the world to be peace. It's an urban fantasy with a mob/syndicate-esque organized crime sort of government. I absolutely loved that the epithet for this book was from Vicious, Schwab's first adult novel. 
 This story is set against a backdrop of a world at war with itself. This boy and girl pair, of course, come from opposing cities. I think it's interesting that in the end, it's almost impossible to differentiate between the humans and the monsters. Greed can turn humans into monsters and compassion can turn monsters into humans. I love the way Schwab uses music - normally appreciated as an art - as a weapon, as something that can cause fear and horror. 
 I've only read Schwab's adult fantasy novels, so this was my first experience with YA from Schwab. For me, Schwab's books have always held a crossover appeal between adults and young adults. She's a rare talent in this world, and I hope we'll continue to see these levels of ingenuity as she continues to share her stories with the world.

I tried with this one. I really did. But I think I might be in the minority here when I say that this was the most interesting book I did not finish. 
 I don't know if it was that we're thrown into the story too fast, with little explanation of the setting, or that the explanation comes much too late, or that I found the male protagonist a tepid bore. All I know is that this had all the elements of a good story, but somehow missed the mark. 
 There's a lot going on in the backstory - maybe too much. A lot has already happened before our story even begins. There is a city, Verity, rent into two, each side controlled by one family. There are monsters surrounding this city, but even halfway through the book, we don't really know where the monsters first originated from. One of the families is led by a man who seemingly controls the monsters/demons, and in doing so, makes people swear fealty to him in exchange for safety from them. The other family, their rivals on the other side of town, hunts the demons that creep into their domain. 
 This is a simple enough concept, but it is not delivered that way. There's just a lot of detail crammed in sporadically, almost in a way where you are expected to get through it without a lot of it making sense at first, and though it does eventually make sense, I feel that it actually began to distract from the current plot, and even worse, from the protagonists. If that makes sense. 
 The protagonists...were not all likeable. Both come from one of the rival families, Kate from the side controlling the demons, August from the side fighting them. When we first meet Kate, she's setting a church on fire, which I thought was daring and intriguing. Kate is trying to get home to Verity, and her method of choice involves getting expelled from every fancy boarding school to which her dad sends her. The daughter of one of the families running half of Verity, Kate is calculating and clever, and probably the only reason I kept reading. Kate is willing to do big things to get her father's approval, and though she is nowhere near as bloodthirsty as she pretends to be, she tries. 
 August though, is kind of an overemotional sissy. I don't want to use that description, but a lot of his chapters made me want to stop reading out of sheer frustration with him. He mops and broods continually about how he doesn't want to be a monster, how his life is hard, etc. etc. Even though his whole backstory is actually really interesting, his personality absolutely kills it. 
 I will say this. There are some truly intriguing side-characters around our protagonists. August's siblings, for one. Both of them are badass but significantly less inclined to brooding. Well, one of them is presumably evil incarnate, but at least he kept me awake. 
 I think there was supposed to be some romance here, but again, there was zero chemistry between Kate and August. Maybe it was my dislike of August, but I just could not see them together. Which made it hard to care about their whole family rivalry being a problem. 
 Another big hurdle for me: I'm not sure where the plot was heading. Presumably to some all-out battle between the families, but I could have surmised that just from the West Side Story-ness of this. I didn't understand it any more than that. It seemed to meander in two directions. In one, Kate's dad is trying to take down the other family by killing off their three monster kids. In the other, August's family is...protecting people? Sending August in to infiltrate the enemy by pretending to be a high school kid, seduce Kate...and then what? Kill her? Use her as a bargaining chip? Maybe I missed the endgame, which is likely because my eyes started glazing at multiple points. 
 In short, great premise, but the delivery just made this seem too drawn out to continue. The too-late arrival of an explanation for the setting, the slow meandering plot that was further hampered by me trying to still figure out why things were as they were in this world, and the utter lack of real chemistry between the protagonists just made it too hard for me to bother finishing this. The sad thing is, I see the raw potential of this story, I really, really do. So maybe it's just me. 
 TLDR: not for me. Maybe for someone else, though.

reference_books.title: The 100 (The 100, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Full Rating: 3/5 
 I think the fact that I watch the TV show actually kind of worked against me here. The book wasn't bad--it's definitely a quick, easy read--but its just not as complex as the show. I still love the premise, and the book definitely did add some interesting things about life on a spaceship. But, This book is very relationship-based, which sometimes was very interesting but other times was a bit boring (especially when the show had me expecting epic battles). Bellamy and Octavia's backstory was my favorite; it had the most depth and was the most compelling. The Glass and Luke plotline had some interesting points, but it also felt like the kind of forbidden love story I've read a thousand times. Plus I'm just generally against teenagers proposing. And while I liked Clarke as a character, the way she yo-yoed between Wells and Bellamy got on my nerves. Overall this book was decent--it just didn't quite have the action I wanted from it.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades Darker (Fifty Shades, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Full Review Here: http://likeakidinabookstore.tumblr.co... 
 Real Rating: 0.5/5 
 Truth be told, I really didn't start this book thinking it was going to be any good. Yet, it still managed to be worse than I expected. 
 All the characters were unbelievable (especially Jack, Leila, and Elena). Anna (and her subconscious and inner goddess--*head-desk*) were as indecisive and repetitive as ever. The attempt to delve into Christian's psychological problems was laughable. And, the new love struck Christian was even more insufferable than the creepy, controlling, dominant Christian of book 1. 
 Plus, the implication that a man hard set in his ways will change for a woman he met a few weeks ago made me want to cry. 
 Don't even get me started on that stereotypical, soap-opera ending. Like wtf? Really? I just cant. 
 I could basically go on for days just listing out all thing things I found wrong with this book. So I'm not even going to try. 
 In fact, I'm just going to focus on the only positive thing I can say about this book, which is that E. L. James can still write a pretty hot sex scene. But, the fact that Christian goes vanilla and they still have sex every few pages, meant that even these scenes became repetitive. After awhile, they were actually boring and they definitely did not come close to making up for the rest of the novel, which was either eye-rollingly mushy and/or stupid. 
 Basically save yourself the time and trouble. This book is barely even worth skimming. I do not understand how on earth this series got so popular. There are much much better books out there, even if you're looking for something unabashedly smutty.

reference_books.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
reference_books.review_text:
Full Rating 4/5 
 This was my first time reading one of Dick's books--and honestly I've had very little experience with the genre in general--so I wasn't really sure what to expect. For the most part, I was pleasantly surprised. The premise and characters were interesting and compelling, there were plenty of thought-provoking scenes, and the beginning was even pretty easy to read; the plot flowed easily from one point to the next in a logical and exciting progression. However, this book does take somewhat of a weird turn near the end, in such a way that I'm not entirely sure I understand what really happened. Like, can someone just explain how Mercer just kept popping up at the end? Were they all just delusions, or was it something more? And what was with Rick's Mercer-filled trip to the desert?! I feel like I could take a college class on this book and still not catch all of the intricate symbolism. But, I also feel like that's a mark of a good book. Overall, this Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep was interesting and a relatively accessible introduction to the genre, but I'd definitely recommend reading it with someone else, because you'll want to discuss everything that just happened.

Etta and Nicholas were believable, relatable characters, and it was not hard for me to get invested in their fast-paced lives. My only minor complaint is their romance did start a bit insta-lovey. But, as they continued to interact, there relationship became more and more compelling. Plus, the making out was pretty hot. Overall I found this book unique, exciting, and romantic, and I can't wait to see where Bracken takes it next!

reference_books.title: The Assassin's Blade (Throne of Glass, #0.1-0.5)
reference_books.review_text:
I was torn over whether I should write a book review for this, because, on the one hand it really is just a series of novellas, but on the other, it has the length and feel of a full on novel. In the end I decided I needed to say something... so here it goes! 
 Basically my two major thoughts were: one, how the hell did Celaena ever become a notorious assassin? I mean seriously, I have yet to see her successfully assassinate a single target. While at the same time I have seen her make stupid mistakes, get caught tailing someone, completely misjudge people, and almost die. I believe in her ability as an assassin even less than I did during Throne of Glass--and that's saying something. 
 My second thought was: this is just too long. Normally novellas are just a short break from the main story, not an entire novel in themselves. And, I found that I could do without having read most of it. 
 Don't get me wrong. I absolutely adored learning more about Celaena and Sam's romance. In fact I think I may like Sam more than either Chaol or Dorian. He was just so sweet and kind and wonderful all while still being a bad-ass assassin. In fact, I believed Sam as an assassin way more than I ever did Celaena. What happened to him was also totally heart wrenching and nearly brought me to tears. 
 I also liked getting a bit more context for Celeana's life in the assassin's guild. Although, I now have a newfound and intense hatred for Arobynn. 
 Really, this book is almost worth reading just for the Chaol and Dorian cameo in The Assassin and the Underworld. 
 But, I basically could have done without everything else. I hated The Assassin and the Desert. It was just completely cliched and predictable and did little to advance the story. (I mean really? an exotic master that teaches her a fighting style based on animals? Now where have I seen that before?! Not to mention the impossible-jump-on-horseback and the-sword-so-close-it-cuts-her-hair scenes). The Assassin and the Healer also added very little, but at least that one was short. I think if I were to read it again. I would skip those two entirely. 
 In the end, I'm still happy to know more of Celaena's background. I just wish it didn't take 400 pages to do it.

reference_books.title: The Thousandth Floor (The Thousandth Floor, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Full Rating: 3/5 
 Anyone considering reading this book for the futuristic aspect of it should probably just walk away now. The plot mainly consists of money problems and teen drama, and 90% of it could have been exactly the same even if it were set in present day. Most of the future tech is cliched anyhow, and some of it barely makes sense. However, if you don't really care about world-building and petty romantic drama is your thing, you have a chance of actually enjoying this book. It follows a whole host of different characters like an all-teen Love Actually, and there are definitely a few interesting storylines and poignant moments. Yet, I personally found many of the characters highly unlikable, many of the situations contrived, and many of the romances rushed. Avery's storyline was by far the worst offender, and none of the others stood out as being particularly fantastic either. As a whole, the quick pacing and variety of plotlines/characters ultimately tip the scales more toward entertaining than terrible, and the ending created an interesting enough situation that I will most likely pick up the next book, but I wouldn't tell anyone to go out of their way to read this story.

reference_books.title: Hollow City (Miss Peregrine’s Peculiar Children, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Full Rating: 2.5/5 
 This book disappointed me. While Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children felt unique and magical, Hollow City felt cliche and contrived. Jacob and Emma's relationship either bored me or made me want to gag. The new peculiars introduced felt one-dimensional, underdeveloped, or just unoriginal. Wow. I just finished the book, but I think I'm going to be absorbing it for a while longer. It was quite wonderful. I really liked how Zusak tells the story from Death's point of view, complete with gallows humor and a quaint way of speaking which made me view everyday things a little differently. Liezel's story would have been touching and powerful on its own, but having Death as a narrator brings this book to a whole new level. I liked how that perspective made the reader react a little like the characters themselves: even during Hitler's insanity, there must have been moments when life was fun and hopeful and perfect, but only for a brief time. Before they could get too comfortable, Death would come around again and the harsh reality of Nazi Germany would drag them down once more. Highly recommended.

This is one of those novels that I put down after a few chapters, came back to it later, and I'm SO THANKFUL that I did. I admit that the unusual narrative technique threw me off at first, and I nearly lost interest altogether if it hadn't kept popping up on my Goodreads update feed. 
 But after giving it another try, I have concluded this might be one of the most rewarding literary experiences I have ever had. The last few chapters -- and even the very last line -- of this book will stay with me for the rest of my life. 
 I have no idea how the film version turned out, but regardless, absolutely everyone should read this book. While that mandate might evoke some of the constructs and real events depicted within the novel, the world might be a better place if people acknowledged the truths learned by the narrator that are so obvious (and tragic) when you just sit down and think for a second.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? I'm a little divided about the cover. The title is mostly what caught my attention, and while the dominoes now make more sense than they did before reading the book, I still don't quite get why it was chosen for the cover art. Hmmm. 
 Characters: Death as a character is a concept that doesn't always work, but I liked him quite a bit in The Book Thief. He made for a very interesting and surprisingly good narrator, and I enjoyed his odd sense of humor. While never truly a direct character in the story, he was perfect for seeing the events through his eyes. Hans Hubermann, Liesel's foster father, was my favorite character. I loved his easy, quiet manner and gentle teasing. If I could have an ideal uncle, I'd want Hans Hubermann. Rosa, on the other hand, took me a while to get used to. Verbally abusive, rude, and sour, I didn't much care for her form of affection, though in the end I did come to like her a bit. I loved Max and Rudy and of course Liesel. Rudy had a defiant streak and Liesel was spunky. She didn't always behave well, but she always felt horrible afterward; it was hard not to forgive her. 
 The Romance: Rudy and Liesel have a bit of a childhood crush on one another, though neither would ever admit it. With so much going on in this book, it never takes forefront. 
 Plot: This is a character-driven book. Many things do happen, but there isn't a main plot. When Max arrives at the Hubermann home, it is definitely a turning point in the story, but it is only one of many in Liesel's life. The Book Thief goes from 1939 to 1945, and follows Liesel's time in a little town outside of Munich. We meet the people who influence her life, witness the events that change it, all through the eyes of Death, who takes an uncanny interest in Liesel for many reasons. Liesel is forced to leave her home and her mother when her father is arrested for being a Kommunist, and when her little brother dies on their way to Himmel Street, where they are to live with the Hubermanns, Liesel turns to book thieving for comfort. She can't read, but there is something about books that she cannot resist. Life with the Hubermanns isn't easy. They are barely able to feed themselves, and Hans Hubermann isn't exactly in agreement with the Nazi Party. But Liesel likes her foster father and she makes friends with a neighboring boy, Rudy. But every once in a while, she still feels the need to steal books, and she soon finds herself taking them from the bonfires and the mayor's house. When a Jewish man shows up at Himmel Street one night, seeking refuge with the Hubermanns, Liesel discovers someone she can share her books with. But Max can't stay forever - not with the war looming ever closer to Himmel Street. Despite the lack of definite plot (because again, Max and even the book thieving is only a small part of the story), I couldn't help but be drawn into The Book Thief. The characters are interesting, I love the era, and the narration style is just so unique and emotional. This is a feels book, and I definitely had a lot of feelings going through me as I read - sometimes laughing, but mostly sad. 
 Believability: Nothing to complain about. 
 Writing Style: First person, past tense. Though every once in a while, Death would kind of start talking in present tense. The narration took me a little while to get used to. It comes across as choppy at first; Death doesn't have a linear way of thinking. He will jump around quite a bit from one event to another, and sometimes this event has happened before that other event. But in about 50 pages, I got used to it, and was able to follow Death's thought process. And I must admit that I really enjoyed it. His dry, dark sense of humor and sometimes bizarre metaphors and similes added an extra layer of bleakness and emotion to a topic that is already very bleak and emotional. 
 Content: 15 s-words, 8 g--damns 
 Conclusion: The Reader will see the end coming fairly well in advance, because Death keeps dropping hints. But it still hit me very hard when I finally read it. I was a little stunned, and for a moment I debated whether or not it completely ruined the book. What was the point, after all, if that was just going to happen? But I honestly liked it, though I cannot exactly say why. I just did. I first tried to read The Book Thief when it initially came out. A story about a young girl who steals books during Nazi Germany sounded like the sort of thing I would love. But I couldn't get into the narration and I thought it was a little too weird, so I didn't pick it up again until recently. The movie is being releases soon, after all, and I hate seeing movies without reading the book first. Now that I'm older, I was able to enjoy The Book Thief a whole lot more. It is a little odd because of Death's narration, and it can feel a tiny bit slow. But I honestly didn't want to put it down, it captivated me so thoroughly. And what exactly it was that captivated me, I'm still not entirely certain. The characters were good, the era was good, the narration was very interesting, and it was an extremely emotional read. But I can't say that the characters were my absolute favorites, or that this was even the best WWII novel I've ever read - or even the most emotional read I've encountered. And yet, there was something about it that just stuck with me. The opening lines and the ending lines will always stay with me. 
 Recommended Audience: Girl-and-guy read, better for teens seventeen and up, and adults. Anyone younger than seventeen probably won't stick with it for long just due to interest level. Fans of WWII, Holocaust, and emotional novels will like this.

The Book Thief is an extraordinary book. Narrated by Death, it chronicles Liesel Meminger's life from 1939 to 1943 - the time in which she lived with her foster family, the Hubermanns, in Molching, Germany, a suburb of Munich. Liesel is not Jewish, but an incredibly reluctant member of the Hitler Youth. Her daily life, at the start of the war, continues in much the same way as life before and after the war. She plays soccer on the streets with her friends, she attends school, she reads books, and she delivers laundry for her foster mother. But as the war progresses, her life changes in the ways one would expect a young German girl's life to change due to war - rationing, air raids, knowing people who have been drafted into the army, etc. 
 However, Liesel's story is not the typical WWII era narrative as it is, on the surface, the tale of the ordinary German, not very sensational or particularly moving. But Liesel is a literary powerhouse of a protagonist. Her brother dies and she copes by stealing a book - a book from which she learns to read. And learning to read, that changes the course of her entire life. 
 It was an interesting choice, on Markus Zusak's part, to have Death narrate the book - it adds a sense of foreboding but also a tone of almost "hyper-reality" - giving a voice to the one fact that we all know but don't like to confront - everyone dies. Death is exhausted by World War II, between the soldiers, the Jews and the civilians, he's exhausted. But Death is touched by Liesel, the girl who seems to see him and a girl he encounters more times than he believes he should (I use "he" because I listened to The Book Thief and the reader is male). 
 Personifying Death takes away the fear, Death narrates the book like Liesel's old friend, not as an inevitable outcome and I believe that makes Liesel's tale all the more profound and moving. My words are inadequate in describing the suffering Liesel endures but Markus Zusak does so with a great love for her, for all his characters. Throughout The Book Thief, Liesel is moved herself by the power of words and though she starts as an illiterate child, she quickly becomes a voracious reader. She recognizes the power words have, the words that stay with us long after they are spoken or read and she learns some valuable life lessons from her words and the words of others. Death reveals the outcome of the book long before the final pages but that doesn't make the end any easier to accept. While not a direct story about the Holocaust or a novel of expected and imminent danger, the outcome is heartbreaking and completely, harshly real to Liesel and the reader.

"Earnest, pretentious and over-rated. I can see the attraction, but it's not for me" 
 That was my initial review. But now, having re-read it, I'm of a slightly different opinion. Zusak does really well at showing the sense of panic and confusion faced by the German People during the Second World War, a perspective not often seen. His characterisation and plot is superb. But I just wish he didn't use that stupid 'death-as-narrator' device. It ruins anything. 
 If you want truly great Holocaust literature, read "Schindler's Ark". If you want truly great experimental fiction, read "If on a Winter's Night a Traveller". The problem with this book is that these two genres don't work as well together as Zusak obviously hoped.

I wanted to love this book. When I read the first few pages I thought I would. Sadly it did not meet anywhere close to my expectations.  I also found some of the descriptions odd. Where I thought the book was supposed to be about a girl who saves books from being burned, she only does that once! The other books she stole was from a kind woman who was in debilitating depression from the loss of her son, and this is after Liesel chews her out for being in depression.

If it wasn't for the last 100 pages or so, I don't think I would have enjoyed this book as much as I did. I spent most of the book trying to find some sort of an emotional connection with Liesel, but I found it difficult. Thankfully, by the end, I was finally able to feel it, and I now want to re-read to pick up on all of the little things I had missed the first time around. I have two small complaints with this book. First, the length. It's a hefty story, and at over 500 pages, it's a lot to sort through. I would not recommend this to anyone who isn't much of a reader. While some bigger books are fluffier and a quick read, The Book Thief definitely is not a quick read. My second complaint is that Death is pretty cocky, and while I get that it needs to be mentioned, it got old after awhile to hear how fantastic he is that he's able to pick up so many souls. Fantastic characterization, because it was very believable, but at the same time, I wanted to punch him and say, "We get it already! Now move on!" He reminds me of one of those people who gets a new car/house/relationship/baby and that's the only thing they want to talk about because they have nothing else going on. Still, I would definitely recommend this book to anyone who's not afraid of a challenge.
I enjoyed the story. I hated the prose.

The Book Thief has many of the common elements of a World War II narrative. There are children trying to grow up, to learn, to form friendships against the backdrop of hate and cruelty. There's a Jew hiding in the basement. There's the inevitable violent end of the Nazi regime, followed by confusion and guilt. But this story is told from the perspective of Death as he encounters, again and again, a little girl by the name of Liesel Meminger. 
 I've noticed that books written for young adults seem to be, on average, so much better than books written for adults. They tend to be more imaginative, better written, and far more thought-provoking. The Book Thief is no exception. 
 Like most books written about World War II, there was no lack of horror. There were times when I had to read through tears. There were also times when I laughed out loud. I found the characters to be very compelling and I truly cared about what happened to them. The writing style was fantastic and the gimmick of having Death be the narrator, which could so easily have become absurd silliness, was actually well pulled off. 
 I highly recommend this book for the young adult crowd, and I think that us old fogeys would do well to read it too.

Oh my. This book. I find it very unique because a lot of Holocaust stories revolve around the Jews. Everyone thinks that all Germans were part of the Nazis. I'll tell you that the Hubermanns were related to them but rarely agreed. I never even thought of what the Germans felt during the Holocaust until this book. I always had sympathy for the Jews. 
 Needless to say, I am a huge fan of learning more about the Holocaust. 
 This book is so beautifully written yet simple to read. It is more of a morbid read just so you know. This book withholds a deep meaning but the deep meaning is also uncovered on the surface. If that makes any sense. 
 Such a beautiful read. You do have to dedicate your time to this book but you will not regret it. A guarantee. 
 Personally, I consider this book a classic. Hopefully, it will be considered a classic in the future so that young readers may enjoy. 
 Also, this book is marketed as young adult but I believe that any age can read this. There is no explicit content (besides German swearing), but you younger readers, it is a bit dark but not too dark. Let's just say there is light at the end of the tunnel.

I think this is a fantastic book for young adults to read that deals with World War II in a very real and appealing way.

Reading this for my daughter who teaches 6th grade. Only about 1/6 of the way. Good writing and an interesting narrator, but don't think this book is for 6th graders. 
 Well on page (I would tell you, but I can't find the book!), I have had to put The Book Thief aside. While I found it interesting, it has taken too long to read.

I picked up The Book Thief three times. The first two times, I didn't even make it past the prologue before I put it back down. Sure, I heard good things, but it just wasn't grabbing my attention. There were other books to read, ones that were more interesting at the time. But I always heard great things. Not a bad word about The Book Thief was to be heard. So I tried again. And once again, it was boring at the beginning. So the narrator is "Death".... big whoop. It's something a lot of people found fascinating, but as someone who reads/has read a lot of fantasy, it's not that hard to believe. So that wasn't a hook for me, but I stuck it out. Made it through the prologue, at long last. 
 And found myself really enjoying the book. I've come to find the narration style engaging. I like the bolded sections. It makes it clear that the story is not being told first person, it feels almost as if I'm listening to a bedtime story, or sitting around a campfire. I keep getting frustrated, though, as Death skips forward in time and then doesn't explain himself (Death sounds masculine, to me. But hey, I could be wrong). 
 As for the plot itself, it is interesting. I've read a couple of novels about the holocaust before, fiction and non-, but nothing quite like this. It even took me a little while to realize the time period it was set in. We see the remains of the Jewish area of the town, but there is no talk of actual violence, and instead more focus on this little girl-the book thief-and her daily life, growing up in a foster home and learning to read and write. 
 It dragged on a little. I had to put it down for a day or so. But since I picked it right back up, it obviously kept me sucked in. It was interesting. At times it was cute, heart-warming even. But at others it was tragic, made all the more so by the knowledge that even though it is fiction, it might as well be true. That and much worse happened in the years leading up to and during WWII. 
 But I truly enjoyed it. Somehow, though I didn't love the narrator, and wasn't always captivated, the story drew me in, played on my empathy.

I'd heard mixed things about this book, but I have to say that I loved it. It was brilliantly written, and I fell in love with the characters and their stories. The idea of a book written by Death was just too interesting to pass up, and while I was mildly irritated by how the narrator revealed the ending of the book ahead of time, by the end I really didn't mind so much. It still had the same effect on me - which is to say, I cried my way through the last forty pages or so. This was definitely worth a read, and I thoroughly recommend it.

*Death narrates this beautiful tale of Liesel, a young girl, who has lost everything, but finds a home in a small community on Himmel Street with her foster parents outside of Munich, Germany during WWII. Death is fascinated with Leisel because she brushes Death three times in her life and he is interested in her life. The Book Thief is the story of Leisel's three brushes with death. 
 Liesel begins her "career" after her brother dies and she steals The Gravedigger's Handbook from by his grave. His death, on the way to being taken to live with foster parents because her parents are in trouble with the Nazi party because they are communists, is something that haunts Leisel forever. Soon after, Leisel gets dropped off at Hans and Rosa Hubermann's home and never sees her mother again. However, the Humbermanns are the beginning of a large number of people that make a huge, loving difference in Leisel's life; as well as a number of books that make an impact in her life. 
 Just a warning: This book made me sob. It did make me smile, laugh, and think as well, but there was definitely sobbing as well.
What an AMAZING book. There simply aren't any words for me to say.

I hate to leave a book unfinished. I really do. But, after 200 pages in which absolutely nothing interesting happened, I decided I'd given the book enough of a chance and now I was done. Which I really wouldn't have expected of a novel for teenagers, since with teen/YA books, even if they're long and even if they're not a great story, they tend to be fast-paced and easy to read. That was definitely not the case with this clumsy, plodding narrative. 
 When I was considering reading this book and I heard it was narrated by Death, my first thought was that that seemed gimmicky. But, people seemed to really enjoy this book and I'm a big fan of historical fiction, so I decided to give it a try. 
 I should have trusted my instincts. Not only does the narration-by-Death not really work here, but as a narrator Death is horribly annoying. Even more than boredom, it was annoyance that made me give up on this book. 
 Our ever-so-irritating narrator is continually interrupting the flow of the story with random explanatory paragraphs, which for some reason are center-aligned and written in bold. 
 Interruption by Death 
 Fun Fact Time! 
 1: Lemons are a type of yellow fruit. 
 2: This boy's hair was the colour of a lemon. 
 Also, for an ageless, presumably all-powerful being, Death seems to have an unusual penchant for clumsy symbolism and metaphors that sound like they came out of some angst-ridden high school kid's poetry journal. I mean, how many different metaphors do you need to employ to describe the colour of the sky? 
 Another irritating quality of our narrator is excessive foreshadowing. I mean, truly excessive. At one point, I was reading a scene where Liesel was grabbing a book from a fire and I thought it had already happened earlier because it had been described in pretty clear detail once or twice already. (To be fair, I had been speed-reading through some of the particularly tedious chapters to get through them faster, so I'm sure I missed some details). 
 On top of the foreshadowing which is essentially just telling you what will happen ("heads up, Liesel's going to steal another book at the end of this chapter! Keep on reading!"), there's the cryptic, vaguely poetic-sounding fragments spread throughout the books. They're nice-sounding words, but without actually knowing what's going to happen you don't really know what the heck they're going on about. A little bit of that is fine, but this book had great long multi-page series of vague clues and obtuse references that I basically tended to skip over because they were PAINFULLY BORING. It's the kind of thing that might be enjoyable in a re-read of the book, when you actually know what incidents are being referred to. Or if, unlike me, you actually care enough to analyze five pages of clues to try to guess what's going to happen. 
 And then there's the awkward, choppy sentence fragments. Because apparently the author thinks that's deep. Poetic. Sentence fragments are. Very good writing. Beautiful. Like a breakfast coloured sun. And a dark chocolate sky. Not just chocolate. Dark chocolate. 
 ...zzz... 
 {jolts awake} 
 Hm, sorry about that. Where was I? Oh, yes -- I don't like this book. Naturally, my review should be taken with a grain of salt because I didn't read the whole thing. Maybe it gets really good later on, though nothing anyone has said has been able to convince me of that. All I know is that, particularly since the last book I read was vaguely disappointing, I really don't want to suffer through this one anymore. I'm going to go try to find a book I enjoy now.

The Book Thief by Markus Zusak 
 Alfred A. Knopf, 2005 
 550 pages 
 YA; Historical 
 3.5/5 stars 
 Source: My sister bought it and now I have borrowed it. 
 Summary: (from goodreads) 
 "It's just a small story really, about among other things: a girl, some words, an accordionist, some fanatical Germans, a Jewish fist-fighter, and quite a lot of thievery. . . Set during World War II in Germany, Markus Zusak's groundbreaking new novel is the story of Liesel Meminger, a foster girl living outside of Munich. Liesel scratches out a meager existence for herself by stealing when she encounters something she can't resist-books. With the help of her accordion-playing foster father, she learns to read and shares her stolen books with her neighbors during bombing raids as well as with the Jewish man hidden in her basement before he is marched to Dachau. This is an unforgettable story about the ability of books to feed the soul. " 
 Thoughts: I saw many rave reviews of this before I started reading it so I had high hopes. Alas I must be an exception for while I can see the strengths of it, it didn't work for me. 
 I liked the idea of Death as narrator but Zusack's Death isn't as good as Terry Pratchett's Death. I liked the idea of a young girl in Nazi Germany. Despite the popularity of WWII in film and fiction, I still feel as if there isn't as much in YA (in general I feel like there isn't much historical fiction in YA at all). Another problem was that despite the little moments in the book, the overwhelming feeling I got from it was depression especially as Hitler and the Holocaust are referenced frequently. I know the Holocaust was an awful event and I do not want anything of that kind to ever happen again but I personally had trouble handling that aspect. I also didn't like the use of German, followed by a rough translation of what was said-I found it annoying, perhaps because I have studied German and didn't always need the translation so it was like having something repeated to me. 
 My favorite part was the descriptions of books and the joyful experience of reading. Liesel certainly needed some good in her life and I think book bloggers will appreciate those passages. The ending did make me cry. The death all around was too much and practically everyone dies. 
 Overall: While I recognize this as a book that is kind of book that wins awards, I didn't particularly like it. 
 Cover: The dominoes are a good choice for the cover.
Incredible. One of my favorites. It felt so nice to reread it, to revisit the characters, like Liesel wished she could've. A must-read

Bookclub read. Rating: 3.5 stars. 
 So, how do I review this book? I am torn because I really liked the story but in some parts it was a little tedious. I think the problem for me was the author's style of writing. I found the layout sometimes distracting. Too often I needed to re-read passages to keep my mind on the storyline. Yet there were times where I was totally engrossed. 
 The story is narrated by death, which is original. Death is prevalent in World War II and so "he" is busy collecting souls throughout the novel as "he" presents "The Book Thief's" story to the reader. 
 Leisel Meminger is the book thief. Her world is Nazi Germany. We follow her life over a few years from when, at only 9 years old, she is taken to her new home in Himmel Street Molching. Her foster mother Rosa Hubermann has a foul mouth, but as the story progresses, one realizes that deep down, she is a decent human being. Leisel develops a special bond with her foster father, Hans Hubermann. He is a sensitive, loyal and caring human being who does not approve of Hitler's propaganda. Her foster family do not hate Jews and are not followers of Hitler, although they must frequently put on a facade when in public, for their safety. 
 Leisel's life revolves around the relationships she builds with those closest to her, her desire to learn to read and write, and her fascination with books which are largely condemned and burnt by the Nazis. Rudy Steiner is her neighbour and a fellow school student who becomes her best friend and accomplice thief. He is always teasing her about receiving a proper kiss from her, something she does not yearn for until it is too late. Leisel befriends Max, the young Jewish man whom her family hides in their basement. The town's mayor's wife Isla Hermann, who allows Leisel to "steal" books from her library, also develops a friendship with her. 
 Leisel's relationship with Max highlights the fact that, regardless of age, gender, race, colour or religion, we are all human beings and we can uplift or destroy each other through words and deeds. Words can be used to instruct, encourage or destroy. Max shows Leisel through the book he writes for her, that words are like seeds which are implanted into peoples minds and they can be used to breed love or hatred. 
 The suffering of the local people when the "enemy" planes bomb Germany reminds the reader that there are no victors in war. Innocent people suffer on both sides of the fence. 
 Overall this book was a good read. The Holocaust was a terrible time for humanity. Unfortunately, even in today's world people are still swayed by extremist teachings and are taught to hate and kill each other. Will human beings ever learn from past mistakes?

Full Rating: 1/5 
 THIS BOOK MADE ME SO ANGRY. One does not read a series like this for the writing, because in all honesty, a child could write prose with the same level of finesse and imagery (or lack there of). One reads a series like this for the entertainment factor--for shameless romance and fluffy action. And because of this, it tends to make one irrationally angry when said series devolves into ridiculous, thinly veiled Christian propaganda. Not only does Higgins imply that consensual sex before marriage taints the soul (a somewhat harmful notion to be pushing onto impressionable teens), Anna's biggest challenge in this book is a literal test of faith and the big epic battle was won by, again, literally praying the bad guys away . So, as someone who is not particularly religious, I found most of the book preachy and anti-climactic. Even the things I enjoyed from the first book were ruined in Sweet Reckoning! I liked for the most part Kaiden and Anne's relationship; their chemistry was believable and compelling--until they rush straight into marriage JUST SO THEY CAN HAVE SEX. Not only that, but Anna is ridiculously dumb about the whole thing, believing for one hideous moment that even sex after marriage would taint her soul (which is not just dumb, but harmful for sooooo many reasons). And after they're married, it seems as if all Kaiden wants to do anymore is have sex (to the point that they make excuses to leave family gatherings just to do so)! ARRGH. Not to mention the whole supremely rushed debacle that was Marna and Jay's relationship. Or the fact that Anna and her "allies" literally never did anything to plan or prepare for their impending battle against evil. OR the fact that Anna can drink to drunkenness and lead others astray, and still be considered "pure" but having sex is out of the question. OR the fact that their supposed all powerful weapon, the sword Anna must stay "pure" to wield, is never used to kill a duke. OR that Patty dies for basically no reason as Anna could have started the whole praying-the-evil-away business AT ANY TIME. Basically, this book was not entertaining enough to forgive it's blatant and at some points harmful preaching of Christian ideals, and at this point, I'm sorry I even picked up this series in the first place.

So I've had to find out the hard way that the conclusion to the Sweet trilogy is nothing but a sappy, melodramatic piece of trash that's hardly worth reading - except maybe for hardcore fans of this series. But even if you do make it through the agonizingly bad writing, be warned that your nerves will probably be in hell. 
 So you might wonder what happened between this absolutely amazing, gritty debut and the end of the trilogy? Well looking back now, the first book was the only one with a remotely interesting story line and character development - the rest was just the drawn out showdown of a deus ex machina scenario that could easily have fitted into the first book, but apparently the author insisted on milking as much money from this cash cow as possible. The thing is, I wouldn't have minded had she at least been creative about it and given us something remotely interesting to read about - but no. The solution to 'the problem' had been here all along - Anna just needed to pray. And no, I don't fucking count that as a spoiler because the author told us that from the beginning. So what kept her from praying at that first summit in book 1? Don't ask me, but it sure as hell would have spared me some nerves. The only other excuse the author maybe had to continue this series was the love 'triangle' but that got resolved so quickly that I cannot take this excuse seriously. The second book was already pushing it in my eyes because the plot was seriously lacking, but the third was was juts a cry feast - happy people eveywhere, everything's perfect, and you even begin to question yourself why the hell am I reading this if the author cannot even come up with a proper conflict? This plotless, over-the-top-sappy Breaking Down wannabe doesn't even deserve to call itself book. 
 Moving on to the themes dealt with in this book (again, note the similarities to Breaking Down here). 
 First, teenage marriage. So let's clear up one thing: no matter how much you think you are in love with your boyfriend, it's not a good idea to marry him at 18. And I'm not even saying that because 'you can't say if you really love him at such a young age' - that's bullshit. I'm saying that because at that age you still have so much to learn and so much to see that you will be missing a whole lot of crucial experiences if you've settled down already and bound yourself to another person in such a way. And you'll be missing those experiences later in life. 
 Next teenage pregnancy - another topic that's greatly romanticized in YA novels. Ask yourself honestly: How thrilled do you think a teenager will be at discovering they have an unplanned pregnancy, considering they are not quite grown up themselves, would like to go to college (you know, have a life), and are lacking a husband or a steady income to provide for the baby? What basically all YA authors fail to see is that teenagers simply aren't ready at this stage to have a baby. You can't take care of someone else if you don't know how to take care of yourself yet. So cut the bullshit and spare me the oh-I'm-a-pregnant-teenager-but-I-still-absolutely-love-my-baby because that's not how it's going down in real life. In real life, it's either abortion or your parents and priest pressure you into having this baby because an abortion is a sin or whatever. As a matter of fact, I can't remember ever reading a YA novel where any teenager has ever gotten an abortion. Because that's a taboo in our society- but society fails to realize that in some cases sparing the baby of growing up with a teenage mom who never wanted them in the first place is the better solution after all. Don't get me wrong, I don't support abortions, I think you should use contraception and use your brain to prevent such scenarios, but just don't write such bullshit about how great it's to be a teenage mom. Because it sure as hell isn't. 
 So cutting a long story short, this book is messed up in so many ways that I've lost count. I really can't recommend this horrible conclusion to an otherwise good series with great potential to anyone except maybe hardcore fans of Breaking Down who can overlook the major issues. I have to say I'm majorly disappointed in this author, and will probably stay away from her in the future. This series could have been so much better, but this conclusion left me with a bad aftertaste.

An advance copy of this novel was provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review. However, this review is based on the audio version borrowed from my local library. 
 This review can also be found at The Starry-Eyed Revue. 
 After loving the first book in this series, I had high hopes for the end of it. But after the somewhat disappointing sequel last year, I was hesitant to finally get to my copy of this novel. Which is why I ended up borrowing the audiobook from my library a couple of weeks ago. And maybe that was also a mistake because this book was narrated by Erin Mallon, same as the others, and though she does a great job of making Anna sound all sweet and Southern, Anna shouldn't still sound so naive. She has a higher purpose, a calling, and yet I still found her so annoying at times. 
 And I know I'm going to get beat over head for this, but I much preferred when Kaidan was denying his feelings and acting a right arse toward Anna. I did like the genuine sense of togetherness in this final installment, with all the Neph working in tandem to defeat the Dukes, but I think because of that, the banter and general fun have gone out of the series in favor of the impending battle between Good and Evil. I get that that's where the series has always been headed, but the tone just changed so much between the three books. 
 There are some seriously shocking twists in this final book, and it's loaded with action and tension and everything that a series finale should include. But I just didn't connect with the story in the same way that I did Sweet Evil. I wanted to...I wanted to go back to loving the dynamic between Anna and Kai and the other Nephilim, but it felt a little forced to me. I also dislike when premarital sex is made into such an issue, and though I understand why in this particular instance, I'm still frowning at the result of the whole ordeal and why it was necessary to begin with. 
 The romance also seemed especially cheesy this time around, probably because of the aforementioned issues and how everyone else seemed to be coupling up, too. The stakes were high, too, in this last book, and yet it still didn't feel like enough. I can't really put my finger on it, but it just lacked that certain je ne sais quoi. 4.5 to 5.0. I really liked Sweet Reckoning. I liked it so much that I read the whole book in one evening. I just couldn't put it down. Without spoiling anything, there were a couple of unexpected surprises that I know some people will not like, and at points, I was even skeptical. Some will say that everything was too neatly tied up. I would definitely recommend reading the Sweet Evil Extras (especially 2.1) on Higgins' site prior to starting this one. They added to the believability of the situations. 
 Plot: 
 After Flynn's murder, the Nephilim know that the dukes suspect a traitor and that they need to prepare for a war. Anna is the prime suspect, so the dukes try to trap her by proving that she is 1) not working, 2) still a virgin, and 3) still tries to do good. They even involve Kaiden in their plan. Through it all, Anna knows her purpose, and she becomes more determined to protect everyone and ensure that good triumphs over evil. 
 Characters: 
 I really liked Anna in this one. It was nice to see that even though she had the occasional doubt, she tried to remain positive. Some people might be critical that she believes that she has to maintain her virginity in order to be considered righteous. Having read the Bible and having been raised in the South, I see why Higgins chose to go that way, but I do understand both sides of the issue. Oddly, I was actually bothered more by Anna's constant desire for alcohol. 
 I can't say enough about Kaiden (swoon!). He was a changed man in Sweet Reckoning. He finally admitted his true feelings at the end of Sweet Peril, so throughout this book, he was able to express himself and the way he felt about Anna. There were a couple of times he had me worried, but all in all, he was amazing. 
 The other Nephilim - Marna, Ginger, Blake, Kope, and Zania - returned, as did Patti, Jay and Belial. It was nice to see that all of these characters supported Anna and each other. There was a little bit of drama between Marna and Ginger, but as a character, Ginger made amazing progress in this book. 
 Obviously, the Dukes return, too, and most of them are grosser and more disturbing than ever. They make perfect villains, and I love hating them. 
 Writing: 
 I had to re-read the first two because it had been a while. I had forgotten how much I enjoyed the series. Higgins did an incredible job of drawing me in and making me feel what the characters were feeling. Also, and I know this is more of a "thing" for me than for others, the books are really well-edited. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 There is a war, and sadly, it's not without casualties. A couple of the losses made me really sad, but in the end, everything happened that I wanted to happen. The epilogue really solidified some of the choices that Anna made, and it was interesting to see how the different relationships played out. While I am so happy to get some closure on the Duke/Nephilim conflict, I'm really kind of sorry to see this series end. I will be honest.... When it comes to books, I'm not usually a crier, but my eyes even started watering at the end.

 So yeah, I was very apprehensive starting this. I love Kai and Anna and I wanted them to be able to be together, to love one another openly and lovingly. I wanted them to have their happily ever after.

Paper towns by John Green... 
 I've always heard about the endless rave of John Green's books, especially "Paper Towns". 
 Since I have never read any of John Green's work, I decided to start with what most people claim is his best work and that is Paper Towns, but for some reason I didn't feel like I wanted to spend money on this (even though I buy ALL the books I read) so I was very fortunate when one of my friends recommended it to me and gave me her copy to read! (Thank you friend). 
 So lets start with the positive things about it, I have to admit there were parts that were really fun and also quiet funny, It actually made me crack up in public a few times (and I never laugh out loud while reading, a smile will usually do). 
 I like the writer's message about the difference in personalities, and that just because you love someone it doesn't mean that you also like who they truly are inside, or that you will change for the sake of the one you love.. now I think those are powerful messages that can somehow benefit the younger, less experienced teenagers who may be confused as of what "love" really is. 
 Why did I give it 2 starts? 
 Will even though few parts of the story were fun, most of the story was actually really really boring, sometimes to the point of frustration! 
 I also thought the story was slow, and I did not like the characters at all!! I mean they were very generic and boring, I did not care for them at all, I also did not care where or what the hell happened to MARGO ROTH WHATEVER. 
 Even though the writing style was Okay, I found the writer to be trying very hard at times. 
 I am sorry but I just can't see what all the hype is about, I mean really?! 
 Probably 14 year olds who don't usually read and have never read anything better might like this! 
 I have to mention that it is only 305 pages so you'll fly through it in one sitting, thank God I didn't have to tolerate it any longer than that. I am also very thankful that I didn't spend money on this. 
 Please don't take offence, it is just an opinion. 
 Happy Reading. :)

I really wanted to love this book and ended up only liking it. Q and Margo both bugged me throughout the book, and I ended up liking the side characters more. That being said, the storyline was intriguing and I was very much looking forward to how it was going to end, but the ending just left me feeling bleh. Looking forward to the movie though!

Paper Towns follows Quentin on his journey to find the mysterious Margo Roth Spiegelman after she disappears right before high school graduation. They were friends as children and drifted apart over the years, but Q has always held a candle for Margo. She comes to his window one night and convinces him to help her get revenge on some of her "friends" with some well-planned pranks - the next day she's gone and no one knows where. But she's left a few clues for Q and he decides to follow them and on the way discovers more about Margo and himself than he thought he would. 
 What I liked: 
 I like John Green's writing style. Period. Perhaps I'm biased, but I'm not sure that he could write a book that I would truly dislike. I especially enjoy the male characters he creates and Q is no exception. He's a mixture of awkward and charming and despite having graduated high school several years ago, I felt he was relatable able and was someone I'd like to be friends with. I also liked Q's friends, and the fact that they had fairly different personalities and interests from his own - I find too often in young adult novels there's a group of characters and they're all so similar it's hard to tell them apart! They're diverse but without being your Breakfast Club bunch of cliche stereotypes - the jock, nerd, badass, etc. [Side note: I'm not having on the Breakfast Club in any way; I love that movie!] 
 I also liked Q's relationship with his parents, who are psychologists. He's a good kid, gets good grades, obeys curfew (most of the time) and his parents trust him. Yet he's not afraid to be daring, to sneak around and take a risk and he's also very honest with his parents about certain issues too. I think that once again, it's a good mix. He's not a perfect little angel, but he's not the type to hate his parents or constantly whine about how they don't understand him. I just really enjoyed Q's perspective - as much as I love reading young adult/teen fiction, I do find myself getting easily annoying with main characters. I'm not sure if this is a reflection on myself, because I'm just not in that mindset anymore, or if there aren't enough well-written teen characters out there, but Q kept me invested in this book. 
 What I didn't like: 
 Margo Roth Spiegelman. 
 I don't think I'm the only one with this mindset. Honestly, she felt really pretentious and reminded me a lot of Alaska. She didn't seem like a real girl. I'm not saying that there aren't teenage girls out there who are adventurous, mysterious, and poetic, who are able to socialize with the jocks and nerds alike, who like all genres of music and read Whitman's poetry and don't care about their looks. But I certainly never knew anyone like that, nor did I ever hear stories about a teen like this either. It also annoyed me that Q uses her full name almost every time he refers to her, although I realize this is part of how he sees her - as this amazing girl whose full name deserves to be used because she's so much more than any other girl. 
 But Q is clearly idealizing her because throughout middle school and high school they've drifted apart to the point where she barely speaks to him, despite them being neighbors. He's in love with the idea of MRS and even Q starts to realize on his journey to find her that he doesn't know her the way the thought he did. 
 This however, doesn't really change Q's opinion of her overall. He is still convinced he loves her (and maybe he does!) and he still seems to be wearing rose-colored glasses where she's concerned. I enjoyed the way the other characters grew and interacted, but Margo just annoyed me. 
 The ending also left me unsatisfied. It felt unresolved and while I realize this can work in some cases, here I just felt like I needed closure. It wasn't a very emotionally strong or moving ending and I had higher expectations. 
 Overall, if you're a fan of John Green, I think you'll enjoy this, though it's nowhere near as moving as Fault or even Alaska - but not all of his books have to make me cry, so I'm okay with this. If you've never read John Green, this might also be a good place to start. I think it's an excellent display of his character development and will give you a feel for his style. 
 For a longer review with quotes from the book, check out my blog

** spoiler alert ** 
 I'm not too sure what I expected from this book. I enjoyed the beginning - going on the adventure and playing the pranks. I ejoyed the chase - where Quentin tries to find Margo, the never ending clues and twists. What I didn't enjoy was the ending. I'm not sure how I wanted it to end, maybe with them both going back to Orlando. But I was disappointed when she decided to go to New York. Even with the promise of keeping in touch and writing... it felt too general, like Green had written this masterpiece and then run out of ideas and decided that he didn't want to continue it.

I originally rated this book a 3 out of 5 stars. With Only An Abundance of Katherines left to read, Paper Towns is my least favorite so far. I didn't think that the story was that great. I read through the entire book in one sitting. I thought I liked Quentin and his friends and I thought I liked this story, but the more I worked on this review, the more I realized that this just isn't the case. 
 First off, John Green has pretty much recycled the characters from his first book Looking for Alaska and inserted them in a new story. Alaska for Margo and Miles for Quentin. It was very hard to read about Margo dramatically leaving vague clues when she decided to run away and not think, "Yup, that is what Alaska would do." 
 We are introduced to younger versions of our main character at the beginning. Still in grade school, young Quentin and Margo are walking to the park together when they accidentally stumble upon the body of a man who had committed suicide. When I first read this my mind went "oooo!! This is cool!" But this scene contributed nothing to the story line. It was some weird prologue that meant nothing. 
 We fast forward to Quentin and Margo's senior year of high school. Although the two characters grew up next door to each other, at some point after the discovered suicide in the park, they drifted apart. I'm not sure if it's the idea of the girl next door, but Quentin has this fixation on Margo. For some reason, he fancies himself head over heels for this girl that he doesn't talk to. I feel like Quentin doesn't even try to approach Margo or get to know her, not because she has a boyfriend (although that seems to be the excuse he uses), but because if he were to express his feelings for her she would shoot him down. So he's content to worship her from a distance. 
 The only part of the book that I found 100% believable was the night of shenanigans. I completely accepted that a young man, whose life long crush crawls through his window after dark and asks him to help her with a project, would totally agree. I especially liked how Margo presented her case. Eleven tasks, no laws will be broken (serious ones, at least), live a little! However, as the tasks were being checked off, it became clear that Margo was nothing more than a manipulative mean girl. I get wanting revenge because find out your boyfriend is cheating on you with your friend. But the third fish, the one that was smashed in Lacey's car; that was just malicious. Margo assumed that Lacey knew about her cheating boyfriend, but she never actually asked her. We find out later that Lacey didn't know a thing about it. The worst part is Lacey just forgives Margo! 
 When Margo runs away, Quentin is determined to find her, which is admirable, but lost its charm quickly. Quentin becomes obsessed with finding her, with reading as far into these supposed clues that Margo scattered before she left. It wasn't the first time she's done this either. Shortly after she goes missing, a case worker shows up at Quentin's house and tells him that the last time she ran away she left the letters M, I, S, S in her empty bowl of alphabet soup. She had run off to a town in Mississippi. Her parents didn't get the message; they just cleaned the bowl and reported her missing. If that's not narcissistic, I don't know what is. 
 Then there was the flop of an ending. I enjoyed the build-up, these friends skipping their high school graduation to go find Margo. But, of the four people who are traveling to a paper town in New York (from Florida, mind you), Lacey is the only one can truly claim to be Margo's friend (and I've already stated my opinion on that definition of 'friend'). Upon being discovered, Margo admits that she didn't want to be found, that she didn't think anyone would know where to find her. Although impressed by Quentin's detective work, Margo just brushes them off; like I said, manipulative mean girl. That's it. That is the end of the book. I thought the buildup was great and then was so anticlimactic that it hurt. 
 I love YA books. I don't always like what is popular, but I love what these books are doing. With all the technology in the world today and other fun distractions, the target audience these books aim for can sometimes be hard to encourage picking up a book. I love author who can get a young person's attention and I respect an author who can influence that same young person to pick up another. I first accepted this book because it was YA. But now, after really sitting down and thinking about it, I'm going to have to say that I didn't care for this book. It romanticizes abusive relationships and glorifies the abuser. Margo may not have hit or verbally assaulted anyone, but she sure did send them into a frenzy. That is just not something that I can, with a good conscience, recommend.

Forced and contrived, I hated Margo and didn't care if they found her. The road trips were fun though. Took this long to read because halfway through I got annoyed and stopped reading, finished it because my students were yelling at me. Tomorrow, I will yell back.

This is a story about a "socially inferior" senior, who has been in love with his neighbor, Margo Roth Spiegelman, since they were children, and when she disappears, he learns a lot about her, himself, and the people who surround them, as he finds the clues he hopes will lead him to her. 
 So while I read this book within a few hours, and I laughed aloud a few times, I felt that the characters were all very flat, and that they all speak with the same voice-John Green's. The best quotes in this book are those he quotes from outstanding authors such as Walt Whitman and Emily Dickinson, otherwise I felt as though in attempting to make the novel sound "profound" John Green says a lot of things in metaphor, but none of these are indeed profound, and are actually quite superficial, and so wouldn't be, and isn't, elevating in the least. You can see where he is layering, to try and make a more full novel, but with an execution that is poorly done, it lays as flat as his characters.
