I wish there could have been more growth as far as him being pretty pretentious, an example being him at the party seeing people who were enjoying prom an senior year and parties as just paper people. Though there was the one line at the end where he was like the stuff maybe paper but the memories are real. I wish there had been more of that. And he wasn't a very good friend for most of the book. I like to think that over the summer after the book ends he improves on that too.
Waste of my sweet precious time
Didn't even want to finish it- boring and a repetition of his other stories.

Not as good as his other two books for reasons other reviews have said. I'm going to read a couple other non-Green books before I read Will Grayson, Will Grayson. So far I've read the last 3 of Green's books in row-- maybe that's the issue.

This book just frustrated me. I was literally forcing myself to read it. I was thinking "it's a John Green book keep reading". I felt it was pointless and lead to nothing. The ending was not satisfying. I felt like Q's journey was pointless and Margo was just a selfish bitch. A little annoyed that it's now going to be a film just like TFIOS (which did NOT disappoint).

Meh. I LOVED John Green after THE FAULT OF OUR STARS, which is pretty much an impeccable book, even if it is for young adults. But now I've read three of his other books (one of which I couldn't even finish), and have to say, they all pale in comparison. I think they're just too young-adulty for me, which is a bad sign, because I usually like young adult books. This one, in particular, has some kids gallivanting across Florida in search of their missing friend, and, well, I just didn't care.

I must say, this is one of the worst novel I have ever read. Though I quite like The faults in our stars of John Green, when comes to Paper towns I completely lack of interested. I found the story-line started stuck at the point when Margo disappears out of blue and Quentin tries to find where she is. Maybe if I was Q, I wouldn't do things like him, that's why I find the story-line somehow unrealistic and stupid.

I was honestly very disappointed in this book. This book had such a big build up which resulted in a very anti-climactic ending. John Green said that he wrote this book to try and break the stigma of the "female character who is ethereal and no one really knows" but I felt that in doing so, he made Margo one of those girls but even worse because she was so vague that the only things we knew about her were what the main character thought about her. The adventures that were present in this book were great, but I just felt that this work could have been executed better. John Green shouldn't have made the book revolve around Margo if he didn't intend on using her character for much at all.

Al principio por el prologo pense que era una historia de terror o algo asi, pero es la historia de un chico eternamente enamorado de una chica que es eternamente loca, unica y apasionada por la libertad. Muchas de las cosas de este libro me hizo recordar a "Buscando Alaska", porque 1) el ambiente en Orlando, estaba muy cerca del ambiente donde se desarrollo "Buscando Alaska", 2) Alaska y Margot, son muy parecidas, lo unico que las diferencia es el final que tienen las dos, 3) Los amigos de Quentin y Miles tienen como el mismo fin y las mismas caracteristicas (a mi parecer) 
 Quentin, es un chico super dulce, que piensa a cada rato en su futuro y en las consecuencias de sus actos; Margot, en cambio, es como dice antes, una loca que lo que quiere es ser libre y alejarse de todas las presiones que tiene en su alrededor. 
 Le doy a este libro un 4/5 porque al principio de la historia me parecio lento la transicion al nudo de esta y por la originalidad, no me gusto mucho que se pareciera a "Buscando Alaska", de resto, es una lectura muy buena y recomendada .

I'd been hearing a lot about this book, so I decided to give it a try, and I have mixed feelings about this book. This book was really good... for about 290 pages of it (I don't actually have the book in front of me to know if that number is correct). I liked the whole chase for Margo and her whole midnight adventure with Q, but I feel like the overall book ending was very anticlimactic. It sorta made me feel like the whole book was made for no reason. 
 I did really enjoy this book tho, and if the ending was better, it definitely would've gotten 5 stars.
It's finished yahhhh!!

I just...I don't know. Maybe I was a shallow high school kid, but I just don't think that any teenager could be so philosophical. I appreciated philosophy in high school, and had many a chat with friends over hot chocolate about philosophical ideas, but I don't think any of us ever went so far as to apply these ideas to our lives, or uproot ourselves to fulfill some abstract idea. 
 Maybe my friends were all too void of early childhood trauma... 
 Who knows. 
 At any rate, I didn't dislike this book. It was entertaining, and I loved that it gave my daughter and I something to discuss.

Whiny, attention-seeking teenager seeks validation that she is memorable. Okay, okay. So that's not far off the mark of how I recall my own teenage years...but the great Margo Roth Spiegelman annoyed me. I certainly wouldn't be driving across the globe for her anytime soon. I liked Q (in a cute puppy-doggish way)and his friends were a riot. I give this 3 stars because I liked trying to decipher the clues along with Q. John Green didn't disappoint with the Minivan-Mad-Dash-to-Margo scene. That, at least, was pretty epic.

The majority of the book is about trying to find a person who does not want to be found using clues that she leaves behind. This book felt like it was Looking for Alaska all over again, but in a bad way. Margo is a very selfish person who does not think about the consequences of her actions. The ending of the book was not what I was expecting and I did not really care for it. I can't help but feel sorry for Q because it appears that his long journey was a complete waste of time.

If I'm going to be honest this book was not good. It dragged out to much, and the ending rewind everything. Why go to all that trouble, then leave her there? I did not want to just drop the book, because who knows it might have picked up a bit. I read this thinking it was going to be as amazing as the faults in our starts, buts its not even close. It's also so unrealistic, yes I know it's a book, but still who could do that all in one night and get away with it. I'm not going into detail because I don't want to spoil it for anyone. Basically if your reading it because you like the faults, you're gonna be disappointed!
Love love love this book. This was the first book I've read by John Green and I just love his writing. I couldn't put it down I literally read this in one day.

Extremely disappointed. After reading TFIOS and hearing only great things about this book I was just not prepared to such boredom and lack of interested in the characters relationships. Q is one of the most annoying characters I have ever encountered, he is obsessed and only thinks about himself and Margo. The deeper meaning of the book gets lost, forgotten. It had everything to be fantastic but John Green got lost somewhere and wasn't able to deliver.

I'm not sure why I keep reading John Green...I guess in the hopes that the novel will be as good as The Fault in Our Stars? Well, let me assure you, this book doesn't even come close. 
 The beginning of Paper Towns was promising and I found myself liking Margo Roth Speigleman through Quentin's eyes. Actually all the characters were likable even Ben. But holy smokes! The plot! The plot was so slow and boring. By about 65% of the way in, I was like, "who cares if he finds her?! Just end this book! Get on with your life Q!"

I love John Green. No other author can turn a phrase quite like him, and I greatly respect his refusal to create novels that assume teenagers are not capable of reading about real issues they face in a frank manner, even if that includes sex and questionable language. I expect excellent work from him, and he did not disappoint me with "Paper Towns". 
 Part of the brilliance of this novel is that a teenager can read it and get an entirely different story from it than an adult who reads it. Neither are inferior to the other, it's simply that some of it is viewed differently when time removes you further from the days of high school. I literally cried from the overwhelming sense of nostalgia it created. 
 Quentin Jacobsen is the "every man" of high school. He is not popular, nor is he quite on the bottom rung of the social ladder. In short, he is smart, but average. Then there is Margo Roth Spiegelmen, the girl who was larger than life in Quentin's mind. The girl on the pedestal. Haven't we all had that person in our lives at one point or another? Of course, eventually we learn that they are just as human and average as the rest of us, and that is the point of the story. 
 The lessons to be learned in "Paper Towns" are good for teens and adults. People are not always who they present to the world. Some are better than they let on and some are worse. The best memories aren't what you think they will be. Everything has a beginning and an end. All of this is woven into a thoroughly entertaining story that is filled with humor and tenderness. I highly recommend it for those who like Green's style of writing.
Yes, his books are aimed at teens, but I find them funny and often quite profound. Always entertaining.
I liked the beginning and the end. The middle dragged.

I did not like this book much. Thankfully I got it for Christmas last year so I did not have to spend money on it. Having absolutely loved The Fault In Our Stars, I was really disappointed by Paper Towns for the reasons listed below. 
 1. The foul language. Yes I'm aware that YA books have cuss words in them but do you really need so many? I'm ok with mild curse words but I think that the one used on pg 17 that was used by Chuck was extreme. I overlooked some of the profanity used in TFIOS because the story itself was really good but Paper towns didn't draw me in as TFIOS did. 
 2. The story. The story itself is somewhat boring. It has exciting moments but there were times when I couldn't get myself to keep reading. I didn't connect with any of the characters. I found Margo to be reckless and annoying. I understand she wanted a new life but just disappearing in the blink of an eye is not the way to do it. She does not care about anything or anybody except her goals and her life. It made me mad that she almost cost Quentin his future by asking him to come on her revenge mission. It also made me upset that Quentin goes along with Margo's plan just because he is in love with her and that Q becomes so involved with Margo that he stops caring about everything else. 
 3. I found the ending section a little confusing because of all the philosophy or whatever the right word is used by Margo and Q 
 I would NOT recommend this book to a friend

Not the kind of book I expected....the story was just too dull. I just don't get what the point of writing a story of the missing girl and the author who is trying to linger on the boy's effort to locate her.
THE BOOK IS BETTER THAN THE MOVIE

I first want to state that I enjoyed this book. It was a refreshing break from all the post-apocalyptic books I've been reading lately. It was a lighthearted, quick read. However, I do feel as though the novel fell a bit short of something... it was quite anticlimactic. I couldn't relate to the characters, especially Quentin. I just wanted to tell him the whole time to stop worrying about Margo and enjoy his last month of high school with the people who truly mattered! I just didn't enjoy this novel as much as I wanted to. I fell in love with everything about The Fault in Our Stars, and I was hoping to fall in love with Paper Towns as well. If you're looking for a novel to cleanse your reading palate, or something you can finish in less than two days then I would highly recommend giving Paper Towns a try.
A very fast paced read, I was genuinely interested in the mystery contained within the novel and I loved the main character Quentin. I also liked his friends Ben, Radar and Margo herself.
I did not like this book. It was too much empty teenage angst for my liking.

Georgie and Neal's marriage is in trouble. When he takes their daughters to his family for Christmas, she tries to call him and ends up talking to him 15 years earlier, right before he proposed. I am a sucker for timey-wimey-ness, so I really liked the premise. I struggled because while the writing was engaging and the characters felt so incredibly real, I didn't much care for Georgie, or 1990s Neal. I sympathized with her, mostly, and it's so easy to see how things slowly fell apart in spots, but I found it hard to like her. I did like her parents and Heather a lot, though. (And mentally cast Andrew Rannells as Seth, which automatically made me like him.) 
 I felt bad for Neal because although she so badly didn't want to trick him into proposing, she did, because she was able to have open, emotionally mature conversations with him that her 23 year old self could never have had, which essentially promised him a relationship that wouldn't actually develop for another 15 years. But he also got to start their marriage with more knowledge/security in their relationship than she did. I liked at the end that she noted nothing had actually changed, and wouldn't until they actually talked now, because grand gestures are so often a cheat to a happy ending. Seems like they'll figure it out from there, though, and that was the perfect ending.

Erm, I don't know about this one. I loved everything I've ever read by Rainbow Rowell up to this point but I was not a fan of this character or storyline. I wanted her to calm down a lot of the time. I wanted her to be less obsessed with her husband and I wanted her to use a phone to the past to do way cooler things than revert to teenagehood and be needy. 
 Not a fan of this particular book but will still look forward to other reads by Ms. Rowell...

I read to the obligatory first 100 pages and had to stop. Georgie gets a shot at a her dream job as the writer for a new comedy show, but is under pressure to deliver four episodes under a tight deadline. To do this she has to drop out of the family's planned Christmas to the in-laws and the hubby is in a snit. He passive aggressively won't call or answer his cell. I kept wondering what this story would feel like with the gender roles reversed. Then Georgie starts using the magical landline. Really liked Fangirl, but this one was just annoying.

I think I'm too old to read these type of books anymore. It was entertaining, I guess, but there really wasn't anything memorable about it, plot or character-wise. Generously giving it 3 stars because it managed to get me out of a tiny reading slump after a couple of super busy weeks!

I love everything by Rainbow Rowell, and I think this new one may be my favorite. Some of her books are YA and some are adult. They are all essentially romances (though I don't think they are classified as such) but are a bit more literary in style. This is one of the adult ones. 
 It's about an already-married couple whose marriage is struggling. She's a TV writer, writing cheesy sitcoms but also writing an original show with her writing partners and trying to get it picked up by the networks. Her husband stays at home with the kids and is frustrated by her long hours and always putting work first, and he's jealous of how close she is to Seth, her longtime writing partner. 
 They're about to head off to his mom's house in Omaha for Christmas when a network shows interest in their original show, and they need to write 4 episodes over Christmas break in order to be considered. This is her dream come true--maybe--and she feels she has to stay home and work over Christmas instead of going to Omaha. The husband is furious and takes off without her, and the book takes place over Christmas week, while she's away from her family, trying to furiously write, and wondering how to save her marriage. 
 This is a very real conflict. So many families struggle with this, whether it's the dad working the long hours or the mom. I really identified with this book. George and Neal truly loved each other; I never doubted that they did, but the book raises the question, is love enough, when you can't make your lives fit together? 
 On top of that, neither of them are perfect people. Georgie clearly is too focused on work (for understandable reasons, since it's hard to make it in Hollywood, and writing an original show is her dream). And Neal has his difficult traits: he's passive-aggressive, he stonewalls, and he tends to be negative in that he seems to hate a lot more things than he likes. He won't even watch Georgie's sitcoms. But he has so many good traits that he's absolutely worth fighting for, and Georgie knows it. 
 Adding to the complexity is Seth, Georgie's writing partner, who seems to be of critical importance to her career in that they write everything as a team and are more creative when the other is present, but who is toxic to her marriage. He's possessive of Georgie and tries to monopolize her time (often successfully) while engaging in a parade of one-night stands with other women. Georgie had a crush on him for a while, but wisely realized he was never going to be in a relationship with her, so she fell in love with Neal instead. But Seth insults Neal, calling him a hobbit (he's 5'6") and just generally being mean, and yet Georgie is not really in a position to stop working with Seth since they make a great creative team. 
 This is a moving, compulsively readable, and often funny book (I laughed out loud in places). I loved it.

Considering I read Eleanor & Park first, I was supremely let down by this book for the sole reason that I just didn't like the characters. None of them were people I would have liked being around if they were real, and because I couldn't really root for any of them it drastically reduced my enjoyment of the novel. 
 Summary: Georgie McCool is afraid she is about to lose her husband when she stays behind during Christmas to work and he and their two girls go back to Nebraska to visit his family. 
 Where Landline comes from: A really convenient magical phone that just happens to work right when Georgie needs it. Do we question it? For all of two seconds, then we move on. Would this have worked just as well as just a story about relationships without magic phones? Yeah. 
 Why Georgie's marriage is in shambles: Neal, her husband, is still a fucking teenage boy in the early 2000s. He's all angst and judgment. Nothing is good enough for Neal, and his way of showing that he appreciates something is to tell you he doesn't hate it. All he needed was skinny pants and eyeliner and he would have fit the bill perfectly. I never once saw anything in him to make me believe Georgie could have fallen in love with him, so the entire marriage seemed like a rickety setup. 
 How it's resolved: It isn't. At all. We are quite literally right back where we started, with no resolution, no conversation between the characters to even TRY and solve it, nothing. Instead we have way too much time inside Georgie's head while she does "what if" scenarios over and over and over again. 
 I'll try Fangirl next, see if I have better luck there.
I couldn't even finish it :/
Different from her other books. Not great not terrible, but still as well paced as everything else she's written.

I liked it.. but it was kinda depressing. Could be the narrator of the audiobook, who had a low, soft, slow voice... could also be the book itself. It wasn't a sad ending.. just a depressing book. It was still interesting enough that I'm going to read other Rainbow Rowell books.

There was a lot of hype surrounding this novel so I thought I would give this author a try. She has previously written two beloved YA novels Fangirl and Eleanor & Park which I have not read. The premise of this novel is that Georgie McCool is able to talk to her husband in the past on a rotary phone during a time when they are having marriage troubles in the present. Georgies husband Neal has gone to Omaha for a Christmas vacation along with the couples two daughters. Georgie was supposed to have gone on the vacation but she got the break of a lifetime at work writing her own sitcom and has to work through the vacation much to her husbands annoyance. 
 I read the book straight through without putting it aside so the story did keep me engaged. The problem for me is that I could not stand Georgies husband Neal. He is described as short and miserable but for some reason Georgie who has so much going for her is madly in love with him. Neal is always miffed about something concerning Georgies career and he is threatened by her writing partner Seth even though they never engaged in a romantic relationship. Personally I don't see what the big deal was about skipping a family vacation to Omaha but apparently it is a deal breaker for Neal. Neal by the way has no career of his own because he could never get his professional life together. He is a stay at home dad which is fine but he does not seem very supportive of the bread winner Georgie. I get the author's point that family should come before career but in this economy you do what you have to do to keep the money coming in and sometimes sacrifices have to be made and one parent has to step it up so the other can make money. I think Neal was unfair to Georgie and it tainted my enjoyment of the story. The magical phone was an interesting plot device. It took Georgie back to the time in the relationship when they were the most in love. Even though Georgie loved Neal with all her heart she finally had to face the fact that she couldn't change who she was and past Neal would have to decide whether he could accept her as she is. I think that is the take away point from this book. We try to be our best selves for the people we love but we are who we are and the people in our lives have to have a certain amount of acceptance. You cannot change your partner only the way you chose to deal with them. Anyone in a long term relationship will probably find a lot to relate to in this book. Everyday life problems have a way of eroding your tolerance for your partners quirks and it is important for couples to remember why they came together in the first place.

I love Rainbow Rowell, but I did not love this one. Just could not get into it, way too drawn out, not very compelling, didn't really like either of the main characters. I'd still pick up anything else she did without hesitation though!

What I wanted Attachments to be but it still fell short for me. I think she's a wonderful writer who is trying to cover up weak plots. I didn't especially like Neal. They both seemed like hot messes. I did like her talking about being a parent though... I think I just want to listen to Rainbow Rowell talk about stuff and not necessarily have to make it cohesive.

Like every Rainbow Rowell novel, I want to shout "Must Read" when I finished it! I loved the magical realism in this very realistic depiction on a marriage and family on the brink of falling apart and how much we need a landline to help us find out way home again. Great women's fiction that's beautifully and thoughtfully written.

What an empty, unfulfilling book. 
 Look, I can empathize with a character who pours too much into work, who prioritizes work life over personal life. I've done this at times in my life (and one could argue that I'm doing it right now as I'm in the middle of a 14 day work trip). But Georgie as a character is fairly unlikable. She takes her husband for granted, despite loving him, and acts like she has no choice but to ignore her family. No choice! If you want to prioritize your work over your family, the LEAST you can do is own it. 
 And at the end, she abandons her commitments to Seth and Scotty to make a last minute grand gesture for her family. YES, she should've prioritized her family more, but screwing over your business partners (and friends!) is unconscionable. The solution is not grand gestures. The solution is keeping your family top of mind and not committing to things you can't/shouldn't commit to. 
 The fantasy elements of this are so boring and reminiscent of the terrible movie, The Lakehouse. THE LAKEHOUSE. Ugh.

Rainbow Rowell's fourth novel is a fun romantic comedy with a time twist that makes it even more interesting. The characters are instantly loveable and one you jump in, it's hard to put down. Rowell's stories are like marzipan on a Saturday night, delicious and almost sinful, but you just can't get enough!

Crisp writing. Elegant, HILARIOUS! Emotional gut-punch. A haunting meditation on long-term love that left me wide-eyed in the middle of the night, talking over the book with my partner...hoping he'd help me figure the angles on the MC's tale.

Because I adored Fangirl, I wanted to love this book. I clamored to get a galley at the Book Expo. I was intrigued by the premise of Georgie being able to have conversations across decades, to talk to herself at a younger stage, through her landline. I was game for some teenage awkwardness, some comedy, and some perspective 
 That wasn't what this book was. 
 Georgie McCool is a television writer, whose dream of launching a sitcom is about to happen. So she and her best friend, Seth, are digging in and working for hours on the scripts that they have to finish to give to the network exec for their big break. Georgie is married to her college sweetheart. They have two adorable daughters. They are also having a rough patch in their marriage. Complicated by the approaching Christmas holidays and the TV pilot deadline. 
 Ugh, there was so much awkward and so much misery in this book! Georgie spent so much time moping over her husband and their relationship... and, honestly, I wasn't getting him as a love interest at all. He comes off as a jerk, and he and Georgie come off as not terribly well suited to each other. Which, I guess is an interesting way to play the romance setup, as a "should they even be together?" 
 So, on some level, set against the usual romance trope, I appreciate this as a counterpoint. 
 And there were a couple of moments where I laughed. 
 But, mostly, this was not the book for me.

Taken from my Save The Date on the blog (full review to come later) 
 Why You Should Be Saving The Date for Landline by Rainbow Rowell: 
 1. Rainbow Rowell continues her trend of being able to write poignantly and candidly about all sorts of love: Every book of hers I've read (all but Attachments) just perfectly captures some intricacy of love in different stages/forms and all the beautiful messiness that comes with it. I loved that, while this was partly a story about a love going wrong, it's also a story about falling back in love and remembering the first time you fell in love with that person as well...especially in the face of maybe losing it all. She makes love just come alive and feel true. 
 2. GOD HER WRITING: I just love how Rainbow Rowell writes and Landline is no exception. I love her dialogue. The insertion of some humor. How it makes me feel. And these beautiful sentences that just make you stop in your tracks. I even read a passage to my husband and I NEVERRRR read him things from what I'm reading. 
 3. Lots of thinking re: my own marriage and really any relationship that's important: It's easy to be complacent and take people for granted. To not try harder to keep your love ignited and fall into bad habits. I'm early on in my marriage and things are wonderful but this was such a raw and honest portrayal of how one day you could wake up and be in a place you don't want to be in your marriage because little by little you let it slip away. 
 4. She just keeps proving she can write anything: This is her 2nd adult book and 4th book total and everything of hers I read is so wonderfully different and I never know what to expect with her but each time I fall in love in my own way with the book and the characters. They are the books that linger for me and keep me up at night. 
 5. She makes this THING work: There's an element to this book, how Georgie communicates with him in the past, that COULD be super corny and she just makes it WORK. So well. Never felt corny. 
 Who Should Save The Date: Rainbow Rowell fans, people who also read adult fiction, people who like love stories that are a bit messy but beautiful 
 A Sneak Peek: "You don't know when you are twenty-three. You don't know what it really means to crawl into someone else's life and stay there. You can't see all the ways you're going to get tangled, how you're going to bond skin to skin. How the idea of separating will feel in five years, in ten -- in fifteen. When Georgie thought about divorce now, she imagined lying side by side with Neal on two operating tables while a team of doctors tried to unthread their vascular systems" (this is taken from the advanced copy and could be subject to change)

Really amazing book didn't think I was going to love it as much as I did. I love the magic that is thrown in there so good and I love all the relationships that are intertwined. I have always thought about how parried couples where once like dating...which I know is dumb like duh they dated but it's weird to think about how a married couple was once just a single person...I don't know it's weird. I absolutely sped though this book in one day and i look forward to reading more of Rainbow Rowell's books soon!

I just really wasn't feeling this one for some reason. It's not like it was horribly written, it was written very well, but it just felt too...Hallmark? too Lifetime? I don't know. I found the ending incredibly corny, absolutely nothing about what Neal was up to in Omaha (I mean...was he doing anything with Dawn? Old Neal wouldn't do anything with Dawn...but would new Neal?). I would have just liked a little scene where they just discussed their problems. Nothing seemed very...resolved to me. What was the magic phone? Why? Was Georgie following the timeline or did she change it? I STILL HAVE SO MANY QUESTIONS!!!
Cute, just like all of rainbow Rowell books, and Ioooved the Cath and Levi cameo<3

I am probably in the minority here, but I could not get into this book. 
 I read all her others; devoured "Fan Girl" in a way I haven't devoured a book since I was a teen. 
 The blurb sounded exciting and different. A woman, whose marriage was on the brink because of her job, figures out a way to talk to her husband in the past and hopefully this will help fix their relationship. 
 By page 50 this really hadn't happened yet. I found myself skimming most pages where info was dumped on me. I didn't really care how she and her co workers moved up into the sitcom world, I didn't really need to know how Georgie and her husband chopped their cheese quite loudly. I think most of this background info could have been spread-out throughout the book or given away in conversations between her and her past-husband. 
 This story moved slowly and was boring most of the time. The writing was not as mature or exciting as "Fan Girl" or "Eleanor and Parks". I feel like Rowell has the pulse of YA/New Adult better than the adult fiction genre.

With this premise I thought this book was going to be a bit ridiculous but I loved it. Read it in 4h (a great way to not start this important project I should be working on). It might be my favorite from this author so far.

More reviews at www.nikkithereader.tumblr.com. 
 Georgie's marriage is falling apart. Neal, her husband, has promised his family, who lives in Omaha, that their whole family will be there for Christmas. But Georgie has a lot of work to do at home and she stays where she is, despite the fact that she thinks it may make things worse. After Neal and their daughters leave, Neal becomes unreachable and Georgie wonders if she has finally ruined her marriage. But, while staying at her mother's house, she finds a way to communicate with Neal from the past. Is this a chance to get her marriage back? 
 This book was kind of a mess. You get thrown into conflict almost immediately but you don't yet have a grip of who the characters are or what's been going on before this conflict. Eventually you get flash backs to tell you what's been going on, but it's still jarring to start a story out like that. 
 It was also pretty predictable. I could tell what was going to happen and what the plot line was going to be even without reading the description. Not to mention the main characters are kind of boring. Especially Neal! Ugh, he's like a robot the way he's written. He doesn't show emotion, or speak with any certain tone of voice other than barely moving his mouth. He's just very dull and I didn't see much in him. I think my favorite character was Seth but only because he had a lot of personality that made up for everyone else's mess of a character. 
 I was hoping this book would have been so much more than it was. It's kind of lame to read a really good book by an author just to have the next one be less than great.

I loved the Attachments. I liked Eleanor and Park. And I don't fully understand all the hype about Fan Girl, as I thought it was just okay. 
 I eagerly bought Landline when I saw it on the shelf (I thought it didn't come until July!), and read it in 24 hours. About halfway through, I started feeling disappointment, and that continued until the end. 
 I will do my best to write without spoilers, but there may be small spoilers: 
 I found it extremely difficult to care about and emphasize with Georgie. She vacillates between adoration for Neal (repeating his name ad nauseum, like a grade school girl, her thoughts trailing off in ellipses), then is talking about how difficult he is, how he growls in arguments and totally brushes her off. And why would he love Georgie? She's just as difficult as he is - working all the time, coming home late, constantly distracted by Seth, her "best friend." 
 Why is Seth even in the book? He serves no purpose, but to push Georgie and Neal closer together in their dysfunctional relationship. As they say, if you're going to show a gun in the first act, it better go off before the end. Therefore he serves no point. His role could easily have been filled with a female friend, except for when he's (obviously) jealous of Neal in college, and Georgie is too oblivious to notice. So what's the point?! 
 I understand that Rowell is attempting to speak about marriage, and the truths of it; that once you have kids, you grow apart from your spouse, working mothers, kids are difficult, etc. But Georgie is not very relatable, and I didn't care whether she stayed with Neal or not (not saying either way). 
 I think the problem may be that I don't relate to Rowell's writing style, which becomes very stream of consciousness sometimes (such as when Georgie is lovingly thinking about Neal) or maybe I'm just too jaded to understand a sweet love story. She also tells rather than shows, through tons and tons of dialogue, that isn't believable. I keep reading her books, expecting a sweet story like the Attachments, but perhaps these expectations are too high, and she is attempting to write more "real" stories now. But other than the trials and tribulations of marriage shown in this book, it didn't ring true to me at all.

Oh GOD!!! This is an absolutely useless rant about a woman trying to save her marriage through a magic/time travelling landline phone. Just a book version of The Lake House using a landline. 
 Rainbow, saying things three times doesn't make the thing anymore desirable... 
 Hate how Rainbow "trys" to show love by using presumably "cute" words like meow-meow or Neal,Neal, NEALLLLL!!!! 
 It doesn't matter that Georgie could have stopped 9/11 from ever happening. NOOOOOO!!! She wanted to save her "marriage", absolutely a horrible novel and a waste of time. Don't waste even a minute thinking about reading this novel, it is absolute SHIT!
This was a cute and charming book, and I enjoyed it, but cute and charming isn't enough to make me love a book. Neither is the author being amazing in person, which Rainbow is.

I loved Eleanor and Park so damn much. Really, really loved. then I read Fan Girl and thought that was pretty entertaining. Landline, however, was not my cup of tea. I trudged through more than 200 pages before I had to give up; not to mention that it was only my intense love for E&P that got me past page 50. I didn't care about the characters and the dialogue felt clunky.
Rainbow Rowell has done it again. Cute. Clever. Funny. Adorable. So relatable (even with a magic phone). So real (ditto). So emotional. Love it! Meow.

Georgie and Neal are married with two children, but neither are happy in their marriage. They both are unhappy for different reasons, Neal feels that Georgie is more focused on her career and Georgie feels that Neal has changed and is not the same man that she met in college. One day, Georgie finds the old yellow rotary phone in her childhood bedroom and calls Neal. However the Neal that she calls is from the past, before they got married. 
 This is a very interesting premise and as always I enjoyed Rainbow Rowell's writing style. As a character, Georgie is likely and funny and found myself enjoying her interactions with her friends and family. I cared about her life and was rooting for her and Neal. I did at times find this book a little slow and felt that it lacked something that I can't put my finger on. I adore Rainbow Rowell and the past three books that she has written. However, this was probably my least favorite of her book, but I still really enjoyed it. 4 out of 5 stars

But then, I see Landline, and sigh at that yellow phone, and am both proud of myself for reading it in the intervening time (checking it off my to read list) and makes me a fan anew of RR. My friend Margaret Willison told me recently that you love a comedian because you trust that even when they take you on a wild journey with questionable jokes, you know they'll bring you into the light by the end of the set. After Eleanor and Park, my love for RR was solidified, and I'd go with her on any winding book journey she wants to explore. She could make the phone book interesting. Get it? Georgie McCool is torn between her career as a TV writer and her devotion to her family. Christmas is looming, and Georgie is terrified that her husband, Neal, is ready to leave her. When Neal takes the kids to visit his parents and Georgie chooses her writing deadline over her family, things hit bottom--until Georgie discovers a way to contact Neal in the past through an old landline phone. 
 This is not the kind of book I read. Ever. But I couldn't pass up trying Rowell's latest book, even if it is adult realistic fiction about a middle-aged woman in an unhappy marriage. This goes to show how much I respect Rowell's writing, and in many ways I enjoyed Landline a lot more than I thought I would. Georgie and her TV show co-writers are incredibly, lovably real characters. Rowell's dialogue practically breathes with life. Though I didn't really relate to Georgie, I do think that Rowell ultimately painted a real, aching, changing romance between two believable characters. Without the frequent connection to the past, the main plot would have been pretty boring, but between the dialogue and the interesting contrast between past and present, the pacing moved forward at a steady rate. 
 I wouldn't recommend this to teen readers, even if they loved Fangirl or Eleanor and Park, just because the focus of this novel is so much on adult problems--marriage, work conflicts, being a good parent. That said, it is a wonderful book in many ways, and a good title to keep in mind for adult readers looking for a unique story set around the holidays.

LOVED IT! So so sweet and magical! Rainbow Rowell is just such a perfect author and this one doesn't disappoint! Her writing is so fantastic and addicting. I couldn't get enough of Eleanor and Park and Fangirl and now Landline! I loved the time travel aspect and how it all came together. Christmas is known to be a magical time of year and this love story really captures it. So magical and so beautiful. I loved how there were flashbacks and we got to see how Georgie and Neal's relationship was started in the first place and all the little defining moments of their relationship. The parallel between their relationship then and now was so interesting and I loved how Rainbow Rowell connected it. I loved seeing them when they were younger and awkward around each other and how they got to being married with kids. So fun! But Georgie and Neal had a lot to work through and I loved seeing how it played out. Its about them reconnecting and Georgie figuring out what she want's in her life and remembering why she fell in love with her husband. Ahhh it was just so heart warming and cute but definitely had a sadness feel to it because it's about a marriage falling apart but then figuring out how to put it back together. I also really loved some Harry Potter references that were thrown in there and some of the silly humor like between Georgie's mom and her pregnant pug. So hilarious! Oh and OMG! CATH AND LEVI had a cameo and it was so wonderful and I got so emotional! Ahhh! Anyway, I absolutely loved every second of this book! Highly recommend anything by Rainbow Rowell! Perfection!

 This book continues the saga of the first book, during which you want answers. If you've continued to this book, you've committed yourself to another dragging plotline led by Thomas, the boring main character of this series. You get a few answers, but none that really answer the really big questions. Like what the hell is wrong with the people that decided this was a good plan? This question is never answered, but I think you can safely assume because they've lost their minds. 
 This book is more of the same as the first book, but less interesting. There is no stability to the book and new characters are introduced that ultimately do no good to the overall plot. 
 Newt and Minho are the only saving grace and the only characters you will care about at all when you're done with this book. 
 I think the thing that differentiates this book from the first book is that there is a set goal very early on in the story. Whereas the first book was kind of like an escape the room game, this is more of a survival game like Oregon Trail, only with much more random and high tech obstacles. The forced love triangle that has zero chemistry is also totally unnecessary and makes an otherwise boring book even more grating.

What I did get was the same characters that I have established no connection with interacting with some new characters that are equally not to my liking in a less interesting environment. 
 At the halfway point I was determined to not read book three even if I still had questions. My problem is I am not a fan of quitting in the middle of a story. Unfortunately I have read some pretty bad books because of this and have a feeling this series is going to end up in that category. But at this point I think it would be more irritating to give up than to waste a another few days and figure out what I want to know.

So I finished this book three days ago and I took some time mulling over what I would say. I wanted to like this book. I was intrigued by the mystery and events of the first book, wanting to know who WICKED was, what was going on with the Flare, and why they all had no memories. 
 That intrigue was lost in the this book. Dashner gives very few answers, asks more questions, and add a lot of gore to the mix. I was more angry at the characters than curious, and felt like each new plot twist was more absurd than the last. 
 This was an exciting book--the action starts from the very beginning and never lets up--but I found myself skimming way too much. Thomas's thought vary over three topics: where's Teresa (or the Gladers, when he's separated from them), how much he hates WICKED, and what does he make of Brenda. The whole book. I can't take 300 pages of the same thoughts over and over again. And the descriptions? Most of the book is spent dealing with killer lightning storms or horribly disfigured Cranks (people with the Flare). How many detailed descriptions of festering sores, falling off body parts, and crazy people do I have to read? 
 This book had so much likeability potential, but it went over the top. 
 Clean Factor: language (Dashner's swear words aren't "real" four-letter words, but you know exactly what they stand for--that's swearing in my book), violence, gore

Though this book does absolutely nothing in providing closure with the events that happened in the Maze, it does dwell on a new set of trials that the group must face. Whether WICKED is good or not is still a looming question for this book as it was in the earlier one. What's really redeeming about this book is the sense of adventure with which Dashner tackles this story telling. Agreed that Thomas does keep on getting unconscious enough times, I think the way his past memories trickles to him during this time is much more important for the plot line. Of course, in no way do those memories help him, but still, it's fascinating enough to see for yourself the relationship of the Gladers with WICKED. 
 All in all, a brilliant read and an equally amazing follow up to the series. It does the trick of keeping you glued with its twists and turn.
One word. Betrayal.

The problem with journey stories is it is so easy for them to turn into a sequence of encounters, connected by little more than the travel between them. The Maze Runner was a mystery to solve in a strange situation. The only challenge in this story is to stay alive while random bad things happen. Much of the trouble is impossible to resist: such as getting across a desert in a lightning storm without getting killed. So if all you need to do is stay alive, and there's nothing you can do to improve your odds, there really isn't any story. 
 The only mysterious bit, the role of Theresa as "betrayer" just comes across as wildly contrived. Apparently, Group B is exempted from all the trouble and danger, and armed, simply so they can stage the "betrayal," which, without giving any spoilers, all I can say is its not worth all the build up. 
 Not to mention the "seductress." Come on, please.!

I became really annoyed with the story line toward the end of the book. Like Thomas, my trust and loyalties are broken with certain characters. You don't mistreat friends like that, no matter what, even if authority figures tell you you have no choice. You find a way around it. Needless to say I am completely miffed by this turn of events in the story line. I can't trust any of them anymore. At the end, just like the ending to The Maze Runner(book 1 in the series), I was left with an Are you freaking kidding me?! feeling. 
 No matter how annoyed I am at certain events and characters in this book, I have to admit that I was sucked in from page one. It is a definite page-turner. The visuals that I got while reading were exquisite. If I had to compare this series to another series, I would have to say that it has a slight Hunger Games feel to it, though nothing can compete with my love of The Hunger Games series. This book has fighting for one's life, death, and a high-octane need for rebellion. 
 The Scorch Trials may trigger some people to have psychological grief. It contains violence, blood, death, betrayal, hunger, and disease.

Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice...well, you know how it goes. In the first book, you spend the whole time wondering what's really going on, what the kids are supposed to be doing, what's the big picture, and at the end, you find out nothing. Or, you're told one thing, but something happens to make you question it. No mystery solved. Then this second book comes along, basically the same as the first but with much more gratuitous violence, and at the end you find out nothing. Or, you're told one thing, but something happens to make you question it. No mystery solved. So now you've spent two books, like 600 pages, following around this kid, and besides four "clues" in Thomas's memory, your understanding of the Big Picture on page 600 is frustratingly similar to what it was on page one. 
 There's a lot of action. There's a lot of drama and violence and death and fear, and it gets you nowhere, plot-wise. It reminds me of Alice in Wonderland: memorable imagery independent of character development and story arc. I know I said I wouldn't continue with this series, and then I read this book, and that's my own fault. But it's two books now and so far my sense of satisfactory ending (not one that wraps everything up but I need SOMETHING) is 0 for 2.

Lo lei por pura curiosidad. Y lo odie, porque era todo lo que sabia que podia ser. De verdad me desagradan los libros que son predecibles. 
 Y me desagrada, lo vengo descubriendo recien, ese tipo de novela donde todo sale mal y cuando algo parece ir bien, paf que empeora, !y al rato se pone aun peor! No me entretiene, sino que me estresa. 
 No voy a dar ningun spoiler. Si te gusto el primer libro, este te va encantar. Yo pase al tercer libro porque lo tenia, pero casi que lo lei sin leer.
it was good. got annoyed by the end since I wanted them to be saved and not have any problems.
Didn't finish. The story got ridiculous fast. Contrived plot to torment the characters with no point or objective other than don't be the random one killed every now and then. Done with the series.
I stopped reading when I realized I was forcing myself through it. Boring. Repetitive.

My main reason for finishing this book was simply to see how it played out. This one provided more details about the world they live in, but became less interesting as the trials were not as interesting. I'm currently in the middle of the third one, and it continued along the same lines as this one.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Considering the circumstances and plot of the book, some things made no sense in terms of furthering the storyline. Namely, Teresa 'betraying' Thomas and then trying to take it back. I get that was a Variable given to her by WICKED, and perhaps Thomas would have understood it more had he chosen to get his memories back. However, it did nothing to further the storyline. Throwing Aris into the mix just created an incredibly awkward love triangle that lasted approximately 7 pages and then ended. It wasn't even as though it made Thomas stop liking Teresa and go to Brenda exclusively. THERE WAS NO POINT. Okay I'm done. Interesting book, another take on the ever popular 'I'm a teen and the world has gone to hell but more importantly two people are in love with me' archetype.
It's a bit confusing but I think that's partly because I'm remembering bits of the movie which i think ended differently.

The Maze Runner was overflowing with suspense that built up to that cliff-hanger at the end. I rushed to read The Scorch Trials ready to have my mind blown. Instead, the ticking time-bomb fizzled weaker than a flat soda. First of all, the atrocious dumbed-down writing is offensively insulting to YA readers. Secondly, I couldn't care less about the characters -- with the exception of Newt and Minho. Why ruin a post-apocalyptic adventure with vurping love drama (*rolls eyes at Thomas, Teresa, Brenda & Aris*) Lastly, what the shuck was the point of these trials?!? No offense LOTR fans, but Frodo taking a stroll to Mordor had more action than this piece of klunk! The only reason I rated this book 2 stars instead of 1 is because I'm hoping the purpose behind The Scorch Trials will make more sense in The Death Cure.

The Scorch Trials was so much more intriguing than The Maze Runner. I had to put the MR down after a couple of chapters because I was bored. However, with the ST, I couldn't put the book down. My heart was beating rapidly the entire time. There are so many twists and turns; I felt like my mind was being manipulated by WICKED as well. I hope the next book to this trilogy is just as juicy!
Should call this the Reading Trial.
it is an amazing and thrilling book and the maze runner series is a must read series

I'm just a few chapters into the book and I can't finish it. The writing style is horribly weak. I remember liking The Maze Runner when I read it a while ago, but how this awful writing slipped past me, I don't know. There is far too much telling to facilitate a connection with Thomas, the main character. A few examples: 
 "He felt a now-all-too-familiar clench of apprehension..." 
 "He was eager to make contact with Teresa..." 
 Stuff like this could have EASILY been rewritten to have more of a connection. "His muscles clenched in preparation to run/fight/sing karaoke; it was instinct, now, after the maze..." (I honestly don't remember what the rest of the original sentence was.) "Desperation clawed at his stomach as he tried to contact Theresa, and panic squirmed in his chest at the thoughts of what could have happened to her." 
 It just seems like shoddy writing all around, and I can't take it for the length of the book.

I was really disappointed in this book after reading The Maze Runner. I loved the first novel, and I had high expectations for the second, but sadly it did not live up to what I had hoped. I had wanted another action filled mystery/thrilled type novel that made me hold onto the edge of my seat and not want to stop reading, but sadly I was bored out of my mind and saw every turn coming. 
 While The Maze Runner was predictable, it was still action packed and a fun read. This book was even more predictable, and pathetically boring. I didn't even know why I was reading it or what the point of the book was because I was so bored out of my mind. 
 The plot was predictable, but it was a well thought out plot. There weren't any major errors in the book that I could find. 
 Overall, I was really disappointed in this novel. I will still finish the series, but I now have low expectations and I don't want to finish the series. 
 One out of five stars.

The second installment of the Maze Runner series is a quick read, but it is less satisfying than the first. 
 Thomas and his crew think they're safe now that they've escaped the maze, but they quickly find out they've only been duped into another trial. Not only are their surviving members put at risk, another maze group (of females) is revealed and pitted against the males. Little by little, Thomas gets memories back in the form of dreams and his relationship with Teresa is questioned. The groups are thrust into the harsh desert and exposed to Cranks, people infected with the Flare at various stages. They are told these trials will help them arrive at a cure for the Flare and give hope to humanity, but the participants have learned to question everything WICKED tells them. 
 This story brings up more questions than it answers, and tries to craft a love triangle between Thomas, Teresa, and newcomer Brenda. The strength of the first book was in the relationships between the male characters, and people like Newt and Minho fall back into the role of auxilliary support to the forced romance. This is the downfall of this book, but I am interested enough in the story to see how it ends.
I wasn't a huge fan of the first book so me not loving the 2nd in the series isn't a huge surprise.

Continuing the story of Thomas and Teresa, kids from the Maze are still running, still not sure why they are still going through trials. This segment introduces new character Brenda whom the author implies are/will be important. Teresa alternately helps and betrays Thomas, with the "WICKED made me do it" excuse. At the end of this segment we are no further in our understanding of the reasons behind the "whys" of this world. We do not know who WICKED is. Teresa reminds us to remember that they are "good." No major character is killed. 
 Really, we know that the middle book in a series is a "bridge book," but we should be closer in our understanding of the world and look forward to completing the series. Do yourself a favor and stop now. This book gives us no compelling reason to finish the series. 
 Originally recommended by a fourteen year old, this same student says he won't finish the series either!
Excellent sequel. I have never read a YA series with better mystery or flat-out creepiness. Can't wait to read the third book.

book_b.user_review: At first i wasn't sure i was going to like this book; started slow but as i read further in....i had to find out what happened. I think part of the reason, without spoilers, is that it is a little dated 1959. Things that scared us backed then are not so scary today.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is one of my favorite books. I have read it twice and both times it gave me the chills. It is a very well written haunted house tale that leaves the reader looking over a shoulder. In my book, it is a classic.

I did not like this book at all! I found it really tedious... 
 I didn't like the style of writing or the story line. 
 It did not live up to my expectations.

Picked this up on Halloween after seeing it listed as one of the scariest books ever. I waited for the scary to start but it never really happened for me. I struggled to get through it. Thinking the "scary" is more psychological or theoretical on some levels and perhaps I missed some of the deeper points? Oh well. Not so scary in my opinion.

It's the home I've dreamed of," Theodora said. "A little hideaway where I can be alone with my thoughts. Particularly if my thoughts happened to be about murder or suicide--" 
 Houses catch a bad rap. Some curse them as conduits, others as tombs. The shelter provided leaves a record of sins and scars. One could imagine the sum of voices gathering as well. Huddled and harboring. Echoes vie with whispers as dust motes measure the empty turn of the seasons. The curse of Hill House renders certain voices eternal. They don't just speak, they inquire and condemn. 
 Ghosts are absolved, at least in my book. Life's cruelty is the villain of The Haunting of Hill House. Elenor was a brilliant character of human failure. Her missteps and insecurity were impeccably realized. I also liked the presence of Mrs. Montague; she and Mrs Dudley maintained a gothic smirk, an antidote of the psychological parlour games occupying the chief characters and their "research." 
 Fear has a smell. Shirley Jackson achieves the impossible by conveying such to the page. 
 4.5/5

I'm beginning to think Shirley Jackson just recycles 3 or 4 different characters in every one of her stories - the unstable younger woman, the slightly older/slightly more stable woman, the arrogant playboy misogynist and the cruel/angry townspeople. No more, Shirley, no more. I loved The Lottery as a teenager, but I'm quitting you now.

 Dr.Montague, a scientist, sets out to pursue an investigation of paranormal activities at a possible haunted house, Hill House. He invites 3 quests/assistants, Eleanor, Theodora, and Luke to stay in Hill House for some of the summer to prove the existence of paranormal events. When they get there they find a creepy house but is it haunted and filled with paranormal activities?

 Dr.Montague didn't do much investigating, he mainly drunk and played chess with Luke. Luke wasn't interesting. 
 Theodora and Eleanor was drama queens. Eleanor was so insecure at times it made me roll me eyes.

 What? The crazy girl is just like all of us? No way! :)

This was a weird, spotty little book. Parts of it I adored (Eleanor, the group's dynamic, the descriptions of Hill House), parts of it terrified me (holding hands in a dark room, the closing doors), and parts of it felt off-kilter and baffling (though I'm sure this was purposeful on Jackson's part). I can see why The Haunting of Hill House has become a seminal ghost story for so many contemporary horror writers, but, overall, I found its conclusion to be less satisfying than I had hoped it would be.

Don't get me wrong. Shirley Jackson is a fantastic writer. The world she creates--of the gothic, imposing Hill House, nestled at the base of hugging hills--is stark, dark, troubling, and surreal. She has an intriguing knack for getting inside the head of her protagonist (although that tends to be uncomfortable, as the protagonist is a couple of cards short of a full deck); and her dialogue is clever and often engaging. That said, Jackson's classic "masterpiece", THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE, misses the horror mark by a phantom mile. Why? Because it's little more than a 182-page pity party/catfight. 
 While I'm ambivalent about Dr. Montague, the other characters in this novel are completely and irretrievably unlikable. Luke is an immature playboy, while Theodora and Eleanor are 24/7 drama queens competing for not only the attention of the men they are sharing Hill House with--but for the attention of Hill House itself. And then Jackson, late in the novel, introduces two even more unpleasant characters in Mrs. Montague and Arthur; I so disliked all of them I kept hoping some manifestation would cart them all off. (Alas, it didn't happen.) 
 Spoiler alert. There are no monsters are ghouls who appear in this novel, and there's nothing wrong with that; a horror novel doesn't have to have a physical entity growling about to be effective. What we do have are bumps in the night, freezing cold air, invisible laughter and voices, and scribbling on walls--yet we don't know if they are real, or products of a psychotic imagination. Furthermore, we get to embark on a most uncomfortable trip as shy, insecure, unstable Eleanor steadily goes bats--a trip having Eleanor pay the ultimate price. In the end, Hill House wins, but as a reader trudging through THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE I was much too ambivalent to care.

This is Shirley Jackson's pivotal ghost story about a girl named Eleanor Vance who is summoned to the haunted establishment called Hill House by a Doctor Montague, an earnest and intelligent psychologist. Beautiful and so stylistically unique, this story has quickly become one of my favorites. Utilizing terror rather than horror, the chilling paranormal aspects of Hill House ingrain itself upon the residents, mostly Eleanor and her friend Theodora, creating a stunning balance between beauty, peace, and disconnect. The audience is left wondering what exactly the haunting is and what the connection is between Eleanor and Hill House, but this just amplifies the amount of fear in the reader. Definitely a must read!
The story as a whole was just ok, but it has one of the best first paragraphs I've ever read.

This book was NOT scary or eerie or creepy but just plain boring! Wasted time getting to know characters who would never matter in the plot. So much detail of the house and the landscape and character thoughts when it's advised as a thriller... I just didn't get it. I'll probably never pick up a S. Jackson again... Major let down.

Four strangers are gathered at Hill House, a decrepit old residence, to see if they can find some actual evidence that is is haunted. Well, it wouldn't be much of a story of no evidence appeared, would it?

** spoiler alert ** 
 Supernatural thrillers have certainly come a long way since Shirley Jackson penned this novel in 1959. I liked "We Have Always Lived in the Castle" much better. But Hill House is considered a classic of the genre, so who am I to dispute that. I've seen several movie versions of this story, and since they are far more dramatic than the book, I think the movies have influenced my expectations of the story. In the end, Eleanor simply crashes her car into a tree. Her spirit wasn't taken up to become a permanent resident of Hill House; she just crashes her car into a tree and that's the last we hear of her. A recent movie version of the story did a much better job. The book is very good at illustrating how a writer uses the omnipotent voice and merges it with the second person voice. At any rate, it took me a long time to read this book because I read it mostly at bedtime and not every single night. I think if it weren't for the 1960s version of the story, I wouldn't be able to imagine the creepiness of The Haunting of Hill House and its events.

I have chewed on this book for a long while. As I've been reading the recently published Shirley Jackson biography, by Ruth Jackson, it has come back to me; it's truly the definitive Jackson book. 
 Franklin writes this: "In Hill House, which appeared in 1959, Jackson gathered powerfully all the objects of her longtime obsession: an unhappy, unmarried woman with a secret trauma; the simultaneous longing for a mother's love and fear of its control; the uncertain legacies handed down by previous generations; and finally the supernatural as a representation of the deepest psychic fears and desires. The result, a masterpiece of literary horror on a par with Henry james's The Turn of the Screw, is arguably her best novel, and certainly her most influential." 
 Eleanor is the young protagonist of the novel. She is neither woman nor child; she is homeless, although she dreams often of the perfect home that will belong only to her. For many years Eleanor has been sequestered in an unhappy home; caretaker to a sour mother who she cannot ever please. When her mother dies, Eleanor seizes the chance to participate in a paranormal experience. Her own background hints at 'sensitivity' to paranormal phenomena, as she and her sister were subjected to three days of a shower of stones (not quite a literal stoning, but close) after their father's death. So Eleanor steals her sister's car, and drives herself to Hill House - whose ghosts include a mother, tragically killed, and two squabbling sisters. 
 There are many brilliant descriptions in this book, and one of the most memorable is that of the physical building of the house which defies symmetry at every turn - every angle and line of it just wrong. Its oddness, and deliberately unnavigable quality, make it the perfect counterpart and foil to Eleanor. The four participants in the experiment - and inhabitants of the house - include Eleanor, the insouciant Theodora, Dr. Montague and Luke (a young man who is the future heir of Hill House). From the beginning, Eleanor seems the most affected by the house - the most sensitive to its ghostly messages. But neither the reader, nor Eleanor herself, ever quite knows what is external and what is internal; in other words, is the entire story just Eleanor splintering, and losing her tenuous hold on reality? Interestingly, the other characters - particularly Theodora - accuse Eleanor of seeking attention. Like a child who blames an imaginary friend, Eleanor seems to be the perpetrator (or is it the victim?) of a series of small yet malevolent mischiefs. There is also a death-wish in this book, a decidedly murky one. We never know quite for sure if Eleanor is merely making 'a call for help' which she desperately hopes will be heeded, or if she has an inexorable impulse to self-destruction.

I got this book off of a "10 most scariest books to read" list & there was nothing scary about it at all. Apparently there was a movie made after it was written & I can already imagine how boring & flat the acting would be. Don't waste your time, unless the thought of an ugly looking house scares you.

Meh. I don't get all the hoopla. I expected an exquisitely creepy story from everything I've read about this book. It should have occupied my mind even after I set the book down at the end of reading sessions. I was very disappointed. 
 The story took forever to get to the actual starting point and was still slow after that. The description wasn't all that amazing, so many opportunities for creepiness were missed, and the ending was a let down. There were interesting crumbs sprinkled throughout the book, but none of them were followed up on. Maybe I'm just jaded on horror or skimmed over the important bits.

A book club choice because it was written by Shirley Jackson, whose short story The Lottery used to be required reading by many high school English students. We were all disappointed, and it wasn't just because this novel, published in 1959, seemed dated. Set in an old house, this is a not-very-compelling ghost story without real ghosts. Not only wasn't it scary, but the characters were unlikeable.

As a voracious reader - and specifically the horror genre - I follow a lot of blogs and websites about books. Just about every list of "Top horror books you must read" includes The Haunting of Hill House. I finally decided to give it a try. 
 I can only say I truly must have read a completely different book than the authors of those lists read. The plot was nonexistent, the characters were cold and forced, the dialogue pedestrian at best, and if some knocking on walls is considered horror then let me bang out a bunch of best sellers. 
 In a nutshell, there is a supposed haunted house that a doctor and three students stay in to document the goings on. Eleanor - the stories "central" character starts to have a breakdown. That's it... End of story... Oh, there's an unexplained cold area in the nursery, some banging and wall shaking, and words written on the walls in blood. If anything, this was more a psychological thriller - not horror. And I really didn't care what happened to Eleanor at the end. All I did hope for was that someone would slap the hell out of the Doctor's condescending wife, who came to visit in the last quarter of the book. 
 While this wasn't the worst piece of drivel I've ever read, it certainly ranks up there with one that I wouldn't even give a second glance to. Had someone actually slapped the Doctor's wife, I would have given it two stars. 
 I have never done this before, but I need to ask - if you've read this book and enjoyed it (or think that it belongs on those Best Lists), please, for the love of all that is written, write me a note telling me what I missed. 
 If you are even the least bit curious and are thinking about reading this, do yourself a favor - paint a wall and watch it dry... It's more entertaining.

I had a hard time making myself finish this one. 
 I love Poe's psychological horror and mentally unstable protagonists, yet Jackson's psychological horror with a mentally unstable protagonist did not interest me much. The plot was too slow for my liking, and Eleanor (the protagonist) seemed weak and silly instead of threatening. Mostly, I just wanted to tell her to grow up and get ahold of herself. I found her annoying, and that made me dislike the book.

No one ever did it better. And Stephen King says it best: "Shirley Jackson, who never needed to raise her voice." 
 I've read this book multiple times and it never, ever fails to disturb me.

While Shirley Jackson's ghost story The Haunting of Hill House is very well written, I found it to be a bore. I was expecting a really easy, pulp-horror, type of novel...based off the two films, base off the novel, that were mediocre at best. I was wrong, Shirley Jackson knows how to write. Descriptions were interesting, passages were eloquent. I just was bored throughout ninety percent of the novel, which is not what I want from a ghost story.

I've wanted to try Shirley Jackson's work for a long time, and now I have! THE HAUNTING OF HILL HOUSE is billed as a horror classic, though in my opinion, it was eerie but not scary. After finishing the book, I'm left with several questions without definite answers, like who (or what) exactly was doing the haunting -- the house itself, the doctor and his test subjects, or something else? Was anything supernatural actually going on, or were the unexplained events a figment of an unreliable narrator's imagination? I have my own theory, but I won't share because of spoilers. 
 THOHH is a well-crafted psychological thriller that makes readers decide for themselves what went down at Hill House. I enjoyed Ms. Jackson's straight-forward writing style, and how she was able to make something as innocuous as a cold spot on the floor downright spooky. The characters were okay. They all irritated me to some degree, and I also thought that the dialogue between characters could get pretty unrealistic and silly, like "Oh, Nell, my Nellie!" or some such. The character I liked the most was the housekeeper, Mrs. Dudley. I loved her totally weird ways. 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading THOHH, and I can see why the book has been a big influence on the horror genre since its publication in 1959.
This was so boring and not scary at all. It's not that it was badly written, it's just that the story was impossibly bland. Nothing happened. That's the bottom line. Absolutely nothing happened.
Eugh.....very badly written so quite honestly, can't be arsed.

Absolute classic Gothic horror. There are bumps in the night, strange writing on the walls and mysterious 'cold spots'. But this is not a cliched read. Recluse Eleanor, is the main focus. Having looked after her invalid mother for years, she now has the freedom she longs for when she accepts an invite to stay at Hill House along with psychic researcher Dr Montague, flamboyant artist Theodora and lovely Luke, amused by the whole set up. Over susceptible, Eleanor is almost absorbed by the house; begging the question, is the house haunted, or is she?

I read this book after seeing the black and white film when I was younger (my dad brought it home for me) and for a 7 year old I was pretty terrified.I read the book and was surprised how much was NOT in the movie. I guess at the time the original movie was made the censorship issue was what kept a lot out even if not much in the book was offensive (really nothing if I remember correctly). Eleanor kind of annoys me as a protagonist, I like Theo better. It's spectacularly chilling and I do recommend that you check it out!

Sigh!This book supposed to be a scary book but I didn't find it spooky at all.I am speechless at how this can even get a 5 star rating from anyone.After reading the synopsis(very interesting),I was expecting a lot from this book but I was disappointed and felt irritated with the characters(especially Eleanor).Meh.
This story is so atmospheric. I found it to be a creepy, slow burning horror novel. The characterisation is excellent.

Shirley Jackson knew how to write really scary books and this is one of her best. I read this when I was much younger and it terrified me. I can still remember passages very vividly. The way the house seemed to overtake the character of Eleanora and the description of the oak tree that almost seems to call her is one of the creepiest things I've ever read. Shirley Jackson lived in Connecticut and her astute views of the creepy New England landscape are brilliant.

Although it's not nearly as scary today as it undoubtedly would have been at the time it was published, what this book is is a lot of fun. The characters are witty and the dialogue is engaging and brilliantly written. The pacing works very well. The characters, especially central character Eleanor, is relatable and easy to care about as are the other haunted house explorers. Some of the plot and narrative seems cliched to a modern reader, but the likeliest explanation is that this story is a prototype for much of what followed. Don't dismiss this as genre fiction or judge it by the awful film version. This is a psychological horror story of great literary merit that is well written and developed. Jackson is an underrated writer who deserves more attention.
It was horribly disappointing. Not at all as creepy/scary as you're led to think when you see it in any kind of "top scariest novels" list.

Ok, this book defined a whole genre. Ok, Shirley Jackson writing is fine. Ok, this is a horror classic that every fan of the genre must read. BUT, I just found it boring and dull. The main character is just annoying! I was waiting all the time that somebody just force her to shut up.I was annoyed by her from the beginning of the book, and I felt the same way until the end. 
 I didn't like this book and I trully think it's quite overrated. But hey, everybody loves it... so maybe I just skipped the good part of it by mistake.

This took me way too long to read despite its short length because I didn't really enjoy reading it. It made me very uncomfortable, so I suppose Shirley Jackson succeeded. I liked We Have Always Lived in the Castle a lot more.

This book had me interested right up until about the halfway mark, although I'm not really sure I would characterize it as horror. I finished it. Barely, and then I was ashamed of myself for reading it. It was almost as if the author had given up on the story.

"Journey ends with lovers meeting" Eleanor kept on saying then and now, which is to become true in a tragic way, a one line story to mull over. "No live organism can continue for too long to exist sanely under the conditions of absolute reality" and there it starts, a conspiracy to dull the expectations down in order to unleash the horror on oneself. 
 The characters were dull and confusing and so many things were unexplained or left to guess, which is great but not on this magnitude. There were not more than instances where it felt a little scary. The book is moderately written and the description of hill house was beautiful in a horrifying way. 
 Mrs Montague, a woman of high elegance annoyed me with her every sentence, Dr Montague, (Mr Sassy) is not good enough, Luke was whiny and Dudleys were creepy for no apparent reasons. Theodora was funny and okay until the first hundred pages. Eleanor,on the other hand kept feeling sorry for herself and ended up meeting her lover in the end finally, death. 
 Hill house, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within; it had stood so for eighty years and might stand for eighty more.
