book_a.title: Allegiant (Divergent, #3)
book_a.user_review:
I do not give this low rating because of the ending (which I didn't love but will not spoil) My problem was: 
 1. How there was great build up to the main conflict of the series that was discarded in this book and rendered pointless by the introduction of "the agency." Which made all of the conflict in the previous books unnecessary. 
 2. The process of the characters discovering conflicts on their own and overcoming them was replaced with information dumps by newly introduced characters that readers had no investment in. 
 3. Did not think the opposing POV worked-could not discern between the two voices and had to always check back to see who's I was reading. 
 I don't give low ratings usually. Even if I don't love the books, I respect the authors work enough to at least give it three stars, but this time I couldn't even do that. I don't disrespect her authority to do whatever she please with her own work, or even thinks she owes the reader a certain ending. I do think she doesn't stay true to her plot or characters and in essence does negate the entire series. i wonder if the movies will rewrite this entire book-would be a huge selling point to the fans of the series. 
 But that's just my opinion.

sample_reviews.review_text: Loved first few books but this one was predictable and a bit boring.
I so wanted to like this book. But for me it was just okay. I had a hard time with it from the beginning and the ending sealed the deal.

Double ugh. I can say I read the series now but it was work getting through this one. Divergent was the best of the three, but nothing ever developed past the interesting idea of the Factions. And the love story became creepy Twilight-ish. On to something better!

I have a lot of feelings for this book. Not all of them bad. But there are a few. *QUITE* a few. 
 The good parts: The character writing is detailed, complex, and realistic. Each character isn't thrown into an archetype that they must adhere to or challenge. They are allowed a wide range. Each of them. Even the ones about whom the readers don't hold any hope. Well, except for one character. And also except for the ending. Saving for later. 
 The relationship that Tris and Four have is very well done. It's probably the best writing for a relationship I've SEEN in a YA book, and that's saying quite a lot. 
 I understand *most* of the twists, even if I really detest some of them. 
 The bad parts: WHY WOULD YOU WRITE A CONFLICT THAT SPANS TWO BOOKS AND THEN COMPLETELY INVALIDATE IT?! WHY WOULD YOU TAKE EVERYTHING THAT IS ORIGINAL, FUN, AND EXCITING ABOUT YOUR SERIES AND THROW IT AWAY TO BECOME ANOTHER RUN-OF-THE-MILL SERIES?! WHY?! WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT? 
 ALSO THAT ENDING WAS BULLSHIT. EVERYTHING ABOUT IT WAS BULLSHIT. 
 My advice to people who enjoy the series, is to read it through Insurgent and then ignore the last 5 or so chapters. Those didn't happen. Those aren't real. That's Jeanine playing with your head. Don't listen. You'll be more satisfied that way. 
 Overall, I'd give it a 4/10. The series is over, I guess, but I'm really, REALLY dissatisfied. 
 **SPOILERS** 
 Tris grows as a person, trying to grapple with grief and her identity while in the Bureau compound, but then at the end she falls RIGHT BACK into the "must be selfless must be selfless!" stereotype that Four accused her of going into the Erudite Compound in Insurgent. She fervantly denies that this is what she meant by going into the death series Weapons room, but it is. She's wrong. Instead of letting her brother reach atonement like he had asked, she HAD to be selfless martyr and go in. Yeah, David was there. Whatever. It's dumb. 
 The fact that the series builds SO MUCH into the factions and then just goes "yeah, it's all meaningless, we're not going to talk about the main setting and any of the conflicts anymore, that's all just an experiment" is EXTREMELY poorly done. Instead of being ground-breaking like the "everything you know is a lie" tactic we've seen in better books like The House of the Scorpion or The Giver, this whole stupid twist just took a giant dump on everything Roth built. Everything she said during the other two books was just thrown to the wind, which is EXTREMELY inconsiderate to the readers. She tried to get it all back by throwing parallels everywhere between the outside compound and inside, but it felt half-assed. I feel like her original plot for the series was much better, that Tris was going to be the voice of the factionless and that she was going to lead them out of Chicago / The City, but then realized "Oh no, I can't write a Hunger Games" and changed it. 
 Last point: Tris' death didn't make a difference. Yes, Chicago / The Fourth City, made peace, but if Caleb was the one to go in and sacrifice himself, that STILL would have happened. The fact that Tris did it instead of him would be completely meaningless were it not for David. Her sacrifice did not carry weight. She changed almost nothing, and that infuriates me the most.

The book itself is good. I flew threw it as fast as the other two. There are many twists, turns, and adventure. 
 However, without spoiling anything to anyone who still intends to read this, I have never been more angry/disappointed in some of the things that happen over the course of this trilogy finale. 
 I actually no longer know if I want to see the movies after reading Allegiant. It depends on how long my anger lasts.....

I struggled between 3 and 4 stars. I both loved and hated the book. It got a bit confusing to me. And I absolutely hated the way it ended. It was a disappointment. But it was also really good. It didn't draw me in like the first two books.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Okay. To start this review, I have to tell you that I liked Divergent and grew aggravated with Insurgent, during which I felt Tris was just wallowing in guilt a lot of self-whining which lead her to sacrifice herself and led her to realize, almost too late that, that she wanted to live. Also, she realizes that her and Tobias have to be honest with each other after both withheld information from each other that, surprisingly (note: sarcasm) almost got them killed . . . again. 
 I am not going to rehash the story but here is what I had problems with. In both the other books, Tobias had trust issues and the only person he seems to trust in the world is Tris. Then, he thinks of himself as genetically damaged because people he DOESN'T know told him he is and he suddenly has an identity crisis. Then, he makes friends with someone he barely knows and plans to overthrow the scientists who believe that only the genetically pure are worthy. Of what, I don't know. Tobias tells Tris of this plan and she thinks it's a bad idea and tells him this but he goes along with it anyway. Again, he only trusts Tris but he won't listen to her advice when this flimsy excuse of being "genetically damaged" motivates his actions, even though Tris tells him it changes nothing about who he is. This attack mortally wounds one of his friends and even though he knows he was totally wrong, he yells at Tris, saying she's not his parents and she can't tell him what to do. I know that the other books didn't cover his POV, but when did he turn into a whiny bitch who yells at, again, the only person he trusts and loves. 
 The other main problem isn't really Tris's death, but how it came about. Since Tris is divergent and part of her aptitude is intelligence, you would think that she would come up with better plans than to put herself in harms way for what she believes is a sacrifice for the people she loves. 
 When Tris dies, I was so tired of her spewing that she sacrificed herself for "love" that there was no sadness in me. (This comes from a person who cries at everything, I mean EVERYTHING!) When Tris and Caleb are getting shot at going to the weapons lab, she sees the person her brother used to be, or who she thought he used to be, and decided then and there, she wanted him to live. But what about her, she seemed to forget that she wanted to live to. For herself, for her friends, for Tobias, but is seemed like a nothing decision for her because she did it for love. 
 Sacrificing yourself for someone you love is fine, but not if you put yourself in a stupid situation without thinking it through. Yes, you might be brave and selfless and intelligent but it doesn't mean that you should give up your life for a plan you just put together on a whim, which is what they seemed to do. And during her sacrifice, Tobias was giving Evelyn an ultimatum to be his mother or the leader of the city and she chose him. And Tobias admits, when he is told that Tris went in the weapons lab instead of Caleb, that it would be like Tris to do that but yet he let her go into a deadly situation alone. 
 There is no character development throughout the series, there is just her trying to find a way to, not really become a hero, but frustratingly, put herself in the way of danger to find the truth or to save people she loves, when in the end, it doesn't really matter. Nothing changed that came about because Tris sacrificed herself. It came about because Tobias asked his mother to choose him over power and they made a treaty with the Allegiant. I don't even know if the memory serum that Tris released before she died would have been necessary, they should have just killed David. 
 This is just my opinion and you can take it with a grain of salt but I wasn't upset Tris was killed. I was upset at the lack of cohesion in this book, the total lack of sympathy I felt for any of the characters because of the lack of character development, and the little sense it made. I liked the concept of the factions but it should have been more developing the characters rather than killing them off to add more emotional baggage to Tris's shoulders until she finally "sacrificed" herself for the love of her brother. At the end of the book, even Tobias after two years, didn't understand why she died for her brother. 
 I wouldn't recommend this book or even the series unless you want a lot of frustration.

 As the third book in Veronica Roth's Divergent series, I think it was the one I was most excited for. We were finally going to get explanations for why the dystopian world was the way it was and why the divergent were divergent! How could this book not be good? But of course, I hadn't actually heard good things about it, so I was a bit weary heading in. Unfortunately, hearsay was right, and I must say I was disappointed in this book. 
 What I Liked 
 I liked that we did get the answers, even though I wasn't actually that thrilled with the answers themselves. I don't really believe a lot about the land beyond the Pale, as it were. I mean, I believed it, in the sense that I don't think there was an unreliable narrator, but that I really wish there had been more information about how it got as it was so that I could believe that modern America could somehow become a propaganda state. Like, what happened to all of the books? The Internet? Canada? 
 Actually, I think what I really would have liked to have read, instead of the Divergent series, is a book about the Purity Wars themselves. Are there any good novels that actually explain the process of how we get from Modern America to Dystopia? If so, I'd like to read those. 
 What I Didn't Like 
 1. I don't like books that alternate POVs between characters when the other books in the series haven't done that - I'm looking at you, Breaking Dawn. It just seems like a cop out. Now, if this had been the case throughout, it probably wouldn't have bothered me so much, but if you can't tell the whole story from one character's POV like you did before, then I just kind of think that you didn't try very hard. Although I wouldn't be surprised if Roth was under pressure from her publishers to get this out quick, so I don't know if I entirely blame her for this and some of the other problems. 
 2. Tobias and Tris's voices sounded so similar, I forgot whose POV I was reading and would have to go back and check. I think this probably could have been fixed with extra editing. 
 3. The pacing just seemed off. It dragged up until the last five chapters, and I just never felt like picking it up and reading. I didn't feel like it was going anywhere and therefore was not enticed to read more of it. In fact, I'd been reading this since January, so that shows just how slow it went.

I'm not really sure where to start with this one. 
 I wasn't a massive fan of the first two books even though they were very simply written and easy to read they were very slow going and nothing really happened until about 80 pages from the end in both books. This book was very much the same in my opinion but some how much worse. 
 The first thing that frustrated me was that it was told from the perspective of both Tris and Tobias. This was probably a good idea in theory but in practice it made it confusing in parts as both Tris and Tobias are pretty much identical with the exception of gender. I had to keep flicking back a couple of pages to see whose perspective I was reading from as it was all the same to me. Also the constant display of affection from the pair got unbearable to read about, I was hoping for more of a well thought out story line and instead all I got was a ridiculous excuse for a teen romance and a little bit of story in between a lot of kissing. 
 The story changes quite dramatically in this last book compared to the first two and flips everything on it's head. I know others might enjoy this but to me it was executed really badly and nothing made sense, there were contradictions flying about all over the place and it just went on for about 200 pages too much. I felt like the author had got bored with what she had already written but felt like she had to write a 3rd book. 
 There was so much wrong with this book that I would be sat at my computer all day and still not be finished writing about it all. I think the most frustrating points for me are what I have already mentioned above and that it was dragged out way more than what was necessary I felt like giving up a lot while reading this and now I wish I had because the end was just incredibly bad. There was no need for an epilogue either, really another 26 pages of how thing unrealistically turned out hunky dory in the end!? 
 I'm not sure what stopped me giving this only 1 star (I may need to re-think this) but I would definitely not read this series again and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone either.

Oh boy - this book is just a mess. 
 Divergent walked a comfortable line of mediocrity. The story was just interesting enough; the characters were just fleshed out enough. Everything was just enough to keep you vaguely interested in what would happen next.

 Then book 3! Again, Roth trots out a whole new slate of characters (most of whom die and none that I could be bothered to care about). Then there is this brand new storyline that spirals all over the place and out of control before sputtering to a senseless end.

I mean, how do you take two incredibly strong, and independent and mature characters and turn them into whiny, and insecure and childish brats? HOW?!?!? It just really is a travesty that i won't be able to recommend this series to people anymore because of how BAD this book was. The only saving grace for this book was the ending. Fractured, uneven, but ultimately, I guess. True. No spoilers alert, so I'll be vague in my comments, but if you've read the book, you'll know what I'm talking about. 
 The theme of forgiveness is a strong thread throughout this book and probably one of the most discerning and thoughtful presentations of this theme in almost any YA book (and perhaps many adult books)I've ever read. Tris has good reasons not to forgive a lot of people in this book, including herself, but especially her brother Caleb for his role in her torture and almost death in book #2. The minespace they tread sometimes carefully sometimes not was fascinating. In turn, many of the characters have good reason not to forgive Tris for her previous actions, justified though they might have been. Forgiveness is a tricky, slippery concept. It works for two seconds and then suddenly, it's gone and the process has to start all over again. Roth gets that. Tris ponders this when she says, "Or maybe forgiveness is just the continual pushing aside of bitter memories, until time dulls the hurt and the anger, and the wrong is forgotten." When Caleb asks if she has forgiven him, she responds, "Yes, I have...Or at least, I desperately want to, and I think that might be the same thing." Nails it. 
 As for other elements - have the dual perspective (chapters written from the perspective of Tris and Tobias) felt strained at times and took me some time to feel comfortable with it. I'm not sure of Roth's reason to change the point of view in this manner unless it made for tidying up the ending, but that does not seem justified. More importantly, the ending - or rather the ending that I'm not being specific about. It was true. It felt right. I was still disappointed. I must have reread those couple of pages quite a few times looking for ...something - I'm not sure what - a piece was missing, but I can't define it. 
 Other questions - I wish I found out what made Tris so immune to all serums, etc. Perhaps evolution? I'm obviously in the Erudite camp and like all of these pieces tied up. 
 But overall - a good read - sorry to see the series end.

***SPOILERS*** 
 This book is a real let down. Although the plot itself isn't too bad, the book has two issues that really torpedo it. First, Roth has decided to use two voices to tell her story, both Tris and Four. While everything was just in Tris' voice, it sounded good, but there is no voice for Four. He sounds so exactly like Tris that sometimes I had to leaf back to the beginning of a chapter just to find out who was speaking. The second issue, of course, and the reason why she uses two voices, is that she kills off Tris, the major character that the reader has been following since the beginning of the first book in the series. 
 I've got to say, when that happened, I flipped ahead just to make sure she'd actually done it, and then I closed the book. Frankly, I just really didn't care what happened after that. Now, I understand that she set up Tris for this going back into the second book (a plot device I hated at that time) and that it is certainly within her prerogative to end the trilogy however she pleases, BUT after I've invested a considerable amount of my life reading probably around 500,000 words, been brought to care about a character, I simply cannot react well when she'd killed off. I'm sorry. Intellectually, I understand. Emotionally, I don't. Period. I've been given to understand that when Veronica Roth wrote the book, she stated that she really didn't take her fans into consideration. Well, I imagine she's discovered by now that writers must always take their fans into consideration. Summer gives me time away from studying and gives me time to immerse myself in stories - particularly fantasy ones. There is nothing better than the opportunity which novels such as The Night Circus give where I can escape the comparatively mundane world that we live in and go on a journey of the imagination. As such I am very grateful for the summer (and for my local library's recommendation emails) otherwise I would have been deprived of this wonderful novel for at least another long year. 
 There is no other word for it except: magical. It is not unusual for me to finish a book of similar length in one sitting, especially if the book in question has me simply wanting to reach the end so that I can find out what happens. And so, when I read The Night Circus' blurb I was hooked, knowing that I had been promised at least one night of good reading. Instead I have been given so much more than what the blurb had been offering. I was torn between finding out what happens as quick as I can and my longing for the story to last like an endless dream (for those of you who've read it, you'll know what I mean :P). As such, it has taken me over a week to finish reading - to savour this amazing story. 
 I love Erin Morgenstern's style. The Night Circus is so beautifully written. Others may not agree - I have read other reviews complaining about how slow the story is, about how confusing it is, etc. Personally, I found the pace to be perfect - the plot does not overpower and take control of the book, but gradually unfolds just as it should. Sure, I was a little confused here and there but I believe this adds to the allure of what is The Night Circus - Le Cirque des Reves. 
 Every aspect of the book is delicately and intricately woven together - parts of the story are told with different 'whens', 'wheres' and 'whos'. You expect the romance between Celia and Marco (which is absolutely lovely, sad, breath-taking and painful all at once) but you also get to know so many of the other characters; their stories are not brushed aside. Then there are the excerpts of Friedrick Thiessen's writing, allowing you to become a 'Reveur' should you wish, and splashes of 2nd person narrative allow you to experience the circus for yourself. It is definitely the descriptions so full of wonderful imagery that makes this book what it is. 
 I could keep writing about The Night Circus but then I'd be here all day. So on a last note: if you choose to read this book (and I truly believe you should), I hope you come to love Le Cirque des Reves just as much as I do.

The Night Circus - Erin Morgenstern 
 Rating: 
 Celia Bowen (a naturally gifted girl trained by her father Hector) and Marco Alisdair (an orphan boy taken under Alexander H-'s tutelage) are pitted against each other in the newest wager made by their guardians, who adhere to different schools of thought when it comes to magic. The Night Circus becomes the venue for their competition, where they outdo themselves by creating more and more elaborated tents. To ensure the circus's continued existence while ending the game without either of them dying, a young man named Bailey becomes the new Proprietor before Celia and Marco both vanish. 
 The premise of this novel was intriguing, but the pace was incredibly slow, the events weren't told in a chronological way and the time period was easily forgotten. The game was not the epic duel it was made out to be and the different magical methods used in creating the tents weren't explained nor shown. The romance was another deception. Many questions about the day-to-day life in the circus remained unanswered. The parts I enjoyed were the Midnight Dinners, the conception of the circus, Herr Friedrick Thiessen's passion for the circus and the reveurs. The circus was also described beautifully.
Visually delicious, painting word pictures and imagery that was exciting. Dreamscape or not? I would like to discuss this book with other readers.

reference_books.title: One of Us Is Lying
reference_books.review_text:
*This book was sent to me by the publisher in exchange for an honest review* 
 When a group of teenagers from different social groups end up in detention together, they think nothing could possibly get worse. Until Simon, the school gossip, dies an hour later. As the only people in room when it happened, the group become persons of interest. Who is telling the truth? And who is lying? 
 The initial start of this book feels very much like The Breakfast Club and I worried that the story would feel too similar but once the driving force of the plot -Simon's death - kicks in, it started to move away for that and grew to become its own story. While the unexpected death shakes the school, leading to threatening tumblr posts and a media frenzy, One of Us Is Lying is more about the characters. The use of multiple perspectives allows the reader an insight into each of the character's lives and does a really good job of breaking down preconceived ideas we have of people based on how they appear from the outside. 
 Personally I've been having a lot of problem with plot-length in books this year and One of Us Is Lying is one of those. In a "who done it" type of story it's hard to get the balance between the investigation elements and the getting-to-know-the-characters element and, for me, there was too much of the latter. But I think a lot of that played into the fact that apart from Bronwyn (who I could really relate to), I didn't really connect to any of the characters enough to want to know more about their lives outside of the school walls. Which was more fault of me than the book itself. 
 One of Us is Lying proves to be extremely well thought out and fantastically well written for a debut novel but just seemed to fall short for me.

Zombies are not for me. 
 There has been a recent surge in Zombie Apocalypse books recently, and I wanted to see what all the buzz was about. When I read the blurb for WARM BODIES, I thought, ok, zombie love story? This doesn't sound too horror/creepy. I'll give it a try. It also didn't hurt that Stephenie Meyer gave the blurb on the cover! 
 This book has been sitting on my shelf since May, but I figured this was the perfect time to pick it up, especially with Halloween just around the corner. Stephenie Meyer wasn't the only author whose work I admire that loved this book - Maggie Stiefvater also raved about it. I wish I shared their love for WARM BODIES. 
 First the good. 
 The writing. WARM BODIES is written in the first person (not always my favorite) from Zombie R's perspective. I would have given up on page 5 if it weren't for Isaac Marion's innate ability to turn a phrase and make the thoughts of R not only interesting, but enlightening. I didn't think it was possible to root for the zombie, but I did. Marion didn't take the story too seriously, though. There were definitely times I gave a chuckle, and appreciated a little levity when the future of M was looking bleak. 
 The gore. There wasn't too much horror for me in terms of eating brains and spilling blood; although, there was some of that. What's a zombie story without some old fashioned brain-eating? 
 "R". R has more consciousness than your average zombie. He is driven by more than eating brains; in fact, he is evolving into another kind of zombie. I enjoyed seeing his transformation, and the spark that ignited it. 
 The relationships. There was a friendship between R and his friend, M, that I really loved. The relationship between R and Julie reminded me a bit of Stephenie Meyers's The Host - memories of someone else's relationship guiding the beginning of their connection. 
 Now the not-so-good. 
 Zombies are not sexy. They smell like rotten meat, their skin is gray and slowly disintegrating off their bones, they are not strong, they moan, and their body parts *ahem* don't work. Marion himself said zombie sex was like "slabs of meat slapping off of one another." I lost my appetite over that one. 
 I couldn't get passed the zombie thing. I found myself repulsed by the idea of them. I understand that the zombies are metaphorical for something greater, but I could not get beyond the literal zombie body. I know, I know, suspension of disbelief and all that, call me shallow. 
 Vampires - they might want to drink your blood, but they're sexy. Werewolves - strong and vicious, but sexy. Faeries - mischievous, but sexy. Fallen angels - flawed, but oh so sexy. 
 Zombies are not for me.

It's a shame this book is frequently described as "Zombie Twilight," sure it's in the same genre of "Young Adult Monster/Human Love Story" and so it's the easiest comparison to make when explaining it to people but it deserves so much better than a Twilight comparison. The female lead is so much stronger than Bella, the love story aspect is not the main focus of the book it's more about survival in the zombie apocalypse. Instead of the male monster turning the human girl into a monster, the human girl makes the monster human. R isn't an unrealistically flawless partner who just happens to be dead. Perhaps I shouldn't have seen the movie before reading the book, but then again, I probably wouldn't have picked up the book without seeing the movie first. I very, very rarely like film adaptations more than their literary counterparts, but this was one of those cases. 
 Some notable choices the author made that I thought felt off when contrasted with the movie: Not allowing Julie's father a chance at redemption, not letting the corpses have a chance at redemption, attempting to make the Boneys more than just husks of zombies who'd given up, all of the scenes with R and Julie in the Stadium. 
 Where the movie had heart, a bit of fun and plenty of poignant moments, the book felt like quite a few half formed thoughts strung together into a loose narrative. I did like the stronger connection to Perry, and how R seemed to find himself again through the experiences of another. It's something that was lacking in the movie and felt like a half-formed thought in that adaptation. The characters were likable enough, the plot compelling enough, and the concept interesting enough to keep me entertained for what was ultimately a pretty quick read.

This is one of the most amazing, beautiful and gorgeously written stories that I have ever read. I do not say that lightly. I was immediately drawn into this story and couldn't stop myself from reading even though it took me into very late night hours. 
 I found it to be so much more than what 'zombie love story' would make you think. With entire passages devoted to what existence is supposed to mean versus what it actually does mean - all from the mind of a zombie, it's more difficult to dismiss this book. 
 Even if you aren't a fan of the zombie genre, this book will engage you in ways you never imagined. It's sharp and witty with syllable counting dialogue that will stick with you long after you've read it. It's revolutionary, beautiful and engaging in brilliantly imagined ways. This book has settled firmly onto my favorites of 2011 and I can't recommend it highly enough. Do not miss this book. You'll be glad you took the time for it.

Truth be told, I didn't know this book existed until I saw the movie trailer posted on one of my friend's Facebook status. The movie looked interesting, but I wasn't interested in another YA zombie novel - I have been burnt before on a YA zombie/human romance and I wasn't interested in trying again. As it turned out while reading the novel, I was pleasantly surprised how well written this novel is and the fact that I actually cheered for a zombie. I was told to take a chance with the book because it is an Adult book and not a Young Adult romance, but also because it gives a new perspective on zombies that has never been seen before. This new perspective (don't worry, I wouldn't give it all away), is that zombies are slowly evolving back into the living for some unknown reason. No one knows how it's happening, nor why it's happening, but the fact is some zombies are no longer chasing after people for their brains. 
 I loved this book and recommend this book to people who love anything written about zombies. This book has everything you can possible want in a novel - a bit of romance, sarcasm, dry humor, action, and of course, and a touch of horror (i.e. zombies eating brains). You will not regret picking up this book--especially if you love zombie stories.

The world is screwed up") and then by the end I really didn't care anymore. 
 About halfway through the book, I noticed all the Romeo and Juliet name parallels (and it's embarrassing that it took me that long, really, because they are NOT subtle) and I groaned out loud. Because...really? Really? 
 I expected the author to play up the funny aspects of the story (this is probably because I saw the trailer for the movie first, and judging by that, the movie goes for more humor), but instead he just went for sort of sappy and vague, especially by the end. Which is too bad, because I feel like this story could have been a lot more fun (in a dark humor sort of way). 
 Also, this is just a quibble, but Julie's dialogue really bothered me. Basically, she just says "fuck" a lot. And swearing doesn't normally bother me, but in this case it just felt so awkward and tacked on, like the author was trying so hard to make Julie seem badass and non-cardboard. In my opinion, it didn't really work. It was just weird. 
 All in all, a bit of a let-down, because I think this story could have been really cool.

Being a zombie is an endless cycle: eat flesh, fall down, wander around mindlessly, repeat. In the midst of the apocalypse, zombies are regarded as the enemy while the living are automatically revered as heroes. Little do these living humans know that zombies have their own thought processes and emotions as evidenced by those of R, the narrator of this story. As a zombie, R has no idea what the hell he's doing half of the time nor does he have any recollection of his former life. His life regains purpose when he rescues a beautiful salvager named Julie and the two of them form an awkward, yet important relationship with one another. The more time R spends around Julie, the more human he becomes in his thoughts and emotions. 
 The first thing I'd like to applaud Mr. Marion on is the sheer creativity it took to write such a novel. The words zombie and romance don't normally go together so easily, yet the author made them fit perfectly. R is a sympathetic character despite being a dingy zombie and Julie is the perfect friend for him since she doesn't concentrate on any of his obvious flaws. Even though R only speaks a few syllables at a time, he makes more sense than most of the military officials who want to shoot zombies left and right without second thought. You know the apocalypse is on its way when a budding relationship between a zombie and a human seems more natural than going with their own kind. Breaking down barriers is the first step in healing this screwed up world. Love of all kinds will save us in the end, both in this novel and in the real world. 
 The second thing Isaac Marion deserves praise for is his system of rules regarding zombie behavior. They have no memory of their past lives, they walk around with a gimp, the only food they care about is human flesh (even though its tasteless and bland), they only speak a few syllables at a time, and their thoughts (though they do exist) are as limited as their speech. The author sticks to these rules all throughout the book and any surprises we do get come naturally instead of being forced. As an author, it's good to have a set of rules your creatures can live by. Otherwise, the reader will assume the creatures can do whatever the hell they want without limits and can basically end the story anytime. If it wasn't for the strict set of rules, we'd have flying zombies who could shoot lasers and fart lightning for all we know. 
 The final thing I have to touch on is the way this story is written. Because of the poetic and descriptive nature of R's thought processes, the pacing is slightly taken down a few notches. But thanks to the present tense storytelling, it doesn't have to be that way all throughout the book. When you're reading "Warm Bodies", you're thrust into the moment and you can never leave until the author says you can. That is what I call true storytelling: showing the readers why R is a likeable person instead of shoving it down their throats. Trust me, you're going to have enough problems with your throats after reading the painful descriptions of how necks and chests are eaten with such brutal violence. Yes, this book is romantic on so many levels, but let's not get complacent when it comes to the fact that zombies are zombies and they crave human flesh and organs. 
 It should come as no surprise that this novel was made into a movie. The descriptions are picturesque and the youth of it all makes R and Julie into perfect movie stars. I don't visit Rotten Tomatoes that often, so I wouldn't know how well the movie has done in theaters. The book, on the other hand, no question about it: Isaac Marion is an A+ student of the literary game and he gets a passing grade for it.

When I went into my zombie crazy, everyone told me I should read Warm Bodies. They said that R, the lead zombie, was adorable... So I caved and got the audiobook. Not only Warm Bodies had great recommendations, there also was an upcoming movie! 
 In general, the book lived up to its expectations, however high they were. R is, indeed, too cute for words. The whole time were in his head, and hes actually a smart, sensitive, caring individual. The zombie plague acts as a filter between his brain and his mouth, though, so talking in complex patterns is beyond him, but that only serves to make the reader simpathize more with his plight. 
 Now, even though in the end I loved Warm Bodies, I spent more than half the book dreading the end. I could feel the tragedy in the air. It was coming my way, and it was going to be devastating... but my friends had liked it, and I was pretty sure theyd not have told me how lovable a corpse would be if he didnt had a chance at a happy ending... right? Right? 
 Thats how I felt. R starts out as a pure zombie with an inquisitive mind, but after a certain incident he begins to reach out to othersto Julie, who is broken enough, and later on brave enough, to listen and to see that theres more than a walking corpse in him. And R responds... little by little, excruciatingly slow, but he begins to question what it is to have the zombie plague, to ponder a future, to dream of changes. And as he grasps, I couldnt help but fear that itd not be enough, that happiness would flee his questing fingertips. 
 Now, I cant say much more without spoiling the whole thing. Suffice it to say that R is touching, moving; that Julie is a lead female worthy of him, with a spark that might leave the reader wondering where theirs went and why, and that their tale was absolutely beautiful. 
 Im not too sure I buy the whole reasoning behind the plague, behind the changes, behind the bonies, as they call the walking dead who have turned to full skeleton. The explanation is a bit convenient, a bit easy, a bit too emotional. But, honestly? I dont care. It worked, its a symbol in a bleak world and I want an ending like that one in real life. 
 Theres a bit of gory violence at first, because this is a zombie book and remember that at first R is pretty normal for a zombie, but if youre okay with your local friendly undead eating a brain or two you should definitely read Warm Bodies. 
 P.S. I had a funny annecdote while reading this one. I was talking to a friend and the dialogue went like this: 
 Him: What are you reading? 
 Me: Another zombie book, its called Warm Bodies. 
 Him: .... Are you possitive its a zombie book?

Well, I liked it. The idea was original and really interesting, and I loved the clever Romeo & Juliet feel to it. 
 That said, I had some problems with it. R is poetic and philosophical. Too much so, and at the wrong moments; we never really get a break from his musings on nature and such. It also feels like other characters have the same inner philosophical 'voice', as well, because when they talk about their thoughts it sounds like his own speech patterns.  So, some pros and cons, but a decent read.

So this book taught me something about myself - I don't like zombies. 
 Which is weird, because I love blood and gore as much as the next girl. Seriously, Game of Thrones? One of my favourite series, and anyone who's ever seen the tv series will tell you how graphic it is. So maybe it wasn't the zombie part of this book I didn't like. Maybe it was just the whole 'this-book-is-literally-a-parody-of-Romeo-and-Juliet.' And i hate Romeo and Juliet. Absolutely and completely despise it with every fibre in my being. You wouldn't think a parody would be worse, but dear Jesus where Romeo and Juliet made me want to throw the book across the room this book made me want to burn the thing then bury the ashes and make myself forget I ever read it. 
 Our main character's name is R (Get it?). He falls in love with a girl named Julie. His best friend's name is M (Romeo's best friend's names is Mercrutio). There is literally a balcony scene, down to the 'what's-in-a-name' part that had me making a finger gun and shooting myself. The scary zombie R, who eats brains, kills Julie's boyfriend Perry and saves Perry's brain so it could be munched on throughout the novel. He ends up falling in love with Julie (surprise, surprise) and suddenly we have a lion-fell-in-love-with-the-lamb scenario where R wants nothing more than to feel and be human. Eventually he gets his wish and they all live happily ever after after a battle that was probably meant to be climatic but I was too busy being grateful that it was almost over to feel the adrenaline. Unlike Romeo and Juliet, no one dies. 
 I have no idea what the sequel to this is going to be seeing as everything was pretty much wrapped up in this one. Maybe it'll be better, seeing as there's no Romeo and Juliet 2 to parody (Romeo and Juliet being dead kinda prevented a sequel from happening). Honestly though, the only way I'm reading the next one is if R reverts to his original self, kills Julie and ends up eating her brain. 
 Sorry?

Not terrible for a Harry Potter ripoff, but the writing could have been better and the rules of the magic system are almost nonexistent. Pretty much if something cool like a fireball is required, the mage in question can do it if they concentrate really, really hard. It isn't so much magic as telekinesis. 
 And come on. The "Enemy of Death?" Really? If you're going to steal from other authors, at least try to cover your tracks a little bit.
It is a good middle school fantasy.

This is a Harry Potter rip off so obvious the authors didn't even try to hide it. It's about a scarred child with a dead mother getting recruited into a prep school for magic. But, for all that, The Iron Trial lacks any of the charm of Harry Potter. The mythology isn't as well thought out, the characters aren't as complex or interesting, the plot isn't as intricate and, worst of all, there's no magic in the story. There's nothing appealing about Callum or his journey into the world of mages. 
 Holly Black is an excellent author, but The Iron Trail just isn't up to her usual standard. I won't be bothering with any of the other books in this series. 
 Not recommended.

Okay, let me say, I've read Mortal Instruments by Cassandra Clare and while it isn't staggering genius, on the whole I enjoyed the series. I'll probably read her next one too just for the heck of it. I've read Doll Bones by Holly Black and I thought it had moments of such surprising depth. So a book written by the two of them, I thought, couldn't be all that bad. I wasn't expecting groundbreaking work, but something entertaining. 
 This book seriously took me 3 months to finish. I'd pick it up, read a few chapters and set it down and just not think about it. Soon I felt like I had to finish it, not because I was so enamored with the story but because there it was, some dude in a metal mask and a dark cape (but not a Death Eater, no no no) and our three wizard/mage heroes, two boys and a girl, staring off at their adventure in their new wizard/mage school. Mocking me. 'This isn't as long as That Book That Shall Not Be Named!' 'You can finish it!' 
 And lo, did I. 
 The thing is, I just didn't care about the characters, I didn't care about the school, I really didn't get the whole school set up or who the Enemy of Death (yep, that's his name) is and what he wants. I didn't care that sometimes the mages need to eat sand or drink blood to get the elements into them, I didn't care about sarcastic, angsty Call. I tried, and I just didn't. 
 Two stars because I always appreciate when I can hand kids a book and say 'this is definitely a Harry Potter readalike' and because there are a few moments of cleverness.

I went into this with super low expectations, because of all the reviews that mentioned it being a Harry Potter rip off. While it does have some very obvious similarities, I wouldn't call it a rip off by any means. 
 The beginning was quite good, but then there was a part in the middle that felt like nothing happened, and it dragged the story. I'd say the first and last 20% were the best. Writing is very simple, world building is quite limited. We could have done with a little more background. I did like the main characters. I've come to appreciate when authors choose MCs that belong to a minority, like Call here, who has a sort of disability. I particularly like the fact that it happened here, when this is a middle grade book. I also really liked the personalities of the three kids. 
 So, it wasn't a perfect book, but I still enjoyed it more than I thought I would. I will continue with the series. I'd say, if you enjoy these type of stories, give it a try, it may surprise you.

 REVIEW 
 Few books make me want to start drafting a review right after I finish reading them. This is one exception. Huzzah for loopholes! To put it bluntly: this book is good. And... I read it in one sitting, okay? There, I admitted it. There are so many things to love about this book. 
 Callum is our main character. I thought I knew what I was getting with him: the typical tragic past, then the boy discovers he has magic powers. It's a predicable MG fantasy, right? Wrong. Then a plot twist occurred that changed my perspective entirely. I can't say what it is because I don't want to give any large spoilers, but trust me, there's no way I saw that coming. At all. 
 I was actually really surprised by some of Callum's backstory. In the prologue, Callum's mother is hiding out with her newborn son and is viciously slaughtered in a mass murder by the enemy. As Callum's father is walking through the cave that his wife just died in, this happens: 
 "As he bent closer, he realized they were words -- words his wife had carved into the cave ice with the last of her dying strength. As he read them, he felt them like three hard blows in the stomach. 
 KILL THE CHILD" 
 How suspenseful is that? I had to keep reading to find out what happened next. Speaking of characters, the antagonist was someone I really loved reading about. The antagonist was called the Enemy of Death. I've heard people call him Ed, though. Despite his rather unoriginal name, the character of the Enemy is something that captivated me, especially as the story progressed. One of the things I was particularly curious to learn about was, who was the Enemy of Death exactly? No one had seen him in decades, yet he still sent out his army to wreak havoc on Magisterium. Hmm... 
 Do I have anything to complain about? Not really. But I read an ARC of this book and since the next book releases late in 2015, it feels like ages until I can find out what happens next. I'm still very excited for book two (it's called The Copper Gauntlet) and I can't wait to read more about the world of Magisterium. Five stars for sure!

This is the story of a boy, who survived after being attacked as an infant by the enemy of the magical world while his parents fought in a magical war. His mother died during the attack and he was left damaged and physically scarred by the experience. 
 He gets into a magical school, despite a seeming lack of affinity or knowledge about his heritage and is mentored by a strange and enigmatic mage who will never give a straight answer. 
 While learning, he makes friends with two of his classmates, a boy and a girl. The girl has studied magic for a long time and is particularly talented and the boy is loveable and well-liked by others. 
 This boy discovers he is possessed of a magic that is connected to the evil mage that lead the other side in the war his mother died in. 
 His father, who may not really be his father, treats him coldly and is angry that he is a part of the magical world. 
 He has a strong connection with his magical pet, and he thwarts a plan by the evil mages underlings to bring him back to his former place of power with the help of his friends. 
 Sound familiar? If not, you should really read Harry Potter. You can skip this series, there is very little new here and it isn't as well-written as HP.

 ''The Enemy was a great mage - maybe even the best - but he went crazy. He wanted to live forever and make the dead live again. That's why they called him the Enemy of Death, because he tried to conquer death. He started pulling chaos into the world, putting the power of the void into animals...and even people.'' 
 Sigh. 
 I'm thinking that this reminds me very much of someone in the Harry Potter series. You must be annoyed of seeing this being so much compared to that series but...there are so many similarities! ...To say the least. 
 It wasn't 100% ripped off but you can't just stop comparing it to HP while reading it. I have actually no idea what Cassandra Clare and Holly Black are thinking about their work, themselves, but I wonder how they did to NOT see (or perhaps they just didn't care?) the 'that-belongs-to-the-Harry-Potter-series' elements. 
 The beginning, I actually enjoyed. It was interesting and I had a good feeling about this book but that only went on for a maximum of 40 pages. Then, it all went VERY downhill and I kept thinking stuff like ''Come on, you can do it. Only 200 pages left...150 more...100, you're almost there, 50 thank god...'' and then it was 50% reading and 50% skimming. 
 There were those silly sentences that made me cringe or just annoyed or confused the hell out of me. Seriously, this was a bad reading experience. 
 ''You're closer to the element - like you're doing magic, you eat rocks or sand, fire mages can eat matches, air mages might consume blood for its oxygen.'' 
 SERIOUSLY??? Who would eat rocks, sand, matches or BLOOD, to gain more power? A sick sick person. 
 The writing was absolutely not impressive nor pleasant. If only it had a better and more beautiful one, I would have enjoyed this maybe A LITTLE more. See, the story takes place in our Century so the language is pretty urban. I was expecting something different and wanted this to feel like a true fantasy book. 
 As much as I love witches, magic, wizards and boarding schools, those elements in the story weren't, surprisingly, enough to make me enjoy the plot. That quite rarely happens to me. The Magisterium didn't even feel like a school, more like a camp. 
 The events are predictable or just darn boring. And, to be honest, I was just not convinced. Not convinced by the characters, the friendship, the dialogs, the TWIST. I don't even see how this series might get interesting with its sequels. It just lacked or contained too many, as I said, similarities to the HP series. 
 So, I would certainly recommend you stay away from this, in my opinion, awful read that will only anger you (if you're an HP fan) or steal your precious time. That was harsh, I know, but it doesn't change that I felt-and still feel-what I said in this review. 
 PS. There are illustrations in this book, mostly at the beginning of each chapter, but, unfortunately, they're not always pertinent.

I bought this one as soon as it came out but just haven't had the time to read it. I'm glad I finally found the time though, because it was a great read. The story follows Callum Hunt as he attends his first year at a school of alchemical magic, a school his father always warned him would be the death of him. When he arrives, however, Callum falls in love with the school and the magic his father had always warned him against. He even makes friends, something he has never had before due to his crippled leg making him an object of mockery at previous schools. But the longer he stays the more he starts to uncover about just how dark this world of magic can be. Just how dark he might be. 
 The concept of a chosen one and magical schools is one that's a bit overdone as of late, but Clare and Black manage to keep it interesting with plenty of new elements. I've always been a lover of alchemy ever since I was little, but in most stories about magic it is mentioned off-hand and never really focused on if it is mentioned at all, so it was awesome to see it take center stage here. There's also some hints at a decent explanation of the magic and where it is drawn from, something that generally seems to be lacking in other books of this sort. 
 It was also refreshing not to have a love triangle of any sort hinted at, but if I know Clare there's a decent chance something of the sort will show up in the later books of this series as the characters get a bit older. I do sort of hope it doesn't though. It really isn't needed. Either way though, I will certainly be eagerly devouring the rest of this series as it comes out.

Ten Second Synopsis: 
 Call fails at failing the entrance exam to the Magesterium and must face his first year as an apprentice Mage. 
 So, for starters, this is basically an American Harry Potter redressed for a new generation. I won't go into the similarities here because they'll be apparent from the very first chapter to those who have read the Potter series. This isn't altogether a bad thing, because, hey, the Potter stories were fantastic - but it is mildly off-putting to read bits that seem overly familiar. I know others have mentioned that there are a couple of twists in the tale that take it in a different direction, but event the big twist at the end has shades of one of the big reveals of the Potterverse. 
 Having said that, this is a reasonably enjoyable book, and I think it will appeal greatly to middle-graders and YA readers - particularly if they haven't read the Potter books. The second half of the tale is far more interesting than the first. Given that it's taken me over a month to read it, and I finished more than half of it this morning, I feel pretty safe in saying that the first half of the story is pretty mediocre. Initially, Call has a chip on his shoulder the size of Alaska and just generally seems like a snarky little snot. As the story unfolds he loosens up a bit and friendships develop that give depth to the characters, and by the end I liked him a lot. 
 I also particularly enjoyed the animal characters in the story. They were a nice addition that added a bit of light to the shade of the events. 
 There are plenty of one-liners here that are both funny and memorable, and overall, I enjoyed the tone of the book. I think I will be more interested in the next book in the series as it will be fun to see where the authors take the revelations at the end of this book.

 I wanted to like The Iron Trial (Magisterium #1). Really, I did. I enjoyed Cassandra Clare's Shadowhunter series, and although I haven't read any of Holly Black's books yet (shame on me), others have told me what an amazing author she is. Granted, the synopsis of this book read like a summary of Harry Potter, and I saw the similarities, but I still hoped the book would be different enough. Alas, turns out it wasn't. 
 The basic plot eerily resembles Harry Potter. A young man, Callum Hunt, goes to a magician's school to learn control his magic. Except, Call doesn't really want to go - all his life, his dad told him to stay away from magic. His dad wants him to fail The Iron Trial, the rest that allows certain kids into magic school, called the Magisterium. But despite Call doing everything he can to fail, he gets accepted anyway. He'll discover what secrets the Magisterium holds, and if it's really as horrible as his dad warned him about... 
 All right, so I'm all for how people should still be allowed to write books about kids going to magic school. Harry Potter did it, sure, but it's been done before, and it's been done after (I'm thinking "The School of Good and Evil, which was also about a magic school). But...There's a difference between having the same basic plot (kid goes to magic school), which is no biggie...and rehearsing just about every single thing from the Harry Potter books. 
 The villain here is a one-dimensional baddy called "The Enemy", supposedly because people are too afraid to say his name. Ring a bell? The main character has two best friends: a boy and a girl (again, Harry Potter similarities). And then the most OBVIOUS one - at birth, called was marked by the Enemy. The parallels are MORE than just 'kid going to magic school', and they're annoying. They made me roll my eyes. They even made me upset. I can only tolerate so many similarities, people. 
 On top of that, the book just doesn't have anything original. Not a single thing. The plot is boring and overused, bordering on cliche. The characters are stereotypes and two-dimensional. The magic system is flawed, the world building needs serious work. Connecting to any of the characters, even Call, was almost impossible. The pace is slow, especially from the moment Call enters the Magisterium, and it drags on for pages on end, even taking some detours in the plot. 
 The surprise at the end was a fun twist, but one that I saw coming from miles away. I know I'm not a middle grader and that middle graders might love this, but I seriously doubt it. Kids are picky nowadays. They too want good world building and characters they can root for. So even if the writing isn't always stellar, they at least want a decent plot and plenty of action, none of which they've given here. 
 If you want a good fantasy book for middle graders, pick up the Lockwood & Co series. It's infinitely better than this one.

Call's disability seems like a real part of his life and the way that he moves through the world, but it's by no means the only featured trait about him-- far from it. 
 True to Holly Black books, the plot had some nice twists, though maybe it was all a bit more simple since it was middle grade. But really! I liked this book :) I'll be giving it to my little cousin because it was a solidly enjoyable read.

Callum Hunt has been told by his father that he should never trust a magician. He hasn't really had to worry too much about it, that is until he is told that he has to take a test to see if he will be accepted into the Magisterium. His father gives him one instruction: fail the test. That doesn't sound too hard to Callum, after all getting into trouble is something he happens to be good at. But things don't go according to plan, and Callum finds himself at the Magisterium, trying to pass the Iron Trial. It is every magician's dream come true... and Callum's nightmare. 
 Cassandra Clare & Holly Black's Book One of the Magisterium series, The Iron Trial, is an action driven, magical tale with some dark undertones. I'm sure there will be some Harry Potter comparisons: it is set in a magic school, it follows the protagonist and his two friends (a boy and a girl), and there is a "big bad" antagonist who isn't seen much on the page. Cassandra Clare's writing origins in Harry Potter fanfiction won't help either. But (and this is a big but) that is no reason not to read The Iron Trial. Similarities aside, this book had plenty of twists that I did not see coming, and Callum is such an unusual but likable character that he draws you into the pages. Firstly, he's not big on making friends, and he takes a while to warm up to his new ones (and them to him). He also has a mild disability - his leg was injured at birth and he cannot walk fast, or properly. That doesn't stop him however, and he doesn't sit around waiting for things to happen. Callum is an exceptionally action focused character - there is no sitting around moping for him... 
 Read the rest of my review on NZ Booklovers.

reference_books.title: Hell House
reference_books.review_text:
Ok, here's the thing. The writing was fine. And the plot was pretty good (standard haunted house, group of people comes to check it out and possibly de-haunt it sort of thing). So the two stars are really more of a personal preference, as I don't handle dark things well. And this was really, really dark. It forces you to think about things that humanity has the capacity for that, in my opinion, don't need to be thought about. They don't need to be thought about, because one of the things we should be working towards as a society is to eradicate even the notion of those things. 
 I'm talking about stuff like necrophilia, etc. I don't need that in my head. So it's not so much an 'I don't want to think about unpleasant things' as 'Writing about this feels unnecessary to anyone's betterment in any way.' 
 I do like Richard Matheson. And there were some things, like the character of Florence, the medium, that I really liked. And it was pretty readable from a writing standpoint. But I just wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

reference_books.title: Twilight (Twilight, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I didn't want to post that I was reading this until I was done, because it would've been too prolonged an embarrassment. 
 I've hated this book with a passion that exceeds my hatred for all other books, except maybe that one that said Elizabeth I made a pact with the devil to become queen. But no, that was written well. 
 Stephenie Meyer...words cannot express (but cliches can) how amazed I am that she was published. Published! And then caused some kind of vampire phenomenon with her writing! 5/6 of the way into Twilight, it gets interesting for about 50 pages, and that's it. If you can read the rest of the book sincerely, then I do not understand you. 
 Bella Swan is the most selfish, irritating, and yet somehow boring heroine I've ever come across. She and Edward have nothing in common. Except maybe the fact that they're both boring. I read the entire, huge book and they don't have a single interesting conversation. Bella spends all her time with him "gazing at his perfection" and he's usually sitting there with a pissed-off look on his face. THERE IS NOTHING APPEALING ABOUT THESE CHARACTERS. Why read it, then? Because, to quote Cheers, "hate is not the opposite of love -- indifference is," and I've hated it so long I know way too much about it. 
 I'd like to spend the rest of the review posting awful quotes: 
 "I wasn't interesting. And he was. Interesting...and brilliant...and mysterious...and perfect...and beautiful...and possibly able to lift full-sized vans with one hand." 
 "Jessica babbled on and on about her dance plans -- Lauren and Angela had asked the other boys and they were all going together -- completely unaware of my inattention." (Bella's a horrible person) 
 "I didn't feel like mentioning that my stomach was already full -- of butterflies." (omg the bad writing, it burns) 
 "I tried to keep up better this time through the woods, so naturally I fell a few times." (Bella's primary characteristic is that she's clumsy. To the point where she might be developmentally disabled, but no one ever seems to call that into question) 
 "I dug through my desk until I found my old headphones, and I plugged them into my little CD player." (Did I mention this is apparently set in 1997?) 
 "Something outside the possibility of rational justification was taking place in front of my incredulous eyes." (I just hated that sentence) 
 Bella's essay topic for her class: "Whether Shakespeare's treatment of the female characters is misogynistic." HOW IRONIC. 
 "I shambled along behind Jessica, not bothering to pretend to listen anymore." (Horrible person) 
 "My favorites were Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility." (Oh, you mean the two most famous ones? And you quoted the beginning of Genesis at the start of your book, Stephenie Meyer? And which Shakespearean play does Edward quote? Romeo and Juliet? HAVE YOU EVER READ ANYTHING THAT HAS NOT SEEPED ITS WAY INTO POPULAR CULTURE?) 
 "He walked to the door of the restaurant and held it open with an obstinate expression. Obviously, there would be no further discussion. I walked past him into the restaurant with a resigned sigh." (Oh yeah, Edward's like an abusive husband, btw) 
 "I wondered if it should bother me that he was following me; instead I felt a strange surge of pleasure." (WTF) 
 ""You remember?" he asked, his angel's face grave." (AGGGHHHHH) 
 ""You were going to fight them?" This upset him. "Didn't you think about running?" "I fall down a lot when I run," I admitted." (Who does that?? Does anyone know anyone who does that? That doesn't have a disability of some kind?) 
 "It was a colossal tribute to his face that it kept my eyes away from his body." (Stephenie Meyer...I'm not even going to say it) 
 "'I'm absolutely ordinary -- well, except for bad things like all the near-death experiences and being so clumsy that I'm almost disabled.'" (Oh yeah, I forgot that she admits it at one point) 
 "If I had to, I supposed I could purposefully put myself in danger to keep him close. . . . I banished that thought before his quick eyes read it on my face." (I would like to add that not only is this the thought of someone PSYCHOTIC, but also that she spends most of the next book doing just that) 
 "I would have been angrier if his laughter wasn't so fascinating." 
 ""What do you want to talk about?" he asked. He was still annoyed." (Edward is always annoyed) 
 "He shook his head, still gazing morosely at the heavy clouds." (Aahahahahahaha) 
 "Good morning." His voice was silky. "How are you today?" His eyes roamed over my face, as if his question was something more than simple courtesy. (When I read this, I immediately thought of all the 15-year-olds reading this and thinking how amazing it is that Edward really cares. Stephenie Meyer is making the next generation of idiots worse) 
 "'Darkness is so predictable, don't you think?' He smiled wistfully." (My friend and I practiced smiling wistfully after this) 
 "He grinned his crooked smile at me, stopping my breath and my heart. I couldn't imagine how an angel could be any more glorious. There was nothing about him that could be improved upon. "How did you sleep?" he asked. I wondered if he had any idea how appealing his voice was." (I count four references to Edward's perfection in that paragraph. STEPHENIE MEYER YOU HAVE ISSUES) 
 "We were silent for the rest of the drive. I could feel the waves of infuriated disapproval rolling off of him, and I could think of nothing to say." (But obvs despite his constant irritation/anger, he's still perfect) 
 "I tried to keep my eyes away from his perfection as much as possible, but I slipped often. Each time, his beauty pierced me through with sadness." 
 "The meadow, so spectacular to me at first, paled next to his magnificence." 
 It's a terrible, terrible book. I can't defend my reasons for reading it, as they are convoluted even to me, but...just horrible.

reference_books.title: Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit
reference_books.review_text:
This book was seriously up and down for me. Jeanette Winterson would suddenly come up with some brilliant flash of insight and I'd think 'This is amazing!' and then she'd spend a chapter or two being maddeningly vague about EVERYTHING. 
 She has this theory about history that it shouldn't necessarily be studied or tried to be laid out nicely in a timeline/history book, because that's just inaccurate and we can never get it right. I'm assuming the way this theory plays out in her writing is indeed this total lack of detail that at least her first book contains. Speaking as someone who spent their formative works reading 19th c. lit, as it was guaranteed not to be 'dirty', I need detail. Preferably heaps and heaps of it. I'll settle for the occasionally nice descriptive paragraph. But no! She denies me this. 
 The main parts of this book I did like, actually, aside from the infrequent bursts of brilliance, were when she told allegorical tales. She is mightily good at them. Hopefully her other novels will be more of that and less of this vagueness. 
 Finally, a quote I liked: "Romantic love has been diluted into paperback form and has sold thousands and millions of copies. Somewhere it is still in the original, written on tablets of stone."

Or possibly that's just my own asshole reaction. reference_books.title: Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded
reference_books.review_text:
This book sucks so bad. It's all about a young lord named Master B-- who spends most of the novel trying various ways of bedding servant girl Pamela, only to finally 'realize' that he wants to marry her, despite their extremely disparate social situations, especially for the 18th century. 
 Most of the exchanges, which happen whenever Master B-- isn't thrusting his hand into Pamela's bosom (it's not as exciting as it sounds) go like this: 
 Lady Davers: Pour me wine, you hussy! 
 Pamela: Shan't! 
 Lady Davers: You pert and insolent saucebox! 
 Lady Davers's Nephew: I say! 
 The subtitle is "Virtue Rewarded", and so Richardson is basically saying that if you keep your virtue, etc., you'll be rewarded in *this* life, which, as the introduction to Shamela quotes from Tom Jones: "to which we have but one objection, namely, that it is not true". 
 Sucks.

One is entitled something like "The first in a series of love letters to Amy Poehler," so I was hoping this would be a recurring theme throughout the book, but no such luck. ** spoiler alert ** 
 Hmm, I'm sort of conflicted about this book. 
 What I expected: A laugh out loud book about a comedian's life and life in Hollywood. 
 What I got: A somewhat interesting left-leaning treatise that wasn't laugh out loud funny but made me smile in parts. 
 It's clear Tina Fey and I would likely not agree on anything political. She openly worships Alec Baldwin and his influence on her career which seems fine to be gracious but there's being gracious and groveling and the latter became evident. 
 Based on reading this book, if I had to guess I would say that Ms. Fey would come down on the side of the protesters against the police in these recent shootings and gun ownership. Against profiling. But then an interesting thing happens on page 49-50 of her book where she is describing advice from her father. 
 "Conversely, he would tell us things like 'If you see two black kids riding around on one bike, put your bike in the garage.' This wasn't racism; it was experience. Those kids were coming from West Philly to steal bikes. The social factors that caused their behavior were irrelevant to a Depression baby." 
 Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Really? Because I'm pretty sure if a cop today said and did that she would not say the same thing. And, the chapter on her father, she only referred to him by his first and last name-- All. The. Time. That was just weird. 
 Some chapters I did find pretty endearing-- such as the one about her honeymoon. Also, the chapters on SNL and her impersonating Sarah Palin were interesting as well. I did appreciate the fact that she did try to protect Sarah Palin and give her a good experience on SNL. 
 What was most interesting but not really fully divulged was how she got the scar on her face which evidently happened when someone slashed her with a knife when she was five-years-old. She doesn't delve into the topic at all except to say that all the attention she got after that incident falsely inflated her ego to the point where she was willing to try anything and everything. It felt like a lot was missing from this autobiography not to talk more about that and the impact it had. 
 If you're left-leaning and enjoy all things Hollywood then I think you'll really like this book. All others, there are interesting parts but definitely get it from the library.

At any rate, I'm giving it 3.5 stars because of the writing itself. It came across as if it were written for the screen and not the page, so it was short and disjointed. Yet, it was still entertaining, funny, and a personable insight into Tina Fey's life. I admire her ability (struggle) to balance work and family, especially when the SNL Sarah Palin "side gig" appeared in her life. The book is not an instant classic or something you'll fall in love with, but it's worth a quick read if you need something for a flight or the beach.  Tina Fey narrates her own audiobook - and I wouldn't have wanted it any other way. Bossypants was already on my TBR list, but when I heard Tina Fey was reading the audio, I knew that I would be listening to the book instead of reading it. Let's be honest, there is no way I am going to deliver Tina Fey's words in my own head better than Tina Fey herself. (Great move on my part.) 
 Sitting in Tunnel traffic heading into Manhattan has never been so entertaining! My traffic mates probably thought I was a crazy person, but I didn't care. When my commute didn't allow me to finish the book, I found myself taking the long way home from little league baseball games and parent-teacher conferences just to listen to more! 
 Tina Fey talks about everything from the awkwardness of puberty to working for the Improv group, Second City; from the thrill of her years working for Lorne Michaels at Saturday Night Live to the Internet haters (to which she responds!); from the 2008 presidential election that catapulted her to celebritydom, to the Teat Nazis she encounters after becoming a mother. (SNL allowed the rights for her to use the audio clip of the opening with her as Sarah Palin and Amy Poehler as Hillary Clinton. I don't care who you voted for, this clip is HILARIOUS.) I have tried to come up with which chapter was my favorite - but I can not. 
 My only warning: Don't listen while the kids are around, or download onto your iPod for your own personal enjoyment. Tina Fey does not censor herself...nor should she! 
 Tina Fey is honest, insightful, and funny as hell. I am so glad I listened to this book, and highly recommend Bossypants!

I am a latecomer in terms of appreciation of the hilarity of Tina Fey. I once thought she really wasn't all that funny. It took half a dozen episodes of 30 Rock (watched when all my other shows were off season) for me to appreciate it. But then? I couldn't get over the wisdom of Tina Fey's character Liz Lemon. I was spouting off Liz Lemonisms way too frequently. 
 So when I quoted her one too many times to my brother in a text, he asked if I had read Bossypants yet. Which, of course, I hadn't. I promptly paid much more than I ever do for an ebook ($7.99, if I recall) and began reading. By afternoon, I was finished. 
 Bossypants is, as many collections of personal essays are, a bit all over the place. The writing isn't phenomenal. There are moments when it isn't even that funny, so don't go in expecting early David Sedaris. That said, Fey's story of her life prior to her run as Sarah Palin on Saturday Night Live and Liz Lemon on 30 Rock is pretty special. It's more of an insider's view backstage those two shows than anything else, so if you aren't familiar with either, then Bossypants may not be for you. 
 And she does bring the funny: 
 Q: Is 30 Rock the most racist show on television? 
 A: No, in my opinion it's NFL football. Why do they portray all those guys as murderers and rapists? 
 ***** 
 (By the way, when Oprah Winfrey is suggesting you may have overextended yourself, you need to examine your fucking life.) 
 ***** 
 We began our breast-feeding journey in the hospital under the tutelage of an encouraging Irish night nurse named Mary. We tried the football hold, the cross-cradle hold, and one I like to call the Bret Michaels, where you kind of lie over the baby and stick your breast in its mouth to wake it up. 
 ***** 
 Lesson learned? When people say, "You really, really must" do something, it means you don't really have to. No one ever says, "You really, really must deliver the baby during labor." When it's true, it doesn't need to be said. 
 ***** 
 I have a suspicion - and hear me out, 'cause this is a rough one - I have a suspicion that the definition of "crazy" in show business is a woman who keeps talking even after no one wants to fuck her anymore. 
 The only person I can think of that has escaped the "crazy" moniker is Betty White, which, obviously, is because people still want to have sex with her. 
 ***** 
 At times, such as in the last bit of dark humor, Bossypants seems to bemoan the fact that women in television haven't come all that far, but by virtue of Fey's prominence (and I would include Amy Poehler here), it's evident that the strides, though small, are being made. And I plan to review Mindy Kaling's book tomorrow, a similar book but one that varies in pretty significant ways, i.e. generational differences. [Tip: Everyone I know who has read this has raved about the audio, and as I could hear Tina Fey's voice as I read, I can imagine it'd be a pretty good listen.]

Here's the thing about Tina Fey- SHE KNOWS WHO SHE IS. And how awesome is that? I love this book- it's part memoir, part sketch comedy in book form, part self-help book. Chock full of little vignettes about the things that shaped her life and how she got to where she is (America's foremost comedy writer- I was going to say "female comedy writer" but Tina wouldn't want me to do that, and honestly, I can't think of anyone who makes me laugh as consistently as she does- she wrote the "Moms Jeans" sketch for cryin' out loud!). 
 And lest you think it's all Hollywood anecdotes all the time, it's not. She writes about things that all women think about- body image, working mom guilt, overcoming the horrible decisions we make in our lives, balancing it all so you don't go crazy, and those triannual cries we have when we just know that we have ruined everything and it will never be any better and you're sick of dealing with stupid people and you're so angry that you're crying it just makes you cry even harder. Yeah, I've been there. 
 And do you want to know the best part?? This book is hilarious and snarky and sweet and subversive. It's just awesome. Just like Tina.

This book is really a 2 1/2 star, but since that rating is not available and since I'm in awe of Betty White--89 years old and starring in a sit-com and guest starring on just about everything else--I'm bumping the rating up to a 3. A nice little book to read if you have an extra two hours. Betty White is, of course, adorable and she includes some wonderful stories--especially from the past 15 years--you know, since she was a youngster of 74. The "chapters" are about two or three pages long and are reflections on a variety of topics. However, much of the material was repetitious. I know, I know, she's 89, but where was the editor? My hat is off to Betty White. Judging from the stories and philosophy included in this book, she has not only lived a long life, but she has lived a fulfilling life. We should all be so lucky.

This book is so random. LOL Just kind of a bunch of ramblings from Betty White that someone asked her to write since she is so popular right now. But you have got to give this woman props for writing a book when she is 89. I learned some interesting stuff about her though.

"If one has no sense of humor, one is in trouble."

sample_reviews.review_text: Anya's Ghost was a great read. I liked this graphic novel because of the supernatural mystery...there were a few twists I did not see coming! As well, I liked how the author incorporated issues regarding coming-of-age and cultural identity. These elements added layers, elevating it to more than just your average "ghost" story.
