It's been awhile since I've read a graphic novel that wasn't a memoir. This is a ghost story/teen angst tale of a Russian girl trying to seem as American as possible so she can fit in with the popular kids at her private school. One day she falls down an old well that is inhabited by the ghost of a girl who died there 90 years ago. When Anya gets rescued from the well one of the girl's bones ends up in her bag and now the ghost girl is following Anya around. Initially, it's kind of cool, the ghost girl, whose name we later learn is Emily, is able to do all kinds of ghosty things. She helps Anya cheat on tests, she sneaks into the locker of Anya's crush and finds out his class schedule so Anya can bump into him, and she helps her find out about a party. But then Emily gets more demanding and more scary. Totally imaginative and fun.

Apa yang membuat saya tertarik membaca buku ini saat berada di toko buku (iya, bacanya numpang aja) adalah adanya endorse dari Neil Gaiman, salah satu penulis favorit saya. Jika Gaiman saja bilang masterpiece, terus saya harus bilang apa? 
 Novel grafis ini menceritakan tentang seorang gadis remaja yang berasal dari Rusia dan pindah ke Amerika sejak berusia lima tahun, bernama Anya. Anya berusaha keras untuk menjadi lebih langsing, menghilangkan logat Rusianya, dan bergaya hidup sebagaimana remaja Amerika supaya dapat diterima dan tidak mengalami bullying sebagaimana saat dia baru pindah. Namun, apa pun yang dilakukannya tak pernah cukup. 
 Suatu hari, dia terjatuh ke sebuah sumur dan menemukan hantu gadis seusianya, Emily, yang meninggal 93 tahun yang lalu. Anya pun berteman dengan hantu itu sejak Emily mulai membantunya dalam pelajaran sekolah, juga membantunya mendekati anak laki-laki populer di sekolah yang disukainya. Semakin lama, Anya menemukan ketidakberesan pada Emily, dan menyelidiki kasus kematian yang terjadi di masa lalu. 
 Kisahnya ringan dan cocok sekali untuk remaja yang sedang 'peduli-pedulinya' dengan pendapat orang-orang di sekitarnya, yang berusaha menjadi orang lain demi diterima di komunitas yang (katanya) keren. Sayangnya, saya agak kecewa dengan penerjemahannya. Saya tidak (belum?) dapat menikmati gaya penulisan yang menggunakan bahasa gaul. Mungkin, seandainya saya membaca dengan bahasa Inggris, atau bahasa Indonesia yang lebih bisa saya terima, saya bisa memberi kisah ini empat bintang. Tapi, entahlah. 
 Pada akhirnya, kisah Anya dan Emily menunjukkan betapa tidak pentingnya penampilan luar dan latar belakang sosial. Ilustrasi dalam novel grafis ini sederhana, tidak terlalu banyak detail, namun cukup cantik. Oleh karena adanya beberapa kata-kata kasar, materi seksualitas remaja, serta sedikit potensi kekerasan, buku ini tidak cocok dibaca oleh anak-anak.

This review was originally posted at Classics Without All the Class. 
 I discovered Vera Brosgol's graphic novel, Anya's Ghost almost by accident. I was at the library perusing the "Teen Section" where they have conveniently placed all of the comics and graphic novels, making me look terribly out of place in the process. I was scanning the shelves and title after title read "Marvel" and "DC." While superhero comics are fun and popular, that's not what I was interested in. I wanted something I hadn't seen before, something a little different, and Brosgol's novel stuck out like a sore thumb. So I picked it up. While the old adage, "Don't judge a book by it's cover" can be useful, it wasn't here. A judgement was rendered -- it looked interesting -- and it came home with me. 
 Anya's Ghost is a young adult graphic novel centered around a high school girl named Anya, her struggle for normalcy as a Russian immigrant living in America, and her friendship with a ghost named Emily. But the moral of this story is about perception. Things aren't always what they seem, but Anya just doesn't know it yet. 
 At the beginning of the story, Anya is like many other teenagers -- self-absorbed, insecure, and a bit mean to her family. She sees only what is happening on the surface. It's at a typical high-school party that she has the experience of peering into another reality to realize that all is not what it seems. Anya begins to change through a series of events involving her ghost friend Emily, a classmate named Dima, and her family. Anya becomes stronger, more self-confident, and selfless through these experiences and over the course of the story. 
 The graphic part of the novel is beautifully drawn and shaded in three main colors: black, white, and purple. The lines Brosgol uses are heavy and dark while the artwork is a bit cartoonish -- it's reminiscent of Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis. The cartoon-like quality of the drawings makes the novel accessible to readers of almost any age. 
 While I especially enjoyed the beginning of Anya's Ghost, things were muddled in the middle with the fight involving Anya's best friend, not to mention her inaction while watching Dima get bullied, or her attempts to garner the attention of her popular crush. Ultimately, Anya learns her lesson that things aren't always what they seem. 
 The Verdict: 
 Library bag. While I enjoyed Anya's Ghost, it's heavy midsection kept me from running down to my local comic shop to pick up my own copy. However, I think it would be a great read for most adolescents and teens. It's beautifully illustrated with a lesson that all of us could take care to remember.

As many graphic novels are prone to be, this was a really fast read, but with lots of interesting depth. Anya's challenges in coming from an immigrant family are not lost on the reader. Early on in the story we find Anya tossing out her mother's ethnic food, in favor of what she deems more "normal" and then heading off to school. Along the way, she falls down a well and meets the ghost of a girl that died from falling down the same well. What seems like a sad little ghost of a previous sweet girl though, might not be all she's led Anya to believe. 
 Obviously, Anya is saved from the well, but her little ghost friend is not left behind. Rather than helping Anya to fit in better, this ghost has not been as forthright about her death as she should have been, leaving Anya with way more on her hands than just her cultural difference. The story does turn spooky, giving Anya bigger things to worry about than her own ethnic background. In true graphic novel fashion, this spooky story still has a light-heartedness about it that we know will somehow lead to a happy ending. 
 I really liked Anya's Ghost and found the story to be one that I fell into pretty quickly. The pictures are well done and the dialogue propels the action forward. Besides the action, we still understand the emotions felt by many of the characters. Anya just wants to feel "normal" like most teens, but with a ghost hanging around, that leads to more abnormal than one might expect! In the scope of storytelling, graphic novels, and the supernatural, this was a fun and spooky tale that pulled me out of my own little reading slump. Thanks to the creativity of artists and authors combined, their vision came together in an engaging story that plays with the modern and old, with the dark and the light. If you're looking for a fun ghost story that still gets marks for being creepy, then this is a nice one to try out.

Plus side: the illustrations are cool and I liked Anya. 
 Negative side: The twist did little to advance the themes and seemed a little cliched. I didn't think so much plot was necessary due to the aforementioned strengths.

Another one of those books I never reviewed! 
 Anya's Ghost is so wonderful. From Anya's spunky Irish friend Siobhan to that deep, deep well- everything is so incredibly interesting here. 
 Anya is a Russian-American girl, which was super fun for me to read just because, well, I am Russian-American. However, my parents are Jewish, so instead of being bugged to go to church, it was synagogue for me. 
 Overall, I felt I could oh-so-much relate to Anya. And I think she's the type of character anyone can feel the same about. 
 Please, anyone who is a fan of cute ghost stories or graphic novels, read this book!

I'm very picky about my graphic novels. The story in this one is, though a bit fantastic what with the ghost and all, really very universal. Anya is going through that life lesson when it seems that everything is wrong with your life and so much worse for you than everyone else. Then you find something/someone that you think will fix everything. You do some stupid stuff as a result of thinking you have new power. Then you eventually wake up and realize that the whole world isn't about you after all. Anya's just learning this in a slightly more dramatic way that most of us. 
 What so impressed me with this book was the expressiveness of the illustrations. The range of emotions that the characters showed was amazing. I could read volumes in one of their glances. 
 This book is well worth reading for teens. (There's also an important life lesson about respecting yourself, ladies!) Enjoy!

First thoughts: I woke up at 5:00 this morning and, after tossing and turning, decided going back to sleep just wasn't happening. Instead, I tore through some library reads - Anya's Ghost was one and was a book I had been curious about for ages! 
 While this turned out to be completely different than I had expected (for some reason I assumed this would be more of a girl-and-ghost-bestie-and-their-wacky-hijinks read) I enjoyed it all the same. HOWEVER, Anya was absolutely horrible. She's rude and nasty to her family (they left Russia for America when Anya was 5 and she can't deal with her mother's Russian ways or her cooking or accent or...) and joins in on ridiculing the only other Russian transplant at school. Until, of course, she needs his help, then she happily plays buddy-buddy. 
 Because of several elements (Anya's worries about her weight, her mother's upcoming citizenship test, her little brother's seemingly constant hobby of burying "treasure" aka Anya's jewelry in the yard, etc) I expected a big turnaround moment where Anya came to accept herself/her Russian heritage - or at the very least a few twists (her brother could have buried the bone necklace, for example) and they just weren't there. 
 Not bad and certainly a quick read, but not as great as I had expected.

It's a colorless graphic novel and the drawing is not "great" in particular, again... it's OK. The story follows a not likable character named Anya who is not popular, who doesn't have a boyfriend, doesn't have interesting experiences, etc. One day, she falls into a well where she met a ghost of a young woman who fell into the well on 1990-ish, or 1950-ish (I don't really remember). Later on, some guys helped Anya to get out of the well. The next day, the ghost of the young woman follows her to school. Turns out, the ghost follows Anya because there's a small part of her skull that is in Anya's bag. Suddenly, Anya's life has become more interesting and Anya likes it. But it doesn't last long... 
 The premise is good actually but again, the execution is failed. I yawned many times when I read this book and I was not really interested with it anymore after 100 pages. Too bad.

Based on how well I liked the movies, I thought I'd try out one of the books. 
 From what I've read, this book (and the recently released movie, which I have not seen yet) is not your typical Nicholas Sparks story. ** spoiler alert ** 
 There's only one way to start off this review... 
 ...Nicholas Sparks, WTF were you thinking?!?!? 
 Ok just had to get that out. 
 I haven't read a book by NS in awhile. I used to read more of them when I was in high school/early college partly because I wanted an outlet to pour my teen emotions into and partly because everyone else was doing it. For the most part, I've only ever thought his books were okay. All of them are pretty similar, love story mixed in with a tragic element, books you can pretty much finish in a snap. The one I enjoyed the most was True Believer but then the sequel At First Sight was god awful so that illustrates it for you. Since Hollywood seems to be on a kick to make all of his books into movies, Safe Haven being the next, I thought why not give that book a shot. 
 The book's storyline is pretty good, despite being a little predictable: Katie, woman who's being abused by her husband runs away, changes her identity and starts a new life in a small town. She's afraid to get close to anyone but little by little she gets sucked into the town. She moves into a cottage, starts making it her own, and is lucky enough to have a neighbor by the name of Jo to break her from her isolation. Jo helps Katie open up and becomes a good friend to her. Alex, the town's general store owner, also befriends her as well as his two children. His wife died and he finds himself attracted to Katie, the first woman he's looked at in a long time. Katie's attracted to him too but doesn't know if she should let him into her life....you see where this is going right? 
 Yeah so they fall in love. Everything's great. Meanwhile Katie's crazy husband his doing what he can to track her down to no avail. When a neighbor dies he realizes his beloved Erin has assumed the neighbor's dead daughter's name, Katie, and has relocated to Southport, North Carolina. He packs his bags, gun and all, and goes off to find her. He literally burns down the new life Katie has, almost kills Alex, but then Katie is able to get his gun and kill him. The sad part is the whole time he was so confused, he barely knew what was going on. Not an excuse for his behavior, but clearly he was mentally unstable & it's sad that someone like that didn't get help before it was too late. 
 So cheers all around the bad guy dies. And I actually enjoyed all of it...until the last two chapters. Hence why the WTF to NS. Instead of leaving the story as it was, he decides to make it so that Katie IMAGINED her good friend Jo, who actually turned out to be Alex's dead wife. AKA Alex's wife basically befriended Katie and made her realize she could be happy with Alex and the kids. Just to show you how the book deals with this: "Jo had been here and she felt her throat begin to tighten. Not because she didn't believe it but because she suddenly understood that her friend Jo - her only real friend, her wise advisor, her supporter and confidante - would never come back". So you're telling me all that time she had an imaginary friend? SERIOUSLY? AND IT WAS HER NEW BF'S DEAD WIFE? SERIOUSLY? How did she even know the woman's name? Was it a ghost then that was actually "there" but not alive? Wow just wow. That was when the whole story just went right out the window for me. It was like NS needed a way for the whole story to be tied into a perfect bow. Alex can move on because his dead wife said its okay and Katie can move on and be with Alex because the dead wife said it was okay. WTF!!!! There was no need for that, no need for Katie to imagine that Alex's dead wife was approving her. It's a twist that just makes NO SENSE. Way to kill a perfectly nice story NS. 
 While I'd definitely recommend this book over At First Sight or The Notebook, I wouldn't ever read it again. Nicholas Sparks shame on you for thinking you need to elevate this decent novel by throwing in a twist because "it's edgy and everyone else is doing it!". Instead you wrote a decent book with a craptastic twist for your ending. 
 I'm half wondering how the movie will handle this "imaginary friend" but I'm not wondering enough to pay money for it. See ya on Netflix Safe Haven. Maybe.

This story surprised me. Once a huge Nicholas Sparks fan, I've given up on him in recent years. I feel that his writing has become somewhat cliche and predictable and often the characters are just not that likable. 
 This story surprised me though, because even thought the basis of the story is somewhat cliche (abused woman tries to escape her abuser), the main character is extremely pitiable. I found myself rooting for her and at the same time understanding the way she guarded herself around new people. 
 This novel is also much more graphic than I expected from Sparks. The descriptions of abuse that the main character endured are so heart-wrenching, that even though this general story has been told many times, I was interested to hear her story. I thoroughly enjoyed the elements of suspense too. I read the book in a matter of days- listened to it in my car even, and could not wait to hear what was going to happen next. 
 If you haven't read any Sparks before and enjoy a good chick-novel, I would recommend this book. If you're a Sparks fan and have been waiting for his next "good one," this is it.

I'll start off by saying that before this book I have never read a Nicholas Sparks novel. I have seen movies of Nicholas Sparks books such as A Walk to Remember (my favorite movie btw), The Notebook, and Dear John (so sad!). Now I have heard things about his books; some are really great, some are cliche, some suck etc. Typical things people say about any other authors books, novels, series etc. Anyways, I was intrigued by this particular book when I saw the trailer for it about a month ago. After I saw it I immediately got on my laptop logged onto goodreads, and read reviews for this book. Then I put it on hold at my local library. 
 So now for my review: I loved this book! I absolutely loved it, and actually want to own it. 
 -What I really enjoyed about this book was the different point of views; its not just one characters perspective, and thats crucial for a story line like this one simply because you have to read the characters perspectives to understand why they do/did what they've done/are doing. 
 -The story line is really good. I loved how when Katie tells her story you feel her emotion, and her fear. I find it fascinating to see the inside of an abusive relationship. It's nothing positive by any means, but I was just so interested in how, and why her husband was so abusive. 
 -The character Kevin (the abusive husband); His point of views, and all of his chapters were just fascinating. I think i found it that way because I want to be a criminal profiler, so be allowed to get inside his head really made me exited. You learn so much about him in just a few chapters. 
 -The ending of the book! Holy balls, just completely unexpected (at least for me). However after reading it, it makes so much sense. 
 -It was a page turner, a little slow in the beginning but as relationships develop, and so forth it just gets better. 
 -The e only negative thing: I feel that both characters fell in love a little too soon. But that's just me so dont be offended. 
 I honestly recommend reading this book BEFORE the movie comes out. It really is good, and a great read.

reference_books.title: Down the Rabbit Hole: Curious Adventures and Cautionary Tales of a Former Playboy Bunny
reference_books.review_text:
I quit at about 40%. I grew weary of the "poor-little-me" routine. Get over it girl. You asked to move into the Playboy mansion because you were virtually homeless. You were given an allowance,lavish gifts,cars,etc. 
 Now you have the unmitigated gall to write a tell all and place yourself in the role of the victim. 
 It became a whiney trope about how horrible her life in the mansion was,how her confidence was eroded,how awful Hef was to her,how all of the other girls were "mean girls". Where are the violins. 
 I felt this book was a way to payback anyone who has ever slighted her. I have absolutely no judgement about her choices,you were an adult,my problem is the lack of responsibility for said choices. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone.

reference_books.title: Behind Closed Doors
reference_books.review_text:
THIS REVIEW MAY INCLUDE SPOILERS,PLEASE PROCEED AT YOUR OWN RISK. 
 Grace meets the man of her dreams. He is charming,chivalrous and is kind to her sister,Millie who has Downs Syndrome. It is a whirlwind romance,he asks her to marry him within a few months. 
 Things begin to go downhill when Prince Charming shoves Millie down the steps at the wedding,unbeknownst to Grace, and she is knocked unconscious,with a broken leg. 
 Prince Charming's behavior begins to unravel and on the honeymoon in Thailand he confesses his "evil" past and devious plan for Grace and her sister. It just keeps getting more ridiculous from here forward. 
 I had so many issues with this book. Grace was such an frustrating,unsympathetic ,ineffectual character. 
 I cannot fathom having a sister that relied upon me and I couldn't get it together enough to formulate a plan. Grace was a moth slapping against a lightbulb most of the time. As a matter of fact,Millie formulated a plan to save them both 
 Jack aka Prince Charming ,the husband,wasn't scary,he was just over the top. He wasn't diabolical,he was pathetic. He lacked the impact that a well written villain should have. 
 The ending of this book was abrupt and just odd. 
 This book lacked believability, flow, continuity...I'll just stop here. I just found this reading experience incredibly frustrating. Would recommend to no one.

reference_books.title: Wonder (Wonder #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book is a gem,and should be required reading in school. 
 This is a book about August who was born with severe facial deformities. Deformities so severe, that there was doubt that he would survive when he was born. He had a plethora of surgeries to repair his deformities so that the things we take for granted,like chewing,would become easier. 
 He was bright and homeschool by his Mother up until 5/6 grade when his parents decided he should go to private school with children his own age. 
 This book is about an extraordinary family, a lionhearted child and a wonderful,supportive cast . 
 Of course,there are bumps along the way and a bully or two,but overall this was a feel good little book. 
 Would highly recommend.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book disappointed me. I really fell in love with Dean Koontz's books back when he wrote Watchers. I love that his books include some sort of mystic animal story. While I was intrigued at first, I was growing wary when 2/3 into the book nothing had happened, and then suddenly it ended. I feel that the ending was rushed and left me wishing I had not paid $25 for it. I liked the characters--I think his character development is usually good, but the story lacked any sort of "wrapping up".

The third Dean Koontz book I read, and although not as amazing as Watchers, Breathless is still pretty good. I like his writing style and he has a talent for character development. Die-hard Koontz fans rated this one pretty low, but given I don't have huge expectations, I liked it well enough for a 3.5 to 4.0. Watchers is still his best, and one of the best books I've ever read. I'll definitely be reading more by him.
I've a love hate relationship with Koontz. This ended up on my Hate list. Seriously, what was this book about?
This book was too scattered for me to really enjoy it; really untypical of his work.

A convoluted plot with an unbelievable resolution. This story leaves me baffled. The loose argument of mathematical evolution versus Darwinism is an interesting premise not fully explored. And the wonderful and mysterious creatures discovered in the book barely make an appearance before the very abrupt, illogical conclusion. A very disappointing read. I'm glad I wasn't very invested in the characters.

Wow. This was an interesting book. It definitely creeped me out quite a bit...I've been hearing strange noises in my house for the past week or so, and I'm pretty sure it's because of this book. 
 This book was well-written and definitely a page turner. However, it gave such a good look into the minds of pure evil, that I sometimes wasn't sure I wanted to keep reading. 
 In the end, I'm glad I kept going. I liked the overall message from the book. I could however, have done with a bit less of the crazy, scheming evil that came along for the ride.

 Recently, I acquired the e-book copy of Breathless by Dean Koontz. I used to be a huge fan of Dean Koontz. In High School I would be checking out his books almost every week until I gulped up the entire collection ...or so I thought until one day I discovered there was other names that Dean Koontz wrote under such as David Axton for Prison of Ice, Brian Coffey for several titles including The Face of Fear (one of my favorites!), Surrounded, The Voice of the Night and the Wall of Masks, there is also other pen names including some you may have heard of like Deanna Dwyer (yes, i was shocked too!) who wrote Children of the storm (excellent book!), Dance with the Devil, The Dark of Summer, Demon Child and Legacy of Terror, then there is K.R Dwyer who wrote Chase, Dragonfly, Face of Fear *re-released under Koontz* (I own this copy and Koontz), and Shattered *re-released under Koontz* ( I have not had the privilege of reading yet), John Hill's the Long Sleep, a variety of books by Leigh Nichols, Anthony North's Strike Deep, Richard Paige's Door to December, Owen West , and Aaron Wolfe. All of these authors and probably more are really Dean Koontz. 
 I have really enjoyed all of Dean Koontz works. Something I think happened when Trixie, his beloved dog, passed on. His writing grew a little weary and I started to really not enjoy his books anymore. I really enjoyed " Your heart belongs to me" that was a great book and I gulped that up in just a few short days. It was one of those books that I wanted more at the end but for good reasons. Then, I decided since that book was good I bought a copy of " Relentless". I read all of it. I read every single page of that book in just a few short days as well. I thought it was leading up to something, that something good was to come at the end. I found nothing good. I was bored and disappointed and wanted to cry for even making myself lose time reading this book. That same day I finished reading it I listed it on Ebay. Someone bought it, I hope they liked it better than I did. There was also the " Husband " book. It also had the same feel that it was actually leading somewhere and then boom another disappointment. I think Husband came before Relentless though. 
 This all leads up to the newest book I decided to give it a go and read " Breathless" . It was a little dry in the beginning and I still decided to give it a chance. I was really enjoying all the cast of characters. It started to feel like the old Koontz. I thought perhaps I could actually get into this book. It had that old Dean Koontz energy you find in most of his writings. It was one of the Koontz books that starts with some random guy that leads up to other characters that somehow all are tangled in one web with each other somehow. 
 Breathless starts off with this random guy Grady Adams. He is just your average everyday Joe that makes furniture for a living and has a dog named Merlin who seems to be an awesome dog. Then we have Camille Rivers who is this everyday average veterinarian who has had a bad past (they never say what) and basically has sworn to protect all living animals no matter the risk. I really hate to say this I don't know why Camille was even in this book except for that Grady found some "creatures" that were of interest to a veterinarian. I was lost about where these two met, how they knew each other,etc. Plus, when Camille came in the picture we lost interest in Grady right away. His story was done and that was that. 
 There was a lot of unanswered questions in this whole book. I wanted to know so much more about everyone and I was just brought to a loss about it all. I wanted to really know more about Puzzle and Riddle the "creatures " that Grady found or rather they found him. I wanted to understand the nature of these beings but at the end it is poorly wrapped up to no satisfaction what so ever. It pretty much ends that things are "okay" now and they all live happily ever after . Why were those creatures there? Where did they come from? What is behind those eyes that he talks about so much? How were these creatures going to make life on Earth more better? I mean the end of this book wrapped up so poorly that if it had been an actual book and not my e-reader I might have considered throwing it against the wall. 
 OH and Mr. Koontz who were the random twin characters in here Henry and Jim? We have an awesome bad guy, a semi-plot that might actually trickle down to something but instead have nothing to do with Puzzle or Riddle or anything for this matter except the fact that he just happened to live next door to Grady. OH! I also don't understand that when Camille finds Jim's wife dead in the cellar how she just walks away and tells Grady, " I think Jim killed his wife," nonchalantly . There was no police involved? No one wondered what happened to these guys they just sort of disappeared at the end. I have no idea what their purpose was in this book at all. I think, however, that it would make a great book in itself. It just felt like ideas he was tossing around and decided to throw it in the book for good measure. 
 There is also Tom Bigger who has also nothing to do with anyone and meets a nice Jewish couple who decide to help him find his parents and he winds up saving one of the characters in this book. There was also no mention to him or the Jewish couple after that. He had also nothing to do with Puzzle or Riddle and I still am confused about why he was even there. 
 I just wanted so much more from this book and I was so disappointed to find out my time was wasted thinking this was a classic Koontz. Instead, it was just another failure by him . In my opinion, I would hold my breath to read this novel. It is up to you.

Wow..this book should have been titled "Lifeless". Is this really a book written by the successful Dean Koontz? I have this weird rule that if I start a book, I have to finish it. I need to change that rule I think because this one was torture. It truly is horrible. The characters are uninteresting at best. The end is horrific (which is probably the only reason it can be found under Horror in your bookstore). The only possible way you might find bits and pieces of this book interesting is if youre a HUUUGE dog lover. I personally am not, but Dean Koontz apparantly is because the dog is the only character in this book with any personality and since he can't talk it doesn't really do much for me. Ugh...i'm so angry that such a proven great writer gets away with writing something this bad and makes alot of money doing it. I think he even realized how bad this book was which explains the rushed ending. I'm gonna move on to another author for now till this book is long gone in my memory bank

I started this book, got 3 pages in and then wasn't able to read it again until just last week. I was a little concerned at first because this book seemed to really jump all over the place, but then I saw the pattern and it really kept me turning pages to get to the next chapter! This was a really hard book to put down.
Really, really quick read. Intriguing kind of story, doesn't hold together but then that's not what this kind of book is for!

The one thing I liked about this book was how there were so many stories intertwined that weren't obviously connected in the beginning. However, I felt the ending was anti-climactic. Was my first Dean Koontz book and I'm not quite sure I'm sold on him yet...
I'm trying to think of a good thing to say about this book. The part when the one supposedly intelligent character talks about evolution was pretty funny, I guess.

The fact that it is called "Breathless: A Novel of Suspense" had me confused. Where was the "suspense" exactly? Needless to say I was disappointed with this book. There was a large amount of characters that you don't get to really know and when Kootz finally gets to the point in the book that you understand why they are there, the book is basically over. I wasn't interested in finishing the book but thought I should because I had spent the money on it. He could have gone more into what Puzzle and Riddle were and why they were all there. I felt that the plot was underdeveloped and could have been so much better and more meaningful.
Mark my words - I'm done with new Koontz books. The next time I feel the need to read something by him, I'll pick up an old one like Lightning.

Probably my least favorite Koontz. I kept getting further and further in the story and I had fewer and fewer pages left and I just kept waiting for something to happen. I've been kind of disappointed in his more recent books. My favorites are his older one such as Watchers (my all time fav!), The Bad Place, Night Chills, Shattered, Lighting, Funhouse, Tears of the Dragon, etc. One of my friends recommended The Taking so I think I'll give that one a try too. Hopefully it's better than Breathless.
This book was awful. It built up to an anti-climatic ending that was complete nonsense. What a waste...

I am a huge fan of Dean Koontz because he writes with such passion and you are always being forced to turn the pages to find out what happened next. Compared to every other book of his I've read, this is flat and dull. It just gets good at the end and then it's all over; I felt like I had just started it. I wanted to learn more about Puzzle and Riddle and the influence they were going to have over the world and the future. 
 There were too many side stories that really didn't have any reason to be there; yes they all coincided, but it felt like fluff. 
 I hate to criticize Dean Koontz because he is usually amazing and I am addicted to his books, but I felt completely let down by this one.
I read as much as I could of this book. His writing is just not my style. The story dragged in too many places. Not enough suspense to hold my interest. But I did try.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I liked how he made the characters come together, but what were those things? If you're going to invent a species, make sure you where they came from, what they mean, etc. Don't leave the reading wondering these things.

Frankly, I find this book a real disappointment. The conclusion was very unsatisfactory; Dean Koontz's explanation for how the strange creatures came into being and why evolution doesn't work displays his ignorance on the theory of evolution. His idea seems plausible when you first read it, but he completely ignored the part about natural selection. I love fiction, and especially science fiction, but I do not like to read misrepresentations of existing working theories.

Dear Mr Koontz, 
 1) I totally noticed hat this whole book was a thin dressing for your mathematical argument against evolution. 
 2) That mathematical argument assumes genetic mutations happen in serial, when in fact they happen in parallel. Ooops. 
 3) Edgar Allen Poe already wrote "The Tell-Tale Heart" Your tired rehash didn't add anything to the book. 
 4) Half of your sub-plots didn't add anything to the book either, and the way they got pulled into the main story about Puzzle and Riddle didn't help. (So the murdering brother was in the next house over the whole time? Who cares??) 
 The only reason I finished this book at all is because a penpal of mine read it and liked it, so I felt obligated to give it a shot. Hoo boy. Nevermind. No more Koontz for me.

I love Dean Koontz. This book left me feeling let down. Good writing and I was engaged until I reached a certain point. Don't need to say more. I'll finish the other Dean Koontz I'm working on!Breathless

I did not like this book at all. The last 3 pages were it's only redeeming qualities. 
 Complete and utter waste of time.

If it wasn't for the awful ending of this novel i would of given it 3 stars. This novel will make you wonder if Mr K ran out of time on his deadline and thought 'screw it' A lot of reviews state that it started off good and then tapered off. I started getting into it and then it ends abruptly, kinda in a way if you bought the first Twilight Eyes and never knew there were a second part to it. 
 Also 
 Dear Mr K 
 Enough of the dogs already(unless you are going to write a sequel to watchers) 
 Yours 
 Mr R

Who wrote this?? I am a die-hard Koontz fan, and this is the first of his novels that I have read that didn't "feel" like his. 
 I love Koontz because his plots are plausible, always involving some kind of psychopath that is playing psychological mind games to terrify his victims. This book is not at all like that. I didn't even find it particularly suspenseful. The book is more sci-fi than anything. 
 The beginning of the book was very confusing with six different storylines. They do, in the end, come together but I found it hard keeping track of all the different people (one of the downsides to listening to audiobooks is that you can't easily flip back and forth in the book). The main character, Grady Adams, is going out for a walk with his Irish Wolfhound, Merlin, and they spot two furry animals as large as dogs but as nimble as cats that aren't like anything previously known to science. The sudden arrival of these creatures seems to be linked to other strange phenomena. 
 I kept waiting for the "action" to occur, but it didn't happen. I did not feel totally captivated by the story, as I usually do with Koontz. For me, this but was just "ok". This is a more recent novel, although nothing like Velocity which was the latest Koontz novel I read in January which is much more like his earlier works. 
 I hope that this is not the new Koontz! I'll go back to reading his older novels. 
 MY RATING: 2 stars (this is the lowest rating that I have ever given, and it saddens me to give it because I'm such a Koontz fan)

Dean Koontz needs to stop writing and retire while he still has a decent reputation, one that he nearly destroyed writing this book. Out of sheer desperation I forced myself to read at least a 1/4 of the book before I became so irritated with the NOTHING that was going on, I wanted to literally throw the book against the wall for making me waste those hours of my life....hours I will NEVER get back. What a shame. Koontz used to be such a great writer. I used to brag to people about how he was even better than Steven King (not that Steven King can write anymore either). What happened? I guess all good things must come to an end. Ah well, I still USED to love you Koontz. But, seriously, this is not good.

I love Dean Koontz. Some of his novels are better than others, and this one falls somewhere in the middle. This is a very thought provoking novel, with some very interesting theories and ideas, making it unique. But, there were some characters involved that I just didn't get what the purpose was in putting them in the book. This could also be considered a cautionary tale. Never involve homeland security. Power does go to the head, and can make an otherwise intelligent person stupid. There were also some pretty cool quotes, but the math went over my head. I do recommend the book, but there was something lacking, I just can't quite explain what.
I finished this and thought "huh?" I thought there surely must be more because the story seemed unfinished.

I often enjoy Mr. Koontz's books. This book did not have the character development that most of his books do. The plot seemed not as tight as most of his books. The intent of this book was lost on me & the ending seemed abrupt. The book had some interesting characters & ideas but they never seemed fully realized.

At some point of reading this book I wanted to find the author and slap him. 
 1. Having short chapters is nice, having a cheesy cliff-hanger at the end of each and every goddamn one of them is annoying to an extreme level. 
 2. When you have a good paragraph, you truly don't have to add any extra detail that make you look like you're a 6th grader in a writing exam. 
 3. I get the concept of Chaos that was being aimed for in this novel but introducing a chacter that is so useless in the middle of the novel seems rather useless. 
 4. Thank you for adding an entire chapter showinv us with graphical useless metaphors how thirsty Tom was. 
 5. The ending is shameful. It's too bad I can't even. 
 However it's well-written so that makes it a well-written waste of your time.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It was a nice change of pace to have Koontz write about another kind of dog, besides his beloved goldens. I love this, the wolf hound, and the 2 main characters that were human. The story moved along at a quick pace, kept me interested even though there were a couple too many characters, until near the ending. Then things fell apart for me. 
 I realize that all the characters end up connected in the story, but it seems to pat for me, how things were woven together. It's like Koontz ran out of steam near the end, and just threw something together. I would have loved it if his creatures were a little more fleshed out, and their escape a bit more interesting, or even harrowing (that was way too easy). One of the main character's past was glossed over, and things were left out of that story line. Another's was quite short, and missed most of his background as well, while his feelings & difficulties with his fight with alcoholism, & his reasons for self-maiming. Why did that one man give away all his gambling winnings? 
 Too many lose ends for me, unanswered questions, characters never mentioned again, and an un-finished-feeling, easy ending. I certainly would not minded having to stick around for another hundred pages, while all of this was explained. 
 1-30-15 - novel reread, accidentally. review still stands.
I normally really enjoy Koontz's books, but I just didn't get this one. I thought everything would come together in a cohesive way--but it just ended without making a point.
This is a wonderful fiction book.

Seriously Dean, I mean, seriously? This was your idea of a story? I was hoping the bad reviews were exaggerated but I was sorely wrong. When you're good, your really good & when your bad, you're oh so very very bad. Better luck next book.
I used to love Dean Koontz, but not anymore. His books are increasingly the same and unfortunately that sameness isn't very interesting.
Ended way too abruptly. It felt like the author hit his page quota and just stopped writing. And while I'm all for a good X-File-ish non-explanation, this needed at least a little bit more of one.

This is the first Dean Koontz book I hacve read. It seems like a waste of descriptive talent. 
 In Breathless he paints this picture with a lot of characters. A character is introduced clearly and quickly as say, a female veterinarian who suffered childhood trauma and finds it easier to relate to animals than people. By the end of the book, the most we may know is a little more about the trauma. The veterinarian is still the same cardboard cutout of a person described and acting in the same way. 
 Dean Koontz has a real talent for narative: vivid imagery, believable internal dialogue, clear, concise descriptive talent. It is wasted. 
 One dimensional fluff with a storyline to match.

This book wasn't great, it was mediocre. Lacks the connection to draw characters together. Storyline was confusing at times. Characters were not relatable. This was my first Koontz book read, so I expected more, but my high expectation was not satisfied, fell short.

The first Koontz book I read was Velocity. Which I adored. There are only two kinds of people I have heard from. People who like genre fiction and insist that Koontz is the same as King (which I always thought was ridiculous. King is The Man), and literary readers who can't stand Koontz, no matter how they feel about horror or thriller books. 
 So I picked up a second book. Then I put it right back down. The back flap read just like The Stand in miniature. But since there is nothing new under the sun, I took a stab at it anyway. 
 There are few cardinal sins that make me put down a book on page 2. 
 This one was the use of the word "suddenly." 
 Moving on.

Oh dear. Where do I begin. First of all, trying to pull off multiple converging character storylines in a book this size rarely works, and in this book it did not work. Nearly every character of focus ended up being the ridiculous complication in someone else's storyline, sometimes with only a momentary interaction that made me wonder why half of these people were even in the book. Cammy is the only character who had any depth at all, and even she wasn't well developed. One or two of the other characters were promising but left me wanting more information. 
 Two very different characters had names starting with the same letters, causing me to be confused during a few scene changes. New characters are introduced far too late in the book. It seemed like the action didn't start till way after the halfway point. The "big reveal" was... lame. The idea had promise but the execution was lacking. The "big standoff" was so anticlimactic it was silly. 
 Feds come in with guns blazing only to stop when they realize the story has broken on TV? Really? With no word from anyone? Just... give up? And no consequences or follow up on what Cammy, Grady and Lamar did? 
 I've been a Dean Koontz fan for a long time, but this just wasn't a very good book. It felt like he was just trying too hard.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ok -- I've never read a Dean Koontz novel before, but my girlfriend conked out early last night and this book (a gift from her cousin) happened to be lying around her apartment. I don't think I've read a novel before that has averaged two and a half stars on Amazon, but I'm also surprised by all the one-star reviews. Those I usually reserve for dull tripe, and even then I usually won't get past the first few pages to know I wouldn't like the book. 
 I understand what folks are writing about the ending: it seems terribly rushed, a couple of subplots are weakly resolved (if at all), and Koontz manages to shoehorn a didactic bit about a thinly-veiled creationism. But one star, really? The fact that I read the whole thing in one sitting, the fact that Koontz effectively stretches out the suspense in Grady's cabin, or that he manages to capture that sense of wonder that the characters undergo -- well, that takes a bit more narrative skill. It's like people who started pronouncing they hated "Lost" because of the unsatisfactory conclusion. Surely the journey to get to the ending was worth it, and that's what I thought of Koontz's strange mix of horror, religious fable and speculative fiction.

I have read about 15 Dean Koontz books. Out of those 15, about 5 are great, 7 are good, and three really stink. Sadly, this was one of the ones that stinked. 
 This book is a lot like the movie Crash, in that for the first 200 pages it has about 5 different stories going. The problem with Koontz and this book is that each chapter is about three pages at times, so you never really feel you get to know the characters. Out of the five stories or so going on at the same time, only two are good. Without telling the end, yes, they all sort of, SORT OF, come together at the end...in the last 20 pages or so. And then it's over. There is basically no plot in this story. Nothing happens at all for 200 pages.I don't know what else to say about this book. He has other great books like Odd Thomas, Life Expectancy, the first two Frankenstein books, just to name a few. Read those before you read this one if you want to get into Koontz.

I was kind of surprised that I didn't really care for this book - since Koontz is one of my favorite authors and generally I really, really like his books. This one just didn't do it for me. I kept waiting for the action to pick up and it never did. The teasers on the back cover, which make the book sound exciting, don't even enter the picture until halfway through the book. Disappointing.

Koontz should never take on Darwin, Creationism, or the like. The sub-plots went no where and really had absolutely ZERO baring on the story, the characters were boring, and things really didn't even end...there just really was no real end. 
 Oh, it's about a new being that was created and plopped into the world with the same emotions and reasoning and souls as a human being, only the people don't know what the hell they are, and they don't ever really figure it out 
 They say it's the journey and not the destination....well this journey sucked ass.
I am a big fan of Dean Koontz but this one wasn't my cuppa tea at all. It just did not grasp my attention at all and I wanted it to be over and done with.
A lot of build up to a let down of an ending
Oh dear.......

I have read some really good books by Mr. Koontz. This was not one of them. I kept expecting it to get good. I was 100 pages into it and said "It's going to get good." 200 pages into it. "It's gotta get better, right?" About 75% of the way through the book I decided to start skimming. I'd had enough of the descriptions about the weird animals and the sick, twisted, paranoid mind of some guy who just killed his twin brother. All the stories were random and came together in loose ways that didn't really make sense. 
 Okay, let me back up. 
 Let's talk about the characters. 
 Grady. Love the name. I have one of the main characters in the book I'm writing named Grady. It may sound silly but that was part of what made me want to read the book. This Grady is so blah it's not even funny. There is nothing to him. He just wanders around in his mountain home with his dog named Merlin. I was not impressed. He is supposed to be the hero in this book and, yeah, not so much. He's a bland character that gets sloppily pulled together at the end where suddenly two or three of the characters are connected to a Marcus Pipp. This Marcus guy was never mentioned in the story until about 200 pages in. I'm sorry but if Marcus is so important, even though he's dead, he needs to be brought up way before that. 
 Cammy. Supposedly the heroine in the story. Another sloppy character. I'm thinking that a woman who, as a girl, grew up on a boat with a drug addict mother and a sick, twisted, abusive stepfather would not turn out all that normal. She was forced to kill her stepfather when she was 15 or 17. Right. This fact is mentioned in such a casual and bland tone that it hardly makes the impact I think Koontz wanted it to. 
 Tom Bigger. A weird and random addition to the story. The scene with the coyotes is never really fully explained. He seemed to be following some sort of intuition or magical sense that he had but it never really got explained either. And somehow he ended up at the house of a lawyer who had hired someone to kill his wife. I was so confused about that twist that never really got answered as to the how and why that I just about stopped reading right there. 
 Lamar. An interesting character. Probably my favorite even though at the end he has some cheesy moments. 
 Henry. The sick, sadistic, antagonist in the story. The whole time I kept expecting it to turn out that he was schizophrenic or something, but I wasn't that lucky. And, unless I misread, he blew himself up with a hand grenade? Wtf? I felt like his story was just ended just to end it. Although I did like the twist and how Cammy and Grady ended up at his house, but it just seemed anticlimactic when that happened. 
 Puzzle and Riddle. All I have to say can be summed up in: WTF? The names: Seriously? They talk: Are you freaking kidding me? I just don't get it. 
 I had to laugh because underneath the title on the cover it says "A Novel of Suspense." When I got done, and partially while I was suffering through it, I thought of No Doubt's song "Suspension without Suspense." There was no suspense in this novel whatsoever. Each chapter ended in a laughable cliffhanger moment that really didn't have the umph to make me want to read more. 
 I have spent far more time with this review than I had anticipated. The plot is sloppy. The conclusion is terrible. The writing leaves a lot to be desired. Sorry, Dean Koontz, but this is definitely not your best work. I will read more of your work, but not until I get this sour taste out of my mouth from this book. I gave it 1 and 1/2 out of 5 Breaths.

This book was not one of Dean Koontz's best that is for sure. The elements could have made a good book. There were many parallel plot lines which I think is fine however they were only loosely brought together in the final pages of the book. It seemed as if the author was on a deadline and just had to finish the book. I usually love Dean Koontz's books but this one I could have done without.

I've never read anything by Dean Koontz, my grandma passed this off to me because I requested some "mindless" break reading. I was surprised that I got so into the story, an intriguing read, I really like how Koontz developed multiple characters and alternated the viewpoint between them. I'll probably pick up Koontz again when I'm bored.

This book was bad, and not in a good way. 
 I wish I had known it was based on Twilight fan-fiction before I bought it, because then I would have saved the money. But thank God for Barnes and Noble coupons, so at least I didn't pay the full retail price for this stinker. 
 There are a lot of things that bothered me about this book, but I don't want to go into them too much. But I will say that the author and her editors needed a thesaurus while they were polishing the fanfic series into a book. The use of the words "beguile," "mercurial," and "clamber" far exceeded the number of acceptable times they should appear within a span of 514 pages. For example, she could have utilized a myriad of words for beguile/beguiling including, but not limited to, the following: intrigue, enticing, fascinate, enchanting, seductive, manipulative, and allure. Mercurial also has a number of synonyms, such as temperamental, capricious, impulsive, and unstable. I don't care if she was trying to conjure an image that fits with the fifty-shades of gray theme. It was excessive. Also, with the number of times Ana clambered somewhere, you would think she was not the least bit coordinated. What is so "beguiling" about a slow-moving, lumbering oaf? I don't get it.

There is not enough memes or gifs to describe my feelings right now. I wasted two days. Count 'em two. One. Two. One. Two. Two. One. ( See what I'm doing here?) They're gone and what do I get for reading this? A numb mind and a desire for Fifty Shades of Grey settled next to a raging fire -_- That last part would be good though, save a soul or twenty. 
 So much dang repetition! I loathe repetition unless it has purpose. No purpose here! None. No purpose! Not one purpose-filled moment. Where is the purpose? Oh wait, there is no purpose!! *rubs temple* See how annoying repeating words and questions are Ms./Mrs. James? Every single page. Lord, at times I just wanted to jump into the scene and grab both of them by the ear and shout: "Murmur one more time! Cock that damn head to the side again!" I eyed scissors thinking I could cut out all the repetition but then would just leave the front and back ( exaggeration, don't correct me). Probably be better to give the dang thing a thesaurus for words andd phrases andd sentences. 
 I get that this is suppose to be a BDSM relationship but I do believe in that kind of relationship the feeling is a mutal thing between a couple but I just don't see that in this book at all. It comes across as the guy taking advantage of a girl who lacks self-esteem and he mistakes that for a submissive quality (unless that actually is one, I don't know). The only times I liked Ana was when she seemed like she was putting her foot down --- standing up for herself--- but it never really lasted long. 
 This is absolutely terrible. The novel, quite honestly, ---seriously it's true--- is a book lover's website posted fanfic written in a terrible manner. 
 Really avoid this fanfic and read better ones on Mibba or something. Now those have good sex scenes. And a plot -.-

Well, thank God that's over! Not sure how I managed to finish "Fifty Shades of Horrible Writing and Bad Storytelling". I suppose that I just wanted to see what all the fuss was about, but I came away horribly disappointed. 
 Anastasia is a most pathetic, unlikeable character. I had a strong dislike for her and her limited vocabulary consisting of 'Oh my' and 'Holy crap'. I wanted to smack some sense into her (or else just smack her). And why was she always so tired after sex? It's not like she did anything except lie there. 
 Let's face it...women who read this book read it for the sex, plain and simple. I know that's why I picked it up. It's clear that the author (and I use the term loosely) knew she wanted to write about BDSM, and then tried to wrap some semblance of a plot around it, only she failed miserably. Even the sex scenes were poorly written and far too frequent. More often than not I found myself thinking 'Really? Again?' Those who gave this book a 4 or 5 star rating undoubtedly had Fifty Shades in one hand and their vibrator in the other. 
 It should come as no surprise to learn that I won't be reading the remaining books in the trilogy. Quite frankly, bamboo shoots under the fingernails would be less painful.

By the time I finished the first chapter, I was asking myself if Ana and Christian were teenagers instead of two adults in their twenties. The grammar and use of words leaves a lot to be desired, but E.L. James does know to cause some intrigue. At least I'm intrigued to know what happens next. I'm not saying the sexual relationship between Ana and Christian aren't interesting to read. But, personally, I'm more interested in finding out where the personal relationship between the two characters goes from here. I want to see if Mr. Grey can "surrender" himself to Miss Steele and trust her with his darkest secret.

I can't believe I actually bought this book. I gave up pretty nice shirt just to buy this and I now want to pull my hair out and scream! 
 A friend of mine told me it's great and brilliant and blah blah blah and I read so many good reviews and ... Oh, IDK, I guess I hoped to read something different from what I usually read and have fun exploring all that BDSM stuff. I'm not into it, but I was curious to see what's all the fuss about. 
 All I want to do now is permanently erase this sh.. from my memory. I really have to stop reading books that have something to do with Twilight - this was my third ''everyone loves it, so maybe it'll be good'' time and now I am officially done. I'ts just not for me. Period. 
 OK, Fifty Shades of Grey: 
 Writing is horrible. I have a copy in Croatian and after only few pages I had to stop and find a sample in English just to make sure that I'm reading the same thing as everyone else. Sadly, it's equally bad in English as it is in Croatian. Awkward sentences, tons of cliches, clumsy descriptions, poor dialogues... it goes on and on. 
 Maybe I'm too old fashioned, but I think that a bestselling writer should actually have talent and know at least some basics about writing. Silly me! Turns out - all you have to do is sit and copy type whatever piece of sh.. you want and a bestseller just jumps out of your monitor/notebook/whatever. 
 I am no expert, I'm just a reader who enjoys all kinds of books and maybe I'm not the one to judge, but come on... This is just not OK. 
 The story is dumb. With other (stronger, smarter) characters it could be interesting, but with Ana and Christian, it's just not working. Before reading, I thought that my biggest problem with this book will be sex, because BDSM is complitely unfamiliar to me. I was wrong. I am not shocked/disgusted with their sexual preferences or their lifestyle (although some scenes were too much - tampon!?!). 
 What I find very, very wrong in Fifty Shades of Grey are WRITING and character development. That ruined every chance for me to like it. 
 Ana is annoying as hell. 
 Seriously, she is now number one on my black list, right next to Julia Mitchell from Gabriel's Inferno. I never liked Bella Swan either, but now - after reading this - she looks pretty good to me. 
 This girl Anastasia is so stupid that I felt sorry for her in some chapters - there, there girl, it's not your fault, someone else made you like this - but mostly, I just wanted to slap her. I still want to slap her. 
 Her thoughts were ridiculous, she blushes all the time, acts like an idiot and has no character. Oh, and she has a goddess hidden somewhere in her and she allways does some crazy stuff, like jumping, yelling, dancing, lying on a carpet, hiding behind sofa, talking to her subconscience (her subconscience is also very talkative)... WTF! 
 And she's BITING HER DAMN LIP EVERY SECOND OF EVERY HOUR. We got it! No need to repeat that in every paragraph! That was more annoying than everything else. STOP BITING YOUR LIP,DAMN IT! Stop, stop, stop you fu..ing idiot! 
 I just can't get over this 'wonderfull' writing - you are such a gem E. L. James! 
 Anyway, our dear Ana is, of course, very beautiful but she doesn't even know it. Her friends are inlove with her, she calles her car Wanda and she likes Jane Eyre and Tessa D'urberville, so she is also supposed to be smart(?). We can't forget that she tripped when she met Grey, so she's clumsy(?), but in a cute way. We should all love her for that because now we know that she has a flaw. 
 Lovely. Just lovely. 
 What a characterization! (Remember, E. L. James is a bestselling author.) Argh! 
 Ana was a virgin (ah, what else) when she met Christian. Of course, she was never even attracted to someone before he came along. She didn't masturbate, didn't think about sex and she kissed only two guys before him if I remember correctly. After a lot of blah blah (he's so hot, he's hot, he's hot...) they end up in his room and she tells him she's a virgin. He acts like a jerk and wants to ''rectify that situation'' so he can fu.. her hard next time. You see, he doesn't make love. He fu..s. Hard. 
 Now this innocent, sweet, cute girl is very comfortable with him acting like this and she wants him so bad that she doesn't even blink for a second to realise the way he's treating her. She doesn't run and scream when he shows her his torturing chamber playroom and clearly explains that he wants her to be his sex slave. She stays with him (because he is so hot) and wants to get it on ASAP. In fact, right after he kisses her, she forgets everything and boom - she's an expert in sex. To be 100% honest, I really don't even want to admit to reading this series....it was that awful. A few pages into it, I saw someone on twitter describe it as "the writing is bad and the smut isn't good enough to make up for it." You can pretty much stop reading right here because that is it in a nutshell. 
 The only redeeming thing I can say is at least my copies were free so I didn't waste money on this garbage. 
 But, since I suffered through it, I feel entitled to have some fun trashing it, so here goes. 
 1.) Characters were supremely annoying, unbelievable, and waiver from alleged brilliance to frightfully stupid throughout. Ana is not believable as a 21 year old, or really as an innocent virgin when the story opens. By the third book, we are supposed to believe, after acting like an inexperienced and extremely, comically clumsy person that she magically knows self-defense and how to shoot a handgun well enough to hit a mark. And can do it in 5 inch Louboutins. OK SURE. *eyeroll* 
 2.) Dialogue is horrible. If the author had taken the time to read any of her prose aloud, this would have hopefully been painfully obvious to her. No one talks the way these characters do. 
 3.) Stupid running dialogue between Ana, her self-conscious, and her (barf) "Inner Goddess". For all three books, you are subjected to horrible atrocities like "My inner goddess tipped her sunglasses down, and peered at me from over the gossip magazine she's reading on her chaise lounge". Or "My inner goddess clicks her tongue and fans herself with a feather boa." Seriously, WTF? It makes you downright stabby after the first time. I found myself thinking, more than once, that the real crazy person in the series is Ana and not Christian because she sounds like she has 3 personalities. 
 4.) The smut isn't very good. In fact some of it is downright gross. (The tampon scene? What woman dreams of that? Blech.) And for a book that's supposed to be about S&M, it gets pretty dull because basically the heroine spends the 3 books trying to tame her partner's tastes and then explains all his fetishes as psychological trauma. I'm guessing kinky people everywhere take some issue with this. It's also repetitive, the sex scenes are so frequent that there is no room left for any kind of plot. 
 which brings me to number 5.... 
 5.) The plot sucks. Any problems the characters face are resolved in about 2 pages, so there is no suspense and it's hard to really care about anything that happens. The most dramatic event in the first book is probably Christian's helicopter going missing. I was hoping he would be missing for days, I wanted to see if his panty-disintegrating gaze could part the growth in the wilderness he found himself stranded. But no, we he's missing all of 8 hours. 8 HOURS. Who cares? That whole story arc was resolved in about 5 minutes. Lame. 
 6.) The writing is horrible. Descriptions sound British, and it sounds like the author has never visited Washington, which she frequently describes as sunny. There's also this stupid connection to Detroit in the book (because all crack whores MUST be from there!) where she mentions that Christian was in the care of Michigan State. Michigan State is a university, the State of Michigan is the phrase she's looking for. A tiny detail, but an annoying one. But mostly I think using Detroit at the origin of the crack mommy was just a pathetic and over-obvious move. (Perhaps I am little bit sensitive to this as I was born there.) 
 I could basically go on forever because there is so much snark-worthy goodness in this entire series. And yes, I am painfully embarrassed to admit, I did read the whole series. I have this problem where if I start something, I just can't stop, no matter how dreadful it is. I have to gawk at the trainwreck. Plus, given the current popularity of this series, I felt like if I kept reading, maybe I'd figure out what all the fuss is about. 
 I will close with this - from about 50 pages in, I started thinking about how much this book seemed like a bad Twilight rip off. As I got further in, it irritated me more and more. It wasn't until after I finished the series and googled it did I realize this series is a fanfiction rip off. And it truly is a rip off, the author made no attempt at originality. Let's compare: 
 -Control freak, over-protective, obsessed with safety male character 
 -Inexperienced, super clumsy, "plain jane" who's also super hot (???) heroine that's book smart, into classic lit, but also makes stupid decisions. 
 -Hero's family is super wealthy, and all siblings are adopted. 
 -Both take place in Washington state. 
 -Male character has a parent that's a doctor. 
 -Female character refers to her dad by his first name, except to his face. 
 -Female character's mom has had multiple husbands, and lives in a warm southern climate away from the action. 
 -Male character struggles with feeling he's a bad person while taking the high moral ground in all matters. 
 -Gratuitous amounts of fast sports cars throughout. Male character buys female character 2 sports cars. 
 -Female has huge problem accepting gifts or compliments. (And can I seriously just say for a minute, who really has this problem in real life, especially the money part?) 
 -Male character has "dark secret" (vampire vs. BDSM aficionado) 
 -Physical character descriptions are basically the same as Bella and Edward, down to Christian's "copper" hair. (Was Edward's "bronze"? Same difference.) 
 -The totally unnecessary and uninteresting post-epilogue re-telling of chapter 1, book 1 from Christian's viewpoint at the end of the series, a la Midnight Sun. 
 I am sure I could think of more, but you get the picture. And for what it's worth, Twilight looks like a literary masterpiece compared to this series.

Especially after finding out that Goodreads made this novel a finalist for "Best Romance". 
 The novel started fairly normal enough: A woman by the name of Anastasia Steele is getting ready to interview a big, pompous and rather important big shot for for her sick best friend who couldn't do the interview and is asking Ana to take her place for the School newspaper. The novel is in complete first person and we see Ana's nerves creeping up on her since she's not used to doing this type of one on one interview (especially when she actually meets Christian Grey, the man who made a mark of himself at the age of 27). 
 Right off the bat, we are introduced to a handsome man with tousled hair, grey eyes, and a mysterious charm that is radiated off him. Ana is indeed attracted to him and it is obvious that he is interested in her as well...After several encounters with one another and going on several dates does Ana realize that she wants to become more involved with him (and Christian with her as well) but he has several terms and rules that he wants her to abide by and thats where the weird things/events start happening... 
 It isn't until page 100 or so that the writing of the novel takes a shift from attraction and endless flirting to some serious, hardcore, raw emotion and the input of 'Erotica' is held at a plate. I have to admit it wasn't as explicit as I thought it would be but nonetheless there were moments while reading where I had to pause what I was reading and either laugh, cringe, shift uncomfortably, curse, or do all the above and also take a breath. Christian is seriously a complicated, disturbed, charming man who is haunted by his troubled past which explains his actions and his BDSM lifestyle (BTW I have no idea what this means and am frankly to scared to find out but because it's referenced so much in the book I thought I'd mention it here). It's amazing how many sexual scenes are in this book but surprisingly I found out while reading through the book that the scenes shared between Ana and Christian aren't just put there for audience pleasure but this dark, erotic, and complex relationship also puts to question an issue that raises within the characters (which I won't mention) but seeing that complexity has made me realized how this book challenges to look deep within ourselves (the good and bad parts) and having to find this out through an Erotica genre baffles me but has made me a little bit more open-minded about this genre. 
 Now for the breakdown: 
 In all, I fairly enjoyed this book despite the sexual innuendoes, and references of heavy, passioned, detailed writing that went on between Christian and Ana. I found the description of the book fairly accurate and actually very humoring, interesting, dramatic, romantic, disturbing, but most of all I found that this book acknowledges the "demons" that people carry (some more than others) and how one woman, Ana tries to understand the mysterious Grey. 
 I HATED the way the book ended however! It was left very open and after THAT certain situation occurredi I didn't think it was nice for E.L. James to leave her readers hanging by a thread and biting their nails over what went on...I know what I'll be doing next: Picking up Fifty Shades Darker and continuing on Christian and Ana's passionate affair and secretly wishing that they become "more". 
 My rating for this book is more like a 4.5/5 but because I felt this book surprised me in more ways than one and left me open-mouthed for most of the time and the story was surprisingly deep and meaningful (plus I feel like I relived my high school sex education once again...except this time it was much more explicitly detailed). reference_books.title: Beautiful Disaster (Beautiful, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
To understand my thoughts on this book, one only has to look at any of the 1-star reviews others have written and I can say I concur almost wholeheartedly. This is not my first New Adult book, but it is my first I have read in quite a few months and I can honestly say that as of very recently (maybe the past six months) my tastes and tolerance have changed DRAMATICALLY. Other New Adult novels I tolerated because overall I enjoyed the characters even if the maturity levels bothered me. But for some reason this one I could barely get through and I think it may have taken the top spot of books that have annoyed me to no end (overcoming Catcher in the Rye-mostly because it was double the length). 
 Now I understand why everyone hates Fifty Shades so much (aside from the terrible writing), it's because of the weak idiotic heroine, and the crazy, obsessive, violent hero-which is EXACTLY what this book is. I almost stopped reading so many times but I have this problem where I have to finish books, so I suffered through. 
 Reasons this book annoyed me: 
 Characters-ugh the main characters sucked and even quite a few of the supporting characters as well. 
 Dialogue-not flowing or realistic. 
 Plausibility-this entire book was so unrealistic, straight from the nitty-gritty details to the overblown events-SO unnecessarily dramatic. 
 Age-perhaps I am getting too old and far removed from college, but a lot of the new adult books exaggerate the atmosphere of college, IMO 
 Writing-so much more juvenile than even Young Adult novels (and this goes for other NA books). Even though NA is supposed to be written for more mature levels than YA books are, they are written poorly, and frankly most YA is leaps and bounds better. 
 I don't usually rant much, but this one warranted it. I am so sorry to any one of my friends who loved this book, because a year ago I might have liked this, but right now it is a book that I cannot stomach and wanted to hurl across the room.

reference_books.title: World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War
reference_books.review_text: I liked the way in which this was told, an oral history, but despite not being a super-long novel, it dragged. Maybe it was because I was interested in some stories or even parts of the war, and not others? I can't tell what it is that just didn't "do it" for me. But because there were places that were interesting and it was a unique telling of a story, it still gets a solid 3.

reference_books.title: Summer Days and Summer Nights: Twelve Love Stories
reference_books.review_text:
Overall, I think I liked the previous collection just a touch better, but this still had some good stories. And most from authors I have never read before. 
 "Head, Scales, Tongue, Tail" by Leigh Bardugo -3.5 
 This one was such a strong story, until the end where it got too fantasy for me. I just wasn't really expecting it and so I knocked it down a half star. I'm still pumped to read Six of Crows though, because I've heard nothing but good things! 
 "The End of Love" by Nina Lacour - 4 
 This was a sweet story by an author I have never read. It was one where I wish there was more to it at the end, not in a bad way like it felt too short, but because I wanted more of the story and the characters. Could easily be a full novel. 
 "Last Stand at the Cinegore" by Libba Bray - 3.5 
 Likewise, I've still never read anything by Libba Bray, but I am definitely interested after this story because this story was ridiculous and funny. A horror-focused story with lots of humor and mockery. 
 "Sick Pleasure" by Francesca Lia Block - 2 
 Another author I've never read, but to me, this was the weakest of the book. I wasn't a fan of the story or the way it was told. Just wasn't feeling it. 
 "In Ninety Minutes Turn North" by Stephanie Perkins - 5 
 No surprise that I liked this one. It was just too cute, and I love this couple. They were in the previous anthology and their story was one of my favorites in there as well. 
 "Souvenirs" by Tim Federle - 4 
 Really liked this story - it felt the tiniest bit more juvenile, but it was an interesting take on a story for a "love story" collection - about a "break-up day" between two high school boys who work together at an amusement park. First read of this author, and I may pick up some more. 
 "Inertia" by Veronica Roth - 4.5 
 The few reviews that were out about this anthology before I read it had people not liking this story that much, but I thought it was unique and touching. I really loved the idea behind this and of course, I'm always a fan of a friends-lovers trope :) 
 "Love is the Last Resort" by Jon Skovron - 3.5 
 I should probably make this a 3 because of it's too large cast of characters, and "too perfect" ending, but it was still cute and fun. Honestly, I think it would make for a very interesting full-length novel. I've never read anything by this author, so I might try something else by him. 
 "Good Luck and Farewell" by Brandy Colbert - 3 
 This one was really just okay. Nothing super special in my book, but a decent story. Not motivated to pick up something else by her though. 
 "Brand New Attraction" by Cassandra Clare - 2.5 
 The setting of this was fantastic and perfectly described, but the actual romance felt out of nowhere and unnatural. I expected more from Clare because of how much I adored the Infernal Devices trilogy, but this was just way too overdone. Maybe short stories aren't her thing. 
 "A Thousand Ways This Could All Go Wrong" by Jennifer E. Smith - 4 
 Have a novel or two of hers on my TBR, but still haven't gotten around to it yet, but I certainly will pick them up. This was a sweet, yet unexpected story in this anthology and I really liked. 
 "The Map of Tiny Perfect Things" by Lev Grossman - 5 
 A fantastic wrap-up to the anthology, and a bit of a surprise as well. I've heard many mixed things about Grossman's The Magicians and so wasn't expecting a whole lot, but wow was this a great love story of two teenagers caught in this Groundhog Day-esque world. I didn't even mind the possibly too cheesy bit at the end. I think this was probably the best of the anthology, IMO.

reference_books.title: Dracula
