 I saw this book at 600 pages and went "holy shit, what even..." but never could have imagined that so much could happen so succinctly in 600 pages. This is a story I have enjoyed immensely since the beginning for its originality, its skilful telling, and its absorbing plot and characters. 
 First of all, it's been a long while since I read Gathering, and Conjuring did a good job of reminding the reader what happened last in a way that isn't info-dumping or annoying. 
 I think most of what I have to say regards the characters, because they are all so good. I liked Holland since the beginning. He's been that tragic character, and this book was his redemption arc. I felt that stab of heartsickness for him at the end, but you kind of understand since the beginning how his story has to go. 
 Alucard and Rhy got so much fleshing out in this book, and I think that I would call this book Holland's AND Rhy's. Rhy was also heartbreaking, just seeing what he has to deal with, but that is the theme of these books - loss and living. The more we learn about Alucard's side of things, the more I liked him and his personal quest. 
 Lila and Kell have been rock solid for me since the beginning, and this book gave them so much development that made me happy. I like how their relationship is a subtle one (I find those to be rare). Despite a couple scenes where they are obviously NOT subtle, the nature of their relationship is. Kell may say that he has a hard time truly trusting Lila's actions, but there is a whole lot of trust going back and forth between them. It lets them be who they are, fight, plan, and win TOGETHER, without one sacrificing anything to the other. Kell's love was honest, and for all Lila's brashness her love was just as honest. 
 This book on the whole was much bleaker in mood than the others. Bleakness, in great amounts, in stories is not something I generally care much for, but given my love for this story and the plot circumstances, this factor was handled marvellously. 
 Another fantastic story from Schwab. I will always read her.

EDIT: I'm reducing my rating to 3.5 stars. Partially, I've read more at this point and have reduced a lot of my book ratings. Partially I just feel my opinion of this drop every time I think about it. This book was really so bland and so flat compared to the other two. Yes, it's a good conclusion, but I don't feel it added enough character development, enough plot, enough intrigue, enough anything. V.E. Schwab can do better. She HAS done better. This book offered me a fairly bad reading experience, and I can't ignore that, no matter how much I love this series. 
 I really only have one complaint, and it's nothing new for this series, so I shouldn't feel disappointed at all. But I can't ignore that this... took me over a week to read. I NEVER take this long to read books. 
 MY LOVE-HATE RELATIONSHIP WITH V.E. SCHWAB'S PLOTTING 
 I love so much about this series. The plotting is not one of those things. The plot is directionless. This is an issue I had with all three books of this series, and it's actually the one thing about this series I actively dislike. On one hand, I love the extended character work. On the other hand, there's no urgency behind the plot. That was tolerable in Gathering of Shadows, but here, the five main characters are trying to save the war, and yet they spend 400 pages screwing around. This book took me over a week, and I usually finish books in three days. That's kind of an issue. 
 Usually, I'd ignore that ONE flaw, but I can't lie, I really hoped and expected Schwab would fix it here. Instead, it got worse. 
 I just generally found the action of this book so meh, so lukewarm, so uninteresting. This conclusion felt like unnecessary drama that everyone was coming home from. It felt pointless. Without my love for the major characters, I don't know if I would've liked ANYTHING about this book. 
 Also, and I'm nitpicking here, I still don't understand why Lila, Kell, and Holland don't just carry a ton of white and grey London trinkets with them. Why don't all of you just carry coins from Grey London? C'mon, wouldn't Lila have stolen enough from Grey London at this point? Do the trinkets have to be emotionally significant? 
 BACK TO YOUR REGULARLY SCHEDULED I LOVE THIS SERIES MONTAGE 
 * V.E. Schwab's writing style is incredible. It flows super well and manages to break my heart, but isn't annoying or pretentious at all. That's a hard balance and her books are worth reading for that reason alone. 
 * Schwab's talent for describing setting especially stands out here. Usually I can't picture any settings in books, but I have such clear mental images of every moment in this book. 
 * Kell is such a realistic character. He never seems like a caricatureaEUR" he's a bit morally imperfect, not always the nicest, but loyal to the nth degree. He's just so interesting and fun to see on page. 
 * Lila is STILL my chaotic neutral wife. She's a bit more mature here, but with the same reckless streak. I love her development. She's great to see on pageaEUR" her dialogue is funny and entertaining. 
 * Rhy's character development is perfectly executed. Again, he's such an imperfect person but he's still so lovable. And I cry. 
 * Holland is so morally bankrupt and yet I love him so, so much. His ending made me both smile and cry. 
 * Alucard may have suffered a bit from I-have-an-archetypal-tragic-backstory syndrome a bit, but he was still a great character. I wished his sister could've been addressed a bit more. 
 * I love the complex dynamics between all the characters. V.E. Schwab does an incredible job with the platonic relationships here. I especially loved Rhy and Kell here. And Kell and Holland have the best, most complex friendship ever. 
 * The romance is built up very subtly and not the major focus. But oh damn, the romance is well written. I was so, so happy about Lila and Kell's relationship ending. Schwab knows how to write romance in a subtle but still swoon-worthy way. There's a sex scene in here that I actually genuinely kind of... enjoyed?? I hate sex scenes in books. Hate them. And yet... ya girl liked a sex scene. I know, I'm surprised too. 
 * Also Rhy and Alucard were maybe one of the few new things in this book and they're really good?? This update is a complete callout for them.

2.5 stars, rounded down because this book should have been a whole lot better based on the author's previous work and skill level. 
 I normally really, really don't like to leave unfavorable reviews: "If you can't say something nice, don't say anything at all." But I ADORED this series up until this last book (as in, it was already becoming one of my favorites of all time), and perhaps that's why I feel more inclined to write this, perhaps even as constructive criticism. 
 First off, if that's supposed to be Rhy on the cover, I can't imagine why, since he really does not have much of a role to play in the story. When the cover was first revealed I assumed it was Holland, because he's the third Antari (fitting the pattern, though admittedly Rhy also fits because he was always the third main character), because this story focuses more on him just as the first two books did for Kell and Lila, and because he was also a king. But given how Rhy ends the story as king and Holland just goes off to die, I have a hard time thinking it was meant to be Holland (in spite of the fact that Holland was much more the driver of the story). This actually bothers me for a bigger reason than simple aesthetics - Holland was more of a protagonist in this trilogy than Rhy was. Not that I don't like Rhy - I do - but having him be the third main character, and worse, having the grand finale book be all about him, didn't work. It was like taking a supporting character and forcing him into a main character's role, while pushing a more major character into a supporting role. It just didn't work. 
 There is some good stuff here, such as Holland's backstory and development, as well as Rhy coming into his own as king. Kell largely remained unchanged, but that's fine, he's still awesome. The writing itself continues to be amazing, almost poetic. Very frequently scenes are intense, emotionally and otherwise. 
 But other than that, the book has some major, major issues upon scrutiny. This is the kind of book where you definitely get drawn into the story and ride an emotional high while reading it, but once you put it down the problems start becoming apparent. 
 There's simply too much going on, too many people involved, and too many new elements/people introduced for anything or anyone to get the proper attention, explanation, and development it/they deserved and result in a satisfying conclusion. Which is notable considering the length of the book and the relative simplicity (and dare I say predictability) of the plot. Normally I am wholeheartedly against authors splitting books in two, but in this case it might have been warranted. 
 Characters acting stupidly was a significant problem: namely Maxim (literally what was the point of his sacrifice?), Rhy going to confront Osaron near the end when there's literally nothing he can do (other than impede Kell, that is, which he does), the various crazy things Lila does (though admittedly she's always been that way), and the sudden and rather pointless betrayal of the Veskans (um, obviously not really a good time for this, guys? What you did wasn't beneficial to you either?). 
 Character deaths in books can serve a good purpose, but here it was just out of control, to the point where it didn't serve the story as well as having a handful of deaths built up for maximum emotional impact would have been. Maxim and Emira's deaths in particular were completely pointless, as was Lenos's. Anisa's, Holland's, and Hastra's were pretty needlessly cruel too, in spite of the fact that they were tied into important (some less so, some more so) plot points. Why Hano and Iso were killed wasn't even explained. 
 Lila fortunately redeems herself a little (her excellent scenes with Holland after he saved her life and when he calls her out on being a murderer were astounding), but she's still an overall unlikable character. Add to that the fact that she's the protagonist who gets screwed over the least (practically not at all) rubbed it in further. I'm starting to think the story would have been better served with her dying instead of Holland, as it would have shown her realizing her need to redeem herself when Holland clearly already had. 
 I'm totally down with the Alucard/Rhy ship, but the issues in their relationship (mostly on Rhy's end) seemed... I don't know, manufactured and drawn out for drama's sake? As for Kell and Lila getting together, I didn't feel much chemistry there and the story probably would have been better with them as friends, but it's cool, I guess. 
 The floating market and Maris were cool (probably the only genuine bit of worldbuilding in this book), but otherwise everything that came out of it was a deus ex machina or a copout. Alucard giving away four years of his life for that mirror seemed... I dunno, kind of unnecessary. I'd think Rhy would be pretty pissed if he found out Alucard traded time he could have had with Rhy for it. The rings and the Inheritor were both complete deus ex machinas that basically came out of nowhere. The "unreveal" is a device that can be used well in fiction, but here it felt closer to a copout in regards to Kell's backstory (or lack thereof) and connection to Maris. 
 Given the premise of this series, I was rather disappointed that the other worlds were more or less ignored here - the characters don't even visit the other Londons except at the beginning and near the end. This final novel feels very insular, with the majority of it taking place within the Red London royal palace or on a ship. That creative decision really took the "epic" out of this sprawling fantasy universe. On top of that, it was disappointing to see even Grey London get more of a conclusion than White London did, when White London played a considerably larger role in the story. 
 And then there's the fate of Holland and White London. The book keeps it pretty vague what really happened, and other reviews here certainly seem to have opinions of what that last line meant one way or the other. Either way this conclusion is viewed, however, it's problematic, and it really boils down to one of two possibilities: 
 1. That White London is going to die and there's nothing anyone can do to save it. (Basically indicated throughout the denouement) 
 2. Somehow, White London will recover. (Possibly implied by the last line of Holland's final section) 
 If option 1 is the case, then damn, our heroes are assholes. Not even a mention or a suggestion to attempt tearing down the barrier that cut off Red London from White London that Red London put up in the first place against a threat that no longer exists so the magic might flow again? Not even a thought to bringing as many people over as they can if White London is truly unable to be saved? Not even survivor's guilt? Without further explanation of their inaction, Red London and its leadership is now essentially indirectly responsible for the genocide of an entire world. And the reader is supposed to be happy it and its system of government was more or less preserved? I sure am not. 
 If option 2 is the case, then... how? Why? Without further setup and explanation, that would be right out of left field, especially if somehow tied into Holland's sacrifice (which you could interpret as being implied by how his eyes are described at the end, maybe?). It's always been carefully shown just how magic in this universe works, and how it isn't just a miracle cure for everything. And yet, if option 2 is the case... that's exactly what happened. The only explanation I can come up with is that the magic might return now that Osaron's no longer around, but there was no indication of this or why that might be the case whatsoever. And it still doesn't excuse Red London's complete and utter disregard for the world and people they screwed over. 
 I do hope Victoria realizes the problems in this novel and continues to better her writing, because she is an amazing author.

This book gutted me. 
 I cried (like, actual tears) a lot. I laughed and there were moments where my heart was all warm fuzzies. Everything about it is so spectacular, and this was such an incredible finale. From the moment I started reading the first book I knew this series would be one of my favorites, and as I read I fell in love with the characters and this world. My soul hurts and this series will forever hold a special place in my heart.
A compelling and impressive finale! This series certainly gets better with each book. Start to end action packed and just delight to read. Highly recommended!

Chudesen krai na edno strakhotno prikliuchenie! 
 Zapochnakh p'rvata kniga trudno i s malka doza dosada. No ot sredata na tomcheto do kraia na tretata se prev'rnakh v edin ot nai-golemite fenove na poreditsata. V'lnuvashcho gradsko fent'zi, obaiatelni geroi, mog'shchi vragove i mnogo khumor izp'lvat sagata "Niuansi Magiia". 
 Cherveniiat London e chast ot edna ot chetiri paralelni vseleni. Toi e p'st'r, v'lnuvashch, izp'lnen s v'lshebstvo. Grad't e dom't na Kel - predstavitel na izchezvashch vid mag'osnitsi - Antari. Te vladeiat ne samo elementite, no i magiiata na kr'vta. Samo Antari mogat da se pridvizhvat mezhdu svetovete, chiito vrati sa otdavna zatvoreni. 
 V sveta na Siviia London magiiata e otdavna zabravena chast ot choveshkoto s'shchestvo. V'v vselenata na Beliia London tsari borba za nadmoshchie i zhazhda za vlast i v'lshebstvo - svet't zagiva. A Cherniiat London e prichinata za tova - toi e chast ot chetv'rtata Vselena, koiato otdavna se e prev'rnala v zhertva na vsemog'shchestvoto. 
 V trite chasti Kel triabva da se prebori da spasi ne samo svoiata vselena, no i Siviia i Beliia London ot parchentse brutalna magiia, koiato se smiata za Bog. Poreditsata e razvlekatelno chetivo, no vse pak postavia i niakoi v'prosi za liubovta mezhdu khorata, za loialnostta i doverieto, za opasnostta da otvorish s'rtseto si, za vlastta i samouverenostta, za znachenieto na korenite. 
 Moga samo da se nadiavam, che niakoga "Niuansi magiia" shche izleze i na b'lgarski ezik, no dotogava - koito mozhe da chete na angliiski, neka go napravi. Struva si :)

reference_books.review_text: I really enjoyed this because in so many ways it really challenged my own views on faith. I especially appreciate the frank discussion that EVERYONE picks and chooses which parts of the Bible they're going to live by. An extreme experiment, and completely admirable.

reference_books.review_text: Read ions ago, can't believe I never added it here.

reference_books.title: Columbine
reference_books.review_text: Unfortunately, I have a bit of an obsession about what happened at Columbine. This book is a really masterful handling of all of the tragic events that went down there. I highly recommend it to people who think they knew what happened--you will be amazed to find out just how much of that was myth.

reference_books.title: The Emperor's Children
reference_books.review_text: Honestly? I'm mad at myself for sticking through the whole damn thing. All of the characters come across as incredibly unlikable, which I know was probably the point of it, but at the same time made it incredibly hard to really care about what happened to any of them. The book ends on a very ambiguous note, but again, since I didn't care about any of the characters, that was completely fine by me.

reference_books.title: No One Belongs Here More Than You
reference_books.review_text: I know that I'm supposed to LOVE Miranda July. All the cool kids do. But god, there really is a difference between stories about outsiders, and stories about, well, people who do some really freaky ass shit. A couple of good stories, but really, I could have cared less whether I finished it or not.

reference_books.title: Dreams of Joy (Shanghai Girls #2)
reference_books.review_text: I loved See's "Shanghai Girls" so much, and she clearly left the door wide open at the end of that one for a sequel, so I was thrilled to see her come through. Except ... This one in no way comes close to the original. It was simply too pat. Really? An American girl could get into China in 1957 with no more trouble than this? The explanations of communism also seemed too simplisitic, especially given that I just finished another book set in communist Russia that seemed to do a better job laying out the realities of the time.

reference_books.title: Goodnight Nobody
reference_books.review_text: Overall, just didn't find it as fun as her other books.

reference_books.title: Jane Eyre
reference_books.review_text: This is book #2 in my classics project. And unlike "Tale of Two Cities," I had never read "Jane Eyre" before (as embarrassing as that is to admit). I fell in love with this book. Yes, I pretty much knew the entire plot without ever having read the book, and yet I still found myself anxious to discover what was going to happen next. Some of the observations struck me as still being relevant even today, and I appreciated Jane's strong, no-nonsense view of the world. I may also possibly be in love with Mr. Rochester myself. Too often in books of this era I find myself wondering what in the world the heroine sees in a particular man. Not here. Jane, girl, I totally get it! ;) I also wanted Jane to tell St. John that he was a complete douche, but chances are fairly strong that if Charlotte Bronte ever heard that phrase, she wouldn't have the slightest idea what I was talking about lol.

reference_books.title: Canada
reference_books.review_text: This book was ultimately very disappointing to me, as I am a big fan of Ford's "The S[portswriter" and "Independence Day." I kept waiting for more to happen. The book jacket alone tells you that there's going to be a bank robbery, and a murder, and you're going to know exactly who did what. The insights of the narrator aren't really anything that revelatory (there are differences between Americans and Canadians, borders are both physical and mental, etc). And then there's the cringe-inducing sex cene between the two main siblings. Any incest plot of eeeeew, but this one is especially so.

book_a.title: I Am Malala: The Story of the Girl Who Stood Up for Education and Was Shot by the Taliban
book_a.user_review: So, just as other reviewers have mentioned, I am critiquing the book, not Malala the person. We can all agree that she is a phenomenal young woman who is doing real things to change the world. That being said, the book itself is not all that well-written. Yes, the historical sections are necessary to provide context, but most people are coming to this book to learn about her and not the history of Pakistan. I admit that I didn't know much (or anything, really) about her background until I read this. I didn't know that she was already a national celebrity at the time of her attack, or that she was the specific target. Her father is a hero in his own right too. Overall, an important read, but not what I was expecting.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'm sure there have been some additions and expansions with the presence of a co-writer but said co-writer does a great job in letting Malala's voice shine through. For most of the book it felt like a sixteen year old girl talking rather than a journalist. It's a great book both because of the shooting and not and I am curious to see what else she accomplishes in her life. 
 You hear lots about India and lots about Afghanistan but not too much about Pakistan so I really liked that too.
Learned a lot about what it is like to live in Pakistan for a girl. Made me grateful for all the freedoms I have.
It had a very slow start and only got better towards the end.

I Am Malala by Malala Yousaf 
 Mala grew up in the Swat Valley of Pakistan. The daughter of a passionate educator, she came to become a voracious student. When the Taliban established a stronghold in the valley, educating girls became a dangerous proposition. Malala and her father refused to remain silent and spoke out against the Taliban, demanding all children deserved access to education. This eventually attracted the attention of Taliban leaders and on October 12, 2015, armed men boarded a bus on which Malala was traveling and shot and two other young women. 
 Let me start by saying I feel a bit guilty rating this book so low. The rating is not a reflection on my view of Malala. I followed her story as it unfolded and have seen her speak. There is no doubt that this is an incredibly impressive young woman. She is intelligent, compassionate and brave. But the book was a huge disappointment. First, the writing is very choppy and often sentences are structured in a confusing manner. I often had to re-read sections to make sure I understood what was being said. I understand. Secondly, since I've read a wide range of books on the Middle East has already had grasp on the history of the area, much of this books felt repetitive for me. Surprisingly, the vast majority of the book is on the I history of the area. I was really looking for a look at Malala and her father. In fact, I would really like to read a biography on him. It is a fascinating man who, in spite of all the death threats, has raised a young woman with the must courage. I always wonder what I would have done in WWII. Would I have done the right thing or been too frightened. Here, a father is willing to put his daughter's life on the line in order to take a stand. Finally, I had to really work to stay focused on the book. My mind often wandered and that's very unusual for me. I just never felt engaged.
What an incredible young woman.
I learned so much about Pakistan and the world Malala comes from. She is a very special girl. Lombard AAUW is doing a book club meeting next week on this book

In 2009 Malala Yousafzai was shot in the head while riding a school bus in Pakistan. With the Taliban in control , she and her father had the courage to speak out about the importance of education, especially for girls. Her story is heart wrenching and inspirational, as after her recovery she continues to advocate change in the world, and is the youngest person ever nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize. I really enjoyed the second half of the book, feeling like the first half was weighted down by political details. 3 stars for the book 5 stars for Malala !
Very moving. Words in a review couldn't capture the gratitude and guilt I feel for being lucky enough to be born in a free nation. We are far from perfect, but we are much farther along than others.
I'll explain my rating in an upcoming book trio.

This 2 star review doesn't reflect my feelings about Malala's story at all. Her story is one of bravery, sacrifice and love. Her story is inspirational and devastating all at the same time. 
 My 2 star review reflects the book itself. The story is written in a way that evoked no emotion from me whatsoever. The mood and feel of the book was cold- and try as I might- I felt no connection to Malala or her story. I struggled to get through the book- because I wanted to hear her story- her voice, and I felt like I was reading a robotic retelling of the events. 
 Too may names, too much history... her tone came across as braggy, not humble and courageous (which is how I imagine her to really be.) The book was not written from the perspective of a 16 year old girl... may be the author put her voice in the book too much..

Everything I've been reading lately feels so relevant. I know I'm coming late to this but book but I'm glad that it found its way into my hands at an incredibly pertinent moment. 
 I hope this is required reading. I'm so grateful for hearts like Malala's. What a truly profound human being. I hate what ugliness has touched her life but I am thrilled she has been given this platform. 
 I highly encourage everyone to read this book. It is the most nuanced book I've ever read about Islam, the middle east, the Taliban, and a woman's modern fight for education. 
 I know it's only February but it's the best book I've read all year.
Important words from an important woman, but I suspect her best is yet to come.
Great first hand account of a life behind not only a veil, but misogynistic customs.

I can't remember if I first heard about Malala before or after she was shot, but I know it was right around that time. I remember being sad that she was shot, but being glad at the same time that she was standing up for the right of children, especially girls, to get an education. 
 I learned so much from this book. I feel it was more than just a biography of Malala, but more of a history lesson: not just of Pakistan, and Swat (the region where Malala is from), but a history of the culture as well.I really enjoyed reading it, and though Malala writes with a 'co author', I felt that I could hear her voice coming through, and pleading for the people of the world to allow her and her friends their God-given right to learn. 
 I hope she'll be able to return to her beloved Pakistan someday, and that her campaign for education never ceases!

After searching for the book for months, I finally bought it in England on a trip. I just took it and sighed in relief. 
 The moment I started reading, I was intrigued by the story. The hard times, but also a reminder, she is human. 
 In the news, they portray her as this (well) holy person. As if she could never do anything wrong. Suddenly, she makes mistakes. She is a person. I did the same things when I was that age. Stuff like that. 
 This book was a great reminder for me that she is a person with a big heart and a lot of courage. 
 The best thing about the book is that you really get to know her, not only as the wise person you see on television. She is a teenager with two little brothers, a father that tries to cook and a mother who tries to fit in.

This book is so bad, that it is hard to find even where to start. It reads about 50% as a really boring history book, or a really boring survey of the events of the Taliban taking control of the Swat Valley in Pakistan. The other half is mostly Malala arrogantly telling the reader how amazing, smart and generous she is (and a bit about how amazing her mother and father are), which is also very boring, but also doesn't make her likable in any way. (By the age of seven I was used to being top of my class... "Malala is a genius girl", my class fellows would say. I was also known for practicing everything - badminton, drama, cricket, art even singing, though I wasn't much good. Or "Malala was a lucky girl," says Hidayatullah. "When she was born our luck changed.". And On some shelves were all the gold-coloured plastic cups and trophies I had won for coming first in my class. Only twice had I not come top - both times when I was beaten by my class rival Malka e-Noor. I was determined it would not happen again.. 
 Coming to the question of what exactly a ten year old has to talk to the media all the time, and why would her father push her to do so knowing that this is a real risk and people are getting shot for less around them. It is not clear to me. I am voting towards changing reality, but not using children and putting them at risk. 
 Now, let's continue with some facts. Since the mantra says "One child, One teacher, One book, One pen can change the world. While this saying might be true, this is one hundred percent not relevant to the story of Malala. I have checked the published statistics of girls going to school in Pakistan through the last decade from several resources (yeah, I know, a bit OCD, but the book really pissed me). She was shot in 2012, and the statics show almost no change whatsoever about girls (or boys) attending schools in Pakistan overall, and in Swat specifically (with even a drop between 2013 to 2014). Even the literacy rate did not go up in the country. I would suggest never take credit that is not yours (even if it would make a good story, which it hadn't). 
 I believe that education is a key to make the world a better place (while it is also very important what do you teach). I believe that we should strive to allow everybody to acquire it. Any type of oppression and terror is despicable, and the situation in Pakistan with the Taliban is no different (unfortunately, there was and there is too much of that in the world). I am happy that people are speaking up and working towards fixing the education situation. But I do have a problem with the overall arrogant entitled attitude. 
 Not sure of Malala is very naive, or just trying to look like a saint. Both are not good if you want to put a dent in the world: 
 I thought if anyone attacked me it would be on those steps. Like my father I've always been a daydreamer, and sometimes in lessons my mind would drift and I'd imagine that on the way home a terrorist might jump out and shoot me on those steps. I wondered what I would do. Maybe I'd take off my shoes and hit him, but then I'd think if I did that there would be no difference between me and a terrorist. It would be better to plead, "OK, shoot me, but first listen to me. What you are doing is wrong. I'm not against you personally, I just want every girl to go to school." 
 Shoe would not stop a terrorist, and you wouldn't have much time to explain that they are wrong. I hope everyone knows that. Especially if they have a real chance to meet a terrorist in a dark alley (or steep steps. 
 There are very well written books about the situation of women in extremely religious area (such as The Pearl That Broke Its Shell or Khaled Hosseini's books). Read them instead. 1 star, and I feel ultra generous.

One of those books where I felt almost duty-bound read. It is very difficult to read about the unjust treatment of women in this part of the world, but the story of Malala and her father's is quite compelling.

Malala has become a 'known' stoic figure which she was always. Throughout the book, you will realise that she is just a child who has silly fights with her siblings, classmates, worries about who is going to come first in class. You will see the child who has stood firmly for her principles. She talks very fondly about her father, tells his story too. She talks about how education has always shaped her life and probably she is trying to live the dreams of his father, like many of us. She is daunting and heroic and yet you can remember her as that girl in the school. She has and will inspire generations of women and men because she stands for a cause which has only one side - the side that enabled me to read her story and talk about her.

The four stars that I rated this book was more for learning the story about this exceptional person. Of course, I had heard about Malala and saw her interviews on The Daily Show with Jon Stewart. It was easy to think that she was thrown into fame merely by the fact that she was shot by the Taliban on her way home from school. What I did not realize until this memoir was that she had become a target because she had written and spoken about her belief that every child deserved an education starting when she was only 12 years old. Her father was a poor man who thru his strong beliefs and hard work established a school in the Pushtun area of Swat Valley. He continued to accept girls as students even when there was a rising tide against educating women. This was during the times that the Pakistani government was increasingly controlled by more conservative Islamic forces who created a more oppressive society especially for women. Women were not even allowed outside without being accompanied by a near male relative. What struck me in her story were also the small moments that Malala relays which makes you realize the universal themes as a pre-teen/teenage girl. She tells stories about competing for first place with her best friend and having tween fights with her girlfriends, having a boy leave her notes and the others teasing her about it (although it is a much more dangerous act in this conservative nation) and her feelings about it, joking with her school bus driver and playing pranks with her friends. Alongside these moments was her real fear that her father would be killed (she did not think the Taliban would target a young girl) and watching her classmates being married off at 14 and 15 years old. This a book worth reading to understand this tumultuous area but gives the message of hope that there are people like Malala and her family in this world.
Interesting look at what life is like for women in Pakistan.
Amazing <3

This book gives you insight to what's going on on the middle east. And I say insight because it gives you a place to start doing your own research on the subjects at hand. 
 This was a well written and narrated account of Malala's upbringing, life, and her wish for her and young children around the world to have adequate education. 
 I wanted to give this at least 4 stars but I found myself getting jumbled in the midst of all information because I couldn't quite pin which prospective to follow. This absolutely shows the hardships of many developing nations and especially those nations that have experienced genocidal events within the 21st century with governments that struggle to gain control over terrorist groups. 
 Malala is a marvel and is blessed to have a father who allowed her to follow her dreams. She took the opportunity and owned it and I, and I'm sure many others, respect her greatly. Although this book is meant to bring awareness to what's going on in the world's of Malala's I believe holding out on publishing the book would of made this a better read. I feel like they jumped on her as soon as she was able, and had they waited we would of gotten a better pieced together read.

I respect and admire Malala. She is a courageous and idealistic young woman. The book is a mixed bag, but is interesting nonetheless.
This is such an important book, a must-read.

This was a wonderfully enciteful book. I loved listening to the audiobook and hearing it in her own words. It made the book even better. My heart goes out to what this girl has gone through, and it amazes me what came out of it.

This is not a reflection on Malala - she is an extraordinary young woman from a highly evolved family. I just was not that interested in the history of Pakistan and the Taliban. Some is okay, but way too much time spent on it in the book. Her mother is illiterate, but is passionate about education for girls, and defies so many cultural taboos to support her daughter and husband. I think we will continue to see great things from Malala and she is a tremendous spokesperson for her people. I also loved her devotion to her faith, even in light of what some Muslims are doing in name of Islam and personally did to her. It not only injured her for a lifetime, but has forced her and her family to live outside their beloved home country. We would all do well to remember that there are millions of Muslims who are peaceful and pray to the same God that millions of Christians do. As I live in St. Paul with the priest sexual abuse scandal in our papers every day, I have to ask as Jesus did - he who is without sin cast the first stone.

I did enjoy this book but it was definitely written by a 17 year old girl - I think her story is quite empowering, but I would have liked to have the background on Pakistan presented more coherently and the story jumped around a lot.

A very informative book and amazing story of a young Pakistani girl. Malala is truly an inspiring young woman fighting for the great cause of education for girls. I'm sure we will be hearing more from this incredible young woman in the years to come. 
 While the narrative is written from Malala's perspective, one does wonder just how much of the voice is that of Malala's vs that of the ghost author.

***4.5 stars*** 
 I absolutely loved the way she tells her story. She's an ordinary girl who loves to tell jokes, who fights a lot with one of her brothers and who loves her family more than anything in the world. Her biggest desire is to learn and to go to school. She's also a girl that suffered something terrible, but who found in that situation the strength to continue fighting for her cause: education for every girl and boy in the entire planet.
I found Malala's story to be incredibly inspiring and courageous. I have a lot of respect for her, not only because of what she's gone through, but because of her strength and conviction.

I don't know why it took me so long to finish this book. Okay i didn't like that she have been saying negative things about her society and country even if it's true i think it's wrong to show to the world how bad my community and society. Second, for a child it's not good and dangerous to talk about political things even if it's for a nobel cause like hers. Finely i think if she weren't a young muslim girl she wouldn't get all this fame and attention although i appreciate her courage to speak out but not like this she should be more mature to know more about life

At the age of 16, most young women haven't lived enough of a life to be worthy of an autobiography. Most young women haven't been raised in a young, violent country, addressed the United Nations, been nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize, or been shot in the face for defending their right to an education, either. 
 That said, only a small part of the book is actually focused upon Malala herself as an individual; much of it centers upon the history of Pakistan, the turmoil as one leader after another has been overthrown or assassinated, the changes that took place in the country, and specifically, in the Swat Valley. 
 It's important background; ghostwritten by a British author and targeted (I assume) for an English-speaking audience, most of us are pretty ignorant of any country's history or geography that is not our own. Malala's love for her home country was revealed early in the lush, homesick-sounding descriptions of the Swat valley (which was once an independent country, like Texas in the USA), the always-crowded-with-visitors homes in the city of Mingora. 
 The oldest of three children, and the only daughter, Malala was named after a legendary Pashtun heroine, definitely a "Daddy's Girl," who loved books even as a toddler and squabbled with her little brother and sometimes with her best friend. 
 Her father, Ziauddin Yousafzai, was a fervent advocate of education for men and women even before he completed his own. He began many schools, many which were not a financial success, before Malala reached her teens. What I did not realize was what a mishmash of culture Pakistan was and is; Bollywood movies, Taliban radio programs, Ugly Betty DVD's... while at the same time electricity service is intermittent, and many homes consist of only two rooms: one for family to sleep in, one for guests. 
 The book reads smoothly, even if it is difficult as a parent to read of violent attacks upon children for the "crime" of wanting an education. And I had to wonder how much was toned down or softened, so as not to upset an American, British, or Pakistani readership, not an easy task. 
 I felt like I got a much better understanding of what it must be like to grow up in Pakistan as Malala did. I know that her favorite color is pink, her best friend is Moniba, whom she still talks to via Skype, since she and her family are now living in England, and that she deeply wants to return home to the Swat valley. Occasionally there was a hint of her voice and personality, but since she is still such a young woman, and experienced such a life-changing event, it was hard to tell who Malala is, or will become. 
 "Peace in every home, every street, every village, every country - this is my dream. Education for every boy and every girl in the world. To sit down in a chair and read my books with all my friends at school as is my right." I would love to see her dream realized.

What an amazing young woman. I was constantly reminding myself how old Malala was throughout her story telling. Obviously she has a bright mind and spark in her heart to accomplish great things in her life. It was enlightening to hear her story.

Va recomand sa cititi cartea scrisa de Malala, o foarte tanara activista pentru dreptul fetelor la educatie si detinatoare a numeroase premii pentru pace, inclusiv Nobelul de anul acesta. Marturia ei, scrisa impreuna cu jurnalista Christina Lamb, este in egala masura informativa si emotionanta. Datele istorice, politice si geografice sunt numeroase si detaliate, pline de nume de lideri politici sau religiosi, de denumiri de factiuni si interpretari ale islamului, destul de greu de retinut pe alocuri, dar acestea sunt necesare pentru a intelege contextul si a afla lucruri care poate in mintea multora sunt destul de alambicate. In plus, ele se imbina armonios cu povestea Malalei, a familiei ei si a prietenilor lor, cu viziunea ei pacifista si evoluata asupra lumii in care traieste, cu anecdote legate de scoala si prieteni, cu relatari despre popularitatea ei crescanda si, mai ales, despre rolul imens jucat de tatal ei in formarea Malalei si in lupta pentru drepturile fetelor la educatie si pentru eliberarea de sub regimul talibanilor. 
 Recenzia intreaga pe http://mihaelaburuiana.com/cartisical....
So much ignorance, cruelty and violence.! Hard to plow through.

I love Malala! She is inspiring and I love what she stands for. If you are going to read this book, get the young readers audio version like I did. For one, it is edited for young readers so it concentrates entirely on Malala's story. Second, the prologue and epilogue are read by Malala herself which I enjoyed. And third, at the end of the book you get to listen to Malala's speech to the U.N. There are times when an audio book trumps the print version. This is one of those times.

I applaud Malala for her courage and for being the strong woman she appears to be even at this very young age. Her story is an inspiration. However, I found the book difficult to get through. To me the writing got in the way of the message.

Did not finish. I seriously wanted to love this book. However, the story does not read like a memoir. It's more like a brief history of Pakistan with some family anecdotes added in. This book has not stopped me from admiring Malala for her bravery and activism, but unfortunately it was just not something I could get into to.

The three stars is not because I don't admire Malala. I admire her bravery and what she stands for. I admire all that she's had to overcome and all that she will continue to do. 
 However, her story was overshadowed by mishmash of historical tidbits and cultural facts (some of them were more important than others). It was pretty hard for me to get into because I think that really messed with a story that could have flowed better. 
 It also kind of bothered me that I felt like I was just being preached at instead of allowed to form my own opinions on it based on her experiences and her story. I often felt her tone was condescending, which reaaaaaaaally doesn't jive well with me. 
 In short, powerful story that could have been even more powerful if told in a different way.
I'm not usually into non-fiction/biography stuff. Although this book got a little boring sometimes, I really enjoyed it.

This was a great read. She's very inspiring. I'm amazed how positive and upbeat she has remained despite what she has gone through. She's a shining beacon for not just females, but humanity in general.

A powerful book showing the history of Malala's journey to get educational equality, the challenges & successes she had, and then the emotional aftermath of the shooting. A wonderful story, touching & emotional, and a look into the threats that the Taliban can have, but how we can rise above it.

I learned a lot from this. I liked the voice of the narrator. She has such joy and she takes such terrible things in stride. She has an indomitable spirit and that really comes across. I can't wait to hear from my book groups.

It took me about a month to read this book but that was simply because I have been in a reading slump. I was looking forward to reading this book since it came out and I was NOT disappointed. Malala's story is one of inspiration and a realism that is just unmatched by any fiction that I have read. Now I know this is a true story and I want to say the best part of reading this inspiring story was how this remarkable young woman took something that could have made her so angry and bitter and turned it into not only something positive but a lesson for everyone. She had already learned the lessons she is trying to teach but as I read this story it became clear that she was not only fighting for girls to get an education in her country but also for the rest of the world's young women. 
 When I finished this book and read the final chapter it brought many thoughts to my mind, the first of which was it would be an honor to meet this young woman as I have already heard her speak via a wonderful interview on 20/20 and she is just so insightful and full of life despite having hers almost ripped away from her. I applaud Malala for her efforts and I know she will not see this review but I wish her true happiness and that she may return home to peace and wholeness for herself and those she holds most dear.

I just couldn't stomach the tone of this book. Writing an autobiography has got to be one of the greatest challenges an author faces--to grab our attention without too much self-aggrandizement, or too much pity. This book had way too much I. . . I. . . I. . . and unfortunately came across self-aggrandizing. Too bad. I only finished it because it was chosen for bookclub, otherwise I wouldn't have. (1.5 stars)
This is a good book,but not for me I was hoping something else.

Once I started reading this book, I could not put it away. What a remarkable person. She is still so young but has done already more great things in her life than most other people. 
 I was really impressed by her story and her fight for womens rights and girls access to education. 
 Unlike some in recent years, she truly deserved the Nobel Peace Prize.

book_b.title: Dare Me
book_b.user_review: I love Abbott's writing, and this particular genre she seems to have created of teenage girl noir. Her "The End of Everything" was absolutely brilliant, and this was too. I swear, the woman understands teenage girlhood better than anyone else I have ever read.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book just never got it's hooks into me. I wanted to love it, I loved the idea of it, and there was certainly some fun to be had in this fast paced plot. There was nothing notably "wrong" with it but I just couldn't get into it. It was well written to the point of being slightly overdone, for every moment I thought Abbott had really nailed it there was one where I was questioning her choices. Bottom line, "Dare Me" is a fun read but if you want high school noir watch "Brick".

I did not like or care about this book at all (the characters are all cliche cardboards without any explanation about motivation) which makes me think that perhaps the one book by this author that I enjoyed was a lucky, unique event and that I should atop trying to read her..

Glorifies disordered eating. Promotes girl on girl hate to a very vulnerable age group. Purple prose, which I personally don't mind every now and then, but here it really detracted from the story and made everything very convoluted. Do not recommend.

I didn't enjoy this book. 
 Actually, it demanded quite a lot of self disciple to even finish it. 
 Not that it was poorly written (for this kind of book, I think it was above average), but neither the characters or the plot ever caught grasped my attention.
Disturbing, yet compelling.

Ooh...mean girls! Now here's a movie 
 I look forward to...a new Heathers...

Yikes. This was NOTHING like "You Will Know Me", which I loved. I had to skim my way through the last half, so boring. 
 Full Review To Come

It's a great story and would make a terrific movie... but it's told in this flat continuous present tense that makes what little reflection there is on a given moment sound stilted. "Something has passed between us, a secret knowledge about us, and what she needs from me. But I blink and miss it." Aside from the confusing and erroneous second comma, this idea phrased this way makes sense only in the past tense, in retrospect. If the blinking is happening in the present and the "something" is so obvious to the reader, it's stupid for the narrator not to think on it a little longer. It makes more sense to notice some overlooked significance of what is said in the moment only from some future date of greater self-awareness. Authors of the world, stop hamstringing yourselves by writing in the present tense!

I made it 50 pages and that's all I could do. I couldn't stand the writing. It was all disjointed and had no fluidity. It was driving me bonkers! Then you have her using weird descriptors for things, like wishbone arms, or hair like a taffy pull. Ummmm okay? What exactly do you mean by that? I've never looked at someone's arms and said, they look like a wishbone. Are the skinny? Bowed? What?! 
 It was too annoying for me to put up with, so unfortunately I won't be finishing this one. This is my first book by her as well, and I'm not sure if I will read her again if this is how she writes.

In some way, the tone and voice of this book reminded me of "The Virgin Suicides" - lyrical, moody, almost hypnotic. Why this worked against the book for me was it made Addy, our central figure, indistinct and shadowy as a character, whereas even more peripheral characters felt more real and fleshed out to me. Imbued with a type of omniscience that I didn't buy from her character. 
 The beauty of it pulled me along through the story (too much time spent dithering on the Beth vs Coach who-is-a liar line) to a resolution I didn't quite see coming. Solid story well told, but it didn't make me fly the way the girls did. 
 I agree with another reviewer that the title didn't work for me. And UGH to that cover.

I'll probably sound pretty prudish writing this, but if this is what high school is like now, I'm home schooling my kids. 
 I'm pretty sure though that this is only a small, sad microcosm of reality. And even giving it that much credence, I find the actions of the characters, particularly the young coach, pretty unrealistic. I like fantasy just fine, but not when it's presented as reality. 
 But it wasn't the overall "bad behavior" in this book that finally made me call it quits. It was the bizarre, meaningless dialogue and exposition that I just couldn't handle. Long rambling senseless sentences about nothing or about how the characters were "feeling" that I couldn't relate to.

I would give this book 2.5 stars. The premise was interesting and I haven't read a book like it before. That being said it started out strong but then lost me the further I read. In the end I was mostly skimming through the pages trying to still get a sense of what was happening but also just wanting to hurry up and finish it. It had some interesting twists at the end but it wasn't the type of book to hook me in and never let go. I would recommend this book to anyone wanting an insiders look at high school cheer leading and how dangerous bored teenage girls can be.
Not really interested in teenage angst; not even sure why I ordered this book

** spoiler alert ** 
 I am not sure if I liked this book or not. I didn't have a real clear idea of what the book was about before I started reading it. I knew it was about a group of cheerleaders, but besides that I had no idea. 
 The opening scene of the book takes place 4 months in the future. You know something awful is going to happen, but you don't exactly know what. 
 The main character, Addy, is likable right off the bat. You feel sorry for her because she is always playing back up to head cheerleader, Beth. Once the new coach arrives, things start to change for Beth. She is quickly cut down and put on equal ground as everyone else. I liked Coach right from the beginning. I liked that she took Beth out of the captain position and didn't take any crap from Beth. You start to see Coach and Addy becoming friendly and Beth starts to get jealous. I knew Beth would do something drastic to get Addy back on her side. Addy becomes blind to everything and everyone around her when Coach is involved. Beth goes insane trying to take Coach down. Coach falls in love with another man other than her husband. Beth finds out and makes it her mission to ruin Coach's life. 
 Beth starts to blackmail Coach. I so wanted Coach to not give in to Beth and rise above, but of course she doesn't. She gives Beth exactly what she wants and soon Beth is fully in charge of the squad. Coach stops showing up altogether. Coach's affair gets blown up when her lover is found dead. Beth desperately wants Coach to be at fault and almost loses Addy in the process of proving Coach guilty. Beth will stop at nothing to get Coach behind bars. 
 For their last match, the squad is trying a complicated stunt. There was originally another girl who was going to do it, but Beth scared her and now Beth is the top girl. Beth ultimately gets everything she ever wanted. I really disliked Beth at the end. She is a nasty girl. I wanted Addy to not believe or listen to her. Once Coach was out of the picture, Addy turned back to Beth for good. I saw what Beth was going to do before she did it. She failed her difficult stunt. I think she fell on purpose. I think she wanted the attention and wanted out of cheer altogether. Beth falls and goes to the hospital. Coach's husband is found to be the cause of Coach's lover's death. Beth got Coach's husband to practically kill another person. Beth is evil. Addy, it turns out, was not all that innocent. She ends up becoming the captain when Beth is out of the picture. You might even think that Addy had this plan all along. I'm not entirely convinced that Addy always wanted to be the leader. I think the idea got planted in her head and it sounded good to her- to have someone else believe in her. I definitely think Addy wanted to be out of Beth's shadow and now that she has the power, she will not give it up.
Compulsively readable, but still meh at the end.

Actual rating: 1.5 
 So... I didn't like this book. Dare Me had the opportunity to be raw and intense but only ended up being a let down and kind of boring. I'm thinking back to when I was reading it and all I can really say is "meh". The writing felt too choppy for me, like it was trying to have shorter phrases in order to repeatedly emphasize the point. 
 I had zero attachment to any of the characters. I was hoping to like Addy but she never really felt like her own person. I mean, I understand that's part of the point, that she's always associated with Beth, but her thoughts and decisions felt so dumb and meaningless. I tried to understand Addy's attachment to Beth and Coach, but I couldn't. They're so unappealing. Beth at least had some sort of unpredictability, but that quickly lost its lustre as the story progressed. Coach was just boring as hell. 
 I bumped the rating up half a star because of the premise and potential. I love the idea of a high school cheer squad and the reality of its grittiness and desperation. I love when books delve into the intensity between girls and how their relationships with one another are so much deeper than most people think they are. One should never underestimate the power of a female friendship and its unpredictability. I thought this concept could really go somewhere, especially with the tension between best friends, Addy and Beth. Unfortunately, I read this book with glazed eyes and didn't put it down only because it was so short. I'll continue to seek books out with these ideas but this one just didn't work for me at all.

This was an incredibly fast easy read. And I would consider it a guilty pleasure and not something that takes too much brain exercise. There were certain parts of it that was fascinating and insightful into the world of teenage girlhood and cheerleading. I wish it had been ever darker. I realize that she was narrating as a teenage girl so a lot of what happened we saw filtered through that character. But I would have liked it to be a little more bold in terms of the dark subject matter. But then again, I'm kind of a twisted character so it might just be me.

This book took forever to read, because simply put I lost interest and Christmas music was more appealing. I soldiered through the end in one day, so I could start my 75 books for 2017. 
 Abbott is very good at speaking from a teenage perspective, which was the problem for me. I felt too old to care about the drama surrounding the characters. I didn't really care about who would win flier or who was most popular etc. Sadly I didn't feel like some of the characters were developed enough for me to understand or believe their motivations. There was promise here but in the end the book was okay. I would recommend to some younger or possibly a former cheerleader.

This is the first Megan Abbott book to read. The first few chapters (the setup, if you will) took longer than I think it should have and I found myself having a hard time getting into it. Once the actual storyline kicked in more, I loved it! Looking forward to reading more of Megan Abbott's books!

It's hard to start with why I hated this book- 
 I have no patience with adults who want to be cool and friends with teens so abdicate their adult responsibilities 
 It makes it look like school administrators and teachers are all morons 
 It stereotypes high school students as all drinking all drugs 
 It has NO positive role models.

Full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. 
 I kept meaning to review this book but kept forgetting, that's how quickly it fell off my radar after I finally, midway through, decided to skip to the end. 
 Intensely disliked this book. The basic premise surrounds a couple of "mean girl" types and the way in which their relationships and dynamic change after they get a new cheerleading coach. Oh, there is also a whodunit mystery revolving around the death of an Army Sergeant recruiter dude. The resolution to this mystery portion of the plot is blindingly obvious, which alone would be fine with me, but when combined with all the horrible red herrings, terrible characters, and the prose, it just combined into one hot mess for me. 
 There are others who have commented on the prose in this book. To that I say see the first line of this review. Abbott's sentences sound beautiful and cool, at times, talking about their "wishbone arms" and such, but right after you read it, there's a moment of "wtf did I just read," and "wtf are you trying to say?" It feels very try-hard. I don't think a writer needs to fill their pages with flowery passages that say, really, nothing at all. It's pretentious and overwhelms the story. You can keep it simple, you know. 
 I think there were only two characters in this book who even had a semblance of a personality. The rest were background noise. Even the ones who had some personality did not make any sense. Coach, for instance. One day she is mysterious, refined, and reserved around the girls, and like three days later, she's inviting them to her house for wine and gossip? What?! 
 Most of the girls, too, are almost immediately enamored by her in a pseudo homoerotic way. No relationship development, no character development, just bam! Coach is the goddess of everything in the world, so let's go to her house, drink wine, tell secrets, and help her cover for her secrets. What?! 
 The worst part is, at the end of the day, this book is about the relationship of two best friends essentially torn apart. the one best friend is queen bitch. Though we get a couple flashbacks, nothing in this book explained to me A) why they were friends; B) why they remained friends throughout the years; C) especially why they remained friends after Coach comes into their lives and Queen Bitch turns into Empress Bitch of the Bitchtonia galaxy. 
 There's no explanation for this girl's immediate hatred towards Coach throughout the book, other than something to the effect of "I've got a hunch she's hiding something." Then out of nowhere (it's not entirely nowhere, since Abbott telegraphs the hell out of her plot) we find out that all the bitchy and horrible things they do to each other go back to one moment years ago when *maybe* the one friend thought she might be in love with the other? What?! 
 I hated this book. The plot was terrible. The writing sounded pretty, but meant pretty much nothing.

This has been compared to Gone Girl, but it lacks the subterfuge of character. There is no curtain of 'cool girl' covering Beth and Addy. They're Cheer Girls, just not the ones you remember from high school, or maybe they are but to the nth degree? This smacks more of Cruel Intentions than Gone Girl to me. Except there's no innocent virgin saving any protagonists. In fact, now that I think of it, there is no moral compass at all. I found it to be a riveting thriller and sped through to the end. I love dark and complicated characters, and this was chock-full of them.

I really did not enjoy this book at all. I don't know what I expected but the writing was hard to follow, the plot just annoyed me and the characters made me cringe. Maybe because I've been a cheerleading coach and the actions of that woman gave all of us a bad name.

My eyes are going to fall out of my head because I have been reading this straight through the night but it is so worth it! You could not pay me a million dollars to be a teenager in this day in age. The backstabbing,jealousy,vindictiveness!! I was surprised with the ending, I somehow never suspected the person that it was.

This book was pure torture. I stayed with it for as long as I could, before throwing in the towel. I hate giving up on a book, and I rarely have to do that. But I couldn't stick this one out any longer. Talk about boring story telling. If you can even call it story telling. The author writes in her concept of prose. Atleast that is how I interpreted it. It's awful. The story just drags, and it's basically a tutorial in how to achieve a in sync toe touch while on a Cheer squad! Hoorah! I even skimmed through the rest in hopes of finding out what happened, and I lost interest while skimming!! It's just a terribly written book. If you don't feel the need to read this, then pass. It's awful.
Vague and melodramatic.

I was really looking forward to this one after enjoying Abbott's last book (much to Tony's surprise). I downloaded the audio version and listened. I don't know if this was the best choice. I don't remember that the book was very long, but the audio definitely dragged. Just when I thought it was over I realized I still had over another hour of listening left. So, I don't think the format suited the story very well. As for the story itself, I didn't find it as compelling as Abbott's last novel. I thought the "cheerleaders gone bad" storyline would be interesting; even though it may be a bit played out, I imagined Abbott would do something unique with it. And, I suppose, it's not exactly your typical story. But it wasn't as good as I hoped.

Disturbing, but not in the "oh, how clever I totally get the point of this" sort of way. I couldn't wait to finish, mainly because I found myself viscerally reacting to these characters...and it just made me feel sad and icky, which I will now call sicky. I can handle one or the other of those feelings, but not both at the same time.
Forsokte och forsokte, men det var inget som var bra med den har boken

Ugh it was simply terrible. I should have known better than to pick up a book about cheerleaders for Pete's sake. The mystery, the obsession, and the badly handled body image issues added up to nothing if not infinitesimal disappointment. This book happens to be something I wouldn't want to touch with a ten feet long poll and would suggest others to do the same. That being said the prose was probably the only saving grace, it's beautifully written. I will hand Miss Abbott that, certainly.
Horrible.

God, this was such a rollercoaster. I was excited to read this book and I must admit I was interested in reading the ending but god it dragged on for so long... I was bored and jumped several chapters to find some juicy parts. This was a disappointment.... i'm not even religious yet this made me groan 'god ' several times of annoyance..
I HATED THIS! I can't believe I read the whole thing, waste of my time.
Bleck! Every character in the book is awful and I didn't really are what happened to them.
I did really like it but I was thinking it more of a twist at the end. I did guess it but I did not think it was the best ending, but still very addictive of a book. Cheerleaders BE crazy
A dark, unique story with a dreamlike quality and a fascinating take on teenage girls, cheerleading, and the desires that drive us.

I hated all the characters, except possibly the antagonist. I kept reading because I was curious to see if I was correct about the level of unreliability of the narrator: I was. 
 There's a team of cheerleaders, in the old version of cheer where you give a few yells and dance moves and that's it. Suddenly they have a new coach, who immediately turns them all into the level of athlete needed to do tricks and to be competitive, who has a 4 year old daughter but is somehow capable of having her team of teenage girls over to drink (and perhaps smoke up, I forget now) every night. None of the cheerleaders have parents, siblings, other friends, romance. 
 There's a murder and some obsession and none of it works because the narrator is so far from sane or reliable that none of the characters act like actual humans would. This may well have been a deliberate choice, but it didn't quite work out.

In Dare Me we meet a group of cheerleaders, they are around 16 years old. Captain Beth and her loyal co-conspirator Addy seem to run the squad. Their old coach has moved away and they are meeting their new coach for the first time. The squad seems to love the new Coach, all except for Beth. When Coach begins an inappropriate friendship with Addy, Beth is teeming with jealousy. Addy is thrilled by her new friendship with Coach. Addy seems the type who wants to attach herself to someone new when the opportunity presents itself. This isn't the first time that Addy has stepped out on Beth. Though Coach's attention on Addy is completely inappropriate even for a 27-year-old, I understand that a 10 year difference in adulthood doesn't seem like much but even a 2 year difference is adolescence is a world of difference. 
 When Addy and Beth catch Coach having an affair on school ground. Beth is delighted to have leverage. While Addy is delighted to have a secret to share with Coach. The story begins to spiral out control, Addy is witness to something that is way beyond her maturity. She is pulled between who to believe Beth or Coach. 
 This was a strange one. On one hand, I feel that Abbott has a great hold on teenagers. I found the behavior and vernacular to be completely believable. Maybe thats due to her being a professor at NYU. I found a lot of the story to be believable, but I really did not care for Addy, and being that she is the narrator, that's a tough spot to be in. Addy felt empty and undeveloped, that may be the point, however, it took me out of the story. 
 I suggest reading the last few chapters slowly, I was so caught up in what was happening that I had to read it twice to fully understand the ending. 
 Favorite quote: 
 "I never gave anything to anyone before. not like this. 
 I never was anything to anyone before. 
 Not like this. 
 I never was, before. 
 Now I am. " 
 For more reviews, please visit iamjanesheart.com.

So, I read to about page 50. When a book is put in the thriller genre and it doesn't have me hooked on the first 50 pages, there is no way I'm giving it the time of day past that. Sorry. 
 That said, Abbott has a very elegant, easy to read writing style. I feel as though that's a rare combination to find with authors these days. Unfortunately, the plot is just something I'm not interested in.

Usually some mean-girl bitchiness can be fun to read about if there's some substance behind it too. However, 25 pages into this book about cheerleaders scrabbling for rank and attention(I know, I even abandoned my Nancy Pearl, try 50 pages of any book before abandonment, rule), I was left with only the urge to punch all the main characters in the face. Including the coach. Not my cup of tea.
It was hard to finish this book. I just couldn't find anything to enjoy. The story just wasn't there.

This is a pretty good book, but I didn't enjoy it the way I enjoyed The End of Everything and Abbott's earlier noir novels. Perhaps it was the subject matter (the world of cheerleaders) which didn't interest me? The plot is taut, but I thought that the writing was often lacking in real pizzazz. Not sure why I thought that, when I was wildly enthusiastic about The End of Everything.
Horrid! Who are these girls? The characters were so despicable and not believeable. Content is definitely not suitable for a young adult audience either.
I don't even care what you think about this book. It was just a stupid teenage story. Sorry.

This has been on my TBR list for too long. I loved the psychological aspect of it. I thought the characters were very realistic. I have certainly known the manipulative queen bee types, as well as the wannabes and lackeys. There were times I felt a little lost as to what was happening, but overall I loved it. You are constantly questioning who is lying, or is everyone a liar?

reference_books.title: Bird Box
reference_books.review_text:
Is there anything scarier than the thought having to do without your eyesight? Not to me there isn't. 
 This book was definitely a page turner! The final chapters were manic, but absolutely fascinating. I don't usually read this type of genre, so maybe that's why the story seemed so original and fresh to me? For whatever reason, I found I was compelled to keep reading and just couldn't put the book down. 
 However, we were left with several unanswered questions, which is NOT my favorite way of ending a story. Here are a few of mine: 
 *	What ever happened to Gary? 
 *	Who was following them in chapter 38? (Boy thought they were in a boat and rowing with their hands) 
 *	What the hell was with all those dead birds falling from the sky in chapter 41? 
 *	Who was trying to pull that blindfold off of Malorie's face? 
 *	Was it indeed a creature that was "right next to them"? And why did it just go away? 
 All this stuff was just kind of put out there, but then nothing! I must admit that I don't like manufactured drama intended purely to heighten the tension. 
 NOTE: I didn't think that the book affected me or scared me too much, but maybe I was wrong. I was home alone when I finished reading the last several chapters, and I was in the bathroom when I heard a noise somewhere in my house. It flashed into my mind that my screen door was unlocked, and before I knew it I had locked myself in my bathroom and stood there with my ear pressed against the door, listening as hard as I could. It took me a couple of minutes to gird my loins and stealthily creep out (while holding a curling iron as a weapon - HAH!), phone in hand ready to dial 911. So... maybe the book affected me after all. 
 DISCLAIMER: This was not the first time that I have barricaded myself in a room after thinking I heard a strange noise in my house. It wasn't the 2nd or 3rd time either! :-) 
 Read with SBC book club September 2016

** spoiler alert ** 
 Had a happy jaunt back into this classic murder mystery. Inspector Alan Grant of Scotland Yard is recuperating from an on-the-job accident. Bored out of his mind in his hospital room, a friend brings him a stack of pictures of different historical figures. Grant enjoys faces, and goes through the stack with enjoyment. He comes upon a painting that challenges him. It is a painting of Richard III. However, the painting does not match the evil villain history has painted Richard III to be -- the wicked uncle who arranged for the death of his two innocent nephews in the Tower of London. Grant starts an investigation "a la Scotland Yard" into the age old murder to see if Richard III really could have been the one responsible for the death of the Two Princes. 
 Who benefited from the death of the princes? What did contemporary reports say about the crime? Who wrote the history that depicted Richard III as a hunchback and as the murderer of his nephews? 
 The result is refreshingly new, and well presented! I can never read Shakespeare's "Richard III" in the same way ever again. *SPOILER* The answer is that Henry VII benefited most from the removal of the two princes. Contemporary reports about the crime were non-existent because all evidence pointed to the fact that the two princes were still alive at the time of Richard III's death. Sir Thomas More wrote the celebrated "wicked Richard III" history that Shakespeare based his play on. And Sir Thomas More supported the Tudor kings. Richard III was the last of the Plantegenet kings. Go figure! 
 So, now go read your history anew and see if you can figure out "who-done-it" yourself!
Ha! Do you think Richard III is completely evil? This one might just change your mind.

A police detective, confined to bed while a serious injury heals, takes up delving into history to help the time pass. Without really meaning to, he stumbles over what seems to him a possible miscarriage of justice, and with the help of a young research assistant, he takes it upon himself to investigate. What really did happen to 'the princes in the tower', and was the last Plantagenet king really the monster that history has painted him? 
 An absolute classic of a detective novel, in a quite unusual form, 'The Daughter of Time' explores how history is constructed, and how certain versions of events come to be widely accepted as the truth, despite a lack of evidence. The title is taken from a Francis Bacon quotation "Truth is the daughter of time, not of authority.' Published in 1951, shortly before the author's death, the book sparked both praise and controversy from the moment of it's publication, with no lesser personage than Sir Winston Churchill weighing in on it's merits. While certain elements of the story mark it as being a work of it's time, it absolutely stands up to modern reading.

http://andalittlewine.blogspot.com/20... 
 When I don't know, I turn to Wikipedia: 
 In 2012, Peter Hitchens wrote that The Daughter of Time was "one of the most important books ever written." 
 On its publication Anthony Boucher called the book "one of the permanent classics in the detective field.... one of the best, not of the year, but of all time." 
 Dorothy B. Hughes also praised it, saying it is "not only one of the most important mysteries of the year, but of all years of mystery". 
 This book was voted number one in The Top 100 Crime Novels of All Time list by the UK Crime Writers' Association in 1990. 
 But why? 
 I am not a mystery reader, but The Daughter of Time came up in my book club, so I read it. 
 Most mysteries fall in one of two camps: the transparent mystery, where we know the guilty party by the end of the third chapter and merely mark time until the hero figures it out; or the deus ex machina mystery, where the hero has deduced some vital clue that is withheld from the readers until after the final confrontation (you could also call this The Sherlock). 
 Daughter of Time is neither of these. Our hero is bedridden, convalescing after being injured while capturing the last baddie. Stuck in his bed, Daughter... breaks one of the cardinals rules of story-telling: almost none of the action happens in front of us. Instead, characters enter the hospital room, tell the hero what's happened and then leave to have more adventures while hero stays home. 
 In this way, Daughter... has elements of psychological thriller and melodrama. I was far more interested in how the hero handled his incapacitation than I was in the mystery that he was engaged in. 
 Maybe we live too much in the reality tv era. CSI and Law & Order regularly take their fictional characters into contact with "real world" cases. But I'm sure this must have been a novel approach for a novel in 1951. 
 Is that what made reviewers hail Daughter... as an instant classic? Or is there something else I'm missing?
