 What a delightful book! This is maybe the third time I've read it, but now with a better background in medieval history, and historical theory in general, it made a lot more sense. The standard view is that the young princes Edward and Richard, the sons of King Edward IV (brother of Richard III) were murdered by their evil uncle. This is the story that went into the history books until revisionists took a closer look at the historical evidence & made a different claim, that it was actually Henry Tudor (the father of Henry VIII and the first Tudor king) who framed Richard III for the murder of the princes. This is the focus of Tey's novel. She introduces it by having her detective hero (Inspector Grant) being laid up in the hospital dying of boredom while he's there, giving himself the puzzle of who really killed the princes to work on during his stay. Tey points out that Tudor historians wrote the main and popular theory about Richard III, because they certainly wouldn't have been able to be objective under the Tudors. Based on the Tudor accounts, Wm. Shakespeare wrote his famous (and excellent) play, Richard III. 
 Grant has as a partner in his "investigation" a young researcher who is able to find answers to Grant's questions based on the non-Tudor historical narratives. While it sounds very boring, the author is able to turn Richard III into a human being and we, the readers, begin to question the time-honored theory of the princes' deaths. What I found most intriguing were other examples of what was supposed to be time-honored historical "fact" that was really manufactured for political reasons. 
 I would recommend this to someone who enjoys history, and especially the history of Lancaster & York (The Wars of the Roses). Otherwise , the reader might find it dull. Furthermore, I think that people who would gain the most from this particular book would be people who are willing to question long-standing historical views & even if you don't agree with the author, at least be willing to consider her point of view. Written in 1951, it still has the power to hold the reader's interest.

I've never read a book with Inspector Grant before, but in this one he is bedridden with a broken leg and investigating a historical mystery to pass the time. He has nurses, an actress, a museum researcher, a doctor, and colleagues to bounce ideas off of and get information from and ends up solving a very cold case. I found the writing to be excessively...British. :) I had a hard time understanding some of the references and slang from 1950's England and had to look up quite a few things as I read. The book read more like a novelization of someone's graduate thesis paper instead of a typical mystery. The information was thrown out very fast and I might not have followed this book as well as I did if I hadn't already known something about the historical time period being described. I liked the idea of "Tonypandy"--ideas that are taught and enmeshed in the public knowledge but didn't ever actually happen. It's neat that there is a word for that, though it is an odd word. 
 Forty million school books can't be wrong. 
 Why, yes. Yes they can. 
 It's an odd thing but when you tell someone the true facts of a mythical tale they are indignant not with the teller but with you. They don't want to have their ideas upset. It rouses some vague uneasiness in them, I think, and they resent it. So they reject it and refuse to think about it. If they were merely indifferent it would be natural an understandable. But it is much stronger than that, much more positive. They are annoyed. 
 And that is the biggest problem with humanity. People get ideas in their head and then won't change them for all the evidence in the world.

After going through all of the Nancy Drews in the Seldovia Public Library in about a month when I was eight or so, I didn't read mysteries much. My mother loved mysteries, especially those of British authors, including Ngaio Marsh, Dorothy L. Sayers, and Agatha Christie. Perhaps, in the perverse way of children, because she did, I wouldn't. It took her twenty-one years of patient persistence to get me to read Josephine Tey's The Daughter of Time. 
 It was a revelation. To this day, The Daughter of Time remains the finest crime novel I have ever read, and one of the finest novels I have read of any kind. In it, a policeman is confined to a hospital bed, literally unable to sit upright, and from that bed he solves a double homicide committed four hundred years before. The crime scene is sixteen generations out of date, there is no surviving forensic evidence, and the chroniclers of the time only prospered through patronage, which could and did color their reporting. 
 And yet, Tey's hero prevails. Satisfying on every level, character, plot, and scene(s).

A famous quirky book from The Golden Age. An interesting and persuasive defense of Richard the Third against the charge of murdering the princes in the Tower dressed up as a detective novel. A thought- provoking companion to The Winter King, the excellent biography of Henry the Seventh which I read recently.

This is a marvelously different mystery. The detective, an inspector from Scotland Yard, is flat on his back in the hospital and very bored, so one of his friends suggests he unravel a historical mystery from the past -- and he picks the unsolved mystery of whether Richard III of England murdered his two nephews in order to steal the crown for himself. With the help of a researcher Inspector Grant delves into the 15th century, researching the eyewitnesses and the motivations of the alternative suspects and comes up with some fascinating answers which I won't reveal. But it is the unique style of this novel that has made it such a classic. It is pure mental/intelligence work, and all the more impressive for that. A true tour de force, especially for those of us who are history addicts.

Police detective investigates Richard's III's supposed murder of two boys while laid up in a hospital. And guess what, he finds out that a lot of history books are wrong. I guess I found this kind of predictable and kind of glamorizing academic research, when I've never experienced something that thrilling in my research. People who like the history of British monarchs and academic detective stories would probably like this book, but it's not really for me.

This would be a 4, but I thought the book could have been over by page 150 and it went on and on. It was actually a very interesting book if you are interested in royalty of the past. Its all about the theory of Richard the 3rd and whether or not he killed his nephews. I learned a lot about Richard the 3rd, and Henry the 7th and Henry the 8th. Hopefully I'll retain some of this for once.

I see that the average rating for this book is 3.95, and all I can think is, who didn't like it?? It takes a really masterful writer to create a sense of page-turning suspense in a novel set entirely in a hospital room, with a hero who only gets out of bed at the very end of the book. The pacing was excellent, characters well-drawn, and the story itself fascinating. Of course, she chose a good story to work with -- Richard III and the princes in the tower -- but even so. And it is wholly my own fault that I miscounted the II's in Henry VII and so thought we were talking about someone entirely different until almost the end of the book. But then I'm really horrible at keeping English history straight. 
 Will have to look up more books by Josephine Tey.

if you want to know whether Richard III was a deformed monster or simply a much maligned monarch, give this entertaining and informative performance of Tey's well-respected investigative mystery a try. It's stood the test of time.

I approached this book with only a slight knowledge of Richard III and the awful murders of two innocent children. I'm afraid to say my limited knowledge came from movies or TV series, not the best source. This book was very interesting, though it can feel slow and non-PC, which in itself is interesting since you get to glimpse at the style and wording used in the 1950's. One thing I don't understand is the title since the main characters from the investigators to the suspects were all male.
Pretty clunky as a piece of literature, but it does put a convincing case, apparently based on historical facts rather than accounts of historians through the ages.
Well written

My shelf for this book should be "Read ... sort of". I just couldn't get through this book and really wanted. The premise is interesting. The writing - not so much. I'm trying to figure out what is was about the writing that put me to sleep. Literally. And I still trying to figure out why this book is listed as one of the top ten mysteries of all time. Have I become so accustomed to excitement in books that I can't get through an intellectual mystery? Do I have to have modern day writing styles in order to enjoy a book. I don't think so. Two of my favorite books are Bram Stoker's Dracula and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Daughter of Time however, was just not the book for me. I wish I had been in on the book club discussion because it would have been interesting to discuss why this book was so ... well ... boring.

What if Richard III wasn't the vile monster most history books claim him to be? 
 Police inspector Alan Grant is jaded from his long hospital confinement on account of a broken leg, and takes up the suggestion of a friend to go over historical mystery to pass the time. From a stack of given portraits he is inexplicably drawn to the face of Richard III, whom he thinks (based on his claim of being a face-reading expert) looked rather too forlorn and in a "dreadful pain" to be a cold murderer. With some outside help, he ventures into the life and reign of King Richard III, and as he learns more about the man he also begins to wonder if history has been ruthless to the last Plantagenet king. 
 This book is an interesting overture into Richard III's life and the mystery behind the disappearance and/or the alleged murder of his two nephews (the Princes in the Tower). Josephine Tey gave plausible claims clearing King Richard of his supposed crimes by presenting who the man was before he was king and laying down his perceived personal and political motivation for claiming the crown. The author seemed to be critical of histories as told by the victors and referred to watered-down versions of truth or misconstrued historical facts as a "Tonypandy", after the riots in this particular South Wales village during the 1900s were said to have been inaccurately chronicled. 
 This is a good investigative read, although not decidedly appealing for me as it took me over a week to finish. I guess I got a little bored at the part where the characters muse over seemingly unimportant things, but on the whole it did not dull my appreciation for this book and Richard III. A Ricardian through and through! :)
Listened to this on CD..so hard to follow. Did not enjoy this at all.

I have been wanting to reread Josephine Tey's The Daughter of Time for quite a while now. The more I read on Richard III, the more I want to read. I just find this time period to be oh-so-fascinating. And the more you read, the easier it is to keep track of who's who and who's loyal and who's not. In this Alan Grant mystery, a bed-ridden Grant turns to solving a historical mystery since he can't be working on any actual cases. A friend knowing of his boredom, of his whining, brings him a stack of portraits, hoping that one face will interest him more than the others perhaps. Grant chooses Richard III. He vaguely remembers his story, but, he wants to refresh his memory. So he begins by reading school books, then historical fiction, and then biography, etc. Grant becomes very opinionated on what he reads, judging that what passes as historical fact wouldn't be acceptable as evidence or proof in court. In other words, he finds the history books to be all gossip. For example, the biography that is supposedly so esteemed, the author would have been FIVE years old when Richard III was on the throne. Yet he writes as if he was an eyewitness to the dramatic events. Grant argues (mostly with himself and perhaps also with his two nurses) that at best the man's facts would be just stories he'd heard from others and written down. Since the biographer grew up and came into power during the Tudors--who had every reason in the world for hating and slandering Richard III--then the stories passed down to him would have bias to them. Who would make a hero out of Richard III when Henry VII or Henry VIII reigned?! He finds a kindred spirit in an American researcher named Brent Carradine. Since Grant is stuck in bed, Carradine is the man doing the hard work, digging into research. Together they discuss the facts as they see them, Grant arranges the facts seeing what he can piece together, seeing if he can make a narrative that works. He just can't believe that Richard III murdered his two nephews. Grant believes that Richard is the one with the least motive to want them dead. For their deaths do him no good whatsoever, just harm. 
 The Daughter of Time isn't your typical mystery novel. The detective essentially just stays in bed and reads one book after another after another. He also discusses Richard III with anyone who enters his hospital room. (His nurses don't find Richard III as fascinating as Grant does.) For readers who do enjoy history, historical fiction, this one can prove satisfying. There is a chance that mystery lovers may enjoy this one too, after all Grant himself HATES history or hates reading history, but, it may not be for everyone.
As a mystery story, I don't think it's all that great. But as a work of popular history and an explanation of how scholarship works, it's really clever.

I found this book intriguing because it combined two genres -- mystery and historical fiction. Scotland Yard Inspector Grant is bedridden due to an accident. Out of boredom, and with the help of a young researcher, sets out to look at the murder of the young princes under Richard III through the eyes of a detective rather than a historian -- to discover who their murderer really was. Such an approach makes a historical event most interesting.

If your passion is English history, specifically the Tudor & Plantagenet dynasties and 15th-16th century succession to the throne, then this is the book for you! It satisfies academically, but is definitely not entertaining fiction. The "daughter of time" is not a person, but "truth," as opposed to "authority." Tey, the author, presents a convincing argument: the "princes in the tower" were *not* murdered by their uncle, Richard III, and he was in fact a competent & highly revered monarch. This of course is in opposition to public school history books, Shakespeare's famous play, and popular thought. Henry the VII was the real bounder. I liked it very much; but then I'm a bit of a nut for this kind of thing & wouldn't recommend it to casual readers.

A fabulous read. 
 This book written in the 1950s has not aged at all despite the 70 years that has passed since the writer penned it. 
 In this the protagonist attempts to solve a crime that occurred 700 years ago. Did King Richard III kill the Princes in the Tower or not?No wonder it ranks as one of the best crime novels ever written. 
 It would be easy to say, that a book written about a crime that happened 700 years ago cannot really age. I think otherwise. After the rage that Da Vinci Code became, there were several me too novels that were just plain tired. You would feel having read one, you've read them all. Even Dan Brown became repetitive and boring. This book however stands out, in the writing and the logical flow of deduction the story takes. 
 The only flaw - the original premise and constant badgering of 'He has a nice face, he couldn't be a murderer'. 'He has a careworn face, he cannot be a murderer'.

book_b.title: Gone Girl
book_b.user_review:
2012 GoodReads Best Mystery & Thriller Winner 
 2 1/2 stars 
 So I REALLY wanted to read this book. It was one of the IT books of the year. Everyone was telling my how much I would enjoy it! 
 I put my name on a waiting list at my library, and was something like 845th on the list. After waiting forever, I get a notification that the ebook is available, and I have to check it out by Dec 21st, or go back to the end of the line. I dutifully check it out, but have no time to read it. I am hosting 2 separate Christmas Days (my family's on Dec 22, then my husband's on Dec 25) and like I said, I have NO TIME TO READ! I was thinking that I would start reading this book right after I cleaned up the mess from all of the festivities at my house. It would be an extra Christmas Gift, just for me. 
 So, on Dec 26th I wake up to a bomb of a house, and a scratchy throat. As I'm running around putting away platters and wine glasses, I'm feeling worse and worse. I collapse into bed that night, thinking that TOMORROW is the day I get to start reading Gone Girl. 
 I wake up on the 27th, and feel like an elephant is sitting on my face! My eyes are tearing, I'm sneezing and coughing, my sinuses are killing me, and I've got a granddaddy of a headache. And Gone Girl is going to disappear from my Nook on Jan 3rd! Did I mention that I REALLY want to read this book? I start to read... 
 And I didn't much care for the book. I mean, it was ok, but certainly not GREAT. I actually had to force myself to keep reading it. Now perhaps my perception was clouded by all of the preceding rig-a-ma-role, but I don't think that's it entirely. Even after I started to feel a bit better, I still wasn't enjoying this book. 
 SPOILER ALERT 
 First of all, the two main characters are not together for most of the book, so there is no dialog between them to speak of. And I like a book that is fueled by conversations between characters. (I guess I'm like Alice in Wonderland in that regard, but I can't help it, that's just the way I am.) I like characters that interact, not just dwell inside their own heads. 
 Secondly, I didn't like either character. He is a cheating slime ball, and she is a psychotic bitch. I wasn't thrilled with spending time with either of them. 
 Thirdly, I didn't like the ending, nor did I find it very believable. Are the police really that stupid? Is Amy really that smart? Is Nick really that gullible? Didn't he know that she was going to pull something on him at the end? If I could guess what it was, couldn't he? COME ON! 
 I'm going to round up this book 3 stars because I think it may have been the wrong book at the wrong time for me. I can see how others would like the book, but it was not my cup of tea.

sample_reviews.review_text: One of the best books I've read. I was completely hooked and couldn't stop thinking about the plot when I had to put it down.

I was so keen to read this..but found it an enormous let down. Kind of clever, but in a self-conscious and showy off kind of way. Kind of unpredictable but in a kind of predictable way because of the alternating narrative viewpoints. Characterisation is unconvincing. Awful Amy is odious and nasty Nick is a good pupil. Desi and the supporting cast are transparent and insubstantial. Little literary merit and even less narrative tension. But... Couldn't give up on it!
What was with the last quarter of that book?

This was an interesting psychological thriller, more psychological than thriller. Nick and Amy are a typical American couple; in their late 30s, married, celebrating their 5th wedding anniversary, recently lost their jobs to the recession, and moving away from their adult home and closer to Nick's childhood home to care for his aging parents. It would seem they are average in every way. But when Amy disappears, the cops begin digging below the surface, and each piece that is revealed paints a different picture of their marriage. 
 Gillian Flynn has created a unique story, with characters that are incredibly different and... psychotic. I recommend this book for anyone who likes a good character study.
Liked it. Had some memorable quotes throughout. Interested in the film version and how they are going to change the ending
It's a sneaky page-turner, and now I wonder why did I let it steal any of my time.

This book was brilliantly written. It probably deserves a 5 star review. But it won't get one. Why? Because fuck Amy. And Gillian... well you're on my list with George R.R. Martin, Nicholas Sparks, and Karin Slaughter for robbing me of my happy endings. Hell I'll just take a satisfying ending. So one star is all you get from me.

Great twist in the middle - and the twists keep coming! Once you get through the first half, it's a thrill ride! 
 My one criticism is that the author seemed to only have one voice for her characters, she sounded like a woman trying to see things from a man's point of view. Overall great read though!

Sometimes there are times where I wish I could quit a book half way through, and not finish the rest. However, when you're already half way through the book you want to finish reading it and see what the ending is like. With Gone Girl, I wish I quit the book for good. I am going to try and write up this review because I haven't read a book in a long time where it just makes me so mad. 
 Gone Girl is a story of Nick Dunne whose wife goes missing on their 5th wedding anniversary. It was a who did it type of novel, and what made it different is that you saw the events from his point of view and you were able to read journal entries from Amy's point of view leading up to her disappearance. 
 The first half of this book was great. It kept me on my toes, and I want to read more. I wanted to find out what was going to happen to Nick. Will Amy ever be found? Nick became their first suspect. I can see where people were finding this sexist, but in a way it was like all other major crime stories. It goes to the person you think is the most accountable. Nick had holes in his story from the start, and he was hiding things from the police. It's no wonder they suspected him. I first started rolling my eyes when the affair was announced. How predictable. Then, once we found out that Amy's personality was just crazy is when I really started getting mad. I don't know why it just infuriated me. This also goes with Nick. He was starting to get on my wrong side. 
 The book continues on. You find out about Amy's past, and how she has framed people before. Nick tries to use it against her. The only sum what redeemable thing was Tanner and his wife. The rest just I can't even. 
 I stopped reading the book fully at about 88% left in the book where the rest of it I just scanned. I couldn't handle it any more. The sad thing was I have read more enjoyable young adult fiction books then this book. The ending made me even madder. You sit there and want to frame your wife, your wife uses you for a pregnancy so you are trapped, and yet you stay with her?! Worst ending in a novel since Jacob and Bella's baby became soul mates in Twilight. I apologize now for those that I recommended this book originally too in the beginning. The first half was great, but ugh.
I'm torn on what to rate this, I really loved it as I was reading, total page turner, but the ending fell so flat, all that building and then nothing. So liked the book, hated the ending.

This was a pretty cool book. As you get into it, you see that something is amiss with the narration provided by one of the characters. Then, as it goes along you see why, and the gradual horror of the situation is revealed. More literary in it's presentation than most, I thought this was a good, unique thriller/mystery. Kind of reminded my of Donna Tart's The Secret History. 
 Read it.

well...it was not as compelling a story as the hype had suggested and i will admit i did a bit of skimming in certain sections. not large chunks, at all, but i would notice myself doing it. like, sort-of tuning out when someone, in real life is going blah blah blah... 
 i knew going into the story there was a twist. i didn't know what the specific twist was. but i figured it out long before it was revealed and then i kept thinking -- maybe that's not the twist? so was waiting for something else to happen. 
 the book is okay. fine, even. it was a quick read and an interesting premise with some moments that were totally fascinating - the stagnation of a marriage and the crazy in people's heads. but it wasn't as dark and twisty as i thought it was going to be.

Amy and Nick...what do I say... 
 Amy loves to control everything and everyone around her. She loves Nick to death, literally. This book started off being funny and I could understand where she was coming from when she discovers Nick's secret. 
 But her level of deceit was cruel and unbelievable. She turned Nick unto his father.

This book didn't change my life or anything, but it did make me stay up late two nights in a row. 
 *yawn*

I liked it. I did. 
 I don't read a lot of contemporary fiction, but sometimes I just want to see what all the buzz is about. B&N is really pushing this book, and several of my GR friends have read it and liked it, so I jumped in. 
 This book is a good illustration of why I don't read a lot of contemporary fiction. 
 It's about (seemingly) normal, everyday people living their normal, everyday lives, when suddenly, the wife goes missing. It's a little bit mysterious, it makes you question your initial assumptions. I liked that about it. I can see why it's getting good reviews. It's twisty and fast-paced and hard to put down. 
 But. 
 There could be an opening here for something heroic, or something miraculous... an opportunity for someone to be beautifully honest, or understanding, or to deal with grief in a really constructive way. But there's none of that here. 
 I don't really like these characters so much. They are young, attractive, and clever. Boy, are they clever. But I don't want to know them. They're not admirable. They use vulgar language, and behave badly. Nobody in this book is admirable. Nobody has a lesson to teach, unless you are interested in a lesson in deceit and trickery. The smallness of these characters, their lack of contribution to the benefit of society or its ideals - that's not who I want to read about. It is real, it is current, it is page-turning and engaging, but ultimately, it is disappointing. Not my favorite kind of fiction. 
 Give me a book about a soul in search of God. Give me the victims of the Holocaust, heroically enduring their fate while holding on to their faith. Give me hard-working pioneers enduring the harshness of the West and forging a nation, or adventurers on a quest to defeat dragons, or the stories of important people from history, or a charming love story. Reveal to me some beautiful hidden truth about contemporary society. Show me teenagers who love and support one another against all odds. I'll even take war-mongering barbarians ahead of contemporary smallness. It's time for me to read some Tolkien, or some Austen, or some Marchetta, or some Russell. Something with hope for humanity... 
 So, it's good. It is.

It is a page turner that can suck you in, I'll give it that, in the same way you can get sucked in to watching Jersey Shore. Lowest Common Denominator entertainment made even worse because the author clearly finds herself very clever.

This book is hideously awful. Psychotic people with psychotic lives doing psychotic things. And no one killed that demented freak in the end. What the hell?! I don't get the appeal of this book. Can someone please explain it to me?

There's a point in Gillian Flynn's Gone Girl where your whole body squirms. It's an involuntary movement that reacts to the intense depth that Flynn reaches into vanquished lives and psychological gamesmanship. She nails destruction onto the headstone of marriage so forcefully you won't want your partner to read this book. At least not in the same bed you're sleeping in. 
 I haven't read a book exposing such twisted human psyches since vintage Stephen King from The Stand, It, Misery era. Like King, who could introduce subtle terror that weeps into your core (not the George Romero branch of terror that relies on splintered doors and grasping hands) Flynn takes you on journey of a zero sum game of what's not. This is marriage at its vilest, thriller at its best. 
 The husband and wife team of Nick and Amy Dunne are about to celebrate their fifth wedding anniversary. But things go awry. The wife goes missing, the husband is the main murder suspect and public opinion weighs in like a bludgeon. But this is less about a great mystery finely played out then about a stunning examination of the slow twist of faded expectations. 
 This is the kind of psychological mystery that Margaret Millar was so good at. Millar's Beast In View is a great example of protagonists losing touch and spiraling off to hunt down and kill reality. Millar was insightful and fair to her characters and much like Flynn you believe in the justice played out until justice becomes just a little too close to the crazy bone.

A psychological thriller with one-dimensional characters. Ditto the main characters, except you can add that they are dull, unexceptional and unsympathetic. We are repeatedly told how brilliant the main character, Amy, is, but I didn't get a real sense of that. For me, the entire first 1/3 of the book was the excruciatingly boring and tedious details of a cardboard couple's marriage. I continued reading and finished the book only because I thought it had to get better, since the book was a best seller. The author explains what is going on in the second 1/3 of the book, but to me the characters still had no depth to them so it was difficult to care. The last 1/3 of the book tied the loose ends up and brought a resolution, of some sort, but seemed far-fetched and too unrealistic and unbelievable to me. And the victim of the story had become almost as repugnant as the victimizer, so I felt no empathy. Possibly I expected too much from the book. It would make an ok vacation read. It's just not anything to reread.

I tried to like this one; I really did. And I know I probably gave up on it too soon but I just can't get past the stereotypical "chick-lit" first five percent of the book. The girl isn't even gone yet, and I have to discard the book. Life is too short to be as irritated by a book as I am by this one so far...
Again, Flynn puts out a novel that is absolutely insane and yet I cannot put it down. I really liked it more than three stars, but the part of my brain that eats it vegetables cannot give it four.

Blech. Contrived, kind of blindly flailing about for anything lurid that will increase shock-value without actually exploring or doing anything of substance. It was just .... too ... much? I kept hoping Flynn was building characters and plot to be revealed as more subtle and complex than on first blush, but no. But I read the whole thing, so I guess that's something.
Couldn't put it down! Addictive story.

Hilarious! Insane! The brilliant start to Part 2 totally won me over to the side of a villain who is dangerous and delusional but with so much wit that you worry when said villain appears to be in peril. Yes, divorce would have been cleaner but not so manipulatively entertaining.
What a bizarre dark and twisted story. A bit too screwed up for my liking.
Wound up feeling like I had been sold a false bill of goods. Ending is preposterous--there's no other word for it.
I'm thouroughly mind-fucked. Holy shit. I did NOT expect any of that.

Well chapter 1 was great. Really grabbed my attention. Think I am going to enjoy this 
 But then I read the rest of it... A sick book about sick people... Not believable really as even the most astute criminal leaves some clues behind.. And the police are really not that stupid! Really ended up hating the pair of them and feeling sorry for their eventual child. I won't be reading any more from this author.

If Mr. and Mrs. Smith had been directed by Afred Hitchocock, with Steig Larsson on for technical supervision, you'd get this. Sometimes surprising, some times far-fetched. I enjoyed the satire of marriage, feminism, and misogyny through a mystery, even if the result was all kinds of horrifying.

This book wrapped itself around me for two days, and after I finished it, I felt a bit disoriented, like I'd woken from a lucid dream. I recommend it to anyone trying to write suspense; it should be on a suspense writing class's reading list. Also recommend to anyone who wants to get lost in a mysterious, often disturbing story.

I must admit I hated reading this. The book is basically a marriage that is a totally disaster. Although there were some fantastic twists, the story just ended with a big disaster of a marriage than it started. This guy would be a great writer for criminal minds, but the beauty of that show is that the story only lasts an hour. The story was creative, but UGH too depressing

I can't rate this novel yet because I'm in the midst of reading it; however, after the first 120 pages, I am hooked! I love the different points of view, the turns. I know it can only get better from here and I have 300+ pages to go!

I'm not a fan of this book. I read it for my book club, and finished it for my book club. If not for that, it would have been a book I stopped reading after the first couple of chapters. I just could not get into it. I tried, but it took me weeks to get through it. Then when I finally get through it, I did not like the ending. When I walked away from this book it left me feeling nothing but frustration that I spent all that time on it. This book was just not for me.

B.O.R.I.N.G !!! 
 Maybe i just watch the movie instead

I enjoy Gillian Flynn's books but this one was brilliant. An enjoyable roller coaster ride in this psychological thriller. She pulls you in by making you think everything is normal but it is not. The book was fill with twists, new information and you simply have to keep reading. Thrillers aren't my favorite genre but I do like to read a couple a year. 
 This is a book about a marriage and that is about all I will say because the not knowing what is next is the best part. Enjoy.

Well, this book will take you on a ride. The writing is cleaver and you will easily get pulled into this story and the minds of these characters. If you are looking for a happy ending, this is not the book for you.

This book is a thriller, one that gets fairly high ratings from what I'd heard before making the mistake of picking this up. I've just come off forcing myself to get to the end of this book and I am feeling a little bit emotional. Why? 
 Trigger warnings. Great big, fat trigger warnings. Wish someone had given those to me before I'd picked this book up. Here, let me offer the favour. 
 First of all, I've been struggling through this book since the revelation at the Part 2 mark. I thought the writing was really ace until then; it made me wonder whether Nick, the husband, had actually done the Whodunnit. And then there was the twist. Which was likewise amazing. Almost as amazing as Amazing Amy. And we got to get a really good look at Amy who was became a bit more complex than originally estimated. Okay, I thought, nothing wrong with a complex character. 
 And then it continued. Thriller isn't usually a big hit with me, but every so often I'll pick one up to expand the horizons. Boy, do they feel expanded. I've read books where a sociopath is one of the main characters before. I've also read books with very unlikeable mains. The one that always comes to mind when I think of this is the main character out of Philippa Gregory's Wideacre. I loved that book, and could even get past the horrid behaviour of the main character, because I could understand why they were doing what they were doing. 
 No such luck in this book. I just watched on in horror as Part 2 wound around to Part 3 and at around the point where I was reading about someone plan to make it look like they had been raped in order to get off a murder charge, I asked myself what I was doing. When that person started to explain--with threatening language, no less--why there was nothing wrong with what they had done, started gloating about it.... that's when I put the book away. Because no pay off is worth that.
What fresh nonsense is this?!

Loved the pacing, complicated characters, twists and turns. Definitely a page-turner. I've read complaints about the ending being unsatisfying but I have to say that I thought it was perfect. Will definitely be reading more from this author!
I couldn't put it down....
Loved this book. It was the complete "thing": mystery, thriller, drama, romance, and really just a terrifying story of a sociopath. But so excellent.

I admit that the plot of this book was excellent -- I knew who was telling the truth fairly early in the book, but I still wanted to find out how it all ended. And the ending was well done. 
 But, I found the language excessively crude. I read books with graphic violence, with sex scenes, with swearing. I don't have to approve of every word in a book to approve of the book. But these characters, who were not the type of people one would expect to be so vulgar, were just... filthy. I can't think of another word for it. I realize that their attitude toward sex was part of the characterization. But did EVERYONE in the book have to treat sex that way? Is that really the way the entire world views sex? It was a manipulative tool or a physical need or a form of abuse - for every character in the book, even the peripheral, so-called-good-guy characters. It got old. 
 I'm not sure who I'd recommend this book to -- a great plot, a great ending, but I wouldn't want to wade through the rest of it again. I feel like I need a shower.

I have been wanting to read this for a really long time....not my cup of tea. The story was brilliant. But the language and graphic explicitness made it hard to move on to the end....and the end was so disappointing..seriously, i read that whole thing for that ending? I don't know, i was just disappointed. Clearly not my kind of book.

I liked the parts about the recession. The ways in which the shift from digital to print has displaced so many people, including the men who used to create the blue books we used to take tests in. The ways that's made so many people angry and made so many of us vulnerable. 
 That's pretty much it. 
 But it's a lot, because I read this book a while ago and I'm still thinking about that part. 
 The rest, meh. I was interested in the wife's frustration with her disappointing husband. But then she turned out to be kind of an idiot, too. 
 So, scratch that. 
 While she was victimized (according to her) by her narcissistic parents as a child, she also has a ridiculous sense of entitlement and contributes nothing to the world; nor does she think she should. She blames everyone else. The husband is a loser, too. 
 Really, the only interesting people in the story are the Blue Book Boys, and we only meet them in passing. It IS sort of satisfying to watch the upper middle class destroy itself in this way, however. If that's her point, onward. 
 Meanwhile, Lauren Grodstein's Friend of the Family was more interesting, I thought.
Right now, I think that Gillian Flynn might be my favorite writer. So clever, so dark, so much fun to read.

Book lived up to its rave reviews & will be on my Ten Best Reads of 2013. Difficult to say too much about it, without spoilers. Suffice to say its a brillian exposition of the Revenge Plot, with skilful twists and turns. Another Highly Recommended.
Very enthralling! Couldn't put it down. The end surprised me and that's not easy to do. Steer clear if you don't like the f-word.
So, so, so good. Liked the writing. The story itself was not predictable. The characters were so intriguing. Hello crazy, unexpected twist.
review to come.
I don't often read current best sellers. That said, Gone Girl is definitely a page turner. Twists and turns abound. I did not see the ending coming!

reference_books.review_text:
See full review here: http://ilayreading.com/2016/04/26/sle... 
 There's no denying that Sylvain Neuvel is an excellent writer. The plot was well thought out, the omnipotent narrator was extremely strong and complicated. I did struggle, though, with the interview style. I was constantly having to go back and look to see who we were talking to, what the timeline was, where we were, etc. Files could skip 5 minutes, or 5 months.There were also a few things in the plot that left a few big confusing holes for me-things I cannot talk about without spoiling the story. It seems Neuvel is leaving a cliffhanger open for a sequel, but there's a hole the size of the Puerto Rico ocean trench that I'm staring into, and I'm drowning in it 
 I didn't hate the book. I'd go so far as to say I liked it. But I won't continue with the sequel if there is one to come. This just isn't a format that serves my taste.

reference_books.title: The Impossible Knife of Memory
reference_books.review_text:
I want to title this review: The Impossible Mediocrity of Mental Illness YA. For as complex and nuanced as mental illness is-you'd think that we would get more than just textbook representation in our stories. Unfortunately, time and time again, it's all I see. So rarely do I find a novel about mental illness that truly shows what it is like to be in the thick of it-instead the depiction is flat and gray. 
 PTSD is such an important subject, and finding good help for our soldiers is a crucial, difficult task. That is one thing about this book that I did agree with: how Halse Anderson wrote Andy's character refusing help or medication. His characterization wasn't incorrect, I think I just had a hard time with Hayley's narration of it. 
 Something else stuck out to me-Finn and Hayley were going through such a similar situation: they both had family members who were addicts. But instead of talking about it or having that bring them closer together, all they did was fight and scream at each other. Their whole relationship was a weird dynamic, but that really seemed off kilter. Also, it wasn't lost on me that Gracie continuously suspected Topher for cheating on her as a projection from her dad...though I think everyone else in the story missed that detail. Those sort of plot holes bug me. 
 But mostly, it's Hayley that bothers me. Her attitude is horrible, and she's an unreliable narrator of the worst kind. And maybe that's the problem. I don't mind unreliable narrators if there are ways to fill in the holes, but I felt like that knife just cut through the plot until I had an impossible amount of memory to fill. 
 Trigger warning: PTSD, Panic Attacks, Knives, Blood, Suicide Ideation/Thoughts/Planning, Drowning, drugs, alcoholism

reference_books.title: The Black Dahlia (L.A. Quartet, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I've been trying to read The Black Dahlia on my phone a chapter at a time and I have just not been having it. I finally gave up. Noir just isn't my genre, generally. It's dark and gritty and incredibly sexist. And it's always got this horrific voice to it. You know what I mean-it's always the SAME voice. Cocky-ass detective in a floppy fedora talking about some bird with the legs, trying to solve some murder on poor innocent females. 
 BD is the same exact voice, same exact theme, except it's true crime, not something made up. Two boxers-turned-cops in the 40s worked a horrific murder. I didn't get much further than that, mostly because of the voice. I just couldn't stand it. 
 So, nope for this one. At least I can mark it off on the Boxall's list. Making some progress with that!

 I'll be real honest with you. By page 13, I was absolutely sure that there was no CDF space military, and that this was just a government conspiracy to rid the country of the overpopulation of elderly people. I'm not sure if I have just been reading too many dystopian novels...or just living in a society where my social security benefits are disappearing. Either way, I think I'm jaded. 
 Also, I wasn't completely wrong. But I can't tell you any more without giving away spoilers. SO HA! You'll have to just read it and find out.

reference_books.title: Legend (Legend, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Can I tell you how weird it is to read a dystopia right now? WEIRD. We are basically living what used to be dystopian fiction, so to read it is very creepy. 
 Thankfully, Legend is still a ways off, and the world June and Day live in seems to have been created originally by natural disasters first, and horrible human government second. Our natural disasters are getting worse...but at least we haven't had a super volcano yet. Right? 
 I'm trying to find a silver lining here guys. I'm trying. 
 (Hopefully by the time I post this review there hasn't been a super volcano. You never know. Italy has had some pretty serious earthquakes lately, and there was one in New Zealand this week too.) 
 I'm scaring myself. What was I talking about? Oh, right. June and Day. 
 Real life nightmares aside, I can understand why this is so popular. It's young adult fiction for young adults. Sometimes, as an adult reader, I forget who the audience is supposed to be while I'm reading books like this--the writing seems juvenile--but this was written by a very young author for a young audience. And for that, it fits wonderfully. Are the characters the deepest I've ever read? No. Is the plot totally unique? No. But I was instantly wrapped up in June and Day's dual POV plot lines. I loved the idea that these kids were brilliant, and that they had such different life experiences. 
 This series goes back in my TBR jar so I can read the rest of the series. We can only hope our government looks a little less dystopian by the time I get around to finishing it. Fingers crossed (plus a whole lot of letter writing, calls, twitter rants, etc). 
 Update 2/10/2017--This has now been added to my shame list, and the rating has been changed to reflect that. A friend pointed out today that June is described as "She was either Native. Or Caucasian." That is unacceptable language. It is incredibly harmful. I have removed the other books from my TBR, and moved this to my DO NOT READ list.

book_a.user_review:
It's no surprise that Pride and Prejudice is an all-time favorite of mine. So many of us fell in love with Mr. Darcy at a young age, and we just never really let go of that crush. But I've had a hard time getting into some of Austen's other books. Emma I like, but everything will always fall short of P&P. 
 Sense and Sensibility probably would have been better titled as Nonsense and Secrets Destroy Your Life. 
 I. 
 Was. 
 So. 
 CONFUSED. 
 Everyone is love with the wrong person in this book, which seemed that it would have been solved simply if they would stop keeping secrets from everybody else. Oh, this person is engaged already to this person, and this person is engaged already to this person, but not really because no one knows it and they aren't ACTUALLY engaged, he just has a lock of her hair. 
 WHAT THE WHAT. 
 The only honest person in the whole freaking book is Colonel Brandon-who I might be even more in love with now than Mr. Darcy. If we all had a Colonel Brandon in our lives, we'd all be SO much better off. 
 Instead we all have Willoughbys and Wickhams. 
 By the end of this, I was skimming, so I took to Hulu to watch the 2008 version-and it made much more sense in movie format. Still, the only real result is that I fell even more in love with Colonel Brandon, and everyone else seemed much more the mess. Of course, in true Jane Austen fashion, it all turns right in the end, but goodness she does like to torture her lovers, doesn't she?

Sadly, this was not my favorite Austen book. (I haven't quite read them all yet, but my current favorite by far is the mature and insightful Persuasion, for what it's worth). That's not to say I disliked it outright--the author's wit sparkles here as ever, and there are plenty of laugh out loud moments, especially when society women imply the meanest insults through the most gracious of dialogue. But S&S didn't work so well for me in the story department. Unlike P&P, the eligible bachelors are all rather forgettable, and Marianne's perpetual histrionic fits left a juvenile aftertaste. And while the final plot twists are not quite M. Night Shyamalan worthy, they do come out of left field and stretched my credulity to the breaking point. Which is too bad, because as an older sibling myself, I identified with the responsible, non-risk-taking Elinor and was rather hoping Austen would squeeze a bit more agency out her by the end.

"Sense will always have attractions for me." 
 Reading a classic novel and a Jane Austen novel was a bit of a different experience. This is the second time I've read this book, (the first time time I read it was during my college year for my literature class and had to write a paper about it) Maybe that's why it took me almost three days to finish this. It was a a great read and an enjoyable one. It's an exuberant, well- written that gets the readers involved on a gut level. 
 Austen labels her the two central characters. The heroine (Elinor) is ruled by "sense"--she's the responsible one. Her sister (Marianne) is ruled by "sensibility" or emotion. It's the classic dichotomy between logic and passion. 
 Marianne and Elinor Dashwood are two sisters who couldn't be more different from one another. Elinor is sensible and reserved and she also does not believe in giving way to emotion, while her younger sister Marianne is passionate and spontaneous and believes that it's best to give way to emotion constantly. So it was no surprised how vocal Marianne was with her feelings towards the dashing John Willoughby. While Elinor kept quiet with her feelings towards Edward Ferrars. And when Marianne's relationship gone south, she was hurt and devastated and so was Elinor when she learned the truth with regards to Edward. But she didn't even try to show how hurt she was. She exerts herself to be strong, and act with dignity even at the expense of her own happiness. 
 I really really enjoyed it. It was nice to see how the two women approached romance and love differently. And it is Austen's ability to tap into human emotions that gives Sense and Sensibility its power. It may take a good many pages, but in the end the two women finally end up with the men they love. My favorite scene was at the very end, when Elinor finally bursts out with strong emotion for Edward, a few moments before he proposed to her. 
 Sense and Sensibility is undoubtedly one of Jane Austen's best works. And one of my favorite books of all time.

Bad girl. I didn't really finish this one. I went to see the play and since I knew the ending, I had no motivation to finish the book and became impatient with the way Austen writes. I know I am supposed to love this type of classic but I need to stop kidding myself--Austen's writing is just not "my thing." I am not sure why because I have read other books from this time period and have thoroughly enjoyed them, such as Jane Eyre.

Ah, how much I love the Austen world. Where only problem of a girl is dance at balls, sing, play music and find a rich husband! Sarcastic tone in Austen's writing really takes the story to another dimension. Loved it!

Definitely not my favourite JA. It is hard to warm up to Elinor, our heroine, because she seems very cold and reserved (she's not, but that's just the way she portrays herself). Her sister, Marianne, is the opposite, but likewise not easy to like because she is too over the top. And the hero, Edward, is weak and smarmy and spends too much time off the page, only existing in Elinor's thoughts.

Favorite quote ( I really don't plan to bother all my classmates with another review so) 
 Marianne: Always resignation and acceptance. Always prudence and honour and duty. Elinor, where is your heart? 
 Elinor Dashwood: What do you know of my heart? What do you know of anything but your own suffering. For weeks, Marianne, I've had this pressing on me without being at liberty to speak of it to a single creature. It was forced on me by the very person whose prior claims ruined all my hope. I have endured her exultations again and again whilst knowing myself to be divided from Edward forever. Believe me, Marianne, had I not been bound to silence I could have provided proof enough of a broken heart, even for you.

'Sense and Sensibility' is the Austen novel I liked the least. For quite a while I wasn't sure why I couldn't get into the story or connect with the characters. I believe the book was just not what I expected it to be. To be honest, there are some differences between this book and others I read by the author. I just didn't expect them to put me off like this. I later learned that this actually was her first published work - maybe this is one reason for the change. 
 The book follows the lives and love stories of the Dashwood sisters, Elinor and Marianne. When their father dies they have to leave their home as their brother inherits everything. As sad as it is, I really liked the beginning because reading about their family dynamics just was hilarious. Having said that I got bored shortly after because the usual 'let's-find-a-well-off-man' dance started. I'm not really interested in this part and although I know that it'll always play a bigger role in Austen's stories it never annoyed me that much in the past. 
 My biggest problem with the book was the main characters. For quite a while I tried to understand if the story centered on Marianne or Elinor. I missed having a strong and interesting main character as Austen presented in other books. Throughout the book, I stayed distant to the storyline and the characters which is why the ending didn't surprise me or offer any kind of consolation. I was not impressed with the ending (especially Marianne's part) and there was a feeling of 'it's-finally-over'. 
 However, I still liked some parts of the book a lot (talking about Fanny here) and while others bored me they were still easy to read and fit whatever was my expectation. In the end, a solid two star rating makes sense and I hope that I can enjoy the next book more.

Full review 
 Why, you ask, did it take me nearly a month to read the mere 266 pages of Sense and Sensibility? The full explanation is lengthy and will be the focus of the paragraphs that follow, but as for the cliff's notes version: I'm really not a fan of Austen. Context: I enjoyed certain aspects of Pride and Prejudice, namely the underlying themes of reading/misreading and the meta elements they invoke, but overall I was left with a rather bland impression. It all seemed a tad trite and banal, and while the writing is clear, concise, and often witty, I found the experience somewhat lacking. As a student of the postmodern, Victorian (and pre-Victorian) literature can only really fascinate me via defamiliarization and Austen is nothing if not a thoroughly familiar writer, at least in my limited experience with her work. So going into reading Sense and Sensibility, I admit a bias. However, failing fascination, I'm always happy to be entertained and diverted. Not the case here, unfortunately. 
 Sense and Sensibility was Austen's first published work, and I wager that most readers would be able to discern this without much prior knowledge; it's not as polished as Pride and Prejudice and certainly doesn't approach some of the complexities of Persuasion. It's a simple story; the reader follows the elder Dashwood sisters, Elinor and Marianne, and the bourgeois lifestyle of late eighteenth century England, in which marriage is the primary concern for all socially mobile young ladies. Elinor stoically loves Edward Ferrars (a more animated character when portrayed by Hugh Grant in the 1995 British film than in the actual text) and Marianne is involved in a passionate and tempestuous love triangle with John Willoughby (a somewhat less reprehensible version of Wickham from Pride and Prejudice) and Colonel Brandon (the quintessential knight in shining armor trope, cleverly subverted through Willoughby's over the top introduction to Marianne). Standard interpretation of the title assigns sense to Elinor, the rational and pragmatic sister, and sensibility to Marianne, the emotional and spirited one. 
 Of course, the standard interpretation is generally the simplified interpretation, and while there's no doubt that Elinor and Marianne act as polarizing forces throughout the novel, the line of demarcation isn't so absolute. Marianne may be labelled as the default passionate diva, but this does not necessarily condemn Elinor to an emotionless life of Vulcan logic; she feels, but is less inclined to overt displays. Thus, the movement of the novel is directed at finding some balance of the two, since both extremities are depicted as emotionally unhealthy, and, in Marianne's case, ultimately physically unhealthy as well. The sisters must reconcile this divergence in order to grow and achieve the neat, Austenian happily-ever-after. It is a novel that requires the conceit of in-depth character studies in order to depict growth, and I suppose this is the first issue I have with Sense and Sensibility - Elinor and Marianne feel very static until just prior to the swift happy ending, during which a degree of psychological reconciliation is jarringly applied. There is character change, but it's sudden and seems born of authorial intervention and not realism. 
 For me, this is forgivable; deus ex machina plot devices and conclusions (and in this case, character growth that facilitates a satisfying conclusion) are so frequent in narrative that I generally only begrudge the most egregious examples. What dooms my enjoyment of the novel is Marianne. This is a character I cannot stand, one of the most unlikeable twats I have ever had the displeasure of reading. Quick explanation: she's whiny, childish, idealistic to a fault, self-absorbed to the point of sociopathy, manic, and narcissistic. Moreover, through frequently referencing Marianne's preference for epic romance literature and poetry, Austen inadvertently portrays Marianne as thoroughly lacking on this grand scale; she's a poor man's Criseyde . Buckle up folks, the long explanation is called the long explanation for a reason. First, before I continue, let me state a few things. 1) Certain genres of fiction (satire, black comedies, absurdist, pulp, and speculative fiction, for instance) are very apt to present the reader with an unlikeable, sometimes even villainous, protagonist. Think Vanity Fair, A Clockwork Orange, and The Picture of Dorian Gray. 2) Such books generally succeed only if that unlikeable protagonist was constructed for a specific, well-executed reason (to reform, to satirize, to condemn, to name only a few possibilities), because only the satisfaction produced as a result of this reason would counteract the reader's general disdain for the protagonist. 3) Thus, books that seek primarily to entertain rarely have unlikeable protagonists since this accomplishes no purpose other than to alienate some subset of readers (this paradigm does not account for incompetent writers who can't craft characters, and obviously personal taste factors hugely in what is deemed likeable/unlikeable). 
 Granted, Sense and Sensibility has some mildly satirical elements, particularly in the characters of Fanny and Lucy, but overall Austen's style is better characterized as deadpan with an added bit of occasional snark. Regardless of tone, I can say for certain that Marianne is not a satirical character, and thus I can only conclude she's purposelessly unlikeable; she does not realistically develop, she does not satirize, and I don't believe that we readers are meant to condemn her as a foil for Elinor. Her terrible attitude serves no reason other than to make me slam the novel down in anger! 
 While Marianne does occupy far too much of the novel for me to even remotely enjoy it, Elinor's character does partially alleviate some of my hatred. I appreciate that she's not an archetypal heroine in that she has priorities that don't involve Edward; her entire being doesn't revolve totally around some guy, and while this isn't a significant leap forward in terms of early nineteenth century literature (one doesn't have to look past the fourteenth century to find the Wife of Bathe), at the very least she's a nice break from Marianne's wailing. 
 I'm sure most readers are familiar with the Bechdel Test for movies. For the uninitiated, it's a simple measure of a movie's female presence consisting of three criteria: 1) The movie has at least two named women in it. 2) These women talk to each other. 3) These women talk to each other about something besides a man. Applying a twentieth century test to Sense and Sensibility is totally nonsensical of course, and in any case it passes soundly, but I reference it here for some context, given that Sense and Sensibility's two female protagonists are utterly obsessed with men. Marriage dominates the lives of these two women and consequently their sisterly relationship, and while conversation is certainly had on other topics, romance is still dominant. Elinor may appear somewhat more independent, but thanks to Austen's always efficient third-person omniscient narrator, the reader is aware that she is merely obsessed quietly, whereas Marianne is obsessed outwardly. 
 If Sense and Sensibility were a satire, this would be praiseworthy. Look at the lives of these oppressed women! Look at how their only chance in life is marrying well! Look at how this consumes them! Look at how they feebly try to balance this practicality with the prospect of marrying for love and happiness! But Austen is no satirist; she's very sincere. And this is why I must finally conclude in emphasis of the importance of interesting characters. It's a traditional narrative, one that was written long before Austen and thousands of times since, no defamiliarization or baring the device in sight. At a base level, this genre of fiction is diversionary entertainment, and for me, Sense and Sensibility did not succeed even in this because of Marianne. I was not diverted. I was bothered.

I CAN FINALLY MOVE ON TO ANOTHER BOOK 
 Update: sorry to Jane Austen fans, I didn't hate it. Just been wanting to read a new book because this one took me so long to finish. Not because I hated it, I always have a hard time reading classics.

Okay, so I am a sucker for Jane Austen, but truly, her books are fabulous. In fact, they make me a little bit giddy just even thinking about them. In my life of toddlers and babies and husbands, and laundry, and dishes, and...I need a little bit of Jane to keep me sane. Sense and Sensibility has my second favorite character of all time, next to Mr. Darcy of course, Colonel Brandon. Oh how he makes me happy. This book is another of Jane's that I have read on numerous occasions.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Enjoyable book, although I was a bit unimpressed with who Elinor ended up with! I personally would have liked to see her with Brandon, he was the better man. I suppose that's the whole point of it though... that sense and sensibility is more realistic and prudent than a wild fantasy.
I read this in a phase of trying to pick off classics so that I knew what they were about. I can see why they were novel, but it wasn't something I'd choose to read.

After reading everything Austen for a seminar this semester, I found S&S to be my favorite. Hands down. Forever and always. It is absolutely amazing. 
 I loved Elinor and Marianne and the growth they go through, and I really enjoyed all their romantic mishaps along the way. It always amazes me that Austen can write relationships that are still relevant today. Who hasn't fallen for a guy who is a complete jerk and leads a girl on for his own amusement? Or who hasn't fallen for a guy because they believe him to feel as much as they do? These are common relationship blunders and Austen shows they've been happening for nearly 200 years. 
 I also love when Austen writes dialogue that shows the reader what is going on instead of just telling them, which I felt is what she did the majority of the way through Mansfield Park. She writes such clever conversations and witty jabs. I could read dialogue by her for days, especially when it's Marianne, who practically has no filter. 
 It was the first of her novels that I found I didn't want to put down. And I am already anxious to read it again.

I wasn't exactly thrilled with this book, but it was better than I first expected. Unfortunately Sense and Sensibility seems lik Pride and Prejudice an Emma, in the fact that you have beautiful girls/women, who wish to marry or relations wish them to marry, but they have little to recommend them and small, if any, dowries. I Emma, you have poor Harriet, who has no living relation and whose father was a merchant. I Pride and Prejudice, ou have the Bennet sisters who are very beautiful, but poor and have a rather obtuse family, including a cousin who will swoop in upon their father's death to claim their own possessions. I Sense and Sensibility, you have the Miss Dashwoods who are very pretty, well liked, well-mannered (even if Marianne is a bit of a recluse), and who have been wiped off the slate by their half-brother and his wife. How unfortunate. 
 There was one thing that made me like this story, however, and that was a connection with the main character, Elinor. I feel like there is a lot of myself in Elinor, or rather Elinor is in me (whichever way you prefer to look at it). She is extremely kind and feels obligated to be kind and patient, often over-exerting herself and going out of her way to make people feel appreciated. She easily feels guilt and is often hurt by Marianne's dislike of and impatience with others. Elinor also bears things very well, often concealing her true emotions. She feels for everybody, including herself, but she is very adept at putting others before herself (I'm not saying this is a good thing). She bears her yoke in life with fortitude, courage, and generosity and is thankful for what she has, rather than what she has lost. 
 I believe Miss Austen did very well in making Elinor her main character rather than Marianne. If that had been the case, I would have dropped the book within the first one hundred pages and never picked it up again. Marianne is a selfish, melodramatic brat who I believe deserves the lot she received from Willoughby (though he is no better, really) and does not deserve such a good man as the Colonel Brandon.

Suprisingly, I didn't like this book. I didn't mind it for the first bit, but the last twenty or so pages totally destroyed it for me. You can tell it's Austen's first book. It doesn't have the depth of P&P or even Emma, and unlike them, it comes off as a stright up example of chick lit. Both the main characters are annoying as heck, way too consending and ready to condem people at a drop of that hat. They're self obessessed and seem to think they're the best ever (they're certainly not). (some spoilers) Take Lucy for example. Up until the last two chapters (before they villianized her out of nowhere)she hadn't done a thing to actually earn Elinor & Marianne's hate- yes, she was with Edward, but it's not like she knew that Elinor was in love with him (and he was the one keeping secrets). She didn't do anything besides be an actual friend, and Elinor A. thinks the worst of her, B. never gives her a chance and C. pretends to be her friend in order to get information. 
 And while they villianized Lucy they went and semi-redeemed Willoughby. He was a jerk who dropped Marianne because he wanted to be rich, and now he's unhappy and I'm supposed to feel sorry for him? Yeah. No. You made your choice buddy, so suck it up.

It's weird; I miss the sea monsters, but I also find myself staying up way too late, blowing past chapter stops, basically inhaling this book as fast as possible. Tough to review a book that has been out for over 200 years. No doubt there are literally thousands of reviews out there, most of which will be better than mine simply because I have a favorite Jane Austin book, Pride and Prejudice, which will never be topped by any of her other works in my opinion. 
 However, this book does leave you thinking alot about love and passion and reason and the inter-relationship between the three. Which is what makes the title Sense and Sensibility so fitting for the book. 
 If you haven't read Victorian period English writings, the style will be a bit difficult for readers, especially since Austin was a female writer writing in a man's world and had ALOT of dry humor and tongue-in-cheek quips that if you are unfamiliar with the culture of the time, may be hard to pick up on. 
 I personally really like the book, but 4 stars is all I am giving it.

At the risk of being considered blasphemous by my many Austen-loving friends, I must say: I didn't like this novel. Unlike P & P, I had trouble finishing this one. It took me over two weeks, and I finished a few other books in the interim. 
 There are two main reasons for my dislike: the writing style and the characters. The writing style reflects its time, of course, but even so, I had to wade through some convoluted sentences, sometimes reading them four or five times and parsing clauses to get at the meaning. This tendency towards complicated and often incomprehensible self-expression was especially chafing in dialog. Did people really talk like that 200 years ago? 
 The characters were even worse. There were very few I liked in the entire book, and all of the likable ones played second fiddle. 
 Marianne, one of the protagonists, was rude and self-absorbed, a typical egotistic teenager throughout the story without even one redeeming quality. For her, anyone over twenty seems only one step from absolute decrepitude. Everyone around her is inferior, coarse, unfeeling, or unforgivably old. Nobody could understand her suffering. Everybody is vulgar. She is so tactless herself, so uncivil to everyone, so blind to everyone else's problems, she made me want to slap her silly face. 
 Elinor is much more gracious and accepting on the surface, but deep inside, she is even snobbier than her younger sister. She must have true friends stashed somewhere, but of the people she socializes with in the novel, everyone is beneath her, at least every female: ignorant, uneducated, too loud, less intelligent, not refined enough, etc. The only ones she genuinely respects are Edward and Colonel Brandon, both males. 
 Edward, Elinor's love interest, seems a nice guy, but he is not given much page space. We mostly see him through Elinor's eyes. Colonel Brandon talks a bit more, is given a bit more characterization, but with him I have a bone to pick. He is twice Marianne's age, and she hardly considers him male. He is an old geezer for her, somewhere on the level of her grandfather. How could he possibly love her? They don't converse. They don't have anything in common. 
 He seems a sensible man, but his pull towards Marianne is obviously lust. He wants the fresh and pretty girl for himself and he gets her in the end, but who is talking about love? The guy wants to have his hands on her young skin and his dick inside her (pardon my crudity), but his persistent attraction to her seems almost indecent from my 21st century perspective. 
 The two most interesting personages in the novel are Lucy Steele, the delightfully manipulative and utterly bitchy villainess without a shred of conscience, and Mrs. Jennings, a kind woman who despite her kindness doesn't command any deference from either Elinor or Marianne. Fortunately, she is pictured as having thick skin, so she doesn't feel their hardly veiled scorn. Or does she? 
 And then there is Willoughby, a totally repulsive human being. He even tries to explain and justify his beastly behavior in the end, and both Elinor and Marianne seem on the way to absolve his sins. They are ready to take his sop story at its face value and forgive his treachery and duplicity, but they wouldn't forgive the well-intentioned foolishness of Mrs. Jennings? Something was wrong there. 
 In the back blurb, the book is called "comedy of manners" but it didn't seem like comedy to me. It wasn't funny. It was dated (of course) and it presents all its characters in a very unflattering way. I didn't care about any of them. 
 I'm set on reading or re-reading all Austen's novels (I have already read P & P a couple months ago) and I hope the others will be better.
Good but a tad hard to read as is all Jane Austin novels.
