 I don't have to write about this book but that it is about "Sense and Sensibility". It is a nice book. However, I think that I saw much of the story in many romantic and drama movies.

I enjoyed Pride and Predjudice so much I decided to read something else of Jane Austen. I enjoyed the book right away. I am reminded when I read her books of how unfair her times were. Money seemed to be the driving force behind most marriage choices. Love was important to some, but money seemed to be more important. There were so many characters in this book it seemed a bit difficult to follow and keep everyone straight.

I felt like Sense and Sensibility ended extremely abruptly, and without the painful detail that was otherwise abundant in the book. I also felt like I was reading a different authors version of Pride and Prejudice... two sisters, one more opinionated (although in this book that meant more frivolous), both love struck, a "villain" of a man who one of the sisters falls for but then gets heartbroken (whose name even begins with W), snotty in-laws, a family scandal, and everyone ending with the right man in the end. 
 This is a simple story arch, and makes sense to duplicate, but not so obviously, and by the same author! I enjoyed the book, but could not fully take in the enjoyment without reservations without thinking about the similarities between it and P&P. I know this book was written before P&P, so technically I should be complaining the other way around, but I can't help the timing of which book I read when. 
 The only real difference I saw in S&S was the relationship between the girls and their mother. I appreciated the love they had for their mother, although Austin still gave her some of the ridiculousness she offered Mrs. Bennett. 
 All in all I liked this story, just as I did P&P, but I thought it was more a retelling than anything and I was expecting to read something more.

When I read read Austen, Persuasion was my favorite. Rereading her novels 20 years later I was surprised by how much I loved Pride & Prejudice. I couldn't put it down and read in giant gulps. So I had high hopes for Sense & Sensibility . . . but I didn't care for it nearly as much. I found it easy to put down and I didn't connect with any of the characters. It was Austen's first novel, and as an initial effort it is of course quite good, but I hope I enjoy the others more upon rereading than I did this one. (I didn't remember the plot of this novel at all, and indeed, until the end, I thought Elinor was meant to end up with a different husband altogether. Oops.) 
 I am rereading Jane Austen's novels as part of the Jane Austen Project, where bestselling authors of today are rewriting Austen's stories. Next up: Joanna Trollope's take on Sense & Sensibility. 
 https://www.waterstones.com/booklist/...
Story is extremely similar to Pride and Prejudice, but much weaker. I didn't care at all about any of the characters or their predicaments.

I will probably not reread this one and obsess over it the way I did "Pride and Prejudice." I enjoyed reading this book, for some reason I would have liked to have read it from Marianne's perspective and see the full of her courtship with Colonal Brandon.
Jane Austen's classic is a favorite of mine. Love the movie and have read the book a couple times.

Wow, well this was a monster I have been for the longest time putting off/avoiding and now that I have finally finished this book all I can say is eh? I know this is Jane Austen's first novel, but if she didn't write Pride & Prejudice everybody would have said she ripped it off (never mind that this book came out first) and in a way she DID rip off herself. 
 Male love interest is wealthy/but can't (for whatever reason) be in charge of his own life 
 Asshole second m/love interest whose name starts with a "W" 
 Other women who get in the way 
 Misunderstandings that otherwise would stall the plot 
 Chapters that over explain what was said already 
 Happy ending 
 I say this fully liking P&P, clearly when Ms. Austen got most of the kinks out. Not to even go into that deus ex machina ending real convenient that Lucy just suddenly didn't want anything to do with Edward, and went with his brother Robert after chapters of her going on about how much she loved him! I mean I know Jane Austen wanted her characters to have happy lives but damn, slapping an ending together where Colonel Brandon (who was almost a minor character) and just throwing he together with Marianne because everybody else wanted her to be with him even though she didn't give two shits about him.... I'll stop.. 
 god, don't even get me started on the unhealthy relationship between Edward and Elinor. I honestly don't get his appeal, he straight up lies to her and she rewards him with her hand in marriage.. WHAT???? 
 Well I didn't really care for the book, I think it was the weakest of Austen's novels but as a first novel its not god awful (there's so much worse out there that's for sure) but it she definitively improved with time, I don't consider myself a Austen-nut (or whatever they call themselves) but I do think she was a good writer and one mediocre book doesn't mean one should never read from an author again, give at least two books.

Ok, I'm not sure if this book really deserves one star, it deserves 0. I hate this book. This is not a romance novel, this is a soap opera. Seriously. I am so angry for having read this book. It took me ages, reading every page has been a torture. I just hate it.
This book was totally lost on me! I picked up an edition by Vivo Books, the only thing I liked about this book was the pretty cover!

book_b.title: The Slow Regard of Silent Things (The Kingkiller Chronicle #2.5)
book_b.user_review:
I don't often give 5 stars to a book, even though I love many. So rarely do I call a story perfect. This is a perfect story. Now, it does help to be familiar with the Kingkiller world in advance. Things do fit better that way. But, even without it, I think people will enjoy this. They don't HAVE to know who "he" is to feel the wonderful sense of anticipation that is coming. The naming is in the story, but not in such a way that they will be confused, because Auri is so different from the other Chronicle characters. 
 Guys, read this novella. It is simple, it is sweet. Auri is one of the loveliest characters I have ever read. I want to read it again already. 
 To see my full review, go to https://ilayreading.wordpress.com/201...

sample_reviews.review_text: I love Rothfuss' other two Kingkiller books, but this one? No me gusta. I appreciate the reviewer who wrote "Rothfuss's new novella, 'Things Are Picked Up And Then Set Down Elsewhere' certainly lives up to its title." I get that words are important and all that and that Auri will probably prove to be an important character somewhere in the series but *YAWN* - this type of story is clearly not for me.

As my friend Luke said, you have to be in the right mood for this story. 
 There is no action, just a discovery of silent things. Ari personifies everything, and her keen insight into normal objects is fun to read. She is set on following the way of things, which makes her abnormal quirks into admirable character traits. Interesting things happen, though none of it is out of the ordinary. I guess that is the draw of this story, though. 
 And at least we saw nothing of Kvothe or his promiscuous ways.

So . . . this is disappointing. It's just not any good. I gave it 58 pages, and just gave up. We get it. Auri is insane. And she anthropomorphizes everything. And it's quickly tedious AF. Really Tedious. Not cute. Not endearing. Tedious. Skip this, and you missing nothing of the wonderful Kingkiller series. Really. Save the $19!

The author warns both before and after this story that you might not like it. I did like it. This one contains only one character, Auri. I have read too many books since I finished his last novel to remember Auri or the world in which she resides. His most recent story about the boy who provides answers for a fee also concerned one character, but at least he interacted with others. 
 Auri seems to have a bit of OCD, and subscribes to something like feng shui. She attributes emotions and characteristics to objects. She also senses things such as "this will be a making day," and "HE is coming in seven days." Auri fancies herself a caretaker, fixing leaky pipes and ensuring that the mirror is happy by putting it facing the window. She also conducts herself correctly at all times even though no one is observing. 
 The author wields words as a painter would, and creates something here poetic and lyrical. He uses archaic and obscure words I often had to look up. My only tiny complaint was that he used a couple words too many times: sweet and maybe grin. 
 In the end notes, the author states that there is no plot and very little action. I disagree. Auri is constantly busy, and the overall theme is preparing for a special visitor.
Just wasn't for me.

I count myself among the few that enjoyed this book. This story is not for everyone. It doesn't do things that most stories do. But what it does, it does brilliantly. The Slow Regard of Silent Things is a sweet, heartsick and all-too brief glimpse into the Underthing and the sweet, broken little girl who dwells there. If you're looking for more Kvothe, look elsewhere. Reread Rothfuss's novels. But if you love Auri, if you've ever wanted to play "A Gift of Three Things", if you've ever examined a thing for its true essence, pay Auri a visit. Savor this book. See the world of Temerant and the world of storytelling a little differently.

Literary fiction at it's best. 
 Pretentious, incoherent, and pointless.

Touching, sweet and sad, The Slow Regard of Silent Things is really a gift for fans of Rothfuss' KingKiller Chronicles. Auri was without a doubt one of my favorite characters in the series and to spend this time with her in the Underthing was a complete treat. Sparse, intimate and without a speck of dialogue we follow Auri through her world while she waits the seven days for "him" to arrive. Like Auri, Rothfuss is careful with his word choice, stepping between moments much like Auri walks in the footsteps of other people. Quiet in its telling and simple in its execution it is a work of magic. It's only a matter of time before Rothfuss finishes his series and if the other goodreads reviewers are any sign, he better get on it (man are they impatient) but I believe in the end, this book 2.5 will become a small good thing within the larger world that he has built.

Auri does things. Inanimate objects have feelings. The end. 
 Every wanted to know how boring your day to day life would be to someone else? That is what this is.
A lovely, quiet vignette about one of the trilogy's more mysterious characters.

E um livro estranho. Patrick Rothfuss e o autor de alguns dos meus livros preferidos. Mostrou que sabe escrever historias para todo mundo de forma fabulosa. Pois bem, neste livro, optou por escrever uma historia para si. Ele avisa! "Malta, cuidado que isto pode nao ser do vosso agrado!". Pede desculpa tambem. Mas escreveu-o e foi, de critica em critica - todos apontando o mesmo, que o livro nao seria para o grande publico mas que, de alguma forma, lhes agradara - chegando a sua editora. 
 E um livro intimista. Nao e bem uma historia - e e disso que Rothfuss se "queixa". E antes um pincelar do mundo de uma personagem que entrara na saga que o celebrizou. E uma personagem doce, fragil, num mundo a parte. Nao conta uma historia. Nao ha accao propriamente dita a nao ser as 8 paginas dedicadas a producao de sabonete por Auri, com as quais o autor brinca, quase envergonhado. E, no entanto, sao momentos deliciosos. Nao e daqueles livros que nao consegue parar de se ler. Nao e dos melhores livros que li. Mas estou estranhamente grato por o ter lido.

This may be one of the most beautiful books I have ever read. This tale from a broken girl, about her life in the Underthing, living underground at a university is more than just a story of a lost soul trying to survive, piecing her days together as best she can. And although there is not a lot of plot in the book, a lot HAPPENS. 
 Fans of the Kingkiller series know Rothfuss's books contain lots of cool things. You don't have to ferret them out, they are there in plain sight, but they require a lot of thinking. You have to make connections, think, ponder, pay attention and then wham, the significance and implications of objects/situations/people and above all names, rises up to crack you in the face. 
 So too with Auri. She is something more than just a girl with OCD and a traumatic past. But you never really know what, and you never really know why, at least not in this book. You get hints and suggestions and possibilities...kind of like in real life where there are no easy or obvious answers to the important things. 
 Is Auri in touch with a deeper sense of the connection of things, or is she just crazy? Is the connection what makes her so messed up and broken? Or was it something that happened besides the magic in her? 
 I wanted this to be ten times longer than it was.

This was a sweet little story that had many more hints about Kvothe than it let on. 
 Auri is a favorite character and spending 30k words in her head was a pure delight.

O que ganhou o livro que meu ver foi a nota do autor. 
 Sou uma pessoa que nao se encaixa e e estranha a outras, como todos aqueles que a historia no fim foi dedicada. 
 Mas, ao mesmo tempo, sou daquelas pessoas que a historia nao serviu. 
 Confusa e um pouco vazia, realmente, prestei mais atencao nos objetos que e todo resto, ou tentando entender o "para que" de quase todos os eventos. 
 Entenda que sou quimica e ver alguem descrevendo sobre fazer sabao nao e uma das maiores magias que ficcao fantasiosa pode oferecer... 
 Talvez em uma segunda, realmente o livro ganhe seu significado :)

A one-man circle-jerk without a climax hacked out by an author far too in love with his own pen and delusions of grandeur. An echoing paean to the worst sort of amateur 'art', doubly embarrassing for having been written by a competent professional who is suffering from a possibly-terminal. Err. Ermine. Urinal. Case of writers' block. 
 This is, without a doubt, the single, signal, Pringle, worst book I've ever read, and by far the most grating and annoying, and I've read the Qur'an and Book of Moron. 
 If there is any philosophical point, it is despicable (though there is very little of one that isn't eisegeted in by a mind trying to make sense of the worse than senseless); it is inanity, insanity, bananity of the very worst sort, a character more than loathable and a flow of unicorn-fluff brimstone, meandering nowhere - enough to make the sensible rage and curl the lip, and wish that a price ten times as great could unread the horrid tripe and recall the hour worse than wasted. 
 Recommended for fans of pretentious fanfiction with pretensions of adequacy who tire of poor plotting and character development and wish both were forever banished. No stars.

I just don't understand why this even exists. Honestly, it's useless - I don't feel like I've learned a single thing about Auri, whom I love as a character in the Kingkiller Chronicles, that I couldn't have already gathered, or that couldn't have been told in a much shorter five page short story. Ten pages at the most. The writing honestly isn't even up to par with his other books. It's not that it's boring, it's not that it's confusing, it's not that "it doesn't do what stories should do" (as Patrick Rothfuss says in the Endnote); it's that it's pointless and just doesn't add anything to the character or the world this takes place in. I like Patrick Rothfuss as a person, but there are times - the last third of The Wise Man's Fear, for example, or the entirety of this book - that I just can't tell if he knows what he's doing as a writer. There are such meaningless little "metaphors" in this book that just reek of trying-too-hard, like, "Foxen was frightened and full of mountains." Don't even get me started on both the Author's Foreward and Endnote - at first seeming to be a harmless justification for this book's existence, fine enough, but then becomes a statement of, "If you don't like this, you just don't get it. It wasn't for you. It's for a special club of people who are oh-so-special because they like aimless stories, like I do." The thing is - I completely get the feeling he describes; that feeling of being alone, of being slightly or totally broken depending on the day or the hour. It's just that it wasn't written very well. Don't sit there and try to make the reader feel bad because they didn't "get" what you wrote. 
 The best thing about this book is the cover, the hardback itself, and the illustrations inside. Meh.

I enjoyed reading this, rothfuss is a good writer and I was swept along having feelings for inanimate things and worries about Auri. 
 But I'm glad I checked it out from the library because $20 after tax for a 150 page novella I don't need to come back to again and again would have infuriated me. Someday I'll probably pay for the trilogy, brand new, even. But this was just an interlude. Also maybe it's just my current mood, but the author really didn't need to apologize. Insecurity is annoying.
Love his work, care about Ari as a character wanted to like this, I didn't, but it in now way will deter me from reading book three in this fantastic series when it comes out

The Slow Regard of Silent Things has been on my TBR for three years. For three long years I told myself I was too busy to read this short novella, in part because I wanted to re-read and enjoy Rothfuss' earlier works, The Name of the Wind and The Wise Man's Fear, despite having read them countless times. I have never been more angry with myself for waiting to read a book, as The Slow Regard of Silent Things was wonderful. 
 I have read so many bad things about this book. Too many people expected Auri's novella to be the third book in the Kingkiller Chronicle series. Others didn't pay attention to what the book was really about. They didn't think about who Auri is as a character. If they had, they might have realized just how brilliant and wonderful The Slow Regard of Silent Things really is. 
 Slow Regard is not a regular novel. It is not normal by any means. It features a single character, for one. When paired with the fact that the novel has no real plot, it goes without saying that Rothfuss did something clever and unique with Slow Regard, which follows Auri's day to day life. 
 If you take the time to read Slow Regard and appreciate it for what it really is, you will learn a great deal more about the world that Rothfuss created. Instead of being a novella centered around a specific event or action, it is a novella that encourages you to pay attention to the world around you. It is a novella about places and names and language. It is a story about a broken girl learning to cope with the only thing that she knows. It uncovers the pain and loneliness of being broken and alone and the difficulties of living with mental illness. 
 But at the same time, it's innocent and charming. It maintains the whimsical and sweet nature of Auri, who is described as a bright young girl who looks as if she is from the Fae. And despite it's lack of traditional story components, it is worth your time. It's short and sweet and beautiful. It is everything that I could have hoped for in a story about one of my favorite characters. 
 For a full, detailed review, check out Paperback Paris!

This is a 2.5 stars. 
 I could tell that it was not for me - it's a very slow story, rich in worldbuilding, a sense of plot (of Auri waiting for Kvothe to come), and it deals deeply with Auri's character/worldview. So those are good things. 
 But: it's too slow for me. I just didn't feel engaged with Auri's story - I didn't care for her point of view. Because of that, I can't rate it highly. This is a good story, but it's not for me. 
 By the way: the illustrations were lovely though.

I feel incredibly guilty giving this two stars. I love Patrick Rothfuss's writing, I love Kvothe as a character, and his world as a setting. And I really disliked this story. 
 This is a novella, quite short. I knew it was written about Auri, the girl who lives in the warren under the university. Okay, cool, I'm game. We know she's got issues, only, told from her perspective, we quickly see that she is living under a serious mental illness. I'm no doctor, but if I had to guess I'd think OCD, obsessive-compulsive and no small bit of autism in there. 
 The recitation of her thoughts, in small detail, were okay at first. A clever approach, and she's cute and whimsical. But honestly, such an unhealthy internal monologue, without cease, was painful. And her self-care is sketchy at best. She almost drowns herself. She is all but starving. She forgets to get warm. I just want to give her a hug and a prescription. I had to force myself to read through. Perhaps I have enough unhealthy thinking, without needing hers too? 
 What I liked: 
 The setting, very rich and neat look at the underground. 
 The craft behind the story, Rothfuss can sure write.

Nope, not for me. I kind of scoffed when Pat wrote a blog post reiterating the prologue, which warns that this is a very different kind of book from the Kingkiller Chronicles. I figured that was fine, it would be a different story, no problem there. But it is a VERY different kind of story, and definitely not the kind I enjoy. Seems more like a free-association writing exercise than a story, to be honest. Oh well, I'm glad I didn't buy the book and instead got it from the library, at 32% I decided I had given it enough of a chance and that I was not going to like it. 
 Lots of people rated this book 5 stars, and that's fine; some people may enjoy this immensely, but I am not one of them.

Thank you for this Patrick Rothfuss. It made me cry, and laugh, and sit in silence. I was also nicer to all the silent things in my house. Oh so gentle to my coffee mug and oh so thankful to the cream and sugar that went into it. Your story that isn't really a story is kinda a beautiful thing. Here's to being a little broken and all the better people because of it.

I became more engrossed and wistfully, sadly charmed than I expected, but still--there was entirely too much grinning happening in this book.

This novella is quite beautifully written and listening to the audio version, read by the author himself adds an additional layer to the atmosphere and beauty of the writing. That being said, the story itself is just Auri walking around describing objects she finds and moving them around. You get to know Auri and understand her strength and fragility but... I don't know. In the end I liked it.

I really enjoyed reading this novella. Auri is such a powerful, tragic, and brilliant narrator. The way Rothfuss tells the story suits her character, and allows us to glimpse the interior life of her mind. 
 The story follows Auri over a week as she makes right The Underground, beneath the University, and prepares for Kvothe's upcoming visit. It's hard to explain the book beyond that, to do so would minimize what makes it special - experiencing the silent everyday actions that keep the world turning. Auri is like a clock-smith, hidden behind the gears, keeping everything on time. It's fantastically imagined. 
 While the book is a beautiful read, I would not recommend it unless you have read The Name of the Wind and The Wise Man's Fear. It's best considered as part of the larger series, not as a standalone novel.

The writing in this novella was so pretentious. It read like a creative writing paper written by someone who didn't know what they wanted to write about and needed to meet a word count. They also used the thesaurus, a lot.

This book was reviewed on Dark Matter Zine; for more reviews, interviews and articles, go to Dark Matter Zine. Alternatively, this link is just to Dark Matter Zine's reviews. 
 A review by Nalini Haynes 
 I have a confession to make. Up until The Slow Regard of Silent Things, I hadn't read any of Rothfuss's books. Shortly after Name of the Wind came out, I edited a one-off issue of a zine for a club. A teenage girl gave me some notes for a review scrawled on both sides of a scrap of paper. I spent over an hour deciphering the notes using the internet as my Rosetta Stone and putting the notes in some kind of logical order. After this experience I was not keen to actually read the book. 
 Fast forward a year or two. My son read Name of the Wind and loved it. I acquired a hardcover copy with the intention of reading it but postponed the actual reading until the trilogy was complete. Wise Man's Fear came out; my son again nagged me to read Rothfuss's work but the feminist critiques of book 2 were off-putting. My son looked awkward as I cited, in detail, criticisms I'd read. 
 "Yes, but the PROSE!" he replied. "You must read his work FOR THE PROSE. You will kick yourself when you finally read it." 
 The Slow Regard of Silent Things allowed me to enter Rothfuss's world from an unconventional and -- according to the author's note -- not recommended point, by reading a novella that is much less of a commitment than a doorstopper. 
 Plus my son took David Mitchell's Bone Clocks and hadn't given me a review by the time The Slow Regard of Silent Things reached publication date, so someone had to review it. [shifty eyes] 
 So. Here we are and here is my review: 
 Auri is a solitary creature, a girl obsessed with Kvothe (the central character of the doorstopper trilogy) although he's never mentioned by name. When she's not obsessing, Auri tends her underground world, setting things to rights. It is her slow regard because she is a silent thing; it is also the slow regard of inanimate objects in Auri's world. 
 Rothfuss's voice in The Slow Regard of Silent Things is part Neil Gaiman in detailed simplicity and part Isobelle Carmody in her Red Wind children's SFF series for eloquent lyricism coupled with simplicity. Rothfuss's larger series (pun intended) is not suitable for younger readers, but The Slow Regard of Silent Things is suitable for a wide range of ages as it's quite chaste. It has one animate character who is, herself, quite modest and proper although there are implications for the future of her relationship with Kvothe within the story. 
 The black and white artwork provides points of interest to the story, enhancing the misconception that this may be a story-book for primary school children (who could read it if they can cope with some stretching language but who aren't the target audience). Pipes trail across the page as Auri follows pipes to ensure she does not become lost. Footprints trail a path cross-wise through the text as Auri fearfully recalls an incident -- an invasion -- that occurred some time ago, motivating her to action. Auri's halo of dandelion hair catches the eye as she sits on a chimney stack reflecting on the night scene. Artwork enhances this quaint novella. 
 The Slow Regard of Silent Things 
 is a descriptive novel of an odd creature's life, her solitary existence, her feelings of isolation and possible mental illness. Told in the very close third person, this novella delves into Auri's world and world-view, including her struggles to remember to eat, needing to give herself permission to eat and difficulties finding food. Without traditional plot arcs or character development, the entire novella is Auri's 'moment'. Tension focuses on Auri's belief that she must tend the world while denying herself, simultaneously seeking to provide sumptuous gifts for Kvothe whose visit is imminent. A simple rhythm blends with lyrical phrasing to create prose worthy of reading for its own sake. 
 This novella is too far outside the mainstream to fairly rate it, even from my personal perspective. I have NFI how to rate it or even what measure to use. Read it and judge for yourself. Writers should read The Slow Regard of Silent Things for the prose. 
 Happy now, Son? [image error]

This book is unlike anything I have ever read before, and since there is no action or conflict or dialogue or human drama whatsoever, I think it will not play with most people. But I loved it. 
 The world needs things like this, because most everything else is actually a dime a dozen. Thank you for writing this, Pat.

The Slow Demise of a Mysterious Character 
 To borrow a cloying Auri-ism, this book is all unkilter. It details a week in the life of the enigmatic character Auri, a mysterious subterranean character in Patrick Rothfuss' otherwise strong Kingkiller Chronicle (Book 1:The Name of the Wind) 
 Things begin amiably. We see Auri's world from her vantage point. Every chamber in her underground world has a name. Days and inanimate objects are personified. She has a constant sense of "balance" or "rightness" or "purity" about the arrangement of objects in space, on shelves, etc. It was nice to develop her perspective and the precious way she interprets the world. There is a near-spiritual dimension to her treatment of objects and patterns. 
 Unfortunately, 150 faltering pages pass and the book proves itself a one-trick-pony. Auri simply goes about her business, collecting objects, traversing rooms which she has named, perseverating about things being out of place and so on. The character study was successfully effected after 20 pages. To drag it out into an entire novella, seemingly for no particular reason, was aimless in my eyes. Rothfuss didn't add much to the KC storyline, nor was he trying to. If anything, the repetitive banality of Auri's life, her lack of introspection, and the strict pedestrianism of it all drains her character of some of its mysterious beauty. 
 As an aside, I like Rothfuss and his writing, and patiently I await "The Doors of Stone." However, in his blogs, public speaking, and now foreword and afterword to this novella, he is too self-referential. He makes generalizations about "people who like my books", but he has only published two novels. He has a warning to prospective readers in the beginning of "Slow Regard": that new readers shouldn't start here, and this book is for those who like "words and mysteries and secrets." Since when do fantasy authors provide awkward disclaimers about the accessibility of their stories? As readers, we are more than capable of determining what is done well and what is not. This one was unnecessary and weak.

The only reason I gave this 2 stars was because it really was beautifully written. However, this is a pointless book. If I knew it was nothing but a girl running around moving objects, washing her hands and feet, making sure everything is in it's place and kissing objects, I wouldn't have bothered at all. Over 100 pages of nothing but that. I couldn't even finish it, it was so boring and pointless. I don't know why some people loved it, but I'm moving on to something that makes more sense to read.
Having a plot of some sort may have helped :(

 Ok as a "let's see more of Auri" treat. Interesting as how much of Auri's condition seems like OCD. Fail as in dang, there is no way this will pass the Bechdel test, but does her life calendar really have to revolve around him ? Damn !
