Deeply unsatisfying, however the author did warn me. I liked it though.

The author says, "Don't buy this book". Yep. Right out loud, he says it. Well, in print anyway. And--shockingly--I can see his point. 
 No matter what the pundits say about "don't buy a book by its cover", good designs kick derrieres when it comes to marketing. If the cover to Slow Regard entrances a reader who buys it without knowing Kvothe and his story, this book will disappoint. If the blurb grabs your interest, for Pete's sake, don't start with this book. Find Name of the Wind and "do things proper". 
 If you think you can barge your way into a museum filled with perfect artifacts and expect to understand it, oh, how wrong you are. The best comparison I have is The Lord of the Rings and the Silmarillion. If you've walked Middle Earth behind hobbits and Gandalf, you know who they are. They need no introduction. But to jump feet first into Silmarillion without that knowledge is like diving into a pool without knowing the depth. And the shock might keep you from trying it again. 
 For those acquainted with Kvothe, who have read every line and hold the story dear, Slow Regard is like holding a long-lost present from a beloved grandmother. I can see her gnarled hands stretched out to me, giving me a teacup for my very own. There is no value to the cup. No antique dealer would want the chipped thing. But to experience again the memories is to bring my grandma back to life. 
 Slow Regard for Silent Things is just that precious. Priceless. For those who hold the memories of The Kingkiller Chronicles and want more.

I wanted to love this. I really did. But good fucking God, how many times must we name the rooms we're in? 
 I miss Kvothe.

I should have heeded Mr. Rothfuss's advice about this probably not being the book you should read if you haven't read the other books in the Kingkiller Chronicle series. I had no idea what was going on. I had to wiki characters and locations. 
 In addition, I don't think it was written beautifully, though it was trying very hard to do so. It was like... action writing, but trying to be poetic. I mean... it had a lot of focus on what she was doing (moving around things, finding things, making things), but not a lot of... focus on inspiring emotions/understanding in the reader. It's like... I was watching this TV show, and there was this owl that showed up, and you can tell that it Meant Something. But what? One character stood there contemplating it. But what was she thinking? I have no idea! It was supposed to be A Moment, but it was utterly empty image. Might as well have spent some time on Pinterest looking at the writers' mood boards or something. 
 I guess I'm saying this is Rothfuss's pinterest board about a young magical female character with fluffy blond hair and a broken mind who lives in a series of basements. It has images of broken gears and handmade soap.

Slow and lovely and ethereal. A slip of a dance through shadows. An unseen caress down your cheek. A breeze scented with lavender and longing. The exact moment between being awake and slipping into sleep. All that.

What a beautiful book. Although there isn't much of a plot, the wounded, indiscernible Auri leads a busy, complicated life. We follow her, and are inside her head, hearing her thoughts and rationale for making decisions. Beautifully written, and there are parts of Auri that we can all empathize with.

Rothfuss was absolutely correct in saying, don't read this unless you have read his other two books. That being said, this extremely short story is a wonderful read, giving insight into one of his characters. The idea of "broken" and the worth/respect of items is interesting, making this a great companion to his series.
Nothing really happened, but I was still intrigued throughout the whole book! Liked how everything had a place to be in the world--reminded me of Konmari.
Well written, but literally nothing happens. Nothing. I can see why Rothfuss himself told his fans not to buy this book.

"This story is for all the slightly broken people out there. I am one of you. You are not alone. You are all beautiful to me" - Patrick Rothfuss 
 If you're looking for a masterpiece then look no more because this is it!! I loved this story so much that I can't put it in words! This is not your usual story, there is nothing traditional about it, yet it's so beautiful, refreshing and haunting. Was this a strange story? Yes it was so very strange but I'm a weird person so I liked it. There is no dialogue in here but it is, there is just one character but yet there are more. Strange huh? Just read and see for yourself you'll get me then. 
 This story is about Auri, a mysterious character from the Kingkiller Chronicle Series. She is a wonderful slightly broken soul. I realised that sometimes I feel exactly like her, I dare to say that we all have moments when we feel like her. 
 You may love and understand this story or you may not, but that's ok because the author himself said:"...it probably just wasn't for you."

I absolutely adored the first two books, but I fell asleep Reading this one. Such a disappointing read. The story has no plot, there isn't one at all, and it's just Auri running around. It follows a broken girl, whose past damaged her (it was kind of hinted) and now she doesn't trust the world and blames herself for things that are probably not her fault. But we don't know that because it's not narrated. This novella could have been about her past, about Auri learning to trust Kvothe, about how she met Elodin in the first place. Anything. Everything. There's a lot of ground to cover up and this book just didn't make a lot of sense for me. The drawing and some quotes were pretty great, but overall, the book was boring and plain. I'm really sad and I wish this wasn't the case, but I'm just giving it 2 stars of compassion/pitty in honor to the rest of the series.

I found this to be a poetic glimpse into the world of a fascinating character, and I noticed myself reflecting on my own state often while reading. Five stars for the writing, but only four for the work as a whole - because I just cant help but feel there was a fair amount of opportunity left unexploited with this project.

After The slow reading of a silent book. 
 The best thing about this book is the author's foreword and endnote where he desperately tries to justify bringing this book to print. 
 But I am a fanboy and nothing this author does will change that.
Reads more like an epic poem than a novella, really. Was quite nice to listen to on my long runs, but very insubstantial as a story.
A fascinating character, but a slightly pointless book. Read the first 30 pages, then gave up and went to the kingkiller wiki to read the summary.

reference_books.title: One Plus One
reference_books.review_text:
Nothing life changing here, but a solid little plot and a memorable couple characters. 
 A struggling family of a mom, a very smart daughter, and a socially different step son live in a not nice neighborhood. The mom is a maid. She cleans house for this successful man who is getting sued for insider trading and his father is seriously ill. The daughter gets the chance of a lifetime to go to an amazing school and they need to raise funds, so they enter her in a competition in Scotland. Their car breaks down on the way, in swoops the successful guy and he drives them. The plot is fun and perfect for the beach. I really enjoyed the characters. The stubborn mom who doesn't want to ask for help, the quirky smart girl, the nerdy / heart of gold guy, the distant but observant and loving son.

reference_books.title: Lord of the Flies
reference_books.review_text: I hated this book. Too gruesome for me. And I hated how mean and awful everyone was. Not my type of book!

reference_books.title: Seeker (Seeker, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed this book! It has a weird (read: good) combination of old (samuri, warriors, assassins) and new (modern world, homes on the move, an Asia I don't recognize) that worked well for me. The settings in this book are well done--rich and beautifully portrayed. 
 The plot is exciting--there was a big missing part of the timeline in the middle of the story that seemed to just be cut out and I wish I saw some of that--I felt displaced in the middle but got back on board by the end. There's some magic which added an element of fun and a sense of displacement in a good way. I wish there had been a little more wonder or awe about the magic--it might be cool to have a non-seeker react to their world in a way more than the guy who's name I can't remember did... he just seemed to silently process. 
 And, while I liked the characters, none of them were so different or interesting that they were super memorable for me. I was interested while I read the book, but now, a week later, I'm no longer rooting for anyone or rooting for a specific end result. I was almost more interested in the adults stories than the teens. What made them the way they are?! They seem all sorts of crazy. I thought the interplay between groups in the books was interesting. 
 I'd read the second book in this series.

reference_books.title: Code Name Verity (Code Name Verity, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I really liked this book. It definitely felt like a young adult book to me (some others don't have that feel--I think it was the language), but I didn't fault it for that. It also took me a really long time to get into it, I felt especially engaged at a certain point when Maddie took over the narration. The climax of the story really took me by surprise. I think Maddie was set up to be scared of violence, so her being the perpetrator was a shock, and felt a little out of character (as did the following forgiveness by Julie's family), but at the end of reading this, I was in tears and it kept me thinking, so I found it engaging and a good read.

reference_books.title: Rules of Civility
reference_books.review_text: I liked this book, but wasn't a huge fan. The characters fell flat for me...

reference_books.title: The Prince
reference_books.review_text: This was for my intro to internation relations class which was horrific. And therefore, I wasn't at all into this book. It was fine. It was strategic. but I wasn't that into it.

reference_books.title: The Sisters Brothers
reference_books.review_text: I was so confused by this book at the beginning--I didn't really put 2 and 2 together that it was supposed to be funny, I just thought it was weird. But once I got into the cadence of the writing I finally understood and started enjoying this book--and it was really funny! And bizarre! I've never read a western before, but I liked the fact that I was sympathizing with this giant, weird looking, romantic, killer. The characters were really interesting and well developed. I enjoyed it!

reference_books.title: Wife 22
reference_books.review_text: I really enjoyed this book. I found myself laughing out loud at some of the situations. The characters were beautifully drawn and the story was lovely. It was really the perfect book for the beach, relatively light. engaging and compelling, with great characters you really root for.

reference_books.title: The Art Forger
reference_books.review_text: As a Bostonian, I waited a while for this to come into the BPL! It was a really fun read, I liked the characters and enjoyed the plot. The writing was so/so, but because I'm interested in the heist, I didn't give that too much weight. I used to live in the South End and know all of the (non-fiction) places the author describes, which is a thrill. However, I thought the characters weren't developed quite enough, and the end was a bit too tidy. A fun 'what if?' type of book, and I really appreciated the detail of how mechanically a forgery works, and the detail of the art world and artist's world, too. Just overall, this book felt a little simplistic. Perfect for the beach or a plane ride. Not something I'll be recommending to people, though. Just didn't hit me well enough to be proactive about recommending it.

reference_books.title: Six of Crows (Six of Crows, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was fine, but just not my favorite. The way it ended was just too much of an annoying cliff hanger for me. 
 The characters were somewhat interesting, with the female characters piquing my interest more than the others, though toward the end when we got a bit more backstory on some of the characters I was interested. 
 This book felt like a CW show, if you know what I mean--sort of teen-soap-opera-y. The plot wasn't that well developed, and there wasn't enough character development--it all happened in flashbacks, which felt like a cop out. None of the characters had real arcs-they didn't change that much (if at all) through the plot, so it felt short and like it just covered the surface area, to me. 
 It might be a good beach/vacation book for teens on spring break, but for me it was lacking. I love a good YA book, but this just wasn't deep or developed enough for me. I want some meat in my stories. It felt like it was written for teens, rather than being a great book that was well written that would appeal to teens, if that makes sense. I won't pick up the rest of the series.

book_a.title: The Art of Racing in the Rain
book_a.user_review: I liked this book a lot. It took me a little while to get into it, since I'm not a car racing kind of girl, but I ended up loving that I heard the story from the dog's POV. It was an enjoyable read.

sample_reviews.review_text: If you like car racing or dogs, you will enjoy this book. I knew this book was from a dog's point of view, but it was still not what I expected. I guess I didn't expect the canine narrator to have such a wide vocabulary and brilliant command of the English language. Not that it was a bad thing. Enzo the dog was actually very insightful and sometimes prophetic. The main plot was intriguing as well, exploring such virtues as patience, perseverance, humility, and love. There were some villains in the story who I had hoped would get their just rewards, but didn't. And the aging of Enzo was rather sudden towards the later parts of the book. But overall, I liked it. Once I hit the 55% point, it was a race to the finish as I couldn't put it down.

** spoiler alert ** 
 So I half-read/half-skimmed through this last night. I actually think telling a story from the dog's point of view could be an interesting idea. One of the big problems here is that this is not the dog's story; it's the story of his master-- not only that, but it really makes no sense to have the dog narrate this when the dog is not witness to crucial bits of the plot. Instead of accepting the narrator's limitations, the author forges ahead and tries to wedge those scenes in anyway. It's jarring and it derails the read. 
 The other problem I have here is the plot. 
 *********SPOILERS AHEAD****************** 
 Look, the goal of writing is not to play whack-a-mole with the world's most emotional plot points. We start out with a dying dog. Oh, that's sad. Then we quickly move to his owner's whirlwind romance (which we never really feel, since it's from the dog's POV), the arrival of the baby (AW!), the wife's illness and tragic early demise from brain cancer (BOOHOO!), the evil in-laws (GRRRR!) trying to gain custody of his little girl (NOOOO!), the rape charge (GASP!) by the Lolita that loved him (WHORE!), the reunion with the estranged parents (YAY!) after they disowned him (BOO!) for abandoning the care of his blind mother (BLIND?! HOW AWFUL!) and the family farm; finally, the confession that the charge was a lie-- justice, custody, and the career chance of a lifetime (YAAAAAAAAAAAAY!) all come barreling down on the conclusion like an avalanche of Karma. Oh, wait, did I say finally? Because I meant penultimately-- the dog dies (BOOHOOHOOHOOHOO!) but reincarnates as a little Italian boy (AWWWWYAAAYBOOHOOHOO!) whom Dennis meets, recognizes, and agrees to teach how to race cars (GRAZIEBOOHOOHOO!). 
 *sigh* I just want to smack this book on the nose with a rolled-up newspaper. 
 These elements, when used sparingly, can provide an emotional core to a story, and allow for exploration of character, or show personal growth and change. This book uses all of these elements to develop no character whatsoever. Nobody seems to change, and all of the characters, including our narrator, are flat. Flatness is not necessarily a bad thing, but in a book like this where it's basically an emotional plot point gang-bang, you'd better damn well have a round character or two in there that is capable of surprising me in a convincing way. They didn't-- everyone behaved exactly as their archetype was supposed to. 
 It's effective at tear-jerking... you know, if you're game for that sort of thing. Otherwise you'll probably just walk away feeling a trifle insulted. 
 Finally, I have a big problem with the theme. 
 "The Art of Racing in the Rain", the book tells us, is about making your own destiny, never remembering your past mistakes, and living solely in the moment. This actually means that having the dog be the narrator is not a bad choice: most animals seem to live very much in the moment, and many of them don't seem to have decent short-term memories, much less long-term ones. Even the intelligent ones that are trainable will forget (or "forget") things like not to go rooting through the trash for food, or they'll wind up with a major stomachache. 
 Why, then, is the book primarily narrated by the dog in the past tense? It's bookended in two present-tense narrations, but the majority of it is reminiscence. 
 There's a lot of discussion of racing as a metaphor for life, and a lot of it just seems to fall flat, or doesn't really get supported by the elements of the story.
I really enjoyed this....I see my Daisy in a whole new light!

It had quite a few emotional moments that warranted a sporadic reading of it. If there are dog lovers out there, this book is for you. I think it validates the importance of a dog's like and makes us wonder even more what's going on between the big eyes and wagging tail. After all, they only have gestures to share with us.

The racing and life analogies are good. However, I didn't like it. Too close to life and too many skipped-over racing analogies. However, there were some poignant moments and quotes you could take out of the book.

I have a really bad habit of marking my books. Passages that speak to me or interesting facts, it doesn't matter. This is a fabulous but tough book to read. finished it flying home from Calgary. Not a book to read in public, especially towards the end. I highlighted 16 different passages that I found were truly gifted thoughts. It is very well written and I hope to find something else by this author in the future. The ending was stupendous.

After years of people telling me to read this book because I love dogs I finally relented. Woof. I'm sorry I did. A dog (but really an unimaginative curmudgeonly old man character) narrates a flat and contrived plot that takes place in some sort of misogynistic fantasy land where men are honorable, young women are liars, and life can be described in endless metaphors to car racing. Also, don't market a book to dog lovers and then add a scene where the owner strikes the dog. Not cool. No dog lover I've ever met is okay with that.
Great first chapter, but for me it became less credible and less interesting as it progressed. Skimnmed to the end.

This book was a readers choice book for our library. I read it because sometimes I try to broaden my horizons and read something different. This book takes the perspective of Enzo the dog. The world is rather interesting from an intellegent dog point of view. 
 Some of my favorite quote from the book are, "Can we not will ourselves to achieve the impossible? Can we not use the power of our life force to change something,one small thing, one insignificant momement, one breath, one gesture? Is there nothing we can do to change what is around us?" "Many of us have convinced ourselves that compromise is necessary to achieve our goals, that all of our goals are not attainable so we should eliminate the extraneous, prioritize our desires, and accept less that the moon." 
 This book does have swear words in it and some sexuality (from a dog's persepective).

A must read - especially for any dog lover. Amazing how he captures the thoughts of a dog in such a believable way. I found myself thinking of my own dog, who has since passed, and how he reacted to my moods and different situations.

I love the first line of this book: "Gestures are all that I have; sometimes they must be grand in nature." It's written from the perspective of the dog and tells the story of a family's struggle with cancer and then an ugly custody battle. I certainly liked this book better than Marley & Me (which I didn't like at ALL), but I found the main character, Enzo, TOO human. It was a little weird. (Although I love the part where he unknowingly disembowels one of the kid's toys.) I'm also not into car racing at all, and using it as a metaphor to live one's life was a little too in-my-face to be appreciated. I feel kinda bad about coming down so hard on this book, but it is what it is.

I didn't expect to love this book. I thought it would be too corny: after all, the narrator is a dog and the protagonist is an aspiring race car driver, but I was looking for something to listen to during my commutes and noticed this on the 'staff favorite' display at my public library. It turned out to be the perfect driving companion; not too complicated or obtuse (i.e. It was OK if I didn't always give it my full attention), not too depressing (sometimes sad - but upbeat overall) and included interesting thoughts and ideas to ponder. You don't have to be an animal lover to enjoy the story. Enzo, the dog, is a wise and thoughtful friend (who only occasionally has problems with self-destructive stuffed animals) and Denny, the aspiring race car driver, is a really nice guy who you can't help but root for.
this is a really sad one.....

I picked this book at an airport just because it had a dog on the cover. Writing these comments 4 1/2 years later, I still tell my friends and acquaintances about it and recommend it to all. Car racing is not something I would have chosen to learn about, but thanks to the dog I thoroughly enjoyed the book. Well-writen, it stayed on the best-seller list for three years if I recall correctly. Don't live your life without reading this book!
A fast read - I really enjoyed the story. Initially I was skeptical about dog as the storyteller but it was refreshingly different.
Ispred tebe je ono sto manifestujes.
I usually hate animal books. A lot. But I really enjoyed this one. I found the dog's personality very endearing. I enjoyed the racing metaphors and the way the story unfolded.

I liked the concept and at times I really enjoyed the narration here, but this book felt a little flat to me. Enzo's philosophy and thought process was fun and sometimes comical, but the plot seemed a bit canned. Altogether an easy read and fun enough for summertime.

This is one of my all time favorite books. The narrator dog is so wise and personable, I really wanted to know this dog. He loved his people so much, it was very heart warming. Further, I never thought I could be interested in car racing but when Garth Stein is the author, it is a fascinating toipic! I later saw him at Eugene Public Library, where I was working, and he was fabulous: just as warm and personable as his dog character!

If you're a dog lover, what's not to love about this book? 
 I read it in two days straight and have never before read so many excerpts of a book aloud to my husband. It is, firstly, hilarious, and secondly, heartrending: a fairly killer combination. 
 Anyone who owns a dog should read it. And I challenge you not to be blinking back a tear by the end of the first chapter.
the first 100 pages was a bit slow for me. good, but slow, then about half way in the proverbial shit hit the fan and i couldnt put it down. was cryin by the end

This is one of the best books that I've read this year. The main character is Enzo, who is Dennis's dog. This story is told by Enzo and depicts the trials and tribulations of his owner Dennis, who is a race car driver. I would recommend this book to anyone who likes stories about love, loss and finding redemption.
It made me laugh, it made me cry, and it is one of the few books that I've been compelled to read again, enjoying it at least the same amount, if not more with each time through.
Terrible. Trite, cliche, lame. Self-conscious in all the wrong ways. And its one shtick is so poorly done it rankles.

This was a quick, easy read. It stirred up some emotion and made me think of my dogs in a whole new way. I haven't done any research, but I think the author of this book must definitely be a Buddhist because that philosophy reigned supreme throughout the story.
One of the best books I have read in awhile. I'm not much of a car racing fan but I a runner. I loved the beautiful metaphors and will certainly keep my eye out for the zebra!

This book took me a day to read because I couldn't read it fast enough. By far this is now one of my favorite books of all times. I fell in love with Enzo, Denny, and his daughter immediately and went through the emotional rollercoaster with them. I laughed so hard at some points and then had to set the book down at others to control my crying that had almost turned into weeping. Amazing, amazing book!
A wonderful read with all the emotional impact as Marley Me but it's fiction.

Smarmy. 
 Also: How dare you people shelve this as philosophy.

(This is a review I wrote several years ago...) 
 Garth Stein's third novel, New York Times Bestselling "The Art of Racing in the Rain," is an incredibly respectable effort at attempting to craft a piece of insightful, timeless (albeit fast-paced) fiction. However, upon completion of the book, an "effort" is really all I can call it. "Effort" is the only thing I witnessed in the construction of the prose, from the all-too contrived, predictable plot to the simplistic language surrounding formulaically sprinkled ten-dollar words and cliches. 
 The plot is fairly simple. Meet Denny Swift, an aspiring racecar champion living blissfully with his wife Eve and daughter Zoe. Without spoiling too much of the plot, within the first thirty pages of the novel the reader is overtly told that Eve is destined to die due to a mysterious, mortal illness. Fasten your seatbelts, beloved Reader, because for the next 160 pages of the novel, (roughly half of the length), you get to witness the slow, anticlimactic, hopeless degeneration of Eve while her husband does alarmingly next to nothing to save her (attending out-of-state races apparently ranks higher on Denny's priority list than taking his ailing wife to the hospital). Needless to say, the novel's plot arrives tired and late to the party, as it isn't until you've muscled through this chunk of the book that you are provided with completely new information. The truly unfortunate aspect of this entire 160-page set-up is that the author employs a tone that so desperately wants to be suspenseful and emotional and so utterly fails; indeed, it is almost as though Mr. Stein either a.) forgot that he already told the reader exactly what was going to happen at the opening of the novel or b.) really, REALLY hopes that you skimmed over that part. The remaining plot thread that follows Eve's death unwittingly borrows a tremendous amount of material from a few films you have probably seen in the last ten years. In short, Denny's difficulties have only just begun. What he will have to endure for the remainder of the novel is a series of misfortunes all conveniently occurring simultaneously to the point of farce. If you think this plot seems a bit simplistic and hackneyed- wait!-- I haven't introduced you to "the literary convention" yet... 
 Meet Enzo, the Swift family dog. He will be your narrator on this journey. I have read multiple novels that masterfully adopt the point of view of a household pet in order to uniquely (and oftentimes amusingly) add color and depth to a relatively simple plot. Never have I had so difficult a time accepting the fact that my narrator is a canine. Indeed, Enzo, in addition to occasionally commenting on wagging his tail for good nature and his efforts to hold his bladder for long periods of time, spouts such rhetoric as "That which you manifest is before you" (his chief maxim which looks better on a fortune cookie than within the context of the plot) and "Oh! The folly!" Is this a dog or an oil painting of a wizened great uncle? And the author's explanation for Enzo's flashes of human-like profundity? Denny's furry friend watches TV. A lot of TV. Add incredible technological optimism to the list of motifs. 
 Make no mistake, the book is entertaining. It has its share of wonderful, heart-felt, laugh-out-loud moments, specifically concentrated in its opening and later chapters. But these moments aren't enough to elevate the novel to any status beyond a solid beach read. At the end of the day, I never felt fully encapsulated by "The Art of Racing in the Rain," chiefly because I was constantly aware of Mr. Stein's dogged (pardon the pun) attempts to impress me with his "literary prowess." It had so much promise. By the end of the book, even the title devolved from sounding intriguing to maudlin and pretentious.

I really enjoyed reading this story as told by "Enzo." Being a dog lover, and reading most if this with my own dog beside me, I know made it feel more alive. This is a must for dog lovers and a great read for anyone looking for a good family story. Heart-wrenching and hopeful, this is a book I'll remember.
Blech.
This is one of the most beautiful stories I have read. I actually forgot that I have the flu while I read it this afternoon.
It's from a dogs point of view, it's Tuesdays with Morrie, The Notebook, and The Christmas Box all rolled into one.

More like 3.5 stars. I didn't like the racing/life metaphor, but I loved Enzo, the narrator. As a dog lover, his wise observations goes along with my belief that animals have souls and are more human than we realize.

I believe a good writer shows you things and makes you reach your own conclusions. This book not only tells you exactly how you are supposed to analyze something, but it then proceeds to beat you over the head with it. I can't even count the number of times I rolled my eyes while reading this - all of the philosophical observations made by the dog and the tedious racing analogies drove me insane. This book is obviously beloved by lots of people, and I guess the relationship between the dog and Denny was kind of sweet, but yeah - definitely not for me, and if I didn't have to finish it I would have quit 10 pages in.
I only read 2 chapters... it was kind of weird and the words/scenes were a little out there for me... it's my Book Club's pick for next month - curious what the other ladies are thinking...

Four stars, but why four stars? .The writing is maudlin. The plot is soap opera. The philosophy is simple minded and I'm not all that crazy about car racing analogies. 
 But then there is Enzo and everything else is unimportant. Enzo is a mutt on the last days of his doggy life and is reminiscing about his life with his human family, eagerly waiting to become a man because that's what he thinks happens what dogs complete their time of existence. The Art of Racing in The Rain is told from Enzo's perspective and the canine narrator turns out smarter than most humans in the learning-from-experience department. He is wise, he is lovable, and he is loyal and there is no way you cannot love this canine Sancho Panza. It is Enzo that pulls meaning into his and his beloved family's life. Enzo even reminds me that sometimes the best truths are the simplest... 
 "That which we manifest is before us:. We are the creators of our own destiny.Be it through intention or ignorance, our success and failures have been brought on by none other than ourselves." 
 Not bad for a mutt, huh?

2.75 stars. 
 "Here's why I will be a good person..." 
 The main character of this books name is Enzo, who is a DOG. 
 Enzo is striving to be human so that when he is reincarnated in the next life (hopefully as a human) he will be ready. Enzo comes off as more human than most people we encounter in day to day life. In many ways, he defines what it is to be human better than any of the actual human characters in the book. No small feat, considering his life and the main story really revolves around his master, Denny who is as likable of a character as you're likely to find. Denny is one of those characters that isn't special because of his amazing racing ability, he isn't special because he has supreme intellect or anything else. He's special because in the face of overwhelming diversity he always stands tall and never fails to do what is right. 
 Although this book is often marketed for "dog-lovers,"(guilty) it is definitely not only for dog lovers. It's more a story of love and life. And I don't normally care for car racing, but if you share that feeling don't let it dissuade you from reading "The Art of Racing in the Rain". I admit I was curious and maybe even a little skeptical how the art of race car driving would serve as the anchor, the source of instruction for living life successfully, for navigating the twists and turns and all the curves life throws at us. But now, having read the story it makes perfect sense, works so perfectly, so brilliantly, I marvel at the wisdom contained in each and every reference. 
 "This is a rule of racing: No race has ever been won in the first corner; many have been lost there." 
 "There is no dishonor in losing the race. There is only dishonor in not racing because you are afraid to lose." 
 The Art of Racing in the Rain has inspirational moments, but the overall story was so-so for me. I was intrigued by the story and enjoyed the life lessons sprinkled throughout and I did want to finish but I did have my issues with it. 
 Minor annoyances: 
 -Enzo goes from being believably canine to being overtly human. Any continuity problems, exaggerated events, or over dramatizations can be explained away because Enzo is only a dog, after all. 
 -Profanity! There were close to 15+ words I didn't enjoy reading that made me loss the feeling of what the author was trying to build. And can I just add that a cursing dog is just weird. 
 -How many Enzos did Denny meet in Italy before deciding he'd met his reincarnated dog? Just saying... 
 The writing was simple which at times I enjoyed and other times felt was unfortunate. With a dog narrating, the author can get away with brief, underdeveloped simple sentences and fragments, and many cliched catch phrases. Nonetheless, I did love Enzo (the smartest and most interesting character in the book) especially when he is giving some insight into the "dog world." Enzo reflects on and empathizes with Denny's difficulties, and relates them to his own world. It was fascinating to see what he thought of people, their life situations and problems but also how he reflected about a dog's life and the struggles they face too, the things that people overlook. He has this strong desire to be human because he can empathize with what the human condition is. The Art of Racing in the Rain does make you think about your pets and the importance of building a solid bond with them. What are they thinking? What is important to their world? I will admit that right after I finished the book I started to think about WHAT I was saying to my two dogs and HOW I was saying it! 
 As you can probably tell, I'm not in love with the book but I think it is worth reading at some point and you may very like it much more than me since the majority of reviews I read were 4 of 5 stars. Enzo's take on life is refreshing and insightful and the analogies he makes between life and race car driving are poignant and eye-opening. It's charming, funny, and touching and you may need to use a tissue as a bookmark. 
 "Here's why I will be a good person... 
 Because I listen. I cannot talk, so I listen very well. I never deflect the course of the conversation with a comment of my own. People, if you pay attention to them, change the direction of one another's conversations constantly. It's like being a passenger in your car who suddenly grabs the steering wheel and turns you down a side street. For instance, if we met at a party and I wanted to tell you a story about the time I needed to get a soccer ball in my neighbor's yard but his dog chased me and I had to jump into a swimming pool to escape, and I began telling the story, you, hearing the words "soccer" and "neighbor" in the same sentence, might interrupt and mention that your childhood neighbor was Pele, the famous soccer player, and I might be courteous and say, Didn't he play for the Cosmos of New York? Did you grow up in New York? And you might reply that, no, you grew up in Brazil on the streets of Tres Coracoes with Pele, and I might say, I thought you were from Tennessee, and you might say not originally, and then go on to outline your genealogy at length. So my initial conversational gambit - that I had a funny story about being chased by my neighbor's dog - would be totally lost, and only because you had to tell me all about Pele. Learn to listen! I beg of you. Pretend you are a dog like me and listen to other people rather than steal their stories."

I know people love this book, and forgive me, but not all books are for all people, and I found this to be literary drivel. It's entertaining enough. I read the whole thing. But it is based on an already dicey proposition. The narrator is a dog. And then it descends into embarrassing descriptions of how humans have sex, and the dog's complicated yet Hallmark ideas about souls and missions, etc. It's Nicholas Sparks from a dog's perspective. Not my cup of tea. The whole idea of writing from a dog's perspective is questionable, and unless you're Tolstoy writing Anna Karenina (wherein there is one of the most remarkable examples of writing from a dog's perspective) it just simply is not for me. 
 In its defense, if you like romance, if you love Nicholas Sparks, this is well written enough that you will love this. This dude's the Mitch Albom of dog-whisperers, so is you love Mitch Albom Or Nicholas Sparks, run out and buy 30 copies and your Christmas shopping is done. But for me, it held little to no literary interest.

Found the book to be emotional moving - a great story about the relationship between a man and a dog, as told by the dog. It's a hard luck story for both the dog and his master and each helps the other. The other charaters in the book - the girlfriend and the daughter were also well developed. Strong book on character development and it tugged at the heart and caused me to feel and empathize.

** spoiler alert ** 
 What sentimental nonsense. And let it be known that I'm not just saying this because the book is narrated from the point of view of a heavily and in the end literally anthropomorphized animal. Yes, the dog is reincarnated as a human in the end. . I mean, I loved this popular New Yorker short story narrated by an elementary class's pet hamster http://www.dinnerpartydownload.org/si..., for example. No, this book is nonsense because it features flimsy, delusionally irrational people as its heroes, and a dog who (this is important) is never convincing as an anthropomorphized animal; that is to say, it's not Stein's cutesy conceit, it's his execution. 
 I've never found something so intent on being positive and uplifting so entirely hateful. I can see why enough Americans loved it to make it a bestseller - people here get crazy about humanized pet narratives. A lot of the reviews are clearly from that special type of pet owner who gets unsatirically teary-eyed imagining their beloved Spot or Fido thinking about identity, existence, happiness and love. You know which type of person I'm talking about: the ones who, when asked whether they would save a stranger or their dog from a sinking ship, would unhesitatingly choose their dog and not be deeply embarrassed to say so. 
 This book, to me, was a male version of "Twilight" - not that there's anything wrong with that, I'm all about wish-fulfillment through art; but why is it treated by critics and the media as anything more than the fairy-tale tripe that it is? In any case, read this book if you think that dogs are exactly like miniature people, like cloying cliches about changing reality with the mystical powers of your mind, have a spiritual connection with race cars, believe doctors are inherently evil, and think that women are the source of all men's unhappiness.

As a former dog owner, I'd like to believe my childhood pet was reincarnated as a (wo)man for her next life. I would like to shake her hand and acknowledge how much I needed, and appreciated, her companionship through the years. 
 The concept of this book, told from a dog's perspective, could've easily flustered a writer. Additionally, I was worried the racing analogies would bore me, as I hate the sport. I actually found them interesting and relatable. Stein handled Enzo's narrative with ease, often bringing me to tears with his insights and aspirations. 
 As one who has had to say goodbye to too many family members in this life, it astonished me to get perspective from the other side. I only know the loss I feel and the fear of the afterlife, but to hear Enzo's acceptance of death and his willingess to go, made me realize that death is not always the end, nor does it have to be heart-breaking. 
 It hurt my heart whenever Enzo would say that he was useless because he didn't have thumbs or the ability to speak our language. Just because we have perceived disabilities does not make us any less capable of loving or providing comfort. 
 I couldn't put this book down. Rather than leaving me sad and overwhelmed, at the end I found myself with a sense of peace. 
 "I am ready."
Listened on audible - well done - laughed, cried- sobbed actually - but not sorry I stuck with it - even though I knew from the beginning that I would be crying

This is a unique and brilliant book, told from the point of view of a dog, Enzo. I can't give it less than 5 stars, even though it's not flawless. 
 I love dogs and Enzo is a wonderful dog. Because of how I feel about dogs, and reading this for a speculative fiction book discussion, well it didn't seem to properly fit that genre, but I'd had the book on my list for ages (recommended by a few friends with similar taste) and I'm glad I got motivated to read it, as my to-read books often languish unread indefinitely. 
 I was so afraid this would make me horribly depressed because I knew that it would be sad, and it's about a dog. I don't believe in reincarnation and I am sad. 
 However, it was also hilarious. Very, very funny. I actually do have a favorite passage, which I will not share in this review (I'd have to paraphrase actually) because I want readers to be able to read it for themselves. It's one that struck my funny bone with its truth. 
 It was sort of a weird book though. The first long part I was amused a good deal of the time, then I was mostly angry and sad, and finally mostly sad. I wish it had been the other way around, first crying and then laughing, and I keep thinking that would have been possible for the author to accomplish this because there are sad and funny/happy things during the beginning, middle, and end of the book. Ah well. 
 What Enzo's voice/story does is give a perfectly perspicacious commentary on the human condition. His perspective is so wise. 
 I don't care at all about automobile racing, but the way it was described was a metaphor for how to live one's life, and that was done so well. 
 I do hate it when books' (and television's and movie's) stories get jazzed up unnecessarily, and a great middle part of the book irked me a bit. Also, I often didn't enjoy the scenes as much where Enzo was not an eyewitness. 
 Readers who know and love dogs will especially appreciate this story and its narrator. I guess non-dog people can enjoy it too, but they're going to miss a few things, I think. 
 My Goodreads friend Chrissie thinks she wouldn't like this because it would be too soppy but I'm going to encourage her to give it a try. Maybe not though since she did read a part/parts and wasn't impressed, and I was spellbound from the first line onward. 
 ETA: I have to add that this is a beautifully written book! Dog or no dog. 
 ETA again: The whole time I was reading this I longed for a dog to pet as I was reading!

I really liked this book. It was an interesting way to write it, from the dog's point of view. I liked the characters I was supposed to like and disliked the ones I was supposed to dislike. Good book.

Drivel, mostly. I found this book to be way, way below my reading level despite my lack of an advanced education. The primary function of this book is to elicit an emotional response (which it did, thus two stars instead of one) and did not challenge me on any level whatsoever. Worse, as a dog owner and dog lover I had the distinct impression the writer has never had a dog given that no dog owner would ever attribute the types of thoughts and behaviors to a dog that the author did. The fact that it had over 600 five star reviews on Amazon really threw me off. I expected it to be better.

I couldn't even finish this book. Too depressing. I kept saying to myself- just one more chapter and it will get better. But, about half way through I gave up. Too much language(f-bomb dropped at least 4 times in the first half of the book) and even too explicit for me, as well. I am very sensitive, tho, and I know a lot of people who really enjoyed this book.
got to pg 100 and couldnt read anymore-tired of reading about manifest destiny, reincarnation, spiritualism from a new age perspective. i have better things to do with my time!
A painful story with a cheesy ending that offers the feel good indulgence of a Disney movie in a page turning novel.

book_b.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
book_b.user_review: This book was a little odd for me. The characters weren't likable, it was a weird mix of fantasy and self-conscious adolescent angst which took me out of the fantasy part of the book and made me aware of there being an author, which I found distasteful. The writing wasn't my favorite, but the plot was interesting. It felt like the author was jealous of the kids in Narnia and always wanted to go there himself, so he wrote a story about making it happen. Everything felt a little fast for me, large swaths of time just passed without any description. I'm sure there are people this appeals to, but I'm not one of them. I was looking forward to this, so, it's a little sad for me. Oh well! Won't read book 2.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really wanted to like this or love this, but the whole thing was just so slow. Really, I don't like Quentin at all, I get him, but at the same times its not an excuse for him to get away with half of the stupid things he does. The first 300 pages consisted of Brakebills, learning magic, them turning into geese, and really the arctic fox intercourse? And all of the unnecessary drunk, sex, and party scene that happens in this book. The first 300 pages can have been written in maybe 150 pages or less and then finally in the last 100 pages of this book we get something! We get Fillory and finally some actions. But boy, did this book really put me to sleep! I fell asleep reading this book because it was just so long and slow. What I did took away from this book is that you can never be happy, you will find something new to be excited about, but sooner or later the excitement will die down, and you will be just back to square one, back to feeling lonely in your life, and wondering why are you not content with your life. This book is depressing, whining, dark, slow, and really of just Quentin whining 75% of the time. I am however curious what will happened in the next two sequels, but I'm not willing to put myself through that misery again. I will probably just read some summaries online and maybe put the next two books on the bottom of my to-read list. Really disappointed with this book. I really think Grossman could have make this such a better book than it is. And again I speak for myself, entitled to my own opinions. You may enjoy this book, a lot of other people did! But this was just not my cup of tea.(

I hated this book the first time I read it, but when it was chosen for book club I decided to try to give it a second chance and try to be more objective. It didn't work. I still hate it. 
 When I first read it I thought I only hated it because of the way it completely twisted some of my favorite novels from childhood (The Narnia Chronicles) but I realize now it's much more than that. This novel has been described as being "Harry Potter for adults" but that statement couldn't be more wrong. This is Harry Potter for adults who have become completely disillusioned by books about magic. There's nothing even magical about this book - Grossman turns magic into science and takes away everything that's magical about magic. The book feels completely sterile and antiseptic, with no heart or imagination at all; instead of the creativity and color Harry Potter inspires in my imagination, I pictured this whole world dreary and grey. The style and tone of the book made the narration feel toneless, and uninterested, which made it hard for me to care about what was happening or get into the story. I didn't like any of the characters in this novel - not because they were unlikable, but because I simply didn't care about them at all. 
 And I haven't even gotten into the minor things that bugged me, like the fact that the school's calendar is randomly 2 months off from the rest of the world for no apparent reason. I've discussed this book with some other people who defended it based on the fact that the tone is intentional and the author is trying to make a statement on these types of novels, but even if this is the case it just put me off the book entirely. If you're looking for Harry Potter for adults, do not read this book. Check out Jim Butcher's Dresden Files instead.

I'm still not entirely sure how I feel about this book. The structure is unusual in a way that might be flawed, or it might just be different from what I'm used to. There isn't a conventional story arc, but it's not arranged as a series of interludes connected by a device, either. Normally, a story with school at its center will be structured around the school time frame, but this isn't. Sometimes a lot of time passes with the narrative just skimming and skipping over things, then other times we stop and zoom in on things that don't necessarily move the plot or develop the characters, although they aren't really objectionable to read. And then the whole school thing turns out to be not so important, in a way. 
 I think the protagonist is problematic for me. I don't really like Quentin, but then he is an anti-hero and I'm not really supposed to like him. It's more that, while Quentin may be more realistic than a conventional hero, he doesn't feel real to me as a fully developed character. After everything he experiences, I still don't feel like I know him or understand what makes him tick. In some cases, I might say that was the desired effect, or I was just not connecting to that particular character, but in this case I'm afraid it's because the character isn't whole. 
 Overall, I still enjoyed the book to a reasonable extent, and I'm looking forward to seeing how the second book picks up the story and pushes the characters in hopefully new directions. I guess I'm supposed to talk about how the book is and is not like Harry Potter, or how Fillory is or is not like Narnia, but really, that's tiresome. It's refreshing to see the Hogwarts-like situation given such a different treatment, and the Narnia stuff seems like perfectly acceptable and somewhat traditional literary signifying.
Fantastic read. Can not wait to start the next book in the trilogy.
Got halfway through before the Young Adult and "don't think about things that are happening in the book" aspects got too large.

I'm giving up. Not only does this book really have no point behind it but it has stolen so much from other books that I just can't understand how Grossman could do it. First he actually uses some of the same made-up words and ideas from Harry Potter and then the last straw was when I realized that he used the same exact in-between type world as was used in the Magicians Nephew by C.S. Lewis. I mean come on.

Quentin is sort of the lovechild of Harry Potter and Holden Caulfield; this is his magical "coming of age." Q is self-centered, petty, insecure, and awkward...in short, your average teenager. This is a novel of his dreams and fuck ups, both spectacular. I really liked it, tho the pacing was a little off for me, and most of the time you want to strangle the protagonist. I'm not running out to devour book 2, but I'll get to it eventually.

I might change my two stars later when I have calmed down a bit, but good lord this book made me livid! If it was written well, all of the blatantly obvious references to The Secret History and fantasy literature (Harry Potter and Narnia in particular) would have been forgiven as they could be passed as homage or intertextuality. But the writing is so terrible (has anyone heard of an editor?), it came across as blatant freebooting (in print form). 
 A magical land visited by four English children (where only human children can sit on the four thrones)? 
 A wizard's school? 
 A hunt for a white stag? 
 A group of precocious and bored university students drinking themselves to death? 
 Drunken orgies in the woods? 
 A time-turner disguised as a pocket watch? 
 A form of wizard chess? 
 A world-between-the-worlds with ponds to jump into? 
 Seriously - are Donna Tartt and J.K. Rowling getting any royalties from this? 
 And lets not forget the worst line in the book: "Of course it matters, Vix," Quentin said. "It's not like they're all the same." "Vix" was a term of endearment with them, short for vixen, an allusion to their Antarctic interlude, vixen being the word for a female fox.
I really wanted to like this more than I did. I like the idea and might pick up book two to see if I like it any better.

I have no earthy idea why this book is or ever was popular. The idea that SyFy bought the rights to the property and has made a television series from it blows my mind. To me this book read like J. K. Rowling's older, 'cooler' brother mansplaining all the ways in which Harry Potter was juvenile drivel. And true to form, by doing so the quibbler missed one of the very coolest things about Harry Potter: good or bad, rich or poor, gifted or average, cool or uncool, all of the students at Hogwarts are just that: students. The great social rift of girls below and boys above is practically ignored. 
 I tried to give The Magicians the benefit of the doubt. I mean, it is written from the POV of a teenage boy. The fact that Quentin's self-absorbed isn't a huge surprise, nor are his more neanderthal views on women. 
 Where I fell off the joy train was during the Antarctic portion of the program. First up, the Russian who runs the concentration camp they call a school is creepy to the point of vulgarity. The whole 'theft of voices' thing boded ill, but it wasn't until the 'hammer and nail' game that Grossman really hacked me off. 
 The scene is set thusly: a dank stone cell, a table and chair, a block of wood, a hammer and nails, and a fiddly spell so oft repeated to suit various conditions as fill the provided book. Our hero is set the task of completing every iteration of this pointless spell that's purpose is simply to allow the caster to drive a nail into a piece of wood with one whack of the hammer without bending said nail or crushing their thumb. The narrative expounds on the conditions covered ad nauseum: different locations, altitudes, weather -- some examples specific, some not. Finally, only three variables remain to be tested: the caster's gender: male, female or 'hermaphrodite.' Naturally, the protagonist balks over the last option like any genderist prig. 
 Obvious irks aside, why exactly are those the final three options? Wouldn't every iteration of the spell have three versions based on the caster's gender? Is it just a given that only a man would find himself having so much trouble driving a nail into a board 'on a tropical island during a snowstorm' that he would have to resort to magic? How does that even make sense? 
 I actually lasted a bit past that. It was when the entire fourth year class was turned into foxes as an excuse for wholesale rape that I gave up. The protagonist describes how the object of his desire's 'eyes roll in terror' as he penetrates her only to 'fog with pleasure' seconds later. (That was written by a true man...with no real sense of spacial relationships.) Our hero describes how uncomfortable things are the next day, wonders if his lady love is still a virgin...and all the other ridiculous garbage anyone with a lick of sense would avoid voicing at all cost. 
 I plan to return my copy to Audible because I just can't justify giving Lev Grossman a single dime.
ummm

I read a good chunk of this book before I decided it wasn't something I wanted emblazed in my brain. I skimmed the end to figure out how it ended and instantly regretted the time I spent even doing that much. What bugs me the most is the boring interludes on "Fillory", which is really code for Narnia. The first parts of the book introduce this other land by narrating how a guy had read about it. I would have preferred parrallel chapters with the Chatwins in the fantasy land instead of all the third-hand accounts which do not feel relevant to the story until you hit the third major partition. 
 My misery level reading this was on par with my experience with Game of Thrones, except none of these characters are redeemable. The characters remind me of a bunch of Paris Hiltons riding a false high (yeah they all turn out to be substance abusers) to fantasy land where, all of the sudden, you have to remember the boring Fillory stuff I skipped over in the beginning. The main character is no Harry Potter unless you put Harry on the road to hell with a fifth of Jack and a bag of coke. 
 I don't think curiosity will get me reading book two, but if I become one of those self-flagellating monks I'll consider it.

I HATED this book. For the the first quarter that is. Everyone in this book seems like depressed teenagers who are completely unworthy to learn magic. Which they are. So why 5 stars? 
 This book really is not FOR adults per se but it without a doubt is, adult. Alcoholism, drug use, and sex is fairly rampant. 
 I didn't like Quentin at all at first but after getting further in the book I felt he became a very relatable character (minus the magic) as far as his feelings of being lost, not truly believing that things he was witnessing were real, long lost loves and rampant drug use coupled with no motivation. After awhile I started to care not only for Quentin but for his relationship with Alice as well as the rest of the Physical Kids. 
 This is a human story, where magic is real but isn't really magical. At least in the traditional fantasy tropes. Yes he goes to magic school, yes there is a magical fantasy land behind a portal. But non of that crap matters. Imagine yourself trying to get into a college but instead of getting a regular interview your thrown into a crime scene and happen upon a school where you must take completely ridiculous tests in a seemingly regular environment only to be told your a magician and magic actually exists. Couple that with a fantasy land of your favorite childhood book series being an actually reality as well, only not at all what you dream about and is far more violent and frightening then you ever imagined. How would you deal with it? Most people when given the opportunity to rise up and do great things... Fail, matter-of-fact. And I loved this book for the way things wrapped up. Its an incredibly human story told with a side story of magic. 
 Any book that you can get drunk in a fantasy world bar with a magic talking bear, a birch tree and a monkey looking dude serving you beer is a story worth knowing in my opinion.

Grossman is an excellent writer, but I am not sold on his story telling. I enjoyed his style but the plot was thin and the characters underdeveloped. I couldn't bring myself to care about them, not even Alice whom I wanted to like so badly. By the end, I was skimming through just so I could finish it. It seemed like Grossman couldn't decide which direction to take the book, so instead of choosing he took it a little bit in every direction. I couldn't tell whether that was intentional or not, but either way it didn't work. I just didn't believe in his world. He didn't make me long for Brakebills the way that Quentin longs for Fillory. That, I think, made the difference.
One of the rare instances when I think the book is worse than the tv show. I liked part one, in the university, and could have lived without almost everything after that.

I wanted to like this book.... I really did but I really don't like the main character at all... He just got more annoying as the story progressed.... I wish they didn't compare this book to Harry Potter because it is not comparable in my opinion... the only thing they have in common is that there is a wizarding school.... that's it...
A darker older Harry Potter. I enjoyed it.

Sure, it's "college Hogwarts" but does the Harry Potter world exist or not in this tale? The pop-culture references (which included Harry Potter, Narnia and Star Wars, among others) cracked me up, but I was frustrated when I couldn't tell which fantasy realms existed and which didn't. For me, the world-building wasn't strong because of this. 
 At times the story lagged and conflict was sparse overall. And the perpetual need for the characters to be inebriated didn't make me think the novel was dark and gritty, it just gave me high school flash backs. 
 Perhaps most frustrating was the cliffhanger ending. Now I have to decide if I want to invest a couple I'd days to finish the story of an apathetic child or read the synopsis of his tale from Wikipedia. 
 There are a couple of positives: the magic is interesting and I like the high-stakes of the casting itself. If the author mentioned something, it was important and all loose ends were tied up, even though it sometimes felt forced. I cared about the love story and cried a bit. 
 But I'm probably going to finish reading the series by taking a jaunt over to Wikipedia.

I WANTED to like this book--I mean, a boy obsessed with a fictional magical world finds out he is eligible to attend a school for magicians; i.e. Harry Potter meets Narnia? Count me in! 
 Except...I didn't like it much. I didn't like Quentin, the protagonist; I didn't like many of the choices he made, and I didn't relate to him enough to forgive him for being a jerk. Parts of the book were clever, especially the way it satirizes Narnia, but overall I was disappointed.
I was hoping for more. Unfortunately until the last 30 pages the book was a waste of time. The characters were not engaging and the plot was essentially pointless
finally forced myself to push through it.... ugh fucking awful.

I couldn't even get through the first 100 pages of this book--it was THAT bad. Coming from one who cannot stand leaving a book unfinished, it was a big deal to decide to put this one down and never return to it. There were so many missed opportunities to give this book depth and life. Something that could have such potential ended up being one of the most disappointing books I have ever attempted to read.

I hated this book. I really struggled to even complete it. It was fairly boring until the very end when it finally picked up. But for the most part nothing of any importance really happened. The book covered about 5 years total and it was so fast that I couldn't really get to know the characters at all as they grew. This is not Harry Potter for adults but it is not even a good book.
2.5 because that one scene with the beast in the classroom was a little scary
No.

I promised myself that I would finish the next book I started, and that was this book. Which is why I actually finished it, which is why I'm giving it two stars. (If I'd let myself put it down, I would have given it one.) 
 The writing is so flat and uninterested in anything that's actually going on in the book that while it matches well with the protagonist, it's actually a terribly punishment for a reader. Nothing in this world is interesting, nothing has weight. Moments that should have an affect on the reader go off like damp balloons because they're carried by characters that have been woefully under-developed. And most of the characters are. He tells too much, and shows too little. 
 I had the sense throughout this book that everything happens because it's convenient for it to happen, not because the characters had to make it happen. Their strings are never hidden. There's no drive, no sense of inevitablility. Which again, is fine for the environment the writer is creating, but dull for the reader. It felt like a series of wooden blocks being dropped on each other, and every act was the hollow clonk of a block meeting the previous one. 
 The lack of effect would probably have worked better if the book had been written in first person, but as it is I just felt as though the author was embarrassed by what he was doing and wanted to be able to pretend he wasn't writing fantasy. 
 I was really put off by the treatment of the one working class character; and every time a new female character was introduced I immediately started a countdown to her breasts being completely, unnecessarily shown or talked about. 
 I look to fall asleep reading a book, not be put to sleep by reading a book, which actually happened more than once here.

In looking at earlier reviews on this site, I see that the author himself said calling this book a cross between Harry Potter and Donna Tartt's A Secret History was a fair call; obviously Narnia is thrown in there, too. I really enjoyed this book, which approached the fantastic with a more litfic sensibility -- characters are flawed and self-involved and mess up and get through things, but not always. I think some Rowling/Lewis fans will like it a great deal, and some won't like the flavor of disillusion that imbues the novel; things are certainly not comforting or black-and-white here. 
 Some things I especially liked: that the young magicians were all neurotic overachievers; the Hudson River Valley location of Brakebills (v. close to my childhood home and thus with its own magic for me); the fact that none of it is easy and that the characters' paths are often unclear; the ending with the many possibilities it opens up.

Narnia fan fiction gone bad. 
 Imagine taking a pleasant children's story, setting it out in the sun for two months until it's completely spoiled, and then writing that down. That is the promise of The Magicians--and it falls woefully short of even that unimaginative ambition. 
 This book was marketed to me as "Harry Potter for adults." The premise is indeed a school for witchcraft and wizardry, with older and more angsty characters. ALL of the characters, in fact, have so much teenage angst as to be completely unrelatable to an actual adult (presumably the target audience?) I would describe the characters (again, ALL of them) as uninspired, lethargic, and devitalized: this also describes the plot. 
 Finally, the whole book is set around the Narnia mythos laid out in "the Magicians Nephew"--but the incorporation is very clunky. It's as if the author meant to write a "Wicked" for Narnia, but then completely forgot this premise while writing the text, and had to go back and add in a sentence here or there to bolster this limping story along to its rushed, slapped together conclusion.

I spent the first half of the book waiting for it to actually begin. Grossman takes his main character, Quentin, through five years of school so quickly that it quickly becomes clear the book isn't about Quentin's time in school - that's just back story. Problem is, I never really came around to liking Quentin or his friends all that much. They drink a lot, and he is the sort who's always expecting happiness to be waiting for him around the next corner - after I get out of my home town, after I graduate, after this, after that . . . Of course, he never finds it. Reading about someone who's chronically miserable gets tiring after a while, even if it is true to life. I do like Grossman's writing style, the way he uses words and turns a phrase, which is probably the main reason I finished the book at all.

I wanted to like this book. I really did. It's been on my to-read list for a few years. But I just can't say it was good. 
 Despite that, I'll start with what this book did right. I think it's unfair to call it an adult version of Harry Potter. It's centered at a school of magic, but that's basically where the comparison ends to me. Although there are obvious calls back to the Narnia Chronicles, Grossman's overall concept was unique. He has the bare bones of something fairly original, and his perspective on the magic-fantasy world is different. I did want to know what happened in the story, and I kept reading for that reason. There's something THERE in this story, and maybe that's what frustrates me most about the finished product. 
 It feels like this book is a first draft, and it could have used a second massive rewrite to tighten things up and make it more engaging. The book just drags. Somehow it manages to drag at the same time it lacks enough detail. Most of the book comes across as Grossman giving us a synopsis of what the story's about. He has such a high-level narrative that it was hard to care about the details or feel engaged. A lot of the book seemed like he was writing to get to the story he really wanted to tell. 
 I wish we had spent more time at Brakebills and developed the characters and the plot better-- any time something interesting happened, it was mostly glossed over, and we spent pages and pages just reading about them doing the same stuff (drink, stay up late, study, drink, etc). The characters ended up being one-dimensional. I cared about the fate of no one. Details that seemed like they would be important (e.g. Quentin's discipline) are basically never mentioned again. 
 The book seems like a missed opportunity. It needed more complex plotting, characters, events, and decisions. I read to see if things would get more interesting and engaging, but unfortunately, I was disappointed.
Why did I even bother finishing this book?

Lev Grossman has written an "anti-novel", meaning that, where most novels start from the premise of a character who grows over the course of the story, changing in response to challenges and realizations and maturation, this novel features a protagonist who is wholly passive, narcissistic, spoiled, and unaware of his basic unpleasantness, and who remains so throughout the story. 
 The "young adult", Quentin, is a proclaimed, and self-proclaimed, genius, who is chosen to attend a College for Magic called Brakebills; contrary to his characterization by the author, he never does or says anything remotely clever or insightful in the course of the story. It is always difficult for an author to successfully demonstrate genius in a character when s/he is lacking that quality, and from the mess that Grossman makes of this novel, it is obvious why he tells instead of shows. 
 It is as if Grossman wants to subvert and contradict not only any expectations one may have for a novel of this type, but for fiction in general. Where there should be detail and exposition there is instead elision, so that readers have a vague idea of place and incident, as if the entire story was being told from behind a gauzy curtain. The narrative progresses in fits and starts, and nothing much happens in the 5-year course of the education of these students, except for the imbibing of much inferior liquor, and the PG-13 sexual fumblings that some of them get up to. A truly eerie and frightening incident with a spirit known as The Beast is the exception that proves the rule. 
 Once Quentin and his band of poorly sketched graduates leaves the confines of Brakebills for the bustle of the real world, and specifically, New York City, the drinking and general ennui continues, much to the disappointment of the reader. Never have those with so much privilege and power been so morose and aimless. (I'd say that this is Harry Potter meets Less Than Zero, but that would insult both works, since Grossman dares the reader to care for or identify with any of the characters in a way that is antithetical to the genuine affection that readers have for the Potter universe, at least.) 
 The final section of the book finds our kids using a magic button to travel to Fillory, an extremely lazy attempt to incorporate the world known to us as Narnia into the narrative. The author says he started by just referencing Narnia directly, but found that by changing some aspects of C.S. Lewis' creation he could more freely move the story in the direction he wished...by which he must mean off a cliff. Fillory, like Brakebills and New York, is a construct composed of both momentum-killing detail and under-developed geography so that at any particular moment the reader can describe the wallpaper in a room but can't say which of the main characters is actually present. 
 And why are our intrepid explorers in Fillory? Because Quentin is obsessed with the books (though he seems to have no sense of their allegorical or thematic super-structures), and demands that they all go. And they do. And things happen. The risk of spoiling the narrative keeps me from telling you what those things are, along with the feeling that nothing much happens anyway, nothing, anyway, that the author didn't just throw in willy-nilly to provide a semblance of action and consequence. There are sacrifices, suffering and loss, but nary a lesson learned by our poor dejected Quentin, who comes through the other side as obnoxious and boring as ever. 
 And so, it seems, the joke is on us. Grossman has dared us to care about his characters, thrill at their adventures, and learn from their mistakes; in the end, there are no characters, no adventures, and the mistake was ours, in picking up this ridiculous book to begin with.

I was indifferent to Portrait when I read it as a lit major, but a few years later I loved Ulysses, so after finally reading Dubliners, I decided to reread Joyce's first novel to see what difference 40 years might make to that initial judgment. Turns out not much at all. What accounts for this bookworm's indifference to an acclaimed novel by one of the greatest novelists in human history? Preferences, pure and simple. By the time I reached my late teens, I'd lost whatever taste I ever had for coming-of-age stories, and as Joyce's title clearly states, that's the whole point of this story. Although I loved the hyperbole of Stephen Dedalus's determination "to forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race," which clearly should have been the last line of the book, his journey from infancy to manhood simply didn't engage my head or my heart, and there was no one else to care for. For women, Joyce's madonna/whore complex made ciphers of his long-suffering mother and the gilded object of his desire, which left me feeling decidedly alienated from the story. Also contributing to that sense of alienation was the infamous sermon on the eternity of hell that leads Stephen to renounce his wicked ways. From the vantage of 2014, I find it hard to understand how any intelligent being could actually believe in hellfire and damnation, and nothing in the novel up to that point made me believe that Stephen actually did. That combination of preferences, lack of engagement, and overall alienation from the story is what accounts for my indifference. Although Joyce's first novel may be masterful sentence by sentence, as a whole it didn't work for me because it failed to engender the fictional dream that is the hallmark of a memorable reading experience. Times change, and as they do, only a handful of towering literary immortals will be able to always capture the imagination of contemporary readers. Almost 100 years after it appeared, Portrait doesn't strike me as one of the immortals.

This is a book about rebellion into pretentious stupidity. It's the story of a spoiled brat raised inside the beautiful on a quest for beauty. The Catholic Church has its faults. But we have seen this type of story before: a young man is appalled at his own sin and becomes a monk. He sees the hypocrisy and false teaching of the Church and then rebels by trying to correct it. This is courage. This was Martin Luther. Stephen is the one who reacts in the opposite. He throws the baby out with the bath water because he thinks he knows everything. His endless dialogue with his friend stinks of self-aggrandizement. When you reject the Truth, you crown yourself king. Well done, James Joyce. You have shone the spotlight on how unoriginal you really are. Rebellion is old and there are plenty of people in our day and age just like you.

I'll make this brief. Portrait is a simple story. a boy grows up to be a man, drops out of university to follow his dreams and in the process lets go of his religion. Sounds simple enough. It's been told several hundred times in any number of bildenstrums. Except one difference: none of those other stories have been written by James Joyce: literary giant, writer extraordinaire, artiste of the highest order. 
 I admit that much of the descriptive melodies drifted straight over my head. I confess the Catholic sermons and religious metaphors, Dantes allusions were way too complex for this simple Jewish student of literature. Ill freely tell you that I found Stephen Dedalus a bit of a dandy, his father a weak spirited alcoholic and his friends a bit too spoilt and self-important (well aren't all liberal arts university students?). 
 However I am more of a man for reading Portrait. I think I have gained a better understanding of what religion can do to us if we let it (take that however you wish), a more thorough belief in my own visions for a happy life and a clearer concept of what beauty is or can be. 
 Finally I am now in a position to say that to write a book which will out live all of us and then some is perhaps one of the most challenging and difficult things a person could do. To ensure each word is grouped to form perfect sentences, to form perfect structure and perfect phrases. Joyce did just that. It's a difficult read. A really difficult read, but one I'm glad I slogged through. And for that I'm grateful.
