It's one of those books you're supposed to read. It's also on all those lists of books you're supposed to read before you die. Sometimes those are books that can change your life or change your perspective. Sometimes they make you wonder if the people who make the lists have actually read the books or just heard about them. Maybe it just means I'm dense and this book was too deep for me. 
 It's got a rambling narrative, filled mostly with conversation. Stephen Daedalus is a student, having a crisis of faith. He's also young and jovial and has a bunch of friends that he has conversations with. It's a pretty dry read. On the plus side, I'd rather spend a day with Stephen Daedalus than with Holden Caulfield. That guy I just wanted to slap. 
 Even worse, I'm supposed to love this book because I'm Irish. I feel like a total race traitor. Perhaps your mileage will greatly vary and you will love the book dearly. You can call me an obtuse philistine, and I will just remind you that there are lots of books, and not every book is for every reader.

I honestly believe a lot of people say they adored this book or that they thought it was amazing, just to seem smart. Like: "Oh, look, I've read a James Joyce novel! I'm just going to say it was great so that people think I'm smart." 
 I'm not saying everybody is like that, just that a lot are. 
 Personally, (not to be pretentious,) I do consider myself to be a relatively intelligent person and a person used to tackling "difficult" and demanding pieces of literature, but this, seriously, I cannot say that I enjoyed it. 
 Yes, the concept is interesting (how the language and style evolves as the "young artist" gets older), but DUDE, this book is TEDIOUS as hell. 
 Little Dedalus changes his mind quite a lot (for instance from zealous Catholic - who looked all over Dublin to find a priest to take his confession... - to a non-believer that doesn't even want to go to one "Easter celebration" to please his mother. My thoughts on this specific part of the novel: "Oh please, just go and shut up about it! You were brave enough to go to prostitutes as a fervent Catholic, then now at least man up and go to church with your mother...") 
 If everybody talked - acted - thought like Dedalus (aka Joyce) the world would be blown to smithereens. 
 Never rereading this one. Nope.

1.5 stars. 
 Because I loathe, abhor, detest, hate Stephen Dedalus. Joyce's writing is revolutionary because he pretty much invented stream-of-consciousness, but what beautiful writing there is is buried under the field of shit that is called Stephen Dedalus and the earliest recorded case of Speshul Snowflake Syndrome in the world. 
 For a character-driven novel (and this was a character driven novel) to have such an unlikable character is just...no. Couldn't enjoy it at all. 
 ...it was like I know that I was supposed to be loving the writing, and I distantly realized that oh hey this sounds nice here and this sounds nice there but the slogging was just so painful.

In terms of entertainment value, this would have to rank somewhere in between a scholastic text on plumbing and your average phone book. Nothing about this book is interesting. Not the cover, not the title, not the obligatory forward hailing the author's genius, nothing. It's the literary equivalent of getting a vasectomy with even less potential for arousal. Think I'm joking? This is your mind on Joyce: 
 Title Page: Chapter 1. "Once upon a time" -promising enough start- "and a very good time it was" -oh my, I wonder why- "there was a moocow coming down along the road" -a what? does he mean cow?- "and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy" -a what little boy?- "named baby tucktoo..." -baby what? a moocow? a nicens moocow named tucktoo? did I get that straight?- "his father looked at him through a glass: he had a hairy face. He was baby tucktoo." -wait... the father is named baby tucktoo? with a hairy face? and a moocow is involved?- "the moocow came down the road where Betty Byrne lived: she sold lemon platt." -Lemon what?- "O, the wild rose blossoms On the little green place" -a little green place where Betty sells lemon platt?- "He sang that song. That was his song." -How lovely- "O, the green wothe botheth." -ummm... this might have been a mistake... 
 But I, ever persistent in my unfounded optimism that books with horrible starts written by supposed icons are bound to get better, read on... and on... regaining consciousness somewhere around page 105. 
 "'Well now, Ennis, I declare you have a head and so has my stick!'" -oooh, nice one!- "'Do you mean to say that you are not able to tell me what a surd is?'" -Oh, the nerve! my, surely everyone knows what a surd is!- "On the wall of his bedroom hung an illuminated scroll, the certificate of his prefecture in the college of the sodality of the Blessed Virgin Mary." -sodal prefectural virgins in college? Fascinating!- "Quasi cedrus exalta sum in Libanon et quasi cupressus in monte Sion. Quasi palma exaltata sum in Gades et quasi plantatio rosae in Jericho." -oh right, the place where Joshua walked along the wall- Quasi uliva speciosa in campis et quasi platanus exaltata sum juxta aquam in plateis. Sicut cinnamomum et balsamum aromatizans odorem dedi et quasi myrrha electa dedi suavitatem odoris." -oh wait, was that all in Latin? I couldn't even tell! It makes about as much sense as moocows and surds! 
 Enter 50 pages of a Priest talking about hell. Summary: It's hot. Funny thing is, this was the best part of the book... because the writing was actually comprehensible. Just so you're not confused, I don't mean that this part was good. Just that I understood the concept that hell = hot. 
 "April 15, April 16th, April 26th" -me oh my, the days are flying!- "Welcome, O life!"-another exclamation point!- "I go to encounter for the millionth time the reality of experience and to forge in the smithy of my soul the uncreated conscience of my race" -this line apparently is important as it is written on the back of my edition. Yes, that was what the publisher deemed the highlight- "April 27th. Old father, old artificer, stand me now and ever in good stead."-oh, way to end the chapter! real cliffhanger!- "Classic Literature: Adapted Words and Phrases" - wait... you mean that was really the end? That sucks!!! I mean, thank bloody Jesus! 
 Did I mention this is a riveting read? Sure to enthrall and entertain readers of all ages and abilities, particularly the illiterate and those without the gift of sight. 
 I could go two ways on this. 1) Fess up that I am clearly not trained in whatever higher powers of tolerance and obtuseness is needed to even pretend enjoyment while reading this or, 2) blame the teachers who shove books by authors like Joyce and Faulkner down the throats of their pupils and then, years later while curled in semi-retirement on the couch with their hair in rollers bemoan the fact that those former pupils and millions like them no longer read but sit their asses in front of a TV screen watching Real Housewives. Is it any wonder? If this was the only shit I'd read in school I'd be an advocate for book burnings. 
 James Joyce, despite the repeated J which gives his the name of a possible superhero (e.g. Peter Parker, Bruce Banner... i.e. someone INTERESTING) is about as much fun to read on the page as Roman Polanski would be to have photographing your daughter's 13th birthday party. In other words, not much. Funny thing is, Joyce's one-time pupil, Italo Svevo, wrote a very interesting book that I'd highly recommend called 'Zeno's Conscience.' No one gets called on their inability to identify a "surd" in it. Talk about the pupil eclipsing the master. 
 It's not that I don't like classic literature. Charles Dickens, Alexandre Dumas, Oscar Wilde, etc, are all brilliant and, despite having written their final words before last century manage to still remain interesting and relevant. It's just that the only thing classic about this is how old it is. Sorry to break it to you, JJ, but you're about as relevant as milk delivered fresh to your door from the moocow's teat. A real treat for buzzards and dullards, to use carefully refined, Joyce-ian "prose." 
 Highly recommended for the narcoleptic masochists out there.

What can I say about this novel... (?) 
 Reading "A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man" prior to "Ulysses" is, in my opinion, indispensable. DO NOT, in any circumstance, do a "direct assault" reading Ulysses...You'll happily bleed to death... but you'll still end up dead anyway.... Ulysses should be admired not feared or, worse, abandoned... 
 I have now a firmer grasp thinking about the "Proteus" episode after reading this masterpice- why such mood of Stephen's character, why such musings...such depth and scope of Stephen's "internal monologue" (Before tackling "Ulysses", it's better to discover the "why" by reading "A Portrait" first before consulting any "critical essays" Joycean books for "proper acclimatization"). "A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man" offered the base for the character of Stephen Dedalus in Ulysses to "get him". 
 Stephen is a fascinating character... there were brilliant moments of Stephen- profound and erudite, but there were also "Aw, c'mon Stephen!" moments were I find him too philosophical, headstrong and drastic a character for his age, i.e., with life experience- his yoke is already too heavy, bordering to conceived diasporic melodrama. 
 The genius of Joyce is that, he brought me in that period... I read the book like an omnipresent, invisible true friend of Stephen Dedalus. I wanted to interject with his conversations with Lynch and Cranly, to look over the window with Stephen observing Dubliners walking about their business, to amble away with Stephen on his wanderings around Dublin and see life as one sees it. The struggle of finding/ reestablishing the Irish identity against imperialism and the orthodoxy of religion, and Stephen's disgust of his countrymen's degeneracy and servility were genius.

I wanted to like this book and was excited about reading it; I was attracted by the lack of a traditional narrative and the book's reputation and Joyce's reputation. I enjoyed the early descriptions of Stephen's family, the descriptions of his school days especially when he had a fever, the questioning of his faith in particular the vivid description of hell (though this was perhaps a few pages too long), and the way Stephen finally overcomes the pressures of country, family and Catholicism. Some descriptive passages were memorable and powerful, for example the play, and the evening where Stephen Dedalus ends up on the beach. 
 I think the book is probably of greatest interest to scholars and academics and those interested in the history of literature (and in particular the modernist phase). I'd liken it to experimental music whilst it makes an important statement it doesn't necessarily make for a good listen, or in this case a good read. The lengthy university conversations towards the end of the book are particularly tedious. I'm unsure what Joyce was trying to say, and wonder about the point of the book. I don't feel I gained very much by reading it, and would not recommend it. Perfectly fine, but vastly overrated by many.

Knowing this book would not be my cup of tea, I "read" the audio book and finished it today. The sermon within the text might have caused me to put the traditional book form aside (which I almost never do), but multi-tasking with audio, I was able to slog through. ** spoiler alert **

All I can say is: Thank goodness that's over!! 
 I'm sure I really didn't understand it, but it doesn't make me even halfway interested in trying to understand it. At least I know what it's about, and I can mark it off the list!
Moocow! What a beginning

The blurb on the back of my copy says: "Written with a light touch, this is perhaps the most accessible of Joyce's works." If this is true, I am never reading another book by James Joyce. I completely bounced off this, I just didn't get it at all. It's taken me so long to read because I kept giving and starting again, or just putting it down and not having the energy or the will to pick it up again for a few months. I'm probably just stupid, but to me it just felt like a load of incoherent, disconnected thoughts interspersed with a difficult to follow story of someone growing up in Ireland.
Did not appeal to me AT ALL. It was a chore to finish it.

I thought this book was so pretentious when I read it as a teenager. a few years ago, I made it through the first twenty six pages of Finnegan's Wake and hated it. but I just listened to the audio book, and I have to say, that was the key. I adored it this time. and I am actually actively looking forward to reading it again when I teach it this year, and making a go at Ulysses too, though definitely with the audio as a companion. sometimes things are meant to be heard, much in the way Shakespeare was meant to be seen.
Required reading, college. I have no interest in stream of consciousness writing. It drives me mad.
completely ridiculous and really hard to follow.

In the future I probably won't remember anything about this book except that the Catholic idea of hell sounds truly terrifying. I was so not into this book. I've always wanted to read Ulysses but now I'm hesitant. I feel terrible giving it one star but I really didn't like it.
I liked Dubliners, so I thought I might like more Joyce... guess this was not the one for me. Maybe I'll try again someday. Maybe.

A highly cerebral book that is part philosophy, part psychology, and part a reflection of the truth, all neatly wrapped in the presentation of a fictional piece of work. 
 Similar to Joyce's "Dubliners," this novel's conclusion feels dissatisfying and very open-ended.
Classic.

This was a painful reading experience for me. 
 *shudders*
Shows how Irish Catholicism, as opposed to Roman Catholicism, permeates every aspect of a young person's life - not always to their advantage.
I don't remember enjoying anything I read my junior year of high school with the possible exception of Hamlet.
I suppose it's good, but I couldn't stand the language.
I was only a freshman in high school when I read this, so it's probably time to give it another try. I don't know that fifteen-year-olds are really ready for Joyce's style. At least, I wasn't.

book_b.title: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (Millennium, #1)
book_b.user_review: The book gave some interesting insights into Nazi movements and political assassinations in Sweden. What I didn't like was that Salandar isn't a very realistic character: she's so intelligent that she comes across as more of a super-hero. That would be fine for a super-hero novel, but it kind of ruins the realistic setting Larsson attempts to create in the rest of the book. It was a quick read, but in the field of mega-hit murder mysteries I found "DaVinci Code" a much more captivating page-turner.

sample_reviews.review_text: Get past the first 100 pages and you'll love it; I promise!
This book is amazing. Can't wait to read the other 2.

In a word? Overrated. I don't read THAT many "thriller" or mystery books, but on occasion. The first half of the book was exceedingly dull. Yes, it got much better in the second, but compared to, say, The Silence of the Lambs, it wasn't even close, tension-wise. And the "Girl" character... of course the 25-year-old bisexual can't resist the mid-forties protagonist who kept saying "I just want to be your friend!"

My motivation for buying this book stemmed mostly from seeing it on bestseller shelves for a year or so. I was a sucker and fell for the brilliantly applied title. I love mystery books, let's just start with that. I think that the fact that this book centered around an unsolved murder was a great way for Larsson to address his larger theme: men hating women, essentially. The way Larsson frames his story is what made the book for me. I love that he uses the main character Mikael Blomkvist as being the investigatory journalist. Though Mikael is morally ambiguous about many things, Larsson lets the reader see that even Mikael is disgusted with the sexual assaults on these women. What I disliked about this book was its tendency to drag on; I think he could have made an even stronger case for the story in about 100 pages less. Another thing I didn't quite like is the explicit detail of the acts of sexual violence. I do, however, understand that this detail was put in precisely for people to feel bleak and disgusted that such acts are occurring in our world, which is justifiable and understandable. That being said, this book is not for the weak of heart or the weak of stomach. I think this book was well-written with an excellent plot, but did not cater to my style of taste.

So far, I would only give it two stars. It is a difficult read. The translation from his native language to english was a rough attempt to put the novel into classical writing prose. The complex sentences are difficult, feel very forced, and lack continuity. The story, I fear, is getting lost in the translation.

I'm so glad I'm done this damn book. I really don't get all the hype, and suspect it's more popular because Larsson died before it was published. (People love that shit.) Enough weird sex stuff to make me wonder about the author, and a story-line that could have been more neatly composed. It definitely didn't need to be so long. I won't be reading the other "girls" in the series. 
 And was there a woman Blomkvist didn't have sex with in this novel?
Gary Sue, meet Mary Sue; Mary Sue, meet Gary Sue. Enough said. This book may experience a down-grading of stars upon further reflection.[Update: downgrade complete]

Brilliant writing, Steig Larsson has edited the book to perfection. Characters are well developed and are easy to hate/love. The plot kept me guessing right up until the end. 
 One of those rare books that everybody says you must read and one that I actually agree with.

DNF 25% 
 I can't force myself to continue this... Just not my kind of book.
I hated this book. I think the author was sonewhat of a perve.

the first book in the widely-read but over-estimated millenium series does a good job of introducing us to the main characters of the novels, blomkvist and salander, and keeping us interested in them. it also teaches you a lot about corporate crime in sweden. i found the structure of the novel exceptionally exasperating, and my first experience with the dead ends of the book found me exceptionally frustrated. i certainly wanted to know what was going to happen but the road to finding out was arduous, and i kept wishing that somebody had edited the hell out of the book -- i'm sure i would've liked it a lot more. this is the most grotesque of the three books: if you get through the level of violence in this one, you'll find that the other two are staid in comparison.

The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo explores the mystery of the Vanger family and has an intriguing plot worthy of a thriller. However, author hasn't developed the main characters Mikael and Lisabeth in depth and they are less interesting than the Vanger family members. At around the same time, I read Carlos Ruiz Zafron's The Shadow of the Wind and the writing in the latter was much more enjoyable than Stieg Larsson's novel. I read the English translations of both novels, so the difference could result from the translators' skills. The novel has flaws, but I recommend The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo for readers interested in plot-driven novels.

I had no idea what I had bought at the airport when I got this, only that it was a cheap 600+ page paperback and I had no book for my flight back and not much money to do away with. The shelf said 'best seller', but that didn't really reassure me much, given that a lot of the best selling stuff is not for me at all (I'm looking at you, Harry Potter and Twilight!). 
 This is a great crime mystery novel. Every blurb in the back was true for me, it wasn't instant love, but it was definitely instant like, and by the middle of it I was having trouble putting it down at work. The characters are really lively and interesting, everyone has a story to tell, and when all is said and done it leaves you wanting more -and for a 600+ page book that deals mostly in character development and setting, that's a big achievement, I think. The plot is intricate and takes a lots of twists and turns -there's the financial fraud expose, the kidnappings, the murder, the disappearances... all this set in Sweden, which is not a country I know well at all, which gives this the added perk of showing you around a bit of Swedish culture and geography. I also didn't expect a book that deals so heavily about violence against women to be so full of 'hell yeah!' moments. Lisbeth -the female outcast co-protagonist- is so full of the HELL YEAH that I really wish I could see where else she would go. 
 It does haves its failings as a book, of course -the author dates the narrative a lot- but they were minor enough that they barely mattered to me. Of course, I'm not a hacker or a financial expert or any of the occupations that the author takes a lot of time explaining -giving too many details can easily tear your narrative down- so if you're a hacker or a financial expert or a reporter or, I don't know, a detective, you might find more flaws in it than I did.
Just couldn't get into this series
Read this book after watched the film. I enjoy the book as much as the film..

Wish I would have known more about this book before jumping in. An engrossing early plot, but fell flat toward the middle. It wasn't worth the time it took to read and featured repulsive sexual crimes I didn't expect. 
 I was originally 14th on the waiting list at my library. Conclusion: not worth the wait or the time it took to read. My advice: don't bother with this 'international best-seller'.

So... 2 stars say it was okay, 3 stars say I liked it. It would be somewhere in between. The story is amazingly written, and the 700+ pages and small print really pack a lot of stuff into it. I didn't realize what the book was like, I was expecting a very different kind of mystery. Yes it is phenominally written, if only it wasn't full of the f* word, really, was that necessary? I could get the story just the same without all the profanity. That annoys me. And the story is definitely not for the faint-hearted. Very raw, too-honest portrayal of extremely difficult subjects.
GwDT was enjoyable, and the fact that I was able to read all 465 or so pages indicates that it was interesting. But I didn't think it was anything special.
The literary equivalent of a bad hot dog: mostly filler, causes headaches, and just stuffed with assholes.

This is one of those times when you really could have just watched the movie. The movie was so well made that it's kinda boring reading the book. Sure there are differences, but they are so small. I'm talking about the Swedish version of the movie. Both had their merits, but the Swedish version most closely follows the book. All in all, a great read.

I found this story slow, dry, weirdly dark, and convoluted. When I made it 70 pages in and the story still hadn't really started yet, I gave up. I then tried to watch the original movie, thinking that perhaps I could at least get a better understanding of the story-line through a director's eyes, for starters. I gave up on that too. I felt like I was slugging through mud to get through the narrative. I would compare this story to the movie, the "Black Swan." Both have the same dark, nightmarish, and mentally unstable qualities to the characters and scenes. (The ones that I saw/read, anyway.)

One of the best "who did it" type mystery novel that I've read to date. Lisbeth, one of the main characters intrigued me almost as much as the plot did. I don't want to spoil this for others so I'll leave this review kind of bare and simply say that I highly recommend this book if you like a good mystery.

I did enjoy this book, however I feel like there was a LOT of build up in the beginning and it made it hard to fall into the "hype" that I have heard about this book. Even though that isn't a requirement, I was a little sad that I didn't quite understand the hype. However, I did LOVE the book from the middle-ish to the end. Mikael Blomkvist was a great main character and I loved the way that his character played off Salander.

Hearing the hype around this book I decided to give it a chance figuring it was something special. Boy was I wrong. More than 50% of the book consists of just a round about gesture following the two main characters through life as they each go through a transitional period. The point was utterly lost on me and I could not even get far enough to figure out how they come to connect. Unfortunately the author did not weave a tale that kept me reading and ultimately took to long to get to the point of the story, that is the apparent murder mystery. 
 The entire book felt like it was just a setup for another book down the line, which to me felt like a wasted printing of words.

THIS BOOK MADE ME WISH I'D NEVER LEARNED TO READ. 
 okay, my dad asked me to expand on my review. i hated this stupid book, i truly did. there is a long list of reasons why i hated it, the first being that i can't call it trash because what larsson sets out to do is not trash. also i hated how it treated women and mentally ill people, i hated the portrayal of ultra-violence against women, i thought it was totally unnecessary. i didn't like the style of writing -- i hated the precision of every stupid movement every character made. i thought the mysteries were stupid, and i though blomkvist was super annoying and had a pointless existence. the ending made me want to kill everything in face and yeah, i know that it was a cliff-hanger so we'd buy his next stupid books but ugh i just wanted to get that book out of my life and then all of a sudden there was that moment of "maybe i should. . ." before remembering "NO NO NO NO NO NO GET IT AWAY." 
 i also hate that i finished the book in two and a half days, thus forcing me to admit that there was something compelling about the book because it is not every book that i waste two days of my life reading, no matter of disgusting or uncomfortable* or boring or annoying. 
 *(i just want to point out that i'm literature major and i am TOTALLY OKAY being made uncomfortable or disgusted by books if it is to a higher, more important purpose. but this book was all shock and no value.)

I cannot rave about this book and in this genre I think Tana French is a better novelist. It wasn't awful, the plot was decent but the writing was really average; of course that could be the translation. I would not recommend anyone running to grab this read.

Although the financial details in this book get a little hard to follow, it's worth sticking it out to the end and just skimming over them. You need to have a general idea what's going on to follow the plot, but don't worry about committing it all to memory and keeping track of it. This book has a surprising twist at the end. Looking forward to reading the next one!

Content: explicit sexual content, S&M, vulgar profanity. 
 Not my style - didn't finish it.
"What she realized was that love was the moment when your heart was about to burst."

This is one of the most adult content filled books I have ever read. 
 Let's just say it was so bad that I will not even be reselling the book I will be throwing it away.
Well that was disappointing...

I must admit after all the hype about this book I was very disappointed. Not being familiar with Sweden, I found a lot of the story boring. I also found the book to be pretty predictable. It is the story of a family plagued with financial problems, murder and the disappearance of a family member. Of course the necessary sexual issues are there also.

This was a disgusting book, sexually. 
 I didn't finish it. It started out pretty good but got to be more about promiscuity and rape. I'm not talking -suggestive writing and you know what happened. On the contrary, the author is quite detailed. I read other reviews and it turns out there is just more disgusting sex. I'm kicking myself for not reading more reviews before I started. 
 I'm disappointed in society; this book has a high star rating. 
 As a side note, this is one of those books with lots of pointless detail. You're constantly wondering, "Do I need to remember all of these things? Is this crucial?" There's just too much and it often made the book move too slowly.
Almost didn't get through it as it just started out too slowly for me. Ended up enjoying it.

It was kind of frightening kind of book but the mystery really caught me! I enjoyed it to the very end and start the second one right away! Though kind of fantastic it also give the sensation that it could actually happen...

Maybe the hype was a little much for me because I did not love this book like I thought I might. I wonder if this would've been so touted if it was published when the author was still alive. Anyway, it was a touch more character-driven and literary than most thrillers, which was a positive. And there were definitely some un-put-downable parts of the book (but not all the book). In the end, some of the resolutions were too obvious, some were too neat, and some were too far-fetched. Still, though, a worthwhile read. But I have no desire to read the sequels.

In my opinion, this immensely popular book is terrible. Exploitative, poorly written, and pretending to bring up real issues such as violence against women and bisexuality pretty much entirely as an excuse to present them as bad semi-pornography.

I heard so many great things about this book/author. I wonder if someone scrambled the electrons when I d/l from Kindle. It kinda stunk. Long and boring. I guess if you lived in Sweden you'd be a fan.
I loved this book! I can't wait to read the next one when it's released in the states. I recommend it to anyone who likes crime mysteries. Has a little something for everyone.
Pretty decent story, a little graphic and explicit at times ~ was a little challenging for me to get into, but overall, a decent summer read.

I was really excited to read this book after all the hype - but was very disappointed. This book was very long and quite boring. I was hoping after a few chapters the story would pick up some speed and actually get to the point but it didn't!! This book is very, very over rated and wouldn't recommend it. I found the beginning of the book a bit boring and very very very very slow. 
 The first half of the book (almost 250 pages) is slow, with not much happening. This portion could easily be removed and replaced by 50 or 80 pages.
Fast paced, great characters, a very enjoyable read.

I can understand why some people would not like this book; it's a slow-burn mystery about an entire family who is despicable. If you aren't into mysteries and have trouble keeping track of a lot of characters, this book is probably going to drive you insane. That being said, it was really fascinating to me and well done. 
 I read this book years ago (2011 I think) but had pretty much forgotten everything that happened so I picked it up again to refresh my memory. I'm glad I did! All of the curiosity and surprise from the first read were present again and the ending still got me. 
 You can tell Steig Larsson had a huge problem with misogyny because the entire book is about terrible men taking advantage and harming women. If this is going to trigger you, definitely stay away. 
 I'm not sure if I'll continue on with the series to be honest. I feel like everything was wrapped up neatly and I'm satisfied; however, I would like to explore Salander's life more and I believe the next book is in her perspective. We shall see!
good, but a little too descriptive for my liking for violent activites and between the sheets encounters.

I stopped reading after 50 pages. The writing was horrendous. Hated the characters. Thought I'd give the story another chance when the movie came around. Got a little further, but walked out after about an hour. I can't believe publisher foist this kind of crap on an unsuspecting public.
For the full review (including random references to both Arrested Development and Futurama), follow the link to That's What She Read.

I don't get the hype with this book. While I liked the concept, and it started out very promising, the story was like a long boring car ride. They could have edited out half of this book and then maybe it would have sustained my interest instead of putting me to sleep. But I did really like the movie. At least I got to find out what happened in the end because I abandoned the book.

3.5 stars? I guess? 
 I love financial books. I've read plenty of them. But the beginning setup of this book almost stymied me. After slogging through that, the actual mystery was entertaining. I was squicked out by all the violence against women (though I loved Salander's revenge). Lisbeth herself is almost superhero-like, which was annoying, but her inner musings were way more interesting than Mikhal's. I'll read the sequel but I hope it doesn't start so boring.

Lisabeth salander and Blomkvist confrontation is nail-bitting moment!! 
 certain catchy quotes still lingers on my mnd 
 "Consequence and analysis" is imprinted into lisabeth.... 
 No acting on impulses 
 the fact that Martin Vanger raped her out in the cabin or that you're going to do it in print? 
 INTELLIGENT CRITICISM 
 Finally correspondence in e-mail is nice to read
Was this work meant to be comical? I couldn't help but notice the gallons of coffee drank and the endless sandwiches consumed both done to the extreme point of comedy.

reference_books.title: Les Misérables
reference_books.review_text: This is a beautiful classic. I only read the abridged version in high school and have had the full length sitting on my shelf for years. I'm definitely going to have to pick it up again soon and get lost in this story.

reference_books.title: Girls in White Dresses
reference_books.review_text: This book was hilarious and honest. Something every girl should read, especially with her girl friends.

reference_books.title: Why We Broke Up
reference_books.review_text: It would have been nice if he knew how to write a story from a teenage girls POV. I'd break up with Min too. So annoying.

reference_books.title: The Perks of Being a Wallflower
reference_books.review_text: I read this book for the first time right before I started my freshman year of high school. It was so wonderful to read something I really related to. I think it's a great book to read if you feel misunderstood, or awkward, which most of us do at the beginning of high school.

reference_books.title: My Heart and Other Black Holes
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I really wanted to love this book but it fell flat. I found myself more annoyed with Aysel & Roman and their problems when I thought I should be rooting for them. Teenage depression is a close subject to my heart and I don't believe parents are as blind to their children's depression as this book would have you believe. Also the lack of encouragement for seeking professional help made me upset because if teenagers read this book & think getting a boyfriend can fix their depression then they're in for a rude awakening.

reference_books.title: Peter Pan
reference_books.review_text:
Eh I know I'll probably be stoned for not enjoying this. Maybe I expected too much from it. Maybe 18 wasn't a good age to read it at. I don't know exactly what made me dislike it, I just know I didn't feel satisfied afterwards. 
 I think I'll have to pick it up again though because everything deserves a second chance, especially a classic like Peter Pan.

reference_books.title: The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I loved reading this book. It was smart, funny, and there was never a clear idea of whodunit until the end. Rowling is great at drawing you into her world and I really felt like I was right there with Strike in his dingy office. If you're a fan of crime dramas you would probably really enjoy this read.

reference_books.title: We Were Liars
reference_books.review_text: Whiny people of privilege experiencing crippling tragedy does not necessarily make me feel sympathy the way I believe the author hoped I would. And while it's nice to figure out the mystery half way through the book, it made the other half hard to get through. I'm happy that I listened to the audio book at 1.5 speed rather than physically reading it.

reference_books.title: Twilight (Twilight, #1)
reference_books.review_text: all i can say is i think i may have strained my eyes from rolling them so much... and where the heck was her editor? did they go on vacation and forget to edit this book. 500 pages of grimaces and staring at each other. ugh. UGGGHHH!!!

reference_books.title: Tampa
reference_books.review_text: Just holy crap. This book is crazy but I couldn't stop listening. The audiobook makes the sound of the young boys even more cringeworthy.

book_a.title: The Spectacular Now
book_a.user_review: I really wanted to love this book, but I was so disappointed. Sutter is a lovable enough character, and I loved his attitude of wanting to live in the moment, but his constant drinking & blaming others for his problems was annoying. You want him to do better, make better choices, not be so selfish. You want him to learn and grow! I kept hoping right up to the very end that he would have some kind of redeeming quality that would give me hope for him even after the book ends, but no. He's a selfish teenage boy that thinks he's doing some good in this world by befriending Aimee. He never appreciates her support and just writes it off as nothing when she really could have helped him grow up. His Peter Pan complex lost it's fun about 1/2 way through the book and I ended up just feeling sad for him.

sample_reviews.review_text: Am I the only person who thinks Sutter is going to be okay? A lot of reviews said they were fearful that he was going to die in the end. There were definitely times I thought something horrible was about to happen. The Story does feel a little incomplete a coming of age that never really is realized in a way.

I was quite disappointed by this novel overall because it started out so promising. None of the characters were likable and little to none character development. I'm not quite sure what the author was trying to say about teens or what the message was, because honestly it wasn't a positive one. The ending left me feeling empty and hopeless; not how you want to walk away from a story. It was an easy read and well-written, but cannot recommend.
I think my review might be biased since I saw the movie first. I just thought it was ok

Reading "the Spectacular Now" was literary deja vu. From the first time something "really gets" Sutter, to every "helluva," I was reading "the Catcher in the Rye" transported into 2008. Even Sutter's beverage of choice emulates Holden Caufield, and how is wanting to "save" Aimee Finnecky any different from wanting to stand at the edge of a field and catch children before they cascade over a cliff. 
 Despite this, "The Spectacular Now" is enjoyable. I can see how it "speaks" to teenagers in the midst of their own identity crises and is certainly full of sweet characters. 
 However, the Salinger-esque writing, plot, characters, cliches and absence of protagonist character development have left me with a familiar disappointment that I felt in Holdeb Caufield, only this time, it extends beyond character to the entire novel. Surely Tim Tharp could have done better? Could have been more original? 
 Don't let this pessimistic review deter you from reading "the Spectacular Now." It is a novel to be enjoyed at face value and without analysis Sutter is sweet and lively "embracing the weird." But like every angsty YA tale there's an underlying emotional plot, and it's here Tharp fails to bring any uniqueness to his novel.
Maybe I didn't get the point of this book, but it just didn't work for me.

Sutter Keely - he's cool, he's fun, he's the life of the party. He's also irresponsible, unreliable and a bit of an alcoholic. Nothing really matters to Sutter apart from wining back his ex-girlfriend and his next drink. That is until he wakes up one morning on Aimee Finecky's lawn. Poor Aimee has none of the awesomeness of Sutter and so he takes it upon himself to introduce her to his spectacular world. Only it seems he gets in a little too deep. For the first time in his life Sutter has the chance to make a difference but can he handle it? 
 The life of Sutter Keely is indeed spectacular. Sutter, the world's most high functioning teenage alcoholic is a loveable ne'er-do-well who takes us on the journey that is his life. Philosophical, funny and full of heart Sutter is easy to like even if he's cheesy (constantly referring to himself as "Sutterman" in fact that he actually refers to himself in the third person makes The Persnickety Rapscallion roll her eyes. See what I did there? Clever right?) 
 There's also the fact that he is, as previously stated, a high functioning alcoholic. And no one seems particularly perturbed by this fact. While I read I kept asking myself, "Is it really possible that his mother just doesn't notice that her son is in a perpetual state of drunkenness? Or is she really just a crap mother?" Neither of which questions are ever answered, or even broached. Which I suppose explains Sutter's disdain for commitment, in his experience people really don't seem to care so why should he? But he does care. Which is what leads him to do stupid things, like try to "save" Aimee. 
 Aimee Finecky - now there's an interesting character. The complete opposite of our man Sutter, she's quiet, shy, neat and nerdy (at least in Sutter's estimation, I mean sure there's nothing remotely sexy about a giant purple coat, mostly because all it brings to mind is images of Grimace but nonetheless - you know, different strokes and all that.) She's also a doormat, pushed around by her family and her best friend - who possibly comes equipped with one of the best descriptions I've ever read, "Krystal Krittenbrink is what you'd call amorphous - a blob." Amazing. Aimee's also full of hopes and dreams and yet for all her sweetness and intelligence she gets so wrapped up in Sutter and his way of life (particularly the drinking) that you start to wonder if she's going to throw away all that hard work in order to keep Sutter around. 
 Sutter and Aimee's relationship is at times sweet and at other times painful. Sutter, so desperate to bring Aimee out of her shell and and for her to recognize her self-worth doesn't realize the negatives his influence is having on her. And Aimee so eager to please and amazed that the super cool Sutter Keely would even be interested in her is unwilling to acknowledge Sutter's flaws. It killed me every time she apologized to him for his stupidity. 
 There's also the fact that throughout most of their friendship/relationship Sutter's still jonesing to get back with his ex-girlfriend who dumped him, yet he continues to allow things with Aimee to progress towards a relationship. Sutter truly is an ass. (A likeable ass, but an ass nonetheless.) 
 There are some really great minor characters in this story, specifically Sutter's best friend Ricky - who embodies the idea of growing up and maturing, and Sutter's ex Cassidy who recognizes that though he's chock full of good times, Sutter's incapable of providing the stability and reliability anyone would want in a relationship. 
 The contempt Sutter feels towards his mother, the fact that he blames her for his father's disappearance from his life, that he lies to his friends about where his father works offer brief glimpses into the part of Sutter he hides away. When he finally see's his father after so many years and realizes that his mother wasn't lying, that his father was a cheat and a good-for- nothing it's kind of the smack in the face he's needed all this time. It was a glimpse into his future if he keeps on the same path. It also makes him realize he's not what Aimee needs (thank god for that.) 
 The book is littered with references to God (Sutter's mantra: "I am God's own drunk") which I guess goes along with our main characters messiah complex which ironically also happens to be his fatal flaw. Sutter's desire to always be kind, to make people feel good is what leads him to leading on Aimee and taking things too far, even in breaking up with her he beats around the bush and skates over the issue to avoid causing her pain not realizing that what he's doing will ultimately cause her more pain then if he just told her the truth. 
 He's a complex guy, Sutter. 
 Let's talk about the ending, because when it happened I definitely started mumbling under my breath about getting a faulty book. Then when my stupidity subsided and I realized that was in fact the end I found myself cursing loudly and repeatedly shouting, "WTF?" So basically the end was awesome. I love when stories end in seemingly obscure ways, mostly because in my mind it means the story hasn't ended. I'm not suggesting that Tharp plans on writing a sequel - I just mean that Sutter's story continues, on what looks like the exact same path he was heading down when the story first began. Which is incredibly sad because Sutter Keely, despite his obvious flaws, is really quite special, which in turn is what makes The Spectacular Now special. Really it's just a story about a series of events; there are no crazy circumstances, no evil dictatorships to overthrow, or existentially uptight wimpy vampires to fall in love with. Everything that happens is totally plausible. It's just made so spectacular because of an awesome character, and great writing. 
 I'm curious to see how this story has been translated to film (despite the fact that it once again stars Shailene Woodley - apparently the only young female actress suitable for any YA novel film adaptations. Which by the by I totally don't agree with and I'm a little filled with rage that she's been cast in The Fault in Our Stars, but that's a rant for another time kids.) 
 The Spectacular Now is one of those books that seem like a rarity in YA novels at the moment - it's a simple story, about a regular kid who's regular life is made extraordinary because of who he is and how he lives. It's a breath of fresh air and a really great read.

Sutter Keely. He's the guy you want at your party. He'll get everyone dancing. He' ll get everyone in your parents' pool. Okay, so he's not exactly a shining academic star. He has no plans for college and will probably end up folding men's shirts for a living. But there are plenty of ladies in town, and with the help of Dean Martin and Seagram's V.O., life's pretty fabuloso, actually. 
 Until the morning he wakes up on a random front lawn, and he meets Aimee. Aimee's clueless. Aimee is a social disaster. Aimee needs help, and it's up to the Sutterman to show Aimee a splendiferous time and then let her go forth and prosper. But Aimee's not like other girls, and before long he's in way over his head. For the first time in his life, he has the power to make a difference in someone else's life--or ruin it forever. 
 Hrrhhhmmmnnm. 
 I didn't like this book. 
 Sutter Keely is a character who is primed for development from page one. He is an alcoholic who continually puts himself and his friends in dangerous situations. His best friend decides to grow up a bit and do things other than just getting wasted all the time and all Sutter does is whine and complain that his friend is abandoning him. His girlfriend dumps him for being a selfish arsehole and he decides to try and wreck things for her in her new relationship (except he doesn't even see it as wrecking things - he's miles too selfish to understand how his action might impact other people). 
 He refers to himself as The Sutterman. 
 So basically, he's a dick. And so develop-able. And yet, the author decides to not develop him one iota throughout the entire course of the book. The book ends with Sutter being just as much of a loser as he was at the beginning. In terms of whiny, detestable characters, this book ranks right up there with Catcher in the Rye. 
 The plot charts Sutter's meandering life as he bumbles from one random situation to another - the only link being that in every single scene Sutter is in various stages of inebriation. Watching someone literally piss their life up a wall isn't very interesting or fun, so the plot was a bit of a bust for me too. 
 You'd think that, being as Sutter is so clearly an alcoholic, his friends would have staged an intervention at some point. Spoiler alert: they don't. 
 Towards the end, the author shoehorns in a sudden and entirely unbelievable meeting between Sutter and his absentee father in order to show the reader why Sutter is like he is. It was clumsy and forced and guess what? Not everyone who doesn't have a dad acts like a complete arsehole. 
 And yet through all of this, I kept rooting for Sutter. I kept hoping he'd change, see the error of his ways. See that the way he was treating Aimee was utterly deplorable. Do something other than just drink and sing Dean Martin songs (I can't stand Dean Martin, by the way). I kept hoping, even as I saw the page count on my Kindle increase and increase, slimming the chances of any character development down to zero. 
 Such a shame. This book could have been great, but it was just annoying. 
 2 stars (and that's being generous)

I see what you did there, Tim Tharp, by writing a first-person POV wherein the protagonist's problems are obvious to everyone - including the reader - but himself. Instead of rooting for the lovers to live happily ever after, I kept wishing Aimee would get some self respect and a personality of her own rather than becoming the female Sutter.

** spoiler alert ** 
 As I was first reading this, I looked at its rating and thought to myself; why does this hysterical book have such an incredibly low rating. 
 Tharp's writing style reminded me of John Greenwriting, so I had no idea why people disliked it so. 
 Then, as I finished, I finally understood. Sutter doesn't change. All thought he said he would do but you didn't believe he would, he did. All he had been doing the entire book that you thought he would stop, he continued doing. The characters you thought would go through a stunning change, stayed the same. 
 People read books to experience the metamorphisis of characters growing up and understanding the world. Sutter Keeley was a high school snior with no work ethic and a drinking problem. All throughout the book you expected him to develop thought process and stop driking, but he didn't. He hurt Amy just as he always said he would.

As for the writing, the narrative slips between present and past tense constantly and the 'I'm like...and she's like...' sentences drove me bonkers. Originally reviewed at Minnesota Reads. 
 The critics have been praising the movie "The Spectacular Now," and after reading the book I have no idea why. I think this may be one of those rare times when the movie is better than the book. 
 The Spectacular Now is the story of popular teen Sutter Keely, the life of the party. He drinks daily, parties hard, gets along with everyone, is always looking to have fun, and seems like he doesn't have a care in the world. Every guy wants to be his friend and every girl wants to be with him. 
 The morning after one of his drunken nights, Sutter wakes up on the lawn of Aimee Finicky, a loaner, geeky girl from his school. She knows who he is; he doesn't know her. This chance meeting begins a very weird relationship Sutter has with Aimee where he decides he needs to change her life. She's quiet, doesn't have many friends, doesn't drink, and doesn't stand up for herself, and Sutter makes it his mission to change all this so he can better her. 
 My problem with this book is that Sutter Keely is such a loser and Aimee is not, so who does he think he is trying to fix her? 
 I fully admit that I would've had a crush on Sutter Keely in high school. He's always at parties, he's laid back, and he bucks authority. In high school, he is king. He was pretty dreamy when I was a stupid 15-year-old, but looking back on guys like Sutter now, they were complete losers. They were full-blown alcoholics or drug addicts in high school who still get drunk or high every weekend, and probably during the week, too. They didn't have plans for the future and never wanted to grow up, so they still work at the same gas station where they worked in high school. This is where Sutter Keely will end up, because he does not change at all in this book, even though change-worthy things happen to him. 
 In a good story, I want to see a character change by the end. On some level, they should be different than they were at the beginning. Whether this difference is emotional, physical, or magical, and drastic, subtle, or hopeful doesn't really matter, but I should see some sort of change. I kept waiting for something like this to happen to Sutter, but by the end we still have the same old Sutter and I wondered why I read this. 
 I also disliked that I never got a full picture of Aimee, and probably because Sutter tells the story. We get to know him, but Aimee is still a mystery. He judges her, believes she should change, and we have to take his word about her, but I couldn't. With the little I saw her, she was a cool, geeky, shy girl with a crappy home life, but she wasn't a loser. She just didn't act like Sutter and he thought she should. I wanted to tell her to run and run fast. 
 I do think I may like the movie. In the previews they show short scenes that were not in the book that make it look like Sutter is changing or at least thinking about changes he needs to make. They also play up more of a romance between Sutter and Aimee and it seems like Aimee makes Sutter better. I don't care so much about the romance part, but the movie looks better than Sutter's mission to change Aimee. I have no idea if these things happen in the movie, but the preview of the movie is the book I wanted to read.

It's a very well-crafted YA book. Although the story didn't affect me as much as I wanted it to be, I was really emotionally invested in these characters and cared very much throughout the whole book. 
 I also appreciate the topic covered and ideas dealt in the story, about how easily one can be lost in life's confusions, even often times the confusions are caused by oneself. Live in life, make the choices, deal with the confusions, and remember the meaning of lives is all put on by ourselves.

I just couldn't get into this one. I was so bored after 5 pages. The blurb says "comedy and absurdity". I didn't think it was funny at all. I was really looking forward to something that would make me laugh, even just a little bit, and not once. I didn't even smile.
I feel so bad rating this book a 2 out of 5. It has won so many accolades and has lots of high ratings - but I just did not care for it much. :( It was just a strange, strange read to me.

John Corey Whaley 
 Where Things Come Back 
 Atheneum 
 228 pages 
 7.1 
 The winner of Michael L. Printz Award, the most coveted award in young adult literary, Where Things Come Back ventures around magical-surrealism territory. It's quirky and beautifully written, yet it feels void and pointless. Whaley's better work can be seen in Highly Illogical Behavior.

It's not about the woodpecker. It's about how a family in a small town freaks out when their teenage son is kidnapped by a lunatic, religious extremist. The book is slow, boring and dark. Then it suddenly gets all light and happy and uplifting at the very end. It is supposed to be about how we all get second chances in life. 
 This story did not work for me. I only read it because it won the 2012 Printz Award. I expected it to be better.

I did like this story but I think for me the two disjointed stories did not come together. Maybe because I read this in multiple sittings and didn't really get into the story line. I could understand the story with the rare bird, the town gaining publicity and the frustration with the disappearance of Gabriel but they lost me adding the missionary story to it. Maybe I need to read it again without distraction to appreciate it more.

Meh... 
 This had good reviews, but was much too short for me, and took far too long to get me emotionally invested. I like how the stories meshed, but I didn't like the ending.

I loved this book. But it's depressing in that 1) it's Whaley's first novel; and 2) it's brilliant. That's just not fair. That's an incredibly intimidating combination to behold for someone working on her first novel. 
 It's complex (the plot), but straightforward (the tone); funny, but moving (without being manipulative). It's set in a small town, but it has a solid world, view. Every single character was a real person I could walk around, touch, and hear his/her laugh. 
 Yeah. This is really depressing.
This won the Printz??

I'm bummed that I didn't like this one because I loved his other books, but this one just didn't hook me. The only person I cared about in the whole book was Gabriel and he was the only reason I finished it.

When one is reading a book in which a character goes missing for two months, one imagines a more dramatic ending than the missing character simply walking up the driveway, returning home to his family. 
 I loved Collin's "When one is...he imagines..." scenarios. :)
Great writing but the storyline was a bit boring

Go read this book. Now. Please. It's great. Really great. I read this in one sitting & I'm just left with that feeling, you know? That feeling when you know you've got yourself a new favorite. It's a good feeling. Now I'm rambling, I'll get on to the part where I try & make my thoughts coherent. 
 Plot- I really don't want to say much because I think it's best to go into this book knowing nothing, & just taking everything in as it happens. That's what I did, I knew nothing about the plot, & I think that's the best way to do it. I loved the plot, needless to say. It was another one of those books where you don't realize why certain things happen until the end. This book's plot was nothing like I thought it was going to be at the beginning. The way this author weaved everything together was amazing, & you slowly get realization after realization throughout the book, as to why earlier scenes were included. I think this was a masterful plot, & it was truly unique. 
 Writing- I was blown away by the writing. It felt real, the inner monologue & the spoken dialogue. It had a raw feeling to it, but yet it was also beautiful in it's own way. I liked how the author used both 1st and 3rd point of view. It flowed very nicely, & I never got bored of reading it. I thought it conveyed many emotions very well, I was actually laughing at some parts, & I did shed some tears as well. Some of the ideas in this novel were wonderfully written, where it didn't feel like you were reading something else, it truly felt like you were in Cullen's mind when he was thinking these ideas about the world. He wrote these passages as a teenage boy would think, but yet conveyed thought provoking ideas with ease. 
 Characters- Within these short 200ish pages, I grew attached to all these characters. I really connected with Cullen, & I felt like I related to him quite a bit. I loved his friend Lucas a lot as well, he seemed very real; all of these characters did. He crated these characters without using any stereotypes or cliches, they were truly their own person, & it was very refreshing. Gabriel, I don't even know what to say about him, besides the obvious that I loved him, a lot. I want a Gabriel as a brother, or even just a friend. One thing I was curious about; was he just a little eccentric, or did he have some slight form of Aspergers? 
 Overall- I was not expecting to like this as much as I did. I just wasn't expecting anything from this book, I honestly didn't know why everybody seemed to love it, all I knew was that it was about some teenage boy in a small town & a bird? It's so much more than that, & I'm so glad I finally read it. I feel like I could say so much more but it would just be me babbling. It's such a quick, & short read, everybody should just run out & read it.

This is my third attempt at writing this review because I'm having a hard time articulating what worked and didn't work for me in this novel. I am glad I read it and thought it was good, but I'm not sure I'd ever go back and read it again, either. The relationships between the characters (Cullen's best friend Lucas, his brother Gabriel, the love interests, the jock/bullies) were well thought out and developed, but some of them felt a bit rushed or forced or something. Like, I was told how close Gabriel and Cullen were, but Gabriel seemed so strange and phlegmatic, I would have liked to have been shown more why they were close. I didn't like the women in this book much. I'm not a slut shamer, but since I don't know anyone who would try to sleep with a guy they barely know the first time they go out (at least I don't think so), I found it a bit incredulous. I found all the women except Libby (who there's very little of in the story), and also the mom, to be just annoying and not very authentic. 
 Characters aside, I thought the plot was pretty good; I didn't care about the woodpecker at all, but what was going on with Gabriel compelled me to keep reading. I'm not sure about the ending; it made me really happy, but I'm not sure how true to life it was, especially for something that calls itself "realistic fiction." The setting was done well as well. Having grown up in a small town myself, I could connect with the things the author described. 
 I think most fans of YA fiction will like this more than I did and should give it a read.

This book is a heartbreaker. Beautifully written, but very readable. Intricately plotted, but in the end elegantly simple. Haunted and sad, but funny. And filled with hope. I often find that, when it comes to the Printz, I prefer the nominated books to the winner. The winners sometimes feel lifeless and cold. At least to me. (It's quite probable that I'm in the minority here.) Not so with this book. I spent most of the story entranced, and had the book firmly placed in strong four-star territory. And then I read the last handful of chapters. Five stars. And I've got a new author to point to when people say that YA books are simple, silly, or not worth an adult's time.
I liked how everything was interconnected but didn't like how the book just ended. I wanted more closure.

I can see why this book won the Printz. It was lovely. There was mystery, heartbreak, symbolism, words, Sufjan Stevens, etc. And a woodpecker. 
 The double storylines confused me quite a bit--it wasn't til the very end that I realized they were different timelines as well (I know, but I'm not the smart one).

A great read and lovely writing. The book didn't effect me greatly but I'm still REALLY glad that it ended the way it did because Gabriel seemed like the kind of person who doesn't come along too often.

I picked up this 2011 Printz Award-winning debut novel while browsing at the library a couple months back, and I promptly put it back down. I think it was the book's cover - a drawing of a woodpecker on a tree, on a quaint wood-paneled background - that provoked the quick rejection. The cover seemed to promise absolutely nothing of contemporary relevance. 
 And, yeah, 
 Where Things Come Back 
 does have an old-timey, Southern feel to it. It's set in Arkansas, populated with meandering oddballs who have time to lay around and contemplate dozens of what-ifs about life and the cosmos. It vaguely reminds me, 16 years later, of the one Faulkner novel I read in college, a novel I remember next to nothing about. 
 But 
 Where Things Come Back 
 takes place in the present, it reads fast as lightning, and its narrator has a winning mix of heart, wit and skepticism. If it was edited just right, this book could be twice as good at half the length*, but as it is, part of the charm is in the meandering. 
 As the book starts, Cullen, protagonist and narrator, is at the morgue, identifying the body of his 17-year-old cousin, dead of a heroin overdose. Cullen's dad is away often, so Cullen has to perform all the man-of-the-house duties in his absence. That means driving around mom and younger brother Gabriel, and today that means identifying the dead body. Cullen's Aunt Julia, mother of the overdose victim, will spend the duration of the book crying. 
 This is the first six pages of the book, mind you, and we're soon introduced to the book's other key players, all identified by first and last name. There's Lucas Cader, popular kid, defender of the bullied, and hyper-loyal best friend to Cullen. (Seriously, it seems objective to state that being Cullen's friend is ALL Lucas is in this book.) There's Russell Quitman, bully, who will be in a wheelchair by the second act. There's Ada Taylor, the girl Cullen loves from afar, who loves Russell Quitman up close. 
 Then there's the woodpecker subplot, which is the reason for the book's cover and which overtakes Lily, the small Arkansas town where the book is set. There's John Barling, in from Oregon, who claims he's spotted a Lazarus woodpecker - thought for 60 years to be extinct - and he's tracked it to Lily. Wouldn't you know, John Barling, media darling, is boarding in Lily right next door to Cullen's family. 
 The woodpecker subplot was my least favorite element of 
 Where Things Come Back 
 . Would the media and public care about an extinct species of woodpecker possibly not being extinct? Would a guy in a safari hat be able to gain fame from proving the non-extinction of an extinct woodpecker? It helps tie the book together, but it seemed as ludicrous to me as it did to Cullen, Gabriel and Lucas. Maybe that was the point? Don't know, don't care. 
 There's a C-story as well, interwoven, that takes place far from Lily. Benton Sage, college-age Christian kid, is in Ethiopia on a mission trip. He disagrees with the mission in a fundamentally hardcore way - he's here to win souls, not to hand out food, water and blankets. A weird, disturbing kid, Benton, and his subplot eventually ties back to the A and B plot, but it unravels in a weird Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon kind of way. I was willing to buy it and go along for the ride, but I can see how another reader would say nope, uh-uh, no-go, silly, forced, contrived. 
 I was a fan, though. I liked Cullen and most of Whaley's other character creations. I liked being quietly surprised, literally on the last page of the book, by an ending that was different than the one I saw coming. And I went pretty much straight for 
 Noggin 
 , Whaley's 2014 sophomore effort, which was equally good in a lot of very different ways. I'm glad I got past the quick, dismissive act of unironically judging this book by its cover. 
 *And you could say the same for this review, no doubt. I'm half-assing the crap out of this first draft.

Much like Andrew Smith, another popular YA novelist of the same era, John Corey Whaley's narrative style feels wildly different from most others in the profession. He seems to see story paths where few would see anything but unyielding granite walls, impossible to bore through without major excavation. John Corey Whaley finds passage through the immovable stone with minimal effort, so the story takes routes we don't understand are there until the full extent of their network is revealed. That's Where Things Come Back, a novel beyond complete apprehension until near the end. Quirky characters, motivations, and loopy timeline tricks lead us to places we didn't think we'd see. You might doubt the author's competence to draw everything together meaningfully, but stick with it and you'll find yourself somewhere in that vicinity by the end. Then you can judge for yourself whether he ultimately hits or misses the mark. 
 "I can't seem to be a pessimist long enough to overlook the possibility of things being overwhelmingly good." 
 --Where Things Come Back, P. 5 
 Lily, Arkansas isn't markedly different from most small Southern towns. Cullen Witter, age seventeen, and his fifteen-year-old brother Gabriel have designs on bigger futures for themselves than would be possible if they lived and died in Lily, but they and Lucas, a close friend from school, know they'll probably wile away their lives where they were born and raised. Cullen is okay with that if Gabriel is; younger brother is a wise soul where Cullen is prone to blunders, the thoughtful Witter son who gives Cullen reason to pause before acting foolishly. And then Gabriel disappears without leaving a clue behind. Excruciating days eke by as the police investigation turns up nothing. Weeks pass, and Cullen, his parents, and Lucas have no idea where to look for Gabriel. He and Cullen talked often about leaving Lily for greener pastures, but Gabriel wouldn't run away without telling anyone. The alternative is worse, however; if Gabriel didn't take off under his own power, then he's presumably damaged or dead by now. Cullen and the people of Lily don't know what to wish for. 
 Cullen's story is relayed in first person, but the third-person saga of Benton Sage is given equal time, initially with no explanation why. Once a promising candidate for Christian missionary work in impoverished countries, Benton has difficulty fitting in with relief laborers in third-world Africa. Disillusioned that his life goal could be untracked so easily, Benton searches for his true calling, but God feels distant. Has his redeemer abandoned him during the most trying period of his life? When a character or two from Cullen's world pops up in Benton's story, the wheels start turning in the reader's head, but the real connection remains invisible until the time is ripe. Only then do we glimpse the complete picture and its implications. If nothing else, it will make you think. 
 Where Things Come Back is bizarre in the same way as Andrew Smith's novels, and not everything pieces together by the end. There are beautiful moments, most of them observations tendered by Gabriel, a sincere philosopher. I love his take on God's responsibility for the world's diversity of artistic genius, evidence that the Creator loves creativity. From Cullen's point of view: "My brother once told me that God was like the best musician in the world, because he put together all the sounds of nature and gave people like Jimi Hendrix his fingers and John Lennon his brain. 'And he's the best writer, too,' Gabriel said to me. 'Why's that?' I asked. 'Because he gives every good writer something to struggle with and try to work out by writing it down. That's genius.'" Brilliant writers grappling with their demons is what produces illuminating passages in literature, ideas that survive beyond the perishable humans who create them. That's why I love to read, always excited that the next book might offer a memorable truth to guide me through harrowing circumstances for the rest of my life. Where Things Come Back wouldn't have been my selection for the 2012 Michael L. Printz Award, but it has value, and I'm rating it one and a half stars. Will you discern the meaning of life from these pages, in part or whole? It can't hurt to give it a go.

Here's another Printz Award winner that is a really odd book. I hate the cover, I don't think it is appealing to teens at all. And the two parallel stories by different point of view characters seem totally unrelated to each other, which I think might also turn teen readers away. But those who stick with it for that sudden AHA! moment when the two stories intersect, nearly at the end of the book, will like it. I liked the main character, Cullen, who's 17 and has a great relationship with his younger brother Gabriel. There was kind of an odd narrative style change where Cullen describes his daydreams in the third person. Basic plot: Gabriel goes missing, at the same time that the town is aflutter over the possible sighting of a rare bird, with a famous ornithologist come to town to search for it. The other story involves a young man whose failed missionary trip leads to suicide and to an obsession by his roommate. You really have to read it to have all of that make sense...
Damn. That's all I have to say other than this book made me really sad and at the same time it was so smart and amusing.

Wow! This book was beautiful; mainly because the story was so simple yet I found so much wonder in the ordinary. 
 I love books set in small towns and the characters that emerge from the pages. In Lilly, Arkansas the cast of characters are very human. Each has a sense of loss and the hope for second chances. It's a story about adolescent love, family, best friends, childhood, tragedy, and the return of an extinct woodpecker. 
 The metaphor behind this unusual bird was genius and truly touching. For a debut novel this book was outstanding. If you choose to read this book, I hope you are moved by the message and when you reach the last page you realize what you have read is something quite unique.

When Things Come Back is an Ode to Teen Angst. 
 I understand the niche for these books, because, after all, much of the work of adolescence is grieving childhood. This is real work, hard work, and angst is appropriate. I just think a book needs more than angst to glue it together. 
 Cullen Whitter lives in a dull Arkansas town, with dull parents, and few prospects of ever getting out. He is surrounded by people who are depressed about their own losses and slim prospects, and his whole life is stuck in melancholy neutral. Then a birdwatcher shows up and spots a woodpecker that was thought to be extinct, and the rest of the town perks up. Suddenly there is a festival, a burger, and even a haircut named for the Lazarus woodpecker. All around him people find something to hope for. 
 Not Cullen. He can't stand the stupid woodpecker, the fraud birdwatcher, and the people who latch on to a bird fantasy as if it matters. 
 The two bright spots in his Cullen's life are his best friend, Lucas Cader, who is smart and popular and handsome and loyal, and his younger brother Gabriel, whose otherworldly wisdom makes him not care about stuff like who is cool in high school; stuff that makes Cullen miserable. 
 Then comes the Life-Changing Event. At least it should have been a life-changing event. But as far as I can tell, it doesn't change Cullen one bit. When crisis strikes, Cullen just gets more melancholy. He blames the woodpecker, he blames his family. He even picks fights with Lucas. 
 This is a very clever book. Clever enough to win the Printz Medal for excellence in Young Adult Fiction. It is well-written, with snappy dialog, and non-narrative chapters about a missionary in Ethiopia that seem entirely unrelated until they crash-land into the main plot. While I found the passages where Cullen slips from first-person narration into third-person distracting ("When one is sitting in his room thinking about a woodpecker, he suddenly begins to feel as if his life..." you get the idea), and his zombie fantasies irritating, I can see that they are clever. 
 But clever can't rescue a novel. 
 This novel needed some sort of redemption, which it never found. I happen to like woodpeckers, and kept hoping for some redemption there, but I understand that might be too obvious. But when the crisis finally resolves without any real redemption, I felt cheated. Melancholy zombie fantasies and all, I cared about Cullen. I wanted him to learn something, get somewhere, grow, forgive. Maybe spot an extinct bird. 
 I guess he is just too clever for that.
