** spoiler alert ** 
 I really thought I'd love this novel, but I didn't. The reviews described the setting as a quirky small town, the plot as slightly absurd, and the narrator as sarcastic. All these things turned out to be true, but despite these elements usually producing a favorable bias in me and all the awards and glowing reviews it received, I did not like it. At all. I was tempted not to review it, but I made a commitment to myself to review all the books I read and I'm not going to shirk that because my opinion differs from the general librarian consensus and that makes me feel awkward. So here goes: 
 At first I loved the book. The first few chapters of my library copy are covered with post-its marking little passages I found amusing or witty. The book drew me in right away. How could it not with an opening sentence like " I was seventeen years old when I saw my first dead body." Little details like Cullen not understanding exactly what his father did for a living made it easy for me to relate to him. But as I continued to read, quirks like Cullen (the first person narrator) referring to himself in third person out of the blue started to annoy me. It was funny the first time, but the returns on that particular gag diminished rather quickly while the instances of its use only seemed to increase. 
 The next big problem for me was that the central driving force of the plot, namely the disappearance of Cullen's brother Gabriel, did not interest me. I was far more interested in the character of Cullen than I was in whether or not his brother was ever found. This took most of the tension out of the novel. The problem was that as I reader I mostly heard about how awesome Gabriel was instead of seeing it for myself. Cullen seems to idolize him as some quirky hipster god wise beyond his years who walks to the beat of his own drum and doesn't care what others think. Unfortunately he seemed more like a caricature of a misunderstood small town teen than any kind of full-fleshed character, right down to the Pink Floyd and Led Zeppelin t-shirts and battered copy of Catcher in the Rye. 
 That brings us to the alternating chapters told in third person following caricatures of religious zealots. First Benton Sage and then Cabot Searcy. These characters are never really fleshed out in the brief glimpses we get of them and their actions seem completely unjustified to me. I realize that they're supposed to be a bit crazy but that doesn't justify a lack of motivation for their decisions. Enough time was spent on their stories that I felt as a reader I should have some kind of sympathy with them, but that sympathy and understanding was never achieved. Instead these alternating chapters just provided an unwelcome interruption to the narrative even when the seemingly unrelated narratives finally connected (I was shocked!) 
 The end didn't really make any sense, but that wasn't what annoyed me most about it. That honor went to the fact that throughout the novel Cullen occasionally added to a running list of good book titles that vaguely related to whatever had just happened to him. Anyone want to guess what the last title/last line of the novel was? It reminded me of the end of Night Circus that annoyed me so much. I can understand a debut author perhaps not being experienced enough to realize how cliche something like that is and thinking themselves very clever and original to end their novel with the beginning/title but isn't that why we have editors? So there's someone more experienced to say "maybe you should re-think that ending, you're really not as clever as you think." It's almost as bad as the 'and then I woke up and it was all a dream' ending. 
 Despite all of that I really did enjoy parts of the novel. Cullen makes a big deal of his brother's wisdom, but I found Cullen's explanations of why society feels the need to put labels on people and how people respond to the tragedies of others the most insightful parts. I appreciated Whaley's willingness to play with different narrative techniques and his creativity in the way he incorporates the story of the long-lost woodpecker. I admired his boldness in tackling such issues as drug addiction, suicide, loss of a sibling, obsession, and stalking (in a this-is-creepy and not romantic light.) Mostly I enjoyed the character of Cullen and all his flaws and humor and tendency to imagine his enemies as zombies. It didn't all work for me this time around, but I can see why he won the Morris debut award (although I'm still scratching my head at the Printz) and I think I will read his next book. Hopefully he'll work out some of his authorial kinks by then.

Not my cup of tea. I considered putting it down a few times but it's not a difficult read, just tedious. The characters are interesting enough but it just felt like a lot of sitting around and pondering the possibility of second chances.

Ah John Corey Whaley is an asshat for making me cry on Mother's Day. Ha...kidding. I will not use any spoilers because for months, as I knew this book was coming out, I had no idea how it would turn out. And...until the last damn page, I had no idea how it would turn out. 
 This is one of those rare novels that make you sit back and mull life over. I love these types of books because, yes they're rare, but because they are so few and far between. And I don't say this because I know Corey but because what he captured in this snapshot of Lily, Arkansas, was the perfect portrayal of small town living and what it's like to be different. 
 My only question...Dr. Webb...the mysterious Dr. Webb...was my favorite part. Why...because it showed that other things happened that we didn't get to see and that we were getting a glimpse of Cullen...what Cullen wanted us to see. Thank you Cullen Witter...thank you.
I could not stand the writing. I had no idea the sense of time and the characters sucked. I could not finish it. It had potential, but I cannot stand the way the author wrote.
Eh... I didn't really care for the writing. I don't understand why this book won so many prestigious awards. It was just okay.

If this hadn't won the Printz, I don't know if I would've finished it, but I'm certainly glad I did because things got more interesting as the book went along. (And I've heard it's even better on a second reading.) 
 My favorite parts were not the main story about the Witter brothers in small-town Arkansas, but the B story about a young missionary's crisis of faith and its subsequent affect on his otherwise average college roommate. 
 There was something Catcher in the Rye-esque about Cullen's teenage malaise, which I think will have huge appeal for teenagers (duh). As a 29-year-old woman, I'm not the target audience for this kind of stuff, so take it with a grain of salt when I say that Cullen's zombie fantasies and talking about himself in the third person mostly bored me. 
 But, overall, I liked it. I'm excited to see what Whaley writes next and I congratulate him on a very promising debut.
It wasn't as interesting as I expected it to be. It seemed to go all over the place and the story itself moved really slow. The end is a bit predictable.

Review will come but for now: 
 This book is very different from what I'm used to. No contemporary love relationhsip, just contemporary. The story is very intriguing and my face looked like this :O for lots of the time. 
 Really interesting and a must-read for everyone.

one world - boring. i have no idea what i just read and why i even managed to read it till the end. 
 the discription felt interesting enough, i the first chapter was so-so in a good way, but from the second chapter i was like "ergh, what?". Still i decided to go along with it, waiting until the plot made sence. Well, it didn't. Story was boring, characters felt empty and unimportant. As for almost all the books that win some kind of awards - left me wondering how could anyone rate this good. Story just does not hold together, it is so incoherent, that at times i need to re-read the paragraph to understand it meaning.

The only more disappointing than reading a bad book is reading a book that you thought was going to be amazing, only to find that it wasn't as good as you hoped it would be. Where Things Come Back isn't a bad book by any means, it just didn't wow and amaze me as much as I was expecting it to. 
 My friend Cuppalit raved about this book and, based on her other recommendations, I was eager to try it. Then, it won the Michael L. Printz award, which almost guaranteed that it would be a good book, since I've loved every other Printz winner that I've read. 
 Whaley is a good writer, I won't deny that. He's created some likeable characters in this book, which started off with a bang, flipping between the story of Cullen in Arkansas and Benton in Ethiopia. I love stories that tell two parallel stories because I'm always just waiting to find out how they'll end up intertwined. The intertwining of the story was perhaps the best part of this book, and it didn't happen until close to the end. Between the interesting opening and the story coming to an end, I felt like the story flat lined. The story was progressing, delving deeper into the characters' lives, but I found that I just wasn't caring as much. Maybe it was the pacing of the story, or maybe I just can't identify as well with boys in small American towns, but I found my attention wavering. I persevered and I'm glad that I finished this book; however, I'm surprised that it took me so long to finish, considering the fact that it's just barely over 200 pages long. 
 This book is Whaley's first novel so I do hope that his next book will be more enjoyable for me. I won't give up on him just yet!

I know that a book is really, really good when I wake up in the morning and immediately think "I wonder what happened..." and then have to read some more to find out. This one was even better because even after I finished the book I'm thinking "I wonder what happened..." because I had really started caring about the characters and knew that the summer that they experienced would change their whole view of the world and the people in it. Or not. 
 I have to admit that I am the type of reader who sometimes peeks at the end of the book when I'm not really sure how much I like it. And if I peek at the ending and cant' tell how the author got me there, then I keep reading. So as I kept reading the second half of the book, knowing what the author had written, I kept wondering "is this one of Cullen's fantasies or is it real?" Kept me on the edge of my seat and kept me wondering how everything was going to tie together.

I can see why this book won the Printz. I read it in almost one sitting--the narrative voice is so strong and Whaley is great at capturing teenage fascination with the mysteries of life. Would definitely recommend.

reference_books.title: Life After Life
reference_books.review_text: 610 pages in this book, and page 597 was good. (Actually, it's the same as the prologue, so if you just read that, that's enough!).

reference_books.title: The Dinner
reference_books.review_text: The first 100 pages were horrible. Painfully slow. Got better eventually, but not great. Interesting moral discussions. Overall not my kind of book and a waste of time!

reference_books.title: The Last Letter from Your Lover
reference_books.review_text: I really wanted to like this book because I loved "Me Before You." But really it is just a cross between "An Affair to Remember" and "Message in a Bottle" - completely unoriginal. Well written, a fun, quick read but more than anything else - unimaginative and predictable.

reference_books.title: Testimony
reference_books.review_text: I started to read this book because the topic intrigued me - a sex scandal in a private high school. But it seemed that little of the book was actually about that! There was too much useless background info. I really don't need to know about the main character's best friend's sister's aunt in order to follow the plot. There was also too much jumping around in time - before the incident, after the incident, one year after, two years after. I kept getting lost! This is the second book I've read by Anita Shreve and probably my last. Wasn't too impressed with the other one either.

reference_books.title: One Plus One
reference_books.review_text: A little too "Harlequin romance" for me.

reference_books.title: Dark Places
reference_books.review_text: I wanted to like this book more than I did because of all the hype over "Gone Girl." But I just didn't love it. I hate when authors feel they have to have an overly climactic ending and a twist that comes completely from left field just for the sake of the reader saying "I didn't see that coming!" Even a twist needs to be relevant somehow! Most of the book was engaging, albeit dark, but I just couldn't find the compassion or interest for the main character.

reference_books.title: The Time Traveler's Wife
reference_books.review_text: I should know myself better and should never have started this book. To me, the concept of time travel is just too unbelievable AND there are not multiple versions of ourselves out there. The main character actually visits himself as a child!?! Too unrealistic and way too slow.

reference_books.title: Water for Elephants
reference_books.review_text: Not my typical genre of book, but I liked it very much. Can't wait to watch the movie now. My only negative was the use of a lot of circus terminology that I just didn't get what they were talking about. Had to google a lot! :)

reference_books.title: Before I Go to Sleep
reference_books.review_text: Kind of confusing at times flipping between the present and what is written in a journal. Beginning was a little slow - very repetitive. But . . . nice twist at the end I didn't see coming!

reference_books.title: Her Fearful Symmetry
reference_books.review_text: So disappointed. Didn't like it at all. Weird, slow, silly, boring. Not even sure how I got through it.

book_a.title: The Nightingale
book_a.user_review: I have read many fiction books about WW2, the Holocaust and concentration camps, and this was definitely one of the best! A different perspective about this horrible time in history that was very unique and incredibly hard to put down at night. I'm sorry that I read the last chapter while out in public in a coffee shop - I couldn't hold back the tears. A beautiful story!

sample_reviews.review_text: I generally enjoyed this book. It was interesting to read about WWII from the perspective of the French whose towns had been occupied, and I enjoyed the symmetry of the two sisters both doing what they could to resist the Nazis. The ending sort of surprised me but I liked it. Overall an enjoyable (if somewhat depressing) read.
Books rarely make me cry. But oh wow this one did.
Couldn't put this book down. Didn't end the way I thought but still loved it.

I don't understand the appeal of this book. The French stereotypes are awful (walls the color of "freshly baked brioche" and impassioned hairy French men and Mon Dieu!s) that seem designed for mass fiction loving women with romantic notions of France and WWII. 
 The vocabulary, characters, and plot are very simple. For anyone who has read All the Light, this book should feel one-dimensional. Or even better, the Frenchwoman Irene Neremovsky's Suite Francaise: a haunting and complicated contemporary telling of the Parisian diaspora and country towns eating themselves alive under Nazi occupation. By comparison, this book is a pulpish American novel that 14 year olds will love and no doubt will be made into a movie. I've stopped a quarter of the way through, just can't fight through it anymore.

"Vianne didn't hesitate. She knew now that no one could be neutral--not anymore--and as afraid as she was of risking Sophie's life, she was suddenly more afraid of letting her daughter grow up in a world where good people did nothing to stop evil, where a good woman could turn her back on a friend in need. She reached for the toddler, took him in her arms." 
 "Asking yourself a question, that's how resistance begins. And then ask that very question to someone else." (R. Campert) 
 "The Nightingale" follows the story of two sisters who fight their own battles against the Nazi occupation of France during World War II. 
 Vianne and Isabelle are as different as they are similar. Vianne, 30 years old, is a mother and a wife living in the countryside. Isabelle, almost 20, is a student who gets kicked out of any boarding school their father makes her attend. 
 War hits their world and shakes it, changing them. 
 This book tells the story of France - just like many other European countries - during World War II as it is: a country of women who struggle to survive and who try their hardest to save as many people as possible. It's a book that tells the story of local resistance against the enemy, a story that is too often forgotten nowadays. 
 Two strong women that grow and learn to love each other in a time when love is a luxury as much as any other bare necessity. Two women who rebel in their own ways, which shows the many - small or big - rebellions against the brutality of Nazi occupation. 
 I love historical fiction because it takes the big picture of a historic event and analyses it through the eyes of characters which may be fictional, but in the end they are as realistic as you and me. Kristin Hannah talks about the war of women, as they realize that, even if they've never tried to live without a man in their houses, they can carry on even if that's the case. Women who gather their courage and roll their sleeves up as they realize their men will probably never return. 
 This book is about people who wonder whether saving themselves comes at the cost of letting someone else die, but just like any good historical-fiction novel, it also dwells on the subject of surrendering in front of evil when your loved ones' life is at risk, which is the whole point of many wars, specifically WWII. Would you save a stranger and let your daughter die? There is no right answer to this question, and Kristin Hannah makes it clear. 
 France is a country that holds a different kind of beauty, and many authors fail to describe the places, their smells, their colours, their vibe, but not Kristin Hannah. France in "The Nightingale" is colourful, vibrant and fragrant. The author perfectly depicted the contrast between France before and after the war, a beautiful country destroyed by men's hunger for power. 
 Full of suspense, love, family dynamics and grief, this book was phenomenal, atmospheric and nostalgic.

** spoiler alert ** 
 One of the best books I've ever read. I enjoy Kristin Hannah, but I don't usually read historical novels, so I went into reading this book with mixed feelings. The main reason I read it was because it had been recommended to me by a friend. What a great book! Near the end, the situation got so tragic that I had difficulty reading it, but that just goes to show how realistically she could paint a picture of teh events of the war.
wanted to like it...but the first couple pages were so cheesy and didn't get much better 50 pages in
This was excellent. Loved her descriptions of the characters, setting, emotions and history. Fantastic plot. Now I want to read her other books.

Heart-wrenching plot lines and strong women characters are the highlights of this World War II-era novel. Positive reviews from friends kept me going throughout this book, especially as I was debating whether or not to finish it at page 200. However, I persevered and realized that the book picks up in every way about halfway through: the characters become more complex and the story reads better. I very much enjoyed that the primary characters were women and all was told in a woman's POV. 
 Having recently read "All the Light We Cannot See," which is also set in WW2, I did not like this one as much simply because the prose did not compare. However, as is the case with most novels set in this era, this heartbreaking novelization of the horrors of war will make the reader FEEL, regardless of the poetry of the prose.
While I enjoyed the book Because I like that period I didn't give it the 5 stars because of the "read like a romance". Good read though. Enjoy!

Well I ended up liking it more than I thought I would 
 If it has one star I liked it a lot 
 If it has two stars I liked it a lot and would recommend it 
 If it has three stars I really really liked it a lot 
 If it has four stars I insist you read it 
 If it has five stars it was life changing

Loved this so much. I was hesitant to read it for a long time - I've read so many books about WWII and even more book set in France, but this one felt entirely original. It was heartbreaking and heartwarming and made me think a lot about the sacrifices I would make for others: my friends, my neighbors, my family. It was a hard read but at the same time a really beautiful one. Highly recommend.
This is one of the most amazing books I have EVER read.

"If I have learned anything in this long life of mine, it is this: In love we find out who we want to be, in war we find out who we are." 
 This is the first line of a truly remarkable story. It is a work of fiction focusing on Paris during WWII but there is a resonance it carries within its pages that really stuck with me when I was finished reading. 
 There are so many wars we fight on a daily basis and it's important to remember miracles do happen in the midst of despair, we don't always recognize them at the time but they are there laden with hope.

Have the tissues handy. This is a tearjerker or an ending. A very engaging story, well developed characters and an interesting historical perspective of and the risks ordinary people felt compelled to take to survive in Nazi occupied France.

Oh.....My.....God. What a book! Really hard to finish it theough tears AND a persistent Yorkie boy who had to have my full attention while I was trying to get through the last few pages. What a great book! Words fail me....the book was so good that those words just don't suffice. This was a book to savor, but one where you HAD to findut what was going to happen next. The kind of book that keeps you awake at night wondering what was going to come next. 
 What will I read next??,?!?!?! 
 I think I've found something to read....The Orphan Train by Christina Baker Kline.

I picked this up because it was a Goodreads pick for 2015. So good and so heartbreaking. It's an interesting view of WWII through the lives of two sisters living in France. They both fight the Germans in their own ways - one quiet and behind the scenes and one dangerously in the spotlight. Based on a true story of a woman who established an escape route for downed pilots during the war.

I was literally ugly sobbing when I finished this book!!!! It was so good and sad (happy and sad)- this may be one of my top favorite books of all time!!! The author did such a good job of keeping me interested until the end... It was very action packed and interesting. I loved all of the characters... I love the historical fiction piece of this but how it how a lot of history in it- the 1940's in Nazi dominated France... Two very different sisters (Vienne and Isabelle) and the story of how they both survive in two very different ways. Their father, Vienne's daughter Sophie, Ari/Daniel (sobs!), etc... I didn't know how affected France was by the Nazis! I actually loved Captain Beck who lived with Vienne- he was actually a very kind and helpful German... The very end of the book was so good and sad I just can't say enough about this book!!

Another Kristin Hannah book, but this one I loved. Set in France during WWII, it obviously isn't going to be a happy book but I loved it. Highly recommend if you like historical fiction or can stomach a WWII/Holocaust story.
Wow! One of the best books I've read in some time. Very emotional at the end. I just feel for what they went through. A must read!

Gosh, I cannot tell you how much I wanted to like this book. Set in WW II, The Nightingale was nothing but a book that tried too hard to be "cool". The plot is quite inconsistent, it is so slow and there is very little development in general. It is seems like the author just add tragedies after tragedies to impress the readers. WW II is a tough theme, unfortunately The Nightingale couldn't pull it off.

I end up reading a lot of WWII historical fiction and this really was one of the best I've read. The characters are so real, sometimes likeable and sometimes infuriating. The story clips along but still lends itself to plenty of emotion. The characters have to make one impossible decision after another and it was very thought provoking to wonder what I'd have done in similar situatuons. I liked the glimpses of a German officer that disliked what was happening... I think that probably happened more than we realize but they were also faced with carrying out command or suffering death or prison. The writing is excellent, the ending was spot on. Definitely recommend!

Rarely has a book resonated quite so deeply. 
 I cried - and I'm really not a weepy reader.
Heartbreakingly depressing. Not my cup of tea.

The Nightingale is a tale of two women who don't realize how much strength they possess until they're faced with the unimaginable horrors of living under Nazi occupation. There's headstrong, beautiful, willful Isabelle, and her sweet, old-fashioned sister, Vianne. Both have suffered loss before the war: losing their mother to death when they were very young, and losing their father to both grief and alcohol after. Each dealing with this loss in her own way. They also face the horrors of Nazi occupation in a different manner. 
 What touched me most was reading, once again, of how an entire population was "weeded out" because they were different. I kept thinking as I read, "Have we learned nothing from history?" Still letting that sink in....
Interesting book involving family matters during the war in France. Two very different sisters and how they coped. Good read.

I am kind of over WWII books. I understand it was a defining moment for a generation and I understand the horror and cruelty. However, it's becoming hard for me not to feel manipulated when families are pitted against each other and have to make heart rending decisions. I will say I liked it better by the end than I anticipated and I did cry.

WWII era is my favorite to read about in historical fiction. The problem I had with The Nightingale was the storytelling. Her writing is so cliche and isn't high quality it's actually mediocre at best which has been a huge disappointment for me. There were also too many plot holes I'm struggling to understand the overwhelmingly positive reviews. The first 50 pages made me realize that this is a shallow book with simple characters. There are chapters with such crucial scenes but it's all so rushed it made me feel like this story was far-fetched. Isabelle didn't look sympathetic at all to me. The relationship between Isabel and Gaetan has to be one of the most forced romantic storylines I have read in my life. It was all so formulaic. I get that some people might love its simplicity but I care more about the details and this love interests were barely believable. The entire story is corny and stereotyped and I don't think a book has be a literary masterpiece for people to enjoy but it could at least not be full of cliches and inconsistencies. 
 Overall, don't believe the hype. It really could have been better. There are other historical fiction novels set in the WWII era that are much more interesting and engaging.

themes: WWII, French Resistance, Family, Love stories, Hardships, Occupation, Vichy government 
 engaging characters, if a bit soap opera-ish...how many things can possibly happen?

It is a good book, just not as great as the word to mouth implies. Two sisters very young women at the beginning of the second world war, will choose different paths. Though their lives remain totally different during the war, their decisions aim toward the same direction, freedom for France and the threatened Jews. But one opts for a more radical position and joins the Resistance at 18, while the other, with a more settled life, just helps the one in need of it more discreetly. 
 I read this book months ago and forgot to review it here. I'm sure I would have enjoyed it better without the noise around it. It brings subconscious greater expectations, and you are almost bound to be disappointed. 
 The problem is that it's chick lit, not historical fiction. If you look for adequacy, you're fr from it. No one in France would say M'sieur, or M'mselle. Typical of American novels... Ariel is a girl's name. A man named Levy would never have stayed in occupied France. When Isabelle takes the airmen to Spain, no one controls them as they go to the free zone -nonsense! The climbing up the mountains should not be that bad to San Sebastian -only 40 kms and a highway. Of course, they were hiding, but still... Antibiotics in 1942? The Vel' d'hiv' round up was a surprise for the average guy, but resistants must have known. 
 See, that is my problem with American writers. They are good, they can write, but they cannot do their homework properly, and it takes he enjoyment away from me.
Compelling story but often weak writing.

First 5 star rating of the year and very much deserved! 
 Kristin Hannah has done it once again. Still holds strong to those 5 star ratings for me!! 
 The Nightingale is a very different approach to one of her novels. This is her first historical fiction and it's so so so good! Definitely hard to read in parts: beautifully sad. 
 I loved that it was in its essence a love story during World War II, but more about a love between sisters, fathers, friends and children. Those who are fans of Hannah already will only love her more, and those who haven't discovered this author's talent for captivating story lines will immediately want to read everything she writes.

I cannot explain enough how much I loved this book. I cried about 50 gazillion times reading it, mostly because it was sad, but also sometimes because I was happy. This is a WWII book, which I know can get old for a lot of readers, but it was such a new, interesting take that it seemed completely new. Isabelle and Vianne are both sisters from France, which was taken over during WWII by the Germans, and so they were essentially living in German controlled territory, billeting with soldiers, and trying to run secret revolutions. That sounds dramatic, but everything fit, and there was so much personal relationship details that everything felt so so so real. 
 If you read one book this year, I would hands down say that it has to be this one, because it is rare that a book moves me this much, and I couldn't stop listening. One thing I would say is that I sort of wish I read it rather than listening because there were so many pretty, well written phrases that I would have wanted to see in print. But I'm a nerd so maybe that doesn't go for everyone. (plus, I would have finished it wayyyyy faster)... 
 ...There's nothing that could have been done better in this book. The plot alternated 3 ways, between an old woman who was being moved into a nursing home in present day Oregon, Vianne, and Isabelle. My personal favorites were Isabelle's chapters, just because she's exciting and lives life on the edge so her chapters usually had more action in them.... 
 ...YOU NEED TO GO OUT AND GET THIS BOOK TODAY, NO EXCUSES!!!! It was remarkable, wonderfully written perfection. I can't even write because I feel like crying just thinking about it. All I can say is, get the book. And I want to know if you read it and what you think!!!!! 
 Read the full review on my blog: https://writethroughthenight.wordpres...
This is her best book yet. I enjoyed the point of view of Nightingale.
*3.5 stars*

This book is the most emotionally heart wrenching book I've read in a long time. I definitely have a book hangover after this one. I highly recommend it to anyone who loves to read about truly heroic women and for those who love to read historical WWII stories.
Heart wrenching, absolutely heart wrenching
Might be really good but started off too sad for me, not going to read it

I didn't hate it but I didn't love it either. Similar stories have been done many times before. This felt rushed and repetitive promising a twist at the end. Unfortunately the author gave away the twist pretty early on in the book so it wasn't a huge surprise. 
 I normally love Hannah but I don't feel that she delivered this time.

It is with distress and disappointment I discover the Jewish Book Council has listed Kristin Hannah's historical romance, The Nightingale, as among the best books of 2015. 
 My first concern is the meritless book itself. Stuffed with linguistic and cultural anachronisms (it is 1941, but the characters are 'on the same page'), neglecting character development in pursuit of plot (no character in this book can bear to exit a room without slamming the door, demonstrating a remarkable passive-aggressive sameness), piling one cliche upon another (twice, roses tumble over a stone wall - and one of those times the author has forgotten her winter setting), this novel bears witness to the writer's C-grade literary standards and tourist's knowledge of France. Furthermore, since the author's imagined audience is women, her contempt, in writing this poorly, is insulting. 
 Then, I am alarmed at the lack of discernment that went into this choice. I want to feel when I see an endorsement from the JBC that I am in safe hands. If The Nightingale is a finalist in the fiction category, how can I trust the merits of recommendations and winners in other categories? 
 Finally, support for this novel from the JBC constitutes advertising, and with such sponsorship the book's readership will expand, spreading literary ignorance, and encouraging the intellectual frivolity that has historically undermined women's education.
Fluffy, but it builds and becomes more interesting.

Hannah delivers MORE than what's promised in this novel about the French Resistance in WWII. Replete with elements of action, feeling, and history, the content of this book parallels any novel I've read about war and post-trauma stress. It does so while honoring the significant role women played in defeating the enemy and in aiding Allied forces, as well as in protecting the innocent. The author does a particularly excellent job in demonstrating how even the most important relationships in our lives sometimes go unnoticed - how poorly we delve into the hearts of those we love and cherish. In the book's public description, the relationship between the two sisters is emphasized, implying (in the way only modern day sexism can) that this a novel for and about women. And what a tragedy that is. Time and again, men in our culture are treated as dim-witted, narrow-minded illiterates, so that one must imagine if this has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. A work of literature about a subject matter so harrowing and poignant should be shared and read by anyone who considers himself intelligent. 
 The book is well-written, but in the ubiquitous contemporary style publishers seem to love. One criticism I might give is that the author is a bit heavy-handed toward the end when she says (and, unfortunately, it does sound like the writer more than the character) that men tell war stories and that women just get on with things. As a reader, this was obvious enough. Hannah had already shown it to us brilliantly. 
 Another score for Hannah is the character of Captain Beck, who is both complicated and complicating. 
 My favorite line (and I don't quote, due to memory) is: Forget who the Nazis are. Remember who you are.

This book was amazing. The characters were so vivid, as well as the settings and storyline, that I was attached from the first few chapters. The story is impacting, to say the least, but it will continue to gut you again and again until you reach the end.
It took me awhile to get into this book but once I did, I was hooked. The ending was amazing. Beautiful story. All the tears.

3.5 stars
Sigh. Cliche after cliche after cliche. Sloppy writing which is a pet peeve. Read All the light you cannot see and pass on this which is an obvious screenplay straight to movie effort.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was excellent to say the least. It was informative, well-written, heart-breaking, and beautifully written. Something I really needed even though I didn't know it. 
 The book starts off with two sisters I initially had a hard time connecting with, but as the story progressed, so did each of their character development. The last couple of chapters certainly broke me in half. After reading the epilogue, I cried for 15 minutes straight because of the reverberating effects this book has. It is definitely going to haunt me for a while. This book certainly deserves its Goodreads award.

I know better. When books are this popular, I shouldn't bother. It is well written and engaging. It's not for me. It's for the people who don't know about this part of the war. I started zoning out pretty early on. It's almost 18 hours long, so I think I was warranted, but multiple POVs and flashbacks with flash ward, it was a lot to keep track of. As a listener I kept waiting for the part of the story I was engaged in to come back. 
 I know I'm gonna take some hits on this one, but I found it just...eh.
If you are considering reading this book... read it. To me, it lived up to all the hype I had heard.

book_b.title: The Children Act
book_b.user_review: I should have stopped reading this book after the first few chapters when I first thought I wouldn't like it. I was right. The writing is way too hoity-toity for me and very little of the book is actually about the main topic. I was excited to read a controversial book about a Jehovah's Witness refusing treatment and the court case that followed. But, again, the book wasn't really about that. Too much about other cases this particular judge tried, her marriage and other "fluffy" stuff - music, opera, etc. Probably won't read any more by this author.

sample_reviews.review_text: Was I engaged the whole time? Yes. Did the story have a predicable turn? No, not really. This wasn't a bad read, I can see people really enjoying it. But I was left with a feeling of "oh." Non-eventful, not moving, just "oh." I think it spent too much time on Fiona's thoughts, so it was harder to view her relationships with meaning. Perhaps that is who Fiona is, her job doesn't allow her the luxury of close relationships.

It looks like I'm in the minority, but I didn't like this book at all. I felt that the title and synopsis were very misleading. The Children's Act and court case regarding the Jehovah's Witness boy are in the story for maybe 25% (if that) but a more accurate title would have been "The Marital Woes of Judge Fiona" for most of the story centered around Fiona's crumbling marriage and it was extremely boring. I don't want to give anything away, but Adam's disease and court case took up so little time and even taking into consideration the final outcome that we find out at the end of the book, made it almost seem pointless. We have to suffer through the marital strife of the judge and a piano recital that draws out over about 10 pages. This was the first book I have read by this author and I may try another one, but I would not recommend this one.

I finished reading The Children Act by Ian McEwan several days ago. It was an easy read and I liked it but did not love it. When Fiona Maye, leading high court judge first meets Adam, a seventeen year old Jehovah Witness dying from leukemia because he and his parents refused a blood transfusion, the only thing that could save his life, I was drawn into plot and anxiously awaited to see how each character would influence the other. However, I did not expect Fiona's lack of involvement in Adam's life. I did not see a romantic involvement developing but rather a young boy looking up to role model or mentor. I wonder if Fiona had acted differently toward Adam and developed a teacher/student or mother/child relationship would they have lived more satisfied lives?

Oh boy, the man can write. This is second novel in a row featuring a female voice - and I have to say it worked for me, as much as I was thinking he couldn't possibly....wrong! It is like On Chesil Beach - how the simple small things undo us. And I love that. I'll read anything he writes. In Hardback. On the day it is released. Which is what I did here.

Is Ian McEwan just writign fot the sake of it and to melk more money? I don't fell like he has to say anything anymore. 
 Plus this was a realy terrible way of handeling a very serious problem like the Jehovah's Witnesses.

High Court judge Fiona Maye is called on to try an urgent Family Court case involving seventeen-year-old Adam who is refusing life-saving medical treatment on the grounds of religious belief. Just before she got the call about this case Fiona received devastating news from her husband. Her marriage and more come into play with her decision in the case of Adam. Her decision will affect both of them in devastating ways. 
 The first two sections of this book were SO SLOW that I would have quit reading it if this wasn't for book club. The last three sections each get better than the last one. Only at the very end of the book do we finally get to see Fiona as a human - not just a meticulous judge. While I didn't really like most of the book Adam's character is done really well and the very end redeems Fiona. But, overall it was a very slow and cold read. It will be interesting to see what the book club discussion is like.

It was a good book, but I wasn't wowed. I think in this case, my age has a lot to do with my ability to fully understand and relate to the characters, though, or rather my lack of ability to do so. 
 If I remember to do that, I might just revisit this book 20, 30 years from now.

Damn you goodreads, with your flimsy 5 star system. 3.5 stars. 
 This is a quiet, easy paced tale, not overly complicated or eventful, and yet fragments stay with you, and revisit from time to time. The things that don't happen. The stance on religion which doesn't sit diplomatically on the fence. The flawed but genuine, sincere, characters. 
 It lacks the passion of my 4s, but it's certainly not a 3. It's a quiet, worthy tale.

I started this book, and I wasn't really into it. I thought the more I read the more I would get into it, but I ended up forcing myself to finish it (a horrible position to find yourself in, as a reader). All I could think of was that I wasted two days reading this when I could have been reading something else. I am not sure why I didn't like it. There didn't seem to really be a point. The plot of the book wasn't even the base of the book. I couldn't find it in myself to even pretend to care about the characters.

I thought I would like this book more, and I still can't put my finger on what I didn't love about it. There are lots of lines of really great writing like you'd expect from McEwan and the final part where Fiona is performing but slowly processing some terrible news she just received was a wonderful suspenseful crescendo to the resolution of the story. But something about it just didn't work for me, maybe it was how unrealistic everything about her marital situation was to me (really, you're going to ask your wife to grant you permission to have an affair and be surprised when it doesn't go over well?) or maybe it was the preachy quality of parts of the story (preachy about the pitfalls of religion; valid points, but it seemed a little forced in the story). Despite, and maybe because of, my issues with the book I am excited to discuss it with my book club. Good start to reading in 2017!
A bit of a busman's holiday for me as a solicitor but very well researched and a satisfying read

A London family court judge has a difficult case to decide on whether a Jehovah Witness boy should be forced to have blood transfusions and while also dealing with trouble in her marriage. 
 McEwan is as always a good writer. I found the cases that the judge came across interesting, especially in how she handled them -- but the book was short and seemed to end suddenly, anticlimactically, and predicitably leaving me wishing there had been a little more to the whole thing.

Small part legal thriller, large part emotional roller coaster, I couldn't put this book down. And while I couldn't relate to any of the characters, I was still drawn to them. If anything, read it for the poetry and language that only McEwan masters so beautifully.
A beautifully written, but not terribly interesting story.

I wavered between one and two stars because it's not a bad book, I just didn't like it. I felt like maybe I didn't get it , because the whole thing seemed a little pointless. If the entire story could be told to someone in a couple of minutes or less, which this can, there isn't much there. Unless, as I say, I'm just dumb and missing something.

I bought this book on impulse. I was familiar with what has been said about the author and not having read any other of his work thought this would be a good place to start, given the legal background to the story and its relatively short length for a novel 
 I began to read it and after a few pages something began to irritate me about the book. I couldn't put my finger on it but whatever IT was won't go away. After getting to about halfway through the book it finally dawned on me what it was about the book that I found so annoying. It was the sheer pretentiousness of the writing. The underlying story would have been fine had it been left on its own, but the author seems to regard himself has having some brilliant unique insight into the human condition , and the reader was constantly treated to this. Particularly in the moments of introspection by the main character which seem to be where he (the author) regards himself as a psychoanalyst. 
 The impression I get of the author is of someone who considers himself to have a brilliant mind. Underpinning his writing is an aura of his intellectual snobbery and that he is just so much more clever and deep and insightful then the rest of us. Truth be told there was an excellent story in here that was ruined by the authors strenuous efforts to show off his intellect. 
 In short the worst book I've read this year

I like legal dramas and this was interesting from that perspective. I found it lacked the intrigue to keep my interest at some points and I was wondering "why was this in here" not only as I was reading it, but after.
boring *yawn*

Moving. Tragic. Sad. Extremely well written. A judge in Family Court must make a decision concerning an ill boy getting a transfusion and he is a Jehovah's Witness. Her marriage is falling apart as well.

This is a good story written in a very tight and uncluttered way. The characters were compelling and well-developed. I am still pondering what Mr. McEwan intended us to feel toward the characters. Without spoiling the plot, I really liked Fiona, but I thought her husband was selfish and unreasonable, and the ending left me a little unsatisfied because of the lack of resolution of the earlier conflict in the book in juxtaposition with Fiona's conflicted feelings at the end. But that was not enough to take away from my enjoyment of this book.

If ever a book can be downright annoying, The Children Act was. I picked up this book on a recommendation from someone who is a fan of Ian McEwan, and I thought I'd give him a chance. The book was a very quick read, but unfortunately most of my haste in reading it was because I just wanted to get to the end as soon as possible. 
 The story is that of Fiona Maye, a High Court judge who has strife in her marriage and regrets about never having children, who meets a 17-year-old cancer patient named Adam who refuses treatment along religious grounds. She has to make the decision whether to accept or reject his side of the argument, and whether the hospital should give him a blood transfusion he and his parents don't want based on their beliefs. 
 Interesting concept, right? Happens all the time. But somehow McEwan made it boring and lazy. Fiona is hardly involved in the court hearing and discussions at all, instead allowing all of the attorneys make arguments for her--I get that she's a judge and that's how court works, but it seemed like lazy work on the part of the author to not have Fiona, the protagonist, actually do anything to advance the story at certain points. Plus, her lack of religion, or at least lack of expressing it, seemed like some kind of hero story, like her level-headedness in the court of law was supposed to be a counterpoint to religion, and it seemed like something a nonbelieving author would do to give himself a pat on the back. I have no idea what McEwan's religious beliefs are, but that's how The Children Act read. In the end, the book had some good ideas in it, but execution was terrible. I have a few more Ian McEwan books in my lineup, but now I'm not sure if I'll be able to slog my way through any of them.

3.5 Not the best book by McEwan that I've read, but quite interesting. What I found the most interesting were the court cases discussed. The last case discussed by Fiona's colleague was especially timely in light of the recent case at Stanford. As he states, "It's bloody class warfare." Overall, I enjoyed McEwan's quiet ruminations on life, relationships, religion, and the law.

This was the first Ian McEwan book I'd read, and I absolutely loved it. 
 It's the story of a 50-year old London Judge, unhappily married. Before her is a case brought by a hospital regarding a 17 year old boy who has leukemia and needs a blood transfusion. His parents are Jehovah's Witness's so are refusing to allow this. 
 How will she make her decision, and what will happen then?

Genre: drama, law, medical 
 In a nutshell: Fiona, a high court, family judge who is going through marital problems, is tested when she is given the most difficult case in her career. 
 I was expecting this to be a more riveting story than it was and I expected it to suck me in. Sadly, it did not. I can understand how many people would like this book, but for me it just didn't work. 
 Fiona has dealt with many different cases as a high court family law judge. In fact, she just dealt with one that dealt her several blows to her morality. But she is dealt an even more difficult hand when she is presented with the case of Adam, a 17-year-old with leukemia. Because he and his family are members of the Jehovah's witness, Adam is refusing a blood transfusion that could save his life. But Adam is not 18, so the decision of whether he will get the transfusion is not his. In the midst of her husband leaving her to have an affair, Fiona must make this difficult decision. This story is one that makes you question what morality really means when moral decisions are taken out of the hands of capable minded individuals and put into the hands of the law. 
 I feel like such an unintelligent person, but I just didn't find this book interesting. Fiona wasn't an interesting or likable character. She is a workaholic that really has no thoughts or interests outside of work. It's no wonder her husband gets bored. She's so self-involved. And you're supposed to fall in love with Adam too, the young boy, but I didn't. He doesn't know what he wants or even who he is in any capacity. I just didn't feel for either of these characters. And that is the point of this book, isn't it? 
 Beyond that, in so many ways, I feel like this book isn't about what it sets out to be about. The rest of this review will be spoilers so if you are interested in reading this book, maybe think about skipping my spoilers. 
 Finally, beyond the book failing to keep my interest and unlikable characters, I just didn't get the point of the book. It seemed useless. 
 The trial lasted like 20 pages. and then it was over. The rest was just filler. And why did the book end that way? Literally the entire story was useless by then.

I've never read a book by Ian McEwan and I am sure it will be my last. There were elements that I thought were excellent and those that were far from it. I heard a lot about the author's books and maybe I was expecting something spectacular. I didn't hate this book nor did I love it. I can't figure out what all the fuss is about his books.

I wonder if I was reading the same book as the description described. I felt the book concentrated more on Fiona's marital strife than Adam, the sick 17 year old. The book starts out slow, picks up slightly when she's introduced to Adam, and then just falls flat. The book felt shallow and I didn't connect with the characters at all. Luckily this was a short book so I didn't waste too much time on it.

Thank you to Netgalley for letting me read this book. It was a lovely, poignant story. At first I found it tough going - any judge having to deal with children entangled in domestic issues has difficult decisions to make. The book took an unexpected turn when the judge takes a more personal interest in one of her cases, her well-considered judgment having impacts she could not anticipate.

- I still love Ian McEwan as always. 
 - I really feel for this protagonist. Walking the line from protecting the clients and entering herself into their personal lives, but then needing to maintain a sense of distance and decorum due to her profession in the law. 
 - I'm not sure if I would have mandated that Adam get the transfusion in the first place. I certainly don't agree with that belief system but the reality is that he was old enough to make a decision for himself. Maybe he and his family would have regretted it but they have the right to the decision. Turning 18 a few months later doesn't magically mature someone. 
 - Fiona's marriage also tugs at my heart. This is sort of a reverse "Harold and Maude". The death of a young man who should have so much life to live wakes her up to reconnect with her husband to take advantage of what limited time they may have together.

1.5 (rounded to 2 stars for the quality of writing, not the story) 
 McEwan can write and he certainly knows how to string words together in a beautiful way but the subject matter in this book leaves a lot to be desired. I was initially attracted to the story because of similar cases during my nursing career, and I was curious to see how McEwan would treat the subject. My answer, unfortunately, was not well or even believable. a kiss between the 18 year old boy and the 60 year old judge?! This much old(er) woman who no doubt looked like a grandmother to him?! I don't buy it 
 It didn't help that McEwan writes in a way that makes the reader very detached from his characters. So the secondary story of the judge and her husband left me cold. Actually, by the end of the book I can't say I blamed her husband for wanting a passionate fling. 
 I've given this author a fair chance and he's just not my cup of tea.
Beautifully written - every word counts. And a story that matters - about decisions, the impact of decisions and what drives our decision making.

(Fiction, Contemporary) 
 I loved McEwan's Atonement and was prepared to enjoy this book very much. 
 The Children Act by Ian McEwan 
 Judge Fiona Maye is dealing with an impending split in her marriage while she is reviewing a difficult case in her court. The case involves a blood transfusion for a seventeen-year-old minor who is one of Jehovah's Witnesses. 
 It perhaps goes without saying that I was disappointed in her court decision, but I knew it could go either way - that's real life. 
 However, McEwan's portrayal of Witnesses is so off that it was completely wrong. Their vocabulary, their explanation (or not) for their stand, and their reaction to the ruling were all very wide of the mark. 
 It appears to me that he studied only one court document of an actual case like this one, and it makes me question the authenticity of any characters he represents in his other novels. It completely put me off McEwan and I couldn't assign this even one star. 
 Zero stars

I gave this book 4 stars. I like the way Ian McEwan brings to life a certain kind of contemporary character -- educated, reflective. I listened to this book which was very appealingly read. Fiona Maye, the main character is a childless judge in family court who winds up dealing with children's issues all the time. The case of Adam, a 17-year old, refusing medical treatment draws her into a personal relationship just at the time her marriage is in trouble.

Although I have been disappointed with previous books by the author, a blurb of the book intrigued me. Reading it was money and precious time wasted. It depicts the solitude of a female judge, her strained marriage comprising suspected adultery by her husband, her short love interest in a young barely adult male (who was the subject of a case she heard), and contains tedious irrelevant descriptions of walks to and from court. To read it is to conclude that female judges are doomed to be childless and loveless. Damning conclusions.

Interesting read. Took me a while which may show that I wasn't AS invested in the story as the last couple of books I've read! Can't fault it but wasn't dying to open it up every day, 3 stars is probably fair

Not the best and not the worst of his novels, and I suppose I should have guessed how it would end. A nicely reflective style, with references to Victoria Gillick and the Cleveland children scandal from the 1980's to get me reminiscing.
Never really connected with the protagonist or the story.

3 1/2 
 Typically readable and thoughtful but just seems somewhat slight, as has most of his post-Atonement stuff. I kept thinking of Enduring Love while I read this, superficially alike in plot but a much better novel to my mind.

A little disappointed by this having loved McEwan's Atonement. I found The Children Act to be lacking in plot, verbose and containing a lot of 'filler' paragraphs/information that really wasn't necessary except to pad it out. I guess the aim of the book is about making you think rather than a gripping plot...
Overlong short story with too many distractions.

Having grown up in the Jehovah's Witness, and in my opinion it IS a cult not a religion, I was very curious how the issue of blood transfusions would be handled. Most of the public is deluded into thinking that children of Jehovah's Witnesses have choices, and they do not. 
 They must obey the rulers or the Governing Body, and their every command, and that goes from not saluting the flag to being forced to carry "No Blood Transfusion" cards. 
 Ian did a great job researching the realties about life for children in this particular cult, and the isolation and social awkwardness of the children, including the fact they are deliberately left unprepared for life if they leave the cult, and the vast majority do. 
 The subject is handled with class and was a page turner, hard to put down. 
 Was very believable, and that comes from someone (and we are less than 1% of the population) who really knows.

I thought this book would be a deep, powerful discussion of what happens when faith, life, & the law converge...unfortunately the writing was very disappointing. 
 Really could have been great.... 
 I would like to try other authors that write about cases that set legal precedents.

Fiona was three-dimensional from the start, right down to her body image in the author's mind; however, the curling chest hairs of her cardboard-cutout husband, along with the martyrdom togs of Adam, took this story down several notches in the second and third acts. 
 The final quarter of this interesting legal procedural, hitched as it is to a vaguely misogynistic elder wife clings/reconsiders/forgives narrative straight out of 1958, cannot help but disappoint. The telegraphed 'plot' ending is so drawn out as to command its own class action suit, and Fiona's ultimate guilt is so wooden, trite, and without merit as to taint, like poisoned fruit from any tree of illicit evidence, the entire novel.

I was touched by this novel. The conflict between the health and welfare of a young man as judged by a conscientious woman judge and the restrictions of a rigid religion provides an interesting plot. I could empathize with all the characters and I believe that is due to the careful and concise writing of McEwan. Fiona was a character I could easily admire.
Story was brilliantly written, however, I'm not sure how the parallel tales were supposed to connect. Maybe it deserves a book club discussion.

I can't come up with a solid complaint about this book, but it just didn't do much for me - maybe the topic is one I've already thought too much about, with my degrees in bioethics and law, so it didn't spark my interest. Well written, and others would probably find it compelling.
I honestly couldn't figure out what this book was about after going 1/3 of the way through it. I finally gave up...

The prose is good but I failed to be drawn to this story. I did not get the connection between the story of the boy and the cheating husband. There were at most three moments in the story when I was truly interested and kept reading. However most of the time it read like filler, beautifully written filler but pointless nonetheless.
Disappointed. Gave up at Page 155. This book won't be overdue going back to the library.

It just did not feel like a real story. Mr McEwan generally creates strong, realistic and deep characters but not in this book. Everything happens too quickly, leaving the reader alone with uncomfortable gaps...

We definitely had a good discussion about this book at my book club. The morality issues are certainly interesting and worth giving thought too. Some of the personal issues the judge dealt with didn't seem very relevant to the main story, and you can certainly tell the book was written by a man.

reference_books.title: East of Eden
reference_books.review_text: John Steinbeck has to be counted as one of the top American writers of the 20th century. Like many people I had read Of Mice and Men, Grapes of Wrath and possible others, but had never gotten around to East of Eden. I'm glad I did. According to WikiPedia, Steinbeck considered it his best work and I have to agree. It's the pinacle of his skill as a writer -- from the conception of the story to its telling, including an intriguing exigesis of the story of Cain and Abel, to the realization of his characters to his description of Salinas Valley, CA. If this is Steinbeck's best and he's one of the best of the 20th century, that makes this one of the best novels written by an American in the 20th century. If you haven't read it, don't wait too long.

reference_books.title: State of Wonder
reference_books.review_text: There are so many good things to say about this book, starting with Patchett's courage to even conceptualize such a story. Then why not 5 stars? The ending, which will be the point of most book club discussions I believe, disappoined me. It was too abrupt and it drew my focus to the up-til-then small questions I had about events in the story, such as the disappearance of Marina's second telephone and the mysteries of the research project. That said there were aspects to the ending that I liked. Therefore, I recommend this book highly to all readers.

reference_books.title: Cutting for Stone
reference_books.review_text: Extraordinary. A must read.

reference_books.title: Little Bee
reference_books.review_text: Like Steig Larsen, Cleave has an agenda which he hides less well in this strange story of improbable occurrences including a 16 year old's being able to stow away on a commercial liner and a refugee's being released from a detention center because another woman did a 'favor' for one of the keepers. Nevertheless, the problems of Africa are kept in front of us in this almost enchanting novel.

reference_books.title: The Girl in the Spider's Web (Millennium, #4)
reference_books.review_text: A worthy successor to Larsson's stories.

reference_books.title: Kushiel's Dart (Phèdre's Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I won't be reading this book past chapter 16. The subject matter is only appropriate for women age 18 to 30. It's extremely inappropriate for anyone under 18 especially girls. But my problem with Carey is her despicable parodying of Judaism--the only religious or ethnic group so identified. 
 She doesn't make much of an effort to hide her identificatiion of Judaism, using the word Yeshuite instead. On page 13 she writes, "the mind of the One God was much preoccupied with the death of his son, Yeshua ben Yosef, and the course of his chosen people." Instead a man name Elua defies God and creates an alternate world for the land in which the protagonist will be born, a land where brothels are the center of culture, and all is permitted. 
 This book was highly recommended by an agent interviewed in a writers' magazine. If this is the kind of book some agents are looking for these days, I shudder to consider the impact of that outlook on the reading public.

reference_books.title: Outlander (Outlander, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
In a workshop at this year's Tucson Festival of Books, Diana Gabaldon reported how she had to battle with Barnes & Noble, which kept placing her books in the Romance section even after they'd become NYT best sellers. Funny, I can't recall what section of the store she preferred, but it wasn't romance because that presumably is where stories that substitute appearances for substance are placed. 
 She may have wanted her books in general fiction, or perhaps in Science-Fiction/Fantasy, or possibly--if they had such as section back then--historical fiction. 
 The above is preface to a few comments on the well-known first book in what has now become a series totaling a million words (according to Ms. Gabaldon). Reading (or re-reading) Outlander--I'm sure I read some of the books in the series, but since Goodreads didn't exist when I did I don't have a record of which ones--I can understand why B&N wanted to hang a Romance label on the book back 20+ years ago when it first came out. 
 If Gabaldon didn't create the historical fiction category, her books have had a lot to do with making it what it is today--i.e., a genre which attracts thousands of readers and dozens of imitators. 
 Outlander--for anyone who hasn't read it--contains all the elements of a good story: interesting characters, an interesting setting--both place (Scotland( and time (mid-18th century), a plot which keeps the reader interested, sex, and romance in the "heroic" not Harlequin sense. 
 But be careful if you pick up Gabaldon for the first time. You'll have a hard time putting her down.

reference_books.title: The Good Lord Bird
reference_books.review_text: A tour de force--the recreation of the last years and days of the abolitionist John Brown told through the eyes of a young slave who accompanied Brown on his last campaign. But The Good Lord Bird is much more than historical fiction. It serves as a treatise on race, gender, religion, and worthy and lost causes. What makes this novel work so well is the honesty of young Henry whose nickname Onion spared him from having to answer to a girl's name despite the fact that he pretended to be one. Onion "tells it like it is," including his own many shortcomings. Onion/McBride's portrait of Brown, while certainly an exageration, nevertheless gets to the heart of the matter--Brown's willingness to die in the service of his belief that God wanted him to put an end to slavery. McBride's portrait of Frederick Douglas, on the other hand, may disturb some. It isn't favorable, but in that sense it continues a feud which has gone on now for 150 years and is likely to last another 150. Rarely has history been mined so creatively to retell an important story in a manner that allows us to reflect on contemporary society. I'm adding McBride's other novels to my to read list.

reference_books.title: Freedom
reference_books.review_text: Although not a book one "enjoys" while reading it, Freedom grows on you and is worth slogging through. I'd give it 3 & 1/2 stars.

reference_books.title: Eldest (The Inheritance Cycle, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I have to stop reading this one too (along with Terry Goodkind's horror novel Severed Souls). I didn't read the first book in the series, so that put Paolini at a disadvantage in trying to get me engaged. After 100 pages or so, I keep falling asleep whenever I try to read...I don't care about the main character. I can't picture his dragon who seems to be smaller than Shaquille O'Neill. There are too many ridiculous forgettable names and languages whose pronunction is impossible. Sorry, Chris. No sale.

book_a.title: The Yiddish Policemen's Union
book_a.user_review:
You don't have to be Jewish to enjoy The Yiddish Policemen's Union, but it helps. Michael Chabon has blended a police procedural into an alternative universe where the Arabs pushed the Jews out of the promised land in 1948 resulting in 3 million of them migrating to a narrow strip of land in Alaska. However, the land grant was temporary and with only two months to go before the Jews have to vacate, Meyer Landsman, a police detective who is living off of Slivowitz in a seedy hotel won't let the murder of a young heroin addict go uninvestigated despite explicit instructions to drop the case by his ex-wife boss. 
 Chabon's inventive history and heavy use of Yiddish terms -- some of which he invented for this book -- will be tough sledding for some readers. Those willing to suspend their disbelief and learn that a noz is a cop and a shoyfer a cell phone, however, will be repaid with the luxury of Chabon's inventive imagery, imaginative plotting and ingenious insights into the human condition. 
 Alternative histories are not uncommon these days. Harry Turtledove is perhaps the best known writer of this genre, but Chabon also leans on Philip K. Dick, Murray Leinster and Harry Harrison. Chabon's world has a direct bearing on the plot as readers discover when his murder investigation ties into the Chassidic longing for coming of the Messiah and secular Jews desire to recapture their lost homeland. 
 At its core, despite the fictional setting and ethnic flavor of the plot and characters, The Yiddish Policemen's Union is about people trying to do the right thing in a world conspiring against them. Detective Landsman works to forget the son he and his wife aborted which ended their marriage as well as the fact that he sees himself as having been a disappointment to his father. His half-cousin and partner Berko hasn't seen his father in years and the dead heroin addict so disappointed his rabbi father than he buried him in a religious ceremony many years before the young man's actual death. 
 But in addition to the complex plot and the down-to-earth characters, Chabon invites us to see a world where there are shtekeleh (Philipino doughnuts), latke (rookie policemen), boundary mavens, shtarkers and tohubohu, where the "winter sky of southeastern Alaska is a Talmud of gray; an inexhaustible commentary on a Torah of rain clouds and dying light," where "Landman's congratulations are so ironic that they are heartfelt, and they are so heartfelt that they can only come off as insincere," where Landman's ex "accepts a compliment as if it's a can of soda that she suspects him of having shaken," and where "every generation loses the messiah it has failed to deserve." 
 The Yiddish Policemen's Union is about redemption of the kind that you don't have to be Jewish to long for.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Yiddish Policemen's Union is an alternate reality novel where, after the WWII, Jews were relocated to Sitka, Alaska. The lead character is Meyer Landsman, a disillusioned but still occasionally brilliant policeman who wants to make a final effort in solving a case before the Sitka district becomes again an official part of The United States. 
 The alternate history gives the writer an opportunity to set his story into an environment which is familiar from old crime novels but in which almost all of the characters are Jewish. Other than that, though, the history has a limited role in the story; it obviously affects the story and is, in some ways, prominent as a plot device, but with minor tweaks the story could've been set in just about any small town. 
 Chabon uses the opportunity to fill the dialogue with Yiddish (?) vocabulary. Even though you get used to it, it still makes the novel a bit tedious to read - it may fit the characters but it doesn't really add to the story itself. 
 Having said that, though, the crime - a junkie Messiah getting shot in the middle of the night - is intriguing, and the plot thickens satisfactorily. Chabon knows how to create suspects, and he knows how to drop hints - but you'll probably notice them only after they get pointed out.
Eh. I got fifty pages into this and just didn't like it. Too masculine of a tone for my taste.
Couldn't get into it. Abandoned on a airplane, "by accident".

It is part science fiction and part mystery. Or Yiddish Policeman is fully both. Thus just by that it is hard to classify. Whether you have a Yiddish background, or great exposure to a Jewish heritage, or an Alaskan one, the world creation by Chabon elevates this story to a level beyond the common in either genre. 
 Yiddish Policeman's is a very good book. It is a well deserved edition of exceptional literature. An achievement and worth reading. Is the mystery a little weak and perhaps a bit like a television mystery episode, in parts. Is our protagonist too intimately caught up in the details of the mystery, again perhaps. But as the story stretches out, these become small quibbles that do not detract that this is a phenomenal piece of writing. 
 The narrative and detail in creating the world soon has you engrossed in that world so you can believe in it. Would the jews wish to resettle to much safer Alaska, then to the very turbulent holy land? Probably not, but with speculative fiction, once you give into it, then the new worlds builds upon itself. Would oil be cheaper if there were no wars in the mid-east, or would there still be wars there over other issues. 
 Since we are concerned about the Jewish settlement in Alaska, we don't really even care about such. We become consumed about the world Chabon has crafted. Even thinking that perhaps more in this world would be nice to visit again.

I REALLY wanted to like this book. I loved Kavalier and Klay and The Wonder Boys...I even liked Summerland. I like the way Chabon writes so I liked it because it is written like he writes...make sense? Well, neither does most of the book. He did a great job of creating an entirely different world in Summerland, but he just didn't manage it here. Too convoluted. It would have helped if he had explained the history in its own chapter, instead of trying to explain it in bits and pieces through the characters and asides. Even footnotes would have been okay. As it was, I was lost. I did like the main character and the story itself, once I was able to pluck it from all of the history, but it was ALOT of work to do. Disappointing.
Not as compelling as some of his other work, but still a great read. Picks up at the end and has me wondering why I never heard about the perfect red heifer before?

I tried. I really did. I was listening to this book and found I just was not paying attention at all. Hearing so many Yiddish words my Great Grandma used to say was pretty much the best part of the book for me.

The Yiddish Policemen's Union won the 2007 Nebula Award for Best Science Fiction Novel of the year, and the 2008 Hugo Award for Best Science Fiction Novel of the year. 
 What a load of rubbish. 
 The only bit of this novel which might even remotely be considered SF is the fact that it's set in an alternate history where the state of Israel was a failed experiment, and many (most?) refugee Jews wound up in a settlement in Sitka, Alaska. 
 Now, I picked the novel up precisely *because* it won SF awards, and my disgust at how far from SF this novel is really flavored my reading of the novel. 
 So this is a noir-esque murder mystery novel, with a down-on-his-luck detective investigating a killing that took place in the residential hotel where he lives. He and his supporting cast are somewhat enjoyable, and the setting actually is pretty neat. The politics against which everything plays out are also interesting. 
 There may be a lot of this novel that I don't "get," seeing as I've got no Jewish anything in my background, also. 
 This is a rambling review. The book was almost enjoyable. 2.5 of 5 stars.

Set in Sitka, Alaska, a homeland established for Jews following the holocaust, the murder of a chess prodigy junkie propels Detective Landsman and his half Jewish, half-Tlinglit partner,Berko into the world of the ultra Orthodox. It's been 60 years since Sitka was given to the Jews who survived the camps as a safe haven and in one month it will revert to American ownership. The Jews will now have to fend for their own. [return] Meyer Landsman, a depressed. alcoholic detective, goes up against the black hat, gangster Verbovers and meets up with incredible personalities in his quest to find the murderer. Incredible language, atmosphere and characters.

I have to give myself a lot of credit for restraint. I was SOOO tempted to throw this f***ing book against the wall, stomp on it and tear it, page by page. But, alas, as a good librarian, I refrained. This book is SO AWFUL it's GHASTLY. A GANTZEH SHANDA because Kavalier and Klay was SOOO Wonderful. 
 FEH!

I really enjoyed The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay, probably because I was such a fan of comic books growing up. This one, a detective novel, I couldn't become invested in the same way. Chabon is a great writer and his greatest talent might be his ability to world-build and develop characters through their backstory without making it feel like you're being bombarded with information dumps. Almost the entire first third of the book is backstory and yet I didn't find myself growing impatient. That's a testament to Chabon's ability. As the story progressed, however, I never found myself engrossed the way I wanted to be.

The Yiddish Policemen's Union: Larger-than life characters overwhelm noir plot 
 Originally posted at Fantasy Literature 
 I knew I would eventually get around to this book. How can one resist? An alternate history about the US resettling European Jews to Alaska to escape the Holocaust, in a world in which Germany defeated the Soviet Union, Berlin was destroyed by nuclear weapons in 1946, and Israel was destroyed in 1948 in a different version of the Arab-Israeli War. Michael Chabon uses this setting for a hard-boiled detective noir story inspired by the works of Raymond Chandler, Dashiell Hammett, and Ross Macdonald, and adds the most colorful, ironic, and over-the-top narrative voice I've read in years. The audiobook is narrated expertly by actor Peter Riegert, who grew up in a Jewish neighborhood outside New York and whose resume includes two years on The Sopranos. He handles the colorful literary chutzpah of Chabon's prose without embellishment and with cool competence.
