 Chabon revels in all aspects of Jewish culture, both what can be viewed as stereotypes or treasured cultural traits, along with classic detective noir, alcoholic self-destructive cops, sinister and yet comical mob bosses, chess geniuses that may also be the Messiah, Native American tribes, and the cold inhospitable backdrop of the Alaskan coastline itself. It's a very eclectic and enticing stew with different flavors battling for supremacy, and for that reason will not be to everyone's taste, but nobody would deny is unique and memorable. There is also a copious amount of Yiddish terms that add yet another layer of flavors to an already heady concoction, so have your web glossary handy. 
 I won't describe the plot in detail since others have done that already. Rather, I'd like to include some of my favorite quotes from the book, because they are frankly what gives the book its character, rather than the plot itself. In fact, while I really liked the writing most of the time, it sometimes completely overwhelmed the story. Strip out the colorful, larger-than-life character descriptions and alternate history backdrop, and the noir mystery isn't really that memorable. So the charm is in the telling, and as far as that goes, Chabon certainly doesn't hold back. Whether you find it incredibly brilliant, charming but overbearing, or just too much really depends on your literary preferences. I felt all three at times, so I gave it 3 stars overall. Here are some memorable passages that will help you decide if this book is for you. 
 The main character, detective Meyer Landsman: 
 "He has the memory of a convict, the balls of a fireman, and the eyesight of a housebreaker. When there is crime to fight, Landsman tears around Sitka like a man with his pant leg caught on a rocket. It's like there's a film score playing behind him, heavy on the castanets. The problem comes in the hours when he isn't working, when his thoughts start blowing out the open window of his brain like pages from the blotter. Sometimes it takes a heavy paperweight to pin them down." 
 Landsman's estranged ex-wife and fellow detective, Bina Gelbfish: 
 "You have to look at Jews like Bina Gelbfish, to explain the wide range and persistence of the race. Jews who carry their homes in an old cowhide bag, on the back of a camel, in the bubble of air at the center of their brains. Jews who land on their feet, hit the ground running, ride out the vicissitudes, and make the best of what falls to hand, from Egypt to Babylon, from Minsk Gubernya to the district of Sitka. Methodological, organised, persistent, resourceful, prepared... A mere re-drawing of borders, a change in governments, those things can never faze a Jewess with a good supply of hand wipes in her bag." 
 The most powerful mob boss in Sitka, Alaska: 
 Rabbi Heskel Shpilman is a deformed mountain, a giant ruined desert, a cartoon house with the windows shut and the sink left running. A little kid lumped him together, a mob of kids, blind orphans who never laid eyes on a man. They clumped the dough of his arms and legs to the dough of his body, then jammed his head down on top. A millionaire could cover a Rolls-Royce with the fine black silk-and-velvet expanse of the rebbe's frock coat and trousers. It would require the brain strength of the eighteen greatest sages in history to reason through the arguments against and in favor of classifying the rebbe's massive bottom as either a creature of the deep, a man-made structure, or an unavoidable act of God. 
 Some hard-boiled noir description of a greasy spoon in town: 
 The hidden master of the Filipino-style Chinese donut is Benito Taganes, proprietor and king of the bubbling vats at Mabuhay. Mabuhay, dark, cramped, invisible from the street, stays open all night long. It drains the bars and cafes after hours, concentrates the wicked and the guilty along its chipped Formica counter, and thrums with the gossip of criminals, policemen, shtarkers and shlemiels, whores and night owls. With the fat applauding in the fryers, the exhaust fans roaring, and the boom box blasting the heartsick kundimans of Benito's Manila childhood, the clientele makes free with their secrets. A golden mist of kosher oil hangs in the air and baffles the senses. Who could overhear with ears full of KosherFry and the wailing of Diomedes Maturan? 
 On the Messiah: 
 "But there was always a shortfall, wasn't there? Between the match that the Holy One, blessed be He, envisioned and the reality of the situation under the chuppah. Between commandment and observance, heaven and earth, husband and wife, Zion and Jew. They called that shortfall 'the world.' Only when Messiah came would the breach be closed, all separations, distinctions, and distances collapsed. Until then, thanks be unto His Name, sparks, bright sparks, might leap across the gap, as between electric poles. And we must be grateful for their momentary light."

I did not finish this novel. I was listening to it on audiobook and finally gave up at disc 4. It seemed to be a very popular book this year, but I simply tired of waiting for the writer to get to his point. The best that I can recollect is that this novel was SUPPOSED to deal with the murder of a talented, Yiddish chess player, who also happened to be the son of the "head hancho" in the Russian Jewish population. The son and the father were estranged for many years. Meyer, the investigator on the case, lived in the same hotel where the son was found dead. Ironically, Meyer has a great hatred for chess because his father was so obsessed with it when Meyer was a boy. That is the extent of what I could discern about the plot in the course of 4 audio discs. The remainder of the time these discs were playing the reader was spewing all the fancy literary devices used to move the plot nowhere. My mind was constantly wandering off because the story was moving nowhere...I wanted to scream, "GET TO THE POINT ALREADY." Literary device is extremely powerful when used to move the plot...but when the plot starts to move in circles or just stand still, it serves no purpose at all. This author could benefit from reading a little Aristotle. He had far too much "stuff" going on. One plot is sufficient for one novel.
While there were some very interesting elements to this book, including a twisting plot and great premise, I simply have a hard time with completely dysfunctional protagonists...

Ugh. I've heard good things about this author, but after this book I'm not so sure that I want to investigate further. The first few chapters were torture. There was so much Yiddish that, as my friend so rightly said, you almost needed a Yiddish to English dictionary. The storyline was alright, but I kept mixing the characters up and was never really clear as to which time period the story was taking place in. There were jumps back and forth and really, I was relieved to reach the end of the book. 
 We'll see if I can bring myself to crack open another of his books - the highly recommended one.

This was a better book than I expected. I've read a couple of other books by Michael Chabon and have been left with uneven experiences. "The Adventures of Kavelier and Clay" was really good in some places and rather drawn out in others. Somehow Chabon won a Pulitzer Prize for that. "Gentlemen of the Road" was much of the same thing. In certain parts you're really drawn in but most of the time I just read it to get to the finish line and close the back cover. Despite being unhappy with my previous outings with this author I just had to read a book with this title. This book "The Yiddish Policemen's Union" was a much more fun experience. Every time I had to close the book I was unthrilled that I didn't have time to keep reading. 
 Meyer Landsman is the main character in this yarn that happens in a different version of what is today's world. In this world there is no Israel. Instead the Jews are given a tract of land in Alaska to live in temporarily. And it's coming up on the time for their "lease" on that stretch of frozen tundra to expire. Diaspora is at hand again. Landsman is a detective in the Jewish sections of Alaska called the Sitka. He's one sad sack of a man. A divorced alcoholic who really doesn't believe in very much at all. This, of course, makes for an excellent leading character. He investigating a murder that happens in the shitty hotel he's forced to live in. Along with himself he trundles through this story with his partner/cousin the half-Indian/half-Jew Berko and his ex-wife/boss Bina. You'll find that nearly every character in the book could use a slash to separate one facet from another. Much like Indian/Jew, ex-wife/boss, rabbi/spy or chess master/junkie. Meyer is an excellent medium to tell a story through but it's really all the strange characters surrounding him that make the story live. While investigating this murder he finds conspiracies, evil Rabbis, CIA spies, double agents and even a purely red cow. It's really a bit of a strange story. 
 Somehow Chabon makes it perfectly believable that all the Jews that would've been in Israel are actually in Alaska. It's quite a feat really. He peppers the dialogue with Yiddish and Hebrew which kind of keeps you immersed there. Not that I know what any of those words mean but they're given to you in a way that you can dope it out through context. Now I know that "sholem" means gun and "shoyfer" means phone. See, I managed to learn something through fiction.

I wanted to like this book more. It is intricate, thoughtful, funny and well written. It is just not my favorite kind of book. I guess it is the same thing that makes me not care for the CSI/SVU/Bones types of Tv shows. I would still try another book by this author and was grateful for the recommendation (a church member).
I'm too ignorant to understand most of the Yiddish references - had to quit trying to read it. Good writing, though, wish I hadn't felt lost through what I did read, if that makes any sense at all.

I found TYPU to be greatly satisfying. Believable characters in a believable nonexistent world. The writing is TASTY, to quote Jack Black... :d 
 In all seriousness, though, Chabon's imagined Jewish settlement (if you can call a city of millions a settlement) of Sitka, and the world it inhabits, to be entirely plausible and tangible. This is the sort of alternate history novel that I want to see more of, instead of the poorly-characterised but well-conceived timelines of wars and accidental deaths. I can also compare the book to Roth's _The Plot Against America_ and favorably so as the ending to TYPU was ten times better.

This is my second Michael Chabon book after Wonder Boys and my reaction is pretty much the same to both: he's a very talented writer with great ideas but one whose books suffer from being overwritten and drawn out. 
 The Yiddish Policemen's Union suffers from some significant ax grinding in the final third. This is double annoying since he hides his agenda in the first half of the book and tries to make it part of the big reveal toward the end. It's triply annoying since it's done using the tired cliche of taking a non-violent group you disagree with in real life and turning them into violent, murderous terrorists in your novel. 
 At one point the Coen Brothers were attached to adapt this book. While I'm mostly glad they didn't since I wasn't a big fan of it, it would have been interesting to see what they'd have done with the material

I just finished The Yiddish Policeman's Union by Pulitzer Prize Winner Michael Chabon. It is a what if book. What if the state of Isreal had failed and the Jews were relocated to a stretch of Alaska and their lease has just run out. I finished the book. I didn't hate it. I realize that part of being in a book club is stretching your boundries. This book was very hard to get into and the rhythm was difficult to follow. I also found the ending disappointing. 
 Spend your time on a better read.

I picked up this book because I loved The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier & Clay. I very rarely give a book less than 3 stars, but this one just wasn't for me. I couldn't enjoy it. Between the story and the writing, it was a struggle for me to get through.

I read The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay and Summerland by Chabon, both of which I liked infinitely better. I felt that there were a lot of large jumps in the plot progression of this book that made it more difficult for me to follow. I also thought the story was too far-fetched, so I found myself not really caring about it. The ending was also very anti-climactic. I don't know if I had higher expectations for this book, but I finished it feeling disappointed.

Such a great premise (alternate version of history where there is no Israel and the Jewish homeland is in of Alaska), such a crappy book. I wanted to love it, but just didn't find it engaging or interesting at all and didn't even really care about the murder mystery and the center of the novel.
I couldn't even finish this book, I thought it was so boring and hard to get into.
Oof. I'm just not a Chabon fan at all. Got maybe 50 pages in, and hit eject.

This was okay. I liked the story, but for me, the language got in the way -- there's a lot of Yiddish. Not so much that I couldn't follow along, but enough that I felt I was missing something, whether it was another shade of meaning or a funny/ironic use of a word. For example, I just Googled "shoyfer," the word used in place of cell phone. It roughly means "ritual ram's horn," so there is clearly some joke or tease being made in the use of that word. I'm not one to sit with a dictionary or with Google and look up every other word, so I'm sure I missed a lot. And since I don't know much about Judaism, I know I missed some references. Overall, I think the book would have been pretty funny if I knew Yiddish.
Very interesting fantasy tale.

Gave it the 100-page test. It failed to grab my attention, pull me in or in any way interest me in plot, character, setting or writing by page 100, so I'm not going to continue on. I'm sure it's "imaginative," as every review seems to state, but a unique idea isn't enough to keep me going.
boring boring boring...

It's thick 
 with yid 
 Maybe too thick 
 and Sitka 
 with 3 million people? 
 C'mon now 
 8-9K is more like it 
 But I'm reading it 
 and because it was never available 
 on the Kindle 
 the publisher and author 
 both deserve one star less 
 than they even got
This languished as a breakfast-time reading book for a long time!

Its not often that I give up on a book, but I sure as shit gave up on this one. I made it like 4...5? chapters in before I threw up my hands & said forget it! 
 The premise sounded really, really interesting, but I just found Chabon's writing style to be very bland & cumbersome while also never getting hooked into the story.

I really tried with this book. I really did. I love Michael Chabon. I loved Mysteries of Pittsburgh, Kavalier and Clay...this one, not so much. I rarely walk away from a book. I did with this one. Half way through and I just didn't care about the characters or what happened to them.

I wanted to like this book. I liked the title and the premise (a futuristic fantasy about Jews settling in Alaska after WWII, combined with a murder mystery). But I just didn't get it. It was very cleverly written, but I had to force myself to keep reading it. The one saving grace was Bina Gelbfish, the ex-wife of Landsman (the protagonist). I loved her feisty character and could have read a whole book about her.

Picked this one up primarily out of lip service to one of my favorite books: The Amazing Adventures of Kavilier and Clay. Fairly or unfairly it was difficult for me not to compare the two. Bottom line, Kavilier and Clay is the far superior book (it did win a Pulitzer), but there are still some interesting elements here. 
 With Chabon the jewel is truly in the descriptions, the metaphors. Maybe aside from Tolkien he has some of the most visual descriptions you will ever read. Sometimes his metaphors make absolutely no sense and I still love them just for how inventive and original they are. See: "He had a voice like an onion rolling around in a coffee can." The Jewish and Alaska elements and the collision of cultures was probably the most interesting thing that went on here, but that was mostly peripheral. 
 This book just didn't grip me though. The whole plot device of the sad sack detective on a murder mystery feels very tired through countless iterations in pop culture. Many of the chapters were also very formulaic: Here's a clue I failed to notice so I need to go talk to this person. Kind of Meh.

This book was plain AWFUL....too confusing, too much flipping to the back of the book to look at the glossary...awful. 
 I loved the idea....I love reading about Alaska...but ugh. Too confusing, too many sentences to dscribe everything. Ugh. 
 Doesn't even deserve a star....I didn't used to give up on books, but I read 50 pages and was so disinterested by this book that I started finding other things to read when I climbed into bed. Time to say syanora. 
 One less book on my shelf. Don't recommend it AT ALL. Put it down...and go back to the library.

I won't give this a rating because I don't feel like I gave it a fair shake. I couldn't even get through the second disc! I got really confused by all of the characters and I didn't understand some of the yiddish terms used (and I know a good deal of yiddish, or so I thought). Anyhoo, it was due back at the library, so back it went. Maybe I'll try it again later.

This book would probably be much better if you removed the first 130 pages. The author may have won the Pulitzer Prize, but as far as I can tell, he won solely for his adept touch at descriptions. Plot was farfetched and full of navel gazing. There were many Yiddish words dropped in for color, but so many that it became distracting. Not worth the effort!

This is set in Sitka, Alaska, and in this story, there is a large Jewish population living there. There was a murder investigation, a divorced policeman whose ex-wife becomes his supervisor, and I'm not sure what all else happened. 
 My mind wandered and I just didn't find much interesting in this book. There were a lot of characters I couldn't seem to get straight and I think a lot of Jewish references went way over my head. I just wasn't interested enough to really pay attention to what I was reading, and as a result, I really don't even know much of what happened. I did like the ex-wife character and the banter between her and her ex-husband. Beyond that, I was just reading to get through it and most of what I read wasn't sticking.

Usually I read a new book in about a day or two or maybe three if the book is 'literary' - this has taken me weeks (practically forever in my world). I thought since I enjoy a good fantasy novel, that I would understand and like the whole alternate reality thing, but obviously I am not as smart as I thought. I continually felt lost. There were parts that I felt were beautiful but most of the time I was re-reading wondering, 'what the hey is going on?' 
 I read a review after I finished, the reviewer compared Chabon to a person leaving their house and looking in the mirror and taking off an accessory. He should have taken off a few accessories. I loved that review because I agreed wholeheartedly. The bones of the story were interesting but I found the bones lost amongst the twinkling jewels.
I didn't finish this because I didn't understand the dialogue.
Wanted to love it like I do so much of Chabon's work. Couldn't.
Just could not get into it... Maybe when I have more time to work with the Yiddish that is interspersed. Not a "light" read.

Oy, Chabon can certainly turn a phrase. His writing style challenges me and I love the fact that I occasionally have to read a passage several times aloud to fully appreciate how he's crafted the words. This novel was extremely original and chock full of my preferred brand of dark humor. What beautifully frail characters. I wish I hadn't finished it already.

I really wanted to like this book. I had heard a great deal about it and I always love a good mystery. Since this was nominated for an Edgar, I assumed it would fall into that category. I listened to the first 4 discs of the audio version and had to give it up. I had NO idea what was going on. I know next to nothing about jewish culture and was completely in the dark the whole time. I really didn't want to have to do additional research to read a book for fun. So I gave up. But I really wanted to like this book.

The first half of this book is terrific and I couldn't put it down. The ending sucked. It was so completely ridiculous, far-fetched, and political, I couldn't stand it. Chabon ruined what could have been a brilliant book by giving it a terrible ending. 
 Also, he could have done a lot more with the Alaska setting. Alaska is absolutely gorgeous, but Chabon made it sound dismal and gray. I think he visited Sitka before writing the book, but the Alaska of the book is not the real Alaska.

I have read that no two people read the same book. I did not finish it. This is rare for me, but I am not the audience for this book. 
 I found the world-building tedious. I was also offended by the stereotypical portrayal of Jews. When a book is highly acclaimed, I usually feel that I am at fault when I don't "get" it. My multiple use of the word "I" is an indication that that I am not saying it is a bad book.

This would make my short list for the most overwritten novel I've ever read. It's Michael Chabon so of course there are some fabulous lines. But at times I felt like I was reading Thomas Pynchon or Nabokov fan fiction. Several times I was on the point of abandoning it but annoyingly Chabon would suddenly bring all his considerable talents as a storyteller to the table and produce a great chapter. Problem was, that was almost always followed by another five rambling overwritten ones. 
 It reminded me in ways of Jonathon Safran Foer's last book, which is essentially a small-canvassed novel about the breakup of a marriage but given monumental import by inventing an apocalyptic war in Israel as a backdrop. This too is essentially about the break-up of a marriage and this too reinvents history to up the stakes. Such vast world changing premises, often used in science fiction, are an effective device for heightening expectation, promising untold revelations but there usually arrives a moment when you realise what you're reading is just another story about a man and a woman who can't get on any more. Maybe though that's clever as all good storytelling is essentially about raising expectation. It didn't though seem especially clever here because my expectations were quickly punctured by all the grandiose overwriting. 
 A tactic he uses is to often describe the insignificant in terms of something infinitely more significant through high voltage overwrought similes, so the everyday has a kind of bogus epic sweep to it. Again maybe this is clever as the novel has at its heart on the one hand an existence of thrift and on the other a belief in transfiguration symbolised by a Messiah character. But for me it came across as someone indulging in the kind of fun that gets out of hand. 
 It's also about a murder and I'm guessing pastiches or high fives famous noir writers like Chandler and Hammett. 
 There's lots of talk of the great American novel but I wonder if, behind the scenes, there isn't also a kind of competition to write the great Jewish novel. Interestingly, Nicole Krauss in her new novel alludes indirectly to the existence of such pressures. I suspect you're much more likely to enjoy Chabon's novel if you're Jewish because if you're not it's often like eavesdropping on family jokes as an outsider. For me it had an elitist strain running through it which I didn't like. Writers surely should be intent on breaking down barriers, not reinforcing them, no matter how playfully.

I enjoyed his writing style, but felt much too out of the loop to finish this book. As contradictory as this sounds, it was both too much of a straight-up cop story, and too ensconced in Jewish tradition, for me to make it through the book. 
 But it interested me enough to pick up another of his books, which I'm in the process of liking very much.

book_b.title: Olive Kitteridge
book_b.user_review: The main character is not very likeable and doesn't change much during the course of Strout's portrait of life in small-town Maine. To lighten the load she introduces and then dismisses a series of other characters whose lives are not working out much better than Olive's. I guess ordinary folk who do the right thing aren't very interesting, but the problem with Olive's acerbic tongue and hypercritical disposition is that there's no basis for it other than her father committed suicide and her mother wasn't perfect. All that said, Strout is a master at close observations and the right word. I just wish she'd chosen a different set of characters to enlighten us about.

sample_reviews.review_text:
DNF after 50 pages 
 *Phew!* I'm a little bit impressed with myself that I managed to make it this far! Wow is this boring. I couldn't find any semblance of a plot anywhere, and I found myself losing focus and thinking about other things while attempting to read it, because it was so boring that I couldn't even make myself pay attention. I also had trouble understanding why it was even called "Olive Kitteridge" when most of the first 50 pages focuses on her husband...not her. Maybe it got more interesting or found its footing later on in the book, but I'm just glad that I don't feel the need to read on and find out! 
 I was attempting to read this so that I could watch the HBO series based on it, but now that I've tried, I'll be joyfully skipping right on to the episodes without a second thought! Let's just hope they're not as dull as the book.
I guess if you want to win a Pulitzer Prize you should write a novel about sad people living depressing lives with no hope of anything getting better.

One of the fastest books I've read! I really enjoyed this, actually found it hard to put down sometimes. The way the story is told, from a lot of characters perspective, really rounded out Olive as a character and gave many dimensions to this town and this story. Olive grows so much and I found myself crying with her and smiling at her witty remarks. All of the characters in the book you find yourself attached to by the end of their chapters. I found myself rethinking a lot about the way I treat people and how to appreciate the tiny moments. Excellent read!

Even after finishing this book, I could not see what all the fuss was about. It is a series of minimally related stories -- related because they all take place in a small Maine town and the epynomous retired schoolteacher has a role (sometimes major, sometimes cameo) in all of them -- that are pretty bleak. Is the author trying to tell us that into each life a little rain must fall, or that we can't judge someone unless we walk a mile in their moccasins? I persisted through the depressing stories because people I admire -- including smart friends and the Pulitzer committee -- thought this was a great book. If any of my Goodreads friends can explain why, please tell me. Behind the picket fences and comfortable wooden cottages, there is someone who is lethally anorexic,or committing adultery,or in denial that their son stabbed someone 29 times, or about to be jilted at the altar. How anyone kept their spirits up in this town is beyond me -- and maybe Henry, who tried so hard to do so in the face of all odds, was punished for his efforts by suffering a stroke that left him debilitated, blind and speechless. As we say in Yiddish, genug! Enough already.

This sequence of short stories that are connected by the stony New Englanders of a small town in Maine and the central character, Olive Kitteridge, is an empathetic book that forces the reader to understand the motivation of each character whether redeeming or not. I am guessing that I am one of the few who liked the main character right from the start, flub-dubness and all. The dog-loving energy and directness of Olive combined with deep flaws, humanize her struggles of becoming a better person even if it took her seventy years to give up her controling nature in order to live at peace with what life presents to her. Elizabeth Strout is a natural story teller that honors the hidden lives of everyday people.

I couldn't finish this book, simply on the notion that the main character is so nasty and mean to everyone she comes in contact with. I think there is enough of it in the world already. The other characters are interesting, but not enough for me to be in this negative space. Oh well.

Content: profanity, sexual references, adultery, suicide. 
 Did not enjoy this book. Could not get past the first couple chapters. Boring and depressing book.

This novel is a series of short stories and I am reading it as an occasional book. I did not care for the first couple chapters much so am not real motivated to continue. I have it in the car for when I am stuck waiting for something like the dentist.

For me, it is just blah. 
 I rarely read short stories, and when I purchased this book I didn't realize that it is essentially short stories. A reviewer on Amazon describes it as though a chapter was ripped out of 20 different books about Olive and compiled into one book. The characters all disappear from the canvas when the chapter ends. I just began to like the people when the story changes and revolves around another character. Yes, Olive is in each story, but I fond her to be an unlikable character and so this doesn't rescue the story. I will not read this again.

In an attempt to read the more recent Pulitzer fiction winners, I decided to listen to Olive Kitterage. I definitely enjoyed these bleak linked stories. Honestly, linked stories are one of my favorite literary devices and Stout did a great job dropping Olive into each story. I like this one much better than Goon Squad. 
 I loved Olive - her acerbic nature was hilarious to me. She used the phrase "hells bells" which is also one of my routine utterances. Unfortunately, I figure I will be/act very similar to Olive as I continue to age. 
 I am looking forward to reading more of Stouts fiction in the future. (less)

The beginnings of the stories are a bit slow, and I wondered why it was titled such, when she's not the full subject of the stories, but there is a richness in the whole that makes me absolutely quenched by the end (and also drenched; yup, I cried). Strout shows us her understanding of the banal of life, but also the deep hope that is in us all. I left the book feeling touched, and hopeful, and (dare I say it, so you don't think I'm a sentimentalist...) full of love.

My book group read this and we all found it an intriguing portrait of a woman we could all relate to...both as someone we might know and someone we might be. In all her prickly fallibility, Olive has a warm and caring side and also has had an effect on residents of the Maine town of Crosby over the years.

Another one of those books I wanted to like more than I did. I nearly gave up on it. My favorite part was on the last page. "two slices of Swiss cheese pressed together, such holes they brought you this union - what pieces life took out of you".

While this book has an unusual structure, being made up of short stories connected by the titular character, there was something about it I really liked. The writing , sparse in style , was beautiful and the subtle hints we glean about Olive in the stories are a really engaging way of building our impression of her as a character. While she may not be the most likeable person, as we learn more about her, it becomes easier to understand her.

This book has received my rave reviews but I didn't like it. I was hesitant to pick it up because it was billed as a book of short stories and I prefer novels, but the stories held together as a novel with one narrative thread better than I had expected. I found the stories depressing and filled with unhappy people living lives of quiet desperation that they are unable or unwilling to change.

Stuggling through this one... 
 Done, finally. It was a slow stuggle,not my style. Could only get thru 10-20 pages at a time.

Since this book had won a Pulitzer and I kept hearing about it, I wanted to check it out. But I tend to hate short stories. I thought this would have a redeeming quality in that the stories were all related somehow. 
 I thought Olive was an annoying, unlikeable character. She had a few redeeming qualities, but they didn't really come through very often. I had a hard time getting through the book which made me forget who the various characters were and I wondered if I was forgetting prior relationships with some of them. I was happy with the ending, but overall I didn't think it was worth plodding through.

Very well written, and a mostly quick read. I needed to take a few breaks, though. Olive was a little hard to stomach, and there weren't many likable characters. I enjoy complex personalities in fiction, but I like some to be mostly pleasant.

3.5 bordering on 4 
 Overall I really enjoyed the messages but also the approach to displaying the messages. How, instead of putting everything in Olive's view we got a look a who Olive is just by learning from those who know her, even if for a brief moment, and on how she interacted with people. It wasn't necessarily a book I just had to keep reading but it really picked up for me about halfway when reality hit and things started to happen. Yet those things that happened were very realistic. So I like that Strout kept it real. It did it's job in that it made me have multiple feelings for the character: sadness, joy, hope. I especially loved the ending but don't want to say more without giving away any spoilers. This was my dad's pick for our family book club and I'm glad he picked it because it is a lovely story and I probably would not have read it had he not picked it.
The style was different, I'll give it that but the stories did not flow in any progression and it was hard to care. I cared for Henry for 50 pages and when the story moved on, so did I.

A lot of different stories and depending on where you are in your life this may effect how you view this book. For a certain age group it is right on the money. For those beyond its a good memory lane. For others maybe not such a great read. I did enjoy the book but felt as with most of her other books its just not for everyone. But what is?

I rather liked this book, and only at the end did I discover that it's not a novel. I read with anticipation until the end, looking for the common link, wanting to find out what had happened to those characters I had grown fond of early on. But alas, it's a collection of short stories. And a damn good one. 
 Olive struck me deeply. Who is she? A bitter, kind hearted soul who no one likes. why? Because she's bitter and negative. But she doesn't see it at all. The read does, of course, but even then it's a struggle. 
 I don't read books over again - but I might this one. Just to see how knowing what I know now would impact my thoughts, feelings, impressions, reactions to the stories as they are written.

4.5 stars. 
 I tried not to find out too much about this book before I read it, so I didn't fully understand that it's not so much a novel and more like a series of linked stories. More than a few are actually centred on Olive and her family and several are from her point of view, but the rest just take place in the town where she lives and Olive is a more or less peripheral character. 
 Elizabeth Strout is an excellent writer; her characters are beautifully drawn and easy to empathize with, even when they are really quite unlikeable. And she's good at presenting us with unlikeable characters. She's good at examining characters' motivations plainly and unsentimentally, but never without care and empathy. You really get to see the parade of human life in this book--people's secret tragedies and triumphs; the things they think are secrets; the things they wish they could tell their families or friends. 
 There are a lot of lonely people in here, but it is not completely bleak. It just seems to take some people a little bit longer to realize what life is supposed to be about. 
 The reason for the half star is there are a couple of coincidences that required a little too much suspension of disbelief. They're not too bad though, and certainly didn't prevent me from enjoying the book. 
 She knows that loneliness can kill people--in different ways can actually make you die. Olive's private view is that life depends on what she thinks of as "big bursts" and "little bursts." Big bursts are things like marriage or children, intimacies that keep you afloat, but these big bursts hold dangerous, unseen currents. Which is why you need the little bursts as well: a friendly clerk at Bradlee's, let's say, or the waitress at Dunkin' Donuts who knows how you like your coffee. Tricky business, really. 
 (p. 68-69)
I just found this book boring!
Hated this book! Not 1 likable character.
Pulitzer Prize for Fiction (2009) <--- so, yeah

Boken har vunnit Pulitzer Prize for Fiction 2009 och har fatt manga fina recensioner. Men jag gillar inte. Jag gillar inte Olive och kanner ingenting for ovriga karaktarer. Dessutom ar det sa trist sa att mer deprimerad stamning i boken far man leta. Den ar fint skriven, men mer gott om den kan jag tyvarr inte saga. 
 Denna bok skulle jag inte betrakta som en roman, utan som en samling av korta berattelsen.

I have no idea why this book was nominated for an award. There was no plot- it was a series of short, chapter stories all connected by the title character, who I did not identify with at all (actually didn't really like her). Ugh!

I wanted to love this. And it is brilliant. But it made me so sad. It was a beautifully constructed exploration of the ways live intertwine and the way we all carry our own personal tragedies. At one point Olive says, "people endure things." And that pretty much sums it up. Not that it's a trial to read (it isn't), it's just each story is about a trial. It got to the point that whenever people were happy I would start bracing myself.
Excellent, great for book club. No wonder it got a Pulitzer Prize. Many thoughtful insights into ordinary life.

I enjoyed this book but it wasn't remotely what I thought it would be. Olive Kitteridge is the common thread between all the stories in this novel. Set in a small town in Maine, Olive is a retired school teacher who loves her son (too fiercely perhaps), enjoys in the goings on of others, and tries to make sense of her life as she ages. Some of the stories are from her perspective and many others are from other townsfolk as they view her, sometimes from a far distance. She is a bit prickly and stoic but she is also very relatable and sympathetic. An interesting and complex look at an aging woman and then lens through which she sees the world around her and the way that others perceive her as well.
I thought this book was kind of depressing.
Excellent!
Reread this June 2009 for my book club and enjoyed just as much the second time around.

This is my second and last book by this author. the book was well written with provocative imagery, but this was one of the most depressing books I have ever read. it is a series of vignettes, many with little in common except a brief appearance by the title character. There were few glimmers of hope or happiness. Some stories ended without resolution. Most were steeped in regret and resignation. the worst sin is the lack of insight in the characters. Overall, the book was too sad and left too many questions unanswered.

I tried and failed. Olive Kitteridge is one of the few books I couldn't finish, but I can't bring myself to give it a 1 because there is some fascinating writing in it. But I just don't care. The problem might lie with the book's structure. I suspect it might have benefited from a traditional novel structure, but I can't know that as I couldn't finish reading!

While linked these short stories are beautifully written. The main character is flawed and at times 
 really unlikeable. With a lesser writer these stories would be grim and not compelling.
A book club book. Not myt cup of tea, and I found it unbelievable at times.
Hmmmm! Had to finish it so I could get back to something better!
This was rather depressing. I was hoping as I read it, that the pieces would all come together and it would end on a high note. It was confusing at times, even in the first chapter.

On the whole, I prefer the HBO four- part series to this novel. Which is so unusual for me, I have a t-shirt that usually expresses my opinion: "The book was better." Not this time, not for me. 
 I like Frances McDormand playing the title character more than I like reading the internal thoughts of the hateful main character in the novel. Her dutiful and loving husband is played by character actor Richard Jenkins. The actor, John Gallagher, Jr., who plays her adult son Chris, played a reporter in Aaron Sorkin's "Newsroom." In the tv series, Maine looks luminous, even if it was filmed in Massachusetts. The novel meanders. What's with the short story "Criminal" about Rebecca? Sure, she had Olive as her teacher, but is that the only connection to the Kitteridges? The tv series is more focused on Olive Kitteridge. I read this with Messy Houskeepers Book Club for a meeting on May 29, for which I made brownies. I borrowed this from interlibrary loan.

Next time I try to read a Pulitzer Prize winning book, someone please remind me that I usually don't enjoy them at all. This book has an interesting premise. It's many short stories that all have the character of Olive Kitteridge in common. Sometimes her only presence in the story is that the main character in that story runs into her somewhere and they say hello. I like the premise but Olive is a crabby woman and all the stories I read were SAD and hopeless. Lots of swearing, marital infidelity and tragedy. Overall, a really depressing book. I couldn't finish it.
This book was very good although now that I've finished it I would like to reread it.

This book is told as a collection of short stories, Olive is a factor in each story but nor necessarily the primary focus, it runs the gamut from her being the main character of the story to actually only being mentioned as a passing thought in one of the other stories. 
 The first story is told from the perspective of her husband and in truth after reading that chapter I had decided that I did not like Olive at all, she was a terrible person, mean and angry. 
 When I finished reading the entire book I still didn't like her very much but I found that I understood more who she was and why, and as the author says in an "interview" in the back of the book; Olive is ferocious and complicated and kindly and sometimes cruel. In essence she is a little bit of each of us. 
 The stories of all the different relationships is fascinating, especially the marriages, different views on how lives changes over the years, how some people are willing to settle for unhappiness and others are not. There is also something very telling about the fact that no one in the book is "normal"; everyone has their oddities some of which are open for all to see and others that are hidden from the world and only revealed in those moments when we feel alone and safe.
As a compliment the short stories in this book evoke similar feelings that I get while reading Dorothy Parker's short stories. I loved it, very poignant.
This book was not what I expected, but I liked it a lot. The author has a wonderful way with words. I will be reading more of her work.
In the end, the struggle was worth it.

I know it won a Pulitzer, but I could not abide the writing style. The opening paragraph, for example, has 11 lines & exactly two poetic but very boring sentences. I read a little more in the hope of getting accustomed to the style, but it just did not work for me.

This is another book assigned to read in my Lit Fic 2 class that I loved. I would have never found this Pulitzer Prize winning story otherwise (unless somehow I made the HBO leap to read vs. just watch - btw, I've watched a few episodes as well and Frances McDormand nails Olive). Anyway - I love the short stories that make up this longer narrative. Interesting flawed characters with every day stories that are written so well they read like sliced butter. ;)
lovely vignettes

reference_books.title: The Language of Flowers
reference_books.review_text: Don't want to finish this book. Too bad to waste my time on.

reference_books.title: The First Bad Man
reference_books.review_text: DNF - not for me. Started out as a very interesting and original novel, but soon withered into just weirdness for the sake of it and even ugliness. I guess it's too sophisticated for my bourgeois tastes.

reference_books.title: My Name Is Lucy Barton
reference_books.review_text:
I'm sorry, but this novel isn't for me. The idea is good - having a mother and daughter get together after many years of separation at the daughter's sickbed, working out their joint past and their relationship. But the writing is annoying, and the leading of the reader by the nose to the end of the book by hinting of some great secrets of terrible deeds does not work for me at all. What does it matter what was done to Lucy exactly, or in what way her childhood had been monstrous? Isn't it enough to know that it had been? The gruesome details work are a turn-off for me, not an incentive to read on. Since both mother and daughter know exactly what happened between them, the conversations between them, which turn in spirals till they finally get to the center, are not enough to hold a whole novel. The metaphor of the daughter's illness is also highly depended upon by the writer, and I don't find it either original or interesting, nor does it contribute anything to the depth of the novel. Yes, we get it, the obscure illness is the poisonous repression that has to be bled out. 
 I didn't find this novel in any way special or interesting.

reference_books.title: The Graveyard Book
reference_books.review_text: Meaningless. I guess I would never understand what is so great about Neil Gaiman's writing, and what others love about him so much. The writing is disjointed, cold, and based on gimmicks and tiny bits of imagination that never add up to anything that stays with you or makes you feel anything. A waste of time.

reference_books.title: The Jane Austen Book Club
reference_books.review_text: Not for me. And I've tried. Twice.

reference_books.title: Tell the Wolves I'm Home
reference_books.review_text: Stopped at 170 pages. Don't care about any of the characters yet. The only interesting one is dead. Everyone else don't feel real. It is a common mistake of writers to make the child main character speak like an adult. This happens here, but in this novel, she also behaves like an adult, leads close friendly relationships with adult men with whom she has nothing in common. Her parents have no idea what is happening. How is that even possible in a normal family? I still remember the time when the world became aware of AIDS, and it was nothing like is described in this novel. Everyone was mostly panicking or hysterical, not wanting to have anything to do with people who suffer or carry the disease. Yet in this book, the parents are completely fine with their young daughter spending time with an AIDS patient, who is gay, another panic-inducing element at that time. By the way, we readers know its the '80s without having to tell us all the time about rubik cubes and suchlike. Give us some credit. The plot is hard to believe, and although this novel is supposed to be a tear jerker, nothing really moved me about it - no emotion in it seems real enough to do that.

reference_books.title: Funny Girl
reference_books.review_text: Terrible writing - telling, telling and telling again. Very boring. Don't care about any of the characters, who seem like cardboard stereotypes, not real people. Not amusing in any way. Too many details and what's supposed to be nostalgia-raising mentions. No soul or real emotions.

reference_books.title: Ringworld (Ringworld, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Shockingly bad - I can't believe it became such a sensation. So Niven knows science. Great. But he can't write to save his life. The characters are ridiculous - as one dimensioned as they come. And this is without mentioning the degrading attitude towards women. DO NOT READ!!

reference_books.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (Hercule Poirot, #4)
reference_books.review_text: Another treat from the Queen of Crime. There is the usual amount of psychological insights, the subtle but needle-sharp humor, and one nasty trick Christie plays on her readers. Even if you've heard about it in advance, the book still takes you by surprise in the end, and is still very enjoyable. I will always return to Christie for a quick fix between books. She was one smart lady.

reference_books.title: The Girls
reference_books.review_text: DNF - Not buying into the hype on this one at all. Extremely annoying and pompous writing style - "They were a constant couple, porous with each other." Lots and lots of telling and no showing, no activity at all, in fact, only page after page of babbling description. There doesn't seem to be any basis or reason for the protagonist's existence other than to let the writer tell the story of the Manson cult from a different perspective, but she doesn't add a lot to the understanding of it. Dear author, if you really believe this story needs to be told again, just tell it, the best way you can, no need for literary tricks. I'm so fed up with the hypocrisy of some writers who use a sensational historical event or art work that they know will create a buzz around their book, but re-tell it using fancy literary measures so that they can be considered 'literary' and 'intellectual'. What comes out of it here is the turning of one of the most emotional and dramatic incidents of the 1960s into a very boring novel about getting older that we've all read a thousand times before. Don't fall into this trap.

book_a.title: Lexicon
book_a.user_review: As you can always expect from Max Barry, this book has an original and intriguing premise, and kicks of with a great action scene which will pull you right in. You have no idea what's going on in the earlier parts of the story, but are gripped by the Lisbeth Salander-like protagonist and the hint of some huge and secret thing operating behind what's been happening. Later on Barry lets us on more and more of the big picture, but can't always keep up the same level of interest and engagement in the story. A few scenes should've been edited and shortened, and I found myself losing the plot here and there because it became too convoluted and wasn't written too clearly. Yet, the book was enjoyable to the end, and I believe there is a sequel waiting for the pick up after the last page. Hope Barry is already working on it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I read this for a summer reading assignment because it seemed like the most interesting book on the list. I adore reading and doing it for school homework does not bother me. I was excited to begin reading Lexicon but soon this excitement died away. A very good idea was ruined with the lack of details. The way the book is set up is extremely confusing as I had no idea what most of the things meant. As a writer, Barry could have done a better job of world-building in this novel, but it was centered mainly on the characters which weren't all that likeable in my opinion. By the end of the novel, I still didn't understand the word system, the segment system (it would have been helpful in understanding some of the scenes. Since the segment system wasn't explained, I had no idea what the difference between a segment 77 or a segment 108 was.), and many of the other aspects of their poet world. Additionally, I hated his writing which was riddled with choppy and run-on sentences. The plot was okay. I enjoyed reading the testing sections and the process for selecting students as well as some of arguments and dialogue between Wil and Eliot. The ending felt rushed. It would have been great to see more insight into Yeat's reasons and more about the bareword. 
 What was disappointing about this book was the lack of details that really would have brought the world to life.

I did enjoy this book and I can recommend it for a quick weekend read. It has a fun premise, but I feel that the book didn't explore it. For instance, it never explained what the "organization" really was or what they were trying to accomplish. Also, while I am fine with nonlinear storytelling, this book did it in a rather clunky way. There were several temporal jumps that were jarring rather than revealing. The author also took lots of shortcuts in the narrative, as if pages were missing. In short, the technical aspects of the book were subpar. If you can overlook that and if you enjoy mind control stories, then you should give this one a try.

This was my first Quarterly shipment from the good folks at Book Riot. This is an awesome bookish website that curates unique packages for book-lovers. The book included handwritten comments on post-it notes by the author. I was super excited to delve into this but I just didn't love it. I appreciated many aspects of the book, particularly the power of words and the uniting power of a common language. There was some really interesting bits about the rise and fall of civilizations and the splintering of languages. 
 However, I didn't really care about any of the characters, the use of cussing seemed random (other than obvious high-stress situations or characters in pain) and inappropriately placed among the intelligent commentary, and the premise seemed a little weak and didn't convince me that such an event was feasible. I guess I was just a Negative Nelly on this one:-/

I found the writing structure and plot convoluted, confusing and tedious. It took me at least five days to read this book because I had to force myself to keep at it. I would never have finished it, if it were not part of the Hub Challenge and I really did not enjoy it. 
 The duality of Harry was obvious from the second we learned that Emily had developed a relationship in Broken Hill. By the end, I was internally hoping that everyone would be exposed to the bareword and would just drop dead.
Probably more of a 4.5 star read. Not my usual genre but full of suspense that kept me tuned in and circling the block to listen longer. An excellent read. Highly recommended.

This book was rather excellent. 
 Such a novel concept, words as literal weapons. This was fast paced, with very engaging characters. My one complaint, and yes, I do have to put it here (sorry, Max Barry) is the constantly jumping back and forth between timelines confused me. I had to often stop and go "wait, are we here, or are we there?" 
 There were some key plot points and reveals that would have been spoiled by a linear plot line, but it was still a bit confusing for me. 
 Overall, I adored this book, and I want to read everything Max Barry has to offer.

I have always been fascinated by language, by words and meaning and understanding. Pondering how we can say one thing and for another person separate to us to understand the meaning in the jumble of syllables that come out of our mouth, well that's one of those thoughts that I could lose myself in for days. 
 It wasn't surprising then that I really enjoyed this book. I enjoyed its premise, I liked the thought that words had power, and I liked the notion that the power of those went beyond the mundane and into the fantastical. I enjoyed the way the story was set out, a puzzle that you could never quite see all the pieces of until the very end when it all slot into its place. 
 I like that thrillers don't just need to be about cars and spies and girls in bikinis. 
 Mostly I just liked the discovery of each character over and over again as the book progressed. Oh and the Australian element was nice too, us locals aren't find of snakes either...

The first 2/3rds of this book were great, but it started dwindling off a little near the end and it started losing me, so I'm debating between 3 stars and 4 stars. It was really fast-paced for the majority of the story and I enjoyed that. 
 The concept of using words as weapons is an interesting one and I'd love to learn more about it or have a prequel about how poets and the school began. 
 It was a bit easy for me to guess the parallels between Wil and Emily's stories. Like I knew that Emily was Woolf and that the 10 year old would be Raine. It took a bit longer for me to realize that Harry was Wil, but I still figured it out after a while. It just took me some time to realize that Emily's story was set before Wil's. 
 I found lots of the book to be unique, but it started to go into cliche land near the end. 
 This book definitely made me more wary of words. And also whether I'm a cat or dog person.
Very nice. The review quote on the back from Lev Grossman sums it up pretty well: "... reads like Elmore Leonard high out of his mind on Snow Crash."

This showed promise, but really fell flat. I guess the author just couldn't find the right words... heh 
 390 p.
An interesting story about the power of words. A dystopian world controlled by propaganda and a secret society bent on destroying our current Tower of Babel - both a metaphor and a play on words.
Whoa.

Eh, I was hoping for so much more. The reviews and blurbs made it seem like a book I would really like. I like the concept of the book but the actual execution? Not so much. I hated the jumping between narrators and times. It seems like a cop out way to confuse the reader. Also, I did not particularly care for either of the main characters which is a big problem when those characters are being chased and threatened and you're all *shrug* whatever happens, happens. I did not understand their motivations. As for the shadowy group Emily joins, again, it just didn't seem fleshed out. I kept waiting for an understanding of the group and it never came. It was too vague and nebulous. I kept reading in the hope that everything would fall together at the end but it didn't. Finally, while the 13 yr old girl in me was thrilled by the ending, it seemed super sappy and tacked on and not a logical development of characters.

I had originally intended to give Lexicon three stars, but then I read some of the other reviews and I felt much less favorably about it than it seemed the other three-star reviewers did, so two stars. It only gets that many because I love that someone tried to write this novel, the synopsis made me long to read it, and it did actually pick up around page 307 (there are 387 pages in Lexicon, so you can decide for yourself how much of a backhanded compliment that is). The first three hundred pages felt more like snippets of my college linguistics textbooks (but with some things wrong) interspersed with a narrative about characters I couldn't bring myself to care about. I find Emily terribly obnoxious and Wil tedious to the extreme. I couldn't figure out why Emily was attracted to Harry or why Harry changed his mind, but it turned out in the end that I didn't care, so that worked out okay. The best I can say about Eliot is that he was there too. The plot structure was frustrating as well, as each narrative shift had to be accompanied by a mad scramble to figure out where on earth in the narrative timeline this section took place (I recall at one point exclaiming out loud, "But she's dead already! Why does she have to be back again?"). I understand the logic of this choice, as it does keep you guessing what the truth is and who is controlling whom, but I disagree with it. Additionally, for a book that calls itself "Lexicon," it sure has a limited one. I generally have no problem with profanity in books, but if you're writing a book about words, I expect you to be a little bit more creative with your lexicon. 
 To be completely, brutally honest, I only made it through Lexicon at all because I was literally parked on the on-ramp to the highway for over an hour last Wednesday when there was that tractor-trailer accident. Lexicon was the only book I had in the car.

The best of Barry's books (so far), and something of a shift towards the serious. 
 The basic idea has been used before: that it is possible to hack the human mind with very specific stimuli. Neal Stephenson used something like this in 
 Snow Crash 
 , for example. 
 Barry uses it very well, tying it in with today's increasing concern the intrusiveness of social media and the big data that advertisers are accumulating on us. In his previous books, there was a greater element of social satire, and he sometimes overindulged in the silly side of that; here he has kept that in check, to good effect. 
 Get a copy and read it.

Lexicon is a very well-constructed, well executed story with a paper thin premise. The idea is that there are over 20 personalty types and that each type of person can be controlled with a specific set of syllables. An elite group called poets are taught to quickly evaluate the types and have learned all the sounds that will allow them to control others. Thus the poets have all the power. This is not convincing although I can see the appeal to those readers and writers who love words and take literature seriously. But there is not enough real life resonance to the idea to make this story compelling.

I can't remember why I originally picked this as a book to be read, but it sounded really promising. The idea that words have power is not unusual. While there was great promise, I feel that this book fell short in several really important ways. The narrative line is choppy and confusing. It does eventually come together, and things that I feel should have been a big plot twist, were not so much a surprise to me as the feeling that I could finally move on because what I was waiting to have happen finally did. There were long parts of the story that made me feel like I had been reading for 50 pages and nothing happened. There was a lot of violence and vulgarity that was gratuitous (and I am really good at tuning it out and overlooking a lot), and while it was no Stephen King, the same thing I always think when I read one of his novels continued to go through my mind: This was definitely written by a man. Love being the thing that overcomes all--not a new or surprising theme--ultimately is what made me continuing reading a book that I didn't enjoy for most of the text. I will say that once I started reading, I couldn't stop, almost like I was compelled to read until I was finished. Maybe they found my base words and used them early on...I don't know.

Ick. This is one book I'm not going to finish any time soon. Having your novel start out incomprehensible and then change characters to a young homeless woman who is essentially sexually assaulted as a "test" of resistance to mind control is not a way to make me want to read more.
Interesting concept, and enjoyable plot. Lots to make you think about language here, a pet interest of mine, so it was up my alley.

Like a lot of other reviewers, I'll say that this book had a lot of potential. I really liked Emily's half of the first quarter of the book. The rest, not so much. Wil is an incredibly boring protagonist, and his boringness infects Emily's parts in the later sections. Emily starts out really interesting, but then the characterization get wonky and she ends up being sort of disappointing. The plot in general could have been better. Also, the cover with the white and yellow words on the gray background so so unbelievably ugly. I mean, what were they thinking.
Interesting premise. Ending was a let down.

For a book where the main premise is the power of weaponised language and semiotics Max Barry has created a surprisingly enjoyable, high octane thriller that seems to be crying out for a film or TV adaptation. 
 It's an interesting combination of literary and language theory, shadowy conspiracy, mythology and Matrix-style cool kick-assery, bouncing energetically across the globe from the USA to the Australian outback. 
 Barry clearly loves language and knows when to use it in the slow unveiling of the 'poets' of the 'is it good or evil' organisation that's super sharp with use of vocabulary, and when not to waste it when some punchy action set-pieces and 'stuff blowing up' is needed as a brain-break from all those lethal words. 
 The only reason I give it a three, rather than a four is the inherent contradiction above. If you like your books on the 'literary' side you might find all the 'Jason Bourne' running around a bit distracting. If you like thrillers, you might find all the 'language' stuff annoying. 
 If, like me, you like a good mid-range mash-up you certainly won't be bored. 
 Could even make dictionaries cool again!

Vote: 3,95 
 Class: L-C1 (FP) (*) 
 (a stand-alone thriller novel) 
 The idea for the story is original and well developed throughout the book; maybe it is a bit difficult to follow the multiple timelines (I sometimes got confused in the first lines after a plot switch). 
 The characters are not really great and only near the end I begun to feel something for them. 
 All in all a good thriller with very well built futuristic setting and an amazing rhythm . 
 (*) There is some explicit sexual content and too much swearing for my liking

Ye-ah. Great for the price, and really thrilling in places. The story is really interesting to me (think Jessica Jones' Killgrave merged with Hogwortseque elements), but the trouble is none of it feels fully developed. The book doesn't do its inspiration justice; it feels like it's too intent on forging ahead whereas I'd prefer it to linger on what's actually interesting. Still, it is very readable for the most part, and I read it in less than 5 hours. 
 Would love to hear what people thought of the closing sections of the book. To my mind it was way too choppy, and it lost me a few times. 
 Compelling story with some great writing, but ultimately not ambitious enough. Would read a sequel however.

As with Barry's other books, this was a fun read that merged a good story with wry social commentary. It's a sci-fi-ish romantic thriller seasoned with neurolinguistics and the opposing forces of security/control/power vs. vulnerability/connection/love.

Good plot and character build overall, but I wanted to learn more about the power of language persuasion and felt that little was mentioned on this topic. I expected more of a Harry Potter reference to spells, where at times in the book/movie, you would find yourself repeating a specific incantation like "time for Apareceum spell!". The specific words spoken seemed like jibberish with no meaning behind it.

Wow, this was kind of all over the place. There were parts where I was fascinated, and parts where I was bored, and parts where I was confused. I LOVEd the parts about the secret linguistics of "attention words", and how specific phonemes would command a specific personality type. I was less interested in various people racing around in an assortment of vehicles and shooting each other.

I can't believe I continued this till the end. 
 Not only do you have no clue what's happening for the first fifty pages or so (you just have to stick with it until things are clarified later, which to me feels like lazy writing), but the book is 100 pages too long and dissolves into such incoherent nonsense by the end that I'm amazed the editor okayed this. Tough to understand (and I have a master's in English) but even tougher by the end to even care.

If no one already has optioned this, someone is bound to find it and turn it into a movie. It's a fantastic read with lots of twists and turns in ways you didn't expect the story to twist. Tarantino should direct it - the chapters are often nonlinear, so you're not sure where you are on the timeline until you're pretty deep in.
Gripping story, but confusing at times.

This book was probably my favorite this year. Its got a ton of foul language so for those who don't want that its not good but, beyond that, its pacing is terrific and the concept original. The ideas that words themselves can harm is brilliant. Its like a thriller version of Dune and Harry Potter combined. This from the back cover: 
 "At an exclusive school somewhere outside of Arlington, Virginia, students aren't taught history, geography, or mathematics--they are taught to persuade. Students learn to use language to manipulate minds, wielding words as weapons. The very best graduate as "poets," and enter a nameless organization of unknown purpose." 
 I love books that pull me in like this one did, relenting only when it ran out of pages to tell the story. A great read!
Really great thriller.

From one star (my previous review) to five stars. This is an excellent speculative fiction novel - hands down one of the best I've read in recent years. I'm not clever enough to understand all of the literary allusions, but I did enjoy the many twists and turns employed by Barry to keep this book intriguing to the end. I read Jennifer Government many years ago and enjoyed it, but this book knocks your socks off. A contemporary SF novel that should become a classic. And I do so hope they make this into a movie. New York and Broken Hill - now there's a fascinating and complex contrast. Read this!

Originally reviewed at Minnesota Reads. 
 Wow, did I have a hard time with this book. I thought I would love it. I wanted to love it. I still think I'm supposed to love it. The premise is pretty amazing. The characters kind of fascinate me. So why did I moan every time I picked up the book to keep reading? 
 Max Berry's Lexicon sounds like the coolest book. A secret society trains young people on a mysterious way to control others by using words. Not real words, a gobbledygook mishmash of sounds that are reminiscent of what an infant might express when trying to learn how to speak, but words nonetheless. I'm still not clear on why their gobbledygook can control minds, but just go with it, it can. The mind-controlling people are called poets, they take on poet code names after graduation (like Yeats, Eliot, Woolf, etc.), and they are a threat to society...or they help society? 
 This thriller is propelled by a poet gone rogue, other poets looking for her, and a lot of shifting loyalties that will make you question again and again the goodness of the poets and what they do. 
 All of this sounds great, so I'm having a hard time putting my finger on why I didn't like this. Maybe it's because I'm still not clear on what these poets do and why they are so important? And what is the history of this secret society and its training academy? Or maybe it's because I couldn't buy into the idea that the gobbledygook they spew would actually control minds? Or could it be that the shift from the power of words to the power of love was kind of annoying? Or maybe it was just how this book was organized, with great action scenes followed by some boring down time? 
 I suppose all of those things bothered me, but they don't seem like enough for me to not like it, because I certainly have believed in unclear secret societies and odd powers in the past. So I think I'm going to chalk this up to poor execution. The whole idea is great, and the book starts off really strong with a fabulous rescue mission in an airport, but the rest of the book never lived up to what I felt like I was promised with such a fabulous opening scene. 
 Many other people really like this book though, our own Jodi among them, so hey, maybe you'll love it. I didn't, but if you're looking for something completely different, you really will find it here. Or you'll find it in Neal Stephenson's Snow Crash, which this seemed to be kind of a rip off of, and not as good as.

I squealed when I reached the end of this book. 
 It's a satisfying finale, but I wasn't expecting it to be the last page! I was so wrapped up in it, I didn't realize how much I'd read until, all of a sudden, it was over.

Really interesting concept of mind control, but not fully developed into a comprehensible plot point. There were a lot of blanks when it came to the way the mind controlling words work. I had a hard time following it, but that could be my mommy brain in full force.

Great premise; OK execution. The idea that language could be, and has been, used in this way is fascinating. The story itself is a fun summer-read page turner. But I wanted more. What does this say about us as humans? What are possible consequences for our understanding of reality? Stephenson's Snow Crash has visited that terrain before and does it better. There are a few crumbs at the end that point toward the deeper meanings of the premise, but it's too little, too late. 
 The other thing that bugged me about the author's writing style is his use of under-reporting details to keep things from the reader to create artificial suspense. I get the fact that we are supposed to identify with the confusion a character is experiencing in an unfamiliar situation and are called upon to make sense of it ourselves and that that is part of our job as a reader. But at some point, doing so crosses some divide and the author's hand becomes apparent when I say to myself, "The author is doing this so that I identify with the confusion a character is experiencing in an unfamiliar situation, but, really, shouldn't the other character, at this point, simply offer up an explanation so that the main character has a clue what's going on because, if this was remotely real, that's what would be happening here." Another quirk is that there are two main time streams involving some of the same characters, and the author sometimes switches between them with little or no warning, so at each section break the reader has to figure out whether or not such a switch has occurred. In both cases, a few more up-front cues would be helpful. 
 Still, a good summer read. Just not as substantive as I'd hoped for.

This started off very interesting, but a third of the way in I learned from other reviews that this story devolves into a mass of chase scenes. 
 I quickly lost interest after that and I'm not sorry I left it. Not that bad, just not for me.

This book takes the art of persuasion to a whole new level. It postulates a group of people who use words to get other people to do what they want. It starts out with a guy getting kidnapped at an airport, goes on a wild chase across America and winds up in a godforsaken spot in Australia. It is witty and fun and also thought-provoking when applied to the political realm.
Interesting concept that was terribly executed.

High concept fantasy thriller. The high concept (magic words) is a gem and well done but it's not enough to satisfy. Nailed onto a barebones generic thriller structure makes me think this would have worked better as a short story or novella.
Started this on audio on a drive to NYC and just speed read the ending. Wasn't going to "waste" those hours in the car.

Emily is a new recruit into the Academy, a place where people who are good at convincing others with their words are trained and groomed, to categorize people and learn to control others with their words. BRILLIANT RIGHT?? So......An incident in Australia destroys an entire town killing thousands...reason? There is a word that triggered this event turning the town into a graveyard. Eliot is assigned with the mission to extract that 'bareword' by the leader of the Academy.... Emily is deemed uncontrollable and a series of events that take place make her a target.... 
 I have so many mixed feelings about this book. Let me talk about the good stuff first... 
 - The concept, words can be used to control people, brilliant. 
 - The pace at which the book starts - fast, thrilling at so many levels 
 - Main Characters have a solid personality 
 Just when you start to think it's gonna get better it disappoints... the plot seems aimless at one point. Supporting characters randomly appear and disappear with no reason. It's such a drag at one point. The book could have been so much more then what is it. I was disappointed may be cause I expected a lot. 2/5
good the whole way through. enjoyed it till the end, which, reading other reviews, I wasn't sure was going to happen. I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoyed smart thrillers.

A little annoyed at myself that I pushed myself to finish this. I rarely cared about the story, nor the characters.. The premise was somewhat interesting - but never felt was used beyond a fairly uninteresting method. 
 Sorry - just didn't work at all for me. But even 10 pages in I debated stopping, but the reviews, by groups I respect were quite positive. 
 Just didn't work for me: story wise, writting wise; concept wise...
Well it's actually not what I expected. But it was a good read. Not more not less.
Excellent suspense novel for thinking people
The power of words...an interesting premise where linguistics and words are used to control and kill. Reminded me of The Circle, or the killing words from Dune.

I have to admit, most of the pre-publication buzz I'd heard swirling around Max Barry's new novel related to a quiz about famous poets. It's a book pretty far outside my normal reading space and I had no plans to pick it up. Yet somehow, feeling slightly slumpy, I grabbed a copy last weekend and found I had lost an entire afternoon. 
 Lexicon is set in a world seemingly identical to ours, with the addition of an agency specifically trained in the art of persuasion. Identified from a young age, talented students are schooled in linguistics and taught key words to help them persuade, aiming to eventually become an elite "Poet". The novel follows Emily Ruff, a student from the streets of San Francisco, and Wil Parke, a man the agency believes to be immune to persuasion, as their stories collide over a frighteningly powerful word. 
 Though I was apprehensive at first, after letting myself fall into Max Barry's universe I was completely engrossed. With quick witted prose and fast paced changes, Lexicon is a novel that is easy to get lost in, particularly as Emily goes through her schooling and the training process. Perhaps this is why I much preferred the fist half of the book to the second, as I would have gladly read several chapters of persuasion techniques over the novel's climax, which seemed slightly rushed. 
 Still, Lexcion was exactly the page-turner I needed for a quick, fun read. If you are looking for a great vacation book that will keep you thinking, puzzling and reading, Max Barry's Lexicon is the one to pick up. 
 Blog: River City Reading

This book is soooooooo good! Totally unexpected! It was a little misleading at the beginning, the way the story was told, but you start putting the pieces together as you read and it was just amazing how it all came together. I love the character development, and the premise of the book.
