 It is so rare to find a book that has it all. Sometimes you get an interesting premise but that's the only thing the story's got going for it, and the characters don't come to life, and the story isn't well-written. Sometimes you get great characters but a boring story. This book has got it all! 
 Words are magic, perfect for bibliophiles. Perfect read for me!

book_b.title: Swamplandia!
book_b.user_review: Couldn't finish - the writing is beautiful, but the novel is pointless, with characters and happenings being weird and eccentric for the sake of weirdness and eccentricity. Not for me.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I liked the author's previous short story collection well enough, but this was a major disappointment. The eccentricity that enlivened the short stories began to seem more like an annoying stylistic tic on prolonged exposure. And, as other reviewers have pointed out, this whole novel seemed structurally flawed -- the bifurcation into parallel narratives just didn't seem to work at all. I confess to having skimmed the final half just to see if things would get better - they didn't unfortunately. 
 That said, I still think Karen Russell is a talented writer, and look forward to her future efforts.

Some of this book wasn't just good, it was fantastic. Some of the writing was beautiful especially the descriptions of the swamp and emotions dealing with the death of the mother. The premise is really interesting too- a family lives on an entertainment park where the mom wrestles alligators. 
 The major theme of innocence lost as the kids get older without their mom to protect them is a baseball bat to the face, and this is no doubt to highlight the trauma of dealing with the death of the mom but some of it was really over the top and massively heavy handed. 
 Supernatural elements seem to play a part of the story, but they really really don't. It turns out that Ossie is mentally ill and that the Birdman is a rapist and likely serial kill (did you catch the fact that he rapes her on a tarp?) And he is not the guide you think he is. INstead the Birdman is a metaphor for innocence lost in a brutal sad manner. The Birdman/tarp scene is a punch to the face. you see it coming and yet you cannot admit to yourself that THIS IS REALLY HAPPENING. This scene is why you get so many angry reviews, I have to admit that this scene made me so so angry, because up until this point you really believe, along with the character that the Birdman is a spirit guide and not some gross rapist/serial killer. 
 The end of the book would include the children being taken from their father by protective services, because parents cannot leave their kids for weeks on end, not even in the swamps of Florida. Especially when one attempts suicide and the other is kidnaped and raped by a transient bird hunter. 
 This is a horribly depressing book that made me angry and sad.
Couldn't finish it. Kept trying to...felt like I must be missing something... Started strong and quickly fell apart.

The famous alligator-wrestling Bigtree family struggles with the death of their matriarch, fierce new competition, and their own realities in this humid tale. 
 The Bigtrees are alligator wrestlers. Or rather, Hilola Bigtree was a star alligator wrestler-until she died. Scores of tourist would come to the swamp to see her take down a gator. Without her, the ramshackle Swamplandia operation is doomed. The Bigtree children-Ava, Kiwi, and Osceola, all start to go their own directions. The story jumps between the perspectives of twelve-year-old Ava and eighteen-year-old Kiwi. Ava remains on the island while Kiwi takes off for the mainland to chase his dreams of going to school. 
 Russell makes you feel the family's defeat and the secrets in their overgrown surroundings. However, there was a point when the bad choices and strangeness got to be too much for me. She lost me about two-thirds into the book.

I wanted this book to be so much better than it turned out to be. I was really upset that there was (at least in my opinion) a major life event/plot point that Ava is forced to go through that the author seemed to throw in for no reason. I don't want to spoil it for anyone, but it was super disappointing and exploitative to put in something this traumatic and then really not address it beyond the fact that it happened. Honestly, I feel like if this part had been left out I would have enjoyed the book a lot more than I did.

I liked some of the stories in St. Lucy's Home for Girls, but this novel wasn't believable or enjoyable. Gave it a try last year and never bothered to post it until Good Reads friend Spencer Throssel just read and reviewed it.
Expertly crafted but depressing story. Points for being unique and completely original but I just couldn't bring myself to like any of the characters.

This book did not live up to its potential. It felt mostly like preamble or build-up - alligators, theme parks, Florida swamps, odd kids, family dynamics...all of that part was great. But, the climax was totally unpredictable and unfair to the reader (and in my opinion, entirely unnecessary) and the resolution was quick, rough, and unfinished. I wanted more after having spent 250 pages becoming invested in this family.

This is the worst book I've troubled to read in a very long time. The first couple of chapters are intriguing and then the author just starts vomiting words onto the page trying to create something meaningful. Epic fail. It's rare that I actually throw a book away so I guess it gets credit for inspiring me in that vein. If this is what garners Pulitzer attention (and several other literary awards) there is no hope for humanity. Let the alligators take over the planet. It's time for us to quit.
Bluch!!!!

I really wanted to like this book, but just couldn't find it in me. I can't really pinpoint what it was, because the description of the story sounded so fantastical. Swampland! tells us about the BigTree family, known in the local area of the 10.000 Lakes in Florida for their Alligator wrestling show. 13 year old Ava and her siblings Oceola and Kiwi are at a loss when the star of the show, Ava's mother, dies of cancer. The tourists have stopped coming and life as they knew it on on the small island of Swamplandia is in a decline. Grampa Sawtooth moves to a retirement home on the mainland, and The Chief, Ava's father, heads to the mainland for business, but doesn't come back. Now Older brother Kiwi takes off for the mainland to work for the competition, World of Darkness- a new biblical attraction centered around a giant water slide, The Leviathan. Kiwi quickly realizes with no official state education and a head full of book knowledge from the abandoned boat library, life is very different on the mainland when you are trying to save the family home and business. Meanwhile, 16 year old Oceola picks up a book on spiritualism from the boat library, and begins communing with the spirit world to meet boys (in the ghostly form of course). Her midnight "dates" introduces her to Lewis, with whom she elopes to The Underworld. What's Ava to do? She has been practicing her alligator wrestling moves to save the business by taking over the dangerous show stopping act formerly owned by her mother. Ava must go after her sister of course, and thus commences her weird adventure through the swamps with a stranger known only as The Birdman.

I'm giving this book an extra star and a half. After our book club discussion I have a better understanding of what the author was trying to do with this story. I think any book that at first isn't "loved", but generates good conversation deserves some recognition. For me this book falls into the category of good for book club discussion, but not a book for fun reading. If you do read this book consider the similarities of Greek mythology and the river Styx.

Every year brings a crop of young writers who grab the brass ring on the first round, and Karen Russell managed this feat last year. Brilliant language and a fantasmagorical setting, a failing alligator farm and amusement park deep in the Florida Everglades.

I was excited to read this book -- I mean, c'mon, a story about a family that runs an alligator wrestling theme park in Florida? -- that sounded like a lot of fun. However, about a quarter of the way through I was completely disaffected. The only reason I stuck with it is because this is one of the titles in the Morning News Tournament of Books this year. 
 I really disliked this book. I think it's one big weird mess, and a poorly written big weird mess. 
 The following Goodreads review does a good job of describing the many problems with this book-- http://www.goodreads.com/review/show/.... In addition, I thought it was off-putting that although the story was told from two points of view, one was told in first person (the young teenage girl) while the other was in 3rd person (her older brother). A strange and ineffective choice by the writer, IMO. 
 The only reason I'm giving it one star is because I found the story of the older brother to be somewhat engaging, interesting, and mostly believable. The story of his two sisters out at Swamplandia, however, was head-scratchingly weird and totally incredulous.

I'm still trying to get over the disappointment of this book. It started out incredibly slow, painfully slow, but I liked the characters so I was willing to continue. When the narrative branched, I became more interested; I enjoyed Kiwi's story. World of Darkness was hysterically dark, and I liked Kiwi's adjustment to the mainland. 
 Ava and Ossie's story really had promise. I really thought the story was entering the realm of magic realism with the trip to the underworld. But, no, with only 60 pages left, Russel dropped a *huge* bomb with no real resolution to it. 
 Add to that several stories-within-a-story that really had no relevance and came out of nowhere and a resolution that was just rushed, and you've got a one-star book.

This book starts off promisingly as a wacky tale of a family run alligator wrestling show in south Florida called Swamplandia - and ruins itself about half way in with a dark dose of magical realism. The characters are murky and contradictory and the shift of points of view between the different stories was confusing. After their mom dies, Ava and Ossie are left to sort of fend for themselves on their island in the Florida swamp. Kiwi heads to the mainland to get a job at their competition to help make money to help save Swamplandia. I liked Kiwi's story a great deal more than that of the sisters and found him a more solid character. The messiness of the plot was highly distracting and the late addition of a horrifying event was surprisingly ignored. 
 There were parts of this book I liked, but would have a hard time recommending it to most general fiction readers. I would be interested in other things this young author writes as I think she has promise.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Something about this novel seemed very juvenile to me. Perhaps it is the thirteen-year old narrator, but I think it's more than that. Plenty of adult literary novels use adolescent narrators. This didn't feel like an adult literary novel. It was probably more to do with the way the story always seemed compelled to state the obvious. It could have also had to do with the weird way in which things like sex and rape were handled. Maybe it was because all the major characters were precocious children, and none of them seemed particularly complex. 
 I did appreciate the wacky premise, about a declining family-owned theme park that features alligator wrestling. However, I think George Saunders' Civilwarland and also his incredible short story "Pastoralia" do more interesting things with the whole "living in a theme park" idea. 
 Russell does a good job of describing the landscape and history of the everglades and surrounding area, especially the details about regional flora and fauna. It's completely believable that a kid growing up in the environment of Swamplandia(!) would be intimately familiar with these species. I also appreciated the pacing of the long journey Ava takes through the swampland to the underworld. 
 When the plot forks off into two separate narratives, Ava's continuing in first person and Kiwi's in third person, things started going downhill. In Ava's sections, I had a good idea where the story was coming from, who was telling it (Ava, obviously) and why. I didn't have that sense at all in Kiwi's sections, especially because they started relatively late in the story. And then there was the Dredgeman's Revelation, which appeared as a separate short story in the New Yorker a couple of years ago. It didn't make much sense then, and it makes less sense as a very long digression in this novel. 
 The idea of the Word of Darkness is clever, and I'm sure Russell had fun playing with that. It also facilitates duel journeys through the underworld, as required in the hero monomyth that has existed since the beginning of man's storytelling. The twin underworld journeys of Ava and Kiwi mirror each other in ways that are not at all subtle (c.f. the Mama Weeds digression, the losses of virginity, etc.) 
 The ending is incredibly disappointing and disheartening. Even though, basically, we are promised that everything will be okay, all the magic and mystery in the world that makes life interesting and fun for these characters gets yanked away from them with a sudden intrusion of the darkest realities of life. Ava's Birdman turns out to be just a con man and a rapist. Osceola's affair with a ghost turns out to be suicidal depression. I didn't like the fact that the elements of magical realism Russell sets up so beautifully become revealed so starkly as illusions and even hoaxes. Depressing.

If too depressed for words by this much-praised novel, a suitable antidote is reading Matt Novak's delightful, brilliant and classic picture book "Gertie and Gumbo" -- a *happy* book about a little girl growing up in an alligator farm in a swamp. (Surely Karen Russell had it in mind? There are just too many coincidences.) Not that there's anything wrong with a book being depressing, but the "innocent point of view" presented by Ava never felt real to me, and I also realized halfway through that I had acquired almost no visual image of any of the characters. Great premise, but the narrative momentum is quickly - sorry - swamped. Especially in the long, long Birdman section, where I felt guilty for skipping pages of what I knew was supposed to be the emotional heart of the story. For innocent POV done with chilling brilliance, compare Matthew Kneale's "When We Were Romans."

I wanted to love this book. I tried to love this book.. . . but it just didn't happen. I fell in love with Karen Russell's descriptive style but she lost me half way through the story. I stopped caring about what happened to the characters and then when THAT scene happened I was like, "Uggg" and had to force myself to finish. So disappointing.

I did not like this book. I was really excited about it because it's a NYT's bestseller and because the New Yorker has loved this author in the past - that and it was at the front of every bookstore. It kind of seemed like a copy of a much better book, "Geek Love," to me, but I loved "Geek Love" so much that I was willing to try out a copy. 
 It is bad. Where the characters of "Geek Love" were fascinating because of their deformaties, depravities, and extremely narrow worldview, the characters is "Swamplandia" are just pathetic and gross. The children are left alone on an island swamp for weeks on end, where they do not know how to adequately cook for themselves or how to wash their clothes, and they do not bathe. When the brother manages to escape the island, he escapes to only slightly less squalid conditions, but still disgusting ones because he is now living with a group of teenagers who only care about the grossest sex. 
 I think the reason why the New Yorker loves Karen Russell so much is because of her many ridiculous metaphors. While they are extremely creative, some of them evoke irrelevant and distracting images. And you can't go through a single page without them. They become obnoxious and pretentious. 
 And it dragged on forever. I think at least half of this book could be cut out. 
 Unfortunately, the storyline only got better after the protagonist, a tween with very little knowledge of the world, is raped. 
 As an English major, I've read many books where characters are either literally or figuratively raped or molested. It is very difficult to read on an emotional level. But other than "Beloved" by Toni Morrison, this has got to be the most disturbing rape scene I have ever read. And it's not because it was universal or graphic like in Morrison's novel - it's because Ava, the protagonist, just lets it happen. She doesn't struggle at all. It is first person narrative, so you know that she doesn't want it to happen, but she still doesn't do anything to stop it. And it's not because her attacker has fought her or threatened her. It's because she doesn't know any better. She knows so little about the world and sex that she ignorantly believes that this must be what sex is like, the norm for everyone. After the situation is over and she leaves her attacker, she doesn't tell anyone about what happened. 
 The plot goes much faster after that, ending in a somewhat satisfying way. But still, I wouldn't recommend this to anyone. Stay away from it, no matter how many critics applaud it. I have yet to figure out what they are ever thinking.

Karen Russell writes wonderful short stories, but her exquisite style grows surprisingly wearisome in the long form of a novel -- after 75 pages or so, Swamplandia! collapses under the weight of its own preciousness. It's at times like reading a Wes Anderson movie written by a straight-A student with an enchanted thesaurus made of rainbows. A few attempts are made to dirty it up toward the end, but even these final, downbeat moments feel too lovingly and carefully rendered to convey any real darkness or urgency: 
 "Be alive, Ossie, I beamed over the monotony of water. "Be safe." 
 No raw emotion ever disrupts Swamplandia!'s carefully curated universe. Russell is a talented short story writer and part of me wonders if her agent, or the market, or whatever, dredged this novel out of her against her will. It would go a long way toward explaining why the whole thing feels so forced.

Swamplandia! is an eccentric book set in the weird world of an American alligator tourist park. It follows the exploits of three teenage siblings coping with their mother's death from cancer. This may seem like a heavy topic, but Swamplandia! is rather kooky and light-hearted. It features plenty of sly humour, such as every single alligator on the park being called 'Seth' in order to avoid spending any money repainting signs. The swampy setting is evocatively described and the plot is never formulaic. 
 Nonetheless, very little actually happens in the book and what does happen never amounts to anything. The opening pages promise that this is the story about how the family "lost everything" after their mother's death, so I expected a tragic catastrophe. Instead, I got an agonizingly drawn out whimper. The heart of the story is really about the 16 year-old sister who turns to the supernatural to cope with her mother's death and elopes with her ghost boyfriend. However even that bizarre narrative element is neither tense nor emotionally engaging. Likewise, the brother's efforts to earn a bit of cash in a crappy job never amount to much either. 
 Despite the exotic setting, this book tries to remain grounded in the real world where teenagers aren't heroes and struggles sometimes end in anti-climaxes. But at the same time, Swamplandia! doesn't explore deeper meanings or show much insight into the character's lives. So what is the point? If there is no external journey or any internal one, all that's left is a few hundred pages of hollow stuff. There is nowhere near enough humour to justify such a slowly-paced, flat book. 
 Like I said, the setting and premise are fresh and well-written, I just wish the author had done something a bit more interesting with them. 
 Edited to add: Since writing this review I have read the book Geek Love by Katherine Dunn and my opinion of Swamplandia! has fallen dramatically. Author Karen Russell just so obviously read Geek Love, absolutely adored it, and then decided to rewrite it for a YA audience. Russell may have changed the family freak show to a family alligator park and removed Geek Love's adult content, but nevertheless all the most memorable aspects of Swamplandia! are straight out of Geek Love. The quirky tone? The weird family? The tale of how that family lost everything? All watered-down versions of Geek Love. And it's not like Russell is even trying to hide her influence - my edition of Geek Love has an endorsement from Karen Russell on the cover! The reason this annoys me is, oddly enough, because everything that I criticised about Swamplandia! is done well in Geek Love. It's like... if you're going to be so heavily influenced by a single book, the least you can do is actually realise what makes that book good and replicate those things.

I love love loved this book. It's so unique, and I thought the writing was beautiful storytelling. I thought that the hint of magic-realism weaved throughout was stupendous, and I really enjoyed the shifting narration. I'll admit that this book isn't for everyone, but if you enjoy things a little different from the norm, and you can swallow difficult situations, I'd definitely recommend this book.
3 stars for the last 100 or so pages when it finally started to pick up.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Dislike books about children being raped. Don't care how good the book is. That kills it for me. I stopped reading it, and found the ending on wikipedia.

I read rave reviews of this book and had such high hopes for it. And I wanted to like it so much. However in the end it was only ok and I finished it feeling so much more disappointed because I feel like it had so much potential.It had good writing, likeable characters-but it couldn't get it's act together and couldn't decide what kind of novel it wanted to be. Add a crappy ending to it and it was even more disappointing.

Oh, there is a lot going on in this book. Besides the occasional lecture regarding the ecology and ethnography of Florida, there is a story about 13 year old Ava. Ava belongs to a family of faux-Indian alligator wrestlers who operate a home-made theme park on one of the islands located in the swamps off the coast of Florida. When Ava's mother dies, the family begins to disintegrate and the business declines; her father sinks deeper into delusion and debt; her sister begins to commune with sprits: and her brother becomes a fish out of water when he escapes to the mainland. 
 As the book progresses, Ava becomes a female Orpheus, journeying to the underworld of the swamp to prevent her sister from marrying a ghost and her brother literally descends into hell by taking a job at a doomsday themed park called The World of Darkness. Quirky, creative, imaginative are all good adjectives to describe Swamplandia!, but nonetheless, I really disliked this book. I should have stopped reading at page 50. It was all too fantastical and grotesque, lacking in cohesiveness and continuity. And reading the laboriously crafted verbiage was like slogging through a swamp of words. Not for me.

Reading this book so I can back up the usual book group moderator.... Sounds like it has both problems and potential. We will see what my opinion will be. 
 It is finished.... The critical acclaim mystifies me. The book seems overwritten to me, over long, and rather silly - and not in a good way. Granted, I have small.tolerance for magical realism. Calling all alligators "the Seths" because their first gator was named Seth and tradition is important.... Please. 
 I will be interested to see what the discussion group.says.
It was good. I have anxiety about poor money management, so I really found the whole thing too stressful to really enjoy.
While I love Karen Russell sentence-by-sentence and I loved the characters and the setting of this novel, this just wasn't my favorite of her efforts. That title still goes to Sleep Donation for me.

** spoiler alert ** 
 It probably isn't a good idea to try and summarize my feelings about a book when I have just completed it moments before, but I will try regardless. The idea of the book completely grabbed me when my mother-in-law put it simply as "a family of alligator wrestlers in Florida" (Yes! To-read it is!). And Russell builds this awesomely detailed world of the Bigtree family. The glory days when Hilola Bigtree would swim with their "Seths" (love that nickname for the gators), Ava's first-person POV with its glorious use of metaphors that would make an English majors heart flutter, Osceola dabbling in paranormal romances, etc. 
 To add to that, Russell piles on interesting situation after interesting situation. The book is juicy with material. "The Dredgeman's Revelation" was engrossing, and I wanted the Dredgeman himself, Louis Thanksgiving, to have a book all to himself. I, like young Ava Bigtree, secretly hoped to find the Underworld deep in the swamp while she searched for Ossie when Ossie opts to elope with the long-dead Louis. Then... 
 Suddenly, the book feels as though it is interrupted by an impatient hurricane. "Let's wrap everything up in less than 100 pages, shall we?" My heart is broken because there are so many unanswered questions, and I feel that the characters were just starting to unravel the many conflicts introduced in the book when Russell abruptly ends it. I want more! The English major in me could go back and simply see everything as a large metaphor, but there's too much left suspended and it is killing me (And damnit, are we really going to overlook that rape?). 
 Rating this story is difficult because if I'm feeling passionately about it in a good way, then I want to increase the star rating, but my dissatisfaction that there is no more is making me stingy.
I couldn't get into it. Only one person in book club liked it so I am going to skip the end and move on.
Magic realism is not my cup of tea, but I thought I'd give this book a try because of all the good reviews. I should have trusted my instincts.

So, I am probably in a minority here, but I didn't even finish it because I didn't really care about the story or what was going to happen to the characters. The writing is charming, but it just didn't intrigue me enough. Poor Ava ends up all alone on the island and that's where I left her.
Thick/dense writing that's hard to push through and a story that's all over the place.

I was getting into the story all right, and enjoying the ride to a certain extent, but then the language got too vulgar and explicit for my tastes. If it were a movie it would be rated R. Perhaps the HBO series they're making on it won't include so much language and I'll watch that.... righhhhht.... :-)

Thirteen-year-old Ava Bigtree has lived her entire life at Swamplandia!, her family's island and gator-wrestling park in the Everglades. But when Ava's mother dies, the park and her family are plunged into chaos. Slowly, Ava's family begins to fall apart and go their separate ways leaving her stranded on the island alone. Ava embarks on an adventure through the swamp to bring her family back together. 
 Told through Ava's innocent eyes, Russell tells a story of tragedy, poverty and ecology seen throughout southern Florida. While the Bigree family's story ends happily, there are notes of sad reality told through Ava's naive perspective making this story even more haunting. 
 While beautifully and masterfully written, I found this story sad and its unfinished quality makes it even more realistic and tragic.

It begins with such promise -- a very novel setting with great characters, but then, the plot meanders strangely until something unexpected and terrible happens and the great characters have nothing to show for their time spent in these pages.

I had a hard time getting into this, even though it had such a great premise. A family-run alligator theme park. Death. Homeschool. Ghosts. A child narrator. All interesting. I started it twice and got distracted by other books, but didn't blame the book. It had to be outside circumstances. So I thought, I will choose it for my book club, and then I will have a deadline and be compelled to finish it. That was stupid. I would have been better off leaving it forever at page thirty. 
 And not because it was too dark, or too dramatic, or too weird. Because I like all those things. No, this book somehow managed to be boring even in the midst of all its dark, bizarre drama. The characters didn't think things that were interesting, even in the midst of interesting situations. Things happened that didn't make sense and were never explained, as if the author wrote the novel during National Novel Writing Month, writing furiously for thirty days, but then never went back and re-read it. Ever. 
 So here is my big problem. WHO THE F*&K NOMINATED THIS THING FOR PULITZER? AND HOW DID IT NOT IMMEDIATELY TANK? WHO ARE THE FOOLS THAT VOTE ON THE PULITZER? Because even David Foster Wallace's ridiculously long rambling unfinished Pale King was better than this. That one didn't have resolution because HE KILLED HIMSELF BEFORE IT WAS FINISHED! So, Karen Russell, what's your excuse? 
 And now, I will have to go talk about this book with six women in their seventies and eighties, who I am betting are re-thinking their participation in my book club.

Meh. While the book was compelling in the middle, I had a lot of trouble getting into it at the beginning and a horrible time reconciling with it at the end. 
 I was unhappy with the narrative and the characters throughout most of the book. Characters initially painted as resourceful and clever end up exposed as foolish and simple, and characters initially flagged as simpletons come off looking much the opposite. 
 It's tough to pinpoint specific plot problems without exposing too many spoilers, so I'll just say that I found the characters' decisions and ultimate fates deeply unsatisfying, and the narrative jumped from poignant to rambling to downright dull over and over again. 
 I would have given this just one star, but I gave Russell a second because other problems aside, she certainly knows how to turn a phrase. Call it a bad book by a good writer.
I didn't finish Swamplamdia! and I don't feel bad. I don't like the characters, tone, or content of the book. I was bored.

I really wanted to like this book since it's been on my To Be Read pile for so long and, more importantly, I really enjoyed Russell's short story collection, Vampires in the Lemon Grove. However, I just couldn't get into the characters of this book. I didn't feel for them and that's something I've come to realize is important for me to really enjoy a book. I'm actually surprised I even finished the book, but I think because I respect this writer, I felt I must give it its due, which in my mind means reading it all the way through. The one thing I did like is the ending. I felt satisfied with the ending and perhaps gained a bit more appreciation for our main character, Ava, as she finally physically and emotionally broke through the barriers that had been keeping her down.

I did not like this book very much. I found it difficult to believe that a dying mother would not be more cautious and thorough in helping her family to deal with the emotional and economic problems her death would cause. While the children were fairly isolated during their childhoods, they had access to television, and interactions with tourists, that made some of their behavior seem inconsistent at best and unbelievable at worst. The best parts of the book for me were the efforts by Kiwi, the son, to help his family financially, and learn to deal with other people once he moved to the mainland.

Karen's debut short story collection was completely amazing. I still think about the worlds she created within those pages. It left me wanting more, and I thought Swamplandia would quench my thirst. Slow paced tale a family dealing with the loss of their mother. Virtually nothing happens for the first third of the book. Once the action gets going, it's fairly predictable and dark.

Strip away the fancy writing and the literary tributes to Mark Twain and Homer and you have a story of a family plunged into grief by the death of a mother, then faced with financial ruin. The father, unable to cope, abandons his three teenage children and sinks into alcohol dependence and depression. The children try to survive. 
 Swamplandia! takes us through a family's crisis and then ends the tale once the family is back together. 
 While the writing is fun and there are some great scenes in the tale, especially the part about Louis Thanksgiving, I found it disappointing.

reference_books.title: Neverwhere
reference_books.review_text:
After reading and loving "The Graveyard Book," I decided to trying something else by Neil Gaiman. I found the premise of "Neverwhere" to be interesting: the bulk of the story takes place in a shadow London, a world set in the tunnels and underground passages beneath the London we know. Richard Mayhew is a typical Londoner, working in finance and engaged to be married. On his way to a party with his fiancee, they nearly stumble over an odd girl who is bleeding and clearly hurting. Richard wants to help her, while his fiancee tells him to call an ambulance and leave her there. Something compels Richard to help the girl, and he takes her back to his apartment, cleans her up and binds her wounds. His involvement with the girl (named "Door") leads him into this underground world and into fantastic adventures. 
 Urban fantasy isn't my usual genre, so if you're skeptical, well, I was, too. But the story is richly imagined and full of excitement. Gaiman is a terrific writer and his characters jump off the page. I was especially taken with the way he used real landmarks and Tube stations in London as jumping off points for his imaginative underworld. I'll definitely be exploring some of his other novels.

reference_books.title: The Wordy Shipmates
reference_books.review_text: Not her strongest book. An almost academic look at the philosophy of the first settlers in America. Disappointing if you're looking for the chatty, jokey style of her earlier books; assumes a much deeper background of this era of history than I have.

reference_books.title: To All the Boys I've Loved Before (To All the Boys I've Loved Before, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Read this after it was a recommended choice for a monthly read-along. Totally enjoyed this: adorable family, funny narrator, engaging characters, hilarious premise. Escapism, sure, but really fun escapism.

reference_books.review_text: Okay, so parts of this book feel a bit like the Hunger Games but I thoroughly enjoyed it.

reference_books.title: The Replacement
reference_books.review_text: I very much enjoyed this YA book about a teenager who isn't the blood son of his parents, but rather a "replacement" -- the child of an underground people who could be described as pixies or fairies or even demons, but who eschew such a name. Mack grows up under the weight of his family's awareness that he was a replacement but his family stubbornly loves him and he loves them, too, in his own way, especially his sister Emma. The book gets suspenseful as Mack tries to understand where he comes from and how he can go on living a life aboveground with that knowledge. There's a bit of teen romance, a kidnapped child, a grunge rock band and many other interesting developments to keep the plot moving. Yes, you've got to suspend your disbelief a bit and be open to the weirdness of the story, but it's a good alternative for when you're in the mood for something supernatural but are sick to un-death of vampires.

reference_books.title: The Diviners (The Diviners, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Not crazy about this one. I thought the historical setting was interesting but the otherworldly plot was a bit hard to swallow. I never connected with the protagonist Evie, either. Apart from her flapper lingo (she constantly says things like "Pos-i-tute-ly" and "do you have any giggle juice?" which drove me crazy, particularly in the first half of the book), she was shallow and immature and for some reason seemed very flat to me. I thought the book could have used some editing, with dramatic passages that went on too long. Bottom line is that it never sucked me in and made me feel like I couldn't wait to see what happened next.

reference_books.title: The End of Everything
reference_books.review_text: Abbott has a vivid way of writing about things that make the reader uncomfortable, making the reader squirm as well as wonder what's going to happen next but in a way that also makes the reader think. This book is told from the perspective of a 13 yr old girl whose best friend and neighbor goes missing. Lizzie knew the missing girl, Evie, best and uncovers bits and pieces that help uncover the mystery of what happened to Evie. But the book is also a really fascinating look inside the head of a thirteen-year-old girl, half an adult and half a child, trying to navigate the scary waters of both impending adulthood and also the issues raised by her friend's disappearance.

reference_books.title: I Let You Go
reference_books.review_text:
Note to self: consider whether you ever want to read another book that is compared to "Gone Girl." Because this book was, and I didn't think the plot twist(s) were THAT surprising or even worked that well in the context of the book. (Honestly, I felt that it was more gimmicky than anything.) 
 This book is half police procedural, half "psychological suspense." While I appreciate the author's attempt to break free from being one or the other, I didn't feel it worked particularly well. I also felt that the shift in perspective (first-person narration that alternates from person to person, combined with third-person) was clunky and at times confusing. 
 The story begins with an awful hit and run accident in which a young child is killed, and the driver speeds away. We follow the police investigation of the accident, as well as seeing how various other people involved in the accident respond and cope with it. I don't want to say any more for fear of spoiling the plot. 
 Important trigger note: animal abuse (I loathe having that be part of a police precedural) and domestic abuse.

reference_books.title: The Time Traveler's Wife
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book got a lot of buzz and was recommended to me several times. I hesitated to begin it; time travel isn't my thing unless it's extremely well done. It took me a little while to get drawn into the story; the beginning is a bit jarring and the frequent chronological shifts were hard for me to get used to. Overall,I enjoyed the book more than I expected to, although it was a bit melodramatic and breathless at times. Several of the plot elements were a bit too clever by half, particularly Henry's death and several scenes involving his daughter. I probably would have liked the book more if I'd seen fewer gushing reviews of it. I wasn't terribly impressed with the quality of the writing: the strength of the book lies more in the originality of the plot rather than the skill of the writer.

Rating: 2.9* of five 
 Lovely little romance novel published out of its genre and hugely successful therefore. No new ground broken here, and not one single surprise. But it's a charming story, it's nicely told, and it's got something that makes a novel worth reading: A beginning, a middle, and an end that flow naturally from one to the next. The end is the logical consequence of the beginning, and that's all too rare in fiction. 
 Had I bought this book, I would be grumpy, but it was free so who cares? Anyone who likes romances will like this gentle, pleasurable afternoon companion of a book. 
 Rating: 4* of five 
 The Publisher Says: "My name is David Brandstetter. I'm a claims investigator for the Medallion Life Insurance Company." He handed her a card. She didn't glance at it. "I'm looking for Peter Oats," he said. 
 "He's not here. I wish he were. Maybe you can help me. The police don't seem to care." 
 She was April Stannard. Her lover, Peter's father, had died. April believed he'd been murdered. 
 Dave Brandstetter's investigation takes him through the rare-book world, to backstage at a community theatre, to the home of a world-famous television performer. Along the way, Dave soon comes to agree with April. 
 My Review: Small-town California has a lot of atmosphere, according to Hansen; I don't remember it that way, but I was young and miserable, so I'll go with the man who found there something that led to this description of an old mill made into a theater: 
 The waterwheel was twice a man's height, wider than a man's two stretched arms. The timbers, braced and bolted with rusty iron were heavy, hand-hewn, swollen with a century of wet. Moss bearded the paddles, which dripped as they rose. The sounds were good. Wooden stutter like children running down a hall at the end of school. Grudging axle thud like the heartbeat of a strong old man. 
 Beautiful. 
 It's with this book, second in the series, that Hansen's chops come fully into play. He's here to wow you, and he's got the story to keep you sitting right there flipping pages. April, the bereaved, is Rita Hayworth in my mind; Oates, the dead guy, looks like John Garfield; Peter, the son and heir, is Cabaret-era Michael York; and so on and so on. (Eve, Oates' ex-wife, is Barbara Stanwyck.) I do this a lot, cast the perfect movie cast as I read along. But this time it felt as if it was all done for me. Oates' murderer, when revealed, was a surprise to me even though this was a re-read. And the actor I'd put in the role was perfect...no testament to my skills, just an example of how beautifully Hansen draws his characters. 
 Dave's got a man, too...how amazing for the 1970s! I so wish this had been a TV series. Magnum PI only gay! *sigh* What might have been....

This was my second reading of the charming "The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society" which I first read before joining Goodreads. Told entirely in letters, the story is centered around Juliet, a young author who goes to Guernsey in 1946 to research a story after the Nazi Occupation of the island. Some of the islanders had spontaneously pretended to be coming from a literary club meeting when they were stopped after curfew by a German soldier. So they had to create a book club to justify their story, and found a special joy in reading. 
 Juliet discovered a group of quirky, caring individuals in Guernsey with fascinating back stories. While much of the book was humorous, there was also the harsh reality of the German Occupation. Children were sent to the English countryside for safety's sake, people were hungry, some islanders were sent to concentration camps, and prisoners were brought in to fortify the island. The literary society was something to look forward to during a bleak time--a place to meet friends and discuss ideas. 
 This is a heartwarming book that's sure to put a smile on your face. Highly recommended. 4.5 stars.

If you've seen any other reviews of this book, it is not unlikely you've seen comparisons to 84 Charing Cross Road. It's somewhat inevitable, given the format of this novel, presented as it is in the form of letters between the various characters. It is a leisurely and familiar way to go about telling a story, and in this case works quite effectively. 
 As I'm finding it hard to pinpoint what exactly prompts me to give this book 4.5, if not 5, stars out of 5, I wonder if it is the authors' skillful ability to represent humanity not only accurately but optimistically. While the recent history of World War II casts a shadow over the lives of the characters, from the start the reader knows there is more to this story than the devastation wrought by war - there is the constant hope of deliverance and the perseverance of a people not willing to submit themselves docilely to the invaders. 
 Not only does the method work and the story embody reality in a touching and poignant way, the characters pull one in with their life. They truly come alive in the pages of the book, and as the book progressed I think I came to think of them less as characters in a book than relatives who had given me the joy of this window into their earlier lives. We see relationships blossom and the fruits of life-long friendships. We cheer on our favorite character and have to chuckle a little when the busybody gets her comeuppance. 
 Shaffer and Barrows' writing draws the reader into the world of this small island of the English channel. It is not a difficult read, but it is sprinkled throughout with gems of wisdom and wonder. One character observes that "Reading good books ruins you for enjoying bad books." And The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society is a good book. 
 (my review from http://www.read-all-over.net/fiction/...)

Be proud of me. I actually finished this book! 
 On the back cover of this book, an author praises this book as so realistic she keeps forgetting the characters aren't real. While she must have short term memory loss about the characters, she did manage to find the books one strength: it's "realistic." Realistic in the sense that I really did feel like someone reading all the letters someone sent and received over about six months. And that is to say, it was really, really boring. 
 This book has no conflict. Literally, it has no conflict. Conflict years ago is discussed in retrospect, but the narrator's life is 100% peaches and cream. Everyone loves her and she makes tons of money. The only real conflict in sight was my own struggle not to put down the book... and, let me tell you, it was a hard won battle. I rushed through it because I knew that if I put it down, I would never pick it back up again. 
 I couldn't possibly ruin the ending for you because there is no ending to ruin. The only "revelation" is who the narrator is going to end up marrying. And I could have bet you money on the correct person five minutes into the book. The rest of it is just repetitive - the characters state and restate the same things in a way that makes you wonder if they all have short term memory loss. Oh wait, I can tell you one thing: at the end, the authors will realize how inept they are at epistolary novels and will jump to a journal entry in a jarring fashion. So you have that to look forward to. 
 The whole "novel" really reads like a watered down history book. I picture a mother writing it as an attempt to "secretly" get a child to learn history... in the same way she pours his medicine into his apple juice. It doesn't work. It ruins the juice entirely and prolongs the bad taste to an entire glass. Don't get me wrong; I absolutely love history... but this was more boring than my high school textbook. I repeat, nothing interesting happens. The story is not touching or gripping or sad. I did not sympathize with any of the characters, whose stories of sorrow and despair in WWII have been told and retold by qualified first-hand witnesses and far better authors. A few of the characters (Adelaide Addison and Mark) were the height of cliche. They're evil because they *gasp* don't like the stunning and perfect main character. Oh no! We must shun them! 
 This could have been worse, mind you. But it was bad. The profanity, homosexuality, unwedded mother, and talk of prostitutes are all just kind of thrown in there to make this PG-13. I resent the authors for making this sound like a good book... they should 'fess up in a note at the beginning! I feel cheated! 
 Goodreads, your high ratings have deceived me. These prose are not beautiful. The characters sound pretty much the same and are hard to keep track of. The poor malnurshed plot is unrealistic at best. Don't waste your time, fellow readers!

I was smiling by page 4. By page 48, all I could think was, "This is a delightful book". I don't use delightful frivolously... Looking forward to savoring this book. 
 *** 
 Now that I've finished this book, I'm still smiling. At times touching, at times funny, always interesting.

Hard to believe that a story about the aftermath of WWII could be so sweet and uplifting. But, in fact, that is the charm of the book - that the horrors of the war are told in such simple, but positive prose that they are all the more striking. And the characters are inspirational for their lively spirits in the face of so much tragedy. Plus, I loved the letter format - reminded me of those books I love, Griffin and Sabine, the Jolly Postman. It is always a guilty pleasure to read other people's mail :)

I loved this book. The only reason I didn't give it 5 stars was because I thought the ending was a little too abrupt. But this book made me wish letter writing was still more common than texting or email. I think it is so much more personal and fun to write letters!
