 "The lines around his eyes make him seem to be starting a smile even when he's not." pg. 161 
 "Isola doesn't approve of small talk and believes in breaking the ice by stomping on it." pg. 197

This was a charming little story with interesting characters. Every time I picked it up to read, I enjoyed myself. The problem was that I didn't feel a pull to pick the book up and continue reading. The story was a meandering one that made me wonder occasionally what the point was. I liked it overall, but I'm not sure that I would recommend it.

I convinced myself for a long time that I wasn't interested in reading this book -- that it was too old-lady, spinster sounding for me. But once I finally succumbed to the amazing reviews and read it, well, I can see why so many people love this book. The writing is fresh and you can't help but fall in love with the narrator, an eccentric author named Juliet, and all of the quirky and fascinating inhabitants of Guernsey. I enjoyed getting to know them and I came to love them, just as Juliet did. The ending of this book came too quickly, for I wanted to stay in Guernsey a bit longer. But I will remember this book for a very long time.
Thie book is very inspiring. It made me want to visit Guernsey. And I will within the next 10 years!

I LOVED this book. Every so often, an image from the novel, comes back to me. Not only is there mystery and suspense, but there's a real sense of history. It reads genuine and true. I'm a fan of historical fiction, and this novel certainly wasn't a disappointment. I am now reading Ann Barrows' chapter books Ivy and Bean to my son.
It took me a bit to get used to a story told through letters. I really enjoyed the characters. It was interesting to hear a WWII story in a new and different location
A novel in letters .. . I thoroughly enjoyed this book.

Well, the story was interesting and I loved learning about the German occupation of Guernsey and I love letters so, you know... 
 But, sadly, the ending was kind of kitchy.

" 'Life goes on.' What nonsense, I thought, of course it doesn't. It's death that goes on; Ian is dead now and will be dead tomorrow and next year and forever." 
 "Strings of anecdotes don't make a book." 
 "This obsession with dignity can ruin your life if you let it."

This is one of the most delightful books I have ever read. Funny, poignant, thoughtful, truthful, and historically-charged. I loved it! It's set on the island of Guernsey during the German occupation of France. Inhabitants are British. Each character is interesting, realistic, and endearing. The genre is letters. Read it, especially if you love history, WW2, book clubs, and British novels. Just adorable.

I REALLY enjoyed this book. It took me a little bit to get into but once I did I loved it! I loved that I could see Juliet the main character grow and evolve. I fell in love with every single character. I laughed with them in this book, but I also cried with them... The ending came a little to fast but as always with a good book! This is one to buy and read again!

This was an absolutely fantastic book! I very highly recommend it to everyone! It was informative, sweet, happy, and a quick read to boot! :) It is about a woman who is an author and is asked to do a column about how reading helped people during WWII. She comes in contact with some people on the island of Guernsey, and the rest of the story is 'their' story. It tells of their experiences, and then the lady writer goes to Guernsey and... it's just so cute! It's all written as letters written to and from all the people involved. Very well written and fun.

We did this in book club and I am glad we did.Charming,delightful tale of correspondence cross the pond.I quite enjoyed the letter style of format that the book utilized.Came to love the characters who were so well drawn,you could feel you were on the island having a spot of tea on someone's porch,Nice,easy read but lovely,
Really sweet little story. A book I might go back to someday if I just wanted to escape to Guernsey in my head.

Horrible, horrible, horrible. I set out to like this story, mostly because I was eager to learn about the occupation of Guernsey during WWII, a subject in which I was entirely unfamiliar. What I got, instead, was a shallow gimmick that grew more and more tedious as the story progressed. I am not sure I have ever really seen a successful execution of a rotating narrator, but its effect in this case was utterly abysmal. All of the characters shared the same voice, regardless of gender, age, or social class. A story that deserved more care and depth was haphazardly thrown together without subtlety or nuance. I hated it more and more as I read it and more and more in hindsight. Horrible.

This story was predictable but oh so delightful. These letters feel as though they're written by real people, not fictional characters. Everything described was so vivid. There's a perfect balance between humor and seriousness; much of it is very funny. I fell in love with several of the characters, who have their flaws but who are very endearing. This is a very sweet story. It would have been lovely if I could have read it in one or two sittings but I read it slowly and just a few pages at a time at points, which somewhat ruined the flow, but didn't ruin the book for me. I enjoyed it immensely.
Too sappy and sweet for me.
enjoyed following the story line through the letters written between various characters. Loved seeing the main character blossom and gain her voice. Good book.

I was given this book by a freind who simply said "read it." So I did. It turned out to join my top 5 favorite books of all time. I ususally don't gravitate towards epistolary novels, but this one had me hooked instantly. I felt a part of this special group of people.

A book about book lovers from the island of my favorite cows...what could be better? Except that it was written in the form of correspondence! My favorite writing style! (And had quite a bit of historical fact which I enjoyed as well)

This is an enchanting and heartwarming book. Although I figured out the ending midbook, I had to follow the characters to the very end. The setting, and time made the characters very believable. Written in episticle style gave life to the voice of each character. A GOOD READ!
I love everything about this book. I just finished it and I'm already ready to read it again.
Boring. Really, really boring. It may be that I read it just after A Thousand Splended Suns. This was highly recommended by a neighbor. I just couldn't get into it.
Menopause lit.

We read this for our bookclub and i really enjoyed this story told in the form of letters. Compulsively readable but a bit "twee" (or trite) to quote a friend. I mean I was ready to pack my bags and move to idyllic Guernsey after finishing this book.

I could tell in this book when the writer changed. It was at that point that I started to really enjoy the book. I actually stopped reading this part way through and was encouraged by a friend to keep at it a few months later. I'm glad I did because it definitely got better as it went on.

book_b.title: The Girl on the Train
book_b.user_review: There is a very good chance that I am either (A) contrary or (B) prone to get my expectations up too high when a lot of people say they really like a book. Or maybe (C) both. But I really did not care for this book at all. I thought the pacing in the beginning was slow -- it seemed like the first half of the book was entirely reading about Rachel and her hangovers - meh. I also just did not like any of the characters in the book which made it hard to care about finishing it.

sample_reviews.review_text:
How do we appear to an outsider looking in on our lives? This is the theme of this page-turning thriller. It turns out that nothing is what it seems from the sidelines. Over the course of the novel, three young women desperately attempt to appear in control of their lives but each struggles to keep the big issues of her life at bay and keep up appearances. 
 Rachel, a young, depressed alcoholic, creatively imagines the life story of a couple she sees each day from the window of her commuter train. In her often intoxicated state, she fantasizes about the blissful life of love and romance that they share. She had this life herself, once, and believes that she can get it back. 
 Megan is a beautiful and talented artist with a husband who understands her need for time and space. But she is restless and discontent, almost smothered, with her life. She has a need to be seen as attractive to unavailable men and this need is driving her to destruction. And, while dealing with that issue, a long-hidden secret comes to the surface. 
 Anna has the husband, the baby, the house and all the fixings for the ideal life but, hidden from view, she knows that none of these ideals are true. She spends her days ignoring the little truths that keep revealing themselves. She lives in fear of losing her beautiful life even though that life is fictitious. 
 Although many reviewers compare this book to Gone Girl, it is nothing like it. These characters have a depth that makes the reader feel for them in their impossible situations. 
 4.5 stars
I thought it was pretty obvious who the killer would be from the very beginning. They hype over this book right now isn't worth it. It wasn't terrible but it was a pretty standard who done it.
One of the most cliched books I've ever read. Boring. Quite obvious what was going on from the start.

** spoiler alert ** 
 "A book published this year" 
 This was an....interesting book. I did enjoy the plot (even though I saw the plot twist a mile off) and I liked the damaged characters. The narrative was interesting, it was told from Rachel (main character), Megan (the missing woman), and Anna (Rachel's ex-husband's new wife). It was a mix between diary entries and internal monologue. I say this because occasionally the narrator would go back and fill you in on some things that she skipped over. I do talk to myself a lot, but rarely do I give a brief synopsis of what I was doing the day before. So, in that respect, I am not sure if that technique was super successful. Also, after reading this, you will be left with the conclusion that 1)all guys are dicks and 2)all women are either desperately wanting a baby, pregnant, or has a young child.
I loved the audio version of this book! Very gripping and held my interest constantly. As intense as Gone Girl.
Wow! This book takes so many twists. It kept surprising me all the way through the last chapter. So unexpected!

1 star for the predictable story. Ugh and the terrible characterisation. Every female was pathetic, needy and pitiful. The male stereotypes were no better. 
 1 star for the fact that despite the story being crap, it kept me up most of the night wanting to know what happened next. The same part of me that likes d-listed and other gossip websites enjoyed the book and I am not proud of that fact.
Figured it out on page 47.

The only thing I could really say while reading this is, "What the hell is wrong with these people. Their nucking futs..all of them. Not only are they all nuts, they are also creepy as hell. Seriously what sane person does the stuff that Rachael does? How could she and Anna for that fact miss how Tom is a douche canoe. Personally they all were a bit douche, but Tom was head of the pack as Sergeant Douche Canoe. I'm seriously creeped out over this one.

I couldn't put this book down for all the right reasons. There is mystery, suspense and good character development. I was surprised by how the story developed and couldn't wait to find out what happened. 
 Loved the ending and would recommend to a friend.

Meh. I saw the twist coming from the very beginning. However, the writing was awesome; she made all of the narrators unlike-able and lovable all at the same time through the raw emotion she gave each of their stories. If you like to read the novels before the films come out, I suggest it, but if you are looking for a thriller, I feel this one has been overhyped.

If you like unreliable (and unlikable) narrators, you'll love this book. Not one, not two, but three of 'em. And if you like reading about alcohol fueled ways to screw up your life, even better. Nonetheless, the novel goes down easily. 
 A page-turner, a beach read (even in November), and some nice location work, but I don't think I'll remember this one for long.

I can see why a lot of people compare this to "Gone Girl." This time the setting is London (well, more like a less-than-chic suburb, judging by the rattletrap light rail that shuttles the heroine to and fro), but the demographic is the same - young, educated, middle-class married couples who *just can't* - and the reader is again treated to that internal, indecisive flip-flopping debate ("Did X do it?" "I think X did it" "X sooo did it" "Hmm, okay. Maybe X didn't do it.") Both books are solid page-turners, both have main protoganists that behave with a maddening lack of sense, and both (IMHO) end stupidly, although I would say that "Gone Girl" was less predictable, better paced, and much better written.

Loved everything about this book. From the unlikable characters (it's a thing, I like books with those. See: Gone Girl, I definitely understand the comparisons although this was a much more fast paced book, less lengthy descriptions, more frenetic action). I enjoyed the story as a whole and had theories about the end but as per usual, I was wrong. I read this book in less than 24 hours because I simply couldn't put it down- it's my favorite kind of book, the ones I can't get enough of. Loved it.

http://mariesbookgarden.blogspot.com/... 
 I've had this book on my "to read" list for awhile...people have compared it to Gone Girl. But although less gruesome than Gone Girl, this novel was less compelling and gripping. I knew Rachel was an unreliable narrator, but this is because she blacked out and can't remember. Gradually, she pieces the truth together in her mind. 
 Consequently, Hawkins gradually unravels the story rather than diving right in. I thought she did a good job of depicting the harsh reality of alcoholism. But ultimately, I expected more out of this novel than I got. It is very British, and I appreciated that! And a decent read...but not as fantastic as I expected!
I couldn't get into this book at all. DNF'd at 87 and 108 pages.

I don't get this. I'm an avid reader that always finishes a book. It took me almost 4 months to get through this, (I'd stop and read something actually interesting in between and I'd binge read). It was so boring and the characters were just plain awful. Literally awful. Not one in my eyes was redeemable except for Cathy the minor character who has infinite patience,in my opinion. I also liked the red-haired man on the train. He was in it for 4 seconds but I liked him, seemed like a jolly fellow. 
 I don't get how this book is so popular? It's one of the most boring and cringe-worthy books I've ever read. There's a movie for crying out loud? What? How? I hope Emily Blunt makes it watchable, maybe they added interesting plot points to the movie,because this book was barely readable and the drunken binges on every page were so annoying! I threw it down a couple of times! The last few chapters were just plain weird and it felt like I lost years of my life, like I wasted them, trying to get to that underwhelming and ridiculous ending. 
 They market it as having a plot twist? Not much of a plot twist. I don't want to give spoilers away but....the "twist" is who the characters truly are and that's pretty much given away in the beginning and the killer was absolutely obvious. I'd have been so much happier with anyone else in this book as the killer. Something crazy to have made the other wasted sentences worth it in the end. 
 I'm sad about this book. It's completely unworthy of its hype, I feel cheated by buying it and reading it, the plot is awful, the characters are awful-including the deceased--and I just....I'm sad that I'm left wanting. The only thing I "want" to know is why I feel I'm the only person in the world that thought this book was horrible. I feel like everyone should know this. 
 Maybe if I'd gotten drunk like Rachel is on every page I could see its merit.

The prologue of this book piqued my interesting. Then I realised it was about an alcoholic woman who spied on this couple she saw from her train window every morning and evening because they reminded her of what her and her husband used to be like. I was pretty bored by the story, but then Megan went missing so I thought "ooh, a murder" and then it just dragged on. Things started to mingle then and got better, but it was alright. I figured out who the killer was about half way through.. but because the characters were dilly dallying and kept talking in circles, I got annoyed. All three woman were just moaners and had problems and they just pissed me off to be honest. Anna and Rachel just took so long in figuring things out, they were so naive. I didn't feel any connection to any of them, so I didn't care about their stories. I finished the story just to see what happened and if I'd guessed right. I did enjoy the ending though, but overall, it was okay. Oh, and the woman who voiced Anna has the dullest voice I have ever heard.. I don't think that helped with liking the book.
Incredibly depressing ... Couldn't even finish it.

"It's impossible to resist the kindness of strangers. Someone who looks at you, who doesn't know you, who tells you it's OK, whatever you did, whatever you've done: you suffered, you hurt, you deserve forgiveness." 
 I liked it but not as much as I loved Gone Girl. I liked the story, the writing style and the characters were so good written. It is good but I didn't enjoy reading it. so depressing.

I couldn't get into the book at all. It was hard to be sympathetic towards any of the characters. At first I felt sorry for one of them, then all I could think about was how pathetic she truly was. They all were. Even the girl who died, I couldn't really care about her. 
 Then I figured out the "mystery" about 2/3 through. After that, I really could care less. I only finished the book to confirm what I already knew. 
 It just wasn't good for me like it was for so many others.

I found the first part of this book really compelling, and I liked the writing style. Then I got tired of the main character Rachel's drunken bumblings, and as there are only a few characters in the whole story, the whodunit element is pretty weak--I guessed it in the very beginning, but read on hoping for a twist. There wasn't one. Megan's character is not fleshed out very well, with past misdeeds only hinted at except for one thing that is lobbed into the story for emotional impact without much thought, and the mysterious, slightly menacing red-haired man is, of course, a red herring. Anna's POV is introduced in the middle of the book and adds nothing to the story; she is a complete cipher. I'd try this author again to see if she's developed as this is her debut, but I really don't get the hype about this book at all.

I feel as if I have a lot to say about this book. The first is that the plot was fantastic, truly phenomenal. But I gave it only 3 stars because the characters were so incredibly horrible that it was distracting me through the book (which was probably the point- misdirection). I feel as if we as the human race have become complacent about our behavior and this book has a whole cast of characters that were deemed by critics to be relatable which proves my point. Everyone should try and be a better person everyday! 
 ** I'm mad at Goodreads right now because it only saved half of my review and I can't remember what else I wrote.** 
 This will be close enough: 
 The plot twists and turns, moves forward and backward in time, all leaving you without crucial details and a firm point to base theories on. 
 I had guessed half of this mess of a plot twist but not the entire thing. Which is important to me, I don't want to guess what happens at the beginning. 
 I think that if you like suspense/thriller novels and would not care about the characters being fundamentally bad then read this book. Or just read it and deal like I did!
I found Rachel weak and hard to root for and Anna and Meagan completely horrible. I think I might have enjoyed the book more if Rachel was more likeable or Scott or someone.
Dark, depressing people...lots of twists and turns. Fairly fast read - in my mind it did not live up to the hype.

Loved this book, really well written, I was apprehensive at first when I started due to it being a diary style book, but from the first couple of pages I was hooked. 
 I liked Rachel as a character, not her lifestyle but she seemed a generally caring person had a drinking problem. 
 I could visualise the characters well as well as the setting. 
 Couldn't put it down, highly recommend
3.5 stars

** spoiler alert ** 
 3.5 stars. I would recommend it, though. This was a hard one to rate. Story is at least a 4. The likability of the main character (or lack there of) is what brought the rating down. 
 The characters... 
 (The following is not so much spoilers, but it might affect how you read the book, so I'm tagging it as such) I get why she was the way that she was, and it makes sense to the story, but she was really hard to sympathize with. She just didn't have anything going for her. Nothing about her was likable. In fact, I can't think of one character in this book I actually did like. Usually characters make the book for me, so it says A LOT about the story that it was strong enough to still make me walk away from the book thinking I liked it. 
 As for the ending... 
 (The following definitely does have spoilers) 
 so I had guessed from near the beginning that Megan's mysterious lover was Tom. What I hadn't guessed was that Tom was a complete psychopath and narcissist. I thought it was either Anna or Scott who did the deed. Anna because she found out about the affair. Scott because he found out (and to drive home the fact that everyone seems to have a great life from the view of a passing train). 
 I didn't start to suspect Tom until a few Anna chapters in. It was a great twist that
Epic page turner but there was too much useless misdirection to give it five stars.

Take the movie and novel Gone Girl, add a little fatal Attraction, and you have a chair-gripping version of Paula Hawkins FIRST debut novel. Let me repeat. DEBUT, as in FIRST novel. I whipped through all of this EASILY in two days and you have to wonder, if this is her FIRST novel, HOW will she EVER match this one in subsequent writings? 
 Seen on Barnes & Noble bookshelves in the states everywhere rated in GoodReads as one of the top novel as well as in Booklist, I am SO glad I have this in our Upper School Library - I can't even begin to tell you how many times you will be shocked from the page turning plot Hawkins infuses - this is an all star find of the year :) You'll see...

I had very high expectations from The Girl on the Train but it fell short on every account. I haven't read more annoying characters in any book before, especially Rachel. I had no sympathy or empathy for her. By the end I was so tired of her incessant rambling that I thought of abandoning the book but I persevered because I hoped it would get better. I would have tolerated this if the plot was good, but it was almost nonexistent. I had guessed the killer before the halfway mark. 
 Even the pacing was very slow. Disappointed.
What a huge disappointment. Maybe this time the movie will be better.

This female-centric potboiler featured characters that were just so pitiful and/or horrible that I came very close to quitting within the first 20 pages. But I kept on, and eventually got wrapped up in the mystery (though I did guess the culprit about halfway through). Recommended for people who liked Joy Fielding's Still Life.

These characters were all CRAZY. I mean crazy-pants crazy. But that was part of the appeal. With everyone so off their rocker, you just didn't really know how this was going to unfold, who was reliable and who wasn't. It was a fun little psychological joyride.

it's provocative & creepy & remarkably sad. 
 so yeah, I loved it. 
 the story unfolds through the pov of 3 unreliable narrators, all of whom are varying shades of awful & immoral -- Rachel, who is thoroughly consumed by her alcoholism, and who lies, unapologetically; Anna, who (gleefully!) pursues an affair with Tom; and Megan, whose backstory is arguably the most dark & unsettling. I was simultaneously furious with & compassionate towards each of them except Tom; my sympathy does not extend that far , which reflects impressively upon the author. 
 BUT to be honest, I wouldn't reread this; guessing the villain was half the thrill, so I doubt the book would be as gripping the second time around.
Gripping story similar to Gone Girl with unsympathetic characters that keeps you guessing to finale. Rated 3.5.

Weak writing, dark story, poorly developed characters. I never liked the main character. There was nothing to like about her. If it weren't a book club read, I would not have gone beyond the first couple of chapters.

Warning: this book does not live up to the hype! 
 I hated every character. One was more up relatable than the next. 
 The grand mystery was pretty easy to figure out about halfway through. I only continued reading to try to prove myself wrong. (I was right.) 
 It's worth picking up if you have nothing else to read, but by no means should you be rushing for your copy.
the audio worked really great with 3 different female narrators. Totally unreliable characters, but it works! Enjoyed it

This is a very complex plot and I admire the way Hawkins is able to control all the threads and bring it to some sort of a conclusion, albeit a bit unbelievably. 
 I struggled for several early chapters with different voices and different time zones. It was difficult to work out any coherent idea of who these people were and how they interconnected. Overall the story was a reasonable thriller but this early lack of clarity did, I think, affect my overall enjoyment. 
 Not that readers should get off too easily but I think Hawkins just made things too difficult and never quite redeemed herself in the end.
***3.5 Stars*** Excellent audio beach read!

I love books with really messed up characters and this book definitely has that, but at the same time, I felt like this book was trying really hard to be Gone Girl....Maybe I would have felt differently if I read this before Gone Girl, but it just couldn't live up completely to that comparison to me.

I can see why all the hype around this book, but I honestly hated every character. They were all a hot mess, everything was messy. Every character was off and fucked up... 
 The ending felt rushed. 
 It was an easy read tho, if thats what you care about.

Nope nope nope. Not for me. I didn't like any of the characters and there were several issues that hit WAAAAAY to close to home for me right now. I almost don't even want to go to book club to discuss this book. Yikes.

Hated everything about this book. The characters, the storyline, everything. I don't know why it's touted as being so "intense and gripping"- I frankly found it pretty dull and boring. I should have guessed when it was suggested for people who liked Gone Girl, since I think I liked that even less than this.
From the very first page I couldn't set this book down. I love how the story unfolded, how the truth slowly came out. Fantastic story.

Very rarely do I read one of those so called hot popular books and now I see why. It flopped in such a major way with me. I literally found absolutely no redeeming value in this book. From sappy boring to a painfully cliche' and sophomoric dialogue, I don't even see how "young adults" could find this story interesting. I can see that it was actually very well written. It's just that the story and the characters were too awful to contemplate.
I don't know, but first 10 pages I find it annoying already.

Really poor female characters that are mostly defined by the men in their lives. All points of view are unreliable because all women have issues, again, caused by the men in their lives. The unreliability of the main point of view, Rachel, is not caused by a crafted display of events that can be interpreted in different ways but because she is drunk. It becomes very easy to understand where the plot is going. Also women can only be friends if they are hating on the same man. It was a painful read, not expected of a summer best seller.

I like this book but I found the characters quite frustrating. I was reading this book thinking that most of the characters bought these problems on themselves and got what they deserved. Anna was just a nasty piece of work and so was Tom. Scott was an idiot and Megan was selfish. I think we are supposed to feel sorry for Rachel but I didn't. 
 The plot was good though and there were surprise endings which is why it gets such a high score. I did have a lot of unanswered questions at the end. If you get lost, follow the dates.

reference_books.title: Pushing the Limits (Pushing the Limits, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Entah kenapa buku ini sanggup menghasilkan banyak buzz daripada sekawanan lebah dalam sebuah sarang. #apeu 
 Kalau para tokohnya enggak saling ber-fanboying atau ber-fangirling satu sama lain, atau ngomongin soal seks, buat saya ini bacaan yang lumayan. Konfliknya cukup kompleks, dan bikin saya sadar kalau jadi remaja itu enggak gampang.

reference_books.title: Ready Player One
reference_books.review_text:
Ernest Cline 
 Ready Player One 
 Random House NY 
 374 pages 
 10.0 (Best Book) 
 Ernest Cline's debut, Ready Player One, is the most adventurous book that I have ever read. 
 Such claim from me is absolutely shocking, as you probably may have read from my reviews, it's rare for me to give glowing reviews--mostly because I'm not easily impressed. I'm sorry if I sound cocky. I really am--sorry, I mean, not cocky--I don't want to be conceited honestly; it's just that I am coded this way. Since I adopt 0-10 rating system, it's hard to crack the 9 score. An even 10.0 review is more elusive, and so far I only give it to this book. When I first read the book almost three years ago, I made a mental promise to myself to buy the book when I am financially capable. It needs three years for me to buy the hardcover edition, but it's all worth every rupiahs. On my second read, I am still in a complete awestruck. Ready Player One is the epitome of the embodiment of nerdiness and that's cool. Even Buzzfeed recommends it 
 In year 2044, when the world is in an ubershit condition where climate change, energy crisis, poverty keep gnawing the mother earth, every single human beings covet to escape the shit world to a massive virtual reality multiplayer game called OASIS, created by a genius game designer named James Halliday--no, not the wine judge. OASIS is like a sweet escape from a real world, where it has vast environment, beautifully rendered graphics, and anything. So when Halliday passes away, he creates an Herculean Easter egg hunting inside the OASIS. The winner of the contest will inherit all Halliday's wealth and properties of OASIS--it's billion dollars. Of course, people all over the world go batshit crazy. But after five years of no progress in solving the first clue, all the hype dies down. Until our main character, Wade Watts, is able to crack the clue, and gets the first of three keys he needs to get the Easter egg. But, he can't live in leisure. He must race against an evil corporate to get the egg, an evil corporate who wants to commercialize OASIS and ruin the ideology that James built around the game. 
 I am a geek.... I guess. I mean not that kind of geek--who plays D&D (Flash news: I've never played D&D), or watches all Star Wars movies or reads not only all the canon comics, but also not canon ones. I am just simply not cool. Of course, I grow up playing games--I first know Nintendo when I am in kindergarten in 1999, almost a decade late where people have already moved on to PlayStation 2 that year. It's what makes me at least able to correlate with Wade--and Cline, particularly, because I feel like Ready Player One is the ultimate chimera of his. But I salute Cline because his gigantic idea to make such an ambitious book is warmly received. It's not a pioneer, though, because my friend recommends me Stephenson's Snow Crash--which I plan to read later--but Ready Player One is the one book that can penetrate the mainstream media, and people suddenly are drunk in their 80's nostalgia. His idea itself deserves a 10-star review. 
 Reading Ready Player One is a six-hour pilgrimage to the mecca for the nerds and geeks. Once Cline starts to babble geekly, he cannot stop and if you're not familiar with the reference he inserts, you may not be able to keep up. But, this is the place where Cline is having fun; Ready Player One is his playground. You can feel Cline's ecstatic squeal and exuberance when he writes this book. He's not a middle-aged white man in Ready Player One; he's a young kid who's elated after finishing a videogame; he's your best friend in playing games; he's my cousin whom I spend time together to beat Final Fantasy games with; he's your D&D buddies. Cline emphasizes that it's cool being a geek, and before you realize it, you will be taken to a nostalgic ambiance of OASIS, and you're twelve all over again. 
 I am seriously still in awestruck. Looking at the vast and imaginative worldbuilding churns my mind and I really want to be in part of OASIS. Cline makes his readers become a central part of his story--and in a way, Cline is like James Halliday himself, the man behind all of this awesomeness. I know I don't understand most of 80's references in the book. But, that doesn't stop me from enjoying the book. Cline proves that nerd is cool; geek is cool; you can be yourself and it is cool, and it feels really genuine in Ready Player One, unlike his next work, Armada, that feels insincere. 
 I was literally jumping up and down when I heard that Spielberg will direct the movie, and I have huge faith in him to make Ready Player One an apotheosis of pilgrimage to mecca of nerdiness and geekiness. I can't wait to see how he turns the picturesque world of OASIS into a screen. I can't wait to see how these lovable characters played by actors in the screen. I can't wait the world to feel what I feel; I can't wait the world to see what an amazing journey Ready Player One has been. But I must wait two years before it's released. The release date has been pushed back to March 2018 to avoid the competition with Star Wars Episode VIII in December 2017, its initial release date. Until that day, I will only be able to cherish Wade and his comrades' adventure in my heart.

reference_books.title: Enclave (Razorland, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Hello, my name is Deuce, and I am Kristen Stewart of the dystopian world 
 Saya sudah sering bilang kalau novel ini bener-bener gelap, kayak belum bayar tagihan listrik. Sebenarnya, secara konsep harusnya, sih, lebih gelap daripada The Maze Runner-nya Om Dashner, soalnya Enclave ini enggak ada happy-happy -nya (Saya bahkan enggak happy baca cerita ini juga) sama sekali, tapi kayaknya Mbak Aguirre kurang berhasil dalam mengolah cerita ini. 
 Waktu saya jelajah buku di Goodreads, premisnya lumayan menarik. Manusia di Enclave cuma bisa hidup paling banter 40 tahun, dan anak-anaknya baru dikasih nama kalo udah berumur 15 tahun, yang berarti dirasa cukup kuat karena bisa berumur sepanjang itu. Apalagi apa zombie Freak yang menggentayangi di luar barikade Enclave. (O, yeah, Mbak Aguirre, mau bilang Freak kek apa kek, mereka sama-sama zombie buat saya :v) 
 Jadi, si Deuce akhirnya mendapat nama Deuce di usianya yang kelima belas. Oh, iya, satu hal yang cukup saya sukai dari novel ini adalah pembagian kerjanya yang bagus, menurut saya. Jadi, di Enclave ini, orang-orangnya dibagi menjadi tiga kasta kerja: Breeder, yang kerjanya bikin anak dan merawat anak; Builder, yang kerjanya mengurus segala keperluan rumah tangga, kayak baju, makanan, dan lain-lain; dan Hunter, yang kerjanya keluyuran di luar Enclave, memburu hewan buruan, dan menjaga Enclave dari zombie Freak. Si Deuce ini sudah sejak lama ingin menjadi Hunter dan akhirnya keinginannya terkabul. Nah, sama si Silk, preman Enclave, Deuce ditugaskan menjadi partner dari Fade, cowok hawtie yang enggak hawt-hawt amat. Lagi pula, mereka, kan, lagi di dunia dystopia, pilihan cowok apa, sih, yang mereka punya? 
 Fade 
 Si Fade ini bukan cowok idaman mertua dan gemar membelot dari aturan dan sampai akhirnya mereka berdua mendapat hukuman untuk menyelidiki hilangnya Nassau, Enclave lainnya. Ternyata oh ternyata, Nassau ini udah dikuasai sama zombie Freak. 
 Dalam kembalinya mereka, Fade dan Deuce ini ketemu sama peninggalan dari Topside, dan sama Enclave bernama Burrower yang juga menyimpan banyak peninggalan berharga dari Topside. Deuce mendapat penghargaan setelah kembali dan hidup tenang, sampai akhirnya salah satu sahabatnya dituduh mencuri peninggalan berharga dan diancam untuk dibuang ke Topside. Fade dan Deuce membelanya, dan, mereka akhirnya yang dibuang ke Topside. 
 Dari tadi saya bilang Topside melulu, apa, sih, Topside? Jadi, begini. Di dunia Enclave ini, tokoh-tokoh yang disebut tadi ini hidup dalam sebuah terowongan bawah tanah dan Topside itu bahasa gampangnya adalah permukaan tanah. Nah, para tetua di Enclave College, enclave-nya Deuce dkk. ini percaya kalau di Topside enggak ada yang bisa hidup. World-building -nya sebenarnya bisa keren, sih, menurut saya, cuman agak enggak believable dan konsisten buat saya. Kayak, soal air bersih. Nah, di terowongan ini (kalau saya enggak salah tangkep) ada semacam pipa dan keran-keran air yang mengangkut air bersih. Lah, tapi di Topside air aja enggak nyala? Terus, itu air dari mana? w('A'w). Terus, Mbak Aguirre ini kayaknya kurang memperhatikan detail-detail kecil. Yang lumayan fail waktu si Fade dan Deuce keluar dari dalam tanah, dan matahari terbit untuk pertama kalinya. Maak, mereka bisa buta kalau cuma pakai kacamata hitam doang. Mereka udah bertahun-tahun ada di dalam terowongan. Kasusnya, agak-agak mirip sama City of Ember, tapi menurut saya, itu maklum, soalnya masyarakat Ember udah bisa lihat cahaya terang dari lampu. Nah, di Enclave ini orang-orangnya bahkan enggak kenal sentir, dan mereka udah berani menerjang matahari. Inget soal penambang di Chile yang berminggu-minggu terjebak di tambang? Katanya mereka benar-benar ditutupi matanya begitu berhasil dikeluarkan. 
 Yang bikin saya ngeluh ialah jalan ceritanya amburadul banget. Kayaknya semua adegan dipaksain muncul dalam cerita ini. Adegan Hunter yang saling bertarung, misalnya. Saya punya feeling kalau adegan itu dimasukin biar wow-novel-gue-keren-banget-ada-tarung-tarungnya. Masalahnya, itu adegan enggak ada efek-efeknya ke jalan cerita. Lah, orang ceritanya sendiri kebanyakan berlatar di Topside. Terus, waktu mereka ada di perpustakaan, terus si Stalker tahu-tahu ketemu sama mereka, terus tahu-tahu ada Freak dateng. Maaak, si Stalker ini apa, sih? Deddy Corbuzier? Kenapa dia bisa tahu di mana Fade, Deuce, dan Tegan berada? (Btw, Stalker ini nama orang). Lumayan banyak kok adegan-adegan random semacam itu. 
 Karakter-karakternya juga labil bangeeet. Ada alasan kenapa saya bilang si Deuce ini Kristen Stewart-nya dunia distopia. Karakternya lempeng banget. Waktu ada temennya yang mati, mukanya datar banget. Waktu dia diusir ke Topside, mukanya datar. Yah, walau dia bilang kalau dia pengen balik ke Enclave, saya yakin mukanya datar. Waktu ada serangan zombie, dia juga bermuka datar. Gaaah! Sangat menyebalkan! Si Fade ini karakternya semacam pengin jadi cowok cool , tapi gagal. Si Stalker ini yang awalnya memburu gerombolan Deuce, malah akhirnya bergabung sama Fade dan Deuce dan mendadak jadi baik, membantu mereka dalam journey to the north mereka. DAFUQ! 
 Alurnya juga cepat banget, dan timeline -nya lumayan panjang banget. Dalam novel yang menurut saya tipis, untuk ukuran distopian YA, saya yakin banget kalau udah sekitar setahun berlangsung dalam novel ini karena mereka harus menunggu musim dingin lewat (yeah, musim dingin!) selama berbulan-bulan sebelum melanjutkan perjalanan mereka. 
 Adegan yang bikin saya facepalm berjamaah itu waktu si Deuce pingsan dan bermimpi soal Silk, pelatihnya dulu di Enclave (yang saya bilangin preman Enclave itu), dan bilang kalau Enclave udah runtuh karena diserbu zombie . Alamaaak, kenapa jadi novel mistis begini? Saya yakin banget kalau Mbak Aguirre ini desperate buat gimana ngasih tahu keadaan Enclave sekarang? Padahal itu enggak perlu-perlu banget. Dan lagi, si Silk yang bilang ke Deuce kalau mereka harus menjaga api unggun supaya tetap menyala, saya langsung 
 Mak, si Silk jadi cenayang setelah dia mati? 
 Bukan cuma itu yang bikin saya kesel. Jadi, begini, Saudara-Saudara! Sama seperti kebanyakan novel distopia lainnya, pasti ada yang namanya pemberontak yang enggak puas sama aturan-aturan yang ada. Nah, di Enclave ini juga ada. Yang jadi masalah adalah kenapa mesti diceritakan soal pemberontak KALAU AKHIRNYA ENCLAVE INI RUNTUH GARA-GARA ZOMBIE FREAK JUGA? Sia-sia dong pemberontakan mereka -_- 
 Dan misteri terbesar yang ada ialah: 
 ZOMBIE FREAK ITU APA, SIH? MEREKA TUH DARI MANA? 
 Omong-omong saya punya hipotesis kalau zombie Freak itu adalah orang-orang yang terkena wabah . 
 Lagi pula, novel ini enggak punya tujuan global, berbeda dengan beberapa novel distopia lainnya. Ambil, contoh Matched yang isinya tak sebagus kovernya, menurut saya, yang punya tujuan global yakni menemukan si Ky (atau Xander?), jadi biar ada kelanjutan. Saya lupa :v. Nah, setelah saya cermati, Razorland ini enggak punya tujuan global. Serius, deh! Menggulingkan pemerintahan a la Hunger Games? Bukan! Mengubah sistem sosial macem Uglies? Juga bukan. Ini novel enggak ada hal-hal semacam itu dan membuat saya bertanya-tanya kenapa perlu ada sekuelnya? w('A'w) 
 Enggak. Saya enggak akan merekomendasikan novel ini buat jadi bacaan distopia asyik. Buat yang suka City of Ember, The Maze Runner, dan sedikit-sedikit The Walking Dead yang dijadiin satu dan dijejal-jejalin, silakan disimak novel ini!

reference_books.title: The Sword of Summer (Magnus Chase and the Gods of Asgard, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Rick Riordan 
 The Sword of Summer 
 Disney Hyperion 
 8.6 (Best New Book) 
 Riordan exactly knows how to spoil me. Making yet another story based on world myth? Check. A witty and hilarious protagonist with sardonic way of narration? Check. Endorsing Taylor Swift's 1989? Check check check. How the Hel (no pun intended) does Riordan know that I'm a closet case of being Swifties? 
 Riordan still uses his old formula and repeats it all over again, yet I keep buying his books and reading them like there's no tomorrow. Riordan's formula magically always works. I've never felt exhausted after reading Riordan's books, even though all the tropes he's used have been recycled over and over again like an old newspaper. 
 The Sword of Summer still follows typical Riordan-esque premise. A young juvenile who never realized that he's a son of Norse god, and his mother died. So, when Magnus Chase figured out that he's no ordinary teenage boy, his adventure began. He traveled around Nine Worlds, to finish a quest (yes, another quest), to stop a doomsday (yes, another doomsday). 
 See? You may have heard that kind of premise in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, The Heroes of Olympus, and heck The Kane Chronicles. You will find similar theme on The Magnus Chase. But, somehow, Riordan is such a trickster and he casts some kind of sorcery that I don't know of to make his books feel refreshing. 
 It's probably the characters, even though Magnus Chase is just like a carbon copy of Percy Jackson in terms of stupidity, ignorance, and humor. But, Magnus Chase is the hero that we can relate to. He's only your usual guy, you'll never look at him twice, but he's got some hidden power that you probably covet. You may sometimes envy him. Nevertheless, the formula once again works like a charm. Not only Magnus Chase, Riordan also creates a Muslim (?--with a question mark as I'm not sure if she's religious or not. Believing another god--let alone Norse gods can be considered as a blasphemous act, but I'll leave the details for now) girl character. I can say that Riordan's decision is--well--interesting. Especially when Riordan wittily connects Sam's Iranian ancestors with Norse settlements in Northern Europe. But, afterall Riordan is known with creating minority characters--we have Chinese-Canadian Frank Zhang and native Indian-American Piper McLean from Heroes of Olympus. I am fully aware that Riordan has personal mission to make his books can reach more people--not only a white privileged American teenager. 
 The remaining characters provide comic relief, and I never expect to find that a sword will be most hilarious and funny character in the book. Some of the laid-back gods are also funny, yet some of the creepy gods are eerily plain and boring. Yes, Hel, I'm looking at you. 
 I am brought up with Shin Megami Tensei games--Persona, Devil Survivors, Shin Megami Tensei itself--and Norse gods have become the important summon on those games. I know Loki, Thor, Skadi, Heimdall, Nidhoggr, Valkyrie, Surt, etc., but I've never bothered to learn the complete myth myself. Riordan probably knows my negligence and yes, he makes another rip-off of Norse myth so that ignorant people like me can learn and understand the Norse myth. The result is magnificent. Riordan forced me to open Wikipedia page, and read the complete story of the myth (I know, I know Wikipedia is not a complete source of learning Norse myth, but at least it's been summarized and well-indexed). I can say that Norse myth is really fascinating. Not only it is the only myth in the world where the gods will kill each other, the concept of Nine Worlds dangling in a super-giant Tree of Life, Yggdrasil, is incredibly well-thought. I should give credit to Norse people. 
 Well, after I read my review above, it seems that I don't write anything useful. It's just a pointless rambling about the books, it has no point. But, well, it's my habit that comes whenever I review Riordan's books. I will be squealing, fan-boying, and shouting just because it fulfills my guilty pleasure. Riordan's books will get a perfect score on "My-Good-Guilty-Pleasure-Books" list. It doesn't provide something new, unless you count making story based on Norse myth is new. But, Riordan has proven once again that he's a master at twisting and crafting the words, making The Sword of Summer fresh, and somewhat bearable and not cringe-worthy. 
 Oh, and yeah, I'm not kidding about Taylor Swift's 1989 endorsement.

reference_books.title: On Chesil Beach
reference_books.review_text:
Ian McEwan 
 On Chesil Beach 
 Jonathan Cape 
 166 pages 
 4.5 
 On Chesil Beach is literary torture technique that is created to test your attention span and patience. 
 When you venture around the boundless world called world-wide-web, you can check some of the books that will be adapted to movies this year and you'll see another work from the author of Atonement, Ian McEwan. On Chesil Beach, from every side, looks very Oscar bait-y, and if that isn't any indication that this particular work is worth reading, it's a Man Booker Prize shortlist. It should be good, no? Or at least beautiful? 
 Well, an opinion of a goodness of a book is indeed arguable, but a book's enjoyability is universal, and On Chesil Beach is painful to read. The main plot is basically is a just struggle between a newly-wed couple to have sex, the groom is wrapped with lustful passion, while the bride still figures out if she's ready to do it or not. As McEwan picturesquely and explicitly describes the process of undressing woman's clothes, the plot seems to go nowhere. While it's pleasant--the only pleasant thing in the book--to read the scrupulous words that McEwan used to paint the background of these two polarizing characters, the whole book is just plotless. Like the head of Janus, the book oversees past and future events interchangeably, but this feels pointless. It's filled with long and overstretched paragraphs. It reminds me of Gilead, but Robinson's work is visceral; it makes you feel something. On Chesil Beach, on the other hand, will only give you pain. 
 The book may not fulfill what most of people expect, and if you are kind of people who must read the book before watching the movie, then I'm begging your life for once in your lifetime you should disobey your rule. You will save some of your precious time.

reference_books.title: We Were Liars
reference_books.review_text:
I can totally see why people praised this book. The writing style is unique, and the twist is really twisted. 
 But I also can totally see why people hated this book. The writing style is unique, and the purple prose is nauseating. 
 I actually kind of enjoying this, but yeah I agree that the writing style is... annoying, to say the least. It confused the hell out of me. For example, 
 We have been here before. 
 Also, we haven't been before. 
 Or something like that, I don't remember it at all. How can't you be confused with writing like that? So, which one is true? I scratched my head... a lot... that my shoulders are full of dandruff because of it. 
 Even so, as I said before, the twist is really good, and I didn't see it coming. It feels unfair, though, since the clues are placed on the middle-end of the book. The plot is actually not that shallow, but I agree that this could be summed up with three words: White-people-problems. Fighting for inheritance, the kids are sick of their parents, they rebelled, et cetera. But, the Sinclair kids at least stood for their ideas. The Sinclairs learned from them. 
 So, if you can stand the way this book is written, I guess you can enjoy this book.

book_a.title: The Catcher in the Rye
book_a.user_review:
J.D. Salinger 
 The Catcher in the Rye 
 LIttle, Brown and Company 
 214 pages 
 8.3 (Best Book) 
 For me, a good book is supposed to make you feel something, and usually I only feel either sadness or happiness when I finish a good one. I only feel anger when I read bad book that frustrates me with badly written plot and hateable character. The Catcher in the Rye is contradictory. At one place, I really hate Holden Caulfield, but I cannot lie. The Catcher in the Rye is an amazing book. 
 Written from the first point of view of Holden, The Catcher in the Rye tells Holden's three-day experience in New York streets after he's expelled from his posh boarding school. He sees the world with such cynicism that any other character in the literary world ever has, seeing the bad in everything. During his adventure, he spends night in fancy hotel, dates his old girlfriend, engages with prostitute, has an encounter with a gay man, drinks booze, and almost dies of hypothermia. He recalls his adventure with vivid, yet jumpy description, from an institution in California, one year after it happens. 
 The book is full of symbolism. Holden's aspiration to become a catcher in the rye, for example, symbolizes his contempt for adulthood, that he's sick of adult people and wants to remain innocent, proving that Holden is naive. Despite all the adventure that he endures, in the end of the book, when he wants to fall to the cliff of adulthood, his sister becomes the his catcher instead, preventing Holden from losing his naivety. Holden's point of view in seeing this comfortless world which runs by phonies also represents the teenagers' dissatisfaction toward every single thing and their lack of trust and faith in the future. For some of us, being rebellious is just a phase and when we reach the maturity, it will all be gone, but for some others, our lack of faith is still there and it makes us worry about the future. 
 As much as you hate Holden and want to strangle him to death at some point when you read the book, you cannot deny that he is iconic. With his red hunting hat, incessant waft of cigarette smoke coming out from his mouth, and his inexorable unexpurgated train of thoughts, Holden represents the rebellious teenager and the spirit of freedom of an adolescence. Yet, he's hateable. He's a misogynistic and homophobic jerk who complains about mostly everything. The only quality that may redeem him is his love for his little sister. Some of us may not be able to relate to Holden--including me--and see Holden as a ranting and ungrateful bastard. For someone who should be an icon for rebellion, Holden seems so passive. While some the other teenagers out there have fought for their rights and do something real, Holden relentlessly bitches around, criticizing everything and doing nothing. Ironically, doesn't this what most of us do? We rarely walk the talk, and choose to criticize everything. The Catcher in the Rye slaps us really hard. Like it or not, we are the embodiment of modern Holden.

sample_reviews.review_text: Quite possibly I'm missing the point of the book, but whether I like a book or not depends a lot on whether I like the main characters and, in this case, I couldn't stand the kid: I found him irritating and whinny. I do wonder if this book would be regarded the same way had the main character been a woman.

The Catcher in the Rye I picked up this book for the Eclectic Reader Challenge and it ended up doing double duty as a read for a module on censorship and banning in a lit class I am taking this semester. It is one of those "Life List" books that I never read in high school but felt like I should. 
 The novel is a Holden Caulfield's narrative of two days that he spends on his own in New York City. He has been expelled from yet another prep school, failing every subject but one. After a fight with his roommate, he leaves school a few days early and goes back to New York City. However, he knows that his parents will be furious about what happened and he chooses to spend a few days alone in a hotel before presenting himself at home for the holidays. His two-day rebellion is spent going to nightclubs and getting drunk or wandering the city, continually bemoaning the lack of intellectual companionship. He has a date with Sally, a girl from his past, and alternately falls in love with her and hates her... all on the same date. He is a boy who is clearly never satisfied with anyone or anything, continually in a state of discontent. His short time of rebellion has brought him no answers and no relief. 
 I really wanted to love this book, or at least appreciate it, but I just couldn't. It wasn't the dated language or ideas, but the complete lack of a character arc for Holden. With most protagonists, there is a certain arc of growth that takes place as the character goes through different experiences and situations and becomes changed as a person by the story's end. This really didn't happen with Holden and that lack of character growth is something that I came to realize I really appreciate in a novel and really missed in this one. Holden is intelligent, but comes across as a bit arrogant, perhaps a little too obsessed with himself as a barometer of intellect. For most of the book, Holden dismisses others as "phony" and casts aspersions on their worth if they don't live up to the personal standards he expects, standards that generally seem not to apply to himself. Instead of relating to Holden's character, I found myself continually annoyed by him and his seemingly complete lack of self-awareness. There was just no growth for Holden over the course of the novel, no change in behavior or thinking, no development. Other than his little sister, Holden seems to struggle to truly connect with anyone on any level. He spends most of the book whining about the fact that pretty much every person he meets is unintelligent and/or phony. He sees himself as intellectually superior to most people, judging others as phony for their interest in things he sees as inconsequential. 
 There is also much about his burgeoning sexuality and how that manifests itself, but there is never any development or resolution to that theme either. It seems as if he is not entirely comfortable with his own sexual awakening, often commenting about his myriad of chances to lose his virginity that are foiled by himself. He often objectifies women, but it is also clear that there is little behind it, more of an effort to fit in with the other guys in his school, rather than an accurate representation of his true feelings. This is seen in his almost obsessive anger towards his roommate when he finds out that Stradlater's date is Jane, a girl from Holden's past. He cannot stand the idea that Stradlater, a guy with a somewhat sketchy sexual history with women, would be with Jane, whom Holden seems to see as some sort of "above it all" standard of perfection. His thoughts on sexuality seem to be rather disjointed, one moment bemoaning his lack of experience and the next almost frightened by it. He does not push the issue with his dates and even during an encounter with a prostitute, he rebuffs the idea of intimacy, instead wanting simply to talk. In keeping with his rather disjointed ideas are his judgments on others' sexuality, often seeing others "perverted." There are also many moments when he questions the sexual orientation of those around him, showing a certain discomfort with the entire topic of sexuality. 
 In some ways, though, iit was an interesting read. The story is told as it flows from Holden's mind, at times very much of a stream of consciousness feel to it. The flow was often a bit disjointed and almost reminded me of the flow of Anthony Swofford's Jarhead book. But it is through this perspective and style of writing that we become privvy to the inner workings of Holden's mind. Yet, as the story unfolded, I still liked it less and less. 
 My Recommendation 
 Classic literature or not, it just didn't appeal to me. But I also think that is a matter of "to each his own." From a analytical standpoint, it was an interesting read, but it just didnt touch me in any way.
I do not understand the point of this book. Did not enjoy it but very pleased I persevered to finish.

I do not and probably wont ever understand what makes this such an American classic. I don't even know why they teach it in schools because you can't even learn a lesson other than "Gosh nobody likes an over-dramatic spoiled brat who thinks they have the worst life ever." Start: 5 stars (awesome voice) 
 1/4: 4 stars (questionable content) 
 1/2: 3 stars (more questionable content) 
 3/4: 2 stars (is this going anywhere?) 
 Done: 1 star (fell flat) 
 But I'll up it to 2 because I did enjoy the book there for a little bit. 
 Pros: 
 1. When I started this book, I was excited by the strong, new voice. This author knew his character. You could tell right off the bat, that this kid had a personality and opinions. I loved it. I read quite a bit and you get used to the same kind of voice for characters. It's refreshing to come into something like this. 
 2. An unreliable narrator is always fun to read. It becomes a game of wits between the author and the reader. (Now, I know nothing about the author or even whether he wrote anything else, but that's my opinion in general about unreliable narrators, the game of wits.) I enjoyed reading between the lines, trying to figure out what was really going on. What was wrong with the kid? Why did he say he wasn't in the mood to call the girl when he clearly wanted to? I loved analyzing the character and coming up with my own theories about the reasons for his behaviour. 
 3. The representation of teen angst, inner conflict and confusion was spot-on. 
 BEWARE: if your teen years sucked, you should probably steer clear of this if you don't want to be reminded of all those crappy feelings. 
 4. Your heart bleeds for the kid, since you can tell he is suffering and is stuck in a loop of self-sabotage. 
 Cons: 
 1. Cussing. Lots and lots of cussing. 
 2. Lots of blasphemy. Beware. HATED it. 
 3. No real plot. 
 4. Unfortunately, no character growth. When you give me a character like this, a character with issues, you had better show me how he is learning to overcome them. There wasn't much overcoming, but rather quite a bit of wallowing and immature behaviour. 
 5. Really dark themes. And by 'dark themes' I don't mean cool-enchanted-forest-that-kills-people dark. I'm talking seedy bars, womanizers, hookers, vomit, pedophiles, lies, banal jokes, etc. 
 6. Leaves a bad taste. 
 7. Frustrating. After a while you think: kid, just talk to someone. But the rambling and judgments and irresponsibility just continues forever. 
 8. What an ending. Here's the book in a nutshell: A teen is troubled and ends up in a psyche ward. A year later he still feels pretty much the same. 
 For the life of me, I cannot see how this was allowed in schools. I would strictly recommend this to 18+, except in special circumstances, where the reader is mature and responsible, otherwise it might mess up a messed up kid more. 
 I can see why some people might relate to this book, but I can't see that it will do them much good to read it, other than to know that they are not alone. It's a negative story with no real lessons learned, sadly.

There is all this unspoken pressure when one reads a classic, I mean it's a classic for a reason obviously. Which means you either like it as the rest of the masses do, or you don't and you wonder if you have missed out on some major facet that appeals to those capable of understanding. So, without further ado and at risk of sounding like an uncomrephending fool I just did not love this novel. Perhaps the whole meaning was over my head but I saw a plotless tale of a cynical young man who hates all things, including himself (all though he hasn't caught onto that last part yet). It promotes nothing positive, drinking, smoking, failing, running away and foul language. The best part is, if this book was written in modern day with that kind of language people would LOSE IT, but since this is a classic it is not only tolerated it is enjoyed. 
 Perhaps it is just the modern day way of life, I live in an age where it's common to eat your breakfast, chat with someone directly in front of you whilst you scroll your latest news feed and think about what color to paint your toes all at the same time. I mean wow, look at what authors are up against these days, new books are pow pow pow all the way through, and they have to be. If they are not the reader deserts within the first few pages. He did not follow the social norms and it could be amusing. Plus there was a thing or two to learn from his all consuming hypocritical hatred for people who do and say the same things he himself did and said. 
 I'm glad I read it, I must have missed the ship though because I'll certainly never put it on a favorites list or read it again. I gave it two stars only because out of context I really love these quotes! 
 "Among other things, you'll find that you're not the first person who was ever confused and frightened and even sickened by human behavior. Happily, some of them kept records of their troubles. You'll learn from them--if you want to. Just as someday, if you have something to offer, someone will learn something from you.  "What really knocks me out is a book that, when you're all done reading it, you wish the author that wrote it was a terrific friend of yours and you could call him up on the phone whenever you felt like it. That doesn't happen much, though."

All book reviews I write are spoiler-free! 
 Rating: 4/5 stars 
 Blood Red Road is the first book in the Dust Lands trilogy. This was a strong start to the trilogy. 
 Before I say anything else, let me first warn you that this book does not use quotation marks. Yes, there's no quotation marks to discern speech - I think the purpose of this is to symbolize the main character's lack of education. In addition to the lack of quotation marks, the characters have accents and to further emphasize their rural upbringings. I got used to this about halfway through the story, but it's something to keep in mind before going into the book. 
 Saba is the protagonist - she's tough, capable, and unapologetic. I absolutely loved her tenacity and unwavering mindset. Her physical and mental strength may have been unrealistic at points, but that arguably made parts of the book even more fun to read. 
 There's an emphasis on family in this book. It made me yearn for strong sibling relationships myself after feeling the family love and struggles vicariously through the characters. Whether or not you have any siblings that you're close to, you'll feel the despair, frustration, and limitless love that comes with the territory of having siblings. 
 You can find my full review here!

DNF at 178 pages. I don't really know what it was about this book that made me stop. I was enjoying it all right at first. I didn't mind Saba's speech or the lack of quotation marks like some people did. But I eventually got to a certain part in the story where certain details just kind of broke my suspension of disbelief, and I couldn't really get past that. Specifically, it was learning that a king rules this violent world by controlling production of the drug chall and who, in his madness, kills 18 year old boys born during full moons so that he can live longer. I don't know why, but that just ended the story for me. I have too much to read to try and plow through something that's not keeping my attention. So, moving on.

Although the cover didn't appeal to me at all, I saw some strong reviews of "Blood Red Road" comparing it to The Hunger Games and The Road that made me want to chance it. Sorry to say that it didn't come close to either of these books for me. Without a doubt, the voice is strong; Saba is a narrator I can hear, and the prose is a notch or two above par. The plot moves very quickly, with characters fighting and changing locations, if only to provide motion. 
 However, I didn't find enough meat here. All of the characters are thin to the point of transparency. The aforementioned plot rushed past crucial moments that deserved more attention. Life-and-death situations arrive abruptly and then pass just as quickly. Storms, car(sail boat?) crashes, gladiatorial games all come and go far too quickly, leaving me wondering why Young bothered with them to begin with. 
 This isn't a bad book, just so-so. I may read on as other books come out, but I'd still recommend The Knife of Never Letting Go in a heart beat over this one.

This book took me a little bit to get used to as the story is told by Suba who in a post-apocalyptic world doesn't have a strong education. There is no quotation marks and the speech is all in slang. After you get over that the story seems to have a lot of potential but it doesn't quite reach it. It is like a photographer who lines up a beautiful shot but leaves the focus on manual rather than auto and ends up with a blurry shot. You know there is something good there but it doesn't quite come to the surface.

Blood Red Road is an incredibly fast paced book, and it begs to be read in one sitting. There's a lot of symbolism piled up in the story, and it's easy to latch onto. The world Young's created is believable, and it's easy to picture, as well. It's desolate and deserted and red. It feels a bit like a story that could be set in the Great Depression, but it's futuristic, rather than historical. 
 Young writes in a dialect. It's not standard English, and some of the words dropped aren't necessarily in English either. Unlike many books written in a dialect, the use of it in Young's book is well-placed. It really gives a strong character to both the setting and to the protagonist, and it enhances our knowledge of who she is and what makes her such a powerful character. As a reader, I had no problem diving into it, and even found myself believing it made the story read faster. I think if it had been done without the dialect, much of the story would be lost. Likewise, I had no problems with the lack of punctuation in dialog, as it made the story read more naturally. Teens and adults will certainly have no problem with this, either. 
 Blood Red Road had every element for a good story, and it doesn't disappoint! It was gritty, full of battles hard won, but the end will leave you smiling!

This was an okay effort. It had some interesting elements and the world-building was decent. My biggest gripe is how many unbelievable circumstances the author threw in. I mean, Saba lives in the middle of nowhere with her brother and father, right? But on the journey to recover her kidnapped brother, she becomes some sort of bloodthirsty, unstoppable gladiator? Where did she learn to fight so well? There is no mention of her being trained at the beginning of the book (not that I remember anyway). She would have been killed in her first or second fight had this book had any sort of authenticity. 
 My second big gripe was the chemistry between Saba and Jack. There was none. That's about all I can say.

A frustratingly uninteresting heroine, cheesy and confounding relationships, and action that is either bazaar or omitted. 
 Blood Red Road tells the tale of 18 year old Saba who sets out to rescue her kidnapped twin brother Lugh, with their 9 year old sister trailing in tow. Saba narrates and the book is presented as though she wrote it... this means the author didn't use quotation marks and did a find and replace on various words to make it appear less literate (figured is "figgered" and stomach is "stummick"). 
 The setting is post apocalyptic with no explanation. There's a tamed crow. And a love interest pops into the story. And Mad Max cage fights, without any weapons. 
 My first gripe is Saba. Her primary abilities are dimwitedness, violent rages, and emotional dysfunction. She is the least intelligent character in the book, outdone by her 9 year old sister and drugged out criminals every other page (not to mention the other characters her age... who are all comparative geniuses). 
 Second, this book is filled with horribly cliched and goofy movie tropes. The teaser reviews clearly state the movie rights have already been purchased, no doubt for harrowing scenes like this: heroine and crew are about to be attacked by overwhelming odds: "We stare at each other a split second. Then, at the ezzack same time, we yell, Run!". 
 Third, the action scenes are usually tepid and poorly described. Saba enters a series of cage fights... we are given a basic description of one contest... chapter break... "One month later"... Saba has apparently won a crapload of these battles and the story is going to move on. Before you can start to argue that the book values the emotional struggle and may have intentionally avoided describing physical conflicts let me note that Saba will eventually fight a 30 foot tall worm monster in hand to wormy-bit combat. 
 Reread the Hunger Games (loved them!) or check out the Wool series (which will scratch your Post Apocalyptic itch). Blood Red Road did nothing but irritate me from beginning to end.
