reference_books.title: Unwind (Unwind, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
"Would you rather die, or be unwound?" 
 Plot Summary: In a futuristic dystopia, parents of rebellious teenagers have the choice to unwind their children, thereby nullifying the threat they might pose to society. Unwinding is a socially accepted practice and is not legally considered murder because the individual will live on in a "divided state." The story follows the paths of three unwinds from disparate backgrounds: Connor, a rebel with a short temper; Risa, an orphan and talented pianist; and Lev, a tithe who willingly offers himself to be unwound in the name of God. 
 MicroReview: If you can suspend your disbelief at the novel's premise and slog through the opening chapters, you will be rewarded with a satisfying payoff and some interesting food for thought. 
 The Lows 
 Bland Opening: With the exception of the car accident scene wherein the three characters first intersect, the majority of the novel's opening features amateurish writing and almost cartoonish plot devices. The school scene felt especially embarrassing for some reason. I was ready to put the book down a third of the way through, but I became intrigued by The Graveyard and I'm glad I stuck around. 
 Lack of Backstory: Even later in the series, Connor's "troubled youth" phase is not described in a way that convinces me of his past temper. It's all very vague, with the examples being "he got into fights at school" or something equally boring and uncomplicated. If this were a movie, I'd want it to open with Connor duking it out with some guy--give me action, not reaction. His later character development would also feel more meaningful if the reader had seen his initial state before he went AWOL and matured as part of his experiences. 
 Undeveloped Friendship: In the Graveyard, Connor and Lev act like they've been bros all along, but in reality they spent very little time with one another. I would have liked to see more group bonding time in the beginning. 
 The Highs 
 Real-Life Connections: You know what, I'm actually convinced that unwinding is a plausible concept. My first instinct is to question it mercilessly: "Hogwash! The United States would never do something so convoluted and immoral." But as human beings, we do stupid, illogical, morally corrupt things all the time without questioning them. Banning gay marriage. Ruining teenagers' lives for trivial offenses like streaking at football games or conducting foolish but relatively harmless science experiments. The inclusion of actual news article clippings about the selling of organs on the black market lends a sense of believability to the idea of unwinding. 
 Cool Setting: An airplane graveyard, you say? Hellz yeah. In addition, one of the best scenes takes place in the packing crates when the unwinds are being transported to their new safe house. They discuss things they dare not speak of otherwise, from the state of the soul after unwinding to the nature of death. 
 Tithes, Storks, and Clappers: I love that Shusterman doesn't shy away from the religious implications of unwinding but rather embraces them in a convincing way. At first, I thought that storks (abandoned babies) and clappers (terrorists with explosive blood) were a bit cheesy, as all made-up terms tend to feel at first, but I gradually warmed up to them and came to appreciate how Shusterman incorporated them into the main plot. 
 Awesome Climax: The exciting ending more than made up for the unpromising opening. The reader even gets to witness the unwinding experience, and there's a good twist in the resolution as well. This really feels like a standalone novel, which makes for a satisfying read. 
 The Bottom Line: I'm already working my way through the sequels because others seem to recommend them.

reference_books.title: The Lost Gate (Mither Mages, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I honestly didn't want to read The Lost Gate, given the mediocre reviews, but I was desperate to find an available audiobook and eager to finally read my first Orson Scott Card novel, despite his anti-LGBTQ leanings. The afterword by the author about the writing of the book was the best part. It was interesting to me that the idea kernel for this book took 33 years to pop into a full-fledged work. But I think this one should've stayed in the expired ideas pile. 
 By the way, this book is not appropriate for young children, despite what the plot synopsis, character ages, and writing style may suggest. 
 The Highs 
 Gate Magery: The magic system was awesome. Period. Portals are an inherently fun concept. The premise of the story is also fairly attention-grabbing: The gate between Earth and the land of Gods (Westil) has been hidden for centuries, making it impossible for the mages left in the human world to return home. There is an intense rivalry between the different mage families, and to prevent war, the groups have promised to rid themselves of unfair advantages. Thus, any person who shows signs of gatemagery must be killed to ensure that no family can return to Westil and strengthen their powers. 
 Wad's Story: I was confused by the alternating perspective at first because I thought that it was a flash-forward sequence for Danny. On the third POV shift, I finally realized the story was that of a completely different character, Wad. His story truly begins when the king and queen come into the picture, as that's when things get really interesting. As other reviewers have noted, Wad's story was by far more engaging and felt more believable than Danny's, with its royal drama, betrayals, and secrets. 
 Unpredictability: I'm not sure if this should be labeled a pro or a con. Maybe I'm just trying to come up with positive qualities so that this review doesn't seem too scathing. The plot takes many unexpected turns, but more in a "well that's fucking random" kind of way rather than a "wow, the plot is morphing into something bigger" direction. 
 The Lows 
 Inconsistent Protagonist: I don't mind unlikable characters, but if someone's personality is all over the place, I can't get a sense of who they are. At first, Danny seems like the bookish underdog, but he quickly becomes an expert liar who feels no remorse for the consequences. He is at times portrayed as highly intelligent and noble, but we only see those traits when it's convenient to the plot. 
 Key Characters Arrive Too Late: We never really get to know Danny's new guardians or the Greek girl. Eric is the one we see the most, and yet his character is inconsequential to the larger plot (although he arguably contributes to Danny's character arc). 
 Setting: This may have been the book's biggest problem. The story mainly takes place in ordinary locales, and it didn't work for me at all. With so many cool avenues to take with the gate magic concept, the story moves in ridiculous directions instead. Danny uses his powers to shoplift from Walmart, pass toilet paper through a stall, and...go to high school? 
 The fantastical storybook tone in the first chapter differs wildly from the rest of the book, which was disappointing, but I should've known to expect it based on what other reviewers have said. I wish that Danny had been less knowledgeable about the human world; I would've preferred a fish-out-of-water story, where human culture is completely alien to Danny. With that approach, there would be all sorts of opportunities for humorous misunderstandings and interesting conflicts. 
 Lack of Cool Factor: The action scenes felt forced and require great suspension of disbelief, most notably when Danny finds a family tied up in their basement as well as when he and Eric confront the black market dealers . The revelatory moment and climax occur in a high school gym class. Quite frankly, those parts of the story reek of amateur writing, and I'm surprised to see that from a Hugo Award winner. 
 Passive Plot: External factors drive much of the plot, mainly by someone finding Danny and confronting him about his powers. Not much happens as a result of Danny's own volition. That type of structure made the plot feel random and disconnected. It seemed like Card was writing by the seat of his pants and went with the first ideas that came to him. As comedians know, the first idea is rarely the best one. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 Unfortunately, Card does not deliver on his interesting premise of a lost gate and awesome magery; it'll be a long time before I read another one of his novels.

reference_books.title: Career of Evil (Cormoran Strike, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I am in despair. My heart has been broken in the best way. I wish I could put the next book on pre-order right now. 
 With this third installment, the author has firmly established what the Cormoran Strike series is and is not. These are not Hollywood mysteries filled with mind-bending twists and explosive action sequences. Instead, the story tries to remain firmly rooted in realism, making the mundane aspects of private investigation work fascinating in their own right. The climactic reveals are not always as dramatic as one would hope, which is perhaps another way of maintaining the realism. However, every small conflict and small victory has its own quiet intensity that makes for a strangely addicting read. 
 Compelling Writing Style 
 The focus of the writing has much improved since The Cuckoo's Calling. There are fewer lengthy setting descriptions, although geography is still a big part of Galbraith's signature style. Street names and counties are featured heavily, making me wonder if this series is a love letter to the United Kingdom in some way. There is a more balanced mix of dialogue and action as well, and the people who are interviewed present more conflict, although it can still be difficult to keep track of everybody. 
 While the writing is often hyper-focused on the minutiae, I never felt bored. In fact, I anxiously looked forward to listening to more at every opportunity. Rarely do I listen to audiobooks without something productive to do (walking, cleaning, etc.), but I found myself just sitting and listening at times, wanting to finish the chapter. Much of my love for this book probably stems from the audiobook narration by Robert Glenister--he has such a talent for voicing the different characters and the tone of the dialogue. I think I might have enjoyed the first book more if I had consumed the audiobook version instead. 
 More Robin Please 
 Robin and Strike's dynamic is what carries this story more than the plot itself. As with The Silkworm, I had no idea what the premise was going in, and I much prefer it that way because everything comes as a surprise. The opening chapters of Career of Evil hooked me right away. I especially enjoyed the chapters told from the killer's perspective, where we get to see the world from his twisted lens. 
 We also learn more about Robin's past and her ambitions, turning her into a full-fledged, living, breathing person in my eyes. She proves to be an indispensable partner in crime, able to coax answers out of leads with her acting and people skills. She is emotional but strong in her resolve to do what is right and pursues her goals with a conviction and rashness that I admire. Admittedly, I may be a little in love with Robin, as I feel both of the main men in her life are undeserving of her attentions. 
 Exploring Important Social Issues 
 Sexual violence toward women is the pervading theme, which can be seen in both the main plot and the struggles of the minor characters. No matter the circumstances, each individual is portrayed with empathy rather than patronizing pity or scorn. Those who have suffered from abuse are victims, but they aren't always likable or helpless. They can't be saved by a kind word or the promise of rescue; they aren't the types to save themselves. 
 There is also a lot of discussion about Body Integrity Identity Disorder within the story, which is a controversial and thus fascinating topic. I remember learning about the disorder in high school health class and being shocked at the scope of human desire (like Robin, I pursued a degree in psychology). 
 A Lackluster Ending 
 As for the grand reveal, the killer's identity was disappointing in that he seems like the suspect we know the least about and is also the least interesting, as his personal connection to Strike is much weaker. I had also hoped that Robin would have more involvement in his unveiling. In addition, the plot point with the most build-up--the killer's confrontation with Robin--also played out differently than I expected. As mentioned before, I think the author was trying to avoid a Hollywoodized murder mystery in favor of a more subdued and realistic version of events. My expectation was that Robin would be kidnapped and have to escape the killer's lair, potentially with Strike helping to rescue her. I also thought that the killer might kidnap Robin's mom. 
 The ending left me with many questions about the characters' futures and much to look forward to. There will undoubtedly be more conflict with the police force and a potential court case; new clients for Strike's business; and the escalation of the elephant-in-the-room romantic tension between Robin and Strike. For a while, I thought the ending was going in an entirely different direction, which would've been heartbreaking but intriguing: Robin would go on to become a detective, competing or consulting with Strike on cases. Their relationship would have a sour dynamic until they softened toward each other again by the end of the next book...but becoming a detective takes at least five years, so that would be quite a time jump. 
 What Do The Characters Look Like? 
 Considering that the series is set in London, I'd suspect an all-British cast for any movie adaptations, but it's still fun to pick out celebrities that most resemble the characters. Strike is always described as a bit of an ugly bloke--large, hairy, and constantly smoking, not to mention the impact of sleep deprivation on his appearance. Despite his gruffness, he has a strange allure that entices even the most beautiful of women. After some contemplation, I think the best real-world correlate for Strike would be Russell Crowe or perhaps Sean Bean, although I wonder who the author had in mind while describing him. 
 As for Robin, it's hard for me to think of an actress who perfectly matches her in age and personality. Blake Lively has the height and perky attitude I associate with Robin, so she's my best approximation for now. 
 Bonus: Woody Harrelson as Shanker, who is an extra useful character this time around.

reference_books.title: Ready Player One
reference_books.review_text:
I'm not sure if I would've finished this one if I hadn't been reading it with my wife. The beginning has its ups and downs, but the '80s references were too grating and cheesy for a '90s kid like me. However, my wife declared it "the best book we've ever read together" and said it changed her perception of what she likes in a book, so obviously it has enough redeeming qualities to warrant a three-star rating (or perhaps a three and a half). 
 The Highs 
 Easter Egg Premise: In his will and testament, eccentric billionaire James Halliday promises his wealth to whomever unlocks the three gates he's created for an elaborate video game Easter Egg hunt. That sets up the story to be one of competition, mystery, action, and adventure. Well, theoretically. 
 Virtual Reality: I'm fascinated by virtual reality concept stories, and Cline explores the potential of this technology in really interesting ways. He notes its applications in the educational system, personal fitness, and, of course, entertainment. Doesn't playing the star of your favorite movie sound like a blast? 
 Admittedly, the OASIS pales in comparison to the VR world imagined in the anime Sword Art Online, which I consumed concurrently with Ready Player One, although I think Cline's version is much closer to how the system would actually play out, with the different themed planets. Also, one of my favorite books as a kid was Heir Apparent by Vivian Vande Velde, which focuses on a girl trapped in a virtual reality game, and every subsequent VR book I read is matched up to my enjoyment of that story. 
 Post-Apocalyptic Future: The OASIS is a way to escape the dismal reality of Earth. The environment is dying, the economy is at its lowest point, and the poorest of the poor live in the "stacks," skyscrapers made of trailer homes. Honestly, the parts set in the real world were more enjoyable than the ones set in the OASIS. It was also cool to see my hometown Columbus featured as the lair of an evil corporate conglomerate. 
 Art3mis: Wade and Art3mis's first meeting was one of my favorite scenes, and my wife loved the romance throughout. I liked Art3mis's nervous way of speaking and Wade's idolization of her, even if the rest of their relationship is summarized in a fast-forward fashion. 
 Side note about the other characters: The mystery of Aech's real-world identity made me more curious than the hunt for the egg (my theory was that he was actually Ogden Morrow ). Halliday seemed loosely based on Steve Jobs. Sorrento was a two-dimensional corporate villain, but that fits with the video game theme. Daito and Shoto seemed like Japanese caricatures designed by someone who has never actually met a real Japanese person before (addressing Americans with Japanese honorifics, mixing Japanese phrases with English on occasion, etc.), although I appreciate the inclusion of other nationalities. 
 The Lows 
 The '80s: Whenever my wife and I go to restaurant trivia nights, the host is inevitably some 40-something whose questions all pertain to '80s pop culture, and it annoys me like nothing else; I'm sure I'll feel the same sense of rose-colored nostalgia about the '90s and 2000s in a few decades' time. The references are probably fun if that's your era, so I'm obviously not the target audience for Ready Player One, since the story relies self-indulgently on the '80s conceit. 
 This story is for people who wish all their obscure '80s video game and movie trivia could serve some practical purpose and make them look badass in the eyes of society. Ready Player One is the epitome of "write the book you want to read," although in this case it's directed at a rather niche group. 
 Dumps on Dumps on Dumps: I didn't mind the exposition in the opening chapter, but even as the story goes on, the majority of plot information is delivered through Wade expounding on aspects of the OASIS or Halliday. For example, when Wade is attending school, there are no actual classroom scenes; it's just Wade going from room to room and telling the reader about the school system, his life, and the contest. The novel is almost framed like a pseudo-memoir, but the tone and presentation don't really match up. 
 Not only were there infodumps, but much of the information presented was redundant. We get a whole chapter on the life and times of James Halliday, even though most of that information appears in the previous chapters. 
 Lack of Foreshadowing: I wish the Easter egg hunt had been more interactive. As a reader, I want to play too! I expected it to be more like a murder mystery, where you can try to put together the clues yourself to guess at the killer. But in Ready Player One, there's no interactive element. How does a person figure out that a gum wrapper and the word "test" = the origami unicorn from Blade Runner?! Seriously. ). If you've ever done an escape room before, the puzzles in the room follow a logical coherence and an outside observer could connect the dots--that's what I wanted from this competition. 
 MacGuffins: The plot relies heavily on items that appear randomly early on and then later become integral to solving the conflict. I'm fine with Chekov's Guns (in fact, they're part of the reason I love Harry Potter), but that approach just didn't work for me in this story. As other reviewers have probably mentioned, it also doesn't make sense that IOI would conveniently keep footage of Daito's murder on their servers. You know, instead of erasing all the evidence . In addition, I was hoping for a big twist at the end and there almost was, but maybe that's being saved for a sequel. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 Ready Player One presents a fun concept, especially for '80s babies, that shouldn't be taken too seriously. Just don't ask questions and enjoy the ride. My wife and I are stoked for the movie, and I wish they were filming it in Columbus so we could be extras. 
 P.S. An audiobook read by Wil Wheaton, a movie adaptation directed by Steven Spielberg, and a real-life Easter egg contest with clues from the book for a DeLorean--sounds like a dream debut!

reference_books.title: The Girl on the Train
reference_books.review_text:
The Girl on the Train Drinking Game 
 Take a swig every time a character: 
 *	Uses a vague pronoun instead of someone's actual name 
 *	Ambiguously hints at some deep dark secret, like "I tell lies" or "No one knows" 
 *	Drinks alcohol 
 *	Drinks coffee 
 *	Rides the train 
 *	Describes sunlight or weather in general 
 *	Describes how shitty they slept 
 *	Repeats an observation they made a few pages ago 
 *	Makes the same exact observation another character made in a different perspective 
 *	Leads you to believe there's going to be a twist, but it turns out that things are exactly as they seem 
 Okay, I can see why so many people enjoyed this one. This was one of my before-sleep books that I read aloud to my wife. Fully expecting our minds to be blown because of the rave reviews, we had fun trying to guess at the characters' secrets (My personal crackpot theory was that Megan's brother Ben had faked his death and was her secret lover. The officer did ask Rachel if the kiss she'd witnessed had been "platonic," but I guess that was a red herring ). Still, there were too many annoyances for me to ignore. 
 For funsies, my wife and I decided to re-read the critical acclaim on the back of the book after we were finished to compare our expectations with reality. One mentions "unreliable narration." Eh, maybe there was some unreliability, but it wasn't strong enough to make me suspect anything interesting. One reviewer calls it a "propulsive narrative" and another says that it "roars along the pace of, well, a high-speed train." I think they just wanted an excuse to use train-related metaphors because this is not a fast-paced book. The plot doesn't pick up until around page 70 and even after that, it feels as suspenseful as trying to get a drink of water from a leaky faucet. 
 That was the worst and best part of this book: There was a distinct trend of the author building suspense, building mystery to the point where you're on the edge of your seat and you're at the top of that rollercoaster--but then you realize there's no drop. It just flatlines. The path is completely perpendicular. 
 The twist is that there are no twists! It's nearly genius. 
 Hawkins' novel does have the same vibe as Gone Girl, but I didn't read this expecting a clone. I wanted something new, something fresh. And, admittedly, The Girl on the Train was different. There are three first-person perspectives featuring women with similar relationship problems whose lives become interconnected. Initially, the comma-heavy writing style made it difficult to distinguish between each voice, but their personalities became more distinct over time. 
 Still, the characterization is limited to only one aspect of their lives; they have no other stray thoughts, relationships, concerns, or dreams, really. As far as I can tell, this book is about women who do nothing but sit around and mope about men. They're somehow vividly portrayed yet lacking in some crucial way. Perhaps this type of characterization is meant to make the narrative seem more focused and to demonstrate a key theme, which seems to be the boredom associated with domestic life. Hawkins certainly makes the reader feel the listlessness of alcoholism and the monotony of a mundane existence. That kind of immersive experience is difficult to achieve, and so for that, I applaud her. 
 The psychological aspects were also quite fascinating, particularly the motivations behind adultery, the craving for power. This was probably an intentional parallel, but certain characters were nearly identical, namely Anna/Megan were both cold-hearted nymphomaniacs and Tom/Scott were both abusive assholes. Also, Kamal was a really shitty, unrealistic therapist. Why does your patient know where you live? Why are you even remotely attracted to her when she's got some serious psychosis going on? Boundaries, man. Rachel, though. Rachel is my fave. 
 As for the grand reveal...Well, let me just say that evil villain speeches (especially ones that reveal zero new information) are one of my biggest pet peeves in fiction. Plus, it begs the question uh, why would you marry someone when you've never met their family? And I feel that I at least know my spouse well enough to sense whether or not they have sociopathic tendencies...or do I? 
 What frustrates me most is that Hawkins has great potential. The writing has a strong ambience, the characters are interesting, the emotions complex--but the story structure is just WHACK. 
 Still looking forward to the movie.

reference_books.title: Carve the Mark (Carve the Mark, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
"I am a Shotet. I am sharp as broken glass, and just as fragile. I tell lies better than I tell truths. I see all of the galaxy and never catch a glimpse of it." 
 In the universe of Carve the Mark, everyone receives a special ability from the colorful current that flows through space. For Cyra, this is the power to inflict pain; for Akos, it is the power to nullify the effects of the current. Certain individuals also have fates--prophecies about their role in future political shifts. 
 Because of his fate, Akos is kidnapped from his snow-covered home of Thuvhe and taken to the other side of the planet, to Shotet, a militant nation bent on conquering Thuvhe. Akos is forced to use his powers to nullify Cyra's pain, and Cyra is forced to kill traitors under order of Ryzek, her brother and leader of Shotet. Cyra and Akos' relationship blossoms as they give each other the courage to sow the seeds of rebellion. 
 Carve the Mark isn't as engrossing as Divergent, nor is it as mind-bogglingly frustrating as Allegiant. Roth presents a strong writing style, imaginative world-building, and likable protagonists. Although the plot lacks cohesion, and somehow the connection between the reader and characters feels tenuous, this book is undeserving of certain criticisms. 
 Sci-Fi or Fantasy? 
 I want to establish the fact that this book should be classified as fantasy, not sci-fi. Yeah, it takes place in space, but it doesn't much resemble our own universe or laws of physics. There are superpowers that are not humanly possible. Google defines sci-fi as "fiction based on imagined future scientific or technological advances and major social or environmental changes, frequently portraying space or time travel and life on other planets." Divergent is sci-fi by that definition, but this isn't. 
 The distinction doesn't really matter, but if you're scared off by the sci-fi label, don't be. Treat it like high fantasy. And if you're looking for a sci-fi read, I'm not sure this fits the bill. Personally, I prefer space fantasy to hard sci-fi because it makes the world-building more interesting. 
 Better Writing Than Most YA 
 I would never have guessed this was by the same author as Divergent if her name wasn't plastered on the cover. Not that the writing in Divergent was at all bad; it was just more action-oriented, whereas in Carve the Mark there is more focus on the details and emotions. Roth's writing has improved significantly, and it's hard to believe that's she's only 28! (Proceeds to weep about being 24 and unpublished) 
 "There was a hunger inside me, and there always had been. The hunger was stronger than pain, stronger than horror. It gnawed even after everything else inside me had given up. It was not hope; it did not soar; it slithered, clawed, and dragged, and it would not let me stop. 
 And when I finally named it, I found it was something very simple: the desire to live." 
 Side Note: I would have preferred Cyra's POV to be in third person. I suspect that Akos was once in first person as well, judging by the stray "I" in one of his chapters, but that his voice might've sounded too similar to Cyra's. 
 Kill 'Em with Kindness 
 Cyra and Akos are good people. Similar to Elias and Laia in An Ember in the Ashes, however, they are always the innocent victims and full of angst. I almost wanted them to have a darker side (like Cyra enjoying her kills, or Akos making the final selfish decision to save his brother). It's hard in YA to create characters that are both likable and interesting, as readers are quick to criticize protagonists whenever they are too cruel or make stupid mistakes. 
 I keep thinking of how intriguing Helene was from An Ember in the Ashes. In this book, the equivalent is Sifa, Akos' oracle mother who allows her family to suffer for the greater good. 
 Is it moral ambiguity in the protagonists that I'm craving? Less good vs. evil, and more gray vs. gray? Maybe that's one reason this book felt like three stars. 
 Villainous Villain Doing Villainy 
 Villains rarely interest me, and Ryzek is your garden-variety dictator. He's meant to be a slightly sympathetic character because of how his father tortured him as a child, thus he's not exactly two-dimensional. However, I would have liked him to actually care about Cyra or have a soft spot for someone else in his life. Vas would have been a more interesting villain (I even thought at one point that he might be in love with Cyra, which would have complicated their battle scene ), but his character was unfortunately underutilized. 
 Recipe for Romance 
 The teasing exchanges and lingering touches between Akos and Cyra were fun to read, but I'm not sure about the romantic chemistry. Rarely do I come across a couple that has me cheering them on out loud, and I've been trying to pinpoint why that is. Is there something about our storytelling culture that makes it difficult to feel chemistry between two people unless they're in a love-hate relationship? Jack and Rose from Titanic are one counterpoint. I'm sure a dozen others could be named. 
 Is it the lack of pining? The sitcom-level of delay it takes for the two leads to get together? That heightened, all-present tension--will they or won't they? I have no idea. Cyra and Akos seem to have a perfectly healthy relationship with how kind and understanding they are toward each other. It's not an unrealistic relationship at all, and they do have their arguments, which are always related to the plot. 
 World Built on Details 
 I've seen some gripes about the world-building. Did we read the same book? Not only do we have the different beliefs surrounding the current, the unique currentgifts (extracting memories, deconstructing items, etc.), but there are also hushflowers, the Shotet festival and sojourn, a visit to a water planet, mentions of larger Assembly politics, oracles, advanced medicine, foreign musical instruments, and various languages. Oh, and the tradition of carving marks after a kill that the book takes its title from. So I'm really not sure what else could have been shoved in there to convince people that there's a high degree of original world-building here. 
 Admittedly, the constant world-building sometimes felt like an attempt at shoehorning every cool thing possible into the story. Even so, the universe that Roth presents is colorful, well-developed, and easy to appreciate. 
 Herky-Jerky Pacing 
 This book didn't feel slow at all to me, but perhaps it's a matter of relativity, given that I'm currently reading The Obelisk Gate and it's one of the slowest books I've ever read. In fact, most adult fantasy novels move at the speed of molasses, but if you're more of a YA reader, then this book might feel slow to you. 
 After mentally outlining the events of each chapter, I found that a lot happens across a short time span, especially in terms of character development and the rebellion plot. However, there was a lack of flow--a lack of connectivity between events. I didn't feel much tension or build-up or expectation. My guess is that chunks of the story were cut out to speed up the pacing, leaving no scenes to bridge plot points. I would have preferred a plot built like a staircase, something interconnected that is always building upward. 
 The Ending 
 I truly expected Akos to sacrifice his life for Eijeh, only to find that Ryzek essentially traded bodies with Eijeh, thus Akos dies for a Noavek after all . Maybe that's being saved for book two because I doubt Roth would go with the obvious choice. I liked the last scene in the arena, although when you kill a character I don't know that well, I'm not going to care much . 
 The final twist with Cyra and her father was cliche, as if it was added in at the last minute to ensure that the book had some additional "gasp" moments. 
 Racism, Ableism, and Bullshit 
 I'm not sure that people understand the definition of these words anymore. The claims that this book is somehow offensive is WTF-inducing at best. Upon reading the book, you will find that not all Shotet characters (who are of mixed race) are categorized as evil or emotionless or whatever negative adjectives you wish to apply. In fact, the characters from Shotet are more fully developed and involved than those from Thuvhe. There's Cyra, obviously, along with Jorek and his family, the Shotet storyteller, and literally all of the other Shotet renegades. Who, I should point out, are trying to reclaim their own nation from a power-hungry dictator. 
 We also hear claims that Thuvhe once kidnapped Shotet children, which hints that Thuvhe is not the peaceful nation Akos remembers from his childhood. From a plot perspective, I agree that Roth could have elaborated more on the truth behind Thuvhe's morally reprehensible behavior. But are people implying that mixed race individuals can't ever be villains without an evil white counterpart, even if all the peripheral mixed raced characters are the "good guys"? 
 To say that other races can't be villains or have unlikable qualities or flaws contributes to marginalization. This is how we end up with grossly positive stereotypes like noble savages and token black friends--by not allowing these characters to have complexities and to be human. 
 As for the ableist accusations and finding strength in chronic pain, just because a character's experience doesn't perfectly align with your personal experience doesn't make it any less true. One of the most positive people I know is someone who has been hospitalized for most of his life. I'm sure there are other people who relate to that, including Roth's friends, her inspiration for Cyra's characters. In addition, there's no doubt in my mind that Roth would have been similarly excoriated if Cyra lacked character development and agency because her chronic pain was only labelled as a curse (and Cyra does consider her "gift" to be a curse for pretty much the whole novel). 
 Why is anyone trying to delegitimize someone else's experience by claiming it to be "problematic" or "false"? That is like saying you need to meet certain criteria in order to call yourself black or bisexual or a woman. The fact that people are making generalizations about entire populations based on one depiction is hypocritical. Would you make generalizations about romantic relationships based on Twilight? Or about gay men based on the actions of Milo Yiannopoulos? 
 Just because a book doesn't align with your personal experience doesn't mean it doesn't speak to someone else's. We need more positive representations of minority groups in literature, and if readers are going to condemn any well-intentioned work that attempts to be empathetic and genuine (and the authors did their research), then I don't see many writers wanting to climb that hill in the future. 
 The Bottom Line: 
 While I'm not interested in reading the sequel to this series, I would pick up whatever Roth's next project may be.

reference_books.title: Not a Drop to Drink (Not a Drop to Drink, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Micro Review: A quiet survival tale about finding human connection during a time of self-preservation--a refreshing albeit slow-to-rise take on dystopian fiction. If you're expecting an "overthrow the government" plotline or battles between factions a la The Walking Dead or The Hunger Games, you will be thoroughly disappointed. 
 The Highs 
 + Realism: The dreary atmosphere and Lynn's simple way of life were an immersive experience. The author definitely convinced me that she'd done her research on hypothetical survival scenarios, though I can't vouch for the factual accuracy of anything. 
 + Dialogue: McGinnis has an ear for human speech, and I was especially impressed by how easily I could differentiate the characters based on their mannerisms. 
 + Humor: Lynn's naivety about the ways of the modern world (i.e., sex) makes for some interesting exchanges. Despite the bleak setting, the novel is filled with lighthearted moments that feel genuine. 
 + Romance: Unlike a lot of YA fiction, this novel features a well-portrayed and authentic relationship. They had chemistry, and I liked that they came from different backgrounds. 
 The Lows 
 + Repetition: Characters often have circular conversations or must inform other characters of what they know, which may be necessary for the plot, but it's boring for me as a reader. As are descriptions of the weather, no matter how important climate conditions are to the protagonist. 
 + Slow Pacing: The flipside of realism is that it can make for some low-intensity conflict, such as finding ways to preserve meat. The story focuses on the more mundane aspects of survival, which I did appreciate. Still, I initially expected that there'd be constant tension between Lynn and those attempting to overthrow her lake and that she'd eventually be forced to leave her farm. The novel was actually more about Lynn learning to develop meaningful relationships. I wasn't disappointed at the actual events per se, but I do think the novel has a slower pacing than its book jacket or opening chapters suggest. 
 + Unsatisfying Ending: So there was an action-packed climax, but Lynn's emotional responses to the novel's most intense moments did not have enough of an impact. Certain significant moments felt underplayed. 
 The Bottom Line 
 Although I'm not interested in reading the companion novel In a Handful of Dust, I wouldn't hesitate to try Ms. McGinnis's future works.

reference_books.title: Hidden Bodies (You, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book could have been so much better than it was. 
 I was hoping that the different pieces of the plot would collide spectacularly at the end, but instead it was as if the writer had just gone with the flow and done no plotting whatsoever. I wanted to see Joe rise to true Hollywood fame and have that fame create closer scrutiny of his past. I wanted Amy to impact the plot in a more significant way than just causing Joe to move to Los Angeles. I wanted the investigations into Beck and Peach to affect the story sooner. The story just seemed...improvised. 
 Joe's narrative voice saves the story, but it's not enough to make up for a plot that repeats the same events over and over, in different skins. In addition, Joe is a more passive character in this book than the first one; things happen to him, instead of him making active choices. There were a few scenes toward the end that were great, although Joe's serial killer plans often seemed unrealistic rather than clever. I did enjoy the characterization of minor players in the story, though; Kepnes has a talent for picking out telling details. 
 Despite the lack of suspense in Hidden Bodies, I'd definitely read another book by Kepnes, even if it's a third installment in the world of Joe.

reference_books.title: The Painted Veil
reference_books.review_text:
"Some of us look for the Way in opium and some in God, some of us in whiskey and some in love. It is all the same Way and it leads nowhither." 
 Because of the audiobook, I mistakenly thought the publication date for this novel was 2006. During the end credits, the narrator announced that the original copyright date was 1925, which makes much more sense given the themes of female independence and the romantic writing style. 
 For the first chapter or two, I felt a little lost, but I quickly got sucked into the drama of Kitty's life. Desperate to marry before her sister, Kitty accepts the proposal of bacteriologist Walter Fane, a reserved-but-dignified man who is very much in love with her. She does not return his ardor, however, and has an affair with another man. The incident leads to Kitty and Walter traveling to China in the midst of a cholera epidemic. 
 As the focal character, Kitty proves herself to be not only shallow and judgmental, but also impulsive, emotional, and surprisingly self-aware. She fascinates me in the same way as Blanche from Tennessee William's A Streetcar Named Desire. I expected her to undergo a transformation by the end of the story, and she did, but not quite in the way I expected (mainly, I thought that Kitty would grow to genuinely love Walter ). In fact, what happened in the third act came very much as a surprise to me, but even with its sudden end, the story somehow tied together all the threads of Kitty's life. 
 Walter is an easy character to sympathize with, and his combined qualities of brilliance, snobbery, coldness, and passion all coalesce to create a complex figure. Charlie, Kitty's lover, is perhaps one of the best villains I've ever encountered; his sociopathic charisma makes it clear why Kitty fell for him. The conversations between Kitty and Charlie made me stand in the middle of the room with my headphones in, doing nothing else, so intent was I on focusing on their repartee. And then there's Waddington, an affable man Kitty meets in China, who is of course the most likable character of them all. 
 Reading the two poems alluded to in this book enhanced my reading experience, one of them being Percy Shelley's sonnet, the other "An Elegy on the Death of a Mad Dog", which plays a crucial role in the story. 
 I look forward to watching the movie adaptation and reading more of Maugham's works!

reference_books.title: My Horizontal Life: A Collection of One-Night Stands
reference_books.review_text:
To preface this review, I have seen at most two episodes of Chelsea Lately, and I tried listening to her standup after I read this memoir, but the material overlaps far too much. Also, I'm not the type to laugh out loud; I just sit with the book in hand and a stoic expression, while inside I'm going, "That's so funny." I'm officially Julie from Scrubs. 
 MicroReview: As a sitcom-esque series of one-night stands, My Horizontal Life will definitely offend most sensibilities, but if you have a high threshold for crude comedy, you might enjoy reading this, even if you've never heard of Chelsea Handler. 
 The Highs 
 Consumable: Each chapter is a short, self-contained story that makes it easy to pick up again after a few days or weeks of not reading. 
 Interesting Details: Handler knows how to pinpoint the most interesting features and flaws of a person. For example: "Turtle was more laid-back than the Dalai Lama...He fixed bikes at the gas station for the summer, and he definitely didn't go to college. He had a vocabulary that could battle my six-year-old nephew's." 
 Strong Narrative Voice: I felt like I was inside her head at times. She's straightforward and doesn't try to make excuses for her behavior (conversely, that means there's little introspection). She retells her sexcapades with a shrugging indifference, except toward the end, where she has a moment of self-reflection and wonders if she should change her flippant lifestyle. It's unclear whether Handler feels this way because society (and the reader) expects that of her or because she genuinely believes she should change. 
 I realize that this book is almost a decade old, so there's that lingering "where-are-they-now" curiosity. In a 2014 interview, Handler stated that she's not "the marrying kind," and it's just interesting to see that comparison. 
 The Lows 
 Pop Culture Allusions: Too many for my taste, mostly because I have to Google every other so-and-so. Dylan McDermott? Harvey Fierstein? 
 Mean-Spirited Humor: Her jibes are targeted at specific individuals and involve shallow, soul-crushing comments about their appearances or perceived intelligence. To be fair, there is a touch of self-deprecating humor throughout and rare glimmers of humanity, but I wouldn't be surprised if Handler had been one of those brutal schoolyard bullies as a child. 
 Supports Stereotypes: This is to be expected from any type of comedy, but Handler frequently reinforces common societal expectations for men, which kind of sucks; I sympathize with all small-penised, hairless, toupee-wearing poets everywhere (clearly, I don't fit into any of those categories). These stories would be equally--if not more--off-putting if written from a male perspective. However, I bet reviewers would be significantly more outraged at the objectification of women than of men. 
 Questionable Morality: I don't mean the promiscuity (really, what kind of person would read a book about one-night stands and get upset over that?), but rather the driving while under the influence of ecstasy; collecting unemployment while being paid under the table; and trying to trick a roommate into losing her virginity to a male hooker. That sort of thing. Shit, man. I'm hoping some parts were exaggerated. 
 The Bottom Line 
 Handler isn't the most likable narrator, but the clever writing style and unfamiliar experiences made this worth reading.

 Probably the thing that bugs me the most about A Wrinkle in Time is this feeling: 
 That, published in 1967 when divorces were becoming more popular, the book seems like it could be speaking to kids whose experience is separated parents. But is the book helping those kids face the real issues of a single-parent household, a community full of malicious gossip, and a father who's never coming home? No. It encourages them to slip into some fantasy where Dad didn't really leave Mom; no, he's on a top-secret mission to a foreign planet. I can just picture my dad, whose own dad left his mom in 1961, reading this book as an 8-year-old and the feelings he might have had about it. A Wrinkle in Time is like The Brady Bunch: it wants to address the issue of separated parents, but it just doesn't. At all. 
 This book doesn't address much other than good vs. evil and what it's like to be a misunderstood genius. And of course the all prevailing power of love.

Very CS Lewis 
 L'engle's writing felt...silky almost. The words flowed beautifully around her unique characters.

It's probably telling about Ms. L'Engle's own moral beliefs that she can't imagine anything worse than people bouncing balls in sync. Especially since people actually die in her stories. Whether her fear of similarity but lack of objection to murder reflects her own lack of morality or just a deep immersion in her own clumsy message is hard to say. Does the book get bogged down under the weight of it's incessant pushing of christianity and it's constant, rather cartoonish depictions of bad anti-communist propaganda? No question. Would the book have been better without it? Hard to say. If it hadn't been a thinly disguised sales pamphlet, it almost certainly would not have achieved "classic" status. It was those very features which allowed schools to feel good about talking it up and encouraging young people to read it. The thinking went "If it rambles on constantly about the evils of communism while trying to shove christianity down the young reader's throat, what could be wrong with it?" Poor thinking, but pretty common in all historical periods. Besides, if you take away the heavy-handedness, I'm just not sure what's left of the story to try to save. It's sort of all there is to the story. 
 One of the things that is interesting when re-reading the so-called "childhood classics" when an adult is that you begin to realize how little of anything was about a story and how it almost always boils down to religious and/or political propaganda. This is both. The point, it seems, is to actually manipulate people into believing in a very real way that being similar is far, far worse than, say, people starving to death. What's remarkable is how often it works. Take a look around at modern society and you will see endless commentary on how socialism is evil but almost none of why it's not morally acceptable to let people starve to death. Trump doesn't talk about how there are starving people who need help, he talks about how "big government is evil." That's the meme that people buy largely because of propaganda like this being inserted into their brains when they are too young to notice that they are being asked to get rid of any real sense of morality and to replace it with a kind of obsession with anything-is-fine-as-long-as-it's-not-socialism. Of course, almost none of those people can tell you what socialism is. 
 To be clear, I'm certain that if I had been raised in a socialist nation, I would find that their "children's classics" all seem to confirm that worldview and condemn any other. It's not a question of whether one side's propaganda is right and the others' wrong. I'm not advocating any view here. I'm just pointing out that it's pretty hard to find a decent story that's taught anywhere up through the high school years that isn't dripping with propaganda and that it is really impossible to separate the fact that people end up believing the same things advocated by these books from the fact that people in positions of authority (teachers and parents) made them read manipulative books that aimed at tricking people into exactly these beliefs. 
 Despite having radically different actual meanings in many cases, books like 1984, Fahrenheit 451, Animal Farm, The Chronicles of Narnia, The Giver, and this one are all used routinely to indoctrinate children into a certain mindset. What's profoundly interesting is that people will often express exactly the views they are told in these types of works to express but deny firmly that they have been manipulated at all. 
 People do the same thing with religion, don't they? People will swear on a stack of bibles that their religion is the real true actually true one and that all others are lies or misunderstandings, but convince themselves that there is just some small coincidental relationship between the fact that they just happen to have a religion that matches their parents and/or community growing up. What unites people is that they all deny that connection's true impact. The belief that 'my belief is true and that everyone else may have been tricked but not me' is far more universal than the beliefs themselves. What does that say about us? 
 As for the book, does it count as the coup de grace that eventually, as always seems to be the case with these things, it is not the angels ("Mrs. Whatsit" & co.) who do the actual fighting themselves? As usual with political and religious dogma, it always ends up being someone else who has to make the real sacrifices. Bin Laden himself would never don a bomb and blow himself up. Naturally, some other, more gullible fool must be found. I guess that sums up the book.

How did I manage to go my whole childhood without reading this? This is the weekend for catching up on youth fiction, apparently. I will admit that halfway through, when the main characters are on the planet, Camazotz, I couldn't help but by reminded of The Giver by Lois Lowery. The perfectly, orderly world with the surprisingly sinister governing force was central to both novels (I should know, I read The Giver this weekend), but Lowery was writing in the 1990s, some thirty years after Madeleine L'Engle published A Wrinkle in Time. Maybe Lowery was a subconscious copycat--or maybe authors are just fascinated with human relationships and the differences that define them. I suspect it is the later. *WARNING: SPOILER AHEAD* On Camazotz, IT (also known as "The Black Thing" and "The Darkness" or just "evil") says, "Differences create problems" (L'Engle 140), but the children eventually win by embracing their own differences and using each of their strengths and talents. One comment that stuck out as somewhat true was IT's claim that the people of earth get confused and unhappy because "they all live their own, separate, individual lives" (L'Engle 142). While individualism is not necessarily a bad thing, it is only by having strong relationships with each other--feelings, attachment, and loyalty--that the children overcome evil with good, with love. Charles is saved by his sister's love; Aunt Beast's caring love saves Meg, and so on. Relationships that celebrate individualism are key to defeating the darkness in this story. 
 I was pleasantly surprised by the peppering of Scripture throughout the text (turns out L'Engle is Catholic). It never felt forced and always fit the situation. The interpretation of the verses might perhaps be considered slightly blasphemous, but only by those who see The Chronicles of Narnia as blasphemous for C.S. Lewis' handling of the Gospel story. 
 Overall, this book is one that every child should read and, if you missed it in childhood, it makes for a lovely Sunday afternoon novel that passes quickly at only 211 pages (large print). It is too suspenseful (inasmuch as a child's book can be) to be a "feel good" novel, but most readers will feel good--if only just relieved for the triumph of the children--at the end. 
 "A great book should leave you with many experiences, and slightly exhausted at the end. You live several lives while reading." - William Styron

This is a hard review to write because A Wrinkle in Time is a children's book, but my adult brain keeps getting in the way. 
 I vaguely remember a teacher reading this book to my class when I was very young. It must not have had a huge impact on me because all I remembered about it were the three annoying witches who abandon some children on a dystopian planet. I guess child-me wasn't impressed with this story. 
 Here's a real summary: Meg's father is a scientist who disappeared years ago while studying time travel. The family has not given up hope that he will come home. One day, three mysterious women turn up in Meg's neighborhood and tell the family that the "tesseract"--the scientific phenomenon that Meg's father had been studying--is real. Meg's father is trapped on a distant planet. It's up to Meg, her brother Charles Wallace, and her friend Calvin to save him. This book was first published in 1962. 
 There is so much in this novel that I either missed as a child or forgot. I think this book is read in schools because it covers a wide range of subjects: science, math, language, history, philosophy, and religion. The child characters are extremely intelligent and not ashamed of their intelligence. They are most definitely nerds. Meg is an average-looking girl who loves math and has some anger problems. Charles Wallace uses big words and easily understands complicated concepts, but he's arrogant. I think it's helpful for real children to see fictional children who have a variety of strengths and weaknesses. 
 This book is a fun space-travel adventure story, but after I finished it, I started to feel irritated. It took me a while to figure out why. I think it's because everything in this book is oversimplified. 
 I'm aware that this story is a product of the Cold War, and many people consider it a Christian book that conforms to a Christian worldview, but I have issues with labels like "Good" and "Evil." I don't think the universe is that simple. In the book, there is a villain called IT. IT has turned a planet full of people into cartoonish communist robots. The only explanation that's given for IT's behavior is "IT's evil." That bothers me. Even children's books should have complex villains with believable motives. I have no idea what's motivating IT to create communist robots. 
 The villain isn't the only thing that bothers me about this novel. The educational aspects of the book are so heavy-handed that I think many children would be turned off by them. They disrupt the plot and start to feel like a school lecture. The story also doesn't have much internal logic. It never explains why an adult can't save Meg's father or why the witch/angel/alien ladies can't give Meg and her friends more help. Finally, I'm not sure what purpose Calvin serves in the story. All he does is hold Meg's hand whenever she gets hysterical. I often forgot that he was even in the book. 
 So, obviously this isn't my favorite children's novel, but I'm going to read the next one in the series. I think the next book was published about 10 years after this one, so I'm interested to see if it's different.

book_b.title: Strange the Dreamer (Strange the Dreamer, #1)
book_b.user_review:
This book contains all of Laini Taylor's favorite things: gods, monsters, angels, cake, kissing, clashes between species, and the humanization of murderers. The plot is wholly original, centering on a mysterious city with a dark history that still haunts its people. The protagonist, Lazlo Strange, is a pure-hearted and curious lover of stories, while his love interest is a goddess with incredible powers who is tired of the cycle of hatred and revenge that exists in the world. They are fairytale characters, more myth than real, and their romance becomes the story's focus, much like Kaoru and Akiva's was in Daughter of Smoke & Bone. As expected, the writing style is lush, flavorful, and on the verge of cloying. It's a treat not often tasted in fantasy fiction. 
 The vague prologue and deluge of fantasy terms in the first chunk of the book made it difficult to ground myself in the story, but after the initial learning curve, I was excited to uncover the mysteries of Weep. Taylor gradually unfurls layers of backstory, with each question leading to another question. The world-building was top-notch, although I would have appreciated a thesaurus or illustrations for the fantastical creatures. There were plenty of minor characters, and some were better developed than others. Drave's antagonistic role felt a bit deus ex machina, and Thyron Nero needed to be more prominent throughout. Overall, though, the folklore and landscape were a joy to explore. 
 I went into this novel assuming it was a standalone, so toward the end I kept asking myself, "How is she going to wrap this all up in twenty pages?" The TO BE CONTINUED ending makes this feel like a TV show season finale, with questions left unanswered and the plot shifting toward something different, perhaps bigger. In addition, I get the feeling that DOSB and Strange the Dreamer take place in the same universe; I'm sure someone else has already posited this theory. 
 So, if you're a Laini Taylor fan, this is without a doubt a must-read.

Having found myself rather disappointed by my brief forays into the Young Adult genre, I decided to find the people who had read the most teen books and discover what they viewed as the best of the best. The name Laini Taylor kept popping up, and this book was pointed to as "gorgeous", with flowery language and beautiful characters. 
 If this is what qualifies as flowery writing, I sure don't want to see dull writing. 
 For the first 100 pages, this novel hits the right rhythm; we feel that the story is progressing while Taylor still maintains the everyday rhythm of life. Try "The Westing Game" or "Watership Down" for a mastery of this style. Lazlo as a character is perfectly likeable, but suffers from Protagonist-itis; i.e. "The Luke Skywalker Syndrome". He's boring. He does all the necessary heroic things, but there's no edge to this character, there's no subtleties. He's just a good person, with no immediate flaws, and nothing much to learn. 
 We get an intriguing blend of mystery and story, but the cracks soon appear. We're introduced to a set of half-human children who act like regular 14-year-old modern teenagers. We're thrown lots of unnecessary detail about the creatures of this world. We're given dozens of made-up names. We're given dull, dull, dull prose. 
 I mean, some of the writing is just ugly . She'll introduce some interesting concept, then immediately ruin it. 
 And so the dreamer and the goddess went shopping for a moon. 
 Okay, fine so far. 
 It was like something out of a story. Well, it was like something out of a dream. 
 There, she's just ruined the atmosphere. This is basic show-don't-tell stuff. If you're going to try to create an otherworldly atmosphere, don't break the moon-shopping excursion with, "Well, it was like something out of a dream." 
 Some of the book sounds like a teenage girl's diary. 
 He really, really, really wanted to kiss her 
 Are you kidding me? 
 Taylor soon does what I was fearing. She drops one-hundred pages of soppy romance straight onto her promising plot and drowns the (quite interesting!) ethical dillema in a thick soup of sentimentality. I have no problem with romance, as long as it isn't presented as rainbows and butterflies and kisses, "EVERYTHING IS PERFECT" romance, and this is exactly what I feared. These characters have no problems together, they just fall in love on first sight. It's an unrealistic romance that once again sends the message to readers that 'true love' is all about bliss and has no work or sacrifice involved. Ultimately, it's just cheap. 
 At about page 460, she realizes all of a sudden that she needs a climax. There are many explosions. 
 So the writing. Everyone talked about how beautiful it was, saying it was too metaphorical for some readers! I just didn't see it. Mostly it was just plain old, "He did, she said, there was..." stuff. Occasionally she'd try out a simile or metaphor, but there was nothing to stir the imagination, nothing to provoke wonder. 
 Beautiful writing is not sappy writing. This, "I think you're a fairy tale. I think you're magical, and brave, and exquisite. And I hope you'll let me be in your story." isn't beautiful writing. Throwing abstract similes like, blue as five murders waiting to happen is just incoherent. When I hear about beautiful metaphorical writing, I'm thinking about maybe something out of Peake. 
 The crumbling castle, looming among the mists, exhaled the season, and every cold stone breathed it out. The tortured trees by the dark lake burned and dripped, their leaves snatched by the wind were whirled in wild circles through the towers. The clouds mouldered as they lay coiled, or shifted themselves uneasily upon the stone skyfield, sending up wreathes that drifted through the turrets and swarmed up hidden walls. 
 or maybe Proust! 
 But sometimes illumination comes to our rescue at the very moment when all seems lost; we have knocked at every door and they open on nothing until, at last, we stumble unconsciously against the only one through which we can enter the kingdom we have sought in vain a hundred years - and it opens. 
 Is it unfair to compare Laini Taylor to Proust or Peake? Sure, of course it is. But this book obviously tried at times to reach some level of metaphorical resonance and descriptive ecstasy. Why water it down? Why not go full out? Why not reach for the skies? 
 And here's the main reason I disliked the book; it was drowning in potential. The characters were there, the plot was there, the setting was there...but the execution fell short. Still, it covered the bases, and it wasn't boring, so I'll give her that. I'll read the sequel when it comes out, and hope that it does a better job exploring the places this story could go.

I really loved this book. How can you not like a fantasy that contains good versus evil, angels and demons, gods and goddesses, mythical places, a cursed city with a problem to solve, adventure, a love story, and whose main character is a librarian with a strange past and the power to control his dreams. Laini Taylor is an amazing story teller. I love her vivid descriptions. I loved it in her Daughter of Smoke and Bone series and I loved it equally as well here. I could visualize the entire scene in my mind even though it is a complete fantasy. I enjoyed these characters and the way their story unraveled a little at a time. I thought there were points where there was a little too much info which caused a lull in the story, and at other points it felt a little rushed, but overall the pace is fast and even though it is a long book, it is a fast read. I wasn't really expecting to like it this much because I am not a mythology/fantasy kind of reader, but this story is very well-written. There will be another book in this series, but it wraps up at an interesting point. There are still a lot of unanswered questions, but it is not a cliff hanger. It left me really wanting to know what happens, but not frustrated with the wait.

i have many things to say about this book, but at the same time i'm finding it rather difficult to put into words. i read strange the dreamer twice. the first time, i dnfed it around 50% (idk if others would count this as a first read seeing as i didn't finish it, but i do). the second time, i made it right to the end. i don't think i've read a book that i both liked and hated at the same time. 
 my favourite thing about this book was the beautiful writing style. it was just so poetic. everything flowed nicely and there was loads of vivid imagery. the world building was very well presented, but i often felt a little confused. it was as if i was reading the story from a distance, rather than being immersed in it. 
 the first time i read strange the dreamer, i was so bored and confused. nearly nothing happened. i found the characters really bland and boring. i primarily dnfed it because of the confusion, but i think that's more because i read it while on a car trip and therefore not solely focusing on the story. 
 the second time i read it was much better. there was still some confusion, but not nearly as much as the first time around. i still felt detached from the story and the characters. again, i wanted to dnf and read something different, but i was determined to finish the book. i thought maybe my dislike was slump related, so i picked up the darkest minds series (which i absolutely loved) and realised it was the book itself. i've seen many reviews say that the second half is much better than the first, but it didn't pick up very much at all. 
 as for the characters, i wanted to like lazlo, i really did. he was a main character but it didn't feel that way. as a reader, i feel as if i didn't learn very much about him which made it hard to connect to him. 
 i found the other group of characters very random. their storyline didn't seem to fit or flow with the rest of the book. at first, i was extremely confused as to why we were being dumped into this other storyline with no warning or build up. i found their powers(/abilities?) quite interesting. 
 overall, if i didn't have such a beautiful arc i don't think i would've finished strange the dreamer. putting it in the simplest words possible: strange the dreamer is beautifully boring. i really enjoyed being able to talk with sarah about how i felt reading this book as it was so hard to put into words. based on this reading experience, i don't think i'll read the sequel, nor am i likely to pick up taylor's daughter of smoke and bone trilogy. 
 **FEB 17 REVIEW // first read through** 
 DNF just over 50%. 
 I found Strange the Dreamer extremely confusing and boring. I had no idea what was going on. I don't know who half the characters are as there's just so many and it flicks between the characters. I feel like I missed something. None of the characters are relatable (probably because I didn't know who was who). 
 I really liked the poetic writing style. There's plenty of worldbuilding, but it comes off a little info-dumpy. I think this book is for a certain type of reader, and unfortunately that's not me.

This would be a damn good book BUT THE EXPECTATION OF SACRIFICE PROMOTES FEMALE PAIN and I've decided I have to start rating books that are ok interesting and funny and part of a genre and story telling tradition that I love but that make me uncomfortable in my own body, below a 3

I have a lot of thoughts on this book - namely that the worldbuilding is as impeccable as in DoSaB, and I enjoy Lazlo and Sarai a lot on their own, but I wish they hadn't fallen in love with each other. It's a sweet story clearly destined for tragedy, but I'm just not as convinced of their enduring love as I was of, say, Karou and Akiva's. I would've been much happier if Sarai had fallen for Thyon Nero, or if Lazlo had (and where are all the queer people anyway?) - the innocent perfection of their romance feels a little Romeo and Juliet. However, the ending is a doozy, a cliffhanger of epic proportions, and there's no way things won't get more tangled and interesting in book 2. All in all a great read... I might still go reread DoSaB anyway.

My heart is broken :(, and I need book 2 now!!! What an amazing story!

I really enjoyed this! The writing is beautiful and poetic. I loved the unique worlds Taylor created and the overall concept was intriguing. However it did have some flaws... The first half was very slow and hard for me to get into. I also felt like there was too much filler and the plot jumped around. I wanted a little more character building and keys to our mystery. As much as I loved the "dreamy chapters" we spent so much time there that I felt a little disconnected from what was going on in real life. This book definitely focused more on the quixotic side of things and not so much on the main issues of the plot. I guess I was just hoping for a little more of that. There were some other things going on with side characters that I was really interested in that we didn't explore very much (hopefully will in the book(s) to come). The big issues our characters deal with really bring some great questions to ponder. While I struggled with the first half of the book, I really enjoyed most of the second. The ending was wonderful! I am excited about where the plot is going next and all the possibilities. Strange The Dreamer is definitely worth picking up and I can't wait for the next one.

While it took me a while to get into the book, once I was in, I was IN. I became completely lost Lazlo Strange's world. I didn't want to leave. Beautifully written with characters I want to follow forever. Even though the male protagonist is amazing and there are actually mostly male characters doing cool things (alchemy, explosions, godslaying) I don't think this book will appeal to guys...I could be wrong, frankly, I hope I am. I thought the story was awesome. At 500+ pages it's a commitment, so find a cozy spot and dig in.

****POSSIBLE SPOILERS**** 
 Well I will give the book 3.5 stars. I like that it had an interesting and unique storyline. 
 Usually the main character isn't my favorite but I really liked Lazlo. I of course adored Sarai and even psycho Minya. I really didnt care for the other 3 little "Gods." They were pointless in the story to me. 
 Im feeling a bit sorry for Lazlo right about now. I knew nothing good was gonna come from him asking for assistance from Minya. That little chick is crazy! I can just imagine all the nasty and wicked little things she's gonna make him do. Oh goodie!! lol. I am anxious to read the next book.

I wish I could give this book so many more stars. It deserves it. Laini Taylor deserves it. In fact, she deserves real stars and I wish I could give them to her. 
 This was everything I was expecting and more. This book made me cry and that has only happened a handful of times. I'm not even upset that I have to wait for the next one to come out because then I can have a reason to reread this beauty. (Like I even need one other than how great it is.) 
 I'm also proud to say that I am the proud owner of two copies of this book, the US and the UK version. 
 Please read this book. You won't regret it.

Reading this book feels like a hug. It really does. I don't know what to say; the world Laini Taylor has created here, the characters, the story, feel like magic. 
 I honestly think the best way to read this book is not knowing anything about it. You need to be able to see the world yourself, be surprised by the journey the book takes you on, without having any prior knowledge. Discovering the details as you read this book is part of the pleasure. 
 I long to see this world Laini has created. Her descriptions are so rich, so detailed, that the places just jump of the page. The characters are complex and exciting; they all bring a breath of fresh air to the novel and evoke emotions. I even felt sad for Minya. I hated her at times, my god I hated her, but I understood why she was the way she was. 
 A massive theme of this book for me was the line between good and evil, and whether such things exist. All too often in fantasies you have two sides, one clearly good, and one clearly evil. But in this book the line is blurred. Both sides have done terrible things, and you understand why each group feels the way they do about the other. 
 This was short, but I don't want to say anything more in case I spoil it. All I can say now is you need to read this book.

It has taken me a long time to write this because it seemed so daunting. I still don't know how to put my love for this book into words. The characters are wonderful - Sarai, Ruby, Lazlo, everyone - and their interactions and personalities and everything about them made me so happy. This world is lush, creative, vivid. This book sucked me in and wouldn't let me back out. Lazlo and Sarai's connection was one I loved reading and they made this book. Also, that ending. Holy crap. Laini Taylor has done it again.

Gorgeous book. I would say I actually want to rate it maybe a 3.5 or 3.75, but only because it was SO hard to get into the entire first half. The majority of the first half is just world-building and explaining Lazlo's past and it was just nearly impossible to connect to him because there was all this background and universe info going on and on. It was absolutely gorgeous, but until Sarai came onto the page and Lazlo started his travels, it was impossible to connect to the story in any real emotional way. 
 However, the second half is breathtaking. Sarai brings the story to life and their interactions were written beautifully. Now that I have a connection with the characters, I want to go back and reread the first half to see what I missed because I skimmed through some early parts. I would've preferred that we got to connect with those characters early in the story, but the quality of writing does make up for that. 
 I would highly recommend, but only if you can handle a story that begins VERY slowly.

2.5/5 Stars

Where do I even begin? I could not put the book down. The world the Taylor creates is vibrant and beautiful. Lazlo and Sarai are one of the sweetest couples in all the YA novels I have read. The ending broke my heart and now I must wait forever for the sequel!

"'You think good people can't hate?' she asked. 'You think good people don't kill?' Her breathing hitched, and she realized she'd crushed Lazlo's flower in her hand. She dropped the petals into the water. 'Good people do all the things bad people do, Lazlo. It's just that when they do them, they call it justice.'" 
 I can always depend on Laini Taylor to ruin my life with her books. It took me two weeks to read this, but I think that can mostly be attributed to the fact that I'm taking a very demanding library cataloging course right now that involves reading exceptionally long articles written in the early 20th century about catalog entry and metadata and so the slow and meandering development of this story was just not happening for me. Anyway, Mr. Strange is one of my new favorite book heroes, and I swear it's not just because he's a librarian and I'm biased. Lazlo is tender and devastatingly honest and so effortlessly GOOD and a hero that I don't think we've ever had before. And so, naturally, Taylor must CRUSH him. *sobs* I don't know if there is a character who could be as perfectly tragic as Lazlo, but if so, it's Sarai, with her moths and her empathy and her whimsy. The dream sequences were my favorite aspect of this book; so eloquently crafted and just utterly gorgeous. Weep is a mystery and an entire magical story unto itself which attests to Taylor's impeccable attention to detail and otherworldly creativity. If you read for action and epic pacing, you're probably not going to like Strange the Dreamer, but with its lyricism and beauty and heartfelt message, this story is a treasure. 
 ___________________________

Quite possibly the best book I have read in years... I am embarrassed to have given any other book a 5-star rating, because there is no rating system where this book wouldn't top them all. Lazlo and Sarai are ridiculously endearing, and I can't wait for 2018 for the sequel.

Yeah, feeling attracted in this case is kinda obvious but it felt too artificial here. Especially since we had a whole spectrum of the really nice and organic relationship. Thyon and Lazlo were my favourite thing and I was really dissapointed it wasn't developed further!

If you loved Laini Taylor's previous books, then you are going to love this one. She makes a world that is clever, interesting, full of people you'd love to meet and with interesting quirks. It has been a while since I read a YA fantasy book and it took me a bit to get into it at the beginning, despite the male lead being all kinds of wonderful and on top of that, a librarian. He is obsessed with finding out about the lost city of Weed, eventually he is offered the opportunity to travel there and discovers that there are good reasons why it is such a secret place. We also meet Sarai, one of the remaining few goddesses who have survived a terrible carnage which took place in Weed. There are ghosts, dream invaders in the form of beautiful moths, magic in many forms and flying machines made of plants. There is a lot going on, and it is beautifully described and very real sounding. The world within these pages is scary and gorgeous and I can see that it will have huge appeal to those who love a great YA fantasy.

Sadly, the sequel to this has already been titled "The Muse of Nightmares." I was rather hoping for, "It's Thyon's Turn Now, Bitches, and he's Back for Revenge After the Brutal Cleavage of His Character Arc."

WOW. This is the fantasy novel I have been waiting for! Every aspect was perfect and fully realized--the writing, the lush setting, the characters that drew you in, and of course the romance between the two main characters.
