Just wow..I finished it in the middle of the afternoon but only now did I find myself capable of thinking minimally straight cause this book left me in a complete mess...I felt rage, sadness, hope, happiness, and frustration all at the same time. I needed time to process and come to terms with everything before writing this. 
 This book was amazing, sure it might have been a little slow paced in the beginning but it was in a very interesting and absorbing way, never in a moment did I felt that what I was reading was irrelevant, cause every page was a possible clue to what was going to happen and what was the truth behind so many mysteries, and Laini Taylor still left a ton of them to follow! The development of the characters, the story behind them and their true self as well the relationship between each other, nothing of that was lacking in here. This was one of the few books that I found myself screaming at a certain character (Thyon Nero cough cough) for being such a brat and arrogate asshole, only to find myself after, understanding the reasons why they were like that, and sympathizing a little with him or her.

I don't recall a time before that I have felt so deeply a part of a fictional universe than I did as I read Laini Taylor's Strange the Dreamer. This book is for anyone who dreams, hides away in their imagination, and feels distaste for reality because of it's translucence. It's rare that I could feel at the same time a part of the story as well as a reader. With vivid descriptions and sensual passages that arouse the senses, Strange the Dreamer causes one to reflect on reading itself. As readers we are constantly reminded of the reasons why we are readers, why we daydream, and why we prefer the story world to the 'real' world. This book is a masterpiece of fantastical realism with a twist of romance which I feel will one day become a classic, earning it's spot alongside the Harry Potter and Twilight series. 
 Lazlo Strange is just as his name insinuates, strange. He is a war orphan whose birth and origins are unknown. He is brought up by a group of stale and dry monks in the city of Zosma. By age twenty is a junior librarian. He is infatuated with tails of Weep, or as he likes to call, the Unseen City. He is rarely seen without a book in his hand or his eyes elsewhere than hidden inside the ancient pages of books recounting the stories of Weep. He has spent seven of his youthful years studying this lost city and learning its language. It is not until the Godslayer comes to Zosma in search of assistants to help him give Weep back its sunlight that Lazlo's dreams may just become possible after all. Finally, this faraway land that Lazlo has met only in his dreams becomes something greater, perhaps even something greater than himself. What awaits him in the city remains a mystery and it is not until the moon glows in the sky, lays his head down to rest in the Godslayer's room, and loses himself in a lucid slumber that he discovers the truth shadowing over Weep. 
 We slowly learn the magnitude of the anathemas hiding within the city. Forces of magic, hatred, and sacrifice turned Weep, many years ago, into a city in despair, haunted by nightmares, spirits, and ghostly secrets. On the ground are the humans who suffer the memories of bloodshed and corruption left behind by the gods while up above, in a citadel hovering over the city are four young survivors, godspawn, as well as a number of ghosts tending to their needs. 
 As the novel progresses reality blurs into dreams and dreams become just as inescapably real as daylight itself. The dangers Lazlos confronts are both complex and enigmatically portrayed. There is so much imagery and eloquent descriptions describing Weep that I feel as though I could accurately paint a picture of the city without doing injustice towards Taylor's imagination. I felt myself immersed and becoming one with the story, sometimes perceiving the city from Lazlo's perspective, and sometimes from one of the godspawn's, Sarai's. It's always such a delight to fall into a story the way I did with Strange the Dreamer. When I read I lost touch with reality and, for the moment, only knew of Weep and the fictional world. 
 The romance that blossoms between Lazlo and Sarai is gentle and precious - two young people who are innocent in the games of love, but somehow immediately are aware that they are in love with each other. Sarai, or should we call her the 'Muse of Nightmares' meets Lazlo in his dreams. They begin a kindling romance that is confined to the moonlit hours, held together by moths, and ended when the sun rises and Sarai must return up above to the citadel until the following night. Together, Lazlo and Sarai share a power that could possibly put an end to what lies at the core of the city's collapse: hatred. Each dream of a time where the godspawn can live amongst the humans without being killed on site. All seems possible...in Lazlo's dreams. However, as the story progresses we soon realizes that while dreams and reality do overlap, they still remain invariably opposite from one another. 
 If there is one thing I am to criticize (but only briefly) about this novel is the complexity and effort that it takes to follow each and every vital situation. For example, Sarai lives in the citadel with three other godspawn: Minya, Sparrow, and Feral. Aside from the happenings down below concerning Lazlo and the Godslayer there's just as much conflict passing between these four. The novel alternating perspectives several time in order to account for what occurs in Lazlo's world and that which occurs in Sarai's. This is all fine and dandy, but at times I felt myself a bit lost and quite overwhelmed. There's a lot going on in this novel just concerning the mystery of Weep that I feel as though all the drama and chapters which zero-in on the lives of the godspawns was rather unnecessary and altogether distracting. But then again, that's only what my personal experience reading was like; I'm sure most readers loved the multi-faceted plot-twists with many stories blurring into others. 
 Lazlo was my absolute favorite character, and given that I'm an avid reader and round-the-clock daydreamer, it simple to see why. He lives vicariously through the stories he hears as well as the ones he tells. Through Lazlo's character Taylor wondrously illustrates how it is not simply the wise or most well off of men who succeed but those who think with their hearts and follow their dreams will discover. His infatuation with a city he only knows through myths leads him into a journey that will change his life beyond all logical reasoning, for, this book is not about rationality at all. It's about dreams and what happens when dreams become fused with reality. 
 Taylor's writing style is poetic, but lengthy. Although the narrative moves slowly and their are several times in which the story is paused just to muse on a character's sleeping position, I never felt as though the story was just dragging on. There were so many beautiful standalone sentences on each of these pages that I often found myself repeating the same sentence to myself over and over again just because of how harmonic it sounded. Her descriptions of her characters are magical, realistic, and somehow utterly relatable. These characters can steal rain from other cities, step into each others dreams, bottle spirit in a vial, and even give life to gardens. Plot twist after plot twist had me reading day and night, in anticipation of which of the delegates would bring back Weep's sunlight and where Lazlo's future was headed: alongside Sarai or alone? Taylor captures the very soul of humanity with her thought provoking approach to her characters. Underlying this magical tales she confronts themes such as hatred and identity. Does hatred win? Is identity determined by birth or by upbringing? I really enjoyed the way the author explored these themes without taking the enchantment away from the narrative. 
 Taylor's splendid prose won me over from the very first page. The fluidity of her words melted from the page and made their way into my heart. This is one of those books that I will tuck away in my mind and will always be a part of me. Dreams, stories, books, mythical creatures, magic - this book is all I could hope for and more. Whether or not one is a fantasy, young adult, or even nonfiction reader I believe that Strange the Dreamer is for readers of all genres. There is so much to take away from and give to this book. Taylor describes the fictional world with so much imagery but not too much as to leave the reader without opportunity of imagination. 
 The novel's plot, characters, and writing bring together an imagination that may perhaps indeed be real. We are brought into an intriguing world where noting is how it seems on the surface, but then again is even more deceptive in the dream world. With a stark ending that leaves one hanging, "because this story was not over yet," Taylor has created a masterpiece novel that has been loved and shared, just like magic. She is definitely an author that I recommend, again, to all readers simply because her imagination is so real and full of heartbreaking emotion that it is impossible to not think for at least a moment that everything happening in this book is real. This book is beautiful and full of terror, just like any book of perfection, yes perfection, is.

reference_books.title: The Wolf Gift (The Wolf Gift Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Goodbye Anne Rice. Your vampire chronicles seduced me into loving all things vampire when I was a teenager. Then you "got religious". Ugh, fine, I bid you well and moved on. Now you've recently written a few books not related to your spiritual journey. I cheered, putting your books on my to-read list. 
 I tried reading your other books, but couldn't get into it. I was bored. Then, Alas, The Wolf Gift. I thought Anne Rice takes on the Werewolf. It's got to be awesome. Dare I hope to be enchanted like days of teen aged past. 
 The answer is NO. I didn't finish this, but I did get far enough to know I don't care anything about the boring main character. The vigilante events are borderline ridiculous. The CONSTANT saying of "I smell Evil" with no descriptors made me want to claw my eyes out. (see what I did there). I mean it's a WEREWOLF, an ANIMAL, a distinguishing characteristics of which is a keen sense of SMELL. 
 I mean what does Evil smell like Anne. Is it acrid, sour, corrosive, pungent...? Forgoing the fact that a keen sense of smell is a major part of being a Werewolf, how about it's not good writing, and considering the length of the book.... 
 I've even tried reading your Vampire Chronicles again recently and I was bores out of my mind. Filled with Emo vampires constantly pondering their fate, good, evil, god, etc. I saw the beginning of these kinds of musings in this book too. I've no interest in taking anymore of Rice's spiritual journies. I want a story. 
 I'll always think of LeStat, Louis, Claudia, Akasha, Merrick, Rowan, Quinn, Marius, etc with fondness and nostalgia, but I guess my tastes have just changed. 
 Goodbye

reference_books.title: The Fever
reference_books.review_text: You have GOT to be kidding me. Some top reviews for this book have already expressed my opinions.

reference_books.title: Rosemary and Rue (October Daye, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
3.75 
 A good strong start. It starts off slow, then gets more and more interesting. I'm definitely reading the next one. I usually don't like the Fae, but Toby makes them palatable.

reference_books.title: The Immortal Rules (Blood of Eden, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The book cover is beautiful and the synopsis seemed intriguing. The book started out with great unique dystopian intensity, but quickly deteriorated after she chose to "turn". 
 It started to drag with the whole mentor-fledgling thing. That COULD have been ok, but all of the rules are the same as in other novels. I found her teacher interesting and I would have loved to switch to HIS POV and backstory rather than be pulled along with this uninteresting teenager as she makes stupid decisions by holding too much to her lost human nature. 
 This felt like several different books. First we have the city/ruins. then her time spent learning to become a vampire, then her running into the ruins after her "maker" tells her they must part. 
 It just seems like a disjointed mash-up of ground already covered.

reference_books.title: The Darkest Night (Lords of the Underworld #1)
reference_books.review_text:
1. a poor substitute for Black Dagger Brotherhood. 
 2. The world building is a bit shaky. Some parts about the gods I don't get and don't care to. 
 3. Cheesy, predictable, instant romantic connections. It can be done well, but I found myself rolling my eyes at the dialogue etc. 
 4. Not a lot of depth to the characters.

reference_books.title: Brave New World
reference_books.review_text: Another "classic" that I found too utterly boring to get into or bother finishing.

reference_books.title: Before I Fall
reference_books.review_text: At first I hated this book because the characters were so "mean", for lack of a better word. However, the plot and concept kept me listening to this audiobook. I laughed, cried, and grunted in disgust. I loved Sam's character arc and enjoyed learning the "why" behind Lindsay. Also, I'm in love with Kent. Definitely worth your time in spite of the fact that you might think this concept has been explored before. Lauren Oliver has become an author in which I will read all of her work. (see "Delirium").

reference_books.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
reference_books.review_text: Sigh. I think there's a movie. This has a great premise but gets bogged down in pretentious uninteresting discourse/dialogue of the characters. I couldn't finish.

reference_books.title: What's Left of Me (The Hybrid Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I couldn't get into this. The premise of two "souls" in one body? I can't suspend my disbelief. It was also weird referring to one person as "they".

reference_books.title: Fight Club
reference_books.review_text: This is one of my favorite movies. Unfortunately I can't say the same about the book. This is my first read of Chuck and I found the writing not straightforward enough and a bit to abstract to follow. Had I not already known what happens, I would have been lost.

book_a.title: Bumped (Bumped, #1)
book_a.user_review: I can't finish reading this. The slang/lingo made it hard to get into, even though the plot sounded/sounds promising.

sample_reviews.review_text:
I'll be honest. I had heard from some other people that they didn't like Bumped much. They were quite disappointed by all the hype created for this book. I still found the premise for the book really interesting and wanted to read it. There were definitely some parts to the book that didn't sit well with me, but I don't think I was as disappointed by others. 
 What didn't sit well with me at all was how babies were basically seen as property. Maybe it's because I have an almost 4 months old daughter, and the experience of pregnancy is fresh in my mind. When I would read about how the girls were given drugs to prevent the mother/baby bond during pregnancy and they referred to babies as "deliveries" or "preggs," I found myself feeling upset. That bond is so precious. 
 Another part of the story that bothered me was how the teens were encouraged and paid to have sex and get pregnant. I can't imagine a time when it would be okay for teens to have these masSEX parties trying to get pregnant. Or when it would be acceptable to use Tocin to facilitate sex when one of the partners wasn't quite ready. 
 Even though these parts of the story bothered me, they still made me think. That's the only reason I liked this book. The whole concept of teens being the only fertile part of the population really got me thinking. Could society really end up like that someday? The virus that led to the infertility, could it be caused by something we do now? Is there much difference between surrogates of present day and the surrogates in the book other than age? 
 Something that really stood out for me was how teen pregnancy was glorified in the book, primarily because of the need. It made me think of 16 and Pregnant and Teen Mom that so many people watch. While those shows might be meant to show the struggles of teen pregnancy, in some ways they glorify it. Here are these teen girls who have unprotected sex, get pregnant, and then find themselves with their own TV shows that millions of people watch. Could we eventually be a society that encourages teenage pregnancy rather than discouraging it? Could we eventually be providing teens with drugs to loosen them up for sex when they're apprehensive rather than teaching them about abstinence and safe sex? 
 This book raised a lot of questions for me and really made me think. I'll read the next book to find out what happens with Melody and Harmony.

I was so excited to read Bumped but I was extremely disappointed, so disappointed that I didn't even bother to finish it. That never happens. It's been sitting next to me for the past five days and I have had no urge to pick it up and read it. There were so many things that I did not like about this book. Lets start with the world building. I've read some reviews were people complemented the world building and I keep thinking am I missing something. McCafferty did not go into any detail of what this virus is, when it happened, why it happened. She failed to explain her vocabulary for this new world, she failed to explain a lot of things about this world she created. I only made it 157 pages in but I think that is plenty of time to explain to the reader what the hell is going on. I felt like maybe I was reading a sequel and that all the world building and other things were written in a previous book. This would have been a fantastic story if the writing had been stronger. Megan McCafferty had a great plot and story, but failed to thoroughly develop it. This is just my opinion.

Interesting, though it really doesn't compare to the Jessica Darling series. I will, though, say that the world created is believable and reserve further judgement for the next books. As a book of its own, I'd say that it has a lot more places that it should have gone. I suppose I'm willing to forgive that while I wait to see what is to come.
I'm super bummed. I LOVE this author. I gave everyone I know her Sloppy Firsts series. This was too sci-fi, too complicated from the start and I hated the Jesusy sister. Boo.
A solid beginning, but the complexity was greater than the length permitted at the density the book was written in.

The Little Bookworm 
 In a world where adults lose fertility around the age of 20 due to a virus, Melody is one of the first girls in her class to go pro, as in professional surrogate. Offered a highly lucrative contact to preg for a well-to-do couple, all she has to do is wait for them to find the perfect match for her. Then her long-lost, "Godfreaky" twin sister, Harmony, shows up wanting her to give up pregging for money and move to Goodside, the religious compound, with her. However, when the surrogate parents finally find the perfect donor, things begin to change for the twins in an unexpected way. 
 I feel like this book was saying a whole lot of things. I also feel like most of things went over my head as I was distracted by the onslaught of pregnancy related slang. The sheer amount of it almost overwhelmed me. Since society has now become focused on encouraging teenage girls to become pregnant, of course the slang would move along with it. It made me laugh but it also made me scratch my head occasionally. And if I had a nickel for every time the word "bump" was used, well, then I'd have a lot of nickels. 
 Still this is a very clever book. In fact, everything about this book screamed clever. It is a biting look at society's tendencies to go overboard with an idea and also to commercialize it. From the FunBump available for the "pre-bumped" to the use of "man brands" (sperm donors), everything about this society is focused on surrogates and child birthing. And I mean everything. I had a hard time grasping the timeline of when all the adults went sterile but everything in the books seemed a bit frantic like babies had to be had now or the world would end. And, by making teenage pregnancy not only palatable but extremely desirable, the message of why they were doing it becomes lost in the marketing. 
 As for the characters, I can't say I liked either one of the twins that much. They represent two extremes and it's hard to relate to an extreme. In fact, the only likable character is Zen, the friend of Melody, who acts like the only voice of reason in the whole book. Everyone is a caricature from both Melody and Harmony down to every adult and teenager in the book with the exception of Zen. Nothing in the whole book felt real and I was emotionally separated from the characters' plights, much like the pregnant teenagers from their bumps. 
 It is a quirky and interesting book though. I found myself racing through it, curious to see what happens next. Was I surprised by the turn of events near the end of the book? No, not really. Am I curious to see what happens next? Yes, actually I am. There were things that could possibly develop into something interesting for the characters and I'd like to see if they are addressed and how so. A lot of people really like this book and I'm still trying to decide how I feel about it. It was worth reading and I guess that's the best thing I can say.

Gave me a lot to think about. Very interesting language, though it was a hurdle overcome at the beginning to figure out what was going on. 
 A good read!

This book read like a bad romance novel. I really like dystopia novels but did they barely felt like one. It felt really unrealistic and as though all the characters were just really stupid. Both girls annoyed the hell out of me and I found myself not caring at all what happened to them. That's the sign of a bad book to me. 
 Melody just seemed vapid to me. She didn't have much personality to begin with and she never really for one. Harmony had one, kind of, but I didn't believe how quickly she changed all her morals - or the ending. And the fact that she compared Johndoe (and seriously, wtf at that name) to Jesus...really? Really?? 
 This novel was just a bad romance book with confusing dystopian lingo and a shaky premise. Initially, the idea intrigued me, but it was done so poorly that there is nothing to love in this book.

Well, this is going to be one of those rare moments when I don't have a whole heck of a lot of nice stuff to say about a book. This book, while it has received several great reviews and I heard good things about it from others, just really didn't do it for me. 
 It started off bad when during the first several chapters I kept getting confused as to which sister was which. I was constantly checking back to the beginning of the chapter and even then I couldn't remember which one was Harmony- the Bible thumper or the professional humper? (bad joke) This was an issue that carried over to other parts of the story, I felt like everything was on the surface without a lot of explanation and therefore I didn't connect with the characters or plot. Both Melody and Harmony seemed like stereotypes instead of fully formed individuals and I just couldn't get invested in their journey or their struggles. Even the world around them seemed to suffer from a lack of explanation. Acronyms were thrown out without definition, slang was tossed out in conversation left and right and without any context and it was hard to follow. The intentional spelling changes were irritating instead of lending insight into the world these girls live in. For instance- seeing the word really repeatedly spelled "rilly" was frankly really annoying. 
 I suspect that the author was trying to show the superficial world these girls are living in. That they have been reduced to breeding for profit and how horrifying that is, but I found myself unable to envision a world where this could be the reality, and therefore it wasn't horrifying at all, just laughable. I wish that there had been more context to it all. Where had the virus come from, what had been done to try and stop it, how did it get to the point where girls were treated like breeding stock? Without that background to back up the story I felt a bit lost. 
 Lastly, this book falls into the trap that a lot of books seem to fall into- that of the cliff hanger ending. They are written and set up for sequels and trilogies and there is the risk of the book not being able to stand on it's own. That is how I felt when I hit the last page. There is no resolution. A spectacularly written first book in the series will do two things in my opinion: 
 1. Come to a conclusion of some sort. It will have a satisfying ending that is enough all on it's own without needing the next book to finish the story. Of course there will be some loose ends to tie up, a promise of a next adventure, or some greater story that is waiting (for example- Harry Potter). 
 2. That anticipation of what could possibly happen next will leave the reader wanting more. 
 Bumped did neither of these things for me. There was no satisfaction to be found in the final pages of this book, it's all left for the sequel (or trilogy), Worse then that, I didn't even care about what was going to happen next. I have suspicions as to what choices Melody and Harmony will make next, but I'm not invested in their journeys in a way that when I closed the book I was instantly wanting more.
I just didn't feel pulled into the story as much as I was hoping. More review to come.

I didn't love this book, barely liked it. At first I was very interested as I thought that there was a possibility that the bones of this book - the year is 2035 and a virus prevents anyone over the age of 18 from carrying a child - might have been fun to explore. Amy Kathleen Ryan's "Sky Chasers" series hints at something similar to this and it was a premise that just wouldn't leave my mind. I hoped that Bumped would bring a different perspective to this but it really didn't. Megan McCafferty didn't flesh out her two main characters - Melody and Harmony (identical twins!) - enough to make it seem like a story that I had any stake in. Maybe they'd find happiness, maybe not, but I didn't really care. 
 The book is not without imagination, the technologies and language that McCafferty invents for her story is pretty impressive and occasionally funny, but there is nothing beyond a surface description of how either of the girls are feeling. I think it's a bad sign that I found myself more curious about what the incidental characters were feeling than the two girls. 
 It's a post apocalyptic world with the challenges and changes that make this novels so interesting but in the case of Bumped it just wasn't worth my interest. I can't see myself suggesting this to any patrons but might check out #2 myself just to see if it improves.. I am always hopeful.

Sharp, witty, and poignant, this book came through in the end. At first, I was a little bit disappointed. I LOVE Megan McCafferty as a writer (Jessica Darling for President!) and I had a lot of high hopes for Bumped, so it kind of fell short of my expectations in the beginning. For one thing, the futuristic lingo was hard to digest--all the bumping and negging and REnegging, etc. I also thought Harmony's religiosity was just TOO outlandish (this coming from an evangelical Christian); but I was annoyed with how McCafferty chose to portray her in the beginning. Eventually I warmed up to Harmony and to the whole book in general (especially once the plot picked up!) and I found that I couldn't put this book down even if I wanted to! Definitely an engrossing read from the middle onward, and I can't wait to get my hands on the sequel, Thumped!

I'm not really sure what to write about this book. I'm not sure what I think. 
 First of all, I should research books better before I read them. There is A LOT of talk about sex in this book. It's practically all about teens having sex (though the actual act isn't ever described). Yes, I am rather naive. I did expect some, just not so much. If I had done research about the book and knew this before picking it up, I would never have picked it up. 
 However, I did pick it up. And I got rather interested in this really, EXTREMELY disturbing story McCafferty writes. There were a few times I almost put it down because of content, but I was so intrigued by the story that I didn't, I couldn't. I kept reading. I read it on my nook and for some reason it wouldn't tell me what page I was on, so I didn't know I was at the end until the acknowledgement page popped up. And then I was UPSET! It's such an abrupt ending, like stopping in the middle of the story. And I really wanted to know what happened next. 
 Like I said, not sure what to think about this book! 
 McCafferty wrote a future, dystopic novel that is amazing. One that is extremely disturbing, but utterly believable. I mean, the propaganda geared towards teens about having babies--ack! The young age of these teen mothers and would be mothers. The emotional and physical and social effects of teens having babies so young, just to give them away...so very upsetting. But I really believed it. 
 For example--parent's selling their children's bodies for 9 months at a time to make babies for the highest bidder. I watched 5 minutes of Toddlers and Tiaras the night I finished this book(had never seen it before) and I totally saw how this could happen. Another example--the glamour of being a sperm donor. Think Justine Bieber. How many teen girls would want him to be the father of their baby? How many parents would want his DNA in their babies? Imagine the paparazzi attacks!!! I can see it. 
 Everything was meant to be disturbing and make the reader think, so that was good. But the religion bothered me differently. The two religious viewpoints were very extreme. It bothered me in a more personal sense. Where's the more rational religious look at infertility and rampant teen pregnancy? 
 So, yeah. Read at your own risk. But very interesting. And rather addictive.

Didn't like the characters. Didn't like the plot. Didn't like the annoying slang words that were so, so trashy and ridiculous. I barely managed to finish reading it. I was intrigued by the description, but it wasn't what i had hoped for.

This was an interesting concept. I wondered while reading it if our society could really end up there--and then I remember shows on TV like "16 & Pregnant." *shakes head* 
 I do like the idea I definitely find this idea interesting but I think my inner word-nerd snob took over a lot while I read this book. The slang drove me crazy. I have said "for serious" a few more times than I'd like to admit but it showed up at least once in every "Melody" chapter, sometimes more. And then there was the intentional spelling of really as "rilly." *headdesk* 
 And then there was Harmony--I just felt sorry for her from page 1 to done. There wasn't much growth for her as a character and I have already had a member of my own family have to deal with religious-crazypants. 
 *sigh* Despite it all, I liked the concept and Melody enough to give the 2nd book a chance. Besides I liked Zen, who has book-boyfriend potential.

I am kind of disappointed in the way the book turned. I had such expectations for the book because the premises sounded interesting. However, it was not for me. The characters were lacking for me. The writing style was lacking as well. Also, it was confusing and boring. It is the kind of story that does not retain someone's attention. I thought Harmony was a frustrating character. I do not know if I will continue the series. Overall, a meh read.
ughhhhhhhhhhhh

I wasn't a huge fan of the book but finished it because it was a pretty easy read. It was just too straight forward and crammed their obvious themes down your throat - "religion is controlling and bad": insert female protagonist who lives in a super protective culture that covers women and controls their marriages similar to portrayals of middle eastern culture. The characters are all just too one dimensional and superficial though it does hint that there's something deeper to the characters near the end of the novel. But it comes as too little too late. The novel ends right when it seems to get interesting but not enough that I want to read the sequel. It felt like nothing really happened and there was no character growth, though when I think back objectively, I can see how they did learn some lessons. They just started off so unrealistic that there is no satisfaction at seeing them make obvious revelations. It's not like I disagreed with the themes of the story, it was just not presented very well. 
 The storyline seemed like it would be interesting, but it just wasn't. The science fiction part of the world where most people become sterile around age 18 is glossed over and the repercussions of the world are touched on - such as how young is too young to promote reproduction too. Once again, it's pretty superficial and I don't make much of a connection to the characters that are presented.

Melody and Harmony were born into a world where teen pregnancy is as valuable as money in society. Melody never knew Harmony, but now they've found each other and must learn to come to terms with the upbringing the other has received. Melody has a goal - she wants to bump and receive all the status and money that comes with it. Harmony, however, wants nothing more than to be the perfect wife and mother. But despite their different lives, their identical looks are going to send them on a journey together that's both a blessing and a curse - pretty much the same as their chance meeting. 
 Bumped is another book in the wave of new dystopian novels taking over the YA market. Written by veteran author Megan McCafferty, known for her popular Jessica Darling series, Bumped presents a world that puts an all new spin on the media craze we see today. Whereas we watch shows such as Teen Mom and The Pregnancy Pact, Bumped turns this phenomenon on its head, making teen pregnancy a valuable, enviable and coveted turn of events. It's a unique twist on the dystopian genre - slightly creepy and eerily fascinating, but definitely and completely one-of-a-kind. 
 Promising premise aside though, I have to admit that Bumped fell flat for me. From page one the book is cluttered with the slang of the world Melody and Harmony live in. In fact, it was so jarring that I actually put it down to attempt to digest who the characters actually were. Furthermore, Bumped is written from both Melody and Harmony's POVs, alternating by chapter and furthering my confusion. Then, to add to my confusion, Harmony continuously slammed religious terms around and compared her love interest to Jesus - who she wanted to sleep with (gross & weird?). Now, don't get me wrong, the irony of the world of Bumped is not lost on me. That said, I felt it was like beating a dead horse with an overtly perky voice that didn't fit a story that, I'm assuming, was supposed to be somewhat serious. 
 Now, I'm not saying that Bumped is a bad book, but I'm confused about the audience of Bumped, as well as what I was supposed to take away from it. If it was supposed to be ironic, or a play on what we see today, I would want that to be more apparent and not masked by slang and dialogue that just didn't work for me. I hate giving bad reviews, but I give it a 2 out of 5 for the original premise, alone. I would still recommend it to fans of an upper YA audience, as well as those who enjoy dystopian novels.

Not sure where to begin. I realize it's a young adult book that I pre read for my tween daughter but it was almost too teenie bopperish to stand. Of course, I will read the second book because I need to know what happens now. But I will say that for a young adult book the innuendos and terminology was borderline inappropriate. I know my child is sheltered but there is no way I would allow her to read this book and get the impression that using those terms or what was going on was appropriate.

This book is set in the future 2036 I think and is about two twin teenage sisters who were separated at birth and raised very differently. Melody grew up being raised to prepare to "bump" (have sex and get pregnant) to the highest bidder for he baby, and Harmony grew up in a church community and was first engaged at 13 and is now engaged again at 16. 
 The book is so full of futuristic lingo that it is distracting from the storyline, words and phrases are used but aren't explained until the next chapter and sometimes much later. This book has such a light hearted easy breezy tone to it but it's actually talking about extremely difficult things: a virus that makes people over the age of 18 infertile, rich people buying teenagers kids (even goes as low as ELEVEN!), mass sex parties that teenagers are going to and then talking about in school (that's how they practice their foreign language), oh and condoms are illegal and no one has seen them for 10+ years. 
 I was so excited to read the book because it's a fresh idea and I applaud that, but it obviously isn't written for my level/age (25) and is geared much younger, but that raises some questions as well because of the fun/fresh tone that is taken for pretty serious topics. I would not recommend this book.
Ugh this book was terrible.

What the heck even is this book???? It's so horrendously awful, my eyes hurt. This dystopian universe is completely ridiculous playing off of the the stereotype of crazy religious people and the weirdness of a world where adults can no longer get pregnant. I'm sorry but this book was so terrible, want a better dystopian teen mother book try Mothership.
Omg. I got through 2 chapters and had to put it down - it was that awful.
It was "for seriously" one of the worst that I have read in awhile. Like "rilly". That slang crap made me want to clean my brain out, the worst!
What's with all these books focused on teenagers forced to get pregnant for repopulation of the earth? It was freaky, weird, and I illogical.

I wasn't crazy about the writing or the plot to be honest. The idea of the dystopia is interesting enough, though it's very much like a teenage version of Handmaid's Tale. I did like the ending, and I think the second book, Thumped, is far better so far.

Fast/easy read. Overall, it was okay, but I was confused for the first several chapters with all this invented terminology for this futuristic society. It took too long for the book to finally explain what the terms meant.

Just....not my thing I guessed. I was trying to give Megan McCafferty another try after HATING her Jessica Darling books. I thought something so unusual and far-departed from my normal reading patterns might offer some hope for something good. It was indeed interesting, but not something I will recommend to others.

Total meh. I could have gotten on board with the plot, but I kind of hated all the characters and really didn't care what happened to them. Melody could have been interesting, but I kept having to read from the POV of Harmony who was annoying and full of secrets (that I didn't care about) and bad decisions. The future slang was a little too much. 
 In the end, I skimmed to see how things ended (build up to another book) and tossed it aside. Which is too bad, because I thought my love for Megan McCafferty's books would be universal (loved the Jessica Darling series).

I was intrigued by the premise of this book, but after 45 pages I gave it up. The way that both of these characters drove me nuts! It was too cutesy, smiley, happy, made me want to slap them. I had a hard time getting past it to what was actually going on in the story. In the end this one just wasn't for me.
I was 25% through this book and it went right into the trash. The writing is atrocious and the story is even worse. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone!!!

I agree with most of the reviews that said the first 50 pages are tough to get through. The future slang and overuse of caps lock makes it a painful start. However, once the story kicks in it takes over your annoyance with those things and makes for a very enjoyable story. 
 The rapid changes between characters (with some chapters being barely 2 pages) makes the story move along quickly yet was a but annoying. However, it does keep you reading because you want to get back to whichever scene to see what is happening. Overall the book takes place over the course of only a day and a half so the pace is very quick. 
 I'm not sure if teens would enjoy this book much, unless they were on the older side, mature, and intelligent. The heavy satire of this teen pregnancy based society seems more for adults because you're able to fully understand the message of the book. 
 Overall, I enjoyed it far more than I thought I would when I started reading. It has its pesky issues but not enough to draw you away from the fascinating and somewhat terrifying world. This book is a very fresh, unique read and I look forward to the sequel.

A very strange and shallow look at the future. Sometime within the next 50 years or so, a virus hits all the young people and those born that prevents them from having children after the age of 18 - so getting pregnant (being "bumped") between 13 and 18 is the only way to keep the human race surviving. It has become popular to find agents and create contracts with married couples that want children - they pay for college, offer cars, money, etc., in exchange for these teenage girls to get pregnant as surrogates and give up their children. 
 The idea is interesting, though the book is done poorly. It is very light and bubble-gummy, only showing the emergent issues and producing good writing in the last quarter of the book ... which did make me want to get the sequel, just to see what happens. 
 The basic premise is that the main character is the perfect girl to be a surrogate - smart, beautiful, athletic; perfect in every way. Except one - she has a twin no one knew about that shows up at her door to try to convert her to their version of Christianity (no bumping before marriage!). No longer "original" due to exact strands of DNA, the twin could be a major issue. Mix ups obviously occur, though the ending was a little surprising and helped to save the book from complete obscurity. 
 Eh.

allright, i thought this book was really really weird. It wasnt bad or anything, but it wasnt great. I realluy dont know what to think about this book fro the moment/. i woinder wat the next one will be klike

Melody and her parents have signed a lucrative conception contract years before with a wealthy couple. Harmony, her identical twin, has shown up on her doorstep, she was raised in a religious community and she has run away. A virus has made it so that only teenagers can give birth, so their babies are very valuable. 
 This is all about choice and the lack of same, and the government and private enterprise attempt to control conception in teens and pre-teens. The Handmaid's Tale did it better, but this is easier reading. I can hope that girls who like this book will check out Margaret Atwood's truly frightening novel. 
 (Interlibrary loan, from a short list of YA feminist novels.)

Gave up around page 40. It feels like McCafferty was overly ambitious in creating the world of her story. The slang, especially, fails miserably. A real shame, because her Jessica Darling series is pretty fantastic realistic fiction.
2.5 - If only because the ending made the whole thing ten times better.

It was a really fun read and an intriguing concept. The only reason I didn't rate it higher is that it sometimes reads like the pilot of a tv show, it's more about setting up the continuing story line than having it's own narrative. Still, I'm looking forward to the rest of the series.

Some of the slang took a bit to figure out, which was probably the biggest downside to this book. Overall, it was interesting. It explores, albeit rather superficially, issues surrounding monogamy, fertility, human trafficking, surrogacy, and religion. Religion is shown as being as off-the-deep-end on one extreme as the bumping-for-profit side is on the other extreme. The book hints that morality lies somewhere in the middle, with people's ability to choose their own destiny being key. 
 None of the sides were particularly demonized and you could see reasons for each characters choices. 
 It was interesting, yet rather fluffy. Personally, I would prefer a book dealing with these issues to be a little more serious and really get into the issues at hand, but at least some problems are brought to light, if not as many as perhaps should be. I was especially glad to see the insertion of the character Malia, as she provided a necessary point-of-view. It would also have been helpful to see a Church family that was successful, and not snidely uncharitable and controlling, as everyone who had interaction with Harmony was.

I'm sixteen. Pregnant. And the most important person on the planet. 
 A virus makes everyone over the age of 18 infertile. Teen girls are being paid to get pregnant for those who cannot have children. Melody has been groomed her whole life to make sure she would be paid top dollar for her "delivery." Her plans are interrupted by the arrival of her twin sister, Harmony, a sister she did not even know existed. Harmony has grown up in a religious community that disagrees with the so-called "pregging for profit" and Harmony is out to save her twin sister from committing what she believes is a grievous sin. The two girls try to get along with their very different backgrounds. A case of mistaken identity changes everything forever. 
 This book has a very interesting premise (albeit not an original one, see Wither, although Bumped is a bit more light-hearted -- was 2011 just the year of teens in dystopias having to get knocked up to save the world?). It made me think a lot about the ethics of using teens as breeding machines and an industry that encourages them to get pregnant as soon as they can. There was a lot of uncomfortable thinking, especially about the psychological and physical toll this would take on young minds and bodies. The book was a fascinating read from that stand-point. Unfortunately, the premise was the only good thing about the book. 
 Like other books that jumped on the dystopia bandwagon in the early 2010s, this book lacked quite a bit in world-building, at least at the beginning. You are just thrown into this world mid-scene and have no idea why things are the way they are. It gets a little better near the end but for the most part I was wandering around lost. It doesn't help that the book is peppered with futuristic sounding slang and terms that are not defined. Every other word seemed made-up and there were whole sentences at the beginning of the book that were complete gibberish to me. Some books can pull that off well, but this one went overboard. 
 The characters were a bit lackluster as well, especially Harmony. From the beginning, she is a person of faith with very strong convictions. This seems to be forgotten at the end of the book. I won't give anymore away for fear of spoilers, but it was too radical of a change for me to be comfortable with. The other characters were nothing special. Melody was a more sympathetic character and I enjoyed her friendship with Zen. 
 This is a book that will make you think about the "what if" scenario. It was a highly interesting premise but the world-building and characters took away from that premise somewhat. I doubt I will read the rest of the series though it did end on a bit of a cliffhanger.

This book was just what I was needing. I feel like I've been reading a bunch of mediocre stuff as of late and everything that has hype has proven disappointing to me. Bumped, of course, being the exception. This is one that actually lives up to its hype. 
 The premise: A virus makes everyone infertile by their 20's, so the only ones capable of having babies are teenage girls. Instead of making it mandatory for girls to have babies (or "preggs", the euphemism for "baby", which connotes too much maternal connection), it has become a multi-million dollar business. Our protagonists are twins who were separated at birth. Twin #1, Melody, is adopted by a wealthy family and is bred to be a professional surrogate, though she has yet to fulfill her contract. Twin #2, Harmony, is adopted by a church where members are encouraged to marry young and have as many children as possible. Pregging for profit is considered a major sin. Harmony has left her community to go and meet her biological twin for the first time ever. Both are in for more than a few surprises. 
 What I really like about this book is how many ways that it can be read. On one level, it's a highly entertaining story; a fast-paced satire. On other levels, it's an indictment of the commodification of human life, of capitalism run amok, of social conformity...Lots to think about. Highly enjoyable.
Weirrrrrd, but well done. I definitely wouldn't recommend this to students; the characters are teenagers, but the content is adult.

 The story is quite simple: a young, innocent girl, who is not at all interested in boys (because girls in high school dont give a shit about dating, this is well known), even if her best friend is pushing her (look, her best friend is POPULAR and INTERESTED IN BOYS and she isn't, aww, poor thing), meets a mysterious guy.

Tengo un problema con Hush Hush (con la saga entera). 
 Lei los libros en ingles cuando recien salian. Me gustaron mucho, pero no dejaron ninguna huella en mi. En otras palabras, mas alla de saber que me gustaron en su momento, no me acuerdo de NADA. Recuerdo la trama central de cada libro y lo basico de los personajes, pero nada mas. No me acuerdo ni de la mitad de las escenas o en que orden pasan las cosas. 
 La saga me resulto atrapante, pero es TAN parecida a TANTAS OTRAS sagas del mismo genero, que no me marco en lo mas minimo. 
 Por momento hay escenas que ni siquiera se si son de Hush Hush o de Crepusculo o de Finding Sky o de cualquiera de esas sagas romanticas/juveniles/paranormales en las que una chica "comun" se enamora del chico malo/raro/solitario de su escuela, que por una de esas casualidades es un vampiro/angel/savant/otracosa y tambien se enamora de ella (a pesar que no es una chica especial, ni linda ni nada). Juntos sortean juntos un monton de peligros porque "no pueden estar juntos" o "es peligroso para ella entrar en el mundo de el" o cualquiera de esas cosas. Mantienen una relacion de "te amo pero deberiamos estar separados" en las que durante toda la saga es un "me quiero acostar contigo pero todavia no es el momento". 
 Y no vengan a decirme que no es cierto. 
 Pero es atrapante. Es un buen cliche sin nada en especial. Atrapa, hace que las lectoras se sientan parte de la historia, como si fuesen la protagonista, y se enamoren del chico en cuestion. 
 Para los que no se cansan de leer siempre lo mismo, vale la pena. 
 Para el que no leyo nada en este estilo, es posiblemente de las mejores historias romanticas paranormales adolescentes que hay dando vuelta. 
 Para el que esta harto del tema, ni lo intenten. 
 Para el que busca un libro de buena calidad, JA, este es el sitio equivocado. 
 Para el que quiere pasar una tarde con algo ligero, podria ser. 
 Si sos una mujer de entre 13 y 16 anos, seguramente te guste a pesar de todo lo que dije.

I hardly ever do this to a book - give it one star and imagine that star is about to supernova at any moment. But 'did not like it' is true; it is an understatement.

Seemed like a duplicate of Twilight to me. Instead of vampires, you have angels. Mysterious guy sits next to girl in biology and inexplicably falls for her despite initially hating her. Why does he end up falling for her? There's no explanation. Boring.

Another book involving fallen angels. What did I tell you? It's all vampires and fallen angels out there in the fiction world. 
 I really enjoyed this book, and a twinge disappointed that it's not a stand alone book. Though, I guess I should have figured that out sooner. There are hardly any books that come out recently that aren't set up to be part of a series. 
 Hush, Hush is about a girl named Nora. When her biology teacher forces the class to switch lab partners, she is thrown into the tangled life of mysterious transfer student Patch. From the start Nora is certain Patch isn't exactly what he seems to be--but she's not sure whether to be thrilled or frightened by that fact. The book is meant to keep you guessing, though I think I figured it all out early on. Still, it was enough of a twisty-turny plot to keep me interested. And while it seemed to jump into the narrative at a strange place (though the real story begins there with Nora "meeting" Patch it seems like it just starts with no lead in. Nora walks into Bio. Bio teacher changes lab partner. Patch is Nora's lab partner now. Patch starts flirting shamelessly in a very abrupt, invasive manner. I wonder how we suddenly got here), I was able to collect myself and breeze through the rest of the book as everything came together.

Great secrets, almost predictable, but a super boring start 
 it was a good, but not great. 
 It was the same concept as other stories, that i got bored halfway thru the story. Yeah, the mysterious classmate is hot... yes, he does like me... yes, he said I should stay away from him. (BLEH) 
 The concept's old already, and get this, he needs to kill her, he WANTS to kill her.

This book makes me regret giving Twilight one star. I wouldn't call this a total rip-off but, oh man, is it close. Normal girl meets creepy mysterious boy in Biology class. Girl is uncomfortable by said boy's creepiness mysteriousness but is drawn by it. Fine, sounds like the formula of plenty of other books. My problem with it? Well . . . 
 Now, Nora is in grade ten. She's sixteen. From my limited knowledge of tenth grade Biology class (we didn't study Biology as its own subject until grade eleven, so it was mostly basics), it usually isn't taught by a Coach (who doesn't seem to have a name other than 'Coach'.) Not to mention, a Coach who doesn't seem really devoted to the subject. He's more focused on the next game than anything. Whatever. It's just nitpicking. (Although, since when is Biology purely dedicated to sex ed? Seriously. That's all they seem to be talking about in that class. Also, 'discuss your ideal mate'? NO. You don't study this in Biology!) 
 *exhales* 
 My real issue is with the Coach's utter idiocy. He puts Patch next to Nora, which is fine. Whatever. Have them interact. But after Nora's continuous pleas to move seats because Patch is freaking the hell out of her and making her super uncomfortable, Coach does absolutely nothing. He doesn't care that his student is being harassed? No. He doesn't. So what does he do instead? Tells her to suck it up and tutor said boy that is freaking the hell out of her and making her super uncomfortable (which, I noticed, never actually happens. The tutoring bit is completely forgotten. Plot point, where'd you go?) What teacher does that? At least move Nora with some other non-offensive unnamed classmate. She doesn't need to be beside Vee - aren't there other students in this class? We know they exist but we don't know any of them. I guess it's just a way to keep Nora beside Patch and force some romance thing? 'Look, they're arguing and Nora's uncomfortable. They must be falling in looooooooove!' 
 No. They're not. 
 This brings me to Nora, our amazingly paranoid protagonist. Honestly. She is one of the nosiest and suspicious characters I have ever read. She believes the entire world is out to get her - and for good reason, too, because apparently every shadow and creak in the night is some crazed killer! A few times, she questions her sanity, since a lot of the things she sees ends up disappearing. (Cue creepy music.) Reading from the perspective of someone fearing they're losing their mind is different and can be well-written. Katniss from Hunger Games, for instance, certainly questioned her sanity a few times. And I didn't mind it at all. It was new and cool seeing that development, understanding where the doubt is stemming from, and seeing where the person goes from there. But Nora doesn't continue with the questioning for the entirety of the novel. She just sort of...accepts?...that weird stuff is happening so...why not just snoop around and Google stuff! That always works :D 
 Oh wait. 
 I did not understand her mind at all. It seemed all over the place. Her reactions to seeing not-there things made her do stupid things, which seemed only relevant for driving the plot forward. But jeez, is she nosy. She goes 'undercover' to ask about Patch's 'mysterious' past (with a ridiculous costume and redundant questions to ask his co-workers that a ten-year-old with good sense would probably not write). For a girl who wants to stay the hell away from him in Bio class, she seems awfully keen to creep on him outside of school. 
 Did I mention our lovely heroine is vying to go to an Ivy League school? I think she proves enough times that she does not belong there. She refuses to accept the most logical answers and instead finds alternate explanations that I had to re-read and still not understand! Nora fails at all subtlety. I don't know if that's supposed to make her look endearing, but I find her extremely incapable of making rational decisions and thinking before speaking. Why is it that, when people ask her to do things she doesn't want, she makes up lies instead of telling the truth? She has a horrible lying streak. She's not assertive in any way. Any attempt to get Patch/Elliot/Vee to back off just makes them just laugh, like 'Oh, you silly girl, you don't know what you're saying!' Nora is more or less a doormat. Fantastic. 
 Her 'relationship' with Patch, the creepy mysterious jerk boy I would love to punch every time he opens his smarmy mouth is beyond comprehension. There's no build-up, no reason for Nora to suddenly wuv him. Everything that he says insults or degrades her in some way. He has sleazy pick-up lines and comments that border on harassment. There's a reason why she wanted Coach to move her seat. And yet, in the hotel (the worst-written scene by far, since it practically just forces Nora and Patch together) she loves him. And even when he admits that he's going to kill her, she is certain he wouldn't dare hurt her. 
 Um. Those alarm bells going off in your head? Yeah. They're ringing for a reason: GTFO. 
 Which brings me to Vee. In all honesty, I thought Vee could not be her real name - it had to be short for something. But while we're given her last name, no full name is provided. Which leaves me confused. But I will let that slide. But I will not forgive her personality. So Vee is supposed to be Nora's outgoing, lovable freakin annoying sidekick. Y'know, the person that drags the reluctant protagonist into whacky and fun situations! :D Yeah, well, not really so much with this book. Vee is actually the person who pushes Nora into a kinda-relationship with Elliot, even though Nora repeatedly asserts the fact that she finds Elliot creepy and is uncomfortable around him. See other note about Nora's imitation of a doormat. But anyway, Vee seems to exist simply for the purpose of pushing Nora into stupid situations to push the plot forward. Also, she is sort-of-dating-but-not-really-I-think Jules WHO I TOTALLY CALLED TO BE THE VILLAIN. UGH. Also, she's Nora's only friend (seriously, there is zero mention of other friends). 
 Nora's mother is . . . non-existent for the majority of the book. Nora lives with a German houselady (because everyone knows that only foreigners with slight accents become houseladies). Anyway. Nora's father is dead I find it funny that his death is like briefly mentioned and Nora seems perfectly normal about it in this book. Meanwhile, from what I read in Crescendo she breaks down at the smallest of references to her father. Continuity, Fitzpatrick. You can't revive something because it becomes an important plot point and shove it in our faces and Nora pretty much lives alone. Which is convenient for the purposes of letting her go wherever she wants, whenever she wants. Also, her mother has no idea that Nora has called 911 like 3 times. The police do not like calls that really are of no importance, aka ALL OF NORA'S CALLS. Nora is a minor - shouldn't the mother have been told? I know my mom would have killed me if I called 911 for no good reason repeatedly. But no - the only thing she seems concerned with is Nora's love life. 
 Parenting: You're doing it wrong. 
 Now, Jules and Elliot. Ugh, I can't even begin to talk about them. Jules was pretty much non-existent. There was no suspense, no build-up to the fact he was the villain. It was just . . . there. And Elliot - well, it was awfully convenient that Nora Googled him and that the article about his murdering habits was like the first result. Also, which stupid reporter put his name in that article? He's a minor. There's like this law or something that prevents minors from having their names published, right? I guess not? Whatever. I'm glad the dude Nora suspected ended up being NOT THE VILLAIN and the dude we never saw WAS THE VILLAIN. 
 Sigh. 
 I just find Nora's ways with Google mystifying and appalling at the same time. She practically Googles everything she doesn't know (which happens to be a lot), instead of Fitzpatrick giving subtle hints for her and the reader to figure out. When in doubt, Google's got your back. Oh, but there's this bit when Nora says, "I was pretty sure Australia didn't have diamonds." 
 Guess what. I Googled it. It does have diamonds. 
 Future Ivy League student right here, guys. 
 Now, I can't forget to talk about Patch, our dear protagonist's true wuv. Yeah. Um, well, let's see. I kinda totally . . . hate him. Him and Nora do not work in any universe, alternate or otherwise. See previous note of Biology class & the sleazy hotel. 
 But we can't forget our almost-antagonist Marcie Millar. Sigh. Why are all the bad girls . . . cheerleaders? They're not evil, guys. I swear. I find it funny, though, that we hardly hear from her after her attack. Um, wasn't Nora like a suspect or something? I was actually really confused at that part of the book, because Nora jumped from talking to the police about how she totally didn't attack Marcie, to being with Patch. At this point of the book, I just gave up trying to figure out anything and using logic altogether. 
 The bit with Nora and the bag lady highlighted (once more) Nora's inability to think rationally. She willingly goes into some shady part of the neighbourhood (I can't even remember what for) and when she asks this lady on the street for directions (to a place literally the next street over), Nora is basically stripped of her coat and hat. Okay, maybe your phone doesn't have GPS or something, but c'mon! USE YOUR BRAIN. The dude that dropped you off told you what direction it was in. I know it's a shady place BUT SEARCH. GO FIND SOMEONE ELSE TO HELP YOU. SOMETHING. And not just that, she leaves her phone in the pocket of the coat she gives to the woman. Nora loses two phones in this book. She tells the reader that her family is well off, but not rich. Yet, they can afford the houselady, Nora continuously wastes money at the bistro place, she loses two phones . . . I give up. She doesn't have a job. She's sixteen. The mom is the only provider and they're not too wealthy. Where, then, is Nora getting this endless supply of money? Why would the mom allow her to waste so much? 
 *throws hands up* I am never getting answers to these questions. 
 OH BUT ONE MORE LAST POINT AND THEN I SWEAR IM DONE: Nora's anemia. She keeps mentioning her iron pills and whatnot. But when it comes down to it, nothing happens to her. I don't know what happens exactly to people with anemia that do not take their iron (oh, wait, I could always Google it) but there are not repercussions for Nora. In fact, the only time her anemia serves a purpose is to get into a room to peek at Patch's file (where Vee has the brilliant idea of calling with a bomb threat *headdesk*). Other than this incident, Nora could not be anemic and the plot would follow in the exact same manner. Whoops. Also, from the 11 or so chapters (about half) I've read of Crescendo, her anemia is mentioned a total of zero times. Whoops. 
 I'm so done with this series.

 Regardless of all my criticisms, for some reason, the book kind of hooked me in. As for all the twilight references in other reviews, if you look at any teen romance novel, it follows the same storyline. there's not much originality in regards to romance plots. This story was completely different. Yes it had a dark stranger who had a creepy nonhuman secret, and a curious girl who he managed to fall in love with yadda yadda, but what teenage romance novel doesn't have that these days? that shouldn't be the main point in regards to whether the book was good or not. anywhooo i will read the rest of the series, because i'm pretty curious.

What do you do when you're a fallen angel, when all you've got to offer is bad and dangerous? What do you do when find that the cost of the thing you want most is no longer something you are willing to pay? 
 Nora is just beginning to get back on with her life after her father's recent murder. That was, until the biology seating changed. Her new biology partner is Patch, the senior who just screams danger, and Nora isn't one to play with fire. But Patch seems to know more about her than she is comfortable with and then there are the things she knows aren't right, like people following her, things and people that others can't see. As Nora grows closer to Patch she begins to wonder what exactly is at stake here and who can she really trust? 
 Hush, Hush is brilliantly written and totally addictive, great for older teens and readers of urban fantasy, such as Wicked Lovely. Look out for book two!!!

 First of all, I went on goodreads and was absolutely appalled by the amount of controversy this book has gotten. Literally, the ratings were either 1 star or 5 stars. And I have quite some stuff to say about the book. 
 The Ups: I thought that the book was rather enjoyable during the actual period I was reading it. It was very fast-paced which I enjoyed, because being so incredibly tired and busy these days, it was nice that I could slip in and out of the world of the book very quickly and I thought that it kept me entertained throughout the story. There was a lot of action, suspense, and I got interested in what was happening. 
 The concept of fallen angels, and Nephilim was very fresh and interesting, and I think it was cool to think of good gone wrong, and how even the most holiest or "good" creatures would succumb to desire. I've read a crazy amount of books on fairies, vampires, and werewolves, but angels were a new idea. 
 The Downs: This book is a romance novel. Right? I mean, that's what it's supposed to be. And I fell for Patch the first time that he popped up. But as the book went on, I found him to be borderline abusive and not attractive or nice at all. And when I don't like the romantic interest in a romance novel, that kind of defeats the whole purpose of the novel. I think that if the novel had expanded more on the entire angel/Nephilim idea it would have been much more interesting than just trying to make the romance work. 
 I also think that the actual action happened too late in the book. I understand that it was building up to a certain climax and that there was a lot of romantic building and information that we needed, but I wish that it would have happened at a bit of a faster pace. I just really think that if the book had been primarily based on the paranormal part of the story and not the romance, it would have been much more enjoyable. 
 I found the book very predictable. It just seemed like another generic paranormal story for me. I saw a lot of things coming and it just generally didn't excite me very much. 
 Overall: Fascinating concept, but wasn't written the way I would've liked it

Didn't like it. Nope, not one bit. 
 Nora was dull and annoying. Vee bordered on too-stupid-to-live. Patch was a complete asshole. And the cherry on top - the plot was boring. 
 It seems that all YA paranormals revolve around the same premise: quiet girl meets mysterious guy who is harboring a dark secret, which girl then spends 200+ pages trying to figure out. Then after she's figured it out, they are free to fight some battle against evil and fall in love. 
 Sure, that worked the first dozen times I read it. Now, it just annoys me. When all the strange things were happening with Patch, I just kept rolling my eyes in annoyance. Can we just get on with the plot here, rather than spending this many pages listening to a 16 year old whine about how the boy she likes is hiding something from her? 
 And Patch. Ugh. One of my least favorite love interests. I hesitate to even call him a "love interest" since "self-centered, heartless bastard" seems more fitting. Call me crazy, but I find it hard to sympathize with a guy who spends 2/3 of the book terrorizing/plotting to kill the girl who's falling for him. That doesn't make him a sexy bad boy, it makes him dangerous and unstable. The point of the sexy bad boy is that he's loving and tender to the girl who finally captures his heart, and will do anything to protect her. Kind of defeats the purpose when the girl actually needs to be protected from him, eh?

I just couldn't get into this book. Mostly it's my fault: I'm burnt out on paranormal romances. 
 But it's also a little bit the books fault because I'm tired of books with smart, generally reasonable, heroines who seem to completely lose their minds and fall for not only a dangerous guy who spells trouble with a capital T (no, really, Nora says that in the book more or less in those words), but a dangerous guy who spells trouble and starts off by acting like a complete jerk. The idea of a girl not being attracted to any of the local boys only to become attracted to an outsider jerk is troubling and problematic on many levels outside of the realm of this actual story. 
 Aside from that, and again this is something I should have known already, books about angels are necessarily religious because they borrow (duh) from biblical mythology and lore. Which is fine. But when you are not religious and don't have that foundation it tends to make for a problematic reading. I had similar problems with Halo by Alexandra Adornetto. 
 The writing here feels solid. There's suspense, action, Nora isn't completely annoying (except for the whole falling for a jerk thing), the book will have appeal--just not for me. 
 The book design is also worth mentioning. I don't love the cover but the fonts on the cover are very attractive and the book pages feature a reverse design with the title and author name at the bottom with the page numbers instead of the top.

Aside from the obvious parallels to Twilight--which, I might add, is a better written book than this one--Fitzpatrick shows a lack of subtlety that is both shocking and completely expected. The writing was poor--the book would have been better served with a third-person narration, in my opinion--and the obvious foreshadowing and heavy-handed use of irony were the feather in this ridiculously ugly cap. The moment of true "I give up" disgust, though, came when I paged through the book to the end and discovered that this Nora chick wasn't even smart enough to insist Patch change his name before laying hands on her. 
 What kind of a stupid name is Patch? 
 I am just so done.

Nora Grey does not want to be attracted to bad boy Patch. She simply cannot help herself. Ever since Coach paired the two of them together in Biology class Patch seems to show up wherever Nora goes. Her best friend Vee urges her to pursue the relationship. 
 When strange things begin happening to Nora she believes that Patch has something to do with it. She soon learns that Patch has a dark secret that puts her in serious danger. 
 I read the Twilight series about vampires. Now, I feel like I have read almost the same book, only with angels and not vampires. The similarities are a little too many for me to feel completely comfortable with. My favorite parts of this book were the pieces that strayed away from that same tired plot. 
 Do not take that as me saying I did not enjoy the book at all. The author's technique is solid and with most of the book being dialogue driven, it was a fast read. I believe I read it in just six hours. The tension between Nora and Patch is stimulating and enough to carry you through the story. The author has developed Nora into a strong young woman and you cannot help but like her. 
 I received an advance copy of this book for review and I have heard around the web that the ending is different in the final release. The ending I read felt a little rushed. There was plenty of build up about Patch's secret. In fact, I was not sure that I would learn as much as I did in the book. It looked like most of the answers would be delayed until another book. But, all was revealed rather quickly at the end. 
 I think this series has potential. I know a second book in the series is forthcoming. I really, really hope that it is not a stinker like New Moon. There are strong characters in place here, please give them a good story.
I liked it but I was just a little frustrated how I didn't know who was bad or good until the last quarter of the book, but I am looking forward to the next book.

HUSH, HUSH starts off with an intriguing prologue. After reading it I got really excited wondering how it would eventually tie into the story. 
 The major problem that I had with the book was the characters. I think that if the characters were written differently I would have liked the book more. Let's start with Patch. The story starts with him and Nora getting paired up as biology partners. I couldn't believe some of the things that he was saying to her. It's the first time they've ever talked and he's saying all these sexual things to her. Let's just say that Patch didn't leave a very good first impression on me. As the story went on, it became clear that Patch was not going to be a very likeable character. He has the mysterious, dark, brooding thing down pat but I also thought he was arrogant and a bit of a jerk. Nora and Patch do have a lot of sexual tension going on but I just didn't feel the chemistry between the two. It wasn't believable to me because I couldn't see how Nora could have fallen for someone like Patch. Also Nora's best friend Vee really annoyed me. I don't know why Nora would be friends with her. I didn't think she was a good friend. She wouldn't listen to Nora, she didn't trust her and she just wouldn't shut up. She just can't keep her mouth shut and is always saying things without thinking. 
 The story had a lot of mystery and suspense. I couldn't figure out who was after Nora and for what purpose. Some of the things that Nora went through were pretty scary and had me turning the pages to see what would happen next. From the way the book ended, it'd be interesting to see what's in store for Nora and Patch. The second book CRESCENDO comes out later this year and I'm curious to see how the story will progress.

 I libri nel mondo sono tantissimi ed e impossibile contarli o leggerli tutti, ma da quel poco che ho letto io ci sono varie tipologie di libri. Ci sono i libri belli dai quali non vorresti staccarti mai, i libri carini che ti hanno fatto ridere, i libri con potenziale ma non utilizzato al meglio, libri che non ti lasciano nulla e libri pessimi che non avresti mai voluto leggere, nemmeno nel duemilamai. 
 "Il bacio dell'angelo caduto" e un libro confusionario e che non sono riuscita a capire al cento per cento. 
 Nora Grey e una ragazza tranquilla che conduce una vita tranquilla in una cittadina americana tranquilla. E' sistematica, non varca mai i limiti che sua madre le impone e le piacciono le stesse cose di sempre. 
 Da quando e morto il padre ha avuto un po' di problemi psicologici dovuti al trauma che le si era creato, ha avuto difficolta a portare avanti la sua normalita ed e costretta a vivere quasi da sola, senza una mamma che puo accudirla perche deve lavorare per guadagnare i soldi persi e senza un padre che non puo tornare indietro. 
 All'esistenza monotona di Nora viene aggiunto un largo sorriso da Vee, la sua migliore amica o "gemella", come la presenta lei, con la quale passa tantissimo tempo. Con Vee va a fare shopping, con Vee va a scuola, con Vee esce e con Vee e seduta nelle ore di biologia del suo liceo. 
 Quando un giorno il coach/prof-di-educazione-sessuale decide di stravolgere la classe e cambiare i posti, anche la vita di Nora viene stravolta da Patch Cipriano, il suo nuovo compagno di banco, il ragazzo nuovo tutto fascino ed arroganza che lei non puo sopportare. 
 Per Nora stare accanto all'insopportabile Patch e uno sfinimento e oltre le ore di biologia scolastiche non vuole assolutamente vederlo. Per Patch sembra essere tutto un gioco e vuole passare piu tempo possibile con la sua compagna di banco tutta gambe. 
 Tra doveri, fraintendimenti e sentimenti silenziosi Patch e Nora passano piu tempo insieme del previsto, ma non e mai abbastanza per Nora per riuscire a capire com'e fatto Patch realmente. 
 Nora ha moltissimi pensieri tra la testa fra Patch e le cose strane che le stanno accadendo da quando due strani ragazzi, Jules ed Elliot, sono entrati nella sua vita e sembrano non volersene andare. 
 La vita di Nora e a repentaglio ed ha bisogno di tutta la forza possibile, tutta la mente e tutti i pensieri per poter affrontare rivelazioni sconcertanti, mozzafiato ed incredibili, avvenimenti crudeli e che le faranno affiorare ricordi che non avrebbe mai piu voluto vedere o toccare. 
 La Fitzpatrick sa di certo come trattenere i lettori incollati al suo romanzo dato che ho divorato questo libro in due giorni e tutto d'un fiato, ma non sa certamente dosare le informazioni, i particolari e gli elementi aggiuntivi ma inutili. Durante la lettura avevo il naso incollato alle pagine, ma non riuscivo a incastrare tutti i pezzi del puzzle perche quest'ultimo era davvero piccolo ma i pezzi erano fin troppi. 
 Il suo stile e nella norma e fluido, anche molto limpido, ma niente di speciale, niente che potesse rimanermi impresso nella memoria e nel cuore. I suoi personaggi e la sua storia sono carini, ma appunto non riescono a lasciarmi nulla se non l'amaro in bocca per aver letto un libro semplice senza che mi strappassi i capelli per l'amore.
