 That demend illusive Pimpernel" The Scarlet Pimpernel by Emmuska Orczy 
 This sure sounds like a remake! I'll be interested to see what Cameron does with it.

Ok, so I actually really enjoyed this book. The plot was interesting, if a little predictable, but I liked it. There was enough suspense to keep me interested. And I Loved Renee. Best and most interesting character in the whole book. The traitor in the end came out of left field. Only complaint was the world building. I liked the premise, but wanted it explained more. What explanation there was is very confusing. Overall definitely recommend.

My first thoughts on this book was that it was interesting enough to keep me reading, but dull enough that it felt like the story was dragging. Around the halfway mark though, I was ready to stab myself in the face because I couldn't take it anymore. This was honestly painful to get through. It wasn't so much that the story was outright boring. The issue was that nothing seemed to happen for long lengths of time and when stuff did finally happen it wasn't exciting at all. I'm sorry, but it shouldn't take nearly half of the book for the story to actually go somewhere. I wanted there to be less of the romance and more of the revolution/fighting against the government type of things. There was one part I got to where Sophia was fascinated by the fact that Rene's hair "felt like hair" and I was so close to quitting the book and never picking it up again. 
 I was never able to connect with the majority of the characters because they were either annoying or had no personality. There was something unlikeable about Sophia to me. She didn't choose to be the Rook because she had a strong sense of justice. She was basically doing it because she was bored and wanted more excitement in her life. Her personality was kind of off-putting. Also, for someone renowned for breaking into dangerous prisons, she was a bit of a crappy spy. She was constantly doing things without checking to make sure it was safe and no one was watching or following her. Renee was a bit bland for a love interest. I was so irritated by the non-stop references to his fire-blue eyes and I seriously didn't need to hear about it every couple paragraphs. As for Spear, I did like him at first, but I hated how the author decided to turn him into this possessive attempted murderer . Also, LeBlanc made for a crappy villain. I didn't like the whole Goddess thing. He would go on these longwinded speeches about the goddess Fate and I honestly had no clue what he was talking about half of the time. The one character I truly liked was Tom, but he was barely there. 
 Overall, this was disappointing. The idea was great, but the execution was terrible. I slogged through this 500 page book, only to be left feeling like I'd wasted my time. Admittedly, the last chunk was a little quicker to get through. That said, I was just expecting much more out of the final action sequences than what I actually got.

I flew though the first 50% of the book but the last 50% took me about 10 days to finish. Despite this I quite liked the book, I just felt it could have been better if about 100 pages had been edited out. Overall, I just didn't love the story as much as I thought I would at the beginning.
I really loved this book by the end. The characters were alive and vivid. It took me a while longer than usual to get into it and be absorbed by the story, but by midway I couldn't put it down!
Wasn't very interesting. Couldn't muster the strength to even get past page 60.
Good book. Lots of suspense and twists but slow at times.

i am here to spread awareness about the curse of the dystopian retelling. signs a novel has the curse include: shoddy worldbuilding that is supposed to be overlooked because it is a retelling, predictable and annoying love triangle, poorly done homages to the source material, attempt at religious themes that end up being comical, references and analogies that don't make sense in a dystopian setting, no resolution to the actual background plot about the dystopian world and how it is trying to "rebuild" because after all who cares about that when u can end the book with which love interest the mc ends up with instead. this curse has claimed many victims, and rook is no exception. 
 i really did try to give this book the benefit of the doubt even though my intuition was telling me otherwise, but as usual my intuition was right (damn me for being enticed by it being a scarlet pimpernel retelling) . like most dystopian novels the world building was atrocious, and it was especially bad because the only time the setting was truly explained was in the back of the book in the authors note. this is one of the cardinal sins for me, needless to say i was not happy. the villain was thinner than paper, and his scenes were so bland. i cannot begin to explain how truly bland and transparent they were. now, if you know me then you know how much i love fate vs free will. this book attempted at fate vs free will mixed with religious themes, and it really fell short. whenever someone went off about Fate i just thought "ummm okay" and tried to forget the meaningless monologues about Fate because they obviously had no real importance. there was nothing really unique about this book and i snoozed my way through it. i suppose i can see why some people would enjoy it or whatever, but i can't watch yet another book fall victim to the curse of the dystopian retelling..... oh well

I quite enjoyed this one. A dystopian tale that is actually a retelling of "The Scarlet Pimpernel".A strong female protagonist and a lot of good action. There was a love story worked into this one but it was done very well in a YA offering; very age appropriate.

I agree with the other reviewers that this book felt long. There were some places where the story dragged a bit, but I think that has more to do with trying to fit everything into a standalone novel rather than dividing up a story into two or three books. 
 I found the setting of the story to be quite interesting and not often explored in YA books. The story is set in the future in what's left of Paris. There's been a shift in the world axis, or something along those lines, and technology as we know if no longer exists and people have been reduced to living like they did in the Dark Ages. Things like satellites, CDs, and plastic bottles can be highly valued and are mysterious objects in this future. Having possession of such or anything to do with a "reliance" on technology can also get someone executed at the guillotine. 
 I'm undecided on the writing style. At times the switching back-and-forth from all the different characters did provide insight on what was happening, but there seemed to be too much reliance on this third-person POV to move the plot along. I think it's the transitioning between these POVs that got to be a bit grating about halfway through the novel. It's fine when you borrow a sentence from one POV to another, but when you're constantly doing it, it just throws a reader out of the story. 
 The story overall was decent, and I love the growth between Sophia Bellamy and Rene Hasard and their love for each other in the book, so I have no qualms with the loveline. However, this might be the first time that an author wrote the childhood best friend character into such a crazy, unlikable one. Spear, yes, this is the name of the character, was fine at the beginning of the book, but turned into that nice guy-type person who you wished would get captured and executed. 
 Overall, the story turned out fine in the end and one of my favourites scenes was near the end in the dining room where there nine characters where going about in confusion about what was happening.
A solid 3.5. I wish the author gave more back grounds/detail about the dystopian society and the Great Death! Good story!
I enjoyed reading this.

I can't comment on how well Rook works as a retelling, since I'm not at all familiar with the story it's based on. But I can say that I was completely bored by it. The world is absolutely fantastic and fascinating, but it's wasted on characters with no personality and a plot that just drags on and on. It took me about 150 pages to even get settled into the story, since nothing was happening, and even then it didn't hold my interest. I only perked up when there was more world-building! 
 Rook did not engage me at all. Most of what I was reading simply didn't stick, and I found myself rereading many pages because I didn't know what had just happened. I also just thought the plot was dull. Sophia is the Red Rook; she frees prisoners from the cells beneath Paris. I don't have a clue why there are so many people who need to be freed though. Was it explained? I honestly don't know. Maybe it was just corrupt government, or convenience. Anyway. Her brother is arrested for being the Red Rook and she obviously now has to save him before he's executed. I didn't care about her brother at all. I was never given a reason to. This made it hard to care about the plot at all. 
 As for the world of Rook, it is amazing! It totally reads like a Historical, but it's actually futuristic. It doesn't say exactly how far into the future, but it's after an event known as the Great Death. Basically, there was a polar shift, solar storms killed a bunch of people, then technology failed, and more people died because of their dependence on technology. Now, machines are outlawed and humans live a simpler life. I loved when things from today were mentioned and the characters had no clue about it, or they've heard stories from grandparents and think they're ridiculous. Like CDs containing thousands of pictures and words! Impossible! It was so great! 
 I really, really loved the world of Rook and really, really wished some other story had taken place in it. I just did not care about any of these people! I didn't understand why they were doing what they did! Everyone is lying to everyone, or thinking everyone is lying to them. And it was just not interesting. There was also a problem with repetition, mainly with conversations between Sophia and her fiance. Their first languages are not the same and he was constantly saying the typical "How you say..." before saying anything. It got old fast, especially since she never did that when they spoke his language instead. 
 Read more of my reviews at Pinkindle Reads & Reviews.
It was alright, not much world building and I didn't connect with the characters as much as I wanted.

I took a risk with this one, because I love the story of the Scarlet Pimpernel and I was in the mood for a rompish, lighter read. Scarlet Pimpernel re-telling sounded perfect. 
 So, I am sighing in bland disappointment. It wasn't blazingly awful, but it wasn't good, and it suffered from a lot of the pervasive flaws found in so many YA books these days (I'm super picky about YA and this is why.) 
 1. eye-rolling romance that could have been good if it wasn't all about "his EYES" "his HAIR" and generally lacking depth and development. 
 2. A potentially interesting Dystopian concept which never explores the possibilities, complexities, or implications of the setting that has been created. It's all window dressing. 
 3. A genderswap (the Scarlet Pimpernel...aka Red Rook...is a girl) that is supposed to be innovative but is actually just more of the same. All the retellings have girls in the main roles if they weren't in the main roles already. Genderswaping isn't enough to make the story good. It really isn't. 
 4. So many details that sound like half the other YA books out there. An anti-technology dystopian future (so that it actually looks like the past). Tossed out phrases like "the Time Before" because apparently nobody kept any history at all, and they have no idea what happened or what life was like before the nebulous apocalyptic event (except, in this case, they have a book that tells them how people dressed during the French revolution). We have good records for a couple of thousands of years, and a pretty good idea of how people lived for a couple thousand beyond that. We've had devastating wars and devastating losses of history (Library of Alexandria anyone?) and we still know a lot about the last few thousand years. If people are alive, they know SOME history. 
 Aside from this, the book got right tedious at the end. I actually started out enjoying it. It had potential. But I skimmed hard those last hundred pages. I tried not to at first, because I'm anti-skimming, but there were all these superfluous storylines that I didn't really care about (her father's estate, her father potentially going to jail...he was a non-character for the most part. The childhood friend that wanted to marry her. The love interest's mother being weird and mysterious for silly reasons AFTER THE CLIMAX OF THE BOOK). 
 I wish the book had explored the FASCINATING dynamics of the French Revolution, even if it was in a dystopian setting. I mean it's a common people's revolution against an excessive, privileged, neglectful ruling class (read: something that sounds very noble) that turned so brutally bloody and oppressive and resulted in a dictatorship (as most revolutions--even noble ones--do). But all that was glossed over, given a few scant sentences, and I realize that the author wasn't even dealing with that really. I'm not trying to knock a book for not being something it was never meant to be and it's not like the source material was a deep, deep, pensive work either. But, again...sigh. I just did not enjoy it. Nothing breached the surface, except some nice, vivid scenery once or twice. And the scene where the heroine was injured was okay too. I liked that one. 
 Side-note: I kept picturing the villain, Le Blanc, as Ian Mckellan because he plays Chauvelin in the film version. 
 This actually didn't work because the villain was weird and had this whole "he made up a cult and believes it and is probably insane" thing going on which doesn't really fit with Chauvelin's character at all.

The story plot was good, I enjoyed the adventure and suspense in this book. But the thing I loved most was how the characters were built up, with each their own personalities, and such beautiful images were created from the text. I rate this book 4.5/5 for the beautiful characters, and the beautiful romance.

This book was a struggle to get through. I actually almost put it down several times. However, I made myself power through. And I'm glad I did. The last 150 pages or so were well-paced and worth it, but the beginning was slow and convoluted. Know that you're in it for the long haul, and you'll be better prepared.

Ugh, so I made a major mistake before reading this book, one I usually do not make because I know better. I read other people's reviews after I bought it! I know. Bad, bad, bad. Reviews will never stop me from reading a book I am really interested, honestly, they do not even color my perception of other books, but for some reason after reading a review I put off reading the book I purchased. When I say put off, I mean sometimes for years. Now, I only put this one off for about two months, but still. 
 Going into "Rook," I thought I would either love it or hate it, as the reviews on it were very polarizing, yet I felt myself really torn. I didn't outright hate it (I wouldn't take the time to post a review if I did) but I wasn't "OMG in love." I've got some thoughts: 
 What I liked: Anyone who has read one of my reviews knows I am very character driven. If I can't connect with a character, especially the MC, I'm not interested. I could connect with Sophia Bellamy. Sophia is the type of female character who thinks she knows what she wants, drives into action without weighing the consequences, and generally makes a mountain out of a mole hill. Usually these types of characters drive me nuts, even if they are very reminiscent of real life teens. What drew me to Sophia was that she was written as this bigger than life character, yet she had zero special powers. Sure she was semi-decent in a fight, but her greatest strength proved to be playing on other underestimation of her. She drove the book for me. I longed to see how she would out-think her enemies. Which brings me to my next point on the multiple POVs. Cameron begins the book from Sophia's POV then throughout allows glimpses into secondary characters minds. Originally, this confused me since there seems to be no rhyme or reason to the switch, but soon I understand it's to allow the reader in on information that is necessary for the pacing of the book, especially towards the end when each character is working off their own agenda. Now, I'm a big fan of romance. Honestly, if a book does not have any I'm usually not interested in reading it. While the romance in Rook was a little light for me, Rene, Sophia's fiance was the whew kind of hot. A little dangerous, a little chivalrous, and a perfect match to keep our adventure seeking heroine on her feet. Plus, he was French and accents are tres magnifique. 
 What I didn't like: The world building. This is a dysptopian novel, where the government is bad, but the world building did not really explain the revolts. The book is set in futuristic Europe with France and the UK featured prominently, yet I did not really get a sense of what came before to make everyone so touchy. Parts of the revolution at the center of the book paralleled The Reign of Terror from the France of several hundred (or in this case thousands) of years prior. The world building felt lazy. In a dystopian novel where a character is fighting against an evil government, I need to understand the cause/effect, and here I just didn't. There were points where Cameron dropped breadcrumbs of knowledge, but I'm not interested in spending my time trying to piece those measly crumbs together. Certain parts of the novel just felt stagnant to me and at times I struggled to remain interested. 
 Overall, this book is not the best example of dystopian out there. The characters are very dynamic and Cameron really took the time to think about her form, yet I struggled being invested in a world I felt I knew little about. It's a fun read but at times I struggles to finish. 2.5/5
Will be reviewing it on my blog, link will be posted soon.

Well, that was a disappointing read. The book opens with a break out of prison, but because I never got the chance to connect with the characters, I didn't really care. Thus began a long 400-page journey. There didn't seem to be much backstory or character development. And half the times, other characters were popping up, and I had no idea who they were. 
 The breaks within the chapters were also rather annoying. Scene cuts that work beautifully for movies, on occasion and when handled properly, do not work for books. There were plenty of times when phrases were repeated and items popped up when the scenes had nothing to do with each other, making the book more annoying than connected. My eyes hurt. 
 I gave this book 2/5 stars for its attempt at a story but lack of character development and interesting plot.

This book is a take on Scarlet Pimpernel set in a post apocalyptic Earth where Parisians live in the catacombs. 
 I have to say before I go any further that Scarlet Pimpernel is one of my ALL TIME FAVORITE books. Like ever. And I really liked Across a Star-Swept Sea so I didn't know how this would hold up. 
 And it ends up being pretty ok. Like I liked it. I'd recommend for those into the genre. I probably wouldn't ever re-read. That makes it 3 stars. Maybe 3.5. (I just now decided the star rating. That was a glimpse into my thought process.) 
 This book is much, much darker than The Scarlet Pimpernel. At first I thought it was going to be a chapter by chapter recreation (and I wouldn't have liked that.) But after the first few chapters, it is very different from SP. I liked the direction it took. The whole thing was very creative. 
 I liked the relationship between Sophia and her brother. And I really like how the relationship slowly progresses between her and Rene. 
 I love Rene and his family. 
 I liked the crazy antagonist. Zealots always make the scariest villains. 
 There were just a lot of fun things about this book. But I think it dragged. It was probably a little too long and a little too many pov switches.

reference_books.title: The Secret History of the Pink Carnation (Pink Carnation, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Chick lit meets the Harlequin romance novel. A friend gave this to me as a good escapist read, but frankly I'm too much of a snob to have been able to really enjoy it. I did appreciate the fact that for once, an American-girl-in-Britain novel (the framing device is a Harvard grad student doing PhD research abroad) didn't constantly invoke Jane Austen.

reference_books.title: The Magicians (The Magicians #1)
reference_books.review_text: Harry Potter + Chronicles of Narnia + The Emperor's Children = not my thing. It was a fast read, at least. But there was absolutely no payoff in the ending.

reference_books.title: A Gate at the Stairs
reference_books.review_text: 2.5. I love her short stories, but this was just lost on me.

reference_books.title: Then We Came to the End
reference_books.review_text: It only took me four months to finish this one. I actually enjoyed it quite a bit while I was reading it, but it wasn't compelling enough to make me want to pick it up again once I stopped. A spot-on portrait of cubicle culture, but nothing that really stayed with me.

reference_books.title: A Thousand Splendid Suns
reference_books.review_text: 2.5 stars. Interesting look at the treatment of women in Afghanistan before and after the Taliban, but a little too melodramatic for my taste.

reference_books.title: Stitches
reference_books.review_text: I found the ending to be a little too tidy (the "art gave me a voice" metaphor, although appropriate here, was almost too easy) but the book was tightly written (a common complaint I have with the few graphic novels I've read is that they don't seem well planned or edited) and the art was absolutely amazing. I will definitely be looking forward to his next book.

reference_books.title: The Witches of Eastwick (Eastwick #1)
reference_books.review_text: Well written. Hated every minute of it. That averages out to two stars, right?

reference_books.title: The Pact
reference_books.review_text: I read this one for my sister-in-law, who loves JP. Not quite as manipulative as My Sister's Keeper (the thought of which still induces spontaneous ranting) but the "surprise" twists got old really fast.

book_a.title: The Uncommon Reader
book_a.user_review: The queen of England discovers books when she happens upon a traveling library parked near the palace. This novella is a really quick read (one lunch hour and a train ride), and very funny. I'm definitely going to check out Bennett's other books, including The History Boys.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is a charming little tea cake of a book - sweet, delicious and ultimately a treat, not a meal. The character of the queen is delightful; a sensible no-nonsense woman who becomes familiar with the ways of the world only when she begins reading books (I found myself hoping that the real Queen has exactly this temperament), and the details about the oddness of her world are lovely, and of course, any reader would be delighted by how much reverence is given to reading itself. I found myself starting to wish there was more given of the world outside of the queens books, but that being said this is a lovely little book.
Meh! :/

not a fan of British lit i found this book endearing . just the mention of a traveling library brought back memories of days long ago. not only did i use a bookmobile, i also drove one.i have come to a conclusion- either you love reading or you do not. there is no in between. but to have a life with no reading i can not imagine.

A cute little story that essentially celebrates the lure of reading. The Queen (of England) notices a mobile library parked in front of the palace when her dogs make a fuss about it; she checks out a book out of politeness and things develop from there...
Cute novella about what might happen if the queen of England fell in love with reading.

A book about the pleasure of reading, so it's why I was attracted to it at first, and as it is the Queen of England who is the protagonist, I thought is could be really funny. 
 A pleasant, short and easy read, this book is indeed funny and witty too. It is simple but interesting. 
 The Queen discovers reading and becomes passionate about it. This doesn't please everyone at Buckingham as she grows more and more bored by her duties - which she used to enjoy. 
 Good and very humorous at the beginning but I lost a little of the excitement towards the end. Anyway, I liked it - it reads like a little treat to enjoy with a cup of tea.

1.5 stars. 
 I feel oddly guilty writing this review as a book lover. However, I found this book about loving books unbearably pretentious and wholly tedious to read. The constant name dropping of authors and the (blatant) implication that readers see the world not only differently, but also exponentially more accurately than nonreaders, was akin to reading self affirmation phrases over and over again. The entire book suggests that the reader, as a reader, is making himself or herself better than everyone else by engaging in the activity of reading. It felt to me like being constantly and heavy handedly bludgeoned by "intellectual" propaganda. And while I may agree with some of the ideas behind this propaganda, I find a book, not literary or enlightening in the least, about those ideas to be almost offensive. 
 For those who thought this was just a "fun" little read, I felt it missed the mark there too.

Several people had recommended The Uncommon Reader to me over the last year, but somehow I only got around to it this morning. Don't be as slow as I was! The idea is very simple - the Queen gets hooked on reading - but Bennett handles it perfectly. It's a delight, and takes about an hour to read. 
 Maybe a short extract will do the job:'Exploded?' said the Queen. 'But it was Anita Brookner.' 
 The young man, who seemed remarkably undeferential, said security may have thought it was a device. 
 The Queen said: 'Yes. That is exactly what it is. A book is a device to ignite the imagination.' 
 The footman said: 'Yes, ma'am.' 
 It was as if he was talking to his grandmother, and not for the first time the Queen was made unpleasantly aware of the hostility her reading seemed to arouse. 
 'Very well,' she said. 'Then you should inform security that I shall expect to find another copy of the same book, vetted and explosive-free, waiting on my desk tomorrow morning. And another thing. The carriage cushions are filthy. Look at my gloves.' Her Majesty departed. 
 'Fuck,' said the footman, fishing out the book from where he had been told to hide it down the front of his breeches.
Boring and overly quaint. I had to make myself read this. It seemed much longer than 58 pages. And the ending, blech, give me a break...
Call me stupid if you like but this book had way too many dictionary on hand words. It really took me out of the story to have to look so many up.

This little book is a cute story about what happened to the Queen of England when her dogs led her to the book mobile and she discovered she had an interest in reading. I'm not sure what Queen Elizabeth thinks of having a fictional book written about her, but I'd like to think she would get a kick out of the direction this book went.

In my opinion, this novella didn't quite live up to the incredible reviews it has received (as a 25 year old, I don't think I quite fit the target age demographic, if that says anything). I won't deny that the book was certainly good, but slightly duller and less "spoofy" than the reviews I'd seen had led to believe. 
 The titular "reader" of this book is none other than Queen Elizabeth II. One day she follows her barking Pekineses into a portable library, and ends up borrowing what turns out to be a barely tolerable book out of politeness (the author had been made a Dame of the Empire , so the Queen assumed it had to be good, since she had already done the honors...). Luckily, the Queen's second book is a page turner, and thus she becomes an insatiable reader, to the dismay of the household, equerry, and the Duke. There are some amusing tidbits here: the queen perfects the art of waving from a coach while hiding a book beneath the window. She hires a homosexual kitchen boy--another patron of the portable library--to suggest new reads (some of the titles he suggests one would imagine to be quite shocking to a grandmotherly monarch). It is obvious that the queen begins to think about her duty and her people in new ways as she is exposed to literature (which says much for the value of fiction), although I imagine that using a contemporary and very much alive public figure as the central character would prevent the author from trying anything drastic, unexpected, or *gasp* the least bit unflattering. Which he doesn't. An interesting premise, some humor, a very understated (borderline yawn-provoking) style, and nothing earthshaking. Unlike the books the queen devours, I don't feel this one changed me all that much.

This novella is an interesting and thought-provoking read. It makes the reader think about the daily life of a monarch and what might happen if the normal routines were changed radically by the Queen taking up reading in a serious way. Alan Bennett is such an interesting writer - I plan to read his novella "The Lady in the Van" next.

Cute is the word that springs to mind when describing this book. The Queen of England has stumbled upon reading and is devouring books left and right. Reading has taken over her life, much to the chagrin of those around her. 
 I made the mistake of reading this book in increments. It is very short and I think it would be best to read it in one sitting. I ended up losing a lot of momentum by breaking it up. I did love the queen's voice though.

"Alteta Sa cititoare" este o cartulie extrem de simpatica, o declaratie de dragoste facuta lecturii si o analiza amuzanta a acestei pasiuni care schimba oamenii si perceptia lor asupra lumii. Intr-un exercitiu de imaginatie plin de umor, Alan Bennett nascoceste o poveste despre cum septuagenara Regina a Marii Britanii este prinsa in mrejele literaturii. Nu ca inainte nu ar fi citit, insa pana atunci o facuse impartial si detasat, caci o persoana de statului ei nu isi putea permite sa aiba hobby-uri si preferinte. 
 Intr-o zi, Regina descopera o biblioteca itineranta si imprumuta o carte de Ivy Compton-Burnett, mai mult de complezenta. Romanul i se pare cam arid, dar mai imprumuta unul, The Pursuit of Love a lui Nancy Mitford. Ei, si prin intermediul acestei carti intrezareste placerile lecturii, ceva ce nu mai traise niciodata pana atunci. Daca ar fi dat peste o alta carte nesatisfacatoare, cariera ei de cititor novice s-ar fi incheiat rapid, dar asa, ea continua sa citeasca si o face peste tot, inclusiv in convoiul oficial, unde isi perfectioneaza tehnica de a flutura din mana in timp ce ochii devoreaza cartea tinuta sub nivelul geamului. 
 Desi rudele sunt bucuroase ca nu mai sunt tinute din scurt, noua pasiune a Maiestatii Sale nu este privita cu ochi buni de catre ofiterii Casei Regale, pentru ca Regina isi neglijeaza indatoririle, nu mai da atentie garderobei si - o tragedie - incepe sa intarzie. La intalnirile cu supusii, ea nu mai pune vechile si banalele intrebari, ci se intereseaza ce citesc oamenii in acel moment. Anturajul vede semnele senilitatii acolo unde, de fapt, sunt semnele sensibilitatii. Secretarul personal nu poate intelege de ce Regina, care a vazut intreaga lume, are acum nevoie de o umila reflectie a ei. Dupa parerea lui, noua preocupare a Maiestatii Sale este o retragere din lume, un act egoist si usor snob, caci, desi oamenii stiu sa citeasca, cei mai multi dintre ei nu o fac. 
 Oare cine va castiga batalia? Indatoririle de regina? Cartile? Sau poate o a treia cale ce decurge ca o urmare fireasca (pentru unii) a lecturii? Dupa parerea lui Alan Bennett, cititul este inactiv, iar pentru o fire activa ca a Reginei, exista o singura solutie... 
 Daca aveti chef de citit mai mult decat atat, varianta lunga se afla pe blog: 
 http://lecturile-emei.blogspot.ro/201...

This was an amusing read but not as sharp or witty as I was hoping it would be. Ultimately however it is much more subversive than expected and this is what elevated it from 3 to 4 stars for me. 
 On discovering a latent love of literature, the queen also discovers that despite being considered one of the most powerful women in the world she has no voice of her own. She is merely a figurehead who is trotted out to open hospitals, chat with the common folk and give occasional speeches, but it soon dawns on her that no one really listens to what she says. She becomes increasingly interested in discussing authors and ideas, but the only person she has to share her thoughts with is Norman, a young man who she meets on her visit to a mobile library parked in the palace grounds. Most people around her are hostile to her new-found passion for the written word and they do not want to see the queen expressing an opinion or stepping beyond the boundaries set for her by history and tradition. She begins to rebel against these restrictions, first in very subtle ways and then more openly. 
 One of the great strengths of the book is its potrayal of the cultural backwardness of the political leaders of today which I feel is very realistic. The ignorant prime minster whose eyes glaze over whenever the queen tries to discuss literature with him is a thinly veiled portrayal of Tony Blair. I loved the ending when she announces to her Privy Council that she is going to write a book of her own and quickly disabuses them of the hope that it will be something uncontroversial. "I was thinking of something more radical. More.....challenging." 
 She later tells the gathered minsters: "One has met and indeed entertained many visiting heads of state, some of them unspeakable crooks and blackguards....One has given one's white-gloved hand to hands that were steeped in blood and conversed politely with men who have personally slaughtered children. One has waded through excrement and gore....Sometimes one has felt like a scented candle, sent in to perfume a regime, or aerate a policy, monarchy these days just a government-issue deoderant." 
 Yes indeed! One can only hope the real queen has an opportunity to peruse this quirky little book with a deep message at its heart.

Absolutely lovely: what would happen if the Queen of England (not known to be a reader) stumbled upon the local mobile library van and took a book to be polite and found herself reading more and more and turned into a bibliophile. 
 Alan Bennett doesn't have a mean bone in his body (I think) and his portrait of Queen Elizabeth is both respectful and fond while he spins a good yarn and reminds us all of what it is to be a reader.
This was such a surprising read!

In this short hilarious novella, Bennett imagines a scenario where, following some errant Corgis, the Queen discovers the mobile library parked in the grounds of Buckingham Palace and feels obliged to borrow a book, out of courtesy. One book leads to another (as books will tend to do), and before long, Elizabeth has developed a serious reading habit. The consequences are far-reaching, and very funny. 
 Within this framework, Bennett provides an incisive (and entertaining) exploration of the power of reading. Despite being one of the planet's most-traveled inhabitants, her majesty's horizons are broadened in ways she could not have imagined. 
 A satisfying, highly entertaining, read.

I read the most part of this short novel one Saturday afternoon in the cafe of the Museum of Modern Art in Forde. This very funny little piece is one of those novels you can read everywhere. Hilarious scenes and social criticisms are numerous, and we often laugh aloud of the discoveries of this Queen who starts reading so late in life. On a national scope, the changes that her realisations bring are enormous: every book she reads opens her eyes on the harsh social realities the people she helps to govern live under; she sees her advisers' mistakes, she reflects on conjugal life and her own role. 
 You should read it! 
 On the personal side, it is true that I always wondered about the kind of books the Queen of England was reading. Or if she could grasp the nuances, understand the references... Rumour has it that the Royal Family believes that their country smells like paint, because all the buildings are rehabilitated and given a fresh coat of paint before they visit... maybe she reads books about cars, as she was a mechanic during the war. Who knows? 
 ^v^v^v^v^v^v^v^v^v^ 
 J'ai lu une bonne partie de ce roman tres court un samedi apres-midi, dans le cafe du musee d'art moderne de Forde. Cette petite oeuvre tres drole fait partie de ces romans que l'on peut lire partout, les situations cocasses et les critiques sociales fusent, et l'on rit parfois tout haut, de cette reine qui decouvre les joies de la lecture tard dans sa vie. Les changements que ses prises de conscience apportent au pays sont enormes; chaque livre lu lui ouvre les yeux sur les realites sociales de la nation qu'elle aide a gouverner, sur les travers de ses conseillers, sur sa vie conjugale, et sur son propre role. 
 Je vous en recommande vivement la lecture, en VO! 
 Pour l'anecdote, c'est vrai que je me suis toujours demandee quels etaient les livres que pouvait bien lire la reine d'Angleterre. Si elle pouvait en saisir les nuances, en comprendre les references... La rumeur surannee voudrait que la famille royale croie que leur pays sente la peinture, car les batiments sont repeints et retapes avant une visite... peut-etre lit-elle des livres de mecanique, puisqu'elle etait mecanicienne pendant la guerre. Qui sait ?
While it had its witty moments, The Uncommon Reader failed to capture my interest and I often found myself bored by it.

A sweet charming little (120 pgs) book about Queen Elizabeth discovering reading for pleasure. I haven't read anything from Bennett before and I'll have to check him out. I wonder what the Queen and Charles thought of this! "One" can wonder! Actually, much of what the Queen goes through is how Goodreads has influenced me--I'm reading much more and understanding more, and attempting harder books. But I haven't started writing yet! I had to google the term "bowled a googly."
Eh. Found it kind of pointless.

Queen Elizabeth II discovers a bookmobile and the pleasures of reading novels: something she hadn't done previously. How this changes the monarch's behavior doesn't sit well with her prime minister. As usual with playwright Bennett, there is a delicious twist at the end. 
 This witty novella offers a treat for the book lover or word collector.

It is not a book to read after catching up on A Song of Ice and Fire and being in the middle of The Lunar Chronicles (obviously a condition that is very specific to me at the moment). I think it's worth a reread in my future.
Fist book I've read about the queen, bless her soul. You see her falling in love with reading. Quite an Uncommon reader, and a lovely story that reminds you why you love books.
Elizabeth the reader -- and the palace doesn't like it. The book is a trifle, but good for after dinner.
Elizabeth II becomes a reader, from Dick Francis to Marcel Proust, with unexpected and comic consequences. Short and cute.
This was a delightful read.

This isn't a book I would normally pick up, but I read it since it is this month's book club selection. I enjoyed the author's writing style and found the story cute. Although the book focuses on the queen as a reader, I still don't feel I got to know her that well as a character.
Reading can be a dangerous and life-changing hobby, even on the most sheltered life. A very amusing read, and it's lovely to imagine Her Majesty might take the hint.
Just lovely.
It was cute - it probably deserves more stars but it's just not the style of book that I really enjoy

"The Uncommon Reader" turns on the fateful coincidence of the Queen walking her corgis at the same time as the mobile library van makes its weekly visit to Buckingham Palace. An encounter with the library van driver and Norman, one of her kitchen hands, leads to the Queen borrowing a book. She has never before read for pleasure, but one thing leads to another, and before long she is neglecting her schedule to cram in a few more minutes' reading. And then ... but that would be telling.[return][return]This book is light, playful, beautifully written, and sympathetic to the Queen and the peculiar life she is obliged to lead. Alan Bennett gets in several digs at the British literary scene (and there are undoubtedly many more than I spotted) and Palace life, and includes a delicately unflattering portrait of the Queen's unnamed Prime Minister, who seemed to my jaundiced eye to bear a distinct resemblance to Tony Blair.[return][return]Whether you love or loathe the monarchy, the British political system, library vans, or corgis, so long as you love reading, you will enjoy "The Uncommon Reader".

A lovely short book for lovers of literature. This book imagines the Queen stumbling upon a traveling library and falling in love with books and reading. The newfound passion leads to changes in the Queen's habits and her general demeanor/thoughts. I often find I want books to keep going but, somehow, this one felt satisfying even though I spent only one evening with it. Four stars easily, maybe even a little higher.
Easy short read. Nothing special but a good mindless meandering for a free moment. Mildly comic.

I avoided this book for some time, under the vague impression that it was all about how special books are, how special people who read books are, how Great Literature can change your life. I hate stuff like that. The Uncommon Reader does have that theme, but in a completely unpretentious, charming way. The Queen is a wonderful character and the book is very funny. I love how disturbed the palace staff is by the Queen's new hobby - they can't quite figure out why reading books is a problem, but are sure that it is. And, of course, as the Queen grows bored with her duties and expands her mental horizons, they are proven perfectly correct.
A delightfully fun short little read. The queen come to like books and this is what happens when one finds out they enjoy reading.
Liked the last line best, otherwise an easy, light read. Great palate cleanser after reading a few "heavy" books in a row

I thought this would be much more delightful than it was. I love to read books about the benefits and joys of reading. To be reminded that enjoying a book is like therapy that takes away any guilt I have for wanting to read more and more. So this little novella was a disappointment in that it shared very little on the inner changes happening to the Queen as she took up reading. It was, at times, humorous, but not witty enough for me to recommend to anyone else.

The Queen (yes, that's the Queen of England) unexpectedly drops into a bookmobile and unexpectedly develops a love, a passion for reading. 
 That's the whole plot behind this tiny novel. 
 And does she ever become a better person. She found, as she read more and more, that she could put herself into the place of someone else, that she could understand the feelings of others. "'At the risk of sounding like a piece of steak,' she said, 'they tenderize one.'" 
 She grows to loath her other duties. Her meetings with the Prime Minister are tedious. She finds reading the opposite of briefings, she tells him. "Briefing closes down a subject, reading opens it up." 
 But no one likes her reading. Reading made others uneasy. A conversation between the Queen and her private secretary: 
 "'I feel, ma'am, that while not exactly elitist it sends the wrong message. It tends to exclude.' 
 'Exclude? Surely most people can read?' 
 'They can read, ma'am, but I'm not sure that they do.'" 
 In the end, the Queen turns to writing, but books have had their say. 
 A fun little story for those of us who love books.

This was one of those boring books which you wish you did not start. I was trying to finish it as soon as I could. Probably, this is book is written as a specialty for british people. But for me it was not funny, not sarcastic, not interesting.

There is one specific thing that Alan Bennett did when he came up with the idea of 'The Uncommon Reader' which automatically secured him a high rating from his readership: he decided to write a book about a person who falls utterly in love with reading. After all any bookworm will always love a story portraying people who fall under the spell of literature since he/she will recognize him/herself on every page of the book. More importantly he/she will feel understood and welcome in this fictive world inhabited by one or several likeminded people. In the end the quality of such books do not really weigh in on the feedback that much anymore since as a reader one is too emotionally involved and cannot but publicly praise these books. 
 This being said, Bennett made us all a favour by creating this quick read in which every sentence seems to fall in place perfectly: the story moves on fast and straightforward, the main character (the Queen), whom we love from the beginning for her charming and witty as well as slightly rebellious nature becomes increasingly dear to us (so do some of the side characters) and generally - reading this book is a pure joyride! Although the narrative seems rather simple and superficial at first, driven by the occasional very quotable passages on reading ("What she was finding also was how one book led to another, doors kept opening wherever she turned and the days weren't long enough for the reading she wanted to do."), further reflection on this work leads to the realization that it actually touches upon many serious and complex topics. For instance since the protagonist is the Queen the book casually illuminates certain characteristics of monarchy that are worth discussing in further detail: The public image a royalty such as the Queen is expected to convey (her obsessive reading is discussed by her advisers in terms of its influence on the Nation's politics) and how the relationship between a monarch and his/her nation can become alarmingly dehumanized (e.g. how the Queen and her advisers talk about 'human resources' when they talk about their employees and how the Queen feels as if she's not allowed to be a human being in the sense that she can have hobbies and show weaknesses). 
 The topic which is addressed the most however is a reflection on the perception and role of books. On one hand we have the Queen at the beginning of the book who tells us that reading is basically for people who have too much time on their hands, people tend to be rather passive and who do not pursue a career, like her. At first she takes a certain pride in her lack of time for hobbies, including reading, by stating several times that one has no time for these things and that she is a 'doer' and anyway, more important matters need to be tended to. However as she gets into the habit of reading and is slowly getting a better understanding of the literary world, even dipping her toe into the discipline of literary criticism, she starts judging people based on their literary knowledge. This development of her character represents two specific but opposed stigmas that have recurrently been put on reading: that books (especially fiction) is for the idler versus the notion that literature is elitist, reserved for the academics and scholars. The Queen alternates between seeing reading as a way of acquiring new knowledge about other lives, other worlds versus doing it merely for pleasure whereas Sir Kevin states that reading should be a public duty. Finally our dear protagonist goes on to find out that reading has made her more empathetic, more sensible "because she knew more of people's feelings than she used to and could put herself in someone else's place". Other interesting themes that are touched upon in this short novel are e.g. the overwhelming feeling or even shame an avid reader may encounter when confronted with the pressure of all the (supposedly important) works that one needs to have read and the notion that a book and the characters in it are not to be confused with the writer and his/her personality, which is another topic that can be analysed in lengthy discussions. 
 Be that as it may I extremely enjoyed reading 'An uncommon reader', Bennett's humour being right up my alley, and am glad to have taken some interesting reflections from it. In the Queen's words: "Books have enriched my life in a way that one could never have expected" and, from bookworm to bookworm, I fully agree with her on that one.

sample_reviews.review_text: Guess was over hyped. ENjoyable and interesting, but not as good as I had expected. The theological aspects were not as convincing as could be - though the society with 2 intellegent species definitely made for an interesting aspect.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This is basically a book about mans faith in God and what happens when this is pushed to the limits. The story is wrapped round a Jesuit space expedition to Alpha Centauri and a 'first encounter situation'. I guess overall the story was okay, but it's been done better. As with many books nowadays this would had more impact crystallized into a short story. A lot of the book is fluff that only points out the weaknesses, not the strengths. The author would have been much better off not trying to tell this as a science fiction story. 
 Most reviews point out how great the characterizations are. True, they were pretty good but very inconstant. At the beginning of the book the main characters are all brilliant and there doesn't seem to be anything they cannot do. (The idea of a small group of people equipping the first expedition to another star reminded me of E. E. Doc Smith's Skylark of Space, but that's another issue.) But later, when they get to the alien world, they make some unbelievably stupid mistakes. Even on my own planet I know not to eat strange things. On an alien planet they go right ahead and try it. They were not even smart enough to bring along some mice for testing. 
 Most of the really bad decisions were only there for a convenient way to move the plot in a certain direction. For me that's just bad writing. But the really killer of the book was the actual moment of first contact. The main Jesuit Priest uses slight of hand tricks to make it look to the aliens like he's making flowers appear out of thin air. Now why would he do that? A few chapters on there is some discussion that they don't want to mislead the aliens into believing they are gods or starting a cargo cult. Make your mind up! After that point I was glad that Sandoz got what he had coming to him. Perhaps that simple act of deception is why God punished him. 
 The science in this book was mostly nonsense. Even worse than bad it made statements about existing technology they anyone can look up and see is just plain false. For an academic writer like the author, this lack of research is just mind boggling and inexcusable. For example: She constantly refers to the Alpha Centauri system as having 3 suns, which is technically true, but the 3rd red dwarf star is 0.2 ly from the other two. That would make it appear as a bright star, not a red sun. The Jesuits accelerate an asteroid using a mass driver and the stated logic is 'the bigger the asteroid is, the more fuel they have'. Perhaps she should look up Newton's Laws. And they can also 'circle at 0.2g' using a mass driver... :) 
 There was a good underlying story but I was constantly taken out of it by eye rolling bad science, stupid character decisions and contrived coincidences. I know that in real life the Jesuits are considered the scholars and scientists of the papal world, but this book made them look like arrogant, ignorant idiots. 
 2 stars and I'm being VERY generous.

 I don't remember much else about this book, probably because it was so scarring I blocked it from memory. I'm pretty sure the teacher only made us read it because we went to a Jesuit high school.

I read this book solely based on the fact that it is about Jesuits in space. That's all I knew about it. I have gone to Jesuit schools for more than five years and love Ignatian theology, and the thought of Jesuits in space was too amusing to pass up. Unfortunately, I probably shouldn't read books based on amusing topic instead of recommendations and good reviews. This book was strangely written and switched POV at strange and confusing moments. Really important facts were mentioned as if I were already supposed to know them and scenes that would have been really interesting only took a few pages, or were skipped entirely, while pages and pages and pages were given to sort-of-plots that didn't go anywhere. The alien species were a disappointment, which is pretty horrible for a sci-fi space book. Most of all, I could hardly figure out what "deep questions" this book was trying to discuss. I dunno. It was a strange and unfulfilling read.

I'm still a little confused how I feel about this book. I normally don't read a lot of science fiction, but this was my book club's pick for the month. The plot of the book focuses on a Jesuit priest, Emilio Sandoz, who is the only survivor of a space exploration to find an alien species. The story jumps back and forth between the time spent on the planet and when he returns home and is reporting to his superiors. Emilio finds his faith severely tested when things go terribly wrong. You will read the whole book to find out what has happened to him and rest of the crew. 
 It took almost half of the book before I really got into the story. I almost gave up on it, and that is why I'm giving it only a three star rating. However, the writing is excellent, the characters are great, and once the story really got going I enjoyed it. Overall I'm giving it 3.5 stars.
This was a curious combination of sci-fi and religion. It doesn't reach any definite conclusions.

The Sparrow is amoving and philosophical science fiction novel. It is not hardcore science fiction, so if you don't normally read sci-fi, don't let that stop you from reading this wonderful book. This tale of the people of Earth's first contact with an alien species has a different twist than typical alien encounter stories--- in this book the mission to the alien planet is not sponsored or undertaken by a space program, it is sponsored by the Vatican.

The only reason I decided to read this book is because someone mentioned that this is a first contact story very similar to 
 Father Dure's story in Hyperion (one of my favorite books ever). This book really isn't similar in that Dure's story reads 
 more like a horror mystery. The cruciform still makes me lay awake at night sometimes. 
 The Sparrow reads more like a tragedy. We are told from the very beginning that this mission WILL fail and everyone except 
 for Emilio Sandoz WILL die. Then, Mary Doria Russell decides to really turn the knife by working backwards and introducing 
 us to the most loveable cast of characters you will ever meet in a science fiction novel. This genre often gets critisized 
 for being too "cold" and "sterile", with characters often taking a backseat to the great ideas and inventions the author 
 gets to play with. This is sometimes a fair critisicm, but the next time I hear that, I will just throw my copy of The 
 Sparrow in their face. These people are really really nice, good people, if I ever have a daugther I'd marry her to Jimmy and if I had a son, I would love it if he hooked up with Sofia.. and some really bad shit happens to them. There really 
 isn't an evil protagonist in the entire story.. oh wait, there is an evil disgusting horrible son of a bitch called the 
 Universe. Man I hate that guy. Responsible for me having to wake up early in the morning, paying taxes, genoicde, WWII, 
 and Emilio Sandoz's horrific experience on Rakhat. 
 Do you remember the last awkward date you had? Remember how it felt wondering if they were interpreting you correctly, if 
 you were understanding them, the doubt, the nervousness, the wonder, the thrill, trepidation, fear ect. Multiply that by a 
 thousand and you get Peter Watts' Blindsight. Multiply by a hundred and you get The Sparrow. Imagine that date goes well. 
 You have finally found another child of God as you yourself are (of course), and then imagine someone telling you after the date that you have been dating that species's equivalent of a dog or cow, and the real intelligence and the only reason 
 you decided to to Alpha Centauri on a hopped up asteroid to go on this date is because of a hunter species transmitting "songs" about 
 dominating and raping an inferior species into interstellar space. 
 And this merry band of Jesuits (and non believers) go 
 skipping down the road over. I didn't cry reading this book as some I've read claim they have, but to tell you the truth, 
 if I sit down long enough and think about it, I will also break down and cry because it is fucking heartbreaking. 
 This is Mary Doria Russell's first novel, and I give her mad props. You hard sci fi junkies will find problems with it. The 
 whole jerry rigging an asteroid and flinging it across interstellar space like it was no big thing will frustrate you. As 
 bizarre as the aliens are, they are anthropomorphisized quite a bit. After Blindsight, I will never look at a depiction of 
 an alien quite the same way, because the truth is, when two species meet, it wont really be like Cortez meeting the Aztecs 
 in the 1400s (as the analogy seems to be in this book), it will be more like Guillermo meets a lizard and tries to explain 
 Moby Dick to it. 
 I could keep going, but if you're still wasting your time reading this, I think you should read better reviews that cover 
 all of the bases, and read this damn book if you can.
