This very highly acclaimed novel had been on my list since I read a review on it in rec.arts.books, probably back in 1996. It was pretty good and I was pretty engrossed for half of it...the second half 
 still kept my attention because the structure of the story demands you stay with it: you know something terrible has happened after the lone survivor of a Jesuit mission to a discovered planet returns to 
 tell his story. 
 Frankly though, I found it a little dry in parts, but not so bad that I didn't want to continue. Besides, I'm a sucker for religion/sci-fi mixes.

I enjoyed "The Sparrow" quite a bit. It's not a perfect book, but it's certainly a page-turner, and I appreciate the incorporation of a religious journey into an SF setting. It's not something I see very often - generally, religion pops up in SF and fantasy that focus on diplomacy, but usually as constructed religions and not real ones - and Russell treated it with respect and insight. 
 The premise is first contact, but the story is the story of Emilio Sandoz, a Jesuit priest who becomes part of a Jesuit-led mission to visit an alien planet and contact its inhabitants. The aliens are discovered through a broadcast of a strange song, picked up at an observatory near Sandoz's hometown. Jimmy Quinn, the tech who first recognized the signal for what it was, calls his friend Sandoz and their friends - George, an engineer; Anne, a doctor and George's wife; and Sofia, an expert in AI tech - to listen to it before he tells anyone else. And the group of them realize that together, they have most of the expertise needed to lead an expedition to this planet. Sandoz's Jesuit superiors immediately back the idea (after all, Jesuits were quick to send priests to the New World after its discovery), add a few more priests, and send them off without alerting anyone else on the planet. 
 Russell takes her time developing the relationships between the characters; it's many chapters in before we even reach the alien broadcast. But we know right off the bat that Emilio is the only survivor of this mission, because the story of the origin of the mission alternates with chapters about Emilio's recovery post-mission. He is under the care of the Vatican and the Pope himself, and it's clear some sort of scandalous tragedy has occurred. Emilio is blamed for causing the near eradication of the Jesuits because of something he did 17 years prior (Earth time; for Emilio, not a year has passed since he began his journey back to Earth) on Rakhat, the alien planet. Emilio is a tortured man, emotionally, spiritually, and physically. One of the strengths of the novel is its ability to pack an emotional wallop and nowhere is it more powerful than in Emilio's haunted dreams, his anger toward his superiors, his brooding melancholy. And interspersing Emilio's return with the story of his life before the mission is heartbreaking; what could have made this spirited, witty, charming, devoted priest the miserably broken wreck he has become? 
 I'm a little ambivalent about Russell's ability to write characters. One one hand, Emilio and his makeshift family are warm and hilarious and likeable, and Emilio's misery is believable and evocative. On the other hand, there are many moments of unbelievable wittiness, dialogue too prescient and on-the-nose for any real human to have spoken it, and characters with phenomenal skill sets and personalities but no apparent flaws. Everyone is too good at everything and gets along too well, but damn, is it a pleasure to read. (Joss Whedon comes to mind when I think about the dialogue/characters - everything's too smart for its own good.) 
 I have generally similar but better feelings about the Big Questions that the novel tries to tackle. Russell goes after one of the biggest ones: How does one deal with God in a universe where horrible things happen? In answering that, she also takes on questions on what it means to be a priest, on the value of family, on colonialism. While the characters can feel over-the-top, Russell deals with these Big Questions wisely: by making them small. Nowhere does anyone claim to know the answers for anyone else. Instead, they lend an ear and offer their own contributions. Sandoz tells Anne, who is a firm atheist, that God is "in the why" of things, but his own faith is shaken (to put it mildly) when the "why" is horrific. There are definitely some moments where answers are provided a little too neatly, but again, those answers tend to hold for one character (and are often overturned later in the story). I've read some reviews that indicate the story is too much an argument for belief in God, but I see almost the opposite. If anything, it's an argument for the theraputic benefits of confession. 
 Most of my problems with the book, from characterization to lack of subtlety, are related to the prose, which isn't always elegant but is generally crafted to make the biggest emotional impact. One person described the book as "emotionally manipulative," which I would say is pretty accurate - but isn't that the point of books? To manipulate the reader's emotions? It's not the deepest book I've read, but it has substance and it was engaging, so overall I consider its obviousness an asset, not a hindrance. 
 There were two small aspects of the book that bothered me unrelated to the above. First off, the aliens and the alien world. There are some beautiful descriptions of the alien planet and the time they spent acclimating to the world is absolutely my favorite part of the book. It's pure joy. But. It's not a particularly alien alien world. I wrote that off as "well, in this novel, God probably exists, and the similarities are a pretty good indicator that God created all life," so it wasn't a huge problem for me. The other issue is the construction of many of the interpersonal/group interactions. There are so many times where characters react to something and then we see what they react to. Paraphrased example: 
 "Something that is a complete non-sequitur," Anne said in response to the look on the other characters' faces that had not been described prior to just now. 
 It made it some scenes difficult to follow, and it wasn't necessary except to show how quick-witted and insightful the characters are, which we already know through many other means. 
 One thing I did love above everything else - Russell's insight into the life of a priest and the psychology of priesthood. She handles doubt and conflict respectfully and creates a portrait of Emilio Sandoz, sinner and possible saint, that represents religion well. 
 Overall: engaging, tear-jerking, emotional, fun read, even if you don't like SF or priests. I'm usually one to encourage "killing your darlings" and this book is largely Russell's darlings (she admits to basing Anne and George on herself and her husband) but it works. Not a masterpiece of prose, but maybe one of heart.
Unbelievably bad. Awful writing and worse science. It was impossible to suspend disbelief with this novel.

Wow, the last few chapters were kind of intense and powerful. Not a light/easy read overall. Not typical science fiction, but the author draws you into the world, and the characters are alive. The author approached the religious aspects genuinely and in a manner that should be relatable to all. 
 I'm not sure I'm exactly eager to read the sequel, but I expect I will at some point.
This is a character driven first-contact SF story written by an anthropologist with a philosophical bent. Amazing work. It is in my top 5 list.

I didn't finish The Sparrow, so I can't say definitively that my review of it is entirely fair. I found the premise of the story different and exciting, and felt the writing early on was promising. I liked a few of the characters - and loved Anne - but as I went along, the plot didn't meet with my expectations when I'd picked up the book. I felt it would have been much better as a relationship story without any of the sci-fi. Lastly, the pacing didn't work for me. I felt it didn't move quickly enough in key places to hold my interest and keep me reading into the next chapter. Russel has some beautiful ideas, and several of her scenes are obviously master-craft stuff - this just wasn't my favorite.
Very powerful. Not sure I could appreciate some of the more intense religious conversations between the characters. But overall, very moving and unforgettable.
One of the most well-written, mentally provocative, suspenseful, dark, and elegant science fiction books I've ever had the joy to read.

Thought provoking. 
 A sci_fi story about a Jesuit mission to another world, that becomes a first contact story unlike ant I have ever read before. This book discusses ideas in faith, anthropology, biology and many other topics. The characters are good and the plot and discovery are motivating. 
 It really makes you think...

Despite the adulation this book has received, and the fact that I thought that the first fifty pages of this book were the beginnings of a masterpiece, I began to see the author as ego-tripping and manipulative, loading the book with hip irony and heavy, hair-splitting religious questions that everyone somehow wants to believe are real and important. I just don't see it. I do not trust this author, especially after considering the numerous above it all, flip, ego-tripping quotes from her web site and from interviews. As an example, in the afterword: "I am the author and outrank him." 
 There is something about this book that truly disturbs me. The adulation for its "cleverness," "breadth of knowledge," and "imagination" all seem false. The first fifty pages are brilliant, the last thirty do a good job wrapping the novel up, but throughout the middle I was in a hurry to get this book over with. 
 People seem to want to believe that this book is raising important questions. But the glib statements of belief or disbelief in God, the characters mouthing the author's philosophy, are telling, not showing. There is some "good showing" in this story but also way too much "telling." 
 The religious questions are boring. Emilio and Anne are narcissists, always supremely concerned with what's happening to them or in proving their world view. The author seems out to manipulate, pull heartstrings via the use of irony. The irony of the singing really being pornography. Emilio killing the little Runa girl. How ironic! 
 Ending a section of fiction is like cinching a rope, using a valid emotion or meaning. But too many authors cinch the ending of a section with irony, which is beginning to become a tired cliche. It's cheap, easy, in tune with current American culture, and always seeks to be the flip and easy last word. Surely this is not what real life is all about. 
 The suspense over the condition of Emilio's hands and the true meaning of the singing is contrived. That Sofia manages to trigger a planet-wide revolution with one statement about unequal numbers of oppressor versus oppressed seems a further irony--ain't we humans just so bad that we can screw things up so badly? 
 If the singing is so important, it should have been described in much richer detail as opposed to "just can't be compared to Earth singing." I admit this would be a challenge, but other writers have spent a lot of time describing what music sounds like and means to them. The author may be thinking that a method of "little or no description" may evoke a special awe, but it definitely doesn't work. 
 The Janata are barely described, and the Runa fall too easily back on "cat like." These are shortcuts to describing something that should be truly alien. 
 The author lost me at Jimmy showing others his results and immediately these folks start thinking of asteroid travel, as if this were a Hardy Boys adventure. But: 
 *	It would have taken a very long time to figure out what was received. 
 *	These particular folks would not have been chosen, even by the Jesuits. 
 *	Other space agencies would have moved faster. 
 *	Their contact methods are amateurish. 
 It would have been better to omit a science fiction plot entirely, or to go beyond into pure fantasy worlds. The author obviously knows a great deal in her paleoanthropology and linguistics fields, knows a lot about the Jesuits, but it seems that she "did research" for asteroids, Alpha Centauri, and other sf aspects, but not enough to have mastered it and made it real. 
 Emilio and Sofia seemed real, at least at first, until Emilio devolved into his boring religious bleatings and Sonia inexplicably cast off her childhood trauma and became a loving housewife, but the others just stand for the author's thoughts, or are used as plot convenience. D.W. is an irritating cliche. Anne seems a flattering self-image for the author. Anne is always right, witty, and full of a false-sounding gusto that, again, is somehow always right. She has no shadow. 
 The two societies repeat the Eloi and Morlocks in Wells' The Time Machine. 
 I don't say a powerful writing could not have been brought out of this. But I feel this author is talking down to the reader, attempting to impress with her cleverness and her knowledge, and browbeating with her religious opinions. Why on earth would I want to suffer a repeat of that with the sequel?

I finished this book some time ago, but I remember being disappointed and even disgusted, and not by the disturbing and gratuitous scenes toward the end. The world of Rakhat was indeed interesting, scientifically speaking I guess, but I found her exploration of the 'deeper questions' she raises to be shallow and facile at best. 
 I found her characters to be very grating, particularly the doctor and her husband, whose names I don't remember. I recall skipping over a lot of dialogue...nobody talks like that, among other issues. 
 An infinitely better exploration of why god allows humans to suffer is to be found in The Brothers Karamazov...if you are truly interested in thoughtful and profound literature on this question, that would be my recommendation. Some might argue that i shouldn't hold sci fi to high literary standards....but I do have high hopes for the genre and love to read well-written sci fi. I think Ms. Russell should stick to worldbuilding, as she does a fair job of this. She should have jettisoned the rest...as another reviewer mentioned, the questions she raises deserve much better than she gave them.

The Sparrow is one of those books that, even weeks after completion, sticks with you. And not because some jackass coated it in glue and threw it at my face. No, not this time. 
 The Sparrow starts out with a grotesque mystery that hooked me and never let go. The alternating timeline approach worked splendidly, building a "present" world on the consequences of the "flashbacks," all along giving you revelations that effect your perceptions of these flashbacks. Characters were incredibly well developed, feeling like real people within pages of their introductions. Feeling such instant affection for these characters only compounds the ever present dread the reader experiences as they learn the character's fates early in the "present" timeline of the book. 
 The Sparrow, though, goes far beyond simply good storytelling and solid character. Its ideas on religion, on faith, on science, and on human needs and desires, are never condescending or preachy. They are simply ideas presented to the reader, allowing him or her to think about them and ponder them in their own time. Reading The Sparrow, I feel, is a very personal experience, which is what all great books are. And even if such heavy notions as God and Science do not interest you, there is a fantastic plot driving it all forward, with an ending so shocking I could scarecly believe what I was reading.

** spoiler alert ** 
 There were some really interesting creations in this book and exploration of alien life with evolutionary aspects. However there is a weird rape plot and it cracks me up that I had just explained to the bookstore person that I hated the Kite runner especially because of the weird rape scenes and how all the local housewives were raving about this book with a manipulative sexual scene and strange plot revolving around that. So then the guy recommended this book where it turns out the main character ( a priest) was raped by an alien, repeatedly. I couldn't stop laughing, I mean did he forget how it ended or did he do it on purpose, I'll never know. 
 This is an really freaky book.

i like books that take on characters that are more than either good or evil and complicated with complicated choices and rich histories and futures. and books that take on spirituality and god without playing dogmatic games or end with a checklist of how you should think=happy bruin. scifi in space. with jesuits. and forgiveness. and healing. i'm a fan. i read this book over and over again. one of my favorites.

I'm going to say it. This book is hard. It took me ages, partly because you know how it's going to end (sorta) and partly because some parts are so painful to read. Really horrific stuff. 
 But I liked it. Is that weird? 
 God. Just. God.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was very hesitant to read this because I usually really don't care for science fiction and also almost always really really hate mysteries. This was pretty enjoyable, though. I think it had some weak points, especially in Anne. There were some times when she was supposed to be funny that just seemed forced to me. Russel kept having these scenes where the characters where all laughing and could barely contain themselves. They didn't work. I wanted to call the author up and say, please stop telling me stuff is funny. It really isn't. It's like when someone tells you a story that they think is hilarious and they end up saying, "Well, I guess you had to be there." 
 The strength of the book was in the chapters that occur in Naples. Sandoz's slow revelations were excellent. The minor characters (all priests) were very real. 
 My major complaint about the book is Emilio's claim that God raped him. Yes, you read that right. Emilio is a priest who finally fully experiences God, but then things swiftly fall apart and he is ruined. I felt bad for him, I really did. But it seemed hypocritical. People get raped all the time. And every time, it's horrible. Emilio would never claim that God raped those people--they were raped, it was awful, but God has very little to do with it. What makes him so special? I'm struggling to articulate this correctly, and I don't want to seem like I am victim blaming or, you know, religious (I'm not. At all.). It just seems like Emilio always understood that evil exists, but was surprised when it happened to him. This annoyed me.

The elevator pitch is just funny: "Jesuits in Outer Space!" but this book is actually really interesting and smart. It makes a lot of sense to me to look at what happens to religious seekers when confronted with sentient life on other planets. The novel is more about trauma and recovery than it is about the alien culture, which was somewhat disappointing to me but made sense. I heard there's a sequel, which I'm excited about. So that tells you something.

Initially, it drew me in, but it soon became clear that the "meaning of life"questions raised by the author was driving the narrative rather than evolving from it. The characters devolved into caricatures, the dialogue became stilted and the plot forced to serve the intended philosophical vision. It became a morality tale rather than a modern novel.

The scientists are idiots, and here are the reasons why: 
 1. They went in search of an alien civilisation by -- literally -- flying in the general direction of Alpha Centauri. They figured out the exact location along the way. 
 2. They arrived at the alien planet, THEN attempted to figure out where to land their spacecraft. Imagine if NASA had done that for the moon landing in the 1960s. 
 3. They tested the edibility of alien vegetation and wildlife by EATING said alien vegetation and wildlife. 
 4. When someone died from the alien diet, our scientists couldn't quite figure out why. 
 5. They weren't able to return to their spaceship in orbit because someone literally used up the fuel in the lander just to show off to the leader of the team. 
 6. They didn't have a clue what to do upon meeting the aliens for the very first time. No SOPs, nothing. 
 7. They emerged out of the lander for the very first time, on an alien planet, without spacesuits. 
 8. They disregarded the possibility of contaminating the aliens with pathogens. 
 9. They disregarded the possibility of being INFECTED by alien pathogens. 
 10. They spent six weeks on an alien planet before one of them said, hey, maybe we should start planting our own food -- YOU THINK? 
 11. They plant human food on an alien planet and disregarded the possibility of destroying the local ecosystem. 
 12. They had no way to maintain radio contact with Earth, and shrugged it off because "everyone they loved was on the planet with them". 
 Most of the characters end up dead by the hands of the locals. This is not a spoiler. 
 They deserved to die, anyway. God damn idiots, all of them. 
 These 'scientists' are the dumbest characters in all of science fiction literature.

** spoiler alert ** 
 To those who are offended by profanity, I suggest you ignore the next sentence and proceed to the rest of the review. Honestly, for most of this book, all I could think was "come the fuck on?!" Not, mind you, because I was really impressed with the brilliant writing and marvelous lot, but because of precisely the opposite!!! 
 Let me provide a bit of explanation by providing a partial plot summary. 
 Let's go on a mission to an unknown planet! Coincidentally, our group is a handful of people, which includes a love triangle (!), and we are all qualified to take an asteroid to an unexplored planet financed by the Jesuits! Let's not test the air before we touch foot to the planet! Let's not try to contact the aliens before barging on to their planet! No need to test any blessed (hahaha!) thing because God has willed this mission! Let's roast some "green guys" and feed them to one of our PILOTS to see if it's poisonous and promptly gave the entire crew eat all kinds of stuff instead of waiting for a period of time! If someone dies, let's do an autopsy and get SUPER angry because the rest of the very tiny crew asks about the results of the autopsy! Let's just lay around on the ground, asleep without any protection at all! Let's not bother exploring or documenting anything, so we are super surprised there are two species on the planet! I'm best buds with these here aliens who happen to have one young translator who knows English! These aliens need to learn how to garden! Oopsie, that caused my alien buds to reproduce and get slaughtered and know I'm a concubine! 
 There is no question that some suspension of disbelief is required to enjoy science fiction (or even some general fiction). However, Ms. Russell is asking way too much out of this reader. 
 Every person on the mission frames everything with what we believe to be known on Earth without trying to be the eensiest but interested in being objective and observing. Here's an irritating sentence: 
 "The principle were the same: firm follows function, reach high for sunlight, strut your stuff to attract a mate, scatter lots of offspring or take good care of a previous few, warn predators that you're poisonous with bright colors or blend into the background to escape detection." 
 Fucking seriously?! 
 Sandoz is well-painted and the best thing about this claptrap, while other characters are one-dimensional. Anne and George are always HILARIOUS and she always cooks intricate meals based on a guests' ETHNICITY. Voelker is just plain sinister. Ed is super supportive and helpful in an aw-shucks way. 
 The author took over 400 pages to slap together a real mess. I should have believed my initial reaction to the first few pages where the author tried to wow the reader with the written equivalent of multi-camera shots, not really describing what's going on. The narrative gets a little more interesting for about 70 pages, but devolves into Dan Brown style schlock and never resurfaces. 
 Last year, I read "The Book of Strange New Things," by Michael Farber also about a man of God visiting a planet inhabited by aliens. It is so, so, so much better than "The Sparrow," so I recommend that to those who did and did not enjoy this book.

I somewhat enjoyed the story line but I do not like reading science fiction or religion much which about sums up the entirety of this novel. Russell is an amazing writer, but this just isn't the genre for me.

Mary Doria Russell gives the reader a wild ride through time, space, and to the core of each individual. Her characters must face the questions of extra-planetary life (something we may or may not encounter, who knows) and supernatural life (the question of religion and worldview, which surely every human must wrestle with). 
 Although I don't read much in the way of science fiction, I do enjoy watching it, so that likely frames my experience of this novel (and it's sequel, Children of God). Additionally, I read the second book first, and so already knew the main plot twists. It's a testament to the author's skill in creating a future, alien, other-world that is not only believable but compelling enough to get me to read book #1 even after knowing all the main points. To be sure, the richness and depth of the first book would lead me to recommend others read them in order.

I had to look up some reviews of this book because I disliked it so much. Clearly many others really like it but no part of the story is the kind of thing I like and the writing seemed sloppy. The book may have seemed better if it were 100 pages less. I'm more than willing to accept that I'm wrong but can sum it up thusly: aliens rape Jesuit priest. My advice, don't bother.

Not one sparrow can fall to the ground without your Father knowing it - Matthew 10:29 
 "But the sparrow still falls": 
 is the response of one character in Russell's excellent sci-fi novel "The Sparrow". Unfamiliar with this quote from Matthew, I did not understand why the novel was titled as it was. Near the final page of the novel, though, the biblical quote and its thought-provoking response are included and the author's choice of title became clear. This is not to say that the underlying questions concerning the nature of God and whether such a creature exists were not both obvious much earlier in the story. 
 Regardless of the fact that the basic premise of this novel features a Jesuit mission ("for the Glory of God") to the nearby planet of Rakhat to meet our newly discovered interstellar neighbors, "The Sparrow" is not a "Christian" novel. In fact, the author's treatment of God is wholly ungenerous. Or perhaps God ought not be asked to come to account for the events the excruciating and life-altering events that the visiting humans experience on Rakhat. This is, I believe, the central question of the novel. 
 Far from being simply a meditation on the nature of God, though, Russell's debut novel also stands out as a very entertaining and believable story of sentient life on another planet. Russell's Rakhat, while populated with creatures intelligent and otherwise all very different from life on Earth is equal in measure to the beauty and terror that a visitor might encounter were they to visit us from another planet. The "people" that the humans meet, the way that human action on a non-human planet impacts events there (as Jesuit missions have historically impacted foreign cultures), and the very detailed anthropological study of extra-terrestrial social and linguistic practices make "The Sparrow" a highly engaging read whether the reader cares to entertain the proffered theological implications.
I loved this book so much! My only problem is that it wasn't long enough! The characters are wonderful and the story is heartbreaking but worth the ride
Jesuits in Space. Does it get any better?
Nope. Won't finish this. Boring predictable characters. Blah!

Be warned, this one starts out slow but will sneak up on you. 
 I really struggled through the beginning, varying between slight interest and floating away. In fact, I very nearly abandoned the book. Then, suddenly, I discovered that I was hooked. 
 I think my struggle was due in large parts to science fiction nature of the book, heavy on the science. In the end, however, the heavy science was part of what I enjoyed most about the book. The themes ran deep in this book, exploring relationships, philosophy, anthropology, linguistics....well, the list goes on and on. 
 The story unfolded in a series of flashbacks to the past interspersed with the present day struggle of the protagonist to deal with the past. Father Emilio Sandoz, a Jesuit priest, was the sole survivor of a missionary expedition to visit the first discovered interplanetary sentient life forms. He was found broken in body and soul only to face the ordeal of facing his Jesuit brotherhood's expectations for explanations that he'd rather avoid. 
 Ms. Russell pulled me through a myriad of emotions as I journeyed along with Sandoz throughout the story. The story was full of depth and complexity. The characters were very richly drawn with unique perspectives that often question today's socio-cultural status quo. However, this was accomplished with a subtle touch, rather than a sledge hammer. No, the hammer was saved for a much more poignant moment in the book, but you will have to discover that for yourself, potential reader. 
 If you find yourself struggling at the beginning, again, I reiterate, hang in there. The payoff is most definitely worth it.
I tried super hard. It was well-written and had potential to be good, but I just couldn't get myself to read. I can't waste my time on books this hard to read!

Based on subject matter alone--a small group from earth visits a planet after it's discovered to be transmitting radio signals--I would have expected to like this book. While there certainly are interesting parts, overall I was pretty disappointed, mostly because the book is framed almost entirely as an excuse to delve into the theological questions of the existence of God and the problem of evil. If those are questions that interest you, you'll probably enjoy this book, but for me they made finishing this book far too much of a chore.

The Sparrow feels like old-school, classic sci-fi. It reminded me of A Canticle for Leibowitz and A Fire Upon the Deep, both books I loved that combine big ideas, well-paced plots, and memorable characters. The Sparrow does the first two excellently, but falls somewhat short on character. Father Sandoz is a great character, but I found the other members of the crew much less interesting. Anne was just annoying.

One of those rare books that just demands to be read in one sitting, as it truly is impossible to put down at times. Engaged me from the start and took me on an amazing ride. Funny, moving, insightful and perhaps even touching the tragic, "The Sparrow" manages to paint a broad canvas of human emotion with its characters and situation, but does so in a restrained manner which makes them all the more human. A remarkable novel that demands, and deserves, multiple readings.
I'm abandoning this one. I'm almost halfway through but it just drag too much.

I read this after hearing about it on the "Books on the Nightstand". I did like this book and though I knew going in it was about Jesuit priests in space (I kid you not) having the first contact with an alien planet and race, I was still not expecting a huge underlying theme to be about faith in god. I am not religious at all (pretty much a flaming atheist), so some of that brought on some internal eye rolls, but I tried not to let it overshadow the book. Interesting commentary on our treatment of other people, other races, and other species..and though some of it may seem shocking there are an alarming number of parallels to present day life. the question is...do I read the sequel?

Jesuits in spaaaaaace! 
 This is what the book is about, but not what it's about. This is a thoughtful and brutal look at what it can mean to have faith. You will fall in love with the characters and they will break your heart. This book will stay with you.
Wow, a lot of people like this book.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This has taken me a while to realize what I found lacking in the book. So much of me wanted to like it, and at times I was really engrossed. Mary Russel writes a "good" yet finally unbelievable story, and no, I'm not talking about the space travel. She is highly intelligent and gifted. Mary Russel really knows about the technical issues of which she writes. Her resume is truly impressive. She is a scientist and it comes through. Her story is well written and follows a group of mostly believable souls. Yet there was a gnawing suspicion that something wasn't quite on while I read and it's sat uneasily with me until this morning. 
 In the end I can't believe the characters. They are too idealized, as if created in a lab. Each one has a unique story and they are well realized to a point, and if they remained in the lab I could go along with how they react to circumstances. However, they are not in the lab but in a realized world where hard things befall them and that's the great failing of this book. Each character is too idealized-don't let me get started on Ann. They are all brilliant and almost perfect in their respective fields. Yes, they do make mistakes but the mistakes are almost too perfect, and yes, the issue of Providence could be argued here but it's how the characters are built and presented that offsets the Providence argument. 
 The characters deal with prostitution, rape, death, "cannabalism", slavery, conversion, atheism, death, in ways that are in small portions believable but the main course rings oh so false. The white heat that these boiling issues naturally create and stir is not there for the most part. It's like intillectuals in a parlor discussing crack babies when having just watched a special on PBS. The feeling and depth is not there. 
 The reactions are too steeped in liberal rhetoric, in wishful thinking of an idealized man or woman to be taken with any depth. And in the end I just can't be won over by this story. 
 The author's real believability comes through in the science and fields of study but in fields of white heated pain and human discovery she lacks real exploration. 
 This is no existential masterpiece.

At the beginning, the author is completely honest with the readers. Sandoz is the only member of the first expedition to an inhabited alien planet that survived and returned home. The tale is told in retrospect, and yet the reader still gets invested in the characters and is shocked when they die. Alternating between the story of what happened and the story of Sandoz's grief, survivor's guilt, and PTSD, this is a well-crafted yet painful story. I wanted to keep reading even as I was saddened by favorite characters' deaths and by Sandoz's crisis of faith. It is a very good book, but I don't know if I would recommend it due to the deep sadness it evoked.

It was great until the ending...the author was the one putting the turtles on the fence posts...and she was cruel about it. The writing was great, but the ending was so horrible, I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone.

reference_books.title: NOT A BOOK: Amazingly Broken
reference_books.review_text: this book is stolen from two other authors- do not read

reference_books.title: Lover Unleashed (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #9)
reference_books.review_text: Of all the BDB books, this is probably the most disappointing in terms of story development. The story of Payne and Manny was pretty lukewarm compared to the previous books, and the stories of the other Brothers didn't really move forward by much (okay, a biggie seems to be getting resolved with V, but then, there's the rest of the book ). JR Ward is a good writer, so even this tepid book is better than the offerings of a lot of other writers, but by the standard she sets for herself in the first 8 books, she falls short on this one.

reference_books.title: Dead Ice (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter, #24)
reference_books.review_text: This book was borrowed from my local Library. After reading the last LKH book, from the Merry series, I am beginning to think there comes a point when writing long-running series' when the author can get so caught up in re-hashing the prior books they lose the forward momentum in their current offering. Sadly this was a huge problem with her last book (the title I don't even remember anymore, sadly) and an annoyance with Dead Ice. With over 20 books in this series, it's pretty safe to assume the fans know the past plots and characters really well. This is one of the few authors I re-read, so the constant re-telling of the old story makes for more pages, but no story advancement-- We've been with you for two dozen books, Ms. Hamilton-- WE KNOW the ongoing story lines and the characters. I loved the return to animator roots, and the crazy challenges Anita had to deal with for her job- unfortunately, LKH has started to do the quick and tidy all-in-one-chapter-wrap ups of the police/animator threads, while endlessly drawing out the relational threads. I'd love to see more balance. In this book, there was a lot of emphasis on Anita's looks and self-image, which was fine, if not somewhat overdone. And the polyamorous aspects, while not as focused as some reviews led me to believe, seemed to be drawn out with no relevance to the current book (yes there will be more-- for all the pages, there was no real advancement of the ongoing relationship threads). Now we get to my peeve-- what the heck is going on with the editing? OMGoodness! The editor should be fired - the grammar was shoddy, and if I had a nickle for every time the word "that" was used, I'd be taking myself out for a surf and turf dinner. I expect better from this experienced author. I'm also glad I can check these out at the library, as the last few LKH novels have not been ones I'll re-read, let alone pay for to add to my extensive collection of Anita Black and Merideth books.

reference_books.title: Crown of Midnight (Throne of Glass, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I checked this book out from my local library. I immediately started this book after completing book 1, Throne of Glass. While I found the first third of the book to be a slower pace (comparatively), it did pick up with some great action and intrigue. It is unfortunate, I'd guessed the 'great reveal' at the end of the book, but it was still an enjoyable plot. Looking forward to book three.

reference_books.title: Lover Mine (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #8)
reference_books.review_text: Okay- New favorite BDB book here! I loved the prior book and professed it to be my favorite to date, but I finally read Xhex and John Matthew (Tehrror)'s story, and it was as great as I hoped it would be. I love strong female characters, and they don't get much tougher than your typical sympath assassin. This was a great story that focused so much on the protagonist's storyline, and really helped progress the total BDB saga also... and might I add, some very satisfactory payback in this book! Go team! I also was happy to see the storyline move forward with regards to Tohrment's health (mental and physical) and the Quinn-Blay relationships. Some hiccups with the facts not matching with prior books, but guess what- one of the best things about the JR Ward books is the layers of complexity and multiple storylines; I'm willing to forgive a few discrepancies for the sake of an otherwise satisfactory read! I'm going through library books at this point, but I will be purchasing the whole series in paperback- they're keepers!

reference_books.title: Magic Breaks (Kate Daniels, #7)
reference_books.review_text: I checked Magic Breaks out from my local library. I must say, this had one of the better storylines, although there was so much going on I got lost and had to back track a few times. Great plot, consistent world-building, fun witty dialog (I love how droll Curran can be), and lots of action. Loved the ending (or is it a new beginning?)

reference_books.title: Vicious (Villains, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I checked Vicious out from my local library. Never in a million years would I have picked this book to read, but it was highly recommended on one of my favorite blogs as the bloggers Favorite Book of all Time. Yep- I had to check it out. This book is an exceptionally well written, evenly-paced story of good and evil-- or more correctly, the varying levels of evil, there's not much good to be had. The plot is terrific, completely unique with a perfect blend of twists, turns, and surprises to keep the reader glued to the page. This one is highly recommended for horror fans ala Stephen King, or eclectic readers who enjoy a great book, regardless of the genre.

reference_books.title: Empire of Storms (Throne of Glass, #5)
reference_books.review_text: I checked Empire of Storms out from my local library. Once again, Maas gives the reader another fast-paced thrill ride with enough twists and turns to qualify as a carnival attraction. I was on the edge of my seat as the already complex storyline got tighter and some unexpected reveals added to the tension. A killer ending leaves me anxious to get my hands on the next book. This is one of the great saga writers and the Glass Throne series gets top-rating from this reader. Highly recommended!

reference_books.title: One Foot in the Grave (Night Huntress, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This book is a perfect compliment to the way the first book ended. Excellent character development and storyline. I enjoy reading the banter and slang tossed around between characters, and the story is fun and pulls the reader in for the ride. Enjoy! This is a great book in a great series.

reference_books.title: Deadlocked (Sookie Stackhouse, #12)
reference_books.review_text:
Alrighty then, obviously the honeymoon is over, and Charlaine Harris no longer finds it worth her while to put out a decent Sookie Stackhouse book. I heard rumors that she had wanted to kill off Bill in the series but changed her mind per HBO/TrueBlood pressure. She should have just stopped or written her own story rather than pawn this lukewarm piece off on the fans. 
 The first 8 or 9 books of this series are terrific... then there was TrueBlood. I got bored by the last few books of the series as Harris seemed to start writing for the TV series rather than the fans. I hated how Sookie, who seems so level headed, kept bouncing around with the men in her life. First sign of trouble with Eric (who she's in a vampire marriage with) and she wants to bail on the relationship? We can all see Charlaine is setting Sookie up to move onto a new man (which I'm sure is what the networks will love... nothing like losing your moral compass and embracing promiscuity to boost ratings, right?) No more Charlaine Harris for me.

book_a.title: Silver Borne (Mercy Thompson, #5)
book_a.user_review: Mercy is a shape shifter coyote (4-legged weight of 30 lbs) living in Werewolf territory (4-legged weight somewhere between 150-200+ lbs) and trying to make a place for herself with the local pack. The fact this is written from a non-dominant perspective (you'll notice I didn't use the word submissive?)is probably why it took me so long to buy the first book. Oh silly me! I have obviously been conditioned by this genre to go for the kick#$$ Alpha females, forgetting that the real heroes are the ordinary ones that do extraordinary things. Mercy is brave, smart, and comfortable in her own skin (both forms). This series is a keeper.

sample_reviews.review_text: Suicide storyline really dragged this one out for me and I had to struggle to finish it. Mercy's interactions with the fairies seemed even more deus ex machina than usual. Weakest book so far by a mile.
my favorite so far!
I think it was around this book in the series that it started to lose me. Now, I only read out of compulsion.
This series is sinking fast.

I am a die-hard Mercy/Bran/Samuel/Adam fan, but I'm thinking that this installment in the series didn't quite hit as many buttons for me as the other books. 
 Dare I say it? The excitement was gone. The book hit my "adam/mercy" relationship button, my "cool werewolf" button with Samuel losing his will to live and being taken over by his wolf, but the side stuff with the pack interference with Mercy's place as mate to their alpha didn't quite satisfy me for some reason. 
 The fae big bad also wasn't quite as exciting as before, maybe because we've reached enough books now that we already know the vampires and the witches and the fae and the excitement of discovering them is no longer possible. 
 That said, I still am a loyal fan to the series, and the development of the relationship between Adam and Mercy (and seeing Adam vulnerable in so many ways) was terrific.

Another great book in the series. Mercy gets mixed up with the fae and the evil Fairy Queen in this one. Between saving others and saving herself she barely has a free moment. I love Adam's bond with Mercy. Very tender and sweet.

Back to the fae in this one. I like Zee's character a lot, so more of him is always better. Some pretty horrible things happen in this book that may forever change Mercy. I liked the storyline for Samuel in this one since he has been little more than a hanger-on in most stories. Something had to happen there and I'm glad that is resolved. Overall enjoyable

I'm glad that this latest installment of the series included more character development for beloved secondary characters, like Samuel. I enjoyed this more than the last one, or it might have been the one before last? the one with the ghosts? that one felt like it was from another series. 
 I am worried that this might be the last one in the series. There were some relationships and ideas left open that I find myself still curious, but enough major issues that have bridged the series that were resolved to make me wonder.

Another good book in the series, but I was left less satisfied than normal. Maybe because the last book I read was the A Game of Thrones series, but I think it was more than that. The story didn't really seem to advance anything, although thinking back on it, it did in some ways. There just wasn't enough of it, though. 
 The worst problem was the uneven pacing of the story. The beginning is a slow, meandering build up of issues. Then there are some new elements introduced with a sudden, frantic ending that felt unfinished. It's almost as if Briggs hit her word count limit or due date & just pushed this out the door. 
 The focus of this book seemed narrower. There is a lot going on in the world, but suddenly entire races get a bare mention. Specifically, Stefan isn't seen at all nor is a a single vampire. Actually, only the central cast has any attention paid to them. It's as if they exist in a bubble. That was one of the realistic points of her previous books - the intrusiveness of daily detail, but there was none, here. Mercy, a small business owner, is gone for a month & there isn't a problem? She had no other cars in the shop? What about Gabriel & his mother? 
 There seemed to be a bit of a departure from Brigg's normal, careful development with Sam's problem. I don't think there was that much of a split in the werewolves personality nor did I care for the magical answer to all his problems. Introduced in the last 1/3 of the book, she magically fixes everything. It just seemed too pat & quick for something that has been developing over all the previous books in the series. Now it's suddenly all better? Nope. Too much. 
 So, not a bad read & I'm still happy enough with the series to read the next, but I'm certainly not frantic to get it.

This one was different than the others before it! It's much more focused on the love story and the characters, and I loved it. So satisfying. 
 It's funny, if the series had started with a book more like this it wouldn't have been quite as satisfying because I wouldn't have been as invested. The more action and plot driven beginnings made the character stories here much more satisfying.

Simply amazing. I couldn't put this down once I had begun! Every book explains a little more about the powers surrounding Mercy as well as developing every character in the plot. With so many different characters to contend with, Patricia Briggs does a wonderful job. Fast paced, never boring! Loved the explanation of the pack bonds and incorporating even more fae. Can't wait till I read the next one!
Forgot how much I liked this series, especially Adam and Mercy. Even the pack.
Not the strongest in the series, but read them.

This book reminded me again why I love this series. It was nice to see Mercy become more involved with the pack! It was nice to see her relationships with various members of the pack. Adam, Sam, Zee and Bran get more interesting as the series progresses! I really enjoyed reading this book!

Meh... 
 I ended up skimming near the end. 
 I thought I should give it a 3 but I realized I didn't like the book.. it was just 'OK' 
 Maybe this series just isn't what it was before. I don't think I should continue ..... :/

The fae are attacking. Mercedes Thompson has had a lot happen to her in the past few years. She went from being a quiet mechanic to whom nothing happened, ever, to being the mate of the local alpha and being inducted into the pack (though none knew that was even possible), has killed three vampires (while discovering abilities she never knew she had) and has been magically forced into things she'll never forget. Now the fae are coming after a book she borrowed. One that seems harmless but holds a powerful secret. And they'll stop at nothing to get it. 
 I felt this book, though it was supposed to be more focused on the fae that's attacking, had a lot more to do with the pack problems that have been going on. In fixing them. I hated the part at the beginning where, even just for a second, Mercy doubted herself. (She was being manipulated...won't give away how, or what happened, but Mercy doesn't doubt herself.) 
 Despite the fact that it wasn't as much about the fae as it advertised, I actually really liked this novel. You get to see the intricacies of the pack bonds, and how it can be used to someone's advantage, or detriment. Also you learn even more about the bond between mates. I also feel like the women of the pack got a bit of a step up in this novel, like their worth was truly being acknowledged for the first time, which I loved. 
 Mercy might just be the strongest character I've ever met. And yet, at the same time, she's not. She has survived so much, but she still has her weak moments. Probably why I love her so very much, and want to keep reading about her. 
 I thought we got to see a whole other side of Samuel in this novel (actually, quite literally...) and I'm really hoping that something that happens near the end keeps him happy. I hate seeing Samuel all depressed. (Yep, I realize that we met him that way, and we've only seen him that way, but somehow I can see the happy side of him that we don't get to see until the end of this novel, and I think he deserves to be that way.) 
 Anyway, the point of the matter is, this is a fantastic addition to the Mercy Thompson series. I'm anxiously awaiting the release of the next book.
this one got me hooked

This series always manages to bring out emotions in me because I love it and I feel for each and every character, but this book, this book just about did me in. I can't remember ever feeling so heart broken and sad as I was reading the first few chapters of this and just all the emotions that overwhelmed me, not only from Mercy but from a certain werewolf as well. 
 It was almost too much, almost. 
 I trusted Briggs to make things right though and I wasn't disappointed in the least, not at all in fact. 
 I love this series. It continues to wow me and keep me on my toes and with each new revelation, with each new in depth look into another characters and into Mercy herself, I fall more and more in love with it. It truly is one of the best werewolf series that I've read and one that will continue to be a favorite, even long after the series is over. 
 The characters are fantastic and fantasy or not, they feel real. Like people you would want to know and hang with and fall in love with. Characters that are memorable and strong. Characters that make the series every bit as much as the mystery and plot do. 
 Briggs is a talented author and I truly can not wait to dive into the next book and get more.
As always, Briggs continues to please. Characters continue to develop. I highly recommend this series!
I LOVE this! I ended the book with a big smile on my face. Must read.

I have been having a hard time adjusting to the time change for daylight savings and quickly get exhausted after a long day at work. I was looking forward to reading Silver Borne since the next book in the series, River Marked, has been released last week, but I was afraid my exhaustion would detriment my enjoyment of this fabulous urban fantasy series. I am thrilled to say that this book sucked me in right away. In fact, I had to force myself to sleep in order to get up for work in time, but I couldn't put it down until I found how it ended. Silver Borne is the fifth book in the Mercy Thompson series and currently my favorite book in the series thus far. 
 Briggs has maintained her well plotted mysteries and world building, but also upped the action and romance while furthering character development in this installment. Unlike its previous installments, Silver Borne tackles many different plot lines that left me on the edge of my seat. I tend to frown upon multiple plot lines because they are generally boring or they don't seem to fit the overall tone of the book, but this is not the case in Silver Borne where all the subplots make up not only the plot but also several character arcs. I did not find myself skimming any parts of the book, in fact, I had to slow done into to absorb the snarky humor and the romantic tidbits in the book. 
 Mercy continues to be an awesome and humble heroine. I like that she feels uncomfortable being in the spotlight and finds herself ordinary. There is no air of arrogance surrounding her. She can take care of herself yet call on others for help. In the past books, Mercy has struggled with the mentality of the wolf pack. She's terrified of losing her own identity and power. Mercy doesn't do submission and she never will. In Silver Borne she comes to realize the importance of pack, which I seem to understand in our layman terms would be family. While the pack does have it's social and political structure, it also has intimacy and affection which Briggs excellently demonstrated in the romance and the lack of for certain key characters in the book. 
 I have been a bit disappointed with the mystery aspect of the previous Mercy books, however, with Silver Borne I didn't have any idea of what would happen next. I enjoyed the twists and turns. I was truly in the dark along with Mercy. I did, however, miss Stefan, Mercy's vampire friend, but thought he needed some time off considering what he went through in Bones Crossed. 
 If you do decide to pick this series up (I really don't know why you wouldn't), I would highly suggest that you start at the beginning or at the very least with the second book in the series, Blood Bound, in order to get a sense of how Mercy's world works, and most importantly how the characters interact with one another. I love these characters and can't wait to see what happens next. Silver Borne is a must read for all Mercy fans.

Over the last few months, life has settled into a rhythm for Mercy. Still dealing with the aftermath of her recent trauma, Mercy's taking her newly established relationship with Adam, local werewolf pack Alpha, slowly yet surely forward even if their bond and her position in the Pack only work sporadically at best. Adam's pack has never really welcomed Mercy with open arms (troublesome coyote that she is), but she never would have expected some of Adam's wolves to meddle directly with their relationship. Upset and unsure of her next move, Mercy distances herself from the pack only to discover that her good friend and werewolf-roommate Samuel isn't coping as well as he had claimed to be. Deciding to keep stick to Samuel's side like glue, Mercy takes him on a short trip to return a borrowed book about the fae (a little light bedtime reading) when she determines that what she has, is in fact a powerful and ancient object - full of secrets about the fae - and worth more, to some, than her very life. 
 Patricia Briggs is one of those authors who understands how to deftly compound kick-butt action with emotional turmoil. Her novels always contain a hefty portion of Mercy fighting tooth-and-nail to protect those she loves, but in 
 Silver Borne 
 , she also gave us a Mercy who had to struggle just as hard to keep the emotional aspects of her relationships intact. Mercy and Adam, as a couple, are really put through the ringer this go-round but, dang it, there is just something about those two together that makes my heart sing. Something that makes me want to stand up and cheer every time they get a moment of quiet together. Either that or giggle at every shared oddball joke. Adam has always been a big winner for me, but his selfless actions toward - and defense of - Mercy in 
 Silver Borne 
 , left me straight-up Adam's #1 Fan. 
 And although this is gonna sound like a obvious contradiction after my above statement, I was a tiny (very, very tiny) bit disappointed with Samuel's role in this novel. Ms. Briggs said that would be his book, but the end resolution for the demons he was staring down seemed a touch rushed. That said, I'm more than willing to overlook that small detail due to the enormous amount of goodness otherwise found in Silver Borne. Simply put: it's vintage Mercy. It's about a shapeshifting mechanic who, with brains and a heart, is always willing to go the distance to make things right for those she loves. I just love her to bits.
There's always someone after this girl and she never backs down. Love the relationship between Adam and Mercy! But i feel soo bad for Samuel :(

Whenever I pick up a Mercy book, I get lost in her world. I forget how much I love Briggs books until I open that book and fall in love all over again. I really like her Alpha and Omega series as well, but her original Mercy Thompson series can't be beat! 
 This time around, Mercy receives a phone call about a book she borrowed from her friend Phin. But it wasn't just any book, it was old and powerful that revels the Faes secrets. Phin, the owner of the book, has vanished, his bookstore is closed down and Mercy is up to her neck in problems. 
 Besides being confused of what the book is all about, Mercy is still recovering from the events that occurred two books ago. Her bond with Adam and his Pack doesn't seen to be going as planned. She's in danger and doesn't know where it's coming from, the Fae, her pack? Someone wants her gone, and maybe more that just moving away. Above all that she's having some confidence issues with Adam. It's going to be a rough week or two for Mercy. 
 I think in Silver Borne we see how much Mercy has affected the people around her. 
 Silver Borne is face paced and filled with twists and turns that kept me engaged the entire story. There is always something new and intriguing in each Mercy Thompson novel. I cannot wait for the next installment!
Better than Book 4. This one had some good mystery, some good action, and left enough story arcs open that I am curious to continue the series.
very good book
my favourite so far
Mercy and Adam, I loved how we got a bigger peek into their relationship. Samuel: and how deep his feelings for pack, family and towards Mercy especially!

What I loved the most about Silver Borne is the growth as we circle back to the pack, and the relationships and conflicts that had taken a backseat to the action. I loved seeing Mercy stand up to the choices she has made and take her place in the pack. 
 There is still enough plot action as Mercy matches wits with a Faerie Queen, but even there it is the emotional scenes that take priority. 
 It actually felt like a lot of things were wrapped up or concluded in this book so it will be interesting to see where the series goes next. 
 A fabulous series so far - it will seem like a long wait til Book 6.

In this next installment of the Mercy Thompson series I was definitely not let down! Mercy has been one of my long standing favorites and I am already looking forward to RIVER MARKED #6 to be released in 2011. I love that Mercy has the feel of someone I could see walking down the street, her character has such a rich quality that you feel that she is a friend that you would love to just hang out with. Her down to earth personality and devotion to her loved ones makes her one of the most likable heroines that I have ever read. 
 In SILVER BORNE we get to see a new side to the relationship between Mercy, the coyote shifter auto mechanic, and her main squeeze, sexy alpha werewolf for the local pack, Adam Hauptman. The dynamics of their relationship as they work through the obstacles of dealing with the pack being in on every part of their it causes strain and shows them that they have to work for the things they truly care about. The pack has been through a rough couple of years and these new transitions cause a lot of conflict within the ranks as they learn who they can trust and how to make it work for everyone involved. 
 With Mercy being her usually self she takes on a lot of things by herself, not wanting to make things worse for those around her. When she receives a mysterious message in regards to an old fae book that she has in her possession, she tries to return it to it's owner Phin, but no one seems to no where he's gone... or maybe they're just being evasive, as so many fae can be. Mercy finds herself in an extremely difficult position as she tries to right whatever wrongs have been done in the search for a missing artifact that is the only bargaining chip she can use when up against some of the most powerful magic she has yet to encounter. Her journey to save her friend and not disrupt the pack even more turns out to be more than she bargained for. 
 We also get to know more about Samuel, the Marrok's son and Mercy's current room mate. As a powerful alpha werewolf living next door to Adam and under the same roof as Mercy the tension between the men in her life is thick enough to choke on at times. Samuel is also someone very close to Mercy's heart and with him going through a difficult time she finds herself wanting to help and unable to find a clear way to do so. Afraid of losing him without giving it everything she has she finds a way to keep the problems under wraps as much of possible but with the clock ticking down she doesn't know if she will have enough time to find the answers before it's too late to save him from destroying himself. 
 I loved this book! The plot was exciting, the characters are enchanting and the romance between Mercy and Adam was a soft touch that just made me smile as I read. Patricia Briggs has a masterful way of merging reality with fantasy that makes you want to believe in the unbelievable. I thoroughly enjoyed learning more about the pack dynamics and seeing Mercy progress as she learned how her bonds with the pack worked. I have to say that I loved seeing a softer side to Adam where Mercy was concerned... and then at the end when he showed how animal he could be... wow! Overall, still one of my favorite series!
Not my favorite in the series but still kept my attention

Other than the beginning of this book being very annoying because it was very whiny and in Mercy's head... I rather enjoyed this book. A lot. 
 Very werewolf-y, very fae-y. 
 The 'fix' for Samuel was a little convenient (dripping sarcasm there), but it'll be interesting to see where it goes. 
 I look forward to the next one.

Mercy Thompson is just getting used to being the girlfriend of Alpha werewolf Adam and the subsequent mate and pack bonds that allow others to read her mind when she realizes someone is manipulating those bonds to make her do things she wouldn't normally do. When her roommate Samuel begins to have problems of his own, Mercy's house burns down, and her friend Phin - a fae who gave her a book to keep safe - disappears, Mercy's got herself big problems... again. 
 The pack dynamics are quite interesting and I liked getting deeper into the world of the werewolves that has been so far more explained in Briggs' other series, Alpha & Omega. Because Mercy is a shifter, not a werewolf, it puts her in a unique position with most of the magical folk, and the way she dealt with the fae showed what a strong, clever heroine she is. I also liked seeing more of Samuel.

Silver Borne includes the normal suspects of coyote changeling, werewolves, vampires and an extended assortment of fae including Baba Yaga flying in her mortar or pestle - I'm never sure which part is which (or witch part is witch). 
 Mercy's relationship with Alpha Adam continues,as do her fascinating friendships with Zee, Stefan and Sam/Samuel. 
 This book focused more on the werewolves and was fascinating.

I enjoy Patricia Briggs. Yet, after having read all of the books...(I am half-way through River Marked.) I am done for awhile. A part of me wants the romance to get ugly with Adam and Stephan. There have been hints of that throughout the series, but I am not hopeful for further development. 
 And, I agree with other reviewers about Sam's silly transition from spurned, "not love to love, but not 'in' love with you", relationship with Mercy to "I am in love with my true love," a fae no less. 
 Am I expecting to much? After sampling the next novel, River Marked, I am not sure if the characters will go much deeper. Mores the pity, really. Like others, if I couldn't read River Marked for free, I would not buy it, except at a used book store.

Still a decent Mercy book. I loved the pack interaction. I just felt that something was a bit off about this. I don't know what though. I'm a really huge fan of the Mercedes Thompson books, so rushed to buy this book as soon as I knew it was out. 
 I haven't read any other of Patricia Briggs' books, other than the Alpha and Omega books, which, in my opinion, pale in comparison. 
 Mercy Thompson is a tough car mechanic who also happens to be a coyote shape shifter. This is book five in her series and she has developed from being a single woman with few responsibilities, to mate to the scrumptious Adam, the local pack's alpha. 
 I found 'Bone Crossed' the last book in the series a little disappointing, so I was delighted to be back on familiar ground with this one. 
 This time it's Mercy's connections to the fae and not the vampires that gets her into trouble. But, for me this book was more about Mercy's relationships. With Adam, with Sam, with Adam's daughter Jesse, and with the pack, than the main story, entertaining as it is. 
 This book moves Mercy and Adam's relationship on, exploring the implications of their mating and handling the inevitable ramifications of Mercy's rape, but also shows you some wonderfully tender moments between the two as they grow closer. 
 However, something I particularly enjoyed in the book was learning more about Sam. While I was desperate for Mercy and Adam to get together at the end of 'Iron Kissed', I love Sam and would hate to see him written out of the series. The interaction between Sam and Mercy is fantastically entertaining and written with ease and wit. Mercy's relationship with Sam is as important as her one with Adam, so it was interesting to see how this is going to move on now that she is mated. 
 'Silver Borne' gives you an insight into both Sam's history, but also a glimpse of his potential future. 
 As with the rest of the series, this book was a thoroughly entertaining read and there were times when I could barely put it down, the pages whirling past in a blur. Driven by the NEED to know what is going to happen next. The action jumps out and grabs hold of you, and the characters are superbly written. Mercy is feisty, determined and brave and you can't help but admire her. This series will continue to have pride of position on my bookshelves.
This series has happily taken a turn away from the endless politics of werewolves, which tire me so. I am enjoying it once again.

I am just so happy after reading this book! I love how far Mercy, Adam and Samuel have come in their struggles. They all deserve this! 
 My only complaint is, the artist for the book cover never captures Mercy correctly. dY~(c)

Coyote shapeshifter Mercy Thompson has recently become the mate of Adam, the local werewolf Alpha. Although Mercy has friends among the local werewolf pack, there are plenty who don't see a coyote as a proper partner for their leader. Mercy doesn't realize the extent of this dislike until someone manipulates the pack bonds that tie together all the wolves, and Mercy herself through Adam, to control Mercy's actions. Then Mercy learns that something has gone terribly wrong with her good friend Samuel, and that there's more to the powerful fae book she borrowed than she realized. Once again, Mercy has a lot of her plate to deal with. 
 Silver Borne is a fifth book in the Mercy Thompson series. I would argue that it's also one of the more complex volumes. Much like the fourth book, Bone Crossed, Silver Borne should not be read unless you are already familiar with the series. Much of Silver Borne is concerned with tying up loose ends from the past few books. One of those loose ends is the mate bond between Adam and Mercy, and what that means for the pack. As a result, a big chunk of this book is concerned with pack politics. The second plot thread is concerned with the growing depression we've seen striking Samuel. The third would be the secret behind the fae book. As you can tell from this description, there's a lot going on in this relatively short book. At times, the novel can feel a little disorganized, but when Briggs really focuses on a single storyline, boy can this book be exciting. 
 Much like Bone Crossed, I don't think that Silver Borne was quite as good as some of the previous books in the series (more specifically, Blood Bound and Iron Kissed). In Silver Borne, there can be a sloppiness to Brigg's usual tight prose that kind of alarmed me. Fortunately, this does not happen very often. Another issue I had was that the resolution to Samuel's story. I, just as much as anyone, want Samuel to be happy, but the way that his storyline was dealt with feels a little too convenient for me. Beyond that, I found I liked this book. I loved the section that dealt with Adam's wolf pack. There's a fight for dominance right in the middle of the book that had me literally gasping aloud. The fae storyline has a really attractive Tam Lin element that had me pretty excited. I also really enjoyed the fact that Briggs is completely aware that just because you're writing a fantasy, doesn't mean you have to abandon the reality that all actions have consequences. Mercy and Adam becoming mated last book was a very important step for the two of them, but Adam's position as Alpha means that there's serious consequences for his pack. I love that Briggs addresses that. 
 Silver Borne is a nice addition to the Mercy Thompson Series. Admittedly, it doesn't shine quite as bright as the earlier volumes in the series, but I had a good time reading it. Briggs is working on a sixth book, River Marked, which will be released in January (Note: for Anna and Charles Fans, there will be no Alpha and Omega book this year).

I was given this book as a gift. 
 There are three kinds of books in the world; the failures, the satisfying reads and the life-changing reads. Patricia Briggs' Mercy Thompson series is one of the truly dependable satisfying series out there. These books won't change your life, but they will give you a good, entertaining read every time, and stand up to rereads as well. 
 Silver Borne is the fifth book in the series following Mercy Thompson, mechanic and werewolf-raise coyote shifter with a knack for defying all odds. As such, there's really no way to evaluate this book without spoilers for previous books, so be warned and if you're just setting out in the Tri-Cities world, you might not want to read this review. 
 Last time in Briggs' world Mercy Thompson got mixed up in a vampire plot that, after her brutal rape in book 3, nearly broke her. Luckily Mercy is getting a vacation from the vampires which allows her to deal with the other major things that happened in the last book--her magical mating to local werewolf Alpha, Adam. The attraction between defiant Mercy and overpowering Adam has been brewing from the first page of book one, when the two pretended to not be able to stand each other. But now Adam's past actions--namely declaring Mercy his mate a very long time ago, before he even tried showing his affection for her in order to keep her safe from the very dangerous werewolves that might see another predator shifter as competition--are coming to light. Adam's love and care are helping Mercy come back from the trauma of her rape, and ironically they're causing him some major problems in the pack, since many of his wolves are suspicious that Mercy would show no interest in the pack for years of being Adam's mate, and now suddenly wants a starring role. 
 Add to that Mercy unknowingly being the guardian of a very powerful fae artifact, and being unable to let those who have shown her friendliness and kindness be abused by others and you have a complex twist of plots that don't go linear like most book plots, but blossom and grow into a collection of characters that seem to share bits of their lives with reader in each book. 
 Briggs' books are fleshy and visual, featuring characters who are beyond fun and lovable. Humble and genuine, and dependable Briggs' skill brings readers loyally back for more of this world, which is neither over powered, nor self important, but is simply and truly, entertaining.

I can't believe how little I remembered of this book. And it is such a good one. This time it is Samuel who gets Mercy in trouble. Samuel is a very old werewolf, and he has grown weary. Being a doctor is no longer enough for him, and he decides to kill himself. Lucky for him, his wolf does not want to die and takes over, keeping him alive. Usually, a werewolf with the wolf in control, turns into a savage beast, but Sam is stronger than that, and he can control himself. But Mercy needs to keep this a secret from the other wolves, as it would mean a death sentence. 
 After her disastrous date with Adam, when one of the pack was unduly influencing her thoughts and actions, she has the perfect excuse to keep her distance from Adam and the pack for a while. But when an armed man comes to her garage, looking for a werewolf to kill, Adam drives to the rescue. Not that he needed to do that, as Mercy had everything well in hand. Somebody has send a television bounty hunter after Adam Hauptmann with a fake warrant to kill him. And given Mercy's garage as the address where he could be found. Which is very strange, as Adam is a local businessman who goes to work 6 days out of 7. 
 As Mercy has brought Sam with her to work, Sam is the werewolf almost getting killed. For not telling Sylvia Sandoval that the big dog she brought with her, and that her littlest daughter Maria has been crawling all over and riding like a pony, she looses her friendship. Her son Gabriel is no longer allowed to work for Mercy as well, as it is not a safe environment for her son. And Mercy has no choice but to agree on that, she will sure miss his help though. 
 Is this really an elaborate plot to kill Mercy, and get the old Fae book she has borrowed from Phineas? Tad warned her about the book, he had gotten a strange message from Phin, and now the bookshop is closed and Phin has gone missing, and strange Fae are popping up all over the place. Mercy makes sure the book is in a safe place, and starts investigating with Sam. Which is a good thing when she is attacked by some strange and very strong kind of Fae and Sam kills him. 
 Of course Adam and the Marrok find out too soon about Sam's condition, and they are very concerned about Mercy's safety. According to Charles, Samuel's brother, Sam has perhaps one week left before he fades and dies anyway. With only one half of the soul wiling to live, there is just not enough left. Unless Samuel finds something or someone new to live for.... 
 A very action filled book, and I loved every page of it. The drama with Samuel/Sam, the intrigue with the Fae who is after the book, and the maker of the Silver Borne was a good story line. Add to that the stuff happening with the werewolf pack, Adam having to fight for his life and his title as Alpha while severely wounded, and the traitor in the pack being found out. Jesse is sweet on Gideon, and she helps Mercy find him when he gets abducted by the bad Fae. I really like how strong Jesse has become in this series. 
 Adam proves again how well he knows Mercy, and that he doesn't want her to change. She is loyal to her friends, and he cannot fault her for that. But he will have her back when needed. I do love how their relationship is progressing. 
 This will be the last book I am re-reading for now in this series, on to new books, new worlds to discover. 
 10 stars.

 When Cade is introduced, the author firmly established him as an alpha hottie. The dynamics between the two characters were fun, sexy and at so many times side-hugging hilarious. Not only does Hell's Knights have fabulous one-liners, but it has whole scenes of funny! This teamed with the graphic sex makes the book one hell of a read. 
 The author bravely leads her main character into territory that really pushed my tender nerves. Addison finds herself in a situation, that is far too real, and most definitely disturbing.
