reference_books.title: The Marriage Plot
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This was another of those books that I wanted to like more than I did. I'm beginning to suspect that most contemporary fiction just may not be for me. The general coming-of-age concept is one with which anyone can identify and understand, especially when combined with "the marriage plot." I actually like Mitchell and Madeleine's stages of marriage age, because being around the "Stage Two" age, of course I notice the same patterns. It makes you wonder sometimes about marriage and how it comes about, which is a different story. 
 Or is it? After all, how does Madeleine and Leonard's marriage come about? Because they were in that stage, or because they were in love? In my opinion, it's because they were in anxious denial. Madeleine seems determined to believe that if she just keeps open-minded about mental illness and steady on the course, that will be enough to cure Leonard. He on the other hand, is a scientist who feels like science is failing him, understandably frustrated and anxious to get on with his life. What happens when obstinacy and panic fall in love? A rushed and ill-conceived marriage, which even poor Mitchell, soul-searching in India, can see coming. 
 Yet it's not the relationship woes, frustrating as they are, which make me feel unsatisfied about this story. Given the characters (whom I admit I didn't find easily relatable or likable), their conflicts are sadly true. I read one review which called the book "over-written," which it may be at times, but at others it can be nicely descriptive. 
 I think my main problem with this coming-of-age tale is that nobody comes of age. Nobody ends up anywhere. Nobody does anything. At the end of the novel, the three characters are in virtually exactly the same positions they were at the beginning. The sole exception is Madeleine, in that she finally knows (kind of) what she wants to do with herself. But considering that Madeleine has had virtually no personality for the majority of novel outside of being Leonard's caretaker*, I can't bring myself to feel more than just vaguely pleased for her. Most of that pleasure lies in the fact that I hope she can finally live some facet of her life now. 
 *This made me think multiple times of The Dive From Clausen's Pier, and that question, "What do we owe those whom we love?" Despite my weariness with Madeliene, she demonstrated the struggle with that question beautifully.

reference_books.title: Bossypants
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I may be one of the few, but I did not go into this book expecting it to be laugh-out-loud funny. I expected the "Tina Fey Story," a tale of a girl growing up and landing a gig on SNL, then her own TV show and a run for the Vice Presidency. I didn't even expect her to go too deeply in depth about that, considering how recent it was and how much she is probably sick of discussing it. I was pleasantly surprised to find that while the book wasn't hilarious, there were definitely moments where I laughed aloud to myself (and that's why I tend to read alone where nobody will give me funny looks). 
 I'm not going to lie. Tina Fey's book is not the most amazing book ever, nor is she the most amazing writer ever. But she can tell a good story, and that is where her book shines. The best chapters are usually those in which she just tells the story of what happens, and you can almost hear her voice narrating it in your mind. The few exceptions in my eyes were "Delaware County Summer Showtime!" which had a lot of good in it but maybe just too many messages to get across, and "Young Men's Christian Association" which started well but faded by the end of the chapter. In fact, any part where I felt that Fey was trying too hard faded for me quickly. 
 What readers are likely anticipating most when picking up Bossypantsis the story of "Sarah, Oprah, and Captain Hook." That actually was not my favorite part of the book, but it was a fascinating read to see how the odd coincidence that these two women looked similar blew up into this media party. Fey may be (understandably) biased about the situation, but her overall point about how women are treated in comedy, and how she and Palin ended up on two sides of the same unfair coin, is valid. That is my favorite part of the chapter, other than the awesome Oprah joke and the way Fey puts together a birthday party for her daughter in the midst of pandemonium. 
 The only thing I didn't particularly like about this chapter was its location in the book. The rest of the book seems to flow more or less chronologically, but from this chapter discussing her daughter's 3-year-old birthday party, she jumps back in time to breast-feeding. It's a little bit jarring in a book that more or less has shown good continuity up to that point, apart from side-jumps discussing weight or addressing Internet commentary. My complaints are minimal though, because I love how Fey discusses her family, her approach to motherhood, and of course, her prayer for her daughter. 
 Overall though, I most appreciated the ways in which this book discusses the way women are treated in Hollywood. Some of them are surprising where I suppose they shouldn't be; for instance, men passed over women's sketches not because they were women's sketches but because the men didn't understand them. Some are not surprising and frustrating; for instance, men passed over women playing parts because they thought the men would be funnier. 
 What's impressive (and inspiring) is the way Fey confronts these things in her book with more confidence and humor and a lot less sarcasm than I would have. She's right to do so, of course: it is her determination to ignore labels, limits, and criticisms that makes it possible for her to overcome them. It's advice and an example that would benefit all women trying to achieve a goal. And it's that message, hidden between stories of improvs and tales of Photoshop, that makes this a good read.* 
 *No pun was intended, but that really made me smile.

reference_books.title: The Flame Alphabet
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I finished this book over a week ago and quite honestly, I've been putting off writing a review because I simply disliked it. It was quite a disappointment because the premise was so intriguing. When I'd first read about this book online a couple of years ago, I immediately wanted to read the book. I wanted to know how language could become toxic, why only children were affected, how this epidemic would be addressed. None of these questions were answered. None. The characters were unrelatable and unlikable and underdeveloped. They inspired no interest and no sympathy. The writing is disjointed, which serves the premise, but not to the point that it makes the read worthwhile. I never leave books unfinished, but if I hadn't been reading this for Eclectic Readers (and facilitating the discussion), I would have dropped this one.

reference_books.title: You're Never Weird on the Internet
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I continue to develop my interest in memoirs, which is fun. I began this book as an audio book, but could not actually make it past the first chapter. This is no insult to Felicia Day, but I found that reading it in print helped me embrace it more. Not to mention, there are visual jokes within the book which I wouldn't have fully enjoyed in the audio version (though I may go back and listen now that I've finished). 
 Day leads the reader through the story of her unusual upbringing and education, but what is actually more fascinating is the twist the story takes after her college graduation (though Day's intelligence is incredibly interesting!). Instead of fully exploring her acting career, or even going into any depth about some of her most popular roles at all, she instead chooses to focus on the anxiety and depression that led her into addiction and threatened her success both as an actor and as an entrepreneur. While her descriptions aren't heavy or frightening, they make reference to real threats which anyone suffering anxiety or depression might feel. I almost wish she had gone into more detail, since some things were touched on lightly or lightened by jokes (some I appreciated, some I did not). However, I'm sure these topics were hard for her to share, so I'll simply appreciate the bravery it took to face them as she did. I wouldn't say this is my favorite memoir I've read, but I'm glad I did read it and there were definitely parts of it I found inspirational.

reference_books.title: Narcissus in Chains (Anita Blake, Vampire Hunter, #10)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 If I'm to be quite honest, plot-wise, this book probably deserves 3 or 4 stars. I was intrigued by the possibility that Anita might be a shapeshifter and what that would mean for her work, her relationships, and her future. I really liked the development of Nathaniel's character (thank goodness!)and I was totally intrigued by the new pard in town. 
 Plot-wise, I felt like the biggest flaws were the slow beginning and the complete lack of development of the bad guys and the new coalitions. After Gregory was healed, I honestly felt like the book was going to be over except for apparently more sex until Marco and the snakes burst into the kitchen (also, I don't like Marco as a name for a lion-man, but that's just me and beside the point). My reaction was something like, "Oh, I should still be worried about these people? They're still important?" I simply didn't take them seriously as a threat. Even finding out the truth about Orlando King was only vaguely interesting, as there wasn't enough time left in the book to make him anything more dangerous or intriguing. 
 So if the book was decent plot-wise, what am I going to complain about? That's right, the sex. And no, while I'm sure many would consider me a prude, I'm not against having sex in the Anita Blake novels. I'm not even against having multiple sex scenes in the Anita Blake novels. What I hated was the way they disrupted the structure of the book. 
 I read one such scene straight through, and then expected to continue with plot. Instead, sex scene after sex scene followed, and I ended up skimming through 100 pages or more. I just found it boring to read about the same thing happening multiple times over a good fifth of the book. It would be like reading about Anita arguing with Dolph for 100 pages without a break. It's interesting the first time, repetitive the second, and downright dull anytime after that if it's not broken up by significant plot development. I don't call getting out of the shower, picking up Jean Claude, and taking him home significant plot development. 
 Just to prove my point, I'll point out that the sex between Anita and Richard hit the mark perfectly. They went through several major emotional and impacting events, converse, and sleep together, which felt natural and even beautiful in a way. It had been a long time since I recall such comfort and happiness between them. Then Anita tries to feed off him and he balks, continuing the plot, albeit in a sad way if you're a Richard fan (I am and I'm not). 
 Now... now I am torn. I would like to know more about the wereleopards and how things turn out with Nathaniel and Micah and the shapeshifter coalition. I'd like to see Anita resolve her relationships with Dolph and Ronnie. I would really like to see more Larry and Edward, because their presences were sorely missed in this book (especially now that I know so much about Edward!). I just have heard often that the books begin going downhill from here, and I'm not sure I want to waste another day skimming through most of a book just to get the good parts from it. Also, the preview at the end of the book seems to indicate that the next novel is primarily about Jean Claude, Asher, and Belle Morte, and I honestly am not interested. Well, I'm interested in Asher. He's fascinating. What to do...

reference_books.title: Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I greatly enjoyed this book. It was a lot of fun, filled with interesting and amusing facts, and Roach's sense of humor is (as usual) amazingly hilarious. The levity and tangential stories did distract a bit from the route that Roach was trying to take, but I still got a kick out of it. And so did my husband, for whom I read some of the best passages aloud. I will say this though, it's not always the book you want to read while you're eating. Though it might help me lose a few pounds... And laugh a few more times.

reference_books.title: Wither (The Chemical Garden, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This book is the closest I've been to bailing on a book in a long time. There are world-building issues with the timing of these genetic experiments and the logic of a world where people can only live to 20 or 25 that really bothered me (not to mention the ickiness of children having children! Ugh!), and I got so hung up on it that when my library loan ran out, I basically shrugged. But I'd forgotten I'd put a renewal on the before even starting it, in hopes I'd have enough time to finish it, and so when it became available again weeks later it popped right back into my Kindle. So I persevered. 
 In the end, I found it quite engrossing, though I never did make my peace with the world-building issues. But I really liked Rhine as a protagonist and wanted to know if she'd make it out of the mansion in this book, or if Rowan would find his way to her. She made some foolish choices which bothered me, and I wish she'd just told Linden the truth, but a good protagonist overall. 
 I also particularly liked the way the novel really emphasized female friendships and the sisterhood that can develop. It was a unique aspect to this story that you don't often see in dystopian novels, even when the heroines have sisters. That aspect really appealed to me, and even though I found Cecily aggravating, I appreciated what the author was doing. 
 Honestly, I'll probably never come back and finish this series, but it was better than I'd have expected based on the beginning. 2.5 stars rounded up.

reference_books.title: Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe (Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was so very moving. So moving, in fact, that I'm struggling to review it. I love how it's not just a young adult love story, or another story about a teen learning to handle his or her sexual orientation. It's really about these teens learning to handle their identity as people. They look at so many rules and standards, and how they meet them and how they don't: they're Mexican, but not Mexican enough because they don't like certain things from their culture. They're supposed to talk about all their feelings, because that's what the right and adult thing to do is, and yet their parents have many feelings and thoughts they don't share. It's a struggle to face these many standards, and these are things that continue as people become adults. I love that the author includes that in the trials that these boys have to face. 
 On top of that, I love that the boys are smart and good and respectful, despite these struggles. They are frustrated and angry, but that's not all they are. I found that heartening, and I really cared about them. I wanted them to be able to face their fears and have the hard talks. They had good parents (I LOVE that they have good parents!), and the author paints the parents as real people with struggles, as well as caring and devoted mothers and fathers. It was a lovely picture of friendship and family and love of all kinds.

reference_books.title: Landline
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 I am hovering between two and three stars for this book. I maybe would have given it 2.5 were that an option. As it is, I'm giving it the benefit of the doubt because I've greatly liked the other two Rowell books (and the preview of Attachments) I've read, and also because I really was rooting for Georgie and Neal. I really did want to cry at the end. Also, I really did think the concept was super interesting. 
 This is all leading up to a really big "BUT," of course. And that is the simple fact that I kept waiting for everything to connect. It's fairly early in the book when we learn that Neal drove from Omaha to propose to Georgie on Christmas, and it's within the first few pages that we learn that he's taking their daughters to Omaha for Christmas without her. The time-travel phone and Georgie's work-first tendencies are laid out in the book jacket. It was fairly easy to connect the dots after obtaining all this information, so I dove in to see them come together. And they just... didn't. 
 The flashbacks are excellent, and they do their job well. Georgie and Neal come together and you want them to work, and you instantly see all the quirks in their young selves that will make their marriage tough fifteen years down the line - the quirks we never see in our own lives. It makes so much sense, and it makes you fall in love with them falling in love. We all have these issues, so let Georgie and Neal show us how it's done! But everything in the present is just disjointed. Georgie's a "work-first" kind of person, who does absolutely no work at all throughout this entire story. Instead she spends pages and pages fretting that she's having a nervous breakdown which leads to repetitive passages of anxiety that the reader doesn't need because the reader already knows the truth. She, her husband, and her best friend have lived through fifteen years of romantic triangle frustration, which never gets fully addressed in the present. Her mother is quirky and had an obsession with sexuality and lingerie, and her sister obsesses over pizza delivery (though if I had to pick, Heather's subplot is my favorite). All these things wind together in brief snippets, which also have many repeating patterns, but don't quite match up with each other. 
 Even in the end, things seem rushed and incomplete. Sure, Georgie has the right conversation with Neal in the past, but she and Seth have a two-page discussion filled with ellipses and multiple vague or unfinished sentences which barely address the feelings and friendship that has been ducking between the lines the entire book. She and present-day Neal never actually work things out at all. She shows up at his door and he won't let her talk with him. Perhaps we should be satisfied that she and Neal spoke at all, even from two different time frames, but when you want two characters to work, you want them to be on the same page. The ending didn't leave me feeling like they were yet. You don't recover from a week of radio silence with "I'll try harder" and a hug. You never even actually find out if Georgie and Seth pull off their show or not (not that it's important in the long run, but I'm looking for any kind of plot resolution here. 
 In fact, the most satisfying part of the end was Georgie yelling at Neal that she wanted to lay out everything on the table, even the terrible parts, so they could just get the fighting done. As much as I hate conflict in my own personal life, it can be a bit cathartic, yes? And yet, it doesn't really happen. Part of the point of the magic phone gimmick is that Neal and Georgie don't line up properly to communicate, either on Christmas 1998 or on Christmas 2013 - but their crossed lines do. So what happens to them without the phone? That is the question that doesn't fully get addressed here, and it's disappointing.

reference_books.title: Love Letters to the Dead
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is another epistolary novel about a girl going through the grieving process for the recent death of someone young. (Odd how I ended up reading two of these so close to each other for the staff book club. I wonder if the person who created the reading list realized how similar they were.) While this protagonist still seemed really young and naive and foolish for the age given, I found it more believable in a way. Perhaps because she was so openly grieving and repressing that grief, and because she clearly was so very susceptible to pressures from her friends and family. I also preferred the writing style to the last I read, though the brief biographies the author gave for each of the celebrities became more annoying the more of them I read. I suppose it's to provide a background for the younger audience for which this book was written, but I felt like it was a bit redundant and a bit too obvious, which stalled the actual story. 
 The story itself was an interesting growing-up and dealing-with-trauma type of thing. It dealt with quite a few heavy issues for a book with such a young-sounding protagonist (physical and sexual abuse, grief, depression, mental illness, alcohol, drugs, sexuality, etc.), but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I really liked and appreciated the emotions Laurel was going through, the grief and the guilt and the anger and the sadness. They resonated with me, especially as someone who suffered a personal loss at a young age, and I kind of wished the author had focused more on that feeling than on trying to remind the audience why the particular celebrities she'd chosen were supposed to connect to the story. The end came up quickly, but was fairly satisfying, if a little tidy. It left you in a comforting, hopeful place, which I think is what I need in a book with a theme of grief. I know this is Dellaira's only book thus far, but I think I'd like to read something in a different style from her. The way she handles heavy emotion has tons of potential.

book_a.title: Authority (Southern Reach, #2)
book_a.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 Full disclosure: I'm not quite sure I'm giving this book the fairest review. I really enjoyed where it began. I love Control as our new protagonist, and I even enjoy Grace as our antagonist (Note: two main characters who are minorities! Excellent!). The perspective Control brings to the Southern Reach and Area X is really fascinating, revealing how little the agency knows, even as they are designing expeditions and risking people's lives. Grace's resistance to his investigations is frustrating, but understandable, given the rocky history of the agency. I really did enjoy watching them circle each other at first. 
 The problem came in the middle of the novel. When I picked it up, it went quickly, but so little seemed to happen that it took a little self-convincing to pick it up again. It got to the point that I just wanted to be finished with the book. 
 When the hypnosis twist and the ending arrive, the story does begin to pick up again, and I really enjoyed the way it ends. It was just kind of not enough - too little, too late. I want to know what happens to Control and the biologist, but I'm just not convinced I'm ready for the next book. There will have to be some pondering on that one. So not a bad book, but not a great one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
After ANNIHILATION--which I really enjoyed--AUTHORITY was a bit of a letdown. 
 In AUTHORITY, we shift from the jungles and mystery of Area X to the offices and politics of the Southern Reach. There's little to no action. Some parts were very compelling, like the interview portions with the biologist...but those were vastly over-shadowed by long dragging periods in which Control (the main protag) goes on a wild goose chase for information. There's misinformation and double-crosses. Layers are added to the enigma that is Area X. Answers are provided, however, in typical "Lost" fashion, they're answers that lead to more questions. I won't give spoilers. Just know that this definitely feels like an interim novel purely meant to get us to the final novel. That's what it felt like at least. 
 This, of course, is required reading if you're taking on the entire trilogy...but this installment was a definite labor. I flew threw ANNIHILATION in a matter of days. AUTHORITY took some effort.

Sustains and even improves upon the first book's creepiness quotient. Also introduces actual characters! But a bit of a lackluster/cliffhanger ending. Definitely in for the third, but this doesn't stand on its own as well as the first.

If volume one of the Southern Reach trilogy (Annihilation) brings to mind Patrick McGoohan's The Prisoner - no names just numbers or in this case occupations, volume two (Authority), continues the theme - Johnny Rivers' "Secret Agent Man" meets The Avengers (John Steed, Mrs. Peel, and "Mother"). 
 We know the date: 10 years in our future. The characters have names. The location is still unspecified but the dangling gray moss and the climate suggests somewhere along the Gulf Coast. Every description, every detail is calculated to project a decaying, stagnant environment in contrast to the pristine, flourishing conditions in Area X. None of the suspense in the first volume carries over to the second - all of the action is mundane, despite the author's attempts to suggest the unknowable. The creepy nature of the environment gives the sole color to the story - a monochromatic rainbow of grays. 
 Volume two, written in third person, shifts the perspective to agent John Rodriguez, new director of the Southern Reach. He prefers to go by Control, hiding behind a nickname instead of a job title. He's also a spy for a shadowy agency known only as Central, represented by an equally vague character called the Voice. Control entered the family business, so to speak, following in the footsteps of his grandfather and mother who is also his handler. He is marginally more sympathetic than the biologist, probably because we are privileged to experience his inner dialogue - almost without end. 
 Much of Control's thoughts seem random. Whether this is meant to reveal his character or represents the author's personal thoughts and observations isn't entirely clear. Some of the lines seem like non-sequiturs with lots of incomplete sentences, more than should be noticeable. After a while you have to ask if Control is a dim-wit. It dawns on the reader well before Control that the Voice is exercising hypnotic commands on him. Control's semi-stream-of-consciousness is probably intended to reinforce the sense of a man teetering on the edge of sanity. Too often they come across as lines that may have sounded clever in the author's head but miss the mark on paper. When the author disappears, leaving the character's voice clear and resonate, it works. Mostly it is like a radio signal fading in and out. 
 The administration of Southern Reach is the primary focus of the novel. The military has a part to play but over time its role has devolved into boring routine. After 30 years without real progress, the bureaucracy has reshaped the scientific investigation. The distinct difference between the 60's space-age, rigorously scientific approach has been supplanted by a bureaucratic, institutionalized, decadent, decaying organization. The surviving staff seems to have a collective malaise or shared delusion or fatalistic attitude toward a dead-end occupation. These odd characters are sufficiently well-drawn, Whitby, Cheney, Grace - they are believable, even recognizable as people we know or have met. The situation Control encounters is reminiscent of the business world - staff reductions, low morale, recent failures, and focus on process not product. The enumeration of the expeditions, which we learn is closer to 40 despite the latest being called the twelfth, is similar to how executives decide software releases should be named and for similar reasons. 
 Beyond the incomplete sentences, there are editing flaws like this one on page 218-9: "A lone great blue heron stood solemn and silent in the middle of the pond. Thunderclouds continued to gather, its feathers dull in the fading light." Really? Thunderclouds have feathers? 
 Why are there 3 volumes? Volume 1 is clearly prologue. Volume 2 is set-up and volume 3 must be the big finish. Volume 1 ended at the point when continuing would have made it tedious. Not so with volume 2. The meandering style is beyond wearing. Cutting volume 2 by a third would have improved the story while still permitting the author's stylistic and creative choices. A single novel 600 pages long should be enough to tell the complete tale. 
 Turning page after page, I attributed my concern to Control - wanting the story to mean something but afraid it did not. In spite of the spooky setting and the ominous portents of Area X, the novel describes a rather dull storyline where the oddities of a misplaced cell phone, a dead mouse and undying plant, rummaged desk drawers, and a murdered mosquito signal the 'unusual.' Will I read volume 3? I finished the "Dire Earth Cycle" so I can manage this one. My expectations are pretty low.
Could have easily been shortened by 100+ pages. Fairly boring.

Holy crap, this book was unbearable! I'm trying to think of something good to say about this book...and failing. It reminds me of an unholy blend of the final season of Lost, The Blair Witch Project, Cloverfield, The Office, and Waiting for Godot. Endless trivial descriptions of bureaucracy, oblique dead-end details, and an obstinate refusal to further the plot in any way, other than with fruitless clues. It seems that fans of Annihilation were enthralled by the ominous Lovcraftian horror of Area X and the unreliable narrator, but the real horror is the unreliable author who writes well and teases with no intention of delivering the goods. 
 I am a prodigious reader of SF&F, but I am not a fan of ambiguity or metaphor. I want a novel with compelling characters, fascinating world-building, and a propulsive storyline that makes we want to know more, but whatever Jeff VanderMeer was aiming for, it went straight over my head. This book smacks of Serious Literature Filled with Deep Meaning that Average Joes cannot possibly grasp. As I read for entertainment and to stimulate my imagination, I cannot go another step. I was hoping this book would provide some illumination of the events of Annihilation, but after getting to the 50% mark without the slightest clue, I cannot justify wasting any more precious reading time. People often say, just hang in there and the book will pay off at the end, but I would counter, why can't a story be interesting and exciting from the get-go? Is that too much to ask? Having read fairly widely, I'm pretty certain of what I will like or not, and this series is about as far from my tastes as I've encountered in a long time. My apologies to all the GR readers who loved this book, I respect your opinions and tastes and I hope you won't think less of me, but why torture myself anymore? I'm moving onto something else.

Authority is ALMOST just as good as Annihilation! This time its written from the point of view of "Control" the new director who's come in to clean up the mess at the Southern Reach. 
 At first I wasnt sure that I was giong to like the book being written from control but after finishing it, I realized how vital it was. 
 This series is one big science fiction mystery that leaves you stunned and questioning everything you ever thought before. I cant wait to finish the series!

Answers a bunch of the questions from the first book, but then supplies a lot of new ones. Great ending. It was helpful to switch perspectives, but this one was less...entrancing somehow? I feel like I need to reserve judgment until I finish the series.

I thought "Annihilation" was one of the best sci-fi books I'd read in recent years, so I was disappointed in the sequel. The pace was slow and meandering, and even when it starts to pick up at the end, it still plods along. The plot was sparse and mostly consisted of office politics, meetings, interviews, tours, meal breaks, theorizing, phone conversations, and some hum-drum flashbacks to the protagonist's past. I guess this is what happens when the setting is an office building rather than a mysterious, Lovecraftian landscape. Occasionally there are some tidbits about Area X's history and origins, but we do not learn much more about it than in the first novel. 
 My main criticism is that VanderMeer gives far too much space to the settings. There are frequent, lengthy, opulent descriptions of boardrooms, offices, containment facilities, research labs, living rooms, kitchens, and bedrooms. If you took these out, I bet you'd loose 100 pages. VanderMeer also gives his characters -even ancillary ones- similar treatment. 
 Stylistically, many of his analogies and similes are over-the-top. Here's an example: "A spiraling thread gone astray that might or might not be made of something else entirely - not even as scrutable in its eccentricity as a house-squatter of a nail that stumbled around like a drunk." Sometimes, he clusters them together and it's very annoying. I wish he would have put more effort into creating compelling dialogue rather than in trying to impress us with his vocabulary and figurative language. On that note, the dialogue is rather contrived and insipid. 
 I think the purpose of this book is to set up the next and final novel. That may explain why it was such a lackluster follow-up to "Annihilation". I really hope VanderMeer takes us back into Area X in "Acceptance", because it is a far more interesting place to be.

This was a good book, and I feel somewhat like a traitor only giving it three stars, but there are reasons. Unlike the first book in this trilogy, Authority took on a much slower, calculated progression, due to the introduction of a new vantage point from a new set of eyes. There were times where I felt like the protagonist's backstory lingered on a bit too long. That being said, it was still very enjoyable and is something I would recommend to fellow readers.

This series is frustrating. I love stories that build mystery upon mystery. Lost and The X-Files are two of my favourite shows. And The Southern Reach books do the same. But the amount of expository material is kind of driving my nuts. 
 This book goes through the tiniest minutiae of Control's days as the new Director at The SR Facility where the Biologist is being held. Great! So, we'll get his insight on top of hers as he interviews her. Nope. 
 Instead we read a lot about Control's mother. We hear a lot about Control's grandfather. We get far too much information about Control's formative years. 
 And every once in a while, VanderMeer cracks open the Pandora's Box and lets some fun stuff out, but the revelations are too few and too far between. VanderMeer also has a predilection for never settling on anything. He was confused, yet somehow clear. She was cold, yet felt warm. It was small, yet somehow enormous. On and on and on with this stuff. And there's a whole lot of telling going on. Control was flooded with emotions. Lovely. What emotions? What does that look like? What does it feel like? Show us, don't tell us. 
 So, the first book was a Shirley Jackson/H.P. Lovecraft hybrid. This one was more an Ian Fleming/Michael Chrichton hybrid (without any of the action and twice the talk!), with a seasoning of Lovecraft. 
 One more book to go. Let's see if anything happens in that one.

The mystery of Area X continues with an FBI agent's entry into the Southern Reach. What's going on? Why can't anybody remember anything? Why is everyone so antagonistic? And why does everything smell bad? 
 Rarely have I been so disappointed with a book as I was with Authority. The first entry in this series is a gripping, psychedelic adventure that reads like a nature-gone-wild acid trip. This book, on the other hand, is like going to work with a punishing hangover. You don't know what's going on and everybody is pushing piles of paper at you. 
 "A shadow had passed over the director's desk then. He'd been here before, or somewhere close, making these kinds of decisions before, and it had almost broken him, or broken through him. But he had no choice." pg 18. On and on it goes. No answers, only confusion and bewilderment. I honestly thought, up until the very end, that something mega-cool was going to happen to make up for all of the so-so stuff that had happened so far. Unfortunately... 
 I also got super excited anytime Area X was mentioned, sort of like passing an old fling on your way to a funeral. Take this passage: "But the truth did have a simple quality to it: About thirty-two years ago, along a remote southern stretch known by some as the "forgotten coast," an Event had occurred that began to transform the landscape and simultaneously caused an invisible border or wall to appear." pg 35. Yes! And then we were immediately back into the boring office work/politics stuff. 
 "You've heard of the Southern Reach?" He had, mostly through a couple of colleagues who had worked there at one time. Vague allusions, keeping to the cover story about environmental catastrophe. Rumors of a chain of command that was eccentric at best. Rumors of a significant variation, of there being more to the story. But, then, there always was. He didn't know, on hearing his mother say those words, whether he was excited or not." pg 71. And that, my friends, is pretty much the whole book. Let me save you another 250 or so pages. 
 I exaggerate. A bit. It's just that I'm incredibly disappointed in the turn this story took. I suppose I'll read the last one in this series because I'm a completionist, but that is the only reason.
Dude! I can't wait to review this serious. Onto book 3.
Terrible terrible book a bit better than the first but not by much

This was also very good. It just builds and builds and sneaks up on you until you're like WTF JUST HAPPENED. The only way I can think to put it is that it's subtle...until it's not. Very much looking forward to the next (and last) in the series.
not thrilling.

After an exciting and disturbing first book, this one was more of a slog to get through. I admired the author's ability to change the tone so dramatically, bringing in elements of mystery, espionage, and conspiracy fiction. The main idea seemed to be that the weirdness of Area X had somehow infected the outside bureaucracy designed to control and study it. The characters all have different neuroses, allegiances, and theories about Area X that prevent them from working with each other rationally to understand the problem. But overall there wasn't really much tension to move the story along. 
 It was still OK (2 stars), and I did like it enough to go on to the third book, Acceptance. I'm about halfway through that and am enjoying it much more.

2.5/5 stars -- The first in this series was very intriguing. Unfortunately, this one was just a bit too repetitive and slow paced for me. I put it down often and didn't always want to pick it back up again. I'm interested I. The overall storyline of Area X, so I'll probably read the third book...but I'm going to take a little break from this series first.
I was constantly yawning. All the time. What a waste and so surprisingly after the good start with Annihilation. Unfortunately , I won't be reading the third book.
Yikes! Four months is a long time to find out the craziness of the Southern Reach!
While not as strong as the first book with the plot a little too plodding, parts are engaging throughout making it an interesting second book in the trilogy.

Unfortunately somewhat mundane and lacking the brightness of the brilliant Annihilation. The story is entirely predictable in this instalment, and Control, John Rodriguez, failed to engage my interest or sympathy. But Area X is always there, in the background and pushing forward, and I am now entirely upon its side.

2.5 
 Good heavens...this book took FOREVER to get where it was going. You could have lobbed off 100 pages and not been any the wiser. 
 Here's hoping it picks up in the final installment?!

** spoiler alert ** 
 This wasn't as good as the first book but it still had me engaged, i wanted to know more about the mystery of Area X and some of the old characters from "Annihilation". I'm listening to these on audio and the moment the first one ended, i started this late at night in bed, i ended up drifting off to sleep and started awake while Control was talking "The Voice" and it scared me shitless, engulfed within the darkness of my room. Anyway, on to the last book now.

Book 1 was a great concept, book 2 not so much, and it needed much better editing. Also, the names seemed so cheesy. Still intrigued by the concept, looking forward to the third, hope the series holds up. Not every book concept is best as a trilogy. I am sick of series that don't need to be series.
This book just really didn't work for me but it is really well written, and has a unique story. I just wasn't engaged the way I was with the first book.

Wow, what an excruciatingly boring book. Annihilation, book 1, was strange and fascinating; I gave it 5 stars. But this...I don't know what happened with this. I put up with it just to get to the next book with the hope that the end of the trilogy will be a return to form. Even listening to the audiobook at 125% speed, this is a real slog. Fans of book 1 would be better off simply reading a synopsis on Wikipedia, which could be accomplished with a single paragraph.

At first, I thought this was an interesting insight into the 'other side' of the world introduced in the first book of the series, Annihilation. Authority is set assumably a few weeks/months past where the previous book left us, following the protaganist Control who is established as the new director of the mysterious organisation sending groups into 'Area X'. It is a refreshing difference from what I expected - yet another group being sent in - yet it did not take long for the book to just fall in quality. 
 The first 200 pages could easily be cut out. Mysteries that don't lead anywhere, build-up that is left abandoned almost as soon as it's created. Characters are given opinions and flaws but then they are scrubbed out to null, indistinguishable by half-way through. By the time the book meanders its way to the point of it all, it's almost the end, and the few spine-tingling moments it has left just end on an unsatisfying note. 
 Whatever the point of Authority was, I clearly missed it; I felt it could have improved vastly by being more concise, by keeping up a much steadier pace, and by introducing a context much earlier than it did. It began promisingly but Annihiliation is definitely the better one despite its own flaws.

I enjoyed this less than I enjoyed Annihilation, but it's not bad. Where I wish Annihilation was longer, I wish this one was shorter. It drags rather a lot in the middle, and I feel that Control's angst over his family and his introspection could have been cut a little short. Also, this author needs to pull out a thesaurus and find some other words besides banal. But this is something inherited from Annihilation. 
 I'm re-reading it to see if I can gain more from a second read. 
 Book ends in a cliffhanger! And of course I'm on a waitlist for the next book! Ahh!

Part 2 of 3 and so good I just had to buy the last book right after finishing this one. 
 Southern Reach has a new boss but he is as clueless as anyone of what really goes on and he is just a pawn in the play. I like the lingering events from book one but not too sure about where VanderMeer is taking all of this. 
 Enviromental threat is here seen as an absense of pollution, a cleansing.

Ugh! So frustrated with this book! Read book #1 and was iffy about continuing the series. Read the free trial for book #2 and it hooked me enough to get me to buy the book. Ugh! Wish I hadn't spent the money. A totally frustrating book, so I actually couldn't even finish, which is really saying something for me cuz I tend to have to finish a book no matter how bad. Annoying book!

The second book in a trilogy is always a little tricky. They can't wrap up everything that happened in the first book, and they have add enough mystery to keep you hungry for the next one. Essentially, book two is usually a placeholder, meant to set up the big showdown in volume 3. So right now, I don't want to say that I found Authority, the second book in Jeff Vandermeer's Southern Reach trilogy to be disappointing, but I did expect for it to be better than it was. 
 Book 1, Annihilation, ended with our protagonist known only as The Biologist, rowing deeper into Area X. No one knows (or is willing to say) what happened to Area X 30 years ago, but something about its malevolent atmosphere defies explanation. The Biologist was part of the official Twelfth edition. The first group reported it as a paradise, the second ended in a mass suicide, the third in a mass murder and the eleventh expedition returned mysteriously, only to die of cancer months later. The Biologist set off to find answers. 
 Authority details the bureaucratic aspects of the secretive Southern Reach agency, responsible for figuring out just what the hell is happening in Area X. We follow John Rodriguez, nicknamed Control (a little on the nose there). He's the replacement director and has inherited a largely uncooperative staff, who feel they know how things should be run. 
 We learn a few things pretty quickly-some members of the Twelfth expedition have returned, surprising those of us who remember what happened to them in Annihilation. The women, including The Biologist say they can't remember anything. Control is pretty sure The Biologist is lying, but can't figure out why or how to prove it. We learn that there have been many expeditions, far more than the official twelve. We learn that some working at the Southern Reach know far more than they're willing to say. And we learn that something is looming on the horizon, but the men and women who have spent their professional lives looking for answers can't seem to see it. 
 The book, like most second books do, plods along pretty slowly, answering the questions we didn't really care about asking. It deepened the mystery and introduced us to the people and concepts that will probably be relevant in book three. I was interested, but not particularly engaged as I read...until the final 40 pages. That's when the book builds to a crescendo of insanity that left me genuinely excited for the next book. 
 Authority was a decent read, but I'll have to read the third book in the trilogy to figure out how much I truly liked it. If you liked Annihilation, I'd encourage you to give it a try, even though the books are totally different. But if you didn't read or like that book, I'd give Authority a hard pass.

I finished it, but man it was difficult. I consider myself an intelligent reader, but I honestly had no idea what was going on half the time, nor what sort of mood the author was actually shooting for. This was the second book in a trilogy...it's doubtful I'll finish it up, even if I have to fight the OCD.

in a word, boring. 
 it has none of the newness and wonder of the first book. 
 it reads a bit like the british spy novel. except without the tension of Nazis or Communists or whatever. Just vague conspiracies that don't make sense and almost nothing of the first book's view of the other side.

After Annihilation I was really excited to read this book, but this couldn't have been anything more different. The difference isn't the main problem but more how boring it was. Authority was honestly such a drag to read. The main character Control is not memorable at all and it got to a point where I really didn't give a shit about what happened to him at the end. Whitby and Ghost Bird are really interesting and likeable characters, but they aren't focused on as much as I, and I'm sure many others, would have loved. VanderMeer really has a way with words and writes beautifully and eloquently, but in this book both the characters and plot development fell so flat, and at places where it seemed VanderMeer wanted the reader to be shocked or terrified I had no reaction to. Authority conveys a really meaningful message, which is why I think this book has some fans, but it could not have been in a worse way in my opinion; the best thing about this book was VanderMeer's writing. Despite all this, I'm still planning on reading Acceptance because from what I heard it's much more like Annihilation, more creepy and thought-provoking and with a better pace. I hope the third book will not disappoint.
This is a claustrophobic, confusing book, with only partial information available. This is the point of the book, and I want to read the conclusion of this trilogy.

This book is deeply frustrating. I should have guessed that would be the case when I saw that it was almost twice the length of Annihilation. The atmospheric writing is still there, instead applied to the mystery of the Southern Reach rather than area X except where Annihilation is tightly woven, Authority is overly florid. Control is not particularly engaging when compared to the Biologist and the goal of a lot of the writing appears to be to make the Southern Reach just as shrouded in mystery as Area X. Authority unweaves several of what I thought were the more disquieting moments in Annihilation and in an attempt to make them more disquieting, just makes things confusing. 
 There are several wonderfully vivid moments, the rabbits, the video from the first expedition, the entire last chapter that save this novel from being a loss, but on the whole, it's missing a lot of what made the first novel so effective. Like maybe a good hard edit to remove some of the dead weight.

I absolutely could not put down the first book. It had the eerie ambiance of House of Leaves plus Greg Bear's Blood Music plus a little Lost thrown in for good measure. I savored every page and forced myself to read slowly. Then, got Authority immediately. The meandering nature of Annihilation suited the expedition, but I felt like Authority kind of went nowhere. I found myself wondering when I was going to learn something. I will hold out for the third book, though!

Dreadful. Wasted too many hours of my life reading this rambling and unrewarding book. 
 I continued on to read the final one and it did not improve by much.
It was fine. Felt like a bit of a slog after the first one.

All the paranoia, muted violence, and strangeness of Annihilation stuffed into a claustrophobic office building, a moldering outpost populated with passive-aggressive bureaucrats infiltrated by a spy from the enigmatic Southern Reach Central office. VanderMeer spreads the influence of Area X in such subtle ways, through the repetition of words, phrases, ideas (colonization, wrong thoughts, decay, border, aggression, inevitability). Obsessions old and new run deep in every character, inescapable, guiding, destructive. This series is masterful. I can't wait to finish it, but I also don't want it to end.

I still have no idea what's going on. Is this some sort of alien invasion? Is the Earth fighting back like in that weird Marky Mark movie where everyone jumped off buildings? Is Control a sweetheart or an asshole? Whitby? Cheney? Lowry? What is happening? I want to not care, but I'm dying to see if anything happens and I've already got the third one from the library, so...onward?

This book was really hard to get through. This first half is about the boring bureaucratic workings and interpersonal relationships of the employees at the Southern Reach. You see very little of the biologist and the main character, Control, is rather whiny and unlikeable. However, if you can manage the power through, the last third of so of this book really heats up and leaves you desperate to know what happens in the third book.

I will continue the final book in the trilogy because I would like more answers. This second installment just felt like I was reading about someone doing a super boring desk job for 300 pages and then some excitement in the last 40.

The sequel to the excellent 'Annihilation.' 
 In 'Annihilation' an expedition is sent out to the mysterious Area X by the enigmatic Authority of the Southern Reach. The book does a great job of creating a Lovecraftian, creeping dread of the unknown. Before reading 'Authority' someone told me, 'this is where you get all the answers.' 
 I had doubts that I even needed all the answers... but I read on. 
 Indeed, there are some answers here. The events here follow upon those in the first book - but from the opposite perspective. A new Director of the Southern Reach is appointed, and comes in to take over - to meets a hostile second-in-command, and all sorts of odd and possibly insane goings-on at the base. Are the effects of Area X leaching through the border? 
 It starts off really well - I wasn't upset to find the 'answers,' I thought they worked very well. But - I expected more to happen. The set-up is great, but there isn't much follow-through. Things are weird and complicated, everyone has a lot of baggage to start with, and there are weird and possibly alien influences. 
 Possibly this is middle-book syndrome - I'll still be reading the third installment of the trilogy.

This is one of the most baffling sequels I've ever encountered. 
 Where part 1 was jaunt through an unnatural landscape layered with mystery, part 2 is... office bureaucracy? 
 Our new protagonist, "Control" is appointed director of the shady government organization that was background in part 1. Turns out: he's a pretty bad manager. Over many pages. 
 If the first 250 or so pages of this book were condensed into about 30 and the final 50 pages were continued, it might have been worth continuing this series.
Wasnt a huge fan of #1 and #2 just didnt do it for me.
3.25 rating. Found this instalment more jarring and meandering. Everything continues to be on the left, now with the addition of more 'wary' and 'embedded'.

Phew ok. I read this book straight after reading (and enjoying) book 1 (Annihilation). And that was definitely a mistake. I stopped reading at around 50% on my initial run-through and only just managed to finish the second half over a month later. 
 This book is much heavier, gives little more information, and unnecessarily long. And VanderMeer seemingly decided to replace the 'intrigue' of the first book with 'annoyance' as the primary feel. Large portions of the book do not move the story along AT ALL and seem only designed to produce an awkward uncomfortable feeling in the reader. 
 The new narrator 'Control' is a whiny paranoid mummy's boy who works with dull weirdos. Large portions of the book are spent in his head as he worries about ultimately irrelevant things. This is scattered with a tiny trickle of hints and intrigue about Area X, but with no real direction until the last few chapters as to how much of this is relevant (hint - not much). 
 The small section at the end, where things happen, and we are actually given information instead of just being blandly teased, is quite good. But 85-90% of the book is pointless and boring. I suspect VanderMeer was looking to re-create the kind of classical uneasiness of existentialist works from Camus or Kafka but he had failed to notice that those books are generally shorter novellas at most, not medium-to-long novels. Fire your editor VanderMeer! 
 I may check out book 3 (in the likely foolish hope of some eventual answers) at some point in the future, but unless you were absolutely in love with book 1 I'd advise leaving it there.

I feel that this book is in large part unnecessary. Firstly, the entire main thrust of the novel was given away fairly obviously very early on (two of the team members returned when we know for a fact that they are dead, the odd smell permeating the facility which only the person who hasn't been contaminated either in thought or person can smell) . The majority of the time is spent with Control as he attempts to wade through office hostility and crazy while getting a grip on his predecessor and Area X. The previous book made use of flashbacks during the course of the narrative and I see no reason why this couldn't be condensed as well. I think the subtlety which would have to be employed would better serve the mystery anyhow. 
 Secondly, I don't like the emphasis of Area X as being the sole main protagonist of the series. It makes sense, sure, that area and its mystery is the background and impetus for the whole series. And each book seems to have its own character focus, but split in three like that seems to be reducing the potential emotional connection. What can I say; I really liked the Biologist. I was looking forward to more from her and that she appeared so infrequently is disappointing.

book_b.title: Ready Player One
book_b.user_review:
** spoiler alert ** 
 What a fun book! This book is truly nerd food. At first I was worried because I found it slow to begin. This is likely due to the fact that Cline takes a great deal of time setting up the premise of the OASIS and the contest; however, patience through the descriptions and details pays off if you enjoy 1980s pop culture, old video games, science fiction, fantasy, or any combination of those. I enjoy them all, and couldn't help but smile (or even giggle) at the many familiar references mentioned. (There were a number of unfamiliar ones too, and I think I may have to add a few titles to my various To Do lists.) I was suddenly hooked so thoroughly, I hadn't even realized it happened. Cline mixes all the best things of each genre: the quest of the fantasy genre, insane technology of science fiction, characters you want to cheer for, and then adds those little details and tiny references that (if you catch them, because I know that I sure didn't catch them all) make you feel like this was written by one of your own fellow geek friends, sharing an inside joke with you. He also pokes at more serious underlying issues, such as the role of technology in society and privacy in an internet world, issues that become disturbing when you really consider them. But rather than solving all the problems at once he lets the matters, and the characters, rest for another day's consideration (probably best for my sleep habits). Recommended for those who really love the geek life.

I thoroughly, thoroughly enjoyed this book. Without spoiling anything I find this book to be worthy of a movie. It brought me back to my childhood, my teen years and beyond. It has brought me the desire to watch all the wonderful movies talked about, listen to all the referenced music and die to find an Atari 2600 so I can go back and play all its games. I might just have to drag out the Nintendo 64 although that unit wasn't talked about until towards the end... 
 Such a delightful, inspiring and well written book. Well done Ernest Cline, well done. 
 This will definitely be a book I recommend to everyone, especially those who love all things Geeky. [?] 
 Onward to your next book.
Fanfreakingtastic!

Ready Player One is the most referential book I have ever read. Its pages drip with 80s pop culture references, some of them obvious, many of them not. It's entertaining at first, especially when you understand the reference, but then it becomes a bit obnoxious and excessive. This, in fact, is a good analogue to the book itself. Its beginning is much stronger than its conclusion, and the aspects of the book which were its most entertaining element at the start become tired and worn-out by the end. 
 The book is on the whole enjoyable. I described it to a co-worker as "aggressively okay." The narrative pulls you along at a steady pace, interesting things happen, the mystery of the "Easter Egg" is sufficiently compelling, but it's the finer details that start to nag. As mentioned, the references, the worship of 80s culture, although explained through the narrative, becomes irritating. The details of the story are impressive, and the author's passion for the subject matter screams on every page. The writing and dialogue serves the story fine and provides only a few moments of profundity. 
 Sadly, the author, Ernest Cline, commits one of the most grievous mistakes of any science fiction or fantasy story, which I call "The Magic Wand." Essentially "The Magic Wand" is a narrative tool to magically fix the story's most perplexing problems. (Did you know reversing the Earth's orbit reverses time itself!? Thank you, Superman). Often times authors use this Wand when they've painted themselves into a corner. "Oh, look, now the main character can fly!" or "travel through time!" or some such thing. Ready Player One's Magic Wand is the main character's outlandish sudden ability to perfectly plan and execute a plan of such devious and conniving genius it leaves both the characters in the book and the reader of the book completely stunned. Furthermore, throughout the book, there are far too many instances of the character needing to know some obscure or obtuse fact about 80s pop culture and the main character conveniently notifies the reader: "Good thing I've watched this film exactly 175 times." Good thing, indeed. 
 Having said all of this, I enjoyed Ready Player One for what it was. I was especially interested in the possible and entirely plausible future of virtual reality that the book showcases. It's both exciting and dismaying. Although the messaging of the book is muddled, which is too bad, the fiction aspect of it was very interesting. (It's worth mentioning that according to an article in Businessweek, each new Oculus Rift employee--a company which has created a virtual reality headset--is issued a copy of Ready Player One). A few years ago I was extremely skeptical of virtual reality's ability to be adopted by the mainstream. Although that hasn't happened in a significant way yet, I do believe it will; in addition, I believe it very well could herald a massive shift in how we consume and participate in entertainment, education, business, commerce, and even how we interact with and make sense of reality itself. Ready Player One shows a world that is either terrifying or exhilarating depending on your worldview. I'm not convinced the author knows exactly which one it is. 
 Ready Player One is being adapted into a film by Steven Spielberg, and I think it might have a better chance being a great story as a film than a book. I think the story needs to be trimmed, sliced and diced a bit, and leave behind many of the arcane details meant to be enjoyed by only a few. There is definitely a fun adventure to be found here, but it might take some other storytellers to tell it a bit better.

This was just what I needed to zone out while traveling in Vegas. It filled up all the waiting time (like waiting for the taxi, the plane, the Miss Asian Pageant -- you know what I mean). Definitely a children's dystopia book for Gen X gaming nerds -- no social commentary, implicit reliance on the ultimate justice and protection of the legal system, and straight-up D&D.
Well, I pushed through it, even though I didn't like it. There was barely any action, and the romance between P and A was boring. The ending was boring, too.

Not especially dynamic in terms of character development, and the writing tended to be a lot of "I did this, then this happened, then I did this, and oh-by-the-way, here's a historical summary of what this thing is all about," etc.. But that makes it sound like I didn't like it, which isn't true! It actually was a lot of fun. I think the writing style is probably strongly informed by the fact that most of the story takes place in virtual reality, and our narrator was pretty much alone most of the time. So it makes sense, but still wasn't my favorite writing. Anyway, the premise and the plot were interesting and the end was satisfying, so definitely a solid read.

LOVED this. Started out with the audiobook (highly recommended - Wil Wheaton is a GREAT narrator), got about halfway through, and then switched over to print so i could finish faster -- and read the rest in an evening. Such an imaginative, genre-bending, addictive read.

I liked but didn't love this straight-ahead adventure story clothed in an unreasoning, nostalgic love for 80s geek culture. I am just a little too old to remember the 80s so fondly. I did laugh aloud numerous times, and the story was involving and plotted well. It's pure summer/escapist/goofy fiction, and it's a lot of fun if you have even a passing familiarity with the 80s. I suspect there's a generation for whom this one is as evocative as Among Others was for me.

I really liked this book! Chock-full of pop culture and pop culture references - and anyone who knows me well, knows that I love that kind of stuff - there was even a "Heathers" reference, which is one of my favorite movies! So needless to say, I was hooked right from the beginning. 
 However, there was one particular thing that bothered me, while reading "Ready Player One", and it ultimately keeps me from rating it four stars. Cline seems to tell, instead of show, what happens, A LOT of the time. I realize that sometimes it's easier to simply describe what's going on, versus show it, but the saying "Good authors show, and don' tell!" kept popping into my head, at various times. Sure, this is his first published book, (plus, he's a screenwriter, which I find extremely cool!)...so combine the two, and I'll let it slide. :) 
 One star for the cool, unique premise, one star for the awesome (and incredibly detailed) 80's material (this guy knows his stuff!) and one for the fact that he is a screenwriter. I just love the idea of being a screenwriter!!

A helluva of a nostalgic and high energy/stakes competition through the 1980s and geek/nerd culture. Yes, it's a whole lot of fun but there's a sobering message here too about where the world could be headed. Even though the message is that reality is always better than fantasy, in this world, it's hard to argue for that point. Being plugged is better than the reality of Ready Player One unless you are one of the priviledged few. 
 Fun read.

Futuristic subject in a time where Virtual Reality takes over all the interest of a population living on a decaying planet. The book is at its best when it leaves the video game events to talk about virtual reality and what it does to the real reality. Unfortunately this does not occur a lot in the book.

I read RPO long after the pomp and circumstance surrounding its explosion onto the SF scene a few years back. And as I had hoped from what I'd heard since its release, RPO was a thrilling ride. 
 For me, RPO was the perfect mix of nostalgia, new age technology and action. Throw in a three-tiered epic quest, an immersive technology/creative new world, generous throw backs to (my own formative years in) the 80s, characters you just want to root for, and a sinister institution/master villain and you get this book. Not to mention an engaging Audible performance from Will Wheaton (I read and listened). 
 Getting down to brass tacks, this was an adventure in every sense. What I think took it over the top were the "retro hooks" that Mr. Cline wove into the plot that got readers like me (I'm hoping so, at least), reminiscing about the glory days of a time long forgotten. One where you worried over things like, let's say, getting your homework done, high school dances, or getting to ball practice on time. Not to mention trying to ride a skateboard behind a moving car while causing a manure truck to drop it's payload into Biff's convertible. 
 Easy five stars out of five, net of the deductions for all the Rush references (ugh) :)

This is such a "boy" book, and as I've stated in other reviews, I dislike dystopian settings. But the 1980s pop culture references won me over. Really, it reads like a young adult book, and if it wasn't for the '80s pop culture I think it probably would have been marketed that way.
Love, love, loved this book.
Awesome.

I thought this book started off quite promising. The book is set in a dystopian world that could 100% become reality and I felt like Cline laid down a really good foundation for his story. I thought the initial world-building was really well done, Wade seemed like an interesting character and the references were tiny bits of fun. I felt like what Cline built on top of that foundation wasn't as impressive. For one, I wanted more insight into the actual world they were living, not just insight into the OASIS. I understand that Wade didn't actually live in the real world and he never really did but I wasn't satisfied and I would have loved to have heard more about the real world. Secondly, Wade himself turned out to be quite a boring character. I didn't care for him that much. Lastly, the story ended up dragging a lot. I felt like it was one 80's reference after another after another after another after another aft- well, you get the point. I wasn't born until the mid-nineties so I didn't get a lot of the references that weren't game-related or mainstream. That said, Cline just explained everything and if that was only done a few times then I probably wouldn't have minded but it was constant and I got tired of it, real fast. 
 I thought the world-building inside OASIS was pretty cool and it was cool because I love playing games. The writing wasn't bad either, it was grand. I could have left the romance though, I thought it was quite unnecessary and it didn't really add anything substantial to the plot. 
 I feel like it was a nice idea to write a book that included 80's references. Cline paid homage to everything he admired as a kid and that's lovely, it really is but I'm just a reader who couldn't get behind all those references; there were too many. I would not recommend this book but I would read something else by Ernest Cline.
