A pesar de no tener grandes expectativas de este libro, termino atrapandome en cuanto deje atras los capitulos que te introducen al universo de la historia (un poco aburridos, pero muy necesarios). Es la primera vez que siento que un libro me atrapa por tanto tiempo ininterrumpido y me provoca, al pausar la lectura, una ansiedad similar a la que se produce cuando se deja de ver una serie o pelicula muy interesantes. 
 Aunque no es su enfoque principal, logra retratar un "mundo real" decadente y sumido en la miseria a pesar de contar con significativos avances tecnologicos. La caceria del huevo de pascua en Oasis es contada de forma agil y sin demasiados descansos para mantener al lector interesado en todo momento, lo cual me parecio un gran acierto que provoca que las paginas pasen y pasen sin que uno se de cuenta.
Couldn't make it past page 56, won't be returning.

Take 2 more successful. Can't say it is my favorite book but once you got past all the nostalgia & battled through to the meat of the story it got better. Might make for an interesting movie, since post-apocalyptic is all the rage now.

Meh. Alright book but everything works out too conveniently in the end, the author writes himself out of a lot of corners. 
 Doesn't get any better on the second read through. I like the premise but the execution is really poor. It feels really forced to me.

Everything that is good about this book has all to do with nostalgia and nothing to do with the quality of the author's writing. The author often does a thing I hate in books where he puts an unrealistic character in an impossible situation, and then the character is able to come out of the situation on top (all of this is a normal and good plot) except this book explains ALMOST NOTHING. 
 (imaginary dialog between me and the author) 
 Oh I'm going to do this impossible thing I shouldn't be able to do. 
 How are you going to do that. 
 Well. I just did. See those words I wrote about it I DID. 
 You did, I see but how. How did you manage to do that. 
 I have no idea, but that is how writing a book works. I don't HAVE to explain. Because even I don't know. 
 You should read this if ...... 
 you grew up during the 80s 
 you love 8os movies 
 you would love a commodore 64 
 you have played dungeons and dragons 
 you enjoy books that don't waste time explaining things 
 Don't read this if ...... 
 you are a 90s kid and don't really know anything about arcade games other than pacman 
 you enjoyed the book THE MARTIAN. Because that was a fantastic book and this one sucks 
 you

I originally gave this 4 stars but the more I think about this book, the more questions I have. Looking back, it definitely comes off as an author self-insert fantasy, though it does have awesome concepts. The gaming universe and the thrill of the chase is very well done; it was hard for me to put the book down at points. But the second half of it became tedious and beyond my stretch of the imagination. There's a point where you can suspend disbelief, but it has its limits, and this book went beyond it. 
 Strong female character: eh? sure? he tried. Eventually the character she could have been dies and becomes a fawning fangirl carbon copy of the Dream Girl archetype. 
 POC representation: sure; again, he tried. Japanese and Black American characters put in just for the sake of having them there really kills character development. The Japanese characters became stereotypes and essentially unimportant to the story when they could have benefited it so much more. 
 It was a good book in the moment, but looking back on it just makes me disappointed.

This book blows!!!!! It is not and I repeat NOT interesting! If I wanted to learn about some Second Life virtual reality or some World of Warcraft crap I would have gone on wikipedia. This book is not challenging and it does not lift you away from your everyday life. And I thought it was so idiotic that in this world of 2044 everybody is CONSTANTLY connected to this virtual world and nobody actually lives their lives. Anyway, really bad experience and I don't understand why so many god reviews... 
 If I wanna get in a video game world I PLAY video games I don' read about video games, darn it! I have no idea who this book is targeted to.

I really liked this book. I think I liked the fact that it was like a scavenger hunt, which is fun. The world this takes place in scares me a little bit, because I don't think it's complete fantasy, but hopefully it stays in the fiction realm.
I started this book, but never finished. It didn't interest me. Wasn't my type of book. Not saying it's BAD, it's just not my thing. My husband would love it, though, I think.

John Hughes movies are all the rage. Kids everywhere are firing up Atari games. Billy Idol and Cyndi Lauper songs are blasting in dance clubs. To the average person in the 1980s, this may appear par for the course but in Ernest Cline's sci-fi novel Ready Player One, we're no longer in the 1980s, we're in the year 2044 and the most obnoxious decade of the 20th century is back in a big way! 
 The whole world is up shit creek without a paddle. People are living in crude skyscrapers constructed from stacked mobile homes, crime is at an all time high and the economy is in the toilet. The only escape from this dreary existence is a massive online RPG network dubbed the OASIS. Players strap on a visor giving them full 360 degree vision of a computer generated world in which they design their own avatar and live out a much more pleasant existence. 
 The game's creator, James Halliday, passed away a few years prior and before doing so, hid a prize deep inside the game. Halliday decided that whoever could claim the elusive prize would gain controlling interest in his company and inherit his unbelievable $240 billion fortune (that's billion with a b). Knowing that everyone on earth would be gunning for it, Halliday did his damndest to make uncovering his "easter egg" as challenging as possible. One would have to both know his life story inside out and be a true scholar of the 1980s. Well, unless you're a giant soulless corporation like IOI (Innovative Online Industries) with its sights set on complete market domination. 
 For years IOI have been sending out their army of hunters, desperate to uncover the location of the egg. Fortunately for the OASIS community, IOI haven't made headway in their search. It isn't until a young player named Wade Watts from the stacks in Oklahoma City uncovers the Copper Key - the first step in the search for the egg - that things really begin to heat up. Can Wade complete the quest before IOI claim the prize or will another ambitious player step up to the plate and nab the billion dollar crown? 
 Despite being born in 1984, I'm not quite a student of the 80s. I was six years old when the calendar turned over to 1990 and the following ten years really crafted my sense of humor and fascination with pop culture. Put on an old episode of the CG TV show ReBoot or Pixar's first Toy Story to really get the nostalgia drug following through my veins. While I was worried that the majority of the references within Cline's Ready Player One would sail over my head, thankfully I had enough crap jammed into that "useless-knowledge" part of my brain reserved for Saturday morning cartoon shows, WWF wrestling, Ghostbusters and Top 40 radio to get me by. 
 While the book took a little too long to get going for my taste, once Wade (or Parzival) grabbed that Copper Key, Cline pushed down on the pedal and took this Delorean of a novel to 88mph. In looking around at several other reviews, it's hard to believe people haven't praised the dialogue nearly as much as I feel it's deserved. While Cline isn't doing anything special per se, it should be noted that everything just feels so natural. I'm going to really miss these characters. 
 Bottom line, this is a really fun book. I welcome the person who takes a crack at recreating the ultimate 90s nostalgia trip where all the characters wear flannel shirts, watch Boy Meets World and obsess over Kevin Smith movies.
Muito divertido! Quero jogar OASiS agora! Jogando dinheiro no livro e nada acontece!

Some of the explanations of the world in this book are so incredibly clunky. That aside, I couldn't put it down! An awesome video game adventure for true geeks--a tale that rewards the geekily obsessed for knowing crazy amounts of minutia (the characters have to know the details, the reader just has to appreciate how cool it is to be a serious geek).

I'm not usually a sci-fi reader, but I think this is one of those rare books in the genre that anyone can enjoy. I was kind of hesitant going in because at first I had heard glowing reviews, but as more time passed, I started hearing complaints about the male characters, specifically the main character, and the portrayal of female gamers. Having read this book myself, I can say that I have absolutely no idea where those complaints are coming from. I felt nothing but pity for Wade, and I thoroughly enjoyed seeing his life improve over the course of the story. If there was one character I took issue with, it was Samantha. She needed to take a chill pill. I loved all of the 80s pop culture references. I have to admit that there was a handful of times when it started to border on becoming tiresome, but then I pulled up a playlist of 80s pop music and honestly, it really added to my reading experience. I recommend doing the same! This book started off a little slower than I was anticipating, but it picked up eventually. I feel like the author wrote this story with the hopes that it would be adapted into a film. Sometimes that works. Other times, it doesn't. In this case, it was both. There were many, many times where we were being told what happened instead of being shown. If that makes sense. I was kind of surprised that the book ended where it did, that there was no epilogue. I don't know if Armada is a sequel. If it is, then I don't mind the abrupt ending.

This book was a nice adventure! 
 The ending was pretty predictable and sometimes the story felt like a "it was all a dream" trope since most of it was just a video game. Also, at times I just felt like I was reading some 80's geek manual and it got kinda of boring (but that's just because I didn't get 99% of the references). 
 Nevertheless, I still enjoyed the action and the characters a lot.

LISTEN. It's 2 am and I'm completely incoherent and maybe crying a little because I loved this book so much. The only thing I can say right now in terms of a review is that I have not felt this attached to a cast of characters or to a book in general since the Harry Potter series. No exaggeration whatsoever. This is now one of my favourite books of all time and all I want to do now is re-read it every day until I die. SERIOUSLY. Holy. Fuck.

So much wrong with this book. 
 It is stuffed with unnecessary words ("The Eighties was a long decade. Ten whole years."). It suffers from a shocking lack of imagination--the world of 2044 lacks any notable technological developments, and mostly contains slightly improved VR gear, slightly increased storage (zettabytes!), and slightly improved WiFi signals (but, don't worry, passages of the book are still dedicated to the scintillating topic of someone attempting to connect to WiFi). Its dialogue is often terrible ("We called them suxz0rz. Because they sucked." [light paraphase]). Its plot stutters, too quickly moving through key plot points, too slowly moving through unnecessary world-building about 2/3 of the way through, and too content to simply list references to video games, TV shows, movies, and songs. It also essentially equates real-world violence with fantasy-world violence, and contains a shocking act of violence that is breezed over. It also romanticizes obsession and equates it with love. 
 I almost gave it two stars because it tries to deal with the interesting issue of identity and personality when people maintain both their "IRL" lives and their online lives, but the way in which it deals with this is just too boring (a female character might be male in real life!). 
 Spend your quarters elsewhere.

This book came recomended, but it's strike two for science fiction for me in 2017. This book takes place in the year 2044 and the main character Wade Watts is only alive when he's plugged into a virtual utopia called Oasis, in fact most people are plugged into the game because a fortune is hidden by the creator into the details, and people are all looking for the golden bean. The race is on and to win, a player must survive. If you like 80s culture, this book is for you. I got tired of reading about 80s TV shows, rock stars, early video games, Molly Ringwald and the Breakfast Club, blah, blah, blah. The 80s were boring and fake to live through, why revive them as a favorite? This could actually be my worse nightmare for the future.

Lots of 80's nostalgia utilized in a very unique way. Even though I wasn't much a gamer ever, I still enjoyed the book. There wasn't too much tension, however, because much of what was happening to the characters was happening to the avatars, therefore the stakes weren't very high. The best part of the book is when Wade indentures himself with the evil corporation, and I thought that scenario should have been explored more deeply, but it was just a short side trip to set up the deux et machina ending. Still, a fun diversion and should make a good movie, especially with Spielberg at the helm.
Excellent Book!!!!!!

*insert me kneeling on the ground holding the book above my head and if it's simba* 
 AAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHHH

I never give a sub review meant to deal w/a certain group, but this book is a 4 star if you were a nerdy kid in the early 80's. Ready Player One took my 16 year old psyche and spilled it out for me to revel in. The D&D references, the nerd movies, the sci-fi authors, and the 21st century connection w/Warcraft and its lingo was a hoot. 
 The plot's pretty passive, but the characters are enjoyable and the ending hits the right note of satisfaction. 
 The dystopian future brought on by global warming is tired and like a bad Star Trek episodes says more about what we're living w/today = epic fail.
really funny and entertaining! a must read..really.
This was a really fun read! I'm trying to talk Jake into reading it.

This is the book I wish I would have written. 
 Deep fried in 80s culture, this was a walk through my childhood. 
 I'm sure it didn't hurt that the internet archive released over 700 Jmame compatible browser games, and that I was doing spring cleaning and found my old notes on Zork I, II, and III. 
 Ah, I want to read this to my children and go the arcade with them. 
 A simply wonderful book for those who grew up in the 80s. 
 I was advised to get the Audiobook version, which is read by Wil Wheaton, which I have to say was a perfect choice. It only added to it to hear Ensign Crusher talking about a Star Trek and the current Oasis player presidency.
If you loved the 80s - this is the geek book! Star Wars, movies and a dystopian government all mixed in. Really a 4.5 not quite a 5

I bloody well loved this, it was such a good book. 
 full review here - http://www.afternoonbookery.blogspot....

takes the first 70-80 pages to get going, using those number of pages for context and backstory. (Where was his editor?) Gamer geeks will love it. It's a little light on the plot, 90% of which takes place in cyberspace, so again, if you're not a hardcore gamer freak, you're going to find yourself frustrated at the lack of human action.

Ready Player One 
 I read a few reviews previously before actually starting to read this book. Several reviewers would bring up the various pop culture references and quotes from various eighties flicks. This of course is usually not a good sign, and typically seen as a bad thing, however it was just the opposite of that for me, I couldn't stop reading the book. 
 In this book you have a world in the not so distant future, that has decided to give everyone a virtual world called the Oasis in which they are able to live. Everything takes place here, it reminded much of the film Surrogates other then this was a virtual world and not a physical world. Meanwhile the physical world is turning out into not such a great thing. 
 James Halliday the creator of the Oasis has passed away, and in his will he leaves his properties to no individual in particular. Instead he says their will be a contest and whoever wins the contest will win his fortune and partial control over the Oasis. 
 Enter in Pazavil who in the real world is Wade, he has been trying to win this contest for years. When he finally finds the first key and begins to run into other characters Is where the real fun begins as the sixers begin to try to destroy everything in Wades world and other gamers worlds. 
 The book movies between the two worlds with great ease, though the majority of the book takes place in the virtual world which is filled with several 70s and 80s references. It is an exciting tale that keeps you turning the pages. It is fun for gamers and non gamers. 
 The book is fun and exciting and manages to get its story out in just the right amount of pace. Indeed parts of this book made me think, wow they are referencing stuff from my childhood this type of thing shouldn't happen until your older. Yet every reference seems to bring a smile to the readers face. 
 Get Reading and Enjoy.

I liked the novel's premise of a high stakes treasure hunt that takes place in a virtual reality word and that's what drew me in to this book. Some of the pacing was slow and the writing was sometimes pedantic. But, the pure fun and nostalgia of seeing many of my favorite old movies and tv shows and vintage computers (my first computer was a TRS-80) play a central role in solving the riddles and mysteries of the plot made it a guilty pleasure for me.
It is a complete geek orgasm of wonderful. Read it. Even if you don't feel like you're in the right mood to read it, just start it. You won't put it back down.
full review pending. By no means great literature, Ready Player One is instead great fun, especially for those of us who grew up in the 80s.
This was a fabulous trip to the nerd-fest and I really didn't want it to end. I loved all the 80s references and descriptions of OASIS are some I couldn't have ever imagined on my own.

God, this was terrible. 
 I read this based on a very positive review from io9, and finished it because I don't like leaving books halfway, but I came very close to abandoning it multiple times. The plot isn't much more substantial than the summary on the back, and is depressingly dull - several times things were plodding along in such a formulaic way that I assumed there had to be a twist coming, only to realise that no, the plot really was that predictable. The characterisation is utterly nonexistent, with paper-thin "baddies" and "goodies". There are a lot of references to 80s culture peppered throughout the book, which I think is part of why it's popular - but even the descriptions of game-playing are so superficial and generic that you can't really make yourself care (and I say that as a fan of vintage computer games). Who on earth was this aimed at? Anyone over six years old would want more story than this but anyone nostalgic about the 80s is going to be late 30s at least. 
 I understand that there is a movie on the way, which I fully expect to actually be better than the source.

THIS BOOK WAS PANCAKE FLIPPING GOOD. At first i was hesitant to pick up this book, i knew there was a lot of hype and i'd been meaning to get to it for a while and just hadn't. Also there was the fact that i don't really know anything about the 80s or video games. But my worries were nothing more than that. This book delivered on every level and i absolutely loved it! Definitely pick it up no matter who you are as the plot and idea is so unique and interesting. I was absolutely immersed in this book and couldn't stop reading it!

reference_books.review_text:
I bailed after 58 pages. Plesantly readable, but nothing happens and the characters are not the least bit interesting. A much better title would be The Borings. 
 I realize this is one of those books that people either love or just don't care for - unfortunately this is the second for me.

reference_books.title: The Giving Tree
reference_books.review_text: Tree, find someone who loves you for who you are - like a bird or squirrel or another tree. Or just be happy the way you are and enjoy the sunshine and keep making apples. That selfish boy does not deserve all your limbs and trunk. And getting love that way does not work. You will be used up and feel used and will be lonelier than before... learn some self-respect, damn it!

reference_books.title: Animal Farm
reference_books.review_text:
Parable about tyranny. Precursor to 1984. On every "books to read before you die" list. Required reading. 
 Yawn. 
 Check.

reference_books.title: The Turn of the Screw
reference_books.review_text: Melodramatic, overwrought drivel. Spooky ghosts. Incompetent governess goes into hysterics instead of asking questions or exercising discipline. Ridiculous vexations and overdramatization. And ghostism. How does she know the spookies are bad, without ever trying to communicate with them?

reference_books.title: Casino Royale (James Bond, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The movie is way better. The spy story is good, but the casino scenes and the romance are terribly boring. Clearly, what constitutes cool has changed a lot since 1953. I rather doubt that smoking 70 cigarettes a day and guzzling stiff drinks would keep your mind sharp and your body in shape enough for spy work. 
 I expected misogyny, but not the bloodcurling levels of it: 
 "These blithering women who thought they could do a man's work. Why the hell couldn't they stay at home and mind their pots and pans and stick to their frocks and gossip and leave the men's work to the men? " 
 Vesper is incredibly beautiful, but alternately cold, or feeble, emotional and submissive. Bond wants to screw her from the start (apparently this was ok in work situations in the fifties). Fleming's idea of a sex scene is crude, and he thinks rape is something to spice up your love life with: "And he knew that she was profoundly, excitingly sensual, but that the conquest of her body, because of the central privacy in her, would each time have the tang of rape". 
 I enjoyed the action, and the writing was pretty good, but the rampant misogyny, Vesper's stupid characterization, and the insipid, creepy love story really turned me off.

reference_books.title: Fried Green Tomatoes at the Whistle Stop Cafe
reference_books.review_text:
Fluffy, heartwarming anecdotes of a bygone time, place and family. Feel-good stories, friendships, people helping and loving each other and life. The characters and stories were interesting and well-written. The island of happy acceptance of a lesbian couple and their close relationship with their black help was a bit too idyllic to believe, especially woven into the realities of black existence in the segregationist south. 
 While I enjoyed the writing overall, I found that the multitude of narrators and newspaper bits changed the tone and jerked the story around. The jumping around in time was also unnecessarily distracting. I had to closely pay attention to the dates on the chapters - they could be anywhere within about fifty years. Otherwise an enjoyable, easy read.

reference_books.title: Scarlet (The Lunar Chronicles, #2)
reference_books.review_text: This is even better than Cinder. Really fun page-turner, suspenseful and action-packed. The additions to the cast, Scarlet and Wolf, bring a new and different set of adventures. Marissa Meyer manages to turn the story of red girl, wolf and grandma into a compelling dystopian adventure that stands on its own but also furthers Cinder's story. As with the last one, it ends with a cliff hanger and I think I need to buy it on my Kindle - the library closes early on Sundays...

reference_books.title: In Cold Blood
reference_books.review_text:
Masterfully written. Beautiful, lyrical, and above all, deeply compassionate to all participants, Capote manages to create a chilling account of the Clutters murders by establishing a non-judgmental, personal tone that dwelves into the thoughts and feelings of the murdered family, the stunned community, the investigators, litigators, but above all, the killers. This unprecedented closeness to the killers is what upsets - the description of their careless romp through the continent, their aimlessness, lack of responsibility, and most notably, their complete lack of remorse. 
 Capote weaves parallel storylines of the victims and the killers, up until the latter's capture. We get to know the Clutters, an almost inconcievably likeable family, who always helped everyone, were always nice, even-tempered, encouraging, talented, hardworking, with no bad habits - not even drinking coffee... Perfect kids, Nancy winning pie baking contests, riding horses, active in social groups, smart, joyful, down-to-earth. Kenyon the brainy engineer-type, always working on electronic and engineering projects. Everybody loved them. Mr Clutter was renown for not keeping cash in the house. They were the least likely family to get murdered in the state of Kansas. 
 Yet they were murdered, brutally, and the killers left almost no clues, no motive. The community is shattered, everyone is afraid, news reporters flood the area. We witness the mourning of people close to the Clutters, the shock, the distrust, fear, suspicion. Many install locks and are afraid to sleep. The crime is so egregious and so mysterious - several investigators become obsessed with the case, chiefly Mr Dewey, whose family suffers greatly from his preoccupation. 
 The most fascinating part of the story, however, follows the killers. Dick, a smalltime crook and thief, is from a loving family, but he does not inherit his parents responsibility and caring. He exhibits growing signs of sociopathy - superficial charm that he uses to swindle money out of men and sex out of women; complete lack of responsibility, inability to learn from mistakes, cruelty to animals, pedophilia, ego-centrism, lack of empathy, inability to see consequences of actions. In prison, he meets Perry, whose background is harrowing - broken family, a mother who drank herself to death, two siblings who committed suicide, extreme abuse at hands of wards - nuns who belted him because he wetted the bed; a care-taker who held him in icy water for the same offense, that almost killed him. His relationship with his father is of love-hate - he loves him but he cannot take any criticism and reacts to it violently, which leads to a fall-out with his father. He joins the Army, encounters sexual and emotional abuse, some at the hand of officers. These all enhance his natural tendency to shyness, inability to control his rage and feeling of abused, unappreciated, put upon, being neglected. 
 It took the interaction of the two to become murderers, and our justice system made sure they met in prison. Capote gives away most of the story, yet holds one that surprised me - Perry's confession, the true account of events. The rest of the book is spent on judicial proceedings, and psychological analysis of the condemned men and their death-row inmates. The analysis is the best contemporary psychology could provide, and interestingly quite similar in the case of four death-row inmates - that of what we call psychopathy - inability to feel emotions, regard for other human beings, feeling like only themselves matter, megalomania. 
 The exception is Perry. Even though he is just as a cold blooded killer as the others, we feel - or Capote feels - that he could have been saved. That he was just an overly sensitive kid who needed emphathy, compassion, education, showing the right way - yet kept being beaten up, let down, misled. His lack of empathy was due to disassociation from a situation, not complete lack of feelings. He is definitely not likeable. But he had potential, and we feel sorry for him. We feel sorry for the whole, terrible, sad story - the Clutters, Dick's family, Perry, and ultimately, the author, who have invested so much of himself in this story that he could never write again. 
 A very moving, profound work, that's more chilling than any fiction could be - because it is true.

reference_books.title: Journey to the Center of the Earth (Extraordinary Voyages, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
I enjoyed this fantastic voyage of scientific discovery and imagination. Professor Hardwigg and his nephew, Henry, along with their guide Hans, follow a medieval traveler into the center of the Earth through a crater of an icelandic volcano, and end up traveling back into the Earth's past. Verne has the opportunity to flaunt his knowledge of geology, physics, biology and paleontology, as well as expound on contemporary scientific theories about what's inside the Earth. 
 The journey is well-written and interesting, save for one but very annoying problem - Henry's constant whining and melodrama. He overdramatizes everything and bumbles about, constantly needing rescue by his uncle and the superhuman Hans. Hans, on the other hand, is implacable, never gets upset, tired, never takes a break, and is always there when the other two need rescuing, something built, or breakfast. 
 Overall enjoyable but too much melodrama.

reference_books.title: Dead Until Dark (Sookie Stackhouse, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It is a page-turner - but that's the only good thing going for it. I read it 'til the end because I wanted to know what happens. But otherwise, the story of a small-town waitress with misunderstood, mystical talents. She says she reads a lot, yet there is no one scene in the book where she reads - when idle, she channel-flips or cleans the house for distracting her mind from troubled events. She writes expertly about sexual deviance but she is a virgin when she consumes her first relationship with an attractive vampire.... 
 ...can you say, romantic vampire fantasies of a misunderstood waitress?

book_a.title: The Tempest
book_a.user_review:
This is not one of my favorites from the Bard. The story is convoluted - there are too many devious plots to kill people for no reason; events are shaped beyond anybody's control but Prospero's. I was not a fan of including the antique godesses, nymphs and spirits, it seemed like a copout from writing about people, which I feel is Shakespeare's best suit. 
 I know this is considered autobiographical, and allegorical of colonism, but that's just not my cup of tea. On the flip side, the writing is brilliant, as always.

sample_reviews.review_text: Favorite Shakespeare play yet! He definitely gave a final hurrah through The Tempest!

I read condensed classics version of this story when I was about 15 and was pretty hooked. I borrowed a big huge red book of Shakespeare's stories and only read this one. It's still my favorite, probably because its' s about a bunch of different people and tragic backstories and love and magic messing with people's heads...and everything turns out alright in the end (except for Calaban, they never did explain him :(( ). 
 If you like movie adaptions, there is a really good one with Hellen Mirren. The cast for all the characters is spectacular.

My favorite Shakespearian works are those that have magical characters and a touch of whimsy. Prospero the sorcerer and the spirits he commands fill this story of betrayal and new love with a touch of whimsy.

Simple & short. 
 Daughter falls in love. Drunken men half heartedly try murder (main conflict?). Nobody objects the return of Prospero and his daughter to Milan. 
 No great soliloquy or monologue. 
 I don't even think there was any great magic. Prospero talks to spirits who could confine people, or scared them away. 
 That's all. 
 I'd rather have some Hamlet or Macbeth
Beautifully written, but bogged down by numerous, tedious sub-plots coupled with lack luster characters made for a very boring reading experience. Skip this one.
The Tempest kept me interested, and I wasn't bored reading this but I didn't enjoy it as much as the few other works of Shakespeare that I've read.

It was a Shakespeare book. I had to read it for school. I had quizzes and assignments on it and it caused me anxiety and frustration. 
 What more can I say?
Absolutely awful. This was a complete waste of time and I resent the fact that I've paid money for it.

Even a genius is allowed to be average once in a while. Reportedly the last play Shakespeare wrote on his own, I can't help but wonder if he mailed it in on this. Maybe he needed the money? Maybe he was fulfilling a contract for one more play, much like Hitchcock did with the abhorrent movie Jamacia Inn, his last British production before moving to Hollywood. Whatever the case, The Tempest was neither romantic enough to make me fall in love, tragic enough to make me sad or funny enough to make me laugh. But, it is Shakespheare so even his meh efforts are better than most, but still. Not up to his standards. 
 I read along with the text while I listened to the audio version, a practice I highly recommend. I wish I could have done that in high school. I'll definitely suggest immersion reading to my children as they enter high school and discover Shakespeare.
my favorite quote: "oh! i shall be pinched to death!" -caliban

I didn't enjoy this text at all. It's male-heavy, moreso than usual, and I can't get over the weird magical realism and androgynous aspects of Ariel. There are so many things I believe are better staged than read, so I wouldn't recommend reading this play.

I started with The Tempest which I had not read before as I only have read Romeo and Juliet, I loved how it compassed fantasy, tragedy and comedy and how it uses magic to take back the power and life you once lead and also to make you family happy and it way of using power to alter a person's life years before only to end up were you lead them to end up but now since living of this magical island they now have powers to use against you ends up making it into be a very amusing play.
interesting..but not really relatable
Excellent ... Throughly enjoyed reading ... Very magical ...
There is some philosophy behind each character and short dramatic story under line.

I was not looking forward to reading this play and I certainly never would have picked it up on my own if it wasn't for my college Shakespeare class. Its arguable what category this play falls under, I think in todays terms it would be labled a dramady. Turns out this play is really much more captivating than I would have thought. Prospero ends up getting some pretty serious character development, how Shakespeare deals with magic, and the characters' reactions and treatment of Caliban are all pretty interesting. I kinda want to see Greenaway's Prospero's Books but I'm afraid about all the old man nudity that is said to be in it. Yikes.

I like the revenge Vs forgiveness conflict developed throughout. 
 Shorter than many of his other plays... This one leaves me wanting a bit more in places.

Not my favorite but good times all around. It's got all your classic Shakespearian comedy elements and is a lot of fun to read. I am not sure that I will ever reread this one but I would go to see the play if I had the opportunity.

For many years, my favourite Shakespeare play. I fell in love with Willy when I was about 8 or 9, having seen some PBS productions of Much Ado and some others. I quickly learned that if you can't watch the plays, they are much more accessible when read aloud, particularly if as I was, you are in love with words. I adored Caliban's satisfying curses like rolls of thunder. I related to Prospero: "Me, poor man--my library was dukedom large enough." (I still do.) 
 There are many, many productions of The Tempest, from a strange puppet theatre one (with Robin Williams as narrator) to the latest bizarre version with Judy Dench as Prospera. Take your choice. I'm sure producers and directors love the costumes, the effects, the locations. 
 But as I grow older, a question haunts me: Miranda has never seen another man besides her father--you can hardly count Ariel and Caliban, though they are of course both male. Hardly surprising then that she falls in love with the first sprack young squire of her own age that invites her for a game of chess (there being no etchings or music discs on the island). All's well that ends in a wedding, as per the conventions of Elisabethan comedy and the modern romcom. But--and it's a big but--what happens when Miranda returns to Milan and sees all those gallants? How long would that particular relationship last? "Oh brave new world, that hath such creatures in it!" I bet she kicked herself for limiting her choices, though perhaps she acquired a collection of dalliances once hubby inherited the dukedom from his father-in-law. A Duchess could certainly allow herself a little latitude.

I read this while studying colonisation for my A-Levels in school, and although the premise is intriguing this is just not a story-line for me. Miranda is sheltered and unrelateable as a woman, and none of the characters have any redeeming features. Having to study this made me dislike it even more.

After watching Something Rotten! on Broadway a little while ago, a lot of the way through this, all I could think was "so Shakespeare did write a musical, after all!" But at what cost? 
 This play was so bland, especially when compared to Hamlet or Macbeth. Where was the rising action? What were the stakes? I never felt like there was any actual genuine drama throughout this entire play. I am deeply curious about the circumstances in which Shakespeare wrote this. Was it an easy rehash of old stories? Was he just trying to make a quick buck to make rent on time? 
 The only reason this got an "it was okay" from me is because I got to read the "Full fathom five thy father lies" song, which is a beautiful bit of writing and imagery. 
 The best definitely did not come last.

2015 reading challenge - A play 
 Not really a bad book to read, I just really don't like reading plays and unless it's Hamlet I find Shakespeare very boring to read.
This play needed more pirates. A few monkeys would have helped too.

The Tempest is one of Shakespeare's last plays. Prospero, exiled Duke of Milan, lives on a island with his spirit Ariel, his slave Caliban, and his daughter Miranda. He has the ability to control everyone on the island by use of his staff and his books. A ship carrying Prospero's brother Antonio, his other brother Sebastian, Alonso, King of Naples, Ferdinand, Alonso's son, Trinculo and Stephano, the king's servants, and Gonzalo, a kindly courrtier, is shipwrecked on the island, with a storm caused by Prospero himself. Ferdinand is separated from the group, then meets and falls in love with Miranda. Prospero gives Ferdinand several tests to prove his love to Mirands. Meanwhile, Trinculo and Stephano encounter Caliban, get him drunk, and persuade him to serve Stephano as his new master. Prospero eventually joins Ferdinand and Miranda in marriage, and forgives the wrongs all of the others have done. Prospero then asks the audience to release him so he can go to Naples. 
 This is one of Shakespeare's most lyrical plays. Some have suggested that Prospero is actually Shakespeare himself, saying goodbye to the theater. (He wrote Henry VIII and collaborated on The Two Noble Kinsmen, so we know that's not true.) It has some classic lines, such as, "We are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep." and "O brave new world, which has such creatures in't." (This is where Aldous Huxley got the title for his novel, Brave New World.) It's also been suggested that the island is actually a reference to America. This was written in 1610-11, so some of the reports from the Jamestown colony in what is now Virginia would have fascinated the audience. Another culture reference is Ariel, which is the name Disney gave to The Little Mermaid in 1989. 
 The production was by the the Shakespeare for Young Actors and Designers program of the Great River Shakespeare Festival in Winona, MN. This program is for students in grade school through high school. They had 3 weeks to put the performance together. Some worked on acting, some on design, both of costumes and set dressing. The basic set was that used for Hamlet. 
 The play was condensed to fit in a 90 minute time frame, with no intermission. Since mostly girls had signed up for the program, most of the parts were played by girls. Given that in Shakespeare's time, all of the parts were played by men, this is an interesting role reversal. The actors did well. There were so many actors this year, some roles were played by 2 or 3 different people. (If I leave names out, it is only for space limitations.) Special commendations to the following: 
 Lauren Callahan and Emma Dalen as Prospero. They switched off in the middle of the play, and got back together at the end. 
 Raelynn Peter as Miranda. In the play, Miranda is 15. She's probably about that age, so it worked out perfectly. 
 Anna Scholz-Carlson as Ferdinand. She was able to play the part convincingly. 
 Emma Bucknam, Olivia Templeton, and Emma Wilson as Ariel. They played Ariel as a group of 3. 
 Violet Richardson and Eva Scholz-Carlson as Caliban. They switched off in the middle of the play. 
 Emma Wilson as Iris, Haley Donnal as Ceres, and Qiana Norris as Juno. They had relatively brief parts in this play, but they did well. 
 Stephanie Shaw as Alonso, Emily Schwermer as Sebastian, Jordon Prochnow as Antonio, Alayna Merchlewitz as Gonzalo, and Emma Wilson as Adrian. Extra commendation to Emma Wilson for taking on 3 roles. 
 Jackson Mixon as Trinculo and Jake Carlson as Stephano. The only 2 boys in the cast, they provided the comic relief. 
 Haley Donnal as the Boatswain and Qiana Norris as Master of the Ship. Again, small roles, but effective. 
 The program was started 4 years ago by Andrew Carlson, who plays Hamlet this year, as well as Dr Caius in Merry Wives of Windsor. He serves now as one of the instructors. This year, the lead instructor and director of the play is Tarah Flanagan, who plays Mrs. Ford in Merry Wives of Windsor. It is a tribute to her dedication and effectiveness that she makes time for this while taking on her other roles in the play. I would also like to recognize all of the other cast members who assisted in the instruction. They are Greg Ivan Smith, Gale Childs Daly, Michael Fitzpatrick, Christopher Gerson, John Maltese, Jenni McCarthy, Robert Montgomery, Sigrid Sutter, and Brian White. They helped make this play excellent. 
 For the designers, Lauren Smith was the primary instructor, assisted by Megan Morey and Jenn Oswald. They exhibited their work in the lobby of the theater. It was interesting to see the designs they came up with, then to see how they translated into real life. Special notice to Lauren Smith, who is also the education coordinator for the Festival, and has a lot of other duties. Again, the quality of the production is a testament to their dedication. 
 All in all, a great performance. I look forward in the coming years to seeing many of these actors and designers on the Main Stage at the Festival. 
 For more information on the Great River Shakespeare Festival, including the Shakespeare for Young Actors and Designers programs, visit www.grsf.org. 
 For more information on Winona, MN, visit www.visitwinona.com.

I wanted to like The Tempest, I really did, so much so that I read it twice. 
 Note: The editions I read of this book are not the editions used to shelve this review on Goodreads. 
 READ #1: Late 2015, Lost in Translation. 
 The first time I read The Tempest the biggest problem was not the play, but the edition of the play I was reading. Each edition of a play, handled by different publishers and editors, ends up slightly different. The one I read was a Canadian publication that claimed that it was meant to translate Shakespeare into "Canadian", whatever that means. The result was a translation where the language was stifled and choppy. It was a frustrating read because it ended up removing a lot of what I love about Shakespeare in an effort to make it easier to understand. Turns out I couldn't understand it and I didn't realize that my edition was so screwy till I got to the end and read the editor's notes. Not cool! 
 READ #2: Early 2016, Education Station. (Warning: spoilers) 
 The second reading I did of the Tempest was for school. The version of the play I read was much, much better and I actually enjoyed doing the required analysis. Reading about how the play fit into Shakespeare's other works and the themes it was representing made The Tempest make a lot more sense. I also enjoyed reading about the theatrical meta commentary Shakespeare was weaving into the play. 
 It still wasn't a great play though. I simply didn't enjoy it. It was interesting, but not enjoyable by my standards. 
 I found that too much of the plot hinged on me feeling sympathy for Prospero. I kept asking myself: Why do I care if Prospero gets his Dukedom back? At the beginning of the play Prospero tells us the backstory that while he was Duke all he did was retreat into his studies leaving the actual governing to his brother, Antonio. Then, surprise! Antonio decides that if he's doing all the work he also wants the perks and the title of actually being the Duke. OMG SHOCK! 
 Now, is Antonio an asshole? Absolutely! He sent a small child to her death and tried to talk some other guy into killing his own brother just so he wouldn't have to pay tribute, but I also totally understand his motivations, which makes him an interesting character. If Prospero is the protagonist it doesn't work if I care more about the villain than I do about him. 
 The characters I did feel for were primarily, Ariel and Miranda. Poor, poor Miranda. You hear all this fuss about Romeo and Juliet, but you never hear anyone talk about Miranda. 
 In the end, I think that The Tempest and I just weren't meant to be. I started questioning the entire narrative and once you question one thing all other sort of questions follow. Like, question, if Prospero has these magical powers, the help of a magical servant, and an island full of resources why couldn't he just leave the island? I'm sure there are some assumptions that could be made, but never in the entire play does anyone explain why they remained trapped there. 
 Personally, I think that The Tempest would be much better performed on a stage than read about on the page. It lacks that sparkle that really makes me love Shakespeare and the magic is difficult to visualize without the all important visuals. 
 On the plus side, if you've made it this far in my review, I did discover some interesting Shakespeare resources in my studies. For exacble I found Ben Crystal and his video/talk about Shakespeare's accent. I also learned through watching his talks that I am, indeed, not too old to have girlish crushes. If I leave you with anything I highly suggest checking out his work. It's really interesting stuff!

The Tempest has been analyzed, as most of Shakespeare's plays, as an allegory to religion, colonialism, imperialism, political turmoil, etc. But whenever I read his plays again, after putting them aside for a number of years, I notice more about the relationship between family, which is what I did this time. 
 Prospero, being the main character in his play, is curious. He seems like a wise old mage, as he is, but he also has some alarming traits about the treatment of his daughter, Ariel and Caliban. That is where the imperialism idea comes in: that Prospero could just come over and demolish the natives and make them like his own people. But even with his own daughter, who has no idea about society standards, Prospero makes her into a maid and a housewife, still arranging marriages and vowing her innocence even when Ferdinand enters the occasion. 
 Miranda, herself, is rather unremarkable. As are most of the characters from Milan, in my opinion. The character that propels the play's action forward, literally, is Ariel, the tricky spirit. Ariel is the obedient one, although he constantly asks to be set free and wins his freedom in the end. (That is where the clash between Ariel and Caliban sets in: both have obeyed Prospero but only one really earns his freedom.) I loved reading his trickery again, understanding it more the second time through it. And I'll admit I got a little teary-eyed when he finally earned his freedom in the end, after long service to the deposed duke Prospero. 
 The two things which felt strange to me reading The Tempest again was, first, the banquet scene, which I still do not really understand why that's included at all. This could be Shakespeare's supernatural themes coming back stronger, but it seems completely unnecessary to the plot. And I could never understand, in any of Shakespeare's plays, how everyone could forgive each other so quickly (especially considering the entire plot of the play takes place in real-time, or in about three hours!). Prospero seems to blow everything off and pledge to destroy his own magical powers so he can go home. But wouldn't you think, after twelve years of banishment and betrayal, it would take more than a few I'm sorrys to amend things. Especially when Miranda and Ferdinand, like Romeo and Juliet, would have to unite these two sparring, rival brothers? Although the play is unique in that it takes only three hours, it doesn't seem to set up a real-life situation. 
 But that above angle is where it gets interesting drawing a parallel to Shakespeare's time and career. The Tempest, as one of Shakespeare's last plays, seems to quite obviously reflect the playwright's growing weariness with his job. Through Prospero, he injects his desire to "break my staff," "drown my book," and dissolve "the great globe itself." It's difficult to interpret this as something purposeful, as though Shakespeare was writing his own obituary, of sorts, but it certainly implies the end of Shakespeare's career. Is Shakespeare Prospero? And vice versa? They both were creators and masters, owning characters and places and events -- and plot devices -- all under the control of the mighty book.

Simple yet profound, The Tempest is a heartbreakingly sincere piece of elaborate theatrical artifice. Shakespeare is a magician at the height of his powers, so accomplished at his craft that he can reveal the mechanisms of his most marvelous tricks and still astonish us.

I set out to read this play when I decided I wanted to watch the movie. Even though it started out with an fantasy-like premise, which I like, I quickly lost interest. Prospero wants to avenge his lost dukedom. He utilizes spirits, magic and the power of nature to bring about the demise of the usurper, and anyone with him. We all know I'm a massive Shakespeare fan. I love that man's plays, even if I don't like all of them. And now it seems I have found a play to add to that 'not my kind of Shakespeare'-list. 
 According to some, this is Shakespeare's best play. Of course this si said of many of his plays, but 'The Tempest' seems to have a special place in the hearts of many people and I have to admit, I don't entirely understand why. Perhaps the reason for that can be found in my favourite Shakespeare plays, such as 'Hamlet' or 'Henry V'. These plays have protagonists you can either like or dislike and have a plot that leads to something, that means something. In many ways I found both plot and characters lacking in 'The Tempest'. I did not like Prospero. Many of my reasons to dislike him are reasons why I like other Shakespeare characters. He is, for example, a manipulator. So is Iago, whom I love. In Prospero I saw no honour or loyalty, nothing to truly admire or truly despise. He is degrading to Ariel, but also reliant on her. He loves Miranda, but has no problem using her in his own plans. He despises Caliban, but still claims him as his own. He feels wronged by Antonia, but has done the same to Caliban. 
 But then I didn't really appreciate Caliban either. He has much less time on stage than Prospero, which means he is hardly a true antagonist. He is both rebellious and subservient, desires freedom but wants to be ruled. There are almost too many oppositions to make him a complex character and none of the oppositions are explored or explained enough to make them real. And this is where my true problem with the play lies. I was completely untouched by it. Ophelia's death in 'Hamlet' is heart-breaking, Henry V's St Crispian's speech is rousing, Benedick and Beatrice's battle of wits in 'Much Ado About Nothing' is hilarious. 'The Tempest' left me very calm and placid and, dare I say it, bored. The plot did not help. The concept of a storm stranding these enemies onto the same island is great, but since everything is controlled and orchestrated by Prospero there is hardly any doubt as to whether his plan will fail or not. Antonia, who stole his dukedom, is very easily convinced to return it, Miranda hopelessly falls in love with Ferdinand and Caliban drops his new master in favour of Prospero in a heart beat. 
 Let's return to Miranda for a moment. Shakespeare is often criticized for his female character but I find myself liking most of them. Miranda however is almost a non-entity, a lack of character rather than a character. She has completely accepted the patriarchal society established by her father and is not much more than a tool to him. Yes, Prospero loves her but only because she is his daughter, taught by him. She falls in love unconditionally with the first man she sees on her father's design and has no other role in the play. 
 My criticism of plot and character aside, it is still Shakespeare which means I still enjoyed the language and the occasional jokes. Some things were really fun and Caliban's 'The Isle is Full of Noises' speech is beautiful. It is no coincidence that speeches from this play were chosen for the Opening and Closing Ceremony of the 2012 Olympic Games. Perhaps it speaks to Britain because the play is essentially about love and war on an tempestuous island. I think seeing it live might change my opinion so perhaps I should try to go see it in the Globe next season!

 The French revolution is in full flood, and French aristocrats are executed daily on the guillotine. But the elusive Scarlet Pimpernel carries out daring rescues, bringing threatened nobles to the safety of England. Lady Blakeney, originally French, becomes embroiled in the Pimpernel's doings when she is recruited as a French spy. 
 I liked the Scarlet Pimpernel books when I was young. Dashing adventure, secrets, disguises, drama, they were fun (though not among my favorites). As with much else, however, they may be better in memory. My main interest this time around was in an aristocrat's view of aristocracy. 
 The plot is thin and romantic - Lady Blakeney's estrangement from her husband, her desire to help her threatened brother, still in France. The underlayment is a mixed bag of politics (nobility good, revolution bad) and stereotype (Jews bad, damsels distressed) that was a much better suited to an uncritical child's mind than for an adult focusing less on adventure, more on people. There's a lot of "if she provided the thought, and he the manly energy and pluck," and it gets wearing, even giving Orczy credit for a woman who is intelligent and active (if ultimately dependent on men). The character's motivations are inconsistent, and even the lead couple's back story makes little sense (Percy Blakeney was apparently a devoted fop when they courted, but Lady Blakeney seems surprised by the fact that he's still a (remote) fop now). 
 All in all, a mildly interesting trip down memory lane, but essentially a book that has passed its freshness date, and can safely pass into history.

 The Scarlet Pimpernel is undeniably one of the world's great adventure stories, its hero attaining an almost mythological status in English speaking culture; Sherlock Holmes is one of the very few fictional characters to have higher prominence. It is not the writing which has made this happen - Orczy wrote a great number of other novels which have all sunk into oblivion - but the quality of the idea of the Scarlet Pimpernel, the romance of his actions. 
 Orczy's flaws as a writer are fairly obvious. Her characters are two dimensional at best (the only ones in the novel that even reach this level are the Blakeneys and Chauvelin). Her prose is fairly pedestrian, particularly when descriptive. The plot is obvious; most first time readers will guess the secret identity of the Scarlet Pimpernel pages before its revelation. The historical background is one sided, presenting a view of the French Revolution which is seriously distorted. And yet, the reader is drawn in, becoming engrossed as the climactic confrontation approaches. The drama of the idea is so strong that it overcomes all the barriers to enjoyment of the novel.

Talky! 
 The first thing you should know about this book is that it was originally a play. Therefore, it consists of a limited number of locations and a lot of dialogue. 
 The second thing you should know is that the main character is not the Scarlet Pimpernel; it is a character named Marguerite, whose most notable qualities are dithering, powerlessness, and a stonelike lack of perception. In spite of Orczy's repeated assurances that Marguerite is "the cleverest woman in Europe," she spends half the novel completely flummoxed by a riddle that most readers will have deduced in the first few chapters. 
 The third thing that you should know is that Orzy's writing style seems intended for an audience with severe memory issues. Each character's personality is directly described by the narrator, then indirectly shown by their actions. Every time a character re-enters the narrative, a separate paragraph or page of dialogue is devoted to reminding the reader of their personality. This is why the first third of the book is nothing but exposition. When the plot finally creaks into motion about 1/3 or 1/2 of the way in, Marguerite spends the beginning of every chapter lamenting her powerlessness to deal with whatever happened in the previous chapter. There are entire chapters that consist of nothing but recap. 
 The advantages of this book are brevity and the enjoyable characterizations of Jellyband, Sir Percy, and the French spy. Also, there is a very cheesy romance angle in the last third of the book, which may appeal to some.

In spite of negative reviews, the play eventually became a popular success, running 122 performances and enjoying numerous revivals. The Scarlet Pimpernel became a favorite of London audiences, playing more than 2,000 performances and becoming one of the most popular shows staged in England to that date." {Wikipedia} 
 SYNOPSIS: The story focuses on Sir Percy Blakeney and his French wife Marguerite. Both are fabulously beautiful, fabulously fashionable, fabulously rich, and the "toast" of London society. 
 Alas, their marriage of just one year, although begun in great passion and love, has already fallen on hard times; a misunderstanding has pushed them apart and they are little more than polite strangers. 
 The Scarlet Pimpernel is a mysterious, brave adventurer who has managed to rescue numerous French aristocrats from under the nose of the revolutionary forces and bring them safely to English shores. He is the hero of England, the talk of every party as everyone speculates on his true identity, and the bane of the French who would like nothing more than to capture and send him to the guillotine. "La!" 
 When Marguerite learns that her beloved brother has fallen into displeasure with the French revolutionaries and is destined for the guillotine, she is hopeful that The Scarlet Pimpernel will somehow rescue him. But when events compel her to return to France, she plunges both her brother and her husband into peril. "Odd's fish!" 
 MY THOUGHTS: I'll admit, as some of my book club members also mentioned, that the novel was a bit slow going for me in the beginning. But it takes off soon enough, and the rest of the story is well worth the beginning thirty pages or so. 
 Personally, I only gave it three stars because I don't think the Scarlet Pimpernel is "great literature," but it is a classic, fun to read and can be enjoyed for the escapist literature that it is. Why is he called the Scarlet Pimpernel? It's a small red roadside flower in England. Beyond that, your guess is as good as mine for Emmuska Orczy never reveals her thoughts or symbolism behind choosing the flower. 
 I thought that the language was a little unimpressive. I know it's just an adventure-romance, but I've read other books of that genre with much more literary merit and character depth. If you like sophisticated classics don't read this book expecting it to fall in that category. If you're just looking for something fun and suspenseful, I highly recommend reading it. It's enjoyable, and we must give Orczy some credit for writing the first masked-hero adventure. Did you know that The Scarlet Pimpernel is regarded as the precursor of such famous heroes as Zorro, Batman and even James Bond? 
 My favorite part of the book is at the very end when the Scarlet Pimpernel, disguised a certain Jew, utters a `good, solid, absolutely British "Damn!"' It is funny because the author, Orczy, writes the book in such a way so that soon realize you know that this particular Jew is the Scarlet Pimpernel but you still don't expect him to flat out have a British accent when he is in France. 
 The Scarlet Pimpernel

I love this book. Yeah, the Pimpernel is pretty obvious. I mean this is not Stephen King level kind of mystery, but for a mystery/romance, it's great. I love classics, but I don't read them much because I like fast-paced books. If you're like me, rest assured, this book is the perfect speed. The romance is subpar, albeit it's not Pride & Prejudice good, but I still enjoyed it greatly. If you want to take a rest from all the dystopian/paranormal books, you should give this a try.

This might be the literary equivalent of a B movie. Both profitable and popular, it gave rise to a long-running series as well as (some say) the genre of the disguised superhero (Batman...Zorro ...Superman...etc.), but there's really nothing particularly well-executed about it. The narration and character development reminded me strongly of Harlequin romances. The bit players are all stock characters that might as well be named "The Virtuous Barmaid" and "The Unsuccessful Lover," and the main characters aren't much better. In this volume, most of the action revolves around "The Crazed Villain," "Our Dashing Hero," and "His Worthy Wife." True, what The Scarlet Pimpernel lacks in execution it partially makes up for in imagination and fun; however, what actually troubles me most about this book is its gaiety. The French Revolution seems a bit of a stretch for the scene of even an ironic or black comedy, and this is a bona-fide romp! I'm all for frolicsome fun, but...the book's light-heartedness comes off as indifference to its own setting. 
 In order to make my unease more intelligible, let me compare the Reign of Terror of 1793-94 with a more recent historical event that bears many similarities: the Holocaust. Would we be so enamored of the Superman franchise if the Man of Steel had been rescuing Jews from Buchenwald instead of kittens from trees?

One of the classic historical adventure novels! 
 The heroic Pimpernel and his intrepid band risk life and limb to rescue families from the clutches of the French revolution. 
 There is mystery, intrigue, humor, romance, noble heroes, dispicable villains and no shades of grey. According to this book everyone jailed by the French authorities are poor innocents, falsely accused and in need of rescue. 
 Sir Percy is a fun character, playing the fop as part of his 'secret identity' and his wife is treated as a damsel, but written with more personality than the usual damsels.

This is a rather interesting "hero" story. It has elements of Robin Hood, the Three Musketeers (and a little Batman/Superman secret identity stuff).

I think that may have to do with the age of the piece and the fact that it's a translation so I wouldn't expect a riveting tale but the story is ok and who doesn't like a good hero story? 
 One final thing I will say is that the identity of the Scarlet Pimpernel is obvious pretty early on but then again it's melodrama to a degree so it's supposed to be over the top and obvious to everyone EXCEPT the characters in the story. 
 Don't mortgage your home to get a copy of this to read but it's a nice change of pace and it's pretty short.

I'd been meaning to read this book for a while. I read Less Than Zero last year and loved it. And I've got a couple of Bret Easton Ellis' other books I'll eventually get around to reading, but at least I've read this. I remember quite distinctly, I read a good portion of this while I was holidaying in Melbourne. I was there with a friend and we were staying at backpackers accommodation. We were mostly over there to do a bit of shopping, a bit of tourist things, really just get right into Melbourne, the city and the inner suburbs. And because we're both bookmen (avid readers) we also spent a fair bit of time between doing things, just reading at the backpackers. Now, I didn't enjoy this book as much as Less Than Zero. I love the self-destructive youth culture of that book, where yuppie culture is much more foreign to me. But it is a fantastic book. Patrick Bateman is a brilliantly psychotically fucked up character. The attention to detail, the nonchalance with which he goes about his killings, it's a fantastic portrayal of a culture in excess, it is so saturated that Patrick seems numb to everything around him. I've still got to get around to watching the movie, but at least the book lived up to my standards.

 1.5 stars Don't worry. That's the tame version. I didn't spoil the extreme parts of the story. Trust me. 
 It might be a long, long time before I read something which knocks American Psycho out of the top spot for "sickest thing I've ever witnessed," and I've read books which have had rape, murder, and gore aplenty in them. 
 How often can a person say that the movie was better than the book? I actually liked the movie because it carried the point from the story without being quite as tedious or gruesome. 
 Part of me wanted to spoiler-tag a couple of the more gruesome scenes, just to give readers who were curious something to look at. But I'm not giving anyone any ideas. O.o 
 The first half of the book was overworked satire. Pages and pages of excessive description gave no great sense of entertainment or enjoyment in terms of reading experience. I do understand why the author did what he needed to do in order to set up the character's state of mind to the reader. Many of the conversations and interactions were needed, and a few were actually informative or interesting, but the same point really could have been made in a few chapters. 
 It all comes down to reading preference for me. Half a book of recycled conversation about fashion, society, tanning, etc. is torture for people like me who could not give a shit about that stuff. I hate wasting my time by reading about stuff I don't want to read about, satire or not. Overkill is still overkill, especially when you see the same catch-phrases (hardbody, gazelleskin, etc.) used dozens of times in the book, and you're sort of sad that you're not playing a drinking game to combat some of the repetitiveness. By the time I got to the chapter on detailing Whitney Houston's career, I was downright tired of reading scene after scene of tedious information. 
 Although...the chapter on name brand water amused me, probably because of how I learned that I'm sparkling water poser. 
 Speaking of excessive...let's get to the second half of the book, otherwise known as a precursor (no, not really) to the show 1,000 Ways to Die. 
 Try thinking of the sickest way you could kill someone. Chances are, you aren't even close to thinking about what Pat put his victims through. 
 Did Pat become the way that he was because he was so rich and bored, and had nothing left to achieve or desire, or was his mind so completely ordered and methodical about everything from the start, that he viewed murder without emotion as just another thing he could organize and categorize? 
 I get why American Psycho has a good portion of its ratings on either one end or the other of the spectrum. Since the subject itself doesn't lend itself well to words such as "love" or "admire," a reader is either going to respect the method of writing, or hate the product of the writing. 
 I wanted to fall on the respect end because I understood why others rated the book high. But I can't overcome the fact that I hated reading the repetitive formula of : character talks about meaningless shit, character talks about or participates in unappealing (and super-extreme) sex, then character makes a gruesome kill. 
 The end of the story gave the reader nothing to wrap up the madness of it all. 
 The guy was a psycho. That's about it. At least the book was aptly named.

For a book about a serial killer, American Psycho is surprisingly boring. It's about Patrick Bateman, a 20-something year old bigoted narcissist who's deeply afraid of turning 30. He works on Wall Street, does a lot of cocaine, and also likes torturing people to death, especially women during sex. 
 Patrick Bateman's narcissism may have been satirical in 1991, but his intense superficiality has become tediously mainstream in 2016. There isn't anything particularly outrageous about a man who is obsessed with going to the gym, drinking mineral water, rejecting food because of its nutrient content, getting tans, having manicures and wearing designer clothes. Contrasted with Bateman's materialism are many scenes of horrific murder. These murderous acts have no purpose, and they are described in a graphic but also incredibly curt, matter-of-fact way that actually makes them extremely unconvincing. The violence is cartoonishly over-the-top and yet depicted in such an understated way that it has no real impact. The many scenes of sexual violence against women are especially notable examples because they are so gruesome but also so ludicrous (eg, murder by acid + broken glass + cheese + rat + chainsaw, with sex before, during and after). The more elaborate the murder, the less I could maintain attention. I found myself rolling my eyes constantly and sincerely questioning why I was wasting my time with this book. 
 The story doesn't have much of a narrative and repeats itself to the point of pure tedium. It doesn't work as horror, it doesn't work as satire, it doesn't work as a black comedy. I wasn't even offended by it because it's so patently ridiculous. I thought American Psycho was wearisome.

American Psycho is probably one of the most exhausting books I've ever read. I feel a little torn on my overall feelings toward it, so am going to first list what I appreciate Ellis attempted to accomplish while then sharing why -- for me -- it didn't work. 
 First off, know that this is a book of utter extremes. The sex and violence are taken to levels that make Chuck Palahniuk look like he's writing Dr. Seuss stories. Misogyny, rape, cruelty, cannibalism, sadism, torture. If you've got a light stomach, you're better off settling for some lighter hors d'oeuvres. 
 This, however, is NOT the focus of the book. What I liked about Ellis' approach is that it's the Wall Street yuppie mentality of wining and dining and knowing where a tie-clip should be on your tie or what type of socks should be worn with a cashmere suit that SCREAMS psycho. The real American psycho isn't the mass murderer, it's the guy who's concerned with having the latest stereo or getting in to the newest restaurant or who's handling "the Fisher account." In a way, this book is really about coming to terms with the fact that we're ALL psychos, that we've lost touched with things that matter, and in today's world, it's a message that probably bears repeating. 
 The other thing that Ellis excels at with this novel is in the way his subject matters are treated. Patrick Bateman's blood pressure remains the same whether discussing the newest Huey Lewis and the News album or cutting off a prostitute's head with a chainsaw. The ease with which the scene changes occurred was fascinating and provided a truer picture of his psychosis than the over-graphic nature of the scenes themselves. 
 Why it didn't work: 
 Ultimately this is a book in which nothing happens. 
 Well how could you say that, considering all the murders and scandalous undertakings you've described so far in your review? And are you sure YOU'RE not the psycho, considering you're now talking about yourself in the third person?!? 
 This book is like watching someone play with a yo-yo for ten hours. Sure, they may be able to do some cool tricks and pull off some impressive feats, but ultimately that ball is just going down and back up over and over again. The conversations are repeated a hundred times as the same group of friends discuss fashion, or where they want to eat, or what "hard-body" they want to get with. We have the same chapters where Bateman reviews the latest albums or discusses every feature of his new stereo. We have the same inner monologues replaying, along with the same senseless crimes and acts of violence, and the characters Bateman surrounds himself with are so analogous - from both his Wall Street friends to the women and prostitutes he dates - that one scene becomes a mirror image of another. I understand and can appreciate what Ellis was trying to say in writing the book this way, it was just extremely boring. 
 I think this is a large part of why both the sex and violence were so alarmingly graphic, but rather than adding complexity it too became more white noise, with one scene attempting to top the other. With a "less is more" approach, using subtlety instead of shock-voyeurism, I think not only could the same message have been attained, but there could have been a story here that moved in an actual direction. Whether Bateman's episodes of violent destruction and self-actualization are all in his head or actually realized isn't as important as the need for the story to go somewhere. By the time we got around to the third or fourth album review, I was looking for someone to murder myself ... 
 Obviously the shock-factor is a play that's worked for the author, in getting his work recognized. Whether it works for the reader is another story entirely. For this reader, sadly it did not.

 LO QUE ME GUSTO: 
 La forma en que esta escrito. Me gusto la manera en que Bret Easton Ellis nos presenta la historia de Patrick Bateman, la manera confusa en que se salta de un episodio a otro, pero siempre contandose como si fuera un diario, como si Pat estuviera escribiendo todos sus pensamientos y sus mas intimas obsesiones. 
 Eso tambien fue otro punto que me gusto, la forma en la que Pat esta tan obsesionado por un estilo de vida que no persive nada fuera de este; que no tenga otras aspiraciones o que no sea un "juzgador", ya que lo deja puro como personaje y hasta cierto punto puede resultar que su enfermedad sea mas creible. 
 LO QUE NO ME GUSTO: 
 Aqui viene mi gran problema. Creo que el autor se quedo bastante en lo literal. No se si esa era su intencion (creo que si) pero el resultado para mi resulta bastante corto en cuanto a expectativas. Es un libro cinico y gracioso pero tambien es extremamente aburrido, al no seguir la estructura comun de una historia y con todaaas las interminables descripciones y escenas super graficas, no pude encontrar un punto critico en la trama o alguna indicacion de hacia donde iba esta historia. Tampoco pude entender que es lo que queria decirme el autor cuando leyera el libro y por supuesto, yo no pude encontrar un sentido. 
 Se que peco si comparo, pero tal vez esperaba un libro mas al estilo El Club de la Lucha (que para mi fue un libro que me marco mucho), pues aunque es una historia sencilla resulta mas profunda y un poco mas critica. Tal vez Easton no queria que su libro tuviera ese objetivo, pero entiendo que debe haber uno y sin embargo por mas que lo justifique, si tenia alguno no lo alcanza. 
 El libro no es malo. Creo que es uno sin puntos medios: lo amas o lo odias. O tal vez como el mismo autor lo plantea puede que seas totalmente indiferente a este. Y eso me paso a mi: indiferencia total a American Psycho.
