** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is almost nothing I was promised it would be. Shocking and gory? Absolutely. But original? Exciting? Well-written? A psychological thriller? A "bleak, bitter, black comedy"? Most certainly not. 
 Firstly, this was one of the most boring books I've ever read, which is surprising when one considers the subject matter. There are more details about Bateman's friends' meals, clothes, and pointless conversations than actual plot. While I understand that these details are provided to give insight to Bateman's life and double personality, it doesn't exactly work; I found myself skimming through the first 150 pages because nothing was happening. (Although maybe this is the point? That modern American audiences want the shocking over the mundane, and so will concentrate their energies on finding the gory details, even if that makes us horrible people? It would be an interesting point to make if it had been done well.) 
 Additionally, this novel claims to be gritty and realistic, but in reality it is unbelievable. Bateman commits an enormous number of murders throughout the book ("...thirty, forty, a hundred murders..." (352) ), some in public, many including victims that would be missed. There is even an early scene in the dry cleaners in which Bateman brings bloody sheets and stumbles over his response when a girl from his building asks about them. Why, then, is law enforcement so scarce in this book? Bateman is not careful about his misdeeds. He commits many of them in broad daylight, some in crowded places. He even confesses in detail to a coworker's answering machine. Perhaps this is my optimism speaking, or too much Law and Order: SVU, but I refuse to believe that no one thought to report or even suspect him. There's just no way. 
 What bothers me more than the mundanity and lack of realistic scenarios, however, is its reception. I am not sure why this book is hailed as groundbreaking and innovative when it is a mere shadow of another famous novel. A Clockwork Orange, while considerably shorter, covers much more ground while actually being unique and fresh, even half a century after its publication. This is not only evident in the similarities between Patrick and Alex's immoral and horrifying actions, but in their love of music. In the chapter entitled "Tuesday," Bateman commits his first murder of the book in a vicious, grotesque manner. In the next chapter, "Genesis," he makes painstakingly in-depth comments about music. This is not the only time this happens either; it happens twice more throughout the novel, and several more times in smaller ways. This juxtaposition is directly lifted from Burgess, but not executed as craftily or, obviously, uniquely. Additionally, while Clockwork focuses on three different aspects of Alex's life and psychology (crimes, rehabilitation, repercussions) while raising important questions about society, American Psycho is a one-note gimmick that never challenges the reader to make connections or examine the world in which we live. It is a poor attempt at imitation of Burgess's genius, and does not live up to the hype. 
 Despite its many shortcomings, however, this novel did do some things well. Patrick's first-person narration establishes him as unreliable and insane through the details he gives (especially in fashion comments and hygienic habits) and his narrative techniques. One of the most obvious examples of this is early in the novel when he forces a bum to spill his change: "Did I do this on purpose? What do you think? Or did I do it accidentally?" (82) This serves to establish Patrick as obviously insane judging by not only the action and subsequent questions but the syntax of this section. It also draws in the reader, making him/her complicit in Patrick's actions. This is also evident through his comments on women, before we ever see him commit violence against them. In one scene, we hear his commentary on Courtney, one of the women with whom he is sleeping: "Why, for that matter, do I want to please Courtney? If she likes me only for my muscles, the heft of my cock, then she's a shallow bitch. But a physically superior, near-perfect-looking shallow bitch, and that can override anything, except maybe bad breath or yellow teeth, either of which is a real deal breaker" (157). This is in striking contrast with itself as well as earlier conversations he has with friends and business partners, about how women only serve one purpose and cannot be both attractive and intelligent/funny/talented (91). Again, the contrast between his conversations/thoughts serve to show his delusions and psychopathic nature. 
 This also contrasts with descriptions later in the novel, namely during the police chase scene, in which the narration briefly and abruptly changes to third person. It becomes almost cinematic, and erases all of Patrick's thoughts from the scene, allowing the reader to focus on the chase itself and how he is able to escape. It is an interesting choice, but it does not add much to the novel except to show Patrick's breaking point. 
 In all, this was not worth the read. If you're interested in the subject matter, Clockwork is a much better book, and is infinitely more deserving of your time. American Psycho does nothing new, and doesn't even manage to do the old particularly well. 
 * Note: I'm adding half a star because Donald Trump is Patrick's personal hero, which I think is the most fantastic detail. Remarkable foresight on Easton Ellis's part.

Awful, awful book - I wish I could give it zero stars. The first half is so boring it nearly drives you to tears. It's a long list of brand names and clothes items, fancy restaurants and popular bars, people Patrick Bateman knows or just associates with, and the women he abhors but sleeps with anyway. It's just so... boringly superficial and materialistic, and the conversations these people have make me wonder why their employers don't have a mandatory psychological test to weed out the crazies. Then again - Wall Street. We know what psychologists say about the profile of people working there, don't we. Narcissistic, psychopathic personalities thrive in such an environment. I guess the author was trying to tell us about the self-entitled, bored yuppies, but his book is a mess. I wouldn't be surprised if he himself indulged in some special substances while writing it. 
 Patrick Bateman is such a disgusting character that you just wish you could erase him from your memory. And the book is from his point of view - needless to say you can't connect to any character since he doesn't connect to anyone. So why is this book on the 1001 Books You Need to Read list? WHY?! Look, Silence of the Lambs has some pretty gory scenes but the book is structured, it has likeable characters, and you never feel the author himself might try his hand at torture. Here, I'm not so sure; there was some pretty fucked up shit in here. 
 So not only does the book fail to generate any interest in the reader, the sudden gory fantasies the psycho has about killing people (and women in particular) just throw you for a loop. In fact, you aren't entirely sure he goes through with all fantasies he has (and he has more and more of them much to my disgust and horror). He's doped up on cocaine, pills, and alcohol, so he's spiralling out of control and the book is just a list of nauseating scenes. I was skipping those (for my own sanity) as well as the long lists of brand items the author indulged in - why not just giving us a catalogue? And what is it about album reviews suddenly popping up in the story? It's just making an already messy and unreadable book even worse. 
 So I was actively reading and not only skimming the dialogues with the many women in his life and even there he shows himself to be an absolute misogynistic, racist pig. I also wish to pretend half the murders he talks about in the story happened only in his head; please don't tell me it's otherwise. Please. I might say I'm good with mature themes but I don't watch horror movies for a reason. Some things I just don't need to see or know about. Life is cruel enough on its own. 
 Summary: Stay away from this story or you'll be slowly driven mad with alternating boredom and horror. It's just not worth your time and I would have closed the book after the first chapter if it weren't for my reading challenge. I'm firm in my conviction I won't ever watch the movie. Just nope.

Another one of those books that suffered, I think, because I saw the movie first and I adore the film. The violence and graphic killings didn't upset me as much as some people have said. I knew what I was getting into and I like watching horror films and reading horrific novels so if that makes me a sociopath, as someone below has said, so be it. Anyway. Some bits were shocking but not enough for me to put the book down. I was constantly thinking about it and wanting to get back to it and it certainly draws you in. I think I was a little disadvantaged by not having lived through the 80s and therefore not getting everything (something that was more of an issue here than with the film). The only reason this has three stars instead of four is because it just started to get a little long. Everything was spiraling out of control but I just couldn't keep my attention. It's a good read and certainly an interesting one. Obviously not for the faint of heart or stomach but it's an experience. Glad I read it.

 I was actually really surprised by the low rating that this book has received when I first started reading it, but I didn't let this sway me while I was reading. I also tried to go into this book with a clear mind, and not compare it to Jay Asher's brilliant work (Thirteen Reasons Why, which if you haven't checked out yet, I highly recommend that you do). So with those 2 things in mind, I ventured into reading his newest novel, and was extremely impressed. Did it blow me away, no, but this was a cute, quick story that was the perfect Christmastime read. I read this literally 2 days before Christmas, and it had everything that I wanted at that time...Christmas trees, pretty lights, hot cocoa, ugly sweaters, candy canes...I could go on and on! Honestly, I could easily see this being a Hallmark Christmas movie (and I'm a sucker for those things). The story was incredibly heartwarming and just a feel-good, light romance, and exactly what I needed. 
 Jay Asher delivered another book with characters that you easily begin to care about as soon as the story begins. Sierra was a caring, kind person that just wanted the best for everyone. She was down-to-earth, and a great MC to read about. Caleb made me swoon multiple several hundred times, and despite his secret (which wasn't as dark as the synopsis made it out to be), he more than made up for his "mistake." I honestly loved his character, and how selfless he was. Every girl deserves a Caleb in her life. But most importantly, I loved how mature they were in their relationship. When they got into an argument, they actually used their words and didn't just make those snap judgments that every other couple in books these days tends to do. It made their relationship more believable to me because it showed that 2 people can actually be adults and handle an argument maturely. Also, despite how quickly they "fell" for each other, their relationship seemed extremely natural and progressed at a normal pace. Again, this was refreshing to read since this isn't common in books anymore. Caleb and Sierra's relationship is very clean, and it focused more on them getting to know each other than trying to get in each other's pants. 
 I will say that I flew through this book and easily read it in one sitting. In some ways it actually felt more like a novella rather than a full length novel. I'm not necessarily saying that I wanted more pages in the book, but the book just seemed incredibly short to me. Nothing particularly exciting or dramatic happened in the story, which in my opinion would have felt out of place if it did. And those are my only complaints (which really aren't complaints more just observations). 
 Overall, Jay Asher's, What Light is a lighthearted, fun Christmas romance. Sure, you could easily write this one off as "just another holiday inspired story," but it truly is a great novel that takes you into a winter wonderland for a couple hours. It's not as gripping or thought-provoking as 13 Reasons Why, but I never expected it to be. So grab some hot chocolate, cookies, and this book, and read this book now! 
 Happy reading :)

edit: okay. i've thought more about it, and there's nothing holding me back from giving this one star except for the fact that i don't like giving books one stars. so i'm lowering it.

I gave this book 1 star because I did not like it. Two stars would mean that it was okay, but no, it wasn't, I did not like it at all. 
 WRITING STYLE: When reading this, it seems like you're reading all of the most common, mainstreams things collected in one, especially sentences. They are just so ordinary and boring! 
 DIALOGUES: Again, everything is mechanical, nothing new or exciting. Things are said just for the sake of being said, it feels like the author did not think about what he's writing and that brings us to... 
 CHARACTERISATION: non existent! Everyone is compliant, there are a few squabbles, but it's like the author couldn't be bothered to make an interesting story. The author also cannot write a female character at all. We see everything from a 16-year-old-girl's PoV and really, whether it be a robot or a 16-year-old-girl, wouldn't make any difference. (and that goes for every character) But I do have to admit, the author gave all of the best sentences and descriptions to the male main character. 
 DESCRIPTIONS: The same. Throughout the book, we get the same descriptions of the same things. First time they went to the church, "We stop to let a car pull into the parking lot, which is filling up fast.", the second time they went to the church "When we reach the 
 church, the parking lot is full." And this is what I know about the church, that it has a small parking lot! 
 Now, I have many more things that I don't like, e.g. the plot is non-existent, very lazy writing, overall, a very easy book that every person who's written something in their life could also write this book. I do like this author's other piece of work "13 reasons why", but that won't make me go easier on this book. I am really sorry that this book wasn't given better characterisations, dialogues, descriptions, etc. I really wanted to like it.
Really enjoyed this contemporary.

I know, I know... I'm late!! What Light by Jay Asher came out on October 18th but I really wanted to wait a bit to put my review out because this is such a great story to help you get in the mood for Christmas! It's about Christmas trees! Lots and lots of Christmas trees!! 
 Well, not all about Christmas trees. It's about forgiveness and love, not necessarily in that order. This isn't your basic happy young adult romance. 
 Sierra has a unique childhood, to say the least. She lives on a tree farm in Oregon. Every year, the day before Thanksgiving, they drive their Christmas trees down to a lot in California to sell them. Their family has been doing this for years; her mother and father met on the Christmas tree lot. For the weeks leading up to Christmas, Sierra does schoolwork from their Airstream trailer while working on the tree lot. 
 Sierra has her Oregon best friends and she has her California best friend, Heather. It's been pretty easy to split and share herself with her two worlds. But things get complicated this Christmas season. Yep, you guessed it! There's always a guy involved when things get messy ;) 
 When Sierra meets Caleb while working at the tree lot, she sees him for who he is on the inside, not for his past mistake and the rumors that swirl around him. The problems arise when Sierra has to convince others that Caleb is not his mistake. And then there's the pesky expiration date on any sort of relationship they may have... or not have? 
 I liked that the story had obvious good guys and obvious bad guys. I also liked the fact that Mr. Asher used subtlety to bring in some of the good guys and the bad guys, too. For instance, Caleb's parents are subtly the bad guys (IMHO, of course). I'll let you figure out that one on your own. And no, I didn't spoil anything for you :) The story was just well written with many characters both clobbering you over the head with their role in the story and others just glancing by, adding their little spice to the story. Nothing too overwhelming. 
 I haven't read any other story with a "crisis" quite like the one in this book before. It left me at times conflicted. But by the happy ending, which I thought was done in perfect proportion to being a holiday story with substance, I was comfortable with everyone's "happily ever after".

 Jay Asher is the king of YA literature. THE KING. ALL HAIL JAY ASHER. And I bet you all can completely agree with me because of the success of Thirteen Reasons Why, one of the best books ever. I think the show has just boosted the readership of the novel SO MUCH so I'm hoping that people might feel a little more interested in this because of the movie. What Light is a lovely Christmas-y story that made me squeal and freak out over the one emotion that every human being has felt at one point of their life: LOVE. 
 I am really impressed with this story because it's not JUST about the cutesy lovey stuff. It's more than that; it's the usual Jay Asher fluff. He adds so many more topics that we never really aware about into his gorgeous stories. What Light basically showed us that hey: HOLIDAY BOOKS ARE FOR THE SUMMER. They can be read in the spring, fall--whenever. When I began reading it, I didn't expect that this would be entertaining, but it definitely was. Asher's writing was (almost) as good as ever, and I really appreciated the storyline. 
 This is one of those feel-good stories that makes you want to appreciate life a little more. Caleb and Sierra are the power couple of them all. I fell in love with their romance as well and just pined for them to be together. IT WAS MAGICAL. I felt a real connection to the book because I wanted the best for the characters if you know what I mean. The plot, on the other hand, was quite slow-paced which was the reason why I had to stick with a lower rating for this one. Unlike Asher's other books, it lacked something. Something life-changing. How did Thirteen Reasons Why accomplish this? I really don't know. Let's just say that it was a nice story. 
 Want a pleasing, adorable story? Read this. That's all I can say. 
 *A review copy was provided by the publisher via BookExpo America in exchange for a honest review. Thank you so much!*

I definitely recommend reading this book during Christmas time. Reading it in March doesn't give you the same feels as it would in December. 
 Sierra's family runs a Christmas tree farm. Every year during Thanksgiving break her family travels from Oregon down to California to sell their trees. It's how life has always been for her, and she wouldn't have it any other way. 
 The family hires baseball players from the town to help out with the trees, but Sierra has never had any interest in the boys. And if she did, the boys would be forced to clean the outhouses. But this year, her California best friend Heather needs Sierra to hook up with someone so they could double date because her current boyfriend is BORING. And Sierra meets Caleb, a boy with a past. 
 It's a cute, simple read, something that could be read in a day. I absolutely loved the dialogue between all of the characters. It felt real and I appreciate that.

I actually really loved how cheesy this book was, especially since it revolved entirely around one of the best times of year. I'm always a sucker for young love because once you grow up you never get it back. 
 I always wondered about Christmas trees, where they were grown and for how long. This book gave me a lot of insight into that aspect of the holiday as well as many others. The selflessness of giving, forgiveness, and even understanding are all aspects we look past on this holiday. This book touched on all of these subjects. 
 I have to commend Asher for his writing with this book as well. He tapped into the female psyche pretty well, writing very relatable characters and very believable friendships. That was probably my favorite part of the book: how close everyone was despite the distances--time and space. 
 It was really a touching book, and much more light hearted than 13 Reasons Why. I enjoyed the complete 180 Asher pulled, and I can't wait to see what else he's going to write for us in the future.

This was a stupid book. First of all, the girl with ridiculously high standards starts dating a boy who is rumored to have attacked his sister with a knife. They sit down and have a heart to heart, and it turns out he repeatedly stabbed the door she hid behind, not her, so it's all good. When she sees his bff avoid him, she confronts him, stating that people change and it wasn't what it looked like (i mean, he was there, but his eyes must be wrong). The bff of 10+ years mentions that she doesn't really know him, but she insists she does. I mean, they've been dating for two whole weeks now. It's pretty serious. 
 And her friends. Her friend from back home in Oregon calls her and informs her that she got a non speaking part in the school play. Then she tells her if she gets on the midnight train, she should be home in time for the performance. When she hesitates, her friend accuses her of choosing the boy over her and hangs up. So, she spends long days working in her family's tree lot selling trees and she had plans to spend the weekend with her other friend and lil bf (albeit psycho, but that's irrelevant here), and her supposed best friend back home expects her to work a 12 hour day and blow off her plans to sit on a train for 16 hours to watch her stand on a stage and be silent, then sit on a train for 16 hours to go back and jump right back into work and school. 
 Are you kidding me? 
 Also, love in 30 days or less. 
 And, the big moment at the end, the best present of all, the piece de resistance, the true measure of the depth of their love - tickets to the winter dance! 
 Nope.

 - The winter setting was appropriate for the time I read it in. 
 - Friendship plays quite a huge role in this book. 
 - Sierra's parents were strict with her which was a nice change from the parents not being involved at all. Sierra's father was worried about her and the possibility of her breaking her heart. 
 Dislike: 
 - Very insta-lovey. I don't quite get why you would try and start a relationship when you know you're only going to be there for a month and possibly never come back. It's setting yourself up for heartbreak. 
 - Not sure if I feel the friendship aspect was done well. It almost feels like all of these girls were there to further along the plot and help the main character get her boyfriend. 
 - Caleb, the love interest, has a tragic backstory. I don't mind tragic backstories, only I was quite shocked by what he did. Especially for the short time the main character knew Caleb, it felt unrealistic for her to just accept it and move on. I know I probably wouldn't have stayed with him. 
 - The ending didn't feel resolved to me. I didn't know if Caleb and Sierra would stay together or if they would break up or what the hell would actually happen after Sierra left. I don't like being left behind with questions. At least, not in a YA contemporary romance.
Cute story warmly feeling

Oh guys. I had such high hopes for this book. Jay Asher's only other solo novel, Thirteen Reasons Why, was one of the best books I read during my teenage years. 
 This book was not made of the same stuff. I DNF'ed it after 100 pages when I realized it really wasn't going to get any better. 
 The plot was entirely one dimensional, the dialogue stilted, and the characters boring. 
 I think this would have worked much better as a short story, but even then, the plot simply wasn't there. This book is a let down, and don't let that beautiful cover fool you. This one isn't worth the read.
Haha, this was so bad. But in a cute, cheesy sort of way.

I came to realize that some YA books are just too...young adult-y for my taste. Frankly, I wanted to read this book because I thought the cover was really cute and so was the title, very christmasy. But after the first few chapters it felt so, idk, immature. Maybe I'm getting too old for YA, or this story is just not so great. All the characters felt too much like teenagers and I know that that's the whole point of the genre, for it too be for and about young people, but I can't make myself finish this one. The plot felt boring and the characters were so blah.. 
 Maybe I'll give it another chance next year around Christmas.

This is the first book I've read by Jay Asher and I have heard such good things about Thirteen Reasons Why so I was super excited to read a Jay Asher book. Let's just say I probably should have started out with Thirteen Reasons Why because What Light turned out to be a real let down for me. It read just like a typical YA Contemporary Romance. There was nothing special about it and in fact I grew very bored of Sierra and Caleb's "relationship". 
 I was also very frustrated to learn what made Caleb such a "bad boy" in everybody's eyes. I do feel his dilemma was serious but I was expecting something different and to make more of an impact. Maybe it's just me and I'm just desensitized at this point in my life, but it just didn't warrant him to be considered a "pariah", to me anyways. 
 The best way for me to describe how I felt about this book I guess is to compare it to those old cheesy after school specials with warnings about teen drug use, pregnancy etc. Not that this book had that serious of an under tone it just felt that cheesy. 
 Even in my disappointment with What Light I'm still looking forward to reading more of Jay Asher. I'm just going to chalk this one up to hopefully being a fluke.

If you're looking for a slap up, quality Christmas dinner kinda book, look away. 
 If you want a take away, kinda festive because it's in a snowflake bag with a Christmas peppermint hot chocolate- stay. 
 Now I knew this would be light, I hoped it would be fuzzy and charming and just a generic quick read. 
 What I got was...well... a good intention that just didn't work out. 
 I loved the idea of it, but it was quite a dark idea for such a small book. I get one of the points was about the trouble of gossip and rumours, but really in this case - the rumours were like...nearly spot on- so you could kinda guess why the other characters were reacting the way they did?!! 
 I didn't like the main character, I found her a bit Mary Sue-ish, and she also seemed to be a bit of a pusher, she literally got in involved in something that didn't concern her in two weeks. And she was a bit of a bitch while doing it. 
 I was hoping for festive, but that lacked as well - the most festive bit about this book was the cover and the fact she worked on a Christmas Tree farm... 
 The words were SO CLUNKY. My god I do not need to know that she cut up her meal with a butter knife and fork, or that she was handed a hot chocolate and then PROCEEDED to put it down!! I mean shgjkdfhgdfjgh- we did not need to be spoon fed... I mean isn't this classed as teen/YA fiction?! 
 I had so many other problems with this book, but if you're looking for something quick, without need of much plot, random story lines and 'okay' making out surrounded by Christmas trees this delivers all of the above. Just expect to be spoon-fed on everything. Even things that aren't relevant at all.
A lovely Christmas read :)
This book is a dumpster fire and took me 8 months to get through

This might have been better had I read it during the holiday season, but beyond the Very Merry Christmas aesthetic, I don't see too much reason that I'd recommend this book to anyone.

 the writing was choppy, no flow, characters forced, no development, couldn't handle the protagonist, insufferable tropes, overall miserable to read. oops, sorry.
An easy breezy read. Not really any depth do it but a nice read if you are looking for something to fill your time.

disappointing. I was expecting something much more real, fleshed out and intense. It was fluffy and saccrine sweet and without any real plot. I loved reading this book that takes place during Christmas, actually during Christmas season! This book was light and fluffy, and had an adorable romance that didn't nauseate me. I loved it and I will defi Italy continue to read more of Jag Asher's books becasue I love his writing style.

"There are so many things prickling in the back of my mind, threatening to take me out of this moment. But instead of worrying about anything, I close my eyes, lean forward, and allow myself to believe in us." 
 Every Christmas, Sierra's family comes down to California to sell the Christmas trees from their farm back in Oregon. Over the years, Sierra has built a seasonal life in California. Her best friend Heather wants her to double date with her and her boyfriend, but Sierra refuses to start a relationship with anyone because this might be her last Christmas coming to California so her days are numbered. One day while she is selling trees, she meets Caleb who made a huge mistake in the past which everyone in the town knows about. She is drawn to him despite this, and has to make a decision to hold back her feelings or give them a chance at least until Christmas. 
 What Light was a simple holiday read. There was nothing that special or unique about it, but it was enjoyable enough because I like the 'we only have X amount of time until I leave, so should we still see what becomes of our relationship' trope. 
 The main characters, Sierra and Caleb, weren't my kind of favorites. I didn't really care about what happened to them, and I was really just along for the ride. I was more interested in Heather and Devon's relationship than theirs. Also, I didn't find anything about them particularly compelling. Caleb's: 
 was a strange choice. I don't know why Jay Asher specifically chose that type of thing to happen. It didn't really fit with the story, and made it kind of awkward. I think the story would've been served better if any other type of mistake was made because I don't think stabbing a door a bunch of times qualifies as that type of thing. I would've been okay with it if it was developed better, but it wasn't (the story is around 250 pages so it was understandable). Because I wasn't satisfied with the handling of it, Caleb's mistake and journey to self forgiveness wasn't as good and heart wrenching as I wanted it to be. 
 I didn't like the characters that much, and the plot wasn't anything truly special, so why did I enjoy it? Well, I was in the mood for an easy read. Even though I don't really believe in half stars, What Light was really a 2.5. It had enough holiday spirit to balance out the things I didn't like, and it helped that it was based on a trope I liked and had an open ending.

Written for www.theradbooks.blogspot.com. 
 Summary: 
 Sierra's family owns a Christmas tree farm in Oregon; each year the family travels to California to sell their trees at Christmas time. She has dealt with having a separate life in each state her whole life; this means adjusting to splitting time between her best friends, schools, and homes. Sierra usually spends her Christmases selling trees and hanging out with one of her best friends, Heather. That is, until she meets Caleb, a kind-hearted guy who made a huge mistake in the past. Sierra becomes determined to help Caleb find redemption in the eyes of the community and his family. 
 Pros: 
 *	Following the life of a girl whose family operates a Christmas tree farm sheds light on a profession that not many people think about. 
 *	Caleb is a likable main character with some redeeming characteristics. 
 *	I enjoyed the Christmas setting. 
 Cons: 
 *	The plot was rather predictable and boring; the whole time I was reading I kept wondering when something interesting would happen. 
 *	Sierra fell into the romance novel trap of pursuing someone who, in the long-run, will probably not work out and using the L-word far too soon. 
 *	The parents seemed to cater to Sierra the second she complained and were wishy-washy. 
 Final Thoughts: 
 I really wanted to like this book; I loved Jay Asher's other book Thirteen Reasons Why. I just could not get into this one. It felt like there were so many interesting plot lines that could have been explored, yet the author went with the more cliche plot. It felt like the story and the characters fell flat. Perhaps if the plot was less predictable, I would have felt the intended heartbreak and cared about the romance in it. If you want a quick holiday read, maybe this book is for you.

"...there are two types of people in the world: those who prefer to be sad among others, and those who prefer to be sad alone." 
 It is perhaps unfortunate that I read this book so soon after reading Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close, which happens to be written by the author's husband. Some of the themes are so similar that I cannot help but compare, and most of the time this book is the one coming up short. While it is in some ways an easier read, I did not find it as moving or as satisfying. (One thing I did like better about History of Love was that some of the characters and especially the young people were portrayed a bit more realistically.) 
 Trying to review it for itself without comparing: I liked the main character Leo Gursky, the old, lonely man afraid of dying without anyone noticing. (At the beginning we are told that he goes out of his way to make himself seen, but aside from the few examples given at the outset I didn't see him really acting this way through the rest of the book.) 
 The unusual ways the story is told (like Alma's story being written out in lists) just didn't work for me. The mysteries of the novel within the novel and how all the characters were connected frustrated me instead of just keeping me interested. And one point revealed at the end (no spoilers) made me feel cheated. 
 There's a writer with some talent here. The book is not bad. But it's not great, either.
Funny, I have read this book. It was written by her husband, Jonathan Safran Foer. Oh, and the title was Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close. Yeah. Her writing is a sad rip off.

I read this the first time during freshman year when I thought I was in love with a boy. It was gifted to me by my very best friend (she didn't know I had previously read it) on my graduation day. I just reread it. What a gift to learn that love manages to find you, in so many peculiar ways, time and time again. Such proof that life imitates literature - or perhaps the other way around. Having read 'Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close' by Jonathan Safran Foer, I found out that he is married to Nicole Krauss and many criticisms levelled at his book were that his story was incredibly similar in themes and technique. I decided to read 'The History of Love' so that I could compare the two. 
 True, both stories feature an intelligent youth who sets out on a quest in New York City - both having lost their fathers. In Foer's story, Oskar encounters a survivor of the Dresden firebombing and in Krauss's Alma meets a Holocaust survivor. Both of the elderly men in the stories are mourning the loss of their estranged sons. However, for me, that's where the similarities end. 
 Yes, Krauss and Foer may have lived together when writing these novels but there are thousands of books that feature people who lived during World War II. If you have a shared history, as partners often do, it is possible you could write about similar things. For me, Krauss's novel is far more confusing in its attempts to weave a mystery. I enjoyed Foer's novel immensely and found the characters easy to empathise with but with Krauss's, I found the characters as confusing as the plot. Perhaps I just wasn't concentrating. 
 I think Krauss was determined to use this novel as a vehicle to demonstrate her intellect and knowledge of writers but it just didn't appeal to me. For a book called 'The History of Love', it lacked heart. I didn't care enough about the characters and the disjointed narrative only distanced me further. 
 This book is meant to be about love, loss and friendship but it seemed to me to be about betrayal, confusion and insanity. 
 There are some genuine moments in the book where I had to stifle a giggle but all in all this book did not come close to 'Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close'.

I loved the writing style, a story within a story within a story. 
 But couldn't complete it. Got boring a little in the middle. I don't even care to know how it ends.

I read this book while on vacation in Hanoi, Vietnam and somehow the combination of the exotic locale where I was staying and the very Western milieu of the novel bound me up in a strange cocoon of longing. The themes of loss struck very close to my heart. The writing is dense and layered and I had to surrender myself completely to the writer and trust that she had good reason for choosing the varied paths through her story. I wasn't disappointed in the end. If you're a black and white kind of person, you probably won't enjoy this book. But if you long for or can tolerate all the shades in between those two colors, I heartily recommend this wonderful work of art.

Oh dear. This is one of those books everyone has been telling me to read. It's reviews having been gushing in the extreme - heartbreakingly wonderful, written by an angel, restores your faith in fiction... you know the sort of thing. 
 I should have known better. This was terrible. It had no story to speak of, its characters were totally 2-dimentional to the point where I just didn't care what happened to them and the writing style was indescribable, and not in a good way. 
 Nicole Krauss, I realise that you are trying to write in the conversational style of your particular characters but "And yet" is not a sentence. It should certainly not appear as a sentence on practically EVERY DAMN PAGE OF THE BOOK!!! 
 I also realise that Jewish authors are hot to trot at the moment, each making their own amends with history. That does not necessarily mean everything they produce is good. This, sadly, is not.

I read about two thirds before I gave up, and there were parts that I did like...the pieces from Leo's point of view were interesting, but I just couldn't fully understand, relate to, or become in any way involved with Alma or any of the other characters. Wow, not really sure what to think! Except... awesome story!

"...right now, at this exact moment, you are the happiest and saddest you've ever been in your entire life." 
 I didn't want to read this book. So many people had told me I needed to read it, that I knew I'd be disappointed. Also, I wasn't sure I could deal with another story about Holocaust survivors right now. But, there was another plane in my future, so I grabbed the book while heading out the door. And I'm so glad I did. 
 The writing -- so evocative of place, and thought. 
 The themes -- invisibility, grief, searching for connections. 
 The characterization -- I want to see Leo at Starbucks, and to pay Bird for a glass of lemonade, and to help Alma put up her tent. 
 It's the kind of book I could see being assigned in an English class to discuss structure and characterization. But I don't want that. It's not a book that should be forced on someone; it needs to be found when they are in a position to appreciate the prose, and reflect on the themes. 4 stars because it's not for everyone at every time.

LOVED this. And it broke my heart a little. I don't remember ever crying as hard at the end of a story. 
 Second reading (which i don't ever do): still love it, still beautiful, still crying.

What an eloquent, captivating, and curious book! I thoroughly enjoyed every part, each voice, the mystery, the way Krauss writes about love, heartbreak, loss and everything that makes us human. Looking forward to reading more of her work in the future.

I give up. Nicole Krauss is an incredible writer, her imagery is imaginative and beautiful, but her stories confuse the crap out of me and never end the way I hope they will. This one is about a man who wrote a book and a girl named Alma who he loved once. He had a son who was also a writer. Beyond that I can't tell you what happened. I read this book, was thoroughly confused by the angles of the story and half the time had ZERO idea what was happening, what time frame we were in, and where the heck it was leading. This was more frustrating than enjoyable, and perhaps I am a simpleton who just doesn't read enough into things and appreciate symbolism or whatever, but I'm pretty sure this style of writing just isn't for me.

I loved this book--enjoyed it all of the way through and was sad when it ended. There is only one thing I disliked that is revealed in the last few pages, but other than that I highly recommened it. Others may be put off my the way that it's narrated by Alma, but I found it refreshing. She seemed like a 14 y/o, unlike, in let's say, The Elegance of the Hedgehog, where the narration of the younger person is ridiculous and unbelievable. Whatever I read next will likely be a disappointment after this.

I would have liked more from Leo and less from the other narrators that just made it drag...I like Leo so that's the only reason I will even give it 3 stars. I can't really recommend this to others
great novel full of life and remorse...characters will engross you

This novel is sad, but sweet. You will laugh, but also feel a little heartbroken for the characters. The characters are easy to love, especially Leo and Bird. This book is very smart, and the connection between the characters is revealed very slowly. Highly recommeneded.

God I loved this book. I finished it on the subway, which is sometimes unfortunate, but it seemed fitting for this book because of the lostness of the characters (also it was set in New York, and I was taking the subway to Brooklyn). The ending just killed me. 
 But really, the best part of this book was the characters. There three perspectives throughout: Alma, a teenage girl, Zvi, an Author and immigrant to South America and Leopold, another Polish immigrant in Brooklyn who made his living as a locksmith. The character descriptions are so specific, so heartbreakingly realistic and paired with these subtly crafted sentences that are just perfect. My copy was full of post-it notes by the time I finished. There are moments, so simple, that bleed with this rich, unfiltered humanity that just leaves you feeling raw, unsettled yet full of this immense amount of hope. 
 This book does what all books should do. It's the re-examining of your own life through another world. It is tender; it is unbearably true.
Absolutely one of the best books in the world! Beautifully written.
Critically aclaimed, did get it.
You need a flow chart to keep up with the characters and names in this book. For the first time ever, I had to read a wiki to understand the plot of a book!
Awesome book, follows the life story of a man who thinks he's left no mark on the world and the lives of the people he's influenced. Well-written, at times the book is poetic.

book_b.title: Her Fearful Symmetry
book_b.user_review: Liked the story...kind of creepy. Weak ending

sample_reviews.review_text: Just another reminder of why I HATE ghost stories. It was terrible. First off it was slow and it took at least 1/3 of the book before I was some what interested. There was a small twist that kept me going and so I keep reading. Then finally when the twist was revealed I was excited. Then the book ended and it ended BADLY. OMG it was probably the worst ending I've EVER read. I really hated this book and would NOT recommend it to anyone. I HATE GHOST STORIES THEY ALWAYS END STUPIDLY.
Though the actions of the characters became unbelievable towards the end, I loved this book. AN just does it for me with her fascinating relationships and descriptively elegant prose.

You know it's bad when you're sitting in front of a blank screen, trying to figure out what to say about a book. This is how I feel about Her Fearful Symmetry, Audrey Niffenegger's long awaited follow-up to her fantastic debut The Time Traveler's Wife. It has taken me a full six days to slog through the meager 400 pages of this story. Never once in almost a week, did I experience that "can't wait to get that book open" moment that makes for a good read. I had to force myself through the entire thing. 
 Her Fearful Symmetry begins with such promise, but the story quickly goes downhill. I thought I'd be really interested in the twins, Julia and Valentina, but I just couldn't make myself care about them. Up to about page 275, I was just bored. Then the story took a dark turn (involving an innocent kitten) and I was disgusted. Valentina's plan to live as an individual away from her sister is not only incredibly selfish and horrifying, but also ridiculous. Whatever small redeeming quality the story had, it lost somewhere between the incident with the kitten and Valentina's plan. 
 I kept reading, hoping at least for a satisfactory ending. Not a "happy ending" - there was no way that was going to happen - but at least an ending that made the reading worth while. I did not get it. The ending was pointless and without any kind of tangible meaning. I was completely let down. 
 I am so surprised at the good reviews I have read about this book. The prose is really beautiful, but that is not enough to make for a good story. In finishing the book, my world is neither better or worse for the reading (unless you take into consideration almost a week lost within it's covers.) I will not recommend Her Fearful Symmetry to you. It definitely lacked the magic of The Time Traveler's Wife, and has nothing really redeeming - no interesting characters, no captivating setting, no fascinating plot line. I am really disappointed.

Stay away from this book. It's not nearly as well written as the Time Traveler's Wife and the ending makes you want to reach through the book and slap the author. Really?! You've got to be kidding me. These are not reactions you want to evoke in your readers and yet, those were my exact words as I closed the book. Starts strong but quickly fizzles into one big waste of time.

ugh, am I going to finish this book? I'm having serious doubts. The writing is so plain and boring I don't know if I'm going to invest any more of my life on this one. I really hate to not finish a book once I begin it. But this book is poorly written. I can't understand this author's popularity at all. sigh. 
 2-23-10 okay, so I stuck with it and finished today and can still say I am not impressed. The twist was predicable in my opinion and a silly plot line of how ghosts need assistance to exit a building left me wondering why did I bother finishing this book. Ah, well.

I feel...undecided about this one. When the author introduced the supernatural aspect, I was like 'hmm, ok, I'll go with this for a bit', but then once it got too complex, with Valentina and her "plan", I was definitely not on board with that. I thought it was just kind of weird. I read a lot of reviews that said none of the characters were particularly likeable, and I don't know that I necessarily agree with that. I think that the only character I truly didn't like was Julia, and then at the end, Elspeth. I can't believe she did that!! Also, I honestly could not wrap my brain around the whole Edie/Elspeth confusion. I couldn't figure out who was actually who and what happened years ago. And the relationship between Julia and Valentina made me feel uncomfortable. Generally, I feel sort of flat after reading it.

An over the top plot (I'm not entirely familiar with fantasy or whatever this is). But, it worked. You could get into the various characters trying to change places or struggle with their settings. Fun to listen to on tape.

Having really enjoyed Niffenegger's first novel, "The Time Traveler's Wife" I was expecting much more out of "Her Fearful Symmetry." Things started off well enough, but I couldn't get past the sinister, morbid and distasteful turn the narrative took on toward the end. I almost didn't want to finish it, which is a very rare thing for me, but I kept on reading in the hopes that the story would somehow redeem itself. 
 I rated the book 2 stars here because I can't even begin to say that I actually liked it. I suppose it was more of a 2.5 for me. I was definitely disappointed.

Interesting idea, but I wasn't crazy about the story. I think it's hard to not compare it to the genius that is the Time Travelers Wife, and unfortunately it fell a little short for me. I did however love the Martin character.

I really liked this book at the beginning. I liked Elspeth, Martin and Robert. I love the setting - London and Highgate Cemetery. And at first, I enjoyed the plot. But about 3/4 of the way through this book, it just got really dumb and over the top. I can do magical realism; in fact, I really enjoy it. But what happened in this book just doesn't make sense. Valentina's plan was silly and the fact that Robert went along with it is just preposterous! The twists and turns with Edie/Eslpeth and who the real mother was = soap opera. Come on!!! Are we educated people here or what? And the ending? What was all that mess? No, this book just did not work for me. Really silly and unbelievable.
read up to the last few chapters, trying to see if it would get interesting but it never.
Don't waste your time on this book. It started well and them about 200 pages into went downhill.
Started out a bit slow, but picked up speed and had a big plot twist that I didn't see coming. I really enjoyed it, but I would say that The Time Traveller's Wife was better. Glad I picked this up.
This was an easy and fun and unique read but the ending was terrible. The last 2-3 pages ruined the whole book for me.

I hadn't read her previous book but was intrigued by the "twin" stories & moved it to the top of my pile. I felt that the author tried to include too many sub-plots which didn't serve to move the story along but did take up time & space. It was ok but not a favorite.

With great Gothic possibilities, the author muddled everything up with characters that were either undeveloped, unlikeable, or underutilized. Niffennegger likes her parallel universes, and what better than life/death. It got silly.

I've got to echo the other folks her: A batty plot with even weirder characters. Also there were times that Niffenegger's writing sounded contrived, like something she might submit in a creative writing class. 
 If you find your appetite for a modern Gothic not whetted from this, I recommend you try Diane Setterfield's "The Thirteenth Tale." "Twinness" plays a central role in this novel, which is also set in Britain, but chances are you won't be rolling your eyes and shaking your head as you read.
Interesting, but the ending annoyed me! Characters lacked depth and believability.

Mark Magro's review of this book sums up my own feelings all too well. Stock characters that are not likeable, with heavy doses of WHAT? thrown in on a weak and meandering plot. Add to that a very adrupt and incomplete ending, and I'm left with a book I don't like. 
 I really hoped for more from this book after the Time Traveler's Wife. I'm not sure why a man with a gene for time travel and the woman that puts up with it were more believable and more likeable, but they were. And bonus for the plot and gripping story in TTW. 
 I'm also puzzled by some odd inconsistencies. In the acknowledgements, Ms. Niffenegger thanks an editor for correcting her Americanisms. Ms. Niffenegger was born in America. Has spending a few years in London made her British? Her spelling throughout the book was British English (colour not color), and I thought it especially odd when commenting over and over that the twins born in Chicago were American. I thought it would be a decent touch to give them accents on the page, if not in the ear. Ms. Niffenegger took the pains to color most of their speech with "like", so I don't imagine that working out the details would be too hard. 
 Finally, the twins. I'm a twin, so perhaps I'm a bit over sensitive. My guess is the research for Edie and Elspeth as well as Valentina and Julia came from a combination of watching The Shining and the newer seasons of The Girls Next Door or reading back issues of Playboy. She does not write twins well at all. 
 As with the over use of "like", thanks for the inappropriate "twins really do want to be the same person / do everything together!!!" idea. Way to promote unrealistic ideas of twins and American speech.

I was about half way through this book and commented to someone that I wished something would actually happen in the story. I can deal with suspension of disbelief, but by the time I got to the end of this book, I found it so unsatisfying that I had to read part of another book to wash this one from my brain. I'm glad I checked it out of the library, rather than having to decide whether to inflict it on someone else or just throw it away.
Decided to give it a try, despite the bad reviews. The story was just weird and it took too long to get going.

i loved The Time Traveler's Wife. loved it. i love Niffenegger's writing style. the way she composes syllables when she is describing a scene or a feeling is musical. 
 that said, this story fell flat for me. not enough development, ended too short and it i found it to be predictable. it took me awhile to get into it and then when i did, i felt cheated by the experience. 
 this in no way means i will not read her next book. like i wrote, i love her writing style.

A gorgeous and moving piece centered on what truly makes one oneself and how much of personality is bound up in our relationships with others. Every twist of the ending was telegraphed from the beginning, but despite that (or perhaps because of it) each piece is still extremely poignant. If this book has a draw back it is that Niffenegger still has a somewhat heavy hand with the English language. Long passages in Portuguese are written in full and then occasionally translated below (a gimmick which smacks of arrogance), thoughts are typed haphazardly in italics and some sentences simply fall flat. 
 Overall, an extraordinary second novel.
I wanted to like this more, but couldn't get through the book the way I did with The Time Traveler's Wife. Perhaps I'll pick it up again and will feel differently.

I eagerly anticipated reading this book because I enjoyed the author's previous book, Time Traveler's Wife. I also was quite intrigued by the blurb that I read when it was published because it said that it centered on the lives of twin sisters who were daughters of twin sisters who had been estranged. They never knew their aunt, but she left everything to them when she died in her 40's. The younger twins leave their life in America to head off to England to live in the aunt's "flat" for a year, as required by the terms of her Will in order to inherit. I can't say how disappointed I was. The books is a really strange, twisted ghost story that has turned me off to Niffenegger. I think my greatest problem is my inability to relate to the relationship between both sets of twins and what transpires as a result.
The book is interesting at the beginning, but then it gets so boring and dull.

Spooky and atmospheric. Two 20-year-old American twins get a letter telling them they've inherited their aunt Elspeth's London apartment, provided that they live in it for one year and don't let their parents enter it. The girls find out that their mother Edie and Elspeth were also twins, but estranged for many years. When they move into the apartment, they meet a variety of interesting characters, including Elspeth's lover Robert (scholar and cemetery tour guide, who might be able to explain the peculiar condition of the will if he ever will read Elspeth's diaries that were left to him). They also discover that Elspeth may not be altogether gone after all. The novel is about secrets, lies, love, peculiar twin relationships, and also about Highgate Cemetery, next door to the flat and vividly described. 
 Great for book groups in that there will be much discussion about the characters and the ending - and whether the ending was telegraphed and if that matters.
I read this last year, unsure why I didn't review it at the time. Pretty good ghost story and tale of living with mental illness. Niffenegger gets mood and place, for sure.

After loving The Time Traveller's Wife, I was convinced that this would be equally as good. I was so eager to read it that I bought a hard bound copy upon release rather than wait. HFS began with such promise: mysterious foreign setting, quirky sisters, a long-kept secret. Unfortunately, the secret was pretty much self-evident before it was obvious to the main characters, any hope for a love story just never materialized, and the ending felt felt both rushed and never developed at the same time. Not a total waste of time but I was definitely disappointed.

This book is so well-written and sooo good. I won't give anything away, but it has to do with two sets of twins and deals a lot with what it's like to be a twin (although I'm guessing both of the relationships in the book were a lot more dysfunctional than the average set of real-life twins). It is set in London in an apartment building next to Highgate Cemetery, which was founded in the Victorian era of England and has several hundred thousand bodies buried in it (I've never been there but it must be a huge place). Several of the characters in the book are volunteers at the cemetery, and one main character is writing a thesis about the cemetery, so obviously the cemetery plays a huge role in the book. And another of the main characters is a ghost. In the last few chapters there were several twists, one that I kind of guessed and two that I did NOT see coming at all. I had a few moments of saying "Oh my gosh" out loud. I would recommend if you liked: The Time Traveler's Wife (obviously, as both are by the same amazing author), The Book of Lost Things, The Woman in White, or In the Woods.

My goodness. 
 I'm not sure if this was a happy ending or a sad ending. It was interesting to step into the supernatural but...hmm.

SO different ...a different flavor that I've never experienced. One cannot compare this book to Time Traveler's Wife as it's completely different. I'm still processing this book. Liked it, but didn't LOVE it?

Very disappointing considering that I loved the Time Traveler's Wife. After they inherit a London flat near Highgate Cemetery from their aunt Elspeth Noblin, two American twin teenagers move in, but they soon discover that much is still alive at Highgate, including, perhaps, their aunt, who can't seem to leave her old life behind. Gimmicky and far fetched.

I'm glad to see that I was not the only one who did not enjoy 'Her Fearful Symmetry'. I agree with many of the previous reviews, I could not connect with the characters, the plot line was limited (at best), and the decisions made by the characters were unrealistic. By the end of the book I had come to expect that the characters would make the worst possible decision available to them and I really didn't care when something horrible happened to them; they deserved it. 'Her Fearful Symmetry' was frustrating and unfulfilling. There is absolutely no way I would recommend it to anyone.
Started off interesting, but the characters lacked motivation.

I loved this book for a few hundred pages and then it completely tanked for me. It made no sense and the ending felt like the writer (THE Audrey Niffenegger whom is so very talented so there's no real excuse for this) just gave up and threw in a bunch of crazy, unbelievable wrap ups seemingly just to finish the book. This ruined the entire book for me. It made no sense. Such dissappointment. Truly hope she has a better editor on the next book.

When I completed this book I was just plain mad. It took 300 pages to get to the point of the story, but then it was so quick once it hit the climax it was like snapshots from there until the end. I really wanted to like this book, especially since I enjoyed her previous novel and this one was more toward the genre I enjoy. However, the story, while having a great premise (only reason for earning 2 stars), was not executed smoothly. It was unblanced, and then the very last sentence threw me for a loop; totally unexpected and not really a conclusion. What was the point??
Interesting book, but didn't quite grab me the way Time Traveller's wife did. I wasn't thrilled with the ending.

Reading the first couple of reviewers, I'm in complete agreement. I think this book is what unscrupulous publicists might call HIGH CONCEPT, i.e. unbelievable cobbled together nonsense. As some other reviewers have pointed out, there isn't a character that you could identify with, like or enjoy hating. Why did I plough on through to the end?

I really liked the Time Traveler's Wife and wanted to like this book but just didn't. I read half the book and realized I was still waiting for something to happen. I just couldn't bring myself to read the rest. The characters were boring and the plot was anemic.
terrible terrible terrible ending. However, I did like the setting of Highgate Cemetery in London. It was a great place to visit, especially after reading the book.

I really wanted to love this book because of my "Time Traveler's Wife" obsession but I sadly did not. The characters were not appealing at all, none that I could champion or truly even buy into, which is also what I felt about the plot. A ghost story is rather a difficult sell anyway so it must be extremely well done to be believable - this was not the case. I found the whole novel rather tedious and uncomfortable while trying to get to a big reveal that finally seemed silly. I am aware of how important the theme of identity was in the novel but the relationships were not fleshed out enough to delve deeply enough into this theme. I am still a fan of Audrey Niffengger's in spite of the disappointment of her second book and look forward to her next novel (which I hope is not a ghost story).

This book reads like a souffle pulled from the oven too soon. On the surface it seems appealing. Twins, odd ball characters, ghosts...what could go wrong? Alas the innards are mush. The story doesn't maintain an internal logic, the characters are not consistent nor is their behavior...the plot...well that gets lost in the collapsing walls of part cooked eggs. 
 Disappointing.
A curious idea, but it would have been much more compelling if I had cared about any of the characters. Did make me want to visit the cemetery though!

Compelling but irritating. I was totally inconvinced by the story which started off ordinarily enough but then veered off into the ridiculous. The characters' actions were not in keeping with the way they were portrayed and the 'dark secret' was, frankly, disappointing.

I had high hopes for this book after The TimeTravelers Wife, but boy-oh-boy was I disappointed. I would tell you how much I hated it, but I don't even know where to start. The writing itself isn't terrible, but the characters are irritating and the plot lines don't make any sense at all. Honestly, I expected better from Niffenegger.
What a weird, depressing ghost story. I wasn't crazy about The Time Traveller's Wife, but this sounded a bit interesting--twins, ghosts, England. Disappointing.

I truly do not understand what happened. The Time Traveler's Wife is one of my favorite books ever. I was expecting Audrey Niffenegger's next book like the second coming. 
 And it was... atrociously boring and stilted with paperthin characterization...? I still can't believe it. I still can't fathom how the same writer wrote both books. 
 Maybe a third novel of beauty and subtlety would help me get over my shock?

I was so disappointed by this book. Unlike Niffenegger's previous outing, The Time Traveler's Wife, this book was filled with bland characters, weak dialogue and a boring plot. It sounded exciting -- twins bequeathed their dead aunt's flat in London, an estrangement between the girls'mother and aunt (also twins), a devastated lover and a famous cemetery. But it just didn't come together. The best characters in the book, OCD neighbor Martin and his decamped wife, would have made a better book. Like the poem from which the title came (Blake's Tiger, Tiger Burning Bright), this book is trite and annoying. Maybe it's just because I had to memorize that poem in 8th grade and have despised it ever since, and that ruined it for me, I don't know. But the twins seemed devoid of personality, as did most of the characters in the book. People seemed to have loved Elspeth, the aunt, but her incredible selfishness made me wonder why. The idea was definitely there, but not the execution.
I wish this book would have been about 50 pages longer. It ended quite abruptly. TOO abruptly for my taste, but excellent pieces throughout.

reference_books.title: The Strange Case of Origami Yoda (Origami Yoda, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
What a fun little bit of silliness. There have been many times where I would have loved having an origami Yoda of my own... in fact, in the back of the book there are directions so that I CAN make my own! Yippee! 
 Dwight, the unique (although unique is really an understatement) and strange boy in the sixth grade, makes an origami Yoda. This Yoda seems to have a mind of his own. He makes predictions and gives advice that almost always works out for the best. 
 Some of the kids in his class are trying to figure out if its all nonsense or if Yoda can really predict everything. That's when one of the kids in Dwight's class decides to put together a file of all the things that Yoda predicts. 
 Is it really Yoda? Or is it Dwight, acting weird as usual?

reference_books.title: The Summer I Turned Pretty (Summer, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I loved it! The characters are real. The mom's are sympathetic and loving and the emotions the characters feel are true and raw. Everyone has their own issues of course, but they aren't outrageous or trite. Prepare yourself. This is another weepy one, so keep the kleenex handy!

reference_books.title: The City of Ember (Book of Ember, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
As someone who is claustrophobic, this book even started pretty creepy. The community lives underground, and apparently, has been living underground for a long time. Honestly, at this point, they probably should look like mole people, with big eyes and pale skin. 
 The descriptions of what was happening to the community was giving me the heebie jeebies... running out of food and supplies and often losing power. Ack. 
 Thank goodness for the curious Lina. She's not satisfied that there isn't anything out there past the lights. And then when she finds a cryptic message in a box that her grandma had, she knows she needs to decipher it and figure out what it means. 
 With her friend Doon, she tries to find a way to save her family and all the citizens... of course it might be too late. 
 This was really good, but I think it might have been better if it was beefed up a little so that it was more for teens and less for kids. However, its a great read for 6-8 graders who aren't yet ready for some of the meatier teen books.

reference_books.title: Heart of Darkness
reference_books.review_text: Maybe I should reread it, because so many people give it a high rating. Not me. All I have is memories of wanting to poke my eyes out.

reference_books.title: Breaking Dawn (Twilight, #4)
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 So far I can't stand this book. This is the worst of the books. I'm really going to try and get through it, but boy oh boy are they annoying... and pregnancy by vampire? That's just too much. 
 Bleh. I didn't give it one star, because I was happy when it was over. I love a good vampire novel, but this was not it. Everything just goes completely right for Bella. Neat and tidy. Bleh bleh bleh. 
 UPDATE: 04/28/09 
 I changed my mind. I wish I could give this book negative stars, but I can't.

reference_books.title: Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)
reference_books.review_text: What a wonderful book. I'm just sad that the trilogy is over. There were some interesting twists and turns.

reference_books.title: Stitches
reference_books.review_text: This was an intense piece of work.

reference_books.title: Before I Die
reference_books.review_text: I love love loved this book. It could be because I'm pregnant, but I don't think a book has EVER made me cry so much. I listened to it and the reader was so good. I just wanted to reach out to Tessa and hold her. All those things that she won't get to experience that so much of us take for granted. It really makes you think.

reference_books.title: Austenland (Austenland, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
What a lovely light read. After reading tons of tragic teen novels, its nice to read something harmless now and then. 
 The characters are humorous and you're never sure who's real and who's "acting".

reference_books.title: Divergent (Divergent, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
It's been a long time since I've stayed up until the wee hours of the morning to finish reading a book. This was one of those books. 
 I cannot believe (and this is not to say that young people can't write well) that this was written by a 22 year old. Its wonderfully written. 
 The main character is very complex, which I really like. She has struggles just like the rest of us, only magnified a million-fold. :) 
 I find it interesting that while it's a future world, because it has common elements that let us know where in America it takes place, it's made more real for the reader. 
 Really great book. Now to pick up Insurgent!

book_a.title: The Looking Glass Wars (The Looking Glass Wars, #1)
book_a.user_review:
This is a fascinating take on Alice in Wonderland... or in this case Alyss Heart from Wonderland. In this story, your imagination really can create anything your heart desires... physically! The Queen of Hearts, used to be Alyss' mom, until her Aunt Redd murders her and steals the crown. Alyss tries to escape through the Pool of Tears, but in doing so, she ends up in Victorian London; alone, depressed and unable to use her imagination anymore. 
 While Alyss grows up in London, Wonderland becomes a horrible place, thanks to the evil mind of Redd Heart. The ordinary people of Wonderland are treated horribly and either killed or sent off to work camps. A small group of people band together and hope that someday Alyss will come back to save them. 
 Having read the original book, I thought that this was a delightfully imaginative take on the story. This update would appeal to girls and guys since there's a little bit of everything; violence and killing, love and romance, carnage and warfare, magic and fantasy. 
 I'm definitely looking forward to reading the next book!

sample_reviews.review_text: I enjoyed the first book in this series; though based on the ending, not quite sure why it's a series rather than a standalone book. The pacing was a little uneven but I remained generally engaged. Jury is still out on if I will complete the series.

While I understand the feeling of necessity to start at the beginning and progress through Alyss' journey to show her development, it led to poor pacing throughout the novel that really bogged it down and made it hard to slog through, made tougher by most characters (other than Alyss) being one-dimensional and generally forced word choice designed to make Wonderland seem, well, Wonderful, this novel ended up being a flop for me despite countless positive recommendations.
I LOVED LOVED LOVED it =] a really good twist on the Alice theme & a must for all fantasy fans. Looking forward to the rest of the series x

The Alice books are my all time favorites, so my dislike for this book was very disappointing. The tone of this book was terrible. The distant narrator seemed so disinterested and presented every detail so matter-of-factly that there was little to no connection with characters or the events. There was little to no description of places or characters. All of the whimsy of the original was gutted and abandoned. The story was slow going and the 'action' scenes were written in such a lackluster manner that I practically missed them. Instead of paying homage to the original it craps on it. The 'magic' is cheesy, impractical, and unimaginative. The setting is some cross between cyberpunk and renaissance cosplay. 
 The names of the characters and places makes this feel like really terrible fan fiction, Wondertroplois? Are you serious? Instead of Tweedle Dee and Dum you have General Dopple and Ganger, oh aren't you clever. Princess Alyss, why? And the worst of the worst Bibwit Harte! An anagram? Really!? And then you mention to the reader that it is an anagram, in case what, we missed your cleverness?! Here's an anagram for you, hist kucdes! It felt so unintentional juvenile in was painful to read.

Alyss (Alice) is real. Not the imagination of Lewis Carroll but the a real place where wars pits the Deck families against each other. Frank Beddor authors the tale of a violent world were Redd, the Queen of Hearts, tries to take-over Wonderland. Wonderland is ruled by Queen Genevieve, who rules her Kingdom through White (good) magic. Alyss is her daughter, princess and future ruler. 
 Beddor uses the major characters from Lewis Carroll's novel with many elaborate physical changes to weave an alteranive variation to the classic tale.
I enjoyed this read. An interesting twist in the Alice in wonderland tale. It was a nice read.

I learned that young adult fiction isn't all patronizing and stale, and some of it can be utterly fantastic and a joy to read. I'm a young adult librarian that is not a big fan of most young adult lit, including the Harry Potter series. Most young adult lit I've read have plot lines that are predictable and just a general underlying self-consciousness on the part of the author, as if they're writing the book while constantly thinking about the age of the reader, the marketability of the book to that reader, and everything else second. Maybe people won't agree with that, but there it is. Anyway, this book was very different. It had real substance and creative twists of plot that made the story delicious to both me and my young adults at the library. Kids told me that other kids they knew at school who never read loved this book immediately. It's just a damn good story--and you don't have to be 14 to be totally enthralled by it... which, in my opinion, is the mark of truly good young adult literature.
2.5 if I could give it that. Review at www.forgedempires.wordpress.com

Audio. This was read by the master, Gerard Doyle, so I know we can't blame it on him. What can I say besides this was just torture. I barely finished it about six times. I would have liked this to have been more true to the original, but ok. That's not what the author wanted to do. I would have been fine with that too, had there been good writing, interesting dialogue, coherent plot, or believable science fiction. None of that. The last time I felt like this was when I read "Wicked; the Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West".

I had such high hopes for this book, having loved Alice in Wonderland since I was a child. 
 Disappointment set in almost immediately, and I finished the book purely because I hate to leave books unfinished. 
 The execution of what could have been an incredible story line was poor to say the least. 
 I will not be buying the sequels.
so far, I'm finding it a bit bleh. Simplistically written and a bit less gripping than I'd hoped. I may not pick it up again. We'll see. There are so many good books to read.
So far I love, love, love this book.

I've never heard of this book before. The only reason I picked this book up was because I heard the author, Frank Beddor, was coming to Tucson, and I wanted to meet him, but, I reasoned with myself, I must read his book first. 
 The Looking Glass Wars, once reading the back, sounded so good. But, alas, I guess the back hyped it up too much. Or, maybe it was my fault. Perhaps my hopes were too high for the book. Whatever it was, The Looking Glass Wars wasn't what I expected it to be. 
 The Looking Glass Wars tells the story of what "really" happened to Alyss and Wonderland. No, that is not a typo. That is how her name is really spelled. Alyss Heart is a princess that one day will be queen of Wonderland. However, her aunt Redd does not want that. One day she summons an attack and kills Alyss's parents. To protect her, Hatter Madigan, bodyguard, takes her away into our world. Along the way, though, she and Hatter get separated. In our world, with no one that will believe her, she meets the one and only Lewis Carroll who will listen to her. He writes "Alice in Wonderland," though his story doesn't follow ALyss's at all. To protect and save Wonderland from the evil Redd, Hatter must find Alyss before it's too late. 
 It sounds good, right? The plot, yes. The writing, not so much. I felt that Beddor's writing style was trying too hard to sound...fantasy-cal, or young. For me, because of the writing, it took me forever to finish. Now, that's only my opinion. Other than the plot (which I really liked, but felt could have been so much better with better writing), I sincerely and utterly adore Hatter Madigan. Why? Because he's dark and mysterious, and stealthy and loyal, among so many other characteristics. Only his character brings up the overall rating of this book. 
 Now, as much as I want to know about Alyss and Dodge, and Hatter's secret, I don't think I can put myself through the second book. 
 And, as it played out, schedule conflicts didn't allow me to meet Frank Beddor after all. 
 Rating: 
 30/100
