I have seen this title recommended for teens that ask after the original Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, or have seen and liked the recent Tim Burton movie. I made it almost halfway through before I became too annoyed to continue. Beddor has an occasional good idea, but each one is summarily drowned in poor writing as it occurs, allowing considerably more stupid ideas to take their place. 
 The general thrust of this book is that it contains the "real" story of Wonderland, told by Alice (a.k.a. Alyss Heart) herself to Lewis Carroll before he allegedly mangled it for his book. This version of the story has no whimsy or wonder; it's all violence and war, with some wizard battles, super-advanced crystal computers, and secret magic societies. Or something. Truthfully, I'm hard-pressed to give an accurate description of how this parallels the classic Wonderland, aside from the talking flowers and all of the cleverly changed names of the classic characters. 
 Here's the problem with this book: it's written in exactly the same way that a 10-year-old boy would tell you about an epic game of pretend he played with his friends yesterday. On some level, that captures a bit of the Wonderland spirit, since imagination is what this story should be all about. The thing is, a 10-year-old's story gets intensely irritating very quickly, as anybody who has spent time around a 10-year-old can tell you. This is because most of those stories involve making a lot of random shit up in the middle of the story, and stealing a lot of shit that they heard somewhere and think is totally awesome and hilarious, regardless of whether or not it actually is. 
 Take, for instance, Beddor's treatment of imagination. In the world of Alyss Heart, imagination refers to some nebulous thing that is half simplistic fantasy magic system and half device for indulging the author's random whims. There are some basic rules ("black" vs. "white" imagination, not being able to imagine someone dead, etc.), but they appear to be enforced completely arbitrarily, and only seem to apply when Beddor wants them to apply. I guess black is evil and white is good, but apparently white imagination wizards can conjure flying swords, which are more "good" than man-eating vines, or some such. And since there is apparently no limit on what the queens can imagine in Wonderland, I don't really know why there's a conflict in the first place. 
 But I guess the only answer to that question that matters is because fantasy war is cool and edgy and totally badass. The kids like dystopias these days, so let's make Wonderland a dystopia! Which, I have to admit, is a decent idea in theory; the bizarre dreamlike qualities of Wonderland lend themselves excellently to a nightmarish darker version. American McGee's Alice is a particularly good example. Beddor does have a couple of interesting twists on the setting, but on the whole, all he really does here is take the surreal adventures of the original and turn them into a boilerplate pulp story. He doesn't really experiment, or explore the source material any deeper than the surface. He instead piles pop-culture cliches onto one another in a fairly transparent attempt at pandering to the young-adult bestseller crowd. I think this is what bothers me the most about this book, and I can't tell whether it's due to the author being inept, callous, or actually as culturally tone-deaf as a 10-year-old boy. Regardless of which it is, that is why the reader ends up dealing with things like the Cheshire Cat delivering the "you talkin' to me" scene from Taxi Driver. Or a Mad Hatter that sports helicopter blades on his wrists (like Wolverine, but rotating!) and a spring-loaded backpack apparently filled with pounds of Victorian-era metal weapons (because steampunk is cool, right?), but still manages to completely eschew walking in favor of doing a series of super-sweet backflips every time he needs to get from point A to point B. 
 Those are the most egregious examples of crap character writing I saw before I stopped, but all of the characterizations are pretty bad. Alyss at seven years old channels none of the innocence of that age, but manages to somehow nail teen angst. This version of the White Rabbit talks to himself for the sole purpose of delivering awkward exposition. Supporting characters range somewhere between flat ("I speak with the exact same mannerisms as the narrator!") and stereotypical ("I drink wine and eat cheese because I am FRENCH! HONH HONH HONH!"). The ninja steampunk assassin version of Mad Hatter is apparently a complete idiot, but still manages to capture the hearts of an entire nation. Presumably because of his super-sweet backflipping skills. 
 In fact, this laziness extends to almost all corners of the writing. The book is obviously derivative of its source material, but even the "new" stuff that Beddor comes up with is tired. All of the character arcs, all of the interpersonal interactions... they've all been done better in other works, and they're all secondary to the action, anyway. None of the characters exhibit behavior that is consistent or believable. And Beddor's writing style is gratingly amateurish. Allow me to digress and send a quick personal note to the author: Frank, I'm not sure if you were trying to put a "NOT!" joke in your narrative on page 126, but you did, and it was really dumb. Clever repartee with the reader doesn't seem to be your strong suit. If you intend to amuse, please go back to describing your characters' wildly inappropriate reactions to their surroundings. Thanks. 
 I don't know. I don't think I hated this book, but it really didn't do anything for me. It reads like a script for a low-budget SyFy special. The portion that I made it through seemed less like a story and more like the portfolio of someone attempting to start a movie franchise, complete with action figure line. Considering that the author is apparently a film producer who is already in the process of turning this into a movie, I don't think I'm imagining that sentiment. In my opinion, Beddor took something with a lot of imaginative depth and made it pedestrian. It's not a total loss; I would still recommend this one to younger teens who are looking for a fantasy book. But this really doesn't have much of substance to offer anyone outside its target demographic. Which, I think, is comprised of younger teens, and people who liked the pew-pew-car-chase-shiny-shiny movie reboots of Transformers and G. I. Joe.

First in a series, this appealing retelling of Alice in Wonderland posits a real Wonderland, but with very real villains and heroes, and with Alyss as the only princess that can save that world from forces of evil conspiring to seize and rule it in dread and bleakness.

After a bloody coup topples the Heart regime, Alyss is exiled to another world entirely, where she is adopted into the Liddell family, renamed Alice and befriended by Lewis Carroll. At age 20 she returns to Wonderland to regain her sceptre, battle Redd and lead Wonderland into its next golden age of imagination." (From Amazon)

Listening to this on audio again to read the rest of the series. After "reading" this one again I would give it 3.5 stars - 4 STARS the first time.

The Looking Glass Wars is a retelling of popular Victorian children's story 'Alice in Wonderland' written by Lewis Caroll. We all know of How Alice Fell Down the Rabbit Hole and What She Found There, but this, ___ tells us, is not so. Lewis Caroll cruelly and absurdly twisted Alice's true story of betrayal and loss into a nonsensical children's story... 
 Okay, sin number 1: trashing the original story and the original author. 
 If you're an author attempting to flesh out little explored recesses of a fictional world, or explore another perspective of said world, or add depth or whatever... you gotta respect the original canon. Describing Alice In Wonderland as silly trash for kids feels less like character Alice (Heart, here, not Liddle!) expressing frustration at being once again mocked by an adult who won't believe her fantastical tales, and more like an author trying to shade a respected author. I mean, yes, on its surface, Alice in Wonderland is a nonsense tale, but I think we all know by now that's just one level of the story? Anyway, it felt like a cheap shot, but I kept going. 
 Sin number 2: shoddy world building. Alice lives in a magical monarchy of Wonderland, which is actually a queendom- not a kingdom! More on that Later. Also Imagination is in a sphere and it powers the world and also all the other worlds in the multiverse? Sounds like something out of like Maggie and Ferocious Beast...? I thought there wasn't enough fleshing out of this concept. 
 Sin 3: heavy-handed moralising about female empowerment was misguided and transparent. Setting up a monarchy as YAY WOMEN BECAUSE QUEENS is always going to get a side eye from me because... the institution of a hereditary monarchy is oppressive of women in and of itself. The expectation that one's body is not one's own and is a tool of state is one of the least empowering phenomena of all. Your ability to refuse sex and refuse pregnancy is reduced to virtually inexistent. Consent doesn't exist for either the man doing the impregnating or the pregnant queen. Even if the queen herself lives a charmed life, the nature of a sovereign monarch means that all the hardworking women (and men!) underneath her have no real prospects save marrying rich... how is that fun? I mean, Alice's royal Father the king Consort Nolan is presented to us as a decent dude, happy to help his wife rule, which is fair enough but like... yay for not assuming that this is not the natural order of things? When he's sent on a diplomatic mission to a neighbouring country, that King is presented to us as boorish and chauvinist - which he is - but answering Women shouldn't be queens! With yes they should! Instead of 'the institution of monarchy serves only to oppress the working classes-' is just. Not the one. 
 Sin 4: Alice's power, as a divine monarch (YAY...?) means she has power to imagine whatever she wants. This is the equivalent to knowing that your leaders, whom you can never replace or hope to become, have the wherewithal to utterly decimate you and the fact that they don't depends entirely on their goodwill. Sounds delightful. 
 I actually really wanted to enjoy this book but did not finish. I felt the concept was interesting but the execution was lacking. 1/5
An interesting take on the wonderland story but a bit predictable at the end.

I was not the biggest fan of this book initially, but it grew on me. I also can't say enough nice things about the author, who came to our library and was gracious and engaging with our teens. And since 6+7 Book Club gave it the highest rating of any book this year, enough said!

I don't think I can finish it. 
 It was recommended to me by Beta; Alpha hadn't liked it when he first read it (in author's proof, which is what I am reading). Beta insisted that _Seeing Redd_ must be read, and thus, I had to read this first. That, plus the TABarron series on Merlin, and of course, the Tree of Avalon. 
 Well, started it. Want to like it. I do like the premise, actually. But I think, now that I have gotten almost half-way through, what just makes it unbearable is that the writing is so bad. Not bad in the sense of ignorant, but bad in the sense of craft and flow. It feels almost as if it were scenes plotted out along a time line, with the back story (what you might tell an actor) plugged in where it best fits. Forced; maybe that is the word that I am looking for. 
 An example might be the naming of characters, to fight the Carroll's story yet work with Bedor's--the White Rabbit is one prime example, and one that Bedor has to point out to us as well (which makes it even more forced--- you get it don't you? see? see? We are being clever about our concept)... 
 So how do I rate this, never mind shelve it? 
 Read, I guess, and two stars. 
 Sorry, Beta.
I wanted to like this but it was bothering me. I didn't get very far before putting it down. Alice seemed to whine a lot and it just didn't capture my imagination.

Although the author's writing can sometimes be a bit pedantic, I enjoyed this book. It was relatively fast-paced, and I think it's something people in the young adult genre would generally enjoy. The last third of the book was, by far, the most exciting and suspenseful. I liked it well enough to read the sequel. I hope it doesn't disappoint!

I remember a while ago when I first heard of this book -- which was before they had a synopsis or mentioned the intended audience and was intrigued. And by intrigued I mean that I kept it in the back of my mind and then managed to forget all about it. So imagine my surprise as I'm hunting for a children's version of Alice in Wonderland and I come across this. 
 The book was a quick read, it's intended for the younger crowd (young adults) and well catered toward that group. Nonetheless if you're an adult reader it is a different take on what really happened to Alice during her time in Wonderland. Actually it's a nice departure of the whole book though it does loose the whimsy. The interesting part is the striking similarities to the recent Burton movie to it. Neither of them follow one another mind you, but there are a few things that are parallel. 
 Important thing for the seasoned readers is that the syntax, the overall flow isn't top notch. I'm not attempting to put the book down as it merits a good idea however it reads as a young adult, I'd peg it to a grade school level. Another thing is that you can easily figure out what's going to happen so one thing I kept wondering was why wasn't it going any faster. I am hoping to read the rest of this series as it's a nice departure from the normal adventures of Alice.

I didn't really like this book. I have read Alice in Wonderland to my kids...the original, and I just didn't like how dark and twisted this book was. I mean did have to be a conspiracy theory type thing?
Mmm

I'm obsessed with anything to do with Alice in Wonderland. I have several T-shirts, two purses, four lip glosses, two necklaces, the AiW collector's Barbie, and the American McGee's Alice soundtrack. So of course when I saw the title of this I had to pick it up. Thank God the book's price was VERY reduced. 
 What a disappointment. I liked the idea behind it. It COULD have worked. Unfortunately, the writing style leaves much to be desired, and Alyss is a huge Mary-Sue. The portrayal of Charles Dodgson as an ignorant man offends me. And I couldn't get into all of the battling. Maybe this is better for ten-year-old Star Wars fans who didn't know much about Alice to begin with, other than by watching the Disney movie. I don't know. I do know I'm not the only one who felt this way about the book. I read it a few years ago and thankfully I don't remember much so I can't go into much detail here. Suffice it to say that this book failed as a spinoff of a beloved novel, much as Ophelia failed as a Shakespearean play spinoff. Normally I give books a second chance by reading the second in a series, but I hated this so much I couldn't consider doing that.
I could not get into this book, and finally after several weeks of trying, gave up. Love the idea, maybe another day it will appeal to me more and I can actually finish it.
I love this series! Such an interesting and unique approach to the original story!

Prologue: oh my God, I'm already annoyed at this book. I hope the rest of the book has an editor. 
 Rest of the book: nope! No editor here, either! Just a magic system with no limits except it can't get rid of wrinkles. 
 Skip to the end: this is truly a book about a special snowflake. Done. Done. Done. I will not be reading the sequel.

The think that bugged me about it was the onomatopoeias. >_> 
 Something along the lines of "They knocked into each other -- BAM -- and Alyss fell down." 
 He does stuff like that a lot, and I can't decide if it ruined the book for me or if I want to read the next two in the series... >_> Unfortunately, I own both... I feel obligated to read them. >_< 
 Also, he did a lot of "Then the princess did this, and then this..." 
 >_> I'm tempted to count how many times he did that. It would be a very high number, I assure you. 
 Just saying, his editor sucks.

Removes the wit and nonsense, and puts a male character in the forefront -- takes everything special about Alice and makes it mediocre. 
 From my LiveJournal, upon rereading: 
 Rereading The Looking Glass Wars and as unimpressed as last time, though I have the two sequels sitting on deck and I'm hopeful . . . Beddor plays with the Alice mythology credibly, but I keep feeling he could have done it so much better and cleverer, and the story itself is fairly routine and uninteresting, but as it's perhaps largely setup, I hope to like the others more. When I read it the first time I went to his website and there was all this email from children telling him how much *better* it was than Carroll, which just annoyed me. It's every narrative that kids read nowadays, and of course they like it because it's just what they're expecting. But it strips out the cleverness and it seems Alyss needs several males to protect her through much of the narrative and ultimately it feels to me like taking something unique and turning it into something less so.

I couldn't get more than ten pages into this book. The writing was trite and the author couldn't leave anything unsaid. It felt very amateur. I was very disappointed as I love a classic retelling and was really looking forward to starting this series.

book_b.title: The Giving Tree
book_b.user_review:
Wow! I just re-read it and I thought it was AWFUL! The tree gives and gives and the little boy take and take and gives nothing back. The tree gives until there is nothing left to give. 
 It made me very sad, and wonder what kind of lesson this is meant to teach children. Not a very nice one.

sample_reviews.review_text:
There are plenty of wonderful Shel Silverstein books and poems, but this isn't one of them, in my opinion. 
 It's the story of a selfish little boy who grows up to be a selfish and self-involved man, and the (female) tree who gives up everything, including whole pieces of herself to please him. At the end of her life she is content to be a stump for the selfish man to sit on. Bleh. If I had a little girl, I certainly wouldn't give her this to read.
I HATE this book! I hate everything about it, from the message to the language to the ending. Ugh!
The tree is enabling the child! This is the story of a dysfunctional relationship, and it's made to look attractive.

A great book...IF you view it as satire. I would read this to my kids to show them what an unhealthy, codependent relationship where one party does all the giving and the other does all the taking looks like. I certainly never want to see my kid become the Giving Tree or the Taking Brat in a relationship of any kind.

I don't get it. 
 I guess the idea of unselfish love is great and all...but... 
 Does the boy learn anything? Does he even feel regret? 
 And it's hard for me not to read this as saying it's okay to destroy trees - that's what the trees want. 
 Huh? How are ecologically minded people not up on arms over this book? 
 I really don't get it.
I kept waiting for a moral, for the boy to learn a lesson, but it never came and he never did.
A great learning tool for children on how real life is. There are people that will give, give, give and others that will take, take, take. Such a sad and beautiful story.

I always loved this book as a kid, but when I looked through it recently I felt kinda strange. Then one of my friends mentioned how she thought the book was a wretched thing to have kids read. I read through it again and thought about it more. The thing is, I think if the reader doesn't look at the tree as having the completely correct opinion (complete self-sacrifice), then it makes more sense. In the end, I really still think this is a good book; more people need to know how to give, and that doing so is just plain good.
I'm so sorry, but I think this should be renamed The Taking Boy. I know the message it's supposed to give, but I just don't agree with it.
One of the first books ever read to me as a child. Classic!

I didn't take this from the perspective of the tree being the motherly figure. I took it in the literal sense that yes we do this to nature and it's rather selfish to take and take without ever giving back. 
 I found this book disturbing and sad.

I hate this book. I have always hated this book. While unselfish sacrifice is absolutely an important, even necessary part of love, giving and giving and giving until you are nothing but a stump to be sat upon by someone who could've used your gentle guidance more than your gifts is a horrible, false ideal. Ugh.

"One of my favorite childhood books ever!! My mother read it to me a thousand times when I was such a little kid as a goodnight story. I bursted into tears. Then I started reading it alone everyday after school. It only got better and better every time."

No disrespect to Shel Silverstein and all of the wonderful books he has given us, but I've never liked this book. I think the message that you are supposed to take from it is that there is pleasure in giving, but that if you are selfish you will end up unhappy and alone - as well as potentially hurting the people around you. 
 The problem is that the story is too ambiguous, and it can easily be interpreted as the boy taking and taking, and the tree happily enabling in a self-destructive manner. This is not one that I would read to my kids.

When I was a bookseller I would occasionally try to dissuade a customer from buying this book, never with success. I agree with the other reviewers who find this book extols sexism (the tree is a she who gives everything to the boy), selfishness, and misguided self-sacrifice.

By the time the tree was a stump I was in need of serious therapy. For some strange reason, I took this one very seriously. 
 I cried so hard that my lips and nose swelled up and I looked like I'd been stung by a hive of very hostile bees.
Disturbing book. It's beautiful and heartbreaking, certainly, but with a message that makes me too uncomfortable for, well, comfort.

I wish to respectfully agree to disagree with those that love this children's book. I read it when my children were little and disliked it so much that I threw it away. The notion that ideal love is one in which you allow another to selfishly use you up is just wrong. In this case, real damage is being done to the child who is allowed to be so self-centered.

I hate this book! Why does everyone love it so much? The tree is a female character that gives and gives and gives to a male character that takes and takes and takes, to both of their total detriment.

I know this is going to probably earn me some hate, but... I cannot STAND this book. 
 Seriously. I cannot stand it. 
 What happens to this tree and this selfish, horrible child is something that grates on me terribly, because I have been in this position. Do you know what happens when one person gives into a relationship and the other doesn't? 
 Bad things. Very, very bad. 
 This doesn't teach children to give. It teaches them one should give until that one has nothing left, and ends up getting sat on. 
 I adore every other Silverstein thing I've encountered. This one, however, is dreadful.
This story kinda creeped me out...
One of my all time favorite children's books

This book gets five stars from me for being beautiful. 
 It was very upsetting when I first heard it, as a teenager, I hate crying. It became a family joke and every time I would come and visit this book would get pulled out of the pile.
Seriously, people, what's with the 4+ Rating?

3.5 
 When I first saw this book I thought it was going to be sweet, meaningful and centered around generosity. In reality it is quite melancholic. Reading other reviews, it seems this simple book is very controversial and subject to many different interpretations. According to one reviewer, Silverstein meant for the book to be subversive. The world is full of awful things and I would have loved if this book had a more positive message rather than commenting on how we use each other and allow ourselves to be used by others. That aside, this story is a good allegory for that.
That tree should have bitchslapped him.
Intensely meaningful and sad.

Aww, damn. I forgot this book makes me cry like a little bitch. 
 Shel Silverstein will always hold a place in my heart because, you know, childhood. Sigh.
I get a lump in my throat when I read this book. So good.

this book is a magnet and enabler for every current and future martyr and I hate it. I gave it two stars for the possibility that this is some kind of sick joke on Silverstein's part, which would be genius.

is there no way to put zero star? the book's message, especially to kids is horrific. It is "how to create a sociopath" and people like it???? 
 Now I am frightened by the idea someone can read that to little kids and what it can do to their minds. To make you understand better, replace the poor tree by a pet. Do you see what you teach your kid? use and abuse people around you, if they really love you, they will accept it. Or from the opposite point of view, the tree's, love means giving your life for the people you love, not to save them, just to fulfill their selfish desires, love will (and must) destroy you. Is not that sweet? 
 t scares me that someone wrote something that bad for kids, it upsets me that the tree got to be a "she" (a paradigm for mother's love?), it terrifies me that people put the book on the list of books you must read. 
 Books you must burn would be better. I will try to put it on the list "if you liked that book, we are not compatible".

** spoiler alert ** 
 It is a really sweet book but when taking a Ecocritical view, it shows the human's dependency on nature but also misuse of it. We take nature for granted and do not consider how we affect nature. The tree is all giving yet we never give anything back. Even when the tree thinks she has nothing left to offer, the boy still finds a way to use her. It shows the human/nature binary in which humans continually take and harm the environment.
I think this should be called, "The Taking Boy."
I cry everytime I read this book!!

After reading this book to my daughter, I immediately shut it and vowed to never read it again. I then went to bed and had dreams of my daughter harvesting my organs and selling them on the black market for cash.
Maybe if I'd read this as a child and not a jaded adult I would have enjoyed this more. All I saw was a kids' book on codependency.
The central character is a selfish shithead who takes complete advantage of his woody friend until only a stump remains.

I love Shel Silverstein. But I can't abide this one. It's like a form of persecution to read it. It's so painful. I can't escape the notion that the tree is the mother in our society; she is expected to give and give and give until there's only a stump of her left. That doesn't help the boy in the long run, or the mother. Maybe I'm being churlish about it. But ugh.

A polarizing children's book, I fall squarely in the "do not like" camp. The boy was selfish, the tree was an idiot. Even decades after I first read this book, I still find the story more than mildly irritating.

This book drives me crazy. I think it sends the wrong message to kids, and I don't understand why everyone gets so excited by it. 
 The message that one should give to others without expecting anything in return is a good message. My problem lies in the last few pages where the "boy" comes back and the tree has nothing left to give. Instead of being thankful and grcious, the "boy" sits his old butt down on the tree's remaining stump. WTF?
This book made me feel guilty, sad, and angry.

This book is messed up. The tree gives and gives, hoping to regain the affection the boy once had for it, and the lose-ass boy takes and takes well beyond the tree's ability to give. This is a codependent relationship if I've ever seen one, yet I'm supposed to think it's heartwarming or something. I think not.
Dysfunctional relations, anyone?
The point of self sufficiency is more important than sacrifice for the well being and comfort of others.
3 stars
This is a book I've always valued because I think the message is fantastic!
As a child, the selfishness of the boy made me sad. As an adult, it shames me because I can see myself in the child.

For book reviews and more, please visit my book blog, The Book Stop 
 The Giving Tree. What can I say? I didn't know how serious some people took a little children's tale. I personally think it's a cute story. We'll see how this goes. 
 'Once there was a tree...and she loved a little boy.' 
 So begins a story of unforgettable perception, beautifully written and illustrated by the gifted and versatile Shel Silverstein. 
 This is a tender story, touched with sadness, aglow with consolation. Shel Silverstein has created a moving parable for readers of all ages that offers an affecting interpretation of the gift of giving and a serene acceptance of another's capacity to love in return. 
 So, I heard about The Giving Tree on goodreads. It seemed very popular, and I was thinking, What's all the hype about? It seemed so short that I thought it would be just a silly kids story. So anyway, I rushed through it a bit the first time, but I thought I was missing something. So I read it again. After reading it a second time, I still thought I was missing something. I wonder why? 
 The story was, in my opinion, was quite touching. It was also very odd, in a good way. Who would've known that I would ever feel sympathy for a character who was a tree? I liked that a child's tale could be so unpredictable. I was anticipating the happy ending, but it never came. That's what was missing for me. I expected there to be a happy ending, but there wasn't. its nit that i didn't want it to end the way it did, it just surprisd me a bit. You could probably debate for hours about whether it was a happy or sad ending, but I think this story means something different for everyone. 
 There's probably a deeper meaning that represents this book, and people will have different opinions and ideas for what that meaning is. I won't be going into that, because I want to review this book as a children's book, which is what it is. I don't want to get caught up in all the fuss that goes on with what message the author wanted to get across. 
 "... and she loved a boy very, very much-- even more than she loved herself." 
 The tree really did love the boy. But how could the tree have known? From what we read, she only ever had any experiences with this little boy. She gave him everything she had. To make the boy happy? To make herself happy? Who knows? The tree desperately wanted to help the boy, and that made her happy? 
 This is where I felt sympathy for the tree. So naive, so innocent. Jeez, I never thought I'd be writing about a tree so deeply. See, thats what this story does to you! It's special. Anyway, the point is... Well we don't know the point do we. As I said its different for everyone. Different people will interpret this story in different ways, so there's no right or wrong answer. Even the children will take it in different ways. That's the special thing about this book. 
 "And the tree was happy" 
 The infamous line. But was the tree ever really happy? Again, you could debate about it for hours. But, did the tree relly know what happiness was? She was a tree after all. The book said she was happy, so should that mean she was happy? It's up to you. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this The Giving Tree. It was cute, but it felt like something special. Something that you should fully digest. It was touching and I really felt connected to the story. My favourite character wa the tree, of course. And I was surprised I even had a favourite character. I really think this is a brilliant children's tale. And yes, of course I'm going to read it again!

I read this for a challenge to read books from childhood shelf. I read this because I have heard a lot of praises about it but this book appalled me. I could not grasp what exactly are we to teach young children from this book? The first thing that came into my mind was that either its okay to be selfish and keep on taking from people without even wish for giving something back or loving someone very unconditionally. Unconditional love, doesnt exist. Also, there is something called self esteem that should be taught and not self pity [of course with how to distinguish between self-esteem and ego]. 
 I dont think I am ever going to let my kids read it when they are really young.

reference_books.title: Hotel on the Corner of Bitter and Sweet
reference_books.review_text:
This historical fiction novel is well described within its own title. It is a bitter tale of what happened to Japenese Americans during World War II, and a sweet tale of the possiblities for second chances in life. The character of Henry and Keiko endear themselves to the reader by the end of the novel. I think their story will stick with me long after I have read their story for many reasons. I will take away a lot of things from this story, and wrote down some of my favorite quotes so that i will never forget. 
 "The hardest choices in life aren't between what's right and what's wrong but between what's right and what's best." 
 "I had my chance,and sometimes in life, there are no second chances. You look at what you have,not what you miss, and you move forward." 
 to "find the sweet among the bitter".

reference_books.title: The Twelve (The Passage, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book; like The Passage; is a page turning,amazing read that turns my claim that I don't read Scifi-ish stuff on its head. Be warned if reading this book that it is epic in its number of characters, time period and in its frequent changes in Point of view. I needed far more than the lists of characters at the end of the book and the short intro in the beginning; which by the way is written in a biblical style that nearly put me off from reading this book right from the beginning. 
 Short rant------>I love fantasy/imaginative writing but leave the bible out of it. It is blasphemious to me when it is used or in this case (the intro)is written in biblical language. 
 I often felt lost during reading-- knowing the characters from the first book, but not remembering the details, and then finallly feeling like I was back on track with the story and characters only to have it change to another point of view and often in a non linear timeline. 
 Is there a next book? If there is hopefully it will include a better index of characters and a more detailed summary of events that doesn't make me feel uncomfortable mixing my faith up in my reading for pleasure life. 
 By the final 100 pages I just wanted to be finished because the undercurrents of a faith component that I do not enjoy was taking away from my otherwise enjoyable reading experience. So a book that would have been a five star ended up being a battle between a two and three star.

reference_books.title: The Glass Castle
reference_books.review_text:
I didn't give this but three stars not because it wasn't well written or because I don't admire the author's resiliance to be able to live a normal life after the childhood she had. I gave it only three stars because the feelings it gave me personally. I came away from reading so sad everytime I picked it up, and found that it was depressing me and I was counting down the pages until completion. 
 I read it because everyone who I talk to raves about it and because the part about Welch is familiar to me since I grew up not far from the city Bluefild that they mention quite a few times in that section. Thankfully I never had to deal with the conditions that she and her family lived in while in that area. 
 I suppose that the anger from witnessing Walls and her siblings life made it worth finishing because you know from the beginning that she makes it out of there. I just wish she would have given herself credit and not felt bad about her feelings about her mom in New York. Her parents had many oppourtunities to make their life better and didn't.

reference_books.title: White Hot Kiss (The Dark Elements, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Being alone, yet surrounded by people is never easy. Add to that all the usual teenaged angst and that is Layla's way of life. She is half Warden (gargoyles whose purpose is to protect the human race from demons) part demon, and on top of that she just wants to be a normal teenager.....Well that IS a predicament! 
 This was so far out of my reading comfort zone. First it's a paranormal romance,so a story about gargoyles, demons, zombies etc. is difficult for me- I picked this up not knowing it was paranormal, but it's good to try something new sometimes so here I am. Second this is a teen romance and they tend to drive me insane with the scenario that is so common---- I hate this boy...but he IS so hot...but he's a bad boy...but I think I like him...wait he is my soulmate I can't live without him. Not to mention he is a DEMON; things like demons, zombie, vampires etc are bad news and to spin them in a light where they are someone you would want to spend time with ;much less cuddle up to....is crazy. 
 I don't see myself finishing this series and blamed my compulsion to finish any book I start for not quitting after only a few chapters,

reference_books.title: A Rogue by Any Other Name (The Rules of Scoundrels, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
If you listen to the Book Riot family of podcasts then you have heard them rave about this book/author. The books have been said to be "smart romances"....what does that mean? I had to know. I read some romance so I am familiar with all the tropes of the genre. Victorian England historical romances are generally my least favorite to read because I hate all the emphasis on the female staying busy with her needlework/music, and aristocratic gossip while the rest of her life is left to the mercy of her parents and then the man she is matched to. There is very little swoon worthy moments when you know the characters have no romantic feelings for each other. So this book glides along the edge of everything that such a romance book is, but the character of Penelope breaks the mold. She resists the life of being married off after being dumped by a Duke who was actually in love with the other women. Penelope thinks that it might be possible to have that something more too. Adventure, heartbreak, and swoon worthiness ensues. 
 The only thing that ruins it is that not all the romance tropes were turned around in this one. The stereotypical bad boy who romanticizes emotional abuse while the woman can't help but love him anyway was just too much. Obviously from the title he is a Rogue, but I can't find him lovable as you should in a romance novel hero. It is possible that he gets better as a character in later books while holding on to that bad boy image as a part owner of a gambling house.

reference_books.title: Eragon (The Inheritance Cycle, #1)
reference_books.review_text: So I had to read this book before I watched the movie. I had high hopes that it would keep my attention like a few other fantasy novels I have read, which I still need to add to my list. I kept getting bored with it and thinking that this might be why some people don't like it. For a kid who hasn't read some of the fantasy greats this may be a great place to start.

reference_books.title: The Lovely Bones
reference_books.review_text: It isn't often a novel starts off on such a sad depressing note- death then follows with the downfall of marriages, the day to day life of a serial killer not to mention the ghostly presence of a murder victim watching it all. I found that I was forcing myself to keep reading, knowing that there was some sort of surprise ending coming. I didn't enjoy it when the ending was revealed--more creeped out. The three star rating was generous I thought, but a spark of what the author was trying to bring from all this did strike me as profound.

reference_books.title: Maisie Dobbs (Maisie Dobbs, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
The first in a series of historical mystery novels beginning in the years leading up World War I, and the post war era. The main character is Maisie Dobbs who, as the book opens is starting a private detective agency. The first case leads her to investigate events that took place during the war and leading to the overall theme of the novel: that war lives on in those who experience it long after the physical injuries heal. Maisie herself is haunted by her time as a nurse and the loss of many people she encountered. 
 I enjoyed the mystery, the way that a story is placed among the historical events we learned about, and the meaning behind the story is timely, as war and its physical and mental injuries are again part of so many of our lives. Events in the novel go back and forth in time; however and it confused me in the beginning because I listened to the audio. The switch in time periods may have been more clear in the book. The rest of the series will probably be read instead of listened to for that reason.

reference_books.title: The Lowland
reference_books.review_text:
When I heard about this book I thought "I have heard so many great things about this author. I need to read some of her books so I guess I will start with this one. " Then after beginning to read it and struggling to get through the first chapters I heard a trusted reviewer say it might not be the best Jhumpa Lahiri book to start with. I think that is probably true. 
 The basic plot is about two brothers who are 15 months apart and who begin life very close as most siblings that close in age might be. As one brother; Udayan grows up he becomes part of the Naxalite movement in India so the brothers grow apart. The other brother moves to America. The novel is in third person; however, the point of view changes between each of the characters to show how the events of the novel played out to each of them. The novel is one in which you get to stay with the characters for a long time so you get to see how decisions made affect future generations. 
 I hated the characters! I suppose that was the intention but for the most part each of them is wrapped up in their own life and make decisions without considering the others around them at all. The coldness of Subbash and Udayan's mother and Guari (Udayan's wife) especially make it hard to read without throwing your book or in this case my Kindle. Udayan's involvement in the Naxalite movement is what brings out my fury for politics in all its forms. Each side has their agenda, refuses to hear any other side or work out any kind of humane solution to problems. So the only thing that is accomplished is strife, and violence. 
 I did like the grand scope of the story because I like to know how the characters lives play out,maybe see just a little bit of a happily ever after for some of the characters. It gives you hope. The author does give us just a few rays of hope at the end. 
 Overall this was not the book for me. I did not see a lot of the lyrical writing I had heard about. I found the sentence structure to be choppy at times and a lot of the author saying "He sees...." or "She sees..." telling us what to see instead of showing us what to see. I want to read more from this author however, because I don't believe I should accept one novel as the representive of someone's work.

reference_books.title: The Stupidest Angel: A Heartwarming Tale of Christmas Terror (Pine Cove, #3)
reference_books.review_text: Oddest book ever! It is a darkly comedic tale of a not so Norman Rockwell. small town Christmas...... with a crazy cast of characters in a anything but a feel good Christmas story. It is a perfect holiday read for when you just don't want the standard "It's a Wonderful Life" type of story. The warning at the beginning intriqued me, but the further I read the more the oddness went over the top, and cooled the five star rating down to a three. Consider the characters: A grinchly often drunk town Santa, a guy with a sunglass wearing talking fruit bat, a pot smoking policeman, a crazy lady with the voice of a narrator in her head, a misfit archangel, and did I mention there are zombies? I don't read zombie stories, the whole undead thing doesn't spark my immagination, but otherwise i thought it was a funny escape from all the holiday frenzy.

book_a.title: Blackmoore
book_a.user_review:
In finding this book (a blind date with a book)I may have found a new favorite author. This is a story of 3 childhood friends who both grow closer and further apart. After years of adventuring together Henry and Kate feel themselves falling in love while Sylvia (Henry's sister)and Kate grow apart. The love story does not progress as you might imagine because of the rules of propriety and class that were common during this time. The story is told largely through flashbacks, return to present day, and jumps into future so that the conflict is revealed slowly. 
 The idea of being trapped in a situation is constantly referred to and drawn in comparison to birds tapped in a cage, and finding your own wings to escape with the hints of warning of such a risk through the stories of Icarus and the story of Faust and his deal with the devil. These were 2 stories which fascinated me when I studied them and so this was just one small box that was checked as I became engrossed in the story. 
 I wasn't sure I would like a story so reminiscent of Regency era romances with all the arranged marriages, girls having their season in society hoping to catch a husband, and ladies like Miss St.Claire and her "exhausting thoughtfulness". Finally I realized I liked this story because it was about a couple rejecting all the things I hate about regency romance. This would have been so much worse if told from Miss St.Claire point of view. 
 The romance is a slow burn, but oh so swoon worthy 
 Henry: "your heart's desire is to leave all of us and fly away to India and my heart's desire is to unravel the mystery of Kate Worthington."

sample_reviews.review_text: Maybe 3.5. I really, really, really, really wanted to love this book. I adored Edenbrooke. It was hard not to have high expectations! I enjoyed the story, though it was nowhere near as good as Edenbrooke and for the love of Pete I don't give a flying hoot about birds. Bad pun intended.

I loved this book so much. It came in the mail this afternoon and I finished it tonight. Yeah it's that good! It definitely pulls at your heart strings and makes you want to scream at the same time. 
 I loved the emotions that were evident each time Henry proposed to Kate, it was heart wrenching. And the romance was AMAZING! hehe. 
 Definitely one of my favorite books!l 
 2nd time through: I enjoyed this book just as much as I did the first time. It was cool to read it knowing what was going to happen and the reasons behind why Kate did what she did. She is a great character and I loved her imperfections. Also how can you not love Henry? He is perfect. :) 
 I love how I got the pang in my chest during several scenes. Not all love stories can do that for me anymore since I've become more picky, but this book managed it again and again. My only complaint is, I wanted Kate and Henry to have even more scenes together. I just love them together. Great book and I know I'll read it many times in the future.

Se queda en 3 estrellitas. Es una historia bonita sobre un amor inocente, con un elemento original -los pajaros-. Pero no sobresale. De hecho, estuve tentada en dejarle 2 estrellas, lo unico que me convencio de no hacerlo es que resulta ser una lectura agradable despues de tantas relaciones toxicas que abundan en la contemporanea romantica actual.

Oh wow! Wow wow wow ! 
 I have had my heart stolen, captivated and healed by Blackmoore. Romance and love as it should be. Beautiful, forgiving, patient, healing ,true, lasting, sacrificial, mesmerizing, passionate, disarming and utterly utterly lovely. 
 I have no idea what to say of Henry!!!!! Mover over Mr.Darcy because this one can never be outdone. I love him. I seriously do:) 
 You Ms.Donaldson are a creative genius. Please please please write more books. Blackmoore and Edenbrooke are simply not enough. I need a lifetime supply of these.

DNF at 60% 
 It was too painful to continue. 
 The protagonist is a shocker. Very annoying. Dense. Selfish. Immature. Short-sighted. Short temper. It's annoying how she seems so well versed in literature but then when it comes to making decisions, bargains, her brain seems to be absent. 
 And then you have the too-good-for-her Henry. My problem with him is that I don't understand why he loves her.
Very different from Edenbrooke, but I enjoyed it.

wow it was such a great surprise. i loved this book. it had lots of unexpected turns and it was so very lovely... the hero and heroine were so perfect together... and this book had a very different writing style from all other historical romances. in other books it always feels like you know how everything will end... in this one i wasnt even sure till the end if it would have the HEA xD 
 i maybe didnt enjoy the beginning, but at some point i understood that i was already past half the pages and couldnt stop reading XD finished it in exactly 4-5 hours :D

I read this book in a few hours. To be honest, while I was reading it I thought it was a great book though there were things that confused me. When I got to then end and was sitting considering what had happened in the book though, that's when I started to realize just how much of the I hadn't actually understood. 
 I didn't not understand the book because I wasn't reading carefully, trust me, I rarely misunderstand things in books. I didn't understand why people were acting the way they were. Why was Kate seemingly so oblivious to Henry's affections when the stories about past events clearly show that she knew he loved her and she knew that she loved him? Why would she have asked him to propose to her three times if she knew he had once loved her (and, as any girl who kept noticing a guy watching them would know) still cared deeply for her? 
 Why did there have to be questionable scenes throne in? Like the scene at night by the sea and the scene from her past where Henry claims she loves him. What's up with her mother? What's up with his mother? If Kate's family was really full of flirts and scandalous people, why wouldn't she have just run away with her aunt? Obviously her mother and sisters weren't acting in a way they should and Kate shouldn't have been listen to them...which brings me to the premise of the whole plot. Why would you make a deal with your mother, who flirts with men as a living it seems, to get three proposals? Just the fact that Kate didn't want to marry because of what she had seen from her mother and sisters is enough for me to think the very idea of that proposal would have been revolting to her. If I was her, I would have refused immediately...and most likely run away...as I said before. 
 As to Henry's mother...if she didn't like Kate's mother so much (for very valid reasons...that family is really messed up) why in the world would she let her children play with Kate all the years of their lives? She was just asking for trouble... 
 And this is why I can't find a reason to give the book a good rating. I liked the plot, the idea, but a book should make you ask many questions throughout that are answered at the end, that's what a great book does. It leaves you with an amazed, happy feeling. This book just left me wondering and wondering.
So sweet (and made me tear up)

I actually ended up enjoying this quite a bit and yet had you asked for my opinion three quarters of the way in, I would have told you this was an odd book and I couldn't quite understand why possessed me to keep reading it for so long. The secondary characters, the mothers especially, are dreadful cliches, the heroine's motivations become clear only very late in the novel, the author is constantly on the verge of slut-shaming and there's very little suspense as the main couple is very clearly in love way before the novel starts. So what changed my mind? Simply put - the end. I can't continue reading Game of Thrones because I don't know if Martin means to have Daenerys trigger a revolution that would bring social justice to the world and if he's not, I'm frankly not interested enough to read this story. It was the same with Blackmoore - if in the end, the heroine ended up renouncing her dreams of independence for a man, I just wasn't interested. The end was perfect in that respect and I loved the heroine very much by that point. It's not a splendid novel but it was a very decent read, with some lovely passages and lines and I'm glad I picked it up.

I loved edenbrooke so I was excited to read Blackmoore but I just couldn't get attached to the main character. She seemed so stubborn and silly and not in a cute corky way. I was inlove with Blackmoore (the house) and Henry but other than that it took me a while to get through it.
Cute Rengency romance. Predictable, but a nice diversion. Sigh.
I didn't like many of the characters in this book, I did like the little twist in the end though! I'd give this book 2,5 stars

** spoiler alert ** 
 Definitely liked it a lot. Donaldson creates the best male characters! 
 I think the ending could have been better; it wasn't awful, just no big build up as much as other moments in the book, so at the end I was like, "Welp, I guess they're together now." It was hard not to compare to Edenbrooke, but since the question comes up I think I simply related to Marianne more than I did with Katherine. I felt like most of Katherine's secrets could have easily been discussed with Henry earlier on and it could have easily been settled; like it was all more complicated than it needed to be. Can we just be a little more Type A?? I was glad that Katherine knew she loved Henry and that she wasn't necessarily opposed to her feelings for him, unlike Marianne in Edenbrooke who's resistance went on a little too long. 
 Anyway, all-in-all this was another great romance from Donaldson.

DNF @ 38% 
 I can't do this anymore. 
 I strongly dislike Kate, and don't care what happens.

I read this book shortly after finishing "Edenbrooke" and so I had high expectations. I did find "Edenbrooke" wittier but I still enjoyed "Blackmoore". It was clean and romantic. I found Kate's obsession with India a little irritating at times however I started to understand her frustrations and motives better as the story unfolded. There were some lovely moments between Kate & Henry. Overall it was an enjoyable book.

3.5/5 
 I really enjoyed it but it could have been better. It was well written and I'll keep an eye out for works like it but it's not something I'd be drawn to read over again. The story was just as frustrating as most romances are, misunderstands and lack of communication will be the death of me. But I liked the ending so I guess it works out.

I absolutely loved this book. Easy, fun, clean romance. One of my favorites. 
 Read it again for book club. Loved it again! Five Stars

Good,clean period romance, which I love! Not quite as riveting as her first novel, but still an enjoyable light read. Though I probably should worry when the old German composer was my favorite character, but oh well.
I give it five stars because I love this book, this is so full of emotions and heart touching book and I love this books.

3 1/2, I think. I found it very satisfying and requested her other book immediately, but it took a bit to get into and four or five days later I had to remind myself of exactly what took place. Plus, I think the gothic lover in me expected a little more of that, given how many surface trappings of that genre this book had. And I wish that there had been one female character other than our heroine that I felt sympathetic towards. But the hero is sort of swoony and I quite like how the ending was managed and it's nicely romantic without making one blush.
Perhaps marginally more readable than Edenbrooke, but still riddled with inaccuracies from the period.
Cute book. Kate really enjoyed it. I had a hard time getting it started but then it picked up speed.

4.5 stars. Another clean, fun historical romance. There's also a slight psychological twist to the story that I think makes the tale rather modern without taking away from the authenticity of the plot.

Kate is a 21st century women born into the 1820's. She has the strong desire to travel, be on her own, never marry, and never be "caged". Her mother knowing full heartedly that her daughter is a fool and must get married, strikes a bargain with Kate.... while she is at Blackmoore she must obtain and reject 3 proposals of marriage in order for her mother to give up on her entirely. Kate sets out to do just that and thinks she has her mother tricked when she makes a bargain with her longtime friend Henry. But will her heart win out? Will she get to India? Will she see her hearts truest desire come true? 
 I cannot say enough good things about this book! The portrayals of Blackmoore and the way that Henry can make us feel about a seemingly dreary English estate leaves you enchanted and full of yearning to go there and never leave. I was immediately drawn into the1800 scene and the people that inhabited Blackmoore that I felt like I was Kate taking everything in. Every person played their part stunningly. From the overbearing and disapproving mothers, to the many guests that stayed in the house, It felt ever the picture! 
 Blackmoore is full of secrets, longing, doubt, love, and fears. You get a few chuckles and it pulls at your heart strings. I know that Blackmoore and the story of Kate will never leave me. A promise is such a fragile thing. Words and intentions held in suspense as to whether they will be fulfilled - or will disappointment raise its ugly head and snatch those words and intentions from our hope-filled hearts? 
 When a book begins well, we are offered a promise of sorts: a treat that will last to the end of the story, staying with us forever after. Blackmore started out in just such a way, so that I told my wife, "Finally, a book I can look forward to sitting down with!" The last few books I've read weren't so good. She was glad to hear that, having heard me laughing often from the other room as I read the first chapters. 
 But, alas, it was not meant to be. It became so corny. I would like to know - do women really react as the main character in this book? With all the cliched reactions one would expect in some cheap dime-store romance, just because a man they like is standing before them? And in the case of Blackmore, this is a man the girl has known and considered one of her best friends all her life. Or, if most women don't really act so silly, does that mean they enjoy reading such nonsense? My wife has never been that way, hence my question. Anyone who has read Jane Austen would be repelled by the way Blackmore is written. 
 Don't get me wrong, I know how the human heart reacts when confronted with someone you care about. To this day, I can't look at my wife without that sense of wonder and admiration, and we've been married for over 35 years. 
 Blackmore started with the promise of lovely expressions becoming a wonderful story. I wish I had read it on my Kindle so I could have some of those phrases that were found at the beginning and could put them down here, but I got the book from the library. The idea of the bargain that Kate made with her mother was interesting, but the tale played out like a bad B movie. I can hardly express how let down I was when the story turned sour; I was really looking forward to the promise of a great read being kept.

 This was such perfect, historical fiction, romantic angst. It delivered on basically everything I wanted it to, but I didn't really ask for anything exceptional. The romance was so wonderful, it was this wonderful slow, slow burn with lots of angst and like based on a really sound and wonderful friendship... Kind of an ideal relationship for me, I loved it. (I would have also have LOVED reading from her love interest's point of view.) I felt so angry while reading this, and so frustrated and, honestly, I did feel quite trapped (even if she may have used the word a couple too many times.) So, not super high quality and all, but I really enjoyed reading it. 
 This book is about Kate who wants to go to India and never, ever marry. But, in order to convince her mother that is the best course of action for her, she must receive, and then reject, three proposals while away at Blackmoore. 
 SPOILERS DISCUSSION 
 Okay, so Kate's mom was similar in many ways to Mrs. Bennet from Pride and Prejudice, in terms of being embarrassing. Also, like, oblivious to the shame that she brought upon her family. I thought she was a kind of one dimensional villain which would be my only real complaint about her. I like my villains to be a little more than just straight up evil. 
 Also, I'm sure that there are people who weren't into the kind of slut shaming that Kate does about her mom and about Eleanor, her sister. For her mom, I think its fine because OBVIOUSLY SHE'S MAD HER MOM IS FLIRTING WITH A MAN WHO IS NOT HER FATHER. And then with Eleanor, I'm just kind of attributing it to the time. Which makes it more okay to me, I think? I also kind of got the sense that what made Kate mad was that their only power came from exploiting men, and she didn't like that feeling of exploitation or that feeling of their only power being related to men... I don't know, but though I was aware of it and not totally cool with it, I thought it was fine in this particular work. 
 So, basically, I just loved the romance. That just made everything for me. Like, the fact that Grandfather knew about her and that Henry talked about her a lot and she was so, so kind to him... 
 ALSO HENRY'S ANGST! Like when he made those little comments and you just totally knew that he was talking about her and about how much he liked her... And then when he's talking about the pain of proposing to Kate and saying all those things that he'd meant for a long time out loud and how it was even worse. So wonderfully and delicously angsty. And he was more tuned into his feelings, y'know, so I would have LOVED to read from his point of view. 
 This is the kind of book that I day dream about. Like, I'll put together little scenes in my head of things I want to happen or think would be cool, I play around with all of the characters and essentially write fanfiction in my head and it makes me so happy and giddy. That's why I really liked this book. 
 And then he also teased her like that scene on the beach. And they knew each other so well and could play off of each other in so many ways. They could rely on each other and have fun with each other and keep each other guessing and I JUST LOVED THE ROMANCE OKAY. IT WAS AMAZING. 
 Also, I really liked Kate. She wasn't just kind of a bitter, mean person, which characters like her who are just kind of wholeheartedly opposed to something can sometimes become. Like, she was just genuinely nice in a lot of ways and sweet to those little girls (that scene was interesting. Because you have Juliet walking around giving things out on behalf of Henry [which, let's be clear, is totally a generous thing to do, no matter how we feel about their... relationship?] whereas Kate makes a less important donation to these people's lives, but she makes it on behalf of herself and its much more personal. The contrast worked, I think, though it was kind of pronounced.) She's very likable and I rooted for her constantly. I was OUTRAGED at things that her mother did, or her sister, or Henry's mother, or even his sister. I could feel her anger and horror. She was really, really relatable. And, yes, there were times where she didn't do the right thing, but I don't really care. 
 The romance. The romance. The romance. It just made this book for me. I ADORED it. I cannot say that enough times. 
 So, yes, some of the language and motifs were a little overused, but I don't really care? Like, if I were in her situation, damn straight I'd feel trapped. I'd be talking about it every other second. That being said, this book doesn't really have a lot of balance. The angst and anger levels are over the top (like with Henry's mom... furious) and the romance is basically the best etc. It goes all the way, and, thankfully, I loved the things it went all the way for. Heavy handed, but it definitely worked for me. 
 Okay, so I've raved about it, why is it getting a kind of low star rating? Because though it was a magnificent romance and lovely read, for me, it didn't give me any depth, really. Like, the secondary characters felt fairly one dimensional (I mean, Ms. Donaldson tried with Juliet, but she still felt underdeveloped to me) and the plot was really, really predictable (I predicted kind of all of it? Like, at least the really big stuff) etc. etc. This book made me happy, but in terms of the things that I'll usually judge a book on, it's not really hitting the mark. 
 I will mostly definitely be checking out Ms. Donaldson's other work because wow did I like this. 
 FIN!

Blackmoore was an unexpected surprise. It was absolutely beautiful. The author told it in such a way to infuse a tone of loveliness into the story. I actually felt what the characters were feeling at times. The author gave flashbacks of when the main characters, Kate and Henry, were younger. Those scenes were sweet and filled with emotion. I haven't read a book like this one in a long time. I actually felt touched by the characters. The plot was creative and beautiful in the execution. I got so wrapped up in the characters and the book itself that I forgot where I was and felt as if I were inside of Blackmoore with Kate. I rarely find books like this and am forever on the search for them. I do believe Blackmooore is on my re-read list. There are few books I will re-read but Blackmoore is one of them. 
 There was one thing missing from this book. I read so many Christian fiction books that I greatly noticed the absence. There was nothing of God mentioned, nothing of prayer, nothing of scripture. It was a clean read, however. I had nothing to complain about there. But Kate and Henry never thought about things beyond their own circumstances--or rather Who is beyond and above their circumstances. That was the only part I was disappointed about. The book could have been so much more if God had been in it. 
 Julianne Donaldson has a lot of talent. I adore her writing voice. I definitely want to read her other book, Edenbrooke, now that I've read Blackmoore. I hope she learns how to infuse her faith into her writing. It could be so much better that way. 
 I give Blacksmoore 4 out of 5 stars.

If you enjoy historical fiction, especially the Regency era, you won't want to miss Blackmoore! Kate is determined to get away from her crazy family, especially her mother. She wants to go to India with her Aunt Charlotte, but her mother wants her married and settled down. 
 Kate also wants to visit her friend Henry's estate, Blackmoore. Determined to get her heart's desire, Kate makes a deal with her mother to placate her. If she acquires and rejects three marriage proposals, her mother will let her go to India and that will be the end of it. Her mother agrees and Kate figures she'll go to Blackmoore, Henry's estate. With his help, she should have no problem securing the three proposals so she can begin on the journey she really wants. 
 The problem is that securing the proposals isn't as easy as Kate believed it would be. Fate another plan for Kate, if she's willing to compromise what she believes is her heart;s desire, to be free of her mother and family. 
 With engaging characters and a deftly described world, Blackmoore is a stellar read. Donaldson's characters slowly reveal themselves to their true character as the story unfolds. While I detested Kate's mother, and Henry's for that matter, I thoroughly enjoyed Kate and Henry's journey together. Wonderful read!
A great read!

This was cute. Light. Clean. Almost completely conflict-free. 
 If you need that kind of book, I'd actually recommend Ms. Donaldson's Edenbrooke above this one.

Kate Worthington has been waiting to visit Blackmoore her whole life. Her best friend, Sylvia Delafield and her brother Henry go visit Blackmoore every year, and every year Kate wishes she can go with them. Blackmoore represents an escape from the unending monotony of her life, and she is anxious for the adventure. Her mother tries to stop her from visiting Blackmoore to punish her for her refusal to marry, and so they strike a bargain: If Kate receives and refuses 3 marriage proposals at Blackmoore, then she is a free woman and can go to India with her spinster Aunt Charlotte. If she fails, she has to do whatever her mother wants her to -- which is sure to include an undesirable marriage. 
 So much about Blackmoore is not what Kate has expected. The reality of convincing three men to want her is daunting, but because there are no bounds or moral limits to her mother's opportunism, failure is not an option. She quickly realizes that the shameful reputation of her mother and older sister precede her making it impossible for any man to propose to her. Henry seems to be the only person who realizes that she is nothing like her mother and sister, even if she does share their good looks. Determined to succeed in her plan to escape marriage and flee to India with her aunt, Kate asks Henry to propose to her three times. He agrees to do it, but on his own terms. 
 One marriage proposal per night in exchange for one secret. Henry wants to know why Kate is so determined not to marry and wants this opportunity to try to change her mind. 
 Julianne Donaldson is an amazing author! The imageries of the black bird in the cage and the controlled notes of Mozart leaving no room for passion add so much to the story. The story takes place in present time (by present time, I mean 1820 England), but keeps jumping back to what has happened over the past three years that has convinced Kate that she must keep these secrets, must refuse marriage, and must control her heart so that no passion enters in.

I'm not sure I really felt anything for this book... 
 I didn't connect with the main character and quite disliked her for the majority of the book; Kate is quite a silly, selfish little girl. She annoyed me the most in that she was both selfless and selfish all at once. But perhaps it's no wonder she's a brat, having a slaggy and conspiring mother and a slaggy and disgraced sister. 
 Although that is one of the strengths of this book - it is slowly revealed why Kate is as she is, and she does grow as a character. 
 The setting made me feel even colder than this awful weather should have, so I supposed the descriptions must have been immersing enough. Only I can't remember any of them. 
 The end was a little too happily-ever-after for me. I much prefer more uncertain futures for the lives of characters. 
 Overall this was a moderately pleasant read, fun and romantic. 
 I received a copy of this for free via NetGalley for review purposes.

Title: "Blackmoore" 
 Author: Julianne Donaldson 
 Publication date: 9/10/2013 
 Type of book: Historical Fiction and Proper Romance 
 Is this a part of a series, If yes, which number? No 
 Summary: Kate Worthington is a single woman living in Regency England. In a world where most of her life is decided for her Kate wants only two things, to go visit Blackmoore (A friend's estate/house) and to travel to India with her aunt. Unfortunately for her those two things are being kept from her by her mother who only wants Kate to marry. In order to get to Blackmoore Kate makes a hasty bargain with her mother. With more at stake then just a trip to India, Kate must quickly find out who she is and what she is willing to do to get what she wants in life. 
 Characters: Kate Worthington: I liked Kate. She is spunky and keeps trying to reach her goals even when things seem out of focus. 
 *Henry: He is my favorite character in this book. I love how sweet he is and how much he loves Kate. He follows his heart even when it's difficult. Henry is very swoon worthy. 
 (Normally I would go on a bit more about secondary characters but for me this book was really just about Kate and Henry.) 
 Favorite bits: *I love the description of Blackmoore and I felt like I had walked the halls myself. 
 *I really enjoyed the subtle and sweet gestures from Henry towards Kate. (I love a subtle and meaningful romance.) 
 *I loved the scene where Henry lets the bird out of the cage. I enjoyed the symbolism of it. 
 Problematic bits: *I did find Kate difficult to like at times. 
 *I think that the book could have used more filling out. I'm not even really sure what I would add but I just felt like it was missing something. 
 Overall I found Blackmoore to be an enjoyable read and great for anyone who wants a sweet Regency "proper" romance. Julianne Donaldson is an author to watch.

" I feel caged. Always. I feel like I am this bird, trapped and stifled and caged, and I keep looking for a way to escape, but I am barred at every turn." 
 It's the first time I read one of Julianne Donaldson's books and what struck me instantly was the lyrical and gripping writing. I flew through her words and embraced the gothic feel of her descriptions. I smiled more than I could count while I was reading it and I closed the book feeling satisfied and cheerful. 
 The story is set in 1820, England where we follow Kate whose wish is to go to India. In order to do so, she makes a bargain with her controlling mother: To gain her freedom she has to reject three marriage proposals. 
 The author did an exellent job depicting Kate's feelings. I felt her desires and hopelessness as if they were my own. What's make this book's greatness is that she's not only trapped by her mother but also by the people around her. 
 They refuse to let her change and become the person she wants to be. She's caged in the image they have of her. They see her as Kitty, the sister of the scandalous Eleanor, the daughter of the flirty Miss Worthington. She even restraints herself with her classical music. It's pretty genius when you think about it and that's what makes the connection she has with Henry that much important. 
 He's the only one who sees her who what she really is. He's her freedom and she's so absorbed into her ideas she doesn't even see it. You know the saying, you can't see the frame when you're in the picture. 
 Anyway, this is a light but meaningful romance full of elaborated symbolism. The author guides our hearts gently without ever pushing too hard, she imposes her pace and make her characters charm us with their genuine and vivid personality. 
 I wish I knew more of the side characters' backtories but overall this was a very good read.
I LOVED this book! Oh man, I loved it. I related to the characters, loved the story, loved England.... man oh man. I want to be Julianne Donaldson's best friend. I looooved this boooook.

What a terrific novel by a great new(ish) author!! 
 Kate comes from a family who is often the subjects of gossip and scandal. Her father sits back in oblivion, while her mother flirts with any man she can get her claws into. Her sisters seem to be following their mother's footsteps. Kate is determined to become an old maid and travel to India with her spinster aunt, but her mother won't allow it unless she receives...and rejects...three marriage proposals. Kate asks her longtime friend, Henry, to help her out so that she can live her heart's desire. But some bargains are hard to drive... 
 My heart went out to Kate. She was known as Kitty as a child and no one, save Henry, will let her break that mold and grow up. She is forever correcting everyone on her name. Her family is so selfish and Henry's mother is just plain mean toward her, yet Kate is the most unselfish and kind person ever, always thinking of the feelings of others. I really liked her and felt a connection to her, which for me, draws me into the story even more. 
 Henry was such a gentleman and true friend. He goes against his (mean) mother to help a friend have a dream come true. Those stormy gray eyes... Any girl would be lucky to have someone like Henry on her side. 
 I loved the friendship and chemistry these two have together. I loved the flashbacks to the past that Kate had--they were the strings that tied the story together to help the reader understand what makes Kate tick. This author has a way of drawing the reader in--I really felt like I was a part of their lives. 
 Put this one on your "to-read" list because you don't want to miss out on this one!!
