book_b.title: The Story of Edgar Sawtelle
book_b.user_review: This is an epic story which many, myself included, begin with a sense of a Steinbeck worthy story. Upon reading further it is clear Wroblewski has found his own niche in the literary world. This book has a little of everything:a coming of age story, mystery, a ghost story, and of course the touching story of a boy and his dog. The thing that sticks with me is the bond between Edgar and Almondine is more than that of a boy and his cherished pet. Because Edgar can not talk the two have a closeness like no two characters in any novel that I know of. The clever way of working the thoughts and feelings of Almondine into the story will make you look at the animals in your life in a new way.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is one of the only books I can say that I regret wasting my time on. I spent MONTHS fighting my way through this book, only to have the worst ending I've ever experienced in a book.

I really enjoyed this story. It was very well written. The ending left me a little frustrated, because I like all loose ends tied up. I can forgive this only because the story was so beautifully told. As a first novel for this author, I look forward to reading his future literary endeavors.

I did not know what to expect from this book. I went to the library to pick up a different book and my top 3 choices were checked out so aimlessly walked the library aisles. I saw this book and remembered it was on the GoodReads list of one of my friends, so I gave it a chance. 
 I thought it was going to be a book just about a boy and his dog but it was much more than that. I do not think that I can give it a proper review without giving too much away. There were a couple unexpected twists that kept me engaged, curious about what will happen next. This book brought up some themes such as redemption, self-discovery, and the importance of animals which I enjoyed. 
 Overall this was a good book. I don't think it is for everyone and I will probably not go around suggesting it to random strangers but I am glad I read it.
I do not understand the point of this book. I enjoyed the setting and wanted to find some profound meaning as the book concluded. Instead, I was left wishing I could get my time back.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I kind of think of this book as two separate books. The "first", about Edgar and his family's breed of future intelligent dogs, was pretty enjoyable and interesting, if often meandering and purple. Wroblewski appeared to run out of room or time or patience for the "second", a strange murder-mystery/ghost story/thriller/Hamlet without much motivation, and the book finished abruptly and without closure. I feel like the characters had been assigned actions to complete, but we were never given all of the parts of their personalities that inspired them to those actions. There were a number of moments where I stopped and thought, "wait, what just happened, and why?". The author seems to have taken on too many ideas at once in this book, and a lot of threads were completely lost as a result. Firmly in the tragedy section, because the author can't seem to stop punishing his characters for unexplained reasons.
What a waste of time. What was the point? Hated the ending.
Beautiful writing and thoroughly heart-breaking.
I really wanted to like this book, but it never got going. The ending was completely unresolved and a huge let-down. I have no idea why it's been so highly rated and reviewed.

Okay, so I haven't quite made up my mind if I'm okay with the ending. I have mixed emotions about it. But, I loved the book so much I just can't dislike it. I would have liked it to end a little differently, but I guess I'll have to take it. But, I definitely recommend. It was a really good book. A little slow to start for me, but I did love it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 For me it was 500+ pages of Ambien. I powered through it hoping eventually the tedium would pay off. I made it to the horrible, pointless end and found the entire novel completely meaningless.

Amazing. Truly a work of art. I have not stopped thinking about this book since I finished it several days ago, such powerful characters (some of which are dogs) and such beautiful words. A masterpiece. What a wonderful portrayal of a modern-day Hamlet.

Something must be wrong with me. Several of my friends read and loved this book, so I ploughed my way though it, knowing that my tastes and their's is similar. I hated every single page of this book. That's right, every single page. Sooooo sad.

Wroblewski has created the most unique plot you could ever imagine. It is about a boy and his father that have continued the grandfather's work to compile a complete record of the bloodlines of their special and highly sought after dogs. Their rural kennel and their breeding program is ahead of anything in the world. The surrounding characters are real and vivid. Edgar's mother and uncle are from Mayberry RFD, and the sheriff could be Andy Griffith. Wroblewski's narrative skills weave you through a tapestry of people and places around rural Michigan and Lake Superior as Edgar runs for his life and his dogs.
Marvelous characters. Achingly beautiful writing. Total bore of a story. Didn't know it was a re-telling of Hamlet. Maybe that would have helped. But do we really need a re-telling of Hamlet? Not me!

The story of Edgar Sawtelle was not what I expected. As you read, you grow to love the quiet courage of this young man and all the tragedy he endures. Being wise past his years makes the ending even more bitter sweet. For dog lovers who find a human quality to your pets, you will love this story.

My view on this book is similar to most others on here. I thought the book was great until the last 50 pages or so when it all went to hell. 
 Why???

I just can't do it. I typically read 40 or so pages per night in a book, but I've been falling asleep after 1-5 pages of this one. I'm through 80 pages after more than a week. 
 As a writer, you're taught that you need to have conflict of some sort on virtually every page. There was no conflict whatsoever in this book. Nothing interesting at all. 
 I almost stopped reading before page 36, when Edgar was introduced. The first 35 pages have no discernable reason for being a part of the story. Then the next 44 follow the same pattern. 
 I don't see how this book has an average rating of 4.20. Maybe because it's a "literary masterpiece." I guess that makes me low-brow. Give me Grisham any day.

** spoiler alert ** 
 After the huge media hype about this book, I was expecting something a bit more engrossing. Parts of the book really drag, explanation of dog training and the odyssey of Edgar and his dogs. 
 The human characters in the book are the least developed of any. The dog characters seem more real. And the reason for the deep animosity between Gar and his brother are shown rather than well explained. It still leaves a lot of doubt in the reader's mind. I wondered if this was a purposeful device by the author, demonstrating Edgar's doubts and frustrations due to his muteness, and the way he's friendless, except for the dogs. 
 The last 150 pages of the book, are where the story finally unfolds. Then events move very quickly. Wroblewski writes beautiful description without the trite metaphors many writers fall into. 
 Our book group selected this book, and the facilitator found many parallels to Hamlet, and some to the Odyssey. We were about evenly split over liking and disliking the book. Many felt that it could have been made shorter without losing any important components.

Simply one of the best, most engrossing books I've ever read. I read 566 pages in three days. This book is a great read, especially for those people who have an interest in dogs, and in sign language. Edgar Sawtelle was born without a voice, so he has to learn to sign. The novel follows his life in a unique perspective, sometimes telling the story from the dogs' point of view. The writing style is engaging and metaphoric, and there is always something interesting happening in Edgar's young life. An extremely highly recommended read - one of my top ten of all time!!! Stephen King, in his critique of the novel, said that life was too short to re-read novels, but that this was one that he was definitely going to re-read!

I should have known. Oprah and I are a million light years apart. I didn't like the gaze of the author on the backflap. Also, if Stephen King liked it, that should have been enough for me to know the book was not for me. 
 I felt it was overwritten. The descriptions were not compelling to me. His use of unusual vocabulary didn't add to the story for me. I felt a better story has more poetic sentence structure in order to emote a stronger tie between reader and story.

** spoiler alert **

 This book advertises itself as a re-imagining of 'Hamlet,' which was what interested me most about it. Unfortunately, it addresses exactly none of the themes that make 'Hamlet' a great play. The use of Hamlet's plot comes across not as a clever, modern re-telling, but rather as an amateur borrowing a plot for lack of inspiration. 
 If you're going to re-write Shakespeare's most famous play, it'd better be God's own rewrite. Otherwise, you only set yourself up for unfavorable comparisons. 
 Wooden attempts at poetry ("they ate like starving kings"? At least I understood that particular mixed metaphor. Some are just pretty words strung together like magnet poetry.), flat characters who spend a great deal of time wondering why they are doing what they are doing (why am *I* doing what I'm doing-- reading this?), and, since the plot is borrowed, no great surprises in store. 
 The best part of the book, for me, is Edgar's journey. Since it does not have much of a Shakespearean parallel, that freed the author up to let the plot move more organically. Unfortunately, we all know he's going back home eventually, so the whole thing becomes something of a red herring. 
 In fact, I thought the cover of this book should be-- not a boy, a dog, and a farm-- but rather a large red herring. Or a school of red herrings. Many things are introduced, but very few of them, ultimately matter. 
 Obfuscation does not profundity make.

reference_books.title: New Moon (Twilight, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was painful to read. Like I said in my review for book 1 of this series, I had hope that the series would improve. It didn't. I had no idea the kind of torture I was in for. The list of problems have grown to say the least. 
 A) The whole birthday party scene. What normal human female wouldn't like having a birthday party, even if it's a small one or just a get-together-with-friends-and-have-snacks kind of birthday party? Is this girl nuts with not wanting to spend her birthday with her "friends"? 
 B) Also, why did Stephanie Meyer spend only five sentences (give or take) describing the most important scene in the book? She spent at least a whole page in the previous one talking about Edward's eyes and she couldn't do the same conveying the part where Bella gets shoved into a table? Logic, anyone? 
 C) And another thing: If they had any sense, they would have gone out feeding prior to the birthday party in order to keep from flipping out as Jasper did over a paper cut. 
 D) Since when does a paper cut bleed like that? I've had plenty of paper cuts in my life, being the bookworm that I am, and none of them have bled like that. Not even the ones I got from other kinds of paper! 
 E) And how, exactly, does one get a paper cut that deep from wrapping paper? It's insanely difficult to get one that goes any deeper than the first layer of skin with that kind of paper, and Stephanie Meyer expects me to believe that Bella got one that is deep enough to bleed that much? Again, logic, anyone? 
 F) As we all know, Bella has a poor sense of direction on the best of days. So, why does Edward take her into the woods to talk to her, knowing that she was likely to follow him? He couldn't just make sure she got into the house okay? Of course not. Edward is an asshat. And seriously, if he had loved her, like he said he did, he wouldn't have abandoned her like that. If he did love her that much, he would have ripped Jasper's fucking head off or at least explained why he had to go away for a while. 
 G) Bella shuts down for several months, causing the author to waste several pages that just had the month printed on them. Waste of ink, waste of paper. 
 H) Bella, after being dumped by Edward, becomes a whiny bitch and can't shut up about dear Eddie-kins, and goes on a suicidal rampage, taking up dangerous activity after dangerous activity just to hear his voice. Is it just me, or does this idiot need a therapist? 
 I) Bella actually survives suicide. I'm not one to condone suicide. My first thought when I hear about one is "What happened for this person to think they had no way out?" With Bella's case, I kept think "Hurry up and die so I don't have to listen to you inane whining and your bullshit anymore!" Too bad Jacob saved her. He really couldn't let her drown? 
 J) Alice can't see shifters. Really? You can see everyone else but you can't see a bunch of shirtless cliff diving oddballs who can turn into overgrown puppies? 
 K) Edward couldn't come back to Forks to see if Bella actually was dead and to pay his respects to her? Seriously? The first thing he thinks is "The love of my life is dead, so I might as well die too"? Good grief! Shouldn't he have thought "Show me the body!"? 
 L) Since when is suicide by sparkles a viable option. Last time I checked, people didn't die from sparkling! 
 The only refreshing things about this book were Jacob's support of his friend, which, unfortunately didn't last long enough, and The Volturi, who were a nice breath of fresh springtime air. They were the closest things to the mythology as Stephanie Meyer got in this series and were a nice break from the sparkling faeries she can't shut up about. From here on in, the series just keeps going downhill.

reference_books.title: Allegiant (Divergent, #3)
reference_books.review_text: This book kinda fell flat. It didn't fall as flat as Mockingjay, in my opinion, mainly because the female lead didn't try to shirk her responsibility. I will say that this book, with its flaws, was okay. It would have been better of it wasn't such an info-dump. I feel it should have been made into two books instead of being one. It wouldn't have been a mental dumping of so many facts and the characters would have improved. Also, because of the info-dump, the characters seemed to suffer. Tris was made to be always right. You're gut is right 90% of the time, usually, not 100%. And Tobias seemed like he was made into an impulsive "I don't give two shits" person, unlike the first two where he was pretty cool. The ending could have been better. It would have been nice for a certain character to get a decent comeuppance. And also, and, spoiler, the power of love stopping Marcus and Evelyn from gouging each other out was kinda bullshit. Marcus beat Evelyn to bits. Somehow, I don't think she would have forgiven him so easily and Marcus would have kicked up a bigger stink. In a way, it almost would have been better to give them both memory serum so they could become new people, but only almost. On a more positive note, at least Tris's character got a proper ending, considering how reckless she was. Seems kind of fitting.

reference_books.title: Eclipse (Twilight, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was just as bad as New Moon. The list of problem only gets longer. 
 A) The newborn problem. Stephanie Meyer just touched base with the updates. Nothing in depth, nothing really new. Nobody goes to investigate. What a surprise (not!) 
 B) Newborns again. Why are they a threat? 
 C) The Volturi couldn't come sooner to investigate the newborns? WTF? 
 D) The newborn thread fell flat. The "battle" only lasts one chapter and we don't really see that much action. It was just a yawn-fest 
 E) Did Bella have to be such a bitch when Jacob kissed her? I get slapping him but other than that, there was no reason to get that smug and arrogant about it. 
 F) Bella wouldn't have had to break her hand (which was an accident, in the first place because, once Jacob's shape shifting kicked in, he got stronger as a result which he obviously couldn't have brought up before) on Jacob's face if she had been more forward about her feelings instead of stringing him along. She really couldn't sit him down and tell him they were nothing more than friends and never would be anything else? 
 G) Did she need to set Edward on Jacob? It was her own fault he kissed her and it's her own fault she broke her hand! She never once said to Jacob "You and I are just friends and we won't be anything else, so can you back off a bit?" 
 H) The three book Victoria subplot was really lackluster. It never really came into anything and was just pathetic. 
 I) There's too many Wuthering Heights references for a book that is in no way Wuthering Heights. Stephanie Meyer really needs to stop raping classic literature and making the references so overt. It's called subtlety for a reason, bitch! 
 This series really was a waste of trees, paper and ink. I am designating this series as two things: emergency toilet paper and a fire-starting aid for when you are out in the woods, ready for a boil-up/mug-up. No better way to make a cup of tea than to burn shitty books!

book_a.title: Library of Souls (Miss Peregrine's Peculiar Children, #3)
book_a.user_review: This action-packed novel really packs a punch. Not only was it fun with hardly any breathing room, it was gripping and engaging. I definitely recommend reading the first two books before reading this one in order to follow the action and story line properly with as little confusion as possible. Now that I've gotten this book finished, part of me wishes this series would go on for another book. Another part of me (perhaps that same part) hopes there might eventually be more stories set in this same universe.

sample_reviews.review_text: So, everyone seems to really enjoy this series, so I guess I am in the minority. It was just, blah. The characters were one dimensional and flat. I never really felt invested in the story compared to other YA trilogies. In fact, I heard myself wondering "When is this book going to end?" with no desire to know how it ends, which is never a good sign. I probably wouldn't recommend this book, as there are so many far superior trilogies out there.

I struggled with whether to give this book the five stars I gave the previous book, but ultimately settled on four stars because, though better than the first book in the series (which I gave four stars too as well), it wasn't as good as the second. Don't get me wrong...I loved this book and I highly recommend all three books in the series. I just have some qualms about it, particularly the first 10% and the last 10%. The other 80% was fantastic, but the beginning and the end kind of floundered. 
 Speaking of the end, as the conclusion to the arc of the trilogy, Library of Souls ending was satisfying in how it ended, but not necessarily in how the ending was told. It felt as though the book reached its own conclusion and then was like "Oh, wait...I need to wrap up the trilogy...I guess I'll use a boring and predictable twist to extend myself a few more chapters and I'll follow up my second climax, which will be good despite feeling tacked on and not being quite as engaging as the first, with a grating epilogue." Really, that epilogue was really what cost this book its fifth star. 
 Nitpicks aside, I really loved this series and consider it a real treasure.

Overall, this may have been my least favorite of the trilogy. Compared to the first two books, it feels like Riggs didn't understand the rules to his own world and lost touch with his main protagonists. I think he finishes the book well, and leaves himself open to return to the series if he wishes to. I'd read another book in the series.

I love this tale. Following Jacob and his peculiar friends through all their adventures and struggles is fascinating a thrill ride to be a part of. I love the uniqueness of it, in a world of vampire/ware wolf/ wizard fiction that seems to be on a loop Riggs has found a new form of imagination to be consumed by us right when we needed it the most. Can not wait for his version of what the Tale of Peculiars book will look like and I'm wondering if he'll ever make a Map of Days with all the different time loops mentioned (as well as those that were overlooked). Excited is one word for what these books have left with me.
this was the best book of this series!!

And it occurred to me, standing there, just breathing with her, quiet settling around us, that those might be the three most beautiful words in the English language. We have time. 
 Wow!! This was a very satisfying end the the series. I'm sad to see it end. This novel picks up right after the second and doesn't slow down until the last page. The first major "twist" (if you were to call it that) happens within the first 100 pages. Ransom Riggs is an amazing author. He had the ability to thrust me into the story along with Jacob, Emma, Addison, and the rest of the peculiars. I highly recommend this book and this series to everyone.
This book put me in a reading slump...I only got through the first chapter and I had to stop. I was really wanting to finish it. :(
I can't believe this whole trilogy contain such many boring and dull content. The important event in the whole three book should just be cut out and combine as one.

Something happened when I began reading the third installment in the "Miss Peregrine's Peculiar Children" trilogy and I couldn't finish it, I couldn't get past the first 100 pages or so. 
 Considering the fact that I absolutely adored the previous two books in the trilogy, it seriously terrifies me how I couldn't even finish this book. I guess I didn't find the plot quite captivating and the photographs weren't even placed there in order to make me feel terrified while connecting them to the story. The ones I did look at weren't creepy at all, to be honest. It felt more like Ransom Riggs gathered these photographs and began building his storyline around them. I was honestly bored while reading it and, one time, I actually fell asleep, the book fell off my hands and I woke up hours later completely disoriented, because falling asleep due to a book hasn't happened me for more than a decade or so. So, yes, you know how frustrated I must feel right now. I seriously wanted to love this book, I was so over the top excited when it arrived in the mail and I couldn't wait to begin reading it as soon as possible. 
 But, instead of loving it, it put me into this huge reading slump and made me stay behind on my reading challenge for this year and also not want to start reading other books. Damn. This shouldn't have happened. I've got a great deal of respect for Ransom Riggs and his writing, because he clearly is a very talented author and I'm certain I want to continue reading his work in the future. But this last book in the series didn't work for me, didn't "speak" to me. 
 So, only 1 out of 5 stars and I put it on my "did-not-finish" shelf, even though I hate not finishing books, especially the last installments in a series. I really hope I'll be in the mood to pick it up again sometime in the near future. I recommend it to people who liked the previous books of the trilogy and to those who love reading about paranormal adventures and YA Mystery/Horror literature.

3.5 stars, rounding up to 4. Overall, I really enjoyed the Miss Peregrine series, although reading all three books in a row was probably a mistake. The series has a strong finish in Library of Souls, but the quirky charm of the first book gets a little buried under the non-stop action of the 2nd and 3rd installments. I also got a little tired of the photos. They were unique and original in the 1st book, but by the 3rd, that gimmick felt played out. 
 Still, I'm glad I finally read all three and stuck with it to the end. I recommend the series, but would suggest reading other things in between to keep the reading experience fresh.

Read my Review Here! 
 Just like Hollow City, Library of Souls begins exactly where the previous book ends. 
 After spending nearly a month reading this, I found myself losing interestest quickly. Don't get me wrong, the book was good. However, I lost most of my excitement for the story in the clutter of fluff. Honestly, there was just too much. The story seemed to drag and all I wanted to know was if Jacob and Emma would finally be reunited with their friends again. One possibility that may have had a negative effect on my reaction was the fact that I wrote down what transpired in the story. I wanted to be able to look back at my notes in the future; however, the further I read, the less motivated I became. Yes, things would happen, but they weren't vital critical to the story. Like I said, there was a lot of fluff. Chapters would be fifty or more pages long. 80% would be fluff, such as Jacob discussing their relationship and promising never to leave each other. The remaining 20% was what progressed the story forward. 
 I love reading prose, but honestly, this was just too much. Everything was described in intricate details, which is amazing. But if it honestly has nothing to do with the story, then don't spend so much time describing it. 
 I was not overly impressed with this conclusion. I think at that point I was willing to accept anything if it meant the story would be over. I did enjoy this series; but for me, it didn't necessarily live up to all of the hype.

The main problem I had with this book -- the whole series, really -- is that it isn't an arc of three stories which contribute to one another but are relatively complete in themselves. The story literally continues as if there was no more than a chapter break, which after a couple of months is a bit of a barrier to getting back into it. It does make for a pretty good conclusion though, developing people's motives and powers, bringing things to a turning point climax. The photographs were integrated the least into the story of all the books -- some of them felt like they were there purely as set dressing, which is always a problem for me in worldbuilding. I want more from it. 
 Still, that sounds like damning with faint praise and for the most part, I definitely enjoyed this, and I enjoyed the fact that Emma and Jacob's strange situation is explored: the fact that in many ways, she's much older than him, though she doesn't look it. The fact that he is caught between two worlds. 
 The first ending (in my head), where Jacob went back with his parents and had to go to therapy, etc, felt... realistic. He says he's had crazy adventures, he went missing, and now his parents are glad to have him back but not quite trusting, not quite sure. The ending-after-that seemed like a bit of a cop-out, though; it just made things too easy, with no sting of parting, no difficult period of adjustment, but something like the best of both worlds.

I liked this 3rd entry into the Miss Peregrine's series one star more than #2. The author fixed the sudden drop into the continuing plot by offering some background information and a glossary right at the beginning, which I appreciated. I still found the photograph parts of the story an irritating after-thought in the writing, and the casual parlance of the narrator annoying. 
 Finally, the characters in these books never really cooperate or stick to a plan and I doubt they'd ever survive real trouble. Addison the dog was the worst for this. Always blowing everybody's cover. Glad to say "So long" to this world.
4 1/2 because the ending was rosy.

It's fine Ransom Riggs, I didn't need my heart anyway. 
 I loved this book. I think of all three, it had the strongest writing and the least reliance on photos as a way to progress the plot. I honestly was so engrossed in the story that I barely noticed them this time around. 
 The story took unexpected turns, and for the last 150 pages I was absolutely on the edge of my seat. So much so, I was squeezing in reading times anywhere I could. I could not put it down. The end was satisfying to a degree that fell somewhere between The Series of Unfortunate Events and Harry Potter. I was honestly saddened to stop reading this book and I intend to read these books over and over, and to pass them on not only to my students, but to my own kids as well.
The best in the series. This was packed with action and had better characters then the rest of the series. Then the ending was a grand twist I didn't see coming.

Another series finale. I think this was probably the strongest written book out of all of them. I wouldn't say it blew me away or anything, but it was pretty decent. I felt like there weren't as many photos in this book? I don't really mind but I did notice. 
 I still feel really strange about the Jacob and Emma pairing, it kills my enthusiasm for these books. Like whenever Jacob thinks about the fact that his Grandfather also loved Emma he puts it out of his mind real quick because it's weird to think about for him. Because it IS weird!! He is a child, that is a child's reaction. Emma is also physically a child but like it almost comes off as predatory... how she likes him bc he's like his grandfather. Really I might be okay with it if she wasn't his Grandpa's ex childhood girlfriend. I can't get over that. Also why does this little punk need some everlasting love with this girl? it was irritating & ridiculous. 
 The adventure in this one was much more enjoyable and I think it's because there weren't as many characters crowding the story, when they're reunited the book suffers a bit bc there's simply not enough time. I loved the new character Sharon. Miss Peregrine's brothers or whatever weren't really compelling villains, the ending wasn't that satisfying because of it. 
 I liked that Jacob finally thought about his parents, and how his choices affected them. But no even this goes to shit when the peculiars somehow show up and can stay in present time no harm no foul. I don't know I feel like the right thing to do was end it where they think he's crazy like his grandpa but maybe I'm a downer. Jacob was most compelling when he was struggling through that. All the other times he's just mooning over his grandpa's ex sidepiece. 
 Overall, it was just okay.

Clever with pacing issues. The interesting premise falls flat with predictable betrayals and resolutions. I never felt much for Jacob and Emma's relationship. It felt too forced; too rushed. Though I suppose that was part of the point considering the way the book ended. Jacob's ability was a bit too convenient. It was explored at times in very fun ways at least. All in all a charming end to a charming series.

The ending of this gave me so many immediately conflicting feels! But I'm pleased with how it ended because for a minute there it looked pretty dreadful. 
 This was probably my favorite of the trilogy. Partly because more action based stuff happened, but also because we FINALLY got to learn about all the peculiardom mythos and really figure out what was going on. 
 I still feel that even though the main character/characters are older, it still felt sort of geared toward younger kids. That being said, I still really enjoyed Ransom Riggs' writing. I loved the blend of time periods that he got to play with and the ways he worked around the different loops (the Panloopticon was genius!!). We met more characters in this story (Sharon and Mother Dust being 2 of my favorites and Bentham being one of the most interesting) and we finally had the showdown everyone was waiting for. 
 I do feel like we've been left a little unresolved in the long run. In no way am I expecting or wanting another book or series, but maybe like a book of short stories about what's happened in the peculiardom since the events? Maybe like one story from each of miss peregrines's children? I'd like that. We need to have Hugh go find Fiona and more adventures from the Panloopticon! 
 **spoilers** 
 I almost wish the Library loop hadn't been destroyed because I would have LOVED to know more about it. It reminds me of the place Penny works in the Magicians. 
 Also, I was *so* upset with the ending until the very end. What a freaking fake out. I didn't lose hope, but I was seriously worried. Then promptly so relieved from the solution. ;)

-I feel like this entire series could've been condensed into just one book 
 - it also seemed like the photos were forced into the he story, instead of just complementing the story 
 - the writing just isn't strong. The plot was drawn out, there were too many characters, and the author just isn't a strong author. In my opinion anyway.
Mejor final, imposible.

I was so looking forward to seeing how Ransom Riggs was going to end this series. But i feel let down. This book, unlike the first 2 seemed to be lacking something.While the first 2 had a very natural flow that left me wanting more. This one felt almost forced creative wise and in the flow. It almost rushed like he was in a hurry to meet the deadline. Overall, it was just okay; he definitely could have did more with it.

What a great finale! 
 I loved this book from start to finish. There was drama, suspense, mystery, and such great relationships. I really enjoyed learning more about the culture and lore surrounding the peculiars. It made me even more excited for The Tales of the Peculiar. Once again I loved the pictures! I just love the world Riggs has created, and I think he did a fabulous job wrapping up the series.

What a book! Such adventures. Would recommend to everyone who loves a good adventure with creepy stuff. This is a book that made me shout out in public with absolute joy (or distres) about what the characters managed to do.
This was a good trilogy. I feel peculiar myself.

Well this was surely a huge let down. 90% of this book is literally the main characters running around trying to find something/someone, then proceeding to run into things/enemies/plot holes. Bad things happen, then good things happen immediately after, erasing the bad things that took place. Rinse and repeat.

Pa nemam pojma.. nesto izmedu 2-3-4 za ceo serijal.. uopste ne mogu da kazem da mi je neki deo bio bolji ili interesantniji od drugog, ali sam odlucila da nagradim knjige zbog ideje. 
 S obzirom da na Instagramu i Pinterestu volim da pratim profile raznih kolekcionara, izmedu ostalog i one cije je fotografije Ransom Rigs koristio za knjigu - odmah sam bila privucena ovim knjigama. Delovalo mi je bas kreativno iskoristiti te stare, crno-bele creepy fotografije i izgraditi neobicnu pricu o likovima koji se na njima nalaze. Cak mi je u nekom trenutku bilo krivo sto se ja toga nisam setila i iskoristila jos interesantnije fotke da napisem daleko bolju pricu. 
 Sve price ovog tipa neizostavno uporedujem sa Hari Poterom koji je dokaz da se moze napisati roman o grupi dece, odrastanju i tom tinejdzerskom dobu, al tako da u njemu mogu podjednako uzivati i klinci, ali i odrasli, a da im pojedini delovi ne deluju neubedljivo i prazno. 
 Sva ta cudnovata deca su mogla biti predstavljena daleko bolje kao i njihova povezanost, osim odnosa Eme i Dzejkoba autor se nije preterano bavio drugim likovima i njihovim medusobnim odnosima, a imao je prostora za to. Najtuznije mi je sto mi ni taj odnos izmedu Eme i Dzejkoba nije bio nista posebno, s obzirom na njenu proslost sa njegovim dedom bio mi je cak i bezveze. 
 Film mi je takode pokvario utisak o knjigama jer sam ga odgledala nakon sto sam procitala prve dve pa posle nisam imala nesto ni volje da citam poslednji deo. 
 Tim Bartona obozavam i tako sam zeljno iscekivala da se taj film pojavi, a uopste nemam utisak kao da ga je on radio. Poslednjih sat vremena filma sam bila u fazonu "Jel mene neko zajebava", osim maski i scenografije film je potpuno bezvezan. 
 Sve u svemu.. jos jedna fenomenalna ideja za roman, al ne tako uspesno ostvarena.. steta..

THIS BOOK WAS PHENOMENAL! I am SO happy with how this trilogy ended! I picked it up yesterday and read it in about 7-8 hours, including interruptions from dinner and such. I finished it at about 2:30AM and was absolutely mind blown. This trilogy couldn't have ended more perfectly and I highly reccomend this trilogy to those of you who have not read it yet!
I just couldn't finish this. Not only did the writing bug me I don't care for any of the characters. Sigh. I tried.

Library of Souls is a perfect ending to this trilogy. This book finishes the story of Jacob and the peculiar children as they try to rescue Miss Peregrine. The ending I thought was just perfect and wonderful.

Each book in this series is better than the one before. The only "I wish" is that there would be some reference early on to the book before- to help bridge the gap between readings. All in all, excellent!!

How peculiar! And what a beautiful, beautiful ending! I need a sequel, a continuation, or an epilogue, whatever. Perhaps a new series? This story could go on for ever and I'll forever be a sucker for more peculiarities! 
 Please.

I was glad I finished the trilogy so I could see how the characters and story all wrapped up - but this book wasn't my favorite in the series. The writing felt rushed and the story didn't pull me in like the first book did. Several times I considered just skipping to the end. :( But I still love how Riggs splices vintage photos into the narrative - makes the book that much better and so refreshing.
A fine ending to this tale. I love the idea of this trilogy, the time travel and ancient libraries. The description of every loop always pulled me in.

What an amazing, Suspenseful, creepy and Magnificent book... This series was such an exciting suspenseful,adventure. Hope there will be a 4th book, The author can't leave me like this. Gotta have more of these characters and creepy pictures!

An apt ending to a very cool series with a particular audience. While it doesn't have broad appeal it certainly has a cult following. The premise of the story and arc is phenomenal and the incorporation of the photographs is beautifully weaved and while I enjoyed the characters, especially our main one, I wasn't terribly awed by the plot though I was impressed that everything came full circle and the ending was well-plotted.

This was a great end to the trilogy. Honestly, the beginning was a bit slow and took awhile for me to get through, but then I couldn't put it down. We learn more about the peculiars and what exactly is a library of souls. I still adore Jacob and Emma. The hollows and wights still remind me of Bleach, namely because in Bleach hollows become arrancars after consuming enough souls, which is similar to hollows and wights. I found Bentham to be an interesting character, as he's morally ambiguous. He helped them, but betrayed them, and then helped them again. All of the loose ends are tied up. The photographs are spectacular and as peculiar as ever. 
 The ending though. That is a perfect ending right there. That very last line is so simple in its perfection. This was a great book, and I look forward to Riggs' next one! 
 We have time.
It's a drag of a book but I like that it has a nice closure
Video review on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YP25f...

In Library of Souls, the Peculiar Trilogy comes to a well-built end. 
 I have nothing negative to say about this conclusion: it was the perfect climax to one of the most original trilogies I've had the pleasure to read.

This series had it's ups and downs for me. I liked the unique idea of Jacob's ability and some of the other characters, but I just didn't feel like the characters personalities could hold water. There was no getting to know or growth from anyone and Emma's mood swings gave me whiplash. 
 I had a beach vacation while reading this book and was disappointed when I couldn't get into this story. It only picked up a little at the end. I could go on and on, but I don't want to bash this book too much. The third book brought the series overall rating down for me, but the first two books weren't half bad. Overall I'm glad I read this series, that it is now in my "read" shelf, and that it is no longer in my "currently reading" shelf anymore.
A solid close on the series, but book two is still my favorite. It did seem a bit long occasionally...

Another great addition to Riggs' trilogy. The photographs continue to be mysterious and intriguing. The story line moves along with the mystery and also the thriller feel that will keep kids who love strange characters reading on.

book_b.title: Twilight (Twilight, #1)
book_b.user_review:
This book was pretty bad. I will admit, it's the only one in the series that I could stomach reading twice. It was just as bad the second time. Reading this book, I had hope that the characters would develop and become proper characters but that was before reading the rest of the series. There were also problems. 
 A) Vampires don't sparkle. What better way to get your prey to notice you than by going "Hey! over here! I'm in the sparkles! Now run, I'm dangerous, not a walking disco ball!" 
 B) If the relationship between Bella and Edward is so forbidden, why is everyone (minus Rosalie) immediately so accepting of it? 
 C)The characters have the same personality as a piece of cardboard (again minus Rosalie but she was a bitch). 
 D) Edward is an ass. He calls himself a monster but he never actually kills anyone. 
 E) Is it really necessary to separate Bella from her "friends"? Well, yes, if you're a controlling jackassed asshat! 
 F) She was the "mother" in her relationship with her mom? Social services anyone? 
 G) Anyone else notice that she's inconsistently rude to her parents? 
 H) Can one really get dial-up these days? I know I've had slow internet on occasion, but dial-up slow? Not bloody likely! 
 I) Stephanie Meyer really did her research at the same time as Bella? And it still sucked balls? Bitch needs a brain transplant, preferably from someone who can write worth a darn. 
 J) The coolest character is there for only five pages/five minutes. 
 K) If you are what you eat, does this mean Edward is a sissy, ultra-girly girl now? Talk about giving girls a bad name. 
 L) Does Stephanie Meyer realize this trash has actually made women from battered\abused women's shelters want to go back to their abusers because these women were reminded of Edward? This is an incredibly bad thing! It's beyond incredibly bad. Try a disaster! 
 I found the second reading spoiled by the rest of the series. My hopes were dashed and Stephanie Meyer should join the Red Sneaker movement to learn to actually write, but, then again, she'd probably keep writing and it would still be trash or, better yet, emergency toilet paper.

I pretty much read it just to say i read it.... 
 It just added to all my skeptimism... 
 Ive read PLENTY of books better. An okay kinda book. Waste of time i guess...

This was one of the worst things I've ever read. It was laughably bad. And this is coming from someone who has read all of the Vampire Chronicles by Anne Rice. No redeeming features to be found here. I gave it about 50 pages. I pity those who give it more.

I learned that vampires are attracted to clumsy idiots, and that clumsy idiots are attracted to extremely creepy jerks! 
 Blech. Boring story; only the thinnest sliver of plot; puerile writing; a heroine who is a weak and stupid damsel-in-distress cookie-cutter character; completely unmotivated characters. All in all, a perfect example of how NOT to live your life/ handle your relationships/ write a book for teenager girls. 
 That this book has become so popular makes me despair for our next/current generation of women. Seriously, ladies-- go read Jane Eyre or something.

I very much enjoyed this book! I didnt really like the movie however it was quite different from the book. once I started reading I just couldnt put it down. if you have seen the movie and have not read the book, I suggest that you get off your lazy but and read it i give it a ten star!!:)
Vampires do not sparkle. Hate it
I just can't believe that this series is anywhere close to a list of best books of all time. It's insulting really.

Vampires that sparkle? What about exploding into flame in sunlight? And if you can live forever, why the hell would you choose to be in high school, which most of us hated? I rate this book a huge yawn.

Im going to give it two stars because, out of the four books, this one is the best. This one has the original story and, well, if youre into young love and that sort of stuff, this will keep you interested. Also, the vampire is quite a gentleman, thats a plus. Its an OK book.

I don't like romances, and the whole idea of a vampire being totally un-dangerous being the PLOT of the story is just boring. Perhaps if Edward was a more classic vampire that eats flesh and pounces on anything and everything, then perhaps I would have enjoyed this better. One star. Could have done better, Stephenie Meyer...

EUGH. 
 there is no end to how much bad I can say about this book, but what I hated the most was just how badly written it was. 
 I understand that it's YA, but there's no excuse for how simplistic this book is. 
 The characters are obtuse and Bella's only personality traits are "clumsy" and "in love with Edward." She is a perfect example of a Mary Sue protagonist. 
 I just... 
 I can't even think about this book long enough to review it properly.

I'd walked past the book stand in my local supermarket a few times and each time the movie cover of twilight caught my eye (I know, you should never judge a book by its cover but hey, its too late now) and after a couple of weeks my curiosity got the better of me and I ended up buying it and boy, am I glad I did. 
 I was sucked into the story completely and ended up reading it in one sitting. My inner fangirl was definitely jumping for joy! I've always been a sucker for love stories and have always enjoyed delving into fantasy and horror, so this book sort of merged the two. I felt that Bella was easy to relate to in certain aspects and Edward certainly filled the role of the mysterious love interest. 
 I hadn't felt this excited for a book since Harry Potter, and was glad to give my bookworm a jump start back into the reading world.
I was skeptical at first considering that these books were not meant for a twenty something male, but I love it. Its fun.
a really good mental potato chip . . .

Teen-angsty love affair between a sexy, brooding vampire and a smart, loner every-girl? Yes please! Sure it's cheesy and cliche, but it's also entertaining and gratifying. Total guilty pleasure, esp. when I didn't dwell too much on representations of race and gender, didn't read too closely or ask too much from the characters, and did read with an overactive imagination to fill in the gaps. I'll admit it--I can't wait to see the movie.

oh where to even begin? i've read this book 1 and a half times. the half time comes from me trying to read it again, trying to see if maybe i just hated it on principle, nope. i couldn't make it past the first 1/4 of the book. (i didn't even get to vampire baseball! dang!!) so here goes... 
 the characters are horrible. 
 bella is whiny. edward is broody, emo and a stalker. (did i mention he freaking sparkles? what the freak!!) 
 the writing is horrible.

 this book is just horrible.

 if you want a good YA series read Harry Potter. want a good YA/Supernatural series? read The Mortal Instruments. there are so, so many other books out there that are so much better than Twilight! read them :)

I was obsessed with this series in junior high, and then the movies came out and I realized how weak the story actually is. Then I grew up even more and realized how HORRIBLE the story actually is. The only reason any of the books get two stars is because my younger self was quite entertained by them.

Very tween stuff; a fast read for those who can wade 
 thru the odd observations of the clumsy protagonist 
 chick. The only new twist on vampire lore (spoiler 
 alert) is that they glitter in sunlight. The movie 
 was not that off from the book, with the exception 
 that no human actor could ever look as good as 
 described in the prose. Overall: eh. But I'll 
 read the rest just so I don't miss the hype.

Lo dejo en tres porque lo que este libro significo para mi en su momento. Cuando lo lei hace cuatro anos, pasaron muchas cosas. En primer lugar ame la saga, me indujo a escribir, me volvio adicta a la lectura (un gusto que siempre estuvo ahi pero nunca recibio el empuje necesario hasta ese momento) conoci mucha gente maravillosa en el fandom... Sin embargo, anos despues y millones de libros leidos, mis gustos han cambiado y mi percepcion es otra. Los vampiros nunca me gustaron en primer lugar, pero me gustaba esta saga y por eso los vi con otros ojos. Sigo pensando que Eclipse es el mejor libro de la saga, pero hoy dia soy capaz de encontrarle millones de errores, cabos suelos... personajes que me gustaban los veo con otros ojos. Cuatro libros fueron innecesarios, se pudo haber contado todo en dos, maximo y hubiese sido mejor. Me importa un soberano pepino lo que digan por ahi, me gusto mucho y eso nunca lo negare, sin embargo, si hoy dia me ofrecieran un libro de la misma tematica, dudo que me caiga de la misma manera.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Alternately boring and annoying for the first 3/4 of the book. The dramatic tension that finally makes an appearance toward the end has an unsatisfying resolution, as the point of view character is unconscious while the conflict is resolved, and only hears about what happened after the fact. 
 Many of the supporting characters are really intriguing. Sadly, neither the protagonist nor her love interest is.

Well, one of the worst books I've read lately. Such of waste of time. I was just about to say that I just don't get how in the world it became a world success, but then I remembered that human kind is so unpredictable. The book is so boring; the silly story could have been told in 100 pages, but the author decided to torture us with more than 500, full of shallow and repetitive conversations between Bella and Edward. I assume it was aimed to female teenagers who dream about falling in love with a gorgeous and perfect guy, but I wonder if all of those girls think of themselves as Bella does: a silly, insignificant, ugly, unattractive girl. I would expect that an author would show a little bit more affection towards his/her characters, but Mrs Meyer seems to hate Bella. Or is Bella a self projection? My question all along the reading was "Why in the world Edward, as perfect as he is, can fall in love with such a waste?" And why in the world a common girl would fall in love with a vampire, risking her life (which she doesn't seem to really appreciate) in just two ore three days and just because "he is so perfectly handsome"? Isn't that as shallow and stupid as it can be? My God, this is the only case I know in which the movie is much, far better than the book... and I hated the movie! And yes, I know Mrs Meyer is making a lot of money with these books. So are doing drug dealers around the world and they're not making any good either.
Not my usual reading material but found the young adult viewpoint intriguing

Honestly, I was a little disappointed after all the hype. By the end of the book I was fed up with the relationship between Bella & Edward, even feeling saddened & disappointed that the author made Bella such a co-dependent, weak young woman. She is certainly not a role model for the millions of pre-teens reading this. Edward comes into her room and watches her sleep, eavesdrops on all of her conversations, threatens her life daily, and she just sucks it right up. In real life, she'd be looking for a restraining order. It is sad that she is willing to give up her life & family for him without even looking back. Also, a little sickened by the fact that she panics every time he leaves the room. And jeez, with all of that, they're not even having sex! I did read it quickly and turn through the pages as I had heard I would, but I'm not really inclined to read the other 3 books and feel I'd be just as happy to have someone fill me in on what happens.

I just picked this book (just before its movie release) out of curiosity. I wonder why everybody is very crazy about this book and I had that urge to find it out myself. But after reading the book, i told myself that it was just an OK book. I somewhat felt that it was over rated.
Loved the characters, loved the fantasy. Team Jacob;)

Read the whole book one day while I stayed home sick from school. 
 I should have just slept.
I gave it a chance I can't say I liked it. it just wasn't my cup of tea.

This over-hyped and over-discussed book is pretty terrible. It's not that Edward is a misogynist or that Bella is a loser of a "heroine." And let's not even get into the reasons why this should not be a teenage girl's idea of a perfect relationship. 
 No, the problem with the Twilight series is that Stephenie Meyer is a truly horrendous "writer." 
 This is a prime example: 
 "I quickly rubbed my hand across my cheek and sure enough, traitor tears were there, betraying me." - Bella, p. 90 
 However, unless you want to be an outcast in middle/high school/college/the office, you probably need to read this book so you can form your own opinion and keep the conversation going when the weirdo in the skirt-suit and Team Jacob shirt in the cubicle next to you starts in on the subject.
I couldn't make it past the second chapter. This book is absolutely horrendous.

Drama, Stalking, Emotional Abuse, Intimidation, Saying Who Your Spouse Can and Can't Hang Out With, and Dying Without the Other Person... etc... etc... 
 This series has all the elements of an abusive relationship! Congratulations Stephanie Meyer... What does it really matter though, right? It's only young impressionable minds reading this garbage. Our youth are going to have a hard time determining what a normal relationship is even considered.

Read this so that I would be able to speak knowledgeably with students about it. I can see why young girls are drawn to this story, but I personally have concerns with the obsessive nature of the Edward/Bella relationship. The book provides parents with a good discussion with their daughters about what IS love... and what they see in this book? It isn't love

I couldn't put it down when I began reading this book. The subject is interesting: vampire and campus romance. Especially the latter, the author has wonderful writing skills in describing the mental working of a 17-year-old girl. 
 I sort of didn't want the early stages of the romance to end. I knew there would be some violence. Vampires were living there anyway, there had to be some bad guys to fight. 
 I was not surprised to find out later that the violence part was less thrilling than the romance part.

My god!! What a horribly written book. The level of english was pathetic, the story line was very interesting though. I prefer watching the movie of course but what a waste of my precious time. This book is ideal for 12 - 14 year olds only. 
 Did not even complete this book! LOL!
Why boher? This is a teen romance book... lots of longing glances and heavy sighs...

The Twilight books were the type of amusement, I needed at a very busy and stressfull time, but I doubt I will read the books again. It is no great litterature nor future classic, nor a story that would be interestning the second time you read it. 
 When all that is said, I have to confess, that I enjoyed the four books about the grat love story between Bella and Edward. It's an exciting story, it's interesting, the passion and love are all-consuming and the danger is always present. 
 When reading the books, you have to remind yourself, that they are young adult books and you have to leave all your usual litterary criteria behind - beacuse Twilight is a young adult series, and you can't expect nothing but just that! And with that knowledge in mind, I think the books are great! 
 All in all - great for young adults and good entertainment for the rest of us.

Mesmerizing! I forgot how fun it was to pick up a book that you really didn't want to put down...and I was so pulled in that I finished the entire series over the next couple days. 
 Before I started reading I was put off by the subject matter, I love fantasy, but falling in love with a vampire...please. And yet, Twilight started out so human and high school. New girl, normal insecurities, regular high school concerns. Then we meet Edward and I was just as fascinated by him as Bella was. I loved the tension, the danger and the dialogue of their relationship. I really enjoyed this book!
I loved it.

Is it me or this book too dull for words? Or maybe I am just to cyncial and bitter to enjoy it ... Officially stopped caring and will be donating this and volumes 2 and 3 to the Library. I may need to add a note: dear reader, not all men want to suck the life out of you ... don't use this book as a guide for your future boyfriends.
1.5 stars.
Much better than I remembered. Appreciate more now I'm older.

I stayed up very late to finish this book. There are only a handful of books that I read in under a week or in the span of a few days- and this one was one of them. 
 And then after I finished the other two books currently out I re-read this one in the same month. Safe to say I really like this. Mad Props Stephenie Meyers

I didn't really have much interest in this series, but I decided to see what all the fuss was about, and what fun it was! There's nothing like your first love, but adding the human/immortal twist makes it interesting. This was also an interesting take on vampires, not exactly going against all myths, but explaining why they exist.

Given this book as a gift. 
 Shoot me if I ever pick it up and read it again. 
 Got maybe about 3/4 of the way through it. Characters were vapid, and childish.

Thanks Miriam for the recommendation - it's always somewhat insightful to read what many girls in my World Lit class are reading. I can't say I really loved it though. It was a fun read - I stayed up to 4am this morning to finish the thing. (I wish WW2 history books had the same effect on me and I wouldn't be so behind in my grad reading.) But I didn't feel like there was anything too complex about the book. I think I remember a time in my life when the "way-too-obsessed-about-a-boy" theme really struck a chord, but at this point it became a bit annoying. And the whole adolescent awkwardness, fitting in at high school stuff got a little tired for me. The end of the book was probably the best part - lots of action, some good vampire bits. Overall I enjoyed the book - it provided a nice break from heavy, dense text, but I'm not going to read the next one in the series until Winter Break because I can ill-afford to burn through two nights that should have been devoted to history. It sure was nice though!

** spoiler alert ** 
 The fact that so many millions of people have read this story leaves me to wonder a bit about the human race. What bugs me even more are the people that want to read about "strong heroines" and still adore this novel. 
 Bella Swan is truly the weakest wimpyest heroine I've had the misfortune to read about. From the start of the novel she makes no sense. Her family life with both parents is utterly ridiculous, and the fact that Stephanie Meyer chooses not to explain why she's gone to live with her father, Charlie in Forks until the story is about a quarter of the way in, just proves what a lousy storyteller she is. 
 Then there's the fact that Bella doesn't quite grasp vampires. Now I know this is fiction, but its present day fiction, where people have heard of vampires, mummies and the holy ghost. How does she not understand in the least about Edward's hunger and why she might be in danger from it? 
 I find very little about Bella to endear her to me. Mostly I just want to punch her in the face. I was actually cheering for the tracker vampire at the end to finish her off, but I knew it would never happen what with 3 more books in the series ahead. 
 And then there's Edward. Perhaps if I could see the real attractivenes in the actor, which so many find sexy I could understand Edward's appeal on paper. But that said I can't. He's a stalker! And he talks down to Bella the whole time, though that's understandable, because Bella begs for it. 
 She's the classic dutiful woman..cooking for her father, obeying Edward most of the time and generally being disgustingly docile. 
 Oh and then there's the whole Cullen clan, denying their existence as vampires for the most part. Why does every vampire not want to feed on the human race! Dammit that's what they are supposed to do. And the sparkly vampire shit is damn damn annoying. Turn into dust please!! 
 If this sage (melodrama) weren't the most popular piece of tripe out now, I would seriously say that only the tweens would find it enjoyable. I'm not sure how to explain off the adults that bought into this, except that years of reality tv have turned so many brains to mush.

I remember when Twilight first came out. Suddenly, everyone hated it. It was sexist! It encouraged domestic violence! I saw the movie a few years ago and didn't think much of it. 
 I read a few pages of the book back in 2012, but couldn't get past my own prejudices. So when I found a free copy of Twilight a month ago, I was determined to read it and decide for myself. Was it really as bad as people were saying? Surely I could be open-minded. 
 So, here's my review. As far as books go, it's not so bad. It's a Young Adult book. The main character is a high school girl, and the book laboriously details everything from homeroom to gym class to the final bell at the end of the day. Will Edward be in school that day? What will Bella's friends discuss at lunch? And so on. I give the author credit for making it seem like the life of a high school student. I know when I wrote Deathskull Bombshell, I was guilty of the same mistake a lot of TV screenwriters make - writing the high schoolers like college students (see also Dawson's Creek, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, etc). So it's nice to see a book written about a normal person who goes through normal everyday things. I would call this a slice-of-life book if it didn't have the supernatural vampire elements. 
 One problem with this book? It's really, really slow. I got about halfway through and then gave up. The plot sort of drags on. Entire conversations are written in great detail, even when they seem not to have much relevance to the plot. I quickly saw a pattern of Edward taking Bella out so Bella could grill him with questions about his mysterious life, which is cool if you like chaste interrogation scenes, but even the ridiculousness of this book or the twee baby cuteness of Jacob Black couldn't save it. 
 I tried, I really did. 
 Personally, I feel that all this hate for Twilight is unwarranted. While I'm not a big fan of the book, I don't see much a point of griping about it either (except in this book review, lol). Some of the Twilight haters are just as enthusiastic, if not more so, than the Twilight lovers. I don't find it especially sexist. It's a book about a girl who reads a lot. Her reading list includes, what, Jane Eyre? Sense and Sensibility? The author obviously wanted to write a character that appealed to nerdy girls who felt they were plain-looking and wanted an imaginary superhero boyfriend to whisk them off their feet. I see no shame in that. 
 I also feel that the people who are complaining that Twilight encourages domestic abuse aren't giving young people enough credit. Most kids, once they reach a certain age, are able to distinguish between fantasy and reality. I watched Aaah! Real Monsters a lot as a kid, but I knew it was fake. Because I wasn't a dummy. I think (I hope) the vast majority of today's youth know vampires aren't real and no vampire is going to date them. And while the commandeering presence and dominant personality of Edward Cullen might be a concern, let's pause and remember: this is a vampire we are talking about here, and no matter how "pretty boy" they are written in this book, they still have to have some "creepy Lothario" qualities in order to seduce their victims and suck their blood. This whole book is basically about a vegetarian who suddenly craves meat, told from the point-of-view of a strip of bacon. 
 That's my review. :P Thanks.

This book just sucked me in. I liked the characters and the plot moved quickly. I thought that Bella's clumsiness was played up a bit too much and Edward was a bit too perfect, but I liked them both anyway. Meyer's did a great job of making it seem perfectly possible that a family of vampires could be living in a small town. I can't wait to start the second one. Sometimes, you can't beat a good romance novel!

Anyone who compares this to the Harry Potter series is unequivocally not my friend. 
 I get the allegory between teenage hormones and vampires' desire for blood. It is a somewhat interesting premise but NOT at all a clever microcosm of fantasy in the way Harry Potter is. It is like a Sweet Valley High novel except the popular high school hunk happens to be an amiable nocturnal beast. Precisely HALF of the book is about how dreamy Edward Cullen is. I sort of want to finish the series out of sheer morbid curiosity but dammit life is too short to read bad books. 
 I can understand why it is a teenage phenomenon but NOT at all why it is an adult phenomenon. I feel like I just drank an entire gallon of Capri Sun.

Yes, I liked it. Other people's reviews are fun to read though, because it's such a mix bag. I read the book for pleasure and it was entertaining. Besides, my teenage daughter thinks its cool I read it and we can have interesting discussions.
A perfect summer read. A humorous and fun look at vampires in a Northwest community.

Goodreads needs a sixth star - "HATED IT". Or, if they need to be nice to the authors, "hated it". "Didn't like it" is so much nicer than this book deserves. 
 Horrible writing, boring and dim characters, and vampires that sparkle. 
 I tried writing a review where I didn't rant about how abusive the relationship is between Edward and Bella, and I couldn't. Ignoring the actual vampire bits (because Edward is just...NO. Across the board NO.), the romance is non-existent and bland. The only chemistry between these two people lies in looks and smell. Oh, and the fact that Edward wants Bella's blood. 
 Props to Meyer for getting people to read and putting a new, albeit horrendous and somewhat hilarious, spin on vampires. But that's all I can thank her for. 
 I'll read the the other books in the series one day, mainly because I need to know how much worse this train wreck gets before it's over. I definitely won't be paying for them, however. These types of books are why libraries exist.

reference_books.title: Crave (Fallen Angels, #2)
reference_books.review_text: So I REALLY like JR Ward's other story lines for the most part (The King excepted), but I just can't get into this series and won't even finish this book. The language - the slang, the abbreviations, the use of unnecessary expressions - is all very distracting. Forget pulling me out of the story - I couldn't get into the story long enough to care. I don't understand the story line either - Devina didn't show up until quite a ways in, and then not to harm the subject of the story, but to torture Jim. By the time I gave up she still hadn't even connected with Isaac. Aren't they supposed to be fighting over him? How can you fight over someone when you haven't even met them? I did appreciate that the human female was intelligent and capable, and didn't want to go straight to "I want to have your babies" the second she sleeps with her guy. Nor do I get the point of being an angel.... We don't spend enough time learning about what an angel is in this world.

reference_books.title: Bite Me (A Love Story, #3)
reference_books.review_text: Gave upon it.... Couldn't get past the valley-speak.

reference_books.title: Pale Demon (The Hollows, #9)
reference_books.review_text: I suppose I shouldn't have read this one first - should have started with the first in the series. Too many unexplained characters and story-lines. Too long. Didn't really care about the main character, who couldn't seem to make up her mind about anything.

reference_books.title: World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War
reference_books.review_text: Only took a day to read, because I ended up skipping most of it. No way to emotionally invest in a series of disjointed "here's what happened to me" reports. The only thing that was moderately interesting was the introduction of a few interesting survival techniques, but since they weren't created by or used to save any characters I cared about, they were only moments of interest, lost in the multitude of "maybe this next report will be more interesting..." I have no idea how they're going to make a movie out of this.

reference_books.title: The Forest of Hands and Teeth (The Forest of Hands and Teeth, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Enjoyed this and have just realized there are more, so I will read those. The one frustrating thing about this one is the dichotomy between the main character's overwhelming internal fear (which appears to be near-paralyzing) and the way in which others perceive her.

reference_books.title: Tears of Tess (Monsters in the Dark, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Made me angry; stopped reading it. Found the subject matter to character development ratio not worth it.

reference_books.title: Fallen (Fallen, #1)
reference_books.review_text: A frustrating read. Lots of hype, so I wanted to check it out. A YA novel, which already makes me bored. A storyline that isn't clear, and which takes forever to start unravelling. And when it finally does start getting some action, it's unclear exactly what is happening, why, and who the players actually are. I know there are others in this series, but frankly, Scarlett...

reference_books.title: Linger (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I don't really see why this needed to be a YA series - hard to imagine teenagers being so self-aware as to be able to deal with the issues in this series in any reasonably adult way. Enjoyed the writing, though.

reference_books.title: The Hypnotist (Joona Linna, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Confusing.... Whose perspective was I supposed to identify with? The time frames jumped around in contradiction to the chapter titles. Why two story lines? It just felt like they were forced together without a natural connection. I felt lost about half-way though.

reference_books.title: Rooms
reference_books.review_text: Couldn't finish - couldn't get through all of the points of view.....

book_a.title: Committed: A Skeptic Makes Peace with Marriage
book_a.user_review: When I married, I did so because I "had to" (moving to another country and couldn't take him with unless we were married); but we had been happily living together for years, and I had never wanted to get married at all. Ever. I have never wanted children (ever), and I did not want to sacrifice my own identity into a couple. I had no role models of what a good marriage looks like - only ones where the parties turned each other into bitter, angry people. I went into it with very bad grace. I wore black, insisted on no rings or flowers and didn't invite any family, just two very close friends to be the witnesses. Now, 25 years after the marriage, I still love my husband more than anything in the world, and cannot imagine life without him. But I still don't want to be "married". I still just want to live with him as we did before. At this point, though, what am I complaining about? Since I have absolutely no intention or desire to leave him, what's the difference? I'm in, whether married or not. I see people every day who have been married 50, 60 or even 70 years in my work, and cannot grasp how they do it. I don't know how to reconcile these feelings, but maybe, as Ms. Gilbert suggests, I am not alone, nor do I actually **have** to reconcile these feelings. An interesting and (for me) comforting read. Only three stars because I can't identify with all the travelling and rootlessness the author seems to need.

sample_reviews.review_text: High expectations for Gilberts' follow up. Not what I expected and felt she was over-thinking and over-writing at times. She wanted it to be SO good and it was meh. I'd like her to release a work of fiction as her short stories from earlier in her career were exceptional.

Ok, so if you saw my review of Eat Prey Love you are probably wondering why would I even consider picking up the sequel to a book a gave such an average rating. 
 Well, I was in a (so long it was years) reading slump and this was on my sister's shelf. Again, as I said in the aforementioned review, I was starting to get back into reading for pleasure so instead of going crazy on what to buy I decided to pick whatever was close by. 
 I may or may not pick up more of Elizabeth Gilbert's books, since her writing is good and compelling, but my problem with this and Eat, Pray, Love lays in the topics and characters (and yes I know is a memoir). 
 To make this story short, 2.5/5 rating and mostly because I appreciated her research of marriage in different cultures, but that was about it.

I love listening to Gilbert narrate her autobiographical work. I decided to read this one this week after learning that the reason she separated from her husband was that she fell in love with her best friend and decided to live out the rest of her life--she has cancer--as partners. 
 While I do not doubt that Gilbert loved the man who became her husband, this book made me wonder if she was in love with him. After all, what lies between its pages is a persuasive essay to herself.
