 In the memoir Committed: A Skeptic Makes Peace with Marriage, Elizabeth Gilbert approaches the topic of matrimony from a variety of angles: historical, sociological, psychological, and emotional. The idea behind the book holds promise, particularly in a time when marriage is scrutinized and on the cusp of evolution. Unfortunately, Gilbert never makes sense of all the facts and views she collects, and the book leaves the author confused and readers unfulfilled. 
 When the United States Department of Homeland Security denies her Brazilian lover and life partner access into the country, Gilbert must reexamine their relationship. Until that point, the two had maintained a fulfilling but unconventional relationship that satisfied their desire for companionship and independence. As survivors of painful and tedious divorces, the two had mutually rejected the concept of marriage altogether. In Gilbert's words, "We had sworn with all our hearts to never, ever, under any circumstances, marry." Faced with the choice of legal commitment or separation, they reluctantly agree to wed. 
 Playing off the momentum of her well-received 2006 book, Eat, Pray, Love, her latest account follows a similar formula. Anticipating the lengthy legal process before them and unable to be together in the United States, the couple travels through Australia and Southeast Asia. Gilbert capitalizes on this experience by interviewing women she meets in her travels on the topic of marriage, and she combines these first-hand accounts with research into the history of marriage as she attempts to make sense of a concept she wholly rejects. 
 One cannot fault the author for her skepticism. With outrageous divorce rates and the changing landscape of relationships, many question whether marriage is still an essential function of our culture. Historically, men and women took vows out of economic necessity or religious obligation. As Gilbert points out, today we benefit from more social, financial, and spiritual freedoms. Why, then, are we still choosing marriage? 
 Gilbert seeks not only clarity but also reassurance, claiming, "This entire book--every single page of it--has been an effort to search through the complex history of Western marriage until I could find some small place of comfort in there for myself." Fair enough. Where Gilbert struggles, however, is creating a story meaningful enough for an audience. 
 In fact, the author admits she wrote the book for 27 women in her life, including her stepdaughter, mother, and friends. She spends much of the book airing her views on companionship, marriage, and motherhood, much like one would vent frustrations to a close friend. More than once, she admittedly falls into rants. At times, her arguments produce thought-provoking and interesting points for the reader's consideration. A bride-to-be could benefit from contemplating a personal definition of marriage based on Gilbert's research of wedlock throughout history and cultures. However, many of the author's ramblings come off as self-indulgent tirades. 
 For example, Gilbert's diatribe on motherhood comes across as unbalanced and unnecessary. Though not a mother herself, she conveys the strain motherhood places on women. By divulging the personal sacrifices made by her mother and grandmother in the name of family, Gilbert resolves that an independent career woman like herself might better fill the role of "auntie." The entire section, though, feels like an excuse for Gilbert to justify her choice to remain childless and adds little to the overall discussion on matrimonial commitment: 
 I can see where I have been vital sometimes as a member of the Auntie Brigade... there are people I've been able to help, sometimes fully supporting them for years, because I am not obliged, as a mother would be obliged, to put all my energies and resources into the full-time rearing of a child... thereby freeing up resources to spread more widely across the community. In this way, I, too, foster life. 
 The lack of authority and reliability from the author detracts from the more interesting features of the book, such as the conversations with married women from different cultural backgrounds. She only scratches the surfaces with her interviews and then quickly drops the subject, as if she doesn't know how to process the information. Gilbert readily admits that she is not a "professional academic, nor a sociologist, nor a psychologist, nor an expert on marriage." The jumbled facts and figures presented throughout the book are interesting bits of trivia but also incomplete. For all her rants, interviews, and research, Gilbert achieves no clarity. She remains a skeptic until the end and concludes that marriage has changed throughout history and the dynamics of commitment differ between every couple. It required a journey throughout foreign lands and a year's worth of research to reach such an ironically noncommittal conclusion? 
 In Eat, Pray, Love, Gilbert inspired readers by emotionally connecting with them through her personal triumphs and losses. In Committed, her constant bellyaching and condescending attitude distance her from the audience and bury the smattering of noteworthy discourse. By the end of the book, readers will feel more sympathy for her patient husband than the confused and pessimistic Gilbert. Perhaps the book should have stayed between the 27 intended readers because it ultimately offers little wisdom or weight for an audience at large.

Its amazing how much I liked Eat Pray Love and do not like this book. It is self-indulgent about whether or not she is going to marry the guy she meets at the end of the first book. In between the self-indulgent scenes is really well written research on marriage that was written in the most boring way possible.
Slow read. I liked her as an author but enjoyed "Eat, Pray, Love" much better!

hm - langweilig - nur was fur historische anthropologie fans :) 
 wo sie doch an sich so nett und und lustig schreibt- und dann aber uber mist :( sie sollte in zukunft romantic comedies schreiben oder so :)

I will admit I picked this up because I read Eat Pray Love but I didn't enjoy it as much. It is mostly about her. How she feels about getting married and her troubles with immigration etc. Sometimes she goes on and on. There is only so much one can listen to someone else who is not in your inner circle complain and whine. Her "interviews" on marriage with south Asians is some what interesting but not sure how it relates to her which is what the narrative is about. It gets better as it goes when she includes information on marriage. I say it is ok if you skip chunks of it where she rattles on. Her other novel was about her but at least there is an escape from average life fantasy. This one seems better suited to a blog.
Seriously.

I really wanted to like this book since I enjoyed her earlier, "Eat, Pray, Love" and Brent liked "An American Man". However, I found it plodding and self-absorbed. Instead of meaningful insights into her conflict regarding marriage, Gilbert comes off as whiny and immature. This book was difficult to get through - I started and stopped a few times- and the history interspersed with personal vignettes was dry and boring. It felt as though because Gilbert ended "Eat" happily unmarried, she needed to write a book to justify her later decision - based on legal necessity - to get married. A big disappointment!
Started reading this book but couldn't get into it - will try again another time
What an exercise in over-thinking. I appreciate the concept, and I did enjoy reading it (at times), but it mostly seemed self-congratulatory and self-involved. Nowhere near as good as Eat Pray Love.

I read this book about 2 years ago and still think of its passages often. The journey of Elizabeth Gilbert is authentic, which is perhaps why I gravitated to it. It may also be because I, too, have often wondered what makes marriage official. She researches in much the same way I do, scouring the internet, buying random books and videos, and talking with other people. If you, too, wonder about the history of marriage and are curious about one woman's journey to find out it's meaning throughout history so she can make peace with the institution on her own terms, this book is definitely worth a read.
I enjoyed this as a 'research' into the concept of marriage as well as her take on it, modern life etc etc. Not for everyone.
Perhaps a bit more relevant for people actually contemplating marriage.

This was not a good story. The problem is that Elizabeth and her partner both DO NOT want to get married yet they have to because of immigration laws. That is the first problem- forcing two people to do something they don't want to is going to end badly. The second problem is that she is somehow convinced that she can demand unbelievably high expectations of the man she marries and the type of relationship they have. She openly admits she will not settle and has crazy ideas of how a relationship must be perfect or not at all. That is part of the reason she got divorced and *spoiler* eventually left 'Philipe' for a woman. 
 Anyone who is married or enters into a committed, long term relationship knows that you must be willing to accept the ordinary. Asking for perfection from your partner is insane and that's her problem. Elizabeth goes around the world asking friends and different cultures about marriage and basically why they chose to get married to somehow convince herself they are all 100% happy. Soon she realizes the truth- no one is 100% happy but that's life. Even her parents, who had a strained relationship, were not totally satisfied but they chose to make it work. That is what a relationship is and how you will survive marriage- you have to work at it and you have to admit and accept marriage is hard work. If you demand high expectations that are so unrealistic as to be laughable (the children narrative and how women must give up their careers or have kids, they cannot do both), marriage probably isn't for you. 
 Seeing her point of view, it's no surprise both marriages didn't work out for her- she was not able to make peace with the fact that life is made up of ordinary and mundane and accept the fact that is ok.
this book has received really bad reviews, but I loved Eat, Pray, Love, so i gave it a chance. About halfway through - very interesting concept, and quite a decent book on the concept of marriage.
Just get on with it and get married already...sheesh!!!

I know that I should not compare this book to Eat, Pray, Love yet we know its kind of inevitable.. Considering the fact they are tied so closely together. Im not sure exactly what I was expecting, but by the end of this book I wanted to throw it across the room... Perhaps that is just me in my naive singleness, but I pretty much did not want her to marry Felipe, if she thought it was going to be such a miserable experience. I think its very rare in these days that people have fairy tale ideas of marriage, many of us know that it is destined to be atleast a challenge from the start.. but seriously this book was depressing. It felt like such an agenda was being pushed, I was very dissappointed. Often I find it hard to criticize a book because you are in fact criticizing the writer, who has invested so much of their time and life... Perhaps someone who has been through a divorce might see this book in a totally different light, but in my never having been married I found the book quite negative.
Reading this kind of felt like being married for 10+ years: Mostly boring, often irritating, and occasionally baffling as to why you even bother.
Amazing. Just so feminist and intimate and real . . . so much of this book spoke to me (and I'm pretty picky about which books I say this of) and I would recommend it to EVERYONE.

Told with Gilbert's trademark wit, intelligence and compassion, Committed attempts to "turn on all the lights" when it comes to matrimony, frankly examining questions of compatibility, infatuation, fidelity, family tradition, social expectations, divorce risks and humbling responsibilities.

I hate to say it, but I really did not enjoy this book! I have never not been able to finish a book, so this is a first. I read about a quarter of the book and had to put it down. I was so thoroughly bored by it. I enjoyed Eat, Pray, Love enough so I figured this book would be a decent follow up and I was excited and happily anticipating to see how Felipe and Elizabeth were doing. I knew they had decided to get married because of Felipe's immigration status and it seemed maybe Elizabeth would get a second chance at happily ever after, and I was excited to read about their possible union. But instead I was reading about all the many cultural differences in weddings and marriages. Which would have been fine for several pages, but Elizabeth kept going on and on, page after page. It began to feel like a research paper instead of a book. 
 When I finally put it down I figured I just needed a break and would pick it back up and read it later. Unfortunately everytime I thought about reading it again I would start to cringe. There are just too many other books out there to read so I have to pass on Committed.

I'm not sure what to think of this memoir, written by the author of "Eat, Pray, Love." In one regard, Gilbert has an easy way with words. Her writing is conversational and personal, which makes you feel very included in the discussion. She also is adept at mixing history and HER-story (ha ha ha Gilbert, you're not the only one who can make corny jokes...) 
 However, I can't detect if there's any truth in her representation of the history of marriage, or is it just random facts she's picked up without any formal literature review? When she opens the memoir with facts about how marriage has evolved over time, she claims 'South Indian brothers share the same bride', yet this is so untrue (...it may be true in ONE particular small sect, but to generalize it as a South Indian tradition without any further explanations is ignorant and inaccurate). Everything that followed made me skeptical about the stats and factual information. 
 Another criticism is her condescending attitude, which comes out during her so called 'keen' observations. For example, while she thinks she's being open-minded, so LIBERAL!, and non-judgmental, her description of her Laos driver's 'poor' hut was unbelievably patronizing. She thinks she's so worldly because she's traveled everywhere, but her attitude is that of a privileged American: "Look at that cute, oh-so-delightful little straw hut! How precious!" 
 I gave it three stars: it's interesting to read about Gilbert's perspective, but I wouldn't take her discourse as the last word on the institution of marriage.

I think there is probably a context in which I would have enjoyed this book much more. For instance, if I were dating or engaged and giving the whole "should I get married" question a lot of thought. However, in the context of my current life, this book did very little for me. It is dissatisfying as a non-fiction study of marriage (very journalism-lite) and as a memoir (a bit of a yawner). After the initial set-up, I found myself reading just so I could finish it- never a good sign. Definitely a let-down after "Eat, Pray, Love," which I admit to enjoying quite a bit.
This was the best book I've read in a long time--personal, insightful and full of historical facts about the institution of marriage.

Bad... plain bad. what a cheesy, insecure, self centered little drama queen juvenile who shamelessly dares to write a book about sth that even an average american teenage would be ashamed to write on her blog... get over yourself, seriously! 
 also, what an appalingly western/american centered judgmental, colonialist mind! the passages that she is talking about the marriages in other cultures are no different from the mentality of the first colonialists; otherising and assuming that the world she belongs is better. the parts she talks about vietnam, it is so patronising she could also write it in the format of a diary of a 19th century anthropologist who is observing the "savage" or "uncivilised" people!!! 
 you are neither an anthropologist/sociologist, nor a historian. you are just a bitter divorcee and not an authority to talk about these things. 
 can i go puke now?
Not that engaging. I was lulled into reading this book because I enjoyed Eat, Pray, Love so much. It wasn't bad, I was just not that into it.
I couldn't finish this. It was equal the rating of EPL and I feel I was generous with my rating when it could have had one star.

I couldn't finish this book. The bookmark is set on page 185 and I just can't keep reading. 
 I read Gilbert's Eat Pray Love awhile back and loved it. I was excited when Gilbert wrote another book - I figured it would be a continuation of her previous stories, adventures, and travels. I was sort of right, but mostly wrong. 
 Committed does continue where Eat Pray Love left off. It is somewhat the story of Elizabeth and Felipe and their decision to get married. But really, this book is an essay of the history of marriage. And frankly, it's a boring essay. I mean, yeah, I learned some interesting tidbits in the 185 pages I read about our traditions of marriage, but I didn't quite feel like reading a history/sociology paper. 
 Gilbert is not an expert on marriage. Her first failed and she had no intention of entering the second except for immigration reasons. And that's fine. Her relationship issues aren't what I'm judging. But her writing a book about marriage when she is no expert in the subject was dull.

I feel like I made a friend with Elizabeth Gilbert, the kind where you get blackout drunk and feel like you understand everything about each other, but years later it might be that you had similar circumstances or were both buried under heartbreak. Ergo, I felt like I saw my old friend at a party and she made no sense and got boring. My brain relates to her difficulty committing and is very happy for her and Filipe and hopes they work it out. My heart wants to get in a spiteful argument about denying tradition blah blah blah and then tell her we're not friends anymore and why can't we just go get drinks???????? Why would you think your grandmother was happier with a nice coat and being some rich woman's assistant than raising a family? Fuck nice coats. Fuck planning parties. Fuck being a waitress in Montana, it's not that amazing. 
 See? I just miss her. Don't read this if you're single. She glosses over people who don't have her dilemma, but duh I guess. This is a book about marriage. It should be presented next to a book about how hard it is to be rich and another one about how hard it is to have such a clear purpose in life by a troll who says "choose your poison."

Don't bother. So sad and disappointing after her book Eat,Pray,Love. 
 It seems as if it was just time to write a book so she hurried and picked a subject which she knew nothing about, asked some villiagers for their opinion and called it a book. 
 Our book group disliked it so much that three did not show because they didn't like it enough to get through it. I read it and dreaded it. 
 Read something else.

Elizabeth Gilbert is my best friend, or would be if I knew her! I can't tell you how much I loved this book, maybe even as much as EAT PRAY LOVE, although you can read from the other reviews how totally different it is. 
 Maybe because my life somewhat parallels hers and she and I think so similarly, or maybe just because I love her style of personal narrative or maybe because I love learning about history through literature and essays and art, but this book was hard for me to put down. I wish I had read it before my marriage last year, just for the extra confirmation it would have provided. 
 Who should read this? Everyone contemplating marriage... heck, anyone in a marriage. Enjoy!

I love Liz but I think the reason this book didn't do it for me was because it was all about Marriage. I thought maybe i would have enjoyed it more than I did. Oh well.... EPL is still my top book EVER.... :)

After reading about this story in Gilbert's Big Magic, I thought the concept sounded great and immediately requested it. I was disappointed when I picked up the book. The idea is great but it falls flat. The actual story drags on too long and Gilbert's interviews and research at times take away from the story.

Not a favourite. It is amazing that an author assumes we should be so interested in her personal struggle to accept marrying a second time. Most of what she "researches" is not new. The amusing thing is that it is the good old Department of Homeland Security that forces the couple to marry in order to stay in the US.

Gilbert's writing style is very conversational, which is a style that usually bothers me. But not in this case. Maybe because the topics interest me: both the history/institution of marriage and a single woman's struggle to decide whether to continue living her life as a legally single person or as a legally married person are issues consistently on my mind. Her story is compelling, accessible, and hopeful. I don't know if I'll ever find my Felipe, but I'd like to think that I know my heart and mind, as well as have the strength of character to make a lifelong commitment if/when I do find him. 
 If you liked Eat, Pray, Love you will probably like this one. If you didn't like Eat, Pray, Love you might like this one. Might depend on how you feel about marriage.

So wow - Liz is getting married. So, what does she do? She writes a book to try and figure out the conventional wisdom. 
 Totally hokey and totally awesome. Her research doesn't reveal anything earthshattering, but her insights are great food for thought. My favorites are the brigade of aunties or sparents (childless women) and the commentary around cheating. Good cocktail conversation. 
 But on a more serious note. The book isn't a search for "why" or "why should I" and it barely touches on her relationship with this seemingly dreamy Phillipe. It's more about her coming to peace with the fact that marriage is what you make of it, and not all marriages are the same. And that seems like a very valid conclusion.

I'm sorry, Elizabeth Gilbert, that I wanted a repeat of the swirling storm and whirly dreamery of Eat, Pray, Love. But I did, and this book far from completed me! 
 I am a little puzzled, still, on the premise of the book. I understand it, but it was piecemeal and sludgy. 
 Well, I will look forward to the movie version of Eat Pray Love and pretend that was the next book effort instead. Then you will still be a modern romantic goddess to me.

I never quit books. I could name every book I didn't finish. There are two...now three. I was just not engaged at all. It felt like a lecture but just didn't bring the info to life for me. Maybe it's because I never read Eat, Pray, Love. I felt like there was very little that helped me feel engaged in their struggle. This book as a stand alone dies little to help you feel invested and get to know Gilbert and her partner.
I read this for book club. It's not something I ever would've picked up on my own. I loved it though. Funny and interesting.

page 180 of the large print edition... interesting that as marriage becomes an institution based in romantic love rather than merely a means to achieving social order, it is increasingly fragile (divorce rate goes up)... not much introspection yet....

I gave up on listening to this book when I realized that what begins as a self-indulgent story about why and how she and her lover had to get a "green-card" marriage after being avowed anti-marriage people, then morphs into a history of marriage around the world, a subject I'm not all that interested in. 
 I didn't like "Eat Pray Love" unlike seemingly everybody else in the world, so it probably makes sense I wouldn't like this even less-interesting book. 
 I guess I'm tired of books that are written for the sake of writing another book. It just felt like, OK, I wrote a book about getting divorced and traveling. Now I'm getting married so I'll write about that. Who cares. Not me.

I loved Elizabeth Gilbert's, Eat, Pray, Love. When I decided to read Committed, I went into it with high hopes that Elizabeth had moved on and was happy again. But, I literally could not get through the first few chapters so I didn't even finish the book. 
 I guess I was looking for a great follow-up to Eat, Pray, Love...it just wasn't in Committed.

I thought this book was better than the reviews I saw before reading it. It isn't on my list of books to pick up and re-read when I'm bored, but it was well written and the continuation of Ms. Gilbert's personal story. Anyone expecting the highs and lows of Eat, Pray, Love will likely be disappointed, but that doesn't mean it isn't good!

2 and a half. After Eat, Pray, Love, I suppose it was tough to come close in a second book. I enjoyed the histories and philosophies of marriage across the ages, but I found her extreme reluctance and ambivalence to get married got old after a few hundred pages.

I didn't read "Eat, Prey, Love". At first, I thought, "Wow, I must have been really busy this past week - I didn't read at all." But then I realized I was avoiding reading because I didn't want to read this. I made it through the first chapter (maybe) before setting it down & deciding that I didn't care enough to see how things turned out. With a little bit of guilt: Dullsville.

Along with millions of other people around the world, I fell in love with Liz Gilbert and her divorce recovery story through her charming memoir: Eat, Pray, Love. That sort of instant success is a tough act to follow. Liz explained in the Foreword of Committed that she was not trying to write a book like EPL the second time around, nor to repeat a formula just for the sake of pleasing her new audience. This was a wise disclaimer. 
 I expected to like Committed more than I did, because of my admiration for the author and the fact that the subject matter fascinates me. We have a lot to learn about marriage, especially successful marriage, considering the divorce rate in the US. What didn't work for me was the hybrid form. We are led to believe this book is going to be another memoir in the beginning chapters. It morphs into a book report of the author's compulsive study of marriage while she and her Brazilian fiance untangle mounds of red tape with the INS. They are "sentenced" to marriage, so he can come back into the US. 
 I love memoir, and I write memoir myself. I love it because a good one takes personal experience and shows us how each person's journey is also universal. While Liz Gilbert hit a home run in that regard in EPL; Committed left me irritated with a book that suffers from genre confusion. A shorter chronicle of personal experience is sandwich bread for interviews and book reports about marriage--the middle "meat." If Committed were presented as a straight nonfiction study of marriage, I wouldn't have minded, but I also might not have bought it. I wanted more Liz and Felipe, less details about what Liz read and who she talked to about their own marriage or marriage customs. I'd have read a textbook for the latter. 
 The language seemed strained except in the more personal parts, and I was thrilled when the author slipped back into the voice of the Liz I know and love (around p. 189). The "marriage study" lacked the flow and authenticity that enchanted so many of us in EPL. Because I was expecting that same perspective, voice and more heart- than head-trip throughout, I'm sad to say, I was disappointed by its unevenness. 
 From a structural standpoint, I found the 8 chapters too long. This was in stark contrast to EPL which had extremely short chapters--108 of them--based on the 108 mala/prayer beads. I love it when authors find clever conventions for titles or other writing mechanics, and that one really rocked. I wanted more natural "breaking off points," since like most busy modern people, I read a book over numerous sittings. 
 I was left feeling that the book was written before its time. We got as much as she could produce on her journey from skeptic to the point of her actual commitment and marriage ceremony. Perhaps if she had waited a year or two longer, she would have had enough material to write a book primarily about her's and Felipe's own personalization of the institution of marriage and her new experience of it the second time around--older, wiser, and very well read. Her most profound insights are in the penultimate Chapter 7, Marriage and Subversion. In it she realizes, thanks to some offbeat reading material, that the secret to surviving marriage as an institution is that people have always made it their own. The research in this chapter is the part I'd keep--and continue the story to the point where we could see this charming couple well on their way to doing just that.
Blah!

book_b.title: A Discovery of Witches (All Souls Trilogy, #1)
book_b.user_review: There were parts of this book I enjoyed, but frankly it was all over the place. It took me a while to get into, as the underlying world kept changing - we start with witches, then all of a sudden we have vampires. Then, hey, demons. Then, ghosts, and goddesses. Talk about deus ex machina. She starts with no powers, then has all sorts of powers. The plot line didn't feel like it got going until the end. Not sure what to say.

sample_reviews.review_text: Witch falls in love with vampire and they try to solve mystery of old manuscript, that all kind of powerful paranormals want to obtain, but because of her special combination of powers and a spell placed on it by her late father while time traveling, it will only open its secrets to her. Are you getting the impression that this book is just a bunch of garbage thrown together in the cauldron and stirred, 'cuz that about nails it! I really didn't enjoy this book at all. It was like Harry Potter crossed with Twilight and went in search of the Davinci Code, and it was long and often very dry, boring, and dragged out. It did have some original material, and the author obviously did her research to try to avoid anachronism and historical error, so thus my extra star. I didn't feel the characters were well-developed, sympathetic, or had any romantic chemistry, unless you happen to be a necrophiliac because the vampire's coldness and rarity or heartbeats and breaths were supposed to be erotic turn-ons, that frankly did nothing for me.
The main character did a lot of sleeping and wondering what the hell was going on.This went on for over 600+ pages.It was rather boring.

I couldn't finish this. The multiple-page info dump that chronicled the main character's life story within the first 1% of the books should've been a big enough red flag to save me from wasting several more hours of my life, but I pressed on, hoping for an improvement. There wasn't. After trudging through to the half-way point, at which I'd endured more conversations about wine, tea and yoga than I thought possible, I gave up. It's clear the author did her research -- that's great, but it doesn't mean we have to wade through her notes. Part of effective story-telling is to weave the research into the story without dragging it down. Harkness missed the mark there. 
 I also saw no good reason for the alternate POV's, other than to give the author a chance to over-explain and suck all the tension out of the book. It was like a glaring neon sign -- "Hey, just letting you know...there's no danger from Matthew...'cause he loves her. Already. After two days. Two days of drinking wine and tea and hanging out in the library." His entire first POV chapter is pointless -- multiple scenes where he and his friend blather on about nothing, in the form of 'as you know, Bob' dialogue, and we get more information on how to play various games of pool than necessary in anything other than a book about how to play pool. 
 I'm incredibly grateful for this site, because I considered trying to go back and finish, but after coming here and seeing this is only the beginning of a series I know stopping is the right decision. Had I forced myself to read through the rest only to find a million hanging threads I would've thrown the book at the wall. Which would've been a problem, because I have it on my kindle.

I never thought I'd run across a book that contained not only my interests in witches and vampires, etc., but would also contain my genetic love, mitochondrial dna, replete with references to the seven daughters of Eve. Well played, Ms. Harkness, well played.

Also Found On: A Book and A Record 
 Oh goodness, question: who hasn't read this book by now? Answer: basically no one. I even saw a old man (like eighty) reading it on the bus the other day. So am I wasting my time reviewing it? Maybe. But I will say this: I'm officially adding my voice to the lovers. The way that Harkness has structured her story is pretty incredible in the fact that it didn't read like an adult novel. It read like popular fiction, extremely popular fiction, which I wasn't expecting from a history professor. Although at times I found this book to be bogged down by stats and facts that I didn't particularly care for, I did feel that Harkness gave a well rounded account that was intellectual and moved forward effortlessly. I adored all of the supporting and main characters and was quite intrigued by the story line. And the setting, oh my goodness don't even get me started. Pack me up in a box and send me to Oxford, because I want to live in that freaking library. Definitely one I would recommend for a summer vacation read, if you haven't already read it. And I can't wait for the sequel to come out in just a few weeks! Sidenote: I hate when the word sensual is used on book jackets. Seriously? This book isn't sensual, it spends like thirty pages talking about the construction and mutation of genes.

Ummm...wow. What to say. The cheesiness is overwhelming. I think I cringed every 2-3 minutes while reading this book. Which is A LOT of cringing, given the 600 or so pages. This book is bad. It's really, really bad. Also, I can now understand why many women seem to think that when a man is a possessive, jealous asshole, it's only because "he really really loves you! A LOT! Like, really! You should be so happy that someone loves you THAT MUCH, and you should obey everything he tells you to do! Because that's attractive and manly and it means he is super into you!" Ugh. Matthew is a jerk. I wanted to punch him in almost every chapter, but I was too busy wanting to smack the s*** out of Diana, who made the lamest attempts at standing up to Matthew, but somehow just kept giving in to everything he wanted. Also, he marries her without her knowledge or consent. I'm not kidding. I wish I was making this s*** up. And they get married after knowing each other for 3 weeks. Really??! You know you're fated to be together after spending 21 days around each other, especially after he's been lying and keeping things from you, like the fact that he killed a lady for sending a letter and murdered past lovers?! Oh yea, he sounds like a DREAM! This was definitely Twilight: The Oxford Years. The book was somehow able to include just about every high society cliche: Oxford, ancient English mansions, yoga, Porches, crew, French castles, helicopters, loafers, perfectly-aged red wine, horse riding, and silent, dignified men with anger issues. General conclusion: if you loved the Twilight series, then you will probably love this book too. If not, there are about 1,000+ better things you could be doing than reading this book.
This is to long,to much not need it in this book.

!!Spoiler Alert!! 
 Twilight Redux. Ugh. Same plot playbook: 
 Rebel girl meets hot vampire. Denies feelings, sworn off relationships. Girl needs protection. Vampire comes to her rescue. Sexual tension, unfulfilled. Vampire world against their love. Vampire leaves girl. Girl mopes. (Thank goodness this didn't last an entire book. Lesson learned from Twilight series.) Vampire returns declaring devotion and his mistake for leaving. Girl welcomes Vampire back. Girl must find power within herself to fight evil forces against them. Witches (werewolves) and Vampires (vampires) must work together. Brings tension, but everyone loves girl so they overcome differences... 
 Make it stop!!

I am intrigued by the book and will continue in the series because I must know what happens. That being said, I feel like there was a lot of wasted time focusing on things, in my opinion, that are irrelevant or unnecessary to the story. 
 I didn't realize that this book was about vampires and demons, so it's much more along the line of mythology/sci-fi than I typically like, but the story interests me enough to continue with the series. If you love cheesy love stories and vampires and witches, then I think you would rate it higher than I did.
Silly. I gave up after about 100 pages.
A long and involved book but extremely well-written. Beautiful research and story-telling of history and culture, science and fantasy while exploring a romance of a vampire and a witch.

I'm not sure where to start on this one. My thoughts on it are as haphazard as the main character. I wanted to love this book - what's not to love with daemons, vampires, and witches rolled into a story that spends a ton of time in a huge library? 
 Except that 300 pages in, and it still feels like nothing has happened. 
 In 300 pages: 
 1. A witch who refuses to use her magical powers (but is really lying to herself about it as she does) discovers a "lost" book sealed with magic and then sends it back to the stacks, afraid of her own magic. 
 2. A vampire who wants the book makes friends with the witch while other witches threaten her for the book and for being friends with a vampire. 
 I should add that Diana falls in love with the vampire during this time too, but I just couldn't see it. She says the words. She pines like a school girl. The romance, however, simply wasn't there. I didn't see it. I didn't feel it. 
 That goes for a lot of who Diana is. I don't understand her - her actions, her motivations, her desires... 
 She sticks her head in the sand as witches, vampires, and daemons congregate around her, threatening her for this mysterious magical book. She pretends to be brave by continuing her routine, such as rowing on the river first thing in the morning, but she does nothing to help herself. She pretends nothing is happening and continues her research on alchemy. The plot is propelled forward (at an excruciatingly slow pace) by the vampire love interest, and he, like most vampires, is secretive, so we, the readers, are at a loss as to his motivations (beside the fact that the story is narrated by Diana, so she only knows what he wishes her to know, thus we too are hampered in understanding him). 
 I tried to get into this book. I love the concept of paranormal beings living among us vying for the secret knowledge believed to be hidden in the book. I see many good reviews, and my husband loved the book, but I simply am not enjoying the story despite the magic. 
 While overall, I could not enjoy this story enough to finish it, I will give the author kudos for a story that uses witchcraft in a respectable manner. Sure, there are bad witches, but there are in real life too. The magical aspects of the story were interesting, but could not support the story when the main character fails to assist. 
 The magic, the world building, and the setting descriptions bump this up from a one to a two. Also, the writing is good, even though the storytelling didn't draw me in. Perhaps readers who prefer a more leisurely pace will find this more to their liking than I did.
Absolutely loved it!

Not going to finish this. I just can't with it any more. This book started off so interesting, and yet somehow it's just literally Twilight. So glad I just got this from the library; the character of Matthew makes me want to hit things.
I never really got into this book, it took me way too long to read it

This turned out to be a grown-up version of Twilight. The writing was much better, but still, not of interest to me. 
 All of the promise of the first half of the book is lost in the second half as it turns into a weirdly premised romance. The driving conflict in particular is a bit trivial.

Eug. A VILE, VILE, BOOK! It is basically a crappy version of Twilight, whereby instead of having a 16 year old girl fall for a 1017 year old vampire, it's a 30-something woman (who is of course, a witch, but with 'issues') and a blah-years old vampire who is frozen at about age 40 (but is super sexy). The plotline disappears 1/3 in, and they have all sorts of weird arguments about feminism and sexism, and frankly it just comes across as annoying semantics sexism. There is a point where they do special yoga (but only for vampires/witches/demons, because they need their OWN yoga), whereby she admires his yoga abilities to such a degree that by the end I feel like I should have a degree in yoga. They go to France (?0, meet his family, and she has a bunch of weird 'cat stand offs' (the characters glare at each other, and circle each other like angry cats, yowl, but ultimately do nothing), and then, at the very end, there's a bad guy? Somehow? Eug. Vile books.
Ugh, such great potential but no action and pathetic back-and-forth pull with the "heroine's" desire to do magic.
I ended up really enthralled in this story after a slow start. I will definitely try to read the sequel.

This book is really well written. Harkness choices of words and flow are fantastic. This is not a book that I would choose to read and is a book that was given to me by a girl at work and on page 368 I gave up. The story was killing me and I gave up. I hope Harkness keeps writing but just about something else.

I wonder if I picked up a copy of Twilight fanfiction by mistake because A Discovery of Witches felt like Twilight posing as an adult novel minus the werewolves. Actually, I daresay that Twilight was a better novel--at least you could finish the thing in two days, and the pacing was fine. A Discovery of Witches takes slow pacing to a whole new level (though I have to admit the writing was a lot more refined), and Bella can't hold a flame to Diana's annoying personality (before today, I didn't even think it was possible.) I don't even know how this made New York Times Bestseller lists. But if a forced love story between wimpy, annoying witches and extremely possessive, handsome vampires are your thing, this is your book. 
 Plot: 
 Diana Bishop is one of the last descendants of the powerful Bishop family line of witches. She is a PhD in alchemy, tall, and lived three decades shutting out magic from her life. She falls in love with a mysterious vampire, discovers a mysterious manuscript...and find out there's a group set out to destroy her magic and more importantly, break up her and her beloved, Matthew Clairmont. 
 Pace: 
 Major downfall of the novel. I can't believe I was able to muster enough energy to last through all 580 pages (believe me, I was already counting pages from the 200 page mark.) If I can last through this, I am convinced I can last through anything (bring it on, Tolstoy!) To Harkness' credit, the beginning was interesting: I was intrigued with Diana's world of magic, vampires, witches, and daemons--and then it just slid downhill, boring me to tears about horses...tea...wine, fancy rich stuff I don't care about. Did an editor trim this novel down at all? 
 The story moves at snail pace until the climax (finally, I thought something interesting would happen)...which resolved on the next page. So much for building up tension. If the rest of the novel moved as fast as that climax, I would be done in less than a fifty pages. 
 Point of View: 
 Much of the story is from Diana's point of view, though there are two chapters from Matthew Clairmont. I find Diana's point of view suddenly shifting into a passive third person. I was confused when Diana "heard" Matthew conferring with his son, Marcus, about keeping a secret from her--and she didn't do anything except telling the reader that it happened. I would have expected all hell to break loose from her. 
 Characters: 
 There are characters galore and I am sure by the time you are at 300 page mark you will have a headache just remembering names. 
 When I only had about sixty pages to go, I thought for sure that no new characters will be introduced--and boy was I wrong. 
 Diana: I am having difficulty understanding why Harkness made her protagonist so unlikable. Despite much of the story being from her point of view, I couldn't relate to her at all. I admire her intelligence, she must've had something special to get herself a PhD and Yale...but I am doubting her rationale. 
 She's a crazy woman. The only thing that matters in her little selfish world is her love life. I feel sorry for her family. They keep calling her to make sure she's safe and she ignores their calls, dismissing her aunts as being paranoid because she can't be bothered to answer her phone. I am surprised her aunts haven't flown out in worry to make sure she isn't dead. She's blessed with such caring family members and yet I am sure she will throw them under the bus in a flash if she had to choose between them and Matthew. At one point she threatens to burn the house down when her aunt questions her. What kind of person threatens to kill the woman that raised her? Diana has no respect for her elders, and someone needs to slap her across the face pronto. People need to stop telling this chick that nothing is her fault and she's perfect. 
 Perhaps it's because of her impressive education that her pride blinds her. She is adamant that she isn't a "damsel-in-distress," but that's exactly what she is. She's also annoying, whiny, rash, wimpy with no patience whatsoever...and maybe too horny. It's such a waste that has so much potential in her genes, and she incessantly claims she "can't" do anything before even trying. What kind of heroine is this? And why does Matthew have such poor taste in women? In the second half, i couldn't last five-minutes reading without putting the book down to strangle her in my imagination. And she has poor fashion sense. Can she just die already? She spends much of her time being severely injured anyway. 
 Matthew: Diana's love-interest and a voracious, overprotective, 1500 year old vampire. He is supposedly extremely sexy in anything he wears, but I wonder if it's just Diana being blinded. I am not sure how a vampire can be sexy in yoga pants, but whatever. He is also conveniently rich (does he pay taxes?), with personal jets, helicopters, cars, yachts, castles, mansions...I am surprised he won't just buy a tank and kill everyone in his way. 
 Matthew is no better in the family department either. He tells Diana that he would kill his son in an instant if he threatened her. I pity his son, Marcus, who despite his loyalty and friendliness is no competition with some ungrateful, annoying witch. 
 The main problem with Harkness's vampires is that they are too perfect. Classic vampires fear sunlight and sleep like the dead. But these vampires have none of those flaws--they can even survive off animal blood if they wish. So basically they are all beautiful, immortal superhumans. 
 Romance: 
 I am utterly sick of hearing them profess their undying love and how early they fell in love with each other. Apparently they are destined to be together anyway. This romance story goes from passionate to just plain annoying in seconds. 
 Plotlines: 
 The plot went from crystal clear to a confusing hodgepodge of sub-plots. It's a complex plot with every itsy-bity thing squished in somehow, and I hope that it will somehow work out. At first I thought the novel was about uncovering the mysteries of a bewitched manuscript, then it turned into a forbidden love story, then they had to run away from the evil Congregation...and then Diana discovers her powers...and then time travel. I give up. 
 I can't even begin to explain the letter Diana's mom left for her...just how many papers are there anyway?!? And why would you ask to your seven-year old daughter if their "shadowed man" is with her? 
 Research: 
 Harkness's background as a history professor shows--whether you like it or not. I admire Harkness's knowledge, but at times it gets too much and drags down the plot, making me go from intrigued to exhausted. There are a lot of quotations/poetry from a lot of historical texts. Obviously Matthew and Diana have a much better grasp than I since they are both PhDs. I'm sure Harkness is passionate about history, but the onerous history lessons often alienated the reader instead of supported the plot. The scientific DNA, twins stuff left me with a headache--I gave up trying to comprehend it after the 3rd re-read. At one point I thought Diana was a hermaphrodite (which would have made the story a whole lot more interesting.) 
 Language: 
 Why there aren't translations (footnotes? glossary?) is beyond me. Or was I supposed to Google translate the Latin, French, German, and Occitan? 
 World-building: 
 One of the few redeeming factors I can think of. Excessive and seemingly never-ending descriptions...but still some fascinating concepts and scenes nonetheless. I enjoyed the Bishop house that had a mind of its own and screamed "Beauty and the Beast" to me. I was half expecting plates and cups to start singing and dancing. 
 If you are a historical fiction and Twilight fan, you will eat this up like candy. And if you hate Twilight, you will want to hurl A Discovery of Witches out the window in no time. I originally picked up A Discovery of Witches because I won a Shadow of Night giveaway, and Penguin Viking will be sending me a galley of Shadow of Night (the sequel to A Discovery of Witches.) However, despite the lovely word-building, strong historical research, the book just did not work for me: the main characters felt flat and the pacing was awkward. Deborah Harkness's fascinating world is captivating, but the delivery was just lacking. Admittedly, I whacked the book twice on the floor after I finished out of frustration. I went from being excited to read Shadow of Night to shoving it in the unreachable depths of my bookcase. For me, A Discovery of Witches is like an alchemy experiment that went terribly wrong.
1 star for the great cover. The first half of the book extremely engaging; However, the heroine became whiny in my view and too dependent.

I just re-read this first novel in the All Souls Trilogy for about the tenth time. It is, without a doubt, the best trilogy I've ever read and, as is every book lover's dream, book one, A Discovery of Witches, is currently being adapted for television, with options for the remainder of the series. 
 The stills from the production were so tempting I had to read ADOW again. It's like comfort food for me, and every time I read it, I discover something I missed, some subtle foreshadowing or a tiny fact that adds to this fascinating story of forbidden love and destiny. Honestly, this book has it all. It's so intelligent and complex it makes me feel more intelligent for having read it. It weaves a compelling, powerful story that seamlessly combines history, magic, evolution, family, culture, genealogy, mystery, suspense, the supernatural, and romantic love and makes even the most abstract concept believable. It's an epic series that engages from beginning to end and has drawn a worldwide audience that's become a fandom. 
 If you haven't read it -- don't prejudge based on your previous experience with historical, paranormal, or romantic novels. This genre-bending series defies all conventions and deserves its place as one of the top contemporary novels in modern literature.

I cannot say enough bad things about this book. I dont know if its because I had such high hopes for the book or because I had a free 4 day weekend to read and I couldnt continue reading this book and by the time I realized what a piece of tripe it was, the library was already closed and now I am without a book and angry. The characters were shallow and underdeveloped. The plot was a rehash of other, equally terrible books but for some reason, Deborah Harkness decided to add several hundred extra pages of immensely terrible writing. It was almost as if she had read numerous other awful supernatural books and decided she could do a worse job. The amount of times I rolled my eyes with the historical name dropping, asinine character interaction and pages of unbearable description about aspects of the book that had no significance on the plot are innumerable. Honestly, if I could write a review that in some way would make the author tear up a little, I would be ok with that. Thats how bad this book was.

This book was upsetting because I went in expecting a mix of suspense, history, fantasy, and romance. Instead I read a wannabe Twilight novel with some witches and history thrown in. Initially, I couldn't put down. I stayed up late into the night turning the pages and loving how the plot was set up. Then suddenly the two characters are madly in love after three weeks and I find myself reading a cheesy romance novel by the middle of the book. I like romance, but this was downright corny and unbelievable. The protagonist shifted from a strong and interesting woman to a frail and vampire-dependent girl. The character evolvement of Diana was done poorly. I suddenly didn't like her anymore. And Matthew switched from an interesting and well-rounded love interest to a stereotypical vampire. It just didn't work for me. 
 I was really disappointed. I enjoyed it immensely in the beginning and then found myself bored by the last half. I couldn't put it down and then it became a chore to pick up. I can see how this is her first novel. I am baffled by the poor editing and pacing of the novel. 
 I truly don't know how this novel is getting so many rave reviews! I thought is was mediocre, unoriginal, and cheesy. The characters became one-dimensional and annoying. It almost felt like two different authors wrote the beginning and second half. 
 I won't read the second novel and want to warn readers that this is a sappy romance novel, NOT a suspense novel.

Not thoroughly impressed, though I did very much enjoy the settings of Oxford, France & Madison County. Well-researched and fairly original, but not gripping, and the writing seemed a little juvenile. I'm only slightly curious to pick up the next in the series; I don't think I'll have a real problem leaving this behind.
Characters are ridiculous...so slow and goes nowhere for ages...a lot of eating,drinking, napping, and celibacy. I liked nothing about this book.
I couldn't finish it! Everyone was way too perfect, even for a paranormal world. Boring!

I have never considered a book that I didn't finish "read", but after 350 pages of repetitive nonsense I thought I earned it. This book was not my thing at all. The characters are so perfect that there is nothing interesting to them. Mary Sue meet Gary Stu. Oh, now you are in love? How convenient! Ugh. I think that this book is for a reader who wants to wake up one day to find out that they are magical and perfect so that they can meet their superhuman dream partner that afternoon and fall madly in love by dinner. Not my idea of an interesting life or an engaging story. If I could give a book zero stars this one would win the prize.
Dnf because I felt like I was reading Twilight all over again
Got to page 189... Realized it was a trilogy and didn't want to spend that much time with the characters. Didn't finish it.
A good juicy read! Totally sucked into the whole fantastical realm of witches, vampires and daemons. Biggest drawback: next book not out for a year.

I got this at the library after hearing the author interviewed on NPR. Since I'm working on a fantasy about the intersection of science and magic, I was curious to see how Harkness would approach it. But I'm sorry to say, I couldn't finish it. It was intriguing at the outset, and I liked the academe setting, but nothing really happened.  I don't know, I'm torn on this. It's too long to be borderline unreadable but still compelling. Maybe not enough for me to read the next book though.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I was terribly disappointed by it. 
 It started out really good & even through the end, I liked the main idea of the book & the fact that it was actually written by a real historian made it even more interesting. 
 But the main character, Diana (a witch), was So Annoying. She started out fine, but 5 minutes after the gorgeous male vampire shows up, she's a quivering mass of stupidity & desire. (Such a CLICHE! There was even a scene where the vampire carried her piggy-back through the woods - IN THE TWILIGHT! I almost hurled it across the room at that point.) 
 Then there were the long (chapters-long) stretches of scenes that had nothing to do with anything & did nothing to carry the story along. Perhaps if it was half the length, it would've been better. I can think of at least 50 pages that can get almost completely cut & it would improve the story. 
 It didn't start getting bad til I was interested enough to just keep going on, hoping it got good again (it didn't). By the time I was 3/4 through, I was just skimming it. I needed to finish, but I didn't need every word. 
 I would not recommend this book, unless you REALLY like history &/or alchemy. That was mostly what kept me reading. The other characters were pretty well done too, and the mythology was interesting. It was just Diana that I hated. And the cliched relationship between her & Matthew - the entire book took place over the period of 40 days & they were already married & ready to die for each other & she'd already made a deal with a goddess to save his life - sacrificing someone else (she doesn't know who/what she sacrificed yet, her deal was "take anyone as long as he lives" - REALLY?) to save him. 
 BEEN THERE, DONE THAT.
DNF - life's too short to read crappy books.
Oh my... how did this even get published? Lots of eye rolling on my part. I gave up when the witch and the vampire went to yoga class.

A Discovery of Witches actually involves witches, vampires, demons, and ordinary humans. The romance at the center of the book involves a witch, Diana, and a vampire, Mathew. Diana is a successful college professor and expert on ancient manuscripts. While on a research trip to the Bodleian Library, Diana winds up breaking the spell on a very important manuscript that other witches, vampires, and demons want to possess. Mathew shows up in the library and protects Diana from a vicious witch. Then he invites her out to breakfast but he doesn't eat anything. Their relationship breaks the rules of the ancient Covenant prohibiting relations between creatures, so everyone is out to get them, especially the most evil ones of each race. 
 Diana thinks she can handle whatever comes along. However, many times in the course of the story, she falls apart and needs to be rescued by Mathew or other allies. 
 Mathew is a handsome, brooding, powerful vampire, who is 1500 years old. Oddly, in addition to drinking blood, he enjoys fine wine and sometimes soup. He has a first edition of Darwin's On the Origin of Species and a Gutenberg bible in his library. 
 For a break between adventures, the Diana and Mathew go to yoga class. While they're on the run from various enemies, they go horseback riding. He buys her birth control pills. 
 This is a pleasant story, and the Recorded Books version kept me company on a long drive. However, the love story seems to lack reason and depth.

Rating: 0 stars. negative stars. 
 I was so confident that I could finish this book. I was so determined. Even if it features a Mary-Sue type protagonist who has "hair all the colors of the rainbow" and is a super-genetically gifted witch, who, surprise surprise, is an orphan and is trying to deny her heritage as a witch. There's also the typical overprotective love interest. Who is a vampire. Of course. There are other characters... but they don't seem to matter too much, being flat cardboard characters, so I guess we'll just ignore them? That's the impression I got, at least. It also bears mentioning that although detail is usually welcome in fantasy stories and worldbuilding in general, I DON'T FREAKING NEED A PARAGRAPH DESCRIBING HOW THE PROTAGONIST LIKES TO MAKE HER TEA. OR HOW THE CREEPY-ASS VAMPIRE WATCHES HER WHILE SHE SLEEPS. STOP. PLS. 
 This book adds a whole new level to the term 'racist'. Essentially, the world described in this book includes four races. Witches, vampires, demons... and humans. The latter are inconsequential and feeble and we are reminded of this every now and then. You know, just so we don't forget how amazing our protags (witch and vampire) are in comparison. The other three races refer to each other as 'witch', 'vampire', 'demon'; their heritage is of more consequence than their personalities. I guess this setup could work in some cases... but it really doesn't add anything to this story. And this is just personal preference, but 1) the human-bashing really annoyed me, and 2) aren't witches inherently human, despite their magic powers? Eh well. 
 All in all, this book is somewhat Twilight-esque in terms of subject matter, protagonist character development, and romantic relationship. HOWEVER. I enjoyed Twilight more because at least, at least! There was more ACTION. Fighting and shit. (Although, admittedly, since I dnf-ed this trilogy, I don't know if the plot picked up later on) 
 So anyway, I almost finished this book- as I said, I was determined!- and then I learned it was part of a trilogy. I'm out. 
 *extra point #1* Authors, please stop using 'vampires' as an excuse to make your characters (especially the male ones) rich, gorgeous, alpha, and perfect in every way. Is that really all the vampire mythology is good for nowadays? Also, I was so annoyed by the way that this author in particular had the vamp/'love interest' meet all the significant people in history, like Napoleon and Newton and Charles Darwin and a whole slew of notables... a little bit heavy handed in trying to prove this guy's superiority, no? But at the very least, don't use history/the cliche of eternal life to do it. Jeez. 
 *extra point #2* It's one thing to say that the protag is an 'independent woman.' It's another to prove it with action. And that DOESN'T mean wilfully ignoring reason and jumping at any chance to argue for arguing's sake. If the protag doesn't like how overprotective and secretive the love interest is being, then all she has to do is clearly and calmly cut ties with him. Not whine about how he never listens to her, or try to prove her own capability. (besides, she's apparently perfect at everything- she rows, rides, runs, is a history professor at Yale, has more raw magical talent than anyone in the history of witches, has rainbow hair... yeah I think we get the point.) 
 Oh, oh! Even though I disliked the book itself, I was EXTREMELY impressed by the narrator (I listened to the audiobook version). Gaaaahh I don't remember her name at this moment, but her British and Scottish accents were on point. I was able to distinguish between all of the (flat as cardboard) characters, and her rendition of the love interest's voice (I won't deign to use his name, since he's basically just there as the 'love interest') was pretty sexy haha~ I'm hoping she's narrated other books in the fantasy genre!

Quirky smart woman falls for super-sexy sullen vampire (is there any other kind?) who steadfastly refuses to eat her. (Twilight for grown-ups?) There was some interesting world-building, such as the emphasis place on how vampires live for so long and are therefore so patient and stalwart, and how witches can physically feel other beings looking at them. 
 Most notably, however, this book broke The Third Rule of Heroes, which states: "If any book will feature a hero or heroine with special powers, then the hero or heroine must spend (minimally) 50% of the story using or exploring said powers." In other words, we don't need to watch Spider-Man 2 where Spidey spends the bulk of the movie not being Spider-Man. Similarly, Diana is a witch. In fact, a super-witch. With every possible witch power (I'm not even going to invoke the sub-paragraph to the aforementioned Rule about balancing a character's super-powers). And yet she spends almost no time in the book exercising her powers. 
 That said, my favorite element of the book was its setting. The Bodlein Library, rooms at Oxford, a French chateau, and a New England house are all rendered with beautiful detail to the historical and physical details.

I'm torn over this book. Alas, another book about a romance between a vampire and another entity--in this one a witch. While I did enjoy the author's writing style, there were times when I felt the book should have ended before it did (I probably could have cut it down by at least 100-150 pages). I also didn't love the ending. I felt it should have concentrated more on Matthew and Diana and not the aunts, but I guess it's a set up for book 2, which I will read on one condition: it has to be shorter. It wasn't tragic, but it could use some editing help to tighten the story.

sample_reviews.review_text: This is one of the only books I can say that I regret wasting my time on. I spent MONTHS fighting my way through this book, only to have the worst ending I've ever experienced in a book.

This book brought up some themes such as redemption, self-discovery, and the importance of animals which I enjoyed.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I kind of think of this book as two separate books. The "first", about Edgar and his family's breed of future intelligent dogs, was pretty enjoyable and interesting, if often meandering and purple. Wroblewski appeared to run out of room or time or patience for the "second", a strange murder-mystery/ghost story/thriller/Hamlet without much motivation, and the book finished abruptly and without closure. I feel like the characters had been assigned actions to complete, but we were never given all of the parts of their personalities that inspired them to those actions. There were a number of moments where I stopped and thought, "wait, what just happened, and why?". The author seems to have taken on too many ideas at once in this book, and a lot of threads were completely lost as a result. Firmly in the tragedy section, because the author can't seem to stop punishing his characters for unexplained reasons.
What a waste of time. What was the point? Hated the ending.
Hated the end!

My view on this book is similar to most others on here. I thought the book was great until the last 50 pages or so when it all went to hell. 
 Why???

I just can't do it. I typically read 40 or so pages per night in a book, but I've been falling asleep after 1-5 pages of this one. I'm through 80 pages after more than a week. 
 As a writer, you're taught that you need to have conflict of some sort on virtually every page. There was no conflict whatsoever in this book. Nothing interesting at all. 
 I almost stopped reading before page 36, when Edgar was introduced. The first 35 pages have no discernable reason for being a part of the story. Then the next 44 follow the same pattern. 
 I don't see how this book has an average rating of 4.20. Maybe because it's a "literary masterpiece." I guess that makes me low-brow. Give me Grisham any day.

** spoiler alert ** 
 After the huge media hype about this book, I was expecting something a bit more engrossing. Parts of the book really drag, explanation of dog training and the odyssey of Edgar and his dogs. 
 The human characters in the book are the least developed of any. The dog characters seem more real. And the reason for the deep animosity between Gar and his brother are shown rather than well explained. It still leaves a lot of doubt in the reader's mind. I wondered if this was a purposeful device by the author, demonstrating Edgar's doubts and frustrations due to his muteness, and the way he's friendless, except for the dogs. 
 The last 150 pages of the book, are where the story finally unfolds. Then events move very quickly. Wroblewski writes beautiful description without the trite metaphors many writers fall into. 
 Our book group selected this book, and the facilitator found many parallels to Hamlet, and some to the Odyssey. We were about evenly split over liking and disliking the book. Many felt that it could have been made shorter without losing any important components.

 This book advertises itself as a re-imagining of 'Hamlet,' which was what interested me most about it. Unfortunately, it addresses exactly none of the themes that make 'Hamlet' a great play. The use of Hamlet's plot comes across not as a clever, modern re-telling, but rather as an amateur borrowing a plot for lack of inspiration. 
 If you're going to re-write Shakespeare's most famous play, it'd better be God's own rewrite. Otherwise, you only set yourself up for unfavorable comparisons. 
 Wooden attempts at poetry ("they ate like starving kings"? At least I understood that particular mixed metaphor. Some are just pretty words strung together like magnet poetry.), flat characters who spend a great deal of time wondering why they are doing what they are doing (why am *I* doing what I'm doing-- reading this?), and, since the plot is borrowed, no great surprises in store. 
 The best part of the book, for me, is Edgar's journey. Since it does not have much of a Shakespearean parallel, that freed the author up to let the plot move more organically. Unfortunately, we all know he's going back home eventually, so the whole thing becomes something of a red herring. 
 In fact, I thought the cover of this book should be-- not a boy, a dog, and a farm-- but rather a large red herring. Or a school of red herrings. Many things are introduced, but very few of them, ultimately matter. 
 Obfuscation does not profundity make.
