Wroblewski's writing was just beautiful. So many "mundane" seeming things were really put into a new light. I liked the book up until the "ghost story" aspect was introduced. It was so REAL, so vivid, so retro-feeling that I really empathized with the characters. And then a sort of surreal element was introduced. I don't mind it, normally, especially being a reader of fantasy -- I suspend my disbelief a LOT. But, to turn so drastically. I don't know, I felt a little betrayed. Like he had sensationalize some of it to make it interesting. Overall I liked it. But ... there was just that something that bothered me.

book_b.title: The Shining Girls
book_b.user_review: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo meets The Shining, complete with a Lisbeth Salander type of heroine - but definitely not as cool as Lisbeth. No one can be as cool as Lisbeth. Lisbeth vs. Jack Torrance? Full review: The Shining Girls Book Review

sample_reviews.review_text: I spent so much time trying to connect dots that weren't meant to be connected. Entertaining, not a favorite.

The Shining Girls is one great idea that is unfortunately poorly executed. My main issue with the book is that at no point do any of the three main characters - Kirby, Dan, and Harper Curtis - ever become more than descriptions on the page. All three exist only insomuch as the author is telling you they do so: they don't become real or three dimensional in the mind of the reader, and neither does their world. The Harper character in particular was annoying because he never achieves any sort of depth: he's a serial killer like pretty much any other serial killer you've ever read about or seen on television. He does bad stuff just because. We know nothing about his background or anything about his life before or after his experience in the House that somehow just pushes him over the line from really bad guy to serial killer. The author offers up one scene that describes some minor animal torture and watching his brother get crushed under a tractor but again, it's par for the course for any serial killer and it offers nothing insightful about *this* particular serial killer. 
 At the start of the book, Harper is running away from a group of people out to do him some sort of harm but it's basically irrelevant in terms of learning anything about him. It's a very drawn out sequence of events, the purpose of which is just to get him to the House where he has this sensory experience while high on morphine that somehow just puts him on this path to hunting and killing the 'shining girls'. And that's about it for Harper in the character development front: he spends the rest of the book stalking and killing girls, and a few other people along the way because that's what serial killers do. At no point does he question what that transformative experience might have been about, or the very idea that this house is somehow a time traveling device/portal. He just immediately goes along with the entire situation. Alrighty, then. 
 Kirby isn't much better. She's a typical alternative/punky kind of girl who doesn't really fit in with mainstream society. Her history with the serial killer doesn't help matters but really, we're not offered much in the way of character development to know her better or sympathize with her much more than that. We get some scenes from her life as she grows up with her flakey, artistic mother Rachel. As an adult she's on the hunt for the man who tried to kill her but the sleuthing/mystery aspect of her story is woefully underdeveloped. Much like the characters in this story, the meat of the plot doesn't get much deeper than the page it's written on. Kirby doesn't really get far at all in terms of finding clues or making connections to Harper until near the end when the whole thing suddenly comes together for apparently no other reason than the author figured it was time to wrap things up. There's a really jarring chapter near the end where Kirby is in the House (which up to this point she didn't even know existed), hiding upstairs as she hears Harper (she doesn't know who he is then but knows he's the man who tried to kill her) coming in and up the stairs. This scene just pops up out of nowhere, and I actually flipped back a few pages to see if I missed something, or if this was supposed to be something she was dreaming about. No, it's just a weird prelude to later on near the end of the book when Kirby actually does find the House and goes inside. It was just a very strange choice structurally as the reader gets thrown right out of things. 
 Another small bit that frustrated me was an exchange near the end between Kirby and the police - she's pointed them to where Harper is living and having been in the House herself, she's seen how it's so different inside than out. Of course, the police go there and it's just a dilapidated abandoned house, inside and out. But when Kirby goes back, this time with Dan, and they both go in, Dan sees the House in the same way as Kirby and Harper: so why does it 'work' for him and not the police? Well, that's another cliche, isn't it? The protagonist tries to convince those in authority about her theory but they are unable to verify what she's said or what she's seen etc. So they think she's crazy and she has to go off to the scary house/location whatever and deal with it herself, thus triggering the final battle between plucky heroine and bad, evil man etc. etc. 
 I lost interest about half way through and just skimmed to the end. I figure if you haven't made the characters come alive and be more than descriptive words on the page by the halfway mark, then there's a problem. This book is big on its ideas but is woefully short on its ability to deliver.

A serial killer that moves through time and his only surviving victim who refuses to give up on finding him. Avoids the confusion that accompanies most tales that flip through time. Engrossing and believable characters lend weight to a fantastic tale. Some moments of true horror, not for the squeamish, well worth the time and accolades.

Well, at least I can say I've dipped my toe into the world of serial killer fiction though I don't when I'll have the stamina to revisit it. Still, this was interesting despite the usual hang-ups that accompany writing time travel. I'm looking forward to reading more of Beukes' work I have waiting in the ranks.
I was really looking forward to this book but it was a big disappointment. Great story idea but it didn't fulfil it potential. Disappointing ending.

This was not a good book. It was an interesting concept, but I found that I was not actually interested in any of the characters, and didn't really care about the plot, and none of the plot twists were surprising or even vaguely amusing. 
 It was billed, in the library, as a thriller, with a time travel twist (the part that makes it spec fic) - it was not thrilling. There is a time traveling serial killer, but even though we get many interminable scenes from his perspective, it's a little hard to say exactly why he was motivated to be a serial killer. (Not good. The guy is basically a Murder Hobo.) The house that allows him to time travel is cool, but is a concept clearly ripped off from Dr Who. Why are these particular women targeted? Why only women? They "shine". No more explanation. 
 The pacing also needed work - it was very choppy, the POV character switched constantly, and there were not very many cliffhanger moments, as there should be in a thriller. Scenes were overlong, without adding much to either characters or plot - inanimate objects and scenery were described in excessive detail. 
 I was disappointed that I picked this as a book for a long car ride.
Flojo, una forma mas de desaprovechar un argumento prometedor.
So good, but I need someone to put this in chronological order for me. Get to work, Internet!

This falls outside of my typical genre but I was intrigued. I ended up not really liking it. It felt so disconnected and I never really understood anything about his motives or The House. Maybe Im not into time travel enough and sometimes you just have to go with it but the book left me with basic plot questions that I feel like should have been addressed.

interesting and involving, but ultimately not satisfying. it felt a bit like a jigsaw puzzle that you feel compelled to finish but don't care what the final image turns out to be. 
 the characters were lively and the relationships were well crafted. the writing shows promise and I'd be curious to read another book by the writer.
A really interesting premise. I thought the plot worked well and loved the protagonist, Kirby.

I was really excited when my book club chose this book to be one our picks. I was thrilled at the synopsis and eagerly dove into this book. However, even though I loved loved loved the idea of this one but the execution was seriously lacking. I loved the idea of the narration completely through the eyes of the serial killer; I felt this was really unique but then it went all sci-fi on me. I was not impressed. 
 I found myself spending most of my time reading and re-reading pages to try and reorient myself within the text and just felt like the narration was all over the place. 
 I really wanted to love this one but it missed the mark for me.

I wanted to love this book. It's about a freaking time travelling serial killer. What more could I ask for??? 
 But I just didn't. 
 There was no explanation given for the house or the time travel ability. It was just there, and we were supposed to accept it. It was so underwhelming that it could have been pulled out of the book and it would have still been about the same. 
 The settings... I struggled with the cues given for time periods and often wouldn't have realized when he was without the chapter titles. 
 The killing... no real explanation given for why he killed these particular girls. Yes, they shined for him, but there was no exploration of why or his motivations for killing. It just seemed like it was destined, because of the house and time loops and nonsense. 
 The romance... I did not go into a book about a time travelling serial killer looking for a romance. Especially not one so weird. I very rarely enjoy relationships between a very young woman and an older man because I shudder at the power imbalance implied in that sort of dynamic. Also the idea that women are valueless once they age. Ick, ick, ick. 
 I ultimately found the book confusing and looked forward to putting it down, which was such a shame considering how excited I had been by it.

I couldn't understand why or any motive in any of it. And the intensity just added to the confusion. I gave up on this one and didn't read past page 55. I'll be honest, it's not quite fair to say "read" on this book. I wish there was a category "gave up" to pick on the goodreads menu. As I age I just KNOW time is too short to read paragraph after paragraph of described confusion when all I get out of it seems increasing irritation. 
 Ironic since time-travel is one of my top 3 scenarios. 
 What is a shining girl?
Well written but about nothing.
Really wanted to like this book, but none of the characters engaged my interest. Skip it and read Zoo City instead.
Unique, quirky characters, suspenseful, creepy, and interesting facts about Chicago.

Meh. I only finished it because I was hoping there would be explanations - and I was disappointed. 
 I won't classify this as science fiction at all; borderline fantasy, because the House is essentially a Magic Mirror. 
 If you expect your murder stories to include repeated, loving descriptions of knives and intestines, you can check that off. If you expect the Hollywood movie older-guy-younger-girl-gradually-drawn-together, yep, it's here. 
 Plus one: thorough research on several areas covered. Maybe a little too thorough, because as so often happens there's a bit of shame-to-waste-this-I'll-put-it-in. 
 So, back to the House, which may have been telling Harper to do things (assuming Harper still has a shred of sanity). I mentioned that it's essentially a Magic Mirror. Now, put those together and let's say that the House is inhabited by a trapped evil wizard. NOW you've got a five-star story. 
 The afterword suggests that Beukes simply wanted to write a time-travel story. She put some work into it, but it might have been better to read more previous stories to see what other, expert writers have done with it. As others have noted, this novel could have been written without the time travel. 
 I never quite got why Harper felt the need the distribute the various, er, let's call them mementos, wherever he went. There were some temporal anomalies, never explained. 
 I wanted to know why the House existed, and how. The explanation can be the silliest handwaving, but gosh darn it, an author has to try. Just tell me it's a spillover from a dimension where magic works, or something. In the afterword, Beukes mentions wormholes, but that's well-explored ground (as is magic) and authors have to respect what's already out there. It's the only one? It links vastly-separated parts of an infinite universe ... and it's used to let one deranged psycho wander around stabbing people? Nah. Wormholes are for moving galactic battle fleets, and reaching distant civilizations. 
 I can allow the ending. We knew from about page 10 that there'd be a showdown, and there'd be a "you can't go in there alone!" and someone would nevertheless go in there alone, and so on. 
 In the end, there's a decent enough story here except that it's totally missing How and Why. 
 I can only guess that those who liked just wanted to get on to the next gory stabbing, and see if Kirby gets it on with Dan.
absurd.

OK this book was violent & at times gruesome. But I couldn't put it down. 
 It is about a time traveling serial killer. I can't believe that I liked it.

A killer travels through time picking his victims and leaving mementos behind. 
 I thought I'd venture outside of my comfort zone with The Shining Girls and I certainly managed that. It was far too gory and violent for me. 
 The trouble is that almost half of the story is told from the killer's point of view. The reader gets a front row seat at the crimes, usually immediately after a series of passages describing the girl so that an emotional connection is formed with the victim. 
 I was on a run listening to the audiobook... now, let me be honest. I was on a mildly taxing walk listening to the audiobook and I had to turn it off when he attacked Kirby. It was simply too much with all of the horror, violence and the bit with the animal too. 
 Perhaps if I had been reading a physical book, I could have skimmed the awful bits. But even then, I think it would be safe to say that this was not the book for me. 
 I was really excited when Beukes introduced the reader to the newsroom of the Chicago newspaper. Her description of the reporter's cubes all stacked up on one another with the sports and feature writers off to the side was eerily accurate to where I work. 
 I also enjoyed the interactions between Dan and Kirby- those two were snappy and fun. 
 Overall though, the gore of the story was too much for me. Only recommended for readers who can handle that type of thing.

"The Shining Girls" was a real page-turner for me! The concept of a time-traveling serial killer may sound hokey, but the story was well-written, with some unexpected twists and turns. Although the very idea requires suspension of disbelief, the pace of the action is so fast that you don't really have time to over-analyze the concept & logistics of time-travel. I can't say much more without giving too much away, so just sit back and enjoy the ride!

The idea of time travel in this book just doesn't work well. There are few books where it does, especially few where it fits into the plot naturally (best is Replay, and very good in The Time Traveler's Wife). 
 Other than that, flat characters, and boring writing style. Definitely not as shining as I expected it to be. And not an "it" book for me. 
 A time traveling serial killer is a fine idea, but you can find better serial killer books too. Specifically, the reasoning of what exactly attracted the killer to the "shining girls" is not actually clear, which makes it less believable. Serial killer, tend to have pretty clear agenda and reasoning, as twisted as it sounds. Harper didn't. 
 About 1.5 stars.

The Shining Girls Lauren Beukes 
 4 Stars 
 So where to start with this one the book is about a time travelling serial killer, when you say it out loud it either sounds silly or fantastic depending on if time travel is your thing, guess what its mine, even if the outline sounds silly to you I would recommend you pick up the book and read the first few chapters you may find yourself hooked. 
 So without giving away too many spoilers Harper is man who discovers a house that allows him to travel in time in return he fells compelled to murder a series of girls who in his own words shine, he meets them when they are children and then hunts them down years later when they are adults to kill them. 
 From the start we know Harper is the murderer, we know the names of the shining girls but what we don't know is when he will kill them or how he will choose to link them all together. As the story progresses we leap around in time forward and backward with Harper as he sets up his kills and as he discovers that there can exist a place outside of time. 
 I love the ideas of time in this story and how we are given hints and clues to put together not to guess the murderer but to connect the victims and to make you want to shout at them when you know what is coming and they remain blissfully unaware. 
 If you fancy something different give this a try

"There are patterns because we try to find them. A desperate attempt at order because we can't face the terror that it might all be random. He is undone by the revelation. He has the sensation of losing his footing, as if the whole damn world is stuttering." 
 "I'm scared, Mom." 
 "We all are,"Rachel says. She hugs her head to her chest and rubs her back as Kirby's whole body racks and shudders. "Shhh. It's okay, honey. It's all right. That's the big secret, don't you know? Everyone is. All the time."

Edit: Wow, my 500th review! 
 For the longest time as I was reading this, I was wondering at the average rating of the book sitting at 3.47. Pretty low for what was one of the "It" books of a few years ago. 
 Now that I've finished the book I can check out the lower rating reviews (my experience has shown the lower the rating the higher the risk of spoilers), and what I've found is that most people had issues understanding motive and that the story dragged. 
 I couldn't disagree more. As far as the story went, I could hardly put the book down. It seems that Ms Beukes has been heavily influenced by the master of storytelling. This reads very much like a Stephen King novel, and I thought the characters were very well described. 
 As far as the killer's motive goes? I can explain that very well: 
 He was a sick fuck. How's that? 
 Okay, you want deeper? He's a misogynist who wants to kill these "shining" girls because they are above the norm of society and it gets his rocks off to visit them when they're young girls and link them with tokens, all the while knowing something they don't: that he will butcher them (and already has in his past). 
 Better? 
 Now, be warned that the whole time travel thing isn't going to be explained to you. So don't worry about it. Accept it as a magical plot device and move on. 
 This was a very cool book with a fantastic premise and executed brilliantly. I think it deserves 5 stars for keeping me so hooked, and that's exactly what I'm going to give it. I will look forward to Broken Monsters.

Imagine if Doctor Who were a psychopath and instead of a police box he had a house and couldn't travel through space, just time. And instead of having young female companions, he hunted down young females to kill them. And instead of being an alien, he was from the Great Depression, in Chicago. 
 So yeah, nothing really like Doctor Who. 
 Lauren Beukes is a great writer and story teller. For that reason alone, I'd recommend any book she's written. If you're a fan of her previous two books Moxyland or Zoo City you should know that this one is very different but you'll probably still like it. It is about a serial killer who hunts down girls as he travels through time and is very graphic so if any of those themes bother you then you'll want to avoid this book.

A serial killer travels through time, dispatching of his victims: young women he refers to as "shining girls". Finally, a time travel novel that makes sense. Sort of. An interesting premise and no real faults in time travel logic - but no real answers either. Why is this house a time machine? What motivates the serial killer to murder these women? What makes them "shine"? They're developing this book for television so maybe the t.v. series will have the answers. But probably not.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The premise of this book is super interesting, a time travel serial killer, but I wasn't captivated. While the writing is definitely a step up from traditional horror novels, it bothered me that the time travel is never explained. Although the murders are disturbing, Harper is a lackluster character that just seems to be going through the motions of killing (which I guess is horrifying its own way.) In contrast, Kirby is a great character. Overall, this horror novel is decent, but not the best book of the summer.

Started this one today. I'm not a huge fan of novels that plunge me into things with no explanation of what is happening. I like a few signposts. 
 If I navigate my way further I'll update as usual. 
 Blah. Not for me. It's too tortuous and the writing isn't holding my attention.

This was so unorganized and hard to follow, but surprisingly a quick read. Just took me 8 days to make it the first 60 pages. There was so much going back and forth between not two but many many times you couldn't keep up with who was where and what was going on. Too many characters and none fully developed. Plus a sad dog scene I had to skip.

After listening to the first CD of this book, I took it out of the CD player very carefully, making sure to barely handle it, put it back in its sleeve, and will return the whole thing to the library as fast as I can. 
 I guess I'm squeamish, but I found the amount of guts and gore in the first CD both so unbearable and so tedious I couldn't stand to go on. (From other reviews I gather the graphic murders continue endlessly through the book.) Plus, I found the heroine's home situation so depressing that although she IS plucky, it just didn't counterbalance the gruesome grizzly murders and the horrible psychopath who perpetrates them. And while I guess it's very hip start a novel with a 15-year-old deliberately losing her virginity to someone she only sort of likes, I found it emotionally deadening. 
 The idea of a time traveling murderer and one of his almost-victims pursuing him in the current day sounded great, and I liked the title "The Shining Girls". But there was nothing shining about this experience. 
 Don't take it personally, Lauren. I didn't like "Gone Girl" either.

If there would be no comparison to gone girl before reading it I think I would of enjoyed this book more. Not as spooky as was promised, not as complex as could be with all time travel, so I was disappointed in a way it wrapped up.

What was this, a thriller? Not very thrilling. The fantastic elements were not very fantastic. The horrific elements were not that horrific. The way the book was written, you knew what was going on, so while it made it interesting, it never paid anything off at the end. I wanted a giant alien spider at the end. Or something. Sorry, spoiler. There is no giant alien spider at the end.

interesting concept, dark, disappointing 
 I'm a first time reader of Lauren Beukes. THE SHINING GIRLS was a buddy read in my book club, Sweeter Reads. The book had a good premise and I was looking forward to reading it. 
 I have been a fan of the mystery/thriller genre for years. Nothing gets the blood flowing more then playing Sherlock Holmes while sitting on the edge of the edge of my seat. I can't read about violence all the time, however when I select a book that's brutal, I have no problem reading about slashing and murder, blood doesn't bother me. Having said all that, its really hard to enjoy a story when the main character is a serial killer with no redeeming qualities whatsoever. There wasn't one thing likeable about this guy. Usually, authors who write books like this give the killer a tortured past whether it be abuse or a traumatic event, and this triggers what they come to be. Now for the reader, that troubled past or that single event is the one little spark of sympathy we bestow the antagonist. Not the case in this book. 
 I thought the idea of time travel was interesting, however we weren't given any details of the mechanics of it. The reader's given a magic house and a key and I guess we're supposed to fill in the blanks. "That Don't Impress Me Much." (I'm not fan of Shania, but I'm sure you get my point) 
 Now, this novel jumps back and forth in time, however, regardless of what decade, all the characters seemed the same ... and flat - definitely not memorable. I didn't even catch on to Kirby, our sweet-little-escape-artist-victim. Her mother was terrible too. She's a wild women, doesn't even know who Kirby's father is. We're given hints; Kirby wants to know who her daddy is, but it's something we - the readers - are left hanging on. 
 I could write more, however I'm growing tired of typing. I wanted to like this book, but for me, it just fell flat. I hurried myself along just so I could finish and move onto something else. Don't let my review stop you from reading the book. Everyone's tastes is different, so at least try it.

This book was honestly confusing for the most part. It was very interesting that the serial killer was able to travel back and forth through time, but it could have been executed better. Most of the book, I was constantly flipping back and forth to remember where the heck I was being taken to now. Switching constantly from 1931, to 1988, to 1950, to 1990, etc... I wouldn't say this book was bad, but it takes a lot of effort on the reader's pet to understand what's going on. At the end it starts to tie itself together. 
 I would NOT recommend this book to those who can't take gore. I had to force myself to read the horribly graphic parts and it was not enjoyable to me.

This book had a great premise, but the tag line is more exciting than anything that actually happens in the book. It was kind of boring, and while I'm fine without pages and pages of exposition, a LITTLE explanation wouldn't have gone astray. 
 Mostly just a police procedural, and there's a reason I don't read mystery. I like my sci fi. But the fantastical element in this story really didn't do or matter much. The whole book, while well written and a page turner, left me feeling unfulfilled.
I wonder if this started as a short story or novella, because it didn't seem fleshed out enough to merit a full book. The bonus story at the end was atrocious.

This is just a nasty, nasty book which I will not be finishing. I'm sure it's well conceived, if you like this sort of thing, but the comparisons to Gillian Flynn and Tana French border on absurd. I see none of French's devil-in-the-details, plot-weaving wizardry and fascinating antiheroes, nor do I see Flynn's brilliantly gleeful, gallows humor-style take on sociopathy. This is merely a series of horrific murders, every one of which prompts only sympathy for the victim rather than a detached interest in the crime or the surviving characters involved in the plot. I'm sure that just as is the case in the Dragon Tattoo series which this books mimics, the heroine will get her revenge. But I felt much too manipulated by and disappointed in the story to stick around to find out.
I really wanted to like this book. Too many loose ends, but I found I really didn't even CARE.

Electronic ARC provided by NetGalley. 
 The Shining Girls is a rather straightforward thriller (as straightforward as anything involving time travel can be), about a time traveling serial killer and the one victim that got away. The perspective in the book is mostly divided between the killer, Harper, and his victim, Kirby, with various other characters--including other murder victims--picking up the narrative for a chapter here and there. I found the story compelling, and I enjoyed Kirby as a main character. Beukes does a great job of showing that while Kirby has survived her attack as well as can be expected, she is certainly a bit damaged. Her actions throughout the novel are frequently impulsive and lacking in maturity, while remaining mostly sympathetic. Kirby feels like a real, though young and inexperienced, girl. 
 I found the writing creepy and compelling, and loved the atmospheric bits of 20th century history that were inserted every few chapters. The Shining Girls is a decently quick read. The writing is solid, characters are well drawn even if they only appear in a single chapter, and the story is compelling enough to carry the reader through to the end.

The idea of a time traveling serial killer is hard to sell, but I bought it because it was something new, something different, something that I had never come across before. The storytelling is good, and in the first few chapters I was hooked. However, the constant switching of narratives left little time to feel acquainted with the characters and the story ended flatly, leaving much to be desired. Another thing that left me baffled was "The House". Curtis constantly talks about The House's need for killing - how it pushes him to look for the shining girls that will become his victims....but why?

There are a lot of great things about the book. The plot is interesting. I love all the characters. The setting is full of details that add to the story. Unfortunately, it feels glacially slow. It is one of those books where you look up how long it is when you're reading the e-book, because it feels like it may never end.

I found this book very hard to get into. the only part I enjoyed was the courage if the main character Kirby to try and find her killer. other than that the time travel theme in it just made it difficult for me to enjoy. sorry lauren beukes

Kind of creepy, but mostly just meh. 
 I was most interested in the why and how, but these were never explained or elaborated on. Much more focus was placed on the romantic sub-plot, which was boring, unnecessary, and just annoying. 
 It seemed like the author was just going down a list of things that would make a book successful, and then using them in the most basic, elementary ways. 
 It could have been so much more, and maybe there was something deeper to it that I am just not getting, but, overall, it was forgettable.
Frustrating

Strange, counter-intuitive, painful, twisted, a great reading experience. A murderer from the 1930s finds a house who exits in different times and travels there to kill special girls, shining souls whose potential might change the world. He visits them twice, once when they are little girls and presents them with token objects, and then later, as young women, when he kills them and takes back the token given, leaving another in their place, thus creating a sick circular story to satiate his killing frenzy. One of the women survives, becomes a reporter and, although broken and suffering, she relentlessly becomes the hunter.

This book is amazing. Like, I am actually tempted to bump other books' ratings down so that this one can stand out more. Well-written, well-researched, and even with a pretty large cast of characters all of them feel distinct and memorable. It kept me up two nights in a row to finish, but it was totally worth it.

A sub-par Stephen King set-up is enlivened by Lauren Beukes fine writing and concern for women as characters rather than plot points. The Shining Girls lacks any sense of suspense, as Beukes runs through her tally list of kills, with thinly drawn interest; however she does seem invigorated by the setting, running from Hooverville to 90's Chicago. The novel has a fairly straight-forward plot once you get into its structure and it is just good enough to make you want to read to the end. A little airless, sometimes imaginative.

I thought this was such a neat little premise and it delivered on those aspects. It's a nasty little thriller but clever and quite riveting. What's a little more satisfying here is that the characters and victims are fleshed out rather than them being paper thin characters up for the slaughter - and each of them comes with the timeline to explore in Chicago. It does become repetitive with it's structure but still an entertaining read. A thriller that stands out and above from most of it's ilk.

reference_books.title: Playing for Pizza
reference_books.review_text: Not bad. I never pictured John Grisham as a sports writer, and really, that was the poorest part. His legal stuff is better.

reference_books.title: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe (Hitchhiker's Guide, #2)
reference_books.review_text: I really love this series. This book is definitely not as good as the first, but I do love the question to life, the universe, and everything. And the truth about who really rules the universe. Douglas Adams was a genius.

reference_books.title: The Red Pyramid (Kane Chronicles, #1)
reference_books.review_text: Good story. I don't think it was quite as well-written as the Lightning Thief series and the constantly changing author was at times confusing, as I neglected to read the "author" of each chapter when I'd start reading. I do wonder how they'll work the second book, as it seems they were trying to recruit the reader. The characters were likable, the story made good use of Egyptian legend, and the plot moved along at a fairly decent pace. I enjoyed it. Somewhere, they alluded to the Greek Gods, so I wonder if we couldn't see a merging of the two series at some point.

reference_books.title: The Well of Ascension (Mistborn, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
I lost many nights of sleep over this novel. That's saying something when I stayed up til 1:00 several nights in a row to read.... 
 After read two, I still love this book. It had a slower start than I remember and an annoying cliffhanger, but I love it nonetheless. That's a mark of a good story.

reference_books.title: Dangerous

sample_reviews.review_text: I'd read it years ago, and have seen the movie many times, but coming back to the novel as an adult, I was struck by the poignancy of the back story as I'd never been before. Agatha Christie wrote so feelingly, imbuing what would have been stock characters in the hands of a lesser writer, with real humanity.

This is an amazing story because even though the inspector figured out, over two other amateur professionals that all the suspects did it -- he also saw the foresight of allowing the train official decide to allow a willing suspect to take all the blame for the murder, as does all the other suspects. 
 This is a story that ties hope, courage, self-sacrifice and bravery with the authority being "wise" enough to cover up a sensational story and thus ruin the least amount of lives... because some criminals are that horrible. This is a world in which man -- not God decides what is correct. That even with technical accuracy and precise reasoning, man still decides to do: what is in his own self interest -- that all choices are a personal matter and not founded/justified on universality. 
 This is how the horrors and the sublime justices are one and the same: that power is bestowed by position and not by some universal good. This is a world where beauty and evil require that we forget one or the other, and in the end this is what is most shocking... Agatha Christie takes us to a deep place that is not easily left. In a sense the mystery unresolved through reasoning so clear, we see everyone's (except the dead's) point of view, so that the evil are the dead only because having all other points of view on the same page establishes what is real. That's how all the weak good guys need each other to defeat the evil bad guy. That's how ideology excludes one of us. That's how only acceptance is good, and the material body of the spirit is the consensus of those who count. 
 For us to be all spirit, we require an invisible reminder to be excluded. The evil marks the border of a transcendental bubble that contains only what can be accepted as being a certain way. This necessary nothing is what is required to establish the minor difference between differences. The question then becomes, what nothing is each nothing -- or are they all the same? Did society truly condemn this man to die, or is the authority afraid of this group? We shall never know. 
 This is a rich book that can be seen in a variety of ways. The solution to this mystery and its subsequent resolution crystalizes the relationships in a way that is undeniably true. In this sense, a mystery is a very detailed account of truth through pure reasoning, but only because the book ends, and then we cannot know everything or anything. We then know the limit of this reasoning, which is what the detective is supposed to find -- exploit and then present the deeper Truth which is reasoning. 
 In that sense, the Godel number as the limit of reasoning is the detective finding another person's will as their undiscountable difference.

I recently went on a 5 day vacation to the Caribbean and wanted to read something completely different from all the other books I am currently reading so I chose Murder on the Orient Express. It was the perfect book for a jam packed vacation with family where I knew I would not have the time to get lost in a book but I wanted a story that would take me to another place. This classic did exactly what I needed it to do. It swept me away back in time in the opening scene - set in Aleppo, Syria - when Aleppo was known for its grandeur. The stage - from the elegant train itself to the high society passengers evoked a romanticism unmatched. The setting without cell phone, computer, even fax machine makes the story all the more richer. H Poirot stays one step ahead of his reader and the pages can't turn fast enough to keep up with him.
I never saw it coming. Hit me like a ton of bricks how it ended. I kept wondering, which one did it? Never figured it like that.
I love Agatha Christie mysteries and this is one of her classics. Nice to revisit her mysteries. #AuthorKarenJeanMatskoHood invites everyone to read and enjoy Agatha Christie mysteries.

I love just about all things Christie, especitally if they are Hercule Poirot, Christie. This is one of her best, even the movie was good. I loved the fact that she put everyone on a train and than had a murder, and what a murder it was. I'll say no more you guys just need to read this one.
I usually love the great mistery-detective, but those long stories of Agata Christie didn't catch my attention. The only book of A. Christie I would read again is the book of short stories.

This book has such great reviews and is getting another of many adaptations, but it fell flat for me. I found the characters difficult to relate to and the writing itself left me wanting more. I found it difficult to stay focused on the story since I never was really invested in the outcome and the plot never grabbed my attention. 
 The story seemed to progress in jumps with information coming out of nowhere, which happened because the protagonist kept the information to himself but also because he seemed to know the information purely by guessing for the most part. Unlike other mystery/crime novels in which the reader is given enough to come up with an idea of the murderer, this book left too much out and instead of being surprised, I was just annoyed. 
 The characters were each too uninteresting and unreliable to connect with or suspect and in the end the true murderer/s were a disappointment. I felt like rather than it being a twist ending, it was merely lazy writing, as way the giveaway of knowledge to the protagonist. There is things one expects from a novel of this genre, and I'm sad to say that this contained very few of them. Yes, there was a murder and therefore a murderer, but there was no resolution and no shocking twists or character development. 
 This is a part of a series but I don't think it necessary to read the book before or after this one in order to grasp what was happening. Perhaps it would make this book more interesting, but I don't think you need to pick them up to read this. 
 I didn't enjoy this book, but I may attempt another of Christie's books in the future and hope for better results. I do think it's worthwhile to give it a chance, though, since this is only my option and the book is well-loved by many so it could be loved by you as well.

Murder on the Orient Express was a bit harder to read because it had some references to European things that I wasn't totally familiar with and possibly period things as well but that didn't take away my enjoyment of the work. 
 Poirot is brilliant and I really loved him. It was interesting how he didn't have the answer right away and seemed stumped at some places but then finally worked it out. I prefer when the detective has to figure things out slowly. 
 I did not guess the ending so I was very surprised by how things turned out though I wasn't crazy about the solution. It reminded me too much of And Then There Were None in some ways that I can't get into without unnecessary spoilers. I also don't know if I felt that justice was done in the end. 
 I can say that I look forward to reading other works by Christie and while I don't know that I will become the level of fan many other mystery readers are, I do expect she will become one of my go to authors when I am not sure what to read.

Great expectations approaching this legend.... I liked it, found it an enjoyable and still modern book, even if the final is really too fantastic (12 people all linked to each other and all participating in a murder).
Somehow, one of Poirot's toughest cases takes place in the closed environment of a train with only about a dozen people that could be involved.

I didn't know the ending! I was so sure I was going to know who did it and then she changed it up on me! Usually, it is the opposite- she does something in the beginning that tells you who it is. Then tries to devise ways for you to second guess yourself and then goes, just kidding! Not this time. 
 That said, I didn't find the characters as fully developed in "Murder on the Orient Express." Usually, I get a strong sense of personality from the Agatha Christie books from everyone involved. Not so much this time. There were strong characters, but there were also characters that I completely forgot about until the end and that hasn't happened to me before. 
 I also found some of Poirot's jumps in logic just a little bit too much. A lot of the time, I felt like he got an answer from absolutely nowhere. Just because a lady says she can cook does not make her a professional cook. It was too big of a leap- there were others, but that is the example that leaps to mind. 
 Still, it was an enjoyable read. Perhaps it was made a little bit better for having read some of her earlier works and assuming that because she seemed to set everything up the same way, that I knew exactly who had done it and then was so very pleased to find out that I didn't. I actually think I preferred some of my Nancy Drew books to this though, but it is definitely worth reading at once.

My first Agatha Christie novel! In it, we follow Detective Poirot's attempt at solving a murder in a train from Istanbul to Calais, the Orient Express. Things take a strange turn when the man who died turns out to be the culprit of one of the most heinous crimes of the century. 
 Oh, how I loved this! The writing is not beautiful or enchanting, it's quite simple and straight-forward, but I was reading this for plot anyway. Everything, from characters to facts to evidence, is laid out very neatly in front of us, but it all gets pieced together in the most impossible way. 
 I picked this up mostly for the cover (it's gorgeous), but it's a really engrossing read. I sped through most of it in an afternoon, and I loved it. The premise seems quite simple, but there's so much to take into account. I love how Christie organizes everything, and she doesn't let any of it become confusing. 
 You know that feeling when you're watching CSI or some other crime show, and you just know who did because it's so obvious? Doesn't happen here! There's such a long cast of characters that every time one speaks, you immediately change your focus to him or her. It's brilliant, keeping the reader on the edge of their seat like that! 
 Also, Poirot is kind of awesome, being all stealthy and super smart like he is. I'm looking forward to read more of her novels.

A classic Agatha Christie, with an interesting difference: most of the mystery is told from the point of view of a group of three non-English (specifically Belgian and French) characters, which for once allows Christie to poke as much fun at her English suspects as the foreign ones.

You have this impression of Agatha Christie as a kindly old lady who writes generic mysteries featuring tea and knitting. 
 And she was that, but before she was that she was this lady 
 who is significantly younger and looks like a little bit of a badass, and in fact she was one. 
 The central question of a mystery is "Who done it," right? And what Christie did is she took that question and said, "How far can I take the answer? How weird can I make it?" And she comes up with these wild, experimental, metafictional reveals. I don't want to spoil this particular book, but I didn't see it coming. It's actually crazy stuff, and this is why she's the queen of mystery: she took mysteries to their absolute limits. No one has been able to take them farther. 
 I mean, look, she's not Borges, she's not going to blow your mind on contact. Hers is a quieter magic, and it's constrained by genre. She's straining the limits of mystery novels; Borges is straining the limits of reality. But it's still audacious. 
 Christie created two (!) of the greatest sleuths in the genre: knitting busybody Miss Marples, and the hero of Murder on the Orient Express, smug Hercule Poirot. He bills himself as a sort of opposite to Sherlock Holmes: "I am not one to rely on the expert procedure. It is the psychology I seek, not the fingerprint or the cigarette ash." If Holmes represents science, Poirot represents intuition. This case takes place in a closed room - the train is stuck in a snowstorm, with no communication with the outside world. No one's identity can be verified. Poirot resolves to solve it entirely through sitting around thinking. And when he does: 
 "How did you get wise to all this? That's what I want to know." 
 "I just guessed." 
 The evidence was there for us - Agatha Christie never cheats, her puzzles are airtight - but it's a pretty impressive guess anyway. And it's an impressive book.

While this is not the first story or novel in which Poirot appears, it is certainly the best known. The plot has been adapted, spoofed and plain ripped-off by any number of writers since it first was published. I remember seeing the 1974 film, starring Albert Finney as the Belgian detective, with a huge cast of well-known actors playing the other passengers. This led to later films with Peter Ustinov taking over the role of Poirot. 
 I read the book years ago, but have recently begun re-reading a number of the Christie novels and short story collections. 
 The plot involved Poirot taking an unexpected journey on the title train and becoming involved after one of the passengers is murdered. Saying anything more would give away too much, so I'll only say that things are not always as they appear. Old fashion but still enjoyable.

Obviously one of Christie's best and most famous Herculean Port whodunit, but the clever plot was so familiar through previous reads and the film that the red herrings, clues, etc, seemed to be signalled. Still enjoyable. 5* for a first read, 3* for me now, so I have averaged the two!

"The murderer is with us - on the train now..." 
 Something about this solemn line renders chills through my nerves. Anyway!! 
 There are some things you are as sure as you can be when you pick up a Christie book without which you miss on the Christie-mystery feel. 
 I mean, you know there is going to be a 
 hot-shot, intelligent-brained detective by the name - POIROT, more than at least two or three couple crime suspects, round table gatherings, ponderings and suspicions, and some brilliantly amazing under-lying cause for the crime. 
 Without these, a story is not a Christie-mystery and quite honestly, I would hate to miss that style of detective-suspect game that our lady of mystery is just so good at. This book is another grand example of the same. 
 Hercule Poirot, Samuel Ratchett, A murder, 12 suspects, dozen fake evidences. And the Orient Express. 
 Samuel Ratchett, the big-shot millionaire is threatened of murder. He approaches none other than our extraordinary brainy Poirot expressing as much to him about his insecurity. Poirot declines his offer to help. The same night Ratchett is murdered in his cabin with a dozen brutal stabs with some fake evidences to support the murder while the Orient Express runs into a snow-drift and halts for an indefinite period. What does that mean? 
 "The murderer is with us - on the train now..." 
 And begins the investigation of our beloved Poirot who will travel to world's end if he has to bring justice and evict the murderer. 
 The story is one of Agatha's regular styles, but if you think you can even make a guess to predict what happened exactly or who the real culprit is, you can well do to put that thought to rest. 
 Because life isn't that simple and easy, my friend and obviously not for our Poirot who in-spite taking every leap and turn to bring the case to rest with his intuitive prowess at work, must come to a conclusion that after-all it 
 cannot be a coincidence 
 that all the travelers on the Orient Express are Ratchett's enemies, that he is amidst of a well-planned crime that was put to action. 
 Having said that, I'd still prefer And Then There Were None over this book any given time in life. It just doesn't climb up that ladder as And Then There Were None and that is the reason I feel it deserves four stars not five. 
 Murder on Orient Express is a thoroughly enjoyable, finish-in-one-sitting, mystery read, best done Christie style, as all you Christie lovers would agree. 
 Read this book if you are looking for a light-headed mystery that does not require much of brain-whirling attention and still manages to have you stay-put.

Solid 3.5 stars. It's Sanderson Lite -- tastes great, less filling. Entertaining follow up to book one.

** spoiler alert ** 
 If you haven't read Steelheart stop now! You've been warned. 
 Maybe it isn't entirely fair but I often think of Sanderson' Reckoners series as his "taking a break writing." That isn't to say both Steelheart and Firefight are bad novels, they're both fun adventure stories, but Sanderson's work on this series lacks some on the intricacy and detail seen in his other fiction. Firefight follows Steelheart almost directly picking up only a little while after the previous novel's explosive climax. David and Reckoners have organized a new government in Steelheart's metallic Newcago. Unfortunately, their actions have made them the target for other High Epics looking to move in to the vacuum and to make an example of what happens to those who raise arms against Epics. David and the rest of the Reckoners take the fight to a new High Epic, one targeting them, Regalia who is camped out in the mysterious ruins of flooded Manhattan known as Babylon Restored. 
 I enjoy David as a main character despite often feeling like I shouldn't. He's a goofy, unbelievable earnest teen who I feel should be just too silly to like. Yet, despite that his consistently terrible metaphors, straight-forward attitude, and incessantly optimistic outlook is infectious. In an world that could easily be written in a manner far more grim and gritty David's almost cartoonish disposition elevates the novel to a level of fun that I'm not sure would otherwise be possible. While David might be a lovable nerdy goofball Sanderson also includes the bouncy and incredibly silly Mizzy into the mix. She lacks some of David's angst but seeing another wonderfully silly character surrounded by people who seem to be professionally serious upped my enjoyment of the novel. Sanderson isn't really known as a humorous writer but Firefight definitely proves he can light comedy well. 
 Where Sanderson is typically known for his complex magic systems and intricate world building the Reckoners series tends to feature a lighter touch. They mystery of how Epics work, why they go bad and what their weaknesses are is a major background mystery that David started exploring in Steelheart and continues contemplating in Firefight. Sanderson is admirably restrained when it comes to the explanations and it makes for an engaging read. It's sort of refreshing to see the major focus on character and action over plot and world. While there is a meta-story going on, further developed in Firefight, it is secondary to the trials and tribulations of the lead character. 
 Sanderson also nicely counters the homogenous cityscape of Newcago with the flooded streets of Manhattan rechristened as Babylon Reborn. He does a wonderful job of using the goals and attitudes of the High Epics governing the cities as a means to influence the cultures of its inhabitants. Steelhearts paranoia and isolationism is reflected in the citizens of Newcago while Regalia's aloof hands-off nature combined with the strange traits of Babylon Restored, abundant glowing vegetation, serving to produce a population more open and celebratory. It's interesting to watch David, so used to scurrying beneath the oppressive gaze of Steelheart and his regime, be so utterly baffled by the borderline care-free nature of Babylon Restored. The population, accepting the potential for death by an Epic, lacks much of the outrage and aggression seen in Newcago. There is air of religious fervor in Babylon Restored that contrasted directly with the stoicism and cynicism of Newcago. It's a great change of setting and watching familiar characters interact with the change in attitude makes for some great reading 
 Firfight proves that even absent of complicated magic system and detail world-building Sanderson can still spill a damn fine yarn. Lightning-paced and speckled with humor Firefight is a novel for anyone looking for a book that is just plain fun. I look forward to seeing where David and the rest of Reckoners go next.

Firefight is the second book in prolific wunderkind* Brandon Sanderson's YA series, The Reckoners, which is about what would happen if the world suddenly developed superheroes, only the superheroes were all of them evil, power-hungry, maniacal psychopaths. The Reckoners are a group of normal people (well, mostly) dedicated to bringing down those superheroes, called Epics in this world. Nineteen year old David is our protagonist and POV into this world. When he was a kid, he watched as infamous Epic Steelheart killed his father, and he swore revenge. The first book in this series was all about David achieving that revenge. This book is all about the fallout. 
 *I will ask this question for the hundredth time: How does he write so many books so fast and they are all of them GOOD? (When asked this question, not by me, at the Tucson Festival of Books last year, he responded that it helps that not only is writing his job, but it's also his hobby. His idea of taking a break from a book he's working on is to start working on another book (or story or novella, etc). So yeah, I suppose if I didn't spend so much time reading, writing book reviews, baking and cooking, watching all the TV etc., I might have the time to be as prolific as Brandon Sanderson. Man, that guy must love writing. 
 For me, that fallout was very emotionally satisfying. Instead of being even more gung-ho about killing Epics, David has responded to being "Steelslayer" by beginning to feel BAD when killing Epics. He feels empathy for them, and he has this new crazy idea about their weaknesses that could totally change everything. This is not an attitude his fellow Reckoners understand AT ALL. Firefight even addressed some of the concerns I had about the first book, most notably it lacked the annoying character Cody who insisted last time upon using the contraction "y'all" to refer to a singular person; it gave David an emotional arc (he was too focused on revenge last time); and it did this while moving the world and the story in an even more interesting direction. (His vision of post-Epic New York City was also fascinating.) David's metaphors were more bearable here than I found them in the first book, probably because I've really grown to like the kid. (Also, they're not metaphors! They're similes as Megan points out to him late in the book .) 
 At this point, saying the Reckoners books are my least favorite of Brandon Sanderson's novels is like saying cookies and cream is my least favorite type of ice cream. It may not be my top choice, but if you gave me a half gallon of it, it would be gone within a couple of days, and I would have enjoyed every bite. Firefight was just as good as I was expecting it to be, but in a different way than I was expecting, if that makes any sense at all. Up next from B-Sand, the second Wax & Wayne novel in December, followed closely (like, within a couple of weeks!) by the third book in January. 
 [4.5 stars]

 For those who have read Steelheart and enjoyed it, I think you would find this book just as enjoyable. I would say the action level is the same as well as the number of reveals. It's a fun enough story to read and brings up some interesting themes and ideas to consider. In fact, David's internal struggle to either hate or sympathize with the Epics was one of the most enjoyable parts of the book for me to read. That along with any scenes involving David and Megan, although I must admit some of their dialogue was cringe-worthy for me. 
 Overall, the writing was pretty underwhelming for me. Sanderson is not especially know for his ability to craft beautiful prose, but I really enjoy the writing style of his adult books. The writing style of Firefight, along with the fact that I found the main character too annoying, made it hard for me to fully engage with the story for most of the book. 
 But the world building was REALLY fun. Not up to par with the Mistborn books (or I assume the Stormlight Archives which I have yet to read), but he had some really unique and interesting touches that I thoroughly enjoyed. 
 I am looking forward to seeing how Sanderson will end this trilogy because his ability to craft fantastic endings is what sets him apart from so many other authors.

 This Review was first posted on Keep Reading Forward. If you want to see more, check out our other locations as well as here. 
 In the second book in the Reckoners series, David and the Reckoners move onto to New York, now called Babylon Restored, after a mysterious pattern of Epics come to attack the team. 
 In Babylon Restored, it is like another world. Imagine New York flooded to the highest points possible, only leaving a couple floors for each of the highest towers. The main mode of transportation are by bridges and by boats. This is all due to the work of the new Epic brought in, Regalia. Regalia is a water epic, an epic who can control water and see through waters as well like a Seer. 
 Now, the second book wasn't a good as the first book was, but it was still relatively enjoyable to read and it continued to hold onto the mass amount of action and suspense. I remember in the first book, I had great excitement for every scene and every scene drew me in. This book, not all of that scenes had that excitement. 
 The new characters were brought in were interesting to read about. I loved Mizzy, a Reckoner, and Dawnslight, an Epic with the abilities to grow plants, highlight colors, and send messages in the form of fortune cookies, despite his unfortunate condition he is currently in. If there was a thing in this world called Good Epics, Dawnslight would probably be the only one (with that official title). 
 Overall, this book was just as good as the first, but fell short in a couple of areas. I still can't wait to see how the series ends. I do have a few theories of my own.

Rollicking. There's not a lot of depth here, although David is making a case for some of his crazy theories, and there's a glimpse of a larger pattern showing through, true to Sanderson's form. 
 The metaphors, when attention is brought to them by David, are terrible and annoying. When he doesn't point out how terrible they are, they can be a bit amusing. As before, the David-Megan interactions steal the show. 
 Entertaining.
Didn't expect this ending.

 Will finish the third book but can't wait to be done with this series.

I admit I preferred Steelheart :( I was really excited to read Firefight, but it didn't make as much of an impact as Steelheart did originally. I also found the metaphors incredibly cheesy and distracting from the story, although perhaps I noticed these more as I downloaded the audio edition, whereas I read Steelheart in Kindle.

SO GOOD! 
 And now I have to wait until Spring of 2016 for the finale? Yeesh.

I guess this series is just not my cup of tea. It just doesn't measure up to his other series. Brandon Sanderson is one of my favorite authors so I am surprised by feelings about this series. It might be because the book really didn't build on itself. It was only when the end came that everything came together. I know that sounds silly since that is how books usually go, but It was just situation after situation until the very end. No small increments or revelations on the way. The characters are likable, but nothing like the character development of Kaladin or Dalinar.

There's something extremely comfortable about reading a book done by one of your favorite authors. It doesn't matter the age range, the subject, or even the characters - you know it's going to be a well done story. 
 That's the case with Firefight. It was comfort. It was familiar. And I enjoyed the hell out of it. 
 I am constantly amazed how Sanderson can create so much out of very simple ideas. He gives us so much, but in the end, it's the simplest things that form the ideas surrounding any of his books. And I can't wait to see how the trilogy ends given all of the info we learned from this book.

As expected, Brandon Sanderson has delivered another fine piece of boundary-busting, action-packed, well-plotted, well-paced, character-driven fantasy/superhero/supervillain story-telling goodness. I ran out of praiseworthy adjectives for Mr. Sanderson's work long ago. 
 This second novel in the Reckoners trilogy does just what a middle book is supposed to do. It drives the overall plot forward allowing for much more detail to come out about just what the characters are facing. It continues the style and concepts of the original but at the same time turns everything upside down to keep it original by changing the locale, adding new characters and new threats, evolving previous characters, etc. And, of course, it sets up the third and final volume perfectly. 
 I won't go into plot details because it would be easy to spoil this one. Suffice it to say that if you enjoyed Steelheart, you won't be disappointed by Firefight. As always, Sanderson's ability to write interesting characters whose courage and ability to reason things out overcomes their own innocent blunders and provide unique solutions to seemingly impossible situations is right at the forefront of this book. Be aware that the final third of the book sprints along at a pace that doesn't let up for a second so be prepared for that and don't plan on going to bed or whatever commitment you may have had before starting that last part.
I'm such a Sanderson fan, I can give his books five stars before reading them and feel pretty confident. I have read one, however, and it's excellent!

reference_books.title: The Miniaturist
reference_books.review_text:
I really enjoyed the writing and a lot of the characters were interesting especially Marin whom I found to be very intelligent and strong minded. 
 She was independent in a world where she couldn't afford to be. At the beginning she appears as a very strict, closed up and pious woman but as the story progresses we get a totally different description of her personality. 
 Nella at the beginning of the book is (thanks to her mother) convinced that the only way to exist in her society is through marriage. Nonetheless she wish to find love is determined to be a good wife. But as the story unfolds she soon realizes how high her expectation were. Miserable and alone she takes confort in the deliveries the Miniaturist sends her. But soon she realizes that the miniatures she receives are more than perfect replicas. They tell stories and secrets. 
 I felt that Nella grew a lot in this book. She become strong to take control of the impossible situation she has to face. Furthermore faced with the existence of Marin she realizes that marriage does not make you valid as a woman. 
 Overall I enjoyed my read even though I wish to have known more about Marin and the Miniaturist. The mystery in itself was interesting but I was disappointed when it unfolded.

The most recently hyped book on booktube, We Were Liars, pushes the themes found in Wuthering Heights but fails to deliver. The attempts to weave in and out of a memory re-consciousness left me feeling tired rather than intrigued. I listed to the advice and read the book without learning of any spoilers, but I would have been better off hearing the less than special ending and reserved my time for something with a bit more substance. Basically, E. Lockhart's structure came off forced and failed at delivering the shock-surprise endings once trendy by creators like M. Night Shyamalan. 
 We Were Liars captures the story of a privileged family who spends summers on a private island near Martha's Vineyard and is at the height of society. The story is narrated by the eldest of the grandchildren, Cady, who spends her time trying to remember something far forgotten. As she comes closer to her truth, she realizes her family is not the picture of perfection and that she has done something she can never take back. 
 I can't decide if it was my failure to connect with any of the characters, the endless fair tale metaphors, or the predictability of the story's end, but I just didn't react in any sort of way to this book. The only feelings that arose out of me were those that came when I was faced with the sad and wasteful death of a household pet. Nothing else moved me when it came to reading this family's story, and when I finished, I was left me feeling flat, bored, and frustrated.
Did not see it coming...

I think my biggest problem was how much my brain had to work to make any kind of sense over this book. I really had to pay attention to every little detail and even doing that, I still found myself confused at times, wondering if the narrator was just exaggerating or if certain things really happened. I suppose that was kind of the point though. It had a very Gossip Girl feel to it. (I feel like I say that about a lot of books...) But another one of my problems were how strange the characters were. Really not your typical teens in my opinion. Some of the things they said just didn't feel right at all. 
 My mind was completely blown at the end. I did NOT see that coming at all. It was a fun book to read and a quick one at that. I read it pretty much from start to finish unable to put it down. And I definitely enjoyed it. I'm really somewhere between like and love. 
 Should you read this? Definitely. It was one of the most interesting books I have ever read. I kind of want to read it again right now to see if I can straighten out some of my confusion.  I am sorry Night Circus, I love you with all my heart and will always cherish you but this is my favorite standalone book of all time 
 I mean, seriously. It talks about love, and friendship, and self discovery, and family, and strength, and bravery to face every inner demon we all have, and summer, and winter, and just everything I could wish for. It is the story of a boy named Ari Mendoza, a person who wouldn't admit his love to himself, and another boy named Dante Quintana, a person who had come to terms with who he was and would always stand for it, even if people hurt him. 
 It was the story of these two guys who fell in love, a love so beautiful and strong, so inspiring, like a poem. It was a love so true, so raw and full of honesty, so full of intimacy and discovery of both each other and themselves. 
 The plot was flowing like the way rain rolls down the windows. It was heartwarming and heartbreaking, addictive and compelling and utterly enchanting. I still find myself in utter shock that my favorite standalone of all time is a contemporary novel. The writing was poetic and wonderful and I found myself longing to jump back in this book seconds after I left it to do other things. It has so many inspirational quotes and explored so many issues that it opened my mind and heart to the world in ways I find myself unable to explain. Some of my favorite quotes were: 
 I got to thinking that poems were like people. Some people you got right off the bat. Some people you just didn't get--and never would get. 
 Another secret of the universe: Sometimes pain was like a storm that came out of nowhere. The clearest summer could end in a downpour. Could end in lightning and thunder. 
 To be careful with people and with words was a rare and beautiful thing. 
 And it seemed to me that Dante's face was a map of the world. A world without any darkness. 
 Wow, a world without darkness. How beautiful was that? 
 The characters were also so perfect. The book treated them all with such kindness and fairness, with such love and care. I just loved every single one of them and wanted them all to be happy. I wanted Ari to realize his love for Dante, Dante himself to be happy and proud of who he is, Dante's parents to have a healthy, wonderful baby that would live to be Dante's sibling, Ari's parents to heal, in their own way each one and I could honestly go on and on with how deeply I fell in love with all these characters and how much I wished I could give them all a world without darkness. 
 In general, I strongly believe this book brought so much light into my life and even when I finished, I still had the weird urge to reread it right then and there. I really, really needed something to remind me that we shall never be afraid of who we are and, no matter what, we shall never turn down the people we know are important for us and will always bring brightness to our life 
 I recommend this to every single person out there, whether you want to read a nice LGBTQIAP tale, or a story about finding yourself, or something poetic, or just something that will put you into thinking and will keep your heart warm and your mind content till the rest of your life 
 Until our next review, keep being strong, and bold and brave. 
 And explore, until you figure out all the secrets of the universe 
 ~Mary

THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR ARISTOTLE AND DANTE DISCOVER THE SECRETS OF THE UNIVERSE! 
 Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe by Benjamin Alire Saenz is about two 15 year-olds who become unlikely friends. The book basically follows Aristotle's life, and the problems he faces. 
 I enjoyed Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe. I thought that the beginning of the book was slow and (at some points) uninteresting. While reading this book (at the start), I thought that I would give it 3/5 stars, but after reading the last 'part' (All the Secrets of the Universe), the book deserved 4 stars! 
 The things I liked about this book were: 
 -(Some of) The Writing Style: At some points the writing style was beautiful, poetic and extremely relatable. One scene in particular stood out to me: 
 "If I had been braver this is what I would have said: Angry? What have I got to be angry about? You know something, Dad? I don't really care that you can't tell me about Vietnam. Even though I know the war owns you, I don't care that you don't want to talk about it, but I do care that you

"Another secret of the universe: Sometimes pain was like a storm that came out of nowhere. The clearest summer could end in a downpour. Could end in lightning and thunder." 
 Als ik mijn bookish vrienden om een goede recommandatie vraag, krijg ik Ari & Dante naar mijn hoofd geslingerd. Het boek heeft mij echter nooit zo aangesproken en om die reden heeft het een paar jaar geduurd voordat ik besloot het boek te kopen en te gaan lezen. 
 PLOT 
 Ari vijftien, weet niet goed wie hij is en heeft vrijwel geen vrienden. Dan leert hij Dante kennen, die hem leert zwemmen. Er ontstaat een vriendschap waarin beide jongens elkaar beter leren kennen, maar ook andere dingen leren kennen. Zo leert Dante Ari alles over poezie. 
 Hun vriendschap wordt al snel sterker en ze vormen een diepere bond. Beiden vinden bij de ander wat ze misschien wel in zichzelf zoeken. Ari is 'jaloers' op de relatie die Dante met zijn ouders heeft, terwijl Dante ervan opkijkt dat Ari voor zichzelf durft op te komen en niet bang is om iemand een klap te geven. 
 Ari is op zoek naar de geheimen van het universum, maar misschien weet hij de antwoorden al wel. 
 PERSONAGES 
 Voor mijn gevoel leerde ik Ari meer kennen door hoe anderen over hem spraken (bijvoorbeeld door zijn moeder, of door Ari) en niet door hemzelf. Wat ik wel leerde, is dat Ari erg met zichzelf in de knoop zit. Hij is boos, maar weet niet precies waarop. Nu is de puberteit al geen fijne periode, al helemaal niet als je ook niet weet wie je nu precies bent. Al met al was Ari mijn favoriete personage. Hij was grappig en zijn onzekerheid was erg herkenbaar. 
 Aan Dante irriteerde ik mij nogal. Het is een doorzetter, maar soms op een nogal... agressieve manier. Ook Dante is erg onzeker; zo twijfelt hij enorm over zijn Mexicaanse roots en zijn seksualiteit. Wat ik daarentegen weer geweldig vond, was dat hij over alles zo open is. Over zijn angsten, wensen en behoeften. Dante is, ondanks zijn onzekerheden, enorm enthousiast over het leven. 
 Graag had ik meer van de ouders van Ari en Dante willen lezen, en dan vooral over de ouders van Ari. Hoewel hij niet de meest hechte band met zijn ouders heeft (althans, niet op de manier als dat Dante met die van hem heeft), vond ik de conversaties tussen Ari en zijn moeder ontroerend. Ze is een sterke vrouw met emoties. Ook de vader van Ari vond ik een sterk personage, alhoewel hij niet vaak 'in beeld' kwam en zich meer, door zijn trauma's, op de achtergrond hield. Een scene, tegen het einde van het boek, was erg speciaal en hartverwarmend: deze scene laat zien hoe veel Ari zijn ouders wel niet van hem houden. 
 POSITIEF 
 + De schrijver weet hoe hij moet schrijven. Ik zie de poetische schrijfstijl waarvan sommigen zeggen dat die aanwezig is zelf niet, maar desondanks leest het boek vlot weg en lopen de zinnen vloeiend in elkaar over. Ik had het boek in drie dagen uit; iets wat mij sinds mijn leesdip sinds Dreamology niet meer is gelukt. 
 + De personages reageren naar hun leeftijd; Ari gedraagt zich als een vijftienjarige op zijn vijftiende, en als een zestienjarige op zijn zestiende. De diversiteit bij de personages vond ik geweldig; niemand lijkt op elkaar en toch zijn ze allemaal hetzelfde. 
 + Hoewel er niet echt een plot is, vond ik het voor de verandering eens fijn om geen boek met veel druk/haast te lezen. Voorbeeld (nee, geen spoiler): op pagina 50 is een gevecht, op pagina 58 rusten ze even, en op pagina 60 komt de slechte tovenaar opeens tevoorschijn. Het had een rustig tempo, wat ik wel kan waarderen. 
 NEGATIEF 
 - Al met al voelde het boek nogal ongevoelig en onbewogen aan. Voor mijn gevoel toonde Ari te weinig emoties om hem echt goed te leren kennen. Vooral door wat anderen tegen of over hem vertelden leerde ik de 'echte' Ari kennen. 
 - Ik had graag gewild dat er dieper op de tijdsperiode waarin het verhaal zich afspeelt werd ingegaan. Hoe werd er met homoseksualiteit in die tijd omgegaan? Was het nog heftiger dan nu? 
 - Het einde was, hoe mooi ook, ietwat te gehaast. Opeens komt Ari erachter dat hij Dante leuk vind. Natuurlijk zag je het wel aankomen, maar er werd nogal mysterieus over gedaan. Ook was het verhaal opeens voorbij. Ik had graag een wat geslotener einde willen zien. 
 CONCLUSIE 
 Het is zeker geen slecht boek; allesbehalve, zelfs. Helaas voelde ik echter te weinig tijdens het lezen. Het las oppervlakkig, bijna emotieloos. Het deed mij allemaal niet zoveel. Bovendien vond ik Ari een ietwat nietszeggend personage, ook al kon ik hem op bepaalde punten ontzettend goed begrijpen. 
 Ik vond dat het boek veel potentie had, maar dat daar vrij weinig mee gedaan werd. Er zijn namelijk veel 'onopgeloste' zaken/situaties waar ik graag meer over had willen lezen: ik had graag gewild dat Ari en zijn vader elkaar beter leren kennen en dat Ari zijn broer te zien krijgt. Ik bedoel: het hele boek heeft hij het over zijn vader en broer 
 Maar ondanks de oppervlakkigheid is dit een dikke aanrader. Het boek is geschreven in een realiteit die niet in veel ya-boeken te vinden is. Alles en iedereen voelde echt aan. Het leek wel alsof de gesprekken zich voor mijn neus afspeelden. 
 Al met al is het een goed boek en vind ik het zeker een aanrader. Het behandelt onderwerpen als onzekerheid, geaardheid en vriendschap.
