While reading this book I was imagining all of the people I would recommend this book to, and then just like that it was ruined. 
 I cannot muster the energy to recommend gay books where one of the kids gets beaten up for being gay anymore. Cheap. I know it happens, but at this point it is just too damaging to include in so many books. When I was a kid I was pretty sure I'd end up tied to a fence and tortured to death because Matthew Shepard was the only young gay person I had ever heard of outside of my group of friends. There was no other representation. Obviously it is important to acknowledge the horrible injustice of violent homophobia, but it is really important to make sure kids get the message that it is not inevitable that you will be brutalised because you are gay. LGBT YA is saturated with violent homophobia already. Find another contrived bonding situation for your love story. 
 The final nail in the coffin for this book was the brother's backstory. We've already had anti-gay violence that ends up hospitalising one of the main characters, but now we get to the brother's backstory, where a trans woman is used as a prop to give the brother an unforgivable past. Completely unnecessary to include a trans woman's murder as a little "surprise!" at the end. I'm not using spoiler tags here because any mystery that exploits anti-trans violence for a cis character's development doesn't deserve to be preserved. I was devastated when I got to this point in the book. And not in the way I challenge all good books to devastate me. I was devastated to be reminded that even in fiction trans women will be murdered for someone's cheap thrills--and I don't mean the brother, I mean the author and the panels of my fellow librarians that so praised this book. Gay and trans suffering is cheap, but I guess it wins awards. 
 I would be hard pressed to recommend this to any teen.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was so very moving. So moving, in fact, that I'm struggling to review it. I love how it's not just a young adult love story, or another story about a teen learning to handle his or her sexual orientation. It's really about these teens learning to handle their identity as people. They look at so many rules and standards, and how they meet them and how they don't: they're Mexican, but not Mexican enough because they don't like certain things from their culture. They're supposed to talk about all their feelings, because that's what the right and adult thing to do is, and yet their parents have many feelings and thoughts they don't share. It's a struggle to face these many standards, and these are things that continue as people become adults. I love that the author includes that in the trials that these boys have to face. 
 On top of that, I love that the boys are smart and good and respectful, despite these struggles. They are frustrated and angry, but that's not all they are. I found that heartening, and I really cared about them. I wanted them to be able to face their fears and have the hard talks. They had good parents (I LOVE that they have good parents!), and the author paints the parents as real people with struggles, as well as caring and devoted mothers and fathers. It was a lovely picture of friendship and family and love of all kinds.

I don't know what to say. Finally a story equally focused on love, family, identity, it didn't feel like the other ones were any kind of background for the main issue which I found very relatable as in real life every aspect of it is as important as it gets. It was genuinely a wonderful adventure with two fantastic characters and I'll miss it so much.

I wanted to like this so much more than I did. It was recced to me by two people within a couple days (people I usually trust!). And if you had just told me the plot I would've thought I'd be into it. But I found it really hard to connect with the characters, mostly because the dialogue was often unnatural. So much referring to each other by name! In casual conversations! When I'm talking to people - especially a one-on-one conversation - I rarely, if ever, use a person's name unless I'm trying to get their attention or something, but the dialogue in this book is filled with people calling their conversational partner by name constantly ("That's not going to happen, Ari"/"They'll always love you, Dante" - followed by Ari using Dante's name in four of his next five sentences!). I kept finding myself rewriting the dialogue in my head to get rid of all the names which is a pretty frustrating way to get through a book. 
 Also, I wish Ari had come to understand himself without his parents sitting him down and telling him he was in love with Dante. Like, good on them for being supportive, but that was awkward and unsatisfying. After everything he'd gone through, I just wanted him to figure it out on his own.

This is such a lovely book. It was a little slow getting started for me, but picked up in the second half. A great summer read!

Ugh, 
 SPOILER 
 The first 50% of the book was a friendship between two boys. The next 40% is about one of the boys coming out. The next 8% is about reuniting, learning family secrets and then BAM! We are both gay. Parents encourage it. THE END.

During the summer after their sophomore year in the late 1980s, two boys meet and begin a friendship. The story of Dante and Aristotle is not cliched, though it is a coming of age tale. It's unique and lovely. The characters are all well drawn and the story moves at a fast pace.

https://aliterarylion.wordpress.com/ & http://literary-lion.tumblr.com/! 
 "I bet you could sometimes find all the mysteries of the universe in someone's hand." 
 Aristotle is a loner, he has no friends and he may as well be an only child. May as well be because his sisters are both adults with their own lives and his brother is in prison. Dante is a quick witted intellectual. When the two boys meet at a pool they being forming a friendship to last a lifetime. 
 This book is beautiful in a way. The writing was very poetic. Unfortunately there was quite a few repetitive phrases that started to feel a little tired. The writer could have found another way to phrase some of Ari's thoughts instead of using the same foil for all of them. 
 Between the plotline with Dante and the plotline with Aristotle's brother it's very hard to find a dull moment. There is an element of mystery woven in through all the scenes depicting Dante and Ari's relationship. 
 Speaking of the relationships in this book they're all fantastically woven. Never does it feel like the book is suddenly dropping a relationship upon you. This book also had a lovely showcase of positive family relationships, even when working through the hard things. It's rare parents are given such real depth in young adult novels. From the main relationship between Dante and Ari to their relationships with their parents and minor characters everything feels organic. 
 There was a bit at the end about how romantic love was somehow stronger than friendship love that was a bit of a put off. In fact there's barely any positive friendships in the novel, which is a problem romance novels tend to run into. Dante and Aristotle's deep connection did make up for it interest wise but it made their world feel smaller somehow. 
 In fact despite the relationships being well written the characters were a bit of a problem. They felt flat. Aristotle himself was a bit of a complex character. He jumped from mood to mood, from love to hate to irritation to love again. It was a little disconcerting. In strings of conversation it was hard to distinguish which character was talking because of how similar the voices were. Characters seem very quick to jump to extreme emotions as well, this goes for Aristotle, Dante and their parents. 
 There were several scenes that felt completely out of place and unrealistic. The main boys feel awkwardly written. It's the sort of book that focuses on the main cast so hard that it damages their ability to feel real because the world they exist in is so flimsy. The relationships progress well but the characters barely feel like real people and it does hurt the novels impact terribly. 
 While I did admit that the writing is poetic it's not always a good thing. At times the writing feels clunky. At times it feels like it's trying too hard to be something deep and beautiful, so hard that it becomes a parody of itself. 
 It's easy to see why a book like this would win awards. It deals with some difficult subjects without letting the writing become too dark or gritty. It's a good book. Beautiful even, but there are definitely things I would have wanted to see done differently.

reference_books.title: City on Fire
reference_books.review_text: Incredibly over-written and much too long. Literary fiction set in 1970s featuring a diverse cast of characters - from wealthy WASPS to punk street kids. A weak motivating mystery - who shot a college student on New Years' Day 1977? - and frequent detours into the backstory of the unhappy, wealthy WASP brother and sister duo of Regan and William made this an uninvolving and slow story. Hallberg's ten dollar words and the similarity of dialogue between characters coming from different socio-economic backgrounds was aggravating. I only made it thru the entire book because I have a very long commute and wanted to see what all the hype was about. Not recommended.

reference_books.title: The Kitchen House
reference_books.review_text:
Cliched melodrama about slavery. This novel is told in alternating voices between Lavinia, a white indentured servant from Ireland, and Belle, a slave fathered by the plantation owner on the plantation on which both women live. After her parents die on the voyage from Ireland to Virginia, 6 year old Lavinia is taken in by the Pike family and assigned to the Kitchen House of the large plantation. The black slaves on the plantation become her family and as she grows to adulthood, Lavinia is caught between the white and black world. Belle's trajectory is equally confused. She is the daughter of the plantation owner and a slave mother who died when she was born. In her early childhood, she was raised with love by her white grandmother. However after her grandmother's death, she is shunted aside when her father marries a white woman unaware of her parentage. Belle becomes a cook in the Kitchen House where the slaves know she is the master's daughter but her father's wife and children do not. 
 This was a very plot based book. There are constant love affairs, lots of babies, abuse, drug addiction, violence, and rape. The evil characters (Marshall, Belle's half-brother and Lavinia's eventual husband, and Rankin, the plantation overseer) are dastardly and evil because it fits the narrative. Lavinia, the heroine of the story, is flat and blandly good as well as being incredibly stupid at times (such as when she plans to ease the burdens of her black family after marrying Marshall--does she not understand the concept of slavery?!) 
 The author seems to argue that there were good masters in slave times who treated their slaves like employees. The abuses and cruelty were a product of bad, evil masters. Whites and blacks got along just like family! 
 I listened to the audio book version and felt both narrators did an excellent job, although the reader for Lavinia had a light Irish accent which didn't make much sense since the character would probably have lost her accent soon after arriving in Virginia as a child.

reference_books.title: Rebel Belle (Rebel Belle, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Light paranormal novel with strong romance elements. Harper Jane Price (think Election's Tracy Flick meets Buffy Summers) is a type A personality who runs the elite private school she attends in Pine Grove, AL. One night just before Homecoming Dance (where she is sure to be crowned Queen), Harper is left with strange supernatural powers. Harper discovers that she has become a Paladin, an ancient guardian with super strength and fighting abilities and that she needs to protect an Oracle. The Oracle turns out to be Harper's least favorite person, David Stark, editor of the high school newspaper and Harper's primary sparing partner. Can David and Harper work to together to prevent a horrible disaster from ruining Cotillion? 
 There is lots of snappy dialogue and Harper is a fun, appealing main character. The novel balances romance and fantasy and is a good light read for teens. The ending of the book sets up more adventures and trials for Harper and David.

reference_books.title: Hotel on the Corner of Bitter and Sweet
reference_books.review_text: I didn't care for this book at all but for some reason I kept listening (probably because I didn't have another audio book handy). I found the story sappy and sentimental. My main problem was that Henry was too emotionally mature for a 12 year old and his relationship with Keiko was that of an older teen rather than a young one. I realize that people were forced to mature at an earlier age in the past (especially during a war) but Henry seemed very unbelievable. The plotting was very predictable and the scenes set in the 1980s with Henry and his son didn't add much to the story. Lisa See's Shanghai Girls was a better book about the Chinese American experience during WWII and Farewell to Manzanar & Snow Falling on Cedars were better books about the Japanese Internment camps.

reference_books.title: Looking for Alaska
reference_books.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 A fairly explicit young adult novel narrated by Miles "Pudge" Halter about his year at a boarding school in Alabama. Miles quickly makes friends with the roommate (nicknamed "the Colonel") and develops a strong friendship crush on the smart and feisty Alaska. Their adventures including drinking, smoking, and coming up with complicated pranks. After the death of Alaska in a car accident, Pudge and the Colonel try to discover if Alaska's death was an accident or a suicide while dealing with their grief. I enjoyed this book and found parts very funny but I failed to see the attraction of Alaska, who seemed to hover between manic-depression and dream girl. While the emotional experiences of being a teenager were realistically depicted, other parts (such as Pudge's memorization of famous last words) were less interesting. Green is very gifted at creating intelligent humorous male teenagers. 
 I listened to this on audio and the narrator did an excellent job of creating voices for the different characters. I did have a slight problem with my Ipod jumping between sections and I listened to some parts out of order before I corrected the problem.

reference_books.title: American Housewife
reference_books.review_text: A darkly humorous collections of short stories that all interrogate the notion of a housewife in contemporary American society. Some of the stories were as short as two pages but they were all biting and witty.

reference_books.title: The Nest
reference_books.review_text:
Contemporary fiction about a dysfunctional New York family. The Plumb family is a group of upper-middle class white people with definite white people problems. Years ago, their deceased father invested money in the stock market and created a nice nest egg for the four kids. The money was promised to them on the 40th birthday of the youngest daughter and over the past several years, the Plumb siblings have been counting on the nest to help them out of their financial over extensions. However, after Leo, the eldest, injures a young woman in a car accident, their mother has depleted much of the money to pay off Matilda, who lost a foot in the accident. 
 Over the course of the novel, Bea, Jack, Melody, and Leo will have to deal with their diminished expectations and other personal problems that have been festering under the surface. The chapters are told in third person omniscient and shift the focus between the siblings as well as several other people in their lives (children, an ex-girlfriend, a boss). The characters in this family drama can be selfish and unlikeable but most of them have a definite character arc and learn to let go of the negative character traits and improve their personal relationships. This book was described by reviewers as funny which I didn't really find - it was slightly satirical but not very comedic. Sweeney's writing is heartfelt and the pacing was swift. Several of the secondary characters (such as Stephanie, Leo's ex-girlfriend) were very sympathetic and more appealing than the Plumb siblings. Strangely the character of their mother sets the plot in motion by taking money out to help Leo and then largely disappears from the narrative. At the end, the author reveals very minor details about what will happen to certain characters in the future but not others; I thought this should have been applied to all characters or removed. 
 Readers who enjoyed The Vacationers by Emma Straub or The Middlesteins by Jami Attenberg will like this similar contemporary family story.

reference_books.title: Born a Crime: Stories From a South African Childhood

reference_books.title: Ordinary Grace
reference_books.review_text: I enjoyed the strong sense of place in the novel but thought the characters could have been better developed. I figured out the mystery of who killed the narrator's sister fairly early on. I agree with the Booklist review which stated, "This coming-of-age story is obviously an attempt to show how grace can work through the fissures of suffering. While the setting is well rendered, the characters are too flat, and Krueger keeps striking the same monologist's meditative note throughout, while most readers will long for variety in style."

book_a.title: The Zookeeper's Wife
book_a.user_review: My initial reaction to this book was conflicted. I liked certain parts of the book (the insight into Polish customs, the information about Nazi efforts to back breed animals) but found other parts frustrating (the digressions, the lack of an ending, the lyrical writing style). After the book discussion, I have a greater appreciation of what the book accomplished. I also have thought more about poetic non-fiction (of which this book would be a prime example). While I prefer my history more straight forward and footnoted and I see the strengths in Ackerman's approach. I wouldn't necessarily recommend this book but reading it had its rewarding moments.

sample_reviews.review_text: I couldn't even finish this book. I think the story in general was good but there was so much random information that I really lost interest.

This novel was good; however, it has lulls in it where the author spends chapters discussing things not relevant to the telling of the story, such as describing an entomologist's bug collection, describing the different kinds of beetles. Looking forward to the film adaptation.

I know I should have liked this book. The content is one of those that makes you seem like a Nazi sympathizer if you don't (which always just peeves me anyway). But I could not get past the poor writing! Seriously. Just couldn't finish it. 
 I applaud the author's thorough research, but come on! If you are writing a research paper, then write one. If you are writing historical fiction (no matter how closely based in fact), then write that. The main character does not speak in quotation marks. The tense and narrative does not switch around willy nilly. If she thinks the damn flowers are beautiful, don't put it in quotations simply because it is a direct quote from her diary. If you truly must prove your facts, put in a footnote. I don't need in-text citations in APA format. I have my own papers to write, thank you very much. 
 I found myself, a third of the way into the book, barely able to remember the main character's names for all the loopy descriptions of animals and insects. Antonia, right? 
 Ms. Ackerman's editor did her no favors. When I see things like this, I honestly blame the editor/publisher. Their job is to help the author transform their novels (or whatever this qualifies as) into decent publications. Why these issues weren't caught or resolved is beyond me. 
 What could have been an absorbing read left me feeling bored and uninspired. Too bad.

I was tossing between a 3 and a 4 for this book. At points I found it really interesting, seeing a different perspective of Poland during WWII and German occupation, but it was nothing that kept me wanting to finish it quickly. 
 It's set in a polish zoo just before the Germans came in in WWII and until Russian occupation. Around one family, hence the Zookeeper's wife. 
 I love books where you can learn something. for this book the main points were: 
 1. That 92% of Europe's jews can be traced back to the DNA of 4 women 
 2. That the Nazi's actually thought interbreeding was the way to go (and they were meant to be scientists) 
 3. That a lot of people documented their time during the war, including a group hidding documents in barrels in the Getto 
 4. How many people risked their lives and their families for strangers (how many of us would do the same?) 
 5. The story of Korczak and his orphanage , a story I really want to know more about... 
 SBC: The XXX's XXX
this book is non-fiction and is very illuminating about Poland's resistance during World War II. Most interesting. It makes me want to go to Poland - which I never had any interest in before.

Setting - WWII Warsaw Poland. Ackerman identifes her sources to create a factual narrative. 
 Antonia takes care of the animals left at the zoo and keeps her home active with family and friends. Empty cages hold a different kind of guest.

I'd go two and a half stars if Goodreads would let me. I'm very interested in WWII, but this book kept losing the plot. It's an historical story bogged down with huge passages not at all germane to the tale. It's worth a read to be awed by how hard Warsaw took it in the pooper during the war, but you'll be skimming sections. A lot.

I read this history because it was this year's One Book One San Diego, choice. I believe it got the vote because it is nonfiction and the other nominees (the outstanding Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close and Dave Eggers' What is the What) are fiction and there is a clear belief that people should not waste their time reading things that aren't true. Anyone who knows me, knows that I don't subscribe to that bias. Fiction is the lie that tells the truth and I shed tears over Jonathan Froer's 9-11 "fiction" where Diane Ackerman's holocaust survival account left me cold. 
 I have read/learned a great deal about WWII and the hiding of Jews from the Nazis, but this account did offer some new information. The Zookeeper's Wife takes place in Poland, at the Warsaw Zoo, during the occupation. Antonina's husband is active in the Underground resistance and they hide many "guests" at the zoo, despite its proximity to a German soldiers outpost. Many plot points are compelling - the ingredients for a riveting story are there - and Ackerman does a good job characterizing five main characters. Yet as a whole, the book falls flat. A naturalist by trade, her descriptions of plants and animals are strong. Her language can be over-the-top poetic at times and seem off-topic. I think restricting herself to depicting only what had been documented - through interviews, entries in Antonina's diaries, and eye witnesses - really shackles a writer and hobbled the pacing of what should have been a dramatic account. 
 Of course the book is not without some merit. It is an important story to tell and provided facts I did not know. But it took an act of will to get from cover to cover. I do look forward to reading A Natural History of the Senses where I believe the writer is in her element and indulges in the details and historical tidbits she loves, but that felt like chaff in a war story meant to flow like a novel.

I read this book having no idea what to expect other than more World War II and the Holocaust (and so soon after reading The Book Thief). This book balances is a nonfiction historical piece, but it tells a story as it incorporates extensive research and real quotes from diaries, letters, friends and family. The zookeeper (of Poland's Warsaw zoo) and his wife used their demolished zoo to help hundreds of Jewish people flee Poland. This book contains so much interesting information (which keeps it from being the sort of book you get sucked into but does make it much more fascinating) about Poland and the underground resistance, yet it still manages to focus on one woman who is immensely powerful in her own way. 
 If you are interested in World War II, I highly recommend this book. Even if you are not a nonfiction war-book fan, The Zookeeper's Wife is interesting and beautiful in its own way, and it is worth reading simply to learn more about the main character, Antonina Zabinski. I love reading about buried heroes, and the everyday people that can make positive differences in the world.

I was not properly prepared for this book. I thought it was a novel and don't ask me why I thought this. Perhaps with different expectations I would have enjoyed this more ... I don't know. I felt it was very disconnected and not edited well. The content was interesting but not what I thought it was going to cover.

Disappointed. Only pushed through so I could use it towards my reading challenge! Very slow, text book details about the animals and historically accurate but those details overshadowed the human story.

I made it through, somehow. It's bad. It's so bad. I went into this expecting to love it, considering the premise is just SO good. This isn't a novel - it's a work of non-fiction, a history book, masquerading as a novel. It's not well-written and it drags on with endless pages of absolutely useless descriptions of things that have no place in the story. We never learn HOW they did these things. They just HAPPENED. It's written like a 300+ page high school research paper, and I really, REALLY struggled to get through it, even with the skimming I was able to do for the entire second half. I made it through, and I'm sure the movie will be so much better, since they're definitely not afraid to get creative and imagine feasible conversations and situations that add to the story. This was so underwhelming and awful, and I'm really disappointed.

I haven't finished this book yet, and it's going to be tough to do so. There is just too much flowery description that seems to have no point. The story is good, when there's action, the book is intriguing and well-written. It just doesn't hold my attention, especially in audio format, where I can't skim past the Nathaniel Hawthorney goodness.

While there is no question at all that the Zabinskis were heroes, the book is subtitled A War Story. Well, it isn't a story, it's a hisory text. This is one author who will never be accused of plaguarism of any sort. If she used the word the in a sentence, she explained where she got the reference. Which made it tedious to slog through. It was amazing what this couple did and lived through but it should have been more interesting.
Was like reading a history text. Should have been fascinating, but to tell the truth, I was bored. Apologies to anyone who really liked it.

This could be a great novel, an informative and compelling read. However, the writing is TERRIBLE. I stopped time after time to read and reread sentences that made no sense at all. And then the character development. I should say lack of character development. In my opinion, this book reads like an early draft of the novel it should/could be. You don't get to know any of the characters and by the end, you know the animals better than the people. The author tries to weave the research she did into the story, but it's like she can't decide if she wants to write fiction or non-fiction--and she doesn't have enough information to make this an interesting non-fiction read. To be honest, I finished reading it because I couldn't believe how bad it was and I kept thinking it had to get better. Way to take a great topic and utterly ruin it.

Everyone raved about this book, but personally, I did not care for it. I thought the tid bits of history were interesting but overall I thought this book lacked connection between the reader and the charater. That being said, it was excellently writer and researched which I appreciate. Just not my cup of tea.
Can't do it. This is just a painful read. Too bad, the premise was so interesting.
I thought this was going to be a "story" in the normal sense, but it was more of a documentary. Don't let that steer you away, though. It was still an incredibly inspiring story.

This novel is about a zookeeper and his wife at the Warsaw Zoo who bravely helped to save many Jews during WWII. Although the topic was fascinating, and the novel was thoroughly researched, the way in which the author told the story, bored me at times, particularly in the latter part of the book. Overall, it was a bit of a disappointment, even though I learned a lot a long the way.

Por calidad narrativa podriamos decir que dos y media, pero es que en realidad no es mi tipo de literatura... empezando por aclarar que, desde mi punto de vista, ni siquiera deberia estar catalogado como novela, sino que deberia ser ubicado en la seccion de otra narrativa, puesto que se trata mas de un libro tipo ensayo o memorias que de otra cosa. 
 Asi pues, la narracion no fluye con la misma ligereza que en una novela, aunque hay que decir que es bastante amena y, desde luego, altamente informativa y descriptiva de una epoca y un suceso: la invasion germana de Polonia durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial, los guettos de Varsovia y como la familia de guardianes del zoo formaban parte de la Resistencia y contribuyeron a salvar la vida de muchos judios. 
 Transmite bastante bien la atmosfera de la epoca, pero le falta cierta dosis de emocion, que no por tratar este tema se tiene que caer en el sentimentalismo, pero tambien existe el punto medio. El toque "animal", curiosamente, humaniza la narracion, le da vida...

What should have been an interesting story, but hampered by overly-flowery writing, repetition of facts, random bits of unimportant information that didn't advance the story, and list of really boring stuff (over a page of which bugs were in the bug collection? WHY????). 
 In the hands of another author, to bring home the occupation of Poland, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, etc this would have been hard-hitting.

Details galore! A story that shows the secret hopeful and helpful side of humanity. Wish the characters had been more alive for me. I will always remember the beetle collection and the sick joke the Nazi soldiers played on Antonia and her children, and friends. Ackerman, while hailed as one of the most exquisite nonfiction writers of the last few decades, did not awe or thrill me with the Zookeeper's Wife. Reading this book did however remind me to tell others about Centropa and inspired me to read Abraham Joshua Heschel. 
 I wish the Zookeeper's Wife was a more potent reminder that 90% of the Jews in Poland were wiped out by the Nazis during the Holocaust. 
 Survivors and others - Jewish bios and stories. Well done. Teachers, please use! 
 http://www.centropa.org/ 
 I hope On Being never takes down this podcast 
 http://www.onbeing.org/program/spirit...

The historian in me feels conflicted, because I genuinely enjoyed a lot of the historical background information that Ackerman provided, but every other part of me really struggled with this book. I did not enjoy it at all up until page 100-ish. After that, it didn't get "better" per se, but just "less bad." The story was interesting, I guess, but I wish the author would go on less tangents and stop filling paragraphs and pages with fluff words about nature. I almost wish that someone had taken the diary of the zookeeper's wife (which Ackerman bases the book off of) and used it as inspiration to write a really good story, maybe even in the historical fiction category? Instead this book sounded like a high school student's persuasive research paper for a history class. I did not enjoy it. :(

Looking through the eyes of a Zoo-keeper's wife's eyes of WWII; how they survived as a family and helping others survive. I did not realize before this, the Polish underground, the spirit of the people in their resistance to the Nazi's and helping as many Jewish people possible. Another side of WWII told. I would recommend to others who find that there is always goodness amongst evil.
http://kathleensbookreview.blogspot.c...

Ackerman is such a sensual writer; the details give the readers such a deep impression of the setting. She presents facts in stark contrast to her lush descriptions which makes them more hard-hitting. Though she brought tears to my eyes countless times, I was buoyed by the courage and spirit of those whose stories are told in this book, especially Antonina's.

Warsaw Zoo during WW2? Sounded really intriguing especially upon hearing that they were a halfway house from the Ghetto. I think that the story of Jan and his wife is an amazing one, but unfortunately Diane Ackerman screwed up the telling. I couldn't tell who was relating the story much less who the main character was. I was not invested in the Zoo nor the lives it saved. I already knew of the Nazi obession with developing a pure race in people, plants and animals. I didn't need a lesson especially since it had nothing to do with the Zoo. I wished it was a better book.

Got a little tired of the long poetic descriptive language but this true story of the Warsaw Zoo during WWII is a must read! This book made me ask hard questions of myself - would I put myself or my family at risk to save the life of someone else?

A friend recommended The Zookeeper's Wife, by Diane Atkinson, and I tried the first 60 pages. I don't doubt that it's a great story in essence, but there's something very irritating to me about the way it's written. Maybe that the author kept interrupting the flow of the story by tacking back and forth between direct quotations from Antonina Zabinski's diary and clumps of Ackerman's research. Maybe that it disturbed me to read about wild animals, especially large predators like lions, kept in close captivity, no matter how much the zookeeper's wife said she loved them.
This was not as interesting as I thought and hoped it would be. Still and interesting story and it did have it's high spots.

This book was awful :( I was very excited to read it - I love WWII stories and I think it's great that "ordinary" people put their lives in danger so that Jews had a safe place to stay. That's beyond awesome. However, the first half? 1/3 of the book was about her zoo. I don't care about the zoo. I really only needed to know of it as a backdrop - hey we live in a zoo. When we finally start in on them housing Jewish families and other members of the resistance - I felt like I was half told the story. The book was based from the wifes view and from entries from her journal / memoir. But it seemed that the husband was the mastermind behind it all. She just welcomed them and cleaned the house. I was very let down.
Not as good as I had hoped - just too dry

As I have mentioned before, any story about the Holocaust really interests me. It is amazing to see what disgusting travesties people are capable of, but also how people will risk it all for human kind. 
 The story is about a zoo in Poland that is destroyed in World War II. The zookeeper and his wife hide refugees they call "guests" in the zoos many cages, houses, etc., to keep them safe from the Nazis. While a great story of what people are willing to do for others, I found the book to be dreadfully boring. I really got in to the last 75 or so pages, probably because I was excited to almost be done with it, but also because I thought it got a little more interesting. 
 I don't know if I have an early copy of the book or something, but I was SO turned off that when I went to read the jacket (I had already picked up a copy somewhere along the way) the very first word of the second paragraph is "drawinag" instead of drawing. I mean, really? On the book jacket?!

I couldn't even finish this one! Arg.... There was barely any dialog or interaction between characters on page. The author just tells you (and not very well) about the characters and what they do and how they feel. I have never seen so many commas, and's, or's, but's etc... I mean wow "holly run on sentences batman!" I just couldn't handle this! Too bad, it is such a great concept and could have been really great I am sure if executed well. Oh well.
I listened to this book on tape. It was interesting, but not totally engaging. I may try reading it instead.
Just couldn't get into this one, so I gave up after about 50 pages.
2.5 stars. This is a really interesting story, but the execution was lacking. There were lots of tangents, so I found the narrative really choppy and hard to follow at times.

I could not finish this book. I had high hopes for it and wanted to read it before watching the movie. However, as a history major, I was appalled at the lack of focus and citations for this book. One minute we are inside Antonia's head and learning about what is happening at the zoo, to the next randomly hearing about someone else. You would be better off reading Antonia's memoir. This will probably be the only book that I will say is worse than it's movie...

I'm usually drawn to Holocaust literature, but this book failed to engage my interest. I liked Ackerman's description of the zookeepers' relationships with their animals and her detailed historical account of the German occupation of Poland during World War II, but she neglected to explain other essential parts of the story. Exactly how and where at the zoo did they hide so many people? Why did the Germans never discover their hidden guests? Why did Jan leave zookeeping two years after the war ended? I'm sure that his war experiences influenced his decision, but Ackerman ends her book abruptly without explaining it.

Around the World in 52 Books: Poland 
 This is one of those interesting true stories, made even more compelling by the inclusion of photographs. I loved the storyline and the spirit of the book, but the actual writing was lifeless in places, which made it drag on a bit, keeping me from a 5-star review.

This is a story of the holocaust from the perspective of the Zookeeper's Wife. They ran the Warsaw Zoo in Poland. It is written from the journals of Antonina and personal interviews with many people this couple helped while working for the underground effort to stop the Nazis. They helped so many from the Jewish community and saved many lives. There were many unknown heros risking their lives each day.

This book was an interesting read, but slow. This is a true story about a zookeeper and his wife in Poland during World War 2. This couple used their zoo property to hide and help many Jews during the German occupation of Poland. Unfortunately, the author's writing style was a bit dry and it wasn't as engaging a story as it could have been.

One of the best books I have ever read, a touching true story that bears witness that goodness is alive and well even in impossible circumstances. 
 I learned so much from this book.

book_b.title: The Martian
book_b.user_review: I normally don't read science fiction but due to the rave reviews and upcoming movie, I thought I would try this. This is a very plot driven book about an astronaut stranded on Mars and his efforts to survive until rescue. Action moves between Mark's (the astronaut) log entries about his time on Mars and the action back in Houston as NASA works to rescue him. There is a lot of science as Mark Macgyvers his way through near death situations. I am a reader who reads for character not plot so most of the appeal of this book was lost on me. I found the characterizations (mainly developed through junior high level humor) remedial and didn't care about all the science (and there is a lot). I can see this being more successful for me as a movie, especially with Matt Damon as the star.

sample_reviews.review_text: I don't have anything against the book. I get how a lot of people would like it. But if this is what purists call "sci fi" then I probably don't enjoy sci fi as much as I think I do..

A good book with plenty of action. I'm not keen on the diary style entries, but i can understand why it was used. Great humor throughout. Nice characters. Its worth a read. Dont be lazy and wait for the Movie. The book is always better!

This is one of the worst books I have ever read. This books is written in boring and mediocre (at best) prose, with two-dimensional characters, and with unsophisticated and banal school yard humor at which a 10 year-old would turn his nose.
Ugh. I could not finish this book. Too many confusing abbreviations and math! I don't want to read math in a novel. I made it halfway through and gave up.
I

This book blew my mind Andy Weir. I fell in love with the story and and the whole idea of an Astronaut stuck on Mars where his survival skills are tested. Overall my thoughts on this book; 
 - All the characters were believable, 
 -the writing style was cinematic( can't wait for the movie- Matt Damen all the way!), 
 -Loved Andy's sense of humor in this book, 
 -Pager turner, 
 -The scientific aspect of The Martian was spectacular,( gained more knowledge about space!), 
 -Watney and his hatred towards disco was understandable, 
 -the list of problems NASA had faced in order to save ones life.( and spent millions and millions of dollars) 
 -the Martian trip on the rover and trailer to Ares 3 to Ares 4 MAV was extremely dangerous and risky!!!! And offcourse exhilarating even from a readers POV. 
 I cannot recommend this book enough, I thoroughly enjoyed this book. And to even think a debut Novel could have such an impact as a stand alone,....Andy Weir has definitely mastered The Martian Story.

Hace tiempo que no leia algo tan interesante. Un tipo esta de lo mas bien en su mision en Marte y chan! queda abandonado por su grupo, que lo da por muerto. El unico humano en Marte, sin agua, sin comida, y con escasos recursos para sobrevivir. 
 Esta lleno de informacion tecnica detallada, al estilo de la CF dura que me espanta, y al mismo tiempo se trata esta informacion con un tono de idiota sin nada que perder que me ha sacado varias carcajadas. 
 A ratos intecala el relato del equipo en Tierra y del equipo que lo abandono, y al principio pense que era relleno, pero no, llena las expectativas del relato y su desenlace. Sobre este punto, el autor tiene buena pluma pero no es muy prolijo con algunos aspectos de la narracion, saltando de punto de vista a un narrador omnisciente a ratos. Es desconcertante pero, ?saben que? !NO ME IMPORTO! Me entretuve a montones, vivi claramente cada detalle y estuve pendiente de todo el proceso. 
 Ojala lo hagan pelicula, seria mil veces mejor que la mayoria de las peliculas que he visto acerca de las misiones a Marte. Esta lleno de humor y de informacion tecnica y cientifica cientificamente precisa. Hay un tema con lo de la peligrosidad del viento en un planeta que tiene tan poca atmosfera... pero bueh, es FICCION.

And done! Took me much longer than it should have to finish this slim volume. Characterization was lacking. I didn't care much about the romance subplot, and Watney's humor grated on me half the time (though it was pretty funny the other half). Slogged through the ending. The technical parts kept me reading it slowly in hopes of understanding how Watney fixed this problem or the other, but between my lack of appreciation for toilet humor and my not-NASA-caliber mind, I was lost for a lot of the time. Still. Learned about torque, Mars' atmosphere, flammability and other things. Definitely going to watch the interviews with Chris Hadfield and Adam Savage to check the plausibility of some of the solutions used. Two stars and a half. Better dialogue/characters that have more than speech tics to tell them apart would have given it three. I am impressed by the fact that the author is a fan of NASA rather than someone who works there because he got a lot of things right. Would try his next book, would try more "hard" sci-fi.

Ok, I'll admit it. I watched the movie first. The horror, I know. I normally prefer to read the book first, but in this case, I didn't know about the book until after. But for once, I found the movie didn't take away from the experience of reading the book. So if you loved the movie I'd recommend giving the book a go.
Interesting format. A little language heavy for me, but it was an intriguing idea. The idea of being stranded in a hostile environment like that was powerful

I thought, originally, that this book had been written in the 90's. Not really SciFi at all. Some of the science is interesting, but one assumes that there will be changes in society too. Will NASA be all male if we even manage a Mars launch? (Oh yes, sorry, there were three women characters. One who couldn't operate a vending machine, one who 'toughened up', and a captain who was so devastated at the loss of one crew member that she failed to lead.) Will "gay" still be a pejorative? Will the US really be the lead in exploration of our solar system? (We've spent generations of accrued capital on wars. Where will the money come from?) And really, calling someone Mexican or Asian isn't the same as actually writing a character from that background. Finally, in real life many people will die in space exploration, just as many died in exploring our oceans. 
 I'm anticipating enjoying the movie more. Movies are so good at fluff.

What a perfect summertime beach read! Total thriller in a sciency nerdy way! Loved it! Thanks for the recommendation Lori! 
 Can not wait for the movie!
Una de las mejores lecturas y es una lectura obligatoria.
GREAT!!! Very technical, but FUNNY!!
Weir reminds me of Michael Crichton, the good parts of Crichton. I couldn't put this down.

"How about Watney? What did he do?" 
 "He's our botanist and engineer. And don't talk about him in the past tense." 
 Watney is also a survivalist. After incidentally being stranded on Mars by his astronaut team, Watney must learn to harvest potatoes and collect water in order to survive several sols (a.k.a days). Can NASA find a way to bring him back home safely, or is it better just to leave him for dead? 
 A rescue of this magnitude can not only be expensive, but also dangerous for any crew members who would have to use their fuel to return to Mars. Five lives can be lost in order to save one. Although, the story is alarming, Watney maintains a humorist tone throughout. Not to mention his positive attitude. Let's face it, loneliness alone could have brought him to commit a sad crime against his life. As to whether this story is actually realistic, who cares, it's fiction. 
 Here's to Watney -- making all astronauts out there seem even more heroic.

One of the best hard syfy books I have ever read! 
 I read an advanced proof of The Martian not knowing what to expect at all. At the beginning of the book, the storytelling had the feeling of those first-person short story narratives that are only all too prevalent in the genre, but boy did this book have some surprises in store for me! 
 First off, the main character Mark, is just a damn like-able guy. I mean, when you read this book, there is no way you can dislike this guy. Mark is put into one of the most challenging and dangerous, and downright hopeless of situations, and somehow, he comes across as pretty good-natured about the whole thing, and has a sense of humor that will make you laugh out loud at times. 
 However, do not let the great personalities that have been created in this book take away from the technical prowess of the author as Weir tells his tale of an astronaut being stranded on Mars for an extended period of time. We are not talking about some distant future time period where everything just happens by magic, but rather in a very, very near future time period, circa 2020-2035 time period. Where things are not much different than they are today. 
 The amount of knowledge of chemistry, biology, physics, astrophysics, and science in general that are put into the book do not detract from it at all. This is RARE. Most times all of the geek stuff that only a few people can stand only serve to detract from the story and the casual reader. Here, it Enhances the story tremendously. It shows not only the ingenuity of the main characters and the supporting cast, but the thoroughness and thought that went into scripting a story so believable and real it is scary. Scary that someone could come up with so many ingenious circumstances and solutions in such a harsh, limited environment. And there are few places that humans will be able to reach in the coming decades than the surface of Mars. 
 Mark is not only funny, he is a damned McGuiver on Mars. (In fact, maybe Weir should consider changing the title before hardback publishing.) 
 I read this entire book in a day to the frustration of my wife and kids who I shamelessly neglected as I tore through this story. There was no stopping the pages from turning on this thing! 
 There are a lot of hard syfy books out there, but none of them have been as approachable and as fun to read as this one! I am truly amazed to come across such a gem and great piece of writing. I am going to be recommending this book to many people over the coming years! 
 Best syfy book I have read all year, bar none! Weir made me lose several hours of sleep. For an author, I don't think there could be a greater compliment.

This book. This book. Atmospheric, action-packed hilarity. I wanted to read the book before the movie came out and... wow. Diverse, realistic cast of characters, loveable, relatable protagonist, and gorgeous description. I couldn't tll you if the science is soft or wonky, but I can tell you it's a damn good read.
Too much science and not enough fiction.

Awesome book! A real love letter to the folks at NASA for their skill and dedication and just plain smarts. In a nutshell, this book is MacGyver Goes to Mars. A freak accident ends up leaving a surviving astronaut alone on Mars with no way to communicate. It's a real survival story and I worried the entire time that somebody as NASA was going to sabotage his rescue or that he would die. So many of today's books seem to be that way. But this was a pure adventure story with no unlikeable characters and no bad guys. Mars is the only 'bad guy' you need in this book. And in Mars' defense, Mars is just being Mars. Highly recommended.

Yes! I finished a book! I knew I hadn't lost my ability to do that. And one that's been on my to read list for a long time. This is great. 
 Anyways, this book was okay. I get the hype. It's very readable and okay, I'll say it, it's so freaking cool. I'm a huge space nerd and I just, Mars and adventures and ahh, it's so cool. I don't know enough but it seems the author has certainly done their research. 
 So what went wrong? First of all, I got bored. I do like science but today, I wasn't quite in the mood to open the Internet and actually read about everything I didn't understand. It was easier to simply skim by. I'd think "okay there's a problem" and then a few pages later go, "okay, he solved the problem". That bored me. 
 Maybe the author should have attempted making the science a bit more friendly to us non-scientists. Maybe I should reread this and that time around, stop be lazy and make a bigger effort to understand. Either way, in the first 100 pages, I tried understanding and it was cool but eventually, I just skimmed over the science which unfortunately was a significant part of the book. 
 So once I stopped focusing on the science, I was left with meager descriptions of characters which all blurred together. None of them were actually three dimensional and honestly, I can now only remember there was a hot astronaut who had a romance with another astronaut, some Chinese people, and an unhappy space paparazzi. The team dynamics were also a bit lacking. 
 Mark was a different story. He's very likable. I just love the nerdy corny smart characters. That said, I was rooting for him in a "I want you to be on my side in the zombie apocalypse way" and "fuck, that was a cool idea". I don't feel like I know him or anything about who he is. His character is utterly defined by his struggle. And yeah, I get his thoughts would be focused on that but I still feel we'd hear something about him, be it his favorite type of beer, how college was for him, why he is an atheist, how the doorknob reminds him of his mother, or something dammit, anything, who is he even? 
 Personally, I haven't left the house in three days and I haven't talked to anyone and I'm already feeling a bit depressed (three days is the limit of my introversion). So damn, I'm impressed his attitude is so great. I can't stand my own mind after three days. This (fictional) guy can be completely alone for so long and be fine. 
 I liked this book, don't get me wrong. I agree with other reviews that another author could have made this into a philosophical masterpiece instead of a nerd fest. Do I recommend it? If you're up for a lot of science talk, sure. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to read up online to see if any scientists have commented about the scientific legitimacy of this book. 
 things I'm taking with me 
 * I don't want to be an astronaut. 
 * Astronauts are nerds with too much power and money. 
 * Anyone can write a book using their knowledge to cover a lack of plot and characterization. Does anyone want me to write a fiction book about art history?

A geeky, gleeful, sci-fi survival story that's saved by the likable smart-ass astronaut Mark Watney who keeps a log of his life on Mars after getting left behind by the rest of his flight crew. It reads like a lab notebook given the experimental nature of having to solve all sorts of problems by himself based on an impressive if implausible engineering-agricultural-astrophysics skill set. Unfortunately, we get very little feeling of what it would really be like to be stranded on a distant planet, just a lot of instructional scientific talk. Here's a typical example: "Heating the gas is what takes most of the energy. Why is that important? Because I'm just one guy and the oxygenator was made for six. One-sixth the the quantity of CO2 means one-sixth the energy to heat it." See? Just like science class! Where's the fiction part of science fiction? Did it get jettisoned so as not to weigh the story down? There's no real character development - all the NASA types are just that, types. The only living, breathing soul is Watney, and much of the time it's quite literally about how he accomplishes that feat on Mars. As he remarks toward the end, "My terrifying struggle to stay alive became somehow routine." Ditto for the reader! Still and all, I found his resourcefulness appealing and of course found myself rooting for him all the way.

Middle-of-the-road space disaster story. I'd say "below average", but I'm not sure how discriminating I was when I was young enough to enjoy this stuff. Oddly, I found some questionable science, while all the reviews talk about how scientifically accurate it was (e.g. I'm pretty sure cooked potatoes digest better than raw ones because cooking breaks down the complex carbohydrates, not the proteins.) Cardboard characters, implausible dialog and action, what's to like?
I could not put this book down. What an adventure of a read.

Science! Technology! Engineering! Mathematics! This fast-paced thriller about an astronaut stranded on Mars accomplishes the feat of conveying the badass awesomeness of STEM fields. Watney, the stranded astronaut, solves problems and troubleshoots his way through surviving on Mars and it's completely riveting. Most of the novel is told in the form of a daily log he keeps, with straightforward language and some funny one-liners. 
 Every once in a while I will read a book and be like, "My husband has to read this after I finish." This is one of those. I think I mentioned it to him about four times already.

Loved it. The genius ideas that the protagonist, Mark, comes up with are crazy. 
 Science fiction full of real science (really totally full of science) I have felt compelled to finish it and loved it. 
 I would say the quantity of scientific information might be off putting for some people. Luckily I'm a total geek and so it was fine for me :) 
 The central character is so resourceful (unbelievably so at times) but is really relatable due to his relaxed tone and sense of humour. It would take an exceptional person to survive and he really is but we can like him too, he'd be a great person to go to the pub for a beer with. 
 While reading it I did wonder if some of the brilliantly creative ideas from 'Illuminae' would have made an even more enjoyable read? I'd love to see some rocket schematics, engineering drawings of his equipment, anything geeky really. But it's a minor point. 
 Engineering friends, science geeks, strongly recommend this one :)

This is Weir's first novel and I would rate it from pretty good to excellent depending on parts of the story. Since I'm not a real science fiction fanatic, I did think this book gave me some exciting moments. Even though there was a lot of technical information on how a person would/could survive on Mars, I don't know how much of that info was actually real. It would have been nice if there had been a glossary/info section to help explain in more detail what was actually happening. Good story though and well received by readers everywhere. Mark is stuck on Mars after an emergency evacuation by the rest of his crew members. Thinking that he was dead they leave. Even NASA is unaware that he is alive since there is no open line of communication since the dust storm that almost destroyed everyone. Most of the book is the log that Mark keeps and what he does to keep himself a live for over a year and a half. So if you're a science fiction lover, I'm sure this book would give you much enjoyment. Weir is an excellent writer and creative story-teller.

Maybe just slightly under 5 stars, but what the heck. Wow, I loved this book! It really appealed to me from a story perspective as well as an engineering-geek perspective. There were some goofy bits of writing, but it didn't take away from the story at all.

Quick, spoiler-free summary: Funny, mildly amusing, but not riveting. 
 SPOILERS AHEAD: 
 I didn't understand most of the science events in the book. It felt strange how sometimes they were accompanied with a simple explanation, and at other times there was no simple explanation whatsoever. I think the book wouldn't be as gripping without the science parts, but I think Weir could have added some simple more simple explanations to help the layman and laylady alike understand it better. 
 The humour was enjoyable, even if at times lame. I probably didn't understand some of the early TV references, but there were plenty of other witty humour remarks. The humour was my favourite element of the book. 
 I think there wasn't much in the way of character development. Lots of them felt quite bland. I get that the focus is on Watney, but I still feel that more could be done, particularly with the Ares 3 crew. I think then Watney could have monologued more on his relations with each fellow team member. They sacrificed a lot to go back for him, but it seemed more like they duty than camaraderie. People like Venkat, who we hear a lot from, seem quite bland. I think supporting characters like him could have distinguished themselves more by the language used and the things said. Easier said than done, I guess. 
 The plot was quite dull. After a few setbacks, I came to the prediction that Watney would just survive anything on Mars and get home safely. No deaths and not many major problems that were unfixable (the food launch was the only one, I think). 
 It would have been more compelling had there been even more struggle. It might sound horrible, but a death or an injury would have made more of an interesting read. Or, if Ares 3 came back to reduce Watney, but were stranded as NASA had pulled funding. I find it difficult to come to terms with NASA, in real life, paying billions to save someone's life with the risk level as high as it was. 
 Watney did face adversaries. Plenty, you may say. I might be unreasonable. I just reckon it was a bit too simple how most things were resolved, and some of it a little too quickly for my liking. 
 Towards the middle, it seemed less likely, and even the likelihood decreased as the book progressed, that Watney would have to wait for Ares 4 after all. That was disappointing because it seemed for a while as if an Ares 3 rescue wasn't a viable option.
This book is everything that I want in a book to be. It's funny, serious, indulging all at the same time
Once I got past most of the technical NASA speak this turned out to a great read. I couldn't put it down.

This was a fantastic audiobook. The story was interesting and the characters great. My only complaint was it did get a little long at time and was technical. I love technical, but I can see many people not enjoying that aspect of it. This is one that will stick with me for a long time.

Remember watching "Apollo 13" and during the movie there was that long period where, after the explosion, they are problem solving how to survive and get back? 'The Martian' is that times ten. This book doesn't always have the most amazing writing (weaknesses more apparent when focusing on what's happening on Earth), but it makes up for it in spades with all of Wateny's descriptions of his survival on Mars. 
 Really enjoyed this one. 4.5/5 stars

I liked it but it was too heavy on the technological and scientific aspects for me. I either had to reread a lot or I just skimmed a lot of Watney's descriptions of what he's up to in terms of modifying the technology and all those things. 
 The ending was a bit anticlimatic too.

The Martian was an incredible story of survival with just enough sarcasm and black humor to make it one of the most enjoyable books I've read so far this year. I was on the fence about this book because I knew it was about one guy who was stranded on Mars. I thought it would be dramatic and ridiculous. But when I saw the blurb from Ernest Cline, author of Ready Player One, which was one of the most fun books I read last year, I knew I was wrong about The Martian being dull. True to his quote, The Martian was funny in a way I never would have expected and it made all the difference in the world. 
 The summary/synopsis for the book is so incredibly misleading and way too serious. The Martian was funny and brilliant and not quite the dramatic and serious survival thriller described. 
 Mark Watney was left for dead when a sandstorm caused problems during his manned mission on Mars. His crew left, thinking he was dead. But convenient circumstances led to Watney surviving. He was the crew's botanist and engineer and had to rig up the few supplies left to help keep him alive. He knew the next manned mission would take 4 years. So he just had to make it that long. 
 The Martian wasn't a heartwarming and serious story of survival.. thankfully. It wasn't depressing or tough, even though times were difficult and shit went wrong. Watney approached every problem with a sarcastic attitude and his personality made for an entertaining book. Who else could go through the details of how he would create a potato farm without boring the reader? He made it so much fun. And anyone who is familiar with engineering and being hands on knows the struggle of doing things the way that makes sense versus doing things the way a handful of guys in suits at a table says it should be done, so Watney's "go F yourself attitude towards NASA cracked me up. 
 Seriously, The Martian was incredible. Mark Watney was a character the world was rooting for. I loved the way he handled his situation. He could narrate his whole boring life anywhere and it would be the funniest shit I've ever read. But I do love that the story took place on Mars, as any lover of science fiction has a certain fondness for the planet. It's where we've always imagined our astronauts going. The Martian was refreshing science fiction and I highly recommend it to any fan of the genre or even fans of humorous narratives. Still, regardless of how you feel about science fiction, Mars, or space, I think The Martian is enjoyable all around. I had so much fun reading it. 
 I'm not conveying my love of Mark Watney enough. To get an idea of what made him such a likable character, I'm posting a handful of quotes. He tops the list of my favorite male characters ever. 
 The first line of the book is, "I'm pretty much fucked." 
 "If the oxygenator breaks down, I'll suffocate. If the water reclaimer breaks down, I'll die of thirst. If the Hab breaches, I'll just kind of explode. If none of those things happen, I'll eventually run out of food and starve to death. So yeah. I'm fucked." 
 "The screen went black before I was out of the airlock. Turns out the "L" in "LCD" stands for "Liquid." I guess it either froze or boiled off. Maybe I'll post a consumer review. "Brought product to surface of Mars. It stopped working. 0/10." 
 "I need to ask myself, 'What would an Apollo astronaut do?' He'd drink three whiskey sours, drive his Corvette to the launchpad, then fly to the moon in a command module smaller than my Rover. Man those guys were cool." 
 "What must it be like?" he pondered. "He's stuck out there. He thinks he's totally alone and that we all gave up on him. What kind of effect does that have on a man's psychology?" He turned back to Venkat. "I wonder what he's thinking right now." LOG ENTRY: SOL 61 How come Aquaman can control whales? They're mammals! Makes no sense." 
 "They say once you grow crops somewhere, you have officially 'colonized' it. So technically, I colonized Mars. 
 In your face, Neil Armstrong!" " 
 I'll spend the rest of the evening enjoying a potato. And by 'enjoying' I mean 'hating so much I want to kill people.'" 
 "In other news, It's seven sols till the harvest, and I still haven't prepared. For starters, I need to make a hoe. Also, I need to make an outdoor shed for the potatoes. I can't just pile them up outside. The next major storm would cause The Great Martian Potato Migration."
This book is unlikely to win any literary awards, and it has plausibility gaps aplenty, but if you can suspend disbelief, it's a really fun, impossible-to-put-down read. A great vacation choice.

In the trailer for the movie, Matt Damon says, "I'm going to science the shit out of this." It's not a direct quote from the book, but it should be. This is a story about sciencing the shit out of a terrible situation. Mark's ingenuity, stubbornness, and drive to survive is incredible. The book also takes a ton of science and makes it incredibly interesting. 
 That being said, it isn't perfect. Mark is a gem, but the other characters are sketched very broadly. Mark's teammates suffer most here, reduced to one or two characteristics. There were several science-y things that I couldn't even visualize, and were consequently impossible to understand. I also wanted more from this book. Mark spends over a year on Mars, and it's science the entire time. I don't expect him to be Ray Bradbury, but there's no introspection, no deeper insight. 
 For a novel about sciencing the shit out of a situation, it's a damn good novel. But it could be better.

reference_books.title: Hush, Hush (Hush, Hush, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
There was very little I liked about this book. My initial reaction was "I hated it" but that's not entirely true. However, I honestly believe it's one of the worst pieces of fiction I've ever read. Strong statement? Maybe. Right now though, I truly believe it. 
 I normally write down my immediate thoughts upon finishing a book. My reaction (read: anger) was so strong this time, I decided to wait about 24 hours and see if I felt the same way. 
 I do. 
 This book infuriated me. Nora is the stupidest, weakest protagonist I've ever encountered. Ever. And! These qualities were unintentional, which is quite unfortunate. She's intended to be intriguing and pure...no. Just...no. She's pathetic and makes no sense. Much like the plot. 
 I was initially interested because I liked the idea of fallen angels. It's a refreshing change from the usual topic in YA lately, if you know what I mean. Too bad that aspect has little to nothing to do with the plot. You wait and wait and wait and then FINALLY at the VERY end do we get any insight on the mythos at all. Unfortunately, all that waiting isn't even rewarded because the explanations are sloppy, poorly researched, and overall unsatisfying. 
 The angel himself is a whole other issue. He's greedy, manipulative, misogynistic, and cruel. One minute he's all "in love" and the next he's completely psychopathic. He's not the only character with such erratic behaviour. Elliot suffers a very unmotivated personality change into a very stereotypical creep. It's seriously out of nowhere, and only happens to further the plot....excuse me, the "plot". 
 Back to the "plot". It's pretty much 3/4s of an annoying back and forth between Nora and Patch who have no real chemistry or any reason at all to even be attracted to one another. That's followed by a bunch of angel mythology that's been slapped in clumsily at the end to tie up those dratted loose ends. 
 Speaking of the end. I nearly threw the book. All the conveniences, the complete lack of consequence, the completely unsatisfying resolution...UGH. I just did not see the point of anything that happened. Really. I didn't care about Nora, or her mom, or Vee, or Patch, or Elliot, or ANYONE. I actually took the side of Jules, the supposed villain. He had been completely violated and manipulated repeatedly by Patch AND was a relative of Nora's and she STILL chose Patch over him. What the actual fuck? 
 In summary: Awful book, terrible characters, no plot, mediocre writing....pathetic. The cover IS gorgeous, though.

This book has a lot of potentials. I love how J.A. Redmerski created something different compared to other romantic and contemporary novels. At first, I expected the story to be quite dull and boring. Two strangers traveling together? It sounds cool but I don't think it encourages romance between the two characters, yet I was wrong because all the while, the romantic development between Camry and Andrew was fascinating. 
 The first portions of the book was quite slow and a bit tedious but during the middle part, the real picture of the love story was clearer, so somehow I was able to determine the real sense of the plot. 
 The interesting part of the story is how the author introduced the characters. Camryn, a 20 year-old girl, is in a soul-searching mission and she needed to get away from home and travel alone to find her share of happiness after dealing with difficult circumstances of her life. Andrew, on the other hand, is also in the same boat with Camryn. So it's not at all difficult to make a connection for the two characters. 
 Actually, I love Camryn and Andrew. Their chemistry is very evident and I think they're perfect together. They share the same passion most especially when it comes to music. Their story isn't also an "insta-love" kind of thing since they first got along each other before they actually fell in love. 
 What serves as a drawback here is that there are scenes that are way too hard to believe. I understand that this is a work of fiction but I also get the point that it's also based on reality. But I rather found some scenes quite overly exaggerated. It's also hard to believe that Andrew or Camryn will instantly trust each other after what, two days of being together at the bus? 
 Their friendship-turned-into-relationship thing is special, yet their emotional and sexual dependence to each didn't sit well on me. I also think there's an emotional obsession between them and for me, it's not at all healthy. I can't imagine how Camryn could not breathe without Andrew. It seems to me like she really can't survive the rest of her trip without him. I don't think that's a good character development. 
 Anyways, the book is great. One thing I do appreciate about it is the fact that it's VERY WELL WRITTEN. There's humor to it and most parts are entertaining. And also, the romance is scorching hot you will definitely be carried away. I also didn't expect the twist at the near-end chapter. Whoa, didn't expect that coming! 
 This book, by the way, is the first book of the sequel so there's a second book waiting, The Edge of Always - which is the thing that I'm going to read anytime real soon. :)

1.5/5 stars. Man, this is tough to write because I obviously have a very unpopular opinion of this book. Here comes my rant! The book started off a bit concerning. We had Cam who has been struggling from anxiety who constantly hung out with a very unsupportive bff and her drug dealer and cocaine user boyfriend. The first few chapters were so predictable until the plot takes a 180 and shifted so much that it felt like a totally different story. Cam ultimately wanted to go on a road trip to destination anywhere. Her reasons and the way she went were unjustifiable and unrealistic. You and your bff have a fight and BOOM... You drop everything including your new job, your family, and your responsible lifestyle for a few weeks of escaping?! Speaking of family , her mother wasn't at least one bit concerned of her daughters disappearing act ?! No one thought it odd that Cam was just gone?! 
 Ok so her relationship with Andrew Parish was sweet at first. Their physical relationship was a big old eye roll for me. It was cheesy, classless, and it totally contradicted everything Andrew was vocalizing. Ugh ugh ugh. 
 We find out around 80 percent of the book that something is up with Andrew. We find out at 90 percent what it is. By 95 percent of the book, the worse has happened and boom... We have the last chapter which pretty much served as an epilogue. There was no build up. There was this unrealistic, unjustifiable, and irresponsible feeling to this WHOLE novel until the last 5 percent of the book. 
 The two best parts of this book that gave it a .5 star higher of a rating was 1. Cam's side braid. It was always on pointe. 2. Every time Andrew called her babe. It really warm my cold hateful heart haha. 
 I know this is harsh but I will not be reading the next one nor will I be recommending this to a friend .

Usually I save my 1 star Goodreads ratings for books that I cannot finish. This book I actually did finish, but the reason why I gave it 1 star will soon be apparent. 
 After reading a friend's review of The Edge of Never, I decided to try it out and see if it really was as bad as she claimed. I began reading with a sense of trepidation and with incredibly low expectations. Perhaps this was why The Edge of Never actually had a surprisingly promising beginning. Probably about up to a third of the way in, I was quite enjoying it, and wondering why my friend hated the book so much. I was enjoying the interactions between Camryn and Andrew, and wondering how their relationship would be further developed and really looking forward to reading about said relationship development. Then Redmerski showed her true colours, and there it was: an absolute monstrosity came to life. 
 Annoying, Shallow Protagonist 
 I'm sorry to say that I have absolutely no sympathy whatsoever for characters who say things like "I'M NEVER FALLING IN LOVE AGAIN! *sobs uncontrollably*". Characters that say such things appear to be set up by the author like this so that there can be some sort of observable character growth: i.e. they've now gotten over the horrible loss of their previous partner and come to terms with the new love interest etc. etc. But goddammit, you can't control love, that's why it's called "falling" in love. (Yeah, I'm so incredibly deep, lol jks). 
 Quite honestly, Camryn didn't even seem to be that greatly affected by Ian's (her previous boyfriend) death (don't worry, that's not really a spoiler). She apparently deeply loved Ian and said the above "I'm never blah blah blah" then BAM. Ian is a distant memory, cast off into the land of dreams and suddenly, Andrew is the love of her life. She even says something like "yeah, I don't think I really loved Ian". Well, okay. You forgot him quickly enough...I also really disliked the fact that there was non existent romance and non existent relationship development between Camryn and Andrew. In the span of a few weeks (or possibly even less than that), the two characters go from "Hi, random on the bus" to "OH MY GOD I WUV YOU SO MUCH". 
 Also, the rough sex? What the bloody hell? That was completely unnecessary, and frankly, off-putting. 
 In addition, Camryn didn't really seem close to the best friend. When the below event happens (you can find out what is is if you so choose to click the spoiler tag or if you read the actual book DON'T DO IT), Camryn appears to have no regard for the friend's life, and says to her "OMG I NEED YOU HURRY AND GET ON A PLANE AND COME TO TEXAS". She doesn't even think about how inconvenient that is, not to mention the fact that she was at that point in time fighting with her "friend" (because the friend's boyfriend hit on Camryn and told her he had loved her for forever and Camryn told her friend this and the friend didn't believe her). So basically, it went from "I hate you for not believing me" to "I NEED YOU SO COME HITHER". 
 Stupid, Unnecessary Event(s) to Gain Sympathy for the Couple. (Yeah, no. Just no.) 
 WARNING: THIS PART OF THE REVIEW CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS- they're hidden by a spoiler tag though :) 
 This event was actually disgusting. I think I was probably going to give the book a slightly higher rating (3 or 4) before the author decided to put it in. As soon as it happened, my face exactly: -_- 
 Time for the spoiler tag: 
 BRAIN TUMOUR!? You have got to be kidding me. BRAIN TUMOUR?! Why the hell do authors think that suddenly pulling the terminal illness card is interesting for the reader? Jesus Christ, if you're going to do it, do it well, not as some stupid trick to make the couple seem deeper in love or whatever the f*** is trying to be achieved here.... 
 And if that wasn't stupid enough, wow, MEDICAL MIRACLE! And he's alive! 
 Oh and now she's pregnant. And she's getting married to Andrew. Stupidest. Ending. Ever. 
 I really wouldn't recommend this. I found out the hard way. Just don't read it. 
 For more reviews, check out my blog: http://lookingforthepanacea.blogspot....
