 After I finished this, I thought it was good. However, the more I think about it, there are a lot of low points in this book too, and it definitely could have been improved in many aspects. 
 The Edge of Never is told from two perspectives. We have Camryn, the sweet girl with depression who hopped on a bus to find herself. We also have Andrew, the bad boy who is traveling by bus to see his father. So, they meet, and they soon end up traveling together. They fall in love, find themselves, have some sex, and so on. 
 I'm sick of formulaic books about the good girl that makes the bad boy good (or vice versa). Sure, this book isn't that bad, but it was nothing new. The commonly found plot may annoy readers who aren't big fans of romance. 
 Camryn bored me. She was nothing new or interesting; just the typical good girl that you can find in most books. She did have her moments of dumbassery. This is pretty much how her biggest one went: 
 Camryn: Oh, look at me! I'm a pretty young girl sitting in a bus station all alone. 
 Scummy dude: HOT GIRL. MUST RAPE. 
 Andrew: Oh no you don't! *beats scummy dude up* 
 Scummy dude: Ow, you beat me up! 
 Camryn: Oh, no! 
 Andrew: Come with me and we can travel together. 
 Camryn: Well, given the fact that I almost got raped, getting in a car 
 with a total stranger is a great idea! Ok, Andrew, I'll come with you! 
 I know that Camryn is a grown up, independent woman, but is getting into a car with a complete stranger after almost getting raped really 
 a good idea? 
 But Andrew. Stupid Andrew. Not only is he a shallow bad boy (with a hidden soft side, of course), he also proceeded to piss me off for most of the book. 
 Now, I don't know if possessive boys who beat up other people if they look at their girlfriends are considered attractive to other people, but it sure isn't to me. 
 So, how did I feel about Andrew beating up 2 or 3 people because they wanted to rape Camryn? 
 *bangs head against wall* 
 The fact that three people were close to raping Camryn really rubs me the wrong way. Honestly, I found the theme of rape to be unnecessary, and Andrew's way of dealing with it made his character seem overly possessive, aggressive, and brash. 
 The plot was also nothing new. I've read a few road-trip books, and they were all much better. The plot is very common, and I felt that it was too slow at times. This book could definitely be cut down. 
 The best thing about this book is the romance. Even though I felt very neutral about Camryn, and Andrew pissed me off to no end, I can't argue that the romance is well developed and fleshed out. 
 Also, Camryn has depression. This was never really brought in properly, and it seemed like a half-assed plot device to make up feel sympathy for her. After suddenly giving up her depression meds, you'd think that she'd be having trouble, but no. After making a huge deal about her boyfriend dying, this is pretty much how the depression sub-plot goes: 
 Camryn: Oh, my life is so sad! I am clinically depressed, and it's just so sad! 
 Me: Oh, ok. 
 Camryn: *goes on depression free for the rest of the book* 
 How does someone get rid of depression so quickly? Severe depression (as Camryn claims she has) is usually a lifelong thing. It's incredibly hard to go through, and if it does go away, it takes a long time. The author should have done some more research on this before bringing such a sensitive and serious plot point into the story. 
 Also, due to sexual content and coarse language, I would not recommend this book to anyone under sixteen. 
 The Edge of Never is nothing new. It's hugely popular, and many people will enjoy it. Beware of this book if you do not often enjoy romances, of if "bad boy" types set you off. 
 To end my review, here is one face-palm inducing quote from Andrew: 
 "If you were to let me fuck you, you would have to let me own you."

Writing:J.A. Redmerski is a great writer. She gave me enough history that I felt like I knew the MCs and their thought processes. 
 HOWEVER, she also gave entirely too much. Why is this book over 400 pages? There was no reason for it to be this long. Some of the narratives went on and on. 
 Characters: I had issues with the MCs. Camryn has been through so much in life. Nobody understands her. Her family & friends do her wrong. She is always so forgiving and never judgmental. She is wise beyond her years. And let's face it, her brother going to prison WAS ALL ABOUT HER! 
 Andrew is the perfect, tatted up, muscled, beautiful face, hair & eyes Hero. He is deep and understands everything. His words make you brave. His touch makes you crave. He is the quintessential bad boy. Nobody is better than him. 
 Okay I'm done being facetious. 
 Storyline: The story was interesting. I've never read a road trip novel before. How do you make a road trip interesting to read about? Redmarski did it. I would have enjoyed a few more stops along the way, however I guess the long narratives ate up any more potential stops. 
 Last facetious moment for real. 
 I know you can't tell by my sarcasm, but there were moments of this book that I really enjoyed. The event that triggered Camryn's road trip was intriguing. The way the MCs met was believable and fun. I even enjoyed the talks on the bus and in the car. And many other things, however some of it was overshadowed by the long narratives and the unrealistic MCs. 
 Intimacy Scenes: Camryn's favorite word is slut. But wait let's not forget, she is not judgmental. But their first intimate moment, I was definitely thinking- 
 Then their sex talks in the car and the subsequent sex scenes- 
 Overall: It was interesting. I'm not sure if I will continue with this series. I'm all for secrets, but Andrew's secret came out of left field. But I would like to read something else by Redmarski.

Me sorprendio que la historia mejorara, asi como la forma en como se desarrolla; es mucho mas rapida de leer que el primer libro, claro que en algunas partes en donde Anastasia me aburria demasiado me saltaba hasta donde pasara algo interesante. 
 Al termino del primer libro todo queda como en suspenso, porque las cosas no quedan muy bien entre los protagonistas y no pasa demasiado para que medio arreglen esos conflictos que se traen y darse la oportunidad de intentar otro tipo de relacion. Asi que practicamente desde el principio se puede adivinar que las practicas sexuales de Christian podrian pasar a segundo termino. 
 Siento que todo pasa muy rapido, no solo por la forma en que esta escrita la historia; sino porque creo que la autora va demasiado rapido con todo lo que pasa, no se que tan bueno o malo sea eso, de algun modo permite leer los libros bastante rapido pero hay algo que no deja disfrutarlos como se deberia. 
 De nuevo mi queja va hacia la protagonista, en serio no me agrada nada y eso no es un elemento a su favor, porque me salte algunas partes en donde de plano de aburria leerla. Christian por otro lado me agrado mas, aunque tiene algunos momentos como 3 o 4 que pense que estaba leyendo a algun personaje meloso y molesto. 
 Por fortuna este libro hizo que quisiera leer el tercero, un poco con la sensacion de saber que puede pasar pero no quiero adelantarme. 
 En definitiva mejoro bastante, aunque por momentos sea predecible no le quita el hecho de que se disfruta (sobre todo a Christian), asi que la calificacion sera mejor que la del primero.

SPOILER ALERT. 
 THIS TELLS YOU HOW BOOK TWO ENDS AND THE SET UP FOR BOOK THREE. YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 ~~1/24/14~~ 
 I was too kind yesterday when writing this. 
 I never in all my life have read something intended for an adult audience that showed up so damned juvenile. 
 I love how Ana goes from giving a pro blow job (as a virgin no less), to giving SHY SMILES/GLANCES/GRINS/LOOKS every five fucking seconds! She's just had his junk in her mouth and her body, they've fucked every way from Sunday, and she's STILL SHY?????????????????? 
 I understand this has to be a "bad boy redeemed" story, but to castigate BDSM while you're at it is so cliche. For someone who was in to it the way Grey was to reverse himself 180 over one woman? I don't buy it. 
 It also makes me resent Ana for changing something that didn't need to be changed, and hate Grey for being so spineless. James even goes out of her way to assure her readers that sadism is not a "mental disorder" by telling us it's been removed from the DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders). 
 If you're going to have the balls to assign your character the trait(s) of being into BDSM, have the balls to stick with it and not pussy out and start painting as something your character should be ashamed of. Part of Christian's early allure is his kinkiness. By this book it's starting to get watered down. 
 I've started book three and it gets worse. 
 The more I read, the more I want to tell James, if you wanted to write a billionaire romance, why didn't you? If you wanted to write a story about an innocent girl meeting a kinky guy, why didn't you? But why on earth did you combine the two and water down one to the point of insulting anyone reading it who IS kinky? 
 All right...back to the rest of the review. 
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
 Where do I start? 
 How many times can E.L. James tell her reader how devastatingly handsome Christian Grey is? 
 How many times can E.L. James tell her reader about Grey's gray eyes? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia bite her lip? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia roll her eyes? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia's inner goddess vaulting off/over her chaise lounge? 
 How many times can E.L. James have Anastasia's half-rim glasses/cardigan wearing subconscious scowl? 
 In a way, I almost want to keep count as I start the third book in this mess of a publishing miracle. Yes, I called it a miracle, because it's a miracle it ever saw publication. 
 The characters are made of paste board at best. 
 James must have done cursory research on BDSM. I have to wonder, the first Christmas this was out, how many beginner BDSM kits found their way under Christmas trees to hapless men whose wives had read this mess prior to the holiday? 
 This is nothing more than a mediocre billionaire finds love romance with a smattering of BDSM for spice. 
 If I dislike the series so much, why am I reading the third installment? 
 Oh, call me a sucker for punishment I suppose. 
 I wondered what lame excuse for a cliff hanger ending would bob it's way to the surface for this one? 
 In book one, it was Anastasia deciding there was no way they would ever be compatible, and running out on Christian. 
 During book two, they're only apart for a week before they get back together hotter and heavier than ever. 
 By the end, Anastasia has agreed to marry Mr. Fifty Shades of Fuckedup (her name for him), had a confrontation with "Mrs. Robinson", the older woman who introduced Christian to BDSM, and has landed her boss's job, after he makes a pass at her in the break room at the office - resulting in Anastasia twisting his pinky finger almost off and kneeing him in the groin. He is summarily let go (Christian owns the company- bought it to keep Ana safe). 
 What cliff is there left to hang off of for book three? 
 The ex-boss is in the background spoiling for revenge. 
 Lame, as what power could he possibly have to bear? 
 Can't wait to see how this peters out.

Before I get to a proper review, I want to address a couple of things. First, I agree with many people who said that the first book, Fifty Shades of Grey, differed in may ways in comparison to this book. I agree. Secondly, and perhaps more importantly, I know a lot of people love this series, and there's something to be said for that. I like that people appreciate books and literature, and I really like it when people delve into fanfiction. With any series, but particularly with this one, I feel like you either love it or you hate it. I'm not so sure I would go so far as to say I hate it. But there are some serious problems I would like to address. With that, read on if that's your thing! 
 My version of this book (an iBook on my iPad) was nearly 700 pages. Way too long, particularly for the level and kind of material that made up said 674 pages. It was incredibly repetitive and I started to skim because it was the same lovey dovey language or sexual encounter over and over again (though, to be fair, I recognize that's the allure for the target audience of this book). This book could (and should) have been 100 pages, maximum. Now, I realize that people aren't reading this book for good literature. They want the sex, and yes there's plenty of that, but even then, this book would only be half as long as it actually is. Here's what made up another 300 or so pages of text: 
 "I need you." 
 "I need you too!" 
 "I love you." 
 "I love you too!" 
 "OMG I can't be everything you need!" 
 "Nooooo I have completely changed now, because of you." 
 "It's not fair to you!" 
 "Don't you want to be with me?" 
 "How can I prove that I'll never leave you?!" 
 "You are mine!" 
 "I'm yours!" 
 "I love you! I can't ever be without you!" 
 "I love you so so so so much!" 
 Over and over and over again. Nearly every interaction between Ana and Christian goes this way, and let's face it, 95% of the interactions in the book are Ana/Christian, and that's one thing that bothers me. This book spans a little over a week, and yet we don't get any of the conversation between Ana and Jose, one of her good friends. Ana and Christian hardly talk about anything besides themselves. It occurs to me that I don't even know what Christian does. Ana talks about how he's such a great guy with humanity at his heart, but we see so little of it. We have to take her perspective on everything because, with this writing style, there's nothing else for us to read. So I find the character development to be less than fantastic. 
 Ana's interactions with Christian are troubling, for many reasons. For one thing, she apparently broke down for a week while she and Christian are separated, and then they're suddenly back together. Ana seems chronically unable to eat, which is really unnecessary. Apparently she didn't eat for four days, and suddenly everyone knows she lost weight. When she talks with Christian, it's basically that blurb I put above, complete with Christian getting angry and yelling at her at least half the times. Not okay. Maybe I'm just not willing to be yelled at that way. And then there's the sudden marriage proposal. They've known each other for five weeks. 
 Two more things: everyone "semi-evil" hates Ana. Everyone loves Christian, right? Ana is careful to point out anytime they interact with women, because of course all the women (except the lesbians. Important distinction there. Christian's magical influence clearly isn't so powerfully magical.) are falling over themselves for him. (Ana spends a third of the book talking about how beautiful Christian is. Which would be overcompensating, but apparently not! He's perfect and all.) So of course they all dislike Ana, especially after she becomes the fiancee. Elena/Mrs. Robinson turns into a huge, huge bitch at the end. That and apparently everyone Ana knows is attractive. 
 Last and most important thing: the inclusion of abuse and mental health is absolutely unacceptable. I found Christian's condition troubling in the first book, and it's completely worse in this one. Suddenly he's so much better after five months with Ana? I find that hard to believe. The interactions with Dr. Flynn are deeply troubling. I just can't see any of that stuff happening. The absolutely worst part was the inclusion of Leila. It was totally random. Ana refers to her as this crazy person, and Leila is introduced in such a way that you're only surprised when Leila shows up in Ana's place because it's not near the end of the book. But James turns Leila into this mentally unstable woman who can't even use complete sentences or use big words, and that's infuriating. That she is suffering from a mental well-being issue is obvious, but James blows it way out of proportion and, I think, reestablishes the idea that we as a society have a lot of misconceptions about mental health. She reinforces those misconceptions. 
 Overall: badly constructed characters, no plot to speak of, and Ana is the absolutely best/worst Mary Sue I've seen in quite some time. The next book is 600 pages on my iPad, and I'm unsure about whether or not I'll pick it up. At least I didn't pay for it, but I'm not sure I want to spend another two days on this book. 
 -- 
 In terms of if this ever comes to film, it'll be interesting to see how they do it. I can't imagine ever wanting to waste an hour of my time on this film. Twilight, Harry Potter, and even Warm Bodies have more going on in them, and they have elements of action and a plot. They are arguably YA fiction, which has to include action and some semblance of a plot. Fifty Shades has no action and isn't YA, so it will depend on how they market the film to a particular audience. I'm less than interested, but I expect they'll have a hard time.

If you read my review of the previous book, you know that I have a conflicted opinion about this story. There are definitely some aspects about these books that I don't really understand or like, but I find them strangely compelling and have been obsessed with these characters since I started reading the first book. Anyway, I assume that if you are reading this you have already read Fifty Shades of Grey, so this review might contain spoilers for the previous book. Be warned. 
 Well, Fifty Shades Darker picks up the story a couple of days after the ending of the first book. I have to confess it was no shock the way the author made Christian and Ana reconnect. I mean, there are three books, so it's obvious that both main characters wouldn't be kept apart after just one book, right? So yeah, the book starts, there are a couple emotional scenes here and there and then Christian and Ana are back together. 
 As I mentioned on the review of the previous book, after a couple sex scenes, I lost interest in them altogether. Since I started reading Fifty Shades of Grey, the thing that kept me going was my curiosity to know more about Christian's past and what made him who he is. In this book, the author finally focuses more on his story and we get a lot more details about his past. Of course I won't reveal anything here. It's enough saying that most people wouldn't bounce back from what Christian's been through. It's a wonder that his weird life-style preferences are the only collateral effects of such horrible things that happened to him. 
 Throughout the book we also get to see the relationship between Ana and Christian finally growing into more of a normal affair; no contracts or weird requests. There's no lack of communication bullshit anywhere and I loved it. God knows I hate it when authors keep characters apart pulling the bad communication card. Both Christian and Ana talk and try to discover what is the kind of relationship that would satisfy both their needs. 
 In fact, I thought the compromise Ana and Christian reach in the end was kind of a perfect way to end this series. But then the author came with that shocking epilogue and another cliffhanger! Now I simply have to know what happens next. Overall, this continued to be a pretty interesting experience. I never thought I would be one to enjoy erotica, but it seems that I am. I hope the author finds a satisfying way to end this series on the next book. A bland ending would be a big letdown. 
 Anyway, that's it for this one. Cya.

I was excited to begin this book after finishing the first one, but about halfway through, I became kind of bored. It seemed repetetive and I pretty much knew what was going to happen. There really weren't any surprises, which was a little disappointing, but I pushed on and finally completed it. Overall, I'm glad I read it, but I won't read it again.

Didn't love the first one, but continued because the first one ended in a way where I felt like it was unfinished. 
 I actually prefer the second then the first. 
 I 
 What I didn't like about this one, is she came across a bit pathetic initially. You break up with someone because they hit you, but you are good to go on a date with them because you need a ride. 
 Sure he is going to do all his changing blar blar, but i still don't like either one a great deal.

I couldn't finish it. Anything that made the first one novel and unique (and, admittedly, that wasn't much) was old hat by the time I gave up. Suspension of disbelief was growing ever harder to maintain and, well, I have about 50 other books on my Kindle I'd rather spend my limited reading time on.

I will make this shorter than my previous rant. It's worse. Really I think that the first two books were one long and poorly edited manuscript that got chopped in half. The only thing darker about this was my mood as I womanfully ploughed through it. Once again this is book valium for the brain dead, cand floss for the souless. I iagine it might be moderately entertaining if there weren't at least fifty other books you'd rather be reading. Having worked out that Grey is a crazed stalker who has some serious mother issues, Ana returns from a five day break up and the break up crash diet certain she can't live without him. Hilarity ensues. Except it doesn't because the only thing funny about this and not in a humorous way, is the fact that once again I kept reading. Do not recommend this under any circumstances. Wel played James, you wrote the book you wanted to write and despite everything, it shows.

Eh. This book was, literarily speaking, better than the first. The "oh my" and "crap/double crap" seemed to trail into the night. This book was much better written, although the back and forth in Christian and Ana's relationship made me anxious. I didn't want to be in the relationship... I can't imagine anybody wanting to either be fighting or sexing. Then again I'm about as WASPy as a human gets. 
 Ana and Christian are miserable without each other. They get back together. They decide to have what most of us would call a "normal" relationship with just a bit of kink. Ana gets a job at a publishing company which Christian promptly buys. Her boss starts to hit on her. Christian gets pissed. They go to a ball. Ana meets his shrink. They have a lot of carnal knowledge and take lots of showers. Christian wants to get married. Lots of girls want him. Christians plane disappears. He's okay. They get engaged. Something about Jose. Mrs Robinson is exposed. Grace slaps her. The end.
Just because I always finish what I started
Another page turner, some twists that I would not have thought of happening. Again the writing could have been better in transitions, but still kept me watching the clock for when I could read more.

"There is a darkness deep in you 
 A frightening magic I cling to" 
 Snow Patrol - "All that I have." 
 The Matrix, Fight Club, the Truman Show? And all on Christian' s wall ?!! 
 Well, when things start off with a nightmare, you know where you're heading. 
 Just when you thought it was safe... 
 Christian goes vanilla... 
 Okay, basically here, I am concerned with Christian's change from Alec to Angel.... The Turn (yes as in movie "The Prestige") 
 "As we talk. It strikes me that he's turned from Hardy's Alec to Angel. debasement to high ideal in such a short space of time". Ana - Fifty Shades Darker. Now that's odd. The mention of "short time of space" is a clue. Is his change sincere?(Snort). I know that Alec goes through a change in Tess as well when he becomes a preacher but that isn't sincere. Let's see if I can find out just what caused Christian to change. Angel also goes through a change as well from a hypocrite to a understanding man but it is not as it seems either. I shall reveal that later. 
 Ana is now working for SIP. She has this creepy boss, Jack who is trying to get in her pants. She receives an e-mail from Christian about Jose's exhibition and decides to attend it with him. Stalker Christian already has her e-mail address. Boy that guy is fast. And so it begins again... 
 Separation period - one week. 
 During that one week, Christian was a shell of a man... he was distraught. He wants to "try" to give her more. Can we really believe this ? I mean even Ana can't believe it. 
 "If I haven't left would he have offered the vanilla alternative? " Ana - Fifty Shades Darker. 
 Maybe he should just try to give her more space. Obviously with Christian comes the supposedly great sex, an Audi A3, ipod, Blackberry, Mac and a new ipad - "I shake my head in disapproval because of the expense, but deep down I love it" Ana - Fifty Shades of Darker 
 Coincidentally there is a bar named Fifty's opposite SIP (it must be "fate"). Then "Fate", like in Tess, has it, that Christian buys SIP - crazy bastard. Ana's bf owns her owns the friggin' company she works for. OMG !!! 
 After a small argument, Ana caves in thinking it is absolutely "exquisite" that she is sleeping with her boss's, boss's boss. 
 ANA IS CLUELESS 
 Meanwhile, Ana is still trying to work out Christian, and still is baffled by the obvious. 
 "He thinks he doesn't deserve to be loved. Why does he feel that way? Does it have to do with his upbringing? His birth mom, the crack whore?" Ana - Fifty Shades Darker. 
 "A hundred images dance through my head: the iPad, the gliding, flying to see me, all his actions, his possessiveness, one hundred thousand dollars for a dance. Is this love?" Ana - Fifty Shades of Darker. 
 Something else to be noted: 
 "I've never really looked at them before: all figurative paintings, all religious--the Madonna and child, all sixteen of them. How odd? 
 Christian isn't religious, is he? All of the paintings in the great room are abstracts--these are so different. They don't distract me for long--Where is Christian?" Ana - Fifty Shades of Darker. 
 Hmmm. Very odd indeed. 
 " I can list the salient points-his control freakery, his possessiveness, his jealousy, his overprotectiveness-and I completely understand where he's coming from. I can even understand why he doesn't like to be touched-I've seen the physical scars. I can only imagine the mental ones, and I've only glimpsed his nightmares once." Ana -Fifty Shades of Gey Darker . Yeah, try to find excuses for the asshole. 
 Christian continues to contradict himself. 
 "Ironically, it was Elena who pointed it out to me. She encouraged me to go to Georgia." 
 "You're the only girl I'd fly three hundred miles to see" Christian Fifty Shades Darker... With Elena's encouragement of course not of your own accord ? 
 My personal favourite: 
 "I try to recall the first conversation I had with him about his tendencies when we were in the Red Room of Pain. 
 "You said you weren't a sadist." trying desperately to understand- make some excuse for him. 
 No, I said I was a Dominant, if I lied to you, it was a lie of omission. I'm sorry" 
 No, Christian, you fucking lied outright, there is no omission. YOU DENIED BEING SADIST!!! (SHOUTY CAPITALS). Here's the proof. And Ana is still trying to make excuses. 
 ""You're a sadist?" (Ana) 
 "No, I'm a Dominant." His eyes are a scorching gray, intense."" Fifty Shades of Grey 
 Remember when he told Ana about the fifteen excluding Elana ? Then he mentions there were others that he paid for excluding the fifteen. Well Christian insists he is monogamous in a relationship and so are his women. Yet he pays for sex ?!!! Certainly prostitutes aren't monogamous nor was the then married Elena. Was he really monogamous if there were so many women ? 
 "How could she have known it was my car?' 
 He glances anxiously at me and sighs. ~She had an Audi A3. I buy one for all my submissives- it's one of the safest cars in its class.' 
 Oh. So, not so much a graduation present, then.' 
 ~Anastasia, despite what I hoped, you have never been my submissive, so technically it is a graduation present.' He pulls out of the parking space and speeds to the exit. 
 Despite what he hoped, oh no ... My subconscious shakes her head." 
 Jeez, then why does she look like all your other subs, and why didn't you give her another car ? Huh ? Why did you make her sign the NDP and negotiate the limits ? 
 ANA VERSUS THE OTHER WOMEN 
 At least Tess, a fifteen year old girl can make sense of things faster than twenty one year old, Ana. 
 "My eyes were dazed by you for a little, and that was all." 
 -- Thomas Hardy, Tess of the d'Urbervilles 
 Then just to antagonise our Ana further, the appearance of Bitch Troll, Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Paedo and Leila, Ghost girl. 
 Leila aka Ghost girl is Christian ex-sub gone psycho. Why is Leila stalking her ? Who does she want to harm ? What happened to make her go off the edge ? 
 "Leila wants back in Christian's life and chooses a suicide attempt to attract his attention." 
 Christian left Georgia to be at her side, but she disappears before he gets there. How odd ?" Ana -Fifty Shades of Grey. I am glad to you realised that is odd, Ana, now if only you can put two and two together. Point to note, though is that Leila left her husband and run off with a guy who was killed in a car crash four weeks ago. Why does Christian have her songs still in his ipod after two and a half years or and her paintings too? 
 Ana has this dream 
 "The girl who is standing outside SIP. Hang on- she is me. I am pale and unwashed, and all my clothes are too big; I'm staring at her, and she is wearing my clothes -healthy and unhappy." Ana - Fifty Shades Darker 
 "I'm nobody! Who are you? 
 Are you nobody, too?" Emily Dickinson. 
 Interesting dream, so far I have been noticing Anastasia nightmares. 
 Well, it turns out that Christian has a thing for brunettes who look like his crack-whore mum. Another greek myth, the Oedipus Complex. 
 "Its obvious to me, for the first time, that he loves his mum. Why then his strange strained ambivalence toward her ?" Ana - Fifty Shades Darker. This would be so easy to the rest of us ... But not Ana, who can't seem to understand the obvious. Hint Ana - He loves her but she betrayed his love and there's no ........ ( To keep the suspense, I am going to complete that later) 
 And this encounter with Leila means that Ana has moved in with Christian. After Leila slashes the A3 tyres and sprays it with paint, Christian buys Ana a Saab. Apparently the A3 was given to all his submissives. He tells Ana he loves her to soften the blow of knowing that her graduation present was actually a "sub car ". 
 "Would I ever leave him again now that loves he me ? ... Could I ever leave him no matter what he did to me ? Could I betray him like that ? No, I don't think I could." Ana - Fifty Shades Darker 
 Christian's Mentally ill ? 
 Anyways, Ana is struggling to understand her Fifty shades and Christian is trying to give her more. 
 "He seems to snap out of his vulnerability in a nanosecond. How can he switch so quickly ? He's the most capricious person, I know." Ana - Fifty Shades of Darker 
 Ana thinks he probably is schizophrenic. 
 "He is like several different people in one body. Isn't that a symptom of schizophrenia ?" Ana - Fifty Shades of Grey. 
 Maybe after all that role playing he just is a good actor, Ana. And she is still friggin' making excuses for him. 
 Jealousy makes you nasty 
 Christian's and Ana's jealousy is also apparent here. 
 Christian buying all Jose's portraits of Ana, so that nobody other man can gawk at what's his. His jealousy over Jose, Ethan, Jack, Taylor - the guy who Christian sent to buy Ana some panties. Ana going for a run because Leila is fit enough to keep up with Christian's BDSM antics, and then how dare Elana look so beautiful, just how dare Elena Cruella ?!!! Ana is actually trying to work out so that she can compete with Leila - Leila had stamina to keep up with Christian's activities. 
 GO ANA!!! 
 Christian doesn't want Ana to work, and finally I champion Ana, go girl !!! Come on, you can do it ! 
 ""I have a new job, which I enjoy. Of course I have to go to work. [...] Do you think I am going to stay here twiddling my thumbs while you're off being Master of the Universe?" 
 "Frankly . . . yes." 
 Christian, I need to work for a living, and I'll be fine. 
 No, you don't need to work for a living and how do you know you'll be fine ?" 
 What does he mean ? He's going to support me ? Oh this is beyond ridiculous - I've only known him for what - five weeks ? 
 I sigh, emboldened by my glass of wine. "You really have to let me fight my own battles. You can't constantly second-guess me and try to protect me. It's stifling, Christian. I'll never flourish with your incessant interference. I need some freedom. I wouldn't dream of meddling in your affairs." 
 He blinks at me. "I only want you safe, Anastasia. If anything happened to you, I--" He stops. 
 "I know, and I understand why you feel so driven to protect me. And part of me loves it. I know that if I need you, you'll be there, as I am for you. But if we are to have any hope of a future together, you have to trust me and trust my judgment. Yes, I'll get it wrong sometimes--I'll make mistakes, but I have to learn. "And if you can do that--give me that--I'll move in with you," I add softly. 
 He inhales sharply, surprised. "You'd do that?" he whispers. 
 "Yes." 
 "But you don't know me."" Fifty Shades Darker. 
 Yes, Christian, you can't control Ana, you need to trust her. Finally, Ana, finaaaaaaaaaaaaaallly!!! There is maybe hope for you yet ! Working gives Ana a sense of self-worth, of accomplishment. Let her make her own mistakes- find her own strength. 
 " Jeez- keep your hair on. But his attitude makes me smile. I want to hug myself-now this man, all domineering and short with me I know. I marvel that I would have found it so threatening only a week or so ago when he spoke to me this way. But now, I understand him so much better. This is his coping mechanism. He's stressed about Leila, he loves me, and he wants to protect me." Ana - Fifty Shades Darker. There goes all the hope that I had for Ana. Fuck what did she just do ? Has she just lost her senses. Protect her by controlling her ? Is love about control or trust ? Oh, this just frustrates me about Ana, she can see the problem clearly. She justifies everything that is wrong by stating that they love each other. What kind of love is that ? Let's not forget that the reason Ana is in danger is because of Christian. Leila is a problem that he has caused. I will validate that later. 
 ANA'S COMPLICATED LIFE 
 Charlatan doctor, creepy boss, ex- sub gone crazy, and ex dommes has our heroine, Ana reeling. Tess, never had to deal with all this suffering. 
 Christian goes all submissive and it is hilarious. This is the scene where the reader should be all emotional but it seemed too contrived. It also seems that real emotion is a hard limit for EL. James too or maybe EL, J has her reasons. 
 Christian is buying a house. Just to work in the Tess theme, there is Ana's fear of. "Four legged fiend of Satan" - horses. 
 Jack gets kicked in the nuts, and beaten up Christian's henchmen, Elena gets a martini thrown in her face and faces the wrath of Grace Trevelyn Grey, Christian's mum. Leila goes into a mental institution - if it was good for Van Gogh career, it will definitely be great for her's. 
 Instead of sitting down and resolving all their differences, taking some time to think about it, Ana and Christian decide to get married. You must be fucking kidding me !!! How long have they know each other ? May 9 to June ... What like a month. Wtf. That's too fast too soon... Icarus. 
 Timeline - 6 June to 18 June 
 Points to note : 
 - Christian's male role model is the pimp that beat up his crack whore mum. 
 - the ridiculous timeline 
 - Christian's change in such a short time. 
 - Ana accepted before actually seeing the charlatan Dr, Flynn. 
 - all Christian's subs look like his crack whore mum. 
 - all the nice, expensive things Christian buys for Ana 
 - the pictures on Christian's bedroom wall - The Matrix, Fight Club, the Truman Show all have some element of ILLUSION - appearance versus reality !!!!!! 
 - Mrs Robinson's husband beat her up. 
 - Ana can't put two and two together "His reverie is broken, and he gazes at me as if I don't understand the elementary math of two plus two." 
 - the Charlatan doctor 
 Some points to think about : 
 -Why does Leila want to harm Christian ? She didn't seem to want to harm Ana. So what's her problem ?-Leila left her husband and run off with a guy who was killed in a car crash four weeks ago about the same time Christian started his thing with Ana. She must have been really ticked off when Christian appeared with Ana at the graduation publicity photo. 
 -Why didn't Jack recognise Christian earlier? If Jack has such a great memory, he would remember the most eligible bachelor in Seattle. 
 - what is it that Elena aka Bitch Troll wants to tell Ana ? 
 - why does he keep photos of his submissives? If it is for insurance purposes surely the NDP and the sub contract will help with that !!! Why does he need photos? 
 - why don't we talk about mum's third husband ? Steve- mum's third husband, "I think that's a dark part of her life, which we've never discussed" Fifty Shades of Grey Darker 
 -"You could have a nice brunette submissive, Christian. One who'd say, "how high?", every time you said jump, provided of course, she had permission to speak. So why me, Christian? I just don't get it." Ana - Fifty Shades of Grey. Me too. I don't get what's so special about Ana. 
 The Matrix, Flight Club, the Truman Show ??? 
 I realise I've haven't done much comparison with Tess here but it is for a reason. I just wanted to highlight a few things. Now for the Prestige...
I'm bored
This series continues to disappoint.

Not surprisingly, the writing was poor in Fifty Shades Darker. I found it quite boring, as the book was very repetitive. Even the sex scenes became boring. It takes off right where the first book left off, and James has this annoying way of describing Ana's days from beginning to end. Mundane and entirely unnecessary details caused the book to drag on. The entire book took place in two weeks, which made the happenings seem so unrealistic. Here is a man who is completely fucked up, yet changes dramatically in a few weeks time. If it were reality, Christian Grey would probably need months, if not years, to progress in the way that James made him in two weeks. That part really bugged me. 
 There was a lot of stuff going on in this book, between Christian's suicidal ex sub, Leila (the story could have done without her); Ana's boss, Jack; and Elena. I really did not like any of the characters in this book, except maybe Mr. Grey. However, there is far less "kinky fuckery" and much more "hearts and roses." 
 Also, the "cliffhanger" at the end was annoying. I am not in the least bit compelled to read the third book in this series. I should have stopped with the first book.

I will keep this short. This was like reading the first book.No plot as such a lot of sex ( which I skimmed) and Ana behaving like teenager still can't say the word vagina and Christian still a controlling, self-centred insecure,little boy lost crazy person. 
 She also decides to take the next step which is insane! Christian has a lot of baggage and I feel that we have just scratched the surface. Oh oh I am trying to understand her rationale into making this decision ( I said I will keep it short!) 
 What has intrigued is what is going to happen in the third book with Jack. I want to find out how he is going to deal with Christian and Ana.
The first 3/4 of this book was redundant. Ok I got it. They like S & M. Finally some story other than gobs of sex towards the end!

** spoiler alert ** 
 As in the first book of this trilogy, some aspects of the writing are sophomoric, mainly in relation to periphery characters, but don't let that deter you (!) because there is brilliance here too. The relationship between Ana and Christian is just so good. Their frank and open communication is fantastic and their story is not only totally engaging, but downright addicting! Christian (aka, Fifty) is one of the most memorable, delicious characters I have ever read. His voice is unique and clear and mesmerizing, yet he is revealed entirely through Ana's experiences and perception of him (quite a talent, Ms. James!). For both Christian and Ana, everything they think they know about their lives gets tilted at odd angles and makes their growing relationship feel like a thrill ride. All the usual suspects return to keep the "action" going (with at least 3 different mini-plots), and, of course, there is the continuing fallout from Christian's severe childhood (and possible adolescent) trauma. Issues of independence, trust, acceptance, submission and, most importantly, unconditional love are all in play. Despite the intensity and conflict the tone remains witty and playful and romantic. 
 The sequel, "Fifty Shades Darker," was a better read because I ended up liking the characters much more. Through initial heartache, Anastasia Steele is able to see clearly what she wants and needs from this man. When she is reunited with Grey she communicates more by speaking her mind, which differs from the first book where she was more reserved with her feelings. As a result, she becomes a stronger woman and, to my pleasure, more and more defiant to the control freak that is Christian Grey. The more Ana challenges him the more exasperated and turned on he gets. Grey has spent much of his adult life avoiding feelings and only having sexual relationships with women. He has never wanted "more" until Ana. He grows stronger as well, going from being emotionally shutdown to falling in love with Anastasia without even realizing it. She slowly brings him out of his self-loathing, dark place by making him realize that he is worthy of love.

DNF 50% 
 This series is terrible for so many reasons outlined in my review for the first entry. But I had a masochistic curiosity. 
 This book mostly removes the inaccurate and dangerous portrayal of BDSM culture, and thus the blurred line of consent in the first novel is not nearly as problematic here. Taking that away, this book is a riot. A laugh a page. It's the so-bad-it's-good quality that so many cult films have. Open this up with a clear awareness, sense of humor, and a glass or three of wine, and you are in for a treat. 
 But does it have to be 500 pages? No. I got bored after 200 pages as James just essentially repeats and extends the same 50-60 page structure again and again and again. Even reading this for laughs, it gets harder to find anything funny after reading it so many times.

Well, I can finally say I met the requirements of the deal I made. Luckily the deal only included reading this book and not enjoying it. Ugh. Where to start? How about the whole crazy ex-girlfriend thing? This could have made for some really tense scenes, but nope. It was all glossed over and resolved way too quickly. The "Oh, no!" with the helicopter felt rushed and pointless. I didn't care at all. The end with the pov switch was just ridiculous. 
 My biggest problem with this book was that it was so BoRiNg. All those scenes where Ana was deciding what to cook Christian and her worrying if he was mad at her for something stupid she did should have been cut out with a machete. 
 I won't be reading book three. There are too many books on my TBR list, and there isn't any time to waste on the boring, pointless ones.

Why I am continuing to read this, I don't know. 
 Another novel that tries to tell women that abusive behavior is really love, not abuse. A novel that is extremely judgmental of BDSM- painting it as an 'illness' of Christian's that Ana is sent to 'cure'. Repetitive wording that is so glaringly obvious it distracts me. 
 Yet... I am still reading. I just started the third one in fact. 
 I take small comfort in the fact the books were not purchased and I have wasted no money on this.
The story really starts to pick up here with a little more explanation, mystery and excitement.
Okay, still not great but okay.

I think this is slightly better than the first in that we start to get a real sense of why Christian is the way he is. It takes the book away from it's "mummy porn" tag and into something with a little more depth.

reference_books.review_text:
You know when you glug down cheap Chardonnay with your girlfriends and you know it isn't good for you, and you are going to have a headache later, and really wish you'd put something better into your body instead and skipped the empty calories/pages? 
 That's this book. It's not awful. It takes very little effort to read. And hey all your girlfriends liked it. 
 If you like retellings I think you can do better. (Chris Moore's Fool remains a fav. Or the Hogarth Shakespeare series. Or even better go read Pride and Prejudice and Zombies- at least that book knows it's a white zin and goes full on campy fun.) 
 2.5 stars

reference_books.title: One Day
reference_books.review_text:
I'd like to give it 2.5 stars. I had such high hopes as I love "structure" novels. Cloud Atlas, Possession, If On a Winter's Night a Traveler, Post Birthday World, The Sound and the Fury.... You get the idea. I love them all. 
 So I thought a one day for x many years conceit might be fun. Not so much. this just didn't quite get there for me. Em is generally ok but a bit pathetic and co dependent. But Dex, really are we meant to cheer for this brat? Guess I never had the Save The Bad Boy gene... My high hopes were dashed. Maybe time to re read Cloud Atlas instead.

reference_books.title: An Abundance of Katherines
reference_books.review_text: Fun but not his best. This one is a bit lighter and funnier than say Stars or Will Grayson or Alaska. But I liked all those books better. Perfect for flight to NY.

reference_books.title: The Silent Wife
reference_books.review_text: I liked it much better than Gone Girl. Fun to watch two people both wreck each other and self destruct in such different ways.

reference_books.title: Disgrace
reference_books.review_text: Coetzee isn't always for me. His spartan sentences and emotional distance sometimes leave me cold. But this one is his best. It's an interesting look at human behavior and choices, and what disgrace and dignity mean to the characters.

reference_books.title: Cleopatra: A Life
reference_books.review_text: in a word- SNORE!

reference_books.title: Outlander (Outlander, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I am so embarrassed to say that I read this, but I did at a friend's insistence. This may have created a whole new genre, not historical romance, but hysterical romance. The review to read here is the one by Holly dated Dec 4, 2013. It is accurate, hilarious and way more fun than the actual book, so I won't try to top it. Just read her review. But don't read the book. (Unless, spoiler alert, you like bad dialogue a la Harlequin romance novel style, poor hygiene, weird catholic logic, weirder scots tribal logic, lots and lots of giggle worthy sex scenes, buggery, torture, and a few witches and rampaging cows thrown in.).

reference_books.title: Lean In: Women, Work, and the Will to Lead
reference_books.review_text: She's a lousy writer with a good point. Don't self immolate your career. Got it. Nice that someone said it, but would have preferred for it to be well said.

reference_books.title: My Name Is Lucy Barton
reference_books.review_text:
I truly disliked this book and would never have finished it except that my book group selected it, and it only took a couple of hours to read. Problem one, the dumb and contrived plot. Otherwise healthy adult stuck in the hospital for weeks after minor surgery? Please. Hospitals kick you out as an outpatient. Husband and kids won't visit. Seems she has no fiends. Why the elaborate I'm all alone and sick and sad set up? So a grown woman can whine for pages and pages about whether mommy loves her. I can't even get interested in much less cheer for a main character who is completely infantilized. I fact I didn't like anyone in the novel. 
 The prose also annoyed me to no end. I'm sure she was going for spare and minimalist. I like that style- Coetzee's Disgrace comes to mind. This wasn't that. This was childish and simplistic. I wanted the prose to grow up as much as the heroine. And finally the dark stuff, the big bad skeletons in the closet. Why bother -glancingly- mentioning them if you don't explore them and they don't advance the story? 
 This is a dull little artificial flavor lollipop of a book that tries hard to pretend to be more. I struggle to understand the rave reviews. Perhaps the discussion with my book group will enlighten me.

reference_books.title: The Husband's Secret
reference_books.review_text:
Such ridiculously plotted chic lit. I knew the "secret". I was bored. The characters kept blurring into mundane anonymity. Most of the female characters are weak and pathetic. 
 And dear god the worst bad movie voiceover style epilogue ever. No epilogues! Don't they teach that in creative writing class anymore?? The epilogue took it down an entire star. 
 The booked was not helped by the fact that I just finished reading An Untamed State, which is a fantastic book about family dynamics, loving your child, and what a strong woman can do when her world falls apart. This book was not that. In fact, if you own this book go swap it for An Untamed State, like now. 
 So the plot and characters are wretched (and did I mention the tied up in a pretty pink glitter bow epilogue?) but the one thing this book has going for it is some pretty good writing about how a long term marriage between middle aged people works. Full marks for that. If that's of interest to you. She nailed that. Example: a character liked making apple muffins for her kid - before her utterly typical mid life crisis husband strays. She notes that she and her husband had sex "quick and comforting and perfectly nice, like a muffin. Marriage was a warm apple muffin".

book_a.title: Alice (The Chronicles of Alice, #1)
book_a.user_review: This was not at all what I hoped for. I was looking for a quirky retelling of an already funky classic. This is not that. The story is VERY gruesome, and extremely rapey. Violation, murder and torture in every chapter. The plot makes no sense, even by Alice standards. And worst of all, it isn't even an Alice story. It's just a random horror story using some names from Alice. 1.5 stars.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Had to DNF after like maybe less than 50ish pages because I just couldn't deal with the writing or the characters. Mostly the writing though. Also reading other people's reviews kind of sealed the deal of me never picking this book up ever again. I kind of got a rape-y vibe from it but I was hoping I was misreading, turns out I'm not. So ya know, pass. 
 Maybe one day I'll find a worthy Alice retelling but so far I'm not having any luck with it.

Where to start on this atrocious disaster of a book that both pissed me off and bored me at the same time? With all the rapey stuff, you say? OK, let's talk about the rapey stuff first. 
 As a starting point, I don't mind the use of rape as a plot point in books or movies. Just like murder, cruelty, and other forms of violence, it can be presented in a way that successfully furthers the narrative and provides character development. What I do take SERIOUS issue with is when rape is presented in a titilating manner, where the tone is, "look at how horrible the is" but also "let me describe in graphic detail where he put his hands and how her poor little body trembled." Come on, people, why are so many romance novels written by women, for women, so rapily titilating?? 
 Next, I also can't stand narratives where women's only purpose in the story is to be raped or brutalized by the men. I mean, every woman we encountered in Old City is about 3 seconds away from being raped (or raped while being eaten) by practically every man walking by (because you know men, just can't help themselves with the raping when women are nearby). Even Hatcher, who's supposed to be the good guy, for crying out loud, can barely suppress his rapey instincts. 99% of the women in this book had zero character development, zero agency, and were only play things, at the mercy of horrible, cruel men. 
 Setting aside the overall rapeyness of the book, it just wasn't a good story. It had no unique, innovative, elements, every plot turn was predictable and present in a million other fantasy/horror books. Evil thorns that grab you, creatures that seduce with songs, magicians, mermaids - yawn, yawn, yawn. Been there, read that, seen it done better. Yes, the book had gruesome descriptions, but this only goes to show that graphic violence alone does not a good horror story make. I mean, Christina Henry could talk to me about stabbing some guy in the eye with a sword all day, and I'd yawn and check how much of the book is left. Whereas Stephen King could literally describe a vacuum cleaner to me and I'd be creeped out for days, with dirty floors to boot. That is one of the big differences between good horror writing and terrible horror writing: a good horror story can make you have nightmares for weeks with only a couple of effectively placed details; bad horror writing hinges entirely on the chopping and the ripping (and the raping, apparently). There's nothing else other than the shock of the gore. 
 And don't get me started on the cheesy romance between Alice and Hatcher. How many times did we have to hear about little, mousy, fragile Alice scurrying behind the big, manly, determined, serious Hatcher? (At one point, she described being picked up by him and how she was "no more than a little bit of a thing in his arms" and I almost lost my lunch). And how many times did we hear the painfully cringe-worthy back and forth of Alice declaring that she belongs to no one! To no one, I tell you! But then she's super excited when Hatcher tells someone she belongs to him. GIRL! GET YOUR S*IT STRAIGHT. I know you were only 16 when you entered the mental hospital and are only a little girl in a woman's body (mostly because you kept repeating it every 5 pages), but at some point you need to stop all this "I need a strong man by my side who could TOTALLY rape me if he wanted, but he wouldn't, because he loves me" fantasizing. 
 A few additional observations: 
 1) The main villain in the book - the Jabberwocky - is so undeveloped, and defeated so very quickly and easily, it's laughable. Also, why was he imprisoned under the mental hospital again? 
 2) Christina Henry, you silly little nit!! Your old world English words sound ridiculously corny! 
 3) Tim: Well, that's no ordinary rabbit. 
 King Arthur: Ohh. 
 Tim: That's the most foul, cruel, and bad-tempered rodent you ever set eyes on! 
 Sir Robin: You tit! I soiled my armor I was so scared! 
 Tim: Look, that rabbit's got a vicious streak a mile wide! It's a killer! 
 Sir Robin: What's he do? Nibble your bum? 
 4) I picked this damn book for book club, and now I basically have to cook up a 3-course feast to make it up to these women for having forced them to read this crap.

I typically try to stay from retellings of classic stories, but I was so drawn in by the dark description of Alice that I just had to check it out. It was a quick and compelling read for me. I liked how Alice developed from a meek, scared little girl to a strong and confident woman. Hatcher was the perfect counterpart to her character since both have endured the unthinkable and have determined never to be victimized again. The villains in this story were disgusting, but eerily familiar as there are people who walk among us every day who have the same sick desires and actions. All you need to do is turn on the news or watch an episode of Dateline to see that this is true. What made this less than stellar for me was the abruptness of the ending. The whole book is leading up to Alice's reunion with The Rabbit and their eventual battle with the Jabberwocky. When the author finally delivers us to The Rabbit's doorstep, he is just a mere shadow of the villain he once was. I guess there is some poetic justice in that. Then, after Alice's old "friend" quietly kills The Rabbit, Alice then comes face-to-face with the ultimate of all evil monsters and he is no more than a man in a suit who is so gullible that all Alice has to do is take his hand and turn him into a butterfly in a jar. What the what??? Then Alice and Hatcher go skipping happily ever after into the field of flowers to follow the white rabbit and begin their next adventure??? I was just really disappointed in the anticlimactic ending. Overall, it was an "interesting" read (in the words of Cheshire), but I don't think I'll be continuing on with the series.

Originally reviewed here @ Angieville 
 So. As much as I adore retellings, I recently realized I'd never actually read an Alice in Wonderland retelling. And what with the absolute rash of them inundating the publishing world these days, I figured it was high time. I've always loved the original classic and the Disney film, but I've never seen any of the more recent film adaptations. When Ace contacted me about reviewing Christina Henry's Alice in anticipation of the sequel's release, it felt like the perfect entry point. Funnily enough, I actually read the first book in Henry's Black Wings urban fantasy series ages ago. We didn't particularly hit it off, but I found myself massively intrigued to find out what she might do with a grown-up Alice. Also, the cover. It sends chills down my spine every time I glance over at the copy sitting on my nightstand. Having now read the words behind that cover, I can verify that the chills only increase after you make the acquaintance of Henry's White Rabbit. 
 Alice is mad. Or so they said when they found her stumbling back out of the Old City, having escaped an unnamed horror, with blood running everywhere and the Rabbit's name on her lips. And so they locked her up for ten years in a asylum for those who had taken leave of their senses, who the New City was too impatient to deal with. But two years in, someone whispers through the mouse hole in her cell. Someone by the name of Hatcher, who never takes the powders the orderlies bring, who fights tooth and nail to avoid the regular baths every inmate must take, who awoke years ago surrounded by bodies with a bloody ax in his hands. And so the two become friends and allies, working desperately to keep a shred of sanity in a world they no longer recognize. Hatcher is determined that one day the opportunity for escape will arise. And when it does in the form of a fire, he and Alice fight their way out of the prison that formed every fiber of their beings for so many years. But now they are on the run. Working their way deep into the twisted streets of Old City, they find themselves on a mad mission to escape the evil the fire released from the asylum and to recapture enough of Alice's memories to know who to hunt and who to flee. 
 If she moved her head all the way up against the wall and tilted it to the left she could just see the edge of the moon through the bars. Just a silver sliver, almost close enough to eat. A sliver of cheese, a sliver of cake, a cup of tea to be polite. Someone had given her a cup of tea once, someone with blue-green eyes and long ears. Funny how she couldn't remember his face, though. All that part was hazy, her memory of him wrapped in smoke but for the eyes and ears. And the ears were long and furry. 
 These opening lines sealed the deal, I'm afraid. There was no going back after I met Alice and she met Hatcher and the two of them agreed to hold hands throughout their ordeal. I was completely unable and completely uninterested in not being with them. Which is saying quite a lot, because their ordeal is 
 not for the faint of heart 
 . I repeat, beyond this point there be dragons of the deepest and darkest kind. I want to make this point early, because this book will not be for many readers. The violence factor is high. Hatcher is an actual ax murderer, after all, and he has set his sights on keeping Alice safe from any threat, which means the body count is astoundingly high in this dark fantasy that takes all the unhinged zaniness from Lewis Carroll's classic tale and neatly amplifies it by one hundred percent. Essentially, this book and I had no business falling as madly in love as we did. But there you have it. I loved it beyond reason. I kept waiting for the level of horror to send me packing, but the core--the light that Alice and Hatcher make by the mere fact of their survival--kept me following. Their fight to stop the mindless violence of the Jabberwock, their run ins with each of the unspeakably evil crime lords that run Old City, and the slow and terrifying awakening of Alice's memories are all excellently rendered. 
 My one issue with the novel is the absolute preponderance of violence directed toward women. It is omnipresent in Henry's world and it is massively disturbing. Alice is essentially its only survivor, and I think she is meant to be the seed that grows a revolution. Which I am clearly fine with, as I stuck with her through the entire bloody gauntlet. But I want to be sure to say that while I comprehend the reasons behind the dark world Ms. Henry has created, I feel that the story's integrity could have withstood a toning down of the violence against women (particularly during their sojourns with the Caterpillar and the Walrus) and still retained its spine-unhinging terror. 
 That said, this novel is utterly magnetic. Reading it feels like a madcap sprint to the finish. I swallowed it in 100-page chunks and came back each night just eager to slip back into this nightmare world. And the reason why is the two main characters. Alice and her mad Hatcher. Their heartbreaking connection and the furious way in which they cling to it is everything I look for when I come to a tale. I loved their story in all its brutal, broken beauty. I sense they will never be far from my thoughts from now on. 
 "You remember it all now," Hatcher said, and it wasn't a question. 
 "Yes," she said. She was beyond weeping for the child she once was. "It is, more or less, what you would expect. Except for the part where I escaped. Nobody expected that."
The heroine is in nonstop peril and frankly I couldnt care less if she died. A bit two dimensional of a book, all around.

There were a few inconsistencies, like referring to him as the "Jabberwock" for the first fifth of the book then bouncing back and forth between "Jabberwock"and "Jabberwocky." It did move pretty fast once but I like books like that so I'm not complaining. Again, this is an adult retelling. Man, loved, loved, loved!! I cannot wait for the sequel!!!!

TRIGGER WARNING: THIS BOOK CONTAINS A LOT OF SEXUAL VIOLENCE 
 I have a complicated relationship with retellings. I always want to love them, but more often than not, end up feeling severely disappointed because I hold the original tales at such a high standard (see: The Lunar Chronicles) Like Beauty and The Beast and Red Riding Hood, Alice in Wonderland happens to be one of my favorites, so it was no wonder that I was a little skeptical going into this one. 
 It turns out that I didn't need to be so worried, because I freaking loved this. Alice doesn't take place in the Wonderland we all know and love, but in a gothic-fantasy town called Old City, where Magicians once roamed free, and is now run by many underworld bosses and their respective gangs. The characters in this story aren't the ones we know and love either. Alice is now a twenty-six year old woman who, after disappearing when she was sixteen, reappeared later, with "blood dripping down her thighs", missing memories, hysterically raving about a "Rabbit". Upon her reappearance, she was deemed mad, and locked up in an asylum in the Old City, away from her parents and her home back in the New City. 
 She eventually finds a friend and maybe-lover in crazed ax-murderer in the cell next to hers - a mad, yet kind, man named Hatcher. 
 The story starts with the night a fire breaks out in the asylum, giving Alice and Hatcher a chance to escape their prison and, perhaps, their years of suffering. But they're not the only ones to escape. Something dark and evil is set free that night, something that has an inexplicable tie to Hatcher; The Jabberwock. 
 The Jabberwock is bad news, and his escape means complete destruction. Alice and Hatcher are the only ones who can stop it. Their quest to find the only weapon that can defeat the Jabberwock leads Alice and Hatcher into the lairs of familiar, but completely recrafted characters. Namely, Cheshire, The Walrus, The Caterpillar, and The Rabbit; the bosses who run Old City. 
 The reason why it didn't get a five star rating from me, surprisingly enough, wasn't the rape-y-ness. It was the ending. 
 Let me explain. 
 Rape and sexual violence bother me - in real life as well as in fiction. 
 That being said, it wasn't a deal breaker for me with this book, because I understood the point of it. Sure, this book would have been as gory and as dark without a lot of the sexual violence - but then its villains would have been nowhere near as terrifying. Because that's the thing about the villains in this book - it's not their magic or their power that makes them monstrous, it's their dirtiest, vilest, human qualities. They snatch girls up from their homes, so that they can use them and sell their bodies. 
 If you took away the magical elements, everything that happened to Alice was something that could have happened in our world. And that's what makes this so powerful. 
 I removed a star because the ending was anticlimactic, and the encounters with the bosses were all a little too rushed for my taste. I was happy that the tale didn't end the way I expected, but the conclusion fell flat after the epic buildup, and the pacing towards the end of the book was much too fast. 
 Which is a shame, because this was such a creepy little book, and I was pleasantly surprised by how good it was. Give it a try, if you can stomach the darkness.

I won this book from Goodreads. It was a good book but it wasn't the kind of book I would really read. It is dark and bloody. About Alice who is sent away to a place called Old City. Not a place you want to be. She escaped and something escaped with her. This book was to violent and bloody for me.

Well, that was just about the most pointless book I've ever read. On one hand, I enjoyed it somewhat while reading (because I LOVE the mythos around Alice), but that was with the understanding that all the gore, destruction, rape, murder, blood, and terror was leading somewhere, that it was about learning to deal with trauma or something, that there was a moral to the story. There wasn't. I was pretty disturbed when I got to the end, and there was no closing (other than a shameless plug for a sequel). 
 It ended up, in the end, just being the story of Christina Henry masturbating to women being murdered, mutilated, raped, and tortured. The needless violence was extreme, in the sense that being raped and owned and sold like cattle was the expectation for a girl's fate. And, without a moral or lessons learned, such violence read like a dark twisted fantasy of a twisted individual, and not anything a non-sick person may learn something from. 
 Oh, and the other part of the story was that, along their way through this twisted universe, Alice and her companion killed people in their quest to kill an evil spirit (Jabberwoky). 
 Did I mention the writing was pretty sophomoric, too?

Whoa. Just whoa. 
 Alice in Wonderland is one of my all time favourite books (almost every room of my house is full of Alice inspirations, and my friends always buy me Alice gifts) so I love reading different takes on it which delve into different parts of the world. 
 This book is not for the faint hearted; it's dark, grisly, unrelenting and utterly absorbing! 
 It presents the well known and loved characters in a truly different light, and each of them gets an incredibly original story. I wouldn't know how to describe this as "a really bloody awesome and disturbing re imagining of Alice that every fantasy fan should read immediately." 
 I would strongly suggest buying both books at the same time as even the 24 hour wait for me to get the second book left me feeling antsy, I wanted to know what would happen next immediately. You will not be disappointed!
Unnecessarily dark & grim with nastiness for the sake of it. It is a good retelling of the tale in that it is true but not my taste at all.
This book is disgusting, badly written and entirely overrated. Here are just a few reasons why Rosey and I strongly suggest you stay far away from Alice.

Review: 1.25/5 
 Well, as a retelling, that did a rather curious job. 
 I was so excited to read this book! It's even on my "can't wait to read" shelf. There is something about the idea of a retelling in which Alice has escaped from an asylum that so fits the wondrous aura of the original book. Yet this did not stick to any of the plot-points, truly. Which was very disappointing. I imagine it would be extremely difficult to manufacture a narrative from the nearly unrelated curiosities of the original Alice in Wonderland--Tim Burton certainly struggled--but it seemed like the only thing this attempt did was take some names. 
 It seems that this is not the only shared factor between Tim Burton's adaptation and Christina Henry's. Both focus upon the plotline of Alice defeating the Jabberwocky (which is somewhat ridiculous if you think about it). Both require a certain blade to kill it. Both have weird sexualizations of the plot points, which is so odd because the original Alice is a CHILD. (Especially Henry's--the entirety of the book was centered upon human trafficking for prostitution and sexual assault.) Both have significantly aged Alices, perhaps to fit this. Maybe Henry was adapting Burton's take on the book rather than the book itself. It all came off as very plagiarized. 
 Things, specifically, that bugged me about Henry's take: Alice travels with her middle aged mental-institution-next-door-neighbor, whom she is in love with for some reason? He, to the best of my detection, is not modeled upon a character. The Rabbit is a villain, the main one, and does not share any attributes with the original White Rabbit. In fact, it seems that Henry may have intended the Rabbit to mean the March Hare? Everyone in the book is a villain and there is a strange incorporation of characters from Through the Looking Glass, but not the important ones (Tweedle Dee, Tweedle Dum and the chess pieces, for example, go undiscussed. Maybe in the next books). In general it was so frustrating to try to compare this book to the original, because it didn't add up. And that is all the fun of retellings! 
 After 291 pages of unspeakable violence, the ending of this book was unbelievably anticlimactic. We follow Alice and Hatcher, her extremely old, my-only-character-trait-is-I'm-a-crazy-murderer love interest, as they battle their way to the two "boss" characters: the Rabbit and the Jabberwocky. I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll just say we encounter these guys for a total of the last dozen pages. Very frustrating. 
 God, I'm so upset by how much I hated this. What a cool concept, entirely dashed. 
 Bottom line: if you like very violent books, you may like this. If you like retellings, you will not. I sure didn't.

I finished Alice in a day. In part because I had the day off, and what else was I going to do? And in larger part because I got sucked in and didn't want to put it down. Imagine Alice in Wonderland got smushed together with Sin City and then re imagined entirely into a story where Alice is a reluctant but rewarding hero. Henry's writing is wonderful, best of all when it is examining Alice's own internal thoughts - the thoughts of mental patient, scarred by abuse, removed from the world, uncertain as to who she is. It is a fast paced, forward moving march of a story, and though it was not the best thing ever (the ending may particularly upset some, as it did me) it was compelling and enjoyable and well worth it.

1.5 
 Alice was once a good girl until she came home from the Old City covered in blood and her body riddled with bruises and babbling about a Rabbit and since then she was relegated to the asylum. 
 Her only friend is fellow inmate "Hatcher" who she talks to through a hole in the wall. 
 When an opportunity presents itself Alice and Hatcher escape but their only Place to flee to is the Old City... 
 There is that saying about not judging a book by its cover. In the case of "Alice" you shouldnt Believe that the story is just as gritty as the cover. 
 There are some interesting ideas but in the end this was not a book I could bring myself to like very much. Its set in a dark and grimy World but it didnt feel very consistent. So people have no problem in locking people up in asylums. 
 Why not just execute them it its such an oppresive society? 
 Another thing that bothered me was the exploitaition of Girls,of course in the real victorian era this did happen,but I felt the author really took it to the limit of bearability.Most of the female characters seems to be victims if you dont Count an old woman and Alice. 
 But even Alice is sometimes reduced to the role of victim and having to rely on Hatcher to survive. Its true that she does get a bit tougher as the book progresses but by then I was too tired of the book I couldnt be bothered

I loved this book!! The book would have been good on it's own, but the fact that it had the AIW twist, just made it that much more "interesting". The writing style was very pretty ... which is funny because the book itself was creepy, gross and awful. In a good way of course! I really loved it much more than I expected. I already bought book 2. Can't wait!

I found the writing to be a little corny throughout, unfortunately. I felt the story delt with serious/dark subject matter which would've been a cool take on the classic had I been able to get passed the writing. It read like a dramatic YA horror with generic descriptions repeated on a loop, which was disappointing for me.

Dark, disturbing, violent. 
 Those are the words I would use to describe Henry's ALICE. However if you can see past her warped and unsettling themes it is also an incredibly strange but also bizarre retelling, re-imagining, of Lewis Carroll's story. I've never read the original tale, nor JABBERWOCKY, and had no problem following along with ALICE as it's so different from the source material anyway. 
 Ultimately I'm not even really sure if I did like this. Alice's world is, as mentioned, dark and unpleasant and this book is definitely not for the faint of heart. And yet still.. there is something to be admired about it. Henry took a lot of risks writing her version the way she did but much of it was clever and well thought out, and certainly the ending was not what you -- or the characters -- would come to expect. That being said, due to the subject matter, I don't think I would ever recommend it.
Dark delights in this one. It's fierce.
a nice attempt, but... 2,5 stars I don't want to round up to 3. Shall read the next one, just out of curiosity.

i've wanted to read this book since i first saw it on goodreads. And now that i'm done with it i'm so glad i did. Mad Alice interested me since i played Alice: Madness return. I even think mad Alice is better than the original version.

Like many others, I was initially drawn to the premise of the story. Then I quickly realized that this book is a perfect example of a potentially good story ruined by mediocre writing. Other than coming up with an interesting plot, the writer doesn't seem to have much craft to create a believable fantasy world that draws in the readers. The lack of detailed description (whether this was the writer's intention or inability I cannot say) makes the entire story shallow and boring. The dialogues are often trite and pointless. And I also have this vague feeling that the writer does not exactly know what kind of audience she is targeting. Her writing style and repetitive vocabulary is too simple for the taste of adult readers, but the horrible elements in the story (such as rape, cannibalism, etc) seem all too much for younger readers. The idea of the book is good, so is the plot, I can see how it can go much further than this if not for the writer's disappointing execution.

To those wanting to read this book I must give a big trigger warning, there is a lot of talk of rape in this novel. 
 TW: RAPE 
 "There was comfort in ignorance, in thinking the world a certain way and not knowing any different." 
 In a crumbling city there stands a hospital with cinderblock walls which echo with the screams of the poor souls inside. In the hospital, there is a woman. Her hair; once blonde, hangs in tangles down her back. She doesn't remember why she's in such a terrible place - just a tea party long ago, and long ears and blood. Then, one night, a fire at the hospital gives the woman a chance to escape, tumbling out of the hole that imprisoned her; leaving her free to uncover the truth about what happened to her all those years ago. Only something else escaped with her: something dark. Something powerful. And to find out the truth, she will have to track this beast to the very heart of the old city, where the rabbit waits for his Alice. 
 This book was wildly imaginative. A very, very dark take on Carrol's Wonderland, with lots of blood and death. It was delightfully disturbing. 
 This book did not have great characterisation, but that wasn't the point of this novel. The point was to shock and to disgust the audience. And it most certainly did that! The description of the atrocities that occur were graphic and left nothing to the imagination. The main characters (i.e. Cheshire, The Caterpillar, The Rabbit) were also very well described, a clear picture was printed in my mind. A problem I had (an often problem) was that the world building wasn't wonderful, there was very little portrayal of the surroundings in this book, it was left to our imagination. 
 The writing was easy to read and very simplistic. There wasn't anything particularly special about the way this book was written, there was no interesting POV, it was written in third person but focused entirely on Alice. Not very original at all, I am afraid to say. 
 There was also a lot of references to rape and some of it was very vivid, which was difficult to read and I do not entirely understand why it was so important to write it. I know that the characters were evil, but was it really that paramount to describe rape so often? I don't think so. 
 However, I did like this wonderland, it was dark and horrid. And there were some very interesting characters and interesting attributes to these characters. I liked the plot and I liked that there was plenty of action in this short novel. It was pretty much non-stop actually and I read very quickly. 
 Overall it was on okay read, nothing too special but I would read the second book just for the horror. 
 A 3 star read.
