 When I recently matched with Kyle, 19, I was shocked how well we got along. We bonded over Wicked and moved on to cover all of the novels by Gregory Maguire, which led to a conversation about fairytale retellings. We both were fans of seeing villains in a new light and he understood that I was weary of retellings that made my favorite classics, such as Alice in Wonderland, more gory. 
 When he recommended Alice by Christina Henry, shortly before it was set to release, I didn't know how I would feel about it. He was planning to buy it on its release date and hadn't read it, but Kyle thought I would enjoy it. The cover interested me and intrigued me as I was excited to figure out why the Rabbit had blood over his eye and looked like a collage. 
 Seeing Alice offered on NetGalley made me even more eager to read it. When the publisher send me the ebook, I braced myself for the gloomy tone I knew it would have. 
 After reading the first chapter, I was hooked. Alice is trapped in a mental hospital, unsure of what really happened before she arrived there. Through a hole in the wall (holes seem to be the best place for Alice to meet people), she befriends Hatcher. The hospital catches on fire and Hatcher helps her escape, muttering about a Jabberwocky that was also freed during the fire. 
 In the beginning, Alice and Hatcher have an interesting friendship/romance. They had never seen each other but their feelings were more than friendly but not quite love. I struggled with this for most of the novel, as Hatcher calls Alice hers, she kisses him, and she questions if she will ever get to know him in the biblical sense. 
 On their quest to get rid of the Jabberwocky, Alice and Hatcher learn that they are connected by more than just a shared hole in the wall. They both have dark, twisted pasts and slowly get to remember who they were before. 
 This novel is similar to playing a video game. Every few chapters has a small boss that needs to be defeated before the final boss. Cheshire continues to be painted as her guide to Not-So-Wonderland, the Old City, however, he's much creepier, trickier and villain-esque than he has ever been painted. 
 As Alice discovers she has undiscovered magic, each "boss" becomes easier to conquer. When it comes time for her to face the final boss, the Jabberwocky, it's almost disappointed. 
 Reading this felt like I was playing a video game that became easier the more I played, The first boss was only challenging because Alice was button-smashing and by the final boss, she knew all the combos. It was disappointing. Halfway through the book, I was picking it up only to finish it. I wasn't hooked like I was during the first chapter. 
 I read this for the intriguing cover and my sweet-tooth for reimagined fairytales, but the only things pushing me through to the end were my need to see how the Rabbit was painted and my need to finish books.

If I could rate this book 5 stars a thousand times I totally would. This book is obviously getting a little bit of recognition, because it's up for voting for the goodreads Choice Awards for 2015 - which is where I first heard of this book - but I can see it getting far more than it already has. I can see this book having multiple editions, games, movies, television shows - everything. This book is really that phenomenal and I think it completely deserves any recognition it can get. 
 She must start believing in impossible things, for impossible things kept appearing before her eyes. 
 Being a huge fan of all things Alice, as soon as I saw the cover I was drawn to it. When I read the synopsis it was as if I had been pulled into a book universe mirroring the game, Alice: Returns to Madness. Others have made this connection as well, as I noted when scrolling through reviews and questions. Everyone who had made the connection was also reassured that it was not a cheap copy of the game; that it was a completely new original idea aside from a few superficial similarities. Having now read it, I stand by this as well. Besides, I think the few similarities between the two (the loss of memories, the asylum, the whole feel of the universe itself), I probably wouldn't have loved this book as much as I do. 
 The basic plot for Alice is a re imagining of the original works of Lewis Carol's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, to which I'm sure every one ever knows. The original is a children's story, while this one is kind of a book for the Alice fans that have now grown up. Just like the Alice in the story. 
 It begins with Alice, a woman who is no longer a girl and who's parents admitted into a mental hospital/asylum for reasons she's not exactly sure on. 
 Alice remembered who she was before. She just couldn't recall what had happened to that girl to make her this girl. 
 She is stuck in isolation, being fed powders that chase unwanted memories away and leave her subdued for the most part. A part of her believes what the doctors tell her: that she's mad. But another part almost clings onto the hope that they are all wrong and it is actually them that are mad, not her. 
 Alice knew she wasn't mad. Maybe. Not deep down. But the powders they gave her made the world all muzzy and sideways and sometimes she felt mad. 
 There is a mouse hole in the wall of her cell, one that speaks to her. But it's not a figment of her imagination or proof of her growing madness like she originally fears. There is a man on the other side, who goes by the name of Hatcher. He was called something else, once. There is a reason behind his nickname however, and it's not at all pleasant. The man is entirely mad, and I think that is possibly one of his most charming qualities. When reading about his character I wasn't sure whether I should love him or fear him, and honestly I don't think Alice was sure on that either, which only added to the quality of character development. 
 She knew, also, that even though he loved her, he was not entirely trustworthy. 
 If you can't already draw these conclusions, many of the characters in this book are direct resemblances of the characters from the original story. Alice of course is Alice, that's obvious. But there is also the Mad Hatter (Hatcher, get it?), the Caterpillar, Cheshire, the Rabbit, and the Walrus. The scene descriptions were absolutely gorgeous in a way so that I could imagine exactly what the author was trying to convey without having to read lines and lines of continuous words describing just one thing. It was to the point but it was effective. 
 This book isn't afraid to use crude themes and let the blood flow, and as morbid as it may sound, personally that was like a huge relief. While in the real world it would be wrong, sometimes I think books try to be too realistic and not at all mad enough. It was different and refreshing and while not necessarily 'scary', it was the right amounts of disturbing which were enough to make it incredibly enjoyable. 
 Her future didn't have butterflies and flowers and rain followed by sunshine. Her future slogged through a river of blood to find the well from which it sprung. 
 There is so much more I could say about this, I don't even think I've touched the surface. I've literally been looking for a book like this one for so long it's not even funny. I am so happy that I have found it! Thanks so much, Christina Henry! You are a genius!

Alice by Christina Henry 
 We begin in a mental hospital, where Alice is alone, save for her next door neighbor, who she only sees through a small hole in the wall. Hatcher, so named because he killed using an ax, has been the only voice she hears for years. There is a fire and they escape. (He is also Hatter, as mad as Alice, after taking drugs the nurses put in her food for years, and being alone in her cell with her violent, half remembered thoughts of what happened during her time with Rabbit) 
 Thus begins an adventure where Alice seeks to find the perpetrator of her downfall, Rabbit. Rabbit left her with a scar across half her face, but he did not escape the encounter with Alice unscathed. Along the way she meets the traditional but enhanced characters Cheshire, Caterpillar, Walrus, and Jabberwock. In this extended version of the Alice in Wonderland story, the bad guys are like gang bosses, controlling parts of The New City. The action starts after Alice's adventures down the rabbit hole are over. The traditional elements of the Alice tale, including roses, food stuffs that change your size, talking animals and such, are twisted into a unique story that sails along after a slow start. There is quite a lot of violence and blood, what with a character who favors an ax, but it is not too much to handle. 
 There is enough story left at the end that I am expecting a sequel. I am looking forward to hearing Hatcher's story in the next volume. 
 I received an advance copy for review.

Retellings and adaptations of Alice in Wonderland are one of my things -- I've even committed scholarship about them (www.neovictorianstudies.com issue 5.1 2012). I stumbled across Henry's Alice at an airport bookstall, of all places. 
 One thing that intrigues me particularly are the darker adaptations of Wonderland: Svankmajer's film, the American McGee videogames, Raven Gregory's graphic novels. This one slots neatly into that category. There are traces of earlier adaptations present: Alice in the asylum (both McGee games), Alice's attraction to the Hatter, or Hatcher, here (Tim Burton's film), malevolent versions of her Wonderland encounters (all of the above, plus). Henry brings enough twists of her own that the novel was enjoyable. The writing is fine, but nothing special, and the climax comes oddly quickly. 
 Worth the trip for people who like the darker potential of the Alice books.

I didn't have time to write a review when I finished this last night, but I loved it so much I had to do this now. 
 Alice is a flawed character. Flawed physically, and flawed mentally. And I can't help but love her. Despite the horrible things that have happened, and the terrifying truth of her life for the past ten years, and horror she escapes from currently, she doesn't let it turn her into a bad guy. As you read her internal struggles, it's almost like you can see the scales tipping each way, towards being a fundamentally good person, and back towards being a fundamentally bad person. 
 Besides the fact that I think Alice is a great character, I love the supporting characters. They have magic, they have mystery, and they are... real. These are characters I can get behind. Either to root for, or to cheer when they meet their well deserved end. 
 I think the world building could be more detailed, especially between Old City and New City. But the characters are what make this a truly interesting read. 
 In the end, I loved this book, and it disturbed me greatly. In all, it was great!

"You're only a mouse if you let them make you one" 
 Wow this book was not what I expected, in fact my expectations of this novel was very low indeed but immediately I turned the first page I knew I had dived head first into a sea full of mysteries, horrors and adventure. 
 There was never a second I was not with the good-hearted yet blood thirsty Hatcher or trying to recollect the memories of the rabbit with Alice. I felt these characters and I witnessed the horrors of the Walrus, the Caterpillar and the gruesome lives of those who dwell in the Old City. 
 This book was absolutely magical and it made me love Lewis Carolls original and quirky story of Alice even more. Christiana Henry took the madness in the original and made it her own and this story is surely one to be remembered. 
 If you are looking for a strong female character and an enchanting tale then don't hesitate to read this book; however if you are among the faint-hearted then certain elements in this book might not see eye to eye with you but nevertheless this book is a must read for everyone willing to dive into the rabbit hole once again.

While this wasn't my ultimate retelling, I still very much enjoyed the "wonderland" Henry had created. The worldbuilding is vague, but worked for the novel. There are no long passages that explain the entire history of the City, but the author includes enough simple backstory that the reader understands how it works. 
 Alice has the most character development, and I enjoyed seeing her go from someone who was meek and passive, to being a female character with strong opinions, and who isn't afraid to express them. 
 Usually I don't like romances in books because they're often so forced and overshadow the main plot, but this one was well done. It's realistic and takes a back seat to the action, and I liked how it intertwined with Alice's character development without defining it. 
 The plot was slightly predictable and the foreshadowing a bit obvious, but it was still interesting, My main problem was with the amnesia that Alice and Hatcher both suffer from, because it seemed like it was the only way for the author to add suspense, They remembered things too conveniently for my taste. 
 Even though it wasn't what I was hoping for, I still really liked Alice, and gave it 4/5 stars.

book_b.user_review: This just didn't work at all. It isn't a genre issue, as I LOVE fantasy, (Harry Potter is my heathen bible) and I like sci if, (Atwood and David Mitchell and some of the books mentioned in this book) and I like the whole British boarding school setting, so I really thought this book would work. sample_reviews.review_text: I wanted to like this book but couldn't get past the genealogy near the front of the book. Should is a terrible curse, particularly when applied to fiction. I should have adored this book. It seems right in my wheelhouse, and certainly gives lip-service to a great many novels I've read and enjoyed (and even more that I've heard of but never gotten around to!). 
 Perhaps I come to Among Others too late in my life, having lost my capacity for belief, as reading it I couldn't help but see all the magical realism bandied about by the protagonist as nothing more than a young girl's attempt to cope with the tragedy of her life. But then, that could be because Walton doesn't really bother building much of a world for me to believe in, but rather relies heavily on references to other people's worlds and vague allusions to things that happen off-stage. 
 In short, Among Others has a marvelous, unforgettable voice...which should have been used to tell a story. Pity all we're given instead is a collection of pretty words.

I don't understand why this book is receiving so much praise lately in the media. The only thing I felt when I finished this book today was cheated, cheated out of the time I spent reading it. I could have spent that time reading a book where things actually happened, where characters were developed other than just the main character. The book was boring and there was a whisper of a plot that pretty much disappeared. The author seemed to hint that there would be a climatic reunion between Morwenna and her mother but even that piece of the puzzle fell flat.

I enjoyed the voice of the main character and her experiences as she recovers from the fight with her mother and the death of her twin and comes to terms with the nature of the magic in her world. In some ways the book was almost a catalogue of science fiction reading, which I found got a bit tedious after a while: probably because I hadn't read most of the SF myself. I imagine that if I'd known more about those books, I would have got a lot more out of this one.

[I also reviewed this title on my blog: Ishari's Bookshelf] 
 I was oh so looking forward to this read. Maybe I had too many expectations? 
 I managed to get through about half of it before I stopped and looked up some reviews to see if I was missing something. Maybe that's cheating? I don't know, but I am glad I checked the reviews. It seems like you either love this book for its homage to classic science fiction and the good ol' interlibrary loan days at the library before e-readers came onto the scene...OR...you found this book to be slow and rambling without a substantial over-arching plot. I definitely fall into the latter group. 
 I found myself getting frustrated with Morwenna and her constant reviews and discussions on various Science Fiction books she had read. I like to think I have read several of the "classic" SF stories (not all of which I have gotten around to put up on my Goodreads), but I haven't read as many as Morwenna read...so I didn't get all the references she made and the questions she asked about them. It just got to be tedious. 
 I also found myself wanting Walton to explore the fantastical elements a little bit more. I understand that a major "charm" of this story is the fact that it is so "normal" - it definitely reads like a boring journal from any early to mid-teenage girl...but, I wanted to know more about the fantastical, the fairies, the witch[es], etc. There was too much allusion for my tastes, I think. 
 I guess my main issue is that I had set up in my mind what the story would be like...and then it turned out to be way more mundane than I would ever have imagined. 
 I hate to say it...but this one will earn a spot on my Lemmed It shelf.

In fact, one one point after giving a lengthy run-down of one side of her family tree, she even tells the reader that we don't need to remember all of that! Then why tell us??

So... this book. It is what it is.

Also, I only understood about 1/5 of the book references, which leads me to believe I'm not really the target audience of this book. It took me ages to plow through, and I don't really feel as if very much happened.

I would get interested in something Mor was doing and then it would be dropped or not evolve into anything. I understand that it was about her moving on beyond her sister's death and learning to grow up, but I found the ending bland and not fulfilling. 
 The whole book just didn't speak to me, despite the fact that I love books and agree with the main character about coffee :) 
 I think there are a lot of people who would love this book, but I suppose I just couldn't relate to it enough.

So far, I think this one is at the top of my list for the Hugos. It feels very familiar and true; finding your place is hard and it's worth so, so much when you do.

I loved this book!!! This is the kind of modern fantasy story that deserves to be read in high schools and talked about for years to come. It's also a great primer for anyone looking to get into fantasy and science fiction. Just write down all the books that are mentioned in its pages and dive in.

This was not a fantasy book. It was about a delusional teenage girl who's sister was killed and she was maimed in a car accident. The whole story is told via diary/journal entries. Most of it is mundane but she is constantly talking about her favorite science fiction and fantasy books and occasionally she mentions seeing a fairy. This girl needs some medical intervention. 
 Before anyone says 'but wait, she's not delusional. Her boyfriend saw the fairies also'. All I can say to that is that you don't know for sure that's what he saw. This is not a third-person narration. It's told first person via a journal. She can think he saw the fairy but in reality he could have seen a bunny rabbit. There may not have even been a boyfriend. She could be sitting in a rubber room and this story is her crazy way of passing the days. 
 I know I'm practically alone on this one, and I was almost willing to think I was reading it wrong, but I decided that thought was just the narrator's crazy rubbing off on me. I think the whole thing was bullshit.

The magic in this book is the nostalgia from the familiar, for me it was in Mor's love for books and how she used them for comfort, friendship, and so on. Mor also went to boarding school, and i recognised and empathised with her experience of it since i'd been to boarding schools from the time i was 6-18 years old, i was also in a girls' only boarding school for my O'level education. Mor's write up of her time there was quite an accurate portrayal of my own time too. Her write up on family, sexual development and so forth was complicated and i appreciated it. I don't know if we were supposed to find her father a sympathetic character but i couldn't move from her early assessment of him as a horrible, horrible parent especially that day when he got drunk. So yes, he did somethings like give her pocket money, discuss books with her etc but it doesn't negate the fact that he was a creepy perv. Obviously, my opinion on the character doesn't really matter since we are reading Mor's diary and how her perceptions of those around her develops. Anyway, this was a good book to read and just settle into that melancholic nostalgia and it did that quite well.

Review posted at That Cozy Book Book 
 What a beautiful book! I don't regret reading Among Others at the end of July, BUT this book has made me a firm believer that seasonal reading is a legitimate thing. Meaning, if there was ever a book to read in late autumn it would be this one. I would have enjoyed the overall reading experience so much more if it was cooler outside. The book is warm and just gives off that kind of ultimate cozy reading feeling. 
 I adored Mori. She is sweet but not naive; inquisitive but not disrespectful; knowledgeable but still curious. And, wait for it...she is basically the biggest bibliophile (namely science fiction books) of all time. The story is told through her diary entries, and in nearly every entry she mentions a book, whether it's The Hobbit, Dune, or The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. 
 Not only does Mori mention books, but she really ponders the motivations of characters and how they are applicable to her own reality. She really finds herself within the pages of various novels, and I thought the way she wrote about that was amazing and even powerful in some of her entries. 
 In many ways, this is a coming of age story, which I thought was beautifully told and interwoven The magical elements of the story are there, but they are subtle. 
 The synopsis on the back of the book led me to believe that this was about to be a dramatic and fast-paced fantasy story of great magnitude. That was simply not the case. While Among Others is admittedly very good, it a quiet story. The magic is there and, yes, even fairies exist, but as I mentioned above it is all very subtle. 
 Due to the high expectations I had going into this book, it took me a REALLY long time to get into the groove of the story. I found myself becoming bored and frustrated, wondering when the "big magic" would happen or when the story would pick up. When I finally sat back and relaxed and appreciated Among Others for what it was, it became that much more enjoyable. If you read this book (and you should) I highly recommend that you don't psych yourself up for an epic fantasy tale. 
 I really loved Among Others, I'm just upset with myself that it took me over halfway through the book for that to happen. I recommend this book to everyone who loves a great, peaceful story that they can curl up with by the fireplace during those chilly months. I plan on reading it again soon, next time with a newfound admiration.

Much of this story is inferred, which was irritating at times - I kept coming back to this one. Enjoyed the discussion of older SF. Not sure why it was set in the late seventies - to limit the books available? Recommended by the Book-a-Day calendar.

I liked the characters and the setting. I liked the story. What I didn't like was the way that things dragged on and on in diary format, with little irrelevant details 3/4 of the time. I wanted to like this much more than I did. Very disappointing.
This book was ok. Really hard to follow with all of the SF titles and authors.
Possibly one of the oddest books I've read. I liked it, but not as much as I wanted to.

To me, this book is the epitome of the unreliable narrator. Maybe that should make me like it more. In any case, on a visceral level, I didn't deeply enjoy this book. Possible reasons: 
 1. I don't know enough about science fiction to appreciate the references and possibly grasp some symbolism there. 
 2. The teenage voice was very realistic, which is a wonderful skill, but not necessarily always enjoyable ;] 
 3. Plot???? 
 4. I didn't really find Mor to be very likable (her mother may have a point, Mor seems a tad manipulative and self-interested), or Wim for that matter. Are we supposed to like a boy who calls every girlfriend he's had an "idiot" or a "moron"? No thank you.

Maybe I didn't get it, but I just did not enjoy this book. It was really long but nothing actually happened. It was wordy and she was whiney. It took me ages to read because I really didn't want to. 
 The only defining grace was the depiction of what magic would be like in the real world.

Eu tinha dado duas estrelas pra esse livro, mas reduzi pra uma estrela depois de ver essa resenha no canal Katie Love to Read: https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=6eob8v3... 
 A personagem principal desse livro e uma garota de 15 anos chamada Morwenna. Ela fala com fadas e a mae dela e uma bruxa ma. Ao tentar impedi-la de fazer o mal, a irma gemea da Morwenna morre e ela acaba tendo que viver com o pai. 
 Mais ou menos 85% do livro e Morwenna reclamando da escola e falando dos livros de ficcao cientifica que ela leu. Mas so isso? Basicamente sim. 
 Uma coisa que me incomodou e que a voz da Morwenna e muito infantil. A cada vez que aparecia no livro alguma mencao ao fato de ela ter quinze anos, eu pensava "eita, e verdade, ela tem quinze!", porque o comportamento dela se assemelha muito mais a de uma pre adolescente. 
 Nao ha desenvolvimento dos personagens, nem da Morwenna nem em relacao a morte da irma nem em relacao a mae dela. Os outros personagens estao ali pra Morwenna nao ficar falando dos livros que ela leu o tempo todo. Por isso, os personagens sao superficiais e estereotipados, como a Deirdre, que so serve de escada pra Morwenna se sentir melhor consigo mesma, especialmente, porque a Morwenna usa uma bengala como auxilio pra se locomover e ela se refere a si mesma como "aleijada" ao longo de todo o livro. 
 Enfim, nao recomendo esse livro, a nao ser que voce queira um passeio pela ficcao cientifica dos anos sessenta e setenta atraves dos olhos de uma garota chata de doze anos.

This book is very hard to describe. The best comparison I have come up with is that it is somewhat like the movie Pan's Labyrinth, in that while the book seems to contain magical elements it is also possible that these elements are imagined by the main character. Incidentally, the book contains a fantastic reading list of science fiction books up to the early 1980s.

This was a pleasant surprise. If you like books, especially if you are a fan of classic science fiction and fantasy, there's enough reading suggestions and literary discourse woven into this text to keep even the most dour reader smiling. While this book is engaging, it possesses the property to cause the reader to speculate on things outside of the narrative without fully expelling the reader from the story. Now that I am done, I find myself rather introspective. I will certainly be rereading this later on. This was my first introduction to Walton's writing and I am excited to read more.

I'd heard mixed reviews going in, but I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this book. This is contemporary speculative done in a way I especially enjoy, namely: it's not a "magical" person following "rules of magic", but instead, every element of the fantastical could have another plausible explanation. In this case, every supernatural happening, and many key pedestrian happenings, could be due to an unreliable / unstable narrator. Since the viewpoint is a tight focus within this character's head, scope is proportionately widened for how everyone else around the protagonist might be perceiving the same events. 
 Recommended, but be warned that this has a significant amount of content, of the type sometimes found in other coming-of-age stories.
Another boring coming of age story. I don't need to read this when I LIVED it.

Probably 4.5. 
 I picked this up after it won the Hugo Award AND the Nebula Award this year and despite it being, ostensibly, about "fairies." I got caught up in the net of the prose immediately and had trouble putting it down. 
 At its core it is a coming-of-age story of a teen girl (Wales/England, 1980) who is obsessed with science fiction, but the narrative is enveloped in a mist of magic. There's underlying drama involving her insane/witch mother and those fairy-type creatures, but it's expertly subtle with details revealed piecemeal throughout. There is a perfunctory dramatic showdown at the end, but it is almost secondary to the plot at that point. 
 Besides, how could I not love a book dedicated to, "..all the libraries in the world, and the librarians who sit there day after day lending books to people."

(actual rating: 1.5) 
 In a nutshell: A young girl who is left crippled by an encounter with her mother, who dabbled in dark magic, grieves the loss of her sister as she attempts to lead a normal life of a teenager yet continues to play with magic herself and talks to fairies. 
 Recommendation: As someone who had high hopes for this book, I do not recommend it as I was sorely disappointed by its slow pace and anti-climactic nature. 
 A friend recommended this book a while ago and I had high hopes for it because it sounded so good. I should really take my own advice and stay away from reading YA because all it does is disappoint me... and I've said this so many times that it's not funny. Maybe someday I'll learn. I have yet to find a YA book I enjoy with a decent writing style, story line, and characters I like. For now, I'll sit here, hanging my head in shame and say I did it to myself again. 
 "It doesn't matter. I have books, new books, and I can bear anything as long as there are books." 
 Morwenna Phelps is sent to an expensive boarding school by her father and his three sisters, who were never involved in her life or well-being from the get-go. Most would see her as a normal teenage girl aside from the fact that she is crippled. But what they don't know is that she became crippled after an altercation with her mother, a witch, that also resulted in the death of her twin sister. Mori misses the industrial ruins by her old home where she talked to the fairies, because the fairies around her new "home' will not respond to her. Her only solace seems to be in fantasy and science fiction books. Overcome by loneliness, Mori dabbles in magic herself to make some friends, but worries that her use of magic will draw her dangerous and erratic mother to her once again... 
 First off, this book is written as a series of diary entries. That doesn't always work. this was the case with this book. It just didn't work for me. If the book were written in third person perspective and in a series of chapters I would at least feel better about that. But as a series of diary entries it just didn't do it for me. However, the main character talks about science fiction books A LOT so maybe that stuff is better to write about in first person. 
 But why did the author include all this stuff about how much the character loves science fiction? Honestly it doesn't add anything to the story at all aside from the idea that she believes Tolkien could see fairies too. 
 Anyway, the plot is very slow moving. I was told this book was amazing and that the whole idea of the main character seeing and talking to fairies was a much bigger part of the plot then it actually was. But she jut talks about her love of books and the fact that her leg is sore from what happened with her mother a lot. And the climax of the book (sorry for the spoiler alert) was actually very anti-climactic and I was bored. This book bored me and I just wanted it to be over. 
 I would have liked to have read more about the relationship Mori had with her sister or more about how her mother was crazy. Because most of the book you're waiting for the mother to show up because she is basically the villein of the story; it would have made the book more interesting. The parts about fairies and magic which is basically what the book is about are written in such a vague way that it is lost on the reader or they just aren't interesting. And unless you've read some of the books she talks about you just wouldn't understand what she's talking about. 
 It's such a shame because I wanted to like this book; the premise seemed so interesting. But, what can you do? Just keep reading I guess!

This was an odd one for me. I wanted to like it, and I think, for the most part I did, but I'm not comfortable saying that I loved it. 
 First off, it's definitely marketed as a book for adults, but, the main character is a teen, and I can definitely see lots of teens picking this one up and enjoying it. So maybe part of my discomfort with the lines drawn in the sand the determine what is YA and what isn't. Which really doesn't have much to do with this book at all. Ah, well. 
 This book definitely nails that feeling that you get when you're 15 or 12 or 24 or whenever and you realize that there are other people in the world who are just as passionate about reading and talking about the books you love as you are. Just the giddiness of getting book recommendations and discussing plot and themes and discovering conventions or magazines or websites that discuss the things you love so much! I'm sure there are people out there in the world who never experience this, but, if you have, this book will bring it all rushing back. 
 The fantasy, elf-ish portion of the book was very Turn of the Screw for me. I wasn't sure until quite far into the book, whether Mor was imagining the elves in place of a much darker truth. I kept wondering if her mother was crazy, or if she were simply a murderer, or if Mor was indeed the disturbed one who had created the elves and magic as a coping mechanism. It was only when she met Wim that I began to believe that the elves were really a part of her world. That feeling never went away, though, which left me with an odd sense of discomfort and unease. It is as if I read the entire novel in anticipation of a reveal that never happened.

There's something peculiar about reading a book where all the "action" happened prior to the story being told. According to Morwenna, there was a battle where she and her twin sister Morganna thwarted their mother's attempts to gain power through magic; the sister died, Mori was crippled. But we don't see any of that. We just get a teenage girl's reading diary, and little allusions to the past. I would perhaps have liked to read the other story. Also, perhaps, I would feel differently if I had read the many, many books she mentions; having read nearly none of them, they do not do any work for me in the book - they don't help with characterization or setting a scene. I wonder if this won the Hugo and Nebula Awards merely because it is so fawningly referential to the history of sci-fi books? 
 And, then, there were one-off phrases that alluded to ideas and happenings that I really wanted to know more about. Like this: 
 I couldn't, of course, tell him about those awful days after Mor was killed, the bruise on the side of her face, the days when she was in a coma, the time when my mother turned off the machine, and then afterwards when I started to use her name and how nobody challenged me, though I'm sure Auntie Teg knew, and probably Grampar too. We might have been identical, but we were different people after all. (p. 256) 
 There are a few scattered musings about how she remembers her sister being part of her, but that of course they were separate people who would have lived separate lives and grown differently, but I think it's really interesting that Morwenna took her sisters name. How does that change the magic that she does? How does it change or enhance her sense of identity? (Oh hey, book club discussion question) 
 On a totally different note, at one point it's written: "On the other hand, is this a complete and candid memoir or just a lot of angsty wittering?" (p. 199). And honestly - which is it? Which is it supposed to be? I suppose which you think it is determines how much you like the book...

A love letter to librarians! How could I not give it five stars? 
 It's hard to know what to say without including spoilers. I was concerned all the way through about how the author would end it but I think it was very empowering to Mori. 
 I probably would have enjoyed it even more if I had read more of the books she mentions but I am not much of a SF reader. 
 Favorite quote: "I can read them again and again. I can read them again and again on trains, all my life, and every time I do I'll remember today and it will connect up." I'm not much of a re-reader but I always carefully choose books to read when traveling so the traveling (and the reading) is an important part of the trip. I can often remember what I was reading on which trips years later.

i have seen the previous reviews on this book and i'm not sure what i missed but i do not suggest this book. i couldnt even finish it and that is a rarity, even when it's a boring book i still usually hang in til the end. but i just couldnt on this one. i got halfway through and all i really remember is the names of a ton of old books that this girl has read. i found the story to be very blah.

The best part of the book was so nostalgic -- the idea of combing bookstores and finding The Book! The Amazing Fantasy or SciFi book that you've never heard of before, but it's by your favorite author and it is just so perfect! Finding The Book in bookstores and on my friends' book cases was a huge part of my adolescent years. It makes me kind of want to earmark the authors that Walton name checks that I've never read: (Zelazny, Delany, Tiptree embarrassingly enough) and never Amazon or Google them and only hunt down their books in used bookstores to recreate the feeling. But I know that truly that feeling is a little eradicated, because even if I play by the rules, I know that they're arbitrary and in real life I can get whatever book I want whenever I want, which is great, except that it ruins the mystique. 
 I also liked that "is it real or isn't it?" feel of the book. Reading as a teenager, I never would have questioned that the subtle magic in the book was indeed the highest reality. But I love Walton's depiction of that subtle magic, which as an adult, you can't help but second guess: "maybe Mor is just subconsciously coming up with a narrative to explain why bad thing X happened." I love that the book works on both levels and that it forces you to consider both -- it's such a great way to depict magic. 
 So what didn't I like? Well, I think my expectations were set too high by Jon and Beka, who both said this book was the most amazing thing in the history of books. Also, while reading the book I had an overwhelming, terribly distracting sense of how much I would have loved this book if I had read it back when I was 18. My 18 year old self would have promptly declared it her favorite book in the history of books, too, but since I'm no longer her, I felt almost guilty reading it. 
 Ultimately, I just felt like I didn't "get it." So, there's this girl, and some bad magic happened in her past, and now she goes to a boarding school, where she's a little social isolated, but then she joins a book club and along the way she buys a lot of books and sees a lot of faeries, and that's all well and good, but when is the plot going to begin? Oh, the book is over, so I guess there just isn't a plot? And I can handle a lack of a plot if the character growth and development is well done, but after awhile I got bored of reading about Mor read and go to bookstores, and I would rather be reading and going to bookstores myself.

Jo Walton's Among Others, set in late 1970s Wales, is the story of Morwenna (Mori for short), a fourteen year-old girl with the ability to see fairies and perform magic. She recently lost her twin sister in a fight they were both involved in to save themselves, and possibly the world, from their insane mother. Having run away from home after this, she eventually finds her way to her biological father's house, where he, along with his three sisters, sends her away to boarding school for reasons that she doesn't quite understand. 
 While there, she does her best to cope with day-to-day life, finding solace in science-fiction books but still feeling pangs of loneliness. In her desperation she does a bit of magic, creating a karass to bring her friends. It's successful and she finds some of happiness in the local science-fiction book club and with another few outcasts at her school. Despite this, however, she's not able to completely push aside the troubling thoughts of her past and the consequences it may have on her future. 
 A magic system that makes you think 
 In Among Others, the concept of magic is approached in an innovative way not seen before. When magic is performed, it doesn't mean that something is created out of nothing as seen in most novels. Magic is a means to alter the past in a way that suits your wishes. For example, had Mori never performed the magic to give herself friends, the book club might never have existed. The people who work at the library might not have existed to create the book club. The people she befriends at school might never have been born. Essentially, because Mori did that bit of magic, there's the possibility that she created all of those things herself to suit her needs. 
 This is an obviously an incredibly deep way of thinking, and it takes you awhile to wrap your head around what it means and all of the possibilities and consequences that sprout from it. Mori has to constantly worry about whether or not her seemingly meaningless actions are the product of someone else's magic in the future, or whether or not her very existence is the product of someone else's magic. It is truly a daunting thought, and one that I'll be pondering for quite some time. 
 A unique style of writing 
 This story is told through Mori's diary entries, and it does seem like the diary of a fourteen-year-old girl, even though she has the ability to see fairies and do magic. Mori has to deal with things that every fourteen-year-old has to deal with, and I'm glad that the fantasy aspects of the novel didn't detract from that. There were quite a few moments when I felt bogged down with information--a few pages of family ancestry that play no real part in the novel come to mind--and it was difficult for me to bring myself to keep reading at times, but in the end I'm glad that I did, because this is a very rewarding read. 
 Jo Walton has an ability to completely capture your mind and entrench you in her novels. There's a whimsical melancholy in Among Others that fully engrossed me in the novel and, at the same time, made me want to set it aside so I could think about the concepts that it shows me with every page. I have never encountered a novel like this. 
 A stale start 
 Early in the novel, before I adapted to the unique writing style, I found myself bored. Mori is at school--and that's basically all that happens. She has day-to-day problems that every fourteen year-old girl has in school, as I mentioned earlier, and sometimes that's just not very interesting to read about--even if she does have some supernatural tendencies. I'm sure that upon a re-read I won't even notice these things since I'll be fully engrossed and used to the writing style, but upon my first read it was difficult to adapt to. 
 A lot of SF/F references 
 There are hundreds of science-fiction and fantasy novels referenced in this novel as Mori reads them, and there is absolutely no way that you could have possibly read all of them unless you're the most hardcore of speculative fiction readers. This didn't necessarily detract from the novel, because Mori talked more about what the books meant to her than what the books are actually about, but sometimes I felt a little lost, having read only a few of the titles mentioned. It's not necessarily a fault, but it's something for me to mention. 
 Why should you read this book? 
 Not only is Among Others one of the most deep and thoughtful novels I've ever read, it was crafted in such a beautiful way that I will be thinking about it for a very long time. There are going to be so many re-reads of this book that I will probably have to buy another copy, simply because it makes me think. This is really one of the most provocative novels of our time, and there is absolutely no reason why you shouldn't read it.

Full review on my podcast, SFBRP episode #230.
Obviously, it's just me, as almost everyone loved this. But I didn't empathize with the characters and found the story dragged.

Morwenna keeps a diary as she is at a boarding school. 
 This book is so baffling to me. It was written in diary-style, with most days being absolutely dreadfully boring. All you know at the beginning is that Mor's sister has died, her mother is a witch (literally), and her father is sending her to this school. The diary entries would talk about school and her grades, and all the sci-fi books she was reading. Then she'd have an entry about her going out to talk to fairies or about receiving letters from her mother, who is trying to destroy her. Why the fairies? Why the mother trying to kill her? Why did her sister die? Why why why? Nothing was answered, and I feel cheated by it. I'd get enticed by one diary entry out of every five or six, and then it would go right back to being boring.

I kept waiting for something more to happen. I like Morwenna as a narrator, and even agreed with her in many ways, but this was just too much like a diary for me. I did not think the ending was satisfying. I still have a lot of questions about what exactly happened with the twins and their mother. No spoilers here, I just never felt like I had a concrete grasp on it. Maybe that's the point, maybe it's to put me in her shoes. I think the reason this was recommended to me so much is because of all the references. It's almost like a big inside joke for science fiction and fantasy fans. We can giggle and go "I get it!" and it makes us feel good, but what about the plot? There's only so much reading I am willing to do about a person sitting in a library/bedroom/cafe reading. I am going to seek out more of the books mentioned in the novel. So much for my foray into first-person.

This book looked so sweet and fun to read. For me it was painful. I kept hoping as I got more into it that I would find the appeal. I literally feel asleep right at the end. Nothing to grab my attention. Wouldn't recommend it to anyone.

This book was so strange. I don't even know what to say about it, except that it took me right back to my childhood, when you couldn't get to the library enough. When the only way to find out about other books was to look in the inside cover where they were all listed. Where fandom was like a secret network that unlike this main character, I was never lucky enough to find. Where like the main character says, you spent a lot of time pulling a book up over your head like a blanket to hide and shelter under.

I guess I didn't get this book? It was...just a list and summary of classic scifi published before 1980. With rather lame characters and a poorly developed/indecisive fantasy-ish background "plot." I can find top scifi lists online. And read about female coming of age set within the context of finding the balance between fantasy and reality in Tell the Wolves I'm Home, a novel that creates characters that feel real and doesn't rely on a male/romantic love catalyst for change and development in a female lead.

This book was a love-song to classic sci-fi authors, and I didn't get a lot of the references, but the passion for reading and the love of the world of books came through loud and clear. I did some internal sighing at the beginning as the author introduced magic and faeries--it's been done so many times, and so badly at this point-- but I was delighted by how that aspect of the book unfolded. The author found something new and meaningful about magic's place in the world, and how it can shape a life.

This is an unusual book. What I loved about it was the description of magic as using what is already there. It made magic very real. I also loved that the fairy creatures lived among ruins. I think ruins are haunted, for real. Just visit the Upper Peninsula, the part with the deserted copper mines. I love Celtic mythology. I appreciated the science fiction bibliography the author provided as part of the plot, and I have added a few books to my to read list. I always appreciate a coming of age story as well. This tale of a teen aged Welsh girl sent to boarding school in England, getting to know her estranged father, and falling in love for the first time all following the death of her twin sister qualifies as a decent coming of age story. The flaws here were sins of omission. The ending seemed rushed and out of nowhere. Several of the very interesting minor characters, especially the Jewish grandfather and the English aunts needed further development. Overall, this novel had an unfinished feeling.
I'm going to sound superficial, but this book didn't work for me at all. I had issues with the format- written as journal entries, super annoying. Plus Mo wasn't likable. The book just fell flat.

reference_books.title: The Shadow of the Wind (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books,  #1)
reference_books.review_text: This book was recommended by a couple of friends and now I can add my recommendation too. Young Daniel reads a book by Julian Carax and goes looking for more, only to find that someone is systematically destroying all the copies of Carax's books. So begins the mystery and the intertwined lives of Daniels his friends, enemies, family and loves. It story mainly covers the years 1945 to 1956. Lots of side stories and surprising twists. To top it off the imagery of the writing is wonderful too. Great read!

reference_books.title: Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, #1)
reference_books.review_text: DNF - Gave up after 150 pages. Boring characters! The zombies were the best part of the book. Read it for a book group who's theme was humor. It wasn't funny.

reference_books.title: Playing for Pizza
reference_books.review_text: If you are a Grisham fan looking for a mystery, this is not it. A fun book about an ex-NFL player playing football in italy. I was there last October and knew some of the places in the book - great fun

reference_books.title: The Professor and the Madman: A Tale of Murder, Insanity and the Making of the Oxford English Dictionary
reference_books.review_text: A very interesting book about the fellow who was compiling the Oxford English Dictionary and the murderer who made thousands of contributions to it.

reference_books.title: Lamb: The Gospel According to Biff, Christ's Childhood Pal
reference_books.review_text: One of Moore's best books. A hilarious and irreverent story of Christ's adventures in the years missing from the bible.

reference_books.title: The Handmaid's Tale
reference_books.review_text: A rather unusual book about a future dystopian society where young ladies are held captive to have babies for women who can't. Interesting that the U.S. government was taken over by the army/militia who blamed the assassination of the president and congressmen on Islamic fanatics (the book was written in 1986). The book begins and ends in the middle of a larger story so if you like neatly wrapped up stories this might not be for you. Excellent writing, what one expects from Atwood.

reference_books.title: The Underground Railroad

book_a.user_review: An incredibly interesting book about an early 20th century explorer who was obsessed with the Amazon. He went on one too many trips which lead to multiple groups who went looking for him and his party. Warning: don't read it if you don't like bugs!

sample_reviews.review_text: The premise is fascinating, the research extensive and the picture that Grann draws of the trials and travails of exploration in the heyday of the Royal Geographic Society were excruciatingly graphic at times. This book makes you thankful that you live in the age of modern medicine and advanced aeronautical mapping tech. My problem with the book is in its fizzled ending. He finds what he was looking for and wraps it up within a few short pages. It was such a let down and much less than what Fawcett deserved. If you're going to make me suffer through page after page of maggots eating explorers legs and malarial fever dreams, I want more than 7 pages of "huh, he was right, there WAS a civilization there." Honestly, I had to double check to make sure that I wasn't missing the last 100 pages, but since I was e-reading this, it wasn't very likely. Good effort, but the author seems like he got tired by the end. Of course, if I was tramping through the Amazon, I would be as well.

When it comes to the particulars of Fawcett's expedition, David Grann is adequate. 
 When it comes to the particulars of Fawcett's civilization, David Grann is exceptionally ignorant. 
 Some men promote their own snobberies. They will snap up a chance to prove they are exceptionally well-read, or know every stroke of a pre-Raphaelite painting. 
 Other, lesser, men are obsessed with promoting their own ignorance. 
 David Grann knows nothing about the Victorian era. This, of course, does not stop him from editorializing about the Victorian era. 
 Women wear nothing except "corsets pulled so tight that they could barely breathe" (43) Nevermind that the trend of choking yourself was 50 years old, and even in its heyday it was uncommon. Victorian women were *quite* smart enough to leave room to breathe. In 1884, Dr. Jaeger invented a non-constricting corset. Prior to that time, from the 1860s onward, women were so well alerted to the dangers of a tight corset that they wore them loose. No woman in 1888 would have worn her corset so tight. (see Mel Davies, 'Corsets and Conception: Fashion and Demographic Trends in the Nineteenth Century' in Comparative Studies in Society and History, Vol. 24, No. 4 (Oct., 1982), pp. 611-64}). Grann cannot research even the most basic aspect of Victorian clothing. 
 Perry Fawcett would be surprised to learn that sexual "desires...terrified him" (44) Nothing in his journals or letters support this; unsurprisingly, this statement is uncited. It's quite stunning that a man terrified of sex had a number of children, isn't it? 
 Grann does not stop there. He roars against Victorian sexuality. 
 "Victorian society, fearful that industrialization was eroding Christian values, was obsessed with mastery over bodily instincts. There were crusades against. . .'masturbatory disease' and abstinence pamphlets disseminated in the countryside instructing mothers to 'keep a watchful eye on the hayfields.' Doctors recommended 'spiked penile rings' to restain uncontrolled urges" (40) 
 Bull. Balderdash. Bunk. 
 None of that is cited, by the way, for the excellent reason that it is either stolen from American insanities or, perhaps worse for Grann's ignorance, ramblings from the insane edges of society. 
 To apply penile rings and the 'masturbatory disease' to Victorian English society at large is like taking a very deep breath and, with a perfectly straight face, insisting that the Westboro Baptist "Church" is a perfect representation of what all Ukrainians believe. Attempting to stop masturbation was an American concern in the 1860s (because, goodness knows, we didn't have anything more important to worry about). The English regularly mocked Americans for their insane heights of prudery (the story about a wife fainting because her piano's legs were bare? That began as a joke about Americans). Culture was not universally monotonous, as Grann seems to believe: I wonder if he thinks Victorian Tibetans rushed to be-skirt their table legs as well. 
 As Fawcett was profoundly British, and certainly not American, none of this at all concerns him or his world. 
 If you want a good look into how happy Victorians were to have sex, please see Queen Victoria's journal (even in its expurgated state, which cuts out some *very* sultry passages), Heather J. Creaton's Victorian Diaries, Judith Flander's excellent histories, and Mayhew's London Labour and the London Poor (which was written and circulated in 1840s--yet, even in that stuffier time, showed how much everyone loved sex), or any of the dozens of best-selling porn novels. 
 Why do we perceive the British Victorians as prudes? First, because Americans are shamefaced little buggers over how insane *they* were during the same period; second, because the Free Love worldview is appalled by people who will have wild sex--but only have that wild sex inside the marriage covenant. Attack it all you like, but respect that they believed it. Do not do as Grann does. 
 David Gram's The Lost City of Z: your ignorance is showing. You research is so poor on the topic of society that, frankly, I refuse to trust this book on any of the particulars of Fawcett's journey. 
 An absolute waste of paper, better left unread, unsold, and unwritten.

The author himself is endearing and definitely did his research. I'm just not convinced there needed to be a book about this. The story of Fawcett's obsession is without a doubt interesting but could have been summed up in a magazine in one of those long features. With not enough material the writing got somewhat repetitive: same ideas but different words. I'll give Grann credit to say that he did a good job of pulling it together in the end.
Love David Grann and I'll read pretty much anything he publishes in *The New Yorker.* This felt to me, though, like a great essay that got stretched to book length. Such a shame.

A grand mystery reaching back centuries. A sensational disappearance that made headlines around the world. A quest for truth that leads to death, madness or disappearance for those who seek to solve it. The Lost City of Z is a blockbuster adventure narrative about what lies beneath the impenetrable jungle canopy of the Amazon. 
 After stumbling upon a hidden trove of diaries, New Yorker writer David Grann set out to solve "the greatest exploration mystery of the 20th century": What happened to the British explorer Percy Fawcett & his quest for the Lost City of Z? 
 I will answer that last question quite simply - no one knows. After some 350 pages, this book answers nothing. But, that wasn't the worst part of the book (although it was extremely annoying)... 
 The worst part was just how long it took to find that out. The first half of the book was a mish-mish of history, biography...filled with names and places that are very hard (for me) to keep track of. There didn't seem to be any kind of flow in the narrative...it jumped from one person to another, one place to another, without really going anywhere. 
 And, to top it off...the research must have been meticulous. The author had to have spent an eternity getting all this information together - it is Class-A in that regard. And that is what got this book 2 stars. 
 Paul 
 ARH

This book is as close to non-fiction perfection as I have seen in a long time! Though the story is rather simple, Grann's writing makes the events come alive better than any novel I have read in the recent past. Basically, the tale is about the 1920s explorer Percy Fawcett who has discovered new lands across South America in a time far before satellites, GPSs, and even radio. Fawcett is attracted to dangerous adventures especially those that take place in the Amazon. For years, he had studied the Amazon and determined that there was a lost city inside the tropics that he called "Z". Others may be familiar with this city as El Dorado. For decades, Fawcett had explored in a similar area but was never able to find "Z". Finally, in 1925 (as a man in his middle ages), he decides to find the City of Z or die trying. Along with him, he brings his son and his son's best friend. Without spoiling anything in the book, Grann announces this in his first chapter, Fawcett dies on this expedition. Yet, he does not go forgotten! For decades later, even into 2005, people went searching for Fawcett and the city. However, the majority of these explorers also never returned. After researching Fawcett and his personal life, Grann becomes infected with the "Fawcett bug" as he calls it and decides that he too must follow in Fawcett's footsteps and try to discover the city in Fawcett's honor. 
 Though this seems like a nonfiction thriller, it is so much more. Grann is able to place Fawcett in with his contemporaries and show the reader how Fawcett's obsession with the region made him a better explored than even the man on Shakleton's expedition. Though Fawcett is not an entirely likable guy, Grann makes the reader sympathize with his neurosis and find compassion for the man who basically forced his family into poverty in order to feed his adrenaline rush (of course Fawcett was more complex than that). 
 www.iamliteraryaddicted.blogspot.com 
 What sets this piece apart from others about Fawcett is Grann's ability to give the reader in depth knowledge on contemporary times while still making the piece read like a thriller. In addition, Grann was given access to Fawcett's family members which in turn gave him access to some of Fawcett's journals and letters that have never before been shown to people outside of the FAcett family. Grann gives the reader a history of the Royal Geographic Society that is as interesting as it is informative. In addition, he brings the reader into the Amazon with just background and description that his audience feels a connection to the region in a similar way as Fawcett did. Overall, Grann is an excellent writer and this piece really shows his abilities. In addition, Fawcett is a superb subject that keeps explorers and readers coming back for more. An absolutely delight to read!

I picked this up recently at the Evanston, Illinois public library and read it as a bedtime book. 
 The narrative has two strands. One is about Percy Fawcett, the original, early 20th century explorer of the Amazon, his belief that there had once been a high civilization in the region and his disappearance while looking for it. The other is about the author and how he attempted to discern and then retrace Fawcett's final trek and ultimate fate. The two are interwoven. 
 The stuff about Fawcett is rather interesting as an adventure story, though rather weak in conveying how it was that the explorer became convinced of a lost high civilization. The stuff about the author's own visit to Amazonia is rather pathetic. Where Fawcett walked, Gann flew and drove. Where Fawcett actually made first, or nearly first, contact with autochthons, Gann watched television with them. 
 As regards the lost civilization hypothesis, Gann closes his book with the evidences that indeed such very well may have existed, very much a major thesis of the superior book on the subject, 1491. That he leaves this to the final section of his text is a nice touch, but it would have been more interesting were he to have made the idea of a lost Amazonian civilization, not Fawcett, the topic of his study at the outset.
2 Hours into a 10 hour audiobook and I am bored out of my mind...dnf

Just finished this book and it was dope! Seriously, I bought it in an airport on the way to Brazil and after the 3rd or so chapter I was sucked in just as Fawcett was to the Amazons. I was actually in the Amazons as I read part of the book so maybe that's why I liked it so but I still think anyone would love it as I did!

 Meh.

The source material is so inherently fascinating - one man's obsession with finding remains of an ancient civilization decades ago leads to his disappearance leads to the author's obsession with learning about the man and his obsession and retracing his footsteps- it all fits. I went off with City of Z explorer Percy Fawcett across the Amazon jungle over spring break. Hiram and Percy led us through "insatiable thirst, skull-splitting headaches, and uncontrollable shivering," as we were "spitting up mouthfuls of blood." We tramped through lands with tribes of natives who "captured prisoners...they either kept...forever or roasted them to devour in their banquets." Swimming in the waters of the Amazon were not only the feared piranhas, the so-called "vampire fish of Brazil," but the horrifying candiru, a creature that is known for lodging in human orifices. Some of us contracted espundia, which "destroys the flesh around the mouth, nose, and limbs, as if the person were slowly dissolving" and others found maggots growing inside our open wounds. 
 Delightful, right? 
 Somehow I have survived all these horrors though we never found the golden City of Z.

Do you like true adventure? Then this is a book for you! A non-fiction book that reads like a novel. It follows the career of British explorer Percy Fawcett who led seven exhibitions into the Amazon in the early 20th Century. His reports to the Royal Geographic Society were so thrilling that they inspired Sir Arthur Conan Doyle to write The Lost World, and even base one of the characters on Fawcett. Apparently the story is considered thrilling enough for Hollywood to put it on the screen (a movie is in the works). 
 I heard about this book on NPR's Science Friday with Ira Flatow. The author does an excellent job of alternating Fawcett's exhibition to find a theoretical ancient city with contemporary commentary on his own exhibition to find whatever happened to Fawcett. Fawcett and his companions disappeared in 1925, although there were rumors that he was still alive years afterwards. Several rescue missions also disappeared. So it's a book with a couple of mysteries, not only what happened to Fawcett, but also what evidence convinced him the City of Z actually existed. 
 One of the most enjoyable books I've read in while.

This book offers a more reader-friendly perspective to Candice Miller's The River of Doubt. Grann expertly shifts back and forth from past to present with an adventure and mystery that will leave you too wanting to travel to Dead Horse Camp yourself. The grotesque realities of the jungle could not be any more enthralling than any fiction story. Wonderful research went into this. I would recommend it to anyone. Percy Fawcett is a name I will never forget.

2.5 The parts of the book I liked were the the stories and adventures of Fawcett. What I didn't enjoy was the author's own expedition and weaving those two stories together. Although the book drew me into the topic more, I would rather have read a really good biography of Fawcett. The book seemed confused to me and fell flat, in my opinion. It could not keep me engaged towards the end.

This fascinating book delves into the mystery of intrepid "gentleman explorer" Percy Fawcett's disappearance during a 1925 expedition to search for an ancient lost city in the heart of the Amazon.
