very interesting
Bigger-than-life Indiana Jones and King Solomon's Mines and Gunga Din rolled into one -- but it's fact and NOT fiction!

The Lost City of Z is a very well-done book on the early 20th century explorer Percy Fawcett, and his mysterious disappearance in the Amazon while he and his son were on the trail of Z, another term for an ancient city of great wealth like Atlantis or El Dorado. The descriptions of what the explorers experienced on their journeys were fascinating and horrifying all at the same time, and you just have to wonder what sort of people they were to be willing to put up with such circumstances for the sake of possibly discovering new areas. 
 The book seems to kinda of fizzle out at the end, but at the same time, it closes with fascinating revelations of present-day excavations in the Amazon. Definitely worth reading if you've ever enjoyed fantasizing about such mythical cities and civilizations and the journey into the unknown.

David Grann is a long form reporter for The New York Times. 
 And very unfortunately for him it shows throughout in The Lost City of Z. A novel which attempts to simultaneously tell the tale of Henry Percy Fawcett and his quest for the titular Lost City of Z, a city of a supposed lost civilization in the Amazon akin to the fabled El Dorado. As well as all those that came after searching for Fawcett's fate. As well as Grann's own tale of research into this subject. As well as background on Fawcett to give you a sense of what he was like. 
 And this is where the reporter comes in, instead of the novelist. The book skips back and forth between times and subjects with abandon and not a whole lot of elegance, each chapter feels more like a long form news article than being part of a coherent whole. Grann can't decide between wanting to do a biography of Fawcett, and so ends up doing only half a job of that. Or if it's a fact based tale of just Fawcett's search for "Z". Which is there but only there every third chapter or so. 
 Or maybe he's doing a perspective tale, of him researching this fascinating tale of Fawcett's search, but again that's only every third chapter, which we abruptly switch away from and has no flow with the rest of the story. And the fact that flow and coherency are so bad is what makes this book dull when it's subject matter is so potentially rich. 
 Great lengths are gone to in describing the potential horrors one can encounter in the Amazon. Bloodsucking mites, tiny bees that get into your pupils, electric eels, malaria and yellow fever, giant anacondas, hostile natives. The list goes on and on, but it's all done in a dry, matter of fact nature, removed from the character and personal experience. 
 And who wouldn't want a tale of a lost civilization in the Amazon? Of then a lost expedition by a famous explorer, of people over the years going in search of this expedition and city only to be lost, taken hostage by tribes of natives, or etc.? Yet Grann doesn't SELL any of it as a personal story, even his own feels dry and somewhat uninvolved. 
 And while occasionally engaging in specific ideas and exploits, Grann's failure to put it all together into anything like a cohesive and personal story makes it feel more like a matter of fact report with ambitions of being a personally involving tale, rather than a personally involving tale in and of itself.

I found this book to be enormously interesting and enjoyable. Part mystery-thriller, part history lesson, part adventure tale, "The Lost City of Z" weaves together elements of geography, cartography, exploration, anthropology, archaeology and even more, as it tells the story of Col. Percy Fawcett's doomed and mysterious trip to the Amazon in 1925. 
 Grann builds a broad framework for understanding the significance of Fawcett's journey by providing background not only to Fawcett himself, but also to the numerous other explorations to the area that had taken place over the centuries. It was fascinating to learn about the competition that existed among these 19th and early 20th century explorers, and how their activities fit in with the developing sciences of anthropology, archaeology, and modern geography (not to mention popular culture). 
 In addition, I enjoyed learning about Fawcett himself, a truly larger-than-life character, a gifted but complex man who walked a fine balance between incredible courage and foolhardiness. His relationship with, and advocacy for, the native Indians was rare and admirable. 
 Ultimately, the author's conclusions about Fawcett's quest and the lost city itself are poignant. 
 I listened to the audiobook version of this book (unabridged) and thoroughly enjoyed it. However, I wonder if the paper copy offers maps and/or photos; I would have enjoyed that. I will look for a copy at the library to see if these are provided.
Good writing. Fascinating story. Interesting anthropological studies. Mysterious and thought-provoking.

I don't read a lot of non-fiction, but I found this story about the Amazon well written and very interesting. I felt that I learned from this book. One thing I learned is that I really don't want to visit the Amazon. Reading about it and seeing pictures of the amazing creatures that live there are quite enough for me. The weather, bugs and dangerous diseases that lurk in the dark deep forests of the Amazon scare me to death!
Interesting historical information but the ending lacked any real climax.

I don't usually read narrative non-fiction (I'm more of a how-to NF lady), but I loved this book. It started a little slow, but the action picked up and I started to be obsessed with the mystery of Z, too. Lots of fun, and totally changed the way I think about the Amazon.
I did not like this book at all. I plundered through it all because it was my Book Group's monthly selection but I would never recommend it.

I may have liked this more if I had come to it with the mentality of reading a documentary instead of expecting a "swashbuckling adventure" with images of an exciting action movie in my head. I mean, you see the sticker on the cover that says "Now a Major Motion Picture," and you open the cover and the first media reviews rave with "A thrill ride from start to finish (Washington Post)", "Vividly alive. . . . Captivating (Wall Street Journal)", "A blood-stirring reading experience (Denver Post)", and even "Unfathomably riveting. . . . Grann wildly delivers the goods (GQ)". Well, it really is not any of these. THESE reviews are more accurate: "A smart biographical page-turner (USA Today)" and "A fascinating yarn that touches on science, history, and some truly obsessive personalities (Entertainment Weekly)". 
 Having said that, I did want to finish this book rather than chuck it. I'm glad I did, because I'd never heard of the very intriguing Amazon civilization findings of Heckenberger, and I look forward to learning more about that topic. The Fawcett story is strange to me in that I can't relate to the drive for folks to keep pursuing the matter (outside of immediate family), but Grann handles it well. It's a decent read on its own. Just not an "unfathomably riveting" "thrill ride from start to finish."

Explorer Percy Fawcett made several failed attempts to find the mythological city of El Dorado, rumored to be nestled in the Brazilian Amazon. His first exploration was in the early 1900's. His last was in 1925, from which he never returned. Grann meticulously researched Fawcett's life and travels and became so obsessed with Fawcett that he set out to retrace Fawcett's steps. 
 The Amazon may sound exotic and magical, but this book completely dispels those tourist-enticing fallacies. It is oppressively hot and humid. There are insects that do horrible things like burrowing into skin to leave their eggs. There are giant snakes that strangle and piranhas that will eat you alive. There are indigenous tribes that have still not been documented. They were not known to be friendly to white explorers, with good reason. Fawcett found some of them practiced cannibalism. However, Fawcett was vocal in his views of protecting indigenous peoples rather than enculturating or killing them. This was quite bold and progressive for the time. 
 This book isn't just a straightforward journey. It's a look at the life of a man who was obsessed with finding something. The work is heavily peppered with bits about who Fawcett was as a person, how he lived his life, and his family. There is mention of his contemporaries who were better financed and less polite with the tribes of the Amazon. Fawcett, who struggled financially, became somewhat of a star during his last expedition. Grann throws in smaller amounts about himself and how researching and following Percy Fawcett changed his life. 
 This book is enjoyable. I feel that Grann meanders at times. Lots of men are mentioned very briefly and this got to be a little confusing. I didn't always understand why Grann was talking about a particular person. All I cared about was Fawcett. This story is quite amazing.
Honestly I only read the first few chapters. My mind kept wandering. Too many details. I HATE details.

Probably the best book I have read this year! 
 This is the account of a real life Indiana Jones. If you love adventure and history, the story and mystery of Percy Fawcett is up your alley. I am still in awe of all that he accomplished in the way of exploration. The author sums up his interpretation and the answer to the mystery, but I cant tell you that. You will have to read the book!

The subtitle "A Tale of Deadly Obsession in the Amazon" grabbed me, and I put this book at the top of my "to read" pile. My excitement couldn't have been more misplaced. While the subject matter was marginally interesting, this potentially exciting story read like a history text book, plodding on and on in a suspense-less state. Finishing this book was almost painful, and I frequently took breaks to instead admire the desolate view of Idaho from I-15 because it was more interesting than the book. Sadly, the only truly enjoyable part was when, finally finished, I threw the book on the dashboard and triumphantly stated, "Done."

Enjoyed parts, other sections seemed needlessly drawn out and repetitive. Feels like it could have just been a long New Yorker article instead of a book. Also felt like the historical stuff was much more compelling than the author's first person modern day experiences were. Main takeaway: wow, there sure are a lot of ways the Amazon can kill a person!

This book was phenomenal. As I was looking specifically for some light reading I was wary that I'd be sentencing myself to a book that would be difficult and dry to get through at times. 
 Not the case here at all. From the moment I picked it up I was entranced. Grann has a real gift for giving you the context and history of the time but paces it expertly. It was a perfect mix of history, anthropology and nature writing. A delicious mystery, and so many colorful characters throughout. I'll be recommending this to everyone.

This book knocked me out. The words fell easily from the page, and I was drawn in immediately to the story of Percy Harrison Fawcett. Grann paid equal attention to Fawcett's story, the development of exploration, and his own personal quest, which combined to make a very compelling story. I loved the ending more than anything else. The most amazing thing about this book is how it managed to fill me with wonder, even though it is almost 100 years after his disappearance.

4.5 stars 
 Even though this is a nonfiction book, it reads like an adventure story, great writing. I really liked it, and I'm looking forward to seeing what to do with it in the movie.

book_b.title: The Monuments Men: Allied Heroes, Nazi Thieves, and the Greatest Treasure Hunt in History
book_b.user_review:
One of the reasons I enjoyed this book so much is that it covers an aspect of WW2 that I had never read about before. From a military point of view it was irrelevant but from a cultural point of view it was unmeasurable - and the war wouldn't last forever. Between Allied bombing and Hitler's Nero Decree the art work was constantly in danger. I was amazed at the volume of art work that was stolen and hidden. 
 Hollywood has just made a movie"based on the book". From the look of the trailers I would recommend you read the book and skip the movie.

I actually only made it to Chapter 14 before I gave up and for the first time ever, asked to return a book. How the author managed to make this subject matter boring is beyond telling, but partly because its so repetitive. Author focused far more on what the Monuments men were feeling and very little on what they were actually doing. Finally, when he stated that Churchill was pushing for a cross-channel invasion, I had to question the author's credibility.

While the story of Allied pursuit of stolen artwork hidden in Nazi strongholds is a gripping one, this book is overkill if one has already ready the book dealing with the Italian story. One book covering the Northern and Southern European operations would have been preferable. Make no mistake, this is a history, with much historical detail.

Though they bear the same title, the film that came out earlier this year bears little in common with the book and the true story - so much so that the film had to change the names of all the characters. The subject matter itself is fascinating: how do you attempt to save major monuments and works of art during a world war? Do you sacrifice the lives of soldiers to save a famous cathedral? And in the case of the Nazis, who looted and stole hundreds of thousands of pieces of art, how do you go about finding them? That said, this book was kind of dry and slow moving. The author also did a great documentary that came out in 2007 called The Rape of Europa, covering the exact same topic. My advice? Spend two hours watching a solid documentary instead of slogging through this 450 page book.
Very interesting. I am not a nonfiction fan but I really liked this.

In the final days of World War II, the 'Monuments Men' scoured Europe to preserve the most important art and buildings in Europe - priceless masterworks Hitler ordered destroyed if the Reich fell. 
 The Monuments Men were a group of art experts assigned the chaotic task of assessing buildings and art pieces for damage in the wake of two armies battling through historic cities. Doing their best with no backup, no special rank, and no transportation, the Monuments Men acted to preserve the great works of art the Germans had been looting in occupied territories. 
 Heartbreaking destruction, of not only human lives but also the history of Europe, followed the clash of Axis and Allies. Hitler and his cronies embarked on an unimaginably complex and widespread scheme to despoil the riches of the occupied territories. The Nazis burned modern art by Picasso, stole from Jewish families, and absconded with anything thought to reflect German heritage. War usually entails looting, but the scale of this plot is breathtaking. 
 The more I learn about Hitler, the more he seems like a maniac straight out of Saturday morning cartoons. He coveted great works of art, was endlessly embittered by the Treaty of Versailles, believed in grand symbolic gestures, planned on enslaving eastern Europe and playing in the rest, tried to exterminate entire classes of people, and named his new government the Thousand-Year Reich. He did everything short of strapping on a cape and cackling "I have you now!" to Superman. 
 The list of art the Nazis stole included Michelangelo's "Bruges Madonna", the massive and massively important Ghent Altarpiece, Vermeer's "The Astronomer", Rembrandt's enormous oil painting "The Night Watch", and the Bayeux Tapestry - plus thousands of other works of art, pieces of jewelry, statues, porcelain, furniture, and gold. These valuables were hidden in salt mines and other unlikely places throughout Germany, including the famous mine in Altaussee. 
 Against this seemingly unstoppable machine of destruction and theft stood the few lone Monuments Men, determined to restore order and put the art world to right again. It was a race against time, especially given the fact that many of his stooges interpreted Hitler's infamous Nero Decree to extend to the stolen art he had amassed for his dream of a Fuhrermuseum in Linz, Austria. 
 Interspersed with tales of Monuments Men exploits are letters they sent to loved ones and colleagues (all a cut above the average soldier's letter), charting the excitement and then the increasing jadedness of the Monuments Men as they struggled to do their jobs single-handedly on the frontlines of a horrific war. 
 Edsel also tells the tale of the remarkable Frenchwoman Rose Valland, whose ferocious determination and subtle spycraft ensured that the patrimony of France did not simply disappear into the night. She is the only female member of the Monuments Men (and not an official one), and without her tireless efforts the impact of the war would have been even more devastating to the art community than it proved to be. 
 In fact, the aftermath of World War II is still with us, in lost lives and destroyed artworks. As proof, I offer two recent articles about hoards discovered more than 70 years later. This story is so vast it almost seems unbelievable. The book begins slowly, but soon picks up, with the author's passion for his subject showing through on every page. (He points out, rightly, that we could have used a Monuments unit in Baghdad after the 2003 invasion.) Essential reading for anyone interested in art and war. 
 There are a few other books on the topic of art theft, including 
 The Rape of Europa 
 by Lynn H. Nicholas, also about WWII, and 
 Loot: The Battle Over the Stolen Treasures of the Ancient World 
 by Sharon Waxman that shows just how tricky the provenance of art objects can be. Finally, 
 Stealing the Mystic Lamb 
 by Noah Charney illuminates one of the works most mentioned in The Monuments Men: the peerless Ghent altarpiece by Jan van Eyck. 
 Quotable: 
 "Hitler knew it was impossible to steal renowned masterpieces [...] without drawing the condemnation of the world. While he had the conqueror's mentality - he believed he was entitled to the spoils of war, and he was determined to have them - Hitler and the Nazis had gone to great lengths to establish new laws and procedures to 'legalize' the looting activities that would follow. This included forcing the conquered countries to give him certain works as a term of their surrender." - 150 
 "The Germans had used the [Dampierre] library's renowned Bossuet letters for toilet paper, but after they left, the caretaker found the letters in the woods, cleaned them off, and returned them to the library. Now that was dedication. That was service!" - 202 
 "Just seeing the warehouses the Nazis had filled with 'confiscated' items brought home to him the size and complexity of their looting operation. This wasn't accidental damage or angry retaliation, but an enormous web of deliberate deceit that stretched all over Paris and down all the roads back to the Fatherland and all the way to Hitler's office in Berlin." - 239 
 "To save the culture of your allies is a small thing. To cherish the culture of your enemy, to risk your life and the life of other men to save it, to give it all back to them as soon as the battle was won...it was unheard of, but that is exactly what Walker Hancock and the other Monuments Men intended to do." - 321 
 "No age lives entirely alone; every civilisation is formed not merely by its own achievements but by what it has inherited from the past. If these things are destroyed, we have lost a part of our past, and we shall be the poorer for it." - British Monuments Man Ronald Balfour (qtd. on page 465)

Learned a lot in this account of the Monuments Men during WWII and their recovery of lost art from the Nazis. Towards the end I just wanted to get done with it (partly because 3 books came in from the library at the same time - why does that always happen?!?!). I could not believe the amount of theft and the planning that went into their thievery. Just adds insult to the numerous atrocities they committed during their time. Pretty cool to find out how much was actually recovered and saved. 
 I might watch the movie - I might not...

I really have no reason to write a review, but I have something that I would like to get off my chest. 
 Nonfiction historical books are not my cup of tea. This book, especially. The whole book felt like I was reading out of my history textbook. There were some bits where it was story, but most of it was just dates and stuff. It was like, "George Stout took a sip from his canteen and gazed off into the distance. In his peripheral vision, he spotted a crumbling cathedral off the side of the road. Now let me tell you when that cathedral was built, how it was built, every historical person that walked through it, and how it has to do with Adolf Hitler." It was a serious chore for me to read.

Great book. Have never known or heard about this aspect of WWII. I am astounded at the lengths that a handful of men and women went through to preserve centuries of world culture and history. I have a whole new appreciation for art and history and those who have served our country.

Laborious reading to get to the good treasure hunt. I love the subject matter, but repetitive writing made this lengthy book a chore to finish. Fortunately the goods came at the end so I was forced to keep reading. I think the movie will hit the highlights and show personality in the characters.

An informative, well-written book on a mostly forgotten part of the second world war. One does not usually think of art historians, museum directors, sculptors, and other artists when one thinks of soldiers storming Normandy and fighting the Nazis in Europe. For anyone interested in what happened to the masterpieces and other cultural gems in Europe, this is the book for you.
Just too boring to finish

A decent book that with a bit of editing could have been so much better. A little known aspect of WW II brought to light by Robert Edsel in tons of minor details that detract from the story as a whole. Included photos are a plus however.

Excellently told tale of men who served during WWII in the Arts Preservation unit of the United States Army. These men were responsible for the finding, collection, restoration and protection of all of the art and art works that the Nazi Government had stolen. It is a very interesting and humanistic read. For someone like myself...who is so far removed from the events of WWII it is a reminder of man's inhumanity to man and the need to preserve our legacy.

I couldn't. I just couldn't read this anymore. This is no Unbroken...one of my ultra favorite WWII nonfiction books. It was a chore to read through the repetition of the same type of information over and over. Frankly, save yourself some time and watch the documentary called "The Rape of Europa." It tells most of the information in this book (all 39% of what I read) but in a way more interestingly historical format.
Didn't finish this one. I felt like it just didn't go anywhere.

I gave up a little over halfway. Ditto for the film. It's a fascinating topic but I thought both the book and film sucked ass in equal measures. (Stellar cast. Still sucked.) 
 Just watch raiders of the lost ark. 
 I'm genuinely surprised by how much I didn't enjoy this. I'm usually a history geek but I stand by "this sucked."

This book was so bad, I don't know where to begin. It felt like reading a high school text book, with a little bit of character development, and a sprinkle of drama - and that was it. Horrible, would not recommend - unless you love reading art history books written like text books.

I could say a lot about this book- that despite the fascinating subject the author wrote it perhaps a bit dry, that the subject is very near and dear to my heart, that at time I was confused as to where they were working within the chronological context of the war, that I was so happy a historian finally included a dramatis personae at the beginning of the book, etc. Instead I want to do something a bit different, because I really want you to appreciate what happen instead of focusing just on the book. 
 These are some of the works that the world almost lost forever, works that would have forever disappeared from our communal history: 
 Van Eyck's The Ghent Altarpiece 
 Vermeer's Astronomer 
 Michelangelo's Madonna of Bruges 
 And even whole buildings, like the beautiful Neuschwanstein 
 We almost lost these things, and thousands and thousands more priceless relics that tie us not only to our history, but together as a people of a world that is growing. So I want you to take a moment and thank these guys, that risked their lives to save this beautiful pieces: 
 James J. Rorimer 
 Rose Valland 
 George Stout 
 and Harry Ettlinger, a German Jew who had grown up next to some of these amazing works but never had the right to go see them, but who had the privilege to help rescue them after enlisting in the American army. 
 So what do I really want you to do here? I want you to appreciate what was lost and what was found. Take a moment today to look at something beautiful. To help you, here are some great links: 
 Google lets you virtually walk around several great libraries, and you can zoom in on the pictures 
 View the Ghent Altarpiece in 100 billion pixels- you can actually see the individual brush strokes 
 Read about ongoing conservation projects! 
 Monuments Men Foundation

This one is really hard to follow. Which one is which? 
 This book took me about two years to finish (on and off of course). I finally broke down and watched the movie b/c I thought it would help. It did a little, but 90% of it was NOT like the book. 
 It was just so hard to follow so many different story lines of very similar guys. 
 Also, I keep going back and forth with myself. Is the Ghent altarpiece really more important than someone's life? It's just a thing...and (gasp) kinda an ugly thing at that. 
 With Hitler wishing to be an artist, I get that art was a big target of the Nazis, but war is war. 
 Bottom line: Nazis suck. 
 Thank you.

The work of the Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives section, a group of several dozen museum curators and restoration experts who soiught to save and retrieve artwork looted by the Nazis, is intrinsically interesting, but the book is dogged in its pursuit of the story. Partly I suspect because the book is driven by correspondence, it remains thorough but too workmanlike to carry interest for long stretches of reading time.

Got the book, after I saw the movie. Got me into lot of details about what was happening in Europe, and the men/women who did something about it. 
 War is ugly, no matter where and when it takes place, and although people suffer, people achievement is a victim as well. You can kill a whole nation, but if their culture is left behind they are never dead, but if you steel or destroy their culture you are erasing them from memory. 
 a great deal of culture was saved by the Monuments Men, and great deal was lost, but did we get the lesson - NO, looking at the monuments destroyed in Iraq and Syria today, nothing changed. 
 Great book to read to learn about events not that past, and the human spirit that can move mountains.

was intrigued by this story upon seeing the movie trailer...before watching the movie I wanted to read it for myself! the length on the book was daunting...took me almost 2 months to read, but I was always enthralled by the story and the characters. Being a museum professional myself I couldn't believe the lengths these soldiers went to to protect the cultural heritage of others...something we all aspire to! a compelling story...an ideal December to February read!

I was thrilled to read this part of WWII history that, thanks to Robert Edsel, is finally being giving some long overdue attention. 
 When I was a student in Paris in 1980, I was aware of Hitler's Nero Decree, particularly for Paris, yet the Germans who had lived there for the 4 years of occupation loved the city so much that they disobeyed and refused to burn the city. 
 However, I didn't know that my favorite museum, the Jeu de Paume, in which I spent hours, was once a transitory through which all looted French art treasures passed through on their way to Nazi Germany. 
 Little did I know when staying at St. Lo on a tour of Normandy, that the town was a hiding place for French treasures that were completely demolished during WWII. 
 Little did I know when I was gazing at the Mona Lisa in the Louvre that she was once stolen and stashed away in a Salt Mine deep below Nazi Germany. 
 I thought I was well versed in history and art history, but this small yet essential piece I had not known. Thank you Mr. Edsel for bringing to light a piece of history that is so important that without it, I may not have had a Paris to study in. 
 This story is so essential and I deeply appreciate the knowledge I gained in reading it. 
 The movie, though another important vehicle in getting this story out, was a mere cartoon representation of the remarkable story of the Monuments Men. 
 Again, thank you Robert Edsel.

This should have been a great read; the subject matter -- a small section of the US armed forces devoted to preserving, protecting and returning art, architecture and cultural relics during WW2 -- is fascinating. The authors obviously did a lot of research and had great respect for their subject. Alas, reading this book was a slog. I really had to persevere to get through it all. Dense writing, slow pace, too many extracts from letters and documents, excessive use of the passive voice all contributed to it. I wanted to like it and thought this would be a gripping story, but the book didn't do the history justice. ):

Might be one of the worst books I've ever read. Horrible writer. No sense of narrative structure--no arc of the story. Never puts any life into the characters. I've no intention of seeing the movie, but no wonder it's reviews were bad. 
 Everyone suggests "Rape of Europa", and perhaps I'll try that soon.
Well researched and a fascinating bit of history. However, the prose and the organization of this book leave something to be desired.

The Monuments Men is rambling account of a very fascinating aspect of World War II. Focusing on the recovery of art and the protection of key cultural sites, the book tells the unique story of a group of people dedicated to a particular mission in World War II. 
 As a generally un-informed and somewhat ignorant appreciator of art, this book was mostly about things that I only partially appreciate. While I understand the importance of preserving cultural heritage, I am not conversant to know anything more than names like Vermeer and Rubens, and that there are pieces of art that are invaluable. 
 But the value of this book is in affirming that a mission of saving and perserving such items is a legitimate function of the military. 
 While my mind frequently wandered as a worked my way through this book (not what you would call a page-turner), there is enough here to warrant a recommendation to read it, especially for people who like to read about World War II.

This is the book on which the recent film was based. I've not seen the film, but I hope that it has a more cohesive narrative than the text, which (in my opinion) is very episodic. Some parts seem to be written independently of others, as Edsel re-uses the same situation or descriptions. In the end though it just never caught on for me.
I think that if you enjoy non fiction this may be a great read. I took it on,despite the fact that I normally don't enjoy non fiction, and it felt like an chore for me to plow through.
Rich on historical detail but a little dry at times, the telling of what could have been a truly fascinating tale felt a little dull and sometimes plodding.

Though The Monuments Men starts out very slowly, it is a very interesting read about a little known but important piece of history. I read this on my Kindle, but I think it might be better experienced in print, especially due to the excellent photographs at the end of the book. I'm looking forward to the movie coming out based off of The Monuments Men, though I think it will probably be obscured into a more Hollywood-friendly version of events.
Excellent listen on Audible. I will be more contemplative at art museums, and it made me rethink my trip to the Louvre.
Was very complicated, many characters, and read more like a history book.....very dry.

Before reading this I didn't understand the atrocities of Nazi looting. I thought I was similar to the looting of the French and English during their wars, but Monuments Men pointed out that it was actually much worse. The purposeful destruction of cultural works is simply unconscionable. I was also impressed at the interest in saving the cultural history of the aggressor, in this case Germany. 
 Although I thought the information was fascinating and interesting, I was disappointed in the writing itself. There was a great deal of repetitive information so much so that I would glance to check that I hadn't accidentally lost my place.

An excellent and informative book on the Allies, lead by Americans, took on an unbelievable challenge of recovering stolen works of art from personal collections, churches, and museums stolen by the Nazis. I knew Hitler was an art lover, but not his second and third commanders. For a historical book it was an easy read. 
 If you are a history buff or love stories dealing with WW2, then I highly reci omen this novel.

KENOSHA NEWS-OFF THE SHELF 12/8/13 
 Compelling Books about WW II - Coming to a Theater Near You 
 by Scott Smith 
 With the recent news reports of Nazi-looted art found in an apartment in Munich, German, there is an increased interest in the upcoming movie Monument Men. Produced and directed by George Clooney the movies has an all-star cast with the likes of Matt Damon, Clooney, Bill Murray, John Goodman and Cate Blanchett in lead roles. Based on the book, The Monuments Men: Allied Heroes, Nazi Thieves and the Greatest Treasure Hunt in History by Robert M. Edsel, the story concerns the little known Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives program, an Allied military platoon made up of museum directors, curators, and art historians tasked with saving pieces of art and other culturally important items before their destruction. Read about this interesting group of unlikely heroes and their efforts to save history and art from Nazi ruin. The movie has been pushed back from its original December 2013 release to early 2014.

During World War II the Nazis looted much art from Western Europe. The US and England composed lists of art objects to be protected from destruction and/or recovered following the reconquest of Europe. A small group of men from the art world were tasked with the location and protection of institutional art and monuments on the lists but the lists ignored art from private collections. This book details the struggles of these men and the French woman who worked with them. It is a fair work on an overlooked area of World War II. My main fault is that it concentrated on the activities of only a few of the Monuments Men.

Finally able to answer that questions I have had about the restoration, rebuilding and reclaimation of landmarks, statuary and art from WWII. Edsel writes inspirationally about the men and one woman who's war was saving the beauty of the countries devastated by the Nazis. This was a noble fight and I am grateful for the foresight and courage of the leaders and all the members of MFAA for the true service they performed for humankind!

I did not actually finish this book except by shameless skimming. The subject is fascinating - the attempt by a few low ranking officers in the allied armies to save as much of the art of Europe as they could from the ravages of war and the rapacity of the Nazi elite. The author had done his research thoroughly, but for me he was too reluctant to discard any of it. I found myself wading through turgid prose to find out countless dubiously relevant details of the individuals lives to get to the really interesting points where we learn about how the art was saved. Perhaps I am unfair, but I feel the book should have been about half as long and written without the irritating assumption that one can get into the minds of the protagonists at any given moment, like an omniscient author of fiction. There were some good stories, but I had to wade through too much dull background narrative to get to them. There is a danger in deep research that one ends up thinking everyone is going to be as fascinated by the subject as the researcher. There is a film of this, probably the better bet.
I only made it about half way through the book. It just felt like a chore to read it. I just couldn't get into it.

I was very excited to read this book about a group of men rescuing important artwork from Nazi pilferage. However this book turned out to be a fascinating story told very blandly. It reads like a office memo and I just couldn't sustain my interest somewhere along the halfway mark. There are parts where the story gets interesting but overall this book didn't capture my attention. Sadly, I've read the movie is not that great either.

A great one for all the history buffs out there. I am amazed at what it took (and the key role a woman named Rose played) to save priceless cultural heritage from being looted or destroyed during WWII. I'm excited to see how they will make this into a movie because it's an epic and overlooked part of the War.

"The reconstruction of Europe after World War II was one of the most complicated and comprehensive international efforts of modern times. The identity and infrastructure of the nations of Europe had to be rebuilt and the restitution of artwork was a vital component. To say the war was the greatest upheaval of cultural items in history would be a grave understatement. In the end, the Western Allies discovered more than one thousand repositories in southern Germany alone, containing millions of works of art and other cultural treasures, including church bells, stained glass, religious items, municipal records, manuscripts, books, libraries, wine, gold, diamonds, and even insect collections." 
 This book tells the little known story of the Monuments Men, experts in the art field tasked with locating, recovering, preserving and repatriating art looted by the Nazis. This small band of men faced an almost insurmountable task. The amount of irreplaceable art and artifacts taken by the Nazis was staggering and whole of the Monuments Men consisted of less than 400 people to look after the entire western half of Europe. 
 What I loved about this book was how these men came from ordinary backgrounds and accomplished extraordinary things. They were architects and scholars, working in museums and universities; some had little to no training in the preservation and transportation of precious artwork. The odds were against them from the start but it's their dedication and the fact that they were willing to put their lives at risk to save mankind's art history that make you root for them. They are the ultimate underdogs where they not only fought against the Nazis but against the clock. "What if we win the war, but lose the last five hundred years of our cultural history on our watch?" Much of the art was stored in mines to protect them from bombing but these places were not always suitable for storing fragile works of art for years at a time. They were prone to cave ins and flooding while the art was also susceptible to moisture and looters. 
 I really liked the chronological nature of the book. As the war unfolded, so did the search for the art. I was caught up as much as the Monuments Men were and I found myself filled with anxiety over certain works that were missing. I also got to follow various members of the group as they tramped around Europe, following troops, striking out on their own, stealing supplies, commandeering vehicles, men and the help of local civilians if needed. 
 There are also some great photos and maps to illustrate what Edsel is talking about. A main character crew list with photos and short bios is included in the beginning which puts faces to the men the reader follows. I wish the art photos hadn't been clustered together though but rather interspersed throughout. For example, whenever the Ghent Altarpiece was mentioned I had to keep flipping back to the photo to remind myself what it looked like as there's a wide variety of works mentioned and it's tough to keep everything straight. 
 Learning about these men and everything they went through, I shared in their triumphs and failures. I worried about them and feared for their safety. Edsel made me feel like I was there. It was exciting and nerve-wracking and hearbreaking, a great read! If you like art history and WWII then this book is for you.

Listened to this as an audiobook after watching movie several years ago. It's a fascinating story but not well told in the book. Sometimes too much detail, sometimes assumes too much about characters (and yet doesn't really make them come alive to the reader). But lots of research and information in the book, a very worthwhile story that is now much better known because of this book.

I gave this book 2 stars partly for the content of the book, but mostly for how it was written. The subject matter turned out to really just not be that interesting. At all. I thought it would be about people going behind enemy lines and stealing precious artwork before it fell into the Nazi hands. But instead it was about waiting around awhile until American troops made it to cities and then searching for artwork that may or may not be there. Really not exciting stuff. Also the author was really dry with the story-telling (or lack thereof). There's a good way to write about history (like Erik Larson), and there's a bad way...

So I am a huge proponent of reading the book before seeing the movie, so I confess I really only started to read this book because I saw they were making it into a movie this year. And I'm glad I did! It was a bit slow going at times, but for a completely historical non-fiction book, it definitely held my interest from beginning to end. I have always been interested in WW2 and of course I love art, so the juxtaposition of those two things is right up my alley. I was blown away by the extent of the Nazi looting of art, both from private collectors (Jewish and not) as well as public, state owned galleries. It's almost unfathomable the number of pieces they stole (and hid!). And the Monuments Men is such as interesting division of the military that I cannot believe has never existed since. I mean I know the focus of war is elsewhere, but for the near loss of so much beautiful European history to have been completely forgotten (and not learned from) is insane. I completely understand it being eclipsed by the Holocaust, but for it to still be as virtually unknown as it is...wow. I was impressed by the research presented in this book, the clear development of everything from an idea into the actual MFAA division, and how amazing it was that so few people accomplished so much preservation. Astounding.

The story of the guys who went around Europe during WW2 saving all of those great works of art stolen by the Nazis. Thank you for your service and saving all that cool stuff, but the book about your exploits was boring. Yawn.
I just wish I didn't hear George Clooney's voice. It's so obnoxious.

I saw the movie first and decided to read the book to fill in the gaps. I learned a lot about the monuments fine arts and archives group. It's a fascinating story but the book was dry and repetitive in some places.

reference_books.review_text:
I'm only about 1/10 of the way into this book, but what a breath of fresh air after enduring the turgid crap of "under the Dome". So far this is awesome- reminding me (in a good way) of Gibson, Dick, Stephenson, Sterling- while at the same time being wholly original in its ideas. Rock on! 
 5/5/10 
 now 50% thru this book, raving incoherently about it to all who will listen. LOVE. 
 Finished on the 7 May, REALLY enjoyed this book. To me the measure of a special book is not just good writing, but the kind of originality that 'the Windup Girl' is filled with on every page. This is not a future from a familiar canon (Margaret Atwood's "The Year of the Flood" is the closest neighbouring dystopia)- yet once I read it, I can just about feel it breathing down my neck, so very close. 
 This is a book that works on many levels, I would LOVE someone I know to read it so we could discuss it!

reference_books.title: Reamde
reference_books.review_text:
Please be clear on one thing. Neal Stephenson's ONE star is most authors' three. His four... well it's off the scale for the normal, non NS author. I'm sorry. Since I'm marking on a curve, and the Baroque Cycle was a solid 5 ( that's 555 in the Normal Non-NS author scale), I can only give this three- and add another star because I liked the unabridged audio adaptation I listened to quite a lot. No, I'm taking it away again. Maybe I'll give it back later. 
 'Reamde' has many of the usual NS themes- beefy, nerdy techy hero (two of them actually); super intelligent, dashing female leads- carefully researched swashbuckling; an exploration of currency and value and the ebb and flow of credit and money in worlds real and virtual. The villain is a cardboard-cutout stereotypical scary terrorist dude, which is kind of disappointing, but there is no stereotyping based on culture or religion- only on the type of person who would be drawn to mayhem, to destruction of worlds, rather than building worlds. 
 The writing is as beautiful and exuberantly erudite as always. There was not a sentence in Reamde that made me flinch. Action boils over from the first page, and ends kind of abruptly after 8oo pages or so, but at least with neatly tied up loose ends. I like that, it makes me happy. 
 I'd put this on the same star rating as Anathem- if you enjoyed that, this is just as good.

book_a.title: Stranger in a Strange Land
book_a.user_review:
I keep adding and deleting stars from my rating of this book, as I read. 
 I had forgotten Heinlein's patronising, self consciously learned tone. Two stars. 
 Story keeps grabbing me, I do want to see what happens next. Three stars. 
 Sexist stereotypes make me grit my teeth. Retains three stars due to year of publication and generational issues. 
 Putting the boot into organised religion, in an amusing and original fashion? 4 stars! 
 Oh crap, I forgot the polyamory thing, here it comes. Back to two stars. Dirty old man != social revolutionary. Really. 
 Currently bogged down in a swamp of comparative religion and alluded-to sex. Will I persevere? Who knows. 
 Finished. Such a long journey to a "look, he jebus" finale. sheesh.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Another classic that I can live without. I read this book because it was recommended (by every science fiction source out there). This was one of Heinlein's weakest (in my opinion) and in spite of all these kudos...I "greatly dislike" this one. 
 Why? I really didn't get into it from the word go. It's not really representative of (at least most of) Heinlein's work. It's slow moving, preachy, and for me just flat annoying. I didn't like the "Oh so loved" main character, and didn't get into the story. 
 My opinion...didn't like it, can't recommend it. Decide for yourself I suppose.
This does not age well.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I wasn't sure what to expect from this book. I didn't read up before hand. I just picked it up for 50 cents at the library book sale. 
 When I began the book, I was fascinated with the Man from Mars, and I really enjoyed the character. And even though the sexism had already started to bother me, I couldn't help but like Jubal, as well. The whole first half of the book in which Martians are explained, Mike is only an egg, and the plot revolves around what will become of him, I stayed busy enough not to focus on the sexism or anything else that bothered me. 
 As soon Mike matured and left home, the book changed so that I felt that I was being preached to with none of the redeeming qualities of the story left to keep me interested. The message seemed to be so shaming towards readers who might not share its values, and yet it seemed so ridiculously backwards in its sexism, homophobia, and general 60s silliness as to be laughable today despite the free-loving spiritualism. (I admit, while I may be quite the liberal idealist, I've never been much for free-loving spiritualism, being more of a proponent of fraternally-respecting rationalism.) I had also unwittingly purchased the complete version that contains 60,000 words cut from the original release, and for a while I was feeling every word of it. 
 I soldiered through hoping to grok it in fullness (Okay, so I may not love this book, but I love grokking and you can't stop me even if you make fun of me in public about it.), and I didn't hate the end as much as I could have. I never said I wasn't a sucker for a happy ending. So in the end I give it a 3 for the food for thought, the new vocabulary, and the failure to piss me off enough in the end to give it a 2.

Am I glad I read it? I guess. Did I like it? Not so much. The plot seems to really just be a vehicle to preach some pet ideas, which may have seemed innovative in the 50s, but are now antiquated and repetitive. No amount of orgies is going to make that interesting. 
 I found myself constantly reminding myself, "it was written so long ago. It is a product of its era," but at a certain point it becomes kind of hard to get past the homophobia and misogyny. There were a few lines where, I'm quite certain, if I had had water in my mouth I would have spit it all over; for instance, "nine out of ten, if a girl gets raped it's it's partly her own fault," which, even more strangely, was spoken by a female character. The characters are at some point meant to achieve this state of great enlightenment, but women are still judged almost exclusively on appearance and chided by the men for their love of clothing and dressing up. It's a product of its era, it's a product of its era... 
 Still, I felt obligated to complete it, at least to see what all the fuss was about. I just imagine Heinlein writing it with all the overblown self-satisfaction and dour pomposity of a teenage reading Nietzsche for the first time.

This is a magical, rare thing. The first half of a great book seamlessly fused with the second half of an awful book. 
 It has been many years since I read it, so forgive me some fuzziness here. 
 The first parts of the novel are well written and believable (as long as you can go with pre-space program views of Mars, and--much worse--the idea of a manned Martian expedition that should never have gotten past psychological screening and isn't followed up for 20 years), and does a wonderful job portraying a completely foreign culture. 
 As the main character (Mike Valentine) acculturates to Earth and starts trying to absorb what he can and fuse it with his values, the book goes steadily downhill. The author's main philosophical mouthpiece (Jubal Hershaw) presents several interesting 'narrative essays' (not uncommon with Heinlein) throughout the middle sections, and Jubal himself remains my favorite character from the book. 
 Mike's later views and the religion/cult he founds are where the novel falls apart. Broadly sexually utopianist in nature, it displays a fundamental lack of understanding of the human species in general, and would be unlikely to last more than a couple of years with any meaningful number of members. (Somewhat like early socialist communes which initially did well, and then fell apart.) This might not be so bad, but the entire last third of the novel is focused on this as it slowly drags into the realm of an unrealistic culture, that frankly, isn't even appealing in the first place.
This is the last Heinlein book I read. It read like an old man's sexual fantasy. There's plenty of people who enjoy these, but not me.
They cannibalize each other - pretty much all you need to take away from this book outside of how sexist the author is.

I just can't go along with the description of this being the best science fiction novel ever written. 
 Just a bit campy with its naive embrace of Hef-like 60s free love and a bit of David Koresh religious community added in. The dialogue is written like a 1950s screenplay from a forgettable black and white film. "Dear, get me a drink." "Do be a darling and toss me that towel". 
 Apart from the Martian (sort of) with some weird telekinesis, there isn't a whole lot of science fiction going on here. High tech seems to be the fact that grass grows in the living room. Heinlein seems fascinated by the word "stereo". I guess that was the high tech consumer product of his day. 
 For the most part, the plot hangs together so that the author can preach his favorite brand of libertarianism. I was "fortunate" enough to read the uncut edition, rescued from the editors and published by Heinlein's widow. More that once, I had the feeling that I was reading page after page of words best left hidden by the markup pen. 
 Kurt Vonnegut called this a brilliant, thought provoking masterpiece. That's a pretty tall compliment that I just don't grok.

This is my first foray into sci fi for decades. I had an urge to read some of the "classics" and I started with this. I knew it was 50 years old, and thought it would be amusing to see what predictions for the future Heinlein had. I found the technology was really not a part of the story. I ended up being bothered by the sexism, and the preachiness of the book. Why sexism, when I can read Jane Austen and just take it for what it was at the time? I guess because (a) this book was written recently enough, and (b) it was supposed to be predicting the future, I was irritated by the "swinger" attitudes. Maybe that's what he was saying. I don't know. Anyway, I enjoyed it less than I'd hoped.
It started out interesting but I found that got pretty boring once I was about a third of the way in. It was a struggle to get through the rest of it.

This was required summer reading for my junior year of high school. I suffered through every page and thought it was weird. In the end, however, I was able to see the book as a work of art and appreciate the message.

Ugh. I really wanted to like this book. At first, it was great. The characters were interesting and the situation was thought provoking. The farther along I read, though, the more I resented being preached at by Jubal and the religious leaders. Also, the women are treated horribly. What a sexist book. I'm done.

Interesting idea, but I found it a bit slow. Too much philosophy and long conversations, not enough story and action. I didn't grok it. There was a lot of nudity. But I couldn't actually see it. I had to use my imagination to see the naked ladies.
I stopped reading halfway through, I just couldn't get into it. I may give it another try at some point.
Vastly overrated.

Oh dear. It really didn't work for me. Now that may be because it's nearly fifty years out of date but I think it's more than that. 
 For a start it's a soap box in disguise, Heinlein hijacks his characters and makes them talk a conversation about his views on all manner of things. The characters themselves are cardboard cutouts - bumping off each other socially and sexually like billiard balls on a table. Lot's of writers are passionate about issues of one kind or another, they don't all make their characters shout about it (China Mieville, or Iain Banks for example; both feature on my book shelf and both of whose work is orders of magnitude better than this) 
 The edition I read was the one revised back up to 220k words from the original 170k words, and boy it showed - i think the original editors had the right idea there. There are chunks of this book that do nothing and go nowhere except to indulge the writer. 
 What's frustrating is that H. shows glimpses of good ideas, clever scenes, even characters that could be engaging if only they were ever developed and acquired a bit of depth. I have read 'The Moon is a harsh mistress' which is also full of H's quirky style, and I can see why that would appeal to some (I'd give 'Moon' 3 stars maybe 4 if I was feeling generous) but this book is shallow to the point of irritation.

Even when I first read this novel, in the '70s, I found the sexist attitude of the author patronizing -- and yet I find myself returning to the book every decade or so...something about it appeals to me, or I'd have sold the book at yard sale years ago. Basically it boils down to a boy's adolescent fantasy future of free love...

Stranger in a Strange Land is a classic science fiction novel. My experience with classics is that they are classics for a very good reason. I often start reading classics with a bit of trepidation, but I usually finish them greatly impressed. So I had high hopes for Stranger in a Strange Land. Unfortunately, it sucks. 
 The story is about a boy, Michael, who was raised on Mars. In the world of this book, Mars is inhabited by some super-intelligent and (mostly) peaceful beings, and they end up raising Michael from when he was a baby until basically he's a full-grown man. At that point, astronauts from Earth arrive and are stunned to find Michael. They take him back to Earth, and our story begins. 
 Because of the way he was raised, Michael is very intelligent, but he's also really weird. He doesn't understand any human culture, customs or languages, so it's difficult for anyone to communicate with him. It's made even harder because he has a habit of entering a comatose state whenever he feels a bit stressed. Despite this, everyone on Earth wants a piece of him. Because of some dumb legal stuff, apparently Michael is heir to a ton of money and adventures, as well as, possibly, the entirety of Mars. So news agencies, businesses, the government, everyone wants to talk with him and get him on their side. A few people, though, want to save him from all of this, and that's where we get an adventure. 
 Michael and his friends run around trying to hide from the government and others, who want to capture Michael, get him to give away his fortune, and then maybe kill him. This is all very exciting, and some of the best pieces of the book. The author is trying to create an outsider's perspective of Earth culture, and it can be sort of eye-opening. 
 But then we find out that Mike has magical powers that were taught to him by the Martians. He has telekinesis, and he can also make people disappear from the world. It's about here that the books crappiness really takes off. Everyone problem can be solved by Mike's magical powers, so all the stakes in the story disappear. Then Mike learns super super quickly, so he ends up knowing pretty much everything and starts becoming incredibly arrogant. Then, in the second half of the book, he starts to investigate religion. It is difficult to describe how incredibly cliched these investigations are, but it gets worse, because then Mike starts his own religion. This religion is clearly heavily inspired by the 1960s culture of free love, so we get many, many pages of proselytizing about how this is really a super awesome way to live that will solve all of our problems. That is literally the entire second half of the book, and the book is almost 600 pages so... it was tedious. 
 Tedious describes much of this book. There are tedious diplomatic exchanges, , tedious religious explanations, tedious and shallow character development, and tedious debates about philosophy that are basically one person talking at another for several pages with the other character interjecting periodic "what?"s and "huh?"s. It's really awful, and it's made worse because many of these ideas are picked up and then dropped, completely, for the rest of the book. It's like the author was taking two year breaks between chapters. 
 I can't recommend this book, but if you feel some compulsion to read it, skip the second half. Seriously. There is literally nothing of any value there. Nothing. You may think there is. You may think "hey, he has to explain something about how this happens, and maybe it's entertaining." He doesn't , and it's not, and you should run away from that half of the book as fast as you can.

This is pure crap. I want back the 16 hours of my life I wasted on this novel. This must have been the inspiration for films like Starman, Phenomenon, and K-Pax. A strange spaceman comes from the sky, to teach human beings a thing or too about spirituality and life. Not to mention, Heinlein uses the novel as a vessel to tell communicate his hedonist, free love free sex (yet still misogynist) ideas, complete with characters who live on a commune. His writing seems almost perverse at times.
Another classic Sci-Fi book.

Mind-blowing in high school, but after all these years I've come to be annoyed by what I think of as the Heinlein shtick, which mostly enables men to have lots of adoring women around for whim-catering.

This book is interesting, and has a great take on how humanity attempts to deal with the great unknown questions it faces. However, for the most part, it felt a little dated. I could feel that it was not contemporary as I read it.
Ugh. Far too dated and clunky for me. Rampant sexism throughout.
Ugh.
Like the book of Job in the Bible. Good. I should read it again though. I've forgotten a lot.

I seem to be one of the few people who didn't love this book. I really wanted and expected to like it as it's often name-checked as an sf classic. Instead, I found a book that was somehow simultaneously both hippie dippy and gut crawlingly sexist. In brief: A guy raised on Mars comes to Earth and founds a religion based on orgies. There's lots of talking about grokking and eventually he is killed by an angry mob. And one character-a female no less-says that nine times out of ten when a woman gets raped it is partly her fault. I know, it was a different time blah blah blah. I don't care. This book is overrated drivel. It's on my all-time worst list and I read a lot of books. 
 I have heard his other books are better. I liked the movie Starship Troopers enough to be somewhat curious about the novel, but I hear the book is pretty different and I suspect what I like about the movie is all Paul Verhieven's doing (Interestingly, he claimed he couldn't finish the book because he found it too depressing.) Regardless, I think this book turned me off of Heinlein permanently.
Wow, I just can't do that level of preachy.
The first 3/4ths of the book was excellent; sadly, it didn't end as strongly.

This book had the potential to be something amazing not saying that it didn't turn out to be pretty good but I was a little disappointed. The premise is great, an earth man that gets raised on Mars and then brought back to earth to learn about humans. This book was written in the 1960s and I can see it being very controversial, hell, some of the things Heinlein wrote in there made me think that even if it came out today people would still think it was somewhat controversial. The story itself was good but the extra things he threw in seemed a bit forced at times. It was really interesting what he had to say about religion and society especially that it still applies to today. The book could have been a lot shorter if he cut out all of his thoughts but probably wouldn't have been considered a classic. Overall a good read but not the one I was expecting.
I think this is one of my all time favorite books.
weird science fiction from a time when people actually believed in the future.

I tried really hard to like this book, and I did--like so many others--take away the word "grok" to incorporate into my everyday vocabulary. The problem lies in the fact that I grok this book rather better than the author did. I can see through the shell of egalitarian equinamity Heinlein proposed to the murky, self-centered, patriarchal morass underneath. 
 Heinlein would have done better to have stepped down from his soapbox while writing this, or, in fact, any of his books. If he wasn't trying so hard to espouse his message, he might have actually come out with a spectacular novel.
Enjoyed the first half... not so much the second half

When you consider we have many other sci-fi writers who are not stuck in their own time and do not write all their male characters as sexist, sex-obsessed or sexy, you can clearly understand the view to give this book a very wide birth. The storyline was actually quite interesting, but I'm sure the is someone out there who had written something similar without the added bollocks "of the time".
One of the few books that I couldn't finish. I kept trying but finally decided there were so many good books I could spend my time reading instead of wasting my time.

I guess I'm glad I read it, but it's really not a good book. It's also lame sci-fi, and at this point I'm beginning to accept I will likely never really enjoy anything by Heinlein. He never stops preaching his agenda long enough for a plot to truly develop. The New Historicist in me does appreciate the insight into the culture that bred the hippie movement, but that's about it.

Reading Strangers in a Strange land is a grind - think of some religious text but told all in dialogue with little or no place setting, character development, or even conflict and tension. The author did provide a plot, but a superficial one. i.e. Super endowed man tries to become god. Or "grok" god," as its characters would say. In the end, the god-like leader reaches the same fate all god-like leaders have in the past, he is executed by the masses, and elevated to the height of a martyr, leaving behind a gaggle of free-loving "grok in fullness" characters that never fight, never emote, never in fact grow out of the catacomb of their one dimensional personalities. Or, should I say personality? Because, if it were not for attributions, it would be next to impossible to tell one man's monologue from another. 
 Did I like a single character in the book? No, not one. 
 The men are all virile, extremely articulate, well read people that just love to have a nest of "girls" that take care of their every physical need. 
 The girls are all self effacing sex machines - who can type on the side. 
 Why is the book so famous? Because it broke new ground when it was published, and was soon adopted by the Woodstock Generation as a model for a free love, go in peace, hedonistic lifestyle. Because, it presents interesting, though not unique, arguments for and against organized religion, and government. And, because, at the time of publication, lines such as, "nine out of ten times a woman wants to be raped," were thought to be bold and honest. Today, they are just considered uninformed and misogynistic. 
 Does it deserve to be read now? 
 Only if you like reading long self-indulgent diatribes.

Stranger in a strange land 
 Ok his book is both a 4 star and a 1 star, because on one side you had a great idea mostly put in a great style. But you also had a lot of misogynistic remarks and attitudes that really urged me to just throw the book away and never finish it. 
 So it's the story of a human born in mars, raised by martians who returns to Earth as a young man to try to understand us humans while teaching us about how martians see the universe and think. 
 Bit spoilers 
 So first chapter the martian arriving, being held on a hospital, learning little by little, nurse Jill seeing him, that was amazing, and the scape to Ben house quite an action scene. 
 Then the Jubal house, that is later shown to be like a playboy house, but while later confirmed not to be case for Jubal, he hints to others. But hey if that were the only thing it would be ok, in a way it also helped with the story. This chapter is amazing for it is on the interaction between Jubal and Mike(the martian) that we learn a lot about Martian life, why water is so important, water brothers, the old ones, eating the dead ones as an honor, and the martian powers. Now later they would sound too farfetched but here I was willing to let it go that this human learned telekinesis, telepathy and the power to make disappear things just because martians taught him to. 
 Here is also where we learn the concept of grok, where Mike explain goes beyond understanding, groking I understanding, knowing, interacting, feeling, becoming one with a concept to think and be able to make. Now that was a great concept and how the author explains it without explaining it, by making the people include the new word in their talks was good, problem is he didn't knew when to stop, suddenly they were groking everything. 
 About the church experience and Mike vanishing the high priest that was interesting, the author dissecting religious movements via a weird religion, the fosterites. 
 Then came the troublesome chapter, Jill and Mike on the road, that started ok and promised to be fun, and there is where the author says via Jills voice, that women get raped because they want to, and the later scene with Jill thinking how good the man ogling over her with raping thought was good. That's when you want to throw the book as far as it can go and never think of it again. 
 But the story behind it was good, and well it was written the 60s so you think well it was the way they thought back then, let's give it another chance. The tattoo lady part was interesting and how she sees Mike as a godlike entity. 
 Then comes the part when Ben explain Jubal about the religion Mike founded, and we would later see what Mike really wanted to build, and in a way this help watch how other would see Mike's religious facade as wrong while it was the other way around, because in the inner circle of Mikes church there was sexual freedom, naked people going around and loving each other like in a hippie fantasy, and that's all Jubal and Ben see, the sexual orgy, he even convinces Ben to return not because it was good, but because it was free sex. 
 Also here is where Jubal shows his opinion on the girls in his house, on one side yes he cares for them as daughters, but on the other hand tells women opinions are useless, dismiss them as tools to his work, makes remarks on their pregnancies. It's just wrong, and yes maybe that was the way people thought on the time, but that doesn't help much. 
 Then Jubal goes to make after he escapes prison and his church is burned, and so Mikes explain how and why the nest work the way it does, and why he make it pass as religion when it really isn't, for example he explain how the shared sex is about overcoming jealousy, or the levels are to evaluate commitment, and why the money even when they don't need it. 
 Bigger spoilers. 
 Now in the end Mikes decide to go out and let the mob kill him as a parallel to Christ, that was in line with his thought as a step to stablish his plan and to become an old one. But then he becomes and Archangel under the order of the Foster founder, that was weird. And the martians being able to blow planets just over the edge of the believable of his martian power concepts. 
 So if you ignore the misogyny in the book, it's a very interesting story of how a martian-human might see us, learn from us, and teach to us. Couple of strange things but an interesting idea-concept. A 4 star 
 But as much as one would like to ignore all that, is impossible, it just means the book has become old in a bad way, an example of wrong ideas in women-man relations of the past, of the things we most avoid. And as such we should avoid to read this at face value, and if we do to remember that the ideas behind it are wrong, all wrong. That turns it 1 star(or 0 but that's not available), no averaging.

OMG I'd forgotten just how mystifyingly anachronistic - even just plain terrible, narrow-minded and terrified of all grey areas in humanity's experience - this book is. Read Keith's spectacular review for a reminder/palate cleanser/wake-up call.
cleverly written. plenty of interesting topics of discussion and new viewpoints. last chapter is good.

I originally read this years ago and thought it was great. I recently re-read the unabridged version and didn't like it so much. His protrayal of the female characters was weak. His vision of idealized sexual liberation seemed like an adolescent boy's fantasy. Come to think of it, maybe that's why I liked it back in high school ;)

Top 100 Science Fiction 
 The books started so well. I understand Heinlen took a while to write this and wonder if the 90 degree turns in the story are related to the various times he picked the book back up trying to figure out how to finish it. 
 It went from an interesting sci-fi story into a diatribe against religion and social mores. 
 It did add the word 'grok' to the English language but only those who can 'think Martian' can truly grok anything, so Heinlen's odd ideas about sexuality and religion, I figure, are safely unattainable. 
 Published in 1962, the 2nd half of this book must have raised a few eyebrows and been smuggled into quite a few boys' bedrooms, but it is seriously dated today. The elite share everything in common, even their women (and women are treated as beautiful property) but the masses will not be able to 'grok' this until they themselves become enlightened.

Partially read back in the seventies(?) but put down due to a lack of interest. I liked sci-fi - still do - but didn't get into this one. I read the whole thing recently. Dated and poorly written but still with some fun ideas. Date read is a guess.

Well! This book was nothing like I expected. And unfortunately it was nothing like I had hoped either. I decided to read it because of its repute and status as one the great science fiction stories of all time. So, not knowing beforehand much of the premise (intentionally) I eagerly dove in hoping for wonderful storytelling and timeless discovery. But nope... 
 What I found was a good story and a great premise COMPLETELY drowned in heavy handed themes and nonstop questioning of human ideals. The themes ranged from interplanetary jurisdiction to the purpose of human sexuality; to cults vs. religions and what does 'to be God' mean. Even though I don't agree with much of the author's preaching, I actually would have enjoyed it if the themes were only questioned in snippets and not THE ENTIRE TIME. 
 Oh and I forgot to mention, the book was originally published in the sixties and is set in an undisclosed future (presumably not too distant from our day today) but even taking that into account there was an astounding amount of sexism and racism. I cringed at least a dozen times. 
 Lastly, It was repetitive and slow. I found myself wanting to finish the book and be done. So I did and I'm moving on. 
 The three good things that I felt the book had going for it were: 
 1. I love the idea of exploring humanity through a nonhuman perspective. Really cool. 
 2. The initial storyline is very intriguing: An earth man raised on another planet comes home and has to re learn everything it means to be human. 
 3. It raised some good questions and insight about humanity's flaws. But again, way too heavy handed. It completely bogged down a potentially good story.

I do not grok it or rather I do not fully grok it. (That that word somehow slipped into our culture could only be from the redundancy of its use in this book) The first half or so of the book was actually quite interesting right up to where Michael is set out on his own. From there it takes a nose dive not toward the ground but into a bottomless pit of pain. It was only the first half that qualified the star otherwise I would have assumed leave it at 0. That I recently read A Case of Conscience by James Blish, that was written 3 years earlier and was altogether better despite its very similiar plot, certainly detracted from this reading. Heinlein uses a human born on Mars and raised by Martians, Blish uses an alien born on earth raised by humans. This book is at its core is an examination of morality and religion using the vehicle of a man with neither. The book lacked interesting characters and, as far as I can tell, a plot. From this and other books of Heinlein's I've read so far he seems more interested in his ideas than in the story he uses to expound on them. I you haven't already subjected yourself to this book then don't, your time is better spent doing almost anything else.
I do not grok this in fullness, the waiting is.

I loved the first half of the book - a convincing description of what an alien culture might be like, a great story about how the world might react, and a compelling tale of one person's efforts to adjust to life on Earth. 
 If I was rating the first half alone, it'd have to be four or five stars - it was really, really good. 
 Which made the second half all the more disappointing. I just couldn't get into it. It plodded along at a snail's pace, and in a very odd direction. The plot suddenly got surreal and unconvincing, and the main characters changed in ways that just didn't make sense. The book finished with a drawn out meander through the meaning of religion that seemed to go on forever. 
 Such a shame. 
 Worth a read for the first half alone, though.
