1/5 
 One of the worst books I've ever had the displeasure to read. 
 I only really picked it up because I adore Jake Abel, and he has a part as Mark in I Am Number Four's film adaptation, but it wasn't worth it for several reasons. 
 1. This book is a cliche piece of drivel. It has almost every overdone young adult trope EVER in its tree-killing pages: 1. a mysterious new student with incredible powers, 2. a gorgeous, sweet, popular girl, 3. love at first sight, 4. the popular girl's jealous ex-boyfriend and other muscle-head jocks, 5. a cute, quirky best friend/side-kick, 6. a mentor figure, 7. an action girl, 8. an evil force hell-bent on destroying the world, etc, etc, etc. 
 And the thing is, you can subvert cliches; you can turn them on their heads, poke fun at them, and/or reinvent them into something interesting. For example, look at Kendare Blake's Anna series. It has a ghost hunting boy starting at a new school, where the popular girl and quirky kid are both immediately drawn to him, the jocks hate him, a powerful creature's after him, and so on. But the sardonic self-awareness of the text, and the characterization, makes it all better. Cas tells Thomas he's not looking for a tag-along, because he knows tag-alongs, like Four's BFF, somehow stumble into the protagonist's affairs. He knows Mysterious New Drifters catch the eyes of Queen Bees, but he uses that to find out more about doing his freaking job, and you know what? Carmel wants to know more about him because she's the Queen Bee, she's actually really smart, and she keeps tabs on what's happening in her school. She and Cas become really good friends, instead of a couple! She surprises him with her ability to be badass, her brilliance, and her determination. That's NOT what we get in IAN4. 
 2. Which feeds into my next point: the characters. Anna Dressed in Blood and its sequel, Girl of Nightmares, aren't perfect. I had my issues with both. However, the primary characters were wonderful. Cassio's POV is snarky fun. Thomas is adorable, and not just relegated to sidekick status; often, he's the voice of reason, and there are points where he acts on his own, for his own reasons. He has plot-threads that are only for him, not Cas. The female characters, though, are even more wonderful! Here's something I wrote in my review of the first book (which is spoiler-y): "Anna Dressed in Blood has many badass, amazing female characters, who have agency in their actions, rather than being mere, passive receptacles for male characters. Anna, like Cas describes, is a fierce goddess. She is the one who stops the ultimate antagonist in the end, not Cas, and is aided by Carmel's titanium bat, while a cursed Cas looks on." In the second book, we get the enigmatic Justine, who gives Cas a run for his money when it comes to being a competent hunter. She's beautiful and clever and young, and you know what? This doesn't intrinsically mean she needs to be thrust into the position of romantic interest in order to be valuable. She cares more about being successful at her job than that, though she and Cas do have some chemistry. All the characters of Anna are great! 
 In comparison, IAN4's characters are card-board cutouts of the same tropes. Four and Sarah are perfect and beautiful and meant for each other, really, BECAUSE THEY HAVE NO PERSONALITIES WHATSOEVER. Why should anyone else have to suffer them? Four is one of the most boring protagonists I've ever had to read. He and Sarah have no interesting flaws, like Carmel's inability to easily give up her status at school, and Justine's desire for power, or even Cassio's habit of making the people who care about him unhappy because of his obsession with saving Anna. None of this is accepted by the narrative as good, but it's there as an opportunity for good growth. IAN4 TRIES to give Sarah some depth by saying she used to have an alcohol problem and was mean to the people in her school because of it, before Four came along. You know how? With a dull info-dump. And Mark doesn't have much depth to him, though my baby Jake did manage to make a few expressive faces when his character wasn't being a shallow dick. He eventually helps Four, but he's still mostly a two-dimensional, overly jealous jock. You know where you belong, Mark (and maybe everyone else)? In a 70's flick about mean, poopie-head jocks keeping the odd, but ~oh so speshul guy away from the girl of his dreams. NEENER, NEENER, NEENER. 
 3. THE PLOT. It's a cliche plot, but it could have been SO COOL, if pulled off properly. Motherhugging ALIENS want to destroy other planets and screw shit up! Four is one of earth's only defenses! Instead, most of the story was stupid, romantic, teenage angst about characters I really had no reason to GAF about. Four and Sarah are drawn to each other for no real reason, except that Four thinks she's the most beautiful girl ever, and I assume she finds him hotter than Mark - which, Imo, what? Jake's face > Pettyfer's, any day. BUT that's beside the point. There was no buildup in their relationship whatsoever. Almost as soon as he meets her, Four thinks Sarah is his soul-mate, because on Four's planet, people imprint or something. YES, like in Twilight, because Frey wants to write JUST LIKE TWILIGHT FOR THEY MUNNIES! This is why, I guess, the world-building and explications for why the aliens do what they do is so vague. He just has a shell of a concept that he's trying to sell. 
 4. And this ties into my final point: THE AUTHOR SUCKS. Not only is his writing boring, simple to the point of eye-rolling, filled with no descriptions whatsoever, and the antithesis of show-don't-tell; he's honestly an asshole. He's James Frey, of A Million Little Pieces's infamy. Basically, he wrote a "memoir," and lots of people found it moving, but it came out that he lied through his teeth in it. He's really in writing only for the money. Wanting lots of people to enjoy your work the way they do, say, Harry Potter is one thing. It's nice to dream about. But wanting to write ONLY to be famous and make money? He apparently has a writing factory where he takes naive young writers, makes them sign a contract that hands much of their rights over to him, and sticks his name on their work. He even writes under the pen-name Pittacus Lore, who happens to be the greatest alien leader on Four's home planet. How arrogant can one guy be? He had IAN4 created to be the next big thing in the YA franchise - to get movies and products and all that other crap. Not because of a love of writing. TOO BAD IT SUCKS, FREY. AND THE MOVIE DOES, TOO (aside from Jake Abel's face, of course). ;P

John has been living on Earth with his Cepan Henri since he was 5 years old. Him and Henri have lived moved all over the United States in an effort to stay hidden. His home planet Lorien was destroyed by the Mogadorians and Alex and eight other children are hidden all across the planet Earth until the powers they are supposed to be developing at puberty make an appearance and they can go after the Mogadorians. The Mogadorians are also on Earth, hunting the nine in number order to get around a protective charm that was placed on the children and to gauge whether or not they can take over the Earth as well. At the opening of the book John has just had to move again and now knows that the first three are dead. They move to a little town called Paradise, Ohio where for the first time John starts making friends. 
 The best thing this book has going for it is that is action packed. The pace is quick and never stays in one place for long. It's all developing powers, fighting and giant battles. It definitely keeps you entertained. 
 The background on Lorien and the kind of planet it was and what society was like was interesting. The flashbacks of both the planets destruction and the scraps of John's life were really interesting. I also like learning about how the history of Lorien and the history of Earth have intersected. However I couldn't help but think that some of the things about the planet sounded familiar as if they had been pulled from other stories, books, televisions shows, movies etc. 
 My other source of contention was the relationship between Sarah and John. It was a sweet relationship it really was, however we never get to know Sarah. All we know is she's a nice girl and she was on a bad path but straightened herself out via family and photography. Since we don't really get to know her well, it's hard to figure out exactly what it is that John see's in her.

Entao...a premissa o livro e boa: aliens (lorienos) vem para a Terra fugidos, porque o mogadorianos invadiram seu planeta natal e destruiram tudo. 
 Vieram 9, que ao longo da vida desenvolveriam alguns poderes chamados de legados, acompanhados por seus cepans, uma especie de guardiao/treinador/pai substituto. 
 Cada um possuia um numero e so poderia serem mortos em ordem numerica, a nao ser que se unissem, o que faria o feitico de protecao acabar. 
 Todos os lorienos vivam escondidos, alguns permaneciam em lugares isolados e outros viviam como nomades, caso do Quatro, personagem central desse livro. 
 Comecei a ler essa serie por causa do filme, impossivel nao ler sem imaginar o Alex Pettyfer (-rawr) nas aventuras do Quatro, e nao me decepcionei. A narrativa e meio simplista e poderia ter sido melhor desenvolvida, mas da pro gasto: ler e se entreter. 
 Um dos pontos fracos, na minha opiniao, e a tentativa de prender o Quatro a Sara, seu primeiro amor, quando seu cepan afirma que lorienos so se apaixonam uma vez e e pra sempre...eles sao aliens ou pinguins? u_u 
 Admito que me atrai a ideia de super-herois e ver o treinamento deles e a descoberta de seus poderes, sem falar que as cenas de batalha do livro sao legais tambem. 
 Claro que a serie virou um caca-niquel, saindo volumes a respeito dos outros lorienos, como o numeno Nove, Oito, por exemplo, e sobre os legados, os quais, admito, li e gostei. 
 Recomendo a leitura, desde que nao seja feita com grandes expectativas e alertado que se trata de uma historia infanto-juvenil, da pra ter um bom momento, como se fosse um descanso entre leituras mais complexas e dar uma desopilada.
Un tanto cliche pero como dicen que los libros y la historia en si mejoran, pues la continuare.

A couple of things that bug me here. Lets be clear, I love young adult books. The thing about young adult is that those books hit the ground running and grab you at go. They are typically fast paced, imaginative and usually well done. I am mostly referring to fantasy or science fiction here. What I hate is when it's marketed as those genres but are really just stories about teenagers and all their dramas disguised as fantasy or sci fi. This is how I felt about vampire academy and now this book. 
 John is supposed to be an alien from the planet Lorien who escaped as a small child with his guardian to hide here on earth from their enemy the mogadorians. This is sort of the set up for the series. My problem with John is he is sooooo human. He no way feels like an alien from another world. I get that he needs to blend, but there has to be some differences. The dialogue is wooden, bland, predictable and flat out boring. There is nothing creative here. 
 My other gripe is that I listened to this on audio. I like audio books, but if you are going to have a reader read a young adult book, that reader should either be a young adult or sound like one. This reader sounded like an old man pretending to be a 15 year old boy. I mean come on now. It was very distracting and the acting was horrible. In just couldn't take the story or the voice. 
 One more grumble. There is no Pitticus Lore. The author is actually James Frey. Sound familiar? Yea, he's the fake drug addict from one million little pieces. Just another reason to not read this.

And the bad guys who are after him are straight out of bad-guy-in-campy-sci-fi flicks... dressed in black, with white faces and sharp teeth. Oh, and they have monsters with them! Big scary monsters that want to kill you. Luckily a little collaboration amongst teen friends (somehow) saves the day. It gets kind of garbled at the end. Kapow! Bang! Crash! Hooray we won!

I read this one because of the catchy title and premise. Meh. If I'd read this when I was twelve, and if I'd been a boy, I probably would've liked it a lot. If you get much into the sci-fi genre at all, you'll pretty much have read this story lots of times before too long. I recommended it to my 13-year-old nephew, though, because he'll zip through it, and the protagonist is relatable. 
 I was pretty annoyed by the time I realized that this was not a stand-alone book, but the beginning of a probably way too long series. The author's dippy pseudonym should've tipped me off, but I was flying home from Hawaii and not paying attention. Kindle recommended it for people who enjoyed The Hunger Games Trilogy Boxset, but it's not in the same league.

I smell a huge rant coming on... 
 The synopsis was okay. It was intriguing, dark, mysterious, and it didn't spoil anything. Unfortunately, the actual book was nothing like that. First of all, I didn't like the characters. At all. John was as plain and as boring as his fake name. So was his straight white hot popular kind sweet girlfriend with an equally awful name: Sarah. I couldn't find a way to relate to these kids and, trust me, I tried. 
 I also disliked the fact that the write dragged the action until the last 65 pages. Why? And the action had basically no climax, no interesting stuff, no good parts, and, what's more, it turned worse when the dog turned into...what was it again? A bird? A dragon? 
 The storyline and the idea was just as bad. 9 alien(ish) kids are sent to Earth to...well, to generate Pittacus Lore's story. They are under some kind of spell that only allows them to be killed in the order of their numbers. The first three are dead and-guess who's next? The main character (No. 4) is only stressed about this "next to be killed" thing only a few chapters, because then he falls in love and forgets about it all and Lore kind of just ignore it through the book. 
 Now the worst part of them all: the style of Lore's writing. 
 It sometimes takes a little time for me to get used to a certain style of writing, but Lore's was just unacceptable. I got used to F. Scott Fitzgerald and to James Dashner and even to Garcia Marquez and I thought I could get used to any style. But I was wrong. The book had no emotion from the beginning to the end and it didn't make me feel anything at all. The characters didn't feel real, the words they spoke were so unnatural and every single sentence sounded as if it were written either lazily or in a hurry (not to mention the very frequent typos). The idea was kind of good (not that good, though), but freaking teenage authors could've written it better. Even I> could've done it better (and I suck at writing). 
 The only acceptable parts were two characters that actually felt okay to me: Sam and No. 6. I liked Sam because he was passionate about aliens and he was the geek of the school. I also liked 6 for the fact that she was quite different from the other alien dudes. But still, these characters seemed a little forced. 
 Conclusion: Twilight but with aliens and flying dogs

When it comes to the books I read, or any media for that matter, it can be difficult for me to separate the author''s personal beliefs from the book they create. Or, in this case, make that authors. Pattacus Lore is a character in the book, that actually is also a pseudonym for the team of writers that apparently wrote this book. A man named James Frey managed to assign the basic concept of I am Number Four to a team of writers specifically for writing the next big literary/film hit like Twilight or Harry Potter. Based on the first film's reception, I doubt that is going to happen any time soon, but still, I find this reprehensible. At least Twilight and even Fifty Shades of Gray came from some kind of creative premise based on the idea that the authors wanted to write because they enjoyed it. Here, they are writing a story just to make a multi-million dollar franchise and nothing more. Sure, Myer and James probably aren't sorry that they are making tons of money, but they wrote the things they wrote because they wanted to. They saw an opportunity to tell a story they wanted to write that they thought people wanted to enjoy. This, on the other hand, wants to make money off you at the beginning, and that is what I find to be so insincere about this series. 
 Anyway, all that aside, how was the book itself? Not very good. It feels like a book that has so much potential only to be wasted by writing for the most common denominator. We have to reach the common school boy, so let's not write about the possibility of going to another world completely different from ours. Let's write about a boring school in the middle of Ohio. We have to have a character that our audience can relate to, so we will make him be a normal guy with alien superpowers named John Smith. He has a boring nerdy friend who, of course, is into aliens. And he has a romance with one of the most boring romantic leads since Bella Swan: Sarah. All of these characters are cardboard cutouts, and have little personality in the way they are written to make them distinguishable from a thousand other characters I've seen. 
 Then there is the narrator for the audiobook. As I was listening to this, I could not help but think that this guy was greatly miscast. Perhaps he was only chosen because he can do a french accent for Henri, but the rest of the time, his voice feels grossly out of place. He would work in a kind of action thriller, but not here in a YA novel. 
 Another element that I find kind of annoying is the difference between the perceived audience that this book is for and the actual audience. When I started reading this book, the writing seemed to dictate the audience was for a middle grade audience. It featured many simple choppy sentences complete with bland sentences that had little originality or creativity to them, but were ones that a middle schooler may like. Then a character would say a swear word, you know one of those words you'd get in trouble for saying in class, and I would be forced to bump up the age limit. This disconnect between the writing style and the age limit does not sit well with me. 
 As for the plot, that is boring too. It goes for long times of seemingly nothing happening. Just boring conversations between John and Sarah. Then, probably because the writing team decided they had to add in action somewhere, there is a scene where John is forced to use his powers, and then back to the boring scenes again. This repeats itself too often, to the point where I wondered why this book had to be so long. It easily could have been 50 to 100 pages shorter and I would have been fine with it. 
 It is this reason why I give it a two out of five. Although I can see the potential with this series, I just am not up for reading it. That, and the message that this book stands for is one I can't accept. In terms of series to continue, this series is number zero.

I don't know how to properly rate this book. In one hand, I enjoyed the story, the plot was good and the characters were brilliant. On the other hand, I think I would have enjoyed it more if I have read it before the Throne of Glass series. Why? Because the plot outline of the two books are practically similar(I would list them all when I have the time to make a full review). But I cannot say that this book is just a replica of Throne of Glass since this was published 7 years before ToG. So, which one had the idea first, really? 
 So yeah, I rated Poison Study ignoring the fact that the plot didn't seem quite original to me anymore since I read ToG first. It's a good story. I would have had better experience if I did not have an idea as to what the mystery was, but then I really enjoyed the writing style even when I can already predict what's to come. It's addicting to read and half of the time, I wanted grab food while eating because all those description of food and tasting got me drooling. 
 Anyway, I'll give 4/5 stars. Full review and comparison of outlines with Throne of Glass will be up soon. Promise!

reference_books.title: Angelfall (Penryn & the End of Days, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Wings on the cover and Angelfall as title. This book screams angelic presence. So I was expecting the typical Angels of God story or at the very least, fallen angel-ish--something along the lines of Hush Hush. That's how I got it all wrong. 
 In Angelfall, angels are not the spiritual beings of god that would bring eternal peace and harmony on earth. They are the exact opposite. The world was on the brink of permanent destruction and the angels are behind it. They swooped down in all their mythical glory and waged war against mankind, wreaking havoc and ruining everything in their path. 
 Penryn's family is one of the many who struggles to live on despite the harrowing condition of the world that they were left in. But their situation is a little bit difficult compared to others. With a mother who may be mentally challenged and a seven year-old crippled & wheelchair-bound sister, Penryn's lot isn't exactly the ideal survivalist. 
 One night as they were on the run, they witness an unusual sight--a group of the feared creatures ganging up on another angel and ripping his wings. Things got so much worse when these angels spotted Penryn and her family. In a blink of an eye, one of them caught her sister and took off. With no one to turn to, Penryn strikes a deal with Raffe, the angel who got his wings clipped. The unlikely comrades then went on to save Penryn's sister from the hands of the cruel angels, but in doing so, they might just reveal darker secrets even worse that the apocalypse. 
 --------- 
 So, Angelfall. Wow. Just wow. From the moment I read the first page, I immediately got hooked. The writing is addicting and kept me flipping through the pages like a madman. The world-building was fantastic and so vivid, I can easily picture the surroundings and places depicted in the story. It's as though I was part of the scene itself. Aside from details that are very much feast for the senses, the characterizations were also amazing. 
 Penryn is one of the best female protagonist written for someone who doesn't have any supernatural abilities. I just love her strong-willed personality. Despite having such a problematic family and an entire world full of despair, she was not the typical whiny and irritating character. There wasn't any line in this book where you hear her complain of her situation. Her pure love and care for her family brought out best in her. She was head-on with the clear goal to save her family and help them survive. It was so easy to pine for her because her personality was so admirable. She has a lot of common sense and that pure dedication to fight on in spite of life's trouble. 
 As for Raffe, I was so impressed with his character's uniqueness. I mean, where have you ever read about an agnostic angel, questioning the existence of the supposed almighty one? I thought that he would be the over-cliched angel: gorgeous, super strong, sex-god seductive guy. But I was so wrong. Yes, there might have been VERY subtle indications of his connection to Penryn but it was not anything like what I've read before in young adult books. He was stubborn, sensible, loyal, caring, and understanding. Every exchange between him and Penryn got me laughing my ass off the couch. Their personalities clashed but in a good way. 
 And that was another thing I seriously devoured in this book: the relationship between Penryn and Raffe. It was slow and progressed subtly, building up as they get to know each other throughout different circumstances. Their conversations irked me because at times, I feel like they are going to end up killing each other due to their arguments. But then it would segue to a very witty and comedic banter. Romance was not the main focus of the book but you know that it's there. It's like a tiny subplot that slowly surfaces as the story went on. It gets you thinking if there really is something for them in the end. And it works so well because readers were left to decipher what's going on between them. 
 Aside from that relationship, I also marvel at the relationship between Penryn, her mom, and her sister. Their family is the epitome of dysfunctional. As I've said earlier, her mom is somewhat on the verge of lunacy. She may actually be the reason behind her sister's unfortunate accident, leading to her disability. The descriptions of her in the book creeped me out like hell. She was supposed to be the mature one, expected to care for her family and yet, her mind was so dark and demented that it almost destroyed the dynamics of their family. That, coupled with a crippled sister, made the whole set-up one-of-a-kind. It was unstable, somehow, it worked. And I loved them. 
 I also applaud Susan Ee for such wondrous side characters. Obi, the Dee-Dum twins, the other angels.. all of them added to the air of mystery in the book. We are given snatches of their personalities that left me intrigued and wanting to know more of their life story. 
 And finally, what got me praising this book like crazy is the plot itself. It was so mysterious and full of surprises. It was so so dark and twisted causing a hell of goosebumps to erupt while reading. I can assure you that it was intensely disturbing and gruesome. The writing was so intricate that images are imprinted inside your head while reading, and it's scary beautiful. The book was deliciously honest in showing the worst sides of everyone. Readers are shown the best and the worst of humanity as the hope to live becomes thinner as time goes by. It's simply irresistible because it breaks the norms of typical angel stories out there. I swear, this books is worth it. 
 Aaaaaand one last thing, my respect for the author just leap up a hundred times more when I learned that this books is actually self-published. I mean, how cool is that?! It is such a good book that I am surprised that publishers didn't kill each other over the rights for this. 
 So.. for this book, I give it a 4.5/5. Sorry for the half point short, I just wanted more of that cliffhanger ending.

reference_books.title: Confess
reference_books.review_text:
Exact Rating: 2.5/5 
 Well, that was disappointing. I finally found the streak breaker of CoHo books for me. It's actually more of a personal preference, and I can see why a lot of people may love this book. I guess it wasn't for me. 
 I just didn't like the dynamics of the relationship between Owen and Auburn. No chemistry, so rushed and it felt a bit more of a physical attraction than anything else. 
 And I didn't like how weak Auburn was with the Trey issue. She knew that something wrong was going on, and yet she just let it all happen. It was so annoying. Generally, I didn't like how Auburn was written as a female character. 
 I also didn't like the male protagonist in the story. For me, Owen was just all sorts of creepy. He doesn't know how to respect personal boundaries. I also felt uncomfortable about how he developed feelings for Auburn. 
 Also, I felt kinda iffy with the insta-love aspect, as I do with all other books with insta-love. I just find it a bit hard to believe how intense their feelings built up after the course of merely 24 hours. 
 Oh another factor could be that I had such high expectations for this since I loved all of her other books. I read everything she wrote before Confess and I gave them either a 4/5 or a 5/5 star rating. 
 And then there were these eye-roll inducing moments: 
 "She could walk into a room full of depressed people an all she would have to do to heal them is open a book and read out loud." 
 --Seriously?? Depression isn't as easy as that. 
 "And I need you to remember that anyone can make love. But I'm the only one who deserves to make love to you." 
 --Wow. Just. What the hell. 
 "Say it. I want to hear you tell me I deserve you." 
 --??? That sounds so creepy. 
 He presses his palm against my heart. "And no one else deserves to be inside you if they can't get through here first." 
 --Is that supposed to sound romantic? Because I don't think so. 
 The novel also felt so rushed. They were so many things the author could have explored more on like the backstory of Auburn and Adam. I mean, she didn't even explain the reason why Adam died (don't worry, this isn't a spoiler. This is actually in the prologue). 
 The only redeeming qualities I found in Confess was the artworks by Danny O'Connor and the character, Emory. 
 So yeah, still think Ugly Love and Hopeless are the best CoHo books. 
 P.S. Don't kill me with hate, CoHorts. This is just MY opinion.

reference_books.title: The Hunger Games (The Hunger Games, #1)
reference_books.review_text: It was a refreshing read. Different from all the vampire stories that are scattered everywhere. It a book about bravery, courage and confusion due to love. It was a good read, though the ending did not meet my expectations. It's a good thing that there is a sequel to the story.

reference_books.title: Fifty Shades of Grey (Fifty Shades, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Despite reading a lot of negative reviews from different sources, I started reading Fifty Shades of Grey last night. It's not that I actually liked the premise I got from the summary, no. I am just curious about what really is the reason behind such disappointment. Plus there are also a number of people who gave it positive responses. And so I gave it a try, just to know if it's a good book or not. 
 I wasn't even past a hundred pages when I decided to stop reading. I am not a conservative nor innocent regarding the issue of sex, but this novel is just too graphic for my taste. I know it's categorized as erotica but the book just seem to have no other substance other than the sex. As I've said a few times before, I do watch porn and it doesn't bother me. But then for a book to have this great deal of detailing, I just cannot handle it. It's basically porn made into a book. The characters were so perverted and cannot seem to think of anything but sex. The lead character blushes at the slightest sexual reference, getting so lost in her dirty imaginations. I tried browsing to see if the story would change or the sex would somehow get toned down, but no. So I guess I don't really want to continue reading more sexual expeditions since the scenes were a bit cliche. And did I mention that the words in th ebook as so repetitive? I was like "Uhm, excuse me? Can't you think of other words and expressions to use?" 
 Also, aside from that, even if I ignore all the sex--after all, it's tagged as an erotica--I still feel that somehow, all the elements in the book are wrong. It promotes domestic violence and it romanticizes sexual abuse. It disguises such horrid things, letting people think it's normal and desirable. It's practically hiding rape culture behind the tag 'romance', which is so wrong. It gives people the wrong notion about consent. It's gross and seriously, people should be worried that kids, yes, KIDS are wanting to read this. 
 For me, it seemed ridiculous. It's like a peek on the diary of a man's desperate sexual fantasy. It's like reading a porn blog. Actually, scratch that. I think it's worse than a porn blog. In the porn industry, people get consent. In this book, the notion of informed consent is completely twisted out of proportion. I think the people who loved the story has a serious problem. I mean, it's a bit offensive, I'm sorry, but it's true. A lot of people would hate me for this but I think this book was better off as the fanfiction it was before. I just wish there is some restriction as to who can purchase the book. I think I don't like the idea of 13 year-olds getting the hands on this book and reading it. All in all, I think this kind of book isn't really my cup of tea. 
 And I put it in the "read" category even though I haven't finished it and probably won't. But where else would I put it? I cannot put it in "currently reading" or "to-read" seeing as both I refuse to continue reading and definitely not going to do so again.

reference_books.title: My Name Is Memory
reference_books.review_text:
Ann Brashares is best known for her young adult series, The Sisterhood of the Travelling Pants. I have read those books and quite enjoyed them way back. So when I saw this book, I thought to myself that it might be good. After all, it is tagged as an adult book, and the premise in the summary is interesting enough. 
 And that's where I got it all wrong. From the first few chapters, it felt like another young adult book due to its overly written prose of the characters' love and feelings. It's just too much and I think that it would be better if the author left something for the reader's own discernment. In short, the writing was so detailed that it became so uninteresting. I was so bored that it's a miracle I even finished the book. 
 Also, I felt that the attraction between Daniel and Lucy is too shallow. Even during their first encounter in their past life, I could not quite believe that Daniel fell in love with her the moment he saw her in the burning house. I mean, call me a non-believer of love at first sight, but I really think that it is a very superficial thing. And then there's Lucy obsessing over Daniel without even knowing anything about the guy. I just think that their love lacks enough substance. 
 I also had a problem with the perspectives. The book was alternating with time elements and with Daniel and Lucy's point of view. But then I cannot discern which voice is which. The writing style is very much similar that without the help of the names, I would have a hard time knowing whose narration it was. Daniel's lack the masculinity and felt way more sensitive and contemplative than Lucy's. He was so lost in his past that he could not appreciate his present life. Lucy's perspective, on the other hand, is too shallow. She is so much engrossed with her feeling with Daniel that I wanted to skip pages so badly. 
 All in all, I think this should have been a young adult book for it would appeal to those who want mushy romance books. It's like Twilight without the vampire stuff. This book would have been more appreciated by younger and more innocent readers. I would have liked it if I read it when I was a freshman or sophomore high school student. I was really disappointed with how it turned out to be.

reference_books.title: The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender
reference_books.review_text:
This book is just so lovely. It's haunting and sad, yet it's magical effect is something I marveled in. The title is so true to its content. It's one of those books that are hard to forget, with characters and events that would deeply burrow into a reader's heart. 
 This book is magical realism at its finest, and I would even dare to compare it with the beauty that it The Night Circus by Erin Morgenstern. Although it is not as grandiose, the air of mystery and surrealism surrounding the story is almost at par with The Night Circus. 
 I think, when I look back and remember this story, there would only be this hollow ache inside me because of the sadness it has delivered through its hypnotic and lyrical prose. It's one of those stories wherein almost everything in it feels so dark and heavy, yet you can't help but read on. 
 Despite the absurdities and strangeness of a lot of the characters and events in this book, it was all too honest and real when it comes to depicting life, love, tragedy, pain, and change. It was all too believable how it mirrors the truths we encounter in life, and it made me love the book even more. 
 Needless to say, I absolutely fell in love with Ava Lavender and her peculiar family. 5/5 stars.

reference_books.title: Cruel Beauty (Cruel Beauty Universe, #1)
reference_books.review_text: OKay, those last few chapters really effed me up. I was so confused of what was happening and it took me a while to realize it. Full review will be posted tomorrow, I'll just get some sleep now. Haha.

reference_books.title: Ugly Love
reference_books.review_text:
Painful. Heartbreaking. Breath-taking. Beautiful. Perfect. 
 These are the only words I could utter when I reached the last page of this book. I was so lost and overwhelmed with the story and I was incapable of doing anything else but stare into nothingness. 
 This is the first book I've read of the New Adult genre. I really don't know what to expect since I have no idea what this genre contains. And boy, I guess picked the best one to start with. Colleen Hoover was amazing. I don't know if all her books are as beautifully written as Ugly Love, but one thing is for sure, I'll be looking out for her other works. 
 Okay, to the story now. From the books babble, we know that this is a friends-with-benefits kind of story. Tate Collins move in with her brother and the guy living next to their apartment, Miles Archer, is her Mr. Interesting. And then things happen, blah blah blah. From the start, I know for a fact that along the way, one of them is going to have feelings way more than what their set-up expects them to have. Let's face it, this is the usual course of this type of scenario. It's basically cliche. 
 If you've known me, you'll probably ask why I read this since I hate cliches. Well, honestly? The writing and the characters were that good that I kept on reading. Yes, the main theme is cliche, but the story is not entirely predictable. The twists along the way were unexpected and so wonderfully crafted. The book was written in two-person narrative, each with in a different timeline. I guess this worked so much in this book because it lead to a gradual build-up of the story and the climax was so beautiful. What I thought to be a shallow story took on a different path. Suddenly, I was blasted with characters' difficult issues which--I believe--if were to happen to me, would be impossible to face. It was so realistic. I may not have the same experiences as the characters but the writing made it so that I can feel how it was to be in their shoes. 
 And I know that some people hate the book because of the author's use of the female character. Some believe that her personality degrades the female gender. But honestly, I think she was Tate was such as strong female character. She know what she wants and yes, maybe her feelings get in the way of her rational thinking, but she owns up to her decisions. She never put blame on anyone but herself because she understood that it was her actions that cause such repercussions. So what if she wants sex from a guy she barely know? Guys do that all the time, and judging her for it is such a double standard. She knew what she was doing and made her own choice. And that for me is a perfect example of a strong woman. 
 Now let's focus on my favorite male character of mine, Corbin, Tate's brother. Though he was not a particularly prominent character in the book, I love how his small part depict such a perfect portrayal of brotherly love. He and Tate were very close and it was obvious how much they care for each other. Corbin was the typical silent types, he doesn't talk to Tate much but he shows, in his actions, how much protective of Tate he was. His display of authority over Tate was so enviable that I want an older brother for myself. 
 What I love most about it is that it tackled real-life issues that are so common, yet are considered taboo by many. It's not an original plot for I believe there are many other movies and books that deals with people stuck in past, people trying to move on or people who makes such bad decisions in life. But this is the book that did it for me. It was so complete, there was total closure, full view of each others' perspective, and an honest display of human emotion. It was so believably real and perfect for me. 
 I also love how the book was so sexually graphic yet it was not it a way that it consumes the whole novel. You cannot even consider it an erotica despite how detail some scenes were. Sex was not its selling point. You will get hooked way before feeling the hot flushes caused by the passionate scenes. I cannot completely describe how good these parts were. It's not written in a perverted sense, it's more of a display of their emotions through physical gestures. It was a great read. 
 After reading the book, I was positive that Ugly Love is the perfect title to describe everything in it. It was such an emotional roller coaster that left me struggling for breath at some point in the book. It was sexy, passionate, strong, powerful, painful, heart-breaking, and satisfying all at the same time. It's one of the books that conjured up such emotions that I literally needed a break from reading. This is a true 5/5 for me and may even be the best book I've read so far this year.

reference_books.title: Beautiful Disaster (Beautiful, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Well.. at least part of this book's title lived up to it. It's a complete disaster. I can't believe how much eye rolls I've made while reading it and I only finished it because I was already halfway through and I can't stand not knowing how it ends, no matter how much the story sucked. 
 Cliched. Full of irritating characters. Toxic and violent relationship. I just want to smack some sense into the characters. The story is so whacked and disturbing. I could not fathom seeing the events in this book in real life. I just don't like the fact that the book shows such shallow regard for boundaries. I was so uncomfortable with how the characters cannot grasp the simple aspect of "no means no" because they were so caught up with their emotions. 
 I have read other books that tackled issues regarding anger management, obsession, and violence in ways so much better than this book had.

book_a.title: These Broken Stars (Starbound, #1)
book_a.user_review:
DNF at around page 190. 
 I'm sorry. I have nothing against the authors of this book. But I tried to finish it and I really just can't. The story did not interest me at all. I was hoping to have feels similar to what I felt while reading Across The Universe by Beth Revis but I was just disappointed. I expected an action-packed thrilling space adventure.. but no. Plus the cover is so gorgeous that I really though it would be one of those awesome books. But I guess I was wrong. 
 From the synopsis, I thought the book was going for a sci-fi-ish path. I thought it would be all space and technology, etc. But all I get was half Titanic-in-Space and half a desert/forest journey, which really bored me. I am already halfway past through the book, and there isn't much going on with the story. The pacing was too slow that it felt like a drag. Usually, I would try to finish a book that I don't find really appealing but with this, I just gave up. 
 I also had a hard time connecting with the characters. It feels like I have read the all before. Their personalities were as cliched as it can be: a spoiled rich girl used to getting everything she wanted plus a low-class military boy who's trying to prove himself equals star-crossed lovers. *sigh* 
 Also, Lilac was a bitch. I mean, there may be some redeeming qualities like her badass-ery in technical stuff and all that mechanic thingy. But even for a rich girl, she's too whiny and annoying. What started as an adorable stubbornness turned out to be just a first-class pain-in-the-ass bitch fit. I can't stand her. 
 As for Tarver, I actually liked him in the beginning but as I was getting to know more about him, he just seemed like this love-crazed guy who cannot think straight and just.. he was always taking note of Lilac's appearance which just made me barf. 
 All I did while reading was to roll my eyes because of the characters or the plot, if not, I would just sigh loudly. I'm sorry, but I was really hoping to love the book since a lot of my friends enjoyed it. I guess, this is one of those hyped books loved by everyone except me and few others.

sample_reviews.review_text:
** spoiler alert ** 
 This book is ehhh. 
 The book is really predictable. I don't feel any sense of excitement or anything but the question, What? always pops up in my head. I really like the characters though. How their relationship grows throughout the book is good but Liliac is such an asshole before. I understand the part of her story and how she lost her boyfriend and stuff. I don't feel like reading the last two books of the series because I feel like it might represent the same idea. I would probably try but oh well!

Jesus a fifth of the way through and I couldn't stand it anymore. I hate him/her but oh they're so pretty. The voices of the characters doesn't match their dialogue and Tarver definitely doesn't sound like the Tarver being debriefed/interrogated (whatever is going on between chapters). And everything happens so slowly, the parts with "action/suspense" not even quickening the pace of the plot. This just makes me want to stray from YA even more. 
 I tried, but this book is ridiculous.

This book would have been a five star read for me if it wasn't for something that happened near the end. 
 Firstly I want to talk about how much I loved Lilac and Tarver both separately, and together. I found both to be entertaining, and although both did annoy me at certain bits, I understood where their choices and decisions came from. I loved the chemistry the pair had, and I like the slow burning romance at first ( although I wasn't too sold at the end with how much they depended on each other). 
 I loved the alien planet in the novel, and I loved how intriguing the mystery around it was, however I found the reveal to be a bit meh, and I'm still confused about a certain event that occurred near the ending of the novel. 
 Overall it was a pretty special book, and although I kinda fell into a slump for a week, I'm glad I stuck through it till the end. 
 I can't wait to continue the series and get to meet the other couples, although they'll have to be amazing to top Tarver and Lilac.
What in the heck did I just read, and when can I read the next one?

What happens when you mix the wealthiest heiress in town with a handsome major who has been stationed on another base and doesn't know that she is off limits? Trouble and even more so when there is an accident that forces the two of them to flee a spaceship in distress and find a terra-formed planet where they appear to be the only survivors. The plot is very inventive and we have the budding romance that can't happen with the very real possibility that they may be the only people there for each other. Lilac LaRoux proves to be much more capable than we think a spoiled teen would be and Major Tarver Merendsen feels much more likeable and vunarable than we think he will be. The book is broken up with sections of Tarver's testimony so their survival seems a forgone conclusion. There is a paranormal link as well with Lilac's ability to hear whisperings that guide them but pull them into something they may not want to discover. Not for the preteens as there are adult situations but they are handled well. I was fortunate to get an advance of this book which is due to be published in early December.

What a wonderful, wonderful sci-fi book. Definitely one of my new favorites. I would rather give this a 4.8 for the typical "survival, stranded with a lover" plot but I love the eeriness of it. Very suspenseful and thrilling!

I'm hoping that books taking place "in space" will become the new IT thing to do in YA literature because I am a sci-fi girl at heart (and I'm kind of sick of dystopian novels). True, much of this book takes place after the main pair -- Tarver and Lilac -- have crash landed on a mysterious planet, so they're not exactly in space, as it were, but still. Yay for space books. 
 This book is extremely engrossing. There are so many mysteries to be solved: what are "the whispers" that keep tormenting Lilac? Why was the planet terraformed and then abandoned? What happened to the Icarus (the ship)? Some of your questions will be answered by book's end, but that only succeeds in raising more. I'm terribly curious as to the society in which these two belong. There is mention of colonies, and Tarver is in the military -- are the colonists revolting? Are colonies at war with each other? None of this information is deemed important in the grand scheme of things, and it's certainly not something with which Tarver and Lilac care to concern themselves, considering the circumstances, but I would like to know. 
 I'm quite enamored of Lilac, who seems to be a very complex character. She's not pigeon-holed into one particular category, as most female characters tend to be. Right off the bat we learn that she plays a role, acting like a spoiled princess in public and secretly fascinated by mechanical things. I appreciated that Tarver's surprise at her mechanical knowledge wasn't down to her being a girl, or even a pretty girl, but rather that she is such a public figure it didn't occur to him that she could have a hidden side. I also appreciated that Lilac's mechanical knowledge didn't make her into some perfect character -- she still had flaws and little to no survival knowledge, but she developed as they went along. 
 I wasn't quite as in love with Tarver. He's a fine person, I like him well enough, but he seems to be a fairly straightfoward character, which made him not quite as interesting to read about. As the book progresses, you can see him changing his opinions, going against preconceptions, and that was great. I like that he trusted Lilac enough to do the things he didn't have the knowledge for, and it was nice that he still treated her civilly after she humiliated him on the observation deck of the ship at the beginning. 
 Their relationship was, I thought, nicely done. It didn't feel shoe-horned in, as a lot of relationships in YA novels tend to be. They found each other attractive at first, which is why he approached her on the ship, but they didn't experience inexplicable feelings of attachment after only one glance. Instead, their relationship grew out of their circumstances -- thrown together in a harsh environment and dependent on each other for survival, their relationship naturally progressed. Granted, it progressed at a more accelerated timeline than normal, but I think that's down again to their circumstances. 
 I enjoyed this book immensely and am eagerly anticipating the next book in the series. Also, as a side note, the cover is GORGEOUS. Even if I hadn't heard so many good things about this book before purchasing, I probably would have picked it up based on the cover alone.

Well paced and well rendered, but I found myself skimming through a lot of the internal stuff after a while -- OK WE GET IT YOU'RE IN LOVE WITH HIM/HER BUT YOU'RE NOT SURE HOW HE/SHE FEELS IN RETURN. Also, those little scenelets of interrogation got super old super fast. But, all told, it was good. I like Lilac and Tarver. Yay.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The cover of this novel is gorgeous. I was tempted to buy a hardcover just because it's so pretty. I'm glad I didn't!! The cover and the first couple chapters are pretty much the only good thing about this novel. I was excited going in, but disappointed and annoyed by the end. 
 I don't think I've ever seen such shoddy world building. And I'm not a stickler about world building. Just give me something. If there are a few holes, I'll fill in the blanks. But there were so many things in this book that just didn't make any sense at all, and they seemed to be there for no apparent reason except the authors decided it was so. I'm going to try not to get too in depth with this, because I could go on for awhile, but an example or two... 
 The upper class apparently have balls and wear corsets and big ball gowns and tails and top hats. They have rooms that are replicas of early 1900 architecture and even lighting. The Icarus was essentially the Titanic in space. But they have tons of money and electricity and hover trays and all kinds of technology. So why is there wardrobe and way of interacting with each other reversed back to over a hundred years ago? No one knows. Meanwhile the peasants wear like jeans and stuff but they have no electricity and live very primitively. Except like Tarver's mom and dad who were a poet and a college professor by trade. If they were as rural and "backwoods" as Tarver portrayed them wouldn't they have been small farmers or laborers? Anyway, basically nothing added up. I couldn't ever figure out why the lower class would have no electricity. They didn't seem to be all that poor and certainly weren't downtrodden or starving. I also couldn't figure out if the upper and lower classes even shared the same planets. 
 On the planet that Tarver and Lilac crash on, there is ONE mountain lion and that's it? If the planet was abandoned and mountain lions are the only predator wouldn't it be overrun? Or wouldn't they have all died off because there is no mention of any other kind of animal except "small burrowing things" that didn't sound like they'd be enough to sustain mountain lions long term? Okay, two examples is enough. But there were a lot more. 
 After the big crash, which happens fairly quickly, the book is just Tarver and Lilac wandering alone on this abandoned planet. Nothing else really happens to them. It's not even an interesting, unique planet. They could have been wandering through any random forest down here on regular old earth, except they probably would have run across more predators. Up until about half way through I was interested and even intrigued. Then things started to get a little weird and ridiculous. There was so much potential for Tarver and Lilac to interact, bicker, learn from each other, grow as characters. But instead they just started to seem more and more flat the more time we spent with them. There was more chemistry between them in their first meeting than there was in the rest of the novel, in my opinion. I wouldn't classify their romance as a "slow burn" because really nothing was happening until almost the end when they finally decided "hey I found you attractive before and we've been alone for so long, now we're about to be rescued and split up again, let's get together while we can!" 
 I didn't like the way the "relationship" was handled at all. It all seemed so weird and arbitrary. They were attracted to each other for seemingly no reason. They had absolutely nothing in common. Neither one really had much of a personality at all. And if it was such a huge deal that no one think Tarver was involved with Lilac (like it could cost him his LIFE) why did they find it necessary to sleep together? Is it Science Fiction? YA Romance? A survivalist tale in a foriegn landscape? Yes. Blending all of these things together (okay the science fiction element was a bit light and more whoo-whoo science fantasy) These Broken Stars weaves a compelling tale of two teenagers crossing plains and mountains after the wreck of a spaceship. 
 Lilac is your average, daddy-is-powerful-space shipping-magnate socialite with a secret from her past that makes her rude and biting to boys to discourage their interest. 
 Tarver is a war-decorated soldier only a few years older, but massively more experienced in reality, and decidedly lower on the social totem pole. 
 They meet on the huge ship Icarus for a fleeting moment and both their lives are changed forever. 
 The biggest portion of the book is spent watching the inevitable toughening up of Lilac and the breaking down of the social and emotional barriers these two have erected as they face different challenges surviving in the wild with only minimum gear. And then there's the little problem of the voices Lilac starts hearing (and only she can) just as Tarver is beginning to like her. 
 The chapters are broken up with short sections of dialogue between Tarver and an anonymous interrogator, and some of the interesting tension is created as what we read happens doesn't jive with what he tells the interrogator. Something incredible, terrible, and wonderful happens on the planet before they are rescued, something more than just the YA kissing and touching, and Tarver and Lilac have to keep it a secret. 
 Mostly this is compelling because of Lilac's and Tarver's relationship. I mean, it's the whole "socialite falls in love with a soldier" kind of trope, but it's done so skillfully in both Tarver and Lilac's POV that you just want them to go on traveling the plains and exploring dark, emotional crevices of each other forever. 
 I also appreciate how they both end up saving each other multiple times, so Lilac isn't helpless. The author even turns her girliness into toughness by having her slog through forest in high heels and a cocktail dress! (and bear it without complaining despite the damage it does her) 
 Excellent romance, nice adventure with a bit of science fantasy to spice it up. There's some kissing and touching, but I would totally let my 5th grader daughter read it.as

4 1/2 Stars! These Broken Stars takes place on the Icarus, a Goliath spaceship owned by the powerful LeRoux. Lilac LeRoux is the treasured, pampered daughter of LeRoux who is traveling on the Icarus. As fate would have it, the Icarus goes down like the Titanic and Lilac herself in an escape pod with military hero Tarver Maresden, a man she publicly shunned. They find themselves stranded on an uninhabited planet, the sole survivors of the crash. Struggling to survive, the barriers of social class are broken as these two discover more about each other. In the process, the strange planet also holds secrets and a past that cries out for their help from another dimension. 
 This book really has it all...romance, science fiction drama, the over bearing, powerful father and adventure. I loved the chemistry between Tarver and Lilac and the way their misperceptions of each other were unraveled. There was a little lag in the middle of the book when I felt like the chemistry was lost and the story was just trudging along, but it picked up steam and the ending was worth the wait. Some of the sci-fi elements I felt were not completely explained, but I was okay with that since this story is really about the romance. Overall, very entertaining and a YA winner.

These Broken Stars 
 is a beautifully written story that will absolutely captivate you from beginning til' end. Incredibly heart stopping, you'll find yourself flying through the pages in no time at all. Aime Kaufman and Megan Spooner have definitely outdone themselves, with this shining wonder of splendor and beauty. The romance is just as timeless and gorgeous, as the characters themselves are. You'll find yourself falling for them the instant they are introduced. 
 Action packed and filled with danger and wonder, These Broken Stars, encapsulates everything that I love about a science fiction book. All of the elements come together so realistically and blend so brilliantly well together, it's hard not to love it. The adventure and romance between Tarver and Lilac is the best part of the book, in my opinion. I fell in love with the gorgeous chemistry between the two of them, the sheer intensity, of coming together and building slowly, only to be ripped apart again made it even more incredible. The world building alone, is absolutely phenomenal! It's rife with danger, action, and heart stopping moments that will have you on the edge of your seat. 
 Kaufman and Spooner have done a brilliant job at penning such an originally stunning and gorgeous novel. The complexity of this story alone, is enough to rouse your interest and keep you reading until the last page. If you are a fan of science fiction novels such as the amazing 
 Across the Universe 
 , then this is the book that you'll want to pick up and read. It is, without a doubt, one of my favorite books that I've read this year. The characters, the story, the romance...it's everything that I was expecting it to be and so much more.This is a book that is definitely not to be missed out on.

 However. The book suffers from the predictable love story syndrome. A predictable love story is not a crime on its own but OMG how boring was that? The conversations lacked humour and really did not make me fall for either of the leads. Trevor (I am aware that I failed to learn his name) and Lilac (LaRoux .... insert eye roll here) are characters that leave no impact on the reader. They're just meh.  Also, I could not understand how is it possible that Trevor (yes I am going to stick with using this name) is already a major. He spent two years in the military - two years - no one can possibly advance like that! What would his prospects for the next 20 years be!?!? And really that was the only thing that he had going for him. 
 Lilac is alright I guess but there is not a trace of originality in her. Maybe the weird name but that's hardly an advantage... 
 And then there is their endless walk across the planet. They walk, they argue, they hate each other, he saves her life, she turns out to be tougher than he initially thought. BOOOORING! It really is a struggle to keep following their pointless adventures until the end, until something actually is uncovered but let's be honest - its not mind blowing. I'm not going to put any spoilers here so I'll just finish with saying that I did not feel rewarded for my patience. 
 On that basis 1* only and I will not be spending my time on the next two books.

Imagine Star Trek meets Titanic. Have that image in your head? I'll give you a moment to process. 
 Kaufman and Spooner definitely drew from those sources for inspiration, but at no point in the story did it feel forced or fake. The plot was imaginative and compelling, but what captured me most as a reader was the strength of both Lily and Tarver. It is rare to find a narrative in which the weight of the story is successfully carried by only two characters, but Stars manages perfectly. There were romantic elements, as Lily and Tarver are drawn to each other from the beginning, but it was not a love story in the traditional sense. Stars is about survival, making peace with oneself, and finding the will to carry on when the world seems to be at its bleakest. It was also refreshing to encounter a book sans a love triangle, and one that hinted at dystopia without following in the footsteps of The Hunger Games or Delirium. Stars can hold its own among its YA fantasy counterparts. 
 You can read a longer review at An American in London. I, for one, want to read the next book in the series, even though it apparently has different protagonists!

In between each chapter are snippets of an interview between Tarver and some sort of integrator... which offers an interesting foreshadowing of the chapter to come, especially as you realize how deeply Tarver starts to lie.

I found the opposing opinions of the main characters especially in the beginning of the book so interesting, though at times I just wanted to hit them over the head and tell them to just talk to each other honestly already! 
 Really enjoyed it and I am looking forward to seeing how This Shattered World is related.

book_b.title: Never Never (Never Never, #1)
book_b.user_review:
After reading all of Colleen Hoover's books last year, I am so much looking forward to this new book--aside from Confess, which will be out on March. As I have said before(after I raved about Ugly Love, Hopeless, & Slammed series), I would read anything written by her. All of her previous books were written as contemporaries, either as young adult or new adult. So, reading Never Never came as a bit of a shock for me since it's somewhat different from her previous works. 
 First off, the summary itself was very vague: 
 Best friends since they could walk. 
 In love since the age of fourteen. 
 Complete strangers since this morning. 
 He'll do anything to remember. 
 She'll do anything to forget. 
 It gave nearly nothing as to what the story could be. It was such a tiny glimpse that it's almost impossible to picture a general plot. But I was intrigued enough to read it so I could know more about what the story could offer. And frankly, that was all it took. 
 Right of the bat, the story was full-on mysterious. From the very first paragraph, it was implicitly established that something peculiar was happening. There were two alternating narrators/POV, and both were very unreliable in a sense that both have no idea of the conflict that was thrown upon them. 
 And this actually worked for me. It was very refreshing to read something in which I am completely unaware of how everything would turn out. I have this thing where I more than likely to predict correctly the plot twists of books I read. Which sucks so much because it leaves me less interested to finish a book. But like always, Colleen Hoover never fails to amaze me with her plot twists. 
 Anyway, going back to the story, I think it's best for me not to reveal much of the plot since it would rob other readers of the complete experience. I would just like to share that I absolutely love the air of mystery surrounding the characters and the relationship between two protagonist. The two personalities were so different and contradicting yet it creates this connection that gave way to witty exchanges and hilarious banters, even in between arguments. 
 One thing that kept me wondering while reading: I cannot distinguish which author wrote which character. I am already very familiar with Colleen Hoover's writing, but it was next to impossible to discern which perspective she wrote. On the other hand, I have no idea of Tarryn Fisher's writing style, yet it blends so well with CoHo. It felt like I was reading a book written by only one author. Both POV has such similar feel and I guess that's good because they complement each other flawlessly. 
 Oh, and because it's Colleen Hoover (though I know that Tarryn Fisher owns half the credit), there were numerous spine-tingling romantic moments that got me squealing quietly at work, while I was sneakily reading during my off time. 
 One point of complain though is that since the book ended in such a cliffhanger, it felt so unfinished. Yes, I know that it is the first book in the series but even so, there weren't any resolutions at all. When I reached the final page, it felt like they forgot to print the later half of the book. The final reveal was only the beginning of the revelations, which didn't do much for an ending. It was like it ended at the climax. Well, anyway, this may be their plan to ensure that readers would pick up the next book. 
 Overall, Colleen Hoover & Tarryn Fisher still managed to surprise me with their work. I keep waiting for an obvious generic pattern for CoHo's plotlines (like with Sarah Dessen) & the only trademark I could attribute to her are the heart-wrenching plot twists, which always unfailingly catches me off guard. I'd give this one a 4/5--knocking off a star for that abrupt ending.

Holy COW. THAT ENDING! 
 Never Never feels so much longer than its short page count. The authors pack a ton of story in! There are mystery elements mixed with a little Romeo and Juliet. It's a book you won't want to want to put down. 
 What would you do if you suddenly woke up and remembered more about the Kardashians than your own life? What if you weren't sure you even liked your former self enough to want to remember? Never Never starts exploring these questions and lucky for us, we have two more books to answers the unknown.

I don't know why I thought there would be answers to my questions at the beginning of this book at the end of it. I REALLY, REALLY DON'T KNOW WHY I TRUSTED TARRYN FISHER and Colleen Hoover, but I'm not really much of a fan of Colleen Hoover, so. (Also, I know, unpopular opinion.) 
 So Never Never is a story about two 18-year olds who literally wake up in their bodies without any memory of anything in their lives in medias res (in the middle of things). The story opens with a girl, who jars into her existence in the middle of a crowded school room, with another girl tripped on the floor beside her. Our girl later on learns her name, Charlie Wynwood, from basically context clues around her. 
 And then she meets her supposed boyfriend at lunch, discovering that he too is suffering from a memory loss the same as hers. They both know nothing about their lives, but they do know the basics of living - like motor skills, trivial things, basically the little things that don't really say much about a person as a person. 
 Most of the time in the book, Silas and Charlie were the only characters in perspective. But as they get to know their world, the readers are also introduced to the characters along the side lines that should have been important to them, but they really don't know them either. The readers are only given enough to create a guess or actually, a skin-deep knowledge of everyone around them, but also a feel that there are a lot underneath that knowledge that will later come into major play. 
 The book doesn't really give you answers as to what are they suffering from, how did they get to that point of their lives, but it did give you everything that answers your questions on the periphery of the answers. If anything, that makes the story even more attractive - the mystery that nothing ever really answers, but you do get a lot of clues you don't know how to fit together. You know they do not answer you right now, but you also get the feeling that it's going to bite you in the ass sooner rather than later, and that makes me really, really stoked for the next installments! 
 Fisher and Hoover did a really flawless work with this one. As I writer, I do not really work well in collaborative projects, because I always end up sacrificing my inputs and ideas. I just don't know how to work well in group in the writing scene. So for me, it's really admirable to read such a collab work between two amazing authors. It's seamless and really engaging, and while reading it, I almost forgot that this is a work by two powerful minds. I am really humbled whenever I remember that fact. 
 Also, there is something to be said about combining the creative prowess of Colleen Hoover and Tarryn Fisher. I mean, I love, LOVE Tarryn Fisher because she writes so beautifully, and her stories are really captivating and emotionally fueled. But also is Colleen Hoover. Plus, remember Colleen Hoover is also the author of Slammed, which is a book about Slam Poetry. And in order to write about a book about Slam Poetry, of course, you're gonna be forced to write poems, and dear lord, if that doesn't establish Colleen Hoover's talent with words! 
 There are so many lines in the book that just jump out to me because of how beautifully they were written. But I'm not going to cite any in here because I really did not have the time to copy them, or even highlight them. I just stare at these lines, sighing at the beauty of the English language. And then proceed to kill myself with the mystery of the book. 
 The mystery of the book! So let's talk about that. At this point, after reading the first book, what we basically know, and this is not a spoiler, is that Silas and Charlie both lost their memory at the same time, know just same amount of trivial things, and it only happens to them (as far as the book infers). The book doesn't allude to anything, whether the cause is biological or anything, but the characters, or at least Charlie, lean towards the supernatural. And in that count, we were given at least one proof that there is something freaky going on. 
 Like I've said, we were only given enough things to paint the whole picture. Maybe like 15%. TBH. We do know that they are in a relationship, their families are tied together - in good terms and later in bad terms, but we really do not know exactly how in both accounts, and that they are (almost) star-crossed lovers. 
 SPOILER 
 kind of 
 just to be safe 
 I am going to speculate here, but what I am reminded of by Silas and Charlie is actually the greatest tragic couple of the literary world - Romeo and Juliet. They both have this epic love (which I am going to elaborate on in a few), and the feuding families. Granted, in the book, their families were partners first, but who's to say that they were really in good terms just because they were business partners. If anything, that makes it even more suspicious. 
 They were both obviously in love with each other, and this love, for them, almost feels like larger than them. As I've said, they were both from powerful and influential families. That in itself contributes to the feeling of self-importance to their relationship. It immediately puts them on a higher pedestal, but not level, than any other couple. 
 They are both teenagers, and they are both misguided. It is revealed that they really do not have the pretty trappings of love that most teenagers liked to believe they have. They both have difficult family situations on their own, and together an even messier one. They both have affairs, they cheat on one another. Basically, everyone around them don't believe on them as a couple. They are destructive with one another, but don't all powerful and encompassing epic love? 
 I feel like, in the perspective of these two teenagers in the midst of something that is definitely beyond them, everything is too real and too raw. There is also that extra layer of teenage mentality that everyone is out to get you, and I feel like it always factors into their relationship that I am kind of questioning whether if their problems before they lost their memories really hold enough water to be counted as significant in the grand scheme of things. There is an allusion of a big conspiracy in the book, but remove that, and focus on them as two people in one relationship. 
 (Idk. I still don't have enough things to actually talk about them as a couple from before. But I am really, really interested in knowing more about the them before their memory loss happened! They are certainly a great Flawed Character study.) 
 I guess what I'm really pointing out is, will their love be enough to be about them and not just because of their circumstances. Although, of course circumstances do really factor into anyone's relationship. But. At the very core, it should be just about them as human beings. About Silas the boy and Charlie the girl, and how they survive because they have this big, big thing inside them that just couldn't be contained. And without the trappings of their fancy lives, they are two people in a love that has been sung and written about since the beginning of history. 
 I don't know if my reading though stems from the book itself, or because I already know what I'm going into with these authors. Maybe the experience from reading them before adds bias and ~foreshadowing~ to my reading, but I'd say yeah. The previous experiences from them kind of make me wary of anything they write. It's not a bad thing. But I cannot say for sure how the book would read for anyone who doesn't know or haven't read the author before, either. It certainly would be an adventure to read both of them, in one powerful book, for the first time. :D Bless your soul, though.

 We all have certain expectations of all books, you want some to be fun, some to have amazing characters, etc., but my main request for any book is to make sense. Not for me to be familiar with everything (I mean I'm reading fantasy most of the time), but just to have an idea which makes sense, no matter what way it's been told. Well, this book failed even in that department. Go figure! 
 Before I Fall, anybody? For me this book seems like something I could say been there, done that story. I have read Lauren's book 4 years ago and at that time it was a really unique idea and the story. This certainly is not unique as the idea is basically the same, so there goes that. I'm not saying that that idea should be exclusive for one story, it's just if you're using it, well don't use it in the same way! There are some other things, as for characters who while being well developed (but let's face it CoHo and Fisher cannot fail in that department), still utterly annoying. I dunno for you but I never swore that much in my life, and suddenly all teenagers are swearing all the time! Then there is drama and more drama and even more drama, as you know it's all about drama. 
 What's there to read? Well this book starts with never and ends with never and there is little in between. Our main characters are high school students, and no this is not NA, but very YA! Their whole journey is to discover what's happening to them, when I knew what's going on from the page one, leaving little space for surprises. Don't get me started about cheating part, just DON'T! 
 Here is more? And you get all that within (only...barely) 100 pages of this book, not nearly enough space to give a full story. Bonus is a cliffy you get at the end which killed it. But then again as this in not a full book - more like a number in a serial which will get its next number but probably without me to experience it, I was not surprised.

A lot has been written about this book and the new trend toward erotic trilogies, starting with 50 Shades of Gray and ending -- well, no end in sight. 
 There's no such thing as a new storyline, of course. Every story has been retold many times, so on the surface there shouldn't be an issue about this new formula. In fact, of all the books in this new trend, I think 50 Shades is the least well written. Lots of painfully silly dialogue really ruined any merit I might have found in the story itself. 
 Release Me has a lot of the same elements: stinking rich, shockingly good looking guy, less(er) experienced good looking female with a feisty edge. He's jaded; she jolts him out of that. In this case, the millionaire has been keeping track of the woman he's falling love with for years and he manages a reintroduction when she's newly graduated and arrived in California for her first job. 
 In this version of the story, she's the one with the baggage that gets in the way. A truly horrendous childhood and resulting-self abuse, and trust must be won. 
 Which is done with the help of some very explicit sex. Pretty well written, mind you. 
 So as long as you're comfortable with the genre, go on ahead. It's far better written thatn 50 Shades, but I'm afraid that's the most I can say for it.
