I have dreaded reviewing this book. Dragged my feet, avoided sharing my disappointment....sigh. All of it. I LOVE Harry Potter. I love the book, I love how it is written....the characters, the magical world, how it is a gateway to get kids to fall in love with reading....LOVE IT. I have taught the first two books in class numerous times and melted every time I see my students bitten by the HP bug....but I was not as excited to read this book....it isn't written by Rowling, it isn't her characters....it isn't a novel....it isn't Harry Potter. It isn't. I don't care how you try to explain it....it didn't feel the same and it kills me that this book is now part of the Harry legacy. Gah. I tried my best to go into this book without any pretenses, but it is hard...I was excited to see the play write's interpretation...but the deeper I got into the play the more annoyed I became. 
 1) I don't feel like the play write truly understood JK's characters....I hated his interpretation of Hermione and Ron. Hermione is not that annoying....and Ron isn't the dumb guy that all the jokes are made on....I mean maybe in the movie? But not the characters I fell in love with! 
 2) The play write does NOT know teenagers....no teenager I have hung out with would hug his friend ESPECIALLY when no one is around...that's not how teens act. Nor how they talk....it really bothered me. 
 3) The end was obvious....the villain was obvious....JK is never obvious. 
 4) Just don't touch what is good. Please. I feel very protective of this world....write your own play about your own characters. 
 So....in the end....should you read it? Sure. Should you gush and love every second? No. It is not the same as the original books. This is a whole different world--- I shall pretend this is fan fiction that got published because he knew the right people....but it isn't the same and I am not inspired to go see the play....I prefer to let the characters live on in my imagination without being clouded by someone else's point of view.

 So, I give it two stars - It was ok.

Gaah I never thought I'd ever give anything related to Harry Potter 1 star and yet here I am. 
 SPOILERS BELOW 
 Now if you go in expecting another Harry Potter book, you will be sorely disappointed. If you go in expecting a play which borrows your favourite characters for a story, you'll probably still be disappointed considering JK Rowling's name is attached to this and you expect a certain level of clever writing from her. Alright so she didn't write the whole thing, she did give her stamp of approval. 
 Firstly, no one is in character. Yeah, sure 19 years have passed but there is so much incongruence it's just making my head hurt. I love Ron. I have always loved Ron. But it seems like they forgot how to write Ron. It reads like movie Ron and not book Ron. Do you not remember Ron Weasley who shared his family and home with Harry after only a year of knowing him? Do you not remember Ron who told Sirius that he would have to go through him before killing Harry, when he thought Sirius was a mass murderer? Do you not remember Ron who Hermione fell in love with because he remembered the house elves and went to warn them during the Battle of Hogwarts? But you know, whatever. Let's have Ron only for comic relief, who only thought about food and wore a gravy-stained napkin when his best friend's son went missing. Fuck you. 
 I get Albus. I get it, it can't have been easy being Harry Potter's son and living up to his name. I can understand his frustration and his anger. What I can't get is Harry's reaction to his son. Really, you really think Harry is going to tell him he wished Albus wasn't his son?? Are we basing Harry on his 5th year when he got mad at everything? It's so out of character for him. And don't give me the bullshit that JK Rowling obviously knows her own characters better, because if she did, no way would she treat Cedric like that. 
 Which brings me to Cedric. Cedric Diggory, the boy who was kind above all, became a Death Eater because he was humiliated during the Triwizard Tournament? Is this the same Cedric Diggory we are talking about who wanted a rematch because Hufflepuff won only because Harry fell off his broom? The one who wanted to be fair so told Harry about the Second Task? The one who wanted Harry to take the cup because he felt Harry deserved it more?? Okay, as long as we're clear. This is especially shitty, considering Hufflepuff has almost no other heroes. 
 What about how the only reason Ron and Hermione are together is because Ron got jealous about Krum?? What are you even on about?? 
 Yes, completely murder Draco's character, why don't you?? 
 The worst of all was the plot. The really weird bizzaro plot. Time- Turner? Is this even a plot? It sounds like those memes where people keep suggesting why didn't they just go kill Voldemort when he was a kid? The wacky plot had so many loopholes it'll make you laugh. 
 The only good thing was Harry confronting Dumbledore about leaving him in an abusive household for ten years. 
 Scorpius as a character was really good. He was funny and smart. 
 But the plot. Ugh. 
 My head hurts from all the bullshit. 
 tl;dr I've read fanfics by 15 years old with tighter plots and better characterisation.

Which is fine, I love a good FF as much as the next person, and if I had been reading this online somewhere I would have been like "What a cool fic!". It had it's flaws, but I don't expect fic to be perfect. HOWEVER this is not a fan fiction, this is CANON. And because of that, the flaws are less forgivable to me. And the fact that JK Rowling would sign off on this (or write it herself which is even worse), without even bothering to correct those flaws feels so low, and it makes me question if she even cares anymore. To release such an unthoughtful, unpolished, ridiculous story with the golden seal of "Canon" is a complete disservice to the fans. 
 Again, it was a fun read, and there were definitely things that I loved, but overall, I kind of just feel angry. 
 Spoilers Below: 
 First of all, the things that I liked: 
 1. I loved that Albus was in Slytherin. I loved getting to see a main character, and Harry Potter's own son, as validation that Slytherin is a valid house that real people, good people, can be part of too. 
 2. Scorpius Malfoy is a blessing on this world. He is a sweet kid and I love that he wasn't written as a mini-Malfoy prototype, but as his own unique character. 
 3. I love Albus and Scorpius together, and how they are able to be friends and accept each other in a way that Harry and Draco could never have done. *However, this comes with a negative as well, which I will discuss later. 
 4. DRACO MALFOY in this story was everything that I EVER wanted from him. I always wanted to see him as a redeemed, functioning, respected member of wizarding society, and this story gave me not only that, but it gave me a Draco who loves with ferocity and depth, and would do absolutely anything for the people he cares about. He behaves maturely and has clearly moved on from his past and who he used to be, and I LOVE that he was allowed to do that, because previous JKR statements about Draco's future have been quite unsavory to say the least. I appreciate that this story gave Draco the characterization he deserves. (And also the Dramione shipper in me can't get over him being on a first name basis with Hermione, and hearing Hermione say "Draco..." so many times, and Draco telling her that he mildly enjoys being bossed around by her, I was in DHR heaven.) 
 5. Harry's confrontation with Dumbledore's portrait was so satisfying. For the longest time we have had to struggle with the image we have of Dumbledore, and how complicated his relationship to Harry was. He was a hero, but he was also devious and manipulative, and Harry Potter has so many reasons to feel used, and to doubt whether Dumbledore ever truly cared for him. It was so so SO satisfying to see that confrontation happen, and for Harry to voice those things, and Dumbledore to admit to them, and for them to have that conversation, and then reconcile and end off in a place of understanding and love. Even though it was only a portrait, and obviously not the real Dumbledore, Harry needed that, and so did I. 
 And those are pretty much all the things that made me happy, so now here are my complaints: 
 1. So many things were just not thought out, and did not feel like they belonged in the HP world, or in these characters. I get that it's 20 years later so characters have grown and changed, so I don't expect them to be the same, but I do expect them to be likeable. I do not want to read a story that makes me dislike the characters who have been so important to me growing up. 
 Exhibit A: Harry and Ginny not letting their children have sugar? Annoying. 
 Exhibit B: Harry acting like an absolute child with his prejudice against a teenage boy he has never met, and Harry blackmailing a teacher into stalking/controlling his son for him. I get it, he had a parent panic attack, and he apologized for it later, but it made me feel sick. And Harry threatening Hogwarts?! "I'll come down on this school with all the power of the ministry behind me if you don't imprison my child for me"??!! What in the absolute fuck? Harry Potter, who loves Hogwarts more than anyone in the entire world, who sees Hogwarts as him home, as the place that saved him, as the place that he always belonged, THREATENING TO HURT HOGWARTS? There is no parent panic attack strong enough for me to believe that, or to make it not disgusting. 
 Exhibit C: Ron Weasley being some kind of characterless slapstick prop. Ronald Weasley is a great man, and a loyal and dedicated friend, and this story has reduced him to a food obsessed comic relief joke. If Albus had gone missing in a real Harry Potter story Ron would have been rushing to their aid to help find him, worried sick and ready to do everything in his power to bring his nephew back. But in this story we have a Ron who shows up ten minutes later with gravy on his shirt cracking a joke about he got lost in the kitchen on his way over. His nephew, his best friend's child, his sister's child, is missing and in danger and whoever wrote this story decided that Ron would not care. Fuck off. 
 Exhibit D: Ron giving Albus a love potion as a gift. I get that in the early HP books love potions are more of a joke thing and not really a serious issue, but you would think that after all these years of people pointing out how gross and rapey they are, and especially the inclusion of Tom Riddle's parentage showing the devastating effects of what happens when a love potion is used, JKR would backtrack on them a little? Like maybe just a little bit? Like maybe not make Ron Weasley, a boy who was slipped a love potion himself at Hogwarts and definitely DID NOT LIKE IT, give one as a back-to-school gift to a teenage boy? Like "Here ya go kid, ya know just in case ya wanna rape anyone this year!" It's gross. It's inappropriate. Why. 
 Exhibit E: Alternate timeline Hermione becoming the new Snape just because she didn't marry Ron. Please, if Hermione hadn't married Ron she would still be just as kick ass, just as kind, just as wonderful as she is now. Her morals do not rest on a man, they are her own and I am appalled that anyone would suggest that her not marrying Ron would first of all somehow prevent her from achieving her canon career path, and second of all, turn her into a woman who is rude and abusive to her students, calling them names and making fun of them the same way Snape bullied her when she was a student. Hermione Jean Granger would never. Fuck off. 
 2. I hated how this book tried to be funny, but just wasn't. The jokes were lame, the humor was slapstick, nothing had the witty, whimsical humor that the tone of HP rests upon. 
 3. *To go back to Albus and Scorpius's relationship, I thought it was annoying how it teased and baited at something more, but didn't have the balls to follow through. JKR already receives criticism for claiming Dumbledore as a gay character without actually following through with that "headcanon" and putting any representation into the actual text, so Albus and Scorpius being written with such language and imagery, and jealous confusion about each other talking to girls, only to still end up with their orientations not being explored or acknowledged is like, cool, here we go again. 
 3. And finally, I mean basically this story is just ridiculous in general. It reads like a fan fiction, and a really over the top one at that. It was like My Immortal pt.2. 
 Exhibit A: Trolley Witch, the spike handed guardian who throws cupcake grenades. I love the idea of the Trolley Witch having a sweet backstory, and being more than meets the eye, and being a guardian of the students...but come on. Spike hands? Grenades? Is this the wizarding world or a steampunk robot AU? I read that scene to my husband and he was like "Wow that sounds like a weird anime." I agree. Cool for a fan fic, too hokey for canon. 
 Exhibit B: That time Harry and Draco had a strange duel for honor in Harry's kitchen? "My son's better!" "No, my son's better!" "There's only one solution then...A DUEL!" OOOOKKKKK. 
 Exhibit C: Voldemort Day. VOLDEMORT DAY. Because apparently this is a cartoon. Also, For Voldemort and Valor. LOL. And did whoever wrote this story miss the fact that The Dark Lord's followers do not call him Voldemort?? Like did they miss the part in book 7 when he puts that spell on the word Voldemort, to track his enemies, because he knows that only his enemies would dare call him that? But I guess now his followers are putting it on big banners to hang over the doorway with the cake and balloons while they celebrate Voldemort Day. Insert that gif of Britney Spears going "Very..ummm....cool?" 
 Exhibit D: The Scorpion King. The Blood Ball. Ebony Delphi Dementia Raven Way. Is this book sponsored by Hot Topic? I can only picture Delphi's blue and silver hair as 2007 scene queen Myspace hair. She probably carries around a Hello Kitty doll which she drew eyeliner on and puts safety pins on all her bracelets. I was an emo kid once, I recognize this story for what it is lol. Insert Britney gif again. 
 So you know, like I said, it was a fun read, and there were things I'm eternally grateful for in it, but they weren't enough to justify this being canon. This is a fan fiction and if JKR would call it what it was I would be a lot more willing to love it's ridiculousness. But having this forced down my throat as canon is a disrespectful slap in the face and I can't believe JKR would do that to us.

UPDATE 18/8/2016: The play itself is sublime. The magic of the play is a spectacle to behold. I went to watch Part I with my sister today and the plot seems much less crazy on stage. Some of the sections that may seem weird in script form e.g. the Trolley Witch scene work really well on stage; in the example given my sister told me afterwards she literally couldn't stop laughing (for all the right reasons). Also, the cast is perfect and I really hope they make a DVD of one of this particular cast's performances because they really bring the characters to life! 
 This review contains major spoilers which I have hidden, but I feel like I should include a disclaimer knowing that many people, like myself, just can't resist clicking on them...DON'T DO IT, PEOPLE LIKE ME!!! 
 How can I describe this play? A love letter to the Harry Potter universe? A compelling tale about love, in all its forms? 
 This script has already proved divisive, and it's easy to see why. For me, reading this play wasn't like reading a Harry Potter novel. Personally I don't think it was ever meant to, not just because of the story being told in a different medium - the way I see it, it's a different kind of story being told. Quite often reading this play felt more like reading fan-fiction, mostly because of some of the more "out there" plot twists Cedric Diggory a Death Eater? Voldemort a father? . That last one made me laugh at first, it was so ridiculous, but then I thought about it some more, and realised how symbolic it was.* One of the most major themes of the play is family, and even our villain just wants to be loved by her father at the end of the day, just like Albus . Love is at the heart of the Harry Potter universe, and this play is about the importance of family and friendship. When you start to pick it apart, it's incredibly clever. This story is not about its villain, or about its super crazy/bizarre but also super fun, wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey plot - it's a character driven piece at heart, and it's a beautiful exploration of how family, or lack of, can make and break a person. 
 * While I like the symbolism and parallelism at work here, Voldemort having a child is probably the one aspect of this play that I'll never be able to think of as canon. However, do we really know Delphi is his child? Could she just be a mad girl twisted into believing such a thing by a troubled, loveless childhood? (This would be in-keeping with the theme of trauma brought into the play by Harry's traumatic childhood nightmares too). I'll have to re-read the play to make up my mind. If prophecies aren't set in stone, then surely they are open to interpretation too. 
 I must say I was pleasantly surprised by how the authors of this play brought in the original series. It wasn't what I expected at all! I had heard about the time turners making a return , but never would have guessed where they would have taken our characters. And, speaking of our characters - wow! Scorpius Malfoy might just be my new favourite, alongside Luna Lovegood. And Ron - he's just how I imagined an older Ron would be (though I know not everyone shares that opinion!). As a side note, Ron and Hermione facing the Dementors together in the dystopian world was, for me, one of the most touching moments in the play. I was hoping for an appearance from Professor Longbottom , but even though he doesn't show up, I'm glad his importance as a character in the series as a whole is highlighted by his importance in this story too. Also, I wish there was more Rose , just because the little snippets we get of her are so great. Overall though, the characters made me laugh, they almost made me cry (I find it very hard to cry at books - I suspect I will be a mess when I see this on stage) and basically I loved where our authors took them. Draco Malfoy's development was particularly nicely done. 
 Reading this play, I can't begin to imagine how they've managed to bring it to life on stage. Magic, perhaps? No doubt it will be a spectacle. I can't wait to see it!

That being said, I found myself being pretty critical of the first ten or twelve scenes, thinking they were too short and "what a lot of work for a two minute scene", or "that's it?". I think the new main characters are well drawn and realized, the reason for two stars. They're funny, smart, emotional, and I imagine make for great roles that actors would love to play. 
 I think the cover price is way too expensive for what ends up being a two hour reading of a play. It didn't make me excited to see the stage version...and I've read other plays or stage adaptations which get me excited for the stage version. I felt a little used...excited for another JK book, but getting something different. I think a newbie would be a little lost, wondering what this spell means or what that world looks like, or why it's important to know that character from past Harry Potter books. I think it's entertaining, yes, but lacks the depth and richness that Rowling's books had when it comes to reading a great story and book. I think Potter fans deserve better. Reading some of the other reviews, some seem to get four stars for nostalgia rather than the content or actual writing of this book/play. Don't get me wrong, I liked being transported to that world again...but I want to reread the first seven books again...not this.

 So, here is my long awaited review: contains SPOILERS! 
 I didn't have very high expectations for this book. I wasn't very involved in the hype around its publication either. I saw it in a bookstore and thought "Hmm, I should read this, after all it's Harry Potter." 
 Well... no. Not Harry Potter at all. I had no expectations and I was STILL super disappointed. 
 Plot holes, irrational characters, no moral behind the whole story. I just can't believe how much this sucked. I just sat on the beach with my Kindle and I was furious. Furious that it sucks so bad and furious that I'm reading it at all. 
 For the most part the plot is absurd. I refuse to believe that Voldemort and Bellatrix had a child (I also refuse to believe that J. K. Rowling actually approved this bullshit). The series of returns to the past were also pretty delusional. The lack of character capacity in most of the characters also drove me completely insane. I only liked Scorpius and Draco who seemed to be the only ones whose actions made at least somewhat sense. All the rest seemed off, acted irrational and weird. Even Harry was... not Harry (I don't know how to elaborate exactly, but I noticed a lot of people put it the same way in their reviews). And Albus... don't get me started on Albus. Neville was absent-minded too, but in a cute way at least. 
 We didn't get to see anything new, anything that happened after the closing chapter of the Deathly Hallows. The book just kept us in the whirlpool of the past, bringing back to life characters who don't need to be brought to life (as great a hero as Snape is, I don't think he has any unfinished business in any space-time dimension). Dumbledore also didn't make any sense: "I'm gonna try to be wise and all, but don't trust me, I'm a painting and my intellect is compromised. Here is the one sentence in the whole book that makes sense." 
 I really really really did NOT enjoy this book...
4 1/2 stars, to be honest I did like the different twist to the story. But you will have to get used to reading a script.

** spoiler alert ** 
 "HARRY: Are you okay, Albus? 
 ALBUS: No. 
 HARRY: No. Nor me." 
 I took this book from my co-worker's hands convinced I would hate it. HATE IT. I went through the first few scenes chanting the mantra "it's fan fiction, it's not canon, it's fan fiction, it's not canon..." 
 And it does read like fan fiction. It draws from the movies more than the world of the books, and a lot of the lines are stilted. There are confusing scenes where the characters' motivations suddenly switch for no perceivable reason. That's all very on-brand if you're thinking of this play as fan fiction. 
 The main character isn't particularly likeable either. Harry's sulky, infuriating teenager, Albus, is held back by the poor decision to not make him sympathetic before revealing his over-exaggerated adolescent characteristics. I also quickly grew fond of Scorpius, which made his best friend Albus's flagrant disregard for other's opinions and feelings even more frustrating. 
 "ALBUS: We're ready to put our lives at risk. 
 SCORPIUS: Are we?" 
 As for the rest of Jo's cast, the writers get Ginny right (finally), but few other characters are done justice, and some are, frankly, slandered. Others are redeemed beyond reason to the point of sending them flailing out of character. 
 Interestingly, I found the stage directions more compelling than anything else, which might explain why the play is so much more popular with people who have actually seen it. While a character's closing line in an act is "Our journey has only just begun" (cringe), the final stage direction two lines later is the intriguing "Whispers rise to a roar." It almost feels like the playwrights would have been happy for the characters to talk like the adults in Charlie Brown while the visual and aural emotional impact and special effects continued. 
 "There's a silence. A perfect, profound silence. One that sits, twists a bit, and has damage within it." 
 But it's Harry Potter, and it's Harry Potter with Jo's influence. So ultimately, as a complete "Potterhead," I got caught up in the nostalgia and the series's well re-produced dry humour. I grew to accept the utter ridiculousness of the plot. Would I have finished this book if it weren't HARRY POTTER and such an easy read (being a 300-page script)? No. But, from the stage directions, it does sound like it would be spectacular on stage, and there are some truly wonderful moments. 
 "They were great men, with huge flaws, and you know what -- those flaws almost made them greater." 
 It's not the disgrace I was expecting it to be.
I would prefer that this book did not exist.
Harry Potter and the Curse of Being Literally The Worst Thing I've Ever Read

It's like killing Mark Darcy all over again. 
 Good fanfiction tho. 
 Go see the play. 
 Bye.

Here goes the so-so sequel. I guess every series got at least one, right? Not as good as Cinder but I must admit Captain Thorne is everything my heart goes boom-boom for. That ravishing bastard. My heart always fall for guys with a good sense of humor, that I can't deny. Scarlet Benoit is Meyer's yet again another Disney-with-a-twist character. Red Riding Hood fell in love with the Wolf. Though this book is about Scarlet I still find myself catching up with Captain Thorne because god knows how gorgeous that guy is.

I am ashamed for not reading this book sooner. I read Cinder about 2-3 years ago. I was worried this book wouldn't compare to the first book, even though everyone's reviews said otherwise. I finally read it because I had borrowed my friend's copy of Scarlet quite some time ago, and she deserves to have her book back. I loved this book, and I think it's even better than Cinder. 
 The book alternates between 3 points of views. Scarlet enlists in the help of a mysterious street fighter named Wolf, to find her missing grandmother when the police have dropped the case. Cinder escapes The Commonwealth with a conceited thief, in search of anything to help her with her new Lunar powers. At the same time, Prince Kai is split between having to find Cinder for Queen Levana in order to protect his country, and secretly wanting Cinder to escape. 
 I was pulled into the story from the start. It was fast-paced and intriguing, even when the only thing happening is travelling and hiding. I like all points of views, though I did favor some more than others. I also liked all the new characters added in this novel. Especially Scarlet and Wolf. I loved them, and I loved their chemistry. I shamelessly shipped them from the start. I constantly cried to the heavens, "YES, THE SHIP HAS SAILED!" to "NO, MY BABIES!" to "KISS, DAMN IT!" This is my new otp right here. 
 I also liked how Marissa Meyer incorporated the Little Red Riding Hood story into the overall plot. It fit in well into Scarlet's story of finding her grandmother (the obvious connection) to the continuing story from Cinder (the less obvious connection). It was put in ways I never saw coming, yet it fit well. 
 Overall, I love this book, and The Lunar Chronicles. I forgot how amazing this series is, and will certainly read Cress soon. At least, sooner than I took to read this book.

This was definitely on par with, if not better than, the first installment and many of my lingering questions from Cinder were answered. Scarlet was another admirable heroine, but just like with the whole Cinder-Kai relationship in the last book, I had a hard time enjoying the Scarlet-Wolf thing. I really think it's my fault though - my cynical, crotchety self can no longer stomach cheesy teen romance like I used to. I appreciate that that's the draw in a lot of YA books (particularly series), and thankfully for these books, the girls themselves outshine all of that lovey-dovey stuff. The relationships are part of the plot but don't take center stage. I really enjoyed the introduction of Captain Thorne - who doesn't love a little comedic relief? - and the revival of Iko as a spaceship was also fun and clever. Scarlet's biggest strength was in the twist and turns of the story itself - Cinder was a bit predictable, but it was hard to guess exactly where this book was going and whether certain characters were trustworthy or not. Meyer really keeps readers on their toes in this one, and I can imagine things only get more intense in the next book. (Fingers crossed there's less awkward romance in my future, but I think that would be asking too much).

I've heard a lot of people say they like this one the least of all the Lunar Chronicles, and now, I've only read the first 2, but I loved this one a lot more than the first one, and I loved the first one a lot! 
 The story line picks up a lot quicker than it does in Cinder, which was much appreciated, although it picks up with Scarlet's story, and after having just finished Cinder, I really wanted to find out what happened with her. But Marissa Meyer does a good job of getting you hooked into Scarlet's story that by the time it switches back to Cinder's story, you're a little sad. 
 I am in love with Scarlet's and Wolf's love story. The chemistry between them is so palpable as a reader. I was so excited for their kiss on the train! That being said, when Wolf betrayed Scarlet and turned her over to the pack, my heart broke. Usually, I see betrayals from a mile away; I've read enough books and seen enough movies that things like that don't surprise me. This one however left me with my mouth gaping open. I felt the hurt that Scarlet did. And then to lose her grandmother so shortly after. I know that Scarlet and Wolf work this out and he wasn't planning on feeding her to the wolves (pun intended), but still, I can't believe I was so naive to fall for him turning her over. That's the oldest trick in the book! 
 I'm pretty disappointed in Emperor Kai for marrying Levana, well, at least proposing the marriage to her. I hope that the marriage never comes to fruition because I know that will lead to his untimely death and I just don't think I can handle another death after Peony and grande-mere. And I don't think Cinder would ever be able to live with herself. 
 I'm excited to see Cinder experiment more with her powers as she practices with Wolf and becomes more powerful. I hope to see her be reunited with the doctor, but not until she is more certain of her powers because I know that he wants to use her for his own gain since Levana caused the death of his daughter. 
 I'm also excited to meet the new character in the new book. I'm so glad I decided to read this series, and I'm exceptionally glad I decided to wait until all the books were out so I wasn't waiting impatiently.

 En el segundo libro de cronicas lunares Marissa nos introduce a Scarlet, una nueva y super mejorada version de caperucita roja. Vive en una granja con su abuelita , quien es super bad ass y fue parte del ejercito hace 40 anos atras. Sin embargo, no todo es bonito en la vida de Scarlet... su abuela fue secuestrada hace un par de semanas y ella esta dispuesta a hacer todo para encontrarla. Es en los primeros capitulos de la novela donde Scarlet , enojada con la policia por haber cerrado el caso como un suicidio o simple desaparicion y enojada por los comentarios de la gente del pueblo acerca de que su abuela esta un poco loca, que conoce a Wolf o Lobo, quien es bastante timido e ingenuo , a pesar de su aspecto de luchador y de estar lleno de cicatrices. 
 " Alli estaban, un par de marginados. Parias. Chiflados. " 
 Si bien pense que el libro solo nos mostraria lo que pasa con Scarlet, a medida que avanza la historia nos damos cuenga que no es asi; se nos presenta tambien que es lo que esta pasando con Cinder en su escape de la prision, lo que le pasa luego de saber quien es , de conocer sus raices y de como llego a ser lo que es hoy. Tambien, nos presentan a un nuevo personaje: Thorne. Este personaje es uno de los mas graciosos que hay, es guapo, arrogante, mentiroso y ladron, razon por la que esta encarcelado en el mismo lugar de Cinder , con quien finalmente, se vuelve aliado. 
 Me gusto que veamos la historia de ambas protagonistas. Ya conociamos a Cinder, pero como una mecanica y ciborg, ahora la vemos como una fugada y , ademas como una princesa que, de una forma u otra tiene que reclamar su trono. Por otro lado, vemos a Scarlet, quien tiene una personalidad bastante fuerte, es combativa, no se que queda callada nunca y tiene una ferrea determinacion en encontrar a su abuela, cueste lo que cueste y pucha que le cuesta . Tambien vemos su relacion con Lobo, la que avanza muchisisisismo mas rapido que la de Kai y Cinder 
 De a poco vamos conociendo que tiene en comun ambas chicas y me encanta que TODO vaya calzando, cosas, detalles, nombres que no parecian importar cobran vital relevancia en este libro. sample_reviews.review_text: By the third chapter, I wanted to just toss the novel out a window. Just too much dialogue and not enough narrative to make this a good read.

Compared to Jennifer Donnelly's other YA novels, These Shallow Graves was a large disappointment, full of stereotypical characters, an uneventful mystery, anachronistic dialogue, and obnoxious cliffhanger endings. 
 There was no finesse or depth to any part of this novel, which is a shame since A Northern Light and Revolution were both so brilliant. I definitely skimmed the last 150 pages and feel that I missed out on nothing.

The protagonist in These Shallow Graves is Jo Montfort, a young woman of high social stature in 19th century New York. Though her world is finishing schools, balls, and the promise of marriage, Jo longs to be an investigative journalist. 
 When her father is found dead, Jo sets out to discover what truly happened to him. Along the way, she is thrust into a world she never knew existed, the side of New York life her sheltered existence prevented her from seeing. And she meets Eddie, a young reporter who agrees to help her for the chance of a story, but ends up staying at her side for love. 
 I liked this book, but didn't love it. The characters were really interesting, and the historical setting was well-done. The mystery was definitely intriguing, but I found myself able to call what was about to happen chapters before it actually occurred. And I did feel the book started out too slowly, to the point where I almost put it down. 
 I would say give this book a chance, but don't feel like you need to rush to grab a copy.

3.5 Stars

 Throw in a irresistible murder mystery, a handsome rogue and it was a story that was doubly hard for me to say no to. 
 I'm so glad I read this. I really did enjoy every single thing about it but especially Jo herself. She was everything I was hoping she would be from the synopsis, strong, fierce, brave, feisty, determined, and a woman that wasn't to be shunted and locked away.

 This was well written, easy paced, character and mystery driven and just enough romance to keep you interested. I do wish the ending hadn't been quite so open ended with a few things left to the imagination but it also left it open to a possible sequel, which I truly would love to see and read.

Here's a not so good book by a wonderful writer.

 Now for Jo. While I find her incredible naivete a lot more believable than a lot of readers, who apparently don't know enough about turn of the century New York to believe that rich girls of this period could be this sheltered and childlike--they really were--I find her managing to walk in and out of danger throughout the book and getting a lucky rescue EVERY SINGLE TIME to be totally unbelievable. The "romance" is also too nice and neat and more a plot point than a true relationship. The end is tidy as can be, and again, too perfect. I was expecting a (believable) unhappy ending for one character, and instead Donnelly makes everyone happy. 
 I will note that this particular character seems to be a reader favorite judging by reviews here. But the plot devices Donnelly used with her made me want to scream--one of the worst plot twists of all. 
 The pity is that Donnelly does great research and writes well enough for me to keep on reading. But apparently most modern editors let best selling authors write messes like this, knowing that they will make lots of sales regardless of the quality. That's a sad thing.

4.5 stars 
 These Shallow Graves is the first book I have read by Jennifer Donnelly and I mean it when I say, it will not be the last. I loved everything about this book. The cover and the actual pages are beautiful (There's a MAP), the characters are fantastic, and the mystery...while I guessed what was going on, I didn't care. Donnelly created a story that yanked me in from page one and wouldn't let me go until I finished and knew what was going to happen. 
 Jo Montfort comes from a well-known family and has grown up surrounded by riches and rules. As a member of the elite society of New York City, the only thing that is expected of her is that she not embarrass her family name and she marry well. The thing about Jo is she wants more than that...one of the things she wants is to be able to write - preferably a newspaper reporter like Nellie Bly. 
 When tragedy strikes her family, Jo is thrown into a situation she never expected to face. As she digs more and more into the death of her father, Jo is introduced to people and danger both of which would get her into a lot of trouble if her mother and uncle knew what she was up to. I loved seeing her do what she wanted to in order to find out more. I have read many books about this time in our history and every time I hear how condescending men were to women (they couldn't possibly have a brain or want to use it for more than discussion about weather and parties) it makes me cringe and appreciate the things I am able to do. 
 As Jo digs, she meets a guy named Eddie. At first it was clear he saw her as an opportunity to advance at the paper but when he learns more about Jo, he finds himself drawn to her. The challenge for these two as they start to have feelings for each other, is that they are from different classes in society and definitely not allowed to do any of the things they have been up to. Both romantically as well as journalists. I liked Eddie - he has a past and as his secrets are revealed he becomes more than just the guy who will help Jo. 
 Coming from different classes, it was interesting to see the way they viewed each other and how they came to realize just how different they really were. From a relationship perspective, I loved seeing them realize the differences and try to figure out how they could even make their relationship work...or if they should. 
 There are a number of secondary characters that add to the story and I have to say, the timeframe that Donnelly set the story in was the perfect framework for this book. If you are looking for a good mystery with solid characters and a page-turning story, definitely check this book out when you can. 
 Thank you to the publisher and NetGalley for the review copy!

1.5 stars. 
 * 
 If you're going to bury the past, bury it deep, girl. Shallow graves always give up their dead. 
 This book has a beautiful and creepy cover, but it was suuuuch a disappointment. 
 I was so excited to start These Shallow Graves. I'd heard so many positive things about it from other people, so I know I'm in the minority when I say this book did not work for me at all. I was expecting something just as creepy and scary as the cover, but unfortunately that wasn't what I got. 
 Actually, the prologue was creepy and scary and really exciting, but what followed was one of the most boring and predictable stories I've read in a while. So much so that I only got to the halfway mark before I skimmed the rest and read only the last few chapters to find out if the twists I predicted happened. They did. 
 My biggest problem was Jo. She was naive to the point of looking incredibly stupid. I understand women, especially young privileged women, being sheltered around that time, but as the book went on it was evident Jo had absolutely no idea what went on in the real world that didn't extend past her circle of equally privileged friends. And that was so disconnected from the Jo we saw in the first chapter when she talked about wanting to be a reporter and even wrote an article about girl laborers. I don't know what happened to that Jo, but to me she was self-centered and unlikable pretty much for the rest of the book. 
 Other problems were: instalove, the predictability of it all, the sloooooow slow pace, flat characters. All of that made These Shallow Graves a torture to read. 
 The one ray of sunshine in this book was Fay. She was badass, fierce, was always prepared for trouble or to cause trouble, and she actually had an interesting backstory! In fact, I might have found this a lot more enjoyable to read if it told Fay's story and not Jo's. 
 * 
 Series: Standalone. 
 POV: Told from Jo's POV. 
 Content Warnings: None. 
 Instalove: Yes. 
 Love Triangle: Jo gets engaged to another guy. 
 Cheating: Not really. 
 Cliffhanger: No. 
 HEA: More open ended than happy.

 I struggled a lot with this book, so I'm unsure how exactly to rate it. I decided on 2.5 stars because it was fairly average, and super slow at many points. I think this could have been shortened by at least fifty pages and been much better. 
 I absolutely believe this should have been written in first person. There were long paragraphs of Jo, the main character, talking to herself in italics, and I think the same thing could have been accomplished if the entire story was from her own point of view. 
 Also, beware the insta-love. It's real bad, guys. Real bad. 
 Another thing that I didn't like was how cheesy this was, with cliche lines like, "It had given her no answers, only more questions." I guessed the plot twist from the very beginning. Most people probably wouldn't but I did, which made following the story kind of frustrating when I was sure how it was going to end.

I don't exactly know where this book and I went wrong. I really wanted to like it, and in a sense there were parts in the book that I did enjoy, but overall this was a big disappointment with me. Which sadness me because so many of my friends loved it, and I was so eager to read it myself, that it just turned into an absolute failure. 
 First, when I read the opening chapter I was excited. Grave digging, my imagination ran wild, I had all kinds of hopes for this book that ended up not only disappointing me but it fell completely flat. 
 Where do I start? 
 Jo. I honestly kind of hate her. She is a 17-year old that acts like she is younger, much, much, younger. Not only does she appear obtuse sometimes, but she is also naive, childish, melodramatic, too trusting, and overall not the smartest crayon in the box. Like in one scene while she is in Brooklyn, after facing so much danger already and learning the dark side of New York City, she goes ahead and thrusts some out of the mill older woman who offers her a ride back home, not even contemplating what kind of danger might be facing her trusting this woman and her husband. Now let me tell you something. I was raised in NYC and if some random older woman and her husband offered me a ride home while I was alone in a neighborhood I am not familiar with, I would run the other direction screaming fire. I guess it might just be me, but as an ex-New Yorker, I actually learned how to not trust people - an issue my husband and I choose to agree and disagree on. 
 Conveniently for Jo though there is always someone there to rescue her from her bad decisions, most notably Fay. 
 The romance was lame and honestly felt a little forced and fake. There were a few scenes that left me questioning if Eddie was actually using her for a story like her uncle has mentioned. Which in itself was never explained. When Eddie was confronted about it, he denied ever saying it, but the author never explained how Jo's uncle pulled that one out of thin air. There wasn't any tension and felt kind of instant. 
 I don't understand why the book was over 400 pages long. It dragged a bit at times. I found myself wanting to finish it in hopes of a better ending, but everything I predicted at the beginning of the story came true, which actually only disappointed me more because it was that damn predictable. There had been parts that also felt a bit rushed and not only that but oddly written. In example, this scene, just found weird the way it was written: 
 "Oh, look!" Jo said. "The man sitting next to her just stood up. He knocked her gloves off the counter. Go return them to her, Oscar!" 
 "He's crazy about her," Eddie said as he watched his friend go. 
 Jo smiled. "I never would have guessed. Is she really a medical student?" 
 Maybe I would have to backtrack a little more for it to make sense on here, but stuff happened conveniently and the actions kind of felt odd? 
 There was mostly just the bad side of NYC at that time and good part. Not much in between. 
 I wanted to know more about the Tailor, he seemed kind of creepy. 
 I only really liked Fay in this book. 
 And the prologue or whatever it was that gave us a glimpse into what is happening later in the book, did not really reflect what happened later. It didn't match. I can't go too much into it, but the feelings and actions of the moment just did not match. 
 I also thought this would be more creepy due to the cover, but it really wasn't. I was surprised Jo could not see the answers in front of her as the evidence continued to pile on, since I myself already figured who done it right after it happened. 
 Also, in one chapter her mother sucks.This review was originally posted on Night Owl Book Cafe

"...I've buried quite a few...and I can bury you, too." 
 This book and I were supposed to get married and have 2.5 kids and live in the suburbs together happily ever after. (HEAs stopped working out for me a very long time ago, though.) 
 These Shallow Graves 
 's premise was a truly interesting one. The whole setting had a very Downton Abbey-feel to it; plus, it's not every day you find an author who handles feminism in Historical Fiction as well as Cat Winters does. 
 I find the nineteenth century a fascinating time, though this makes me come across as a romantic and a somewhat starry-eyed little kid, I like this era despite its patriarchy, none-too-comfortable fashion and prejudices. This book takes us to the streets of 1890's New York, inside the slumps, brothels and docks of the city and the secrets lurking in there. 
 The good of this book is these things: it's setting, for one, which is well done. It's fast-paced, and its characters feel full of life. And God, the first half is more or less a shitload of upperclassmen angst, but it's fun to read. There's plenty of feminism and great character development, especially our protagonist's. It's all very likable. But I wasn't completely swayed by it, despite the most perfect ending of all time and the writing's pleasing aesthetic excellence. 
 What's the worst thing about it? Well, I might be in the minority this time, but I knew from the seventh chapter who it was. Reader's intuition, or whatever, but I knew who was the culprit and that lessened my enjoyment of its climax. Conclusion: the mystery was predictable. And giving me predictable mysteries is more or less a recipe for disaster. Next problem, its Main Character, Jo Montfort, though develops in time to a wonderful person you'd have liked to be friends with in real life as you journey with her, fell flat for me because of only one thing: she's got something of a damsel-in-distress complex. Sure, I don't expect every single character of my books turning out to be badass Katnisses or Penryns, but she is saved from one dilemma or another every single time by someone or another, most notably by Fay. I'm all for girl-power, and dude, Fay's an awesome character, but you need to save yourself at least once in order to gain my respect. Another thing, this book ends almost every chapter with a cliff-hanger. I don't have anything against them, Rick Riordan has made them terribly lame for me with time. But the thing is, this takes it to another not-new, pretentious-punchline- 
 Looking for Alaska 
 -level. It annoyed me, sure, and I thought the romance was kind of insta-love-ish? I totally shipped that ship and it's balanced well--doesn't make the plot completely revolve around it, but its beginning seemed kind of...gimmicky? 
 Despite the, err, poor quality of its mystery aspects, I must say, it never once felt like the characters investigating were being handed clues on silver platters at every twist and turn of the road, which has become quite a recurring theme in YA. They worked for it, fought for it, and you know what, it has never once felt easy. Plus, how easy it was for a woman to be considered insane during this time really creeped me out. 
 Did you read 
 A Madness So Discreet 
 and felt like punching walls because of its mystery? Then 
 These Shallow Graves 
 's will probably soothe your angry soul. Is this book life-changing? For some, perhaps. For me, no, but it was an enjoyable read, though I kept losing interest due to thirteen tests and vivas I suffered through this October. Do I recommend it? Yes, I do. But I'd say don't go into it with expectations as high as mine had been. It was a good book, but not to a satisfying extent for me. 
 "Dead people always make me hungry." 
 It's fun, captivating despite the shitty mystery; carries a great message. You're guaranteed to be hooked. 
 Thank You, Random House Delacorte, for providing me with an Advanced Reader's Copy

It is so rare when a book can actually surprise me. This book did just that, and I absolutely loved it. I didn't even want to put this book down, I found myself reading it in every last second of my free time, and sometimes even in class. 
 This book takes place in one of the most fabulous eras in the history of New York City. Before the time of celebrities, people focused on the lives of the rich, recounting their every move in the newspapers the next morning. Jo Montfort is among the privileged, but her world is flipped upside down when her father dies in a gun cleaning accident. Jo is whisked away from school to be with her mother and other family in their time of mourning. 
 Jo has trouble believing that her father would ever make the mistake of cleaning a loaded gun, so she starts looking into his death. Along the way, she meets a reporter, Eddie, who agrees to help her out in her search. They come across many things that are shocking to Jo, and she sinks deeper and deeper into a world that she didn't even know existed. 
 Overall I felt that this book was extremely well written and had a great flow and pace to it. It didn't feel too dragged out, and it also didn't rush by. Not to mention a bunch of surprises at the end that made me quite happy with the book. It was most definitely not the typical ending that I imagined would end up coming.
I love this woman's writing. It's not one of her best, but it was definitely readable!

3.5/5 I received an ARC for review from Random House. This was a good read but it took me awhile to get into it. 
 These Shallow Graves is a historical fiction mystery about a young high society girl Jo who wants to be a reporter and be free from society's constraints on her for being from a good family and being a women. When her father is killed in a accident this triggers a series of events that lead to the realization that it was no accident. To find the truth Jo allies herself with a young reporter and puts her reputation on the line (which was a big deal) to find the truth. 
 It was sadly very predictable for me and I guessed many plot reveals but it was still a good read. Donnelly has very descriptive writing and I like her style. I didn't connect very well with the characters but Ioved the side of New York we get to see where the upper and lower class are so drastically contrasted and explored.

Seventeen-year-old Jo Montfort wants to be a reporter like her hero Nellie Bly, but it is extremely difficult to do when one is a student at a girl's school in 1890. The headmistresses would rather Jo write about kittens and tea parties than the plight of mill girls. Her friend Trudy cautions Jo to wait until after marriage to a suitable gentleman before breaking the rules, but Jo just can't dream of a marriage without love. Then the unthinkable happens- her father is accidentally killed while cleaning his gun. Was it an accident? Jo knows her father was smarter than that and when she hears a newsboy declare her father had committed suicide, she becomes determined to get to the bottom of the mystery. She won't stop until she has answers. Her quest will take her into parts of New York she never dreamed existed and uncover some long held secrets that reveal her proper world is not all it seems. 
 I really wanted to like this book. I enjoyed Northern Light a lot and faith that Jennifer Donnelly could pull this off. It started off good- like Edith Wharton writing for a YA audience. There were some good parts that Charles Dickens would have written. This book is the secret love child of Edith Wharton and Charles Dickens locked in a vault for a modern writer to insert a modern type of heroine and pretty much ruin a good thing. 
 POSSIBLE SPOILER ALERT (for non Good Reads people stop here if you don't want the least hint of a spoiler. 
 This story followed a formula that I've read one too many times before. Even though I couldn't put the book down and doubted the identity of the murderer, I wasn't really surprised by any of the reveals. I figured things out faster than Jo and Eddie. Eddie at least should have been able to piece together the clues even if Jo couldn't. The plot relied on too many coincidences for my taste and the constant emphasis on freedom pretty much gave away the shock value of the reveal. Again, Eddie really should have known. 
 As a mature adult, I could have done without the teen angst romance. I didn't buy it at all. I can see why Jo would be drawn to Eddie, the same way Lady Sybil was drawn to Branson but I feel like Jo saw Eddie as an escape, a means to an end and her heart wasn't fully engaged even though she said it was. She behaved childishly and recklessly whenever he was around. I can't really see why Eddie loved Jo. The romance begins too quickly and there's too much drama. The ending was OK- more realistic than I was expecting anyway. 
 I'm torn between admiring Jo for not putting up with the stifling world she comes from and admiring her bravery and also thinking she is a little heedless. I don't think I could be so brave and I think I would rather NOT know. I wondered how she could hurt her family by making their secrets public. I was sort of hoping the author would make the bold choice of making Jo behave like a person from the 19th century and not as a modern young woman. Jo thinks and behaves like a modern young woman and that makes her easier to relate to than her friend Trudy who breaks the rules but wants that life of ease and comfort. I'm conflicted in my feelings for Jo but I think teens will like her a lot and relate to her. I think I would have enjoyed the story more when I was younger. 
 The secondary characters are the real stand-outs. They seem like they were the creations of Charles Dickens without the humor. I had no idea that such an underworld existed in New York though I'm not totally surprised. I would have been less surprised if the book was set in London. I really liked Fay and how she made the most of a bad situation. Her story is certainly horrifying and more interesting and real than Jo's story. I had to skip a lot of Oscar's detailed medical information. I don't have the stomach for that sort of thing. Forensic detecting is introduced quite nicely into the Mrs. Jeffries series without being gory. Grandmama is a cringeworthy hoot. She reminded me of Aunt Marge (Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban) with all her talk of breeding. Yuck. 
 What saves the book from being a true dud is the historical details. The author did a lot of research and she has the skills to introduce the different parts of New York and the current issues of the day without interrupting the flow of the story. The reader is really transported to 1890s New York City. 
 I would recommend this book to older teens/young adults. Mature people stick to Edith Wharton and Charles Dickens. Younger teens and any older readers who like the idea of the story but not the execution may enjoy A Spy in the House. 
 Content warnings: 
 Violence 
 language 
 discussions about sex 
 pre-marital pregnancy mentions 
 fondling 
 passionate kissing 
 prostitutes 
 gory medical information 
 a seedy underworld
Even though it was fairly predictable in other ways it wasn't and I really enjoyed seeing the time period from the eyes of the main character.

Bored bored bored bored BORED! Oh the inanity! I am really reluctant to give up on books. Sometimes it takes a while for the story to pull together. But I don't care about Jo or Eddie. Jo's mother is ridiculous. Her uncle is annoying. Her naivety is boring. Her Grandmama's vulgarity is just vulgar. And Eddie has nothing to offer. There's no cleverness. No witty repartee. I was tired of hearing about "Daddy's agenda" before we learned what the first reference meant. Not good.

**Thank you to NetGalley for providing me this book for an honest review.** 
 The first pages are all about sex... I know that the time period they didn't talk about that sort of thing, but it seems like it could have done without all of the sex talk, especially if you are pushing YA it seems like you are going to limit what grade levels it will be accessible to. 
 Otherwise this was an extremely long book, felt like it took forever to read.
Too juvenile

First of all, I want to start this review by saying how much I liked "these shallow graves". Probably it's because I love historical fiction, and/or because of the darling characters, I guess both. The story is dark, but at the same time funny and at times even light. I found it fascinating to read about 1890's New York. A Place full of growth and excitement and perdition. The storytelling made it feel very real, It felt like I was actually reading a true story, maybe a memoire. I wonder if the various brothels, newspapers apartments and buildings really existed, I'll probably google it. 
 Anyways, I loved the main characters and their stories, especially Fay and Eddie. 
 The murder mystery was rather boring and foreseeable, every twist and turn I'd seen coming chapters in advance, and all the dead-ends in the investigations irritated me and made the book unnecessarily long and dragging, but the final 100 pages made up for every flaw. I was a little saddened by the open ending of the love story, but it made it feel realistic, for trust is not regained and heartache not overcome in one day. Tbh, I can't really see a future between Eddie and Jo. Eddie was too hurt to really forgive her and I think he will soon dwell so much in his work, that he will un-fall in love with her, while she will always have feelings for her first love.

(From www.pingwings.ca) 
 3.5 stars; source: borrowed ARC 
 I've read one of Jennifer Donnelly's adult fiction novels, years ago, and recall that I enjoyed it. I was intrigued when I heard that she had a YA historical fiction novel coming out, and was really excited to borrow an ARC from a friend. 
 I love historical fiction, and I found myself drawn into the novel's setting (New York City, at the end of the 19th century) right away. I loved reading about Jo's life - the clothes, the customs, the carriages - and I also loved the way she wanted to rebel against what was expected of her as a girl from a wealthy family. While everyone around her expected her to marry, she wanted to see the real world and write about it. 
 As for the story, the mystery itself was not difficult to sort out, but I enjoyed Jo's investigation into her father's death. I liked the romance, too, between Jo and a reporter she meets. 
 However, the story felt really slow at times, and I never got emotionally invested in the book. 
 Overall, this was a good read and if you like YA historical fiction, I'd recommend checking out These Shallow Graves.

3.5 
 This had so much awesomeness. I loved the ideas and deeper arguments presented. 
 That said, there was a bit of a shaky start but I pressed on because I really liked Revolution and I trust Jennifer Donnelly to give me material to feel emotional and passionate about. I felt she did in this work. I liked the plot and mystery. I also liked the characters.

I tried to like this, I really did. But it just did not connect for me and I did not finish it. 
 I may be the wrong age for this story, but I simply could not suspend disbelief sufficiently to buy that Jo not only WOULD sneak out of her house in the middle of the night to go to "a bad part of town" looking for the reporter, but that she COULD manage to get there on her own with no prior experience navigating a city like New York at that time without some trouble finding a young, clueless girl like she is. 
 The feel of Jo also came across to me as "dilettante" as though she wanted to investigate because she was offended about what happened to her father. The book says that she was distraught, but it didn't FEEL that way to me. I could not find any sympathy for Jo, and so I could not relate to, or root for her. And without being able to connect to Jo, I simply didn't care about anything else she did or that happened to her so I gave up on this. 
 As I said, this very well may be a situation where I am the wrong audience for this book, and others may love it. It wasn't for me.

Spoiler Alert! 
 Author Donnelly provides a great opening and conclusion, although the middle is slow, repetitive, and predictable at times. Jo, the main character, relies heavily on friends to help her solve several murders and to get her out of precarious situations. In part, this is a coming of age story for a girl forced to grow up. 
 The timeline seems inaccurate for some situations. Slavery ended in the United State in 1865, yet the father would have been at least twenty when he became involved in the slave trade in 1871. In 1890, he has a daughter old enough to be engaged. A quick web search indicates the average life expectancy for a man of that era was around forty years. In addition, the reporter was using a typewriter in 1891 at a time when few reporters had access to the machines.
It was too long of a murder mystery!

reference_books.title: Existence (Existence Trilogy, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
In my opinion this book was okay 
 I both liked this book and hated it (hates such a strong word, it was more like disliked it). It had interesting parts and parts that made me want to slap the characters, facepalm, and/or roll my eyes. 
 The story line in general was interesting (I mean, seeing dead people! That has to be interesting). But I felt that the story kind of went off track. We begin with Pagan seeing Dank (which is a really weird name by the way!) and then the tutoring and then Pagan is pissed at Leif, car crash, survive, the "relationship" with Dank, goodbye Dank, the trip that had the car accident involved, mental home.... 
 Well my point is that it goes off track and then somehow fits it all together (in a confusing way). 
 What really irked me was the "relationship" between Pagan and Dank. They only kiss like once, they barely talk or know each other, and we have Dank out of the picture for who knows how long (I honestly had no idea how much time went by in this book). But Pagan loves him so dang much that she will risk her life (actually die) for him. 
 *rolls eyes* 
 There were some moments in the book where I felt like I was missing a few pages because of how fast things were going. 
 For Example: 
 "And if he refuses to take your body he will be taken as a result. Are you going to tell her that part, Death? Are you going to tell her how you will be no longer free to roam the Earth as Death but you will be condemned to Hell? You'll be as lowly as the fallen angels. If she lives, you essentially die." Gee stood watching Dank with her hands on her hips. "The choice is now.Once your powers are stripped I'll be transporting you down. And I truly hate to go down." She flickered her gave towards me. "You can live and have an eternal life while he burns in Hell with the rest of the fallen angels and sinners, or you can go with me and live in light and let him continue the life he has lived since the creation of man. For he is, and has always been, Death." 
 *turn the page to next chapter* 
 The dark sky began to churn around a core of light. I grabbed Dank's arm with both of my hands as if he was about to disappear. "What's happening?" I asked over the sound of the wind roaring in the distance. Dank shook his head, with his eyes on Gee. 
 Is it just me or did that happen really fast? 
 And then there's the thing with Leif. Pagan tutors him and then after the accident (with a snap of the fingers) they're dating. 
 But I really liked the fact that there was some originality to this book unlike a lot of teen books and that it didn't have some of the annoying things in other teen books (although it did have a very teeny tiny love triangle but it was little so... HOORAY!) 
 I apologize for wasting your time with this review 
 EDIT: I take that back. I DID NOT like this book.

reference_books.title: That Summer
reference_books.review_text:
This and other reviews can be found on The Psychotic Nerd 
 MY THOUGHTS 
 This wasn't really what I expected from this book. This is my ninth Sarah Dessen book, so I knew what to expect, despite the fact that this was her first book. And this book did follow a lot of my Sarah Dessen expectations. Though, based on the cover and title, I was expecting more of a light-hearted, summer read. While this book takes place during the summer, it's not the fun, summer book that I was expecting. 
 Haven is fifteen years and reaching almost 6 feet. Her father has run off with the weather girl and her older sister is getting married. Haven wishes that everything would go back to the way it was. Back when her parents were happily married, her sister was nice to her, and she wasn't freakishly tall. When Haven runs into one of Ashley's, her sister, old boyfriends, she begins to miss the past even more and question what happened to it. 
 This is a fairly short book, at around 200 pages, so it's not a surprise that this book is actually very uneventful. There are two weddings, the appearance of Ashley's old boyfriend (though, Haven is the only one who notices him), and Haven's job. Overall, this is actually just a coming of age story for Haven. The whole book is very slow-paced and focuses on how Haven has to grow into how much her life is changing. While not much happens, I did like reading it and it was a nice story. Many supporting characters were annoying, but I did like Haven. She doesn't quite know why her life is changing so rapidly and why she can't go back, and I could really feel for her. 
 While this is Sarah Dessen's early work, it still has her usual style. It's the coming of age tale about a girl who is in a tough family situation. Unlike her other books, there is no romance whatsoever, maybe because the main character is younger than her other books. 
 IN CONCLUSION 
 This isn't my favorite Sarah Dessen book, but I still liked it. I liked seeing Haven's journey in figuring out why this is happening to her family and her. Sarah Dessen is still one of my favorite authors.

reference_books.title: Dorothy Must Die (Dorothy Must Die, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This and other reviews can be found on The Psychotic Nerd 
 Actual Rating: 3.5 Stars 
 THE RUN-DOWN 
 When a tornado goes through the trailer park where Amy lives, she's taken to the land of Oz. Only, it's not the happy munchkin land seen in the books and movies. It's a much darker, messed up place. Dorothy is not the farm girl anymore and has taken over Oz. 
 Oz is a mess and the only way for things to return the way things were, is to kill Dorothy. 
 And Amy is the lucky girl to do it. 
 MY THOUGHTS 
 This book was one of my most anticipated books of the year and, along with that, there's so much hype surrounding the book, but this book kind of disappointed me. I did like this book, but I expected so much more! 
 The first issue that I had with this book was how quickly Amy grows used to Oz. Almost right away the tornado takes Amy to Oz, and I was okay with that, but I got the feeling that Amy was okay with this way too early. At first, she believes that she's hallucinating/dreaming because she's in frexing Oz, what else would you think? But she quickly believes that,yes, she's actually in Oz. I just would think that it should take a bit longer to believe that you're in the actual land of Oz, but I guess that's just me. 
 It also took me awhile to get into the story and connect with any of the characters, but this is probably more my fault than the book's fault. I just happened to have read a majority of this book in public places and/or places that I had difficulty concentrating in, so that might have been why I had a difficult time getting into the book. I was, eventually, able to get into it and connect with the characters (probably when I wasn't reading in noisy public places or trying to read standing up). When this happened I was able to enjoy the story and I actually ended up really liking it! I found the screwed up world of Oz oddly intriguing! So, in the second half or so of the book, I really did enjoy it. But I did have an issue with the fact that the whole book was a lead up to Amy killing Dorothy and then... it doesn't happen. It just kind of disappointed me, since that was the whole point of the story, but I guess there would be no sequel if Dorothy actually died. 
 To be perfectly honest, there wasn't much action in this book. It was mostly Amy in training and Amy waiting. That was fine, although it did get dull, I did enjoy it but I kind of wish there was...more. 
 IN CONCLUSION 
 The only reason why this book didn't get a higher rating is how disconnected I felt throughout the book. which is, that I said, mostly my fault, so I'll probably have to reread this sometime. I will definitely be reading the sequel! I did enjoy this book enough to continue! I also get the feeling that what I want, more action, will be in the sequel!

reference_books.title: Never Always Sometimes
reference_books.review_text:
This and other reviews can be found on The Psychotic Nerd 
 MY THOUGHTS 
 I had really high expectation for this book. Adi Alsaid's last book, Let's Get Lost, was phenomenal. It was fun, heartbreaking, and I adored it. So, of course, I was excited for more brilliance from Adi Alsaid, but this book wasn't what I was expecting. It's a good book and I like it, but it's not a 'new' book and certainly wasn't the funny, unique book I was expecting. 
 Dave and Julia are best friends and at the start of high school, they create a list of 'Nevers'. The list includes cliches that high schoolers often get into. Rules like, Never dye your hair a color of the rainbow, secretly pine for someone, run for prom king, etc. It isn't until the list is rediscovered senior year that they decide to do ALL of the things on the list. But Dave already has done something on the list, he's been pining for Julia. 
 I really like the idea of the Nevers and I was very curious to see how they would go about them all. It was indeed very interesting seeing how they did, since it's not like they follow the list exactly to a point, they randomly did things throughout the year and things happened because of them. While I wish this book could've been about the list entirely, it wasn't really the main focus, which I guess is okay. As I mentioned, they do things throughout the year, so it's not like they set out to do the list in a day or a week, that means that other stuff is also going on at the same time. I admit that I was kind of bored by the normal school life and things, but it did make things realistic. 
 I think that is a plus in this book, the realism. This book felt very realistic and, yes, that might have been why I was bored at points. The relationships, both romantic and friend oriented, were very realistic to a point that you don't see often in books. Many relationships, especially romance, are exaggerated in books. I felt this way in Adi's last book as well, so I can definitely say that he can certainly write realistic contemporaries. 
 Now, I was a bit bothered by how ironically cliche this book was, even know I shouldn't be. Why? I just get the feeling that this book was supposed to be cliche. The book is about two teens who are against being cliche teenagers, but in the end are they actually cliche? This is actually an important part about the book and I do believe that the cliche-ness was on purpose. Doesn't mean that I didn't groan at the cliche-ness at points. 
 IN CONCLUSION 
 Overall, this is a good contemporary read, but it's not what I was expecting and not quite as good as Adi's debut novel. I love the idea and wish it was focused on that more, despite the fact that not doing so made things more realistic. If you enjoy such books, pick this one up, but I recommend Adi's previous book more.

Back a couple of years ago when we started this blog, we reviewed the first book in the House of Night series, Marked. The review was mostly positive, praised the characters, and ultimately ended in a recommendation. 
 We deeply, sincerely apologize for that. 
 So, to atone for our sins, we've decided to re-read and review the entire House of Night series from the beginning - all nine books, both novellas, and five comics - so that we can take a look at and discuss exactly what makes them so awful. 
 Like before, we're going to start the review off with our protagonist, Zoey Redbird, a character who possesses just the right balance of Divine Special and Unrepentant Asshole to make us want to constantly punch her right in the face. As obnoxious heroines go, Zoey blows every other irritating character we've ever read about out of the water like a fucking hurricane. 
 Allow us to rant elaborate: Zoey is a raging Mary Sue. Sure, lots of protagonists are, in some way or another, but Zoey ticks nearly every box on the Mary-Sue checklist, and then ramps it up to eleven. She's beautiful, "exotic", supposedly smart, virginal, doesn't drink, smoke, do drugs, or even *swear*, and is at fault for absolutely nothing. Anything bad going on in her life or around it is wholly because other people who are out to make her life miserable - her stepdad, the mean girl at school, etc. From the word "go", she is a super-speshul "vampyre" snowflake, in large part due to her Cherokee heritage, and she is literally the only vampyre in the history of FOREVER AND EVER to be as magically gifted as she is. Boys fall at her feet in waves, everyone important loves her, and the ones who don't are canonically evil. 
 Yet despite having these super-special magical powers, Zoey really doesn't bring a whole lot to the table. In practice, she's not particularly smart, insightful, charismatic, or physically adept, and as a heroine, her agency is almost nil. Zoey may be super special awesome, but she doesn't do a whole lot - bad things happen, eventually the fix magically presents itself, and Zoey somehow winds up being the hero. 
 This alone would be enough to make her an eye-rollingly annoying heroine, but as usual, Zoey turns it up to eleven by eschewing any semblance of a likable personality. 
 We don't even have to go past the first chapter before Zoey's showing us just how stuck up, snobby, and pettily judgmental she really is. In fact, it's probably her defining personality trait. You can't go two pages without Zoey spouting out some snide comment about a group or individual that she finds inferior to herself; one of the first things she says about anyone is that her best friend is shallow, dumb, and prone to "annoying K-babble". This is her best friend, okay, and yet both Zoey and the book waste no time in showing us how this is going to play: our heroine is better than everyone. 
 From there, nearly every character we meet is treated similarly. Here's a short list of the people Zoey encounters and/or mentions throughout the first chapter, and the impressions we're given of them: 
 - Kay, her BFF - stupid, shallow, and - it's implied - promiscuous 
 - Heath, Zoey's ex - a dumb, alcoholic pothead 
 - Dustin and Drew, Heath's friends - closed-minded hillbilly rednecks 
 - Zoey's mother - weak-willed and dependent on her husband 
 - Zoey's step-father - a controlling religious zealot 
 - Zoey's nameless older sister - a "slut" and "Barbie", whose supposed promiscuity Zoey uses against her mother in an argument 
 - Kevin, Zoey's little brother - lovingly* deemed a "troll" 
 *sarcastic tone implied 
 Yeah. It's always a good sign when a book has to turn its supporting cast into cartoonishly awful caricatures of human beings to drum up a little sympathy and source of angst for its heroine. Zoey is probably supposed to look like a saint in comparison, but all we saw was a judgmental asshole who liked to talk a whole lot of shit. A whole lot of misogynistic shit, at that. 
 The misogyny is one of the most infuriating aspects of House of Night. These books take a laundry list of every awful, misogynistic idea that women have about each other, and gleefully perpetuate a world in which they are true... 
 Read full review at You're Killing.Us.

Quite a fun book. Well-written, interesting protagonist, and kind of a strange take on the "vampire" concept. The conceit of this book is a "vampire finishing school," which basically means a private high school for vamps. The "vamps" are as non-vampy as you can possibly get, though, at least in this, the series' first book. In movie terms, think of it as MEAN GIRLS meets THE CRAFT. 
 I read the book because co-author Kristin Cast is a fan of my work. That, plus the fact that the HOUSE OF KNIGHT series has sold a bajillion books and generated a rabid following made me want to check it out. I'm glad I did. 
 If you dismiss this as "just another TWILIGHT," you'd be wrong. Yes, this is high-school vamps, but I felt the characters were far less starry-eyed and more typical of the clique nature of a real high school. These kids are kids, and only really succumb to the broader scope of the supernatural aspect near the book's end. 
 I won't read the rest of the series, but don't take that as a knock on the work -- as a middle-aged guy, high-school melodrama doesn't really resonate anymore (vamps or no vamps). If you're into this type of story, MARKED is a home run. The series just completed, by the way, so you can slam all of the books without worrying about a long wait for the story's end. 
 I hope the Dark Daughters keep on kicking ass.
