** spoiler alert ** 
 Ugh. I HATED this book. It's either the first novel or the first novel in episotarly (letter) form. It was one of the driest things I've ever had to read. I was supposed to read it for an all-about-the-novel class in college, but I didn't make it all the way through. I think the only thing worse than this novel was trying to read books in Old and Middle English (yeah, like that was possible!). 
 In case you're really interested in reading this (why??! why????!!!!), it's about a young servant girl in the house of an a young but attractive master who is lusting after her. Pamela has the protect her virtue, i.e. her virginity, against her master's advances. Though she enjoys the attention a little more than she should and flaunts her figure through clothing that a maid really shouldn't be wearing (in the 17th century, so that could mean that she reveals an ankle when she shouldn't). Turns out the master wants to marry her, but she's way below his station, so he has to resort to abducting her in a carriage on the way to her parents' house, holding her against her will at another one of his residences, and having an older woman servant watching over her. At some point while is Pamela protecting her virtue, the older servant and the master try to force Pamela to have sex with him, but in the end he can't do it. It's a relatively happy ending for both of them, as the master asks Pamela to marry him. But isn't it better hearing it from me rather than trying to read it yourself? (Take my advice, unless you're crazy or something.)

Interested in experiencing long-lasting frustration? Read Pamela. 
 Wanna witness multiple sexual assault? Read Pamela. 
 Ever wondered what Stolkholm-syndrome-like submission to hegemony is like? Read Pamela. 
 Enthusiastic about worshipping Providence and the generosity of the Lord? Read Pamela.

Dive into Jane Austen's favorite novel and novelist, and read along as a cross-dressing rapist pulls out all the stops to snare Pamela's most precious jewel. 
 Jokes aside, this is one of the first records of the reformed rake archetype--Christian Grey, anyone? Where the nearly always wealthy hero goes from desiring the heroine's consent, to desiring her. Don't you know the love of a good woman cures all wounds, or at least all raping rakes. Although Austen gives us a nice twist on this with Henry and his arc in Mansfield Park. 
 Another aside, this is why I really appreciated beta hero billionaire Blake Reynolds in Courtney Milan's cyclone series, and I'm sure since her writing is so smart it's a conscious riff, that Blake always wants Tina's enthusiastic consent--an ingenious send up of the reformed rake. 
 "I want her. But you know what I want most? I don't want her to break down and quash her reluctance. I don't want her to surrender to me. I want her to want to want me, not want me grudgingly aganist my will." (94). Milan, Courtney "Trade Me."

Yes. I am that crazy person who read each page of Pamela. I'm not even getting a masters in 18th century literature. I had no class where this was assigned reading. I am trying to write a novel that takes place in the 18th century for my college senior project and my academic advisor insisted that I had to read some books from the era and listed this one. I read it not expecting to enjoy it. I hated it. I read it with the intention to learn about 18th century culture and values. And I learned a lot. Like that a girl's "virtue" was as precious as life itself. Nobody seemed to mind a girl that whined. And I really got the sense that they truly believed that if a man molested you, it might mean that he truly loved you. And that is a very sad fact of the era.
I finished it. And I feel that that was a pretty huge accomplishment. Probably the slowest (500 page) book I've ever read.

Start to finish: badly-written, moralising drivel. If this book hadn't been as influential as it had been, this would probably have received my lowest rating. It did however prove inspirational to many in its time. I'm sure the world is a better place for it. Absolutely. 
 Pamela is a woman who sincerely believes that the best way to resist emotional and sexual abuse from her employer, Mr B., is to believe the best about him. She seems oblivious to the fact that he is an unrepentant predator nor to the fact that by not removing herself from the situation, she contributes to both the cause and result of what must be, oh, three quarters of the novel. 
 But after being a despicable lecher for most of the book, he suddenly turns over a new leaf and she, dim girl, decides that this is satisfactory and ends up marrying him. They settle down happily and she begins to work on his acquaintances and friends, sorting their debased lives out as well through her pious example. And then, suddenly, 
 right at the end, just when you think things are going to continue in the same vein they have for over 300 pages, absolutely nothing happens. 
 Oh, dear. Now I've spoiled it for you. 
 I thought this was a poor book from beginning to end. At the very least, this is misguided rubbish by a man who had absolutely no idea what it was like to be a vulnerable female in a male-dominated society where women's needs came slightly lower down the scale than those of the family dog. To suggest that women who found themselves subject to compromise from the likes of Mr B., could simply hold fast to their virtue and defeat evil is naive at best and downright dangerous at worst. 
 And it's written in the most laborious and over-elaborate style conceivable. Things happen but the whole thing is so drawn out you feel like nothing does. It's epistolary, which is an entirely pointless structure which I don't think a single author has ever pulled off to their credit. 
 So, I've read it to save you the bother. Go and find an author who can write a moral tale without sermonising and leave Richardson for lit. buffs to analyse.

Wow. Is all I can say. This book will suck the life out of you. It is so repetitive and emotionally draining, not in a good way. I typical love epistolary novels however, Pamela makes it so hard to feel sorry for her. I just could not get into this book.

I really wanted to prove all of the naysayers wrong when I began this book (which I picked up at a used book sale due to Pamela being my mother's name). However, by the very fact that it took me months to read it, it can be determined that this was not a particularly enjoyable read. In fact, my finishing it seems almost as momentous as passing my PhD comprehensive exams last week. 
 It goes without saying that the ideas presented in this novel are out of date and seemingly ridiculous in this day and age; this, I think, is not a weakness, but lends to whatever level of charm it possesses. It is the writing style that is hard to digest at first. I think it will be difficult to go back to reading straightforward prose. The worst part of Pamela is that it is just too long-winded. It is about 350 pages too long, which I assume is why others choose to reach for the abridged version. After one gets past the writing style, the first 200 pages are fairly entertaining mainly due to their absurdity. (The fact of her being about 14 aside...) At times you just want to scream at her to sleep with him already! Her opinion towards the creepy, obnoxious, would-be rapist (I mean she is just asking for it since she's so pretty--eye roll!) Mr. B changes far too early in the book, leaving the last 300 pages as basically a venue for Samuel Richardson to vent his opinions on society, religion, and politics. 
 In conclusion, I'm glad I read it and I'm also REALLY glad its over.

The problem with "Pamela" isn't that it's an infuriating book. It is, but of course you have to read it with the historical context in mind. That makes it a little less aggravating. 
 No, the problem is that most of the book is dull. There's at least some interest in the beginning, with Pamela trying to evade the threat of her employer. But after he supposedly grows a conscience and she tosses her brain out the window, the book is just one long meeting of their mutual admiration society--with the occasional break to let someone else pop up and compliment them for a change. 
 I made the mistake of thinking "it's classic literature, so it has to get better sometime!" It didn't. You may like it a lot more than I did. But I'd strongly advise potential readers to be willing to abandon ship. If you're bored partway through, it's very unlikely you'll find anything to recapture your interest.

I first discussed Emma Chase via my local library, where I found "Tangled" on the New Reads shelves. Best find ever. Finally, a romantic comedy that was actually funny! And I have faithfully followed Ms. Chase ever since (and got to meet her a few years ago at the RT Convention in New Orleans-if you see this, Ms. Chase, my apologies for not having my best manners on display; I was so excited to be there that I forgot to think straight half the time). 
 When Emma announced the start of a new series, I both rejoiced and pondered. Huzzah! More Emma Chase goodness! But no Drew or Kate...and I love them so much...I am sure there are/were others like me out there. 
 Well, having read and reveled in "Overruled," I can say we should relax. The witty humor that had me falling over in laughter with "Tangled" is present in this new series as well. While Stanton's not quite as hilarious as Drew, he is a rather enjoyable ass. Takes him forever to realize the inevitable. And as a native Mississippian (unfortunately), I was amused at how spot-on the descriptions of Sunshine, MS, and life there were. (for the record, I kept picturing the real life Summit, MS, as Sunshine in my head) 
 The plot is fairly simple: Stanton is a successful attorney in Washington, D.C. when he learns that his long-time love (and mother of his child), Jenny, is getting married-and not to him, like he'd always assumed she would. With typical male bravado (and hormones) raging, Stanton races down to Mississippi, with his friend and co-worker, Sofia, in tow. What follows is a story of love, longing, hilarity, gun toting grannies, tractor races and male bonding, lions on a date in the jungle (okay, okay, that's not really a big part of the book but it just struck me as a hilarious description of The Lion King that IS used in the story), and ultimately the wit, humor, and highly entertaining sex scenes we've come to love and expect from Emma Chase. It's a highly different world from Drew Evans (spoiler alert: Drew makes a cameo, and he's as funny as ever and 'makes' the most of his appearance), but yet still familiar and fun.

 In the first book of this author's new series, we meet the sweet southern boy, Stanton, who has a life plan with his girl, Jenny. But life throws them a curve-ball, and the two react in the strangest of ways. 
 Fast forward 11 or so years later. Stanton still has his plan. In his head, Jenny is still his girl. Even though the live in completely different states, and see other people. But have no worries, it's all just casual. Riiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiight, that's how it always starts. 
 Although the L word is only used by towards one person in the beginning, this story is clearly a love triangle. Just not the typical one. 
 Stanton loves Jenny. 
 Jenny has a past with Stanton, but no longer loves him in that way. 
 Sofia has a friends with benefits relationship with Stanton, but its obvious, it means more to both of them then they admit. 
 Throughout the story, I really didn't know what to think of Stanton. He's got all the qualities of the perfect BBF, except one. His heart wasn't were I wanted it to be. And as you read the story, you sense his heart might not actually be where he things it is, he's just so focused on "the plan" that he can't see what's right in front of him. 
 Stanton and Sofia are seriously hot together. This quote alone says is all: 
 I grip my dick firmly, pumping slow, then trace the tip over Sofia's lips, spreading the moisture already there across them. 
 I look into those eyes, eyes a man could drown in if he's not careful - and I tell her, "Open." 
 5 alarm fire, H-O-T!!! Yowza! 
 While I wasn't sure what I thought about Stanton, I loved Sofia. I'll admit, I didn't quite understand how she could do the "friends with benefits" thing without getting attached. She so bravely supported Stanton's quest to get back the "love of his life", not herself. At first I didn't understand how she could distance herself, but little by little, she lets the emotion peak out, and it only made my heart break for her. 
 "We're friends who fuck - that's nothing like what me and Jenn are."

 Sofia remained strong and not a whiny annoying heroine, even as she broke down, so I couldn't fault her in any way. 
 As for Jenny, like Sofia, I wanted to hate her. But it really was just impossible to do. I could totally understand her reasoning for moving on. How she convinces Stanton to do the same, was a bit unexpected, but I like how she pointed out all of the obvious signs he had been ignoring all along. 
 "You're so stubborn - you're so stuck on what you think is supposed to be, that you're missin' what's right in front of you." 
 While this book doesn't have the laugh a sentence humor than the Tangled series did, there are still funny moments, usually from the cast of secondary characters. 
 Nana and her gun - She never did like "that boy" Stanton, but she offers much needed advice to him at the oddest of times.

The love triangle was a bit odd and unexpected, as two people come to realize that there careful laid plains where blown up when their hearts opened up to the idea of love. I'm really looking forward to the next two books in the series, which feature Jake and Brent, who work in DC with Stanton and Sofia.

So Many Reasons I Shouldn't Like This Book, and Yet I Did 
 "You're so stubborn -- you're so stuck in what you think is supposed to be, that you're missin' what's right in front of you." 
 FINAL DECISION: I book I put off reading because it has two things I really tend to dislike lawyers and a hero who believes he is in love with someone else -- yet somehow I found this book compelling. I couldn't stop reading it. My only complaint is that I wanted more. 
 THE STORY: Stanton Shaw, a criminal defense attorney in Washington, D.C. is known as "The Jury Charmer" because he is a man it is hard to say no to. He has a plan for his life. Although he lives in D.C. his heart is in MIssissippi with his childhood sweetheart and their daughter. The two had a child as teenagers and although they were in love, they kept postponing their life together. Stanton, however, believes that they have a special and immutable connection until he gets an invitation to her wedding to someone else. Stanton is determined to go home and convince her to call of the wedding. He decides to bring along with him Sofia Santos who is also an attorney at the firm he works with. Stanton and Sofia have been friends with benefits neither wanting a more serious relationship. While Stanton works to recover his past love, he can't seem to forget the woman of the moment. 
 OPINION: I've had this series on my radar for a while. People keep recommending the books to me, but I'm generally not a fan of lawyer books. Being an attorney myself, I often don't find the tone and voice of the book to fit in my experience. Finally, this book had been recommended one too many times and I was looking for something new to read and I started this book with low expectations. And then I couldn't put it down. 
 I was attracted by the tone of the book. The book begins with the first person narrative of the hero and then switches between the first person of Stanton and Sofia. This book is really Stanton's story because it is his continued expectation of his relationship with his childhood sweetheart that animates the story. Although I am generally not a fan of stories where one of the characters believes themselves in love with someone else, I thought it worked here because of the first person narrative. Having access to Stanton's thoughts gives readers an understanding of how he actually feels for Sofia and for the woman he insists he loves. I just had to smile at his blindness of his own true feelings. Stanton also is incredibly honest in recognizing his mistakes by the time he acknowledges he loves Sofia that I forgave him for his stupidity throughout the book. 
 This book felt deep and emotional and I felt so connected to the characters and felt their connection to one another. The book tackles difficult issues of first love and coming to terms with the loss of young dreams and I ended up loving it. 
 I give high marks to a book that was much more than what I thought when I read the description. 
 WORTH MENTIONING: Warning that the hero spends almost the entire book believing he is in love with his childhood sweetheart. 
 CONNECTED BOOKS: OVERRULED is the first book in the Legal Briefs series. 
 STAR RATING: I give this book 4.5 stars.

Heather's review from Smut MattersThis won't be a very long review. I don't have a lot to say about this book. For the record, I love Emma Chase's books. She has this way of writing heroes who are complete assholes but you just can't help but root for them. As infuriating as Drew Evans (from her Tangled Series) could be, you couldn't help but root for him and Kate. 
 Not Stanton Shaw. He wasn't even an asshole. Ok. He was an asshole. But what I couldn't deal with was how dim-witted he was. He was an apparently good lawyer, so he had to have some smarts somewhere, but none of them were on display here. I suppose there could be some minor spoilers here, so beware if you haven't read this one yet. 
 He and his high school girlfriend ended up being very young parents. Stanton was determined to do the right thing by Jenny, and take care of her and the baby. Jenny insisted he keep the scholarship he had already won and get his education so he could better take care of them. Her family was not thrilled with the situation, of course, but were as supportive as they could be and more than willing to have Jenny and the baby live with them while Stanton went to college and law school. So he did. He left their tiny little town and went to DC for college and law school, then settled there. Before he left, he and Jenny agreed to still be a couple, but not to hold each other to any promises of monogamy. So when the book picks up, ten years have passed. Ten years. Stanton makes it home about once a year to see Jenny and his daughter and the rest of his family, and spends the rest of his time fucking his way through DC. Everyone is happy. 
 Then he gets an invitation to Jenny's wedding and freaks right out. He can't believe that "his girl" would get married to anyone who wasn't him. He drops everything to go back home and convince her that it's bullshit and he's the only one for her. Well, that's not exactly true. He doesn't drop everything. He doesn't drop his current long-running fuck-buddy, Sofia. He really doesn't drop her. He takes her with him. To his hometown. To help him convince Jenny to marry him. This whole part is where Stanton lost me. He genuinely can't see why Sofia thinks it's a bad idea for her to go to Mississippi with him. He's been having sex with Sofia for about six months, they work together, and he can't imagine any reason she shouldn't go to Mississippi to convince another woman to marry him. Between the freak out over Jenny's impending nuptials and this, I was pretty much done with Stanton. 
 And it was unfortunate because I really liked both Sofia and Jenny. But I lost a lot of respect for both of them, especially Sofia. Jenny had been in love with Stanton in high school, but she was smart enough to realize that it was currently a nostalgic kind of love she'd always have for her first love and the father of her daughter. Sofia, on the other hand, was really smart and kind, and generous, and beautiful, and still fell for this dim-witted goofball with only the one redeeming quality. (To quote John Oliver - "Fucking. I'm talking about fucking.") Keep sleeping with him, sure, but to fall in love with this guy was beyond me. 
 Anyway, I'm moving on. I still love Emma Chase's stuff, and I can't wait to read the rest of this series.

Even though Sofia realizes she is starting to fall hard for Stanton, she allows him to talk her into going with him, because he "needs" her. (Gag!) At this point, to me, Sofia was really degrading herself. Sofia does tell him that on the trip they can't have sex because this is supposed to be about Stanton and Jenny putting their relationship back together and it wouldn't be right for Stanton and Sofia to be having sex all the while. But, that agreement lasts about 30 seconds. Whenever Stanton is horny or feels needy, Sofia gives in to him and has sex despite the fact that he is spending time with Jenny, trying to keep their relationship together. 
 By this point, I couldn't stand watching Sofia degrade herself any further and quit reading---about 2/3 the way through. I mean, I want to read about a romantic "hero," not a man who is so immoral that he sweet-talks one woman into screwing him while he's claiming to love---and trying to reclaim---another woman. And, reading about a heroine who allows a man to exploit her makes me feel sort of ill. I mean, these people's behaviors are too close to some sick real-life relationships I have seen and I hate that an author is putting out these kinds of behaviors as "romantic."

Emma Chase is an incredible writer! She knows just the right way to write a romantic comedy, without making it sound forced. 
 There's genuine humor in her books! And Overruled couldn't be different. 
 I really liked this book. It entertained me a lot and I coul't put it down...read it in an hour! 
 One thing though, one of the sentences in Portuguese didn't make a lot of sense, probably because it was tranlated through Google Translate or other translator....those never get phrases right, just individual words (and even those aren't very reliable). I really advise to ask someone before using them, but most of the Portuguese was right and there wasn't much of it, two phrases, actually. So who am I to judge? If I didn't' know Portuguese I wouldn't notice, but since I do, I can't not mention, because to me it always sound a little disappointening to see an author using something he/she doesn't know without proper research, even if it's just one phrase. 
 I'm like that in Portuguese too, I can't stand people using English wrong...the perks of being a Portuguese and English teacher. haha 
 Anyways, that didn't take any of my "like" for this story. Little grammar mistakes don't bother me, I only mentioned this, because I'm Brazilian so it didn't feel right, but Sofia's family names were all so right (the spelling and the use, I oove when an author is considerate enough to use names that actually are used in th countries their characters are from). But I disgress... 
 Stanton and Sofia story is filled with passion, HOTNESS, fun and friendship! God I loved Presleyi, she was adorable and Stanton might make ovaries explode for sure!! :) 
 I definitely recommend this book if you want a story that will make you laugh out loud genuinely. It has a sharp sense of humor and even sharper charaters (Nana was another great character). The heroine is fun and strong, but we get to see her vulnerable side too, so she's very relatable.. 
 I don't agree woth Stanton's behavior during his 10 years between college and the present, but I liked him too!!

Hmm... no where near as satisfying and laugh-out-loud hilarious as "Tangled". May try the second in the series just because it focuses on different characters -- these two are far from appealing, and let's face it, the set up makes it a bit hard to swallow his total change of heart by the end.

So glad to finally get into The Legal Briefs series. I've been meaning to read this for a long time but didn't have a chance. Overruled is about Stanton Shaw and Sofia Santos, both are bright lawyers working in a law firm and they are friends with benefits. 
 One day, Stanton received a wedding invitation from his High School lover and mother of his child, Jenny Monroe. Jenny got pregnant when he's about to leave Sunshine, Mississippi to pursue Law studies. They became good parents to Presley, their daughter. Jenny encourage him to pursue his dreams to become a lawyer instead of being stuck in a small town and they have an agreement to have an open relationship. He decided to go home and asked Sofia to accompany him in the hopes Jenny will change her mind. 
 Sofia is a hardworking woman who doesn't have time to have relationships. She's okay with the arrangement she has with Stanton and when he needs help, she doesn't hesitate to help him. Her feelings for him developed as she gets to spend more time with him. They have an intense sexual tension and chemistry but is he capable of loving her just like Jenny? Is he willing to go beyond their arrangement? 
 I like Overruled because of the angst and humor. There are times it made me laugh and I really enjoy the little drama. However, Stanton was a let down. He may be charming, sexy and intelligent in the work field, but he's an idiot for handling his relationships. He left the ladies hanging and I really feel bad for both of them. Jenny waited so long for him but he didn't come back for her, I understand why she moved on from him and I'm glad she ended up with a guy who will cherish her. As for Sofia, she deserves to be treated better than this. It's obvious she loved him and I'm frustrated Stanton didn't see that earlier. He. Is. So. Damn. Blind. 
 It's still a good start despite of my issues with the male lead. I'm going to continue the series and hopefully it gets better. P.S. It's nice to see Drew Evans here ;) I miss that swoon worthy man. ;)))

Omg 
 Just no, how on earth are you supposed to cheer for the happy couple? 
 1 - he is an asshole 
 2 - his baby mama is a doormat 
 3 - the love interest is sleeping with a married man 
 And the couple are supposed to ride off into the sunset HEA 
 Vomiting in my mouth a little bit
3.75 stars

HNRY 
 The hero, Stanton, spent too much time with his baby mama, Jenny, than the heroine, Sofia. A little over 60% was spent with Stanton fighting for the interest of Jenny. Ugh. These are my least favorite stories. I don't want the hero PINING for his baby mama. I do not trust those type of heroes. Not for me. It may work for you.

This had some funny parts to it like you can expect from Emma, as well as those sex scenes we all lov . What I could not stand is the way these woman were portrayed. They were nothing but door mats for Stanton. I lost complete interest in this book after he acted like a caveman thinking he owns one woman while screwing the other. I was excited for a new series from Emma but this book really disappointed me. I won't bother reading anymore in this series.

2.5-3 stars. I won this book from a FB giveaway. The writing is good. The story is, for the most part, good. The characters... Stanton is an a$$hole. Majorly... I could not pull for him. I wanted Sofia (and Jenn) to find someone who appreciated her. I never believed that Stanton did. He was such a jerk. The series seems good though and I'm looking forward to Jake's story coming soon in the series.

Sustained was a pretty good read. I liked the secondary characters so decided to give this a try. 
 Cussing ensues! 
 Are you fucking kidding me? The hero, a term that could be used loosely, is sex on wheels. Yes, he is. Emma Chase writes exciting, seductive heroes and Stanton definitely falls in this category. Too bad he is an amoral asshole who wants his cake and fuck it too. Sorry. I am angry. 
 He gets his high school sweetheart pregnant, is there for her, but they decide not to get married as he has to go get his law degree in New York. The girlfriend says they should keep things open, and boy does he. Ten years later Stanton is in a friends with benefit aka fuck-buddy relationship with Sofia, another attorney at his firm, but still keeps things open with the mother of his daughter. 
 He finds out that his ex is planning on getting married so he takes Sofia (she of the fuck-buddy relationship) and goes back to get his ex back. Sofia actually goes. Stanton and Sofia have sex as much as possible while he tries to manipulate Jenny back into his life. 
 I am done. 
 Is this supposed to be charming? Who does this kind of crap?

4.5 stars 
 What an awesome listen! It was fun, it was sexy, it was fresh, and it had the unmistakable Emma Chase captivating writing style! Loved it! 
 Simply put, we have Emma Chase's type of hero we got to know and love in Tangled - all cocky smart ass, hot as hell, who manages to be charming even when he's a total jackass and you want to punch him in the face LOL, the lawyer-y type of strong, sassy, independent woman we met in Julie James's books and the romantic, sweet, warm, all around funtastic big family we saw in Jennifer Probst's Millionaire series. Quite the combination if you ask me, and if you like any of those authors, you'll love this too! 
 Either way, fun, quick, perfect summer read! 
 I'll admit, the plot, the twists and the way the hero acted was kind of frustrating, but with this set of characters, this writing style, this world, the humor, you cannot not fall in love with the story and devour every word. :D 
 After Jenny disappears from the doorway, I climb slowly up the porch steps--the way you'd approach a hibernating, crotchety old bear. You're fairly certain it's safe, but it's best to be ready to bolt just in case it has one good swipe of its claws left. 
 I tip my hat to Nana in greeting. "Ma'am." 
 Her eyes thin to razor-sharp slits. "I don't like you, boy." 
 "Yes, ma'am." 
 Her crooked finger juts out at me. "You're a Satan. Slitherin' in to trick Eve out of Paradise." 
 "Yes, ma'am." 
 *** 
 Her eyes go wide, then narrow. She folds her arms and takes deliberate steps toward us. It's her court stance, defense attorney mode--and it's sexy as fuck. 
 "I'm sorry," she says, not sounding sorry at all. "Did you just say, 'It's a maaan thang'?" 
 "I don't talk like that." 
 "Well, that's how Neanderthal sounds in my head. I'm just waiting for you to grunt, pound your chest, and rub some sticks together. Or have you not discovered fire yet?" 
 *** 
 Presley stops in front of me. "We use our words to solve problems around here, not our fists." She paces some more. Then she looks hard at Jenny. "And you've hurt JD's feelin's. You need to say sorry." 
 We nod in sad unison. 
 Getting your ass chewed out by an eleven-year-old is no fun at all. 
 Presley shakes her head and wags her finger. "I'm very disappointed in both of you. I want you to sit here and think about your behavior. And next time, I expect you to make better choices." 
 With a final reproachful humph, she flounces away--leaving us to stew. 
 *** 
 When you're young, you love fireworks 'cause they're loud and bright and thrillin'. But then you grow up. And you see that candlelight isn't so thrillin', but it still makes everything better. You realize that the glow of a fireplace can be just as excitin' as fireworks--the way it burns low, but lights your home and keeps you warm all night long. Stanton was my fireworks . . . JD's my fireplace."

** spoiler alert ** 
 After tedious consideration, I have decided to give up on this book entirely. As much as I love the author's sense of humor and as much as I would love to be consistent in finishing each and every book I decide to read, I simply could not finish this book out of principle. 
 Stanton is an asshole, that much is said and established. But while I love Drew's character in the original Tangled series, Stanton only comes off as an immature and overly entitled dick-head. Sure, there are parallels to their character and the author certainly tried to emulate the classic formula that made her first series widely successful. But, that's all there is to it. The plot is weak, unrealistic, and, frankly, demeaning to women. 
 The problem really lies in the story and the characters. To explain, the plot is really about Stanton who after getting his high school sweetheart pregnant, he goes off to DC to become a successful lawyer. They both have an open relationship and Stanton decides to sleep with all of DC and NY. He does all this expecting Jenny to still love him and accept him every time he goes to visit their sweet southern childhood home. He then goes off the rails when he finds out she's actually found love and is getting married, so Stanton decides to pull a really dick move and convinces his fuck buddy - Sofia - to go with him and prove his love to Jenny. On the way, he tries to get in Sofia's pants too. 
 Stanton shows no signs of emotional maturity. The female lead is also troublesome since she's such a pushover despite being a definite alpha in the work and life department. She certainly deserves better but she's waiting around for a cheater who, by no means, will only spell disaster for her. 
 I find this absolutely disheartening. Women are already subjected to several harmful messages on love and relationships by books such as Twilight and 50 shades of grey that glamorize abuse as healthy ideals for relationships. No, they're not. 
 While there's no physical abuse in the book, there is a definite number of psychological and emotional manipulations that, frankly, I think the leading lady can do without. What's terrible is she actually believes she deserves the crappy treatment. 
 Also, maybe because I like reading between the lines, I cannot enjoy this book because I tend to read the subtext. 
 Bottom line is: Stanton is an asshole for expecting the woman he impregnated to remain loyal to him (and limit her emotional and personal growth for him) while expecting his fuck buddy to be conveniently there for him (emotionally and sexually) while he woos the ex-girlfriend. 
 I know what the author is trying to express here and I know she's sincerely trying to make a point about how we can all move on from making stupid decisions blah blah blah. 
 But - I think the author knows it too - her female characters deserve so much better because they're better than that. That is exactly why she made Kate & Deedee such strong characters in her previous series. I think she's trying to do the same but failed when she made a male character that seems too discouraging to even provide substantial emotional development. 
 But that's just my opinion. My brother clearly likes this series, so that maybe something to consider when I do change my mind and try to finish this. 
 For now, I doubt finishing this book will happen anytime soon. 
 As it is, there are other stories that I will happily waste my time on.
That was depressing

My favorite Emma Chase book so far. I was a criminal defense attorney once and many things rang true to me :) Every single one of the characters was sympathetic and someone you wanted to root for - even the people inadvertently keeping the hero and heroine apart! It's filled with Chase's trademark witty banter, funny, sexy and very real male characters, and uber passionate sex scenes! Can't wait to read the rest in the Legal Briefs series!
3 stars - Contemporary Romance
A fast read. I really enjoyed the book and the characters. It was nice to have a cameo appearance from Drew. Sadly, the cameo appearance reminded me how much I miss Drew!

I didn't want this story to end. It was smart, it was sexy and it was fun. Did I mention sexy? Well more like major sexy. The main male character is macho and alpha, both loving and selfish, and wants what he wants when he wants it. For the first time, things aren't going the way he planned and he's going all out to change it with the help of his "wing woman" who is also his coworker and bed buddy. I adored every character in this book from their smart snarky friends, outrageous family members and a shotgun toting nanny. I don't want to give away any of the hilarious plot points so I'll just say this is a grand beginning to what I know will be a very entertaining series. 
 Well done Emma!

DNF @ 50% 
 I hate to not finish a story, but I feel like I gave this one a pretty good shot. When at the halfway point I still wasn't feelin' the characters, I had to stop. 
 I guess my issues with the story started right at the beginning. I should note - I forgot what the story was about, so I went in blind. It seemed the story was about a couple of high school sweethearts, that had found themselves accidentally pregnant. I was on board with their love... until their 'Open relationship' status was revealed, a year after they welcomed their baby girl. In no world is an open relationship a good idea. It was a recipe for disaster and what happened next was the beginning of Stanton's demise for me, even if it all did start out as his girlfriend Jenny's idea. 
 The southern gentleman transformed into a DC manwhore and I hated him for it. It didn't help that the stories 'heroine' was sprung on me a chapter or so later - ten years down the track - when I was still stuck on what had happened with his baby mama a few pages earlier. In my eyes the heroine, Sofia, was 'the other woman', so I instantly hated her too. I also didn't like the way their friends with benefits relationship was thrust upon me. There was no build up, they were six months into their fucking friendship, and it was clear they were swerving into feeling more than casual, but I didn't care. Then I found out the relationship with Jenny, which I assumed had crumbled and died ten years earlier, was actually still going on. He still considered her 'his girl', even as he lived and fucked his way around DC, many miles away from her and his daughter in Mississippi. What a pig. 
 You could say I hated everything about Stanton, and the story gave me this horrid feeling... that kind of heavy gut you get when something bad is going on... yeah, that's how I felt when I read this. I see other reviews talking about how great Stanton is and how hot they were etc, but all I can think is, HE IS A PIG! And a hypocrite. His reaction to finding out his girl is getting married angered me! It's as if he expected her to raise their daughter, still living with her parents, waiting for the day he decided to come back to her. And what did he decide to do to stop her? Take his friend with benefits Sofia home with him to win his girl back. Oh, and of course they fucked each others brains out on the way home to Jenny! PIG!! And slut. 
 Eww, eww, eww this book just makes me feel dirty - and not in a good way. The more I'm thinking of it the more I'm ranting and the more infuriated I'm feeling. So I should go... My one star rating does not reflect the writing - it was good. In fact, to get me this enraged, I'd have to say it was great! But it has had a terrible effect on me lol. 
 Fuck Stanton! I'm out.

It took me forever to read this audiobook. Part of the problem was I couldn't listen to it if there were other people in the car. Then the male MC was such an egocentric jerk that I would get angry and turn it off. The last third of the book, when it focussed on story and not sex, was much more engaging.

reference_books.title: Linger (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Recipe for InstaCouple, as demonstrated by Maggie Stiefvater 
 Ingredients are as follows: 
 1 melodramatic, moody teenage girl 
 1 angst-ridden, incredibly lyrical werewolf 
 Just add a drop of parental disapproval and let sit for two to three days. 
 Voila! You've got your InstaCouple. 
 Warning: side effects include lyrical, borderline strange prose, large amounts of blood loss, lovesickness in its many forms, and harrowing drama.

reference_books.title: The Reckoning (Darkest Powers, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Sigh. 
 Unfortunately, this final act didn't redeem its predecessors. 
 There were no surprises or amazing plot twists. As usual, everything was too contrived, the dialogue was painful to read, and there just wasn't the spark that marks a great book. 
 The ending was more disappointing than all Disney sequels combined, and that's saying something. By midway through the Reckoning, I didn't even care about the romance because it was so obvious how it was going to work out. 
 Everything was insanely predictable and no matter how hard I tried, I never really believed in what was going on. It was all so improbable and cinematic. I have a good feeling that if this series was turned into movies, I'd actually like the movies better than the books. Because that's what the books already are: geared for a target audience, filled with all these Hollywood-esque twists and turns, and providing nothing more than a distraction for a couple hours. 
 Save yourself the time and energy and just don't read these books. It was only the compelling need to finish what I start that kept me reading these books. 
 I'm not condemning them...they were a nice distraction. But that's all they'll ever amount to in my mind.

reference_books.title: Forever (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
Hmm. I actually kind of cared about the characters...in the last ten pages, anyways. Stiefvater continues to drag readers down a path of soppy, selfish characters and yawn-worthy romances...I was actually kind of glad Sam and Grace were separated. 
 The reinstatement of characters that made brief, brief appearances in Shiver slowed the pace and muddled the plot, Rachel being as annoying as ever. 
 Isabel and Cole were the only interesting couple. And they exchange toy cars and random kisses. 
 This book just happened to be all over the place, the only obvious destination the wolf hunt, which was strange and confusing. 
 "Forever." Yeah right.

reference_books.title: The Awakening (Darkest Powers, #2)
reference_books.review_text:
Hardly an impressive effort. 
 The same things that bothered me in the first book were alive and kicking in this sequel that, in my eyes, serves no other purpose than connecting the Summoning and the Reckoning. It's painfully obvious that it's just a bridge between the books. Since the novelty of the series had worn off with book one, I slogged through The Awakening with no excitement or eagerness whatsoever. 
 I wasn't surprised at anything or impressed by anything for that matter. Compared to its mildly better predecessor, The Awakening won't fail to disappoint.

reference_books.title: East of Eden
reference_books.review_text:
To keep it short and simple, this novel was a spectacular read. It shared some interesting philosophies, kept me gasping and laughing, and paralleled the story of Cain and Abel {found in the Bible, Genesis to be specific} with a modern twist. 
 The only thing keeping me from giving it a five-star rating was the levels of violence, lack of morals, and serious subject matter.

reference_books.title: Shiver (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Urrrrrrgh. 
 I've read The Scorpio Races, so I was expecting this book to match a certain standard. Granted, Scorpio Races was written two years after Shiver, but still. 
 Instead of endearing characters, I found selfish, whiny, bratty, know-it-all Grace Brisbane, lovelorn, angst-ridden werewolf Sam, and a host of insanely annoying characters. Grace just seems to think she knows what's best for everyone. Stiefvater writes Sam as an obvious love interest for her (meaning he's not even his own character, he's simply a furry puppet), and the only likeable character was the enemy. Yeah. 
 Okay, so Grace and Sam fall in love with each other in what, a week? I get that Grace has watched Sam for years, but seriously? A tad obsessive. And she just...ANNOYS me! 
 The plot is riddled with holes. It's just...ugh I am seriously irritated with this book. 
 The voices of both characters were SO immature. Their "love" felt so fake. 
 Alas, I promised that I'd read the trilogy. 
 Here's to hoping it gets better.

reference_books.title: The Rosie Effect (Don Tillman, #2)
reference_books.review_text: All I can say is that I sort of wish this book wasn't written. No devastating repercussions of reading it, but it gave me secondhand anxiety and I was not okay with that.

reference_books.title: The 5th Wave (The 5th Wave, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Short Version: gripping, powerful, and wonderful, this book should be on everyone's to-read list. 
 Long Version: Maybe it's because I read a terrible book before this one, making it even greater in comparison, but I absolutely fell in love with this novel. It's a masterpiece. Hilarious, raw, shocking, well-thought out, intriguing, and so deep. All of those things and more. This was the first real page-turner I've read in a long, long time. I seriously COULD. NOT. PUT. IT. DOWN. 
 It made me feel so much in such a short time. 
 The characters were so unique and beautiful, I loved them to death. 
 While the premise might SEEM tired and overdone, the author brings something very new to the table. Any cliches you may think are in this book...think again! It doesn't feel cliche at all. I knew from the very first chapter that this was something to be treasured. There is violence, no doubt, but the way he writes it makes it work with the story. It's not just mindless, like plenty of other action novels. 
 I will sing this book's praises forever and ever. It's JUST THAT GOOD. 
 As for the plot. My goodness, that plot. It took me by surprise again and again. Every twist was a jaw-dropper and that ending is seriously a punch to the heart. SO GOOD. 
 I don't usually give out five-star reviews, but I truly feel like this book deserves it. 
 I applaud you, Mr. Yancey, on a job well done.

reference_books.title: Wake (Watersong #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Short Version: Simplified YA fantasy that makes me sick of mermaids/sirens. 
 Long Version: I was yet again disappointed with a book that had promised to be so great. I mean no disrespect to the author; I just didn't like the book. There was none of the grace and elegance I look for in a novel. It was written in a very simplistic way, as if the audience was intended to be middle-school kids. There were no new ideas that made me go, "Oh, this is interesting!" The backstory for the mythological creatures featured was very long and dry and unoriginal. The whole siren thing was weird for me. 
 Here's the breakdown. 
 Characters: I didn't like any of the narrators. They were very two dimensional and were very much stereotypes. The hot, ruggedly handsome "bad boy." The brainy, overprotective older sister. The pretty, free spirited younger sister. The geek turned hot boy next door. Etc. They all seemed very shallow and self involved. Example: Gemma seemed to be constantly obsessed over how pretty she was, and if Alex liked her enough, etc. The villains were petty and annoying rather than intimidating. Their backstory came out as stiff and rehearsed. 
 Plot: No surprises whatsoever. It was all very predictable. Nothing shocked me. 
 Dialogue: not typically a subheading, but I just have to comment. I found it very...unrealistic. They spoke so formally. It sounded very scripted and played to their individual stereotypes. It was just dry and uninteresting. 
 Setting: very vague, with the descriptions not overly interesting. 
 Writing Style: She told us what was going on, but she never really delved into how the characters were feeling. Sure, she said they were crying, but that was just an action. She didn't explain the heart-wrenching pain or the terrible loss. She just said they were crying. The action scenes were debatable and didn't do anything but point out how flawed (not in a good way) the characters were. Also, she had so many sentences that would go like, "Gemma was shallow, and this showed all the time." (Not an actual sentence). You know what I mean? She'd have ", and" ALL THE TIME. It seriously bugged me is much. Also she overused words like "really" a lot. 
 All in all, this just didn't sit with me. I didn't enjoy this book as much as I was hoping to; the whole of it was one big cliche. 
 It lacked any kind of depth...and for a novel set in the ocean, well, that's just plain ironic.

reference_books.title: Splintered (Splintered, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
Thanks, A.G. Howard, for totally ruining Lewis Caroll's classic. 
 I can justify that. 
 The book begins with a half-hearted narration that's meant to represent a teen girl's mind. What's more, it's meant to represent the mind of Alyssa Gardner, a girl who I can describe as self-centered, boy-crazy, and stubbornly independent. 
 Then things get crazier when magic is introduced. I felt that there was never a good enough explanation. Things just happened without reason or consideration, which was irritating and distracting for me. 
 Once Alyssa and her {OF COURSE} impossibly attractive sidekick enter Wonderland, the slow destruction of the classic begins. Rabid White? Really? Thank goodness I've already had the pleasure of reading the original Alice in Wonderland, or else the characters would be forever ruined by Howard's irreverent interpretation. 
 Skipping ahead to the ending, it seemed way too Pollyanna to be realistic. There was the sly hint of a possibility for a sequel, but if there is, I will avoid it at all costs. 
 One thing I noticed was that there was NO INDEPENDENT FEMALE CHARACTER. Sure, Alyssa tries to fend for herself, but her thoughts are constantly centered around the males in her life. It's like she can't survive without them. Neither can Ivory, or Red, or any of the other female characters. Their dependency on males to "fill the emptiness" is emphasized. Undermining the adventurous plot twists is the fact that it's basically just a ploy to the real story, which is Alyssa finding a man to, as aforementioned, "fill the emptiness." Speaking of males, both Jeb and Morpheus were reduced to love-crazed sidekicks to the one and only Alyssa. 
 The romance was somewhat enjoyable, but far from a stable relationship. 
 Like I mentioned briefly, the plot twists were excellently executed. It's just that the bland narration and the laughable characters did nothing to enhance or explain those plot twists. 
 Cover: 3/5 
 Characters: 2/5 
 Plot: 3/5 
 Overall: 2/5

book_a.title: Partials (Partials Sequence, #1)
book_a.user_review:
Merrr. 
 I have to say this book didn't agree with me much. The plot was unoriginal to say the least (genetically engineered beings, mysterious ours, decimated population), the writing was thick with boring adjectives and science facts (which were impressive but still, hardly helpful to the plot), and the characters didn't stick with me at all. 
 Yet there was something mildly captivating about this book. The action scenes were well done and I found myself smiling at points. 
 I think my final verdict, though, is that Dan Wells is an average writer with average talent. Not to say I could best him, but compared to other YA novels, his Partials bites the dust. 
 Cover: 3/5 
 Plot:2/5 
 Characters: 2.5/5 
 Overall: 2/5

sample_reviews.review_text: Un punto a favor es que de otras distopias que no se centra en el amor de la protagonista con algun chico. Realmente hay amor pero hacia sus amigos y la raza humana. Kira es fuerte y quiere salvar a sus amigos y hara todo lo posible, asi sea arriesgar su vida.
Overall, this is one of those novels with a really interesting premise that could have been rather promising, but ended up being incredibly boring. Great idea, poorly executed.

Past the hundred page mark and the only thing that happened was one explosion and one camel. 
 People said that this was up there with The Hunger Games. There is only one way I can see that happening. 
 This was actually labeled as a don't miss dystopian series. Well here's me, missing it....
DNF at around 40%
I absolutely love this trilogy. The ending was kinda rushed but I still loved it overall. Adventure, and more adventure.

This book had a lot going for it: great premise, some solid characters, plot twists (some of them predictable, others not), etc. 
 However, it is in severe need of a good editor. To me, this felt like a solid middle draft. Something that maybe a publishing house might deservingly purchase, yeah. But then it would be, you know, edited to remove logical inconsistencies and improve the pacing. 
 There were SO MANY inconsistencies. It got to the point where neither I nor my readalong companions could tell when something was a deliberate clue-type inconsistency or just a gaping plot or worldbuilding hole (most of them turned out to be just holes). 
 The pacing was also a huge issue. If the whole book contained what its last 100 pages or so did, the book would get at least four stars from me, even if the logic holes remained. It was exciting, surprising, and the characters got into a lot of trouble they had to figure out how to extract themselves from. 
 ...And then the book ended. *sigh* I'll definitely read the second one, in the hope that Wells will be able to maintain the momentum that he gathered in the last bit of this book (and hopefully his editor will be more on the ball this time), but I just can't justify giving this book more than three stars as it stands.

I was underwhelmed with the believability of some aspects, but still it makes for a good story which improves in the second half. There are just so many unanswered questions which hopefully will be answered in the next book.

I wanted to like this book so badly. I forced myself to read the entire thing, hoping it would get better. It never really did. This book was a mess, in my opinion. 
 First off, it did not feel like a post-apocalypse story for some reason. I understood that it was, and the characters kept telling me it was, but it never felt like it. Really, it just made me want to go replay Fallout so I could get a true post-apocalypse story. 
 None of the threats felt all that real. The Voice was just there, and never really was. We didn't see them until the very end. We were just told they were attacking, and never actually saw it happen. I honestly didn't even think they really existed. 
 The virus made no sense to me. Maybe it's because I'm not very science based, but I still don't understand why it only affected the babies. That probably was explained, and it just went way over my head. Also, way too much info-dumping about the virus. Way too much. It got boring. 
 Also, I'm still not sure what exactly the Partials are. For some reason, I thought they were mostly robots, but I guess not...? They are part human, but I don't know what the other part is. They seemed more like super-humans to me. So the name 'Partials' felt inaccurate to me. 
 Some of the characters were a mess. Marcus, in the beginning, apparently was never serious, but by the end, that's all he was. And it wasn't character development, it was just bad continuity. Plus, I still don't completely understand who Isolde was. Was that one of Kira's "sisters"? There were just way too many characters that weren't developed, so it was really difficult to keep track of them. 
 Normally, weird names don't bother me. I understand that fantasy characters should have fantastical names, like Legolas and Bilbo, and that sci-fi characters should have sci-fi sounding names, like Yoda, and Spock. Characters from different cultures, or in the future, fine. But there was really no reason for these characters to have such bizarre names. It's only 50 years in the future. I think normal-ish names would survive. And I mean, seriously, the closest thing to normal was 'Samm'. You couldn't have just named him 'Sam'? Seriously? It was annoying. And again, I am not bothered by weird names, but these ones bothered me! 
 The "twist" was so predictable, I figured it out just from the title of the book. Without reading a single word, other than the title, I knew that was going to be twist. Granted, it's a thing that the YA genre is doing lately, so I've seen it before, way too many times. It's not a twist any more, you guys. Please stop doing that. Nobody's shocked anymore. It's just far too predictable. 
 The writing also felt messy to me. Maybe it was because I zoned out so many times, but suddenly the characters would be in a new place, or doing something new, and I had no idea when that had happened or why. It jumped around a lot. Again, that could have been me thinking about all of the other things I would have rather been doing that reading this book. 
 The ending was way too rushed. That last chapter skipped an entire week, and it was not okay. Suddenly the bad guys were doing what Kira wanted them to do, and things were being resolved, far too easily. It was very infuriating. 
 There were times when it was somewhat interesting. It definitely got intense towards the end, but I just stopped caring. I didn't like any of the characters, so I didn't care what happened to them. I just needed to finish the book since I've quit so many lately.

The year is 2076. Kira is sixteen. She was orphaned when she was five by a war against the Partials, a legion of genetically engineered soldiers who turned against their human creators. A violent, deadly virus was unleashed that killed millions across the globe. The survivors were plunged into chaos. A settlement of survivors grew into a society, located on Long Island. They believe themselves to be the only humans left in the world but there is no outside communication so they can't be entirely sure. Power and technology are in scarce supply. Kira has had to grow up much too soon in order to survive the past eleven years in a society that has forgotten much of what it once knew. For eleven years the Partials have let them be, but strife and turmoil amongst the remaining humans threatens their existence again. The deadly virus has a devastating consequence; no babies can be birthed without contracting the fatal virus almost immediately. Kira is a promising medic, a student just learning her profession. She wants to find a way to prevent RM from destroying the human race and time is running out. The youngest citizen is now fourteen. Desperate attempts to increase the number of pregnancies and live births has brought forth no solution but has fomented the unease and unrest of the citizenry who object the Machiavellian decrees from the government. Kira decides she needs to study the Partials to discover why they are immune to the virus if she is to have any hope of understanding how to stop the disease in humans. But the mission is dangerous and forbidden. Headstrong and persuasive, she sneaks away with a loyal group of friends to save the future for the survivors of mankind. Her discoveries may heal or destroy all of mankind. 
 The premise of the novel is good; Deadly virulent virus knocks out most of humankind, evil, genetically engineered partial humans who look human but are sophisticated killing machines, and a set of egotistical, tyrannical government officials who schizophrenically sway between wanting to protect mankind versus controlling mankind for their own good or the good of those in power. 
 The trouble here hinges around a young protagonist who readers are expected to believe has the ability and training beyond her tender years to qualify her to be the one discovering the cure. You may argue that this is just what young adult readers might gobble up, a teen saving the day against improbable odds. And, I would likely concur. But I found myself wanting there to be some explanation or reason that could allow me to swallow that improbability more easily. The author told me several times that Kira was qualified, but I just didn't ever suspend my disbelief wholly. Another problem I had was wrapping my head around the science, virology and genetic engineering. I felt like the author had to connect a lot of the dots for the reader implicitly because, left to their own devices, we'd never make the leap ourselves to the truths you need to have for the plot to spool along. And, finally, I felt that the novel would have benefited from better editing, especially in the first 180 pages. I am often critical of novels that neglect or short cut world building, but in the case of Partials it needed to be more succinct. It's not until Kira and her team head into Manhattan that the action of the story begins to pick up and that's well over 150 pages into the novel. I dare say you will lose a few teen readers along the way with this approach. Still, the novel does pick up steam and does start to elevate your sympathetic nervous system as Kira and the gang race to the finish with a few interesting twists. I think the biggest problem the novel has is that it just doesn't connect on an emotional level the way some other Dystopians have i.e. Hunger Games, Delirium, or Unwind. The trick is creating a protagonist the reader feels she/he really could know, imperfect but rallying, and a slew of other characters who you feel passionately about too. To the point of readers playfully taking sides. Edward or Jacob? Gale or Peeta? But Marcus or Samm? No, they don't invoke the same kind of tension. Still, I find myself looking forward to the next installment! I am curious to see what ParaGen is all about and if the world is really as decimated as it seems.

Genetic Engineering: A fascinating and frightening topic. Should the field of study be allowed? If so, what rules should be in place to govern the participants, who enforces the rules and who punishes the rule breakers? 
 Partials introduces a world clinging to existence in an apocalyptic mess created by the consequences of genetic engineering. The extinction of the human race is a ticking clock, winding down permanently with each newborn's death. Following the same prescribed method of survival isn't working. The ruling Senate, spurred by fear and the quest for absolute control, changes the rules. 
 Citizens of the last colonized city are suffocating under totalitarian rule. Unrest is rampant. And no matter the stakes, oppression always exacts a price. Fighting for a belief is hard. Doing the right thing, no matter the cost, is harder. Some are willing to pay with their lives so others might live. But is the sacrifice enough if finding answers to the most important question is never asked. 
 Who created the predator that destroyed the world before the Break and why? 
 I love stories that don't just resonate with me emotionally but hit me between the eyes intellectually. They make me like (or hate) characters. Root for them throughout the story. Believe the things that they do. Then make me face reality and think. Holy bejesus. Mankind is arrogant enough to push the boundaries of science beyond what we understand just to see if we can without determining if we should. 
 That makes the fictional world of Partials a scary real-world possibility in some form or permutation after scientific experimentation, discovery, and execution. Paranoia? Maybe. Then again, imagine how people would have reacted a hundred years ago to in utero surgery, doctors performing robotic surgery, and stem cell treatments...things not even considered cutting edge by today's fast-paced exploration of medical science and technology.

 I've previously read I Am Not A Serial Killer and enjoyed it very much even though I'm not a horror fan. You can read my review here if you want to. What I enjoyed most was the writing style, and so I had high hopes when I switched to a series in a genre that I actually like. 
 I was not disappointed. Along with the good writing, Partials offers an interesting premise, a lot of science, and a lot of action. It's not necessary as fast-paced as other post-apocalyptic novels (Kristen Simmons' Article 5 comes to mind), but it offers enough twists and turns to keep the reader's interest for the entire time. 
 The characters are great and, as with "I Am Not A Serial Killer", I loved the dialogue. I also liked the diversity, and the great names that came with that. There's one exception to the great-character-rule, which is our main character's boyfriend Marcus. I'm sure he's supposed to be nice, but I can't stand him and his obnoxious attitude and I sure hope there's less of him in the next book. 
 What stood out above all the action and science and whatnot where the questions this book posed. Right from the start the main character Kira is interested in the politics of her small community. She has a strong sense for what should be done for the sake of mankind, but her conflicting emotions make her question herself and the system in place. There is never an easy way out for her, and I actually quite liked it when she developed a thought that might not fit into her prescribed world view and tried to push it away. She's sixteen, and even though her circumstances forced her to take adult responsibilites early on, she still has to find her own answers and goes about that as most young people would. It is fascinating to watch, and impossible not to form your own opinions as well, and I like it when a book accomplishes that without ceasing to be entertaining. 
 Seeing how this doesn't really work as a stand-alone even though the major plotline is resolved, I can hardly wait for the next part. And I don't have to, Fragments is out already :).

I couldn't finish this book. I kept putting it down and reading something else then coming back to it for another chapter...repete until I realized I just don't care about anything that is going on and it is incredibly boring. It sounds like a great idea, but the execution was not good.

Eleven years ago, a biological weapon was released on the human race that killed nearly everyone. The primary suspect was the government engineered cyborgs, Partials. The Partials were created to fight a war with China and Iran. However, when RM was released, it was feared that they finally decided to turn on their human creators. Now, after the majority of the human race has died, the survivors are still struggling with the effects of RM: every baby dies after a few days. In order to save the human race, the Senate, the ruling body, enacts the Hope Act--a law the forces all women eighteen years and older to have as many babies as possible. However, even while the Senate is trying to save the human race, the Hope Act threatens to split the people in half and cause a civil war. After witnessing the death of several infants--and fearing that the Senate will lower the required age on the Hope Act--medical intern, Kira, decides that she needs to try and find the elusive cure for RM. This sends her on a journey to find a Partial and reveals secrets that nobody is willing to accept, including her. 
 From the first lines in this book, I was hooked! After reading many young adult books with insipid heroines who are completely overcome with sexual angst, Kira was refreshing. She was smart, on an amazing career path in the medical field, and had depth. Even though she was in a relationship with Marcus, they had a casual ease about them. There was no sexual tension or angst in their interactions. It was obvious that they have been together for a long time and had the relationship of adults. It was nice not to read the angsty drivel that is usually found in young adult books. 
 In addition, I felt that most of the main characters in the book had a lot more depth than is typically seen. Granted, I wished the author had spent a little more time with specific characters. That being said, it was obvious that they all had a back story that helped to create who they were in the present. Even if the author never gives the back story, as long as he knows what it is, it will come out in the writing. 
 The world building was simply amazing! I was totally engrossed in the Long Island of the future and the Partial inhabited Manhattan. The little touches the author used (clothes, iPods, and so on) helped develop the world further. Honestly, when the teens came across the panthers and antelope, I was instantly reminded of I Am Legend. In some ways, that was able to lend credence to the story. 
 The author tackled some hard issues in this book. I felt that he didn't make the subject matter easy or dumb it down for young adults. The whole concept behind creating the Partials and then forcing them to live in pseudo ghettos, limited their jobs, cutting their wages, and that they could only shop at certain stores reminded me of the Jews in Nazi Germany and how the former slaves were treated in the United States. Further, the forced pregnancy and experimentation on the babies is another big issue. These concepts are heavy hitters! They force the reader to sit down and think about the world they are in. Also, Kira's willingness to die for the cure asks people how far will they go for something that they know is right. 
 It was rather interesting to see that most, if not all, of the adults in the book were all about control and rather dimwitted. Honestly, this didn't bother me too much. First of all, the adults were still stuck in the old world. Change was hard for them; however, it was forced upon them with the onset of RM. They were afraid to look at other possible solutions. For me, the fact that they called all of the teens plague babies was very poignant. Sometimes it takes an outside prospective to find the solution. Granted, I found it hard to believe that some of the adults weren't a little more understanding or ready to think outside of the box. That being said, it wasn't too far outside of a possible reality. 
 This book was an amazing read! It was one of those books that you never want to end. I found myself slowing my reading down while struggling at the bit to read faster. Honestly, when the new book comes out later this month, I will have to scrape together enough money to buy it.

Actual Rating 4.5 stars 
 Originally posted on my blog, Zach's YA Reviews (zachsyareviews.com) 
 Review: 
 Protagonist: While Kira is a really strong heroine, she is lacking in a few other areas. First off she's really indecisive and that really hurts her strong character when she is constantly debating her choices and various elements of her life. This is a flaw that is easy to overlook from time to time as it doesn't really affect the plot all that much, but at the same time there are moments when Kira is debating her relationship with Marcus and it just falls flat due to Marcus' poor character development which I'll get to more later. Overall, I really like Kira as a character and was really impressed with the author's depiction of her and I can't wait to see what comes next with Kira. 
 Romance: So... the romance. I was expecting a lot more out of this romance, which for the record isn't that I expected more romance. So there's a little bit of a love triangle, though I don't know how developed it will become, between Marcus, Kira, and Samm. At the beginning of the novel Marcus and Kira are already dating, which isn't inherently bad, but since there's no real look back at their romance, Kira's confusion of her feelings for him, and no real development for Marcus as a character I had a hard time getting on board with them as a couple. Samm however isn't completely in the running as my choice favorite either. It's not that he's a bad character, in fact he's a great one, but I'm not to sure if his relationship with Kira will cross that thin border to a romantic one. I'm hoping it does because they would work really well together, but I'm not going to go into a shipping rant right now. I think if the author developed Marcus and gave us a glimpse at what drew Kira and him together I would feel like there was something tangible for their relationship to cling to but at the moment it's kind of hanging by a loose thread. 
 World-Building: As usual the world-building was my favorite part of this book. At the beginning of the book the genre is very obviously post-apocalyptic but the further into the book you go the more little themes and plot points from dystopian show up all while keeping the original genre's theme in tact. The circumstances in which this world is set are incredible and very unique. There are plenty of post-apocalyptic novels in which robots have taken over or nearly wiped out the human population but the fact that they are genetically manufactured organic beings is interesting and all of the intrigue and secrets in this book are truly amazing.This is definitely a book in which you shouldn't trust anyone except the protagonist. 
 Predictability: So, I'm not sure how to rate the predictability of this book. Since this is one of those books where I didn't really trust anyone there were so many conspiracy theories going on in my head that some were bound to stick. There were also moments that were so convoluted and out of the blue that I was so utterly shocked, and contrary to many novels where things seem to just come out of the blue, in this one they seemed to really make sense and work well for the book and story. So I guess after working that out the predictability is well written, but then again it's all really a matter of how you approach what's happening in the story. 
 Ending: The last chapter probably threw me off most of all. This book ends in a way like most other first books in series where the biggest hurdle of the book has been overcome and there's an, albeit brief, time of peace, but in this there's a bit of a difference. Most first books in a series end in a plateaued way, making it easier for the reader to wait between installments, but this book ends in a spectacular cliffhanger. I loved it and really added an extra layer of mystery to the story. 
 Rating: 
 This book was phenomenal, but I did find a few problems with it from poor character development to a couple small plot holes. Ah, the apocalypse. Some say it'll come with fire. Some say ice. Author Dan Wells says it comes from a deadly virus that wipes out most of the human population. 
 Wells sets up a spooky, post-apocalyptic hellscape in "Partials." Like a lot of YA dystopian fiction we've got a feisty heroine going toe-to-toe with a corrupt government. And a love triangle. Unlike a lot of YA fiction, we've got more of a military sci-fi vibe and it's not written in first-person present tense. 
 Here's the basic premise: Kira, a teenage medic, wants to cure the RM virus that's killed most of the human population. In addition to the deadly Partials, sort of android/human killing machines built for the military, attacked and killed humans around the same time the virus struck. No babies have survived for more than a few days in the past 11 years. Kira's bestie and honorary sister (there are only two people left in the world who are genetically related) is pregnant. Kira has a gut instinct that the Partials hold valuable clues to curing the RM virus. 
 So, Kira and a ragtag group of friends set off to find a Partial, capture it and study it. 
 Here's what works in the book: finally a YA dystopia has actual characters of color running around and doing things. Actually, most of the characters are people of color and that's awesome. Most of the world building works in the book. There are little details about economics, political power (specifically "The Hope Act") and technology that are simply fantastic. The book also raises some interesting questions about morality. Oh, and the A.V. Club likes it too. 
 What doesn't work: There are times when the plot drags hard. One of the corners of the love triangle goes from likable to annoying abruptly. It doesn't feel like this was intentional. Rather, this seems like a product of clumsy characterization. This isn't the only time this occurs either. Some of the characters read flat and aren't as well defined as they should be. Kira's motivations are clear, but it's difficult to really feel empathy for her. 
 There is also the issue of pacing and awkward prose. There were multiple times I had to reread passages because I wasn't quite sure what had happened. 
 That said, there are enough twists and turns to keep readers on their toes. The set-up and delivery of this book are different and interesting enough to where I'll be checking out the sequel, "Fragments."
