reference_books.review_text: Her third acts never, never wrap up. Every other part of the novel is so good! Why can't she solve her work problem _and_ her love life? Like how come Eleanor can't save her sister, too? How come ...? Resolve all your plot lines! My wakeful hours are in your hands, Rainbow Rowell

reference_books.title: Ender's Game (Ender's Saga, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is the DH's favorite book of all time. And he is my favorite. 
 So, I read it. 
 meh.

reference_books.title: Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus
reference_books.review_text:
One of the dumbest books I have ever read. Reductive, condescending, and almost entirely without humor. 
 Fortunately, I read it as a college freshman and realized, "oh, I'm like, a guy. I do not want to talk about my thoughts and feelings. Or read about them in self-help books." Duly noted, duly avoided for decades now.

reference_books.title: The Corrections
reference_books.review_text: Is something wrong with me? 50ish pages in and I just ...don't care. These people are boring and they seem unlikely to change that.

reference_books.title: The Light Between Oceans
reference_books.review_text:
A melodrama with a unique physical and temporal setting - an Australian island soon after World War I. 
 Thoughts: 
 *Very...Victorian: clean, conscientious, and with a bit too many filigrees for my taste. 
 * I was wishing there was a "Does the Dog Die?" for babies in books. 
 * There was more to talk about for the book club than I expected after reading it alone. Esp. with a group of alternately pregnant, grieving, adoptive, and "regular" mothers.

book_a.title: Water for Elephants
book_a.user_review:
Hmmm. Not bad. Silly ending, and silly beginning to the tale. There's so much unresolved loneliness in a story that seems to be about how you're saved for a litle while, and then it all pretty much turns out sad in the end anyway. 
 If I could have really fallen in love with some flawed, well-developed characters,maybe I could have suspended my disbelief at the crazy coincidences that start this story. Or, if the story had been a warts-and-all look at the people who make up the circus, then I could have ignored the cardboard main characters. Or, if the older narrator had some perspective or wisdom to transmit as he reflected on his story . . . but . . . no. . . . 
 This gets two stars because it didn't make me want to find the author and make him pay me by the hour for the time spent reading like with "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo," but...I just was in the mood for more than a melodrama.

sample_reviews.review_text: A great story with a lot of action and interesting information about train circuses back in the 20s and 30s, but frankly, the animal abuse, sometimes implied, sometimes described in detail, was just too much for me. I won't belabor the point because I know I've talked to all my friends about it already, but this book made me just ache with injustice. If the characters had been real, I think I would have actually hurt the main animal abuser, August. I am so conflicted about circuses and even zoos sometimes. I understand that a lot of these situations keep the animals in caring environments and I like being able to see and learn about wild animals up close. But for some reason, human beings are just too easily cruel in these situations and it absolutely drives me crazy. In short, the book is a good read with some interesting thoughts on growing old, but ultimately made me very glum and I felt like I couldn't read anything for several days afterward.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Wonderful story line. I love how the author actually used events that really happened. Who would have known that an elephant could do that to a person?? I like the jump between Jacob as an old man and then him remembering back to his younger years.

I loved the story, and I really liked the Jacob character, but I couldn't stand Marlena. Her character was so shallow, I couldn't see why he would love her so much and so suddenly. Just didn't buy it, which was unfortunate because it was the basis of the whole plot development. 
 I would like to give this book 4 stars if it weren't so crude. There are plenty of pornography descriptions and f-bombs, which I felt were pretty unnecessary. But I guess it goes along with the "gritty" 1930's circus theme--if it's "gritty" it must be more believable, right?
I really enjoyed this book until about 3/4 of the way. Then I found it was very repetitive

I read this as an advanced copy from work because I dig elephants, but it just came out on paperback and - SURPRISE - it's a huge bestseller! I really don't know how to call 'em. Like everything I give 3 stars to, this was a really enjoyable, readable, but not mind-blowing book. It has a good, sweet story and narrative that switches back and forth between the present day in an old-folks home and circus life during the depression a la "The Notebook" (which I never read, but I saw the movie, so I know). But most importantly, this book did nothing to detract from my love of elephants. I recommend this book to the women looking for a new book club selection at work all the freaking time.

I'd only recommend this book to people who love the circus and circus nostalgia. I've never liked circuses with animals (no one who cares for animal rights ever could). I don't care if these were different times. It's horrible to think what tortures these animals had to go through. The rest of the story was pretty irrelevant.
Great book. Not just an animal story, a well-written fiction all around.

I thought this was generally an easy read - it was interesting to read details of the ins and outs of what is arguably the travelling circus's "golden age," which I know so little about. I appreciate what Gruen was trying to do by making the book alternate between present-time and flashbacks, but I would've actually just preferred for the entire story to be told in the past; at times the old age/present-day segments felt clunky and unnecessary (then again, maybe that was the point in order to underscore Jacob's sentiment of uselessness in his geriatric years?) - I found myself coming close to skipping those chapters (or just rushing through them) so that I could get back to the overarching story. In terms of the characters, none of them really jumped off the page for me - they all just seemed to be lacking in some more depth or purpose that I couldn't quite put my finger on. Sadly, I found the ending to be cheesy and utterly unrealistic - it would've been more believable (albeit convenient and expected) if he had just died. Overall, the book wasn't a complete wash but it definitely isn't a favorite of mine. I don't regret reading it, though - it was easy to get through and served as an adequate distraction for a long commute. I'm interested to see if I like the movie any better.

if you are in love with circus,fond of elephants or adore Robert Pattinson you would probably like this book,other wise you will find it a bit boring and playful (i give it a R Rating).the romance was so not convincing !! the only thing that kept me going is the Author's style and choice of words,they were lovely .
The beginning is amazing. After about a third of the way in ... It drags. And drags. And drags.
Sper recomiendo este libro!
The beginning was a bit slow, and I didn't like the coarse language in particular or the explicit scenes. The book would have been better off without those. Surprise ending.
Thoroughly enjoyed this book
See my review for "A Discovery of Witches" and substitute "paranormal trap of witches and vampires" for "CIRCUS!".

I loved this book. I didn't pick it up for the longest time because I didn't think I would like reading about the circus. I was wrong! I got it because there were so many rave reviews. I love this book and will miss reading about all the characters in the book. You get so involved it makes you feel like you are there with them, feeling their pains, ups and downs. I loved how the story went back and forth from old Jacob in the nursing home to younger Jacob remembering his days with the circus. I love elephants and feel sorry for any animal that is abused. Makes me want to go out and rescue all the elephants. I hope everyone remembers that all animals have feelings and can feel it when someone mistreats them. An excellent book. If you like the circus or not, read this book.

I really enjoyed this book, it was a great story! A 93 year old man is in a nursing home and the circus comes to town. The story is about him remembering himself as a young man and one fateful summer when he stumbles upon working for the circus. Lots of sadness in this book but the ending let me fulfilled and I would recommend it to everyone!
This is one of my all time favorite books.. I became completely engrossed in this story... As it says on the cover, it is both compelling and gritty.. great description... What a good book...

When I first heard of this book I thought it was just about an old guy in the circus. Then I saw the movie trailer and I said to myself,"Oh, I remember. I have heard of this book and never picked it up." I saw it at Walmart and I thought Oh why not. Might as well read the book before I see the movie. The thing is every time I was reading this book, I kept picturing the characters from what I've seen from the movie trailer. There's nothing wrong with that but first of all Jacob's hair is red and they didn't even make Robert Pattinson's hair look red and Marlena is a brunette not a blonde! Oh, Hollywood and the changes you make to books. 
 I thought this book was okay. I didn't like it, I didn't hate it I just thought it waas okay. I liked the story and the message it gets across. I also think Sara Gruen did a good job in portraying an old men coming back to his memories. I have to say though I was not a huge fan of the romance. I just didn't feel the chemistry between Jacob and Marlena. I also didn't like how badly they traeted the animals at the circus. I mean I can shake my head with the men that were left behind and not paid very much but how could they just let those poor animals thirst and starve!!!!!??? 
 One of the literature teachers at my school said we might have a book club meeting on this book but he said there was content in it that would not be appropriate for the younger kids at my school. I can see why now and that's all I'm going to say. 
 Good book but I just didn't enjoy itvery much. I am excited to see the movie and how it stays true to the book.
Great book! Loved the story and the characters!

This review can also be found here - http://thebookboudoir.blogspot.com/20... 
 I picked up Water for Elephants because everyone was talking about it and I knew it was being made into a movie. It took me a while to get into it; although that was MY fault, not the books (I was reading three others at the time). When I made it to the half way point I was able to focus more on it and I'm so glad I did. It's a wonderfully detailed story that I could clearly see playing out in my head. It was interesting, being able to "see" that time period and the train circus. I think that part fascinated me the most because of what I do for a living; working at a center that Ringling Bros performs at atleast once a year. I enjoyed Jacob and his narration. I loved his relationships with Rosie and the other animals as well as the humans. The ending left me happy and satisfied. This book felt so real, as if Jacob really wrote it all himself. I'm glad I was finally able to focus all of my attention on WfE- it's a good read and I can't wait to see it all play out before my eyes on the big screen.

Thought it was a great story line, loved the characters. Could've been more of everything though, ie plot, setting, character analysis. Overall good. Once you got to the ending though the plot seemed really rushed, would have liked the author to slow down a bit and really get into it instead of running toward the end.

This was an interesting read for me, because I couldn't put it down, yet I never liked it. I never really got to where I cared about the characters, or the situation, and yet it was so compelling. Loved the ending, it was such a great fairy tale happy ever after. Good read, but I won't read it again.
I read this book in one day. It is a quick, exciting tale of circus life. However, I was turned off by the sexually explicit scenes.

best novel I've read in quite awhile. couldn't put it down. engaging characters. fascinating facts about the bygone era of circus folk. story spins easily from past to present with a bit of suspense woven throughout.
Very enjoyable read.

Circuses showcase human beings at their silliest and most sublime, and many unlikely literary figures have been drawn to their glitzy pageantry, soaring pretensions and metaphorical potential. Unsurprisingly, writers seem liberated by imagining a spectacle where no comparison ever seems inflated, no development impossible. For better and for worse, Gruen has fallen under the spell. With a showman's expert timing, she saves a terrific revelation for the final pages, transforming a glimpse of Americana into an enchanting escapist fairy tale.
It really wasn't all it's been cracked up to be.
I thought this was pretty poorly written. It wasn't believable and the only reason I finished is cuz the plot was interesting. I was disappointed and skimmed to the end after the halfway point.

This was another book that I listened to the audiobook and I loved it. The voices were spot on and it brought the story to life for me. And what a story it was! I loved hearing Jacob's point of view - both when he is older in the retirement home and when he is younger in the circus. The juxtaposition of the two completely different settings just brought a different dimension to the story. 
 I quickly fell in love with Rosie although it took me a bit longer to warm up to Marlena. There were so many bleak moments of the story and you could almost see the colors as you read it - gray during the most depressing scenes and vibrant reds and oranges during the circus acts. This is another book that I'll be rereading in the future.

this book was...okay. not a complete waste of time, but not a 'must read'. i liked it well enough, but i'd heard such good things from people who's opionions i normally respect that i was disappointed. this isn't one i'd recommend to others, and there is a part me that is saddened by that. i like books about circuses-the potential story lines and cast of characters are so diverse. that being said, i was surprised that the elephant seemed to be the most dynamic of the bunch.

I seriously have no idea why people were raving about this book. It was an okay read, but the language was not inspiring at all and the characters were for the most part one-dimensional. The action was interesting at times, but nothing to write home about (though I am curious as to how often people were really "red-lighted" in real life). I'm not a fan of the Ringling Bros. type circus (lions and tigers and elephants belong in Africa, not onstage doing stupid tricks for our amusement) so perhaps this colored my perception of the book. And I still don't get the title - the old Jacob complains that there's no way someone was hired to be a water boy for the elephants because they drink too much - but then the book never really explains how they are watered. Anyway, as with most of the modern fiction I've read lately, this book does not live up to its hype.

I have learned in the last year that some reasons why I don't read certain books are total crap. I thought this was a light romance and not worth my time. 
 Instead, I find that it is an incredible story and so many things going on, that I can't *quite* label it as a romance, which is great, because.... Well, now that I think about it, I used to think I wasn't a fan of the romance novel. Maybe I am.

I would have given this book three stars if it had ended earlier. The author did a good job setting up a dark world within the circus complete with some huge killer events in the end, but they were all forgotten when they enabled the lovers to lead a wonderful life.

I couldn't finish. This book is totally disgusting, maybe I'm being too sensitive... Actually, no I'm not. This book is utterly revolting. And way too informative about killing all the horses. I'm thowing it away. I really wanted to like it, and I even loved the first couple chapters. But it soon went down hill.
Loved it! Easy to get started, hard to put down. I was sad when it was over, but was satisfied with the ending. Learned lots of interesting stuff about that era (early 30's).
Despite the glowing reviews this one got, I wasn't thrilled with it. It was very slow moving and didn't have enough character development for me.

Gritty as a dirt sandwich...I found the book very appealing because I enjoyed the writing so much(I am always intrigued by a woman author writing from the man's perspective & I thought Sara Gruen was very convincing). I enjoyed learning about the circus-life during the Great Depression era. But with that being said...it is a very adult book and I found myself blushing a few times throughout & flipping ahead.
Loved this!!!

Not my type of book at all but read for a reading group that I hold at the library I work in. 
 The love story for me happened to late and I found myself wondering why I was even bothering to read it, given that I don't even like the circus, I was highly relieved when I finally finished it!

I had high expectations for this book which was probably my own mistake. Although it was an interesting story,and it read quickly, I was disappointed in the flatness of many of the characters and the superficial dialogue. I thought Marlena was in inadequate "heroine." She seems to have no depth, and the reader never learns much about her, besides she has an abusive husband, which only proves her to be some what weak in her decision to stay with him. I also found it difficult to digest some of the dialogue that was just not believable in some situations. Overall, I thought the story was interesting, but the writing was not the quality I expected it to be. To some, this doesn't really matter, but to some, it is everything.
I found it to be a cheap version of "Sophie's Choice" except it had a hollow happy ending. yawn.

Reading this was like running a marathon on bloody stumps. It took forever and it was painful. 
 The subject - a vet recalling his days in a failing 1920s circus - would've interested me if the writing had been up to par. It wasn't horrible, just amateurish at times. Also, the dialogue could've been better. If the characters sounded more like they came from the '20s it might've drawn me more into the story, but they sounded like contemporaries who like to use old timey jargon. Also, I can't get down with the idea that an old man, who can't remember his own age, can remember minor details from 70 years prior as well as exact dialogue that is as mundane as the tripe used to fill out an hour-long soap opera. 
 Why do I read modern pop lit? Oprah's minions shall no longer rule my reading! 
 Maybe I might have disliked this a little less if I'd just read it instead of listened to the horribly narrated audiobook. Never has a narrator squeeze so much melodrama out of the simplest of actions and mildest of emotions. 
 I don't think I've ever taken this long to get through an audiobook. Usually, even if I'm not enjoying it, I can just let it run and bust on through. But with this one I actively avoided listening to it by being inactive. My thing is, if I have a boring job to do like yardwork or servicing my lady*, I plug in an audiobook and both the book and the job whizz by. But not this book. Instead of weeding or going for a walk with Water for Elephants I made sure I had other things to do. The days-long NFL draft came in handy. 
 * "My lady" is the term I use for my car. Get your mind out of the gutter.

Lovely romance and a vivid portrayal of circus life in the 30s. The story is told as the memories of a ninety something year old man living in a nursing home where he is treated as a fragile child, being told what to eat and what to do. The arrival of a circus sparks memories of himself seventy years earlier when joining the circus and falling in love. 
 Is beautifully written and cleverly plotted as the narrative addresses life in the circus during the Great Depression (main character's youth) and life at an assisted living home (main character's old age); secrets of a fascinating past and the creeping helplessness that assaults an aging body. 
 Sweet, moving and emotional.

Wow, what can I say about this book? It garnered 5 stars from me, and I'm a harsh critic. I'll be the first to say that its premise did not interest me and I read it out of obligation to a book a club...but oh am I glad that I did! 
 This book has it all...mystery and intrigue wrapped into a love story with a little added whimsy and an honest story that will tug on anyone's heart strings. 
 Gruen has taken one of the most original stories I could every imagine and flawlessly writes it from a male's perspective, which is no small feat. I laughed, I cried, I even found myself genuinely surprised at how involved in the characters I became. I can say though that after reading this story, I never want to be put into a "home" when I reach my later years.
AMAZING

Water for Elephants is a fascinating novel of a traveling circus in the Great Depression. As an old man, Jacob Jankowski recalls the memories of his youth working in the Benzini Brothers' circus as a vet. From his first day hopping aboard the train, he befriends many of the circus workers including a dwarf named Walter and a stowaway named Camel. His tenderness towards animals pleases Marlena, the equestrian with whom he soon falls in love. Jacob's affection, however, swirls up bitter rivalry with her husband August, a schizophrenic animal trainer. Despite her mischief, Jacob and Marlena also become fond of an elephant named Rosie and shield her from August's wrath. 
 I absolutely adore this book. It's one of the very few books I've read about the circus life and I am delighted that the author captures the time period perfectly with wondrous detail. Everything is so vivid! I can almost imagine myself working alongside the workers to help set up the various tents or tending to the horses. I also find both Jacobs charming- the kind and tender young Jacob and the grumpy but humorous elderly Jacob. It reminds me of the Notebook with the amazing flashback-style narration, a Nicholas Sparks novel that I'm sure many are familiar with. It wasn't hard to keep track of the switch from modern day to flashback to modern day at all. I've never been a fan of historical fiction, but Water for Elephants surprisingly engrossed me. I definitely recommend it to everyone! 5 jillion stars. 
 P.S. Some cringe-worthy explicit scenes featuring one very well-known stripper. Even the sex scene was less detailed than Barbara's moments ha.

Loved it! 
 It was full of jargon that was interesting if a little hard to follow, but the storyline was a classic on a new and exciting stage, and I enjoyed it! (even the unrealistic ending!) 
 Made me want to join a circus!

Really enjoyable, but not quite as profound as the high reviews seemed to make it out to be. Nevertheless, a really good book and very inspiring for those that dream of having their own NaNoWriMo novel published.

I only made it a few chapters in before I had to stop. I wanted to read it, I really did, but when I hit the first graphic sex scene, I had to stop. I am always disappointed when authors feel they have to add smut to a book. It makes me wonder if they're really confident that the story can carry itself.

I downloaded this to my Ipod, and listened too it on my morning walk, a cd each day!!! It made a very boring walk, and adventure. The story is told from an old man's perspective about his life with the circus, around the turn of the century, when the big tops were loaded on trains, and carted from town to town. the chapters flip flop from the time that Jason(main character-is 23 to 90 or is that 93?) 
 One my top 3 reads this year!!!

book_b.title: Olivia Joules and the Overactive Imagination
book_b.user_review: Fun, fast read. Looking forward to further Olivia Joules books.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Ah, gifts from family memebers who assume because you read every time they look at you, that you will like the books they do. Note: This has never worked for me. 
 Olivia Joules is the almost-standard British journalist, like a skinnier, more imaginitive Jemima J. She has possibly the most overactive imagination ever, and imagines herself a bit like Emma Peel or James Bond. She sees conspiracies and drama everywhere. She never goes anywhere without her Rules For Life which she repeats over and over again and a hatpin. 
 This book quickly devolves into a spy fantasy that breaks all suspension of belief, and I have some bloody stretchy suspension of disbelief. Olivia is recruited to M16, and is given with no real training, becomes a essential part of bringing down a terrorist cell, and ends a little bit like Ms. Congeniality -- with less believability. Even if you like chick lit, skip it.
This and Cause Celeb are her best books and I wish they would make movies of these. Olivia Joules has a very clever plot and I enjoyed it very much.
More like "it was ok" but not quite as good as Bridget Jones. I think this author, as funny as she is, is going to have a hard time overcoming her first hit.
Couldn't hold my interest.
I read this book a few years ago. I really don't remember much about it so I must not have been too impressed.

How could the author of "Bridget Jones' Diary" write something so terrible? It seems she hasn't really written anything since, either. I guess she doesn't have to, if this is the sort of drivel she plans to write.

This book pales in comparison to the Bridget Jones duet. It had little of the charm, wit, and humor of the books that I liked and had a lot of...fluff. Seriously, reading it felt like being force-fed a vat of cotton candy: sugary, sticky, full of air, and in the end, ultimately unsatisfying. Don't bother.
FUN FUN FUN poolside reading.
But Bridget Jones was so good! I was pretty disappointed here - just didn't do it for me.
I couldn't finish it. I still don't know whether she was dating a terrorist. I still don't care.
I absolutely hated this book and couldn't finish it. It was my local book club choice. I thought the story was nonsense and the writing poor.
Not her best.

Wow was I not only underwhelmed, but I couldn't wait for it to be over. I'm a fan of the author, and so I set out to read all the things she had written...if this is the book I had chose to read first, I would have never continued to seek her books out. Extremely disappointing.

ALthough I LOVED Bridget Jones, Fielding just wasn't doing it for me with this story. Olivia Joules is a crazy journalist who somehow finds herself all wrapped up with a bunch of terrorists in Honduras. The story is slow-moving, lacks the humor and wit of BJ, and just wasn't that good.
Olivia is certainly no Bridget Jones. While the book isn't horrible, it's not Fielding's best.
Tried, but just couldn't get into it. Wanted to read some brain candy - but this one didn't do it for me.
This was not a bad book, just lacking in depth. If looking for an easy to read mystery then this is your book.
One of the worst books I have ever read. Would give it no stars if possible. Seems like Helen Fielding had one really good idea with Bridget Jones and that's it.

What can one say of a book when you live in a county where finding anything to read in english is a challenge. Well one can say that it was mostly an easy read and as far as entertainment it's passable although often laughable. As far as any complaints the largest would have to be wanting to slam an editor against a wall for letting Fielding get away with random over use of page breaks many times without any change in location, time, or even voice for that matter. Arggg! If I could I would give it 2 1/2 because it's not my cup of tea, but its not terrible so I'll let it fall on three.
En besvikelse. Olivia Joules ar inte pa langa vagar lika rolig som Bridget Jones och jag tyckte inte att boken var underhallande. Slolaste fram mot slutet.

I actually really enjoyed this book. I think I enjoyed it more than the Bridget Jones' series and I wish Helen Fielding would've written more about Olivia. Josephine Bailey did a wonderful job of narration also!
Cheap rip-off of the author's own (better) work.
I like Helen Fielding, but I really did not enjoy what I read of this book before I put it down, unfortunately.
So disappointing, considering my love for Bridget Jones. I only finished this book because I was stuck in the Philadelphia airport and had nothing better to do. Ughghgh.
Lame - Lame - Lame
2 1/2 stars. I may have penalized this book because I really enjoyed Bridget Jones and this just isn't nearly as good. Therefore I was somewhat disappointed...
Unfortunately, Fielding can't seem to do plot on her own. With Jane Austen to guide her, Bridget Jones's Diary was brilliant, but everything else has tanked.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Usually reading Brit chick lit results in eye clawing and mental shrieking. What can I say the phrases used and the regurgitated spunky yet clueless inner monologues irk the depths of my soul. I didn't have those issues with Olivia Joules and the overactive imagination. So pigs must be flying in hell. 
 That doesn't mean I like this book though. Olivia annoyed the sh#t outta me. She is another in the long line of too stupid to live heroines, who taint my reading life. We discerning booksluts ought to rise up and cull them from the literary herd braveheart style. 
 In a commercial break from my murderous rant lets get back to the review at hand. Olivia J-O-U-L-E- S (like the unit of energy not the shiny baubles will be from here on out referred to as OJ the orange of juice not the former football playing murder suspect) is a failing journalist seemingly plagued by attention deficit disorder and paranoid schizophrenia. 
 Her situation translated: Oh Noez, my career is stagnant because I keep handing in articles about the stupid crap I make up instead of my assignment. 
 My response to her situation translated: Bleh,cry me a river. 
 Anyways things kick off when she's subtly demoted from news to the style section of whatever newspaper she works for and is sent to some skin cream launch in Miami. Enter mysterious French Arabic dude who wants to make sweet jihad all over her zexy body. He supposedly makes slug skin cream and movies. She instantly decides he's Osama bin Laden ( <-her words not mine) but then decides he's just an al-Qaeda operative so she's game for tongue wrestling. Stuff is blown up and * shock & awe* our jet setting sheik has dropped it like its hot flying the coop. So now OJ and 4 out of 5 doctors agree slug cream dude is a terrorist . So it makes perfect sense that she follows him to LA then accepts an invitation to his resort in (tropical place). C'mon look at that face of course she can trust him. So what if she doesn't know him from adam and if he continues to lie about being a director? At least he's stopped lying about being french. Now Ladies, that's nothing to shake a stick at. 
 All the while during OJ's travel awkward and clumsy hijinks ensue. I guess they are supposed to funny but they just cement how much I loathe her. 
 Pop quiz time kiddies: You just accepted a strange man and possible terrorist's invitation to go diving at his private tropical resort. En route after some travel issues you find 5 kilos of cocaine in your carry on luggage ( btw why is coke always mentioned in 5 kilo bundles in film and novels? Why not 3? Or 8?). what do you do? 
 Well if your OJ you flush it down the the porta-potty toilet and continue on with you to your death wish destination. Ha ha ha ha.... What a bunch of giggles. This is my stop, time to get of this ride. 
 After 3 failed attempts to finish the remaining 1/2 of this bunk; it's time to throw in the towel. I can't bring myself to read anymore . Someones obviously gonna get eaten by sharks at some point...if only it could be her. If any of you fine folks out there in the e-world possess the perseverance to complete this book; please drop a comment with your take on it. Did it make you laugh? Cry? Tremble with rage and annoyance?

Terrible! 
 Was this supposed to be real story...is it in her head? Is she in an institution!? Because she should be...just ridiculous

Silly fun abounds in this part-spy, part-romantic comedy. reference_books.title: The Crown's Game (The Crown's Game, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
This is my Book Of the Month- June 2016, with GR group- Book Corner 
 The premise of the story is soo cool, two Enchanters fighting a battle to be the Imperial Enchanter and on top of that the story is set in 19th century Russia. Got to be Epic Right! 
 The first half of the book was indeed interesting but it went downhill for me after that. 
 Nikolai and Vika are the enchanters who have to compete in 'The Crown's Game' and Pasha is the Crown Prince. 
 **MILD SPOILERS HEAD** 
 The things I liked 
 Nikolai has his strengths as the enchanter and Vika has her own strengths Nikolai can control Material things and Vika the Natural Elements . They each have 5 rounds and at the end of the game the one who loses dies i.e if they don't kill each other before that... In middle of the game, the king can declare a winner and the loser dies (just auto com-bust) 
 The first few rounds of the enchantments were fascinating. I really liked how Nikolai played on his strength and his enchantments were really brainy whereas Vika was clearly the more powerful one as she could control the natural elements 
 I really liked Pasha's sister as she is really clear in what she wants. I think she is actually fit to be a Queen when she grows up. 
 Introduction of Aizhana was really fascinating. 
 Things that could have been better 
 Now you can see a love story a mile off and I really don't mind it unless the main storyline is not lost in the romance. But this is what essentially went wrong with this book. 
 Pasha falls in love with Vika, Vika falls in love with Nikolai and then Nikolai falls right back in love with Vika (this bit was really really abrupt) & 'The Crown's Game' is lost somewhere in the background. 
 Pasha come's off as a very weak person and he actually did not have any major role to play. I felt the character's potential was not utilized. Actually apart from Vika and Nikolai, the rest of the characters were not very well developed. 
 People who did not need to die, did die for moving the story on a different tangent and this was not in flow with how the story was progressingThe whole logic of killing the Tsar to stop the game did not make any sense as the games would continue if there is a heir! 
 After the third round of enchantments this was clearly a love story. There was no real battle and the story shaped into a fantasy romance. 
 No one in the city knows that the Enchanters exist and the Crown's Game is carried out in secret. Now some of these enchantments were done quiet publicly and not one normal person could relate them to magic. Is the city full of fools? 
 My expectations going into this read was really different but if you want to read a Fantasy Romance (with a love triangle) this is the book to read.

reference_books.title: The Great Gatsby
reference_books.review_text:
Buddy Read with Murugesh. 
 Well this book was a surprise and not what I expected especially that ending! I haven't seen the movie and did not know the plot of this book when I started reading it. 
 The book was first published in 1920's and obviously captures the booming wild lifestyle of the Flapper era perfectly. 
 Going into the book I thought Gatsby would be the narrator of the story but it in fact was Nick Carraway. He was one of the likable characters in the book. 
 This book is filled with unlikable and annoying characters. Starting with Tom & Daisy Buchanan- 
 "They were careless people, Tom and Daisy- they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made..... 
 And then there is Jordan Baker- 
 "She was incurably dishonest. She wasn't able to endure being at a disadvantage, and given this unwillingness I suppose she hadbegun dealing in subterfuges when she was very young in order to keep that cool, insolent smile turned to the world and yet satisfy the demands of her hard jaunty body." 
 And finally there is Jay Gatsby himself and his obsession with his ladylove. 
 "The modesty of the demand shook me. He had waited five years and bought a mansion, where he dispensed starlight to casual moths so that he could 'come over' some afternoon to a stranger's garden." 
 - The enormity of what all Gatsby has done just for his one chance seeps into you casually. 
 And then when he gets his chance.... 
 "He had passed visibly through two states and was entering upon a third. After his embarrassment and his unreasoning joy he was consumed with wonder at her presence." 
 I really did not know at first if I should dislike Gatsby or pity him. But by the end of it all I just felt really really sad for him. 
 The book really high-lights the selfish and self-serving nature of human beings and how superficial and callous people can be.

reference_books.title: Code Name Verity (Code Name Verity, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I want to make it clear that a 2 star rating means that this was an 'OK' read. It's definitely not bad and I can see the appeal this story has for many readers but this did not work for me and I will come to the reasons below. 
 After reading a lot of glowing reviews from other readers I had very high expectations from this story. An espionage novel set in the time of World War II, this definitely has to be the best, right? 
 But I think I should have set my expectations lower or even better gone in without any preconceived notions as to how the story will be and I would have maybe liked this much better. 
 To begin with, the book is clearly divided into 2 parts: 
 Part 1 was a bit disorienting at the start as I could not understand what is going on and who is the prisoner? Is the story from her perspective or is she really narrating the story from her friends perspective? It also started feeling a bit repetitive and I started losing interest at this juncture. 
 Part 2 picked up pace. There was more drama and action and it was well connected to Part 1. But for me the damage had been done. I did not feel emotionally vested in any of the characters. There are some twists and turns at the end but they did not shock me as much as I wished (maybe because I had gone into this state of despondency due to Part 1) 
 Yes, it's story about woman power, female friendship and fight that involved civilians doing daring things for their country but I wish the pacing of the first half could have been similar to the second half and in turn made me connect to the characters. 
 If you like the blurb, do give this one a try. All I can say is this one was not for me......

reference_books.title: Heartless
reference_books.review_text:
This is my Book Of the Month- February 2017, with GR group- Lovers of YA. 
 Well this was a frustrating book for me. I had very high expectations after reading the first 3 books of the Lunar Chronicles but somehow this book did not have that magic. 
 This story is about Catherine. I really did feel sympathy for her and the difficult position she finds her in. 
 "She pictured the king of Hearts standing before her, holding her hand. She grimaced to think of that small clammy hand in hers. And then, his request. To be his bride. To be his wife. There would be no passion, no romance, no love. But she could picture precisely how he would smile at her, so hapless. So hopeful. 
 Her stomach roiled. 
 Could she ever say yes to that? 
 As she took a sip of tea, a more important question struck her. 
 Could she ever say no?" 
 But then the same thing goes on and on, and nothing much happens till more than 60% of the book. 
 The interesting part came in the book too late and you have got to be really patient with this storyline. 
 "Two Rooks, a Pawn and a Queen. That's how the riddle begins, but howsoever shall it end?" 
 This is a spin-off on 'Alice in the Wonderland' but I have to say that it is a very different and unexpected take on the original book. 
 It would have been an Okish read but the ending made me like it. 
 The iconic sentence from 'Alice in Wonderland, 
 "Off with his head" 
 takes on a deeper meaning altogether.

book_a.user_review:
1.5 stars 
 This is my Book Of the Month- April 2017, with GR group- Nothing But Reading Challenges- Category: Young Adult BOM. 
 "Now the days of winter begin, and the Goblin King rides abroad, searching for his bride." 
 This is an interesting plotline for a YA Fantasy book and it could have been a great read if all the possible theories and concepts that were introduced were explored further. 
 Firstly, for any book to click with a reader, the reader has to at least like the main protagonist. Liesl started out as a selfish, cribbing, insecure personality and I did not really like her. But by the end of this book... 
 If this was a re-telling of Beauty and the Beast, Liesl would have been the Beast. She is such a horrible human-being. Always wanting what she cannot have and then if she gets what she wants, she is never happy or satisfied. Always comparing herself with her sisters beauty and her brothers talent. Always coveting what she cannot have. 
 And the tantrums and the sulking just got on my nerves. Here is just a sample of what I had to bear! 
 So I answered the Goblin King's question the only way I could. 'Do you not like my new dress?' I blurted out. That certainly surprised him. 'I-uh- what?'. 'My dress', I said. 'Is it not to your liking?'. His eyes were both bewildered and wary. 'It is lovely, Elisabeth.' 'And me? Am I lovely?'. The Goblin King frowned. 'You are in a mood tonight dear.' He had not answered me. Suddenly I could not bear to remain seated. I rose to my feet and paced back and forth before the fire. I was in a mood- for a fight. 'Answer me,' I said. 'Do you think me lovely?'. 'Not with the way you're acting at the moment.' 
 The Goblin King was a two dimensional character who did not even have a small bone of 'scary' in his body. He was more like a weak, unsure, adolescent boy who does not know what is actually going on. 
 If this would not have been part of a Group Read, I don't think I would have even finished it. 
 Now that I have finished it my alternate preferred ending would be- The Goblin King's love and caring attitude was just an act to manipulate Liesl. He makes Liesl believe that he is letting her go but it's all an act. She struggles to get out but dies with the hope that she will get free. I know it's dark but it would have been preferred to the 'meh' ending we got. 
 The only reason this is a 1.5 stars and not a plain 1 star is for the few interesting concepts that this book introduced. Overall I did not like and would not bother reading the next book of this series.

 You could say that I'm a hardcore Labyrinth fan girl. I love the movie, Labyrinth, and have seen it many times, glitter-dappled set and cheesy puppets aside; it's an interesting story that's clearly inspired by Celtic faerie lore, and (you could argue) the allegorical tale of a girl's coming-of-age through the use of symbolism. In fact, many of the reasons I love the movie are less because of what's in the story and more of what's explicitly left out. 
 Because of that, I was a little skeptical when I heard that there was a book coming out that was inspired by Labyrinth - skeptical and also bouncing-off-the-walls excited. Because another book came out this year that was also inspired by one of my favorite stories: RoseBlood by A.G. Howard, which turned one of my favorite antiheroes into a psychic vampire who owns a rave club. 
 I was not pleased with these developments. 
 WINTERSONG starts out okay. It takes place in historical Bavaria, and is about a selfish brat named Elisabeth who only cares about music. She spends most of the book whining, feeling sorry for herself, and being jealous of her siblings. Then one day, her sister, Kathe, is kidnapped by the Goblin King, and Elisabeth is forced to go Underground to save her because if she doesn't succeed, her sister will be gone forever. The integration of The Goblin Market and Der Erlkonig were interesting, but I've seen Labyrinth fanfiction writers run with this concept before. In fact, one of my favorite authors, Subtilior, has a Labyrinth fanfic called 
 Erlkonig 
 that runs with this concept beautifully. Likewise, Viciously Witty has an excellent Labyrinth fic set in Ireland that is based off and called The Goblin Market. 
 I get that there's only so many famous works of faerie lore, so the possibility of overlap is high, but that just makes it even more important to set your work apart from others' and go the extra mile to make the story interesting and the characters compelling. The Goblin King in WINTERSONG was not compelling. He did not feel like the King of Mischief; he felt like a nervous guy at prom who is afraid that his mean girlfriend is going to embarrass him in front of all his friends. He even blushes and stammers. He's also apparently a christian, or follows christian tenets, since he goes to chapel in his free time and talks a lot about God (especially in the last quarter of the book). This was really jarring to me as a reader, because many of the faerie lore is based on Celtic mythology that predates Christianity by centuries, so it doesn't really make sense that the "Elf King" would go to church.... 
 I looked on the author's profile, and in one of her "Ask the Author" questions, when answering how she was inspired to write this story she says she " 
 decided to write 50 Shades of Labyrinth." So I don't think that it's a stretch to say that WINTERSONG reads like Labyrinth fanfiction, and not even particularly good or original Labyrinth fanfiction, since it primarily relies on ideas that have already been explored by many others in the fandom. Even the sex in this book - arguably the selling point of the premise, since I'm sure many of the hard-core fan girls of Labyrinth wish that there was an alternative telling of the tale when Jareth and Sarah really did end up together - is uninspired and whiny. Elisabeth whines about the sex, that there isn't enough of it, that he doesn't really want her. There are some truly well-written passages in here, but then you also get ridiculous passages like these: "I dip my quill into the inkwell once again, and join up my teardrops into a song" (204). 
 If this book is 50 Shades of anything, it's 50 Shades of a Whining Heroine Who Never Shuts the Hell Up. She is one of the most unlikable protagonists I've encountered in a while because all she does is complain and whine and cry and talk about how ugly she is. The only thing that sets the heroine apart are her musical abilities (a similarity it shares with RoseBlood), and she's even a brat about this. She sets her brother's face on fire out of jealousy because he is able to study music because he's a boy and she isn't and gets mad at the Goblin King for obtaining her a klavier because - she says - it's too beautiful for her and that makes her feel bad, basically. I'm sorry, you want me to root for this twit? 
 This was a huge disappointment for me. The only upside is that it made me want to go watch Labyrinth again and revisit some of my favorite fanfic to read when I was in college.

Wintersong is a dark and poetic story about music, madness, sacrifice, passion, magic, wishes and learning to accept yourself. I absolutely adored this story and I felt a bit sad after finishing it. Besides entertaining me, this story made me feel all kinds of emotions and it made me think about topics like beauty and cruelty and sacrifice. 
 What I liked 
 - The writing style. It's actually the most outstanding part of the book. The author uses formal and old-fashioned words that enhance the overall feel of the story and the descriptions are vibrant and luscious. 
 - The use of the German words like Fraulein and Mein Herr. It strenghtens the setting. 
 - The whole story reads like a fairy tale. 
 - The chemistry between Liesl and the Erlkonig is super hot. The sexual attraction is palpable. However, their chemistry also shines through their passion for music. 
 - The fact that Liesl wanted and liked sex and even admitting it. As a feminist, I totally approve of the way the author handled sexuality. That a woman feels lust too and acts on these feelings and that it's nothing to be ashamed of. 
 - The use of contradictions. Beautiful but cruel. Ugly but seductive. It sounds impossible, but after thinking about it for a while I realised that there can be beauty in cruelty and that beauty can be cruel. Moreover, in a twisted kind of way ugliness can be seductive because it gives power. 
 - Often, the interaction between Liesl and der Erlkonig was on a whole other level than normal communication. They communicated through their music and it was beautiful. 
 - This story had elements of the myth about Hades and Persephone, Beauty and the Beast and Red Riding Hood. 
 - Both Liesl and der Erlkonig changed a lot during this story. Der Erlkonig learnt that true love is letting the other go. While Liesl learnt to accept herself. 
 - The ending. It was bittersweet and broke my heart. Still, it was a satisfying end. However, the ending makes a sequel also a possibility. 
 - Even though the book was 436 pages, it felt like it could've been a 1000 pages. Not because it was boring or had a slow pacing, but because it was a rich and intricate story full of details, secrets and little plot twists. 
 What I didn't like 
 Every few pages Liesl was complaining about her being plain and talentless. In the end it becomes clear why her plain appearances are emphasised and I can understand the author's reasoning behind it. Still, it really annoyed me 
 The verdict 
 I give this story five stars without any doubt. I think I made it clear in this review how much I love this book. And if you weren't sure if you'd want to read it, I encourage you to give it a try. Especially if you like fairy tales, a poetic writing style and a bittersweet plot.

Wintersong is a Grimm Fairy Tale meets Beauty and the Beast meets Hades and Persephone. It's sweeping lyrical passages will enchant you as if you too are stuck in the Underground, where time plays funny tricks on you.  I want so much more. The last chapter wrapped up the book with a nice loose bow, but I felt S. Jae-Jones could expound more upon this world. What happens with Josef, Kathe, and Lisel???? I can't imagine the Goblin King will sit idly by as time marches on. All rules were made for breaking or at least loopholes. Who doesn't love a good loophole? I have questions that need answering, I won't ask them here, in fear of spoilers, but they do exist. Please, give me a second book or novella or something. Please!

THIS BOOK. This BOOK. I had heard about this for MONTHS and upon seeing the description (because yes, Labyrinth movie comparisons I heard around it grabbed me) literally pre-ordered as fast as I could. I had trouble getting started (not the authors fault, mine entirely) but once I did I didn't stop till I finished. 
 S. Jae-Jones knows what she's doing here right down to the lyrical prose, music mentions, and the descriptions of the "goblin" kingdom. Also, I was extremely happy with the tiny little nods (blink and you miss them of sorts) towards Labyrinth (the movie) and also spotted bits and pieces of Hades/Persephone mythology but was also extremely impressed with the way the plot was handled. 
 I started thinking while reading where this book could go and was not disappointed in the least. She, the author, doesn't give the reader a "insta-love" situation (well, she does in a way but it's not as expected - not for the main couple - and aides the plot along) but all of the relationships and characters (Liesl, her sister Kathe, and the Goblin King in particular) in this novel experience over all character growth that makes the novel worth while and makes it stand out. 
 I also loved the Goblin world that Jae-Jones gives the reader, its intricate and well thought out, but it made me curious for more (I hope there is more coming and that this wasn't just a one shot). But, I also enjoyed the journey in the "non-Goblin" world that Jae-Jones gives us. Because at the center of that is Liesl and her feelings towards her family and the love she has for them that propel all the aspects towards a happy but bittersweet conclusion. 
 I hope S. Jae-Jones decides to write more in this universe with these characters. If she does, or doesn't, I'm looking forward to what she writes next.
This is literally copying The Labyrinth.

This book definitely gave me vibes from ACOTAR, Beauty and the Beast, and The Wrath and the Dawn, all stories that I love by the way. With that being said this story still held its own for being unique. It's definitely got complex world building but I loved all the goblin elements to this story. 
 It is a slow paced book which I don't usually like but it didn't bother me too much with this story. I think a lot of the slowness had to do with the topic of music that this book heavily focuses on, some parts seemed to focus too much on the music and it was unnecessary. It definitely could have been cut down. 
 There is a lot of mystery and intrigue surrounding the Goblin Kings past which kept me interested, I really want to know more about it. 
 I liked that it's made clear the female protagonist isn't beautiful. Elizabeth makes it known that her sister is the attractive one and even the Goblin King says he's attracted to her for what's within not her looks. Although I personally do believe you do have to find someone somewhat attractive in looks too which he didn't really say, I'd rather he had said something along the lines of her not being the most beautiful woman on the planet but he loves all of who she is inside and out. Which I think the author was trying to get at just maybe wasn't worded as great. The focus is there's so much soul and passion to Elizabeth that that is what shines through. It's different from the usual protagonist, not that there is anything wrong with being beautiful but I like that the message being emphasised is love is more than appearances. 
 That being said the romance definitely made me feel conflicted. Elizabeth lusted for him and the Goblin King made it clear he had a connection with her from when she was a child. Yet I couldn't really understand how they fell in love I suppose. It seemed Elizabeth was lusting for him from the start even when he put her through his games and she gave up her life for him, they didn't have that deeper personal connection like I wished Elizabeth would have had but it seemed she didn't care about that. It also really bothered me the way sex was handled in this book. Elizabeth refused to give the Goblin King her heart until they had sex, she wanted to 'find herself' by letting him 'break her' so she thought by letting him take her virginity that would somehow fix all her problems and make her become this new woman who could freely love him and show this friendship and personality he's been wanting.  Poignant, painful, and divine, Wintersong is a breathtaking piece I want to experience again and again and again.

Their powerful romance tore me open and laid me bare to myself and the raw honesty of what was written.

Between the flood of musical wonders and the striking burn of lust, it seemed that every imaginable hope and fear was touched and played with; like in an orchestral masterpiece, the ebb and flow devoured me, and I was happily overcome. It was like my childhood and adulthood and all possibilities crashed together inside of me and were turned about by S. Jae-Jones' lyrical, whimsical ways. 
 When I flipped the last page, there was a real, aching weight on my chest and tears waiting behind my eyes. I was amazed and intoxicated by this story... completely seduced. This story truly was a wintersong, and if I can embrace its cold and hold it in my heart, I will not want for spring to come.

 Read my full review on my blog, Turning Pages. 
 Wintersong is a dark, sweeping tale of loneliness, sacrifice, and love. 
 S. Jae-Jones' writing is so lyrical and mesmerising that it's easy to become hooked to the book. The world she crafted is dark and dangerous, and full of pain, temptation, seduction, and love. Sometimes the story is uncomfortable, but I kept hoping that it would have a happy ending. The story talks a lot about religion and beliefs, and who we are. There's a lot of judgement towards Kathe who is interested in fashion and flirts with men for fun. In the context of the setting and the religion of the characters I suppose it's realistic. 
 A big part of this book is the romance. At times I found it hard to root for them, because it seemed like Liesl wasn't even sure of her feelings herself. Liesl is sometimes an inconsistent character, but then as you get to know her it's easier to understand that she's quite flawed, sad, and lonely, but her secret dream of being a composer is what kept her afloat. t times I found it hard to root for Liesl and the goblin king, because it seemed like Liesl wasn't even sure of her feelings herself, she went from hate to attraction to hate, and that made the sex scenes more dark than romantic or sexy. I kind of wish the story had a bit of a different ending only because I'm a sucker for those sappy happy endings where everyone gets what they want, but at the same time the ending suited the story. 
 This is also a story of family and what we'll do to protect them. Liesl struggles to find common ground with her sister, so she instead builds a strong relationship with her musician brother. Over the course of her journey, she learns that her sister was lonely too and that Liesl would sacrifice everything to save her. Love is a powerful thing. There's also an important arc for Liesl as she learns to love herself and be herself despite her parents forgetting her or putting her down. I think that's perhaps the best arc in the story. Liesl confronts who she is, and fights for herself. 
 Wintersong isn't a perfect book, but it was a reading journey I'll never forget. Even now the story is lingering in my mind. The characters are sometimes inconsistent, and sometimes the romance was a little off-putting as were some other aspects. But overall I really enjoyed the book.

I can't quite say whether it's because I read this book on the heels of the (as expected) terrific The Hate U Give, or if it's because this book genuinely isn't as good as A.C. Thomas' debut (apples and oranges though the comparison may be), but S. Jae-Jones' debut wasn't as good as I was hoping for. 
 To be fair, it seems that everyone else went into this thinking it was a Labyrinth retelling, and having never seen that movie might not have helped me, like how not having read A Tale of Two Cities hindered my enjoyment of Sarah Rees Brennan's Tell the Wind and Fire. Well, to be fair, I've also never read too much of Christina Rossetti's poetry, outside of snippets in English textbooks and in Sarah Rees Brennan's Demon's Lexicon, and that doesn't help me going into this book either. 
 My overall impression of Wintersong is that it's a beautiful, haunting book, brought down by its slow pace, interminable length, a plot that has a way of meandering (or sometimes feeling completely lacking), and some pretty awkward romance - borderline new-adult romance, though the book is of course marketed as YA - between Liesl and the Goblin King. Honestly, the impression I got of the Goblin King was that he was another one of those Loki-clone love interests who's pretty, but creepy and hyped to death because of his fantasy bad-boy nature. The Warden and the Darkling come to mind, and Rhysand, and Legend, and especially Morpheus. 
 That said, though, I couldn't stop reading once I got started, and while I'm typically not too enamored with dreamy, surreal-type fantasies that sacrifice plot for atmosphere, JJ writes so well that I couldn't help myself. 
 For sure I'll be reading the sequel, Shadowsong, but I'll be going into that one with a bit of trepidation - and hope that JJ gets the story a little more off the ground, and a little less directionless.

Wintersong is a keen start to a duology that focuses on pretty poetic language, with a pseudo historical story of a girls slow burning love for a fabled goblin king. 
 While I admit the writing is classy and spellbinding in the most, I found the story to be a little drab. Elizabeth is the middle child of two eccentric parents. One who used to be a worldly musician turned drunk and one who's effervescent nature attracts the locals to drink at her tavern. On a night, the towners come to be either entertained or to gossip. 
 Elizabeths sister, Kathe, is the belle of the town. She is a beautiful by nature but we soon learn that she stole Elizabeths love interest, and now Hans comes across as creepy rather than the lover scorned. Liesl, (she has two names in this book) also has a younger prodigy brother who is a marvel when he plays the violin. Liesl herself is a musician too and plays the klavier (piano) but is constantly being put down by her father. She helps Josef train for his audition which will take his to music halls around Europe, if he impresses the Maestro. 
 One day, while shopping in the town Liesl and her sister come across the goblin sellers of the market, and she gets her first sighting of the goblin king. Naturally, she finds him alluring but strange, and she encourages her sister, Kathe, away. But the goblin king tries to lure Liesl to the goblin world by using Kathe. She then makes a bargain to exchange places with her. 
 From here the story is really, really slow. So much that I began to lose interest. There also wasn't a whole lot of story going on, once you got past all the purple prose and constant droning of Liesl going on about how plain she is, and how her music isn't that great because everyone tells her. You see, the Goblin king is enchanted by her music, and even tells Liesl that its her music he wants to hear, not her. 
 Personally, I didn't find the story romantic, or even a slow burning love, the constant flips between emotions made it impossible for me to even like the two main characters. Liesl couldn't ever decide if she wanted to stay with the goblin king. And the goblin king seemed to prefer his 'god' to anything else. This was also a no-no for me. You can't bring this worlds religions into a YA fantasy. 
 At the end, this isn't a faery or goblin story with its wild parties (I think there was one but that was all) and its wild hunts, and its seelie/unseelie versus who's going to rule when someone off's the goblin king. This is really a story which shades on the intricacies of leading a normal boring life to, maybe, living underground with someone who can't decide if he wants you or your talent. 
 So, in short, I didn't enjoy this as much as I'd hoped. Too wishy-washy and drawn out to really get a grips with the little story there was. 
 The writing, however was diverse enough to read in the beginning, but even then I got bored with its over-poetic-ness and lyrical eccentricity.

I just expected that this would be better since it is supposed to have more of a fairy-tale aspect to it with traditional German folklore. What a letdown in that aspect. 
 The characters are stock and boring, it takes practically FOREVER for anything worthwhile to happen in the story, and I kind of had to plod through it because it just wasn't captivating enough. 
 I think I'll just skip the sequel... and probably anything else by this author...

Firstly, I would not classify this as YA, it's definitely NA for me. And those sex scenes, they were awkward from top to bottom, trying to put together old timey austerity and what current readers feel is sexy (reminded me of Fifty Shades from time to time - or rather the quotes I've read from it). 
 I loved the first part as much as I hated the second. At first I really liked the writing, and the story was original. But the voice, the character herself, the type of story, everything changes in the second part and it fell flat. 
 Elisabeth and der Elkoning (why is it written in italics all along?) are not a good couple. Their feelings for each other keep changing, going from hate to admiration to contempt to adoration... It doesn't make sense.
