 Expectations. I have very high expectations for this book since some bloggers levelled it to Hunger Games. I, for one, is a fanatic of that book and that also fueled my desire to read Delirium. Unfortunately, on the first half of this book, it was a little bit dragging and sometimes I canaEUR(tm)t stop my eyelids from drooping because it made me sleepy. Although, the pace will catch up at the second half of the book. 
 The Concept. Well, this is another dystopian novel but this book has a very unique approach to it because it turned love into very disgusting disease. This will be the element that will bind the story together and would probably be the cause of a lot of conflicts in this series. 
 The Dystopian World of Portland 
 It has been sixty four years since the President and the Consortium identified love as a disease, and forty three since the scientists perfected a cure. 
 Love a.k.a Amor deliria nervosa , the deadliest of all deadly things. It produces shifts in the prefrontal cortex of the brain, which result in fantasies and delusions that, once revealed, lead in turn to psychic devastation. What makes this dystopian world interesting is that they consider love as a disease. They believe that love have caused fracture, chaos, and instability to the people infected by it and because of this the case of marriage dissolution increased, incidence of drug-use and alcohol-related deaths also skyrocketed. So the scientists came with a cure that will prevent them to feel it. To undergo the procedure, you have to be at least eighteen or sometimes a little older. Otherwise, the procedure wonaEUR(tm)t work correctly: people end up with brain damage, partial paralysis, blindness, or worse. 
 THE SYMPTOMS 
 PHASE ONE 
 preoccupation; difficulty focusing 
 dry mouth 
 perspiration, sweaty palms 
 fits of dizziness and disorientation 
 reduced mental awareness; racing thoughts; 
 impaired reasoning skills 
 PHASE TWO 
 periods of euphoria; hysterical laughter and heightened energy 
 periods of despair; lethargy 
 changes in appetite; rapid weight loss or weight gain 
 fixation; loss of other interests 
 compromised reasoning skills; distortion of reality 
 disruption of sleep patterns; insomnia or constant fatigue 
 obsessive thought and actions 
 paranoia, insecurity 
 PHASE THREE (CRITICAL) 
 difficulty breathing 
 pain in the chest, throat, or stomach 
 difficulty swallowing; refusal to eat 
 complete breakdown of rational faculties; 
 erratic behavior; violent thoughts and fantasies; hallucinations and delusions 
 PHASE FOUR (FATAL) 
 emotional / physical paralysis (partial or total) 
 death 
 HOW PEOPLE LIVE IN THIS WORLD 
 People are allowed to study. In their senior year, they will have various board exams aEUR" math, science, oral and written proficiency, sociology and psychology and a specialty elective. Then scores will be release. The academic assessors will analyze the strengths and weakness of a person, and then assign him to a school and a major. The last step is the evaluation so they will get paired. TheyaEUR(tm)ll be put in the scrutiny of the evaluators and answer all their questions. After which, evaluators will send a list of four or five approved matches. One of them will become their spouse once they graduate from college assuming that they passed their board exams. People who donaEUR(tm)t pass get paired and marry right out of high school. The evaluators will do their best to match them with people who received a similar score in the evaluations. As much as possible they try to avoid any huge disparities in intelligence, temperament, social background, and age. 
 THE CITIZENS 
 The Cured. These are the people who have already undergone through the procedure. They are not capable of loving though there some who seem resistant to the cure. 
 The Sympathizers. These are the cured people who are still somehow affected with the disease. They can still feel things theyaEUR(tm)re not supposed to feel. They are almost always executed. If not, theyaEUR(tm)re locked away in the Crypts to serve three life sentences, back-to-back. 
 The Resistors. These are the people who resist undergoing the procedure. Most of them are captured and locked away at the Crypts. Others who got lucky run into the wilds. 
 The Invalids. These are the people who live in the Wilds and they also havenaEUR(tm)t undergone the procedure. They donaEUR(tm)t see love as a disease, or they donaEUR(tm)t believe in the cure. They think itaEUR(tm)s a kind of cruelty. 
 The Regulators. They are employed by the government. They patrol streets every night, looking for uncureds breaking curfew, checking the streets and (if curtains are open) houses for unapproved activity, like two uncureds touching each other, or walking together after dark aEUR" or even two cureds engaging in activity that might signal the re-emergence of the deliria after the procedure. They report directly to the government and work closely with the scientists at the labs. 
 The Uncureds. These are the people who havenaEUR(tm)t undergone the procedure yet. These are the minors, since you should be at least eighteen to undergo one 
 THE LANDMARKS. 
 The Wilds. This is the unregulated land that exists between recognized cities and towns. This is where the Invalids live and have been believed as a myth among the people living within the borders. They believe that a place like this doesnaEUR(tm)t exist. 
 Portland. This is the setting of the story. The border is surrounded by electric wires so people fear crossing this line. All the cureds live here. Motto: Safety, Sanctity, Community. 
 The Crypts. This is PortlandaEUR(tm)s combo prison-and-mental-ward. This is where the sympathizers and resisters go. There are six wards in this building, Ward Six is the worst and is considered as the Dead Ward. This is where the political prisoners go. They are kept in solitary confinement no one ever gets released. 
 THE BOOK OF SHHH, The Safety, Health, and Happiness Handbook. This is like the Bible of the people in Portland. Everything that can be learned about their world can be found here. Defacing or destroying the book is sacrilege.

 Title: Delirium (Delirium#1)

 Synopsis: They say that the cure for Love will make me happy and safe forever. 
 And I've always believed them. 
 Until now. 
 Now everything has changed.

 Lena looks forward to receiving the government-mandated cure that prevents the delirium of love and leads to a safe, predictable, and happy life, until ninety-five days before her eighteenth birthday and her treatment, when she falls in love.

Currently, I am super hyped up about reading Pandemonium, and even more the grand finale set to release this year! This Delirium craze is setting upon us deadlier than the deliria...  Anyway. Before reading this I had read Oliver's debut novel Before I Fall. It was really good, yet very depressing - with no sense of a happy ending but more like, "This is going to be my last piece of chocolate." BAM: the end. What if it wasn't? That's how it normally is when you have no self-control with chocolate... You never know... And who is going to eat the other pieces left?.... Or did she leave anything left.... See what I mean? I wanted to know what happened with that chocolate! 
 In Delirium, right before the final chapter, this is what it was like. I felt unsatisfied. The whole book Lena was constantly transforming - just like Sam did in Before I Fall. She was rising up against this adversity taken toll in her life, a situation where she felt like she was all alone until she met Alex. Then when she is captured towards the end or the book and all alone once more she's contemplating how to kill herself to not undergo the procedure. Hello? I thought you told yourself to never give up! Now you're making me feel like I'm giving up too! 
 And then Grace comes to the rescue, her six year-old cousin's daughter (confusing much?) who hasn't spoken a word in front of anyone so her family (except Lena) think 'she's as dumb as a rock.' At Lena's last chance of escape and she gets caught, Grace shouts "Wait!" and momentarily confuses Lena's relatives/hostages, including a couple guards trying to prevent Lena escaping, but in pausing she is able to jump out the window. You always have to watch the quiet ones.. 
 And Alex... Oh Alex, I sure hope you stay how you are and do not become anything else. I felt like you saved me too as you lead Lena to safety, thus ultimatley sacrificing yourself (or so she thinks...) 
 I can't help but admire the many hidden morals in Oliver's novels. Her character's are so life like and realistic that even though I am reading a fiction novel, her writing is able to create empathy for me towards the character. Most cases I can't help but think "what if this happens to me?"

Love, a four letter word that invokes fear and disgust in the minds of every civilized American. It is the deadliest of all diseases and brings with it only pain, loss and heartache. Having witnessed first-hand the disastrous symptoms of the deliria, Lena Haloway eagerly counts the days until her eighteenth birthday, when she will be cured. Then she meets Alex, an invalid from the wilds, and everything she thought she knew about the disease, the government, society and even her past is called into question. 
 Wow! I can't remember when last I read a book this emotionally charged. The entire novel is like a showcase for the beauty of life. The stark contrast between the cured and uncured civilians is spectacular. The sheer splendor of Ms. Oliver's words and descriptions makes every mundane act of living a piece of art and poetry. Very few 'pictures' resonate with me for any length of time after reading a novel, but I cannot get the vision of the Portland bay at sunset out of my mind! 
 The relationship between Lena and her best friend Hana is definitely one of the highlights of this novel. It is so wonderfully natural and Hana's vibrant character leaps off the pages, into your face. Lena's character growth is beautifully developed, her habits are endearing, and her relationship with Alex is exciting and lovely at once. 
 There are so many underlying morals and themes in this novel, but for me, the greatest is the warning against apathy. What an eye opener it is to imagine this world without love. 
 The ending - so tragic and yet real. I take my hat off to an author who is willing to remain true to her story this way. I can't wait to read the sequel! This series goes into my 'Favorite series of all time' shelf!

 However, I liked the way the characters spoke and behave like teens, usually they don't on these kinds of YA books and I also found the writing style surprisingly good. ?Que decir de este libro?  La parte romantica es completamente previsible, pero resulta digerible; la relacion entre la protagonista y su mejor amiga, sigue derroteros parecidos... la sorpresa de lo que realmente le sucedio a su madre entra dentro del patron... el final tiene su toque de drama que no acaba de resultar creible como inesperado, porque uno se imagina lo que pasara en la segunda parte. Aunque, eso si, hay que reconocer que la duda queda sembrada, lo que invita a leer la continuacion, aunque sea por pura curiosidad.

reference_books.review_text:
I liked the first book a lot, and the following year after I read it I couldn't understand the uproar by the Catholic church about the movie. Which I also enjoyed on its own. 
 The books get worse, it's like drinking alcohol, one or two books is ok. But by the time you get to the third book, you may feel nauseous. 
 Phill Pullman reminds me of a long winded Jedi: "these are not the droids you are looking for." weaving a reality distortion field around his story. Where the ultimate message isn't just that there isn't a God, but that it's limiting to believe in God. 
 A quote from Terry Pratchet's, The Hogfather : 
 Death: Humans need fantasy to *be* human. To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape. 
 Susan: With tooth fairies? Hogfathers? 
 Death: Yes. As practice, you have to start out learning to believe the little lies. 
 Susan: So we can believe the big ones? 
 Death: Yes. Justice, mercy, duty. That sort of thing. 
 Susan: They're not the same at all. 
 Death: You think so? Then take the universe and grind it down to the finest powder, and sieve it through the finest sieve, and then show me one atom of justice, one molecule of mercy. And yet, you try to act as if there is some ideal order in the world. As if there is some, some rightness in the universe, by which it may be judged. 
 Susan: But people have got to believe that, or what's the point? 
 Death: You need to believe in things that aren't true. How else can they become?

reference_books.title: The Hypnotist (Joona Linna, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I don't like scary books. :) okay, I do sometimes. This is so far A compelling story, I'm catching some tense switching from the translations, but it's not really too distracting. 
 I really want this story to end well for Benjamin.

reference_books.title: The Amber Spyglass (His Dark Materials, #3)
reference_books.review_text:
"This is how the world ends, not with a bang, but with a whimper." -T.S. Eliot 
 Good bye forever to the world I loved so much in the first book. I enjoyed the first book so much that I hoped to return to the world Pullman built. When it became obvious that the first world was abandoned I kept reading for two reasons. The film was coming out for the first book and I like to form my own opinions when it comes to hubbub. But also the way I saw it, was that I had invested however much time with the characters and the story that I wanted to see where the author would derail his book after he hijacked his own story. 
 I enjoy reading fantasy, and I enjoy the occasional social commentary on religious debates, but this book lacks elegance in both. 
 I dont mind a message, I mind it when the message is written on a hammer and then beaten repeatedly on my head. At that point I don't care what you are selling, I'm not buying. 
 It reminds me of another quote from Terry Pratchet's book the Hogfather: 
 Death: Humans need fantasy to *be* human. To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape. 
 Susan: With tooth fairies? Hogfathers? 
 Death: Yes. As practice, you have to start out learning to believe the little lies. 
 Susan: So we can believe the big ones? 
 Death: Yes. Justice, mercy, duty. That sort of thing. 
 Susan: They're not the same at all. 
 Death: You think so? Then take the universe and grind it down to the finest powder, and sieve it through the finest sieve, and then show me one atom of justice, one molecule of mercy. And yet, you try to act as if there is some ideal order in the world. As if there is some, some rightness in the universe, by which it may be judged. 
 Susan: But people have got to believe that, or what's the point? 
 Death: You need to believe in things that aren't true. How else can they become?

reference_books.title: A Farewell to Arms
reference_books.review_text: I took my family to the only WWI museum in the country, which as you may know is in Kansas City Mo and is probably one of the most under appreciated treasures of the state as its one of the best museums I've been too--and I've been to some great museums. Anyway, I was familiar with some of the images, dates, and players of WWI. But I had a hard time imagining what life must have been like, I found myself compelled to find a good WWI story to paint the picture of what life would have been like for a young man picking up arms and fighting the good fight. I remembered reading the 'Old Man and the Sea' and liking it, so after a few minutes searching for an audio book I could get into I found Ernest Hemingway and the famous book Farewell to Arms. I highly recommend it. The book Beautifully paints a portrait of what life was like a hundred years ago in Europe at the time of the Great War. He's an amazing author and the book is narrated by John Slattery so if your an Avengers fan, he's the actor that plays Howard stark (Iron Man's dad) he does a masterful job of bringing the words to life and the action to mind as Hemingway weaves the tale of life for a young man and his adventures during the war.

reference_books.title: Tigana
reference_books.review_text: I read reviews saying this book was better than Tolkien, a fantasy staple, best in it's class... Perhaps it was the hype that it couldn't live up to for me, but I was bored. This book is very detail oriented and I just couldn't get into it. If you like this book you'll probably like the Imager series. Also detail oriented, only I found the characters to be more fun.

reference_books.title: Theft of Swords (The Riyria Revelations, #1-2)
reference_books.review_text:
This book was really enjoyable, I've read some really good reviews and now I know why. I think I'll have to reread the last few chapters I finished it on a plane while exhausted and distracted by turbulence. So maybe it's not the authors fault I couldn't stay in the story towards the end. Because I was hooked from the beginning and especially enjoyed the first book... Perhaps though it started better than it ended. 
 This book is an omnibus of two shorter books cleverly titled a new "Theft of Swords." Two different swords, two different books, two tales of the same story, and captivatingly told. I'm looking forward to reading more from the author.

book_a.title: The Alloy of Law (Mistborn, #4)
book_a.user_review: I think the mistborn series is by far my favorite Sanderson, this book is a fun addition. I'd gladly read more of this particular series though I miss the characters of the earlier books. If you haven't read the mistborn and are thinking that you probably will, there's a spoiler in this book so I wouldn't recommend it as an introduction, even though it probably stands along without reading the other books first.

sample_reviews.review_text: Fantastic, 2nd favorite Mistborn book so far and I really can't wait for the next Trilogy.
Disappointing.

Phew that took me awhile. Longer than I would have liked, thanks to Fallout 4. I liked it, but I didn't necessarily love it. Then again, compared to most other books I probably would have rated this much higher, but being that it's written by Sanderson and I have such high expectations for pretty much anything he writes, I had to go a bit lower on the rating. I loved the interplay and superb bromance action between Wax and Wayne. Their banter is exceptionally witty and so so much fun to read. However, I did struggle a bit with some of the super long battle sequences and I didn't find the female characters all that engaging. It felt a bit like pulp, which I do like, it just wasn't what I was expecting. Good main protagonists, pretty sweet antagonist, LAME cover. Not a fan of these photo covers, let my imagination run wild! Meh, I'll stop complaining. As long as this man keeps writing, life is good.
A fun western for those of us that don't like westerns. My only complaint is that the book was too short. I hope Brandon continues with these characters.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I really wanted to like this book because I enjoyed the first three. There's nothing hugely and definitively wrong with it, but some of the plot lines were a bit predictable (women kidnapped for breeding, supposedly dead uncle's involvement, etc.) and at least some of the characters were likeable (Wayne) and intriguing (Miles). 
 But oh dear lordy, that Marasi woman was annoying as all hell. Supposedly smart, good with a rifle, sometimes confident with elements of badassery shining through, and then... well, here's a particularly annoying snippet: 
 '"That includes basic healing and some small amount of surgery," Marasi said. "As well as complete anatomy courses." 
 Wayne frowned. "Wait. Anatomy. Meaning, all parts of anatomy." 
 Marasi blushed. "Yes." 
 "So-" 
 "So it was very popular in class to watch my reactions, apparently," she said, still blushing.' 
 She goes to watch an execution alone, fights the Vanishers, but blushes when she sees a man without his shirt on or when she thinks about anatomy... after taking courses on surgery. Really?! 
 Not sure why the only interesting women Sanderson wrote about in this book (Lessie, Ranette, Steris) featured so little. Egads.
Sequel?!?!?!

This was really disappointing compared to the original series, i honestly think that the characters weren't really well developed and the story lacked so many things, now i do have in mind that this is half short compared to the other ones but i don't think that's an excuse. I know that comparison is unfair but i can't help but think that this is not a good series.

Not my favorite of Sanderson's work. It was much more of a western or action adventure novel than a fantasy (though in some ways that's also pretty cool? That the fantasy aspects are a backdrop rather than the focus). And, although the end hints at interesting things, it was largely missing of the cool twists and turns that are part of the reason I love Sanderson so much. There was still some interesting philosophizing though, which is another thing I enjoy about his work. ("Philosophizing" maybe has some negative connotations, but I don't see it that way at all, at least not with Sanderson's work.) 
 And it was a cool advancement of the Mistborn world in general. I'm definitely interested to see where he's taking the larger story. Just wish I'd liked this particular story better.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I enjoyed this book but I have to say I didn't find it as satisfying as the original Mistborn trilogy. I decided the reason must be because it didn't have such an epic story. Mistborn ect was huge system overthrow with major ramifications. Here we have a major bad guy but that's it. Of course much is left hanging in the end and so I think the entire new trilogy will have to be taken in before a true judgement can be made. The writing was of course excellent and the characters were well developed. I didn't care for the female characters very much but then it's hard to top Vin. I really, really wish he had gone much farther in depth with what's happening in the world and what has been happening over the past 300 years.

A nice little tale, set in a land something like London at the brink of electricity, reading a little like a Sherlock Holmes (though with a little more action, and the wild west thrown in for good measure), and a compelling magical dimension. 
 I was desperate for something quick to read last weekend - and this book hit the spot. I've never read anything else by the author, but quite enjoyed the book. It felt well written, cohesive, and I really enjoyed the notion of magic introduced here: Allomancy and Feruchemy. 
 I've since read the first book in the series (this turned out to be book 4), and it wasn't nearly as good. It was too long, and a little loose. This one though, was great.
This came off more as steam-punk than the first arc of the series. Allusions to the past at the end are well done. The new characters are more inviting and ones you want to root for from the get go.
Here's my thoughts about this book, and in case you want a hint, I loved it ;) http://ageekyreader.tumblr.com/post/1...
Good! I couldn't stand the narrator at first, but he grew on me. I wish I had reread the first three Mistborn books before starting this, however. Not as intricate as the first three, but enjoyable.

Continues the awesomeness found in Mistborn. This is set a few hundred years in the future from the last book, so be prepared for some change. It's not something you often see in the fantasy genre, this change of time within a world, but Brandon pulled it off very well. One of my favourite authors currently. 
 Pros: 
 1. Excellent characters. If you love stories because of the interesting characters, then you'll love the Mistborn series in general and this book in particular. I adore Wayne. 
 2. Lots of action. Some pretty cool action scenes. There's one with a train... well, you'll see when you get it to it, why it's pretty awesome. 
 3. Some new uses of allomancy. I was surprised to see the new uses, wasn't expecting it. 
 4. Kinda a western feel. I'm not fond of westerns, but coupled with allomancy? It works. The same with the heist thing, wasn't into it, but Mr. Sanderson added enough other cool stuff to make it work. 
 Cons: 
 1. Not long enough. 
 Look forward to reading the rest. I hear there is going to be some futuristic sci-fi stuff in this series some time... Can't wait.

As always, amazing world-building and pacing--it was so fast. It's unbelievable how Brandon created a sequel for the original Mistborn trilogy with a different feeling but has the same clutch to it. Scadrial (the world of Mistborn) seems entirely new from the Final empire. It's like high-fantasy, steam-punk, mystery/detective, contemporary and action genres are shoved into a single short novel which resulted to this stunning, fast-paced 1900s-era tale.

I've often wondered what a non-medieval high fantasy novel would be like. I've been mostly exposed to fantasy that's firmly Tolkien in setting. This is my first time reading a high fantasy novel with a more 'modern' setting, and as evidenced by the 5 stars up there, I enjoyed it immensely. 
 Not only did I like seeing a western high fantasy, but I liked some of the issues this novel explores. Fantasy novels vary in much, but rarely in objective: the main character or characters are typically charged with saving the world. The Mistborn trilogy was no different in this respect. And it begs the question - in a world that is socially and chemically similar to our own, how will these significant events be viewed and remembered by subsequent generations up through a modern era? 
 It was awesome and fascinating to see how the cataclysmic events in The Hero of Ages (and before) are immortalized in the industrial society that exists three centuries later. It adds a huge layer of depth to the world Sanderson built, and makes me wish I could see canon follow-ups for all my favorite high fantasy universes. 
 Aside from all this, the story and the characters are brilliantly executed, interesting, and, coupled with the interesting setting, make for a great read. I 
 laughed out loud at times, and my pulse was racing through the action sequences. I'll be adding the second volume to my to-read list immediately, and bumping Brandon Sanderson up yet another notch in my estimation.

Listened to the audiobook from Audible. Very entertaining steampunk/western featuring the magic system from the Mistborn books. I've only read the first Mistborn book and yet I was able to enjoy this one just fine, so you don't have to have read the rest of the series.

I've always wanted to write a book combining fantasy and the Old West. Brandon Sanderson beat me too it and did a magnificent job at that! 
 The Alloy of Law takes place three hundred years after the Mistborn trilogy, and the beloved cast of characters we once knew are now remembered only in legend. With industrialism on the rise, trains chugging across the country, and electric lights twinkling to life in the cities, the world itself has apparently progressed in leaps and bounds (or allomantically speaking, Pushes and Pulls). 
 But the wild frontier still exists out in the Roughs and, as Waxillium Ladrian can testify, there's more than enough danger there to keep a lawman and his six-shooter busy. When tragedy strikes, Waxillium hangs up his badge and his revolver and heads to the city, leaving the life of a lawman behind him. Or so he thinks. But with a band of mysterious thieves known as the Vanishers on the loose, the city isn't quite as safe and civilized as it looks. 
 I loved this book. The concept of a fantasy world that is continually developing and becoming more technologically advanced, just like the modern world, is both fascinating and rarely seen. Sanderson seamlessly transitions his magic "Allomancy," "Feruchemy," and "Metalurgy" from a time of daggers and swords to a world of six-shooters and rotator guns. 
 I fell in love with the characters as well. Waxillium Ladrian, the hardcore lawman. Wade, his comical but no less dangerous deputy. And Marasi too, of course. I certainly hope Sanderson is planning more books about these three. I would snatch them up in a heartbeat.

How do you categorize a book that is a sequel to an epic trilogy but also moves the progress of the civilization forward to the industrial age? Three hundred years later and much has changed since the final empire, but not Sanderson's epic story telling. 
 While not my preferred time period (?) the characters and story continue to be masterfully crafted and executed. Absolutely worth continuing after the original trilogy.

Part mystery, part fantasy, part western, is how I would describe Alloy of Law. And amazingly it all comes together nicely into an interesting world and left me wanting more. It's a rather short novel from Mr. Sanderson, unfortunately for us, but an enjoyable read. The main characters are interesting, especially the quirks of some of the characters; the villain is very interesting and his abilities make him difficult to defeat. For those who have read the Mistborn trilogy which precedes this, they'll find interesting bits of geography and old characters mentioned. I'm not sure how well this novel would sit with somebody who hadn't read Mistborn trilogy first. I would recommend this to everyone who has read the trilogy, and suggest those who haven't do the trilogy first then pick this up after.
I promise my reviews wont keep being this lazy but, this book was a fun standalone novel after having hated the second and third books. Look forward to the Shadows of Self.

Unfinished!!! 
 I wish I could give this a 5. I really do. 
 Alas, my book conscience wont allow that. The concept deserves a 5, but the execution is just not all that. I really don't know why I felt this way about this one when all I heard was glowing reviews. I'm a self-confessed Fanderson, so it's even weirder that I should find one of his books to be worth anything less than 4 stars. 
 There aren't any glaring issues with the book, but there are also few glowing strengths. 
 People talk about the banter between Wax and Wayne, and it's not bad, but it's also one of the few strengths. Unfortunately, it's not quite strong enough to really affect my opinion of the book overall in any meaningful way. 
 So, in the "good" corner, we have concept and banter, and in the "bad" corner, we have

I cheated. I read this before reading any other Mistborn book, because the cover is freaking awesome. Was not disappointed. It took a while to figure out how the allomancy worked, but once I got it, it's pretty simple. I also approve of how the end surprised me. I had it all predicted out like I usually do, and I was already rolling my eyes in anticipation and then Sanderson completely goes the other way. Badass. I loved the setting, with the contrast between and Old West type place and a city run by the aristocracy. If I read the first Mistborn books, it will only be because of The Alloy of Law.

3.5 
 Buena novela de Sanderson que funciona mejor vista ahora como introduccion a la nueva trilogia de Mistborn que como novela independiente, claramente inferior a las anteriores. Aun asi es un libro facil y rapido de leer y que nos presenta a los nuevos personajes y la nueva era en el mundo de Mistborn en el que se situara la accion. Muy divertido de ver la evolucion de la magia y su utilizacion junto al avance tecnologico y con un final que deja con ganas de empezar ya el siguiente libro. Lectura obligada para todos los fans de la serie.

I picked this book up without having read anything by Brandon Sanderson before so I didn't base my review on feeling like I was "missing something" here and there. Frankly, my opinion of Sanderson is that he bit off more than he's trying to do too much at once. I felt while reading this story that the "magic" got in the way at times and was the main basis for the personality or descriptive nature of the characters. Given that this book was set many years after the original Mistborn trilogy, it was more removed from the previous characters of the series. However, I felt like there could have been a lot more to this story than there was. The characters were very flat while attempting to be interesting and carismic, while simultaneously changing personality on occasion to to contratdict previous behavior. 
 In short: I like it well enough to attempt the original trilogy to see if reading the previous books would help flesh out the work, characters, and magic. But Sanderson has not, and is unlikely to, make my favorites list. If this was a debute story, I might stick with him to see if he'd improve, but as it's not... 
 I felt like this book had a lot of potential and felt let down by most of it. At times good, but mostly just a little too much magic and that the idea and action of it took precidence over character make up and occasionally plot. 
 Perhaps as a fall back when I'm desperate and have nothing else to read will I turn to Sanderson, but as it stands, I won't be seeking him out as a regular.
Absurdly good times.

Not as good as the Mistborn trilogy. Might have given it three stars, but I'm getting tired of the whole "magic fantasy world moving into the industrial age" trope. I get it, technology is allowed to progress in modern fantasy, can we get back to stabbing people with swords now? 
 Edit: Oh, and it really annoyed me that the main characters were named Wax and Wayne. F&*# off Sanderson that isn't clever it's just stupid.
SO amazing to be in this world again!!!

** spoiler alert ** 
 A strong start to a new series of Mistborn novels, which should keep me entertained for at least part of the time before the new Stormlight Archive book comes out. 
 I freely admit that this book and I got off on the wrong foot -- introducing just the kind of tough, active heroine I love reading about, and then shoving her into that infamous metaphorical refrigerator before the first twenty pages were out. Heroines are, and always have been, a foremost concern of mine, and I wasn't thrilled to see the action girl erased from the page, to be replaced by a pair of girly-girl socialites whom I feared would have little to offer by comparison. I hadn't forgotten my disappointment with the depiction of both heroines at the climax of Warbreaker, and I wasn't sure I could put my trust in Sanderson here. 
 I have been well and truly schooled. While I remain unhappy about Warbreaker's climax, Sanderson does NOT repeat that mistake here. Marasi may not be the tough action heroine that Lessie would have been, but despite her shrinking-violet mannerisms and self-esteem issues, she has won me over. She may doubt herself and her usefulness perpetually, but manages to be helpful at almost every turn, and she comes through at the climax. Steris is also an interesting case. From the standpoint of the plot, she is very much the distressed damsel, unable to rescue herself or even to make it a teensy bit easier for her rescuers to help her. Yet somehow Sanderson manages to endow her with such an intriguing personality that I find myself far less bothered by that than I otherwise would have been. And what would I like to see in future books in the series? More Ranette! 
 Waxillium is a stalwart hero, just flawed enough to keep him interesting, but a hero worth looking up to. Miles is an appropriately chilling villain. The only character I'm not entirely happy with is Wayne, apparently everyone else's favorite. I do like certain aspects of him. I appreciate that he likes Marasi and makes room for her on the team rather than trying to squeeze her out to preserve his bromance with Wax. But darn it, man, that asexual mechanical genius has made it clear a thousand times, in a thousand different ways, that she's just not into you. So back. Off. 
 A solid read, highly recommended for those who like their steampunk with a Western flair.

4.5 stars . I'm so emotional right now because "IRONEYES," HOW???*crying* 
 And Wax chose Steris. Over Marasi. *sobs myself to sleep*

My hubby and I swapped favorite books (we both like completely different genres - romance vs epic fantasy - Yikes!). The Alloy of Law was definitely interesting. Very well written. I see why my hubby loves to read Brandon Sanderson's books. But honestly, for a romance chick like me, it wasn't my fave. I enjoyed it, but probably won't become a die hard epic fantasy fan. =)

It's been about one hundred and six books since I read a Sanderson (the last was April), and I haven't spent any time in the Mistborn world in over 5 years. How crazy is that? 
 Yet I found myself utterly compelled, that 19th chapter was brilliant. If you're not anywere familiar with the world it's probably a harder one to get into than the original Mistborn trilogy, but for a first timer it's well worth the effort and for a fan, it's truly delightful.

Pretty solid book! Prototypical Sanderson style - direct prose, awesome magic system, fast paced action. Didn't quite enjoy the characters or the western feel when comparing to the first trilogy though.

I had this from the library for nearly a week before I started reading it. I just wasn't sure about magic and guns going together, and the picture on the cover seemed kind of lame to me. Maybe I didn't want anything to possibly taint the brilliance of the Mistborn trilogy :). In the end though, it did not disappoint! Here are my thoughts, in no particular order: 
 -I really liked how there wasn't any cheesy romance in it 
 -Some of Wayne's dialogue seemed a little too over-the-top 
 -The "gallery of death" part in the prologue should be skimmed if you want your mind free from disturbing images. (Dan warned me ahead of time so I knew the couple of pages to skip!) 
 -Great characters, engaging plot 
 -Is this really a stand-alone book? They didn't resolve everything!

Kharmoniia, m'gli i kr'v izplitat misteriiata v ,,Splavta na zakona" na Sanders'n. 
 Ne mozhe da se otreche elegantnoto preplitane na deistvieto na niakolko niva, kato Sanders'n ne ostavi nito edin ot geroite si neopetnen - vseki imashe svoite sili, slabosti i greshki. 
 Trista godini sled razpada na Imperiiata i sm'rtta na Lord Vladetelia Elendel e spokoen grad s vsichkite pliusove i minusi. Ima si vsichko - kakto kal i mizeriia v po-nizshite kvartali, taka i balove i falshivi otblias'tsi v bogatite takiva. 
 Grad't obache e nap'lno nepoznat za glavniia geroi Uaksilium Ladrian - dvuroden(m'gloroden-ferokhimik), prekaral poslednite dvadeset godini izv'n grada v opiti da zashchitava spravedlivostta i tova, koeto mozhe da se nareche zakon v pusteeshchite zemi. 
 Uaks se otkazva ot presledvaneto na prest'pnitsi, zashchoto chicho mu umira i toi, po stechenie na obstoiatelstvata, se okazva naslednik na titlata, imushchestvoto i zaemite na semeistvoto si. Preobladavashcho zaemi. 
 Tova imenno e prichinata da zapochne da si t'rsi s'pruga, koiato da se v'zpolzva ot negovoto ime, a toi ot neinite finansi. Nepriiatna, no udovletvoriavashcha i dvete strani sdelka. 
 Za tselta obache se nalaga da zag'rbi tova, koeto vinagi e obichal - presledvaneto na spravedlivostta, ludeshkiiat biag k'm opasnostta i neustoimoto privlichane na zagadkite. A zagadkata ne zak'sniava da se poiavi. Pri tova s gr'm i trias'k. 
 Izchezvashch misteriozno sk'p tovar i niakolko otvlecheni zheni s blagorodno poteklo i alomantichna kr'v v'v venite si sa dostat'chno, za da razbudiat detektiva v Uaks, a kogato otvlichat i potentsialnata mu s'pruga neshchata stavat seriozni. I Uaks se vpuska v presledvane na prest'pnitsite, koito ne ostaviat sledi zad sebe si. 
 Ne sam estestveno. A v kompaniiata na svoia dob'r priiatel Uein, s'shcho dvuroden i liubitel na zagadkite. Prosto ,,zaemashch" nuzhnite mu neshcha i iskreno obichashch k'smetliiskata si shapka. 
 K'm tiakh se pris'ediniava i Marasi - goliama fenka na Uaks i Uain i razkazite za podvizite im v pustoshta, i po sluchainost, blizka na otvlechenata b'deshcha leidi Ladrian. 
 I tuk zapochna prikliuchenieto. 
 Alomantiia, ferokhimiia i prestrelki se zav'rtat v neprestanen potok ot udovolstvie mezhdu 500-te stranitsi na knigata. Sanders'n ne e pestil ot talanta si, kakto ne spestiava na glavniia geroi ranite i nat'rtvaniiata. Osobeno sled bitkata s drug dvuroden, koito blagodarenie na sposobnostite si e pochti bezsm'rten. 
 Intrigi, sm'rt i v'prosi bez otgovor. 
 I, razbira se, Kharmoniiata. 
 Kharmoniiata, bez koiato svet't ne bi bil tova spokoino miasto v poslednite tri veka. 
 Kharmoniiata, koiato ne propuska da se namesi, kogato svet't e iota ot tova da izleze ot relsite na ravnovesieto.

just couldn't get into the setting and environment--as always i enjoyed the uniqueness of the magic system, but compared to the original trilogy it seemedwatered down. Also thought the book was a little corny overall, starting with the title.

I enjoyed this more than I expected. I was a little tired of the Mistborn series by the time the original trilogy ended, but this one was fun. The old Western feel and Wax's and Wayne's banter had a lot to do with it. It was also intriguing to see how things played out from the originals and how Vin and the crew were remembered. All in all good fun and I'm looking forward to the next one.

Pre-ordered this for my son's birthday (in Aug.) and it arrived today. Since I probably won't see him before Thanksgiving, I think I'll read it quickly. Since it's here. :) 
 Mistborn meets the Wild West! Loved this twist. Waxillium (Wax) is a man that can't help but be the hero that is ingrained in him, and his side-kick Wayne (huh -- wax and wane, just got that)is a hoot. Not sure what I think about the little romance twist at the end. Might be interesting to see how things (and people) work out.

A Wild West/fantasy/steampunk/detective/adventure novel? Well, yeah. And it works. The story takes place on the same fictional world as Sanderson's Mistborn trilogy but a little over three centuries later. There are now railways and firearms and even some places with electricity. The protagonist is an aristocrat who went to enforce the law (such as it is) out in, well, mostly lawless regions outside civilization, but he returns to take over the family estate when he hears his father has died. He intends to no longer be a lawman, but situations arise that compel him to do so, with the (comic) assistance of his longtime sidekick. That's pretty much the setting and the start of the plot. 
 I found it an enjoyable story, for the most part. The characters are likeable and fun, the mystery the hero is trying to solve is complex enough not to be painfully obvious at first, and the magic system is familiar from earlier books. The protracted 'action' scenes and detailed rationalizations for the magic, however, are a overly drawn out at times. But all in all, it's quite entertaining. For the first 286 (of 325) pages, I was following the story quite happily, but then.... a moment of 'Harmony'. Someone not familiar with the metaphysics from the other Mistborn stories would have been completely lost, I think, but even then.... Divine intervention? Really? That's got to be about the lamest way to get a hero out of a tough plot corner that there is. I actually paused a moment when I got to this point and thought, "Oh, come on!" 
 Still, I found this a fun, light story. If you liked Sanderson's Mistborn books, you'll like this one too.

Second review: September 22, 2015 
 Not much to add from my first review. I completed my reread of the Mistborn series today in preps for Shadows of Self, which releases in 2 weeks. I can't wait to see what happens with Wax, Wayne, and Marasi! I will say here that I sure hope Wax ends up with Marasi because she is awesome. And they totally make a better companionship than Wax and Steris. 
 First review: May 24, 2014 
 A very good, quick read. The last novel I read was Words of Radiance, so this book read extremely fast. But what I think Brandon Sanderson is so versatile at is writing a good, solid story, no matter the length. 
 I didn't see a lot of things coming, but I did make some pretty good guesses that ended up being accurate. However, there were plenty of guesses that completely missed the mark. This is a good thing, these signify good plots and plot twists. 
 Sanderson's characters were awesome. Wax and Wayne? Epic. Marasi? Cool chick who has a lot more to her than meets the eye (I can't wait to see her character really evolve in the next book). 
 This book is a steam punk western with the awesome magic system I've come to love known as Allomancy. It bridges abilities so that even though there aren't any Mistborn in the book, there are Twinborn - people who have both an allomantic ability and a feruchemic ability. This makes for some awesome action sequences, and has actually opened up the gates even broader for the epicness of the magic system. 
 Sanderson, I'm ready for Shadows of Self. Bring it on!

Hesitating between 3,5 and 4* 
 Very entertaining like all Sanderson books but misses the epicness from the previous ones and something else. Didn't really attach myself with the characters, and with the main one the less.

After finishing Era 1 of Mistborn, I rushed through this book. 
 Sanderson did it again - I loved the world and characters. Wax & Wayne are the duo I didn't know I was missing. Also, I didn't think that the magic system could get any cooler but he managed to do just that. 
 This could be read alone but I 10/10 recommend reading the first three Mistborn novels to appreciate the lore of the world better.

Alloy of Law 
 Another competently written story from Brandon Sanderson, though I have trouble getting enthusiastic. It ticked along as I read it. The world is a nice move along from the original medieval Mistborne books to a sort of streampunk western setting. But I didn't really find the hero all that interesting, the main baddie for this book was sort of garden variety 'I know what's best' type. The love interest (I know, but she is) grated on me. Just added up to, well, easier to finish than stop. Wayne, the side kick was fun though - though maybe the hat thing went of a bit much. 
 Sanderson is good at explaining his magic system and its use in fight scenes, but I feel he has already done this extensively in the earlier books. But his call backs to the previous books is done lightly, so you don't need to have read them first. As you can probably tell, I'm ambivalent and probably more so from writing this review.

It was good. Fast read, sort of a noir novel inside he mistborn universe. 
 Overall i would say that i enjoyed it, although i found it lacking depth or maturity. it was more of a YA read.

I had high expectations for this book because it wss by Brandon Sanderson, but it was very disappointing. I found that this book should have been good because of how good The Mistborn Trilogy was one of my favorite trilogies of all times, but I guess streampunk just don't work with me. This book has too much of traditional streampunk elements that makes me feel that there is always going to have a mystery with a murder. I wish I never bought this book.
Good fun. Glad I was already familiar with the magic of Mistborn. He does great fight scenes, and I loved Wayne's character.

This was my first step into the world of Mistborn, and I expect to be back. 
 Fastpaced frolic in an intriguing world. Run, levitate, or ride the train round the city, as Wax and Wayne (I'm sure there is a pun or two in there), chase a bunch of kidnapping thieves. A fun little romp. 
 Some of the action sequences could have used a little polish, and some of the events had me questioning their feasibility(though I won't go into them as I don't want to raise questions for other readers and maybe diminish their enjoyment). But I am more cynical than most. 
 8/10
The last 5 pages were good. Everything else was crap. Doubt I'll continue the series.
I really liked this series before Alloy of Law. This book really took the Mistborn series to another level and it is now one of my favorite fantasy series.

And he pushed and pushed and pushed a bit more. Slow motion. And pushed again. After that he pushed, rolled and pushed. If it was Dr Seuss and it rhymed it might have been funny. The word "pushed" is used 3 times in each sentence. To the point that it has no meaning and the whole action is just pointless gibberish. 
 The book just doesn't compare to the original trilogy. A pity to see such a capable writer producing mediocre action flicks like this one. 
 If you liked mistborn stay away from this one. If you are thirteen and looking for some easy action book go for it. You will probably love it.

book_b.user_review: Ok it is a cute book and I think it makes every parent cry at least once. But seriously the mom has a weird relationship with her son.

sample_reviews.review_text: I hate this book. WAY too much smoozy sentiment. Not my thing.

"Love you Forever." Or more ACCURATELY, "Love You for a Limited Time Because I Am Going to Die." 
 "I love you forever...As long as I'm living, my baby you will be (or your mommy I will be)." 
 This line, or something close to this, is repeated on every page. This phrasing sounds to me like it REALLY SAYS, "I will love you forever. . . Well, not REALLY FOREVER but at least until I die. Until I die I will love you and we will be baby and momma and I WISH it was forever but I WILL DIE so our love and our close relationship WILL END. But until then I love you SO much." 
 The story line reinforces this showing a timeline beginning with a young mother singing this to her son throughout his life. Eventually the son grows up and lives in his own house with his own baby. At the end the mother is elderly. The son drives to his elderly mom's house, creeping into her room and singing a version of the song to his mom. I don't remember the exact words and can't look it up because I hid my copy at the top of my bookshelf so that my kids don't ask me to read it to them. The language is there, of course, referring to someone's "as long as I'm living" finite life period. In the context of his visit to his mother I find it implied that she is dying or it is a reminder that she is old and will die. After that, the man goes home and sings the song to his baby. 
 To me, this story portrays a heartbreaking love between parent and child. EVERY TIME this deep love and parent-child love relationship is mentioned there is always the limiting condition that this love and bond lasts for a finite time period, "as long as I'm living." 
 This book triggers DEEP feelings of sadness in me and causes me to think about dying and leaving my kids motherless and of losing my loved ones to death. Death is the final and permanent separation between all loved ones and lasts much longer than our brief lives on this earth. 
 ***** 
 Every time I've tried to read it to a kid I end up bawling and the kid ends up crying too. Actually, every time I've read it to anyone I cry and the other person usually starts crying, too. 
 I read it to my spouse. "Look how sad this book is! Let me read it to you!" I said. As I read, tears started STREAMING down my face. Seeing me look so heartbroken caused my stoic spouse to cry and he asked me to please stop reading it. 
 The BIG problem with the book is this. The refrain, repeated on every page, goes something like this, "As Long as I'm Living...my baby you will be (or your mommy I'll be?)." It doesn't really matter about the second part of the phrase, the loving sentiment, because it is conditional on the first part..."As Long As I'm Living...." 
 ***** 
 I love my kids. I don't tell them, "I love you so much but every time BEFORE I tell you this I MUST POINT OUT: THIS LOVE WILL EXPIRE! This loving feeling and our familial relationship is a LIMITED TIME OFFER. GET IT WHILE IT'S HOT!" 
 Every time "As Long As I'm Living. . ." is chanted I hear the corollary "I may be alive now but I AM going to die. As guaranteed as my love for you, so is my death." Worse yet, "You won't be my baby and I won't by your mommy. And I feel I must remind you of this every time I repeat this line and every time we read this book." 
 Most kids are terrified of death and become scared at the thought of being temporarily separated from their parents and are even more scared by the concept of a parent's death. Some kids may hear this words and not hear the implied "death" concept but I promise you SOME KIDS WILL. I do not recommend this book as a gift for ANYONE. Unless, of course, your goal is to emphasize the finite duration of love and relationship between close family members. In that case, this book would be most appropriate. 
 As a kid I would hear this message: "Sorry kids, life really sucks and we're all gonna die. Don't worry I will PROBABLY die before you. If you grow up to become parents one day YOU will probably die before your KIDS do . . . Of course, when you kiddos are parents your kids COULD DIE before you do and YOU KIDDOS could bite the dust before me! Don't worry about that for now. You and I have no control over my or your death. It could happen at any time. So don't worry about it. At least know that I'll love you and stick around as your parent for as long as I can...As long as I'm living! Again, I have little control over the duration of that period. But UNTIL the day of my or your sudden death . . . WE ARE GOLDEN!" 
 I would prefer the words "Forever and ever . . ." "Forever and Ever Your Mommy I Will Be, Forever and Ever My Baby You Will Be." I will always be my child's parent. My parents will always be my parents and I will be their child even after they are no longer on this earth with me. They are irreplaceable. Their love for me goes with me wherever I go. 
 Likewise, I try to instill into my kids the gift of love and belonging. I want them to know I love them now and forever. In my heart I am and will always be their mother and they will always be my babies even when they are grown up. I will love them every day of my life and beyond if that were possible. 
 I share with my kids that my grandparents live on in my heart and in my memories of their lives and of their love for my parents, me and for them. My elders have passed down so much love and knowledge and my children will do the same for their loved one. For me, this is forever love, or at least a love that continues beyond death and THIS is a truer way to teach kids and loved ones that we love them forever.

Creepy book of a mother who can not let her son go. Even when he is a grown man she puts a ladder up to the window and watches him when he sleeps. The most disturbing illustration is when he is a teen and she is crawling up the hall to get in his bedroom. I know I will have "haters" on this review but that is how I feel!
i have and always will find this horrifyingly creepy.
This book just creeps me out.
This book had a lot of potential, and it is without a doubt both a moving experience and worth taking the time to read.
great, childhood book

As a librarian, I was vaguely aware that this book was controversial, but had no idea why. I noticed it in the donation pile one day and paged through it. I concluded that this may be the creepiest children's book in all the land. 
 This is the story of a boy and his very clingy mother. Mom waits until Sonny is asleep, then crawls(!!) across the floor to hold and sing to him in his sleep. As the boy ages, his mother's bizarre form of affection gets more and more disturbing--consummating in Mom driving to her adult son's home across town with a ladder strapped to her car, breaking and entering into the man's house, and holding him on her lap as he sleeps! (Good thing Sonny never has a lady friend over, or a burglar alarm.) The song "Mother" by Pink Floyd came to mind more than once. 
 Besides abnormal attachment, another major theme of this book is the aging and eventual loss of Mom. Pretty deep stuff for a bedtime story that has a picture of a toilet on the cover. 
 The drawings are atrocious soft-focus sap, and bring to mind something that would appear on stationery sold by Focus on the Family. The family cat resembles an overgrown rodent. When the son becomes a teen and goes into a rebellious stage, his challenge to the system is depicted by his wearing a Hawaiian shirt, Elvis haircut, pegged jeans and women's loafers. Oh, those crazy teenagers! 
 The last page shows the adult son holding his new daughter, singing the same song that his mother once sang to him. Ahh! The cycle continues!! The child's mother is nowhere in sight; I wonder what she thought about Mother-in-Law continuously breaking into their home? This would be a fine book choice if your family lives in the Bates Motel.
I know many people love this book...I find it quite weird and annoying both at the same time.

Once upon a time, I read this to my classes. Then my mother died, and I was unable to get through it with them. It's a powerful book, a wonderful lesson, and a resource that I would suggest for every home and classroom.

From my experience, people either love or hate this book (I find very few who fall in the middle) . . . and I definitely fit the latter category. Normally, I won't give a book a low rating if my dislike of the book is largely influenced by the fact that I'm outside of the target audience, but this book is just too creepy to forgive. I know most kids probably wouldn't see it that way, but I could never even bring myself to read this to my daughter.

In this children's book, a mommy reminds her child at different stages throughout his life that she will always be his mommy and he will always be her baby, by appearing with a bedtime lullaby at all stages of his life--beyond childhood into teenagerhood and adulthood. 
 I had trouble with this one because I don't know who it's for. I've read that it has something to do with the author having a dead child, and imagining what they could have had, but as a children's book I don't really know what to do with it. A young child will not relate very well to the idea of becoming an adult and having to interact with his mom in an adult-to-adult capacity, and a parent probably oughtn't find it comforting and cute to see a mother climbing in her adult son's window while he's sleeping to sing him a lullaby (not in a whimsical, Cat-in-the-Hat way). So yes to the idea that a son is always his mommy's baby no matter how old he gets. No to expressing that by infantilizing him and watching him while he's sleeping as a man.

I hate, hate HATE this book. It is incredibly creepy and disturbing, and I am immediatly suspicious of people who get all misty-eyed and weepy while talking about it. The writing is terrible and the illustrations are even worse. With all of the WONDERFUL books out there for children why a parent would subject their poor, innocent child to this tripe is beyond me.
Yecch!!!!
A weeper. Another one I can't get through when I read it out loud. Growing up.
I got this book for my little boy. I have never had a book for children make me cry so hard. I love this story.
My baby is twelve and has severe autism. She attends a residential school far away and I have this poem? Song? on her wall for her when I can't be.
If you were read this book as a child, you probably need to read Understanding the Borderline Mother now that you are an adult.
Touching story for a children's book

I can't believe the negative reviews on this book! There are many comments about the creepiness factor. Certainly people are entitled to their opinions, but to those negative reviewers: "Have you ever heard of symbolism and exaggeration?" 
 No matter the age of the child, the parents are always interested, always watching, always loving. As the child grows towards and into adulthood, it is no longer appropriate to hold and cuddle, but that memory and love is still there. 
 It has been a long time since I have read this book, although I'm sure it is on a bookshelf some place in my house. I do remember when I first read this book. I was really touched by the message and I brought it to my 8th grade classroom the Friday before Mother's Day. 
 At the beginning of the school day we had Homeroom where teachers were expected to do activities on values clarifications, responsibility, study skills, etc. The kids hated it, and none of the teachers liked it either. 
 So that day I told the students I wanted to talk to them about something important they should always remember. I told them to lock the door because I didn't want anyone disturbing us. 
 That action was very different and unsettling to some--I was already different enough as their math-loving, basketball playing teacher. I had a quick flashback to playing 3 on 3 basketball in the gym with 5 8th boys in the gym after school and hearing one guy say to another, "Dude, is that your math teacher?" Yeah, bring it. 
 So I told this 8th grade class that Mother's Day was coming on Sunday and they should think about how much their Moms (and Dads for those that had one)loved them. The kids were older now, and sometimes it is hard for the parents to show that love. It may come out as nagging and disciplining. Blah Blah. 
 Then I read this picture book aimed at 4-6 year-olds to them...and they loved it. We had a little bond going. They were touched and they all planned to go home and let their Moms (and Dads) know they appreciated them. 
 I told the kids to unlock the door and released them to go to 1st period and I would see each of them through out the school day for math. 
 Some of the kids from Homeroom were in my 1st period math and they told the other kids in the class we had a "secret". The kids wanted to know and the kids that were in my Homeroom egged me on. So we locked the door, we talked, and I read the book. 
 This scenario played out for every class. They all loved the book and they knew their Moms loved them. 
 I did this every year before Mother's Day until I got married and became an instant Mom to teenagers and moved across the country as my husband was transferred. 
 I did my best to raise my instant family in love. I guess I did OK. When they call, who do they ask to talk to? They have given me 9 beautiful grandchildren that I love. 
 While raising teenagers, I also gave birth to my son who is 18 now, and is planning to leave in August for BYU (2000 miles away). Moms raise their kids to be independent and self-sustaining, but they never stop watching and loving.

This is a book that I thought was cute at the beginning and very touching at the end, but the middle is just weird. Generally I like weird, but this just didn't do it for me. It's a great book to introduce your child to the cycle of life. I just could get over the suspension of disbelieve of the middle section.

Obviously enough, I'm in the minority here, but this children's book is weird, creepy, disturbing and will probably give me more nightmares than any Stephen King novel ever did. 
 "Love You Forever" is, as the title indicates, about a mother who loves her sweet little baby boy forever, until her baby has grown into an adult and she into an old woman. I'm perfectly fine with the message that mothers (respectively parents in general) will always love their children and will (in most cases - sadly enough, there are always exceptions) do everything for them to be comfortable. But Robert Munsch simply overexaggerated while portraying this message, and finally made me see a totally different message in this book: That a mother's love justifies stalking her children and entering into their lives in one of the creepiest and most disturbing ways - by climbing a ladder to her son's bedroom, entering the house and picking her son up to rock him back and forth while he's sleeping. 
 I'm sorry, but this is so weird, I can't even find it funny anymore. Yes, the book is meant to be understood metaphorically, the book is supposed to be somehow funny and cute and oh-so-sweet (although I only furled my eyebrows in confusion rather than actually laughing). In the beginning, the book was still interesting; everyone can relate to the way children can bring chaos into everything. But then the mother began to enter her son's room at night. Is it okay to go into your two-year-old son's bedroom while he's sleeping with the intention of admiring him and admitting that you will love him forever? Yes, it is. I am totally fine with that. Doing so with a nine-year-old son begins to show signs of creepiness, but it's still acceptable. 
 It isn't acceptable if your son is thirty and has moved on with his own life. You can't just break into his house to admire him, indifferent from how lonely you might feel. (And yes, I understand that this book is not supposed to be taken seriously, and it's not even realistically possible for an old woman to be able to pick up her full-grown son while he's sleeping, but this book pretends it is, so I will too.) There are thousands of better ways to incorporate a message about a mother's love into a book. I wouldn't even consider this one to be a children's book ... calling it a horror novel would perhaps be more appropriate. 
 If you want to read a fantastic children's book, then please skip this and read The Velveteen Rabbit instead, which is an absolutely wonderful story. Or if you want to read two more reviews of "Love You Forever" which I really enjoyed and can whole-heartedly recommend reading, then read this Anne's review or the other Anne's.

I do not like this book.

I know I'm in the minority, but I found the text overly-sentimental and the majority of my former high school students could have drawn better illustrations. But that's just one opinion.

 Edited to add: After reading the other reviews, I've just figured out that the mom in this book reminds me of my smothering father, who also creeps me out in many ways.
