Unfortunately I didn't quite connect with this book. It had all the ingredients right there, but somehow it didn't make me fall in love with it. 
 I did like it though. And as weird as it sounds I think I like TJ more than I like Trent. IDK why, but that's just how I feel. 
 Maybe I'll like the next Maddox book more. I will definitely read it because, hey, after all, they're Maddoxes :)

I was kind of disappointed because I thought this book was going to have Trent's pov to but it was only Cami's. I really hope the author writes one from his pov like how she did with Travis. When the book starts off with Cami's trip to see TJ is cancelled, I was thinking that he was married. When other things started coming up about keeping secrets, I started thinking that maybe he was in the FBI like Travis and his brother Thomas were. The ending of the book was totally unexpected with finding out who TJ really is. Never would have guessed who he really is. Can't wait for the next book

OMG! OMG! OMG!!!! TRENT effing MADDOX and CAMI!!! Plus THOMAS JAMES MADDOX! OHHHHMYYYYYYYYYY! This book just turned my shitty day into one awesome day by reading and finishing it before, in between and after work. AWESOMEEEEEEE! <3 <3 <3
*3.5 stars*

Me Ha Gustado Mucho La Historia de Trent y Cami, Pero Realmente Senti Que Aparecio de La Nada (Aunque La Autora Intenta Explicar que trenton Sentia algo por ella desde el Principio), A Parte De Eso me Encanto Ver El Mundo de Maravilloso Desastre desde los Ojos de Cami, Me Mega Encarine con Los Personajes y Sin Duda La Identidad De "T.J." Me dejo en Shock Total.

I, along with pretty much everyone reading this book, was SUPER excited to get to read a NEW book from Jamie McGuire. I adored (and still adore) Beautiful Disaster - seriously, one of my favorite books of the DECADE. I skipped Beautiful Wedding after being completely bored by Walking Disaster, though. So, maybe my expectations were too high here. Or maybe Ms. McGuire really is a one-trick pony and got super lucky when she created the wonderful Travis Maddox. Either way, Beautiful Oblivion was a gigantic disappointment. The entire time I felt a strange sense of deja vu - Trenton was exactly like Travis (I know, they're brothers, so maybe that could be explained away), but everything else was the same, too. The setting, the girl with daddy issues, the spunky best friend. I think even some of the conversations were repeated. Plus, it was set to take place concomitantly as BD, which was confusing in the beginning, and then redundant to have to see YET ANOTHER retelling of BD from a new perspective. Enough already! The only thing that kept me reading until the end was Cami's big secret - which I guessed right from the beginning - but didn't think that possibly could be true because there were just too many holes for that "secret" to actually be true. But, there it is. Disappointing, unoriginal, and boring.

Jamie never fails to dissappoint! This book is awesome as Beautiful Disaster. The surprise at the end was totally shocking and in no way did i see that coming but it was really great!! I Loved IT! I highly recommend this!

I think I love Trenton Maddox more than Travis. Is it possible? 
 Wasn't sure what the expect from this book but I got way more than anticipated. Didn't expect the T.J. Drama to unfold like it did and I'm not even sure that twist was needed at all because the rest of the book was so good.

I can't believe I'm writing this review right now. Beautiful Disaster is one of my favorites, and it's my go-to book when I have nothing else to read. 
 Okay I tried really hard to give this book more than 3 stars, but I just can't. It felt like there was no story. The main characters were there, but nothing was really happening. I tried to get into this book so hard, but I just couldn't. 
 When Trent claimed that he'd been in love with Cami since they were kids, I just couldn't believe it. Maybe I'd believe it if there were flashbacks to explain how he was in love with Cami I'd actually buy it. 
 The "secret" that Cami had, well I figured that secret out in the first few pages. It would have been a great shocker, if it wasn't already so freakin obvious. That "secret" was what the book revolved around, so since I already figured out what it was, I just wanted Trent to find out and get it over with. 
 So yes, this book made me sad, because I wanted to love it so much. I just hope the next book is better, so I can get my Maddox crush back on.
I felt like I was reading Beautiful Disaster again but from someone who isn't Travis or Abby's POV. It's a nah.. though that part with Toto was really cute.

This is one of those cases where the character(s) know more than the reader and it just didn't work. 
 I really enjoyed the first book Beautiful Disaster. This one was just okay. I liked the love story and the chemistry between these two characters but it was a slow read. Part of the problem is, there is a "secret" that we don't know and really don't understand. I'm sure this was supposed to add tension, but all it did was make the character development confusing and frustrating. 
 I didn't understand Cami's motivation for keeping her ex secret which made me really not like her very much. Trenton is a straight forward character similar to his brother Travis. Trenton really was the best part of this story. 
 I find the Maddox brothers interesting so, if there is another book about them, I will probably read it. This one just didn't work for me.
This is my favorite book of Jamie's so far! I love how real Jamie's characters are. They are regular people who are broken and aren't we all? Life isn't "fixed" it's just done. I appreciate that.
trenton disinda hic bir seyi sevmedim. kurgu, sir hic birini. muhtemelen bir daha bu yazari okumam, saniyorum Travis in kitabini yanlislikla o kadar guzel yazdi.

reference_books.title: Thirteen Reasons Why
reference_books.review_text: I understand why people don't like this novel. I had a very hard time getting through it myself. Don't get me wrong, it's a great piece. But when you've dealt with rejection, humiliation and bullying in high school, it just brings all those thoughts back. To all those who say that she should just get perspective instead of killing herself, maybe it's just because you don't understand or remember how it feels. When you feel so lonely and desperate that you only see one way out. Not saying she was right, but the authore understood her pain and wrote it as real as it gets. That is why I'm giving it 3 stars.

reference_books.title: Carry On
reference_books.review_text:
Hmmmmm... this world reminds me of another book, I think as I pet the Crookshank furry toy I bought at the Harry Potter Studio Tour last week. Seriously, is J. K. Rowling such a fan or Rowell that she didn't bother picking up the phone to slam her with a copyright lawsuit? 
 I admit, I haven't read Fangirl. Maybe if I did, this book would make more sense. But, as it is, I just felt wrong reading this amateur copy. Not only would it make more sense if she had actually written a few more books to give us a better understanding of Simon's journey, but the love story pre-kissing was just non existent. It actually sounded like any fanfiction where Harry and Draco end up together when there's NO build-up for a romantic relationship in the original world. I get the Harry/Draco thing, cause I used to be a big fan of them together (still am a little, reincarnated in a Scorpius/Albus fan). But J.K. never even hinted at a romantic link between those two. And that's how Rowell wrote Simon. No romantic attraction AT ALL. Until the big kiss that just comes out of nowhere... and made no sense... 
 Also, who the hell uses the F-word every few pages? I get that your characters are teenagers, but nobody thinks or says the F-bomb that many times... And don't get me started on the parenthesis... 
 I guess I finished this book for the sake of adding a full read to my challenge, if nothing else. Note to myself: stay away from Rainbow Rowell's books, they're just not for you.

reference_books.title: The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe (Chronicles of Narnia, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
I quite liked it. 
 I saw the movie years ago when it first came out but, at 14, I was a bit scared when I saw how massive the book was (which at the time I didn't realize was the complete edition) and never got around to actually read it. 
 Reading it now made all those movie memories come back and I really liked it. I wish I hadn't been so stubborn as a teen and had read it earlier.

reference_books.title: Before I Fall
reference_books.review_text:
I can't finish it. With every page I read, I find a new reason to want to throw this book against a wall or strangle Sam until she gets some sense knocked in her head. 
 She's an idiot. A selfish, superficial idiot who only follows her friends so she won't have to deal with the world by herself. 
 In the 3.5 days (chapters) I've read, she has barely realized that her best friend is the typical mean girl who doesn't care about anything or anyone but herself. Not only that, but it took her 3 days to learn that being an asshole and starting rumours about people hurts them. Welcome to the real world... 
 I cannot wait any longer for Sam to become a "better person" or however it is that the book ends. I've got a big enough dose of Mean Girl in the past 210 pages to last me for years...

reference_books.title: Go Ask Alice
reference_books.review_text: I couldn't be more disappointed in this novel. Frankly, if I wanted to read a teenager whine about how unfair her family and life is to her, I would read my own diaries. The more I tried to read, the more I felt like this novel had backward thinking minda behind it, which of course isn't surprising for a 1970s book (didn't know that when I picked it at the library). All in all, disappointment and suffering (from the lack of writing talent) all around.

reference_books.title: Girl Online (Girl Online, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
UPDATE: I have been made aware that the book was actually written by a ghostwriter. Since Zoe Sugg came up with the idea, some of the praise still go to her. But it is obvious that any praise on how the story was written go to the ghostwriter. 
 Despite its cliches and lack of diversity, I quite liked this book. 
 The story is quite simple: a girl who seems unable not to make a fool of herself at every turn - and who runs a popular anonymous blog - goes on a trip to New York with her family. There, she meets a really hot guy and a romance sparkles between the two. A perfect Cinderella story, until she learns his secret. Everything resolves itself in the last 10 pages. 
 Famous blogger Zoella took a love story that has been used too many times and found a way to make it appealing to 21st century teens. Penny blogs, has Facebook/Twitter/Instagram, goes viral on YouTube at one point, is subject to fangirls' wrath online... All those are things teens and young adults of the 2010s have seen and done. And there are lessons hidden in all Penny's misadventures. Take her "reveal" by CelebWatch, for example. The 2 lessons hidden there are 1)don't believe the gossips and 2)don't bully girls on the internet because they are in the mere vicinity of your idol (or because they are rumoured to go out with your idol's rumoured boyfriend). 
 My only major problem with the story was that Penny's best friend Elliot is a bit too stereotypically gay. His journey (the parents problems, mostly) redeems him to a certain extend, but there are moments where his gayness becomes caricature. The description of his taste in clothes made me cringe at times. For all the other good things Zoe Sugg brought to her books, the gay-best-friend was far less well executed than the others.

reference_books.title: Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda
reference_books.review_text:
Loved it! 
 This a really cute story about being forced out of the closet, but learning to adapt to a life out in the sun. Simon's friends and family are very accepting and, while not everyone is that lucky, it's a beautiful novel about coming out when you're a teen and so many things happen at once in your life. 
 The ending left me with a huge smile on my face, much like those very cliche romance novels sometimes do when they are well written. I was definitely rooting for Jacques and Blue.

reference_books.title: Rivers of London (Peter Grant, #1)
reference_books.review_text:
3.5 [?] 
 FINALLY! It took me two weeks to finish this book, but I DID IT!! I usually read mostly while commuting, but being stuck at home all week since I've got back in the country, it was hard to do so. But the lack of commuting hours is not the only reason it took me so long to finish this book. I gave it 3 stars because it wasn't bad, but it wasn't amazing either. 
 When I read a murder mystery - even a supernatural one - I want it to be a page turner. I want to be out of breath while reading, eager to know what happens next and how they'll catch the murderer. The problem with this novel is that there is too much description. While it's interesting to learn about Aaronovitch's world of magic and the science behind it (my scientific mind loved it), most of the novel was focused on detailed description. A good part of those could have been less detailed and it wouldn't have taken anything from the novel. A moment that should have been quite important (Peter discovering Lesley is being controlled by Punch ) was almost boring, since I had to skim over all the description. 
 On the bright side, Aaronovitch writes beautifully and is very open-minded. Despite a male main character, there is hardly any sexism, racism or LGBT+ -phobia (if any). That was refreshing and quite nice. 
 If you don't mind a slow building murder mystery and you love magic infused in science, you'll probably love that book.

reference_books.title: To All the Boys I've Loved Before (To All the Boys I've Loved Before, #1)
reference_books.review_text: I could barely finish the first 3 chapters. I don't ask for much from a YA novel, butI certainly ask more than something that looks like it was written by a 12 years old. I had hoped I would like it, because the plot seemed quite good. Unfortunately the writing is just something I cannot pass over when I read a book.

reference_books.title: Empire of Storms (Throne of Glass, #5)
reference_books.review_text:
once again, a good 10 days of struggle to finish this book, with a "WHAT THE HELL IS THIS?!?!" at the end. 
 It wasn't bad. I even liked some parts of it. But the novel in a whole just left me hanging. I hope for the fans sake that this is not really the last (as it seems to be) in the series. Not that I would put myself through another 600-pages of this kind of tortuous reading, but it's just mean to leave your fans on such a disappointing ending. 
 I think the one thing that disappointed me the most was the end-fight. Like really? You went through all of this for that kind of non-fight? 
 I also got tired really quickly of Mass' fixation on having everyone in a relationship. I appreciate the effort for inclusiveness, but if you're going to put everyone together, at least don't just use same-gender couple passively. Except for mentions here and there of gay and bisexual characters, we never actually saw a gay or lesbian relationship in the whole series. The whole pairing thing in general seemed pretty desperate by the end of the novel, though. Let's be real here, not everyone needs to find their soulmate during a war... 
 At least I didn't have to suffer through another scene of Chaol being a complete hypocrite. That was a nice change. And some of the parts between Rowan and Aelin were pretty good. 
 Far from my favourite of the series and the one novel that made sure I won't ever read the sequel, if Maas feels like giving people a better ending than this.

book_a.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (Hercule Poirot, #4)
book_a.user_review:
I am tempted to give it only 2 stars for the ending... 
 The story in general was good. Poirot was his typical self and the murder was unnecessarily complicated, but I am used to that coming from Agatha Christie. 
 What really bothered me was the end. 
 I surprised myself at one point thinking "wouldn't it be different and refreshing if there was a Poirot novel written by the murderer, who would befriend Poirot". Little did I know how on point I was. 
 It could have been a great ending, if Dr Sheppard had some character and emotions. The writing of the last chapter was so gloomy, a robot would have shown more emotion! Remorse, guilt, joy, pride, sadness... any emotion would have made more sense. I have never read of someone committing murder then suicide, yet feeling absolutely no emotion about either (unless they have some sort of personality disorder). 
 Apart from that, the novel was no better or worse than any other Poirot, hence the medium 3[?]

sample_reviews.review_text: Ever since the CWA last year voted it best whodunit novel ever written I've been meaning to read it. it holds up well considering it was published in 1926 and though it's not my favourite Agatha Christie, it's quite clever. And who doesn't enjoy a good Poirot.
NO. There are no words for just how much I despise this book. A zillion clues and very little character development. Ugh

Agatha Christie manages in this book to weave a tale so spellbinding you sit back and wonder how she does it. Do not under any circumstances watch the movie before the book as much of the surprise will be ruined. 
 This book was a rule breaker which uses several literary techniques to achieve its suspense. The murder itself is classic Christie but much of it has a certain darkness to it. 
 The character of Carolyn in this book is the inspiration of Miss Marple by the way. I found her character fascinating.

Ok so my dad and sister told me this book would be amazing, life changing and had the biggest most surprising ending EVER. But on about page 150 I was SOOOO bored with it! Neither my dad or sister would tell me who murdered him! I was in the book enough to where I wanted to know who kille Ackroyd, but I didnt want to finish it. Apparently the ending was so amazing and un called for. 
 So I asked my dad if I guessed it with two tries if he would tell me if I got it right. I got it right on the second try...hehe.

Vintage Christie - all the clues are there! 
 This is one of those books with a realistic village setting. I love the Mah Jong party where everyone gossips (and criticises play!) 
 'I saw Flora Ackroyd this morning,' said Miss Gannett. 'Pung - no -Unpung. I made a mistake.' 
 'Four Circles,' said Caroline.'Where did you see her?'
This book had a great twist! This was my first Agatha Christie book and I think the first of many.

According to me it was too boring to hear it again and again from every characters in the story... The book seems to be complicated at some stage. The words used by author made me to google more frequently. And the story which was tagged to be crime never gave me the feel of a crime story it was more a detective story a boring i would say... I wont recommend this book it was a utter waste according to me to read this.

Even though I knew the ending, I thoroughly enjoyed this book! Considering how obsessed I was with Agatha Christie as a teen, I was shocked that I didn't read this one. Love the twist, love Hercule Poirot, and love Agatha!
One of my favorites!!!

Please note my ratings are only my personal reaction to the book, not meant to judge its quality or what it might mean to someone else! It's just that it's been a long, long time since I came away from reading a book start to finish like I did with this one: as exactly the same person I was when I started. At the very least I usually feel like I met an interesting person or learned about something. (And after reading a really good book, I feel I've actually evolved as a human being.) 
 I give this two stars because if I hadn't known the character of Poirot from Mastserpiece on PBS, I would have enjoyed getting to know him. And the mystery was clever. But not clever like a good plot or story--more just clever like a math problem. I know that is scintillating to some people, but not this reader. 
 And though Poirot was interesting, I never found myself caring about him. I didn't find myself once caring about any one of these characters. 
 I've never been a mystery reader. I did enjoy a Dorothy Sayers recently, and wanted to read this because it is supposed to be Agatha Christie's best. If so, I don't need to try another.

tres bonne enquete, pas de longueurs et beaucoup de details pour s'embrouiller avec les differentes pistes et finir par suspecter tout le monde. Je savais que la fin serait surprenante mais finalement un peu decue.
Not really my kind of thing I guess. All plot and twists and turns, but nothing of any real interest.
I read this when I was in high school. My introduction to both Agatha Christie and Hercule Poirot. A must read for anyone who loves a good mystery.
Nie moge powiedziec ze przeczytalam, ale fabule znam znakomicie.

I read this in one sitting (one of the blessings?? of being sick). It had me guessing the whole time. While I figured out some of connections, I totally missed the the most important one. I may just be the newest Agatha Christie fan. I can recommend this book with no reservations.
Ha! This one got me. I kept thinking I knew whodunit, then changed my mind a couple times. In the end I was like "What!?! Oh. Of course."

One is not deemed to be the Queen of Mystery without good cause, and Agatha Christie is certainly the just recipient of such title, which has endured throughout the decades. 
 The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is perfect in everything; rich and complex characters, with ambiguous personalities and not-so-honorable interests, tense social relations, drama, a slight hint of romance and a seemingly impossible murder to resolve. 
 It will hook you from the very beginning, have you question everything alongside Dr. Sheppard and Monsieur Poirot himself, trying to find an answer to a complex riddle. Although I was not surprised by the ending and saw it coming from quite early-on, I was never sure of what would happen, while being entertained and never bored along the way. 
 The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is a prime example of what a good mystery should be. It is also a prime example of a good book, and an honest reflection of the brilliant mind behind its conception.

I succeeded in reading this book on my second try. And in between the first and second tries, I was told the identity of the murderer. While I wouldn't necessarily recommend it, knowing from the outset who did it put a whole new spin on the story. I paid attention to clues (and they are abundant) and saw the red herrings Christie threw out to us. I thoroughly enjoyed the book on the second go-round. I look forward to more.

It was amazing. 
 How do you say "Thaa Tharu Maaru Book" in English? 
 That was my reaction after finishing this book. 
 I couldnt believe it even after the surprise was revealed. 
 Very, Very few books can have such a profound impact on you after you finish them. 
 Agatha Christie is the Queen of Mystery after all. 
 I just felt Hercule Poirot overthrew Sherlock Holmes a bit by this novel.

In perhaps, one of the finest of all Hercule Poirot mysteries, Agatha Christie crafts an ingenious plot with nothing less than stunning revelations at the conclusion. Her sheer genius leaves the reader breathless. Set in the small town of Kings Abbot, a retired Hercule Poirot becomes involved in solving the scandalous murder of Roger Ackroyd, the town's richest inhabitant. Unable to stay away from mystery for long, Poirot's interest is piqued and he is easily convinced into joining the investigation. Unlike other stories to follow, this one is narrated by the pleasant voice of Dr. James Sheppard, who chronicles the events and accompanies Poirot in Hastings absence. Clues abound and everyone at Fernly Park is a suspect. Only Poirot seems to understand the meaning of what he sees, not the inspector in charge of the case, the polite Dr. Sheppard or the reader can distinguish the significance or the insignificance of the many clues and converstations laid out in the story. This story in particular, in my opinion ,is a sample of Christie's best writing. The way the the reader is manipulated will be emulated in many novels to follow by other mystery writers. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd comes to a stunning conclusion, while the reader simply shakes their head acknowledging that Poirot is indeed master of the "little gray cells."
Enjoyable, not at all scary murder mystery. I figured it out (lucky guess?) on page 100. But still fun to see how it all came about and who was responsible for what.

I went through a phase after my first reading of The Art of the English Murder of trying to read some of the detective fiction put in the "making murder entertainment" category. Reading Doyle was easy--I've read through a massive two volume anthology four times and counting because Holmes is excellent if morbid bedside reading. I tanked with Dorothy L. Sayers, and Christie didn't even get touched before I moved on to the next trend. I finally picked up this one on a whim, thinking it was the first Poirot novel (lol), and breezed right through it. I also watched the corresponding episode on Netflix, and I have to say, the book is definitely better. David Suchet makes a good Poirot, but the man in print is just so much cooler. 
 This story is told from the perspective of one of the resident of King's Abbot, where the story takes place. Dr. Sheppard is the local GP and by all accounts, a citizen of good standing who's in deep with the local money...though Dr. Sheppard himself isn't rolling in it. Dr. Sheppard makes a diary of the events surrounding the murder of Roger Ackroyd (I know, even I didn't see that one coming). Ackroyd's friends and family all had various motives, and the ending surprised me. Agatha Christie is famous for her seats-of-the-pants writing, and she's been quoted that even she doesn't know who did it until the very end (meaning everyone is plausible). I can see now why Poirot is one of the defining detectives of the whodunit detective story. The quirky characters and plot were fun in a way that the TV episode couldn't match.
Don't remember this book specifically but I loved every Hercule Poirot book by Agatha Christie.

This is the fourth in the Hercule Poirot series written by Agatha Christie. Hercule Poirot is retired from the French Police and is content growing vegetable marrow when he is asked to look into the murder of Roger Ackroyd. Murder, blackmail and a few surprises are in store for the reader in this , one of Christie best mysteries.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I didn't...particularly...care for this book. Crazy, I know. 
 See, all I knew about it was that there was a big twist. As soon as I saw it was in first person (as compared to third in Murder on the Orient Express) I thought, the narrator is going to be the murderer. 
 Then I thought, the big, much-hailed twist certainly cannot be that predictable. 
 Oh, but it was. 
 Now, I understand: context. When this was written, it probably was an unheard-of shocker to have the narrator be the criminal. And perhaps if I hadn't just read Murder on the Orient Express, and if I didn't know that there must be a reason for the perspective change (if I had thought that all Hercule Poirot novels had a Watson penning for his Sherlock, for example), maybe I would not have called it so early, and maybe it would have been more of a mystery. 
 But we are not in the 1920s, and I had read Murder on the Orient Express (a far superior novel, in my opinion) first, so here we are. 
 I gave it two stars because there was some meticulous planning involved for the big reveal, and I respect Christie's skill as an author to pull that off. 
 Alas, the big twist itself just didn't do it for me.

I'm so disappointed with the ending- so very, very disappointed! Honestly, isn't there a law against such endings? 
 Every time I thought I knew the murderer, a technicality would present itself against them. Then, Christie slapped me on the face when in the climax she revealed the killer. 
 Dame Christie, I don't know if I love or hate you more for this, but I believe you are the best mystery writer ever!!!

The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is a classic locked room murder featuring Hercule Poirot. Roger Ackroyd is found in his locked study stabbed to death. Hercule is called out of retirement to solve the crime and with the aid of Dr. Shepherd begins to investigate. Love Agatha Christie's mysteries.

Looooved this one!!!! In most of Aghatha's books, I realize who the murderer is, mostly from the beginning, but in this one I've realized who the killer is only when Poirot started to explain the events. I was soo shocked, because I wasn't expecting this at all!!!

** spoiler alert ** 
 If you only read one book by Agatha Christie, make it this one. Published in 1926, this story of Poirot is one of the best written. All the clues are there, if only you could see them the way that Poirot sees them. The book is seen through the eyes of Dr. Sheppard - Captain Hastings being in the Argentine. We start, unsurprisingly with a death. An apparent suicide, if you believe Dr. Sheppard's nosy sister, Caroline. She believes that Mrs. Ferrars [and there's a nod to Jane Austen even] killed herself because she was overcome with remorse as she murdered her husband. It's not the death of Mrs. Ferrars that pulls Poirot into the mix - it's the death of Roger Ackroyd, a wealthy inhabitant of the small town. What's the significance of the chair? What is Miss Russell [the housekeeper - very lucky to have an alibi, according to Caroline] up to? And most importantly - if all the evidence points to Ralph Paton, surely he's guilty? And if he's not guilty, where on earth is he? Fantastic, unexpected and obvious all at once. 
 A number of criticisms have been levelled at this book, relating to internal consistencies and the fact that some people just couldn't handle having the rug pulled out from under them. No book will be completely consistent in every way, but the minor inconsistencies in this book, can be easily explained away. Utterly fantastic, read it, read it, read it.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Warning: I am totally going to ruin this book for you if you haven't read it. If you think you might want to read it, I would say that for a mystery novel, you could do far worse than this one. Stop reading now if you don't want the ending spoiled. 
 I felt like this book was just OK, but then I opted for three stars because I really liked the voice of the narrator, Dr. Sheppard. I decided to read this book after a recent article in Mental Floss recommending it as a seminal work in mystery fiction. Plus, it just seems sacrilegious to consider myself a "serious" reader and never to have read anything by Agatha Christie, who (the back cover kindly pointed out) has been translated into more languages than Shakespeare. ANYWAY, since I read the article, which gave away the ending, I already knew Sheppard was the murderer. This didn't make the book less enjoyable. In fact, it was kind of more fun to pay attention to his "reticence" knowing what he was hiding. 
 What I really didn't like was the ending. It just seemed so implausible to me that Sheppard would 1) not really believe Poirot had figured out he was the murderer 2) when he DID know the jig was up that he'd resign himself to his fate instead of killing Poirot and making a run for it 3)that he'd think people weren't going to figure out it was him after he killed himself. I mean, seriously? His not-so-helpfulness of Ralph was bound to get around, and after Poirot's very clear warning to the killer in front of everyone the night before, Shepherd "accidentally" killing himself and then the case being dropped isn't going to tip people off? Ah well, I could go on in this vein. I thought that ending was a serious cop out. I also didn't like Christie drawing attention to her cleverness in the way she had strictly told the truth (through Dr. Sheppard) but left out some important details. It was clever, and enjoyable, but to point it out to the reader lessened my enjoyment. 
 Anyway, it was good enough, but it will probably be my first and last Agatha Christie novel.

This is a definite must-read among the Christie mysteries, or murder mysteries in general. Unfortunately it was so memorable that rereading it wasn't quite as enjoyable as rereading another novel might be, since I remembered the ending. Still, I stayed up far too late just rereading it.

Best thing about Agatha's books- They are direct to the point, always start with the crime in the first place (soon after the set-up) and end with her infamous twist. Perhaps this explains why they are V.Quick reads reason: there is no unnecessary crap in it. 
 There are doubtless more detective stories which are more exciting than Agatha's works, but still what makes her books more fascinating is "climax" (Shall I say revelation). They seem as if the whole book is worked from backwards (no guessing works). Every time they are just surprising, no disappointment in it. 
 Coming to 'The Murder of Roger Ackroyd': Like in all her books crime in it is simple and perfect. Author opens the guessing game to the reader well in advance (and let the reader suspect all the players involved more or less till the pre-climax). There are full of stereotypes, boring conversations which could have been avoided, too much of Poirot's irritating methods and all. But where things get little crazy is towards the climax and finally, there comes the stunning revelation which is so beautiful and rewarding (perhaps best among all the climaxes I have read of her works) 
 PS: Either you like her books or don't like them at all. There are no '3 stars' for her books.

I have never read an Agatha Christie before, or frankly any mystery from this more "civilized" time. I was surprised by the congenial tone throughout the book, even between the murderer and Poirot when the ultimate reveal came. I think I expected a tense and rushed vibe like so many of our current thriller genre novels have these days, a la Dan Brown. This read more like a social comedy in the vein of a gentler Oscar Wilde or the like. 
 I suspected the ending but only because I had in advance about this book. What I read had not revealed the specific ending, but enough to clue me in. But having guessed did not complete ruin it, especially as I wasn't certain of my guess, so it was still satisfying to see how it all came together. 
 I definitely liked seeing the reveal at the end which made clear that all of the facts really were revealed to the reader during the novel. I was definitely left with a feeling that I might have been able to solve the mystery if I had tried hard (which I didn't at all), and that's pretty intriguing to me. In the other mysteries I've read I usually feel there is no way someone could guess the murderer or it is sooo obvious the detectives in the story are idiots for not figuring it out. I can see why Christie has the reputation she does. 
 I'll definitely be up for reading more of hers in the future.
Read for our podcast www.quincepodcast.com episode 21 and enjoyed revisiting!

Probably hovering somewhere around two and a half stars. I enjoyed it, but I'm also not sure I see myself reading many Agatha Christie books in the future - the last 15-20 pages were fun in a scandalous sort of way, but the rest of the book was a bit dry. 
 This is an especially difficult book to discuss without diving headfirst into spoilers. If you'd rather not be spoiled, my review is basically that this is a decent mystery to read on a rainy afternoon, but it was probably much, much more shocking when it was written. While some of the characters are fun - Poirot was colorful, and I actually quite liked Caroline - most of them are puzzle pieces more than people. 
 Spoilers: 
 Going into this book, all I knew was that this was Agatha Christie's mystery with the big twist ending. I love big twist endings! I was very excited. Unfortunately in this case, knowing that a twist is coming is a bit of a spoiler in and of itself. Everyone is a bit shady in The Murder of Roger Ackroyd with the distinct exception of our narrator, Dr. Shepherd. Reading this work from a modern perspective, he stands out immediately as a hugely unreliable narrator: he attempts to narrate events in a manner that's almost analogous to a newspaper report, always trying to be very detached, fair, impartial. But at the same time, it becomes clear rather early on that he is not being terribly forthcoming, and there are big gaps in his retelling of events. About a quarter of the way into the book I was convinced that he was giving a shoddy account of what was going on, and about a third of the way in I was convinced he was the murderer. I didn't know why, of course - I'm genuinely terrible at trying to figure our mystery plots. I never guess the murderer. But if you know that there's going to be a twist going into this one, it can be easy to guess what's happening from a literary point of view. Of course, that's not meant as a knock on Agatha Christie - I'd imagine that when this book was first published this was a radical thing to do in the mystery genre, and it's a clever idea. But now, when most of us are accustomed to questioning the motives of our narrators, this doesn't quite have the punch that it used to.

A small village where everyone knows everyone and then there is a death of one Mrs Ferrars. Although attributed to an overdose of veronal, people suspect that she committed suicide because of guilt. According to rumors and widespread suspicions, 
 Mrs Ferrars had supposedly poisoned her husband, who died just over a year ago. But there was never any proof to prove any of this. 
 While people are digesting these shady circumstances, Roger Ackroyd, a very close friend of Mrs Ferrars is found dead in his study with the door locked from inside and a letter missing which was speculated to have been sent by Mrs Ferrars before her death and contained the name of the person blackmailing her. This blackmailer claimed to know all about her act of killing her husband and could prove it. 
 Suddenly the complete household of Roger Ackroyd comprising of his sister-in-law, Mrs Ackroyd; his niece, Miss Flora Ackroyd; his stepson, Captain Ralph Paton; his best friend, Major Hector Blunt; his secretary, Geoffrey Raymond; butler, Parker and housekeeper, Miss Russell are all under suspicion. Hercule Poirot, who has retired and now lives in the same village, is urged by Flora to take up this case. Poirot suspects that everyone is hiding something or the other. 
 Why was Roger Ackroyd killed? 
 Did he finally know who was blackmailing Mrs Ferrars and so was killed before he could reveal the blackmailer? 
 What is the mystery of the pulled out and illogically placed chair in the study where Mr. Ackroyd was killed? 
 'An opened window,' he said. 
 'A locked door. A chair that apparently moved itself. To all three I say "Why?" and I find no answer.' 
 Who was the mysterious man Dr. Sheppard saw coming towards the house? 
 Who was Roger Ackroyd talking to at nine thirty when no one seemed to have entered the study? 
 Who called Dr. Sheppard and informed him of Mr. Ackroyd's murder when no one in his house knew that he had been killed? 
 Can Poirot solve this baffling case where suspects are too many and each has a reason to commit the murder? 
 With conflicting statements and unreliable alibis, will this case prove a first time failure for the great Hercule Poirot? 
 A case unlike any other, 
 "The Murder of Roger Ackroyd" 
 is a mystery in the class of mysteries where the concept is so novel that it will shock you and surprise you, leaving you with your mouth hanging open even though decades have passed since its publication! Howsoever, I tried I could not come up with one clear suspect. Agatha Christie expertly shifts her focus of suspicions from one character to another leaving the reader with no clue as to the real murderer. I tried all my 
 "little grey cells" 
 but could not pin point the murderer and when the killer was finally introduced I felt as if I had been punched so hard that no air was left in my lungs! 
 The characterization and story development is exquisite. The interactions between the narrator, Dr. Sheppard and his gossipy and always 
 "scandal mongering" 
 sister, Caroline were just too good and highly entertaining. The wit, humor and outright funny descriptions of Caroline by Dr. Sheppard left me chuckling and looking forward to their playful bantering and Caroline's efforts at accumulating information from everyone. 
 1) 'Caroline can do any amount of finding out by sitting placidly at home. I don't know how she manages it, but there it is. I suspect that servants and the tradesman constitute her Intelligent Corps. When she goes out, it is not to gather information, but to spread it. At that too, she is amazingly expert.' 
 2) 'My sister's nose, which is long and thin, quivered a little at the tip, as it always does when she is interested or excited over anything.' 
 The narration of the incidents by Dr Sheppard was interesting and engaging. I loved his humor and his confusion regarding Poirot's actions. His description of the hobbies of the villagers was outright hilarious. 
 Our hobbies and recreations can be summed up in the one word, 'gossip.' 
 Like many of Agatha Christie's other books, 
 "The Murder of Roger Ackroyd" 
 also has a village setting with gossipy villagers who are more interested in other people's affairs and take great pride in knowing things about others that are not public knowledge. Caroline is the same. She is always nosing for information and so when a new man moves into the neighboring cottage she wants to know everything about him but is unable to do so. The results of her speculation about the mysterious man who happens to be Hercule Poirot are hilarious and very entertaining. The only thing she knows is that he is a foreigner and interested in the growing of vegetable marrows! 
 'To Caroline's extreme annoyance, she has not been able to find out anything about him, except that he is a foreigner. The Intelligence Corps has proved a broken reed.' 
 'But that is certainly not the sort of information that Caroline is after. She wants to know where he comes from, what he does, whether he is married, what his wife was, or is, like, whether he has children, what his mother's maiden name was -and so on. Somebody very like Caroline must have invented the questions.' 
 Poirot is the constant source of discussion between the brother and sister and they come up with extremely funny suggestions as to his profession. 
 'My dear Caroline,' I said. 'There is no doubt at all about what the man's profession has been. 
 He's a retired hairdresser. Look at that moustache of his.' Caroline dissented. She said that if the man was a hairdresser, he would have wavy hair- not straight. All hairdressers did. 
 The character sketch of Poirot is like a caricature with 
 'An egg-shaped head, partially covered with suspiciously black hair, two immense moustaches, and a pair of watchful eyes.' 
 'Clearly a retired hairdresser. Who knows the secrets of human nature better than a hairdresser?' 
 This book is clearly one of the superior works of Christie and recently also voted 
 "Best Crime Novel Ever" 
 is a book with the right mix of light and funny moments coupled with serious, dark and mysterious moments. The dialogues between characters are legendary and remain in our memory long after we have finished reading the book. 
 1) 'The good dog, he does not leave the scent, remember!' 
 2) 'Method, order, and the little grey cells.' 
 3) 'Everyone has something to hide.' 
 4) 'Only one kind- the fool in love.' 
 5) 'it is not easy to hide things from Hercule Poirot. He has a knack of finding out.' 
 The description of the killer is chilling and leaves the reader shuddering at the thought of such a person in reality. A man so normal and friendly that no one suspects him and he often finds himself playing the role of a confidante to many secrets which people, thinking him harmless, kind and understanding, share with him unaware of his 
 "strain of weakness" 
 and 
 "blunted moral fibre" 
 . 
 'Let us take a man - a very ordinary man. A man with no idea of murder in his heart. There is in him somewhere a strain of weakness- deep down...He may stumble by accident on a secret - a secret involving life or death of somebody...Here is a chance to make money..He becomes greedy. And in his greed he overreaches himself...Exposure faced the man of whom we are speaking. And he is not the same man he was -say a year ago. His moral fibre is blunted. He is desperate, He is fighting a losing battle, and he is prepared to take any means that come to his hand, for exposure means ruin to him. And so -the dagger strikes!' 
 'Afterwards.' he went on softly,

In Christies novels, there are no rules. The objective is keep the reader guessing.

The story and mystery are engrossing as always but having found out the result, I can say this was not satisfying result. The reader was duped for the sake of not guessing who did the murder. 
 Christie also mentions through Poirot, that she gives all the facts to the reader keeping the logical deductions to Poirot. Well, Poirot goes to Cranchester to find Ralph there in a mental hospital, of course the reader can't do so. Similarly, the narrator tells that he was unable to find Ralph and we have no choice but to believe him. Otherwise one would easily suspect the narrator from the start. Christie should have pointed doubt somehow in the mind of the reader that the narrator should be suspected only then it would have been fair.
I wonder if I would have liked this more if I didn't know why it was famous. Instead I thought it boring and was annoyed with the "twist."

As someone fed up with trite and cliched Poirot dramas on ITV, I was surprised to be told that the books were really worth reading - starting with this one. I had an inkling what the famous plot twist was, but it still seemed pretty obvious even before the famous Belgian detective arrived. He only served to muddy the waters, creating confusion where none had existed before. It's very formulaic - although we can perhaps forgive Christie since she largely invented the formula - but the book does rattle along nicely and is well-written. All in all, it's what it's intended to be: a light, enjoyable story that can be knocked off in a few hours.

 My friends are constantly trying to force me to read erotica books - the more they think I'll dislike it, the more they want me to read it. I was wary about starting BARED TO YOU for several reasons: one; it's frequently referred to in the same breath as FIFTY SHADES OF GREY, which I did not like; two; I've been acquainted with this author before via her historical romance novels, which I also did not like; and three; it's got one of those vague non-summaries that doesn't tell me what the book is going to be about, which kind of makes me suspect that it's not going to have much in the way of substance besides, well, copious sex. 
 As it turns out, I was sort of correct and sort of incorrect on all three counts. BARED TO YOU is the story of an early-twenty-something and a late-twenty-something using kinky sex to self-medicate their traumas - only, instead of one of them being god-like and rich, they're both god-like and rich...and so is everyone else in the book. I'm still not sure if this levels the playing field, or if it just underscores the vapid, shallowness of these types of books. 
 ***WARNING: SPOILERS TO FOLLOW*** 
 I buddy-read this with my friend Sarah, and I have to agree with her that Gideon is a much better hero than Christian. As controlling and stalky as he is, at least he listens to the word "no" and doesn't beat her with belts and control her eating habits in order to come to term with his own demons. They actually do couple things together, like eat out (no, not just that way) and work out together, and go to charity balls...and other things that normal couples do together. The only downside is that Gideon apparently acts out rapes in his sleep, both on the receiving end and the giving end. Um. 
 The sex - and man, there was a lot of sex in this book - was actually good, for the most part, which was a pleasant surprise after reading ASK FOR IT and being treated to the not-so-sexy image of creamy bodily fluids gushing every which way. BARED TO YOU has some great scenes...but since this book is basically 70% sex or prelude to sex, they lose their power and get repetitive after a while. 
 Also, there's just some really bad scenes in here: 
 ...his powerful body straining with the primal need to mate (91). 
 "I'm so deep in you...I can feel it against my stomach...feel my dick pounding into you" (137). 
 His balls were heavy and big, an audacious display of his powerful virility (162). 
 Gideon battered my tender sex with that brutally thick column of rigid flesh (230). 
 "You're milking the head of my dick with those hungry little squeezes" (237) 
 And some of the worst phrases for buttholes: 
 the pucker of my anus (234) 
 my sensitive rosette (235) 
 that darkly sexual place (237) 
 I did find it a little irritating that the bisexual best friend of the hero sleeps around constantly with people of both sexes and basically comes across as a shallow jerk. The author gives a reason for this behavior, but it's still annoying to see characters conform to stereotypes (I also side-eyed her flamboyant gay boss). I'm all for inclusivity and practice makes perfect, but this is not a book I would ever pick up to fulfill any #diversefiction challenges. Let's put it that way. 
 Likewise, the way the other wom(en) are portrayed in this book made me feel similarly torn. Day tries to give them more substance than just that beautiful conniving temptress who swoops back into the hero's life to still him away from the virginal heroine. In this case, Gideon's women are portrayed with some degree of nuance (more so towards the end). The women who sleep with Cary (the bisexual BFF of the heroine), however, do not receive that same courtesy, and at one point, Eva refers to them as trash or something like that. Stay classy, Eva. 
 The way one of my coworkers described this book to me at my old job made it sound like this book was about assassins, and that title - Crossfire - made me think that I was about to get my hands on some Bastien Toussaint-type anti-hero. I think I know what happens next (based on her spoilers), and I'm curious enough to learn about Gideon and Eva's backstories that I'd probably pick up book 2. If it was cheap. I think my favorite part was when Eva, starry-eyed from her move from San Diego to New York, New York, marvels at the modern wonder of the garbage truck. Because of course, in California, we grind our garbage up and put it into fair trade coffee or smoke it in bongs, I guess. Please, tell me more about this New York-exclusive rubbish-processing behemoth on wheels... -_- 
 Edit: Can I just say that I'm so tickled by the fact that this edition has "discussion questions" in the back of the book? They're absolutely hilarious. Here are some of my favorites: 
 Initially, it's the physical attraction that draws Gideon to Eva, but by the time he lures her to his nightclub there's something deeper involved. What is it about Eva that causes Gideon to pursue her so relentlessly? (337) 
 Gideon's life revolves around his work and his philanthropic commitments; Eva's social life is more personal. How do these differences affect them as a couple? (338) 
 Gideon and Eva have a very sexual relationship. Considering their pasts, why do you think sex is such an important way for them to communicate? (338)

The first time I started this series was when I was in high school and apparently I really liked it, because I read three and shelved the remaining books as Want to Read. 
 ...I have no idea what I was thinking, or what could have made me enjoy these books. I find the relationship portrayed in this series disturbing. I suppose I probably liked the idea that a female victim of sexual abuse has the ability to let herself be vulnerable (particularly with a man) and, as a result of that vulnerability she is now open to finding love and engaging in a sexual relationship that she actually enjoys. Now, those are not bad things to look for in a book. Unfortunately, if these are topics you're hoping to read about, I'm sorry to say that this is not the novel for you. 
 The relationship is toxic and the characters are extremely codependent. I mean, the guy legitimately stalks her because of his need for control. They bring out the worst in each other; their entire relationship is one big trigger and they enable the other's harmful behavior. It's not crazy that two victims of abuse would be able to get involved in a healthy, committed relationship with one another. The problem with this series is that the relationship isn't healthy and it is not beneficial to their continuing recovery (although with Gideon, I think it can be argued that he hadn't even begun to address the traumatic events he experienced). 
 If they were to work on their issues separately and eventually got back together much further down the line, there's a good chance they'd have a mutually fulfilling relationship. I just don't appreciate the idea of them meeting, each having major setbacks, and deciding to work on their problems all in the name of "love." 
 I understand this book is essentially just smut, but that doesn't mean we can't learn things from books we read- even trashy romance :)

reference_books.review_text:
3.5 -- more thoughts to come. 
 11/10 update: okay, here are those thoughts. 
 - Started slow, felt very similar to WYGB, but really picked up. Unfortunately, a lot of that was due to multiple plots being introduced in rapid succession. 
 - stealing the keys didn't really serve a purpose except to just be another signifier of "what a madcap day, I'm stressed." I don't like it when characters do cringe-y things if there's no justification for the writer to include it as part of some larger scheme. Basically, I'm generally wary of books/movies/whatever based on the aforementioned madcap days -- you know, one day of endless things going wrong. 
 - on that note, just scrap the plot line with the former illustrator turned modern artist. Enjoyable scenes but again, focus. 
 - the graphic novella included within and that whole storyline with her sister/father/mother was the best one. I would have much preferred Semple to really stretch her creative muscles to make that the main focus. 
 - For all the descriptions of how Bucky's family is quintessentially Southern & so genteel...then the way they distanced themselves from Eleanor would have been so much different. Much less direct. Think discreet scorn and "bless your heart" vs. demanding a hand-written apology. 
 - I CAN'T BELIEVE SHE LEFT THE DOG THERE, I NOTICED IT IMMEDIATELY 
 - The multiple dropped clues about their fervent atheism and her husband's abandonment of childhood Catholicism should have been obvious markers to me of something to come, but instead I just thought it was weirdly aggressive. That's on me. BUT! I did enjoy the inclusion of Joe's conversion. Semple nicely balanced a perfectly realistic if harsh reaction from Eleanor with a gentle and fairly positive treatment of faith.

 I feel like this review needs some kind of disclaimer (yep, it's going to be that kind of review), so here goes. This is the toughest review I've had to write so far. It's going to be rambling, for which I apologize in advance; I've been trying to organize my thoughts for over a week, and it's just not happening. Normally when I finish a book, I have a rough idea of the points I want to cover in the review, but with Eleanor & Park, I don't know where to start. 
 Before I attempt to articulate why this book didn't work for me, I also feel the need to disclose that realistic fiction is the genre that I read the least often. I usually read for escapism, and though realistic fiction is still fiction, most of the time I prefer to read about a world that's far removed from this one. So why do I still bother with the genre, then? I have had the occasional success with it, and I worry that cutting it off completely would mean missing out on some great books. It's just a matter of finding the ones that are right for me. Sadly, Eleanor & Park was not one of them. 
 I first became interested in the book after it seemed like everyone was reading it, and if you look at the reviews, a slew of them are five star. I took a particular interest in this book when I found out that Park was half-Korean, the son of a Korean mother and a Caucasian father. While our situations aren't quite the same (I was born in Seoul and adopted when I was four months old; my mom was of Irish descent, my dad of Irish and German descent), I was still very curious to read about Park's experiences growing up in an interracial family. I don't know if I went into the book with subconscious expectations of how Park's heritage would be explored, but to me, it was a subject that wasn't probed nearly deeply enough. In fact, the portrayal of his whole family was one of the stumbling blocks that I encountered while reading this. 
 Park senses a distance between him and his father, and he wonders if it's because he inherited more of his features from his mother than his brother, Josh, did. Now, Park also says that his parents are madly in love with each other. If Park's dad is madly in love with his Korean wife, why would it matter if his son takes after her in appearance? I'm missing something here. There's also zero backstory about how Park's parents met other than that his father was in the military and stationed in Korea, and Park's mother conveniently doesn't talk about her life there. It's as if she had no life until she married Park's dad, came to America, had two kids, and started doing hair and nails out of her garage. I found this image one-dimensional and unsettling. 
 As a character, Park didn't strike me as one of substance. Aside from his occasional identity issues, there wasn't much else to him. He alternates between pondering his looks and mooning over Eleanor. I did want to scream at him when he asked Eleanor, this girl whom he's supposed to be absolutely, completely in love with, if she was the one scrawling lewd graffiti on her own textbooks. What?! When she suggests that it might be Tina, one of the girls at school who's been bullying her, Park sticks up for Tina. He was so clueless at times about how hellish Eleanor's life was, especially at home. 
 I wasn't fond of Eleanor, either. Personality-wise, she wasn't the type of character I could connect with, but I also really didn't like the way she saw Park sometimes--as Asian first, as Park second. Before she knew his name, he was "that Asian kid." Even after these two are supposed to be madly in love with each other (which I didn't buy, and the romance in general was too sappy for my liking), she still makes the offhand remark about his appearance, not in a mocking way, but it's like this is the first thing she notices about him. If this was meant to reinforce how lacking in ethnic diversity Eleanor and Park's neighborhood was, I don't think this was necessarily the best way to go about doing so. There was a lot of potential here to examine why Eleanor thinks and says some of the things she does, but there's hardly any follow-through. 
 I get all nostalgic over the 80's, and the geek in me appreciated the X-Men and Star Wars references. And I was ecstatic to see Elvis Costello and "Alison" name checked. All of this was not, however, sufficient to overcome the issues I had with the book, which also asked me to believe that these two characters were the 1986 equivalent of Romeo and Juliet. I've never considered the latter couple to be the paragon of adolescent love, so perhaps that was another reason why I had trouble with Eleanor & Park. Of course, there are many readers who loved this book, and I encourage you not to let my sole experience with it dissuade you from checking it out.

So I had to read this book due to all the controversy. You know how it is....satisfying the sick curiosity. While it did not rate 5 stars for me as it did my friends, I did enjoy it. I think partly the story hits somewhat close to home for me. I can sympathize with Eleanor's familial situation from my own harsh experiences. So for me, this is somewhat of a hard read. On the other hand, I absolutely loved the era and music portrayed in this story. I was in grade-school in the 80's (yes, I am an old biddy) and I grew up listening to The Smiths, Joy Division, Echo & the Bunnymen, Sex Pistols, etc. This story brought back the nostalgia (good and bad) of growing up in the Midwest in the 80's. I did enjoy this story enough to try another one written by Rainbow Rowell.
One of my favourite books ever.

Rating: 4.5 
 "Tell us, why has Romeo and Juliet survived four hundred years?' Park hated talking in class. Eleanor frowned at him, then looked away. He felt himself blush. 'Because ...' he said quietly, looking at his desk, 'because people want to remember what it's like to be young? And in love?" 
 This is the second Rainbow Rowell novel I've read after Attachments which has the same writing style, except that it was set in a time before I was born, or might have just hatched. 
 Eleanor and Park is one of those books which gives you that feel good sensation, that warm and fuzzy feeling you get when you reminisce your memories as a 16-year-old. Of planning your future with that one girl, just because she smiled at you or laughed at your joke. 
 The first few pages itself...I knew this was gonna be a great book. 
 Eleanor has just moved to town, and she comes from a broken home, divorced mom, abusive step dad, and 4 siblings to take care of. 
 She also has weight issues which make her insecure about herself and has extremely red hair, earning her the nickname Big Red. 
 Park is half Korean, half American. His main aim is to fit in with the other kids in town, as because of his Asian looks he feels like an outsider. He's a good kid and doesn't like mixing around with his rowdy class mates. 
 The way both of them bond is over comic books. At first she just steals glances at his X-men comics, until he just hands her an issue one day. 
 Once she starts reading them, they have these sweet and hilarious discussions of each issue. 
 "Eleanor put the comics between her books and stared at the window. For some reason, she didn't want to read in front of him. It would be like letting him watch her eat. It would be like ... admitting something." 
 "She read stuff as fast as he could give it to her. And when she handed it back to him the next morning, she always acted as if she were handing him something fragile. Something precious. You wouldn't even know that she touched the comics except for the smell. Every book Park lent her came back smelling like perfume. Not like the perfume his mom wore. (Imari.) And not like the new girl; she smelled like vanilla. But she made his comics smell like roses. A whole field of them." 
 The only disappointment for me was the ending. You ask anyone who has read the book, they will have the same issue. Why was the ending so abrupt? Why was I left asking what the heck happened later on? 
 I hope there's a sequel. Would recommend it everyone.

Outside of my usual wheelhouse, but I heard good things on the Pop Culture Happy Hour podcast & figured I'd give it a try. And it was decent. High schooly coming-of-age stuff is kind of tricky ground for me, because although I enjoy a "kids take steps into the larger world" story as much as the next person, my own high school experience was such a bland, non-starting, drama-free experience (which I think means that I did it wrong) that I have a hard time relating unless other factors draw me in. 
 Ms. Rowell mostly did a good job with that. She used her 1986 setting very well without constantly beating you over the head with, I dunno, references to Pepsi Free and Miami Vice and Reaganomics. E & P bond and fall in love over comic books and mopey music, and of course I'm gonna dig that. And the characterization is pretty solid. They think, speak, and act in all of the frustrating ways that real teens do, making me like them and sort of hate them all at the same time. That's good writing right there. 
 But all of the overwrought, high drama emotions and the kinda cliche aspect of their romance (he's the nice kid from a solid family, she's the girl from the abusive home in the bad part of the neighborhood)... as I said, this is outside my usual wheelhouse. Not really my bag, but well-done as these sorts of things go. If you enjoy these types of stories, Rainbow Rowell is probably an author to watch.

Oh my god where do I EVEN begin? The blatant racism? The creepy fetishization of Asians? The not-so-subtle body shaming? The exotification and emasculation of Asian men? The extremely sexist objectification of Asian women? This book is an absolute mess. If you want to read a romantic story between people of colour, please go pickup a book actually written by a person of colour (and not from someone with an oppa fetish). 
 One more thing, Park is a last name! No one names their child just Park. Would you name your son just Brown? Because I sure as hell wouldn't name my kid just Chan. In Asian cultures, our names are carefully chosen to represent something symbolic or significant to our family. It's clear that Rowell put minimal effort into researching Korean culture. Rowell's representation of the Korean community offers nothing positive or insightful; she merely reinforces and perpetuates damaging stereotypes. Goodbye godawful book, I am 50 shades of done with you.

Review 
 I wanted to love this one so much. 
 I started this book mainly due to the huge hype and because there were copies of it at the school library. Obviously, if i can get the book without having to wait or put a hold on it, it's a lot better for me. I checked it out, along with a number of other books two weeks ago. Eleanor and Park was the first on the stack. I went into it knowing almost nothing about it. I knew that it was probably a romance novel and that the main characters were Eleanor and Park. From the very beginning, I could tell that I wasn't going to like it very much. But I held out hoping that maybe, just maybe it'd grow on me and that I'd experience the feels and happiness that other readers had felt. 
 It didn't. 
 From the first moment I saw the cover of this book, I had thought that Park looked Asian. I was right; he turned out to be half-Korean. I appreciate that Rowell decided to write about an interracial relationship and an Asian/Caucasian one at that because there's very few books that deal with these types of couples. The problem that I had with the relationship was that it was too abrupt. It's a case of insta-love mixed with bi-polar syndrome. Their first interaction is the moment when Park tells Eleanor to sit down on the bus. It's not a very polite exchange and neither of them are left with positive relations. Eleanor refers to Park as "the stupid Asian". Park is upset about it. I couldn't see how Rowell was going to make a relationship about this without making it ridiculously cliche. My questions were answered when suddenly, the two begin to develop crushes on each other. It wasn't the classic love/hate relationship because all of a sudden a switch flipped in their brains that made them like each other. It comes out of nowhere. I personally feel like their relationship feels like one where they got together because of convenience. They're sitting next to each other on the bus everyday so why not get together while they're at it? If I dated every person I sat next to every day I think I would have to shoot myself. 
 Bi-polor insta-love is one thing, but the rest of the relationship was just as bad. If you ask me, it felt like a really unhealthy relationship. Eleanor was always so insecure about it, constantly getting jealous and mad about the things that Park would do. If they were truly a happy couple, she wouldn't feel so unconfident about it. I understand that she has those family problems, but I didn't think she needed to always take out her emotions in insecurities on Park. 
 The characters in this book were a mixed bag. I hated Eleanor. I didn't like her character or her personality or how even though her family is suffering, she doesn't think to help them at all. If they tell her to not call the police, she meekly doesn't even if she knows that it would help. She could've cared less about what happened to her family as long as she wasn't hurt. It's like she thought the whole world was against her and that she's never in the wrong. Her problems might have been bigger than Park's, but she handled them so badly. On the other hand, I liked Park. I liked reading about his family's banter and the difficulties that he faced. He could have been a great character but he wasn't fleshed out as well as I would have liked. Eleanor's black friends were really fun to read about (even if a bit stereotyped). I loved the interactions that Eleanor had with them. Some characters were good, but the ones that weren't, really really weren't good. 
 This book was one of the most boring books I have ever read. Almost nothing happens besides the relationship Eleanor has with Park and the family interactions they have. The plot is the slow way they fall in love during a school year. *yawn* When I was 1/4 of the way through, I looked at the page number and realized, "Holy crap there's another two hundred pages to read. I'm going to die of boredom." This never happens to me with books. Never. I sincerely hope that Eleanor and Park doesn't get a sequel. 
 I think that there's a problem with a book if I don't realize that it's in a certain time period until I look online. I knew that it was probably set sometime in the 1900's but never did it cross my mind that it would be 1986. Um, please explain to me how Park hasn't been bullied as much as his real life counterparts would have? Even in modern-day America, Asians are bullied for being who they are. I can't even begin to believe that it wouldn't have happened in 1986. The same goes for Eleanor's friends Beebi and DeNice. The fact that they weren't bullied by the white girls in the gym class surprises me. 
 Another thing. How did Park's mom get carted off to America? She most likely didn't know any English and I doubt that her parents would let her be taken. How does Park have green eyes? The brown allele is dominant. All Asians have brown eyes and since her ancestors are all Asian, it's impossible that she would have a recessive gene for green eyes. Therefore, the only possible eye color their kids would have would be brown. 
 I do admit that the writing was well done. It had a John Green feel which most would probably think is a good thing. I could care less because I didn't like his books but his flow was great and Rowell's was too. 
 Not bad but I'm not on the bandwagon for this book. I'm hoping that Fangirl is a better read.

::sighs:: It's not you, it's me. Well, mostly me. 
 I had every intention of giving this three stars, I really did. YA is always iffy with me, and I went into this knowing that and trying to keep an open mind nonetheless. There are plenty of YA books out there that I love, that I even consider favorites, so I know I can enjoy YA books. I was hoping this would be one of those, and while I realized it wasn't going to join my list of favorites, I didn't have any major issues with it. Eleanor and Park are both decently written - teenagers are hard to nail down as characters, and the author did a good job of giving them consistent, realistic voices. I appreciated Eleanor's resiliency and inner strength, and Park's willingness to face down the criticisms of his peers to do what felt right. I really liked Park's parents - now that I'm on the grownup side of the equation, I found myself sympathizing more with them, and hoping I can be the kind of parent who understands when their teenager just needs to do something, regardless of how stupid it may see, and helps them as best I can while still being a responsible adult. 
 But the point of the book isn't the characterization, it's the romance. FIRST LOVE. And just ... ::sighs:: It's not my thing. I totally get why people love reading about high school misfits who beat the odds and find each other and experience the thrills and awkwardness and exultation of first love. But it's not something that particularly draws me. I had my own thrilling awkward exultant high school experience, and I don't really get anything from reliving other people's. And that aside, I didn't really get into the romance between Eleanor and Park. It never grabbed me. They seemed to be laying a foundation for a sweet friendship, and then suddenly they're holding hands and in love. And I know, I know, first love, high school, fine. It just wasn't translating for me. I appreciated the general idea of it, but I didn't really buy it. 
 Still, I like my ratings to be a balance of what I personally think of a book, and what the book is offering outside of my emotional reaction to it, so I was going to give it a fair three stars. But then, that ending. I'm subtracting a star specifically for the ending. Maybe if I'd connected more with the romance, the "heartbreak" of the ending would've resonated more with me, but since I didn't, it just annoyed the hell out of me. I read 350 pages for ... that? 
 Oh, well. I read this to fill the high school prompt of the popsugar challenge, and now it's filled, so that's my silver lining.

3.5 Stars 
 Considering my own personal Midwestern experience with riding on a bus full of belligerent kids from the undesirable part of town (which actually took place in the late 80's-mid-90's) I started out with a solid connection to the more cringe-worthy elements of this story. Heck, I was having flashbacks! (That may have skewed some of my objectivity in the onset, so I just wanted to be upfront about it.) 
 The book starts out with 16-year-old Eleanor tentatively moving back in with her weak-willed co-dependent mother, her many younger siblings, and her drunkard stepfather after a year of being pawned off on a family friend. Plus-sized, redheaded, and nearly destitute in her wardrobe options, her first day at a new school--and first time on a new bus--goes about as well as one would expect. Her one bit of a social break comes when Park notices her plight, takes a sort of irritated pity, and assists by rudely ordering her to sit next to him. From that point on Eleanor both benefits and suffers under Park's unwitting social umbrella. 
 Initially, the two don't speak to each other at all. This oddly believable awkwardness goes on so long, Park doesn't seem to know how to break it once he begins to take a vague interest in the girl. 
 They are both outsiders, in a sense. Park is a music and comic book absorbed loner, who's half-Korean heritage and largely functional family set him apart from all the other kids in their neighborhood. And when he catches Eleanor reading his comics along with him on the bus ride, he immediately starts sending her home with them. This naturally progresses to him sharing his music with her, and this new found comradeship steadily transitions into hand-holding...rapidly intensifying from there into mutual attraction and deepening connectivity. (I've noted some reviewers balk at the speed of their relational development, but given Eleanor's unhealthy home life and Park's insecurities over his self-identity, this reader personally found their relationship rang with hormonal teen authenticity.) 
 Eleanor & Park is more than just a dated, star-crossed teen lovers premise with a lot of heavy 80's pop-culture references. It's a story that revolves around the timeless politics of fickle high school social-strata, juxtaposed to home-life drama--some of it petty and some of it desperately serious in nature. It takes a thoughtful-yet-impactful look at judging and misjudging others--be they friends, acquaintances, or family. There's also a poignant look at the perspective variances that can result from differences in class. But it's ultimately in the handling of Eleanor's horrendous domestic situation that this reader found the most enduring value. 
 The Pros: 
 The prose has a steady, organic flow, with peripheral characters gradually coming into clearer relational focus as the plot progresses. The emotional conveyances are frequently visceral, and the layers of conflict subtly unwrapped--which is likely to keep readers engaged. The main characters are both flawed and endearing in their own unique ways. And the ending, while somewhat flexibly unresolved, could still be considered satisfying. 
 The Cons: 
 I made the mistake of listening to the audiobook. I do not recommend this. While the male narrator did a fine job of voicing Park, his attempts at Eleanor's lines were mind-wrenchingly distracting. But beyond that, this YA book has more frequent use of the F-word than I recall finding in even the grittiest thriller or sci-fi novels I've ever encountered. Yes, it was that excessive--and hearing it over and over poses a problem for audio learners like me (i.e. if I hear it, I tend to have trouble not spitting it back out at inopportune times.) Never mind the fact that I was listening to this in the car and I quickly discovered I couldn't play it with my kids in any kind of earshot--headphones on or no. Could the author have handled that differently? That's not for me to say. To her credit, the language was largely used to both demonstrate teenage immaturity and help reinforce identification of the more villainous characters. I simply regret that it makes me hesitate to recommend the book to the teens it might actually help. (Also, I worry it may inadvertently cause a sort of exclusivity--as not all kids facing abusive situations are accustomed to and/or enthralled with this much vulgarity.) 
 Language choices aside, I also would have liked to see more growth in the relationship between Park and his father--which I felt like we were being set up for but sort of fell along the wayside. 
 On the whole, I appreciated this read far and above that of Rowell's later book, Fangirl--which makes me vaguely concerned. But then again, the stories are so dramatically different, much of the variance could be attributed to that fact alone.
