Beautifully written, wonderfully executed. It brought back the feeling of being 'in love' at sixteen like it was yesterday. Both characters were likable and relatable, and not 'mushy-gushy' at all, especially not for teenagers. I appreciated that they liked each other because they were interesting to the other person, not simply because of looks or other shallow matters. 
 I wanted to punch Eleanor's stepfather in the face the entire way through the book. Or push him down a flight of stairs. Enough for it to hurt pretty badly. I couldn't believe her mom's blindness to it all, either. 
 There were subtle moments with Park and his biracial heritage that I identified with. Although they weren't blatant moments, I found it interesting that Rowell chose to make him biracial, and for his parents to have the history they did. It brings another dimension to why people treat him the way they do, especially during the time period. I felt that the characterizations were just done so well and built perfectly.

You guys...I tried. I tried so hard, but it took me five days to read 80 pages. FIVE DAYS! That's good for some people, but not for me. In-between this book I read Of Monsters and Madness and it was more engaging then this book and that protagonist had the personality of a foot. A freaking foot! Not even both feet, just one! And I still found it more entertaining than Eleanor and Park. 
 So, a little background. I bought Eleanor and Park simply because I could buy Eleanor and Park. I didn't want to read it, I had no intention of reading it, but I finally cracked under the pressure and spent 15 bucks on this book at Target. Everyone was all like "This book was amazing" and "This book made me cry". That is the main reason I hate overhyped books. I get so excited and think it's the greatest thing since Santa Christ when it's not. 
 I hate saying that, I really, really do. I always feel like I'm that asshole who hates everything that's popular simply because it's popular. I want to tell you, that that's not true. If I don't like something, it's because I didn't like it, not because everyone else did. 
 Anyways, let's get on with the review. Eleanor and Park is about (surprise, surprise) two teens named Eleanor and Park. It's 1986 and the two of them are both misfits, and this is during a time where being a misfit did not come with a sense of entitlement because you think you're different. Anyways, Park is a half-Korean kid and Eleanor is the new girl who dresses like Macklemore's "Thrift Shop" and Weird Al's "Tacky" had a kid and then threw up on her. 
 I'm not going to go into depth about the racism that was or wasn't present in this book, mainly because I didn't live in the eighties and I have no idea about that particular decade other then what horror movies have taught me, which trickles down to "Everyone is Stupid as Fuck". What I will point out is that Eleanor and Park didn't make me...feel. 
 I generally avoid romance as much as humanly possible in books, mainly because so few authors can get it right. Rowell did make Eleanor and Park's romance generally believable, but the characters of Eleanor and Park were nothing to gush over. I felt that they were more annoying than anything else. Eleanor dresses weird, she knows this and holds her head up high through adversity, but if you look at it. Really look at it...it wasn't adversity. 
 Eleanor is poor, has too many siblings, an alcoholic stepfather, an abused mother, is fat, bullied, and can't be invisible to save her life. She literally had all of these thing in her life, but I never felt any emotional turmoil in her life. Rather than act like someone with problems, she acts like nothing is the matter. Yes, there can be the argument that this is some type of coping mechanism, but it's not because Eleanor isn't coping with anything. She's content with her life and hasn't done anything to change it. Not. One. Thing. 
 Park...Park likes music, comics, martial arts, and Eleanor. And he's half-Korean. He never develops ANYTHING beyond these traits. He doesn't grow as a character, nor does he do really anything. Sure he's got some really sappy line that I'll admit made me "awwww", but he never...did anything. It was like he was a character we had just to like Eleanor for all her weird quirks. 
 That's all Eleanor and Park are. Quirks. They don't have problems or personalities. They have quirks that sound nice, but get tired really fast. As someone with no interest in the millions of pop culture references in this story, it got old. I don't care about Joy Davidson or The Smiths. We get it, it's the 1980s, you don't to use the word walkman every couple of pages for us to understand that. 
 And that ending? I would have NEVER guessed it in a million years, if we WEREN'T ALREADY TOLD IN THE FIRST CHAPTER. The first line is literally: 
 He stopped trying to bring her back 
 So either a) She dies a la John Green or b) she leaves him. It wasn't rocket science figuring this out and I would appreciate it if I wasn't treated like it was.

"Eleanor & Park" by Rainbow Rowell (yes, Rainbow) is one of the best books I have ever had the pleasure of reading. Unlike most of the young adult fiction I read, this one is written in third person and is limited to the two main characters, Eleanor and Park, as it switches between the thoughts of each of them. This particular narrative style connects the two protagonists in a way so special that you know the characters are in love without the author ever having to spell it out. It takes place in Nebraska in 1986 and focuses on the lives of two sixteen-year-olds who feel like outsiders compared with the rest of their class. Eleanor not only comes from a broken, abusive home, but is also mocked for having crazy red hair and being overweight. Park is half Korean, half Irish and likes to wear eyeliner. From the first time they meet on the bus to school, their lives are changed forever. As their friendship turns into a vigorous attraction that neither of them can deny, they realize that being in love doesn't rid them of their problems, yet they're still brave enough to try. 
 This book. This book.This book.This book. I cannot. 
 It's been over a year since I've read anything that has given me such immense feelings over every aspect of the book. This one grabbed tightly to my heart from the very first chapter and continued to turn it into mush as I faithfully turned the pages. I was so enchanted by the characters' story that my heart crushed near the end and I cried like I was losing a close friend. At the very last page, I literally cried out, hating the idea that I had to go on with my life without knowing exactly where Eleanor and Park ended up. I fiercely crave to read more, even if it's as uneventful as what Eleanor ate for breakfast or what comic currently took up space on Park's lap. 
 All other books seem bland and juvenile and poorly written in comparison. Reading Rainbow's writing is like getting to eat your favorite candy. It's addictive, pure, and intensely satisfying. As someone who aspires to be an author, this book is my gold. I want to study it, learn from it, and steal all her tricks. This is the type of book that will affect the way I write and change the way I think about teenage love stories. I cannot get enough.

"She looked like art, and art wasn't supposed to look nice; it was supposed to make you feel something." (S. 147) 
 "He couldn't buy Eleanor a pen. Or a bookmark. He didn't have bookmark-like feelings for her." (S. 179) 
 Inhalt: 
 Wir schreiben das Jahr 1986. Die 16 jahrige Eleanor ist neu an der Schule und wird von allen gemieden. Vor allem im Bus fuhlt sie sich fehl am Platz. Nur ein bloder asiatischer Junge lasst sie neben sich sitzen. Ein bloder und gutaussehender asiatischer Junge. Park ist koreanischer Abstammung, liebt Musik und Comics und mag vielleicht doch nicht ganz so blod sein. Die beiden freunden sich an und fortan teilen sie mehr als nur Wolverine-Comics und Mixtapes. Sie treffen sich heimlich nach der Schule und nahern sich langsam an. Doch sie wissen, dass die erste Liebe in den meisten Fallen nicht fur immer halt. Dennoch geben sie ihr eine Chance und versuchen allen negativen Einflussen zu trotzen. Eltern, Mitschulern und Fuhrerscheinprufungen. Ob sie den Mut und die Starke besitzen alles durchzustehen? 
 Meine Meinung: 
 Da Fangirl von Rainbow Rowell schon langer auf meiner Wunschliste steht, ich aber bisher noch nicht dazu kam das Buch zu kaufen, habe ich durch Zufall dieses von der Autorin entdeckt. Warum also nicht das vorziehen, wenn es schon plotzlich vor mir auftaucht?! 
 Gesagt, getan. Das Cover ist unheimlich suss. Eleanor auf der einen Seite und Park auf er anderen, verbunden durch die Kopfhorer. Genau wie die Geschichte im Bus beginnt. 
 Ich kam schnell in die Geschichte rein und fand es interessant, dass der allwissende Erzahler immer abwechselnd in Parks und Eleanors Gedanken geschaut hat. So bekam ich einen viel besseren Einblick in die Gefuhlswelt der beiden und konnte mich in sie hineinversetzen. Die Protagonisten waren so sympathisch wie schon lange nicht mehr. Ich habe mit ihnen gelacht, heimlich geweint und manchmal war ich auch peinlich beruhrt. 
 Die Geschichte wird im Rahmen von einem Jahr erzahlt und schreitet nicht zu schnell oder zu langsam voran. Nach und nach werden neue Charaktere eingefuhrt oder weiter ausgebaut. Standig musste ich seufzen, weil es einfach nur ein Wohlfuhlbuch ist. Die Rezension konnte ich auch nicht gleich nach Beendigung schreiben, weil ich alles erst einmal sacken lassen musste. Jetzt, 3 Tage spater, stelle ich fest, dass das Buch mich NOCH mehr beeindruckt hat, als erst angenommen. Das Ende fand ich zu Anfang etwas komisch aber inzwischen finde ich es richti gut =) 
 Fazit: 
 Eleanor & Park ist ein rundum gelungenes Wohlfuhlbuch uber die erste grosse und manchmal eben auch schwierige Liebe. Eleanor & Park sind mir sofort sympathisch gewesen - Nerds mit Herz Jeder auf seine Art und Weise verpeilt und unperfekt. Aber genau as macht sie und das Buch aus. Ich habe mich in ihnen wiedererkannt und konnte sie und ihre Entscheidungen deswegen so gut verstehen. Top 5-Book of the Year!

Eleanor and Park by Rainbow Rowell is a story about first love and how, while it might not last forever, you never forget it. Eleanor's life has never been easy. She just recently moved back in with her mother, four younger siblings, and her drunkard of a stepfather who kills anything that is good. At her new school everyone makes fun of her for her bright red hair and chubbiness, but when she sits next to a boy on the bus, she never new that she would fall in love with him. 
 Park has never lived up to his father's manly expectations. He inherited his mother's Korean looks and prefers listening to music over watching football (even if he is pretty good at martial arts). But when he allows the new girl to sit next to him on the bus simply because no one else would, he never would have guessed his life would be changed. 
 Eleanor and Park would look like a weird couple on the outside, but on the inside they are kindred spirits discovering the joys and pains of first love. This book is both sad and encouraging. Sad because there are severely damaged families like Eleanor's, but encouraging because when you love someone it doesn't matter what other people think.

#12: Un libro recomendado por alguien que acabes de conocer. 
 **No iba a estar en el reto pero de algo debia servirme, sin ofender. 
 Tengo muchas, muchas cosas para decir de este libro pero no voy a hacerlo, no ahora. Siento que si hago una resena voy a terminar haciendo algo muy negativo y ese no es mi estilo, ademas ya me he descargado por otras redes sociales. Estoy sin palabras por ahora.

MOVING, POIGNANT, AND UTTERLY REAL 
 Boy, this takes me back to being 16 and desperately in love--that all-encompassing feeling that just overwhelms you. He's half-Korean in a mostly white neighborhood, and thus, doesn't sit with the cool kids at the back of the bus. He just tries to lay low and fly under the radar. (Been there, done that.) Her home life is a mix of abuse, neglect, and abject poverty. She's "big", has wild red hair, and nothing to work with when it comes to putting together her wardrobe. She sees herself as fat and unattractive. She cobbles outfits together, with ties and squares of cloth pinned in strange places to hide holes and stains on the few pieces of clothing she owns. On her first day at the new school, she knows she won't fit in. When she boards the school bus, she's effectively blocked from seating by everyone. He recognizes her predicament, and although he doesn't want to call attention to himself, he scoots over, allowing her to sit beside him. Thus begins one of the sweetest romances I've ever read. 
 This is no insty romance. They don't even speak for the longest time. He's into X-Men and Watchmen comics and reads them on the bus. She reads over his shoulder. He notices and slows his reading so she can follow. Over time, along with music, their mutual love of comics creates a powerful bond between these two outsiders. Rowell really understands "show, don't tell." She shows this relationship forming inch by inch...beautiful. These are two of the most real characters I've read in YA lit. They're complex, flawed, and utterly believable. Their stories are rich and poignant and their voices realistic. The love they share takes me right back to my teen years where every look, every nuance was filled with emotion. This is a sweet love story...doomed, perhaps, but painfully sweet and well worth reading. 
 Pick it up. You'll be glad you did.

 Eleanor is impotent as times but mostly always a euphoric character. Reading her parts about her family and the way Richie treats the people around him - including herself made my hate towards grow even more. 
 Park is a benevolent boy and his love and need for Eleanor is so addicting, I could never get enough of it. 
 I gave this book a four and a half, simply because I wasn't that pleased with how the ending ended. Although I did like the ending, I felt as though Eleanor and Park should have re-united with each other and Eleanor said 'I love you' to him, just like he did to her. 
 This leads me to my next point. The last two sentences of the book, it says: 
 'Eleanor hadn't written him a letter, it was a postcard. 
 Just three words long.' 
 When I read these lines, I instantly though that she was regarding to 'I love you'. In saying this, the previous pages before the last page, Park was wondering if she had read the final issue of 'Watchmen', and what she thought Dr Manhattan was defining when he said the three words 'Nothing ever ends'. Maybe Eleanor's three words were in fact 'nothing ever ends', and she said those words because she knew that Park would've read the final issue of Watchmen or she was regarded them to her relationship between them both. 
 I definitely consider you reading this book as it is truly the most beautiful, uplifting novel you could ever lay your fingers on. x

All of these rave reviews are a bit baffling to me. That is not to say that the novel is terrible but it failed to win me over like it did with so many other readers. This is a quirky coming-of-age story about two high-school misfits during the 1980's experiencing their first romantic relationship. Rowell's extensive use of the word "like" and "seriously" gets annoying fast. I understand that she is attempting to accurately capture the vernacular of teenagers but it is a bit overdone. However, growing up as an 80's kid, the plethora of pop culture references are amusing and nostalgic: The Smiths, Star Wars, Back to the Future, XTC, etc. Reading this novel continually gave me the urge to dig up my old A-track mixtapes from the basement storage room or go on an 80's movie marathon. At one point in the novel, Park says to Eleanor that he wants to be her Han Salo. Even though it is kind of lame, there is something oddly sweet and cute about this young couple. 
 This is a quick and easy read that doesn't really leave much to the imagination. The writing is simple, direct and sometimes quite humorous but lacks any substantial emotional resonance that is essential to a story about first love. Or maybe I am just really cynical when it comes to young love. At least it did not require a great deal of energy or time to finish.

Okay, this is a typical YA novel, it's unfair to give it 3 stars compared to its own genre but I couldn't get myself to give it more stars to be honest, it's a cool one but I got bored after the first 150 pages. 
 I liked the music references and the "Hey. Hey" thing and yeah it made me realize how I'm no longer a teenager but what I likrf most was the afterwards by the writer

book_b.title: Kiss the Girls (Alex Cross, #2)
book_b.user_review: I read this far too young and it scarred me for life. The snake with its mouth sewn shut? Ugh, scarred, for reals.

sample_reviews.review_text: DNF - I've decided that Patterson's books are very hit or miss for me. I just couldn't read this one so I'm done with the Alex Cross books.

This is the first Patterson novel I've ever read, and it will be my last. I enjoy police procedurals, but not when the writing is so awkward, and the plot so full of holes. 
 The main character is Doctor-detective Alex Cross who is such a hot-shot super detective that he continuously misidentifies the killer, and makes really poor decisions. 
 There are certain chapters which go into excruciating detail (worryingly, the sex assault/murder chapters are included in this), while there are sudden unexplained gaps in time in other places in the book, which make no sense. 
 Avoid.

I never saw the movie so didn't really know what I was getting into with this. Finished it in one night it was that much of a page turner. Definitely not for the faint of heart, or one to read alone though. It is 451 pages of complete creepy, diabolical sadism that will make you want to sleep with the lights on. 
 Would've given it more stars but for a few things...there is a relationship that develops that feels wholly unbelievable given what one of them has gone through. It doesn't seem to give justice to the trauma this person would have gone through. Secondly, how the crime is solved. The initial tip-off to the guilty party seemed to be an afterthought and we're given very little background on how this person ever even came up as a suspect. 
 Solid read, but with some holes. Don't read it alone, or late at night.

This is genuinely the worst book I have ever finished. 
 To be fair, it is tolerable when there is action, which is often. But every time James Patterson tries to put words coming out of a characters mouth, it makes you want to punch yourself in the face. When he writes descriptive, emotional paragraphs, it makes you want to punch him in the face. 
 I actually dog-eared a couple pages because the writing was so bad, I wanted to be able to quick reference it to people to show them how bad it was. 
 Want another example of how bad a writer he is? One of his other books is called, "Night of the Machete." I am not a God-fearing man, but if you believe in God, maybe throw in an extra prayer for James Patterson's English language murdering soul.

Hold onto your hat, this is a roller coaster ride. Does evil get any more horrible? The bad guys are so clever. There were a couple of times when I had to say, "Really Alex? You are not that stupid." But his dumb moves certainly keep the story raging on. 
 This is James Patterson, in the beginning, on his own, making a name for himself with great writing, intense suspense, awesome characters, and the start of a fabulous Alex Cross series.

I can't get enough of the Alex Cross novels by James Patterson!! I own them all, but haven't finished the series yet. 
 I read it because I really liked the movie, and a friend told me that the book was so much more graphic - it was!

A story that is good at building suspense and creating a sense of unease. However, the graphic and gratuitous descriptions of violence against women were deeply unpleasant and misogynistic and it makes me question the author's state of mind. Not sure if I would read another of his books.

There is no question that the story itself was creepy, if not terrifying. I did however find that the constant pop culture references from the 90s made it less timeless as a crime thriller. It also had quite a bit of cheesy one liners, and an unnecessary, almost uncomfortable budding romance between a detective and a victim. Aside from it's cheesy pitfalls, the detail in the process of investigating and hunting down the serial killers, was well detailed, and fascinating.
Read this book years ago and absolutely loved it. One of my favorites by Patterson.

Wow, I can't believe I used to like this book. All of the things I came to hate about the later books of the series are actually WORSE in this book. Spoilers are about details, not the plot so it shouldn't ruin much/anything. Also, fair warning, a lot of this review is a C&P of the first Cross book since a lot of my issues are the same. 
 1. The fact that Patterson spends half the book writing about how evil white people are drives me nuts. Keep in mind that Patterson was a 46 y.o., married, wealthy, while male from Palm Beach, FL writing about what it's like to be a 38 y.o. single father living in a crime-ridden poor neighborhood in DC. Really!? If it were only Patterson's apparent self-hatred, I would just feel pity for him. However, he managed to repeatedly glorify reverse-racism while fitting in more racist cliches than I ever would have thought possible. Check out how many times fried chicken and ribs shows up in the first three-four books. Also, Alex's obsession with white women. To say nothing of the language and the discussions of "the man," slavery and why the blues is the only good music ever created. Oh, and every white cop is an A$$ 
 2. *SPOILER ALERT* The plot is completely improbable. 
 - Cross is allowed in a crime scene involving a close relative that isn't even in his jurisdiction. When that gets far-fetched, the FBI allows him onto THEIR team because of Kyle Craig, an agent that Cross met ONCE and didn't appear to care much for. He is now described as a "close friend" and breaks a ton of regulations to get Cross on the case with no oversight. 
 - Cross breaks at LEAST 3 major laws. The incident of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer is a federal crime and would have been a jail sentence of many decades if committed by anyone else. Also, many areas consider martial arts a deadly weapon, so he might have been looking at a near-life sentence. But they were white and MIGHT have been profiling, so it's okay... 
 - Cross' new g/f is allowed along on VERY dangerous stakeouts, including being on the scene when they hope to arrest the bad guy. At one point she is even described as wearing a short skirt, heels and a "peasant blouse." The first scene where they are hoping she will ID the guy - okay. But after that, WHY!? 
 3. Cross is revoltingly perfect. He balances family, women and job perfectly. He never gets angry with his kids/nana or they with him. He is gorgeous and impervious to beatings, shootings, etc. (sorry, I already forget which violence took place in which book). And he has NO issues what-so-ever except for the occasional "oh ya, and I miss my wife." Another reader said this, but I must take the time to agree - why does every characters have to have crappy relationships? Cross comes from a broken home himself and is a single dad due to a murdered wife. His love interest has a broken home and everyone around her died of cancer. 
 4. Cross' women: This is more of a pattern than anything. Date Alex Cross = end up dead or attacked horrible. Congrats to this one for being attacked, not once, but THREE TIMES in the book. She might be the only one in the series not attacked because of Cross though. Apparently women exist in Cross' life only to be killed so he can have more angst. 
 Also, In this case, he takes a crime victim on as a patient (unofficial or not, he still does therapy with her in an official capacity) and then becomes sexually involved with her. So now he should lose his job, his freedom AND his license as a psychologist because that breaks the NUMBER ONE RULE in psych. 
 5. I hate the writing style. The tendency to go from first person to third person (and MANY third persons at that) drive me tweaky. Pick one. I also don't like the short, abrupt chapters that appear to do no more than lengthen the book. Also, why does Patterson feels the need to RANDOMLY EMPHASIZE PASSAGES FOR NO GOOD REASON? I mean, is there really a need to confuse the reader by adding italics not only for thoughts, BUT FOR SUDDEN BURSTS OF WRITING THAT APPEAR TO MEAN NOTHING? This gets worse in the second and forth book (I skipped #3 this time around), but IT'S PRETTY ANNOYING HERE TOO. See what I means? Oh, and learn how to write a 4 year old's thoughts so that she doesn't sound older and wiser than Nana. Actually, she and Nana might as well be the same character except that the girl is there to be cute and Nana is there to be racist. 'Cause apparently being racist when your old is okay. 
 All in all, a book to be avoided - especially if you actually read and THINK about what you are reading. If you are the kind of person who listens to the beat of the song and has no idea what the words are, you might like it just fine. And if you are white and feel guilty about it, you will probably even find it "deep."

"Kiss the Girls" was one of the best books I have read! 
 Detective Alex Cross is searching for his missing neice, Naomi, who has been kidnapped by a killer known as Casanova. Cross enlists the help of one of Casanova's only known living victims, a medical intern named Kate, who escaped and the killer is now hunting. 
 The plot in this book was fantastic, not to mention the mystery, suspense, and the characters themselves. A must read for all James Patterson fans, and fans of mystery, intrigue, and great storytelling!

I forced myself to read this to make sure I wasn't being too hard on the first in this series. I don't think I was. I didn't enjoy it very much. 
 Alex Cross is trying to be too much of everything. As a result he's not very good at being a cop or a psychologist. He blunders around never seeing the procession of serial killers who are constantly following him. The plethora of law enforcement organisations swilling around this plot just get in the way. The fact that none of them want Cross anywhere near the case makes their subsequent letting him in bewildering. He (and all the other cop's to be fair) can't even look after their best witness against the seemingly invincible serial killer. And in spite of his apparent intellect and forensic abilities he keeps identifying the wrong people as the suspect. 
 I know its fiction and were supposed to suspend our belief a bit....but this overdoes it i'm afraid. The depiction of what happens to the girls is unpleasant, unnecessary and certainly not entertaining. 
 I wont be reading anymore Alex Cross....

The characters are mesmerising to say the least. The positive characters such as Kate and Naomi come out strong and admirable as much as 'Casanova' and 'The Gentlemen' are despicable. The author admirably uses two antagonists without hesitation or remorse( yup, i mean it). Comparable in excellence to its predecessor Along Came a Spider, it reveals more of Alex Cross's identity as a cop and as a man of his people.
I picked this up because Brendan Dassey mentioned it. Now I have more thoughts about Making a Murderer. However, my opinion of James Patterson remains the same.
I don't like this near as much as Alex Cross or Maximum Ride series books.
While the story was completely engaging, the descriptions of the crimes were unnecessarily sexualized and violent.

Only gave it one star because I couldn't give it zero. Awful. Badly written, so many cliches, predictable, a lot of women characters written by an author who cannot write women, unconvincing and obvious. All bad, not recommended to anyone.

3.5 boring stars 
 It was a bland thriller, nothing special. Now that I look back, there is not much I remember, though I enjoyed the book so-so. The writing style was seductive and pin-like. The story was lame,loose and not well researched, I couldn't connect much. 
 -Detective Ruskin is Casanova. (Though the hints were near to none, and as there was nothing much about Ruskin in the book. And the name unravels in the last 10 pages or so,just like that.."Look!Ruskin is Casanova!" Why couldn't Kate recognize the only long brown haired, blue eyed, muscular,tall and strong man walking daily in front of her (remember, she knows Casanova's profile a little too well.) 
 -The author blandly tried distract reader to Craig and Ruskin's partner(lame...I can't even remember the name,he came so,so seldom in the book) 
 -Will Rudolph, a medical doctor is 'The Gentleman' 
 -Gary Soneji from the first book Along Came a Spider escape from the prison.
Waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay too long. In about the middle one phrase was repeated about 50 times. No more Patterson for me.

Another fast paced page turner from Patterson. 
 This one has Alex up against not one but two serial rapists and killers. One is more brutal and on the West coast while the "collector" is on the East coast. It becomes personal when Casanova (the East coast monster) kidnaps Cross's niece. He tries to solve the case before she is killed.
Alex Cross es, por mucho, uno de los personajes mejor construidos que he leido ultimamente. Agradezco a la persona que me recomendo la serie y lamento haber tardado tanto en retomarla.
Like J Patterson. Plan on reading the whole series in order, hopefully.

One of the best psychological thrillers by James Patterson. I had to also buy the DVD along with the book. 
 I love the shorter chapters. This is a very well plotted and paced story. Very suspenseful. I read it in 2 days.

This book is not a good book. This book is a bad book. 
 I feel like I'm spending most of my time saying "shut up" to my book. That's not a good thing. That's a bad thing. When I physically shudder at something that's NOT SUPPOSED TO MAKE ME SHUDDER its a very bad thing. This is written from three main perspectives, the killers', the victims' and Cross's and all extremely annoying. 
 Patterson's writing is even more terrible than the last book of his I read. He's just not a good writer. There's no flow, its all awkward sounding and it's very disjointed. He uses exclamation points in awkward places! I think they're to indicate something profound, but it doesn't work out! It just makes it seem cheesy and dumb! He also uses italics seemingly at random. I'm not sure if he knows what italics are for. 
 (THIS NEXT PART IS A RANT ABOUT HOW PATTERSON ABUSES THE SOUTH AND MY HOME STATE IN THIS BOOK SO IF YOU'D LIKE TO SKIP THIS PART FEEL FREE BECAUSE ITS ALL ME BEING ANGRY.) 
 This book is partially set in North Carolina, again where I'm from and I'm embarrassed. The plot is terrible (really essentially the same as the last book, but I'll discuss that later) and frankly, I really don't want the first thing that people think of when they hear 'North Carolina' to be James Patterson and his horrible story. Not to mention, he screws up so many facts about North Carolina and the universities located within North Carolina. It really doesn't take much effort to look up the name of the UNC hospital or specific information about the campuses. Will someone let him know that State University of North Carolina isn't a place? Its North Carolina State University. And its North Carolina Central University, not North Carolina Center University. Those right there are inexcusable mistakes. GOOGLE IT MAN. He also manages to portray some of the best universities in the south (and the country by the way) in a negative light. I don't appreciate that. He uses every stereotype in the book when talking about the South. Its really quite obvious he's a Yankee because he has no idea what the South is really like. Believe it or not, we're not all hateful racists, most of us are pretty fantastic people. There are racists everywhere in the country, they're not exclusively Southern. He seems to really hate the South because everything Alex Cross says about it is negative. Oh, by the way, North Carolina is two states away from DC. Its not that different. Last time I checked, DC is also below the Mason-Dixon Line. That makes you a Southerner, whether you like it or not jerk. I'm going to hop off my soapbox now, I just felt the need to defend where I'm from. 
 So the plot, same old, same old really. Serial killer with a personality disorder, Alex Cross has a special interest in the case, this time its because his niece (who he helped raise, what a saint!) is one of the possible victims. And Alex Cross once again "falls in love" with whatever woman doesn't realize he's a jerk. 
 The characters are the same too. Alex is still a perfect hero and everybody else is still wrong and racist not to mention, cocky and rude. That got old in the last book. This isn't just old any more, this is bloody and beaten and dead. Alex is alot like our friend Anita Blake. He a racist, a sexist and he thinks everyone is out to get him. Somehow everyone has a personal vendetta against him when they're actually just doing their jobs. 
 Again, its a great thriller! A great crime novel plot! But the writing and the annoying as crap characters and the ignorance on the part of the author just ruins it. I hate this book. I hate this series. Hate is a strong word, but its so, so accurate. And I think I hate James Patterson, mostly because he seems to hate me because I'm from the South. Because that obviously makes me a backwards racist. 
 In summary, to quote Stephen King: "a terrible writer [but he's] very successful" 
 1/5 stars 
 Book review blog: http://thebookgirlblog.wordpress.com/

I guess the almost 4 star rating of this book reiterates the fact that everybody is different and some a lot more different than others. I thought this book was horrible in all aspects, writing, plot, dialogue and story. Some of the lines, for example, "She was murdered beyond cold blood" (what does this even mean?) are completely asinine. Not to mention that the person lived. Suffice it to say I thought it was a superficial, amateurish attempt that wasted a few hours of my life that I can never get back. If I ever meet Mr Patterson I'll try to get him to reimburse me for my purchase and time wasted.

Because James Patterson wears a baseball cap that says, "I'm No. 1," some small part of me is reluctant to write a negative review. But let's be honest, this book is awful. And not as in unreadable, because he clearly has honed in on the formula/language that we can all read and understand. And have come to expect from almost Every. Single. Book. Ever. Published. 
 There are are willful, purposefully disturbing thematic elements in this book, and not in that cool way that say, Pan's Labyrinth is disturbing. The degradation and humiliation of women in painfully GRAPHIC DETAIL did not fall into this book by accident. 
 And Cassanova? **Tea spit-take** 
 I am almost stopped reading right there.
tenses up!

3.5 stars 
 I am becoming quite the fan of Alex Cross, he intrigues me. although so far both books have left me expecting a little more from him. 
 This book was fast paced and was well equipped with memorable bad guys. I will have to keep reading.
A fantastic book which was one of only a handful that genuinely scared me!
To date, this is my favorite James Patterson book about Alex Cross. Isnt there a movie made too?

I read the first Alex Cross book as part of a reader's advisory exercise a few years back. One of my perpetual goals is to finish/keep current with series that I've started and haven't yet finished, so I decided to download the second Alex Cross book on audio recently. I did not particularly enjoy the audio version - books filled with suspense and action are often difficult for me to enjoy on audio because I know I'd be reading a physical copy much more quickly than I can listen to one. Additionally, I didn't particularly enjoy the narrator of this one - someone about his voice and inflections just didn't really work for me. I will probably pick up the next book in the series in print - they are interesting enough mysteries to keep me engaged. Though I don't know how long I'll be able to stand Alex Cross - I find him a bit creepy, and the comparisons to Ali (in looks) seem too frequent.
Sick.

I saw the movie awhile back, so I decided to read the book and see how that compares. It had been awhile since I'd seen the film, so I didn't remember everything that had happened. Good story, keeps you wondering who the bad guy is and how they'll catch him in the end.
Wonderful, Suspenseful BOOK! I could not put it down!!!!!!!
I teally enjoyed this series

Still loving Alex Cross character, and still excited to read the next book in the series, however I thought this book was much weaker than the first, the story was slow and sometimes unnecessary, it felt more like character building and setting up the story for the next book to establish his biggest fears and driving forces. Still a good detective story but I have higher hopes for the next one.

Before giving my opinion about this book, the 2nd one featuring Alex Cross, it is only fair to disclose that I ADORE the Alex Cross/John Sampson duo. I'm convinced that Mr. Patterson could place these two in even the most mundane storyline and still come up with a winning book. Luckily, such is not the case with Kiss the Girls. This is a fabulously written mystery with multiple opportununities for the reader to figure out who, what, when, where and why. The human monsters in this book are ruthless, arrogant, unapologetic and quite dispicable. As the reader, the desire for Cross and Sampson to apprehend the atrocities masquerading as humans is even a bit stronger than the need for the victims to be saved. Having said that, some of the victims are amazing, strong women; leaving the reader with a wish to see the ladies kick butt. Any chance Mr. Patterson is generous enough to give the reader everything he/she hopes for in a book? You'll have to read it to see.

So badly written I couldn't finish it. Reads more like a secondary school student has been told to write a crime novel over the summer. Not helped by the fact that the back cover blurb actually spoils two major plot points. Every chapter is about two or three pages, obviously written for people with very little attention span. Shifts from first person to third person perspective every couple of chapters, robbing it completely of any sense of suspence, and that's BEFORE we get down to all the massive cliches. 
 Ugh. Exceptionally poor.

Note to self: This is what you get when you choose a book based solely on your crush on Nathan Fillion. Please, don't do it again. 
 Okay, I liked this book a lot more than I liked Along Came a Spider, hence the 2 stars. But when I say 'liked' I mean it only took me one month to read Kiss the Girls instead of two like last time. Although I find the plot interesting--I saw the movie back when it came out and I remember enjoying it--I found the book to be way too long, drawn-out and boring. It needed a lot more action and a lot less of Alex Cross's personal life. And I don't like him any more than I did in the first book. I have a tiny crush on John Sampson. I want to know more about Kyle Craig. I found the kidnappers/murderers interesting. Hell, I care about that random guy in the bar parking lot more than I do about Alex Cross. I'm still not sure exactly what it is, but the character really annoys me.
JP is getting so bad.
Great detective story.
So good, very scary.
This book was so much better than the movie. Although, I did enjoy the movie. However, in the book you get deeper into the killers head and he is by far the more fascinating character of them all.
This was BOMB!
Wanna give it 6 out of 5 stars... Amazing trip to the minds of two serial killers, unbelievable twist in the plot in the very end of the book... Wow, what a reading!
Yeah, I just don't like this series. At all.

This is somewhere between 2 and 3 stars for me. I read it as my commute-to-work book which means it's good enough to hold my attention, but most of the time not good enough to stop me breaking off to go to work (although once I did end up walking into to work reading in order to find out what happened..) 
 This is very similar to the first book. The main character (Alex Cross) has a pretty boring/eay personality, so although I didn't especially like him, I did _not_ like him and hence was happy enough to read about his life. The main female character (Kate) is an excellent role model for all girls- able to take care of herself and tough enough not to break down no matter how hard it all got. I like Alex a lot more for the fact that he was able to form such a strong relationship with such an independent woman. 
 I have to admit there were a couple of scenes that were really way too grizzly/disturbing for me. I do hope that no mentally unstable people read these books and take them as an invitation to copy... what a truly horrifying idea. 
 The dialogue is also rather poor at points. 
 I will probably read the next book in the series..

This just isn't very good. I tried to give the series a chance but after the first book the same things that annoy me are still present. The people aren't believable, the events aren't believable and Alex is a superman who solves things without a process I can follow. I've had enough of Alex Cross.
The book is way better than the movie.
